papers.abstract: Qwen3.5-0.8B rarely finishes reasoning in thinking mode: at a 4,096-token budget only 1 or 2 of 500 MATH-500 answers close their think block (two seeds), and accuracy is 15.4%. A recent demonstration had GPT-6 Astra edit 131,072 of the model's weights without gradients and reported MATH-500 rising from 7.9% to 48.1% at a 32,768-token budget. We provide the missing gradient baseline, then combine the two edits. Fine-tuning only the 140 to 139,750 weights with the largest gradient, on the model's own correct answers to MATH training problems, raises thinking-mode MATH-500 at 4k tokens to 39.0-45.5% after 2-9 minutes of training on one GPU; 50 training examples suffice, and 1,398 random positions give only 16.3%. The gradient concentrates the edit on the most nearly constant channel of each of the first three layers. Because the model has no bias terms, an edit confined to those channels acts as a constant vector added to the residual stream: adding three fixed vectors to the unedited model matches the accuracy of such an edit. Under the Astra protocol (32k tokens, presence penalty 1.5), the Astra edit scores 52.1% (finished and correct) in our reproduction and our full-strength edits reach 45.6-45.7%, but ours win at every budget up to 16k tokens (39.5% against 6.7% at 4k). The two edits are complementary. The Astra edit plus our 139,750-weight edit at half strength scores 62.2% at 32k, 10 points above the Astra edit alone (p = 3e-9), with half as many tokens; our half-strength edit alone scores 46.7%.
bullets: The unedited model almost never completes its thinking block within 4,096 tokens and achieves 15.4% on MATH-500.
Fine-tuning only 140–139,750 high-gradient weights on as few as 50 correct training examples raises 4k-token accuracy to 39.0–45.5%.
The gradient concentrates on near-constant channels in the first three layers, behaving like fixed vectors added to the residual stream.
Under the 32k-token evaluation protocol, the reproduced Astra edit reaches 52.1%, while the authors’ edits perform better at budgets up to 16k tokens.
Combining the Astra edit with a half-strength authors’ edit reaches 62.2% at 32k tokens, outperforming Astra alone and using half as many tokens.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates gradient edits to stop reasoning loops in small LLMs, improving performance on reasoning tasks.
papers.title: A Bias in Disguise: Tiny Gradient Edits Stop a Small Language Model's Thinking Loops and Complement a Frontier Model's Weight Edit
papers.tldr: Tiny, gradient-selected edits largely stop Qwen3.5-0.8B’s reasoning loops, and combining them with a frontier-model weight edit substantially improves math performance.

papers.abstract: Since its introduction by DeepSeek, group relative policy optimization (GRPO) has been widely adopted for training large reasoning models and agents, spurring a proliferation of its variants. Yet the group size, a crucial hyperparameter in these GRPO-type algorithms, remains largely chosen by trial and error. Exploiting the U-statistic structure of GRPO's policy gradient, we recast the selection of the group size as a classical statistical problem of variance ratio estimation. This problem is particularly challenging when the denominator of the ratio is small, rendering naive plug-in estimators unstable. To address this challenge, we propose a pessimistic ratio estimator that accounts for the denominator's estimation uncertainty. We characterise the statistical properties of this estimator across three sample-size regimes. Empirically, using %a jackknife-based pessimistic rule on synthetic tasks from Reasoning Gym and real-world benchmarks covering both mathematical reasoning and code generation, we show that our adaptive group size selection reduces the mean squared error of the resulting policy gradient and improves policy optimisation over fixed-group-size baselines, with modest additional computational cost.
authors: Shijin Gong, Kai Ye, Victor Chernozhukov, Xinyu Zhang, Chengchun Shi
bullets: GRPO group size is important but is typically chosen by trial and error.
The authors formulate group-size selection as estimating a variance ratio from GRPO’s U-statistic policy gradient.
A pessimistic ratio estimator handles instability when the denominator is small by accounting for estimation uncertainty.
A jackknife-based rule is evaluated on synthetic reasoning tasks plus math and code-generation benchmarks.
The method reduces policy-gradient mean squared error and improves optimization over fixed group sizes with modest extra computation.

papers.selection_reason: Applies U-statistics to GRPO for LLM reasoning, improving policy gradient estimation stability.
papers.title: U-Statistics-Powered LLM Reasoning
papers.tldr: The paper adaptively selects GRPO group sizes using a statistically robust U-statistics-based ratio estimator, improving policy-gradient accuracy and optimization.

papers.abstract: Zeroth-order optimization has emerged as a resource-efficient alternative to Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) when fine-tuning LLMs, thanks to the inherent low dimensionality of the loss landscape. It relies on a two-point estimate of the gradient that only accesses the function value and not the gradient, bypassing the resource-heavy backpropagation. Recently, it was accidentally discovered that per-sample clipping can improve the performance of the trained model, while running a differentially private version of zeroth-order optimization \cite{zhang2024dpzero} with a very large privacy parameter $\epsilon$ (corresponding to very little privacy). In this paper, we systematically investigate this phenomenon and demonstrate that ($i$) the optimal choice of learning rate $\eta$ is inversely proportional to the clipping threshold $c$, satisfying $\eta c =$ constant; ($ii$) clipping drives the zeroth-order optimization to a different solution with higher test accuracy; and ($iii$) this phenomenon is only observed with per-sample clipped zeroth-order optimization and not other zeroth-order alternatives that also provide robust estimates of the gradient. Further analyses with artificially injected label noise reveals that clipping leads to more robust predictions, which stems from the implicit down weighting of hard-to-fit training examples. Our code is available at https://github.com/SewoongLab/ClipZero
authors: Saket Gollapudi, Elisa Bertino, Sewoong Oh
bullets: The optimal learning rate scales inversely with the clipping threshold, keeping ηc constant.
Clipping leads zeroth-order optimization toward a different solution with higher test accuracy.
The effect is specific to per-sample clipped zeroth-order optimization, not other robust zeroth-order gradient estimators.
Under label noise, clipping produces more robust predictions by reducing the influence of difficult training examples.
The study focuses on explaining clipping behavior in zeroth-order fine-tuning of LLMs.

The results demonstrate that unclipped ZO-SGD performs worse as natural difficult examples (B) and synthetic mislabeled examples (A) are added, whereas clipped ZO-SGD remains completely invariant to natural difficult data (81.1%→ 81.3%) and highly resilient to synthetic label noise (79.4%). Crucially, when both A and B are manually pruned (Subset C), unclipped ZO-SGD (81.5%) fully recovers and matches clipped ZO-SGD (81.1%), confirming that clipping improves generalization by acting as an automatic outlier filter against both natural and synthetic high-loss gradients.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates clipping in zeroth-order optimization for LLM fine-tuning, improving robustness and accuracy.
papers.title: Understanding Clipping In Zeroth-Order Optimization
papers.tldr: Per-sample clipping changes zeroth-order optimization’s solution and can improve test accuracy and robustness by implicitly downweighting hard-to-fit examples.

papers.abstract: Recent work proposes hypernetworks that convert a document into a low-rank parameter update (LoRA) in a single forward pass, enabling fast injection of new knowledge into a frozen LLM. However, storing separate LoRA adapters for each document can be unsustainable in streaming settings. In this paper, we study the problem of composing hypernetwork-generated LoRAs using two representative systems, Doc-to-LoRA and SHINE. We show that hypernetwork-generated LoRAs have a geometry sharply different from directly fine-tuned LoRAs. They exhibit greater spectral concentration and stronger cross-document alignment than next-token prediction and QA fine-tuned adapters, which are diffuse and nearly orthogonal across documents. Guided by this observation, we propose latent-space LoRA merging. We compose the intermediate hypernetwork latents and then decode the merged latent through the frozen LoRA-generation head. We show that latent-space merging techniques consistently improve over weight-space and factor-space baselines while preserving a single fixed-rank adapter. These results support latent-space composition as a promising mechanism for combining hypernetwork-generated LoRAs under a fixed output-rank budget.
authors: Yanlai Yang, Minki Kang, Divyam Madaan, Sung Ju Hwang, Mengye Ren
bullets: Addresses the storage challenge of keeping separate LoRA adapters for many streaming documents.
Finds that hypernetwork-generated LoRAs are more spectrally concentrated and cross-document aligned than directly fine-tuned LoRAs.
Composes intermediate hypernetwork latents, then decodes the merged latent into a LoRA using the frozen generation head.
Evaluated with Doc-to-LoRA and SHINE; latent-space merging consistently improves over weight-space and factor-space methods.
Scope: combines hypernetwork-generated adapters under a fixed output-rank budget.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Latent Merger overview. A shared, frozen hypernetwork encoder maps each document to a latent. The trainable merger adds a gated, permutation-invariant residual to the latent mean. The frozen LoRAgeneration head decodes the merged latent into one fixed-rank adapter for the frozen language model.

Figure 1: Hypernetwork-generated LoRAs occupy a qualitatively different region of adapter space. We visualize pairwise distances between unit-Frobenius-normalized adapters using metric MDS, with 500 passages per method sampled from the SQuAD validation set. In the two-dimensional MDS embedding, directly fine-tuned NTP-FT and QA-SFT adapters form broad shells, while D2L and SHINE adapters concentrate in compact regions. This structural difference motivates latent merging methods that respect the hypernetworkinduced adapter geometry.
Figure 2: Cumulative spectral energy of stacked adapter matrices. Hypernetwork-generated adapters concentrate energy in fewer directions than directly fine-tuned NTP-FT and QA-SFT adapters.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes latent-space merging for hypernetwork-generated LoRAs, addressing LLM memory and efficiency.
papers.title: Latent Merger: Latent-Space Composition of Hypernetwork-Generated LoRAs
papers.tldr: Latent-space composition effectively merges hypernetwork-generated LoRAs into one fixed-rank adapter, outperforming direct weight- and factor-space merging baselines.

papers.abstract: Foundation models are built through large-scale pretraining, often followed by post-training, and are then adapted to specific tasks and behaviors. But, does the adaptation add truly new capabilities, or the base model already holds it? We decompose the update induced by different adaptations into a component shared across all inputs and a residual that varies with the input. We find that the shared component suffices for most of the adaptation gain and can be learned directly: a shift adapter that learns a constant vector per layer, identical for every input, reproduces the behavior of LoRA and full fine-tuning. We call this the potentiality principle of foundation models: the base model already contains the capacity needed for task-specific expertise. To adapt to a new task, the model just needs to be actualized, i.e., pushed in a certain direction via a constant, input-independent shift. We show the implications of this principle on parameter-efficient adaptation, steering, and convergence across models, and how it explains the neural thickets phenomenon.
authors: Fabian Gr\"oger, Shuo Wen, Maria Brbi\'c
bullets: Adaptation updates are decomposed into an input-shared component and an input-dependent residual.
A shift adapter using one constant vector per layer reproduces the behavior of LoRA and full fine-tuning for most adaptation gains.
The work proposes the “potentiality principle”: pretraining provides the needed capacity, while adaptation selects or activates it.
The principle has implications for parameter-efficient adaptation, model steering, convergence, and neural thickets.
The abstract does not specify quantitative results or the scope of evaluated models and tasks.

papers.title: On Potentiality and Actuality Of Foundation Models
papers.tldr: Foundation models often already contain task-specific capabilities, and adaptation mainly actualizes them through a simple input-independent shift.

papers.abstract: Linear attention models exhibit a disproportionate deficit relative to softmax attention in associative recall (AR) in language modeling. We investigate this gap through natural language evaluations, synthetic recall tasks, and targeted training interventions. Using a synthetic setting, we quantify the role of state-size in how many items can be recalled from memory and find a similar empirical scaling across the tested linear-attention architectures. Testing this relationship reveals that even a single layer at scale can learn to retrieve thousands of associations across long distances. Yet, standard language model training does not reliably teach a linear model to copy from context, whereas a comparable softmax model learns to do so. Considering this, we strengthen recall supervision during training through in-context sentence repetition and context-sensitive loss reweighting. Both methods improve recall-intensive benchmark performance and narrow the long-distance AR gap to the softmax baseline without changing the architecture, token budget, or number of optimization steps, at a slight cost to general language modeling. These targeted changes to training can thus elicit substantial but underutilized retrieval capacity in linear-attention models. These findings suggest that, although linear-attention architectures have substantial capacity for recall, their inductive biases and the demands of language model training make it difficult to develop this capability without dedicated incentives.
bullets: The study examines why linear attention underperforms softmax attention on associative recall in language modeling.
Synthetic experiments find that recall capacity scales with state size similarly across tested linear-attention architectures.
Even a single sufficiently scaled layer can retrieve thousands of long-distance associations.
In-context sentence repetition and context-sensitive loss reweighting improve recall benchmarks and narrow the gap to softmax attention.
These gains come without architectural or compute-budget changes, but with a slight cost to general language modeling.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates linear attention recall capacity and training interventions, directly relevant to efficient attention and language modeling.
papers.title: Eliciting the Recall Capacity of Linear Attention
papers.tldr: Linear-attention models can recall far more associations than standard training elicits, and targeted recall-focused supervision substantially improves their long-distance retrieval.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning an instruction-tuned language model on new facts often erodes its general abilities. We find that standard fine-tuning lowers instruction-following, reasoning and coding benchmarks by 35 points on average, and that these losses track a collapse in answer length: fine-tuned models at least halve their responses, and the further a response drifts from the initial model's length, the more often it fails. We propose InstructReplay: the initial model answers a set of general instructions once, and during fine-tuning the model is kept close to the initial model on these answers. Across three model families and two domains, InstructReplay reduces the average decline on five general benchmarks from 28.1 to 2.4 points and keeps answer length close to the initial model's, while learning the new facts as well as standard fine-tuning. It balances learning and retention better than seven adaptation methods in all six settings. Controlled comparisons attribute the gain to replaying the model's own answers to general instructions rather than to the form of the loss.
authors: Xiaofeng Shi, Qian Kou, Hua Zhou
bullets: Standard factual fine-tuning causes major general-ability degradation, linked to sharply shorter answers.
The method first records the initial model’s answers to general instructions, then keeps the fine-tuned model close to them.
Across three model families and two domains, benchmark decline falls from 28.1 to 2.4 points on average.
It maintains answer lengths near the initial model’s while learning new facts as well as standard fine-tuning.
It outperforms seven adaptation methods across all six settings; controlled comparisons identify self-answer replay as the key factor.

papers.selection_reason: Fine-tuning LLMs on new facts while preserving general behavior is continual learning for language foundation models.
papers.title: InstructReplay: Replaying Assistant Turns to Preserve General Behavior During Factual Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: InstructReplay preserves general instruction-following, reasoning, and coding abilities during factual fine-tuning by replaying the initial model’s responses to general instructions.

papers.abstract: Training Transformers requires careful hyperparameter tuning, which becomes increasingly costly for large models. We introduce UDV-Rebalance (UDVR), a reparameterization that inserts an auxiliary diagonal matrix $D$ between naturally paired weight matrices $(U,V)$ appearing throughout Transformer architectures. UDVR periodically rebalances the factors to maintain unit-norm columns in $U$ and unit-norm rows in $V$, with $D$ absorbing the corresponding scales. With rebalancing, a single hyperparameter setting of UDVR remains effective across model scales, architectures, and data distributions. This yields a tuning-free rule that adapts to each weight matrix using only its dimensions. We fit this rule once on ViT models trained on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, and it remains valid when the activation function or the optimizer is changed. The same rule transfers to new image domains in DomainNet, to ViT, Swin, and MaxViT on ImageNet, and to language-model pretraining with up to 1.3B parameters. UDVR consistently outperforms Weight Normalization and $\sigma$Reparam and matches a vanilla baseline whose hyperparameters are swept on each target model.
authors: Yikun Hou, Naomi Graham, Alp Yurtsever
bullets: Introduces UDVR, which inserts a diagonal scale matrix between paired weight matrices and periodically rebalances their factor norms.
Uses matrix dimensions to set a single transferable hyperparameter rule, reducing per-model tuning.
A rule fit on CIFAR-trained ViTs transfers to new image domains, multiple vision architectures, and language models up to 1.3B parameters.
Outperforms Weight Normalization and σReparam, while matching a vanilla baseline with target-specific hyperparameter sweeps.

papers.selection_reason: Transferable Transformer training reparameterization that applies to language-model pretraining, relevant to LLM architecture and scaling.
papers.title: Weight Scale Rebalancing: Transferable Training Recipes for Transformers
papers.tldr: UDV-Rebalance enables a largely tuning-free Transformer training rule that transfers across model scales, architectures, optimizers, activations, and domains.

papers.abstract: The ability to learn and generalize from limited experience, or sample efficiency, is a cornerstone of intelligence. How can we build language models that turn a few user interactions, a few snippets of unfamiliar code, or a handful of experimental results provided in context into knowledge that generalizes? Prior work has found that sleep, a process where the model performs $N$ recurrent forward passes to refine its representations of a chunk of context, can improve long-context reasoning (specifically, within SSM-attention hybrid models). We study whether this method also improves in-context adaptation on general, non-synthetic tasks for transformer language models. To this end, we pre-train language models up to 1.2B-parameters on up to 100B tokens with sleep mechanisms. Notably, longer sleep (i.e., using a larger number of recurrent forward passes $N$) enables the model to learn faster in-context on multiple few-shot algorithmic, question-answering tasks, while also achieving lower next-token prediction loss on out-of-distribution evaluations. On held-out code, models with $N=2$ and $N=4$ match the no-sleep baseline's loss using $2.10\times$ and $2.39\times$ fewer tokens in-context, respectively. More broadly, we view our work as a step toward building models that have better tradeoffs between in-context adaptation and decoding latency.
authors: Sangyun Lee, Zhang Enyan, Michael Xu, Hao Tang, Zinan Lin, Weijia Xu, Chris Quirk, Jianfeng Gao, Giulia Fanti, Xiaodong Liu
bullets: Studies whether recurrent “sleep” passes improve in-context adaptation beyond prior long-context reasoning settings.

Longer sleep improves few-shot algorithmic and question-answering adaptation and lowers out-of-distribution next-token loss.
On held-out code, 2 and 4 sleep passes match the no-sleep baseline with 2.10× and 2.39× fewer in-context tokens.
The approach targets a better tradeoff between adaptation efficiency and decoding latency.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a 'sleep' mechanism for sample-efficient in-context adaptation in LLMs, representing a novel approach to test-time learning and memory consolidation.
papers.title: Sample-Efficient In-Context Adaptation via Sleep
papers.tldr: Sleep—repeatedly processing context—helps transformer language models adapt faster from few examples and improves out-of-distribution prediction.

papers.abstract: Many use cases for large language models (LLMs)---from AI safety to exploration and human interaction---can benefit from epistemic uncertainty estimates. We argue that existing Bayesian Deep Learning solutions, which are often restricted to a fixed model family, fail to capture the full epistemic uncertainty at practical LLM scales. This is because the error due to the bounded capacity of the model family remains invisible to disagreement among models supported by the prior. We relate this error to the well-known power-law scaling of LLM loss with model size. We then show that a second power law quantifies the shrinking disagreement within ensembles as model size increases. Its slower decay relative to the capacity law above suggests that ensembles capture a growing share of epistemic uncertainty and become more competitive as an axis for scaling, compared to a single larger model. Finally, a third power law quantifies the loss of ensemble diversity as members share a larger fraction of training before branching, and therefore identifies a further limitation, beyond the capacity error, for LoRA ensembles and optimization-based or second-order methods that approximate uncertainty around a single training solution. At a high level, these findings suggest diverse ensembles can be a promising axis, both for scaling and uncertainty quantification at larger scales.
authors: Siamak Ravanbakhsh, David Nitchi, Khang Ngo
bullets: Fixed model-family Bayesian methods miss uncertainty from models’ limited capacity.
Ensemble disagreement shrinks with model size according to a power law, but more slowly than capacity-related error.
This slower decay suggests ensembles capture a growing share of epistemic uncertainty and may be a viable scaling axis.
A third power law shows that sharing more training before ensemble branching reduces diversity.
The findings highlight limitations of LoRA and optimization-based ensembles that approximate uncertainty around one solution.

papers.selection_reason: Presents scaling laws for ensemble uncertainty in LLMs, identifying a new axis for scaling and uncertainty quantification that complements single-model approaches.
papers.title: Scaling Laws of Ensemble Uncertainty in Language Models
papers.tldr: The paper identifies power laws governing model-capacity error, ensemble disagreement, and ensemble diversity, suggesting diverse ensembles increasingly improve epistemic uncertainty estimation as LLMs scale.

papers.abstract: Modern large language models (LLMs) keep the feed-forward network (FFN) intermediate width identical across every layer, a convention inherited from the original Transformer. Yet mechanistic work suggests layers at different depths do qualitatively different work, raising a natural question: are their capacity demands also non-uniform, and if so, can a fixed parameter budget be allocated more wisely than uniformly? To probe this, we apply principal component analysis (PCA) to the input of each FFN down-projection and measure, for every layer, its intrinsic dimensionality as the smallest number of principal components needed to reconstruct the activation up to a fixed cosine similarity. Scanning 58 open-weight LLMs spanning 14 families and 70M to 72B parameters, we find a recurring middle-heavy profile in which middle layers carry higher intrinsic dimensionality than edge layers; the profile is robust to the calibration corpus, even across English and Chinese, and is largely preserved through post-training fine-tuning. As a direct test that this signal is structurally meaningful, we use it to guide width pruning in a knowledge-distilled student under a matched parameter budget: the PCA-guided allocation outperforms the uniform-width convention by +2.3 points on Qwen3-8B and +2.5 on Qwen2.5-3B, while lower-dispersion teachers show smaller gaps (+0.9 on Gemma-3-4B, +0.5 on LLaMA-3-8B), and a budget-matched inverted control does worst on all four teachers. Across these four teachers, the size of the gap tracks how unevenly the teacher's intrinsic dimensionality is distributed across layers (a single-number summary we call $\sigma_{99}$), and the advantage persists through downstream supervised fine-tuning. Code is available at https://github.com/naver-ai/lidf.
bullets: Across 58 open-weight LLMs from 14 families, FFN intrinsic dimensionality consistently follows a middle-heavy layer profile.
The profile is robust across calibration corpora and languages and remains largely preserved after post-training fine-tuning.
PCA-guided width pruning improves distilled students over uniform widths on four teachers, with gains depending on how unevenly dimensionality is distributed.
An inverted allocation performs worst, supporting the structural relevance of the measured dimensionality signal.
The advantage also persists after downstream supervised fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Quantization-Conditioned Backdoors (QCBs) cause large language models (LLMs) to exhibit malicious behavior after quantization while remaining benign at high precision. Existing defenses often rely on security-guided configuration selection or iterative optimization, but do not identify which quantization-induced changes should be repaired. We isolate module-local quantization effects from upstream drift by evaluating the high-precision and quantized versions of each module on identical states from the quantized inference trajectory, and formulate QCB defense as repairing the resulting same-state operator discrepancies. We propose ReQOR, a training-free defense that identifies the dominant directions of these discrepancies on benign calibration data and restores the full-precision computation along them in closed form, yielding a factorized residual adapter. ReQOR uses neither attack information nor gradient-based optimization and supports both full-span and low-rank repair. Experiments across four LLMs, three PGD-based QCB attacks, three malicious behaviors, and three quantization formats show substantial QCB mitigation while largely preserving benign utility. In additional experiments on a non-PGD outlier-injection attack, existing baselines largely fail, whereas ReQOR remains effective. Further analysis shows that dominant operator-discrepancy directions provide more effective and rank-efficient repair than rank-matched random, low-energy, or raw weight-error directions, while low-rank ReQOR reduces deployment memory overhead.
authors: Wonjune Seo, Minkyung Park, Saerom Park
bullets: Targets quantization-conditioned backdoors that emerge after quantization despite benign high-precision behavior.
Compares full-precision and quantized modules on identical states from the quantized trajectory to isolate local discrepancies.
Repairs dominant discrepancy directions using a closed-form factorized residual adapter, with full-span or low-rank options.
Across four LLMs, three attacks, three malicious behaviors, and three quantization formats, it substantially mitigates backdoors while largely retaining utility.
Also remains effective against a non-PGD outlier-injection attack; low-rank repair reduces deployment memory overhead.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at medical question answering yet are rarely evaluated on the stepwise diagnostic reasoning that defines real clinical workflows, where impressions are revised as information accumulates. We build Annotated Stepwise Clinical rEasoning for NaturalisTic Diagnosis (ASCENT), a clinician-annotated benchmark and training resource of 3,078 stepwise problems derived from MedQA-USMLE that decomposes each vignette into EMR-aligned steps (Findings, Impression, supporting Rationale), enabling evaluation of intermediate reasoning under incomplete information. Experiments and training with ASCENT revealed insights into how current LLMs handle stepwise diagnostic reasoning. Even strong reasoning models that perform well on MedQA-USMLE leave substantial headroom on ASCENT, and general-purpose frontier models trail further, exposing a persistent gap between fully informed and stepwise diagnosis. Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-7B and 32B on ASCENT yields measurable F1 gains over both pre-trained and HuatuoGPT-o1 CoT-trained baselines, with gains driven primarily by precision. Complementary robustness analyses (counterfactual perturbation, format-vs-content control, judge agreement, and rollout) further show that ASCENT-fine-tuned models rely on the diagnostic content of prior impressions rather than imitating their output format, while error propagation under rollout remains a key challenge for clinical deployment.
authors: Yera Choi, Yeong Hwa Kim, Jaedeok Lee, Taekang Kim, Sangdoo Yun, Seong-Eun Moon
bullets: Introduces 3,078 clinician-annotated, EMR-aligned diagnostic problems derived from MedQA-USMLE.
Decomposes cases into Findings, Impression, and supporting Rationale to evaluate reasoning under incomplete information.
Strong reasoning models still lag on stepwise diagnosis compared with fully informed question answering.
Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-7B and 32B improves F1 over pretrained and HuatuoGPT-o1 CoT baselines, mainly through higher precision.
Robustness tests suggest models use prior diagnostic content, but rollout error propagation remains a deployment challenge.

At each step, clinical findings are paired with a list of suspected disorders (Impression) and the corresponding rationale (Reason). In evaluations with ASCENT, each step is treated as a separate question, and models are prompted to generate either only the Impression or both the Impression and the corresponding Reason.

papers.abstract: Deep search is a critical capability for agents tackling complex, open-ended tasks, where solving a problem requires iterative information gathering, query reformulation, and evidence-based verification rather than a single retrieval step. To address these requirements, we present Bathys 9B and 27B deep search agents built around a training framework that spans verifiable question synthesis, post-training, and online reinforcement learning (RL) under context compression. Our high-quality data construction ensures both search depth and reliability: each clue is reformulated as an indirect reference requiring independent retrieval, and retained evidence chains enable verification that the clues jointly determine a unique answer. Curated trajectories underpin a pipeline of supervised fine-tuning (SFT), Kahneman-Tversky Optimization (KTO), and Compaction-Managed Group Sequence Policy Optimization (CM-GSPO): SFT provides a stable foundation for tool use over long horizons and query reformulation; KTO uses binary feedback on trajectories to improve the selection of answers grounded in evidence; CM-GSPO optimizes execution sub-trajectories with length-normalized likelihood ratios on the recorded rollout contexts and reweights sub-trajectory advantages to correct the extra weighting introduced by independently averaging sub-trajectory losses. Bathys 9B and 27B attain 66.51% and 80.49% on BrowseComp, respectively, under an evaluation protocol with trajectory self-verification and conditional retries.
authors: Zixuan Chen, Shengyou Yuan, Nang Yuan, Ming Ma, Zelin Xiao, Lin Zhou, Siyuan Luo, Jiaqi Su, Chengrui Wu, Tiankuo Yao, Nairong Zheng, Cong Pang, Jiapeng Luo

Builds verifiable training data from indirectly referenced clues and evidence chains that uniquely determine answers.
Uses SFT, KTO, and CM-GSPO to improve long-horizon tool use, evidence-grounded answering, and optimization under context compression.
Reports BrowseComp scores of 66.51% for Bathys 9B and 80.49% for Bathys 27B.
Evaluation includes trajectory self-verification and conditional retries.

papers.abstract: A common occurrence in Large Language Models (LLMs) is the emergence of so-called massive activations. This phenomenon is well known in the literature and has been connected to attention sinks, representational compression, as well as signal propagation. However, the reasons and consequences for their appearance are not yet well understood. In this paper, we explain the role of massive activations in deep learning by showing that they are connected to the region migration phenomenon in delayed robustness. Under the spline theoretic interpretation of deep networks, we show that massive activations push the representations away from the nonlinearity boundaries of the network, decreasing the complexity of its input-output map around data points. Furthermore, we uncover for the first time that this phenomenon is not unique to transformers and actually appears in a number of common architectures performing simple supervised learning tasks. We validate this connection through extensive experiments on a diverse set of architectures including residual MLP, ResNet18, Vision Transformers and GPT and datasets including MNIST, CIFAR10, Imagenette and Shakespeare Text. We consistently observe that massive activations and region migration co-occur with adversarial robustness. Furthermore, we illustrate that this connection holds in the large-scale pretraining of LLMs by showing that the rise of massive activations in LLMs closely tracks the adversarial accuracy of the model under perturbations of the token embeddings.
authors: Tigran Fahradyan, Riccardo Ali, Sergio Calvo-Ordo\~nez, Jos\'e Miguel Hern\'andez-Lobato, Pietro Li\`o, \'Alvaro Arroyo
bullets: Connects massive activations in LLMs to region migration, a phenomenon associated with delayed adversarial robustness.

Experiments across image and language tasks consistently find co-occurrence between massive activations, region migration, and adversarial robustness.
During large-scale LLM pretraining, the growth of massive activations tracks robustness to perturbations of token embeddings.

papers.abstract: As Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale, Expert Parallelism (EP) becomes increasingly important for distributing experts across devices. However, the resulting token dispatch and combine operations can become a major bottleneck during inference. Overlapping these communication phases with computation is constrained by the sequential dependencies of standard MoE architectures. We introduce BRAID-MoE, an architecture that pairs laddered residual connections with early routing to relax these dependencies. Laddered residuals enable each expert combine to be deferred to the following block, while early routing computes the next routing decision from the pre-combine residual, with experts still receiving the updated post-combine hidden state. This creates an extended communication window in which the preceding combine and next dispatch can execute back-to-back on a dedicated communication stream, overlapping attention computation. On Qwen3-shaped MoEs with 0.4B-A0.1B and 2.5B-A0.5B parameters, BRAID closely matches sequential training at matched compute, with validation-loss increases of only 1% and 0.5%, respectively. We further demonstrate that existing MoE checkpoints can be adapted to BRAID with limited additional training, largely recovering their original accuracy. On a converted Qwen3-30B-A3B model, BRAID achieves speedups of up to 1.29$\times$ in prefill and 1.37$\times$ in decode, and at least 1.12$\times$ across diverse workloads and EP configurations on one or two four-H100 nodes. It outperforms competing overlap strategies in all tested settings, with the strongest gains when communication is a major latency bottleneck and its duration approaches the available computation window. These results demonstrate that early routing enables more effective communication-computation overlap in MoE inference at a modest cost in model quality.
authors: John Zarka (MLIA), Danyal Ahmed (MLIA), Eugene Belilovsky (DIRO, MILA), Edouard Oyallon (MLIA)
bullets: Targets token dispatch and combine bottlenecks caused by sequential dependencies in expert parallelism.
Uses laddered residuals to defer expert combines and early routing to initiate the next dispatch sooner.
Enables back-to-back communication phases to overlap with attention computation on a dedicated stream.
On converted Qwen3 models, reports up to 1.29× prefill and 1.37× decode speedups, with at least 1.12× across tested workloads and configurations.
Validation-loss increases are limited to 1% and 0.5% in two smaller matched-compute settings; existing checkpoints can be adapted with limited additional training.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Comparison of (a) Sequential, (b) Parallel, (c) Ladder, (d) Early-Routing (p = 1), and (e) BRAID MoE architectures. Red blocks denote computation and blue blocks denote expert-parallel communication. In BRAID, sharded expert outputs are combined with the residual stream and immediately dispatched to the next layer’s experts, enabling back-to-back communication operations.

Figure 2. Illustrative two-stream execution schedules of (a) Sequential, (b) Parallel, (c) Ladder, (d) Early-Routing (p = 1), and (e) BRAID MoEs. Red blocks denote routing (R), attention (A), and expert computation (E), while blue blocks denote dispatch (D) and combine communication (C). (a) Sequential MoE serializes attention and MoE execution. (b) Parallel MoE overlaps dispatch with attention, since both branches consume the same residual. (c) Ladder MoE overlaps attention with the preceding combine, but routing still depends on that combine. (d) Early-Routing computes routing from an earlier representation, overlapping it with the preceding combine, while dispatch still waits for the fresh post-attention representation. (e) BRAID computes routing from the earlier residual while sharded expert outputs are combined, enabling back-to-back combine and dispatch operations across consecutive layers, with communication overlapping attention. Timings are schematic and not measured.

Figure 3. Communication dataflow in BRAID-MoE. The dashed region highlights the back-to-back combine and dispatch operations enabled by precomputed routing assignments. Sharded expert outputs are combined with the residual stream to produce yℓ. In our implementation, residual addition and MoE RMSNorm are fused into the combine epilogue, with normalization applied only on the dispatch path. The unnormalized residual yℓ is preserved for the subsequent residual update.

Figure 4. Training perplexity for the 2.5B-A0.5B Qwen3-style MoE under Sequential, Parallel, Ladder, and BRAID schedules. Curves are smoothed over a trailing window of 0.3B training tokens. The main panel covers 1B–10.46B tokens, while the inset enlarges the final 1B tokens. All schedules use matched training settings. BRAID uses a separate normalization layer for early routing.

Figure 5. Speedup relative to Sequential for EP=4 (one four-H100 node). (a) Prefill versus global batch size B at L = 1024; (b) prefill versus prompt length L at B = 64; (c) decode versus B at L = 1024; and (d) decode versus L at B = 64. Each curve represents one execution schedule; the shared legend applies to all four panels. Detailed latency and overlap measurements are reported in Appendix C.4 (Table 10).

Figure 6. Speedup relative to Sequential for EP=8 (two four-H100 nodes). (a) Prefill versus global batch size B at L = 1024; (b) prefill versus prompt length L at B = 128; (c) decode versus B at L = 1024; and (d) decode versus L at B = 128. Each curve represents one execution schedule; the shared legend applies to all four panels. Detailed latency and overlap measurements are reported in Appendix C.4 (Table 11).

Table 4. Qwen3-30B-A3B inference for 16 prompts of 1,024 tokens per GPU (global batch 64 with EP=4 and 128 with EP=8). Latencies are the mean of five job medians ± standard error (30 rounds per job, each measuring all four schedules in random order); decode latency is per step. Combine and dispatch overlaps are medians over three Nsight Systems traces of the fraction of each communication kernel’s execution time concurrent with computation kernels on the same GPU. Speedup is relative to Sequential; bold marks the best latency and speedup.

Table 10. All workloads with EP=4: average of the medians of five jobs of 30 rounds ± its standard error, speedup over Sequential, and combine/dispatch overlap from Nsight Systems traces (fraction of communication-kernel time concurrent with computation on the same GPU, across GPUs).

Table 11. All workloads with EP=8 on two nodes: average of the medians of five jobs of 30 rounds ± its standard error, speedup over Sequential, and combine/dispatch overlap from Nsight Systems traces (fraction of communication-kernel time concurrent with computation on the same GPU, across GPUs).

T is the total GPU span, Tm is the summed duration of DeepEP’s dispatch and combine kernels and their epilogues, and TE is expert computation time. We estimate the independent computation window T ov c from the summed durations of attention and other non-expert computation kernels. The last two columns of each phase show ρ = Tm/T ov c and the idealized limit Sideal from Eq. (3). papers.abstract: We introduce reinforcement learning from collective rewards (RLCR), a recipe for jointly training language models to act as agent organisations under latency constraints. A CEO and up to eight specialists share one policy, co-ordinate through a message board and workspace, and are trained with a common outcome-derived advantage. The deadline makes parallel work valuable when it increases the return earned before the cap. We train Avalon-M1-Mini (120B) across 147 environments. For the trained model, eight-hire organisational execution raises IMO-ProofBench-Advanced scores from 23.8% to 39.0% relative to single-agent execution. Across 12 benchmarks, organisations achieve similar average scores at approximately one-third the derived latency of token-matched single-agent execution and just over half that of eight independent attempts followed by selection. The trained model also outperforms Nemotron 3 Super, post-trained from the same base model, across all evaluations when comparing each model's best tested configuration. On EdgeBench, organisations overtake the single agent after approximately 0.4 derived hours. Over the course of training, organisations develop hierarchies to manage communication costs, invest more in peer review, and alter how work is divided. Safety evaluations find near-universal refusal of harmful actions but sustained declines in external reporting in two of three oversight scenarios. These results establish a shared-advantage baseline for studying organisational learning, performance-latency trade-offs, and collective oversight.
authors: Iliyan Zarov, Henry Course, Anthony Hartshorn, Ran Achiron, Louis Roche, Akshit Sinha, Chengxi Taylor, Ross Taylor
bullets: A CEO and up to eight specialists share one policy and coordinate via a message board and workspace.
A common outcome-derived advantage rewards organisational strategies that increase returns before a deadline.
Eight-agent execution improves IMO-ProofBench-Advanced from 23.8% to 39.0% versus single-agent execution.
Across 12 benchmarks, organisations reach similar average performance at roughly one-third the derived latency of token-matched single-agent execution.
Training produces communication hierarchies and more peer review, but external reporting declines in two of three oversight scenarios.

figures.caption: Figure 3 | Message Boards as a Laboratory for Collective Intelligence. A channel from an Avalon-M1-Mini organisation working on a data science task. In this particular task, agents post baselines and model sweeps with their cross-validation scores, create internal leaderboards, share engineered features on request, and build on each other’s results.

Figure 14 | The Rise of Surgical Teams. Share of opening plans that split implementation by component or use a build/test/review pipeline centered on one code owner. Over training, implementations become more centralised reflecting increased hierarchy, increased importance of supporting roles like testing and review assisting "power ICs". Bands are 95% bootstrap intervals over (step, task) clusters.

Figure 6 | Post-training recipe comparison. Avalon-M1-Mini compared on accuracy/score benchmarks with Nemotron 3 Super (120B-A12B) by NVIDIA. Both models are trained on top of the same base model and do not use on-policy distillation from a stronger model. Our RLCR recipe trains an agent organisation mode to create a new parallel inference-time compute setting.

Figure 1 | Collective Inference-Time Scaling. As we train Avalon-M1-Miniwith RLCR, the compute organisations spend on communication grows alongside total inference-time compute and task performance as RL compute increases. Panels show performance averages across environments with different reward scales. We observe similar trends on test and train environments. Compute is in FLOPs. Because the maximum wall-clock rises over training, communication compute is measured per rollout-hour, which the policy can raise by communicating more or by keeping more agents busy. Appendix A explains the motivation as well as alternative measures that show similar trends.

Figure 2 | Reinforcement Learning from Collective Rewards (RLCR).We show the basic ingredients of our RLCR recipe, which consists of agent organisation rollouts operating through message boards, a shared collective reward, a wall-clock timecap to impose latency pressure and reward parallel work, and policy gradient objectives to reinforce successful organisations.

Figure 8 | DRACO score against work time. Mean score over the 100 DRACO-Internal tasks for a single agent and an organisation of up to 8 hires given varying amounts of maximum work time. Stars are the same model and tasks with no time constraint, placed at their mean work time. Standard errors are about 2 points. This ablation was performed on an earlier checkpoint of Avalon (step 170).

Figure 5 | Avalon-M1 RL Environments. We train on 147 reinforcement learning environments, organised into sectors in the chart above. Sampling rates vary over time due to the use of a curriculum, which prioritises learning progress. We train on 30,509 distinct tasks over training, a small fraction of the 2 million plus total tasks available.

Figure 7 | Sequential, independent and collective inference-time scaling against latency. Mean reward over 12 benchmarks against derived latency per trial for a single agent (B0), extended thinking (S8), eight independent agents with a selector (I8) and the eight-hire organisation (B8). All three forms of scaling beat the single agent by a similar margin, but the organisation reaches that accuracy at about a third of extended thinking’s latency and under 60% of the independent agents’. Derived latency rebuilds each agent’s clock from the event log (Appendix C.2).

Figure 15 | Co-ordination Share by Organisation Size. Left: the share of an organisation’s working time spent on co-ordination, against the organisation budget 𝑏. Right: the same measure against organisation size 𝑛 (the CEO plus specialists), with the hierarchy and fully connected cost models fitted. Bands are 95% intervals from resampling environments.

Figure 4 | Learning Long-Horizon Tasks. At training-time, we use a wall-clock timecap based on derived latency to impose latency pressure. At test-time we impose a fixed 12 hour timecap. We see that all organisation budgets improve over the course of training, and organisations additionally provide latency benefits over single-agent execution (Section 3.3).

Figure 25 | Descriptive organisational scaling fits. Collective quantities against the number of specialists hired 𝑁, on log–log axes, for the 35 long-horizon environments in steps 100–200 of training. Large points are means at each 𝑁, faint points are individual rollouts, and the solid line is the fitted power law with its exponent 𝛽 and 95% bootstrap interval. Dashed lines show proportional scaling (𝛽 = 1); for direct-message pairs they show star (𝛽 = 1) and all-pairs mesh (𝛽 = 2) predictions. Panels are ordered from most sublinear to most superlinear.

Figure 9 | EdgeBench reward over time, by organisation budget. Mean best-so-far score against derived latency for the 784 runs of the four-seed EdgeBench evaluation (49 tasks × 4 seeds × 4 budgets). Left: observed curves. Right: log-logistic fits of Equation 7. Dashed lines mark where the best organisation budget overtakes the single agent, at roughly 0.4 hours both observed and fitted; given the small final differences, this crossover time is approximate.

Figure 10 | The Rise of Hierarchy in Agent Organisations. Organisations start with a wheel structure between CEO and hired agents. Over training, CEOs hire lead roles more frequently, creating a middle-management layer. Left: share of hires with lead titles in the software-build training environments. Right: the same share on the EdgeBench evaluation. Bands are 95% bootstrap intervals over environments and tasks.

Figure 26 | Reaction emoji on the message board over training. One panel for each of the 15 most-used emoji, showing reactions per 1,000 rollouts on its own linear scale, as an 11-step running mean over every training rollout. Non-emoji symbols that agents used as reactions are left out.

Figure 27 | GRPO vs GKPO Advantages. Advantage of each training rollout against its wealth relative to the group mean. GKPO keeps the ordering of the Kelly advantages while bounding the negative advantage. The Spearman correlation with Kelly advantages is 0.96 for GKPO, against 0.82 for GRPO.

Figure 12 | Division of Labour by Domain. We divide environments into sectors and analyse hired roles over time. Software engineering environments show a move towards hierarchical roles; business simulations invest more in risk management. Trends are often subtle in some domains, and we anticipate more steps are needed to observe more significant shifts in the division of labour.
Figure 28 shows the momentum Boltzmann sampler of Section 2.2.3 at work.

Figure 28 | Momentum Boltzmann Sampling. Environments are sampled according to their absolute learning progress, which varies over the course of training. As environments saturate in their performance, they get sampled less and other environments get sampled more. Note that some environments were added to the training run later in training as they became available.

Figure 16 | Code output scales faster in open-ended environments. Left: lines of code written against specialists hired, for open-ended and procedural environments. Each point averages environments with equal weight, relative to each environment's own mean, so only changes within an environment count; lines are the within-environment fits. Right: the 45 environments ranked by their own exponent, with 95% intervals from resampling rollouts.

Figure 11 | Two SWE organisations, early and late in training. The task is to make a football management game from scratch. Each organisation is the highest-scoring eight-hire team in its group. Left: every specialist reports to the CEO. Right: a Lead Developer builds the shell that its reports extend, while the data roles and an independent QA verifier work directly with the CEO.

Figure 19 | The Insularity Problem. In each safety scenario, agents recognise the problem at a high rate (the collective-cyberattack share slips to 70% at step 200). But they act on it much less over the course of training, i.e. reporting problems to humans. The decline is durable in the takeover and cyberattack scenarios; in whistleblowing it reverses after step 170. One hypothesis is that this dissociation reflects training incentives and the lack of mechanisms or rewards for reporting externally; the experiments do not isolate this cause. The figure shows a subset of the ten evaluated checkpoints; the text reports all ten. In the cyberattack scenario, confederates for steps 186–200 were driven by the checkpoint under test rather than by step 150. Shaded bands are 95% intervals: Wilson for the per-run and per-agent counts, bootstrap over runs for the per-engineer whistleblowing rates. 𝑛 = 30 runs per checkpoint.

Figure 13 | Organisations Invest in Peer Review. Over time, organisations make more hires with roles like verifier, reviewer, critic, auditor or checker. When counting the number of tokens per hour that are dedicated to peer-review, we see this increase accordingly over the course of training.

Figure 24 | Co-ordination is rewarded in moderation. Mean training advantage by the rollout’s organisation co-ordination share, for each organisation budget, pooled over long-horizon environments. Rollouts are weighted so that every GRPO group counts equally, so advantages balance around zero. Bands are 95% bootstrap intervals over groups.

Figure 22 | Articles per 100 words of reasoning over training. Articles (a, an, the) per 100 words of CEO and specialist reasoning, with code removed. Environments are weighted equally over the 62 present in at least 80% of sampled steps. Lines are centred running means over 10 training steps, and bands are 95% bootstrap intervals over environments.

Figure 18 | Collective Action Experiments. In the public goods game, Avalon-M1-Mini’s contributions peak at step 100, collapse at step 150 and only partly recover by step 200; with a punishment stage they stay near the ceiling throughout. In the stag hunt the share choosing the stag falls steadily after step 100, corresponding with increased reasoning about the safety of the guaranteed payoff. In the intergroup allocation scenario, spiteful behaviour towards the other group collapses after step 100 and only partly returns.

Figure 23 | Specialists co-ordinate increasingly with each other, not with the CEO. Share of specialists’ working time spent co-ordinating with other specialists (left) and with the CEO (right) over training, by organisation budget. Each point is a 20-step bin, averaged with all 21 long-horizon environments weighted equally; bands are 95% bootstrap intervals over rollouts within environments.
Figure 17 | Attitudes towards teammates. Agents increasingly plan to help, explicitly offer help, and attribute work to teammates as training progresses. Centred 5-step pooled shares with a 95% band.

Figure 21 | Total communication compute. As Figure 1, with total communication compute per rollout in place of communication compute per rollout-hour on the third axis. Points are training steps; the line joins the means of six equal-count bins.

Figure 20 | The Uneasy Triangle of RLCR. Long-horizon episodes, multi-agent rollouts and a multienvironment curriculum each stretch a flat advantage over more tokens or spread a batch over more task families. Each raises the variance of the policy-gradient estimate.

Table 3 | Avalon-M1-Mini across organisation budgets and single-agent baselines. B0 denotes single-agent execution; B2, B4 and B8 denote organisations with a budget of 2, 4 and 8 agents. S8 is a single agent that may not submit until it has matched B8’s output tokens. I8 (independent@8) runs eight single agents in parallel with no communication; a selector, the same model, then reads the eight answers and trajectories and submits one. Bold marks the best result for each benchmark across the organisation budgets, S8 and I8.

Table 1 | Agent Organisation Tools. The agent organisation harness provides basic message board primitives for communicating with other agents, including direct messages and public channels. These tools are appended to other tools an agent has available to them, such as environment tools.

Table 5 | Organisational scaling exponents compared with cities. Exponents 𝛽 of 𝔼[𝑍] ∝ 𝑁 𝛽, where 𝑁 is the number of specialists hired (1–8) in the 35 long-horizon environments for agent organisations, population for cities, and the size measure named in each row for human teams and firms. For agent organisations, 𝛽 is fitted to the pooled rollouts and Within env is the exponent fitted within each environment, environments weighted equally; a quantity is superlinear if its whole 95% interval lies above 1.1, sublinear if it lies below 0.9, and linear otherwise. Regimes for cities and human teams follow the classifications in the original studies. City exponents are from Bettencourt et al. (2007), except phone contacts, from Schläpfer et al. (2014). For human teams and firms, the Ringelmann exponent is our fit to the per-person output reported for groups of two, three and eight; the information-consumption exponent is the inverse of the reported fit of employees on records read (0.76 ± 0.01).
Table 6 | What each reaction emoji is used for. The most-used reaction emoji over the last seven steps of training, with a typical post each is attached to.
Table 4 | Evaluation settings. Tasks is the number of distinct tasks evaluated and seeds per task the number of independent runs of each. Notes describe any departures from the full benchmark.

Table 8 | Environment issues found by rollout audits. Envs counts environment repositories with at least onemerged fix in the category; categories overlap. For repeat submissions, it counts environments that pinned the SDK release with the latch. Fixes to the SDK, the sandbox platform and the harness are not counted.

Table 7 | RL Training Environments. We train Avalon-M1-Mini on a diverse range of tasks, with a focus on long-horizon tasks that require sustained reasoning and environmental interaction. We sample hierarchically, first environments and then tasks within them, so sectors with many tasks are not overrepresented.

papers.abstract: If Chinese had been Latinized, as the Latinxua Sin Wenz movement proposed, what would it have meant for Chinese NLP? Homophones and tone marking complicate the answer. We convert Chinese corpora to syllable-separated Pinyin and train superBPE tokenizers from scratch. The resulting Pinyin vocabularies not only exhibit expected homophone collisions, but also show approximately 10% higher fertility than characters. An alternative BPE configuration changes the relative fertility of the two representations. We further pretrain Llama-style models on Chinese characters and Pinyin. The Pinyin models perform worse on per-character perplexity, homophone disambiguation, and overall ZhoBLiMP minimal-pair accuracy. An exploratory phonological probe yields near-chance performance for both representations. The broader implication is that written input representations are not merely neutral encodings. Choices for representations affect language modeling and their downstream performances. Latinization never actually happened for Chinese, but other languages did, such as Hangul and Latin script replaced character in Korean and Vietnamese; the cost we measure is a guide to where modeling effort for those languages should concentrate.
bullets: Pinyin tokenizers show expected homophone collisions and about 10% higher fertility than character tokenizers, though results vary with BPE configuration.
Llama-style models pretrained on Pinyin perform worse on per-character perplexity, homophone disambiguation, and ZhoBLiMP accuracy.
A phonological probe is near chance for both character and Pinyin representations.
The findings suggest written representations are not neutral and may guide modeling choices for languages that underwent script Latinization.

papers.abstract: Specialists post-trained from a shared checkpoint acquire complementary capabilities, and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) can consolidate them into a single model. However, we find that existing consolidation methods, from weight merging to MOPD, fall short when specialists diverge substantially from the shared checkpoint, whereas prior studies mostly examine specialists that remain close to it. We present a unified recipe for multimodal MOPD that consolidates such specialists back into the single student they branched from. The recipe specifies initialization, data selection, balanced supervision across teachers, and preservation of existing capabilities for consolidation, together with a targeted refinement stage for capabilities that still lag behind their specialists. In an industrial setting with six specialists, the student closely approaches each specialist in its own domain and surpasses the perception specialist. It recovers 97.0% of their average gain, compared with 79.8% for IM-MOPD. In the fully open five-domain setting with Qwen3-4B, our method recovers 95.7% of the specialists' average gain after consolidation and 97.5% after refinement, compared with 94.1% for IM-MOPD. We further analyze the full pipeline through mechanism ablations and training dynamics, providing practical guidance for diagnosing incomplete consolidation. Code will be released.
authors: Zihan Liang, Zikun Qu, Ben Chen, Fan Yang, Wenwu Ou, Min Zhang, Zhongxiang Dai, Xinchao Wang
bullets: Addresses the failure of existing weight-merging and MOPD methods when specialists diverge far from their shared starting checkpoint.
Combines careful initialization, data selection, balanced multi-teacher supervision, and capability preservation.
Adds targeted refinement for capabilities that remain weaker than those of the specialists.
With six industrial specialists, the student closely matches each domain specialist and surpasses the perception specialist.

Recovers 97.0% of specialists’ average gain in the industrial setting and 95.7% after consolidation—or 97.5% after refinement—in the open five-domain setting, compared with 79.8% and 94.1% for IM-MOPD, respectively.

papers.title: Branch and Consolidate: A Unified Recipe for Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
papers.tldr: Branch-and-Consolidate is a unified multimodal on-policy distillation recipe that merges substantially diverged specialists into one student while retaining their capabilities.

papers.abstract: Looped language models apply one shared transformer stack several times per token, and every loop is readable through the shared language-model head. Post-training them is hard. Reward-only reinforcement learning needs a verifier and learns from one sparse signal per response; spreading the reward over loops collapses the entropy of every loop; and cross-loop self-distillation, as in LoopOPD, can only teach intermediate loops, because the last loop cannot learn from its own frozen copy: the loss is zero at initialisation. We observe that a looped model already contains a policy that decodes better than its last loop: the next-token distribution extrapolated from the first loop through the last. ELPSD (Extrapolated-Loop Policy Self-Distillation) turns this distribution into a self-distillation target: a frozen copy of the model computes it, and the model's own last loop is distilled towards it on its own rollouts, using the exact reverse KL at every visited prefix. Teacher and student are the same model, so ELPSD needs no reward, no external teacher and no privileged context, and it leaves rollouts and decoding unchanged. We show that the objective pulls the last loop towards the base model's last loop with weight 1+w and away from the base model's first loop with weight w, and that the teacher must stay frozen, since an idealised teacher recomputed from the current model extrapolates without bound. We evaluate ELPSD on Ouro-1.4B-Thinking across five math benchmarks against the base model, GRPO, RLTT and OPSD. Without any reward, ELPSD raises the average avg@8 from 61.15 to 63.69 and is the best method on all five benchmarks, ahead of GRPO (62.32), which uses a verifier, and the self-distillation method OPSD (61.77), which needs reference solutions.
bullets: Looped models reuse one transformer stack across multiple loops, but standard post-training struggles with sparse rewards and cannot self-distill the final loop from itself.
ELPSD uses a frozen model copy to extrapolate the next-token distribution from the first loop through the last and applies reverse-KL distillation on the model’s own rollouts.
The method requires no verifier, reward signal, external teacher, privileged context, or rollout/decoding changes.
The frozen teacher is essential: recomputing the extrapolated teacher from the current model can cause unbounded extrapolation.
On Ouro-1.4B-Thinking across five math benchmarks, ELPSD raises average avg@8 from 61.15 to 63.69 and outperforms GRPO and OPSD.

papers.selection_reason: Self-distillation method for looped language models directly concerns LLM post-training and policy improvement.
papers.title: The Teacher Is Already Inside: Self-Distilling Looped Language Models Beyond Their Last Loop
papers.tldr: ELPSD improves looped language models by distilling the model’s own extrapolated early-to-late-loop policy into its final loop, without rewards, external teachers, or changed decoding.

papers.abstract: Model-aware online data selection prioritizes the training documents that contribute the most given the model's current state. Existing online selectors rank candidates upon gradient-based data utility scores, which requires the full forward-backward pass of the main model on every candidate document. Scoring each document therefore pays as much as training on it, yet only a small fraction is used for the real model update. We introduce DAiSy, a lightweight linear auxiliary model that learns to predict data utility scores from frozen document embeddings, which eliminates the computation overhead and infrastructure burdens. The linear estimator is updated alongside the main language model, fitting to the exact gradient-based utility scores obtained from the backward pass of regular training steps. Consequently, scoring a candidate requires only a linear transformation, bypassing the costly gradient-alignment computation. We demonstrate its effectiveness and efficiency for LLM pretraining in English and multilingual scenarios, with various steering target designs. The improvements from DAiSy can consistently survive the instruction-tuning phase.
bullets: Existing selectors require a full forward-backward pass to score every candidate document, despite using only a small fraction for updates.
DAiSy predicts gradient-based utility from frozen document embeddings using a linear auxiliary estimator.
The estimator learns online from exact utility scores computed during regular training steps.
The approach is evaluated for English and multilingual LLM pretraining with different steering targets.
Reported gains and efficiency improvements persist through instruction tuning.

papers.selection_reason: Online data selection method for LLM pretraining; relevant to large language model research and training efficiency.
papers.title: DAiSy: Online Data Selection by Adaptive Utility Estimation for LLM Pretraining
papers.tldr: DAiSy accelerates model-aware online data selection by predicting document utility with a lightweight linear model instead of costly per-document gradient computations.

papers.abstract: Our goal is to build language models that are steerable by design. Today's language models are pretrained with next-token prediction, which relegates alignment and control to the final 1% of training tokens or inference-time interventions. These models repurpose a single input channel for both instructions and data, leading to common failure modes where the model mistakenly treats data as instructions such as intentional jailbreaks and unintentional in-context alignment drift. To correct this, we propose a pretraining method and architecture that separates the two from the very start, producing Mancelle-3B. An encoder processes high-level semantic features of upcoming text with cross-attention that prevents the token stream from writing back into this control channel. During pretraining, the model learns to rely on these features to predict the next token, turning the channel into an effective handle for steering the model. Mancelle-3B steers more strongly than prompt- and activation-based methods on comparable open models while maintaining fluency, and it withstands adversarial black-box and soft-prompt counter-steering that defeats those baselines. We reproduce this against a more controlled baseline with Mancelle-400M. Our results show that robust control can be built into language models if we do so early and intentionally.
authors: Henry Castillo, Yanchen Liu, Claudio Mayrink Verdun, Dylan Hadfield-Menell
bullets: Motivation: Standard next-token pretraining conflates instructions and data, enabling jailbreaks and in-context alignment drift.
Method: An encoder supplies high-level semantic features through cross-attention while preventing the token stream from writing back into the control channel.
The model is trained from the start to use this channel for next-token prediction, making it a built-in steering interface.
Mancelle-3B steers more strongly than comparable prompt- and activation-based methods while preserving fluency.
It resists adversarial black-box and soft-prompt counter-steering, with the finding reproduced using Mancelle-400M.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a novel LLM pretraining architecture with a separate control channel for steerability, constituting an architectural advance fitting large language models.
papers.title: Steerable by Design: Conditional Pretraining for Robust Control of Language Models
papers.tldr: Conditional pretraining with a dedicated, non-writable control channel makes language models more steerable and resistant to counter-steering.

papers.abstract: Generative reward models (GRMs) make language-model evaluation more explicit by generating critiques, rubrics, or intermediate analyses before predicting a final preference. However, explicit evaluation does not necessarily imply a reliable evaluation process: under outcome-only supervision, a model may reach the correct final preference while producing weak or unsupported intermediate judgments, turning the evaluation into a post-hoc rationalization. We introduce STEP-GRM, a framework that directly supervises the intermediate evaluation process of rubric-based GRMs. In addition to conventional preference supervision, STEP-GRM provides structural guidance for rubric construction and local supervision for criterion-level judgments, encouraging the model to learn not only the correct final preference but also a more reliable process for reaching it. Extensive experiments show that STEP-GRM achieves strong performance on standard reward-modeling benchmarks while improving the consistency and correctness of intermediate evaluations. Moreover, reward signals produced by STEP-GRM lead to better downstream policy optimization, demonstrating that more reliable evaluation processes can translate into practical gains beyond reward-model accuracy.
authors: Qiyuan Chen, Yuze Zhao, Jiahe Chen, Hongsen Huang, Hongxia Xu, Yingda Chen, Jian Wu
bullets: Outcome-only supervision can produce correct preferences with weak, unsupported, post-hoc rationales.
STEP-GRM adds structural guidance for rubric construction and local supervision for criterion-level judgments.
Experiments show strong benchmark performance and more consistent, correct intermediate evaluations.
Its reward signals also improve downstream policy optimization, extending benefits beyond reward-model accuracy.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of STEP-GRM. (A) Structured preference data are constructed and partitioned for probe training, cold-start SFT, and RL. (B) A single-criterion probe is trained to independently judge response pairs under individual criteria and is frozen thereafter. (C) STEP-GRM is initialized with SFT and subsequently optimized with process supervision: privileged rubric self-distillation Lpriv guides the evaluation structure, the frozen probe provides criterion-level reward Rcrit, and outcome and format rewards Rout and Rfmt supervise the final preference and output structure, respectively. (D) At inference time, only STEP-GRM is retained, constructing its own rubric, producing criterion-level judgments, and predicting the final preference without reference rubrics or the probe.

Figure 4: STEP-GRM judge system prompt. The generative reward model first proposes a rubric of instancespecific criteria, each tagged [Hard Rule] or [Principle] and labelled with the response it favors in isolation, and then aggregates these criterion-level judgments into the final preference.

Figure 7: Single-criterion probe system prompt. The probe judges the two candidate responses under a single criterion in isolation and outputs a reason together with a three-way verdict (A, B, or tie).

Figure 3: Training dynamics of process supervision. Left: Removing Rcrit preserves outcome reward growth but leads to a sharp collapse in criterion-level agreement, illustrating post-hoc rationalization drift. Right: Privileged guidance maintains a stable KL divergence with a sparse gate activation ratio of ≈ 27–28%.

Figure 1: Making evaluation explicit is not enough. Outcome-only supervision can yield the correct final preference while leaving intermediate criterion-level judgments unsupported, allowing the generated evaluation to become a post-hoc rationalization. STEP-GRM supervises both rubric construction and criterion-level judgment, turning the evaluation process itself into a direct object of learning.

papers.selection_reason: Process supervision for generative reward models, improving LLM evaluation and downstream policy optimization.
papers.title: Making Evaluation Explicit Is Not Enough: Supervising the Evaluation Process in Generative Reward Models
papers.tldr: STEP-GRM improves generative reward models by supervising how they evaluate, not just whether their final preference is correct.

papers.abstract: Latent reasoning and key-value communication store intermediate information in continuous representations, limiting direct inspection of model behavior. Existing activation readers trade the low cost of task-specific probes against the flexibility of language-model decoders. We propose the Calibrated Latent Reader, CLR, a compact transformer that predicts reasoning outcomes and message content through task-conditioned interactions between states and candidate answers. Source adapters support transfer across models, while conformal calibration provides coverage and false-alarm guarantees under exchangeability. On two CODI models, CLR improves accuracy over MLP and attention probes by 4-18 percentage points for final-answer prediction and reference-value membership. On CODI-GPT-2, it achieves accuracy comparable to a 1.7B LatentQA-based verbalizer using 437-648 times fewer inference FLOPs. On synthetic Qwen3-4B communications, comparing decoded facts with public commitments detects 93.1% of message substitutions at a nominal 5% false-positive rate.
authors: Zixi Wang, Gaohao Zhou, Yubo Huang, Xin Lai, Yushe Cao, Jingzehua Xu, Shuai Zhang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of inspecting intermediate information stored in continuous representations.
Uses task-conditioned interactions between model states and candidate answers, with source adapters for cross-model transfer.
Applies conformal calibration to provide coverage and false-alarm guarantees under exchangeability.
Improves final-answer and reference-value prediction accuracy by 4–18 percentage points over MLP and attention probes on two CODI models.

Achieves comparable accuracy to a 1.7B LatentQA verbalizer with 437–648× fewer inference FLOPs, and detects 93.1% of message substitutions at a nominal 5% false-positive rate in synthetic Qwen3-4B communications.
