papers.abstract: Large language models have shown strong capabilities on complex tasks, yet how to control their reasoning effort remains a significant challenge for practical deployment. This paper provides a systematic investigation of reasoning-effort training, contrasting reinforcement learning (RL) with on-policy distillation (OPD). We find that compressing reasoning and separating effort tiers are governed by different signals. Length-penalized RL reliably compresses a single policy, reducing thinking on AIME25 by 70\% without accuracy loss, but collapses the tiers when they are trained jointly. Multi-teacher OPD separates them: across 33 benchmarks, low and medium use 58\% and 43\% fewer thinking tokens than high, while high improves on the reference policy by 3.1 points. We trace this difference to the training signal. A sequence-level reward cannot tell tier-specific behavior from shared behavior, whereas OPD supplies a tier-specific target at every visited state, including the decision to stop. Building on this analysis, we show that a single token-level KL anchor on the high tier is sufficient to learn separated tiers within one RL stage, and that natural-language effort instructions make this separation emerge from the start of training, yielding a policy competitive with multi-teacher OPD at matched thinking length. Finally, the separation built by dense targets holds only on the states seen in training: it does not carry over to unseen agentic tasks, where effort acts mainly through the number of interaction turns, whereas the compression induced by sequence-level rewards does.
authors: Tianliang Lv, Hao Li, Xinchao Xu, Zhengkun Zhang, Ju Huo
bullets: Length-penalized RL reduces AIME25 thinking by 70% without accuracy loss, but jointly trained effort tiers collapse.
Multi-teacher on-policy distillation separates tiers: low and medium use 58% and 43% fewer thinking tokens than high, while high improves over the reference policy by 3.1 points across 33 benchmarks.
The difference arises because sequence-level rewards do not provide tier-specific guidance, whereas distillation supplies state-level targets, including when to stop reasoning.
A single token-level KL anchor on the high-effort tier enables tier separation in one RL stage; natural-language effort instructions help separation emerge from training start.
Dense-target separation is limited to training-seen states and does not transfer to unseen agentic tasks, where effort mainly changes interaction turns.

papers.selection_reason: Systematic investigation of reasoning-effort training in LLMs, contrasting RL and on-policy distillation.
papers.title: Rethinking Reasoning Effort Training in Large Language Models: On-Policy Distillation or Reinforcement Learning?
papers.tldr: The paper shows that reinforcement learning compresses reasoning effectively, while on-policy distillation better separates reasoning-effort tiers, and proposes a hybrid RL approach that achieves both within one stage.

papers.abstract: Open-weight LLMs are competent software engineers, but they sometimes fail at tasks they are otherwise able to do. Often it is not a failure of reasoning. It is a few small missteps over a long trajectory (repeating a step that has already failed, or declaring the task done while a requirement is still unmet) that make the difference. Correcting this calls for a surgical weight update that steers the model toward the right actions without interfering with its reasoning. Such updates, typically learned with LoRA adapters, are often too small to survive merging into a released checkpoint. In our BF16 release, the median weight change is only 1.5% of a single rounding step, and merging loses roughly two thirds of the update's norm. When the same adapter is merged into the mixed FP8/NVFP4 release of the same model, 93% of the update disappears. Instead of increasing the size of the update, we directly train on the surviving part. We introduce merge-aware fine-tuning. Standard LoRA rounds the merged weights to the storage format only at export, so the loss never sees the rounded weights. We instead round the sum of base weights and adapter update to the release format at every training step, keeping the vendor's quantization scales, and compute the loss on these weights. The forward pass matches the serving engine numerics, and the gradient passes straight through the rounding, so the model we train is the model we ship. The loss optimizes only the model's actions and keeps its reasoning close to the base model. Applied to Nemotron-3.5, the recipe improves agentic coding in both the BF16 and the NVFP4 release, by up to 8.4 points on Terminal-Bench 2.1, and we publicly release both models.
authors: Sandeep Singh Sandha, Prann Bansal, Arvind Sundararajan
bullets: Targets small action-level mistakes in software-engineering trajectories rather than broad reasoning failures.
Standard LoRA updates can largely disappear when merged into BF16 or mixed FP8/NVFP4 releases.
Trains with the merged weights rounded to the deployment format at every step, matching serving-time numerics.
Applied to Nemotron-3.5, it improves Terminal-Bench 2.1 performance by up to 8.4 points across BF16 and NVFP4 releases.
The authors publicly release both resulting models.

papers.title: Fix How It Acts, Not How It Thinks: Surgical Fine-Tuning of Frontier LLMs
papers.tldr: Merge-aware fine-tuning preserves surgical LoRA behavior after quantized checkpoint merging, improving agentic coding while keeping the base model’s reasoning largely unchanged.

papers.abstract: Continued fractions have been shown to be a function class capable of constructing expressive yet parameter-efficient neural networks. These neural networks are not only effective for supervised learning, but also for training LLMs. However, the rational form of this function class introduces poles when the denominator approaches zero, which prior work has avoided by enforcing a small positive (non-smooth) lower bound. We show that performance and training stability can be highly sensitive to the choice of this lower bound. In this work, we introduce a novel transformation of the partial denominators, inspired by its connection to the Green's function in physics, that mitigates the above issue elegantly by constraining the spectra of the constructed tridiagonal Hamiltonian. Our approach further eliminates the need for incremental training used by previous works for stability, thus avoiding involved modifications to standard pre-training procedures. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our reparameterization by replacing FFNs with a previously proposed continued fraction architecture for both language and image generative modeling. Across diverse models, such as GPT-2 XL, (nano) Llama-MoE, and Granite, we show that our proposed method achieves performance comparable to the original (FFN-based) architectures while maintaining ~30%-50% parameter savings as before, and in most cases even outperforms the more complicated incremental training baseline. We further demonstrate, for the first time for continued fraction networks, that their effectiveness also carries over to image generative modeling, that utilize diffusion objectives. On a state-of-the-art Diffusion Transformer, we show that our approach again achieves performance comparable to the original FFN-based models with ~30% parameter savings and significantly outperforms the previous incremental training approach.
authors: Soumyadeep Pal, Amit Dhurandhar, Vijil Chenthamarakshan, Dennis Wei, Karthikeyan Natesan Ramamurthy
bullets: Continued-fraction neural networks are expressive and parameter-efficient but can become unstable when denominators approach zero.
The method transforms partial denominators using a Green’s-function-inspired constraint on the associated tridiagonal Hamiltonian’s spectrum.
It removes the need for incremental training and its modifications to standard pretraining procedures.
Experiments replacing FFNs in language models and diffusion transformers show performance comparable to FFN baselines, often surpassing incremental training.
The approach extends continued-fraction networks to image generative modeling for the first time, with similar parameter savings.

papers.title: Spec-CoFrGeNet: Reparametrizing Continued Fraction Networks for Stable and Accurate Training
papers.tldr: Spec-CoFrGeNet reparameterizes continued-fraction networks to avoid denominator poles, enabling stable standard training while retaining roughly 30–50% parameter savings and competitive generative-model performance.

papers.abstract: Can a language model work in the weight space of a policy network for a repeated game? We put four questions to a mid-size open model, on recurrent networks of 1{,}218 weights with exactly checkable answers. Given a population of opponents described in English, write a policy that is optimal: its value is a finite computation over the agent's information state, so a submitted network has an exact gap from the optimum. Given a network's weights, report its action after each of fifteen opponent histories; recover the state machine it implements, judged on every opponent sequence to depth ten; or repair a network whose output was altered in one place and say which round first goes wrong. The model recovers the program in 62 of 66 replies, reports all fifteen behavioral entries correctly in 34 of 36, and attains the optimum in 20 of 20 when it states a policy the evaluator compiles. Repair is the exception: 4 of 18 repaired, 5 of 18 diagnosed, with a median patch covering one of the two entries needed.
bullets: Tests four tasks on recurrent policy networks with 1,218 weights and exactly checkable answers.
Writes optimal policies from English descriptions of repeated-game opponents; all 20 compiled policies attain the optimum.
Recovers implemented state machines in 62 of 66 replies and predicts 15-step behavior completely in 34 of 36 cases.
Repair is substantially weaker: 4 of 18 repairs succeed and 5 of 18 faults are diagnosed.
The study evaluates exact policy values, action sequences, state machines, and first-failure rounds.

papers.abstract: Multi-token prediction (MTP) accelerates autoregressive decoding through block-wise prediction, but remains vulnerable to error accumulation across sequentially generated blocks. To investigate this limitation, we analyze the distinction between block-wise and sequence-level cumulative information loss (CIL). Specifically, when the model generates using its own previous outputs without access to reference answers, the input-conditional gap equals the cross-block dependence of the reference targets. To improve prediction when these generated prefixes are imperfect, we propose Dual-MTP, which supervises shared prediction heads under full and randomly masked contexts. Together, complete-prefix supervision and context perturbations provide complementary training signals while retaining the MTP architecture. To characterize this training objective, we use the normalized dual loss to bound the divergence between the model's predictive distributions under full and masked contexts. Experiments across five backbones and six tasks spanning mathematical reasoning and GLUE understanding show that Dual-MTP achieves the highest average task score on four of five backbones, with gains of up to 2.46 points over MTP. On mathematical reasoning tasks, Dual-MTP also achieves 1.4 to 1.9 times the decoding throughput of the NTP reference. Together, these results show that dual-context supervision can improve prediction accuracy while retaining efficient multi-token decoding.
authors: Tangyu Jiang, Zhanke Zhou, Haodi Wang, Yiu-ming Cheung, Xiaohua Jia, Bo Han
bullets: MTP suffers from cumulative information loss when generated prefixes contain errors and differ from reference contexts.
The paper distinguishes block-wise from sequence-level loss and links the input-conditional gap to cross-block dependence in reference targets.
Dual-MTP applies shared prediction heads with full-prefix and randomly masked-context supervision.
A normalized dual loss bounds divergence between predictions under full and masked contexts.
Across five backbones and six tasks, Dual-MTP improves average scores on four backbones, with gains up to 2.46 points; reasoning-task throughput is 1.4–1.9× NTP.

papers.abstract: Looped language models apply one shared transformer stack several times per token, and every loop can be read out through the shared language-model head. Post-training them with verifiable rewards is hard: the outcome reward carries one bit per response, spreading it over loops trains intermediate loops on tokens sampled from the last loop, and distillation needs either a teacher that ignores the reward or an external, larger model. We observe that a looped model already contains a teacher stronger than its last loop: the next-token distribution extrapolated from the first loop through the last. ELGO (Extrapolated-Loop Group-relative Optimization) adds to GRPO a dense per-token distillation term towards this distribution. The teacher is computed from an anchor copy of the model, which stays frozen and is replaced by the current model once the student's KL to the teacher falls below a threshold, so the teacher improves with the student without chasing its own extrapolation. The outcome reward splits probability between correct and incorrect responses, and the teacher decides which tokens are preferred inside a response. Between refreshes the objective is KL-regularised RL anchored at the teacher, whose optimum tilts the teacher by the reward. On Ouro-1.4B-Thinking, ELGO raises the average avg@8 over five math benchmarks from 62.32 with GRPO to 64.20 and is the best compared method on every benchmark, while spreading the reward over loops falls below the base model.
bullets: Looped models reuse one transformer stack across multiple loops, but outcome-only rewards provide too little supervision for intermediate loops.
ELGO extrapolates the model’s next-token distribution from the first through the final loop to form a stronger internal teacher.
A frozen anchor teacher is periodically replaced as the student approaches it, enabling improvement without unstable self-chasing.
The method combines GRPO with token-level distillation and KL-regularized reinforcement learning.
On Ouro-1.4B-Thinking, ELGO improves average avg@8 from 62.32 with GRPO to 64.20 across five math benchmarks; directly spreading rewards over loops underperforms the base model.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of ELGO. The anchor copy θ̄ reads out loops 1 and 4 on every rollout prefix and extrapolates them into the teacher πT. The anchor starts at the initial model, stays frozen between refreshes, and is set to the current parameters when the dense loss falls below κ. The trained model samples rollouts from its last loop πθ, as in GRPO. The verifier gives one sparse advantage Âi per response; the teacher gives a dense log-ratio δi,j per sampled token. The loss is LGRPO + β LKD.

Figure 1: Left: GRPO gets one bit per response; RLTT trains intermediate loops on last-loop samples and their entropy collapses; LoopOPD has no reward. Right: ELGO extrapolates loop 1 to loop T of an anchor copy of the model, refreshed when the student has absorbed it, into a dense target for the last loop, next to the outcome reward.

papers.title: Beyond the Last Loop: Reinforcement Learning with a Teacher Extrapolated from the Model Itself
papers.tldr: ELGO improves reinforcement learning for looped language models by using a self-extrapolated, progressively updated teacher to provide dense token-level guidance.

papers.abstract: We compare a MEGABYTE-style byte-patch Transformer with a 64-byte sliding local decoder (local64) to a matched byte-level 8k BPE decoder (BPE-8k) under identical raw bytes, document order, and approximately matched bytes per optimizer step: 350M parameters and 10 billion training bytes. Under matched-span document sliding (identical scored byte ranges), BPE-8k leads with relative gaps of -5.2%, -4.9%, -9.3% and -6.1% in bits per byte (overall, text, code, math; paired bootstrap). Downstream, CharBench equal fine-tuning favors local64 (53.7% vs 40.0%), fact200 favors BPE-8k (16.5% vs 7.0%), and PIQA (raw and length-normalized) and ARC-Easy length-normalized favor BPE-8k after Holm correction at alpha = 0.05; remaining tasks are ties. Evaluation pitfalls that changed conclusions include context-length extrapolation past the BPE training context, bits per token reported as bits per byte, and inconsistent byte denominators. Unlike controlled tokenizer studies that vary the subword tokenizer under a fixed token budget, or FLOP-controlled byte-model scaling studies, we hold the raw bytes, their order and the optimizer recipe fixed and ask whether a fixed-patch byte model can replace the tokenizer at all. Limits: one size, one seed, one 8k vocabulary fixed before the runs, and a known difference in embedding initialization between the twins.
bullets: Both models use the same raw bytes, document order, optimizer recipe, and approximately matched bytes per step over 10B training bytes.
Under matched-span evaluation, BPE-8k leads in bits per byte overall, text, code, and math.
Equal fine-tuning favors local64 on CharBench, while BPE-8k leads on fact200, PIQA, and length-normalized ARC-Easy; other tasks are ties.
Evaluation choices that affected conclusions included context extrapolation, confusing bits per token with bits per byte, and inconsistent byte denominators.
Scope is limited to one model size, one seed, one fixed 8k vocabulary, and differing embedding initialization between the twins.

papers.abstract: Conversational assistants compact older messages into short notes and evict the originals. When the note's language requires a distinction that English leaves open, such as Spanish adjective gender (agotado vs. agotada), messages that omit or explicitly state that attribute can yield the same note. After eviction, later turns cannot tell them apart: taking the inflected form literally asserts an attribute the user never gave, whereas discounting it as routine grammar discards one the user did give. We propose a training-free repair across writing, pre-eviction verification and reading. The writer marks unstated attributes with paired forms (e.g., agotado/a), a likelihood check before eviction rewrites unsupported single forms into paired ones, and the reader trusts remaining single forms as stated facts. On five Qwen3.5 and Gemma-4 models, eviction cuts recall of stated attributes from 90% to 34% in question answering (QA); our repair raises F1 (which penalizes both errors) on every model, by 9-53 points in QA and 12-40 points in agent handovers.
authors: Ian Miao, Fangrui Zhu, Bowen Jiang
bullets: Problem: Compacted notes can conflate omitted and explicitly stated attributes when the target language encodes distinctions English leaves ambiguous.
Method: Writers mark unsupported attributes with paired forms, pre-eviction checks repair unsupported single forms, and readers treat remaining single forms as stated facts.
Result: Eviction reduced stated-attribute recall from 90% to 34% in QA; repair improved F1 across all evaluated models.
Scope: Evaluated on five Qwen3.5 and Gemma-4 models in question answering and agent handovers.
Contribution: A training-free repair spanning note writing, pre-eviction verification, and reading.

papers.tldr: A training-free multilingual compaction repair preserves whether attributes were explicitly stated, substantially improving later recall after message eviction.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM inference by letting a cheap drafter propose tokens that the target model verifies in parallel. Parallel block drafters such as DFlash and P-EAGLE propose a whole block in one forward pass, but they lose the dependence between tokens in the block; DSpark restores part of it with a lightweight correction head that runs sequentially. Measuring DSpark, we find that this head overrides the base prediction on most slots, so the expensive base readout through the target's full lm_head mostly provides a seed. We therefore propose Wavefront, which follows a simple principle: shrink the base and strengthen the correction head. Wavefront replaces the full lm_head with a learned low-rank base, conditions the correction head on the whole drafted prefix within the same block, and resolves it with a few parallel Jacobi passes. A fixed pass budget makes the draft step free of data-dependent control flow, so we capture it as a single CUDA graph in vLLM with fused kernels. On Qwen3-8B, Wavefront improves throughput over xPress, DSpark and DFlash by 2.6%, 10.7% and 23.6% on average across math, code, chat and agentic benchmarks, and by 9.6%, 14.3% and 28.9% on SPEED-Bench long-context prompts. On Qwen3.8-27B it leads DFlash2, DSpark and xPress by 7.6%, 10.6% and 5.0%, and by 7.4%, 5.8% and 6.0% on the same long-context prompts. The gains persist as serving load grows to concurrency 32.
bullets: Targets the limited within-block token dependence of parallel drafters such as DFlash and P-EAGLE.
Uses a learned low-rank base, a correction head conditioned on the full drafted prefix, and fixed-budget parallel refinement.
Implements the draft step as a single CUDA graph with fused kernels in vLLM, avoiding data-dependent control flow.
Reports throughput gains over prior drafters across math, code, chat, agentic, and long-context benchmarks on Qwen3-8B and Qwen3.8-27B.
Gains remain as serving load increases to concurrency 32.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a speculative decoding architecture for faster LLM inference, relevant to efficient LLM serving and LLM architecture.
papers.title: Wavefront: Low-Rank Drafting with Parallel Causal Refinement for Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: Wavefront accelerates speculative decoding by replacing costly draft readouts with a low-rank base and refining entire token blocks through a few parallel Jacobi passes.

papers.abstract: Reasoning models degrade as their context grows, so longer reasoning traces do not by themselves give longer effective horizons. One way to extend the horizon is to compress the reasoning history into a compact state from time to time and continue from the state. Existing methods train the state with the final-answer reward or distill it from a stronger model. Neither signal is tailored to measure the contribution of the state alone. We observe that a reasoning model that degrades over long trajectories still behaves reliably in short contexts. We aim to preserve this short-context behavior when compressing the reasoning history. Motivated by this, we train a separate summarizer with Delta-KL, a reward computed from the frozen reasoning model's token-level predictions on sampled continuations, and run inference by truncating the trace, summarizing it, and continuing from the summary (TruSuCo). Training uses a few thousand questions with 4k-token reasoning prefixes and does not need answers or external teachers. Under a fixed 32k-token budget, the trained summarizer improves on vanilla reasoning and on an untrained summarizer in all nine settings across mathematical benchmarks and Reasoning Gym puzzles, by up to 7.7 points and 12 points, respectively. The improvement over vanilla reasoning grows with the budget. At 128k tokens, our method outperforms it by 10 points on AIME 2024--2026. Analyses show that truncation prevents the collapse of vanilla reasoning and that the trained summaries retain more of the reasoning history.
bullets: Long reasoning traces degrade as context grows, limiting effective reasoning horizons.
A separate summarizer is trained with Delta-KL from token-level predictions on sampled local continuations.
Inference repeatedly truncates the trace, summarizes the history, and continues reasoning from the summary.
Using a few thousand questions and no answers or external teacher, TruSuCo improves over vanilla reasoning across nine settings.
Under fixed token budgets, gains reach 7.7 points and 12 points over vanilla and an untrained summarizer; at 128k tokens, it gains 10 points on AIME 2024–2026.

papers.abstract: Reliably evaluating the capabilities of advanced AI systems is critical for safe development and deployment, yet such evaluations may be undermined by sandbagging, a situation in which a model strategically suppresses capabilities it possesses. Existing work has developed controlled sandbagging settings and methods for detecting or eliciting hidden capabilities, but comparatively little is known about how a model's internal neural computation changes when its capabilities are suppressed. In this work, we study sandbagging through the lens of internal functional organization. Inspired by network neuroscience, we construct functional graphs from attention-head activations and compare their organization under honest and sandbagging conditions while holding the model architecture and weights fixed. Surprisingly, across model architectures and community detection methods, we find a consistent structural signature in which sandbagging is associated with reduced functional connectivity within detected communities. We further demonstrate that this reorganization can guide capability elicitation. Ablating attention heads that exhibit the largest connectivity changes substantially recovers suppressed performance while largely preserving performance under honest behavior. Moreover, incorporating these structural signals further improves existing inference-level and weight-level elicitation methods. Together, our results show that sandbagging is accompanied by systematic reorganization of internal computation and demonstrate that functional network structure can provide both a mechanistic lens for understanding capability suppression and a practical signal for recovering hidden capabilities.
authors: Manzi Fabrice Niyigaba, Ishan Verma Prasad, Sansheng Cao, Zheng Huang, Yujun Yan
bullets: Sandbagging may hide a model’s true capabilities, complicating reliable safety evaluations.

papers.abstract: Frontier models like GPT-6 Astra are increasingly able to do substantial reasoning without a monitorable chain of thought, chains of thought are becoming less legible, and are often monitored asynchronously to reduce cost. With the future of chain of thought monitoring unclear, it may be necessary to design LLMs with monitorability in mind. We propose a modification to existing LLM architectures based on GRAM, SGTM, DEMix, BTS, and similar methods to compartmentalize dangerous capabilities so that their use, especially in combination with dangerous reasoning types that may indicate strategic adversarial use, can be monitored more cheaply than chain of thought in a way that might outlast monitorable chain of thought. We propose several variants of this architecture designed to balance tradeoffs and discuss other benefits, such as capability removal.
bullets: Motivated by increasingly opaque and asynchronously monitored reasoning in frontier models.
Builds on GRAM, SGTM, DEMix, BTS, and related architectural methods.
Separates dangerous capabilities and reasoning types to enable cheaper monitoring of their use in combination.
Presents several architecture variants intended to balance monitorability and other tradeoffs.
Also discusses potential capability-removal benefits; the abstract does not report empirical results.

A monitor reads routing at every stage to detect potentially dangerous patterns.

papers.abstract: Representation quality in pretrained text foundation models is not concentrated at the final layer, yet practitioners routinely probe it there because layer selection without labels has remained an open problem. We present a large-scale empirical study of where layer quality lives across 25 models spanning four architectural families and four pretraining strategies, evaluated on 13 datasets across classification, pair classification, semantic textual similarity, and multiple-choice question answering. Peak probing layers depend systematically on pretraining strategy and architecture: masked encoders peak in late-middle layers, sequence-to-sequence models shift their peak with task type, contrastive sentence encoders concentrate signal at the final layer under CLS and last-token readouts but peak early under mean pooling, and decoder-only models exhibit distinct phase structure tied to depth. We distill these findings into the Stable Geometry Index (SGI), a closed-form, fully label-free selector with no fitted coefficients combining power-law fit quality, effective-rank capacity, spectral stability, and a weak depth prior. Across 383 evaluation groups SGI improves over the last-layer baseline and lifts Hit@3 from 0.39 to 0.52, recovering 40% of the gap to the oracle without using any labels, and exceeds a supervised ELMo-style layer mix on the matched subset despite using strictly less information. Our ablations also reverse a common assumption in the spectral-decay literature: power-law fit quality is a stronger predictor of layer quality than the exponent's proximity to one.
authors: Arnesh Batra, Aniket Khandelwal, Arush Gumber, Krish Thukral, Kushagra Agrawal, Dev Sharma
bullets: Study spans 25 models, four architectural families, four pretraining strategies, and 13 datasets covering four task types.

Across 383 evaluation groups, SGI raises Hit@3 from 0.39 to 0.52 and recovers 40% of the oracle gap.
Power-law fit quality predicts layer quality better than the exponent’s proximity to one, challenging a common spectral-decay assumption.

papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) enables transformers to adapt to new tasks from demonstrations without updating their parameters. However, theoretical guarantees for transformers remain limited in general, and elusive in particular when target responses depend nonlinearly on the evolution of observed paths. We establish an ICL framework for path space, using path signature features. Building on the universal linear approximation property of signatures, we construct explicitly a causal softmax transformer with two attention heads per layer that emulates in-context Lasso. Under sparse signature approximation and suitable moment and concentration conditions, we establish finite-sample prediction error bounds. Our analysis goes beyond the IID data setting in the existing ICL theory, allowing dependence among demonstrations and the query. Experiments on in-context sparse recovery, nonlinear path regression, execution-cost prediction, and financial payoff inference demonstrate robustness to changes in observation grids and adaptation to unseen market environments. Across these prediction tasks, transformers with signatures match or outperform vanilla transformer baselines with substantially fewer trainable parameters, highlighting the effectiveness and efficiency of signature-based ICL.
authors: Ziheng Cheng, Xin Guo, Ben Hambly
bullets: Introduces a path-space ICL framework using path signature features to model nonlinear responses to evolving observations.
Constructs a causal softmax transformer with two attention heads per layer that emulates in-context Lasso.
Proves finite-sample prediction error bounds under sparse signature approximation and moment/concentration assumptions, beyond IID demonstrations.
Experiments show robustness to changing observation grids and adaptation to unseen market environments across several prediction tasks.
Signature-based transformers match or outperform vanilla transformers with substantially fewer trainable parameters in the reported tasks.

papers.abstract: Hyper-Connections expand residual capacity across parallel streams, yet restrict every branch to narrow read and write interfaces: each branch still reads a single stream mixture and writes scaled copies of one output vector to all streams. To lift this bottleneck, we propose Grouped Hyper-Connections (GHC). By partitioning each branch into parallel groups along attention heads or FFN channels, GHC supplies each group with a distinct stream mixture and aggregates their separate outputs into each stream with learned weights. Extensive experiments across dense and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models show that GHC consistently improves upon Identity Hyper-Connections (IHC) with negligible parameter and memory-access overhead, increasing training efficiency by 35% over Pre-Norm and 10% over IHC. Moreover, expanding residual interfaces overcomes the diminishing returns of adding streams, allowing wider residual states to yield further gains.
authors: Tianyu Li, Hongtao Zhang, Dongchen Han, Jingshu Liu, Bojun Wang, Chen Jiang, Yulong Huang, Wei Chen, Tianyu He, Xiangyu Zhang, Gao Huang
bullets: Problem: Standard Hyper-Connections restrict branches to one shared stream mixture and replicated outputs, limiting the benefit of parallel residual streams.
Method: Partition attention heads or FFN channels into groups, each with its own stream mixture; aggregate group outputs into streams using learned weights.
Results: Across dense and Mixture-of-Experts models, GHC consistently outperforms Identity Hyper-Connections with negligible parameter and memory-access overhead.
Efficiency: GHC reports 35% higher training efficiency than Pre-Norm and 10% higher than IHC.
Scope: Expanded residual interfaces reduce diminishing returns from adding streams, allowing wider residual states to provide further gains.

papers.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive language models, enabling non-autoregressive text generation through parallel decoding. Existing dLLMs can be broadly categorized into two families: masked diffusion models (MDMs) and uniform diffusion models (UDMs) In this work, we theoretically show that MDMs are easier to optimize due to their mask-based transition schedule but have lower computational expressivity, whereas UDMs enable iterative state revision and greater expressivity but are substantially harder to train. This trade-off raises a natural question: can we obtain the expressivity of iterative revision without giving up the simple, easy-to-optimize transition schedule of MDMs? Motivated by this analysis, we propose Lookahead Editing (\ours{}), which augments masked diffusion decoding with a rewritable proposal state. At each decoding step, the model performs several lookahead updates to iteratively refine future predictions in this proposal state before committing tokens to the masked sequence. This design introduces a rewritable proposal that uses additional compute to improve expressivity while keeping the simple mask-based transition schedule of MDMs. We fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen3-8B to obtain LED-\texttt{7B} and LED-\texttt{8B}, respectively. Across eight benchmarks, LED SFT yields average gains of $+11.4$ and $+7.7$ points over standard MDM SFT. Moreover, using SFT alone, LED-\texttt{8B} outperforms LLaDA2.1-16B Q-mode, which is trained with continued pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning.
bullets: MDMs are easier to optimize than uniform diffusion models but have lower computational expressivity because they lack iterative state revision.
LED preserves MDMs’ simple mask-based transition schedule while introducing extra computation for future-token refinement.
At each decoding step, multiple lookahead updates revise predictions in a proposal state before tokens are committed.
Fine-tuned LED models achieve average gains of 11.4 and 7.7 points over standard MDM SFT across eight benchmarks.
LED-8B outperforms LLaDA2.1-16B in Q-mode using SFT alone, though the method increases decoding computation.

papers.abstract: Prompting language models to verbalize stepwise numerical confidence during generation is an increasingly popular approach for triggering backtracking and error correction in agentic reasoning. This strategy presupposes two capabilities: (1) in-situ monitoring fidelity (does confidence drop when an error occurs?) and (2) downstream steering control (does an uncertainty token causally steer the model to repair its error?). We evaluated four open-weights models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, and Phi-4, 14.7B) across 15,200 math benchmark attempts, isolating 2,017 reasoning errors within each model's capability frontier. Applying 27,568 counterfactual continuations across these failure points, we demonstrate a consistent decoupling between monitoring and control. On monitoring, all four models fail to detect their own errors. Verbalized confidence does not distinguish mistake steps from sound reasoning, yielding near-chance within-position AUROCs between 0.500 and 0.561. Even at a model's first reasoning error, trajectory confidence remains saturated at 95.1% to 99.9%, with noticeable drops ($\ge 10$ points) appearing on fewer than 9% of errors in Llama and under 1.6% in the other three models. In contrast, models respond readily to external uncertainty: injecting a low-confidence tag (10%) at the error step significantly increases downstream correction across all models (+3.7 to +22.5 points over format-matched 95% certainty; all $p \le 0.0022$), reaching up to 38.5% under active rethinking instructions. However, injecting doubt onto already-correct steps causes models to discard valid reasoning, reducing solve rates by up to 22.8 points. Inference-time self-correction is thus bottlenecked by in-situ error detection rather than downstream repair capacity: models readily steer toward recovery when prompted with doubt, yet fail to self-monitor during generation.
bullets: Evaluated four open-weight models on 15,200 math attempts, isolating 2,017 reasoning errors and testing 27,568 counterfactual continuations.
Verbalized confidence did not distinguish erroneous from correct reasoning, with near-chance error detection and confidence often remaining very high after mistakes.
Externally injected low-confidence tokens improved downstream correction across all models, especially with active rethinking instructions.
Injecting doubt into correct reasoning could harm performance, reducing solve rates by up to 22.8 points.
Self-correction is therefore limited primarily by in-situ error detection, not by the ability to repair errors once uncertainty is supplied.

papers.abstract: Decision models are emerging as fast components of larger AI systems. Yet recent decision models, such as Jev, process options sequentially, leading to different predictions based on their ordering. Across ten open- and closed-source decision models, we find that \emph{order-sensitivity} is pervasive, causing substantial accuracy degradation and unreliable decision-making. These effects become more pronounced as the number of options grows and can compound across multi-step decisions. To address this problem, we systematically compare eight methods for mitigating order sensitivity in terms of robustness, predictive accuracy, and inference efficiency. Among these methods, we find that \emph{tree attention} is a surprisingly effective and efficient method. It achieves order invariance by processing options as parallel branches of a shared context. When used during training, it matches the baseline's average accuracy. Applied to the baseline without retraining, it also eliminates order sensitivity with only a 1.1-point drop in accuracy. Our findings demonstrate that order invariance can be enforced directly in decision models with little or no loss in predictive accuracy.
authors: Bodong Liu, Dongyoung Go, Sofian Zalouk, Kilian Q. Weinberger

papers.abstract: The post-training of pretrained large language models, including supervised finetuning (SFT), direct preference optimization (DPO), and reinforcement learning with verifiable reward (RLVR), is very sensitive to the learning rate, and tuning it through grid search is costly in both computation and memory. In this work, we propose \textbf{TipSweep}, a method to transfer the learning rate across the number of trainable transformer blocks. To do so efficiently, we search for the best learning rate by training only the last $k_0$ blocks (in our experiments, typically $k_0=1$), and provide scaling rules that predict the optimal learning rate when training any set of $k$ blocks, including when $k=L$ (the full transformer). Across experiments with models ranging from 1 to 7 billion parameters, we observe that the optimal learning rate follows precision-dependent scaling rules: the optimal rate scales approximately as $k^{-1}$ with float32 (FP32) master weights, but as $k^{-1/2}$ when updates are applied directly to bfloat16 (BF16) weights without a master copy. We explain both rules using an analytical model that accounts for update rounding, under assumptions supported by profiling experiments. Finally, we develop two prototypes of the learning rate search for a 6.7-billion-parameter model. The first fits the search on a single consumer GPU with 16 GiB of memory. The second speeds up the search on a high-end GPU by evaluating all candidate learning rates in a single pass over the data, so that a five-candidate search takes about half the GPU hours of one full-depth ($k=L$) run.
authors: Nan Chen, Soledad Villar, Soufiane Hayou

Provides an analytical explanation based on update rounding, supported by profiling experiments.
Demonstrates memory- and compute-efficient search prototypes for a 6.7B-parameter model.

papers.abstract: During autoregressive decoding, the deeper representations of the previous token have already been computed, yet shallow layers at the current token cannot read them directly because standard self-attention connects positions only at the same depth. We introduce Attention Latent Feedback (ALF), an architecture that allows every sublayer to attend to the outputs of the deeper layers at the previous position. Training unrolls this cross-position recurrence into two parallel passes, whereas decoding remains single-pass using cached previous-token states. Across mixture-of-experts models with up to 4.0B parameters, ALF lowers held-out loss by 0.022-0.024 nats over the standard residual with about 1.1% decoding FLOP overhead, and consistently outperforms prior final-state feedback across all three scales on both standard and attention residual backbones. On MoE-1.6B, ALF matches a $1.38\times$ larger baseline token budget, and on MoE-4.0B it lifts average accuracy across seventeen downstream benchmarks from 45.1% to 47.0%. Analysis further reveals that intermediate and nearby deeper layers drive most of this benefit, allowing a fixed nearest-window variant to retain 89%-94% of the gain at linear read cost while learned attention widens its margin with scale.
authors: Xuyuan Xiong, Siyu Chen, Mengzhao Chen, Yue Su, Zhuoran Yang, Ping Luo, Xihui Liu
bullets: Addresses the limitation that standard self-attention only connects the same layer across positions during autoregressive decoding.
Introduces cross-position attention from every sublayer to cached deeper-layer outputs of the previous token; training uses two parallel passes, while decoding remains single-pass.
Across MoE models up to 4.0B parameters, reduces held-out loss by 0.022–0.024 nats with about 1.1% extra decoding FLOPs.
Improves downstream accuracy on MoE-4.0B from 45.1% to 47.0% across 17 benchmarks and outperforms final-state feedback across tested scales.
A fixed nearest-layer window retains 89%–94% of the gain at linear read cost, while learned attention benefits more as model scale increases.

papers.title: Attention Latent Feedback

papers.abstract: Updating an LLM adapter should not require replaying the full interaction history of every active session. Yet reusing key-value (KV) cache entries computed under an earlier version mixes model versions, while full-history re-prefill becomes increasingly costly as histories and session fleets grow. We introduce LiveLora, a model-runtime co-design for exact final-block KV cache migration. Frozen lower decoder blocks and fixed K/V adapter down-projections preserve each token's base projections and low-rank coordinates across adapter versions. The runtime reconstructs candidate K/V, reevaluates the latest token through the final block, and commits the adapter, cache, and next-token logits together. We prove continuation equivalence to full-history re-prefill in exact arithmetic under the stated model assumptions. On Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, median paired publication speedups over full-history re-prefill average $68.98\times$ across five runs for 32 active sessions with 8K tokens each. Serving benchmarks show approximately 4.8% decoding overhead relative to native cached decoding. Compared with retained-boundary replay, compact retention gives a $3.42\times$ reduction in additional session storage at 8K, with similar measured publication-plus-decoding cost. LiveLora allows persistent LLM agents to adopt new adapter versions without replaying their full interaction histories.
authors: Tianyi Huang, Samuel Xu, Ivy Gu, Nathan Huang, Siqi Zhang
bullets: Addresses costly full-history re-prefill and the incompatibility of reusing KV caches across adapter versions.
Uses frozen lower decoder blocks and fixed K/V adapter down-projections to preserve base projections and low-rank coordinates.
Migrates the final-block cache by reconstructing K/V, reevaluating the latest token, and atomically committing the adapter, cache, and logits.
Proves continuation equivalence to full-history re-prefill in exact arithmetic under its model assumptions.
Reports 68.98× median paired publication speedup at 32 sessions with 8K-token histories, about 4.8% decoding overhead, and 3.42× lower additional storage than retained-boundary replay at 8K.

papers.abstract: Looped Transformers iterate a shared block of layers to increase computation without adding parameters, offering stronger performance and test-time scaling. However, this power has so far required training from scratch and yielded only modest gains for LLMs. Finetuning existing models into loops is far cheaper, yet also brings only marginal gains over SFT. We propose LoopRes, an effective, scalable, and simple approach that turns loops into significant and consistent gains for pretrained LLMs. Building on Attention Residuals, LoopRes lets each looped layer attend directly to the outputs of earlier loops. Since these outputs are iterates of the same layers and become harder to tell apart, we give each a trainable loop-aware key that encodes its structural identity. Attending to all earlier loops also lets layers skip intermediate ones, so we restrict each layer to a residual window of the latest W loops, forcing every loop to build incrementally on recent ones. Across 6 pretrained LLMs from 3 model families and 9 benchmarks, LoopRes delivers significant and consistent gains: at 2x compute, it improves Qwen3-1.7B-Base by 29.1% over SFT, more than doubling the gain of the state-of-the-art baseline. The gains hold on larger models up to 30B and across all three families. More importantly, from 1.7B to 8B, LoopRes scales more steeply than SFT as compute grows, reaching a higher ceiling while needing less compute on long outputs. These results establish LoopRes as an effective looping approach, delivering both better performance and better test-time scaling.
authors: Xuanlei Zhao, Hailun Xu, Kai Wang, Yang Luo, Yingxuan Ren, Zirui Zhu, Yuxuan Lou, Kun Xu, Yan Wang, Kanchan Sarkar, Yang You
bullets: Addresses the limited gains of adapting pretrained LLMs into shared-layer loops.
Lets each looped layer attend to outputs from recent earlier loops using trainable loop-aware keys.
Uses a residual window over the latest W loops to encourage incremental computation and avoid skipping intermediate loops.
Across 6 LLMs, 3 model families, and 9 benchmarks, LoopRes improves Qwen3-1.7B-Base by 29.1% over SFT at 2× compute.
Shows stronger scaling with compute, higher performance ceilings, and lower compute needs for long outputs from 1.7B to 8B models.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes loop residuals to improve pretrained LLM looping and test-time scaling, directly relevant to LLM architectures.
papers.title: Unlocking the Power of Loops in Pretrained LLMs with Loop Residuals
papers.tldr: LoopRes makes pretrained LLM looping substantially more effective by enabling loop-aware residual connections, yielding consistent performance and compute-scaling gains.

papers.abstract: LLMs typically solve complex tasks with chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, which is also the main tool for monitoring them for misaligned behavior. However, standard transformers can also solve tasks with complete latent reasoning (CLR), carrying out the whole task internally and outputting only the final answer. Theory bounds the depth of CLR, the number of sequential steps it can carry out, and recent work measured it to be shallow. In this work, we ask whether CLR is deep enough for a model to pursue a hidden objective that requires reasoning. Such a model would generate a CoT that appears to solve the given task, while a latent multi-step computation decides its answer based on the hidden objective. First, we show that a simple auxiliary loss allows models to solve a multi-step task latently at least 5x deeper than previously reported. Then, in two common tasks, decision-making and code generation, we train a model to pursue such a hidden objective, which decides a loan or plants a vulnerability. The model's CoT justifies the output with no trace of the hidden objective, and a strong LLM monitor does not flag it. Finally, using activation patching, we find that the latent computation is completed before the model generates its CoT, which takes no part in it. Altogether, we show that a hidden objective that requires reasoning can go unseen by a monitor that reads only the output.
authors: Tomer Ashuach, Zorik Gekhman, Avi Caciularu, Ori Ram, Jonathan Herzig
bullets: Standard transformers can carry out complete latent reasoning and reveal only a final answer.
An auxiliary loss enables latent multi-step reasoning at least 5× deeper than previously measured.
The authors train models whose hidden objectives influence loan decisions and code containing vulnerabilities.
Generated chain-of-thought rationalizes the outputs without revealing the hidden objective, and a strong LLM monitor does not flag them.
Activation patching indicates the latent computation finishes before chain-of-thought generation and does not rely on it.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates latent reasoning and hidden objectives in LLMs, relevant to LLM behavior and safety.
papers.title: Can Latent Reasoning Drive LLM Outputs Without a Trace?
papers.tldr: LLMs can perform deep latent reasoning to pursue hidden objectives while producing plausible chain-of-thought that conceals the computation from output-only monitors.

papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly serve as judges of other models, shaping benchmark rankings and model development. Yet, a judge whose rationale consistently supports its verdict may still disagree with human preferences. To study this, we introduce PRIMEAPE, a multilingual benchmark for evaluating judge verdicts and rationales. PRIMEAPE provides 2,205 response pairs covering 243 instructions in English, French, Spanish, Urdu, Hindi, Norwegian Bokm{\aa}l, and Yoruba, with 11k human annotations of preferences and rationales across relevance, naturalness, truthfulness, safety, and overall quality. Our evaluation of twelve open- and closed-weight judges reveals that aggregate performance conceals differences across languages and criteria, while requesting rationales does not consistently improve agreement with human preferences. Judges also favor the first position, longer responses, and responses from related models, with effects that vary across criteria and languages. Crucially, judges can justify verdicts that disagree with human preferences while maintaining consistency between their verdicts and rationales. These findings show that consistency with a judge's own verdict does not establish alignment with human judgment. PRIMEAPE enables assessment of both, providing a foundation for more reliable multilingual judges. We release our benchmark and all annotation materials under the CC BY-NC 4.0 license at github.com/Toloka/primeape.
authors: Vladislav Mikhailov, Sarfraz Ahmad, Momina Ahsan, Zoia Butenko, Vladimir Dobrovolskii, Preslav Nakov, Erik Velldal, Lilja {\O}vrelid, Ekaterina Artemova
bullets: Evaluates judge verdicts and rationales across 2,205 response pairs, 243 instructions, seven languages, and five criteria.
Includes about 11,000 human annotations covering relevance, naturalness, truthfulness, safety, and overall quality.
Results across 12 judges show aggregate scores can hide substantial differences by language and evaluation criterion.
Requesting rationales does not consistently improve agreement with human preferences; judges exhibit position, length, and related-model biases.
The benchmark and annotation materials are released under CC BY-NC 4.0 to support more reliable multilingual judge evaluation.

papers.abstract: Medical post-training raises benchmark accuracy, but accuracy does not show which internal components a model's decisions depend on, or whether components that support one benchmark also support another. We apply the weight-space intervention paradigm of ROME and MEMIT at the granularity of one MLP down-projection column. Our measurement, Empirical Margin Sensitivity (EMS), replaces each coordinate magnitude of a column by its mean while preserving the column's sign pattern and L1 scale, and records the resulting change in the logit margin between the correct option and its hardest-wrong competitor. This isolates the margin's dependence on a column's fine-grained coordinate structure while the column stays in place. We discover high-EMS columns (anchors) on MedQA in ten public checkpoints (four general-purpose bases and six medical post-trained variants) across the Gemma, Llama, Qwen, and AFM families, and measure the same columns on MedMCQA and PubMedQA. Mean-ablating each discovered anchor set lowers MedQA accuracy in all six post-trained models, by 6 to 28 points. In the two pure-SFT checkpoints, crushing anchors raises the PubMedQA margin on correctly answered items (negative EMS), and anchors with this property sit significantly deeper than the same model's other anchors; the four checkpoints trained with RL or mixed recipes show positive PubMedQA EMS and no significant depth shift. The depth association recurs in each of three held-out checkpoints. Because the checkpoints differ in data and pipeline as well as objective, we report these as per-checkpoint observations.
authors: Aniruddh Shreyas, Aarnav Kembhavi, Minal Moharir
bullets: Post-training accuracy alone does not reveal which internal components drive model decisions or transfer across tasks.

EMS intervenes on one MLP down-projection column by replacing coordinate magnitudes with their mean while preserving sign pattern and L1 scale, then measures the change in correct-versus-hardest-wrong logit margin.
Across ten checkpoints, EMS identifies high-sensitivity MedQA columns (“anchors”) in Gemma, Llama, Qwen, and AFM models.
Mean-ablating anchors reduces MedQA accuracy in all six medical post-trained models, by 6–28 percentage points.

PubMedQA effects differ by recipe: pure-SFT models show negative EMS and deeper anchors, whereas RL or mixed-recipe models show positive EMS without a significant depth shift; findings are checkpoint-specific.

papers.abstract: Large language models can have behaviours which only arise in hard-to-anticipate contexts. These hidden behaviours pose a challenge to alignment audits, which seek to uncover problematic model behaviour but are limited by the scenarios the auditor can anticipate. To address this challenge, we explore limited-parameter finetuning (LPF) on examples of a target behaviour. While training 3-25% of LoRA parameters, LPF reveals whether the model has a hidden behaviour, even when standard behavioural evaluations cannot. LPF succeeds on a suite of model organisms with hidden behaviours (8-14B parameters), and also surfaces naturally occurring hidden behaviours in open-weight models (27-35B parameters). LPF can thus distinguish between models which appear behaviourally identical to an auditor, and does not require the context in which the hidden behaviour surfaces. LPF provides a novel affordance that may be useful for auditing frontier AI models. However, we do not evaluate LPF against baselines in a realistic auditing setting, so further work is needed to determine its practicality.
authors: Boyd Kane, Jo J. Jiao, Elizabeth Donoway, Bryce Woodworth, Alex Cloud, Alexander M. Turner
bullets: Addresses alignment audits that are constrained by scenarios auditors can anticipate.
Trains only 3–25% of LoRA parameters on examples of a target behaviour.

Practicality remains uncertain because it was not evaluated against baselines in a realistic auditing setting.

papers.abstract: We propose loom attention, which allows a Transformer to dynamically rewire its circuits at every token by interweaving a head's vertical attention over the outputs of earlier heads (to obtain its query, key and value) with its horizontal attention over tokens. We instantiate vertical attention efficiently with normalized and gated linear attention over a per-token matrix memory, which stores the compressed head outputs and serves as a second residual stream. This yields LoomFormer, a dual-stream architecture that splits control and content between the vector and matrix streams. Across model sizes and training token budgets in language modeling and downstream tasks, LoomFormer matches Transformers trained with over 3x compute and recent residual-stream baselines (HC/mHC, MUDDFormer, AttnRes) trained with ~1.7-2.8x. For example, trained on the same 300B tokens with only 2% extra FLOPs, LoomPythia-2.8B achieves ~1.6x the average downstream gain of mHC-Pythia-2.8B over Pythia-2.8B, and matches (0-shot) or surpasses (5-shot) Pythia-12B. Code is available at https://github.com/Caiyun-AI/LoomFormer
authors: Da Xiao, Qingye Meng, Shengping Li, Xingyuan Yuan
bullets: Motivation: Standard Transformer circuits have relatively fixed information pathways across heads and layers.
Method: Loom attention interleaves vertical attention over earlier head outputs with horizontal token attention, using normalized, gated linear attention over per-token matrix memories.
Architecture: LoomFormer uses dual residual streams, separating control in vector states from content in matrix states.
Results: Across language modeling and downstream tasks, it matches models trained with over 3× compute and recent residual-stream baselines trained with roughly 1.7–2.8× compute.
Scope: Demonstrated across multiple model sizes and training-token budgets; code is publicly available. ],

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become an important component in large language models (LLMs). However, existing RL approaches focus on final outputs or textual solution trajectories, leading to coarse-grained rewards and unreliable reasoning. Such paradigms focus mainly on what the model outputs while overlooking how the model internally reasons. Therefore, can we reward how a model thinks internally rather than merely what it says? We first reveal the problem of textual reward aliasing in existing reward modeling approaches. Motivated by this, we propose the Attention Process Reward Model (APRM), which assigns internal rewards based on hidden states and attention maps to capture high-quality reasoning patterns. With only approximately 46M parameters, APRM is trained using ranking and counterfactual objectives, and its reward guides RL optimization while being periodically updated to handle distribution shifts. Integrated with representative RL methods, APRM achieved an average pass@8 gain of 2.88\%. Our results demonstrate the promise of incorporating internal reasoning signals into RL for LLMs.
authors: Kairong Han, Nuanqiao Shan, Ziyu Zhao, Xinpeng Dong, Zijing Hu, Dian Jin, Leyan Deng, Junjian Ye, Lujia Pan, Fei Wu, Kun Kuang
bullets: Existing reward models rely on outputs or textual trajectories, causing coarse-grained rewards and textual reward aliasing.
The Attention Process Reward Model uses hidden states and attention maps to assess internal reasoning quality.

APRM integrates with representative RL methods and reports an average pass@8 improvement of 2.88%.

papers.abstract: We report paired-seed architecture ablations from the development of Sophea Artemis, our in-house Greek-English model family. Every arm trains on the same 3B targets with a shared tokenizer and recipe; models range from 54M to 759M total parameters and roughly 54M to 124M active parameters. The main finding is that, at this tiny scale, stored capacity matters far more than mixer design. On a fixed held-out test, replacing the dense feed-forward blocks of a recurrent/attention hybrid with sixteen routed experts, at nearly the same approximate active parameters, lowers loss by 0.079 (Greek) and 0.112 (English) nats per target, and doubling to 32 experts lowers it by a further 0.022 and 0.031, at every paired seed. Reusing a four-layer block three times recovers about 40-44% of the gap between a shallow and an independently deep model, consistent with looped-Transformer results. In contrast, the choice among grouped-query attention (GQA), Gated DeltaNet (GDN) hybrids and a Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) hybrid moves loss by only about 0.01-0.02 nats; a 1:1 GDN/GQA hybrid is the one dense variant that improves on GQA in both languages at every held-out seed. In bits per character, Greek and English held-out losses are similar despite a 74.49%/25.51% training split, and synthetic mathematics, which comes from a collection outside the training sources, is the hardest Greek test component and gains least from added experts. Cached decoding needs its own qualification: trained models passed cached-versus-full logit checks only under a fixed-reduction inference policy, which itself changes 1.4-2.8% of next-token argmax choices relative to native evaluation. All results are conditional on one recipe and scale.
bullets: Paired-seed ablations used the same 3B targets, tokenizer, and training recipe across models ranging from 54M to 759M parameters.

Synthetic mathematics was the hardest Greek component and benefited least from added experts; cached decoding required a fixed-reduction policy and remains qualified.

papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are used in more and more new tasks, context engineering becomes a fundamental method to efficiently steer LLMs by constructing instruction prompts or metadata without intensive training. A growing number of LLM context engineering (LCE) approaches automate the task by casting the LLM itself as the engineer that draws generalizable instructions or experiences from offline trials as context. Although these methods resemble how humans learn from experiences, it remains unclear \textbf{when and how} LLMs can engineer effective context from data. To answer the question, we first establish a benchmark composed of datasets with different reasoning patterns. We compared different LCE methods with different LLM families in 8B size, showing that there is no single winner for all tasks, even compared with simple baselines like chain-of-thought. Even when scaling model capabilities via more parameters or generation iterations, LCEs do not consistently boost existing performance. Across all datasets and models, the performance gains of LCEs are negatively correlated ($r=-0.5, p\le 0.05$) with the diversity of the failure modes of reasoning trajectories. Investigating how LCEs work, we find that (1) the improvement in instruction adherence can explain some success of LCEs; (2) one major bottleneck is whether LLMs can extract effective experiences out of natively diverse failures. Through this study, we uncover the limited capabilities of LCEs in abstracting principled contexts from diverse failure modes and understand how LCEs work, providing guidelines for future work.
authors: Junrui Zhang, Zeyu Xu, Runchuan Zhu, Jie Peng, Long Zhang, Zixin Ding, Jiaxin Lin, Kai Wang, Jianmin Ji, Junyuan Hong
bullets: Introduces a benchmark spanning datasets with different reasoning patterns to study when LLMs can engineer effective context.

Performance gains are negatively correlated with reasoning-failure diversity (r = −0.5, p ≤ 0.05).
Improved instruction adherence explains some gains, while extracting effective experiences from diverse failures is a key bottleneck.

papers.abstract: This paper develops a theoretical account of Transformer attention by organizing existing probabilistic and information-theoretic results. It identifies the assumptions under which attention computes a posterior mean and the additional conditions required for accurate next-token prediction. Posterior-mean optimality under squared-error loss does not by itself establish predictive sufficiency; even a sufficient representation requires a prediction head that uses its information correctly. An excess-log-loss decomposition makes this distinction precise by separating representation information loss from prediction-head error. The analysis clarifies the conditions required for predictive guarantees. Determining when these conditions hold in trained models, and how architectural or training choices can support them, could guide the development of AI systems that preserve and use predictive information more effectively.
bullets: Organizes probabilistic and information-theoretic results on Transformer attention.
Identifies assumptions under which attention computes a posterior mean.
Shows that posterior-mean optimality under squared-error loss is insufficient for predictive sufficiency.
Uses an excess-log-loss decomposition to separate representation information loss from prediction-head error.
Highlights open questions about whether trained models and design choices satisfy the required conditions.
papers.selection_reason: Theoretical analysis of Transformer attention and predictive sufficiency; relevant to LLM architecture understanding.
papers.title: Toward a Theoretical Understanding of Transformer Attention: Bayesian Estimation and Predictive Sufficiency
papers.tldr: The paper clarifies when Transformer attention can be viewed as Bayesian estimation and why posterior-mean representations alone do not guarantee accurate next-token prediction.

papers.abstract: Many large language models (LLMs) use chain-of-thought (CoT) to solve complex problems, but hide their CoT traces to prevent reasoning capabilities from being distilled. While recent studies have shown that hidden CoTs can be reconstructed, existing methods typically require training a separate attacker for each target LLM. This paper studies model-agnostic CoT reconstruction, aiming to reconstruct hidden CoT traces from arbitrary target LLMs using only input prompts and visible final responses. We propose Final-Output Preference Learning (FOPL), which trains a single reconstruction model that generalizes to unseen LLMs without target-specific adaptation. To achieve this, the reconstruction model must learn which reasoning patterns match a given final response without knowing the target LLM's identity. We address this using preference optimization, training the reconstruction model to prefer native CoTs over synthetic alternatives for the same question and final response. By learning these preferences from LLMs with accessible CoTs, the reconstruction model learns to distinguish reasoning patterns based on visible responses. Experiments show that reconstructed CoTs capture distinct reasoning patterns across LLM families, including a family unseen during training. Moreover, students trained on reconstructed CoTs match or outperform those trained on native CoTs across several reasoning benchmarks.
authors: Hongli Shen, Shaopeng Fu, Qinbo Zhang, Jian Li, Di Wang
bullets: Addresses model-agnostic reconstruction of hidden reasoning without target-specific attacker training.
Uses preference optimization to favor native CoTs over synthetic alternatives sharing the same prompt and final response.
Learns reasoning-pattern preferences from models with accessible CoTs, without identifying the target LLM.
Reconstructed CoTs capture distinct patterns across LLM families, including one unseen during training.
Students trained on reconstructed CoTs match or outperform those trained on native CoTs across several reasoning benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a powerful approach for improving language-model reasoning, but its supervision is inherently sparse: a sequence-level verifier reward is propagated only through sampled trajectories and provides no direct signal for alternative actions. On-policy distillation (OPD) offers a complementary form of supervision by providing dense teacher feedback over the full next-token distribution, but this signal is not grounded in verified task outcomes. Simply co-optimizing the two objectives does not couple these signals: verifier feedback remains sparse and does not inform the dense teacher supervision. We introduce Verifiable On-Policy Distillation (VOPD), which transfers sparse verifier feedback into dense, verifier-grounded supervision. Our key observation is that the implicit-reward view of OPD places teacher supervision and verifier feedback in a common reward space while retaining a reward signal available for every next-token action. Under this view, VOPD projects verifier preference onto the teacher's implicit-reward direction and Rao--Blackwellizes the resulting signal over the full vocabulary, propagating verifier-grounded supervision to actions that were never sampled. The resulting objective can also be interpreted as adaptively extrapolating the distillation target according to teacher--verifier agreement. Across two teacher--student configurations and eight mathematical reasoning benchmarks, VOPD consistently improves both final performance and learning efficiency over vanilla OPD and other on-policy distillation baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/juntongshi48/VOPD.
authors: Juntong Shi, Stefano Ermon, Jure Leskovec, Minkai Xu
bullets: RLVR rewards only sampled trajectories, while on-policy distillation provides dense teacher feedback that is not tied to verified outcomes.
VOPD combines both signals in a shared implicit-reward space and projects verifier preferences onto the teacher’s reward direction.
Rao–Blackwellization propagates this verifier-grounded signal across the full vocabulary, including unsampled actions.
The method adaptively extrapolates distillation targets based on teacher–verifier agreement.
Across two teacher–student settings and eight mathematical reasoning benchmarks, VOPD improves final performance and learning efficiency over vanilla OPD and other on-policy baselines.

papers.abstract: Post-training large language models routinely pools reasoning trajectories from diverse teachers or algorithms, yet it remains unclear whether standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can learn such heterogeneous strategies without explicit mode conditioning. We study the learnability and local bottlenecks of heterogeneous reasoning through a formal mixture formulation and controlled experiments. We first formalize the representational compatibility of the optimal autoregressive model with latent reasoning mixtures: the target next-token distribution weights modes by their prefix posteriors and concentrates on a single mode once alternative modes assign negligible likelihood to the prefix. In a verifiable symbolic graph-search environment with paired breadth-first and depth-first search trajectories, no consistent disadvantage is observed for unlabeled mixed SFT relative to homogeneous or labeled baselines under matched token budgets while preserving both modes. Scaling across 0.6B--14B models and data budgets largely eliminates global mode confusion, shifting the primary bottleneck to local state-tracking transitions. Because a local mistake affects the final outcome only when subsequent reasoning is sensitive to that step, we find that only a small fraction of local errors are outcome-determining \emph{Critical Reasoning Nodes (CRNs)}, and that single-step repairs at these nodes rescue failing trajectories across symbolic search and natural language benchmarks whenever the model has sufficient downstream competence to complete the remaining derivation. Our environment is open-sourced at https://github.com/Bowen1911/Symbolic_graph_env.
authors: Sunbowen Li, Dandan Song, Shengkun Ma, Xuanning Cao
bullets: Formalizes how an autoregressive model represents mixtures of latent reasoning modes using prefix-dependent mode posteriors.
In paired breadth-first/depth-first graph-search trajectories, mixed SFT shows no consistent disadvantage versus homogeneous or labeled training under matched token budgets.
Across 0.6B–14B models and data budgets, global mode confusion largely diminishes, shifting the bottleneck to local state-tracking transitions.
Defines Critical Reasoning Nodes (CRNs) as the small fraction of local errors that determine outcomes; repairing them can rescue failed trajectories when downstream competence is sufficient.
The symbolic graph-search environment is open-sourced; results also extend to natural-language benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Professional documents are a long-context workload that retrieval-style benchmarks do not capture. In a ten-domain enterprise collection, a task's evidence is spread across a source document of median length 27 pages (mean 48.8, maximum 873); a third of tasks rest mainly on charts, drawings, and maps; and 70.9% require two or more reasoning hops. We post-train Kimi-K2.7, an open-weight foundation model, at its full context window on 1,465 expert-authored tasks with atomic rubrics from that collection, training rank-32 adapters with one round of privileged-context on-policy self-distillation followed by two rounds of rubric-reward reinforcement learning. We render each PDF as text for training and as extracted text plus selected page images at evaluation. The smoothed RL training reward rises from 0.37 in the first tenth of the run to 0.67 in the last. On the 100-task GDP.pdf holdout, served in a 262,144-token window, strict pass (all rubric criteria met) more than doubles after the second round, from 11.0% to 24.5%, with gains across input lengths up to 240K tokens. Mean tokens generated stay flat (9,803 to 9,733), so the gain does not come from longer outputs. GPT-5.6 Sol's leaderboard strict pass is 30.7% at a measured 3,422 tokens. On 220 out-of-domain GDPval tasks, where the model runs as a long-horizon tool-using agent, mean rubric reward rises from 0.571 to 0.746 after the third round and zero-credit tasks fall from 54 to 10, while messages per task fall 18%, from 70.9 to 58.2. In paired trajectories, the third round replaces a context-thrashing retry loop with one up-front check of all sources, and verification extends from checking that files exist to checking what they contain. We argue that long-context evaluation of agents should report accuracy jointly with tokens and turns, and that datasets of long documents should ship text and image renderings alongside each PDF.
authors: Sushant Mehta, Logan Ritchie, Edwin Chen
bullets: Evaluates professional-document tasks involving very long sources, visual evidence, and multi-hop reasoning across ten enterprise domains.
Post-trains Kimi-K2.7 using rank-32 adapters, one self-distillation round, and two rubric-reward RL rounds over 1,465 expert-authored tasks.
On a 100-task GDP.pdf holdout, strict pass rises from 11.0% to 24.5%, with gains up to 240K-token inputs while generated tokens remain nearly unchanged.
On 220 out-of-domain GDPval tasks, mean rubric reward increases from 0.571 to 0.746, zero-credit tasks decrease from 54 to 10, and messages per task fall 18%.
Argues that long-context agent evaluation should jointly report accuracy, tokens, and turns, and that document datasets should include both text and image renderings.

papers.abstract: Confidence estimation for large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) aims to assess how likely a particular generated response is to be correct. We investigate how learning this assessment can benefit from the model's predictive reliability on the underlying query. Binary correctness supervision, however, assigns identical labels to occasional errors and frequent failures, as well as isolated successes and consistent success. These outcomes can arise from substantially different predictive behavior under stochastic decoding. We propose a confidence-learning framework that supplements realized response correctness with query-level predictive reliability. We estimate reliability through repeated generations under a fixed model and decoding configuration, then combine the empirical success rate with individual correctness to construct a graded confidence surrogate. The surrogate differentiates responses sharing the same correctness label while preserving the average predictive reliability of the sampled response pool. To learn this target, we condition an independent confidence estimator on the query and its full generated response, and optimize backbone LoRA adapters together with a projection and scalar confidence head using mean squared error. Repeated sampling is required only for supervision construction; inference scores an individual response without additional generations. We establish ordering and mean preservation properties of the surrogate and derive a selective-risk bound connecting population surrogate prediction error to the error rate among accepted responses. We evaluate the framework across language and vision-language models, examining confidence calibration and selective prediction.
authors: Chen Li, Xiaoling Hu, Chao Chen
bullets: Binary correctness labels miss differences between occasional errors, frequent failures, isolated successes, and consistently correct behavior.
The method combines an individual response’s correctness with query-level empirical success rates from repeated generations.
An independent confidence estimator uses the query and full response, trained with LoRA adapters and a confidence head via mean squared error.
Repeated generations are needed only to construct supervision; inference evaluates each response in a single pass.
The paper proves ordering and mean-preservation properties and derives a selective-risk bound, then evaluates calibration and selective prediction in language and vision-language models.
