papers.abstract: Next-token prediction relies on learned token embeddings whose dimension $d$ is much smaller than the vocabulary size $V$. Existing analyses of training dynamics either fix the embeddings with $d\ge V$ or train them only in restricted settings. It remains unclear whether jointly training the embeddings by gradient-based methods from random initialization leads to accurate prediction when $d<V$. In this paper, we study this question in the simplest setting where it is already nontrivial, namely next-token prediction with a one-token context, which we refer to as a state-transition model. The model consists of an input embedding and an output embedding, either untied or tied, and is trained from Gaussian initialization by perturbed gradient descent with weight decay on the population cross-entropy loss. We consider ground-truth transition laws whose centered log-probability table has low rank and bounded entries, and measure the prediction quality by the relative prediction gain (RPG). It is zero for the uniform predictor and one for the optimal predictor. For the untied model, we show that when $d=\Omega(\sqrt V)$, with probability at least $1-e^{-cd}$ for some constant $c$, the RPG is above $7/8$ at every iterate in the final $1-1/d$ fraction of training iterations. For the tied model trained on a subset of states, we prove that the RPG on the observed states is $1-O(V/d^2)$, and under a coverage condition on the ground truth and a bound on the learned embeddings, we further prove a prediction guarantee on the unseen states. Our analysis is based on the bounded trace of the Hessian of the softmax cross-entropy loss, which implies that the approximate second-order stationary points reached by training have high prediction gain. Numerical experiments with practical parameter choices illustrate the persistent training gain and the transfer of the tied model.
authors: Yee Man Choi, Fengchi Wang, Ruiquan Huang
bullets: Studies one-token-context next-token prediction with jointly trained input/output embeddings initialized randomly.
Analyzes untied and tied embeddings using perturbed gradient descent with weight decay on population cross-entropy.
For untied embeddings, dimension scaling as Ω(√V) yields RPG above 7/8 during most late training iterations, with high probability.
For tied embeddings trained on observed states, RPG is 1−O(V/d²), with additional guarantees for unseen states under coverage and embedding-boundedness conditions.
The theory uses a bounded Hessian trace to connect approximate second-order stationary points with high prediction gain; experiments illustrate persistent gain and transfer.

papers.abstract: Parallel-trainable recurrences such as Mamba, linear attention, and DeltaNet offer constant-cost streaming inference, but they suffer from two limitations: 1) they struggle to track discrete state, and 2) they read every parameter at every step, tying model capacity directly to CPU latency. We introduce Yggdrasil, a recurrent architecture that decouples capacity from per-step compute by looking up each layer's transition in a large, tree-routed bank of recurrent experts. Each router addresses its bank using the current token and the state of the layer below. We prove that this cross-layer context is necessary---a single token-indexed layer of non-expanding transitions with finitely many reachable states cannot perform conditional resets---while avoiding feedback from the layer's own past preserves parallel-scan training. Because each step traverses one tree path and reads a single expert per layer, active weights stay within a few hundred kilobytes in CPU L2 cache while the full bank resides in RAM. Among the parallel-trainable models we evaluate, Yggdrasil is the only one to solve all five state-tracking tasks. At matched active parameter counts, it achieves the lowest test bits on enwik8 (1.540 bpb) and the human genome hg38 (1.567 bpb), while stepping $3.0\times$ and $3.3\times$ faster on a single CPU core ($6.7\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ and $5.8\,\mu\mathrm{s}$) than the fastest streaming baseline, and delivering the highest GPU throughput of all models at batch 1024. On the Genomic Benchmarks, it is the strongest causal model at matched active parameters (86.0% mean accuracy).
bullets: Addresses state-tracking weaknesses and per-step latency that limit parallel-trainable recurrent models.
Routes each layer’s transition through a tree using the current token and the lower layer’s state, activating one expert per layer.
Cross-layer routing enables conditional resets while preserving parallel-scan training by avoiding feedback from a layer’s own past.
Active weights fit in a few hundred kilobytes of CPU L2 cache, while the larger expert bank remains in RAM.
It solves all five evaluated state-tracking tasks and reports strong language, genomic, CPU-speed, GPU-throughput, and genomic-classification results.

papers.selection_reason: Recurrent expert-routed architecture for state tracking with fast CPU inference; directly relevant to LLM architectures and efficient inference.
papers.title: Yggdrasil: Tree-Routed Recurrent Experts for State Tracking and Fast CPU Inference
papers.tldr: Yggdrasil uses tree-routed recurrent experts to improve discrete-state tracking while keeping per-step CPU inference fast and memory-local.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has demonstrated strong performance in improving large language model (LLM) reasoning, yet its credit-assignment signal remains coarse. Outcome verifiers provide scalable supervision by judging whether a completed response is correct, but they do not directly indicate which intermediate reasoning tokens contribute to success or failure. As a result, policy optimization can be inefficient, especially when training base models directly from sparse outcome feedback. In this paper, we introduce SAEPO, a Sparse AutoEncoder-guided token-level credit assignment method for outcome-supervised Policy Optimization. Rather than treating correctness only as a rollout-level (sequence-level) signal, SAEPO uses a pretrained sparse autoencoder (SAE) to build token-level semantic representations within reasoning trajectories; it scores each token based on the SAE concepts (e.g., penalizing wrong "final-answer" tokens but rewarding correct "reasoning-process" tokens), learned in an unsupervised manner, to achieve fine-grained credit assignment. SAEPO is a plug-in advantage-shaping module compatible with various policy optimization algorithms. We instantiate SAEPO with both GRPO and GSPO, covering token-ratio and sequence-ratio policy-gradient objectives, and evaluate SAEPO across three LLM backbones on six math and two code benchmarks. Empirical results show that SAEPO improves both the math and code benchmark averages over the matched baselines, with gains of up to 6.63% and 5.57%, respectively. On Qwen3-1.7B-Base, training curves also show faster early accuracy growth. Feature and token-level analyses suggest that the SAE-derived signal favors question-relevant concepts and reasoning tokens.
authors: Yusong Zhao, Zihao Zhao, Zirui Zhang, Tunyu Zhang, Ziyan Wang, Yi Wang, Chengzhi Mao, Hao Wang
bullets: Targets coarse credit assignment in outcome-supervised reinforcement learning, where verifiers judge only completed responses.
Uses a pretrained sparse autoencoder to represent reasoning trajectories and shape token-level advantages based on semantic concepts.
Can be plugged into multiple policy-optimization methods, demonstrated with GRPO and GSPO.
Evaluated across three LLM backbones on six math and two code benchmarks, improving matched-baseline averages by up to 6.63% in math and 5.57% in code.
Analyses indicate the learned signal favors question-relevant concepts and reasoning tokens; early accuracy growth was faster on Qwen3-1.7B-Base.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of SAEPO. A frozen SAE encodes token hidden states from grouped rollouts into sparse features. For each token, its counts of similar tokens in correct and incorrect rollouts determine its token-level reward, with higher reward assigned when more similar tokens appear in correct rollouts than in incorrect ones. The token-level reward is normalized and added to the outcome advantage, while the verifier reward, policy-ratio construction, clipping rule, and KL regularizer remain unchanged.

Figure 4 SAE features (concepts) associated with the highest and the lowest SAEPO token scores, computed from rollouts on the “Algebra” and “Geometry” subjects in MATH-500. Feature-level rewards are obtained by averaging semantic scores over tokens where each SAE feature is active. Rows show features with highest/lowest rewards and their top activating tokens; color intensity indicates normalized activation within each feature. Left: High-reward features correspond to subject-relevant concepts, such as spherical and coordinate vocabulary in Geometry, and computation and expression terms in Algebra. Right: Low-reward features mostly capture connectives, copulas, punctuation, stop words, and discourse markers. These results suggest that the SAEPO-derived signal concentrates on semantically meaningful reasoning features.

Figure 1 Comparison of credit assignment mechanisms in outcome-supervised policy optimizations. GRPO assigns the same rollout-level credit to all tokens in a generated reasoning trace, so decisive reasoning steps and incidental tokens receive identical credit. Our SAEPO assigns question-local, token-level semantic credit based on semantic representations from the SAE feature space; therefore it rewards question-relevant reasoning tokens while penalizing uninformative or misleading tokens with more fine-grained credit assignment. Top words of the most related concepts to an example rewarded token “interior” show that our SAEPO can achieve interpretable token-level credit assignment.

Figure 5 Examples of how SAEPO can assign a fine-grained credit signal to each token. For rollouts from different types of questions, we visualize the SAEPO-derived final shaped advantages Aqg,t = Aout qg + αŜqg,t from Eqn. (13) assigned to individual tokens in the rollouts. Green tokens represent positive credit that rewards the tokens, gray tokens represent near-zero credit, while red tokens represent negative credit that penalizes the tokens. SAEPO tends to reward semantically meaningful tokens like question-relevant tokens in incorrect trajectories and reasoning tokens in correct trajectories, while penalizing uninformative or misleading tokens even when they are in correct trajectories, achieving fine-grained token-level credit assignment over the reasoning trace.

Figure 3 Training dynamics on Qwen3-1.7B-Base. We plot training accuracy curves during RL training for GRPO and GSPO, comparing each vanilla policy optimization algorithm with its SAEPO-augmented variant and with credit-assignment baselines (i.e., KTAE, THR, and GTPO). papers.selection_reason: SAE-guided token-level credit assignment improves LLM reasoning policy optimization.
papers.title: SAEPO: Sparse-Autoencoder-Guided Credit Assignment for Policy Optimization
papers.tldr: SAEPO improves sparse-reward LLM reasoning training by using sparse-autoencoder concepts to assign fine-grained token-level credit instead of relying only on final-answer correctness.

papers.abstract: A transformer language model computes a deep hidden state for every token but uses it only to sample that token. Existing latent-feedback designs, which feed hidden states back across tokens, are mostly built in during pretraining and gain little when added to a pretrained model. We introduce the temporal residual, a second residual stream that every sublayer reads and writes and that is carried from each token to the next. It adds 2,752 parameters to a 4.2B-parameter model and starts exactly at the pretrained network. Retrofitted onto Qwen3.5-4B-Base with 5B tokens of training, it beats a standard model trained on the same data by 7, 13 and 5 points on AIME 2024, AIME 2025 and AMC 2023, writes shorter solutions, and stays ahead at matched training compute. The separate stream matters: prior designs that feed state into the existing stream recover at most 40% of the gain when retrofitted. Validation loss can mislead: the recipe with the lowest loss gains nothing at decoding. Trained with filler tokens in place of reasoning, the model reasons in its hidden state: its GSM8K accuracy with no visible reasoning rises from 21% to 40%, and falls back when the carried state is zeroed.
authors: Ziyang Cai, Xingyu Zhu, Sanjeev Arora
bullets: Addresses the limited effectiveness of adding latent feedback after pretraining.
Adds a separate residual stream that each sublayer reads, writes, and carries across tokens.
Retrofitting Qwen3.5-4B-Base with 5B training tokens improved AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and AMC 2023 performance by 7, 13, and 5 points, respectively, versus a same-data standard model.
The approach supports hidden-state reasoning: GSM8K accuracy without visible reasoning increased from 21% to 40%, but dropped when the carried state was removed.
Separate-stream design and decoding evaluations matter; validation loss alone did not predict gains, and prior retrofits recovered at most 40% of the improvement.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a temporal residual stream carrying latent feedback across tokens in pretrained LLMs, improving reasoning and acting as a lightweight recurrent memory.
papers.title: The Temporal Residual: Fast and Effective Retrofitting of Latent Feedback into Pretrained Language Models
papers.tldr: The temporal residual efficiently retrofits cross-token latent feedback into a pretrained language model, improving reasoning while enabling shorter or hidden reasoning traces.

papers.abstract: Policy gradient (PG) methods such as GRPO dominate LLM fine-tuning, yet recent work showed that Evolution Strategies (ES) also scale to fine-tuning models with billions of parameters. Which method needs fewer samples, and on which tasks, remains unclear. We view the two methods as estimators of the same gradient that differ in where they explore. Because ES perturbs parameters, its noise grows with the number of parameters, and because PG samples actions, its noise grows with the number of generated tokens. Only noise along the directions that change the reward slows learning. The cost of ES then depends on the effective dimension, the number of independent skills a task requires rather than its parameter count, while the cost of PG depends on the effective horizon, which counts only the tokens that share both credit and weights with the reward-carrying ones. We train both methods on a synthetic task where the number of skills and the effective horizon can be varied separately. PG is cheaper when the horizon is short, ES becomes cheaper once it is long enough, and this crossover moves to longer horizons as the number of skills grows. We then measure the effective horizons of 20 NLP, math reasoning, and agentic tasks and compare the two methods with Qwen2.5-7B. PG leads on short-horizon tasks, the two tie on the moderate-horizon math ones, and no task has a horizon in the regime where the theory predicts an ES advantage. Terminal-Bench has a far longer horizon. There, in a preliminary comparison with Qwen3.5-4B, ES without any credit assignment reaches a higher success rate than the PG checkpoint released with Tmax, as the theory predicts. ES should thus have the advantage on long-horizon tasks with few independent skills and a nonvanishing reward signal. Current benchmarks are only at the onset of this regime, so ES should become more competitive as agentic tasks grow longer.
authors: Qiyao Liang, Kajetan Schweighofer, Xin Qiu, Risto Miikkulainen
bullets: Both ES and policy gradients estimate the same gradient, but ES explores parameter space while policy gradients explore generated actions.
ES sample cost depends on effective dimension—the number of independent skills—whereas policy-gradient cost depends on effective horizon—the reward-relevant token dependencies.
On a controllable synthetic task, policy gradients win at short horizons; ES wins beyond a skill-dependent crossover horizon.
Across 20 NLP, math, and agentic tasks, policy gradients lead on short horizons and tie on moderate-horizon math tasks; no task reached the predicted ES-favorable regime.
On the much longer-horizon Terminal-Bench, preliminary results show ES without credit assignment outperforming a released policy-gradient checkpoint.

papers.selection_reason: Analysis of evolution strategies versus policy gradients for LLM fine-tuning; relevant to LLM training methodology.
papers.title: Dimension Is Free, Horizon Is Not: When Evolution Strategies Rival Policy Gradients for LLM Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: Evolution Strategies (ES) become competitive with policy gradients when tasks have long effective horizons but few independent skills, though most current benchmarks remain too short to show a clear ES advantage.

papers.abstract: Test-time learning (TTL) enables large language models to adapt to unlabeled inputs during deployment. The model updates a lightweight adapter by minimizing the next-token prediction loss on the input it receives. When these updates persist across conversation turns, every user query serves both as the request answered in the current turn and as adaptation data for later turns. By choosing the queries used for adaptation, an attacker can influence parameter updates and weaken safety alignment through ordinary interactions with a TTL chat service. To demonstrate this risk, we introduce Progressive Test-Time Adaptation Poisoning (P-TAP), a query-only multi-turn attack that jailbreaks the model by poisoning its session adapter through the service's own updates. A sequence of escalating adversarial queries shapes the adapter turn by turn; the final harmful request is then answered under the accumulated state without itself being used for adaptation. Across four open-weight instruction-tuned models, enabling updates raises attack success rates on average by 13.00 percentage points under greedy decoding and by 22.25 points under best-of-10 sampling, relative to matched sessions receiving the same queries without updates. Answering adversarial queries but adapting on unrelated text or on benign text about the same topic removes most of this increase. Among existing safeguards, screening incoming queries flags every attack stream before the final request, while a perplexity-based detector of unsafe adaptation flags none of the successful attacks.
authors: Honghao Feng, Shanhan Qu, Kai Tong, Shuquan Man, Huiping Zhuang
bullets: P-TAP gradually shapes a session’s lightweight adapter with escalating adversarial queries, then uses the accumulated state to answer a final harmful request.
Across four open-weight instruction-tuned models, updates increased attack success by 13.00 percentage points with greedy decoding and 22.25 points with best-of-10 sampling.
The attack’s effect largely disappears when adaptation uses unrelated or benign same-topic text instead of adversarial queries.
Incoming-query screening caught every attack stream, whereas a perplexity-based unsafe-adaptation detector missed all successful attacks.

papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement asks a system to improve the very system that improves it. Today's language models improve themselves through data, training recipes or scaffolds. Whenever their weights change, gradient descent writes the update, not the model. We let the model write its own weights. In SELFWRITE, each generation the current model studies its own reasoning on fresh training problems, inspects its own weights and activations in a persistent Python session, and writes a program that constructs a low-rank weight edit for itself from white-box primitives (singular directions, activation contrasts between its right and wrong answers, rank-one projections, tensor computations), with no training or gradient tool. Every candidate is graded once on a hidden gate set against the current model; the best strictly improving edit is merged into the weights, and the edited model writes the next edit. On Qwen3.8-27B and math problems from DAPO-Math, five generations of SELFWRITE raise gate accuracy from 73.95% to 76.45% and accuracy on a held-out test split that the loop never sees from 76.30% to 77.75% (avg@4) and from 82.60% to 84.80% (pass@4), without a single gradient step. A language model can author useful changes to its own weights without gradients, and the edited model keeps writing useful edits.
bullets: The model analyzes its reasoning, weights, and activations in a persistent Python session to design self-edits.
Edits use white-box primitives such as singular directions, activation contrasts, rank-one projections, and tensor computations.
Each candidate is evaluated on a hidden gate set, and only strictly improving edits are merged before the next generation.
On Qwen3.8-27B math problems, five generations improved gate accuracy from 73.95% to 76.45%.
Held-out performance also improved, indicating that the self-edits generalized beyond the loop’s gate set.

The rank-one edit is merged only if it improves the model on a hidden gate set, and the edited model Mg+1 writes the next edit. No gradient tool is used and no training step is taken.

(3) Select: every candidate is graded once on the hidden gate, paired problem by problem with Mg; the largest strictly positive gain is merged, and Mg+1 becomes the next editor (Section 3.4); gate statistics reach the sessions of later generations. Bars are schematic. The test split is never shown to the editor.

papers.abstract: Reasoning models deliberate over multiple answer proposals, often resulting in excessively long traces due to backtracking, even when the correct answer has already been reached (Across three 32B models, ~87% of rollouts contain 1 unique answer yet still make ~8 answer proposals on average). Given this potentially "decorative" chain of thought (CoT) reasoning, can we look to the model internals to determine if the model will backtrack or commit to an answer proposal? Operating under the hypothesis that models maintain an internal representation of their uncertainty, we seek to extract this representation and characterize its relationship with backtracking behavior at answer proposals. By querying the model's verbalized confidence following answer proposals throughout a response trace, we extract a linear direction for latent confidence that separates high and low verbalized confidence. This direction can steer verbalized confidence as expected, but it surprisingly can also steer the next token probability of backtracking, performing on par with a linear direction extracted directly from backtracking examples. We then test the direction under progressively more realistic interventions. Steering continuously from a mid-trace answer proposal modulates response length (~-1.3k - ~+2.5k tokens) and the number of answer proposals (-4.18 - +4.75) in both directions, with minimal cost to accuracy. Applying the confidence direction from the start of generation, where proposal positions are unknown, still shortens traces at comparable accuracy, and its effect surfaces in the linguistic confidence of proposals. Overall, our study reveals the intricate interplay between a model's internal confidence and its proclivity to backtrack or commit to an answer.
authors: Stephen Cheng, Zahra Sodagar, Sandeep Soni, Dinesh Manocha, Sarah Wiegreffe
bullets: Many rollouts repeatedly propose answers despite containing only one unique answer, suggesting potentially unnecessary chain-of-thought backtracking.
A linear direction extracted from verbalized confidence separates high- and low-confidence states and also influences the probability of backtracking.
Steering this direction mid-trace changes response length by roughly −1.3k to +2.5k tokens and answer proposals by −4.18 to +4.75, in both directions.
Applying the direction from generation start shortens traces at comparable accuracy, even without knowing proposal positions.
The findings link internal confidence representations to a model’s tendency to commit or continue reasoning.

papers.abstract: Multi-step reasoning requires models to preserve and update intermediate information as computation unfolds. State tracking captures this fundamental requirement, but models that succeed within a fixed range of state transitions may not generalize when substantially more updates are required. Recurrent Transformers offer a natural mechanism for addressing this challenge by repeatedly applying shared Transformer blocks, allowing computation to scale with problem length. We study when such recurrent computation generalizes beyond the training range in a controlled state-tracking task, varying operation representation, positional encoding, and recurrent capacity. We find that recurrence alone is insufficient: multi-token template representations and absolute positional encoding can severely limit extrapolation, whereas atomic operation representations enable substantially stronger length generalization. The effect of positional structure also varies with recurrent depth, with periodic positional encoding achieving the strongest mean performance at greater recurrent depth. Most importantly, scaling the recurrent operator extends the extrapolation horizon, reaching 35.1% exact-match accuracy on sequences of 20-40 operations after training only on 2-10, while substantially larger fixed-depth Transformers remain at 0%. Additional recurrent computation at test time can extend the range over which the model generalizes, but does not eliminate failure on much longer sequences. These results suggest that recurrent computation can support length-generalizable state tracking, but that its effectiveness depends critically on whether the learned computation remains reusable across sequence lengths.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is one of the most popular post-training paradigms for large language models. RLVR typically trains a single model under hyperparameters chosen before training begins, while researchers tune hyperparameters across consecutive runs. We introduce Population-Based Post-Training (PBPT), which trains several models in parallel and lets the training process do the tuning through population-based training. PBPT periodically evaluates models on a validation set. High-performers are duplicated and their hyperparameters perturbed to explore new configurations. Low-performers stop training and are replaced by these copies. On reasoning benchmarks (Enigmata, Nemotron) and interactive tool-use environments (Gaia2, AppWorld), PBPT produces stronger agents than compute-matched groups of independent RLVR learners. Furthermore, PBPT is able to recover from poor initial hyperparameters, automatically discovering better settings over the course of training.
authors: Yixuan Even Xu, Aleksei Petrenko, Raja Giryes, Jackson Hamburger, Kevin Chen, Fei Fang, J. Zico Kolter, Philipp Kr\"ahenb\"uhl
bullets: RLVR commonly trains one model with hyperparameters fixed before training, requiring manual tuning across runs.
PBPT trains a population of models in parallel and periodically evaluates them on validation performance.
High-performing models are copied with perturbed hyperparameters, while low-performing models are replaced.
It outperforms compute-matched independent RLVR learners on reasoning and interactive tool-use benchmarks.
PBPT can recover from poor initial hyperparameter choices by discovering better settings during training.

papers.abstract: Frontier language models can now read and edit the weights of a neural network much like code and thereby improve a small model, an approach known as Weight-Space Programming (WSP). We further explore applying WSP to a language model itself, which we call Self-WSP. Specifically, Qwen3.5-0.8B reads its own weights, proposes an edit, and then continues with the edited weights as both problem solver and editor. We find many cases of genuine self-improvement. Self-edits can raise GSM8K accuracy from 11.8% to 62.2% and MATH500 accuracy from 7.0% to 32.2%, sometimes by changing only 16 parameters, and in some cases repeated self-editing keeps improving the model. A closer look, however, reveals that these gains lack interpretability. The model shows little understanding of the edits it makes, and WSP driven by random search sometimes performs comparably. Self-WSP thus holds promise as a path toward recursive self-improvement (RSI), but realizing this promise requires further exploration.
authors: Guoming Ling, Shanshan Zhong, Kaixuan Zhang, Zhongzhan Huang
bullets: Qwen3.5-0.8B reads and edits its own weights, then uses the edited model for both solving and further editing.
Self-edits improved GSM8K accuracy from 11.8% to 62.2% and MATH500 accuracy from 7.0% to 32.2%.
Some improvements required changing as few as 16 parameters, and repeated self-editing sometimes continued to help.
The model showed little understanding of its edits; random-search WSP sometimes achieved comparable results.
The approach suggests potential for recursive self-improvement but remains difficult to interpret and validate.

papers.abstract: In Large Language Model (LLM) pre-training, loss curves can conceal substantial instability, i.e., even small perturbations may lead to dramatically different predictions while leaving loss nearly unchanged. To investigate this phenomenon and reveal the underlying mechanisms, we first formulate LLM pre-training as a non-autonomous dynamical system that jointly evolves model weights and Adam optimizer states. Based on this formulation, we introduce a normalized sensitivity score in optimizer-relative coordinates to identify sensitive training checkpoints. At one such checkpoint, a weight perturbation of only 10^(-5) leads to 35.7% disagreement in top-1 predictions and 16.2% disagreement in benchmark answers after 200 training steps, with only 0.8% of greedy generations remaining identical despite similar validation losses. Furthermore, we find that perturbations to Adam's first and second moments induce comparably large effects, with similar sensitivity patterns observed in OLMo-1B. Finally, guided by our diagnostic, targeted stabilization reduces top-1 disagreement to 0.83% and increases generation exact match to 88.3%, at the cost of a 0.11-nat increase in validation loss. Our findings reveal a hidden form of optimizer-state-dependent sensitivity in LLM pre-training that conventional loss-based evaluations may overlook, while demonstrating its potential for diagnosis and mitigation.
authors: Bo Liu, Yuan Xie, Junan Chen, Fujun Han
bullets: Models are framed as non-autonomous dynamical systems jointly evolving weights and Adam optimizer states.

Similar sensitivity arises from perturbing Adam’s first and second moments, with patterns also observed in OLMo-1B.
Targeted stabilization reduced top-1 disagreement to 0.83% and raised generation exact match to 88.3%, while increasing validation loss by 0.11 nat.

papers.tldr: LLM pre-training can be highly sensitive to tiny weight or Adam-state perturbations despite nearly unchanged loss, but targeted stabilization can substantially improve prediction consistency.

papers.abstract: Looped transformers do not acquire new knowledge during a forward pass. Prior work shows that they store as many bits in their weights as non-looped models. It remains unclear how recurrence makes this knowledge available during inference. We study this question using synthetic factual recall and multi-hop reasoning, measuring depth-resolved readable information in bits with native readouts and tuned lenses. Under final-loop supervision, single-hop facts become readable progressively: heavier memorization loads delay retrieval despite comparable final readable information. Untied baselines of equal unrolled depth concentrate retrieval near the end of their stacks, whereas looped models expose facts earlier. This delay is not intrinsic to the tested recall tasks: training with supervision and depth-specific readouts at every loop makes near-final information readable after the first loop in all tested configurations. Representational analysis shows value-related structure emerging within states organized by the query key. We then study multi-hop chains whose facts are stored in the weights rather than given in the prompt. Intermediate entities become decodable in chain order, and aligned transitions show next-entity structure developing while current-entity structure remains dominant. Interventions in a released six-recurrence model establish a causal role for these representations. Counterfactual replacements of a probe-defined entity component at a single prompt position redirect downstream bridge entities and the final answer. Conversely, replacements from queries that reach the same entity through different preceding relations, preserving the remaining relation suffix, retain the original answer in over 99.5\% of tested cases. These results distinguish a training-dependent schedule for factual recall from the causal role of retrieved-entity representations in subsequent composition.
authors: Fabio Valerio Massoli, Arnau Padr\'es Masdemont, Jordi Ros Giralt, Arash Behboodi
bullets: Under final-loop supervision, heavier memorization loads delay when facts become readable, despite similar final information.
Loopy models expose facts earlier than equally deep untied transformers, while depth-specific supervision can make near-final information readable after the first loop.
In multi-hop recall, intermediate entities become decodable in chain order as next-entity structure develops around query-key-organized states.
Interventions show that replacing a retrieved entity redirects downstream bridge entities and answers; matched relational substitutions preserve the original answer in over 99.5% of tests.
The findings separate a training-dependent retrieval schedule from the causal role of retrieved entities in composing answers.

papers.abstract: We present KMed-31B, a medical large language model post-trained from an open-weight model for on-premises deployment with limited hardware. Post-training a model for diverse medical tasks remains difficult, because improving one kind of task can lower performance on another. We attribute this to differences between tasks in expected output and available feedback. Medical question answering and diagnosis prediction have reference answers, whereas clinical inquiry has no single correct response and is judged with rubrics. We therefore divide medical training tasks into four categories by these two properties, train one specialist per category with a reward that its feedback supports, and integrate the specialists into a single student with Multi-teacher On-policy Delta Distillation (MOPD$^2$). For clinical inquiry, we build Synthetic Health Dialogue, a simulated corpus of consultations with lay users and clinicians whose patient cases span common clinical presentations in primary care. Relative to its base model, KMed-31B raises HealthBench Hard from 22.95 to 41.87 and HealthBench Professional from 37.92 to 50.20 in non-thinking mode, and from 23.80 to 51.48 and from 41.97 to 59.18 in thinking mode, while its scores on four multiple-choice medical benchmarks are maintained or slightly improved. KMed-31B has the highest unadjusted HealthBench Hard score among the compared models, including proprietary ones, and scores higher on HealthBench Professional than every open-weight model we compare, including models with more than ten times as many total parameters. Applied to another base model, Qwen3.8-27B, the same training recipe also raises both HealthBench scores. We describe the training recipe, data construction, and settings in detail so that institutions requiring on-premises deployment can develop medical models from open-weight foundations.
bullets: Addresses conflicting feedback and output requirements across medical QA, diagnosis prediction, and clinical inquiry.
Trains four task-category specialists, then integrates them using Multi-teacher On-policy Delta Distillation (MOPD²).
Introduces Synthetic Health Dialogue for simulated primary-care consultations involving lay users and clinicians.
Improves HealthBench Hard and Professional substantially over its base model while maintaining or slightly improving four multiple-choice benchmarks.
Reports strong HealthBench performance among compared models and transfers the recipe to another open-weight base model.

The pipeline is applied separately to the thinking and non-thinking branches (excluding open-ended QA in the thinking branch), yielding one checkpoint per branch.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented language models answer well when the relevant document comes first or last and poorly when it sits in the middle. Some fine-tuning recipes lift the middle by lowering the start. We show how training contexts teach positional bias. With a uniform answer slot and shuffled distractors, the optimal reader ignores position. Building on this result, Exchangeable Self-Distillation (ExSD) trains a small adapter on shuffled contexts to reproduce the model's answer when it reads the answer document alone. It needs no gold answers and only a few thousand examples. On six models from 1.5B to 32B parameters, ExSD raises both average and worst-position accuracy against the frozen model, including on a held-out test split. In controlled LoRA comparisons, it significantly improves both criteria over Pos2Distill. Against CORD, mean differences are not significant, while worst-position accuracy improves significantly in the 20- and 30-document settings. ExSD also matches or beats gold-answer fine-tuning, changes behavior on other tasks far less, and transfers to unseen tasks. Head probes show greater reliance on content over position.
authors: Qingsen Ma, Dianyun Wang, Jiahong Liu, Irwin King
bullets: Uniform answer placement and shuffled distractors motivate making document position uninformative during training.
ExSD trains a small adapter on shuffled contexts to match the model’s answer from the relevant document alone, without gold answers.
Across six models ranging from 1.5B to 32B parameters, it improves average and worst-position accuracy, including on held-out data.
ExSD outperforms Pos2Distill on both criteria; it matches or beats gold-answer fine-tuning and transfers to unseen tasks.
Head probes indicate increased reliance on content over position, while behavior on unrelated tasks changes less.

figures.caption: Figure 3. ExSD wins all 12 prompt-matched comparisons on both criteria. Figure 2. Exchangeable Self-Distillation. (1) A ranked retriever puts the hardest distractors first. A document’s slot then predicts how answer-like it is, so position itself becomes evidence (Prop. 2). ExSD places the answer document at a uniformly random slot and shuffles the distractors, so every slot looks alike (Prop. 1). (2) The target is the frozen model’s own answer when it reads the answer document alone. (3) A LoRA adapter learns to give that answer from the full exchangeable context.

papers.abstract: To surface "objective" fact-check notes, X's Community Notes uses Biased Matrix Factorization (BMF) on crowd-sourced ratings to separate note quality from reviewer ideology. We show that for any correctly specified model that decomposes ratings into quality and ideological alignment, this separation requires fixing an ideological anchor: a reference point for what counts as neutral. We give a characterization for the standard implementation: with $L_2$ regularization, BMF anchors quality at a point proportional to the mean reviewer ideology, recovering objective quality if and only if the mean reviewer is neutral, assuming note quality is uncorrelated with note leaning. This parallels the Condorcet Jury Theorem: collective judgment recovers truth when the pool is unbiased on average. When that assumption fails, BMF's recovered ranking shifts toward maximizing aggregate reviewer satisfaction, which coincides with social welfare only when the pool is representative. This is not specific to BMF; the rating matrix admits a continuous family of gauge-equivalent decompositions, each implying a different quality ranking, so no mechanism based on ratings alone can recover quality without implicitly choosing such an anchor. What appears to be routine hyperparameter tuning is in fact a normative choice about whose preferences define quality.
authors: David Gamba, Seura Ha, Daniel M. Romero, Grant Schoenebeck
bullets: Quality–ideology separation has a continuous ambiguity: multiple equivalent decompositions of the same ratings imply different quality rankings.
In standard Biased Matrix Factorization with L2 regularization, the anchor is proportional to the mean reviewer ideology.
Objective quality is recovered only when the reviewer pool is neutral on average and note quality is uncorrelated with note leaning.
Otherwise, rankings favor aggregate reviewer satisfaction, matching social welfare only when reviewers are representative.
The issue is general to rating-only mechanisms, not specific to BMF; tuning effectively selects whose preferences define quality.

BMF implicitly selects this shifted frame.

Item-based (γ̂item, circles) and user-based (γ̂user, triangles) estimators (Section D) both track γ∗ of Theorem 10 (dashed; the root of (10) at each replication’s empirical moments, averaged within each µu), which follows µu/2 near zero and bends below it at the extremes. Figure 5: Estimated γ̂ vs. regularization strength λ (µu = 2, κ = 1, σ = 0.1). Dashed: γ∗ = 0.78 from (10). Estimates stay within about 0.1 of it for λ ≤ 0.1; the user-based estimate falls to 0.51 at λ = 1, where the fit trades risk for norm (Figure 6).

Figure 7: Estimated γ̂ vs. regularization ratio κ = λq/λu (µu = 2, λ = 0.1, log scale). Dashed: γ∗(κ) from (10). The item-based estimate follows it across two decades of κ; the user-based estimate tracks it up to κ = 2 and undershoots beyond.
Figure 9: Estimated γ̂ vs. observation noise σ (µu = 2, L2, κ = 1, λ = 0.01). The estimators remain close to γ∗ = 0.78 (dashed, from (10)) across the noise levels tested.

Figure 6: Regularization term (left) and training risk (right) vs. λ. Risk stays near its minimum for λ ≤ 0.1; beyond that, the optimizer trades predictive accuracy for lower parameter norm, explaining the deviation in γ̂ at high λ.

Figure 10: Estimated γ̂ vs. µu under binary ratings (logistic link, Bernoulli observations, L2, κ = 1). Dashed: γ∗ of Theorem 10, a reference only, since the logistic link is outside the theorem. The user-based estimate tracks it; the item-based estimate compresses at large |µu|, consistent with saturation of the logistic link.
Figure 13: Estimated γ̂ vs. mean item ideology µv (L2, κ = 1, µu = 0). The theoretical prediction γ∗ = 0 (dashed) is confirmed: item ideology mean does not shift the anchor.
Figure 11: Quality gap@10 vs. µu under binary ratings. The monotonic increase with |µu| is preserved relative to the continuous case (Figure 4).

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes the non-identifiability of latent factors in systems using LLMs for fact-checking, discussing ideological alignment and quality estimation.
papers.title: Can Ideologues Agree on Quality? From Non-identifiable Latent Factors to Collective Outcomes
papers.tldr: Community Notes cannot identify “objective” note quality from ratings alone without choosing an ideological anchor, making quality rankings partly normative.

papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation transfers capabilities from large language models to smaller students, yet stronger teachers do not always yield better students. Recent studies report diminishing or even negative returns from teacher scaling. We hypothesize that these limitations arise in part from insufficient student capacity to absorb the teacher's knowledge. We therefore investigate loop and recurrent computation as a way to expand the student's effective capacity by modifying its computation graph while keeping the backbone parameter count fixed. Under teacher-forced KD during pretraining, weight-shared looping improves performance but retains teacher-size saturation, whereas cross-token recurrence avoids the observed reversal with larger teachers. In mathematical post-training under both teacher-forced KD and on-policy distillation (OPD), recurrent students scale better with increasing teacher size than looped and vanilla LLMs do. Crucially, we show that a pretrained LLM can be readily fine-tuned into a looped or recurrent architecture jointly with OPD, without repeating pretraining. Our recurrent Qwen model improves with larger teachers and consistently outperforms looped and vanilla LLMs. This suggests a new post-training paradigm that integrates architectural conversion into distillation, avoiding a separate conversion stage while substantially improving student performance and maintaining near-vanilla inference latency.
authors: Zeyi Huang, Jiuxiang Gu, Eli Shechtman, Yong Jae Lee, Zongze Wu
bullets: The work addresses teacher-size saturation and performance reversals in knowledge distillation, partly attributing them to limited student capacity.
It compares weight-shared looping and cross-token recurrence under teacher-forced KD and on-policy distillation.
Cross-token recurrent students scale better with larger teachers than looped and vanilla LLMs, especially in mathematical post-training.
A pretrained LLM can be fine-tuned directly into a recurrent or looped architecture jointly with OPD, avoiding repeated pretraining or a separate conversion stage.
The recurrent Qwen model consistently outperforms the looped and vanilla variants while maintaining near-vanilla inference latency.

papers.abstract: Coupling a property-graph database to an external language-model server imposes a three-part socket tax: serialization overhead dwarfing microsecond graph reads, repeated prefill of verbose schemas, and blind decoding divorced from the live catalog and multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) engine. We present Shoonya, from-scratch commercially clean (0.0% non-commercial or share-alike data) tri-modal (Python, Rust, OpenCypher) small language models (16.8M to 1.07B parameters) co-designed with shoonya-infer, a zero-dependency pure-Rust runtime embedded inside the samyama-graph-enterprise address space. Direct GraphStore references unlock three database-native primitives: (1) an epoch-invalidated SchemaPrefixCache over a copy-on-write PagedKvArena accelerating warm CPU time-to-first-token by 4.91x--13.68x with O(1) DDL invalidation; (2) a 36 us columnar catalog and source-span logit mask enforcing valid ontology identifiers and verbatim spans; and (3) a sub-65 us read-only MVCC gate serving Tier-0 queries inside 389.8 MiB INT8 RSS (59.8--67.9 tok/s) with 0.0% hallucination leak. Rank-factorized tied embeddings (-74.5% vocabulary weights), atomic indentation tokens (0/421 indentation errors), 4:1 grouped-query attention with 2:1 cross-layer KV sharing (-93.75% INT8 KV memory), Warmup-Stable-Decay training, KnOTS SVD merging, Step-GRPO, and Rust Jacobi SVD governance keep 100% of layers heavy-tailed ($\alpha \in [1.88, 2.20]$). Finally, we synthesize nine lessons across v0.1--v1.0, resolving a Reverse-Token-Density Distillation Trap via teacher scaling and zero-VRAM Verifier-Advantage-Gated Knowledge Distillation (AdvKD), recovering +13.61 MBPP points (33.07%) while reaching 100% validity on enrichment, grounded extraction, and tool planning.
bullets: Targets serialization cost, repeated schema prefill, and decoding that is unaware of live catalogs and MVCC.
Uses an in-process Rust runtime with Python, Rust, and OpenCypher models ranging from 16.8M to 1.07B parameters.
Introduces epoch-invalidated schema KV caching, catalog/source-span logit masking, and an MVCC gate for read-only queries.
Reports 4.91–13.68× faster warm CPU time-to-first-token, 0.0% hallucination leak, and 100% validity on enrichment, grounded extraction, and tool-planning tasks.
Verifier-Advantage-Gated Knowledge Distillation recovers 13.61 MBPP points while operating without VRAM for the distillation verifier.

papers.title: Shoonya: Zero-Socket In-Process Small Language Models for Graph Databases with Schema-Epoch KV Caching, Live Catalog Logit Masking, and Verifier-Advantage Distillation
papers.tldr: Shoonya embeds small language models directly inside a graph database to reduce socket overhead, reuse schema context, and constrain generation using live database state.

papers.abstract: We show that an AI agent can write new capabilities into a pretrained language model by adding gated attention heads and MLP neurons inside its existing layers, without backpropagation and without fitting any weight to the answers of task examples. It has a budget of 50 model passes and sees no validation or test instance. Composed in one model, its modules for six BIG-Bench Hard (BBH) subtasks raise the normalized BBH score of Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct from 19.95 to 41.05 (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct: at most 35.01) and that of Gemma-3-1B-it from 10.25 to 32.86. Against the unmodified model at the same precision, both composites leave the next-token distribution on 1,023,000 WikiText tokens unchanged (KL exactly 0), give identical answers on 15,845 items of five other Leaderboard tests and identical scores on the other 18 BBH subtasks. The agent also writes exact multiplication up to 20 digits, running the model only up to 6 (100.0% on the absent lengths of the sealed test in both models; a LoRA with the same budget: at most 2.1%). Sets, rules and report sentences were sealed in git before the first session (manifests timestamped in Bitcoin), with dated amendments listed in Appendix D; a frozen evaluator ran the sealed test once. Verdicts (H5: tracking; H6: composite; H8: one pass vs. chain of thought; H9: fresh and rewritten instances; H10: side effects; H12: multiplication), on the preregistered sealed test, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct: H5 success, H6 success, H8 (web_of_lies) success, H9 success, H10 (composite) success on (i) to (iii), (iv) confirmed, H12 success; Gemma-3-1B-it (H7: H5, H6, H8 and H9 in this model): H5 success, H6 success, H8 (web_of_lies) success, H8 (tracking 3) success, H9 partial, H10 (composite) success on (i) to (iii), (iv) confirmed, H12 success. Not everything worked: 4 of 45 single modules show small side effects and 5 of 50 sessions hit the 12-hour limit without a module.
bullets: The approach adds gated attention heads and MLP neurons within existing layers using at most 50 model passes and no validation or test examples.
A single model composed of modules for six BBH subtasks improved normalized scores from 19.95 to 41.05 on Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and from 10.25 to 32.86 on Gemma-3-1B-it.
The written modules achieved exact multiplication up to 20 digits while the base models ran only up to 6 digits; a same-budget LoRA reached at most 2.1% on the absent lengths.
On tested WikiText tokens and other benchmark items, the composites produced unchanged next-token distributions or identical answers/scores outside targeted capabilities.
Limitations include small side effects from 4 of 45 modules and 5 of 50 sessions that timed out without producing a module.

papers.selection_reason: Directly writes new capabilities into LLM weights via gated heads and neurons, a novel architectural modification relevant to large language model research.
papers.title: Don't Train It, Write It: An AI Agent Writes New Capabilities into Language Model Weights
papers.tldr: An AI agent can add targeted capabilities to pretrained language models by writing internal modules into their weights—without backpropagation or answer-fitting—while largely preserving existing behavior.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is commonly adopted as one of the components in post-training of large language models (LLMs), but in multi-turn agentic tasks we find that the student model increases their reasoning lengths after training. Our empirical analysis shows that the reasoning token lengths is affected by how much the student can distract the teacher's scores. We introduce Muted Distillation (MD), a simple variant of OPD that hides the student's reasoning from the teacher, so the teacher judges what the student does without the interference of student's reasonings. MD takes a few lines of code and adds no extra data or hyperparameters. On the knowledge-work benchmarks OfficeQA Pro and SpreadsheetBench, it reduces output tokens per episode by 57\% and 53\% compared with standard OPD, making the student more concise than it was before training. At the same time, it matches OPD's accuracy on OfficeQA Pro and improves pass@1 by 4.8 points on SpreadsheetBench.
authors: Yuwei Zhang, Ian Miao, Wentao Zhang, Chen Qu, Bill Bi, Jingbo Shang, Donna Schut
bullets: Standard on-policy distillation can lengthen student reasoning in multi-turn agentic tasks.
Muted Distillation prevents the teacher from seeing the student’s reasoning, reducing score interference.
The method requires only a few lines of code and adds no data or hyperparameters.
It cuts output tokens per episode by 57% on OfficeQA Pro and 53% on SpreadsheetBench versus standard OPD.
Accuracy matches OPD on OfficeQA Pro and pass@1 improves by 4.8 points on SpreadsheetBench.

papers.selection_reason: Novel distillation variant for LLM post-training that reduces reasoning token length; fits LLM methods research.
papers.title: Muted Distillation: Sealing Reasoning from Teacher Unlocks Token-Efficient Agents
papers.tldr: Muted Distillation hides student reasoning from the teacher during on-policy distillation, producing substantially more token-efficient agents without sacrificing benchmark performance.

papers.abstract: For on-policy distillation (OPD), more capable models are a natural choice as teachers. However, higher task performance does not necessarily imply greater teachability. A controlled token intervention study suggests that even a model weaker than the student can serve as an informative contrastive reference. Building on this observation, we propose Contrastive On-Policy Distillation (cOPD), which provides dual branch supervision by contrasting strong teacher, weak teacher, and student predictions at student generated prefixes. Our analysis explains how this three way comparison helps select token candidates associated with better or worse reasoning outcomes under an idealized model. We evaluate cOPD across diverse teacher student configurations spanning different training stages, parameter scales, and model families, on tasks including mathematical reasoning, instruction following, and question answering with abstention. cOPD achieves the best or top-tier performance among the evaluated baselines across all three tasks, improving overall Pass@16 on mathematical reasoning by up to 7.51\% over the strongest baseline. Further analyses show that cOPD suppresses undesirable response patterns and suggest that it facilitates exploration.
authors: Zhibo Hou, Fan Zhao, Yiping Li, Zhiyu An, Wan Du
bullets: Motivation: A teacher’s task accuracy does not necessarily determine how teachable it is; even weaker models can provide useful contrastive signals.
Method: cOPD applies dual-branch supervision by contrasting strong-teacher, weak-teacher, and student predictions at prefixes generated by the student.
Analysis: The three-way comparison helps identify token candidates linked to better or worse reasoning outcomes under an idealized model.
Results: Across varied teacher–student configurations, cOPD achieves the best or near-best performance on mathematical reasoning, instruction following, and abstention-based question answering.
Scope: Further analyses indicate that cOPD suppresses undesirable response patterns and may promote exploration.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Teacher takeover experiment. As the takeover budget increases, the negative branch with weak teacher takeovers generally reduces student accuracy, whereas the positive branch with strong teacher takeovers generally improves it. Both effects are larger than under KL-based selection.

Figure 2: Instruction-following response distributions and constraint satisfaction in a shared UMAP space, where each point represents a response and crosses indicate violation. cOPD produces valid responses in additional regions while largely avoiding the prominent word-limit failure region.

Figure 3: Failure mode analysis. (a) Mathematical reasoning accuracy (Pass@16) and truncation error counts. cOPD suppresses truncation failures while surpassing the strong teacher in accuracy. (b) Opening-token supervision for valid and invalid reasoning formats. W2S-OPD excessively amplifies the invalid token’s relative weight, whereas cOPD’s corresponding gap is negligible.

Table 2: Results on instruction following (IF) and question answering with abstention (QA w/ Abstention). All scores are percentages, and Abst. represents the correct abstention rate. Bold indicates the best student result in each column, and underline indicates the second best.

papers.selection_reason: Contrastive on-policy distillation method for LLM teacher-student configurations across reasoning and instruction following.
papers.title: Contrastive On-Policy Distillation via Dual-Branch Supervision
papers.tldr: Contrastive On-Policy Distillation uses strong and weak teachers together to guide student-generated reasoning, improving performance and exploration across several tasks.

papers.abstract: Contribution: This study has shown that a shared prompt-refinement procedure, guided by distinct affective and cognitive feedback signals, can improve held-out reference agreement and multi-label classification while reducing affective-generation variability without executor parameter updates. Background: Industry 4.0 has increased demand for personalized technical education across interconnected computing and engineering domains, while prompt sensitivity and generation variability have complicated dependable interpretation of instructional dialogue and learning outcomes. Research Questions: The study has examined whether task-specific feedback can improve affective-reference agreement, generation consistency, and cognitive classification without updating executor parameters. Methodology: A secondary language model has revised executor prompts using executor-output discrepancies against model-generated affective references for four dialogues and annotated Bloom labels for 70 learning outcomes; separate sets of 100 EduTalk conversations and 1,000 outcomes have supported held-out comparisons. Small refinement sets, unvalidated affective references, and absent learner-outcome measures have constrained interpretation. Findings: Affective mean absolute error has decreased from 0.742 to 0.702 and mean generation standard deviation from 0.307 to 0.238, while Bloom micro-F1 has increased from 0.687 to 0.893 and exact-match subset accuracy from 0.418 to 0.636. These findings have supported prompt refinement as a candidate approach for developing adaptive technical instruction, while its effects on workforce learning remain to be established.
authors: Josh Dean, Karan Patel, Gaurangi Raul, Yu-Zheng Lin, Jesus Pacheco, Sicong Shao, Shalaka Satam, Soheil Salehi, Pratik Satam
bullets: Targets dependable interpretation of educational dialogue amid prompt sensitivity and generation variability.
Uses a secondary language model to revise executor prompts from affective-reference discrepancies and Bloom-label feedback.
Held-out results showed lower affective error and variability, alongside higher Bloom micro-F1 and exact-match accuracy.
The study used small refinement sets and unvalidated affective references, with no direct learner-outcome measures.
Effects on workforce learning and adaptive instruction remain unestablished.

papers.abstract: Standard autoregressive large language models attend to the growing history of generated tokens, making the key-value (KV) cache a central memory and throughput bottleneck in long-chain reasoning and multi-branch sampling. Yet an important class of reasoning problems is naturally first-order Markovian: the next step depends on a sufficient representation of the current state, rather than on the raw sequence of all earlier steps. We develop a unified design paradigm for Markovian-reasoning specialized large language models. At the cache level, the Markovian state interface transforms history-dependent KV storage into constant-size state transfer with respect to the number of reasoning steps. At the learning level, we reformulate long-chain prediction as independently trainable one-step transition objectives, with explicit state bottlenecks, distillation, invariance, and drift-consistency losses. At the architectural level, we introduce a dual-loop Transformer: an outer loop advances the reasoning state, while an inner recurrent-depth loop allocates adaptive computation to each transition through shared weights and explicit memory tokens or recurrent matrix states. We connect this architecture to a three-region cache, step-relative positions, truncated backpropagation, branch-aware checkpoints, and a transition-centric evaluation protocol. The organizing principle is simple: the optimal reasoning system need not remember everything; it must carry forward exactly what the future needs. This principle opens a path toward specialized reasoning engines whose memory footprint is decoupled from reasoning-chain length.
authors: Haibin Tong, Liangliang Xin, Yamei Zhu, Jiang Yu
bullets: Targets KV-cache memory and throughput bottlenecks in long-chain reasoning and multi-branch sampling.
Uses explicit state bottlenecks and independently trainable one-step transition objectives with distillation, invariance, and drift-consistency losses.
Introduces a dual-loop Transformer: an outer loop advances states, while an inner recurrent loop adaptively computes each transition with shared weights.
Integrates three-region caching, step-relative positions, truncated backpropagation, branch-aware checkpoints, and transition-centric evaluation.
Scope is reasoning tasks where the next step depends on a sufficient Markovian state rather than the full history.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Dual-loop Transformer architecture with transition-centric pretraining. The outer loop advances the reduced state (qt,Mt) across reasoning steps and releases step-local KV, while the inner loop repeatedly applies a shared Transformer core for Rt computation iterations. The transition training objectives shape the same shared core to support state evolution and compact cross-step memory.

Figure 1: Structural KV-cache compression for a Markovian reasoning chain. Conventional autoregressive attention retains the entire sequence of previous reasoning steps. In contrast, a Markovian state-rolling interface retains the fixed context Q, the latest sufficient state zt, and the bounded current-step KV workspace, which is released after each transition. With a fixed-size sufficient-state interface and bounded step length, cross-step memory does not grow with the number of completed steps k.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes specialized LLMs for Markovian reasoning using a dual-loop transformer and structural cache compression to decouple memory footprint from reasoning length.
papers.title: Specialized Large Language Models for Markovian Reasoning: Structural Cache Compression, Transition Pretraining, and Dual-Loop Transformers
papers.tldr: A specialized LLM design treats Markovian reasoning as state transitions, reducing KV-cache growth from sequence-dependent storage to constant-size state transfer.

papers.abstract: In dynamic scenes---football matches, traffic streams, surgery, or assembly---actions unfold at fundamentally different time scales: in football, a kick happens in milliseconds, a possession lasts seconds, and complex events such as a successful pass followed by a goal combine multiple atomic actions over extended durations. Models trained solely on visual data struggle to learn effectively across different time scales, lacking a principled way of reasoning across fine-grained instants and broader intervals. Neither point-wise nor purely interval semantics suffices: the former fragments events into frame-level snapshots lacking overall event identification; the latter treats intervals as atomic truth-values, ignoring state trajectories. We introduce Temporal Logic Tensor Networks (tLTN), a differentiable neuro-symbolic framework addressing this duality via a formal, multi-sorted logic where events and states are structurally interdependent. Extending Interval Logic Tensor Networks (ILTN), tLTN grounds state predicates as fuzzy truth-value paths over time points, while events are first-class entities with learnable trapezoidal fuzzy durations and differentiable Allen-style relations. A compositional semantics fuses static, event-structural, and state-dynamic satisfaction into a single differentiable LTN grounding. Crucially, the modalities constrain each other bidirectionally: the interval layer dictates where point-wise constraints (e.g., Until, Since) are evaluated, restricting them to event-defined spans; conversely, the point-wise layer validates interval relations, rejecting them if underlying state dynamics contradict the relation. Through controlled synthetic examples, we show when single-modality learning fails and how this localization reduces frame-level computational cost on long traces.
authors: Edjard Mota, Artur d'Avila Garcez, Maria Azevedo, Odalisio Neto
bullets: Addresses the limits of frame-level and interval-only temporal semantics in dynamic scenes.
Represents states as fuzzy truth-value paths and events as learnable trapezoidal fuzzy durations.
Uses differentiable Allen-style relations and compositional logic to integrate static, structural, and dynamic constraints.
Constrains point-wise reasoning to event-defined spans while using state dynamics to validate interval relations.
Synthetic examples show failures of single-modality learning and reduced frame-level computation on long traces.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The semantic bridge: the solid curve is a state trajectory (point-wise modality). The dashed trapezoids are fuzzy event extents (interval modality). At t = 4.5, the interval for event B (in green) reaches full membership while the underlying state trajectory is near its minimum, a configuration that interval-only semantics cannot express, since it evaluates properties over intervals as atomic truth values, and that point-wise semantics alone cannot localize, since it has no representation of the interval in which the state’s dip in truth value occurs. Between events B and C (in blue), point-wise constraint evaluation is localized to the event spans rather than the full trace, allowing the system to stop reasoning about what should persist at each time step in the absence of an action.

papers.title: Temporal Logic Tensor Networks: Foundations of Temporal Reasoning in Neural Networks
papers.tldr: tLTN is a differentiable neuro-symbolic framework that combines point-wise state dynamics with fuzzy event intervals for more principled multi-timescale temporal reasoning.

papers.abstract: Advances in large language models (LLMs) have expanded their role in high-value productivity tasks, including financial analysis and modeling, while enabling models to play an increasingly active role in their own improvement. This motivates two complementary lines of inquiry: can financial modeling capabilities provide a foundation for model self-evolution, and can self-evolution, in turn, advance financial capabilities? We introduce FinEvo, a self-evolution framework that integrates autonomous experience construction with financial capability improvement. FinEvo prepares financial models, iteratively evolves challenges through self-play, and learns from the resulting interactions using executable rewards, relying on the same model throughout. An end-to-end execution with Qwen3.6-27B shows that solving feedback supports both increasing reasoning demands and identifying specification issues that executable checks can miss. Learning from these experiences raises whole-task success from 22.73 to 29.09 on held-out within-source tasks and from 13.13 to 19.19 on SpreadsheetBench 2 Financial. Comparable gains across task sources and evaluation settings, together with improvement on a task category absent from training, suggest that FinEvo strengthens underlying financial modeling capabilities shared across tasks. These findings support self-evolution as a path toward broader financial competence, advancing the empirical exploration of recursive self-improvement (RSI) in professional domains. Code is available at https://github.com/pcj-sudo/FinEvo.
authors: Chengjun Pan, Shichun Liu, Zekai Zhou, Shihan Dou, Jiahang Lin, Chengsong Huang, Dingwei Zhu, Tao Gui
bullets: Targets recursive self-improvement in financial modeling, with the model generating and learning from its own challenges.
Builds financial models, evolves tasks through self-play, and uses executable feedback for learning without changing the underlying model.
An end-to-end Qwen3.6-27B run improved whole-task success on both held-out in-source tasks and SpreadsheetBench 2 Financial.
Feedback increased reasoning demands and exposed specification issues that executable checks alone could miss.
Gains on a task category absent from training suggest improved capabilities generalize across financial tasks.

papers.abstract: Co-creating layouts such as websites and slides is a useful testbed for evaluating multi-turn instruction following of LLM systems. Since an intended layout's appearance cannot be well expressed in a single turn, the user must wait for the LLM to generate a layout then iteratively refine it with the LLM over multiple turns. We present a small-scale, exploratory (n=6) study of this multi-turn process to compare the differences of human-AI and AI-AI teams on the same layout-generation task. Given a reference wire-frame layout, a participant or a language model 'speaker' issues natural-language instructions to a fixed 'listener' LLM over multiple turns until the speaker is satisfied. Rather than an LLM as the judge, we fit a scoring function over geometric layout features using curated human preference data (n=19). We find that LLMs tend to encode the entire layout in the first turn, while humans iterate over many turns on average, writing much shorter instructions. We also find that human-AI teams consistently scored lower than AI-AI teams. This gap is driven by a limiter of human participants in specifying precise sizes and positions (e.g. 42 pixels to the right). Humans perform almost at par with language models on other features like ordering the elements into nested structures. We then perform interventions on the speaker LLMs to make them more human-like, and find it difficult. This raises the challenge of using LLMs as user models to evaluate multi-turn co-creation tasks.
authors: Rajvir Singh Naginder Singh Virdi, Yewen Pu
bullets: Compares human-AI and AI-AI teams refining the same wireframe layout through natural-language, multi-turn instructions.
Uses a learned scoring function based on geometric layout features and human preference data rather than an LLM judge.
LLMs typically encode the full layout in the first turn, while humans use more turns with shorter instructions.
Human performance is especially weaker for specifying exact sizes and positions, but is nearly comparable for nested element ordering.
Interventions to make speaker LLMs behave more like humans were difficult, challenging their use as user models.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can display sycophancy, a tendency to excessively praise, agree with, or validate a user. Existing studies have tested LLMs for sycophancy primarily through application programming interfaces (APIs) rather than the consumer user interfaces (UIs) through which the public commonly interacts with LLMs. Access mode (API vs. UI) may affect observed sycophancy rates. However, it remains unknown to what extent prominent models show API-UI differences in social sycophancy, which includes behaviors potentially more likely in UIs (e.g., softening warranted criticism). We tested ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and DeepSeek through both APIs and UIs on four dimensions of social sycophancy. Across models, UI access was generally associated with greater social sycophancy, with odds ratios up to 7.56 (95% CI [6.22, 9.20]). However, UI-API differences varied significantly across models for all sycophancy dimensions, including a pronounced reversal for DeepSeek moral sycophancy (43% UI vs. 82.3% API). Overall, our results suggest that API-based LLM evaluations may underestimate the prevalence of sycophancy in corresponding consumer-facing systems, making access conditions consequential for the external validity of LLM evaluation. To facilitate research on access-mode effects, we release 57,000 model responses and SycoUI, a browser-automation pipeline for standardized cross-interface LLM evaluation.
bullets: The study examines whether API-versus-UI access changes observed sycophancy in ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and DeepSeek.
Models were evaluated across four dimensions of social sycophancy using both APIs and consumer-facing UIs.
UI access was generally associated with greater sycophancy, with odds ratios reaching 7.56 (95% CI [6.22, 9.20]).
Effects differed significantly across models; for DeepSeek moral sycophancy, the pattern reversed (43% UI vs. 82.3% API).
The authors release 57,000 responses and SycoUI, a browser-automation pipeline for standardized cross-interface evaluation.

papers.tldr: LLM social sycophancy is generally more pronounced in consumer UIs than APIs, but the effect varies substantially by model and behavior.

papers.abstract: Deploying large language models (LLMs) in long-horizon and continual interactions requires maintaining reusable memory states for future inference, posing challenges for existing architectures. Standard Transformers accumulate layer-wise, token-level KV caches, incurring linear GPU memory growth and quadratic computational complexity as the context expands. In contrast, linear-time architectures compress history into fixed-size states, but struggle to retain fine-grained details. We introduce MemOnce, a foundation architecture that learns scalable memory states for language models. MemOnce is based on two core designs: (a) Memory encoder-decoder: it caches only a small subset of final-layer hidden states as compact memory representations and dynamically decodes them back into KV caches for attention layers; (b) Memory sparse attention: for each continual input, MemOnce adaptively retrieves relevant memory representations, with the sparse indices computed only once across layers. Coupling these two designs enables efficient on-the-fly memory loading and KV cache decoding, drastically reducing the GPU memory footprint and achieving linear-time complexity. We conduct extensive experiments to show that MemOnce outperforms Transformers and other architectures across varying model sizes, context lengths, and training paradigms (pretraining and post-training adaptation). In particular, adapting Qwen3.5-4B with MemOnce reduces memory state cache by 1313$\times$ and prefill latency by 6.9$\times$ at 1M context, and improves throughput by 3.5$\times$ and overall memory performance by +5.77%. Finally, MemOnce generalizes zero-shot to downstream representation tasks, achieving competitive results against specialized models.
authors: Chang Nie, Chaoyou Fu, Songlin Liu, Yiqing Hu, Caifeng Shan
bullets: Addresses the linear GPU-memory growth and quadratic computation of Transformer KV caches, while preserving more detail than fixed-size state compression.
Uses a memory encoder-decoder to store selected final-layer hidden states and dynamically reconstruct attention KV caches.
Applies sparse attention that retrieves relevant memories once per input and shares the sparse indices across layers.
Reports substantial efficiency gains, including 1313× lower memory-state cache, 6.9× lower prefill latency, and 3.5× higher throughput at 1M context in one adaptation setting.
Generalizes zero-shot to downstream representation tasks with competitive performance against specialized models.

This enables a constant active memory state for continual inference, alongside an Lr× cache compression across both depth and time dimensions.

papers.abstract: Transformer performance scales with depth, but layer count merely counts the opportunities for sequential computation: layers could still behave as nearly independent refinements that barely depend on one another. We study how transformers develop functional depth during pretraining, introducing an exact inclusion-exclusion decomposition that isolates the connected component, i.e., the computation that appears only when a specified set of layers acts together under identity ablation. Tracking this quantity across public checkpoints of Pythia, OLMo, and Amber yields three findings. First, write-relative connected coordination strengthens from its initialization or earliest-checkpoint baseline as pretraining proceeds, across all measured interaction orders. Second, these connected components are behaviorally consequential under direct intervention: deleting them damages perplexity more than deleting a norm-matched random direction at the same site in all 35 measured model-order cells. Third, pairwise representation similarity is consistently negatively correlated with pairwise connected coordination across seven models, yet the two signals are not interchangeable: similarity- and coordination-based block-removal criteria often agree in Pythia but diverge on Amber. Together, these results suggest that architectural depth provides the opportunity for sequential computation, while pretraining progressively organizes cross-layer dependencies within that depth.
bullets: Introduces an exact inclusion–exclusion measure of connected computation produced only by specified layers acting together under identity ablation.
Across Pythia, OLMo, and Amber checkpoints, write-relative connected coordination strengthens during pretraining across measured interaction orders.
Removing these connected components harms perplexity more than removing norm-matched random directions in all 35 tested model-order cells.
Pairwise representation similarity is negatively correlated with connected coordination, but the two measures can recommend different layers for removal.
The findings indicate that pretraining organizes sequential cross-layer dependencies within the computational opportunities provided by depth.

Coordination is weak relative to later checkpoints at initialization and progressively concentrates into an early-interior band as training proceeds, across every measured order.
