papers.title: Functional Depth Is Learned: Isolating the Computation That Layers Produce Only Together
papers.tldr: Pretraining progressively develops meaningful cross-layer computations in transformers, making depth functionally—not just structurally—important.

papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) have advanced natural language understanding, their ability to perform complex target-aspect-sentiment detection (TASD) -- a key task within aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) -- in zero-shot multilingual settings remains underexplored. Existing ABSA research predominantly focuses on English or relies on fine-tuned task-specific models, leaving a gap in understanding how open-weight LLMs handle compound sentiment triplet extraction across diverse language families and domains. We present a systematic evaluation of zero-shot multilingual TASD across 12 languages and three domains using seven instruction-tuned open-weight models -- ranging from 8B to 35B parameters across dense and mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures -- under four prompting paradigms: monolithic, chain-of-thought, sequential, and sequential refine. Our results show that direct monolithic prompting achieves strong zero-shot performance, outperforming multi-step pipelines, while dense models consistently outperform sparse MoE architectures. Through fine-grained error taxonomy profiling and step-level pipeline tracking, we demonstrate that initial aspect term recall forms a hard bottleneck, whereas multi-step decomposition degrades extraction quality; iterative refinement only partially recovers this loss on larger models while inducing net-negative over-refinement on smaller architectures. Finally, generation volume analysis shows that multi-step strategies incur up to 2.38x token overhead without F1 gains, establishing monolithic prompting as the most effective and efficient paradigm for multilingual ABSA.
bullets: Evaluates seven instruction-tuned open-weight LLMs across 12 languages, three domains, and four prompting paradigms.
Direct monolithic prompting outperforms chain-of-thought, sequential, and sequential-refinement pipelines.
Dense models consistently outperform sparse mixture-of-experts models.
Aspect-term recall is the main bottleneck; multi-step decomposition often reduces extraction quality.
Multi-step prompting increases token use by up to 2.38× without improving F1, while refinement can over-correct smaller models.

papers.tldr: A systematic study finds that simple monolithic prompting is the most effective and efficient zero-shot strategy for multilingual TASD with open-weight LLMs.

papers.abstract: Current decoder large language models rely on a combination of attention, feed forward and residual layers. The attention used is autoregressive (AR) though this is not strictly correct, as we note. That motivates the introduction of other attention methods that, while also not strictly AR, do enhance the AR character. One is based on a decomposition of mutual information (MI) into a set of Conditional MIs (CMIs) that correlate key tokens with pairs of query tokens. A second, higher-order attention, introduces correlations between contiguous key and query tokens. A third introduces correlations between a set of key and query tokens and uses a Generalized Maximum Entropy Principle to obtain an attention expression spanning a sequence of tokens. All these methods may enhance the information content of the autoregressive probabilities that are used in inference/generation. Applications to contrastive decoding and a systematic analysis of autoregressive probabilities are presented.
bullets: Motivated by limitations in standard autoregressive attention used by decoder LLMs.
Introduces attention based on mutual-information decomposition into conditional MIs linking key tokens with query-token pairs.
Develops higher-order variants modeling contiguous key/query tokens and larger token sets.
Uses a Generalized Maximum Entropy Principle to derive sequence-spanning attention expressions.
Discusses applications to contrastive decoding and systematic analysis of autoregressive probabilities.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes new higher-order attention mechanisms for decoder LLMs, directly relevant to LLM architecture.
papers.title: Enhancing Attention with Higher-Order Attention
papers.tldr: The paper proposes higher-order attention mechanisms to enrich autoregressive information by modeling dependencies among multiple key and query tokens.

papers.abstract: Offline chain-of-thought (CoT) compression creates shorter supervision for efficient reasoning, but per-example compressors repeatedly process similar expressions across traces, wasting compressor budget. Methods that reuse identical text across examples miss longer shared expressions when names, numbers, or formulas change from one question to another. We introduce CRAFT, which abstracts problem-specific details into slots to uncover partially lexicalized expression templates (PLETs) and clusters wording variants into families. Compressing each family representative once yields shared deletion or rewriting edits, which are applied with each occurrence's own details to construct compact, ordinary-text training targets. Compared with per-example rewriting, CRAFT Rewrite reduces weighted compressor budgets by a median 90.7% with a median accuracy loss of 1.21 percentage points, while generating shorter reasoning. Against cross-sample encoding, it shortens reasoning across all eight model-dataset settings by 25.3% on average and improves accuracy in five.
authors: Shibo Wang, Yuzhe He, Yifeng Zhao, Yunjiao Zhou, Zepeng Ning, Hanzhang Zhou, Kezhi Mao, Junlang Qian
bullets: Per-example CoT compressors waste budget by repeatedly processing similar expressions.
CRAFT abstracts names, numbers, and formulas into slots to discover partially lexicalized expression templates and wording families.
It compresses one family representative, then transfers its deletion or rewriting edits to each occurrence’s specific details.
CRAFT Rewrite cuts weighted compressor budgets by a median 90.7% with a median accuracy loss of 1.21 percentage points.
Compared with cross-sample encoding, it shortens reasoning by 25.3% on average across eight model-dataset settings and improves accuracy in five.

papers.abstract: Machine unlearning is an approach to privacy protection: it aims to remove the influence of designated data while preserving the model's behavior on information that should be retained. While a growing body of work investigates this objective in autoregressive large language models, machine unlearning remains underexplored in diffusion language models (DLMs). DLMs generate text through iterative denoising, exposing partially masked states whose internal representations change throughout the generation process. This raises a DLM-specific question: can selective forgetting improve by identifying forget-data-associated features and adapting their suppression across denoising stages? We conduct a controlled investigation of this question in LLaDA-8B-Instruct. To evaluate the unlearning of knowledge plausibly encoded during pre-training, we use WMDP as our forget-domain benchmark. Using top-k sparse autoencoders and denoising-state replay, we compare static and stage-adaptive feature suppression. We find substantial shifts in forget-data-associated features across denoising stages, but tracking these dynamics alone does not reliably improve the forget-retain trade-off at the evaluated operating points. Together, our study provides an initial empirical foundation for developing and evaluating machine unlearning as a post-training privacy mechanism in DLMs.
bullets: Machine unlearning in diffusion language models is underexplored because their internal representations evolve across iterative denoising.
The study evaluates LLaDA-8B-Instruct using WMDP as a forget-domain benchmark.
Top-k sparse autoencoders identify forget-associated features, while denoising-state replay enables comparison of static and stage-adaptive suppression.
Forget-associated features shift substantially across denoising stages.
Tracking these shifts alone does not reliably improve unlearning performance at the evaluated operating points.

papers.abstract: Public benchmarks guide model selection, post-training rewards and claims of progress in artificial intelligence, yet leaderboards report aggregate scores without verifying whether each task's prompt, environment and grader agree on what counts as success. How often that agreement fails in contemporary evaluations, and in which direction confirmed defects move scores, has remained unmeasured across grading designs. Here we synthesize task-level quality reviews of 749 tasks across eight frontier benchmarks and 767 public model evaluations spanning closed-form question answering, document rubrics and agentic execution to assess whether prompts, environments and graders align. Task validity stratifies sharply by grading architecture. Closed-form benchmarks revised after public error reporting reach 92.5% verified validity, compared with 29.3% across six multi-step suites that nevertheless already supply 161 verified complex tasks. Rubric suites fail through mismatches between prompts and reference checklists, whereas execution harnesses add incomplete state assertions, shared-channel leaks and grading-time collisions. Across confirmed defects, 71.7% withhold credit from compliant solutions while 28.3% permit shortcut passes, indicating that raw leaderboard ceilings understate frontier capability on many practical tasks. Grading committed patches inside a fresh container cuts confirmed runtime bypasses from 14.7% in shared containers to 2.7% (a 5.5x drop, and 0% in read-only or static suites), showing how targeted maintenance restores existing benchmarks at low cost. As the initial milestone of the long-term Benchmarks' Last Exam initiative, this synthesis launches sustained expansion across wider benchmark coverage and deeper evaluation-quality dimensions so that pursuing leaderboard gains directly advances genuine model capability.
bullets: Task validity varies sharply by grading design: revised closed-form benchmarks reached 92.5% verified validity, versus 29.3% across six multi-step suites.
Rubric evaluations commonly mismatch prompts with reference checklists; agentic harnesses add incomplete state checks, shared-channel leaks, and grading-time collisions.
Among confirmed defects, 71.7% withhold credit from compliant solutions, while 28.3% enable shortcut passes.
Using fresh containers for grading cut confirmed runtime bypasses from 14.7% to 2.7%; read-only or static suites recorded none.
The initiative provides an initial synthesis and plans broader coverage and deeper evaluation-quality analysis.

papers.abstract: We introduce Tasklets, a benchmark of small synthetic tasks for evaluating the computational capabilities of language model sequence-mixing layers. These tasks probe foundational capabilities such as recall, sequence manipulation, and state tracking. Such tasks are widely used in architecture research, but differences in task selection, formulation, and evaluation make comparisons across studies difficult. Tasklets brings these tasks together, organizing them by the capabilities they test and providing a shared setup for evaluating how different architectural layer types learn fundamental computations. We compare a broad range of layer types through controlled experiments with small models. Our task implementations and evaluation code support reproducible, low-cost testing of new architectural proposals: https://github.com/zaydzuhri/flame/tree/tasklets.
authors: Zayd Muhammad Kawakibi Zuhri, Munachiso Samuel Nwadike, Kentaro Inui, Alham Fikri Aji
bullets: Evaluates capabilities including recall, sequence manipulation, and state tracking.
Standardizes task selection, formulations, and evaluation to improve cross-study comparisons.
Organizes synthetic tasks by the capabilities they probe.
Compares diverse layer types using controlled experiments with small models.
Provides open implementations and evaluation code for low-cost architectural testing.

papers.abstract: Serving engines treat the ways of running a greedy language model as interchangeable: cached or not, padded or not, alone or batched, one token or several verified at once (speculative decoding). In finite precision they round differently. We measure how often the greedy text of Qwen3-0.6B (bfloat16, 128 new tokens, GSM8K and ARC prompts) differs from a reference that decodes one token per pass. Verifying 4 guessed tokens per pass changes 60% of 150 prompts and padding changes 68%; every first divergence has a top-1 minus top-2 logit gap of 0.375 or less. A split of the noise shows that cache entries written by multi-token passes are about as noisy as the multi-token pass itself. A margin gate (fall back to one token when the gap is below a bound calibrated on separate GSM8K prompts) whose fallback reads that cache does not help: 58 of 100 prompts differ, against 61 of 100 for plain verification. Rebuilding the cache with one-token passes leaves 0 of 100 different but costs 7.2 model passes per token, against 1.0 for the reference. Fixed-width decoding makes drafted and plain decoding identical (0 of 100 prompts differ) at 0.75 passes per token. On shifted MMLU and HellaSwag prompts the rebuild gate leaves 0 of 60 different, plain verification 48 of 60. On 138 further and shifted prompts the bound was exceeded at 0.6% of positions and missed 0 of 309 flips. One GPU, one drafter, small models.
authors: Mohammed Nayeem Khan, Navin Kumar R
bullets: Multi-token verification changed outputs on 60% of prompts, while padding changed 68%; divergences occurred only when the top-1/top-2 logit margin was at most 0.375.
Cache entries written during multi-token passes were a comparable source of noise to the passes themselves.
A margin-based fallback that reused the noisy cache barely helped: 58/100 prompts differed versus 61/100 with plain verification.
Rebuilding the cache with one-token passes eliminated observed differences, but increased cost to 7.2 model passes per token versus 1.0 for the reference.
Fixed-width decoding matched plain decoding on all tested prompts at 0.75 passes per token; scope was limited to one GPU, one drafter, and small models.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes rounding noise and cache effects in speculative decoding for LLM inference, directly contributing to efficient inference and cache management.
papers.title: Vega-Fafnir: Is Greedy Decoding the Same Decoding? Where Rounding Noise in Speculative Verification Comes From and What Removing It Costs
papers.tldr: Finite-precision rounding makes supposedly equivalent greedy and speculative decoding produce different text, but fixed-width decoding removes the mismatch more efficiently than rebuilding the cache.

papers.abstract: Laya is a small model that answers a multiple-choice question in one pass: each option has a name and a written description. A new skill costs a training run, so we test whether published recipes for merging fine-tuned models (weight averaging, task arithmetic, TIES, DARE) work for it, and whether the theories behind them hold. All 156 models start from one released checkpoint: four plain fine-tunes, five specialists (each adds one kind of training row), joint fine-tunes on all rows, and prediction ensembles. Items are held-out, synthetic and LLM-labelled. In-family, each skill is scored on new items of its own kind, and "kept" is the share of a specialist's gain over the plain fine-tune. Averaging four specialists keeps 52% [38, 64] with +1.7 points of general accuracy; adding the full vectors keeps 42% [3, 63] with -9.0; TIES, which trims and resolves sign conflicts, keeps 64% [50, 76] with +1.5; joint fine-tunes, which see all the rows, keep 120% [104, 162] and 116% [104, 149]. DARE does not repair the full sum (-0.4 points), and ensembles of the models' predictions keep 26% to 54% depending on how they are combined. Swapping the seed of one specialist moves the average by up to 8 points (23 for the full sum). Of 10 predictions fixed in advance, 1 held, 1 held partly, 7 failed and 1 could not be tested. Out-of-family (benchmark questions, code-mixed tickets), the four-way average, joint models and ensemble stay within 2.6 points of the plain fine-tune, but full-vector sums lose up to 7.7. Labels are LLM-made, data synthetic, one base model.
authors: Mohammed Nayeem Khan, Navin Kumar R, Akhil P
bullets: The study tests weight averaging, task arithmetic, TIES, DARE, joint training, and prediction ensembling across 156 models sharing one base checkpoint.
Averaging four specialists retains 52% of their gains and improves general accuracy by 1.7 points; TIES retains 64% with a 1.5-point gain.
Full task-vector addition performs poorly, losing 9.0 accuracy points; DARE does not repair it, and prediction ensembles retain 26–54% of specialist gains.
Joint fine-tuning on all training rows retains 116–120% of specialist gains, outperforming merging methods.
Results are sensitive to random seeds, and external validity is limited by synthetic, LLM-generated data and a single base model.

papers.selection_reason: Empirically evaluates model merging and fine-tuning techniques (TIES, DARE, task arithmetic) for LLMs, contributing to post-training methodology.
papers.title: Altair-Nidhogg: Which Model-Merging Theories Hold for a One-Pass Decision Encoder? Soups, Task Arithmetic, TIES and DARE Against Joint Training and Prediction Ensembling
papers.tldr: In a one-pass multiple-choice encoder, TIES and specialist averaging preserve some skills, but joint training is strongest while full task-vector merging and many theoretical predictions fail.

papers.abstract: Reliable comparisons of continuous diffusion language models (CDLMs) require evaluating both model fit and the distribution of generated text. Two common practices leave this goal only partially addressed. Likelihood-based evaluation often reports a variational upper bound on discrete negative log-likelihood, whose slack can confound comparisons. Generated-sample-based evaluation commonly combines generative perplexity with within-sequence unigram entropy; both scores can remain favorable even when a sampler produces the same text on every draw. We introduce \textbf{Open CDLM}, a benchmark for evaluating CDLMs and their samplers, and describe the design of an accompanying open-source library to support reproducible comparisons. For likelihood-based evaluation, we clarify which comparisons of model fit are supported by reported perplexity bounds and how those conclusions depend on the evaluation procedure. For sample-based evaluation, we use \textit{Kernel Text Discrepancy} (\textbf{KTD}) to compare collections of generated and real texts, alongside diagnostics for diversity, validity, and coverage. In controlled OpenWebText experiments, replacing a collection of texts with copies of a single selected passage improves both conventional generation scores. MAUVE detects the resulting collapse, and its response to other perturbations depends on the text representation and the type of perturbation. This work marks the beginning of Open CDLM as an open-source project for CDLM research. We will maintain and extend the library over time and welcome contributions from the community.
authors: Hao Jiang, Ruixi Chen, Jiayi Han, Yulei Sun, Yujian Chen, Gen Li, Brian. K Chen, Guang Cheng, Weijian Luo, Tianyang Hu
bullets: Highlights that variational perplexity bounds may obscure reliable model-fit comparisons.
Shows that generative perplexity and within-sequence unigram entropy can reward collapsed samplers producing the same text repeatedly.
Uses Kernel Text Discrepancy (KTD) with diversity, validity, and coverage diagnostics to compare generated and real text collections.

In controlled OpenWebText experiments, conventional generation scores improved under single-passage copying, while MAUVE detected the resulting collapse; its sensitivity varied by representation and perturbation.
Positions Open CDLM as an extensible project for reproducible CDLM and sampler comparisons.

papers.abstract: Byte-level BPE vocabularies retain 256 single-byte fallback tokens. When converting such a model into a pure byte-level model, these tokens provide the starting embeddings. How much training have they received? We estimate byte-token exposure in Qwen3.8 using two independent routes. First, we tokenize 540 MB of public corpora covering 40 domains and 33 languages, then combine per-domain token shares with assumed pretraining mixtures. Single-byte tokens account for 13 to 36% of tokens, mostly ASCII; genuine UTF-8 fallback bytes (0x80-0xFF) account for 0.15 to 0.27% under mainstream mixtures, or about 2 billion occurrences per trillion pretraining tokens. Fallback rates vary by four orders of magnitude across languages, reflecting how well each script is covered by the vocabulary. Second, we analyze embedding and output-matrix row norms for four open models, using untrained padding rows as a zero-exposure baseline and ordinary tokens with known frequencies for calibration. In all four models, the 13 bytes that cannot occur in valid UTF-8 remain at initialization, while every legal high byte lies in a high-frequency band. For Qwen3.8, the norm-based estimate agrees with the corpus estimate within a factor of four. The norm-frequency relation eventually folds, so inversion is useful only as a model-specific, order-of-magnitude estimate. No private data were used.
authors: Liwei Zhang, ZhiMing Tong, Mochen Guan, Linzhe Li
bullets: Analyzes Qwen3.8 using 540 MB of public text spanning 40 domains and 33 languages.
Single-byte tokens comprise 13–36% of tokens, while genuine high-byte UTF-8 fallbacks comprise 0.15–0.27% under mainstream mixtures.
Fallback frequency varies by four orders of magnitude across languages, depending on vocabulary coverage of each script.
Embedding and output-matrix norms provide estimates consistent with corpus-based estimates within a factor of four for Qwen3.8.
Norm-based inversion is model-specific and only reliable at order-of-magnitude precision because the norm–frequency relation eventually folds.

papers.title: How Many Bytes Has a BPE Model Seen? Estimating Byte-Token Exposure in Pretraining from Corpus Statistics and Embedding Norms
papers.tldr: The study estimates how often byte fallback tokens are encountered during BPE pretraining, finding that legal UTF-8 fallback bytes are rare but measurable and can be approximated from corpus statistics or embedding norms.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning enables safety-aligned code language models to adapt to diverse downstream tasks. However, training on untrusted data can severely undermine their ability to refuse harmful requests. Notably, we find that models comply with harmful requests even though harmfulness information remains highly decodable from their internal representations. Moreover, an initial preference for refusal does not necessarily translate into sustained refusal behavior throughout generation. Together, these findings reveal a critical gap between recognizing harmful requests and consistently refusing to fulfill them. To address this gap, we introduce SAFEHOLD, a novel provider-enforced defense framework that preserves safety alignment during harmful fine-tuning by treating refusal as a sustained generation process rather than a single response decision. Specifically, SAFEHOLD preserves the aligned model's full-vocabulary response distribution at the initial generation position through decision-boundary anchoring, while supervising the complete refusal sequence through refusal-path reinforcement. We conduct extensive experiments evaluating safety, utility, and internal mechanisms. SAFEHOLD reduces average ASR by 72.03 percentage points relative to undefended fine-tuning, outperforming five SOTA defenses by 24.32 to 70.87 percentage points. Meanwhile, it improves average HumanEval pass@1 by 10.24 percentage points over undefended fine-tuning, while maintaining an average XSTest over-refusal rate of only 2.73 percent. Overall, these results demonstrate that SAFEHOLD effectively mitigates safety degradation during harmful fine-tuning while preserving benign-task utility.
authors: Miaoqing Tian, Ruohan Li, Qian Lu, Haipeng Qu
bullets: Fine-tuning on untrusted data can make safety-aligned code models comply with harmful requests, even when harmfulness remains detectable internally.
Refusal is not reliably sustained throughout generation; recognizing harm and consistently refusing are distinct capabilities.
SAFEHOLD uses decision-boundary anchoring to preserve the aligned model’s initial response distribution and refusal-path reinforcement to supervise complete refusals.
It reduces average attack success rate by 72.03 percentage points versus undefended fine-tuning and outperforms five compared defenses.
The method also improves average HumanEval pass@1 by 10.24 points, with a 2.73% average XSTest over-refusal rate.

papers.abstract: Tokenization represents one of the most crucial steps in mulilingual NLP pipelines. Yet, tokenizers routinely under-allocate vocabulary to low-resource languages. While improved allocation leads to better performance, it remains poorly understood how tokenization shapes cross-lingual representations and transfer during pretraining. To address this, we pretrain 39 mono- and bilingual 1B decoder-only models on FineWeb2-HQ across English, German, French, Arabic and Chinese, varying only the tokenizer. Our results demonstrate that improved vocabulary allocation (i) substantially raises cross-lingual representation alignment in early-to-mid layers, an effect that prior work measuring only the output layer could not observe, (ii) increases cross-lingual parametric knowledge sharing in feed-forward neurons, supported by correlational and causal evidence, and (iii) an alignment-transfer dissociation, where cross-lingual transfer remains essentially unchanged despite higher alignment. Moreover, transfer is significantly lower for cross-script bilinguals even under fair vocabulary allocation, indicating that the script barrier is not merely a tokenizer artifact. All of our checkpoints and code are publicly available.
authors: Jonathan von Rad, Pontus Stenetorp, Yao Lu
bullets: Studies how tokenizer vocabulary allocation shapes multilingual representations during pretraining.

Improved allocation raises alignment in early-to-mid layers and increases cross-lingual knowledge sharing in feed-forward neurons.
Finds an alignment–transfer dissociation: higher alignment leaves transfer essentially unchanged.
Cross-script transfer remains lower even with fair vocabulary allocation, suggesting the script barrier is not solely a tokenizer artifact.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) capabilities have been associated with localized parameter regions, enabling targeted model editing and intervention. However, it remains unclear whether a region identified before model optimization remains an effective intervention target afterward. We evaluate the functional persistence and parameter overlap of coding capability regions across three instruction-tuned models under quantization, pruning, and LoRA-based adaptation. Although re-extracted regions exhibit substantial parameter reorganization, ablating the original region after optimization eliminates or nearly eliminates coding performance in almost all conditions, while magnitude-matched controls preserve performance. Partition analysis further shows that the shared subset of the original and re-extracted regions accounts for most of the observed ablation effect in the majority of conditions. These results demonstrate that parameter overlap and functional persistence are distinct: capability regions can remain causally effective intervention targets even when their parameter realization changes substantially.
authors: Jiwoo Kum, Chanwoo Kim, Doyun Kim, Seonghyeon Cho, Sihyeon Lee, Chanjun Park
bullets: Studies coding capability regions across three instruction-tuned models under quantization, pruning, and LoRA adaptation.
Re-extracted regions show substantial overlap changes with the original regions after optimization.
Ablating the original regions eliminates or nearly eliminates coding performance in almost all conditions.
Magnitude-matched controls generally preserve performance, supporting a region-specific effect.
Shared parameters between original and re-extracted regions explain most ablation effects in most conditions.

papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly receive high-level instructions about roles, values, interests, and communication style. Such instructions can conflict even when a prompt assigns them equal authority and provides no priority rule. We study co-authoritative persona conflict, in which a single prompt jointly assigns two opposing personas. Across eight conflict types grounded in published source material and five LLMs, we measure conflict acknowledgment, resolution strategy, and directional stance. Models acknowledge incompatibility in 72% of direct checks but explicitly surface it in only 22% of task responses, revealing silent arbitration. Dominance accounts for 45% of dual-persona responses, and 35% of compromise-labeled responses retain directional lean. Prompt framing further changes the visible form of arbitration substantially more than ordinary paraphrase variation. These findings show that evaluating instruction following should assess whether models disclose conflicts, how they resolve them, and which persona their responses favor.
authors: Sihyeon Lee, Jiwoo Kum, Jihun Song, Chanwoo Kim, Chanjun Park
bullets: Studies prompts assigning two opposing personas with no priority rule across eight conflict types and five LLMs.
Models acknowledged incompatibility in 72% of direct checks but surfaced it in only 22% of task responses.
One persona dominated 45% of dual-persona responses; 35% of compromise-labeled responses still showed directional bias.
Prompt framing substantially changed arbitration’s visible form, more than ordinary paraphrasing.
The results motivate evaluations of conflict disclosure, resolution strategy, and favored persona.

papers.abstract: We propose the three-dimensional Skyrme model as a topological benchmark for neural variational methods and construct fully three-dimensional Skyrmions with baryon number $B=1,\ldots,4$ without imposing a symmetry ansatz, with high precision. For $B=2,3,4$, the relaxation of these Skyrmions starts from $B$ unit-charge lumps with random positions and orientations, which carry no symmetry information. The known toroidal, tetrahedral, and cubic Skyrmions nevertheless emerge spontaneously. The resulting variational energies for $B=1,\ldots,4$ lie slightly below the published reference values. The neural method highlights the high accuracy for retaining the topological charge, differing from $B$ by at most $10^{-6}$ in the highest-precision solutions. Our numerical method goes through physical constraint tests such as the Derrick virial relation and the Faddeev--Bogomolny bound, together with evaluation / verification through independent quadratures and resolution sweeps. We then compare Kolmogorov--Arnold networks (KANs) with multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) in more than a thousand training runs, both with and without a rational-map ansatz. With default settings, KANs appear markedly superior, but most of the gap disappears once the MLP activation function and learning rate are tuned. KANs remain more parameter-efficient and more robust at fixed epoch budget, while MLPs with the tuned activation function perform at least as well at fixed wall-clock time. We also argue that continuous gradient descent cannot smoothly change the topological sector of our neural field, clarifying the origin of topological freezing observed in our neural variational solvers. Our results on the neural methods applied to Skyrmions pave a research ground for AI-agentic benchmarks for classical topological solitons, toward AI-assisted soliton physics.
authors: Koji Hashimoto, Masaki Murata, Gakuto Ogiwara
bullets: Skyrmions with baryon numbers B=1–4 are obtained without imposing symmetry, with toroidal, tetrahedral, and cubic structures emerging spontaneously.
The computed energies lie slightly below published reference values and satisfy virial, topological-bound, quadrature, and resolution checks.
Topological-charge errors are at most 10⁻⁶ in the highest-precision solutions, indicating strong charge preservation.
KANs outperform default MLPs and remain more parameter-efficient and robust under fixed epoch budgets; tuned MLPs match or exceed them at fixed wall-clock time.
The study attributes topological freezing to the inability of continuous gradient descent to smoothly change the neural field’s topological sector.

papers.abstract: Model merging combines experts fine-tuned from a shared backbone, such as LoRA adapters of a large language model, into one multi-task model without further training. Existing methods apply one rule to every task, yet the accuracy they lose is uneven across tasks. We show that the lost accuracy remains recoverable from each task's residual, its task vector minus the merged update, and that a task's validation headroom, the share of its expert validation accuracy the merge loses, indicates where recovery pays off. Residuals from different tasks interfere, so they must be merged rather than summed. We propose HR-Merge, a training-free wrapper around any merging method. It weights each residual by its task's headroom, re-merges the weighted residuals with the base operator, and adds the result back at a strength selected on validation, falling back to the base merge when no strength helps. On six NLI adapters of LLaMA-3 8B, HR-Merge lifts TIES from 93.29 to 94.29 normalized accuracy, above all tested bases, mainly by recovering its weakest task. In vision, on three CLIP backbones, up to 20 tasks, and LoRA merging, it generally improves or preserves base accuracy and yields the best model in every setting.
authors: Jiakang Huang, Xueyan Zhang, Renyi Cai, Jingcheng Niu, Jiaru Li, Yining Wang, Josh Zhang, Jiahe Jiang, Jinman Zhao, Gerald Penn, Baharan Mirzasoleiman

HR-Merge weights residuals by each task’s validation headroom, re-merges them with the base operator, and adds the result back at a validation-selected strength.
It is a wrapper around any model-merging method and falls back to the base merge when refinement does not help.
On six LLaMA-3 8B NLI adapters, it improved TIES normalized accuracy from 93.29 to 94.29, mainly helping the weakest task.
Across CLIP backbones, up to 20 tasks, and LoRA merging, it generally improved or preserved accuracy and achieved the best model in every reported setting.

papers.abstract: RL post-training typically produces domain experts that must then be consolidated into one model, and as new experts keep arriving, this consolidation becomes a continual process. Weight merging and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) must re-consolidate the whole model whenever an expert is added, and can erode capabilities outside the target domains. We propose Composable Soft-Prompt Distillation (CSPD), which keeps the pre-RL model frozen, distills each RL expert independently into a soft prompt, and composes experts by concatenating their prompts without joint training. A single soft prompt suffices to distill an RL expert, recovering at least 90% of the teacher's gain in 22 of 23 math, code, and agent settings. Independently trained prompts compose well. In a multi-expert setting, the average rises with every expert added, and the full composition matches MOPD (67.83 vs. 67.79). The composition generalizes best across six held-out benchmarks. Input-space adaptation adds little serving overhead, keeping throughput within 1.5% of the unadapted backbone and reaching 2.40x that of rank-4 LoRA. These results point toward continual post-training on a fixed backbone.
authors: Zhen Zhang, Changyi Yang, Xuehai He, Chengzhi Liu, Yutong Yin, Ziyue Liu, Zhuoran Yin, Yangmin Li, Zhihan Liu, Jisen Li, Mingyu Jin, Chuhan Li, Zhaotian Weng, Ruoyu He, Wenyao Gao, Jiaxin Deng, Chenwei Wu, Hui Shen, Wenhao Chai, Chenyang Zhao, Zhuofan Ying, Kieran Liu, Andrew Chen, Pony Ma, Zhaoran Wang, Alkesh Patel, Zhe Gan, Xin Eric Wang
bullets: Addresses the need to repeatedly consolidate newly arriving RL experts without retraining the whole model or eroding non-target capabilities.
Distills each expert into a single soft prompt and composes experts by concatenating prompts, requiring no joint training.
Recovers at least 90% of teacher gains in 22 of 23 math, coding, and agent settings; independently trained prompts compose effectively.
With multiple experts, performance improves as experts are added and matches MOPD (67.83 vs. 67.79).
Generalizes best across six held-out benchmarks with minimal serving overhead: throughput remains within 1.5% of the backbone and reaches 2.40× rank-4 LoRA throughput.

papers.abstract: Domain specialization of large language models (LLMs) often improves target-domain performance but degrades broad capabilities. Model merging is an attractive training-free alternative, yet common parameter-space strategies (for example, interpolation and sparsified averaging) provide limited control over task-specific interference. We introduce Adaptive Model Alignment via Ranked Inherited Subspaces (AMARIS), a covariance-driven framework that transfers specialist updates only along selected activation directions. AMARIS formulates merging as budgeted subspace inheritance: it seeks high specialist activation capture under a regularized base-output perturbation budget, then builds a low-rank projection gate from ranked generalized eigendirections. This yields a single static merged checkpoint that concentrates transfer in high-utility, low-interference directions. We evaluate AMARIS on Qwen3-based merges (8B and 32B) across finance, instruction-following, and multilingual SEA specialization. In our evaluated settings, AMARIS reaches Pareto operating points that are competitive with strong training-free baselines, including 98.37% specialist retention with 95.16% core retention for the 8B finance setting, 103.55% core retention with 90.28% specialist retention for the 8B instruction-following setting, and 99.20% core retention with 94.80% specialist retention for the 32B SEA setting. These results support subspace-constrained merging as a practical route to compositional capability integration without additional training.
authors: Hwee Young Kang, Irwin De Tao Chin, Wen-Haw Chong, Hai Leong Chieu
bullets: Addresses capability degradation caused by domain specialization and interference in conventional parameter-space model merging.
Uses covariance-driven, ranked generalized eigendirections to construct a low-rank projection gate for specialist updates.
Optimizes specialist activation capture under a regularized budget limiting perturbation to the base model’s outputs.
Produces a single static merged checkpoint and achieves competitive Pareto trade-offs across finance, instruction-following, and multilingual SEA settings on Qwen3 models.
Evaluated retention trade-offs include up to 98.37% specialist retention with 95.16% core retention in the reported settings.

papers.abstract: Long-form generation is increasingly important for agentic LLM systems, yet current reinforcement learning methods typically optimize an entire document with a single outcome-level reward. This delayed and coarse-grained supervision makes it difficult to localize errors and assign credit across semantically distinct parts of the output. To address this, we propose a short-horizon framework that reformulates long-form generation through semantic decomposition into segment-level decisions. Each segment is generated with prefix-conditioned context, allowing cross-segment coherence to be preserved while keeping supervision local. The generated segments are then scored with rubric-based rewards for adherence, coherence, and relevance, enabling explicit local supervision at the segment level. These local rewards are used to compute step-wise advantages, yielding localized policy updates. To isolate the effect of supervision granularity, we instantiate both outcome-level supervision and our short-horizon process reward method (SH-PRM) under the same GRPO framework. Across multiple LLMs and two long-form generation benchmarks, SH-PRM consistently outperforms outcome-level supervision and strong inference-time baselines under the same optimizer and comparable budgets. Further analyses suggest that these gains primarily arise from improved credit assignment. Overall, our results suggest that aligning supervision granularity with the semantic structure of long-form generation is an effective design principle for long-form LLM training.
authors: Heyang Xu, HanWen Hao, Qianren Mao, Zhuo Liu, Qili Zhang, Sheng Yang, Jianxin Li
bullets: Long-form reinforcement learning struggles to assign credit when a whole document receives only one coarse outcome reward.
The method decomposes outputs into semantically meaningful segments generated with prefix context to preserve coherence.
Rubric-based rewards assess each segment for adherence, coherence, and relevance, producing step-wise advantages and localized policy updates.
Implemented within the same GRPO framework, SH-PRM outperforms outcome-level supervision and inference-time baselines across multiple models and two benchmarks.
Analyses attribute the gains mainly to improved credit assignment.

This change in supervision granularity enables more precise credit assignment by penalizing problematic paragraphs while preserving credit for strong ones.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought prompting significantly improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) but incurs high inference costs due to lengthy autoregressive decoding. While previous efficiency approaches reduce costs by discarding tokens or utilizing continuous latent representations, these lossy methods fundamentally sacrifice interpretability and auditability. In this work, we introduce a novel compression framework for intermediate reasoning. We apply Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) to reasoning corpora to learn a compressed vocabulary of Private Use Area (PUA) tokens, each representing frequent semantic spans. After expanding the LLM's vocabulary, we fine-tune the model via strictly 1:1, our method is lossless. We evaluate our approach on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-14B, and Qwen2.5-32B across four diverse benchmarks. Our method reduces total generated tokens by 14.7% on average with reasoning trace lengths dropping by up to 27.1%, while incurring a negligible average accuracy cost of 1.6 percentage points. Crucially, this approach is orthogonal to existing lossy methods, allowing practitioners to stack lossless and irreversible compression techniques. We demonstrate that a compressed intermediate language provides a highly efficient computational resource that accelerates inference while fully preserving the transparency of LLM reasoning.
authors: Rabimba Karanjai, Suryabhan Singh Hada, Hemanth Hegadehalli Madhavarao, Qun Gu, Libin N. George, Wenhuan Sun, Neha Monga, Richard Williamson, Prakhar Mehrotra
bullets: Addresses the inference cost of lengthy chain-of-thought without sacrificing transparency through lossy token dropping or latent representations.
Learns semantic-span tokens with BPE in the Private Use Area and fine-tunes expanded-vocabulary LLMs using strict 1:1 supervision.
Evaluated on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-14B, and Qwen2.5-32B across four benchmarks.
Cuts total generated tokens by 14.7% on average and reasoning-trace length by up to 27.1%, with a 1.6-point average accuracy cost.
The lossless approach can be combined with existing irreversible compression methods.

papers.abstract: While chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting elicits intermediate reasoning steps from language models, it is unclear which words in the context actually steer the CoT. We identify Phantom Context Influence (PCI): language models are disproportionately steered by semantically irrelevant context words, even as the same models deny those words' relevance when asked. To localize PCI, we introduce Leave-One-Out Word JSD analysis, which removes one context word at a time from the otherwise intact context to isolate its marginal effect on the next-token distribution; words whose removal flips the prediction (pivot words) are passed to the same LLM to self-judge whether it recognizes this predictive dependence. Across four models and three benchmarks, language models largely do not know which words steer their reasoning, a mismatch we call the Generation-Judgment Contradiction. Inspired by this phenomenon, we propose Online KV Suppression: it scores every prompt word's influence over the whole chain of thought in a single pass, then zeroes the KV-cache entries of the highest-influence word the model itself judges inert and redecodes. This single-word intervention improves CoT accuracy across four models and five reasoning benchmarks, by up to 8.9 percentage points on math reasoning benchmark.
authors: Yanbei Jiang, Chao Lei, Jey Han Lau, Krista A. Ehinger, Rena Gao Wei
bullets: Identifies Phantom Context Influence: semantically irrelevant words can disproportionately alter chain-of-thought reasoning.
Introduces Leave-One-Out Word JSD analysis to measure each word’s marginal effect on next-token predictions.
Finds a Generation-Judgment Contradiction across four models and three benchmarks: models often fail to identify words steering their reasoning.
Proposes Online KV Suppression, which removes the model-judged inert word with the greatest measured influence during decoding.
Improves chain-of-thought accuracy across four models and five reasoning benchmarks, with gains of up to 8.9 percentage points on a math benchmark.

papers.abstract: Critic-free reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) typically assigns a uniform advantage to every token. Token-reweighting heuristics like the 80/20 mask favor high-entropy tokens, but fail to measure a token's actual impact on the outcome. We formalize this impact as the forking value: the variance of the success probability over the policy's next-token choices. The expected forking values along a response sum exactly to the reward variance. Token credit is thus, in expectation over a prompt's responses, a fixed budget spent at the forks. This motivates weights that redistribute credit within a response. The forking value factorizes into a fork consequence, which requires costly continuations to estimate, and a fork probability, which the softmax provides. On Qwen3-8B-Base, this fork probability decays exponentially with a token's within-response entropy rank at class-specific rates, revealing that most tokens carry negligible forking value. CreditFilter weights each token by an exponential window over the same rank. The window is calibrated to this fork-probability envelope, under an approximately flat fork consequence. CreditFilter needs no extra forward passes and is stabilized by difficulty damping and an entropy-gated fallback. Averaged over three seeds, it outperforms DAPO by 7.7 points on MATH500 and by 10.5 and 9.1 points on AIME24 and AIME25. Its dynamically adaptive variant matches it. The ablations show that both parts matter: ranking tokens within each response rather than across the batch, and matching the window's decay rate to the envelope. Code is available at https://github.com/yoctta/CreditFilter.
authors: Hanqing Zhao, Liuyue Xie, Rong-Cheng Tu, Xu Zhang, Davide Modolo, Dacheng Tao
bullets: RLVR’s uniform token advantages overlook that only a small subset of tokens substantially affects outcome success.
The method defines token impact through forking value and uses softmax-derived fork probability as a cheap proxy.
It applies an exponential weighting window over each response’s within-response entropy rank, calibrated to the observed decay envelope.
Difficulty damping and an entropy-gated fallback stabilize training without requiring additional model evaluations.
Across three seeds on Qwen3-8B-Base, CreditFilter improves over DAPO by 7.7 points on MATH500, 10.5 on AIME24, and 9.1 on AIME25; both within-response ranking and decay matching are important.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces CreditFilter, a method for calibrating token weights in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) based on the 'forking value' of tokens, improving performance on mathematical reasoning tasks.
papers.title: CreditFilter: Calibrated Token Weights over the Within-Response Entropy Rank for RLVR
papers.tldr: CreditFilter reallocates RLVR token credit toward within-response high-impact forks using calibrated entropy-rank weights, improving mathematical reasoning performance without extra forward passes.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates language generation by letting a target model verify several draft tokens in one forward pass. Earlier neural drafters such as EAGLE extend each candidate sequence one token at a time. Recent work has turned to parallel drafters such as DFlash, which predict a whole block at once. Another approach uses n-gram retrieval to find an earlier occurrence of the current context suffix and copy the tokens that followed it directly into the draft. We introduce CoPyro, which feeds these copied tokens into a parallel drafter in place of masks. The drafter learns from context which tokens to keep and which to revise as it predicts the block in its usual forward pass. Across eight benchmarks on Qwen3-4B, CoPyro improves overall acceptance length for all four parallel drafters tested, with gains of 2.19-5.08% when trained on 100K samples. With DFlash trained on 710K samples, overall gains range from 1.08% to 2.00% across the tested model sizes and temperatures. Code generation benefits most in both settings. On Qwen3-8B, processing the proposals adds an average of 0.24 ms per decoding round in Transformers.
bullets: Addresses the limited draft quality of parallel drafters by leveraging tokens copied from earlier matching context suffixes.
Feeds copied proposals into the drafter instead of masks, allowing it to retain or revise them during its normal block prediction.
Improves overall acceptance length for all four tested parallel drafters across eight benchmarks on Qwen3-4B.
Reported gains are 2.19–5.08% with 100K training samples and 1.08–2.00% with DFlash trained on 710K samples; code generation benefits most.
Proposal processing adds an average of 0.24 ms per decoding round on Qwen3-8B in Transformers.

papers.abstract: Local-cloud agent systems pair a cloud model with a small on-device agent that acts on private data, often as the last check before an irreversible action. We identify, for the first time, a failure in which such an agent is led into a violation by its own correct decisions within a session. After it correctly releases an item whose restriction was lifted, it becomes more likely to release the next item that is still restricted. Because the trigger is a correct decision, a history with no faulty step can still end in a violation. We call this failure correct-precedent generalization and find it in 13 open-weight models from nine developers. A single correct precedent can cut the safe rate of the most affected agent roughly in half, and the risk compounds when a refused request is simply sent again in a new session. Interventions on the agent's history indicate that it carries its decision on the released item over to the restricted one instead of checking that item's status. Building on this finding, we propose Paired Decision Distillation (PDD), which distills the decisions of a weakly affected teacher into a LoRA adapter. PDD restores the safe rate to nearly 100% in every distilled model, without extra prompt text or model calls.
authors: Chong Tian, Yu Wang, Steve Liu, Qirong Ho, Xiuying Chen
bullets: On-device agents may violate policies after making only correct decisions earlier in the same session.
A correct release of one item can bias the agent to release a later item that remains restricted; repeated requests across sessions compound the risk.
The failure, termed correct-precedent generalization, appears in 13 open-weight models from nine developers.
History interventions suggest agents transfer the prior release decision instead of rechecking the new item's status.
Paired Decision Distillation (PDD) uses a weakly affected teacher and a LoRA adapter to restore safe rates to nearly 100% without extra prompts or model calls.

papers.selection_reason: Identifies a failure mode in on-device LLM agents (correct-precedent generalization) and proposes Paired Decision Distillation (PDD) to restore safe behavior, offering a technical solution for agent safety and adaptation.
papers.title: Correct Precedents Induce Policy Violations in On-Device LLM Agents
papers.tldr: Correct decisions can create harmful precedent in on-device LLM agents, while Paired Decision Distillation nearly eliminates the resulting policy violations.

papers.abstract: Personalized long-form generation asks a language model to write new text the way a specific user would. The standard recipe, retrieval-augmented generation, places a few of the user's past texts in the prompt but leaves the model to decide what to take from them. We introduce StylePrism, a taxonomy of 28 stylistic aspects in seven categories, and SP-Refine, an inference-time method that makes style extraction an explicit step: the model first fills StylePrism with the user's patterns, quoted evidence, and habits to avoid, then drafts from the user's samples and revises the draft twice against this profile, guided by its own style scores. On the three long-form tasks of LongLaMP with three LLMs, SP-Refine outperforms LongLaMP's retrieval-augmented baseline in 25 of 27 ROUGE and METEOR comparisons, by 10.2% on average and by up to 35.8%. Annotating users' own texts with the extracted profiles shows that StylePrism captures concrete, checkable habits, from the order of rhetorical moves to a reviewer's sign-off. Ablations show that the profile helps as revision guidance, not as a replacement for the samples: writing from the profile alone is worse in all 27 comparisons, while a single implicit-inference call is a cheaper alternative that comes close. Oracle variants that let the reviser see the reference, together with reference-free controls, show that larger refinement gains require information unavailable at inference time.
authors: Jenitha Reddy Patel, Sameeksha Kini, Amulya Rayasam, Anisa Dye, Abhinav Sharma, Sai Karthik Navuluru, Bo Ni, Li Li, Junda Wu, Tong Yu, Nedim Lipka, Xiaolei Huang, Tyler Derr, Yue Zhao, Zhengzhong Tu, Yu Wang, Hongjie Chen, Thien Huu Nguyen, Nesreen K. Ahmed, Franck Dernoncourt, Ryan A. Rossi
bullets: Defines StylePrism, a taxonomy of 28 stylistic aspects across seven categories, including concrete habits and patterns to avoid.
SP-Refine extracts a style profile with quoted evidence, drafts from user samples, and revises the draft twice using the profile and self-evaluated style scores.
Across three LongLaMP tasks and three LLMs, it beats the retrieval-augmented baseline in 25 of 27 ROUGE/METEOR comparisons, with 10.2% average and up to 35.8% gains.
Ablations show profiles work best as revision guidance alongside user samples; profile-only generation performs worse, while a cheaper single implicit-inference call is competitive.
Oracle results indicate that larger refinement gains depend on reference information unavailable during inference.

figures.caption: Figure 3: What STYLEPRISM extraction captures. Only the user’s actual abstract is shown; each highlight marks text matching an aspect in the profile extracted before this abstract was seen, colored by category (Figure 2). SP-PROFILE keeps only step 1 and then writes from π without S; SP-INFER keeps only step 2.

For all three generators, SP-REFINE (vermillion) and SP-INFER (orange) form the outer boundary on the style criteria, ahead of LONGLAMP (tied with it only on Format for GPT). papers.abstract: Manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) extends residual connections to multiple streams and stabilizes residual propagation by constraining stream-mixing residual matrices to the Birkhoff polytope, the set of doubly stochastic matrices. In this work, we investigate how to effectively mix residual streams within the Birkhoff polytope. We reveal a mixing trade-off: when under-mixed residual matrices stay close to the vertices of the Birkhoff polytope, hyper-connections will degenerate into a set of nearly independent streams; when over-mixed residual matrices are concentrated around the uniform barycenter of the polytope, streams will become less distinguishable from each other. We theoretically validate our findings by bounding the cumulative residual mixing, stream difference and gradient difference of mixing coefficients across layers. Motivated by these findings, we propose Contraction for Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (cmHC), an exact doubly stochastic method which geometrically contracts the Birkhoff polytope toward its interior. This contraction mitigates under-mixing by forcing the residual matrices to explore deeper into the polytope, with a provable stream mixing bound and no new parameterization. Moreover, we apply a moderate contraction at the shallow layers to prevent over-mixing, enabling stable gradient propagation on extremely large-scale model pretraining. Extensive experiments across dense and mixture-of-experts models at various parameter scales demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of cmHC. We also develop fused operators for cmHC on Ascend NPUs, reducing hyper-connection execution latency by up to 44.8%.
authors: Haowei He, Ziwen Zhao, Chenshuo Pan, Gang Lin, Zhihao Yang, Chao Wang, Xinzhang Liu, Kaidong Yu, Han Gao, Dongfang Li, Menglin Yang, Shuangyong Song, Yongxiang Li
bullets: mHC can under-mix streams, leaving them nearly independent, or over-mix them, making streams indistinguishable.
The paper theoretically analyzes cumulative stream mixing and differences in streams and mixing gradients across layers.
cmHC contracts the Birkhoff polytope toward its interior using an exact doubly stochastic transformation with no new parameterization.
Applying stronger contraction deeper and moderate contraction in shallow layers supports stable gradient propagation for large-scale pretraining.
Experiments across dense and mixture-of-experts models show effectiveness and scalability; fused Ascend NPU operators reduce execution latency by up to 44.8%.

papers.abstract: Task 3 of the FinReason Cup 2026 scores a system on two values per case, the one an XBRL filing reports and the one its own calculation relationships imply, and labels each failure as structural, extraction or calculation. This report shows that the calculation-error rate so defined does not count arithmetic failures, and bounds how far it is from one using the published board alone. One of the three rules behind the benchmark, DQC_US_0015, has an answer that is the negation of the reported value (in all 110 published practice cases, against 1 of 120 and 6 of 102 for the other two), so a calculation label on such a case records a wrong fact or a wrong route, not a wrong sum. Subtracting the available structural and extraction labels from each entry's error count on that rule gives a floor: the bound is positive for 22 of the 23 ranked entries, and at the top it is sharpest, with at least 11 of 12 and 12 of 13 calculation errors of the two joint-first entries falling on cases where no arithmetic remained. The calculation-error rate of the best systems on this task is almost entirely not arithmetic. The vehicle for that result is an entry that reconstructs the three data-quality rules the benchmark is drawn from, DQC_US_0015, DQC_US_0117 and DQC_US_0126, as a deterministic system with no learned parameters, no training step and no external service, running all 680 cases in 1.4 seconds. It scores 96.62% under the offline judge on development and 95.29% on the published test set, and its residual error concentrates in cases where a concept carries several equally flagged facts and the question names no dimensional member. Reading those error classes against the per-rule accuracies is what exposed the metric, which is why both are reported here.
bullets: The benchmark compares reported XBRL values with values implied by calculation relationships and labels failures as structural, extraction, or calculation.
For DQC_US_0015, the benchmark answer is the negation of the reported value in nearly all published practice cases, so calculation labels generally do not indicate incorrect sums.
A derived lower bound is positive for 22 of 23 ranked entries; for the two joint-first systems, at least 11/12 and 12/13 calculation errors involved no remaining arithmetic.
A deterministic reconstruction of DQC_US_0015, DQC_US_0117, and DQC_US_0126 achieved 96.62% on development and 95.29% on the published test set, processing 680 cases in 1.4 seconds.
Residual errors mainly occurred when multiple equally flagged facts shared a concept and the question specified no dimensional member.

papers.abstract: Code models are increasingly trained on the full history of software repositories, every version of every file, rather than on a single snapshot. The tools that deduplicate training data were built for snapshots, and what they do to a history has not been measured. We measured it on a pre-registered random sample of 306 public repositories, 25 mature projects, and the 12 repositories behind the SWE-bench benchmark. A history is mostly repetition: in the vocabulary of text indexing, a pangenome, one text in many near-identical variants. The history of a typical repository holds the equivalent of 19 copies of its current code, and a mature repository holds 89. The reason is that each edit changes a few lines and leaves the rest of the file in place: nine tokens in ten of a changed file already existed before the change. Exact-match deduplication removes none of these copies, since no two versions are identical. Large training pipelines already deduplicate their snapshots by grouping near-identical files and keeping one. Applied across versions, the same step brings the repetition down to about two copies. But two problems remain. The deduplicator keeps one version of each file, and in widely used implementations, including the one we measured, the rule for choosing that version ignores dates, so for half of all files the version kept for training is an old one. Sorting versions newest first before deduplicating fixes the problem at almost no cost. The second problem is benchmark answers. Benchmarks such as SWE-bench test a model on real bug fixes, and a merged fix survives in a median of 18 later versions of the files it changed. Therefore, removing benchmark fixes needs a separate step that checks every version. We turn the measurements into a short set of rules for teams that train on code history, and release the instruments and frozen outputs.
bullets: Repository histories contain roughly 19 copies of current code typically, rising to 89 in mature projects; nine in ten tokens of a changed file already existed before the edit.
Exact-match deduplication removes none of these non-identical historical versions.
Near-duplicate file grouping reduces repetition to about two copies, but version-selection rules may retain old files when dates are ignored.
Sorting versions newest first fixes stale-version selection at minimal cost.
Benchmark fixes can persist through many later versions, requiring a separate all-version scan to remove them from training data.

papers.abstract: Language models fuse reports in retrieval, multi-agent consensus and agent memory, where treating shared-source reports as independent can double count evidence. A common remedy is an instruction to count each source once. Its value depends on the receiver's raw baseline. Pricing it needs an exact reference. We build the graded-dependence exact reference: binary worlds with single-report reliability 0.65 and four dependence levels, whose disclosed parameters give every world an exact posterior and every rule a target risk. The paired gain protocol scores raw and instructed answers of four configurations on 2,976 worlds. Agreement and gain separate in both directions. At $\delta$ = 0, claude-opus-5-5 and gpt-6.1-sol agreed with the rule within 0.001 in 744 of 744, and the instruction raised their posterior mismatch by 0.044; gpt-6-luna agreed in 165 of 744 and gained 0.0140 (95% interval 0.0064 to 0.0219); claude-haiku-5-5's gain moved from -0.0295 ($\delta$ = 0) to +0.0302 ($\delta$ = 1) (descriptive). The prespecified first-child endpoint contrast, gain at $\delta$ = 1 minus $\delta$ = 0, was 0.0342 (0.0303 to 0.0382). In the preregistered tests, the raw source-weight contrast was positive (0.259, 95% interval 0.182 to 0.337; Holm rejected zero) and the grouping endpoint difference was not detected (0.0004, -0.0023 to 0.0031). This interval excludes differences larger than 0.0031 in magnitude and lies within the registered precision bound of $\pm$0.0046. The reference prices the rule before any model call. The paired gain, estimable as a Brier difference on labelled deployment items, decides adoption per receiver and prompt condition.
authors: Tengfei Shao, Asma Rezaei, Ali Reza Kamali
bullets: Treating reports from shared sources as independent can double count evidence; instruction value depends on the receiver’s baseline.
The study constructs an exact reference over binary worlds with 0.65 single-report reliability and four dependence levels, then evaluates raw versus instructed answers on 2,976 worlds.
Agreement with the exact rule and improvement from instruction were distinct: some models already agreed nearly perfectly, while others gained modestly.
The prespecified dependence-level gain contrast was 0.0342 (95% interval 0.0303–0.0382); the grouping endpoint difference was not detected and was bounded within ±0.0031.
The authors recommend estimating paired Brier-score gain on labelled deployment items before adopting the instruction for a given receiver and prompt.

papers.abstract: Aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences requires simultaneously satisfying multiple, often competing values. Existing preference optimization methods collapse these into a single implicit signal, and even multi-objective extensions optimize within a shared parameter space, leaving cross-value conflicts unresolved. We propose MAPES, a multi-value alignment paradigm in which conflict resolution is a first-class concern at every pipeline stage: it first decomposes supervision into value-specific experts trained in isolated parameter subspaces, then recomposes them via preference-aware value merging and a lightweight harmonization stage that aligns the merged model with the expert ensemble. Across five preference alignment benchmarks, MAPES outperforms strong direct preference optimization (DPO) variants and multi-objective baselines on the benchmark-level average, with no large degradation on GSM8K and GPQA; matched controls isolate the contribution of each stage.
bullets: Targets the unresolved conflicts that arise when LLMs must satisfy competing values.
Decomposes supervision into value-specific experts trained in isolated parameter subspaces.
Uses preference-aware value merging followed by lightweight harmonization with the expert ensemble.
Outperforms strong DPO variants and multi-objective baselines on the average across five preference-alignment benchmarks.
Shows no large degradation on GSM8K and GPQA; matched controls assess each pipeline stage.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) has become a core technique for post-training large language models, enabling students to learn from dense token-level supervision on their own generations. However, even with a capable teacher, OPD training can be unstable, leading to excessive response length, repetitive generation, and severe performance degradation. One example is \textit{spurious agreement}, where the student maintains high overlap with the teacher at the states visited but produces repetitive generations. Although such failures have been observed, the mechanisms behind these failures remain poorly understood. To address this gap, we investigate OPD through the lens of learning dynamics, tracing three mechanisms from local analysis to subsequent on-policy sampling. We first identify states where sampled-token OPD updates fail to correct teacher--student mismatch and characterize them using the student's mass on the teacher's top-$p$ set. We then show that learning from the teacher is difficult at mismatched states and that their gradients can also affect with learning at other tokens. Finally, using a termination-token mismatch as a case study, we study how continued training on mismatched states influences on-policy sampling, suppressing the student's current modes and leading the student toward states where the teacher is unreliable . These findings help explain the benefits of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) initialization and motivate targeted correction of states where student and teacher are mismatched.
authors: Xinnan Zhang, Zeyi Liao, Siliang Zeng, Zhongruo Wang, Jiaxiang Li, Xinyan Zhao, Huan Sun, Mingyi Hong
bullets: OPD failures include excessive length, repetition, performance degradation, and spurious agreement with the teacher.
The analysis identifies mismatched states where sampled-token updates fail to correct the teacher–student gap, characterized by the student’s probability mass on the teacher’s top-p tokens.
Gradients from mismatched states can interfere with learning at other tokens, making teacher imitation difficult.
A termination-token mismatch can suppress the student’s existing generation modes and steer sampling toward states where the teacher is unreliable.
The findings support SFT initialization and targeted correction of student–teacher mismatch states.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes learning dynamics of on-policy distillation for LLM post-training; relevant to LLM training and behavior.
papers.title: When Students Fail to Learn from Teachers: Learning Dynamics of On-Policy Distillation
papers.tldr: This paper explains why on-policy distillation can destabilize language-model training by reinforcing student–teacher mismatches that distort future generations.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training of large language models runs two GPU workloads with different hardware demands: rollout decoding, which is dominated by memory access and whose batch shrinks as responses finish, and a dense learner. Current systems either time-share every GPU between them, paying serial phases and switches, or split GPUs into pools whose sizes change only in whole devices. We present CTRL, which makes co-residency a third RL execution layout: every GPU runs a learner rank beside a persistent rollout engine, sharing the device under CUDA MPS. A host-owned learner makes the layout fit: optimizer state stays in host memory, and policy weights stream layer by layer through a bounded GPU window. A publication gate trains each ready batch first and waits only before releasing the next policy, keeping a dropless staleness bound. A step-time bound guides compute-share selection, and a GPU-time ledger explains overlap and sharing costs. On H100, A800, and RTX 4090 GPUs with Qwen3 models, CTRL achieves 1.11-2.24$\times$ the throughput of the stronger of verl's asynchronous baselines across 24 workload settings with the staleness limit set to two, and 1.23$\times$ verl's colocate_async on eight H100 GPUs. With the same learner, co-residency is 1.10-1.26$\times$ faster than time-sharing on all three platforms and 1.10-1.30$\times$ faster than the best measured whole-GPU split on H100 DAPO-Math workloads at 256-528 trajectories per step, on four and eight GPUs.
authors: Ruijia Yang, Ruikai Li, Zeyi Wen
bullets: Addresses inefficiency from either serial GPU time-sharing or inflexible whole-GPU partitioning.
Co-resides a persistent rollout engine with a learner on each GPU using CUDA MPS.
Uses host-memory optimizer state and layer-wise weight streaming to fit the learner beside rollouts.
A publication gate and step-time bound control policy staleness and compute sharing.
Across reported platforms and workloads, CTRL delivers 1.11–2.24× the throughput of stronger asynchronous baselines and consistently outperforms time-sharing and measured GPU splits.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive Transformers generally fail on out-of-distribution reasoning due to two primary reasons: positional corruption over long sequences and structural state drift across deep execution steps. We introduce ORION, a framework that supervises exact canonical execution states via auxiliary heads to anchor latent trajectories to valid computational manifolds. Across Folding, GridShift, and CLRS-30, a pre-registered 2 x 2 factorial shows that RoPE and ORION address orthogonal axes. RoPE recovers length extrapolation (59.8%), while ORION recovers depth extrapolation (66.7%). Moreover, their combination complementarily achieves strict additive gain in joint length-depth extrapolation, while either method alone offers near satisfactory results. Negative controls confirm that the gain depends strictly on exact canonical alignment; hashed state statistics fail to constrain depth extrapolation.
bullets: Targets two failure modes: positional corruption over long sequences and structural state drift across deep reasoning steps.
Uses auxiliary heads to supervise exact canonical execution states and keep latent trajectories on valid computational manifolds.
Across Folding, GridShift, and CLRS-30, RoPE primarily recovers length extrapolation (59.8%), while ORION recovers depth extrapolation (66.7%).
Combining RoPE and ORION yields complementary additive gains on joint length-depth extrapolation.
Negative controls show that exact canonical alignment is necessary; hashed state statistics do not constrain depth extrapolation.

figures.caption: Figure 7: The ORION architecture on both domains. An exact simulator emits the canonical state Φ(S) = (µ, ν, ω, T, ans) at every execution step; five read-out heads decode it from one shared latent, and their losses are added to the language-modelling objective. The answer head is one probe among several rather than the privileged output. The identical wiring runs on FOLDING and GRIDSHIFT, which is what lets the contrastive term act across domains.

Figure 3: Canonical-state pretraining transfers across domains. Exact match during adaptation to the other domain under an equal 800-step budget, using five seeds. Models are initialized from scratch, from a Transformer pretrained on the source domain, or from an ORION model pretrained on the source domain. The ORION initialization improves target-domain held-out performance over Transformer pretraining by +0.085 ± 0.041 for FOLDING→GRIDSHIFT and +0.035 ± 0.013 for GRIDSHIFT→FOLDING. The improvement is positive in every seed in both directions.

Figure 2: ORION composes with RoPE on depth extrapolation. (a,b) Exact match at execution depths 5–8, after training at depths 1–4, for RoPE alone and ORION + RoPE on FOLDING and GRIDSHIFT. Bands show ± one standard deviation over three seeds. Printed values give the pairedby-example difference at each depth; stars indicate p < 0.05. Across all held-out depths, ORION + RoPE improves over RoPE by +0.016 on FOLDING (p = 0.036) and +0.024 on GRIDSHIFT (p = 0.002). (c) The corresponding difference across model widths in the five-seed scaling ladder. The gains are +0.000, +0.004, and +0.082 at 3.5M, 11M, and 26M parameters, respectively; the largest model favors the combined condition in all five seeds.

Figure 1: ORION + RoPE keeps computing the canonical state beyond the training depth. Exact accuracy of the canonical-state read-outs by execution depth (seed 0; shaded region: training depths). (a, b) The answer set read directly from the latent at the decision position, without autoregressive decoding, on FOLDING and GRIDSHIFT. (c) The occupancy map on FOLDING. With absolute positions the read-outs collapse at the first unseen depth (0.04, 0.19, 0.06); with RoPE they remain at 0.63, 0.67 and 0.85 at depth 5 and decay gradually, so the state is still being tracked where it was never supervised.

Figure 4: Canonical supervision confines the latent trajectory. The final-layer hidden state at each executed operation is one point per step, projected on the two leading principal components of the in-distribution states and expressed in units of their spread. Arrows: mean step-to-step displacement of 800 paths through each cell; bold path: mean position from step 1 (square) to step 8. The baseline moves 1.18 spreads per step with no coherent direction; ORION + RoPE moves 0.44 along a coherent field. The effect comes from the supervision, not the positional encoding (0.45 for ORION without RoPE, 1.36 for RoPE alone).

Figure 9: Layer-to-layer linear CKA within each model on FOLDING (seed 0, 384 in-distribution prompts). Both models show the same smooth block structure, with adjacent layers above 0.97 and the embedding layer the most distinct. Canonical supervision does not reorganise the layer hierarchy. Note the colour scale starts at 0.90; on an absolute scale the two panels are nearly identical, which is the point.

Figure 5: An execution trace in the FOLDING domain. Each operation reflects part of the sheet onto the rest and concatenates the stacks, so layer count grows with depth while the footprint shrinks. The canonical state Φ(St) is the stack-valued geometry at each step; the query is a punch through the final stack, scored by exact set match over the original cells it perforates.

Figure 6: An execution trace in the GRIDSHIFT domain. Cyclic row and column shifts permute origin labels over a grid whose extent never changes, so unlike FOLDING the state size is independent of program length. The canonical state is the origin-per-cell permutation and the query asks which positions hold marked origins after execution.

Figure 10: Degradation on FOLDING, from the reduced-budget surface sweep. (a) Exact match against execution depth at the training state sizes; the shaded band is the trained range and the printed values are the endpoints at 2×. The rotary conditions degrade gradually while the two absolute-position conditions fall off a cliff at the first unseen depth. (b) The joint surface for ORION + RoPE over both axes, every cell labelled with exact match; red lines mark the edges of the training region and n/a marks a combination the generator cannot produce. Reading up the left columns shows depth costing accuracy gradually; reading across to the right column shows the size axis costing all of it at once, at every depth. The size axis is not drawn as a separate curve because all four conditions coincide on it (0.195, 0.190, 0.169 and 0.170 at S/Strain = 1.33).

Figure 11: Per-algorithm exact match on the CLRS pilot (single seed). (a) In-distribution (n = 16). (b) The preregistered out-of-distribution endpoint, the mean of the length and structural axes. Only kmp matcher separates the conditions; activity selector and graham scan are at zero for every condition.
