The preregistered hypothesis was that canonical supervision compresses the execution subspace. The TwoNN estimator is the one measure that moves the other way, so we report the evidence as mixed in direction but uniform in conclusion — no measure supports compression. papers.selection_reason: Improves transformer length/depth extrapolation via canonical-state supervision and RoPE, relevant to LLM architecture and long-context research.
papers.title: ORION: Exact Canonical-State Supervision for Systematic Generalization in Transformers
papers.tldr: ORION improves Transformers’ systematic generalization by supervising exact canonical execution states, addressing depth-related state drift alongside RoPE’s handling of long-sequence positional corruption.

papers.abstract: Language models assign different probabilities to token sequences that decode to the same string. In reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR), a trainer that re-encodes sampled text may train on a different token sequence with the same reward. We ask how far this moves a training update, and whether the movement has a consistent direction. From one checkpoint, we compare updates on the same rollouts, canonical and with selected tokens split into two pieces, against an update on a different batch. On Qwen2.5-0.5B with three-digit addition, splitting about one token in 25 moves the update 0.556 times as far as replacing the batch. The ratio rises with the fraction split in four models and depends on which tokens are split; within a checkpoint, the displacements share a direction across batches. In a tabular model with one table per tokenization and a single sampled string, we prove that whenever two strings below an unsampled prefix differ in probability, only the zero full-gradient step agrees across tokenizations, however it is weighted. In an audit that decodes and re-encodes resampled rollouts, re-encoding touches up to 5.2% of rollouts but at most 0.08% of tokens, far below the split fractions we test. Training on fixed rollouts, the canonical arm finishes ahead in 14 of 18 pre-registered pairs; the interval for the mean accuracy difference includes zero over all pairs and excludes it only under the registered exclusion rule, which favours the canonical arm.
bullets: Re-encoding the same text changes token-level probabilities and therefore the RLVR training update despite leaving rewards unchanged.
On Qwen2.5-0.5B, splitting roughly 1 in 25 tokens moved the update 0.556 as far as using a different batch; the effect increased with split frequency and varied by token.
Update displacements tended to share a direction across batches within a checkpoint.
A tabular analysis proves that, when tokenization-dependent probabilities differ, only a zero full-gradient step is guaranteed to agree across tokenizations.

In an audit, re-encoding affected up to 5.2% of rollouts but no more than 0.08% of tokens; canonical training finished ahead in 14 of 18 pairs, though overall accuracy evidence was inconclusive under the stated analysis.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The ratio R (Equation 2) against the achieved split fraction, for four models on three-digit addition and for Qwen2.5-0.5B on GSM8K (hollow markers, dashed line). Small points are seeds; large points are means over seeds at each requested dose, placed at the mean achieved fraction. The three Qwen models share one vocabulary and Llama-3.1-8B has another (sizes in Table 7). LoRA, seq_reinforce; five seeds for Qwen2.5-0.5B on addition and three for every other curve.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly asked where to center the coefficients of a small-sample Bayesian regression, but the evidence is unclear: benchmarks are often built to match the prior and models may remember them. We audit this practice with one frontier and one flash-tier model, using hidden feature names, post-cutoff housing data and a pre-specified test that gives features the wrong descriptions. First, the models share their errors (correlation $0.92$--$0.99$ across draws, vendors and paraphrases): averaging $20$ draws is no more accurate than one, and treating draws as independent creates overconfidence. Much of this error comes from reporting each feature's effect alone, not with the others held fixed. Second, against the best classical prior, the LLM center helps clearly on one of four benchmarks (RMSE $-5.8\%$), marginally on two, and hurts mean RMSE on the fourth. Third, the LLM's stated uncertainty is unreliable; letting the data set the prior scale cuts the harm of a wrong center four-fold against a unit-variance prior. A pre-specified external test returned the verdict \textsc{partial}: on $18$ rule-selected problems the center helps on six and hurts on four, and a hard trust gate trusts a harmful prior while an evidence-weighted mixture is safer.
bullets: Across models, draws, and paraphrases, prediction errors are strongly shared; averaging 20 draws adds no accuracy and can cause overconfidence if treated as independent.
A major error source is describing each feature’s effect in isolation rather than conditional on the other features.
Compared with the best classical prior, LLM centers clearly help on 1 of 4 benchmarks, marginally help on 2, and worsen mean RMSE on 1.
LLM-reported uncertainty is unreliable; estimating prior scale from data reduces the harm of an incorrect center four-fold versus a unit-variance prior.
An external test found mixed outcomes: the center helped on 6 of 18 problems and hurt on 4; evidence-weighted mixtures were safer than a hard trust gate.

papers.selection_reason: Audits the use of LLMs as priors for small-sample Bayesian regression, evaluating their accuracy and uncertainty reliability.
papers.title: When Do LLM-Elicited Priors Help? A Controlled Audit of Language Models as Priors for Small-Sample Bayesian Regression

papers.abstract: In this paper we introduce a new benchmark dataset, NightmareDiscourseBench, for testing NLP pipelines that identify forms of direct discourse in English-language fiction. We first review existing publicly available benchmarks (providing summary statistics and reviewing available metadata) for this task, identifying theoretical inconsistency and exclusive focus on speech as primary issues in this domain. We then overview our narrative theory-based framework for classifying and evaluating different forms of direct discourse, and finally describe NightmareDiscourseBench, a new benchmark test set of 12 text samples accompanied by metadata pertinent to the task of direct discourse identification.
authors: Claudia Carroll, Gabi Kirilloff, Dashiell Leigh
bullets: Addresses inconsistencies in existing benchmarks for direct discourse identification.
Expands evaluation beyond speech-focused discourse forms.
Uses a narrative theory-based framework for classification and evaluation.
Provides 12 text samples with task-relevant metadata.
Covers English-language fictional texts; broader generalization is not established.

papers.abstract: Multilingual reasoning distillation requires choosing the language in which teacher reasoning is presented, yet existing recipes often entangle linguistic form with differences in generation, translation, and filtering. We construct content-controlled supervision by rendering the same verified English trajectories into English, translated target-language, and language-mixed shells, and fine-tune two pretrained students in three target languages, evaluating them on multilingual mathematical reasoning at two difficulty levels. Even with the underlying reasoning content held fixed, we find that shell choice can change downstream accuracy, with effects varying across students, languages, and difficulty levels. Pre-training compatibility does not consistently track these outcomes, and even when our tests find no clear accuracy difference between shells, their output-language behavior can still differ substantially. These results suggest that the supervision shell is a distinct design choice in multilingual reasoning distillation.
authors: Hoejoon Kwon, Jinhee Jang, Byeonggeuk Lim, YoungBin Kim
bullets: Uses identical verified English reasoning trajectories rendered as English, translated, or language-mixed shells.
Evaluates two pretrained students across three target languages and two mathematical-reasoning difficulty levels.
Shell choice changes accuracy, with effects varying by student, language, and difficulty.
Pre-training compatibility does not consistently predict which shell works best.
Even without clear accuracy differences, shells can produce substantially different output-language behavior.

papers.abstract: Child-safety taxonomies typically characterize safety risks through a predefined set of harm categories, and existing evaluations largely operationalize these categories using prompts that explicitly invoke them. However, child-safety considerations can also arise in seemingly benign requests that lack recognizable harm-category cues. We therefore investigate how child-safety alignment generalizes to such settings. Across six models, we find considerably higher misalignment rates on requests without recognizable harm-category cues than on those containing such cues (80.0, 54.0, and 48.4 percentage-point gaps for Qwen3.5-27B, GPT-5.4-mini, and Claude-Haiku-4.5, respectively). Through controlled behavioral and mechanistic analyses, we find that introducing a single harm-associated word reduces misalignment across most models, with mechanistic evidence suggesting that child-safety reasoning may rely in part on lexical and semantic associations with words in the prompt. Our findings motivate evaluations that treat child safety as context-dependent, and not reducible to a fixed set of harm categories.
authors: Anika Misra, Chimaobi Okite, Rada Mihalcea
bullets: Existing evaluations may overestimate child-safety alignment by focusing on prompts that name predefined harm categories.
Across six models, uncued requests produced higher misalignment than cued requests, with large model-specific gaps.
Adding one harm-associated word reduced misalignment across most models.
Behavioral and mechanistic analyses suggest lexical and semantic prompt associations partly drive safety reasoning.
The study supports context-dependent evaluations that extend beyond fixed harm categories.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) develop rich internal representations of language, but whether their individual coordinate axes carry meaning, or whether meaning is encoded only in directions in representation space, is still an open question. A common assumption is that individual axes in LLMs are arbitrary. We here challenge this view: across 12 LLMs from six model families, the native axes are reliably more aligned with other models' representations, with human brain responses to language, and with interpretable linguistic features than randomly rotated axes that preserve the same geometry. The native axes nonetheless fall well short of the best achievable alignment, so LLM coordinates are not fully arbitrary but also not fully canonical: they are partially canonical. A theory of how LLMs represent language must explain both the population geometry they learn and why individual units acquire patterns of response profiles that recur across systems.
authors: Andrea Gregor de Varda, Ferdinando D'Elia, Greta Tuckute, Evelina Fedorenko, Meenakshi Khosla
bullets: Tests 12 LLMs spanning six model families against randomly rotated representations with identical geometry.
Native axes align more reliably with other models, human language-related brain responses, and interpretable linguistic features.
The findings challenge the assumption that meaning exists only in directions rather than individual coordinates.
Native-coordinate alignment remains below the best achievable level, indicating incomplete canonicality.
A complete theory must explain both shared representation geometry and recurring unit response patterns.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Axis-by-axis alignment under rotation of the coordinates. A. Schematic of the unit matching procedure. Each coordinate axis of an LLM hidden representation X (one axis per unit) generates a response profile across the input stimuli. Each unit of a target representation Y (a unit of another LLM, a voxel in the brain, or an interpretable linguistic feature) is matched to its most correlated axis in X on a training split; the alignment score is the correlation r between matched pairs on held-out stimuli, averaged over target units in Y . B. The stimuli in X are represented as a point cloud in three coordinate frames (with all pairwise distances fully preserved). Left: a random orthogonal rotation (α = 1) moves away from the native axes but keeps the geometry intact. Middle: the native basis (α = 0), where each axis corresponds to one model unit. Right: the optimal rotation Q∗, learned by gradient descent on SO(n) to maximize the pairwise alignment with the target. If the native axes were arbitrary, the matching in A would give identical alignment scores in the left and middle panel; if they were fully canonical, it would give identical scores in the middle and right panels.

Figure 2. Three settings for probing the LLM representation basis. In each setting an LLM’s hidden representation (X) is aligned to a target representation (Y ) via axis-by-axis matching. For each basis of X (native or rotated), we match each target dimension to the single axis of X with which it has the highest absolute correlation on training stimuli and evaluate that match on held-out stimuli. Top: Model-to-model, where Y is the hidden representation of another LLM elicited by the same set of 627 naturalistic sentences (the 384 sentences of Pereira Experiment 2 combined with the 243 sentences of Pereira Experiment 3). Middle: Model-to-brain, where Y is human fMRI responses recorded in the language network while participants read the same 627 sentences across two experiments. Bottom: Model-to-feature, where Y is an interpretable linguistic feature, either a binary well-formedness label from a minimal-pair task (Y ∈ {0, 1}; morphology, syntax, hypernymy) or a multi-dimensional rating vector (Y ∈ Rk; perceptual and affective ratings).

Figure 4. Model-to-feature alignment as a function of rotation. Pairwise alignment of each LLM against five interpretable feature targets that span morphology (Wug), syntax (BLiMP, averaged across 12 sub-tasks) and lexical semantics (hypernymy minimal pairs; perceptual sensorimotor norms; affective valence/arousal/dominance norms). papers.selection_reason: Analyzes the internal representations of LLMs, finding that coordinate axes are partially canonical rather than arbitrary, providing insights into LLM geometry and interpretability.
papers.title: Partially canonical axes in large language model representations
papers.tldr: LLM representation axes are neither arbitrary nor fully standardized: native coordinates show meaningful cross-model, brain, and linguistic alignment, but remain only partially canonical.

papers.abstract: Researchers submitting deep learning jobs to shared GPU clusters need runtime estimates to request time limits, choose hardware, and budget compute. Large language models (LLMs) offer a tempting shortcut: describe the job and ask. We introduce PreRun, a benchmark for predicting deep learning training and inference runtime from information available before execution. PreRun contains 801 training and 1,884 inference records of language and vision models collected on a GPU cluster, paired with workload configurations and explicitly defined timing targets. It also includes 64 text-generation configurations measured under standardized conditions, each in three separate program launches. We compare three LLMs (Qwen3.5-9B, GPT-OSS-120B, and Claude Opus 5.5) with regression baselines and evaluate analytical estimates on a supported forward-pass subset. On 16 held-out generation configurations, the open-weight LLMs underestimate latency by 90-99% on average without examples. Claude's zero-shot mean absolute error is 4.5 times that of a Random Forest fit on 32 configurations. Five labeled examples substantially reduce Claude's generation error, but their benefit varies across timing targets. We will open-source our data and evaluation pipeline upon acceptance.
authors: Ashish Molakalapalli, Kangda Wei, Haonan Duan, Alex Carter, Ruihong Huang
bullets: Targets runtime prediction for shared-GPU scheduling, hardware selection, and compute budgeting.
Provides 801 training records, 1,884 inference records, and 64 standardized text-generation configurations with repeated launches.
Compares three LLMs with regression baselines and analytical estimates on a forward-pass subset.
On 16 held-out generation configurations, open-weight LLMs underestimated latency by 90–99% on average without examples.
Five labeled examples substantially improved Claude’s generation predictions, with benefits varying by timing target.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces PreRun, a benchmark for predicting LLM runtime on GPU clusters, directly relevant to LLM behavior and resource estimation.
papers.title: How Long Will My Language Model Run? A Benchmark for Pre-Execution Runtime Prediction
papers.tldr: PreRun benchmarks how well LLMs can predict deep-learning training and inference runtimes before execution, finding that zero-shot estimates are often highly inaccurate but improve with labeled examples.

papers.abstract: Weight-space programming is a frontier language model's recently reported ability to read and rewrite another network's weights without gradient descent. We investigate how examples can provide a weight update so that a weaker language model performs the task with nothing in the prompt, and study what it edits. Our experiments cover six tasks, four frontier editors and three families of weaker language models, without the editors being told anything about in-context learning (ICL). In most runs, the few-shot minus zero-shot residual is measured at the final prompt token, the ICL task vector, and write it into the weights, at its sparsest into near-silent MLP units keyed to the prompt format. Results reach the accuracy of ICL and of fine-tuning on the same examples, LoRA included, usually leaving perplexity untouched, with worse performance under changes of wording. We also qualify the comparison by counting unfinished runs, observing that one editor falls below fine-tuning; held only to the seen examples, without task pairs of their own, only the strongest editor has similar performance. Given a task and unlabelled inputs, that editor writes its own examples and does nearly as well on unseen items as with labels.
bullets: The study examines six tasks, four frontier editors, and three families of weaker language models.
Editors convert few-shot-minus-zero-shot behavior into a task vector and write it into model weights.
The sparsest updates target near-silent MLP units associated with prompt format.
Performance usually matches in-context learning and fine-tuning, including LoRA, while leaving perplexity largely unchanged.
Performance worsens with wording changes; one editor underperforms fine-tuning, and comparable results on unseen items are limited mainly to the strongest editor.

papers.selection_reason: Weight-space programming writes ICL into model weights, matching fine-tuning.
papers.title: Weight-Space Programming Writes In-Context Learning and Matches Fine-Tuning in Language Models
papers.tldr: Weight-space programming lets frontier models write in-context-learning behavior into weaker models’ weights, often matching in-context learning and fine-tuning without gradient descent.

papers.abstract: Recent work has shown that continued fraction inspired neural architectures (CoFrGeNets) can be highly parameter efficient yet performant for language modeling. In this work, we revisit continued fraction-based channel mixing with the goal of improving its performance and simplifying integration into standard pre-training protocols for language models. We achieve this by two simple yet critical contributions: i) we propose a novel non-expanding gated continued fraction inspired architectural component to replace feedforward layers in established language model architectures that may use vanilla multilayer perceptrons or gated linear units or (vanilla/gated) experts in mixture-of-experts (MoE) type architectures. ii) We propose a way to re-implement divisions -- the non-linearity in these architectures -- in terms of logarithms and exponentials. By experimenting on different language modeling architectures such as GPT-2, Llama-3, Mamba-2 and (nano) Llama-MoE we find that our proposed architecture performs similarly or significantly better than the continued fraction architecture proposed in prior work along with having higher throughput. In addition, our re-implementation of divisions makes training of deeper CoFrGeNets stable without the need for incremental training which was proposed in prior work as a means to stabilize training, but added notable complexity to existing large language model training implementations. Code is available at http://github.com/IBM/CoFrNets
authors: Amit Dhurandhar, Vijil Chenthamarakshan, Karthikeyan Natesan Ramamurthy, Dennis Wei, Rahul Nair
bullets: Targets parameter-efficient continued-fraction channel mixing for language models.
Introduces a non-expanding gated component compatible with MLPs, GLUs, and MoE experts.
Reformulates division using logarithms and exponentials to simplify and stabilize training.
Across GPT-2, Llama-3, Mamba-2, and Llama-MoE variants, performance is similar or better than prior continued-fraction designs with higher throughput.
Eliminates the need for prior incremental-training procedures for stable deeper CoFrGeNets.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Above we see our continued fraction inspired architecture that can replace feedforward layers in dense as well as MoE architectures. Our architecture performs a non-expansive gating of the input that then passes through an (ensemble of) continued fraction ladders. The fact that we do not expand the hidden representation and each layer of our ladders requires only a linear number of parameters we obtain significant parameter savings over typical (gated and vanilla) feedforward layers leading to dense models that are ≈ 2 3 the size and MoEs that are ≈ 1 2 the size. In our implementations we create a different class for CoFrGeNet that has the same api as the FFN class, that is, same parameters are passed and the same size output tensor (equal to embedding size) is returned. The depth and width parameters for CoFrGeNet could be additionally passed or just set in the CoFrGeNet class itself. Hence, no changes are made to the residual stream or other aspects of the original architecture. The input x1, ..., xp in the figure is thus simply the output of the attention or SSM layer where the residual stream is added and the representation normalized in the particular block. In other words, nothing else in the model architectures changes and the input and output tensors are both size embedding dimension.

Figure 3: CoFrNet architecture from [14] to simulate FFNs. Two ensembles are used each consisting of specified number of p-variate ladders. Element wise multiplication is done between the representations coming out of the linear layer of each ensemble for higher expressivity.

The docling data mix of 2 trillion tokens was used for pre-training.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a new feedforward architecture for LLMs, directly relevant to LLM architectural advances.
papers.title: Non-Expanding Gated Continued Fraction Architecture for Feedforward Layers in Language Models
papers.tldr: A non-expanding gated continued-fraction layer can replace feedforward components in diverse language models while improving throughput and stabilizing deeper training.

papers.abstract: Modern language models (LMs) are increasingly deployed with access to search tools at inference. Yet pretraining remains predominantly focused on predicting static text, with search capabilities typically introduced during post-training. We propose Search-Native Pretraining as a practical route to teach search capability during pretraining from ordinary text corpora. Specifically, we augment pretraining corpus at scale with web-search queries and retrieve web response using a local index. Training on this augmented corpus teaches models to generate search calls and incorporate retrieved evidence during language modeling. Across Wikipedia and DCLM-Edu corpora and 360M to 3.3B parameter scales, search-pretrained models ("QueryLM") show improved performance on knowledge-intensive tasks and higher steerability toward the retrieved evidence. Crucially, their advantage persists after supervised fine-tuning of both search-pretrained and conventionally pretrained models, indicating that the tested post-training procedures do not fully recover the capabilities developed during pretraining. Throughout our experiments, we find that a 1.4B QueryLM consistently beats or matches the performance of a FLOP-matched 3.3B baseline model across all knowledge intensive tasks. These results establish search-pretraining as a practical way to develop foundational search capabilities during pretraining. We release the training artifacts, including model checkpoints and data.
authors: Kaustubh Ponkshe, Gyung Hyun Je, Stefan Taga, Colin Raffel, Martin Jaggi
bullets: Motivation: Search is often added only after static-text pretraining, potentially limiting foundational search ability.
Method: Augment ordinary text corpora with web-search queries and responses retrieved from a local index, then train models on the resulting data.
Result: QueryLM models improve knowledge-intensive task performance and follow retrieved evidence more effectively across tested model scales and corpora.
The gains persist after supervised fine-tuning, suggesting the tested post-training methods do not fully recover capabilities learned through search-pretraining.
A 1.4B QueryLM consistently matches or outperforms a FLOP-matched 3.3B conventional baseline on the reported knowledge-intensive tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Search-Native Pretraining pipeline overview. (1) We augment training documents with inline search queries and corresponding search results, intended to contain useful knowledge for predicting original document continuation. (2) We train on (1), computing loss only on original document tokens and search queries (green), while search results are masked (gray). papers.abstract: We show that reinforcement learning (RL) in reasoning tasks can succeed even when the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data is severely corrupted. In a mathematical reasoning dataset (GSM8K), we systematically corrupt training trajectories across 361 configurations by injecting realistic error types, varying error locations, trace-answer consistency, and corruption ratios up to 100%. While aggregated SFT-only performance steadily deteriorates under corruption (dropping from 43.61% to 13.80%), Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) post-training consistently restores model accuracy back to gold-baseline levels (approximately 60%). Crucially, initializing RL with as few as N = 8 minimal, incorrect, three-line "form-only" traces boosts post-RL performance to 69.30%, outperforming standard gold SFT initialization (60.71%) and GRPO without SFT (35.00%). Further, we show that SFT accuracy is largely uncorrelated with post-RL accuracy (r approximately 0), demonstrating a fundamental asymmetry in post-training: SFT primarily establishes structural layout (form), while RL independently discovers functional reasoning (function).
authors: Anika Misra, Shreyas Vinod, Huteng Dai
bullets: Evaluated 361 corruption settings on GSM8K, including errors in locations, trace–answer consistency, and corruption rates up to 100%.
SFT-only accuracy fell from 43.61% to 13.80% as corruption increased.
GRPO generally restored performance to roughly gold-baseline levels (~60%) despite corrupted initialization.
Initializing with just 8 incorrect three-line form-only traces reached 69.30%, versus 60.71% with gold SFT and 35.00% without SFT.
SFT accuracy was nearly uncorrelated with post-RL accuracy (r≈0), indicating distinct roles for structural form and functional reasoning.

papers.abstract: Recent gated linear attention models use state-independent gates, computed from token representations without directly reading the recurrent memory. This design supports efficient chunkwise computation: sequences are divided into chunks of consecutive tokens, with parallel computation within each chunk. However, the same token representation produces the same gate, even when the layer stores different information. We introduce State-Dependent Gating (SDG), which computes element-wise gates from the change in memory over a chunk and applies them at the chunk boundary. This provides state feedback for forgetting while preserving parallel computation within each chunk. We develop fused kernels for Gated DeltaNet, Kimi Delta Attention, Gated DeltaNet-2, and Mamba-3. Our theoretical analysis quantifies the potential reconstruction benefits of state-dependent, element-wise gating under a signal--noise model. We also show that boundary decay is an element-wise ridge proximal step when the gate is held fixed. Empirical evaluation of 1.3B linear attention and hybrid models trained on 100B tokens shows improvements across language modeling, commonsense reasoning, synthetic and real-world retrieval, and long-context understanding. These results demonstrate that SDG is an effective approach to enhancing existing linear attention models.
authors: Renjia Deng, Yuxi Liu, Yutong He, Xue Wang, Kun Yuan
bullets: Existing gated linear attention uses state-independent gates, which ignore the information currently stored in recurrent memory.
SDG computes element-wise gates from the memory change over each chunk and applies them at the chunk boundary.
The approach preserves parallel within-chunk computation and is implemented with fused kernels for several linear-attention architectures.
Theory connects SDG to improved signal reconstruction and interprets fixed-gate boundary decay as an element-wise ridge proximal step.
Experiments on 1.3B models trained on 100B tokens report improvements across language modeling, reasoning, retrieval, and long-context understanding.

papers.abstract: Routed low-rank adapters offer a parameter-efficient means to improve the performance of large language models (LLMs) across tasks. Hence, it is assumed that they can also be used to improve the support of low-resource languages in LLMs, which currently serve English far better than the thousands of other languages spoken worldwide. However, this assumption has never been verified empirically under a shared multilingual evaluation protocol. We address exactly this gap by comparing eight low-rank adaptation (LoRA) methods on a frozen base model, using 146 training runs across 200 unique languages and more than 10,000 evaluations. Our results suggest that a reduced-scale search can identify viable configurations of LoRA methods but does not reliably predict their relative performance, as the top-ranking configuration is never best at scale. LoRA reliably improves language-model fit on translation data, consistently degrades reading comprehension, and benefits low-resource languages most. These findings suggest that LoRA methods should be regarded as targeted tools rather than general-purpose means for improving the multilingual capabilities of LLMs.
bullets: Compares eight LoRA methods on a frozen base model across 146 training runs, 200 languages, and over 10,000 evaluations.
Shows that reduced-scale searches can find viable configurations but do not reliably predict full-scale rankings.
LoRA consistently improves fit on translation data, with the strongest benefits for low-resource languages.
Reading comprehension degrades consistently after adaptation.
Concludes that LoRA methods are best used as targeted tools for multilingual adaptation.

papers.abstract: Natural language autoencoders (NLAs) are a method for generating natural language explanations of LLM activations. We develop evaluations based on auditing tasks that test the ability of NLAs to surface latent knowledge, identify whether a model was misled by a hint, and catch a silent fabrication. We also develop extensions to NLAs that let them use activation information from multiple layers and positions, let us apply them more effectively to long transcripts, and reduce the number of false claims they make. These extensions result in improvements on both our auditing evaluations and auxiliary evaluations adapted from prior work. We also use the evaluations to study how different auditing capabilities change over the course of NLA training, and find that although every evaluation improves early in training, extended training can hurt performance on some of our auditing evaluations.
bullets: Evaluates whether NLAs can expose latent knowledge, detect misleading hints, and catch silent fabrications.
Extends NLAs to use activation information from multiple layers and positions.
Improves NLA handling of long transcripts and reduces false claims.
Reports improvements on new auditing evaluations and auxiliary evaluations from prior work.
Finds that auditing performance improves early in training but may decline with extended training.

papers.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) paired with Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has become the dominant recipe for post-training LLMs on complex reasoning tasks, but has been shown to collapse the policy into a low-diversity mode. Repeated LLM outputs are nearly identical, and pass@k accuracy converges or degrades as a result. We propose ROAM-GRPO (Routed Off-mode Approach Mining for GRPO), an augmentation to the GRPO algorithm which incentivizes exploration of distinct reasoning strategies and aims to increase output creativity during evaluation. ROAM-GRPO detects well-solved problems during training and transfers them to an "off-mode" track. The model is prompted to produce distinct solution strategies to such problems, which are verified for logical validity and distinctness by an LLM judge and subsequently self-distilled into the policy. Training Qwen3.5-2b on a 1,000-problem subset of the MATH lvl5 dataset, ROAM-GRPO implementation increases peak pass@16 by 4.7% and correct embedding cosine distance by approximately 1.5-2x on a difficult evaluation set.
bullets: Addresses low-diversity reasoning and declining or saturated pass@k performance after SFT and RLVR.
Routes well-solved training problems into an off-mode track for generating distinct solution approaches.
Uses an LLM judge to verify logical validity and strategy distinctness before self-distillation.
On Qwen3.5-2b trained with 1,000 MATH level-5 problems, it raises peak pass@16 by 4.7% and roughly doubles correct embedding cosine distance.
The reported evaluation focuses on a difficult evaluation set and this training configuration.

papers.abstract: Does post-training change what a language model represents, or how this representation is read out into an answer? We compared linear probes with the models' own answers, analyzed with signal detection theory, in six open-weight base models and their post-trained versions. For judgments of whether German texts were written by a human or an AI, probes and word n-gram classifiers separated the classes well, but the answers did not and often ordered the texts inversely. Post-training lowered the sensitivity of the answers on average ($\Delta d' = -0.34$ across model families; -0.29 across three prompts). It also changed the use of a stated base rate: Base models shifted their log-odds by less than the stated change in prior odds, most post-trained models by more. In two models with stage-wise checkpoints, the change occurred during supervised fine-tuning, model stitching implicated the early layers, and from mid-depth on internal states at positions after the text, not those of the text, transferred the change between checkpoints. Our corpora cannot be shared, so we add a case reproducible from public data, the truth of negated statements. Here, post-training acted in the opposite direction: Probes decoded truth at or near ceiling in every model, the answers of several base models did not use it, and post-training repaired them; by mid-depth the repair resided at the positions after the statement; below it, the representation of the statement contributed, strongly in one of four models. In a training study, adding 2,000 correctly labeled authorship judgments of news texts to otherwise identical fine-tuning data improved the answers on our newspaper and textbook corpora and inverted them on the chats, where they followed a news-trained probe of the base model. Post-training thus changed how a judgment is read out of what a model represents, and a small training signal can set its direction.
bullets: Across six open-weight model families, probes often decoded authorship information well even when model answers did not.
For German human-versus-AI judgments, post-training reduced answer sensitivity on average and altered how models used stated base rates.
Stage-wise analyses linked the change mainly to supervised fine-tuning and later-layer states at positions after the input text.
For truth of negated statements, representations remained highly decodable while post-training improved several models’ answers—the opposite pattern.
Adding 2,000 labeled authorship examples changed answer behavior across text types, including reversals, showing that limited training signals can set readout direction.

figures.caption: Figure 2. How the interventions work. In panels A, C, and D, the horizontal axis shows the positions of the prompt in reading order (the instruction, the text to be judged, the question, and the position at which the answer is produced), and the vertical axis shows the layers of the network. (A) Information flow: through attention, later positions read information from earlier ones. The answer is produced at the last position. Information from the text reaches it through the positions after the text: the question (dark tiles) and the last position itself, which also reads the text directly at every layer (the schematic shows only the route via the question). (B) Steering, sketched in a two-dimensional version of the highdimensional representation space: human texts (open circles) and AI texts (triangles) differ along an AI–human direction (arrow between the class means). Steering moves the state of one text along this direction (diamonds) and measures how the model’s answer changes; the dashed line marks where the answer switches. The two need not be orthogonal: the angle between the AI–human direction and the model’s decision boundary determines how strongly a shift along the direction changes the answer. If the model read the direction correctly, a shift toward the AI texts would move the answer toward “KI”. (C) Model stitching combines the lower layers of one checkpoint (here the base model, blue) with the upper layers of another (here the SFT model, orange). (D) Activation patching replaces the internal states of one model (here SFT) at selected positions and one layer with those of the other model (here the base model’s states at the question positions).

Figure 1. Brunswik’s lens model, applied to a language model as judge and extended by an internal lens. A state of the world (Brunswik’s distal criterion; the ground truth, here whether a text was written by an AI, whether a statement is true, or whether a review is genuine) is reflected in observable cues of the text, some of which are valid and some of which are not (dashed). In the first lens (encoding), the model integrates these cues into its internal representation; whether the ground truth can be decoded from this representation is measured with linear probes, and whether two checkpoints represent it in the same way with probe transfer. In the second lens (readout), the representation is read out into an answer to the question by weighting internal features. Only one of these features wasmeasured directly: the class direction, i.e., the direction that separates the two classes in the representation; its relation to the answer was examined with steering at the answer position (Appendix D). The other features are schematic. Achievement, i.e., the agreement of the answer with the state of the world, requires both lenses. Post-training changes mainly the second lens (orange), and in several cases also the first (Sections 3.4 and 3.6); model stitching and activation patching locate the change in depth and in the prompt. Splitting the judge side of the lens model has precedents in personality judgment (detection vs. utilization of cues; Funder, 1995) and in neuroscience (information encoded in a neural population vs. read out for behavior; Panzeri et al., 2017). Note: for the authorship corpora, probes were fitted both on the text positions and on the last prompt position; for the truth and review sets, only on the last prompt position.

Figure 3. The authorship information is available but not used. Sensitivity (d′) for separating AI from human texts in the three corpora. Upper rows: classifiers on word and character n-grams and on surface statistics, probes on the average input embedding and on the internal activations at two thirds of the network depth, and an externally trained detector (EditLens). Lines show 95% bootstrap confidence intervals, except for the two probe rows, where they show the range across models. Lower rows: sensitivity of the models’ own answers (raw prompt), one small dot per model, large dot = median. The dashed line marks the maximum d′ that can be estimated with the given number of texts.

Figure 5. Authorship: model stitching and activation patching at layer 16. (A)Model stitching between base and SFT checkpoints (textbook summaries; the numbers of layers that were tested differ between the two directions and between the models). The x-axis gives the number of lower layers taken from the other checkpoint. Blue: base layers below, SFT layers above; orange: SFT layers below, base layers above. Dashed and dotted lines mark the sensitivity of the unmodified base and SFT models; bands are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. (B) Activation patching at layer 16: sensitivity after exchanging the internal states at the indicated positions. Blue: base model’s states inserted into the SFT model; orange: SFT model’s states inserted into the base model. “Unpatched” shows the recipient model without any exchange. Error bars are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Patching at layer 8 (more mixed; text positions contribute somewhat) is shown in Supplementary Figure S1.

Figure 6. Authorship: activation patching across layers (textbook summaries, 238 texts; error bars: 95% grouped-bootstrap confidence intervals). Sensitivity (d′) of the recipient checkpoint after its residual stream was replaced by the donor’s at one set of positions and one layer: the instruction before the text, the tokens of the text, the question and answer cue after the text, the final position only, or all positions. Note that the two rows have different scales. Horizontal lines show the unpatched recipient (dotted) and the donor (dashed). In OLMo 2, the text states had no effect at any layer; in Apertus, they carried part of the difference between the checkpoints up to layer 12. The instruction positions carried part of it in the lower layers of both models. From layer 14 onward, the states after the text carried it in both models. Hybrids can lie outside the range of the two checkpoints.

Figure 4. Post-training mostly lowers the sensitivity of the answers; with 16 labelled examples, most models improve. (A) Sensitivity of the base model (blue) and of the final post-trained model with the identical raw prompt (filled orange) and with its chat template (open orange), per model and corpus. Asterisks mark differences between the base and the final model on the identical raw prompt that survive Holm correction within the family of 18 final-vs-base comparisons; all of them are decreases. The increases of OLMo 2 on the short chats and of OLMo 3 Think on the textbook summaries are significant only without correction or under false-discovery-rate control (the latter in a condition with low answer probability, ≈ .30). Multilevel random-effects summary across all 18 comparisons: Δd′ = −0.33 [−0.53, −0.13]. (B) Sensitivity as a function of the number of labelled examples placed before each text (raw prompt; base vs. final post-trained model). Points show the mean of d′ computed separately for each of four example sets; vertical lines show their range. Whether base models profit more than post-trained models (difference of gains, 0 vs. 16 examples) is tested in the supplement: the base model gained more in four of five comparisons, reliably only for OLMo 2 on the chats; for Qwen3 on the textbook summaries, the post-trained model gained more. On the textbook summaries, only 0, 8, and 16 examples were tested; for OLMo 2 only 0 and 8, because 16 textbook summaries exceed its context window of 4,096 tokens.

Figure 7. Negated statements: where supervised fine-tuning repairs the readout (300 statement pairs; error bars: 95% grouped-bootstrap confidence intervals). (A) Model stitching: sensitivity (d′) of the answers of hybrids that take the first ℓ layers from one checkpoint and all layers above from the other; horizontal lines show the unstitched base (dotted) and SFT (dashed) checkpoints. (B) Activation patching at layers 8 and 16: d′ of the recipient checkpoint after its residual streamwas replaced by the donor’s at one set of positions (the statement, the instruction before it, the question and answer cue after it, the final position only, or all positions); dotted lines show the unpatched recipients. Note that in the truth prompt the question precedes the statement, so that the positions after the statement contain only the answer instruction and cue. (C) The same exchange at 12 layers (100 statement pairs), for base and SFT model of OLMo 2 and Apertus and for base and final post-trained model of Gemma 3 4B and 12B: share of the difference between the two checkpoints that the exchange transferred (values below 0 and above 1 are clipped). Upper row: the base model receives the states of the post-trained model (“into base”); lower row: the post-trained model receives the states of the base model.

papers.selection_reason: Examines how post-training changes LLM readout of represented information, relevant to language foundation model behavior.
papers.title: Represented but misread: Post-training changes how language models read out what they represent
papers.tldr: Post-training can change how language models read out existing representations, sometimes degrading judgments and sometimes repairing them, with small training signals influencing the direction.

papers.abstract: Task success alone does not specify which behaviors post-training should reinforce. Even successful teacher trajectories can contain unsupported assumptions, unproductive repetition, or superficial verification. We propose Skill-FT (Skill-Guided Fine-Tuning), which uses natural-language skills to suppress undesirable habits and elicit underrepresented effective behaviors during teacher rollouts, then fine-tunes a target model on the resulting trajectories. We introduce AutoMaster, an autonomous post-training system in which an LLM agent develops these interventions through trajectory analysis, skill design, data selection, and feedback from rollouts and target-model evaluation. Across Terminal, Search, and software engineering tasks with 4B and 9B target models, AutoMaster improves mean performance over Vanilla SFT on successful unguided teacher trajectories by 1.42-8.99 percentage points, with the teacher, task pool, training set size, and SFT recipe held fixed. Together with the ablations and trajectory analyses, these results suggest that behavioral shaping can make a fixed model a more effective teacher. We further find that retaining skill instructions during SFT yields higher mean performance than removing them across all six settings, despite their absence at evaluation and identical supervised outputs. These findings suggest that preserving skill context as part of a training demonstration can support better behavioral internalization.
authors: Guoxin Chen, Shuang Sun, Fanzhe Meng, Xinyu Tang, Ruihua Song, Wayne Xin Zhao
bullets: Addresses the problem that task success alone does not identify which teacher behaviors should be reinforced.
Skill-FT applies natural-language skills during teacher rollouts, followed by fine-tuning on the resulting trajectories.
AutoMaster automates skill design, trajectory analysis, data selection, and feedback from rollouts and target-model evaluation.
Across Terminal, Search, and software engineering tasks with 4B and 9B models, it improves mean performance over Vanilla SFT by 1.42–8.99 percentage points under fixed training conditions.
Keeping skill instructions during SFT improves performance across all six settings, even though they are absent at evaluation.

figures.caption: Figure 1. A correct result is only part of what a teacher demonstrates. AutoMaster designs natural-language skills to guide teacher rollouts and selects demonstrations for fine-tuning. (a) In this example, both pipelines process all 100 records with four workers. The skill-guided teacher also checks whether the fix holds with fewer or more workers. (b) With the same teacher, task pool, training set size, and SFT recipe, students trained with AutoMaster achieve higher performance than their Vanilla SFT counterparts on all three benchmarks at both model sizes (4B and 9B). Labels above the bars show gains of 1.42–8.99 percentage points over Vanilla SFT. Error bars show ±1 SD over three evaluation runs per checkpoint.

Figure 2. Overview of AutoMaster. An LLM agent designs skills for subsets of a fixed training task pool and tests them in pilot teacher rollouts. It refines the skills as needed, runs promising interventions on larger batches, and selects demonstrations for SFT. In each outer-loop round, the student is trained from the same initial checkpoint, with any skill instructions used by the teacher retained in the training input. The student is evaluated without generated skills.

Figure 4. Contributions of skill guidance and data selection. w/o Skill Guidance retains agentdirected selection from unguided teacher rollouts. w/o Data Selection retains skill guidance on a fixed random subset of tasks but omits agent-directed trajectory selection. Removing either component lowers the mean score in each of the six settings. Task-Matched SFT uses unguided rollouts from the same teacher and matches the final training set of AutoMaster. Even with this match, AutoMaster scores 1.08–10.11 percentage points higher on average within each setting. Points show mean scores over three evaluation runs per checkpoint. Horizontal bars indicate ±1 standard deviation.

Figure 7. Explicit use of skill context in teacher demonstrations. Two examples from the SFT corpus illustrate how skill instructions inform the teacher’s reasoning and actions. (a) The teacher applies a conditional rule to distinguish interpreter invocation from direct execution, avoiding an unnecessary permission change. (b) The teacher references the supplied grammar to derive an expression’s grouping, then implements and tests the corresponding parser. Skill instructions and trajectory excerpts are condensed. Quotation marks indicate verbatim excerpts.

Figure 5. Skill-guided changes in teacher behavior. Each column compares unguided and skill-guided rollouts by the same teacher on the same task. (a) Terminal: Both solvers meet the error threshold. The unguided teacher claims fourth-order accuracy despite evidence of second-order convergence. The skill-guided teacher switches to a nine-point stencil and verifies fourth-order convergence using direct solves on successively finer grids. (b) Search: Both rollouts identify the same episode. The unguided teacher repeatedly guesses the award, while the skill-guided teacher identifies the director from episode credits and verifies the clues. (c) SWE: The unguided teacher reverses the global sort to satisfy a flawed self-test. The skill-guided teacher checks the UTF-16 encoding, corrects the self-test input, and keeps the required ascending order.

Figure 3. Infrastructure of AutoMaster. The agent accesses data and submits rollout and SFT jobs through the MCP interface. After SFT, the execution controller automatically schedules evaluation on a separate GPU cluster, where SGLang workers load the checkpoint directly from storage shared with the training cluster. Linked experiment records let the agent trace each evaluation back to the training set and the skills that guided the teacher.

Figure 6. Retaining skill instructions during SFT improves performance without test-time skills. Both conditions use the same teacher trajectories and SFT recipe. Keep retains the skill instructions in the training input, whereas Remove omits them. All students are evaluated without skills under the official benchmark protocols. Bars show mean scores over three evaluation runs per checkpoint, circles show individual runs, and error bars indicate ±1 SD. Labels give the gain of Keep over Remove in percentage points.

Table 1. Main results with Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B. We report task accuracy for TerminalBench 2.1 and BrowseComp, and mean test pass rate for Doc2Repo, all in percent (higher is better). Results are mean ± SD over three evaluation runs per checkpoint. Bold marks the highest mean in each column. ∆ gives the gain over Vanilla SFT in percentage points.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes an autonomous post-training system with skill-guided fine-tuning for LLMs, relevant to language foundation model research.
papers.title: AutoMaster: Autonomous Post-Training by Making the Same Model a Better Teacher
papers.tldr: AutoMaster autonomously improves post-training by using skill-guided teacher rollouts to suppress unproductive behaviors and elicit more effective ones.

papers.abstract: Decision models enable fast, confidence-aware decisions by scoring candidate answers in a single forward pass, without generating text or intermediate reasoning. Yet reasoning can substantially improve decision quality, raising the question of whether its benefits can be retained without the cost of generating it. We investigate this question with \textbf{GLiDE}, a family of decision models spanning 0.4B to 27B parameters. Building on Qwen hybrid language models, GLiDE enables bidirectional interactions between the context, question, and candidate answers by removing causal masking from full-attention layers. To transfer reasoning capabilities into single-pass inference, we combine soft-target distillation from multiple teachers, including a reasoning model, with progressive post-training on diverse decision tasks. We further explore parameter-free recurrent depth to increase inference-time computation without generating tokens. Across five model sizes, GLiDE lies on the performance--parameter Pareto frontier of the Hugging Face \DI{}, with each model outperforming evaluated alternatives of equal or smaller size. \dmtwo{} (27B) achieves a hidden-set score of 71.52, with an expected calibration error of 2.0\% and a median latency of 92.9\,ms on a single GPU. Further checkpoint averaging and parameter-free recurrent depth yield GLiDE~27B, which reaches 73.37 with an expected calibration error of 2.1\%.
authors: Sahibzada Allahyar, Julia White, Dhruv Atreja, George Hurn-Maloney, Urchade Zaratiana
bullets: Targets confidence-aware candidate selection while avoiding the latency and token generation costs of explicit reasoning.
Uses bidirectional full-attention interactions among context, questions, and candidate answers in Qwen-based hybrid models.
Combines soft-target distillation from multiple teachers—including a reasoning model—with progressive post-training across diverse decision tasks.
Provides models from 0.4B to 27B parameters that the abstract reports as lying on the Hugging Face decision-model performance–parameter Pareto frontier.

The 27B variant reaches a hidden-set score of 73.37 with 2.1% expected calibration error after checkpoint averaging and parameter-free recurrent depth; scope is evaluated on five model sizes and the stated benchmark.

figures.caption: Figure 2: GLiDE V1.2 architecture. Each decision is encoded as a single sequence containing the context, question, coded candidate answers, and an answer prefix. Starting from a 64-layer Qwen hybrid decoder, GLiDE removes causal masking from its 16 full-attention layers, enabling bidirectional interactions while retaining causal recurrence in the 48 Gated DeltaNet layers. A dedicated 255-way readout scores the final hidden state, and a softmax over the offered options produces a normalized probability distribution. Decisions are computed in a single forward pass, without generating tokens or intermediate reasoning. Appendix C details the output semantics and deployment policies.

papers.abstract: Pretrained language models (LMs) remain unreliable on exact multi-digit arithmetic without gradient fine-tuning or external tool interpreters. We introduce closed-form, zero-gradient circuit-grafting primitives that compile deterministic computation directly into pretrained LM weights using zero training examples and zero runtime hooks, while bounding per-layer normalization drift and preserving natural-language (NL) competence. Our construction combines three analytical mechanisms: (1) two-layer Mellin-GLU quadrature over bias-free SwiGLU/GeGLU layers, turning unknown per-token RMSNorm scaling into translation along a log-spaced gate grid ($>250\times$ dynamic range) with IEEE 754 error bounds; (2) cross-token scale cancellation via signed Chebyshev Indefinite-RoPE self-sink attention and memoryless SiLU-antisymmetric GatedDeltaNet shifts; and (3) axis-aligned width extension ($d \to d+K$) with $\sqrt{d/(d+K)}$ norm compensation, Base-1000 canonical BPE emission, and differential $(+254,-256)$ tied unembeddings. An automated 5-stage compiler synthesizes 4-8 digit signed $\{+,-,\times\}$ circuits in constant $\mathsf{TC}^0$ depth alongside 3-literal Boolean (100%, $N=1{,}728$; plus 42-layer Gemma 4 E4B audits) and 5-bit Majority/Parity (100%) circuits. On 6-digit arithmetic ($N=1{,}200$, BF16), IBM Granite 4.2 3B (1.07M-1.33M active non-zeros, $\le 0.036\%$) and Alibaba Qwen 3.5 4B (2.25M-2.39M non-zeros, $\le 0.057\%$) reach 99.17% and 100.00% ALU-prefix accuracy (100% with an FP32 sidecar) and 98%-100% mid-sentence resumption, outperforming 12.8K-sample LoRA (42.2% / 61.7%, 0% inline continuation). A factorized block-sparse sidecar holds A100 memory at 7.89 / 10.65 GiB (4.60 / 8.14 GiB under INT8/INT4 + FP32 sidecar) while passing all 14/14 pre-registered $>2$K-token Tango splits ($N=4{,}392$; 0/11,134 OOD triggers).
bullets: Addresses unreliable exact multi-digit arithmetic without fine-tuning or external interpreters.
Uses closed-form Mellin-GLU quadrature, scale-canceling attention/state shifts, width extension, and canonical token emission.
Compiles signed 4–8 digit addition, subtraction, and multiplication plus Boolean and Majority/Parity circuits.
Reports 99.17–100% six-digit ALU-prefix accuracy and 98–100% mid-sentence resumption on two models; FP32 sidecars reach 100%.
Scope includes specific arithmetic/logic circuits and evaluated models; results rely on sparse weight edits and optional sidecars.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a highly novel zero-gradient method to compile exact circuits into pretrained LLM weights, relevant to LLM capabilities and architecture.
papers.title: A CPU Inside an LLM: Zero-Gradient Compilation of Exact Circuits into Pretrained Weights
papers.tldr: A zero-gradient compiler grafts exact arithmetic and logic circuits into pretrained LMs with minimal sparse weight changes and no runtime hooks, achieving near-perfect reported accuracy while largely preserving language behavior.

papers.abstract: It has been demonstrated that, in certain settings, large language models can perform weight-space programming to directly modify the weights of neural networks. However, it is unknown how dedicated training of these networks can contribute to the successes of weight-space programming. We present a benchmark of LLM-driven weight-space programming on vision models, in which five LLMs edit convolutional networks and vision transformers on relabeling and error-correction tasks on Waterbirds, CIFAR-100, PACS and Entity-30. We report more than 2,600 such edit processes, whereby each edit is scored on held-out images for success, side effects and accuracy loss. We compare standard training with label smoothing, gradient-based editable training, and our Edit-Ready Training (ERT), a novel method that rehearses the direct, closed-form weight edits LLMs perform. We show that preparing networks for editing raises the success of LLM edits substantially where standard networks are hard to edit. ERT further achieves the highest mean score for GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 across all evaluated baselines. We will release our LLM testing framework alongside all tasks, editing trajectories and scores. Project page: https://viscom.uni-ulm.de/wsp
bullets: Evaluates five LLMs editing convolutional networks and vision transformers on relabeling and error-correction tasks.
Covers Waterbirds, CIFAR-100, PACS, and Entity-30, with more than 2,600 edit processes scored for success, side effects, and accuracy loss.
Compares standard training, label smoothing, gradient-based editable training, and Edit-Ready Training (ERT).
ERT rehearses the direct closed-form weight edits performed by LLMs and achieves the highest mean score for GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 across evaluated baselines.
The framework, tasks, editing trajectories, and scores are planned for release.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces Edit-Ready Training (ERT) to prepare vision models for LLM-driven weight-space programming. This explores a novel interaction paradigm between LLMs and vision models, relevant to both language and multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Training Vision Models for LLM-Driven Weight-Space Programming
papers.tldr: A benchmark shows that training vision models specifically for LLM-driven weight edits—especially with Edit-Ready Training—substantially improves editability and performance.

papers.abstract: Attention in large language models (LLMs) scores every query against every key with a full dot product. We investigate whether this dot product must be computed completely for attention to be effective. We propose Hidden Sparse Attention (HiSA), which keeps the query and key projections intact but only computes a partial dot product, following a static, parameter-free rule set by the token positions: attention becomes sparse in the hidden (feature) dimension, an axis much less explored than token sparsity, rather than over tokens as in almost all sparse attention methods. Based on the structure of rotary position embeddings (RoPE), we decompose keys and queries into parts which can be omitted when computing attention. By training LLMs from scratch with HiSA, we find that this partial dot product does not hurt but improves performance compared with the complete product while computing only about a third of the query-key products. During inference HiSA improves decoding speed and shrinks memory footprint. We also extend HiSA to FlashAttention-3 kernels for training and inference. Finally, we motivate our approach by showing that dense attention learns to suppress the attention score parts that HiSA drops. Code is available at https://github.com/ambroise-b/hisa.
authors: Ambroise Borbely, Mathieu Salzmann, Olivier Verscheure
bullets: Targets the full query-key dot product in LLM attention rather than sparsifying across tokens.
Uses a static, parameter-free rule based on token positions and RoPE structure to omit selected query/key components.
Preserves full query and key projections while computing only a partial attention score.
Training from scratch shows no performance loss and reported improvements over complete dot products.
Extends to FlashAttention-3 and reduces decoding time and memory usage; dense attention also learns to suppress the omitted components.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces hidden-dimension sparse attention for RoPE-based LLMs, reducing attention computation and improving inference speed and memory footprint.
papers.title: HiSA: Sparsifying the Hidden Dimension of RoPE Attention in LLMs
papers.tldr: HiSA sparsifies RoPE attention across the hidden feature dimension, reducing query-key computations to about one third while improving performance and inference efficiency.

papers.abstract: Beam is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 501.3B total parameters and 23.4B active parameters, specifically built and optimized for coding, reasoning, and agentic workloads. Beam delivers frontier level reasoning, while requiring 3-4x less inference compute than many models of its class. Pretrained on 23.8T diverse, curated, high-quality tokens, Beam features a 1M-token context window achieved through a novel two-stage midtraining phase, built on verifiable, correctness-anchored data. Post-training leveraged a large-scale, fully asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) campaign across 10.5K GB300 GPUs, generating over 100M rollouts over 4 weeks of training. We believe this is one of the largest scale RL runs conducted by any open lab to date. Across our evaluation suite, capabilities continued to improve as we increased RL compute, with no sign of a plateau. Supported by deep hardware-model co-design, FP8/NVFP4 quantization, and a 1.93B-parameter speculative decoding drafter (DFlash 2), Beam maximizes serving throughput with efficient, flexible deployment. Averaged across conversation turns and harm categories, Beam refuses or pivots on 88.9% of harmful requests while complying with 81.5% of harmless requests, achieving the highest refusal/pivot rate on harmful requests among open-weight models on the Pareto frontier.

Figure 12: This figure demonstrates an overview of the filter-best-fit algorithm. Oversized documents are first filtered out, then a group of bins is allocated for packing. Each sample is assigned to the bin with the tightest fit. If no fit is found, the group is flushed and a new set of empty bins are allocated. The process continues until all data is exhausted.

The stateless gateway places new sandboxes in an eligible cluster using routing policy and advertised capacity; its response identifies the sandbox and owning endpoint. Each sandbox-server replica implements both lifecycle control and command proxying. Pod and Node watches feed the capacity snapshots read by the gateway. Commands and deletion address the owning cluster directly. Each sandbox contains one task container with the daemon and task processes, isolated by gVisor or Kata Containers with Cloud Hypervisor (CH).

papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly rely on extended reasoning traces, yet the training signals used to shape this behavior remain coarse. Supervised fine-tuning on full trajectories forces the model to imitate an entire demonstration, overconstraining its output distribution, while trajectory-level reinforcement learning provides only weak credit assignment, rewarding or penalizing whole completions without identifying where they succeed or fail. We propose edit-based training, a general framework for learning from a model's own trajectories via localized textual corrections. Given a sampled completion, an editor identifies the first point of failure under a specified criterion and proposes a minimal replacement span. The model is then supervised only on these edited spans. By design, this concentrates supervision where the model's reasoning first breaks down and aims to preserve its existing reasoning patterns elsewhere. The method applies both offline and online, with the latter continually adapting supervision to the model's evolving failure modes. We instantiate this approach on reasoning instruction following with Qwen3-32B on the ReasonIF benchmark. Compared to full-trajectory imitation and trajectory-level reinforcement learning baselines, edit-based training substantially improves compliance with the reasoning instruction while largely preserving the model's skills on untargeted tasks. These results suggest that localized correction is an effective complement to these approaches for shaping how LLMs reason.
authors: Alexandra Yakovleva, Luat Gia Khoi Nguyen, Juho Kannala, Harri Valpola, Alexander Ilin
bullets: Full-trajectory imitation can overconstrain outputs, while trajectory-level reinforcement learning offers weak credit assignment.
The method samples a completion, identifies its first failure under a criterion, and replaces only the problematic span.
Localized supervision is designed to preserve the model’s existing reasoning patterns and can operate offline or online.
On Qwen3-32B evaluated on ReasonIF, the approach substantially improves instruction compliance while largely preserving untargeted-task skills.
The abstract reports scope on reasoning instruction following; broader applicability beyond this setting is not established.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Edit-based training within one example. The instruction asks the model to reason in Chinese; the final answer is to remain in English. Each column shows the state of the trajectory after one editing round. The prompt and instruction are fixed across rounds. A red circle marks the first remaining instruction violation at the current round. A green circle is the editor’s minimal replacement span and is used as a supervised training target. Gray circles are model-generated tokens that are uncorrected in the current round. White circles are tokens accepted as part of the final trajectory but not used as edit targets. In the sampled rollout, the model begins reasoning in English, so the first reasoning step is flagged as the first violation. The editor makes a minimal Chinese replacement, and generation resumes from the corrected prefix. The editor applies replacements until the model continues reasoning in Chinese. Once the model adopts the requested mode, it may overshoot and emit the final answer in Chinese as well, which is itself a violation. The last edit then restores an English answer. The trajectory is now compliant.

papers.abstract: AI agents built on large language models (LLMs) often answer questions from incomplete records. Missing information might be interpreted as unknown or false, depending on the completeness of the source. Current evaluations fail to distinguish these two aspects, as they are usually interwoven with other reasoning demands. We present ClosureBench, a benchmark that tests whether LLMs follow the stated rules for dealing with missing information. Every base scenario is tested under OWA, CWA, and LCWA, and only the treatment of missing information changes between variants. ClosureBench provides a verified base benchmark as well as agent extensions for action choice, source scope, and updates. A model is considered correct on a base scenario only if it provides correct answers in all of its closure variants. Across 960 instances, overall accuracy can mask substantial closure mistakes. Models achieve overall accuracy from 71.18% to 99.86% across replicated runs, but their core switch accuracy, measured on the scenarios whose gold label actually changes with the contract, varies between 18.23% and 99.31%. Large discrepancies emerge under LCWA. For example, some agents choose unknown despite the prompt indicating that missing information should be treated as false. Our findings demonstrate that evaluations of AI agents should not only measure whether agents can reason over existing facts but also whether they use the appropriate assumption when information is absent.
authors: Francesco Belardinelli, Flavio Corradini, Matteo Leonesi
bullets: Tests identical scenarios under the open-world, closed-world, and locally closed-world assumptions, changing only missing-information rules.
Includes verified base tasks and agent extensions covering action choice, source scope, and updates.
Requires correct answers across all closure variants and introduces core switch accuracy to expose assumption-sensitive errors.
Across 960 instances, overall accuracy ranges from 71.18% to 99.86%, while core switch accuracy ranges from 18.23% to 99.31%.
Large errors occur under LCWA, showing that high overall accuracy can hide failures to follow stated closure rules.

papers.abstract: Reasoning capabilities in large language models have evolved from prompting-based methods to internalized model behaviors. In this paper, we investigate whether the internal thinking model of an LLM can be deliberately changed and whether such a change is beneficial. Instead of relying on Chain-of-Thought, we train models to follow Question--Option--Criteria (QOC), a structured decision process that decomposes a task into explicit questions, competing options, and evaluation criteria. We present a three-generation development pipeline that ranges from a basic QOC decision core to richer answer synthesis and statistically enriched QOC reasoning. We then evaluate the resulting models with respect to both internal consistency and output quality. Across the reported experiments, QOC-based fine-tuning improves answer quality relative to non-fine-tuned base models and yields particularly strong gains once models are large enough to execute the underlying QOC computations reliably. The results suggest that the internal thinking model of an LLM is trainable and that structured alternatives to Chain-of-Thought can provide a promising path toward more reliable, interpretable, and task-adapted decision support.
bullets: Investigates whether an LLM’s internal reasoning process can be deliberately changed.

Develops QOC models through three stages: decision reasoning, answer synthesis, and statistically enriched reasoning.

Benefits are strongest for sufficiently large models that can reliably perform QOC computations.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) support parallel generation, yet they often require many denoising steps because only a fraction of token predictions are sufficiently reliable to be committed at each step. Existing acceleration methods primarily optimize confidence learning or commitment policies. However, these approaches operate on the outputs of a single denoising forward pass, in which information from the prompt, previously committed tokens, and uncommitted positions may not yet be fully integrated. Consequently, some predictions remain under-refined when the commitment decision is made, and modifying the commitment policy alone cannot improve their underlying representations. We introduce dLoop, which restructures a pretrained diffusion language model into a Prelude-Loop-Coda architecture and recurrently applies a parameter-shared intermediate block to the same partially masked state. Rather than advancing the denoising process, each additional loop provides further latent computation, allowing information distributed across uncommitted positions to continue interacting and become more fully integrated before commitment. Experiments on GSM8K, MATH, MBPP, and HumanEval show that dLoop achieves the highest or tied-highest accuracy on every benchmark. With tokens per forward pass (TPF) adjusted for loop computation, it outperforms Fast-dLLM in both accuracy and TPF on all four benchmarks and dParallel on three, and is more accurate than d3LLM on all four, while d3LLM attains higher TPF; no compared method surpasses dLoop in both. Mechanistic analyses show that extra loops mainly help on slow, unstable trajectories and that updates at uncommitted positions drive changes in token decisions and later generation. Pre-commitment latent computation thus makes predictions more reliable, offering a route to DLM acceleration distinct from forcing confidence through the training loss.
authors: Handa Li, Pengxiang Li, Mingyu Cao, Xilu Wang, Li Shen, Da Li, Lu Yin
bullets: Targets under-refined token predictions caused by committing after a single denoising pass.
Reorganizes a pretrained DLM into a Prelude-Loop-Coda architecture with a parameter-shared block applied recurrently to the same partially masked state.
Uses extra latent computation to integrate information across prompt, committed tokens, and uncommitted positions before commitment.
Achieves the highest or tied-highest accuracy on GSM8K, MATH, MBPP, and HumanEval; it outperforms Fast-dLLM in both accuracy and TPF on all four.
Extra loops primarily benefit slow, unstable generation trajectories, with updates at uncommitted positions influencing later token decisions.
