papers.abstract: Reasoning models often become more accurate when they can generate longer answers at test time. This behavior is known as test-time scaling. However, RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) usually trains them with a fixed rollout cap. We find that this cap changes model behavior, not only training cost. After training, models use few additional tokens beyond the training budget. They outperform the base models near that budget, but their accuracy stops improving and falls below the base model at larger budgets. The rollout cap thus becomes a learned constraint, that limits model's test-time scaling. We call this effect budget internalization. We observe it across Qwen3.5-4B, Gemma4-E2B, and Nemotron-3-Nano-4B and two reasoning training tasks: mathematical reasoning and diverse, procedurally generated problems. This effect also transfers from math training to science and coding tasks. Training-objective level ablations on Qwen3.5-4B show that most changes recover little test-time scaling. Stronger KL regularization and lower training-data truncation preserve more scaling, but stronger KL reduces in-budget accuracy. Forcing an answer on truncated training rollouts largely removes budget internalization, but also removes most of the in-budget gain. SFT on artificially truncated traces reproduces budget internalization, whereas SFT on naturally short traces does not, which shows that the effect is not specific to RL. This result links budget internalization to length-censored post-training rather than to an RL-specific objective term. Thus, a rollout cap does not only control training cost. It can trade low-budget gains for lower performance when additional inference compute is available.
authors: Ilia Zavidnyi, Alexander Kovrigin, Arina Puchkova, Kirill Gelvan, Sergey Titov
bullets: RLVR-trained models learn to stop near their training token cap, treating it as a behavioral constraint.
Models outperform their base versions around the training budget but can underperform them at larger inference budgets.
Budget internalization appears across multiple model families and math, procedural, science, and coding tasks.
Stronger KL regularization and less truncation preserve more scaling but may reduce in-budget accuracy.
The effect also occurs with SFT on artificially truncated traces, indicating it stems from length-censored post-training rather than RL alone.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes how fixed rollout budgets in RLVR affect test-time scaling of reasoning LLMs, relevant to large language model training and behavior.
papers.title: Budget Internalization: Fixed-Budget RLVR Trades Test-Time Scaling for In-Budget Accuracy
papers.tldr: Fixed rollout budgets can make reasoning models optimize for short answers, improving accuracy within the budget but weakening test-time scaling beyond it.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon agentic tasks require a model to call tools over many steps at contexts of 100K tokens or more, yet many low-bit quantization methods are calibrated on short web text and judged on perplexity. This mismatch is costly: existing quantizations of Qwen3.8-27B at or below 3 bits per weight match BF16 on shorter tasks like AIME, yet in published results solve at most 72% as many tasks as BF16 on DeepSWE, a long-horizon agentic benchmark. We propose NariQ, a trellis-coded post-training quantization method that calibrates on tokens generated by the BF16 model in agent sessions. On Qwen3.8-27B, NariQ at 3.0 and 2.5 bits per weight stays level with BF16 on two long-horizon agentic benchmarks, DeepSWE and Terminal Bench, as well as on AIME and RealWorldQA. Our checkpoint at 2.0 bits per weight trails this performance. To our knowledge, these are the first quantizations at or below 3 bits per weight shown to match their full-precision version on long-horizon agentic tasks. We release the files as Qwen3.8-27B-NariQ-GGUF (https://huggingface.co/nari-labs/Qwen3.8-27B-NariQ-GGUF), with inference available through our llama.cpp fork at https://github.com/nari-labs/nari-llama.cpp.
bullets: Targets the mismatch between short-text quantization calibration and 100K+-token, tool-using agent sessions.
Uses trellis-coded post-training quantization calibrated on tokens generated by the BF16 model during agent sessions.
At 3.0 and 2.5 bits per weight, matches BF16 on DeepSWE, Terminal Bench, AIME, and RealWorldQA.
The 2.0-bit checkpoint performs worse than the higher-bit versions.
Releases Qwen3.8-27B-NariQ-GGUF and a supporting llama.cpp fork for inference.

papers.title: NariQ: Sub-3-Bit Quantization for Long-Horizon Agentic Tasks
papers.tldr: NariQ enables 2.5–3.0-bit quantization of Qwen3.8-27B while preserving BF16-level performance on long-horizon agentic tasks.

papers.abstract: Post-training recursive self-improvement (RSI) iteratively improves a target capability, operationalized by a fixed anchor benchmark, through repeated intervention, training, and evaluation. Yet most loops use the anchor's aggregate score as their sole observation, so early gains give way to stalled progress and repetitive exploration. When this anchor-only feedback ceases to reveal actionable gaps, a plateau may reflect an exhausted observation rather than an exhausted capability. We introduce adaptive observation (AdaObs), an observation-side mechanism of harness evolution that keeps the anchor objective fixed while adapting the active observation. At a plateau, a controller refines diagnostic granularity, escalates difficulty, and adds related tasks; validated increments are fused back into training, while every checkpoint remains evaluated against the anchor. Across eight independently optimized anchors in long-context reading comprehension and instruction following, AdaObs raises the mean score from $66.4$ to $73.7$ under a matched data budget, outperforming FixedObs, the anchor-only baseline. The evolved harness further improves the seven-task average on the independent PostTrainBench across two agent backends. These results identify observation adaptation as a missing mechanism of harness evolution for sustaining post-training RSI.
authors: Yinhao Tang, Youqing Fang, Yanan Sun, Xintian Shen, Hanyu Sun, Wenran Liu, Yue Wu, Weiming Zhang, Bin Liu, Wenwei Zhang
bullets: Anchor-only aggregate scores can hide actionable capability gaps, making progress appear stalled.
AdaObs adapts observations at plateaus by increasing diagnostic granularity, difficulty, and task coverage.
Validated observations are incorporated into training, while checkpoints remain evaluated on the fixed anchor benchmark.
Across eight anchors, mean performance increased from 66.4 to 73.7 with a matched data budget, outperforming fixed observation.
The evolved harness also improved the seven-task average on the independent PostTrainBench across two agent backends.

papers.selection_reason: Adaptive observation mechanism for post-training self-improvement of LLM capabilities; relevant to language foundation model training and reasoning.
papers.title: Sage-Evolve-Preview:Adaptive Observation for Post-Training Self-Improvement
papers.tldr: Adaptive observation helps post-training self-improvement escape plateaus by refining diagnostic feedback while preserving a fixed anchor objective.

papers.abstract: Post-training low-rank compression of neural networks must not only approximate the original weights but also preserve the model's input-output behavior. Recent output-aware methods measure the compression error beyond the compressed layer, at the model output, weighting logit changes by the observed next token or by the model's predicted probabilities. We propose Complete-SVD, a method for large language models that minimizes the $L_2$ distance between the logits of the original and compressed models, weighting all logit changes equally. Linearizing the network around the original weights, together with a Kronecker-factored approximation, reduces this objective to a weighted SVD with a closed-form solution. Its output-side factor is intractable to compute; we estimate it without bias from random probes, at a cost of $K$ backward passes per sequence, independent of vocabulary size and sequence length. At matched settings with uniform ranks and WikiText-2 calibration, Complete-SVD achieves the lowest C4 and PTB perplexity in every setting, and at ratio 0.7 under LEMS rank allocation. Replacing the $L_2$ distance by the Kullback-Leibler divergence (KL-SVD), with the same estimation framework, lowers calibration perplexity in most settings and raises downstream accuracy, but raises cross-corpus perplexity. Complete-SVD also improves IFEval instruction-following accuracy over the strongest prior output-aware methods throughout.
authors: Alper Kalle, Theo Rudkiewicz, Mohamed-Oumar Ouerfelli, Mohamed Tamaazousti
bullets: Targets post-training low-rank compression that preserves input-output behavior, not just layer weights.
Linearizes the network and uses a Kronecker-factored approximation to reduce compression to a closed-form weighted SVD.
Estimates the otherwise intractable output-side factor unbiasedly with random probes, requiring K backward passes per sequence.
On WikiText-2 calibration, it reports the lowest C4 and PTB perplexity across matched uniform-rank settings and at ratio 0.7 with LEMS allocation.
KL-SVD usually improves calibration perplexity and downstream accuracy but increases cross-corpus perplexity; Complete-SVD improves IFEval accuracy over prior output-aware methods.
papers.selection_reason: Output-aware low-rank SVD compression for LLMs; reduces model memory while preserving logit behavior.
papers.title: Complete-SVD: A Functional Norm Approach to Low-Rank LLM Compression
papers.tldr: Complete-SVD compresses LLMs by minimizing equal-weighted changes to the model’s output logits, achieving strong perplexity and instruction-following performance in the reported settings.

papers.abstract: When a constraint puzzle has several correct answers, language models tend to give the same one.We study four open-weight models from three families on symbolic puzzles and multi-solution ZebraLogic variants with exactly known solution sets.Repeated samples concentrate on one default solution far beyond uniform sampling, and different models often share it.Yet models usually produce even rarely sampled solutions when added clues uniquely identify them.On held-out symbolic puzzles, we compare visiting entities in name order with visiting those with the fewest initial candidates first. Both searches try values in the stated order. Where their pre-specified predictions differ, the latter matches a larger share of responses in all four models, by 26 to 40 percentage points.Reversing the stated value order or specifying a search order shifts responses towards the solution that the new order favours, on both testbeds. Randomising the presentation or supplying a random search order raises breadth (the effective share of solutions in use) by 26 to 42 percentage points on the symbolic task and 11 to 26 on ZebraLogic. The largest observed validity losses are 3 and 4 percentage points, respectively. Randomised presentation broadens answers more than a random-choice instruction in each of the three main models.
bullets: Across four open-weight models, repeated samples overproduce one solution rather than sampling uniformly, often the same solution across models.
Models can usually produce rare solutions when additional clues make them uniquely identifiable.
Searches that select entities with the fewest candidates better predict model responses than name-order searches, by 26–40 percentage points where predictions differ.
Reversing value order or specifying random presentation/search orders shifts responses and broadens solution coverage, with limited validity losses of up to 3–4 percentage points.
Randomized presentation broadens answers more than a random-choice instruction in the three main models tested.

papers.selection_reason: Empirical study of how search order shapes LLM default solutions on constraint puzzles; relevant to LLM reasoning behavior.
papers.title: Many Solutions, One Answer: Search Order Shapes the Default Solutions of Language Models
papers.tldr: Language models’ default answers to multi-solution puzzles are strongly shaped by the order in which search options are presented or explored.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding has emerged as a critical technique for accelerating Large Language Model (LLM) inference by decoupling generation into a drafting phase and a parallel verification phase. A crucial challenge is therefore designing a drafter that is both lightweight and accurate enough to approximate the predictions of the target model. We present a highly optimized Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) architecture that extends existing backbone LLMs to efficiently produce high-quality drafts. Built around a single shared drafting head, our approach features three core architectural optimizations: target activation injection to anchor semantic planning, zero-copy KV-cache cross-attention to bypass prefill compute and reduce memory overhead, and an efficient clustered vocabulary projection to reduce the cost of full-vocabulary decoding. Testing these improvements with the Gemma 4 model family, our G-MTP shows out-of-the-box speedups for both large server-side setups (up to 3.1$\times$) and smaller models targeting memory-constrained on-device environments (up to 2.3$\times$ on H100 and up to 2.2$\times$ on a smartphone GPU). In addition, we present parameter-efficient fine-tuning recipes for G-MTP that keep the drafter aligned with the backbone LLM under domain shift, requiring up to 1.83$\times$ fewer target forward passes than tuning only the backbone.
authors: Filippo Galgani, Ziwei Ji, Omri Homburger, Ganesh Jawahar, Michelle Ramanovich, Ivan Korotkov, Luciano Martins, Utku Evci, Edouard Yvinec, Pooja Consul, Vivek Kumar, Tal Schuster
bullets: Addresses the need for lightweight, accurate draft generation in speculative decoding.
Uses a shared drafting head with target activation injection, zero-copy KV-cache cross-attention, and clustered vocabulary projection.
Evaluated with the Gemma 4 family, achieving reported speedups of up to 3.1× on server-side setups and 2.2× on a smartphone GPU.
Introduces parameter-efficient fine-tuning recipes that require up to 1.83× fewer target-model forward passes than tuning only the backbone.
Scope: results are reported for Gemma 4 models and the specified hardware environments.

figures.caption: Figure 1 | Architecture of the optimized Multi-Token Prediction (G-MTP) module. The input to the drafter is constructed by concatenating the token embedding (𝑒(𝑥)) with the backbone hidden state (ℎ(𝐿)), both of dimension 𝑑target, and reducing to the drafter dimension 𝑑draft. The draft tokens are then propagated through the MTP layers, utilizing cross-attention against the backbone’s frozen KV Cache to bypass prefill computations before recursively triggering the next forward step. For subsequent drafting steps, the drafter’s output state is up-projected (𝑊up), concatenated with the embedding of the sampled draft token, and down-projected (𝑊down) to form the next input (Equation 3).

Figure 2 | The autoregressive G-MTP drafter (blue blocks) is initialized with activations from the main model (gray blocks) and cross-attends to its KV cache. Across successive drafting steps, the positional encoding (𝑝1) remains constant, as the drafter repeatedly queries a static, pre-computed KV snapshot.

Figure 3 | Empirical scaling of theoretical Block Efficiency (BE) and speculative wall-clock throughput across varying lookahead horizons (𝛾). While longer draft sequences monotonically increase token acceptance, throughput degrades for some models (e.g., 26B MoE) as drafting and verification costs exceed generation gains.

Table 4 | Speculative Decoding Domain Adaptation Performance (Gemma 4 E4B). Fine-tuning the model without updating the MTP (row 2) can lead to regression in Block Efficiency (𝛽). Joint finetuning (row 3) matches or exceeds the 𝛽 of the no SFT reference (row 1), and two-stage distillation (row 4) recovers about 96% of it.

papers.title: Efficient and Robust Drafting with Multi-Token Prediction
papers.tldr: G-MTP is an optimized multi-token drafter that accelerates speculative LLM decoding across server and mobile hardware while remaining efficient and adaptable under domain shift.

papers.abstract: Organizations monitor their workers' activity for insider threats, in which workers misuse their legitimate access, by copying confidential files before leaving. Detectors score how unusual each day of activity is, flagging the most unusual for an analyst to review. Prominent current approaches use opaque neural networks, so explanations of a flag point to internal features: patterns of neuron activity most active on days of misuse. We audit such explanations for language-model detectors trained on CERT's simulated workplace logs. To test an explanation, we see what happens to the detector's score when we remove its features inside the model. We compare this to a control: a change that is as similar as possible to the removal, but without actually removing the features. Because defining "similar" requires choosing a metric, our central contribution is the tipping radius: a first-order prediction of how far that metric must move before the difference between removal and control disappears, a measure of how fragile the result is to that choice. In 33 of 34 runs of seven language models, the tipping radius is at most 18% of the distance between two standard choices of metric. Moving that far removes at least 58% of the difference or reverses it, while random moves of the same size leave it largely intact. The result replicates in thirteen of fourteen pre-declared primary runs on openly released models, though on our trained detectors the difference is often too small to measure. We also find that a flag's score partly reflects who the worker is, not what they did, and that the features named depend on whom they are compared against. Audits should therefore fix the control's metric in advance, report its tipping radius, and disclose that comparison.
bullets: The study audits explanations that identify internal neuron features behind anomalous workplace-activity flags.
It introduces the tipping radius, estimating how much a control metric must change before the explanation’s apparent effect disappears.
Across 33 of 34 runs involving seven language models, small metric changes—at most 18% of the distance between two standard metrics—removed or reversed much of the explanation effect.
The findings replicated in 13 of 14 pre-declared runs on open models, while effects were often too small to measure in the authors’ trained detectors.
Flag scores partly reflect worker identity, and identified features vary with the comparison group; audits should predefine and disclose the control metric and tipping radius.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a 'tipping radius' metric to audit the reliability and fragility of explanations in LLMs for insider threat detection, contributing to the interpretability of large language models.
papers.title: How Reliable Are Explanations of Language Models That Detect Insider Threats?
papers.tldr: Explanations from language-model insider-threat detectors are often fragile because their apparent importance depends strongly on the chosen comparison metric and reference worker.

papers.abstract: Routing states in mixture-of-experts (MoE) models can distinguish correct from erroneous reasoning steps. If changing routing also changes a model's step-level verification judgment, it is tempting to conclude that the judgment follows what routing encodes. We test this inference with RouteVerify, a controlled intervention study that replaces selected internal activations from one solution trace with activations from another, while keeping the evaluated input unchanged. Across nine MoE checkpoints, we compare three intervention interfaces: router logits, MoE outputs, and post-MoE residual states. We vary the layers and token positions at which activations are replaced. We measure changes in a verification margin that quantifies the model's preference for INCORRECT over CORRECT. We also evaluate the same input with activations from correct versus erroneous steps to test whether the resulting judgment depends on the source step's correctness. We report four linked results. First, probes on router logits separate correct from erroneous steps in eight checkpoints (AUROC 0.80-0.88). Second, replacing router logits across all routed layers changes the judgment in all nine checkpoints, and by more than a norm-matched random replacement. Third, this change rarely depends on whether the source step is correct. At one layer, routing from erroneous steps and from correct steps produces indistinguishable margins in all nine checkpoints. Under all-layer routing, their difference is resolved and positive in only one. Fourth, the same difference is positive for local residual replacements in eight of nine checkpoints, so the measure does detect such dependence where it exists. Correctness is therefore readable from routing, and routing replacements move the judgment, but the movement rarely follows correctness.
authors: Yucheng Du, Ryan A. Rossi, Xiyang Hu
bullets: Across nine MoE checkpoints, router-logit probes distinguish correct from erroneous reasoning steps in eight models.
Replacing router logits changes verification margins in all nine checkpoints, more than norm-matched random replacements.
The judgment change usually does not depend on whether replacement activations came from correct or erroneous steps.
Local residual interventions reveal correctness dependence in eight of nine checkpoints, showing the measure can detect it when present.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates routing mechanisms in mixture-of-experts models using controlled interventions to understand step-level verification, contributing to the understanding of LLM architectures and interpretability.
papers.title: RouteVerify: Routing Interventions for Step-Level Verification in Mixture-of-Experts Models
papers.tldr: RouteVerify shows that although MoE routing encodes step correctness and affects verification judgments, routing interventions rarely transfer correctness-dependent judgments.

papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed as LLM-as-a-Service (LLMaaS), where user queries are sent to remote LLMs for inference, raising severe privacy concerns about the exposure of sensitive user inputs. Differentially private inference mitigates these risks by injecting noise into input embeddings. However, existing methods struggle to balance privacy and utility, as stronger privacy protection often leads to substantial accuracy degradation in LLM inference. In this work, we propose DP-SPD, a differentially private LLM inference framework that protects user queries by hiding the real query among client-generated dummy queries. All queries are randomly shuffled before being sent to the server, preventing direct identification of the user's true intent. To improve inference efficiency, we exploit the shared-prefix structure among queries and reuse transformer key--value (KV) caches during decoding. We analyze the privacy guarantee of DP-SPD and evaluate its utility on classification and generation tasks, as well as its privacy protection under QIA, EIA, and GPT-based attacks. Experimental results show that our method achieves strong inference-time privacy protection and near-plaintext utility while improving inference efficiency through shared-prefix KV-cache reuse.
authors: Zhihao Liu, Zixiong Guo, Shuo Shao, Yu He, Wenli Wang, Meihui Chen, Di Wang, Yuke Hu
bullets: Addresses privacy risks in remote LLM inference, where sensitive user queries are exposed to the service provider.
Hides the real query among dummy queries and randomly shuffles the set before server-side inference.
Uses shared-prefix transformer KV-cache reuse to reduce the efficiency cost of processing augmented queries.
Evaluated on classification, generation, and QIA, EIA, and GPT-based privacy attacks.
Reports strong inference-time privacy, near-plaintext utility, and improved inference efficiency.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes DP-SPD, a differentially private LLM inference method that reuses shared-prefix KV caches to improve efficiency while maintaining privacy.
papers.title: Ask in the Crowd: Differentially Private LLM Inference via Dummy-Augmented Shuffling
papers.tldr: DP-SPD protects LLM queries by mixing them with client-generated dummy queries, shuffling them, and reusing shared-prefix KV caches to preserve utility and efficiency.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise as predictors across various tasks, benefiting from their ability to use information from unstructured context. However, when predictions serve as parameters of downstream optimization problems, higher prediction accuracy does not necessarily translate into lower decision costs. We propose decision-focused reinforcement learning (DFRL), a framework for post-training LLMs to predict optimization parameters using negative downstream decision regret as reward. DFRL trains LLM predictors to minimize the costs of the decisions induced by their predictions, without requiring downstream convexity or differentiability, and integrates readily into existing RL post-training frameworks. To address expensive reward evaluation, we develop two approaches. Heuristic warm-starting uses inexpensive approximate rewards during an initial phase before switching to refinement with exact rewards. Reward correction combines inexpensive estimates with randomized exact evaluations, preserving the expected policy gradient while reducing the expected number of exact solves per update. Experiments on three synthetic optimization problems demonstrate improvements over prediction-loss baselines, while a larger knapsack experiment shows faster early improvement under short training budgets. On inventory planning with H&M transactions and product descriptions, our best configuration, in which the LLM reasons before predicting, reduces regret by 31.4% relative to the SFT baseline and 12.4% relative to the strongest evaluated conventional forecasting baseline.
bullets: Prediction accuracy may not reflect the cost of decisions made from LLM outputs.
DFRL uses negative downstream decision regret as the reinforcement-learning reward and does not require convex or differentiable optimization problems.
Heuristic warm-starting and reward correction reduce the need for expensive exact reward evaluations.

Experiments on synthetic problems, knapsack, and H&M inventory planning show improvements over prediction-loss baselines; the best inventory configuration reduces regret by 31.4% versus SFT and 12.4% versus the strongest conventional forecasting baseline.
The method is evaluated within the reported synthetic, knapsack, and inventory-planning settings; broader generalization is not established by the abstract.

figures.caption: Figure 1 DFRL pipeline with RLOO as an example. (1) Context. The input x provides task-relevant information, including text and structured data. (2) Predict parameters. The LLM independently samples K parameter predictions ĉ1, . . . , ĉK ∼ πθ(· | x). (3) Solve downstream optimization problems. Each prediction ĉk is passed to the optimizer, which returns a decision w⋆(ĉk) that is optimal under the predicted parameters. (4) Evaluate regret. Each decision is evaluated under the observed parameters c and compared with the optimal decision under c, yielding reward rk = −ℓ(ĉk, c). (5) Update the LLM policy. RLOO subtracts the average reward of the other K − 1 predictions from rk to obtain advantage Ak. These advantages weight the policy gradients used to update θ, without differentiating through the downstream optimizer. The hindsight cost F (w⋆(c), c) is shared across predictions and cancels from the advantages, so solving under c is unnecessary for the RLOO update.

Figure 2 Test regret comparison during the first five minutes of training on the 96-item knapsack problem. (a) Reward correction with p = 0.5 versus exact RLOO. (b) Heuristic-only training and a heuristic warmstart followed by exact RLOO. Both panels use the same exact RLOO reference. Curves show mean test regret over three training seeds shared across methods; shading indicates ± one sample standard deviation.

papers.abstract: A prompt for in-context learning (ICL) can describe a task in addition to, or instead of, demonstrating it through examples. Yet how task descriptions work remains poorly understood theoretically. Through the Bayesian view of ICL, we model descriptions as informative priors characterized by their specificity and reliability. We adapt the effective sample size (ESS) from Bayesian statistics, quantifying a description's predictive value as an equivalent number of demonstrations. For in-context linear regression, we show that a reliable description's ESS grows with its specificity and with the task's dimension. A description that may be irrelevant, however, gains little from its specificity unless demonstrations are given. In practice, do in-context learners use descriptions as a Bayes-optimal predictor would? Our experiments show that meta-trained Transformers come close to the Bayes-optimal ESS when tested on their training distribution. Pretrained language models, however, make too little use of highly specific descriptions when answering without reasoning; most of them closely match the Bayes-optimal predictor only when reasoning is enabled. These results extend the Bayesian analysis of ICL from demonstrations to descriptions.
authors: Bruce Nguyen, Bei Jiang, Linglong Kong
bullets: Models descriptions as informative Bayesian priors and measure their predictive value using effective sample size (ESS), interpreted as an equivalent number of demonstrations.
For in-context linear regression, reliable descriptions become more valuable with greater specificity and higher task dimension.
Potentially irrelevant descriptions benefit little from added specificity unless demonstrations provide supporting context.
Meta-trained Transformers nearly achieve Bayes-optimal ESS on their training distribution, while pretrained language models often underuse highly specific descriptions without reasoning.
The analysis extends Bayesian theory of in-context learning from example demonstrations to task descriptions.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes in-context learning and task descriptions in LLMs through a Bayesian effective sample size framework.
papers.title: Is a Description Worth a Thousand Demonstrations? Specificity and Reliability of Task Descriptions in In-Context Learning
papers.tldr: Task descriptions can substitute for demonstrations in in-context learning, but their value depends on specificity, reliability, and whether the model reasons over them.

papers.abstract: Combining fine-tuned models by composing their parameter updates has become a standard alternative to multi-task training. We formalize composability as a property of a collection of task vectors and prove that the excess loss of the merged model is controlled by an interference functional of the cross-task curvature overlap and the signed alignment of the updates. In the quadratic regime this functional equals the excess loss, giving a criterion that is necessary as well as sufficient and that measures the angle between task vectors in the curvature metric rather than the Euclidean one. Fine-tuning under a curvature-guided regularizer -- constructed from curvature statistics of the kind memory-efficient optimizers maintain -- keeps displacement in the base curvature metric below a ceiling set by the penalty coefficient at every iterate, at the standard $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ non-convex rate. Under a single Loewner comparison between the base statistic and the task curvatures, this control converts into a ceiling on the interference functional, inversely proportional to the penalty coefficient, so that the curvature term of the bound is controlled during training. A first-order term, present because regularized solutions are not stationary for the task loss, is not reduced in the same way. Experiments on an exact non-quadratic model confirm the budget and the ceiling, show the first-order term dominating for strong penalties, and find the curvature-guided penalty slightly better than an isotropic one. In a three-seed transformer study the functional is rank-correlated with merging degradation, but no more strongly than the Euclidean displacement norm.
bullets: Defines composability through an interference functional combining cross-task curvature overlap with signed task-vector alignment.
In the quadratic setting, the functional exactly equals merged-model excess loss and uses angles measured in the curvature metric rather than Euclidean space.
A curvature-guided regularizer bounds displacement in the base curvature metric during non-convex training and yields an inverse penalty relationship for the curvature component of interference.
The regularizer does not similarly reduce the first-order term caused by solutions being nonstationary for the task loss.
Experiments confirm the predicted budget and ceiling; the functional tracks merging degradation, but is no more rank-correlated than Euclidean displacement in a transformer study.

papers.title: Interference Bounds and Merge-Aware Training Dynamics for Composable Fine-Tuned Models
papers.tldr: The paper develops curvature-aware bounds and regularization for predicting and controlling performance loss when merging fine-tuned models, while showing that first-order effects can remain dominant.

papers.abstract: Argumentation frameworks (AFs) provide explicit, formal mechanisms for representing and resolving conflicts and thus have been incorporated into large language model (LLM) decision-making. The benefits vary and depend on how arguments and their relations are constructed, evaluated, and incorporated into the decision process. {We abstract a workflow consisting of four stages based on existing argumentation-augmented methods} and investigate their design choices over tasks of debate-based decision-making and retrieval-based fact verification. Our evaluation with recent LLMs shows that existing methods do not consistently improve performance across the considered tasks. Motivated by this observation, we develop two task-specific methods. The first is called Qnt-Arg, which organizes arguments around the original speakers in debate materials and aggregates model-estimated argument strengths and candidate-answer priors under gradual semantics. The second is Qlt-Arg that uses credibility estimates to establish preferences between conflicting evidence items and applies grounded semantics to select acceptable evidence for subsequent LLM inference. We examine the roles of generative and decision models within the two methods. In the debate setting, Qnt-Arg consistently outperforms other argumentation-augmented methods across matched configurations; Qlt-Arg improves retrieval-based fact-verification performance compared with the baselines. These findings demonstrate the value of combining formal argumentation and LLM while highlighting the importance of aligning with tasks in argumentation construction, model selection, and the role of formal semantic reasoning.
authors: Bochen Han, Anshu Xiong, Mingyang Ma
bullets: The study analyzes a four-stage workflow for incorporating argumentation frameworks into LLM decision-making.
It evaluates design choices for debate-based decision-making and retrieval-based fact verification.
Qnt-Arg groups debate arguments by original speakers and combines estimated argument strengths with answer priors using gradual semantics.
Qlt-Arg ranks conflicting evidence by credibility and uses grounded semantics to select acceptable evidence for LLM inference.
Qnt-Arg outperforms matched argumentation-augmented methods in debate, while Qlt-Arg improves fact verification over baselines.

papers.abstract: AI systems operating near the limits of their capabilities can maximize utility while minimizing the risk of error by abstaining or deferring questions they are not confident about to a human or a stronger model. Recently, large language models (LLMs) have been post-trained to estimate confidence in their own answers. To achieve this, methods reinforce confidence scores based on the correctness signal to each question-answer pair individually, with rewards that encourage assigning confidence 1 to correct answers and 0 to incorrect answers. However, estimating confidence scores is useful in that it enables selecting only the most confident answers, to maximize the share of solved questions while accommodating the user's risk tolerance. Assigning confidence 1 to correct answers and 0 to incorrect ones is theoretically optimal, but unattainable in practice and detrimental for selective prediction with a non-zero risk tolerance: confidences pushed to 0 and 1 carry no information about how answers compare to one another. We therefore introduce CARE (Cross-question Abstention Reward Estimation), which computes rewards over a set of question-answer pairs: At each of several risk tolerances, the confidences across the set induce an abstention threshold, and each confidence is rewarded for lying on the correct side of it. Since the threshold itself comes from the set, every verbalized confidence is reinforced relative to other questions' confidence, not against its own binary correctness label. On math, CARE increases the coverage at 5% risk (C@5) across MATH-500, GSM8K, and Big-Math-Digits from 0.8% to 42.4%, compared to existing pointwise correctness-matching rewards. When trained on multi-hop Wikipedia QA from HotpotQA, CARE improves C@5 in out-of-distribution general-knowledge, reasoning, and math benchmarks (including CommonsenseQA, GPQA, SimpleQA, and TriviaQA) from 12.3% to 23.6%.
bullets: Pointwise rewards that map correct answers to confidence 1 and incorrect answers to 0 lose useful distinctions between answer confidences.
CARE (Cross-question Abstention Reward Estimation) rewards confidence rankings across question sets using thresholds induced at different risk tolerances.
This enables models to abstain or defer on lower-confidence questions while maximizing coverage under a target error rate.
On math benchmarks, CARE raises 5% risk coverage from 0.8% to 42.4%; on out-of-distribution QA, it raises coverage from 12.3% to 23.6%.
The approach is evaluated for selective prediction and confidence estimation, with reported gains across several in- and out-of-distribution benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Can the allocation used to train experts also predict which expert will perform best on a prompt? Such a connection would make the intended division of labor inspectable before training and allow the allocation itself to guide inference. We introduce InflEns, a mixture of LoRA experts whose training weights and inference routes come from the same location game in a fixed prompt-trait space. Players choose positions to maximize their expected shares of the prompt distribution, without using expert losses. We utilize the game's kernel-general theoretical criterion for when co-located positions become locally unstable to separation. We evaluate InflEns on a corpus assembled from seven safety-related benchmarks, which demonstrates that the highest-share expert has the lowest held-out response negative log-likelihood (NLL) on approximately 90% of prompts across four kernels under a sharpened simplex representation, compared with approximately 15% after permuting allocations across prompts. We demonstrate that the method performs comparably to published learned gates without having to train an explicit gate on the experts. Because the router is fixed, we can trace harmful behavior to a single expert and retrain only that expert, which lowers HarmBench attack success from 0.51 to 0.02 while keeping instruction following. The game also gives us several controls over how the experts specialize, including the kernel choice and its parameters, the trait-space geometry, and the number of experts. Importantly, InflEns is a general framework that can be extended to any encoder and data distribution.
authors: Mark Lovett, Denis Lim, Soroush Vosoughi
bullets: Experts choose positions in a fixed prompt-trait space to maximize their expected share of the prompt distribution, without using expert losses.
A kernel-based stability criterion guides when co-located experts separate and specialize.
On seven safety-related benchmarks, the highest-share expert had the lowest held-out NLL for about 90% of prompts, versus about 15% with permuted allocations.
The fixed router performs comparably to published learned gates and enables tracing harmful behavior to one expert for targeted retraining.
Specialization can be controlled through the kernel, trait-space geometry, and number of experts; the framework is intended to generalize across encoders and data distributions.

papers.abstract: A program-induction benchmark is informative when its examples require the structure it aims to test. Yet a two-rule generator can produce demonstrations that a single rule also explains. We introduce certificate-grounded calibration, which constructs matched tasks with minimum solution lengths of one and two in a bounded string-replacement language. Complete one-rule enumeration and an executable two-rule witness certify the change before model inference. We evaluate 120 reference families with three to six shared examples, using 1,440 new model trajectories and 480 saved trajectories. Across Qwen3-8B and Olmo-3-7B-Think, displayed-task completion is 23.53-45.83 percentage points lower on certified separation tasks, while success on a wholly unshown witness pair is 8.40-13.45 points higher. These witness gains accompany lower agreement on uniformly sampled strings and 1.93-5.78% agreement on inputs that activate both reference rules. Recertification also reveals that a single unchanged example can exclude a shortcut and determine whether two rules are required. Together, these results show how the evidence supplied by examples shapes both the required solution and the programs models produce. The construction provides an executable testbed for comparing program search, final-answer delivery, and behavior on new inputs under verified task requirements.
bullets: Constructs matched string-replacement tasks with certified minimum solution lengths of one versus two rules.

Recertification shows that even one unchanged example can eliminate a shortcut and determine whether two rules are necessary.

papers.title: When Is Program Structure Required? Certificate-Grounded Calibration of Program-Induction Difficulty

papers.abstract: Do standard benchmarks see the architectural differences that matter? We study it with 64 from-scratch pretraining runs of Transformers and three linear-model families at 1.3-8B parameters on 1-2T Nemotron-CC tokens, at a cost of roughly 100k USD per 8B run. In academic-scale pretraining (1.3B parameters, 100B tokens), architectural differences can all but disappear when the models are carefully tuned. Instead, at 1-2T tokens they become measurable: Canon layers, which add local token mixing, consistently improve Transformers, saving about 30% of pretraining tokens for the same MMLU accuracy at 8B. We also introduce GLA5 and GDN2, which improve gated linear attention and Gated DeltaNet with low-rank output gates. Surprisingly, with Canon, the simplest linear model, gated linear attention, matches Gated DeltaNet and outperforms Mamba2 even at 8B/1T. Therefore, the extra machinery of Gated DeltaNet and Mamba2 may do little more than mix neighboring tokens. Even at 8B/1T, however, high scores on standard benchmarks can hide weaknesses in basic in-context skills. In particular, linear models that match or beat Transformers on these benchmarks cannot, in fact, reliably retrieve information from a short 500-token context. Moreover, no model, Transformer or linear, reliably beats random guessing on arguably the simplest two-hop question, stated in a few short sentences, even at this scale. These findings $\textbf{challenge traditional architecture research}$ based primarily on standard benchmark scores. In contrast, small synthetic playgrounds, which predicted the architectural differences above at <100M parameters, can reveal what these benchmarks miss. For practitioners, one lesson is to include in-context reasoning examples in pretraining data from an early stage, rather than reserve them for later mid-training, let alone post-training.
bullets: The study analyzes 64 from-scratch pretraining runs of Transformers and three linear-model families at 1.3–8B parameters using 1–2T tokens.
Canon layers, which add local token mixing, consistently improve Transformers; at 8B, they achieve the same MMLU accuracy with about 30% fewer pretraining tokens.
New GLA5 and GDN2 variants improve gated linear attention and Gated DeltaNet; with Canon, simple gated linear attention matches Gated DeltaNet and outperforms Mamba2.
Despite strong standard benchmark scores, linear models fail to reliably retrieve information from 500-token contexts, and no tested model reliably solves a simple two-hop question.
The results suggest incorporating in-context reasoning examples early in pretraining rather than relying mainly on later mid-training or post-training.

papers.abstract: Computational complexity theory offers a principled framework for characterizing the efficiency of computational problems, and Large Language Models (LLMs) can similarly be viewed as computational systems executing a structured process of input, inference-time compute, and output. In this context, the number of generated tokens emerges as a natural and directly observable proxy for inference-time compute. However, we show that the tempting analogy between LLM token length and classical time complexity does not hold. We disprove the hypothesis that inference-time token usage aligns monotonically with classical time complexity, demonstrating a fundamental divergence grounded in how LLMs actually allocate computation during inference. To this end, we introduce LLM Complexity, a new metric designed to quantify problem complexity from the perspective of LLMs by characterizing the area bounded above by the accuracy-token curve. We find that diverse LLMs induce highly consistent task rankings under LLM Complexity, indicating that the metric captures stable notions of difficulty across models. We leverage this property to construct an easy-to-hard curriculum for supervised fine-tuning, which improves accuracy while reducing token consumption. Finally, we demonstrate that LLM Complexity generalizes to real-world tasks, producing more stable cross-model correlations than human-annotated difficulty labels.
authors: Yu-Hung Wu, Shao-Xiang Yuan, Chan-Hung Yu, Zih-Ching Chen, Kuan-Hao Huang, Shao-Hua Sun
bullets: Generated-token count is an observable proxy for inference compute, but it does not monotonically align with classical computational complexity.
LLM Complexity is defined by the area bounded above by the accuracy–token curve.
Different LLMs produce highly consistent task-difficulty rankings under this metric.
An easy-to-hard curriculum based on LLM Complexity improves accuracy while reducing token consumption.
The metric extends to real-world tasks and yields more stable cross-model correlations than human difficulty labels.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Time complexity does not align with LLMs’ inference-time token usage. We conduct experiments on NEMOTRON-253B and report the relationship between the token budget and accuracy. (a) For problem size 80, sorting (O(n log n)) requires more tokens to reach 50% accuracy than some tasks with higher theoretical complexity. (b) For four sum closest, accuracy at a 10K-token budget does not decrease monotonically with problem size. Together, these results highlight a mismatch between algorithmic complexity and LLM inference behavior.

Figure 4: SFT learns and curriculum improves generalization. Accuracy on seen (training-split) vs. unseen (held-out) instances for each algorithm. Bars compare random-order SFT and curriculum SFT (complexity-based weighted sampling) evaluated on both splits. The dashed line separates algorithms included in SFT training (seen algorithms) from algorithms excluded from training (unseen algorithms). SFT yields higher accuracy on seen instances than unseen instances for seen algorithms, confirming effective adaptation, while curriculum SFT improves held-out performance and transfers better to unseen algorithms.
Figure 2: Illustration of inference utility. We plot accuracy as a function of token budget. The shaded area under the curve represents aggregate accuracy across the budget.

Table 2: Cross-model correlation of task-level complexity rankings. We report Spearman’s ρ / Kendall’s τb between the per-task complexity ranks induced by Model A and Model B (higher is better) on 12 algorithmic problems. papers.abstract: Hybrid attention is rapidly becoming the dominant architectural choice for frontier models. Despite their successes, such architectures complicate model design by introducing additional choices, including the types and locations of layers. This combinatorially large design space has been studied empirically, but given the vast expense of training and evaluating models with different configurations, a principled understanding of the effects of layer selection and ordering is needed. We provide the first such analysis, showing that the dominant hybrid architecture is highly task-specific. Concretely, for any layer configuration, we prove that there exists a task where we can construct a model with this configuration that provably outperforms any other model of any different configuration under fixed resource constraints. Empirically, we observe that for standard training, learned hybrid architectures exhibit separations between layer orderings that match our theoretical findings. For instance, under the same memory budget, the optimal architecture predicted by our theory for a segmented retrieval task consistently achieves perfect accuracy, whereas the next strongest plateaus below 0.5. These results extend to deeper models, where ``containing'' the dominant architecture for a task indicates whether the model attains high performance. In addition, we investigate the mechanisms learned by hybrids, observing that Transformer layers contribute the largest share of performance on associative recall across architectures. This work establishes insights into task-dependent hybrid architecture design relevant to the training and scaling of frontier-scale hybrids.
bullets: Hybrid models introduce a large design space of layer types and orderings that is costly to explore empirically.
The authors prove that for any layer configuration, some task exists where it outperforms every different configuration under the same resource constraints.
Experiments show that learned architectures exhibit performance gaps between orderings consistent with the theory.
On a segmented retrieval task, the theoretically optimal architecture reaches perfect accuracy, while the next-best remains below 0.5.
Transformer layers provide the largest share of associative-recall performance across hybrid architectures.

papers.abstract: Effectively eliciting the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) at inference time remains an important challenge. Existing studies address this challenge through context engineering, which shapes user queries, or fixed steering, which directly intervenes in model computation. However, predefined contexts and fixed intervention strategies may not adequately accommodate the diverse knowledge and reasoning requirements of individual queries. This raises a natural question: Can internal steering in LLMs be made query-adaptive? In this work, we investigate whether query-induced internal activations can guide adaptive steering in LLMs. Our pilot studies reveal subject- and layer-dependent neuron activation patterns and show that amplifying subject-relevant neurons can improve model performance. Based on these findings, we propose Q-NeuS, a query-adaptive neuron steering framework that dynamically determines which neurons to modulate and by how much for each input. Specifically, Q-NeuS constructs a compact subject-guided candidate neuron space and employs a lightweight Query-Adaptive Gate to generate neuron-wise modulation coefficients. To learn effective intervention strategies, we introduce Neu-GRPO, which adapts group-relative optimization to train the Query-Adaptive Gate using the relative performance of multiple neuron intervention configurations. The base LLM remains frozen throughout training and inference, and no task or subject labels are required at inference time. Extensive experiments across multiple LLMs and benchmarks demonstrate that Q-NeuS consistently improves model performance and exhibits broad applicability across model scales and strong cross-benchmark transferability.
bullets: Fixed steering may not fit the diverse knowledge and reasoning needs of individual queries.
Q-NeuS identifies a compact, subject-guided candidate neuron space and generates query-specific neuron modulation coefficients with a lightweight gate.
Neu-GRPO trains the gate using relative performance across multiple neuron-intervention configurations.
Experiments across multiple LLMs and benchmarks report consistent improvements, broad model-scale applicability, and cross-benchmark transfer.
The abstract does not specify particular datasets, numerical gains, or limitations beyond its evaluated scope.

papers.abstract: Most existing approaches enhance mathematical reasoning in large language models (LLMs) as a monolithic capability, despite the fact that different mathematical problems require different reasoning skills. Recent work has explored a more fine-grained perspective by decomposing mathematical reasoning into atomic skills and developing specialized modules for individual capabilities. However, how to effectively utilize these atomic abilities remains underexplored. To address this challenge, we propose Atomic MathReasoner (AMR), an instance-level framework for composing atomic reasoning skills. AMR first trains a library of capability-specific LoRA experts and performs gradient-free optimization over held-out validation subsets to discover a diverse set of low-loss composition prototypes. It evaluates the preference of each prototype using the token-level negative log-likelihood of reference solutions, filters ambiguous assignments through a confidence margin, and distills the resulting pseudo-labels into a lightweight router. During inference, the router selects an appropriate composition prototype for each problem, enabling problem-specific utilization of atomic skills without costly online optimization. Experiments on the AtomicMath benchmark across general and mathematics-specialized LLMs demonstrate consistent improvements. On Qwen2.5-Math-Instruct-7B, AMR increases average field accuracy from 64.4% to 68.1% at Level 1 and from 59.3% to 63.7% at Level 2, while improving average logical reasoning performance from 39.4% to 46.8%. These results demonstrate that effectively composing specialized atomic skills provides a promising approach to strengthening mathematical reasoning in LLMs.
authors: Jiashu Li, Tianyu Gao, Qinglong Liu, Jinping Wang, Ye Wei, Zhiqiang Gao
bullets: Addresses the underexplored challenge of effectively combining atomic, capability-specific reasoning skills.
Trains LoRA experts, discovers diverse low-loss composition prototypes via gradient-free validation optimization, and filters uncertain assignments.
Distills prototype preferences into a lightweight router that selects a problem-specific skill composition at inference time.
On Qwen2.5-Math-Instruct-7B, improves average field accuracy from 64.4% to 68.1% at Level 1 and 59.3% to 63.7% at Level 2.
Raises average logical reasoning performance from 39.4% to 46.8% on AtomicMath.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the proposed Atomic MathReasoner (AMR) framework. Top (Stage 1): Prototype Construction. We first decouple mathematical reasoning into atomic capabilities and train corresponding LoRA modules. A gradientfree optimization algorithm is then applied to the validation set to search for localized capability compositions, constructing a Compositional Prototype Set. Bottom (Stage 2): Route Selection Mechanism. We generate pseudo-labels via token-level NLL and apply a margin-based filtering strategy to obtain a noise-removed training set. Finally, a lightweight router utilizing TF-IDF feature extraction is trained to dynamically predict a suitable combination for unseen problems.

Figure 1: Conventional LLMs treat mathematical reasoning as a monolithic capability, often failing across diverse mathematical problems. In contrast, AMR dynamically composes atomic reasoning experts for each input through instance-level routing, enabling problem-adaptive capability synergy and more accurate mathematical reasoning.

papers.abstract: Language models acquire their capabilities from training data, and developers withhold data during training to keep models from learning capabilities that could be misused. How long this delays a capability, and how much data is needed to acquire it later, is unknown. Here we show that the general progress a model makes on the rest of its training data substitutes for the data that was withheld. We withheld the training signal for individual skills in models of chess, Othello, molecular strings, bracket languages and web text. The delay of a withheld skill in larger models was predicted from smaller ones. A chess model never explicitly trained to respond to check ranked the legal responses almost as well as a model that was. When models were then trained on the withheld data, they acquired the skill with a small fraction of the data needed from initialization, and this fraction decreased as the models progressed. A control rule of equal difficulty was learned much more slowly. A programming language withheld from the training text of a 7-billion-parameter model was regained in the same way. Data filtering therefore delays a capability, and the data required to regain it decreases as models improve.
bullets: Withholding skill-specific training signals delays, but does not prevent, capability acquisition.
The delay for larger models can be predicted from results on smaller models.
A chess model trained without explicit check responses ranked legal responses nearly as well as one trained with them.
Models regained withheld skills using only a small fraction of the data required from initialization, with the fraction shrinking as training progressed.
The findings span chess, Othello, molecular strings, bracket languages, web text, and a withheld programming language.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a common approach for training large language model (LLM) agents on long-horizon tasks. However, learning from sparse terminal rewards makes credit assignment and exploration difficult. We approach these challenges through a policy-induced capability region, the set of states from which the current policy can reliably complete a task. Near its boundary, an agent may need only a few actions to reach a more solvable state, even when the goal remains distant. This reduces long-horizon learning to two coupled subproblems of reaching that state and completing the task from there. We address them with paired advantages and a progressive reverse-to-forward curriculum. The advantages provide separate signals for reaching more solvable states and completing the task from them, while the curriculum expands the capability region backward along successful reference trajectories and then into off-reference states through on-policy exploration. On ALFWorld and WebShop, our method outperforms competitive agentic RL methods at both model scales, achieving success rates of 90.1%/96.1% and 80.2%/82.6% with Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B-Instruct, respectively.
authors: Siyuan Du, Yuxin Liu, Meng Tang, Haoran Li, Yechao Bai, Feiyang Pan, Jia He
bullets: Targets sparse terminal rewards, difficult credit assignment, and exploration in long-horizon RL.
Defines a policy-induced capability region: states from which the current policy can reliably finish a task.
Uses paired advantages to distinguish reaching more solvable states from completing tasks afterward.
Expands capability backward along successful trajectories, then outward through on-policy exploration.
Outperforms competitive agentic RL methods on ALFWorld and WebShop at both Qwen2.5-1.5B and 7B-Instruct scales.

papers.abstract: We introduce Clover-35B-A3B-Preview (Clover), a mixture-of-experts diffusion language model with 35 billion total parameters and 3 billion activated parameters, supporting thinking-mode generation. Clover adapts Gated Delta Networks to block diffusion by combining recurrent memory of previously generated context with bidirectional softmax attention inside the current block. Historical memory readout competes with current-block tokens in a shared softmax, with learnable block-size calibration and a separate, zero-initialized right-context convolution branch. Clover leads the seven evaluated agent metrics, including 73.6 on SWE-bench Verified and 51.7 on Terminal-Bench 2.1. On internal agent workloads, it reaches a reported generation speed of 680 tokens/s using one NVIDIA GB300 GPU at BF16 precision and batch size one. We organize the evaluation around model quality, drafting and verification costs, and deployment under constrained memory. We also describe a decision-model variant that generates answers to related questions in one denoising pass. On an internal set of 500 groups, joint prediction raises question accuracy from 90.37% to 93.88% and all-correct group accuracy from 65.4% to 77.0%.
bullets: Uses Gated Delta Networks adapted to block diffusion, combining historical recurrent memory with current-block bidirectional softmax attention.
Adds shared-softmax memory readout, learnable block-size calibration, and a zero-initialized right-context convolution branch.

Reports 680 tokens/s on one NVIDIA GB300 GPU at BF16 and batch size one for internal agent workloads.
A decision-model variant improves joint question accuracy from 90.37% to 93.88% and all-correct group accuracy from 65.4% to 77.0% on 500 internal groups.

papers.abstract: During human cortical development, functional systems become increasingly differentiated. We asked whether improved reasoning in language models involves a comparable regional reorganization. Applying diffusion-map embedding, used to characterize cortical organization, to matched base and reasoning-trained models from three families, we found broadly preserved gradient profiles with localized changes within a contiguous layer span. Grafting weights from these spans into instruction-tuned hosts improved mathematical reasoning on average, with gains rising with region overlap, while retaining more previously solved problems than grafts elsewhere. Across training, the span formed gradually during the early rise in performance, and grafts from intermediate stages helped. Grafts shifted most hosts partly towards their donors' behaviour and sometimes improved on problems the donors failed; the same analysis located a transferable span in a medical model. Together, these findings identify a reasoning-related region whose weights improve reasoning with low interference in the host's existing mathematical competence.
authors: Donghyeok Lee, Sangwon Yu, Sangkwon Park, Hye Youn Park, Munyoung Chang, Sungroh Yoon
bullets: Reasoning-trained models retain broadly similar global gradient organization but develop localized changes within a contiguous layer span.
Diffusion-map embeddings were applied to matched base and reasoning-trained models across three model families.
Transplanting weights from the span into instruction-tuned hosts improved mathematical reasoning on average, especially when donor and host regions overlapped.
The span emerged gradually during early performance gains; intermediate-training grafts also helped and often preserved more previously solved problems than other graft locations.
A similar transferable span was found in a medical model, though the analysis supports a reasoning-related region rather than a universal mechanism across all models.

papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed, monitoring their behavior becomes important for detecting unsafe or unintended actions. Activation probes offer an efficient approach, but existing methods face trade-offs between accuracy, interpretability, and computational overhead. Probes on raw activations lack interpretable inputs, whereas sparse autoencoder (SAE) probes use interpretable features but often rely on additive classifiers and large SAE encoders, limiting interpretability and increasing memory overhead. We introduce GateWatch, a compact, interpretable classifier that expresses its entire decision rule as an explicit Boolean logic over a small number of binarized SAE features. We explore three approaches to constructing these circuits under a specified gate budget. For efficient deployment, GateWatchServe computes only selected SAE features, enables streaming of their binary values across layers during inference, and evaluates multiple GateWatch classifiers in parallel using compact lookup tables. Across 24 tasks on Gemma-2-9B, GateWatch achieves 80.49% mean test accuracy using only 3.8 SAE features and 3.5 logic gates per probe on average, just 1.17 percentage points below full 16K-feature SAE probes, while matching or outperforming them on 10 tasks and reducing probe memory by 99.98%. Inside vLLM, 1,000 concurrent multi-layer, multi-token GateWatch classifiers retain 97-98% of baseline throughput and 99.8% of KV-cache capacity.
bullets: Targets the accuracy–interpretability–compute trade-off in activation-based LLM monitoring.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces GateWatch, a low-overhead monitoring method for LLMs using Boolean circuits and sparse autoencoders, contributing to interpretability and efficiency in LLM architectures.
papers.title: GateWatch: Low-Overhead LLM Monitoring with Boolean Circuits
papers.tldr: GateWatch enables highly compact, interpretable LLM monitoring by classifying behavior with Boolean circuits over a few binarized SAE features, with minimal accuracy and serving overhead.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting improves the performance of Large Language Models by eliciting intermediate reasoning steps. However, CoT is far from perfect: on some tasks, models perform worse than with direct-answer prompting, and on others they generate a few hundred tokens to reach the correct answer. We start by labelling each CoT hidden state as recovering if patching it into the direct prompt yields the correct answer, and failed otherwise. A linear probe shows that the model encodes these two classes differently. We then show that the representation space of the direct prompt holds a direction for each question that leads the model, in a short generation, to the correct answer more often than CoT does. Specifically, we rotate the direct prompt's last hidden state once, before generation, towards a direction built for each question from its own recovering and failed states. Across 25 tasks, these directions raise the direct prompt's mean accuracy from $46\%$ to $85\%$ on LLaMA 3.1 8B (CoT: $69\%$) and from $52\%$ to $86\%$ on Qwen 2.5 7B (CoT: $77\%$), with a tenth of CoT's tokens. CoT is thus not the shortest route to this accuracy, and these directions can be used in future work to train models to align their states with them.
bullets: CoT hidden states are labeled as recovering or failed based on whether patching them into a direct prompt produces the correct answer.
A linear probe distinguishes these two hidden-state classes.
For each question, a direction derived from recovering and failed states is used to rotate the direct prompt’s final hidden state before generation.
Across 25 tasks, accuracy rises from 46% to 85% on LLaMA 3.1 8B and from 52% to 86% on Qwen 2.5 7B, exceeding CoT accuracy with roughly one-tenth as many tokens.
The approach requires question-specific directions and is presented as a basis for future state-alignment training.

Each CoT state is patched in place of the last state z of the direct prompt and labelled recovering if the model then answers correctly and failed otherwise. The means of the question’s recovering and failed states, c+ and c−, give the task-solving direction d ∝ c+− 0.5 c−. papers.selection_reason: Analyzes Chain-of-Thought hidden states to identify task-solving directions in the representation space, offering a method to improve direct answer generation in LLMs.
papers.title: Chain-of-Thought Hidden States Reveal Task-Solving Directions for Direct Answers
papers.tldr: Question-specific hidden-state directions can steer direct-answer prompting to substantially higher accuracy than CoT while using far fewer tokens.

papers.abstract: Looped language models deepen reasoning at a compact parameter count by iterating a shared layer stack T times per token, turning recurrence depth directly into sequential decoding latency. Conventional early-exit decoding halts after initial passes without cache completion, truncating cached key-value states of past tokens to shallow depth. We study the opposite strategy, late entry, where new tokens skip initial passes and enter directly into the final K T alongside subsequent steps at zero extra serial calls. Projecting these finished T-pass wake states inside the existing output GEMM (Wake verification, governed by logit-margin tolerance tau in [0, inf]) unifies greedy-exact T-pass decoding (tau = 0, matching K = T block decoding within bf16 reduction order), margin-gated verification (tau > 0), and non-rollback lossy late entry (tau = inf) inside a single static CUDA graph. On Ouro-2.6B (T = 4), K = 2 Wake reaches 5.2x greedy-exact speedup at tau = 0 (+26% over K = 4 block decoding on GSM8K) and 6.8x at tau = inf (+16.9 points over trained early exit at matched speed). Scaling test-time recurrence across T in {8, 16, 32, 64} on Huginn-3.5B cuts K = T/4 rollbacks 21.5x with depth, driving greedy-exact (tau = 0) speedups to 6.1x (T = 32) and 8.4x (T = 64, +153% over K = 64 block) and tau = inf speedups to 10.6 to 12.5x.
authors: Ziqi Jin, Jiaxi Li, Weiwen Xu, Aixin Sun
bullets: Problem: Standard early exit leaves past-token key-value caches incomplete, while full recurrence increases sequential decoding latency.
Method: New tokens enter directly into the final K recurrent steps; Wake verification checks projected states using a logit-margin tolerance τ within a static CUDA graph.
Modes: τ=0 provides greedy-exact decoding, τ>0 enables margin-gated verification, and τ=∞ gives non-rollback lossy late entry.
Results: On Ouro-2.6B, K=2 achieved 5.2× exact and 6.8× lossy speedups; scaling recurrence on Huginn-3.5B reached up to 8.4× exact and 12.5× lossy speedups.

papers.selection_reason: Decoding strategy for looped LLMs that reduces latency and cache-related overhead; relevant to efficient inference and LLM architecture.
papers.title: Late Entry in Looped Language Models
papers.tldr: Late entry accelerates looped language-model decoding by letting new tokens skip early recurrent passes while preserving configurable exactness or accepting controlled approximation.

papers.abstract: Manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) extend a Transformer's residual stream into multiple parallel streams with learned cross-stream connections. Prior work trains all streams toward a shared objective. We instead study whether assigning distinct learning objectives to different streams can improve task performance and induce objective-specific specialization. Using complementary lexical (sparse) and semantic (dense) retrieval objectives as a test case, we find that objective-specialized mHC consistently outperforms a non-specialized mHC model across the full sparse--dense fusion range, for both two- and four-stream models and at two model scales. We then examine how specialization changes the model internally using probes of stream representations, residual mixing, objective-specific gradient flow, and read/write gates. The specialized and non-specialized models behave similarly through most of the network but diverge in the final layers: the specialized model develops increasingly objective-specific gradient flow, distinct read/write routing patterns, and reduced cross-stream mixing, and streams assigned to different objectives become increasingly dissimilar while those trained toward the same objective remain highly similar. Fixing the residual mixing to the identity leaves the specialization benefit intact, indicating that the benefit stems from objective-specific read/write routing rather than learned cross-stream mixing. These results show that assigning distinct objectives to mHC streams can improve multi-objective retrieval while inducing structured, depth-dependent specialization in the residual computation.
authors: Shantanu Agarwal, Ruchita V. Maitri, Zhiqi Huang, Vivek Datla, Alfy Samuel
bullets: Tests objective-specialized mHC using complementary sparse lexical and dense semantic retrieval objectives.
Specialized models outperform non-specialized mHC across the full sparse–dense fusion range for two- and four-stream models at two scales.
Specialization emerges mainly in final layers through distinct gradient flow, read/write routing, and reduced cross-stream mixing.
Streams trained on the same objective remain similar, while streams trained on different objectives become increasingly dissimilar.
The benefit persists with identity residual mixing, implicating read/write routing rather than learned cross-stream mixing.

Figure 1: Schematic comparison of the three encoder configurations studied in this work. In all three, streams propagate through the full encoder stack and the retrieval heads read only the final-layer (l = L) stream representations. (left) Single-stream: the standard ModernBERT encoder, with a single residual stream read by both the sparse and dense retrieval heads. (middle) Non-specialized mHC: the residual stream is expanded into n parallel streams with learned cross-stream routing. Both retrieval heads operate on the mean-pooled representation obtained from all n streams, so the sparse and dense objectives jointly optimize the same stream representation. (right) Objective-specialized mHC: the sparse and dense heads instead read disjoint sets of final-layer streams, so each objective selectively trains its assigned stream(s). For clarity the schematic depicts n = 2 streams; we study both n = 2 and n = 4 in our experiments.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a Transformer residual-stream architecture modification with objective specialization, relevant to LLM architecture research.
papers.title: Objective-Specialized Residual Streams in Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections
papers.tldr: Assigning different retrieval objectives to parallel mHC residual streams improves multi-objective retrieval and induces depth-dependent stream specialization, primarily through objective-specific routing.

papers.abstract: Building a small language model requires choosing which published improvements to combine. We compare five changes in the same model, using the same data and training budget. We test selected combinations and repeat each one with a second random seed. Mixture-of-experts layers, Muon optimisation and a Gated DeltaNet hybrid give the largest gains. Extra normalisation also helps, while an attention gate with a matched parameter budget adds little on average. The gains mostly combine, but small interactions between changes appear again in the repeated runs. Repetition also reveals benefits that an initial statistical estimate treated as noise. These findings apply to our small-model training setting; the expert models also have greater total capacity. The practical lesson is to test promising components together and repeat the comparisons before deciding which ones to keep.
bullets: Compares five architectural and optimization changes under the same data and training budget.
Mixture-of-experts layers, Muon optimization, and a Gated DeltaNet hybrid yield the largest gains; extra normalization also helps.
An attention gate with matched parameter count contributes little on average.
Most improvements combine effectively, but small interactions recur across repeated random seeds.
Results are limited to the small-model setting, and expert models have greater total capacity.
