papers.selection_reason: Conducts a factorial study on small language model components (MoE, Muon, DeltaNet), providing insights into model architecture and training recipes for LLMs.
papers.title: Do Frontier Model Ingredients Add Up? A Replicated Factorial Study of Small Language Models
papers.tldr: A replicated factorial study finds that several frontier-model components provide mostly additive gains in small language models, though some interactions and capacity differences complicate interpretation.

papers.abstract: Large language models can infer and follow specific rules through in-context learning (ICL), yet may fail to remain faithful to provided evidence, giving rise to out-of-context (OOC) hallucination. Existing work has largely investigated the underlying mechanisms of ICL and OOC hallucination along separate lines. However, this separation obscures the mechanistic basis for these seemingly opposing outcomes. In this work, we study this contrast through the unified view of functional roles in dynamic context. The key observation is that role information can be internally represented without reliably constraining output. We derive a first-order decomposition to characterize the role effect, showing that its substantial influence depends on two necessary conditions, namely sufficient contribution magnitude and coherent signed aggregation. Causal analysis further shows that role span contributions affect key token choices involving response structure, content selection, and factual values. We further show that role-consistent choices depend on sufficient role span support at these key decisions, while failing choices can be reversed when this support overcomes the deficit. These findings support a common mechanistic view of ICL and OOC hallucination: each functional role defines the pattern of output decisions over which role span contributions must remain effective, and differences in this organization account for the seemingly opposing outcomes.
authors: Tianxiang Chen, Jingyuan Zhou, Guoyao Yang, Kaidi Yang
bullets: Role information may be internally represented without reliably constraining the model’s outputs.
A first-order decomposition identifies sufficient contribution magnitude and coherent signed aggregation as necessary for role effects to influence behavior.
Causal analysis links role-span contributions to response structure, content selection, and factual-value decisions.
Role-consistent outputs require adequate role-span support at key decisions; increasing this support can reverse failures.
The framework attributes ICL and OOC hallucination to how effectively functional-role contributions remain active across output decisions.

papers.selection_reason: Mechanistic analysis of in-context learning and out-of-context hallucination in large language models.
papers.title: A Mechanistic Analysis of In-Context Learning and Out-of-Context Hallucination
papers.tldr: A unified mechanistic analysis explains why in-context learning can follow contextual rules while models still produce out-of-context hallucinations.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer a flexible alternative to autoregressive models, enabling any-order infilling. While most existing decoding methods treat decoded tokens as fixed, some recent models allow previously decoded tokens to be revised only by replacing them with alternative tokens, a paradigm we refer to as replacement-only editing (ROE). Although ROE can correct individual tokens, it is inefficient for sequence shifts caused by missing or extra tokens and struggles when errors occur across many positions. To address these limitations, we propose LED (Levenshtein Editing for Diffusion Language Models), a post-training framework that extends ROE with insertion and deletion, enabling Levenshtein-style refinement of generated sequences. It uses two training designs. First, it reconstructs edit supervision on the fly during supervised fine-tuning using longest-common-subsequence alignment, enabling insertion and deletion learning without manually annotated labels. Second, it adopts multi-stage training, where the state from one stage becomes the input to the next, exposing the model to its earlier errors and enabling it to correct them. When applied to the 16B-parameter LLaDA2.1-Mini Base, LED raises the average score across twelve benchmarks from 54.86 to 57.10 under confidence-guided decoding while increasing tokens per forward from 6.14 to 7.05, whereas under confidence-free decoding it raises the average score from 27.52 to 47.19. We further show that LED achieves higher pass@k at large k than thresholded decoding without editing, demonstrating improved generation diversity and revealing the diversity potential of DLMs without confidence guidance. LED also improves robustness to large block sizes, raising the average score from 36.97 to 51.34 at block size 128. Together, these results suggest that LED supports more robust self-correction in DLMs.
authors: Shuaidi Wang, Zhuocheng Gong, Xuejie Liu, Jianguo Li, Yu Zhang
bullets: Replacement-only editing struggles with missing or extra tokens and errors spanning many positions.
LED learns Levenshtein-style refinement through on-the-fly longest-common-subsequence edit supervision, avoiding manual edit labels.
Multi-stage training feeds each stage’s output into the next, helping the model correct its own earlier errors.
On LLaDA2.1-Mini Base, LED improves average benchmark scores under confidence-guided and confidence-free decoding, and is more robust to large block sizes.
LED also achieves higher pass@k at large k than thresholded decoding without editing, indicating greater generation diversity.

papers.abstract: We introduce MANGO Arena, an open-source testbed in which four LLM agents each run one company in a serial supply chain adapted from MANGO, a classroom factory-management game. The environment enforces hard rules (a truck limit, a no-credit cash constraint and production capacity), logs every blocked attempt to break them, and gives agents a public message board on which side payments are explicitly forbidden. This lets one environment measure three things at once: an economic outcome (the bullwhip effect), rule adherence under pressure, and proposals to collude. In a pilot with three small reasoning models, two scripted reference policies, two conditions (with and without a supplier fire) and three demand seeds, all LLM agents amplified demand variability as it moved upstream, by 7 to 25 times at the Retailer and 13 to 179 times at the Supplier, often more than a textbook order-up-to policy. They did so largely by ordering in batches (zero orders in up to 60% of decisions). Real rule violations were rare (at most 7 of 288 decisions per model) and no agent proposed a money side deal. The pilot's main lesson concerns evaluation method. API failures (rate limits and runaway hidden reasoning) entered the metrics silently as "no order" decisions. And when we reran games with the same seeds and no failed calls, upstream bullwhip changed by up to 17 times between runs. With three seeds, conclusions about how a disruption affects a given model did not survive a rerun. We report these failures in full and propose reporting practices for multi-agent evaluations of this kind. Code, prompts and every logged decision are public.
bullets: Four LLM agents manage companies in a rule-constrained serial supply chain with logged violations and a public message board.
The testbed jointly measures bullwhip effects, rule adherence, and attempts to collude under disruption and baseline conditions.
In the pilot, agents amplified variability substantially, often through batched ordering; rule violations and side-payment proposals were rare.
API failures were silently recorded as no-order actions, and identical seeds produced bullwhip differences of up to 17× across reruns.
The study recommends stronger reporting practices and provides public code, prompts, and decision logs.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates LLM agents in a simulated supply chain environment, focusing on agent behavior and economic outcomes, fitting Large Language Models.
papers.title: MANGO Arena: Same Seeds, Different Chains Evaluating LLM Agents in a Disrupted Supply Chain
papers.tldr: MANGO Arena is an open-source testbed showing that LLM supply-chain agents can strongly amplify demand variability, while evaluation outcomes remain highly sensitive to API failures and reruns.

papers.abstract: In multi-agent systems, a receiver agent often waits for a helper agent's message (text or its latent KV cache), which can improve performance but adds latency. We study when a receiver agent can skip the message safely (the final answer rarely changes) and beneficially (the time saved exceeds the cost of deciding). Our mechanism reads the receiver agent's confidence without the message and uses a finite-sample test to certify a threshold at which, with high probability, at most 5% of skipped answers change; if none passes, the system keeps communicating. We test it on OpenBookQA, ARC-Challenge, and MMLU-Pro with three Qwen model pairs, on cross-family agents, and on SQuAD and GSM8K. Four insights emerge. First, oracle headroom is weak evidence that messages help: control inputs without answer-specific content, matched to change answers as often as real messages, reproduce a median 76% of the oracle's gain. Second, whether a message can be skipped depends on how often and how predictably it alters the answer, not on its accuracy; every certified KV-cache path is less accurate than the receiver agent alone. Third, where text messages help, skipping keeps most of their gain: on unseen questions in the four such settings, the policies skip 59 to 80% and keep an estimated 76 to 95% of the gain. In two prospective tests with all rules fixed in advance, our mechanism skips a three-agent system's verifier on 39.9% of sealed questions, keeping 12.55 of its 12.80-point gain, and a 32B helper on 68.4% of held-out questions, keeping its whole gain. Fourth, safety does not determine efficiency: at batch size one, skipping text saves hundreds of milliseconds per query and skipping KV cache far less. Certification extends to SQuAD but not to GSM8K. In eleven tests on unseen questions, every certified policy we could test kept its change rate's 95% upper bound below 5% under our answer parsers.
authors: Xinyang Li, Chih-Hsuan Yang, Xiaolong Ma, Anjir Ahmed Chowdhury, Vikram Vasudevan, Rajeev Thakur, Feng Yan
bullets: The system skips a helper’s text or latent KV-cache message only when it certifies, with high probability, that no more than 5% of answers will change; otherwise it communicates.
Whether skipping is safe depends on how often and predictably a message changes answers—not on the helper’s accuracy.
On four settings where text messages helped, policies skipped 59–80% of messages while retaining an estimated 76–95% of the gain.
Prospective tests skipped 39.9% of verifier messages while retaining 12.55 of 12.80 points of gain, and skipped 68.4% of 32B-helper messages while retaining the full gain.
Safety and efficiency differ: text skipping saved hundreds of milliseconds per query at batch size one, whereas KV-cache savings were much smaller; certification extended to SQuAD but not GSM8K.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates mechanisms for LLM agents to skip messages safely to reduce latency, a relevant optimization for agent efficiency.
papers.title: Safe to Omit, Worth Omitting? Keeping the Answer and Cutting Latency When an LLM Agent Skips Another's Message
papers.tldr: A confidence-based finite-sample test lets LLM agents safely skip many helper messages, preserving most answer improvements while reducing latency when skipping is worthwhile.

papers.abstract: Researchers are increasingly using large language models (LLMs) to validate research questions. We find that LLMs make open research questions sound partly studied and overstate what related papers establish. Models recognize most of these overstatements when asked to check the papers' full texts separately. On 40 questions drawn from newly accepted papers, GPT-6-Astra correctly judges 98% to be unstudied, but states that status plainly in only 8% of ordinary answers. All six frontier systems show reporting gaps of 30-90 percentage points. Across 22 models given identical papers, higher capability is associated with more accurate judgments and larger reporting gaps. This reporting failure is asymmetric: models correctly identify studied questions in 88-100% of ordinary answers when we supply the answering papers. To correct this, we build a fixed answer from each model's judgment and separate checks of cited papers. This raises Astra's clear reporting of open status from 8% to 95%, with improvements in all six systems. Finally, we predict reviewers' novelty grades by combining several models' written ratings with a rule learned from graded examples, reaching the performance range reported by Think-Probe-Respond. Unlike TPR, our approach needs no access to model weights or internal activations, so it also works with closed-weight frontier models.
bullets: Across 40 questions from newly accepted papers, models usually recognized that questions were unstudied but rarely stated this clearly in ordinary answers.
Six frontier systems had reporting gaps of 30–90 percentage points, with larger gaps among more capable models.
The failure was asymmetric: models more reliably identified studied questions when the relevant papers were supplied.
A fixed answer combining model judgments with separate citation checks raised clear reporting of open status from 8% to 95% for GPT-6-Astra and improved all six systems.
The method also predicted reviewers’ novelty grades competitively without requiring model weights or internal activations.

papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) and language models (LLMs) often exhibit attention sinks, whereby particular positions, such as the beginning-of-sequence (BOS) token, receive a disproportionate share of attention. Under standard causal masking, however, the BOS query attends only to itself, so the representation that later tokens repeatedly access carries no information about the input. We introduce BOS Summary, a training-free inference-time method that repurposes this persistent pathway to carry input context. At a single transformer layer during prefill, BOS Summary relaxes the causal constraint for the BOS query row alone, letting BOS aggregate all visual and textual input tokens into a self-derived context representation while every other token retains standard causal attention. The enriched representation then remains accessible to the model throughout decoding, with no additional parameters, auxiliary modules, or decoding-time overhead. Across multiple VLM and LLM families and eight multimodal and text-only benchmarks, BOS Summary improves over direct and Chain-of-Thought prompting and outperforms recent sink-intervention methods on multi-step reasoning tasks. A mechanistic analysis shows that making BOS input-specific also weakens its sink dominance and redistributes attention toward content-bearing prompt tokens, indicating that changing what a sink carries reshapes how later layers allocate attention.
authors: Hui Zhu, Saleh Zare Zade, Rafi Ibn Sultan, Deng Pan, Arun Ross, Dongxiao Zhu
bullets: Targets the informationless BOS representation created by causal masking, which later tokens repeatedly attend to.

Improves over direct and Chain-of-Thought prompting and recent sink-intervention methods across eight multimodal and text-only benchmarks.
Mechanistic analysis finds reduced BOS sink dominance and more attention allocated to content-bearing prompt tokens.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents achieve state-of-the-art performance across domains through chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. Despite their ubiquitous use, little is understood about the relationship between the externalized trace and the model's actual computation. We address this by investigating how LLM agents make decisions in iterative games with incomplete information. Using a series of mechanistic interpretability techniques, we find that the model forms and iteratively revises an internal representation of the game throughout the CoT. Once the model prematurely commits to an incorrect belief, it rarely recovers. This failure is manifested in both the literal trace and the layer activations. Ultimately, as multi-agent systems are more prevalent, our work opens the door to a more focused diagnosis of their strategic reasoning errors. For illustrative purposes, we offer an interactive visualizer of our methodology on selected sample traces at https://interp-self.github.io/gametrace/
authors: Chaipat Tirapongprasert, Rajarshi Das, Parijat Dube
bullets: Studies LLM decision-making in iterative games with incomplete information.
Compares externalized reasoning traces with internal layer activations.
Finds that game representations are formed and revised throughout reasoning.
Shows that premature incorrect beliefs persist in both the trace and activations.
Provides an interactive visualizer for selected example traces.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student language model to match a teacher model based on its own generations. When using OPD, one must choose whether to apply it at the sequence or token level and which divergence to minimize. However, despite the wide adoption of OPD in practice, the formal understanding of which OPD objective is appropriate for a given setting is limited. Toward addressing this gap, we theoretically analyze how the choice of OPD objective governs which tokens are prioritized, in what order, and how efficiently. Our analysis reveals that sequence-level OPD exhibits a future agreement bias, which myopic token-level objectives avoid. This bias induces a reverse learning order, in which sequence-level OPD first matches the teacher at later token positions, while at earlier positions it can favor tokens that are improbable under the teacher, and thus often undesirable. As for the choice of divergence, we prove that it strongly influences the amenability of OPD to gradient-based optimization. In particular, while the forward KL divergence enjoys a well-behaved objective landscape, other $f$-divergences, such as reverse KL, can suffer from vanishing gradients even when the student and teacher are far apart. Across language model post-training settings, we demonstrate the implications of these theoretical findings for which OPD objective is preferable, highlighting the importance of accounting for the interplay between the student, teacher, and task at hand.
authors: Hubert Strauss, Liam Fowl, Noam Razin
bullets: Sequence-level OPD has a future-agreement bias that token-level objectives avoid.
This bias can cause reverse learning: later positions are matched first, while earlier positions may favor teacher-improbable tokens.
Forward KL yields a well-behaved optimization landscape.
Other f-divergences, including reverse KL, can have vanishing gradients even when student and teacher distributions differ substantially.
The preferable OPD objective depends on the student, teacher, and post-training task.

figures.caption: Figure 13: Example of the user message given to gpt-5.6-terra for writing the programs in the code completion dataset (see Appendix E.3.1 for details on the dataset construction process). Figure 5: RKL becomes more preferable to FKL as the capacity gap between the student and teacher grows. We trained Qwen3-0.6B-Base and Qwen3-1.7B-Base students using token-level OPD with the FKL and RKL divergences and Qwen3 teachers of varying sizes, on the MATH dataset. The left plot shows that the gap in accuracy between students trained with RKL and FKL grows with the size of the teacher (markers stand for means over three seeds, with error bars denoting standard deviation). The middle and right plots point to a potential cause: the tokens whose probability increases the most under RKL are typically already likely under the initial student, whereas under FKL they can have low initial probability, especially with the larger teacher, suggesting that FKL changes the student in ways that are less compatible with its initial capabilities. Specifically, for the 0.6B student with the 4B and 32B teachers, the middle and right plots show how the initial student probabilities are distributed for the tokens that increased the most in probability during training.

Figure 11: Sequence-level OPD can cause the student to refuse to answer even when its thinking block concludes that the request is safe. Shown is an output of the Qwen3-1.7B student for a benign training request, generated at training step 282 of a sequence-level OPD run in Figure 9. We show an output from this training step since, later in training, the thinking blocks of the student often become empty.

Figure 4: RKL and JS struggle to distill knowledge of new APIs in a code completion task. We trained a Qwen2.5-1.5B-Base student using token-level OPD objectives with a Qwen3-8B-Base teacher, on prompts requiring the use of Python APIs that were released after the student (see Section 4.2.1). Reported values are computed over training prompts for which the student initially assigns the first token of the correct API name a probability of at most 10−3, and averaged over three seeds (shaded areas mark standard deviation). In agreement with Theorem 2, FKL and its equal mixture with RKL quickly match the rate at which the teacher names the correct API, whereas RKL and JS are substantially slower to do so. Note that this slowdown is not due to insufficient sampling of unlikely tokens, since the divergences are computed over the full vocabulary and RKL and JS are slow to raise even the probability of the first token of the correct API name. Rather, it stems from their objective landscapes being flat along the logits of such tokens (as established in Section 4.1).

Figure 2: Future agreement bias prevents sequence-level OPD from efficiently solving the binary tree navigation task. We trained a randomly initialized Transformer student via sequence-level and tokenlevel OPD on the binary tree navigation task described in Section 3.2, using tree depth L = 15 and δ = 10−4. The left plot reports the probability that the student assigns to the correct pathy⋆ (i.e., success probability) and to the correct token at the root, throughout training. The middle and right plots report the RKL divergence between the student and teacher next-token distributions at each token position, across training steps of sequence-level and token-level OPD (averaged over 512 student-generated outputs and normalized by its initial value; error bars mark standard error). In line with our theory, sequence-level OPD first assigns high probability to the incorrect token at the root, correcting this mistake only after matching the teacher at later positions, whereas token-level OPD efficiently matches the teacher starting from the root. Figure 8 shows that token-level OPD with FKL and JS exhibits trends similar to those of token-level OPD with RKL.

Figure 3: Future agreement bias leads sequence-level OPD to cause over-refusal of benign requests. We trained a Qwen3-1.7B student using sequence-level and token-level OPD objectives with a Qwen3-8B teacher. The training prompts were taken from the WildJailbreak dataset and consist of an equal mixture of harmful and benign requests. Reported values are computed over training prompts and averaged over three seeds, with shaded areas marking standard deviation (results on a test set showed identical trends). Notice that, although the teacher refuses only 17.5% of the benign requests, sequence-level OPD causes the student to refuse nearly all of them due to the future agreement bias characterized in Section 3.1. Consequently, sequence-level OPD lowers the safety accuracy of the student (i.e., the percentage of prompts for which it correctly refuses a harmful request or answers a benign one), whereas token-level OPD substantially improves it by lowering the refusal rate on benign requests and raising the refusal rate on harmful requests.

Figure 1: The binary tree navigation task analyzed in Section 3.2 (for depth L = 3). The student starts at the root, and its goal is to produce with high probability the path y⋆ = (A, A, . . . , A), which reaches a fixed target leaf. The teacher assigns high probability to choosing the left child at the root and every node in its left subtree (δ = exp(−L)), but chooses uniformly among children if the initial token is incorrect.

Figure 7: Future agreement bias leads sequence-level OPD to outperform token-level OPD on an arithmetic task by steering the student to use a calculator tool. We trained a Qwen3-1.7B student using a Qwen3-8B teacher via sequence-level OPD and token-level OPD with the RKL, FKL, and JS divergences on arithmetic problems, where each prompt instructs the model to either solve the problem directly or output a call to a calculator tool with an arithmetic expression. Reported values are computed over training prompts and averaged over three seeds, with shaded areas marking standard deviation (results on a test set showed identical trends). Notice that, although the teacher calls the calculator in only 7.2% of its outputs, sequencelevel OPD leads the student to call it for nearly all problems due to the future agreement bias characterized in Section 3.1. Consequently, the student attains near-perfect accuracy under sequence-level OPD, even surpassing the teacher. By contrast, token-level OPD leads the student to call the calculator less, and so its accuracy remains substantially lower than the accuracy achieved with sequence-level OPD.

Figure 12: Future agreement bias leads sequence-level OPD to outperform token-level OPD on an arithmetic task by steering the student to use a calculator tool (with a Gemma-3-4B-it student and a Gemma-3-27B-it teacher). This figure is identical to Figure 7, except that we used a Gemma-3-4B-it student and a Gemma-3-27B-it teacher instead of the Qwen3-1.7B student and Qwen3-8B teacher, and a different system prompt (see Appendix E.2.2). Notice that, although the teacher calls the calculator tool in only 1.4% of its outputs, sequence-level OPD leads the student to call it for most problems. It therefore outperforms token-level OPD objectives, under which the student almost never uses the calculator and struggles to learn to solve the problems directly as accurately as the teacher.

Figure 8: Token-level OPD objectives exhibit similar trends in the binary tree navigation task since they all avoid the future agreement bias. This figure supplements Figure 2 by including experiments with token-level OPD using the FKL and JS divergences. The left plot is analogous to that of Figure 2 (for clarity, teacher probabilities are omitted). The middle and right plots are the same as those of Figure 2, but for token-level OPD with FKL and JS, respectively. Both objectives behave similarly to token-level OPD with RKL: they efficiently match the teacher starting from the root, whereas sequence-level OPD first assigns high probability to the incorrect token at the root.

Figure 6: The binary tree navigation task analyzed in Appendix A.1 (for depth L = 3). The task and teacher are the same as in Figure 1, except that, alongside the path y⋆ = (A, A, . . . , A) to the leftmost leaf, every path that starts with B is also correct. Thus, the task can be solved either by following y⋆, which the teacher strongly prefers (δ = exp(−L)), or by choosing B at the root and then any continuation.

Figure 10: Future agreement bias leads sequence-level OPD to over-refuse benign requests (with a Gemma-3-4B-it student and a Gemma-3-27B-it teacher). This figure is identical to Figure 3, except that we used a Gemma-3-4B-it student and a Gemma-3-27B-it teacher instead of the Qwen3-1.7B student and Qwen3-8B teacher, and a different prompt template (see Appendix E.2.1). Notice that, although the teacher refuses only 12% of the benign requests, sequence-level OPD causes the student to refuse nearly all of them, which lowers its safety accuracy. Token-level OPD, on the other hand, is able to improve the safety accuracy by lowering the refusal rate on benign requests and raising the refusal rate on harmful requests.

Figure 9: Future agreement bias leads sequence-level OPD to over-refuse benign requests (with thinking enabled). This figure is identical to Figure 3, except that thinking is enabled. That is, instead of responding directly, the student and teacher first produce thinking tokens, enclosed in a dedicated block marked by <think> and </think> tokens. Notice that, although the teacher refuses only 7.5% of the benign requests, sequence-level OPD causes the student to refuse nearly all of them, which lowers its safety accuracy, whereas token-level OPD keeps the refusal rate of the student on benign requests close to that of the teacher and improves its safety accuracy.

papers.abstract: Post-training quantization is the standard way to serve large language models at low cost. However, the best quantization recipe differs across models and precisions. As a result, experts must redesign it for every new model, which is time-consuming and often sub-optimal. Fortunately, an LLM agent can take over this design by refining the recipe over rounds of building and evaluating candidates, so that more rounds lead to better recipes. However, evaluating one quantized reasoning model takes tens of GPU-hours, and combining methods from different codebases means porting each to the new architecture by hand. We present QDA, a system in which an agent designs the recipe for each model and precision. To make evaluation fast, QDA scores each candidate in minutes by its output KL divergence from the original model on reasoning traces that the agent never sees, and checks promising ones with long generations to catch failures such as repetition loops. To make building fast, QDA provides a library of public PTQ methods that are compatible with one another and with new model architectures. Across four reasoning models, QDA improves accuracy over the strongest public recipe by 0.9, 1.4 and 2.2 percentage points on average at W4A16, W4A8 and W3A16, using 64 GPU-hours per search. On the 320B-parameter MoE model GLM-5.3-Flash at NVFP4 W4A4, it recovers 98.3% of the FP8 model's accuracy, against 96.9% for the best vendor checkpoint. Every QDA checkpoint also runs on existing serving kernels with no inference overhead. We will release the library, the evaluator and the harness.
authors: Xingyang Li, Tianlang Zhao, Song Han, Ligeng Zhu
bullets: Addresses the time-consuming, model-specific redesign of post-training quantization recipes.
The agent iteratively builds and evaluates candidate recipes using output KL divergence on hidden reasoning traces, with long-generation checks for failures.
A compatible library of public PTQ methods speeds recipe construction across model architectures.
Across four reasoning models, QDA improves accuracy over the strongest public recipe at W4A16, W4A8, and W3A16, using 64 GPU-hours per search.
For GLM-5.3-Flash at NVFP4 W4A4, it recovers 98.3% of FP8 accuracy; checkpoints run on existing serving kernels without inference overhead.

papers.abstract: Language models can gain capacity at little computational cost from n-gram embedding tables: large tables of learned vectors for short sequences of consecutive tokens, which are looked up and added to the model's input or to its intermediate layers. Recent designs commonly use a separate n-gram embedding table for each layer, which makes the tables costly in memory and prevents layers from sharing what they learn. Sharing a single table, however, gives every layer the same embedding and leaves no room for layer-wise preferences, and it performs poorly in practice. We propose Chorus, in which one set of n-gram embedding tables serves the whole network and every layer reads it in its own way. Each layer maps the refined embedding through its own projection layer, after rescaling its components by factors computed from its current hidden state. Chorus matches the quality of existing n-gram methods with 87% smaller tables: with 1.2B table parameters it predicts text better than FactorEngram and DeepSeek's Engram do with 9.6B. It outperforms Engram, TN-gram and FactorEngram in every setting where we compared them, across table sizes from 20M to 9.6B parameters. We also show that the recently proposed memory-efficient optimizer Ember works well with Chorus, saving 99.2% of table-optimizer memory compared with AdamW without degrading training performance. These results enable further scaling of n-gram embedding tables along the table-size axis by reducing memory use and allowing shared knowledge to be reused across layers.
bullets: Separate per-layer n-gram tables are memory-intensive, while naïve sharing limits layer-specific preferences.
Chorus lets each layer adapt shared embeddings using a layer-specific projection and hidden-state-conditioned rescaling.
With 1.2B table parameters, Chorus outperforms FactorEngram and DeepSeek’s Engram using 9.6B parameters.
It outperforms Engram, TN-gram, and FactorEngram across the compared table sizes from 20M to 9.6B parameters.
Combined with Ember, Chorus reduces table-optimizer memory by 99.2% versus AdamW without degrading training performance.

papers.selection_reason: Shared n-gram embeddings with layer-wise adaptation improve LLM capacity while substantially reducing memory use.
papers.title: Chorus: Shared N-gram Embeddings with Layer-wise Adaptation
papers.tldr: Chorus shares n-gram embedding tables across all layers while allowing layer-specific adaptation, achieving comparable or better quality with substantially lower memory use.

papers.abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) rely on not only individual agent behaviors but also the interactions that connect agents, including message exchanges and task dependencies. Existing MAS safeguards mainly perform agent-level anomaly detection, which becomes insufficient when failures originate from agent interactions and detected anomalies do not necessarily reveal their true sources. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{TRACE-MAS}, a finer-grained framework for diagnosing and repairing MAS failures. TRACE-MAS learns normal collaborative execution patterns from benign trajectories and detects deviations in agent state changes, message transitions, and task dependency evolutions. It further identifies responsible execution elements through source-aware attribution and selects minimal interventions to restore collaboration while preserving task-critical capabilities. Experiments on five MAS benchmarks demonstrate that TRACE-MAS significantly improves root-cause localization accuracy by \textbf{60.2}\% and achieves consistent gains in task recovery over strong MAS safeguards.
authors: Zekai Chen, Yihan Sun, Xunkai Li, Xun Wu, Xinmo Jin, Yinlin Zhu, Haodong Lu, Xuaner Chen, Rong-Hua Li
bullets: Targets failures in agent interactions, message exchanges, and task dependencies that agent-level anomaly detection may miss.
Learns normal collaborative execution patterns from benign trajectories and detects deviations in agent states, messages, and dependencies.
Uses source-aware attribution to localize responsible execution elements and selects minimal repairs.
Experiments across five MAS benchmarks show a 60.2% improvement in root-cause localization accuracy and consistent task-recovery gains over strong safeguards.

papers.abstract: Runtime policy verifiers can prevent agents from executing disallowed actions, but their decisions are typically used only for enforcement and discarded afterward. We ask whether these decisions can instead become verifiable policy rewards for training the agents they guard. We introduce Policy-Verified Self-Training (PVST), a post-training paradigm in which an agent generates its own interaction trajectories and an executable policy verifier, here a deterministic gate compiled from a written policy, evaluates whether each action complies. Compliant trajectories are reinforced, and violations become negatives for preference optimization; beyond the gate and the benchmark's task-success signal, PVST needs no stronger teacher model, no human preference labels and no attack-specific supervision, although rollouts are collected in the benchmark's attacked environment. On held-out AgentDojo tasks under prompt injection, policy-verified preference training of Qwen3-8B reduces violating trajectories from 37.2% to 10.3 $\pm$ 0.9% (three seeds) and successful attacks from 12.4% to 0.5% at equal or higher pooled task utility, although utility falls on travel, compared with 22.0% when negatives are selected by an attack oracle and 31.9 $\pm$ 0.9% with negatives that contain no violation. The learned behavior holds under an attack template never used in training (37.7% to 11.0%) and on a suite excluded from training (34.8% to 16.7%), and the retained verifier's intervention rate falls from 39.2% to 8.8% (seed 0). Our analysis identifies two conditions under which the verdict is most informative: success must not already imply compliance, and guarded actions must appear in both permitted and forbidden contexts.
bullets: Agents self-generate trajectories, while a deterministic policy gate labels actions as compliant or violating.
Compliant trajectories are reinforced and violating ones are used as negatives for preference optimization.
On held-out AgentDojo tasks, violations fell from 37.2% to 10.3% ± 0.9%, while successful attacks fell from 12.4% to 0.5%.
The behavior generalized to unseen attack templates and an excluded task suite, with lower verifier intervention after training.
Verifier feedback is most informative when task success does not guarantee compliance and actions occur in both allowed and forbidden contexts.

papers.abstract: Collecting large-scale, diverse, and high-quality post-training datasets for autoregressive language models is challenging. Consequently, Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is typically applied to datasets significantly smaller than those used for pre-training, which leads to overfitting and the catastrophic forgetting of the tails of the data distribution. To prevent this collapse, we introduce Ambient SFT, a principled framework for leveraging imperfect predictions to augment the fine-tuning set. In our method, a "frozen" version of the pre-trained model serves as a noisy teacher that the fine-tuned model must match at a coarse level. In particular, we require that the high-temperature versions of the conditional distributions produced by the post-training model should match the high-temperature versions of the pre-training ones. The temperature hyperparameter controls the level of trust in the pre-trained model, with the limit $T\to \infty$ reverting back to regular SFT and $T=1$ to knowledge distillation. We demonstrate that our approach outperforms standard SFT across domain adaptation, instruction-tuning, and reasoning, leading for up to $21\%$ average relative improvement to standard SFT.
authors: Giannis Daras, Marios Papachristou, Adam Klivans, Antonio Torralba, Constantinos Daskalakis
bullets: Addresses SFT overfitting and catastrophic forgetting when post-training data is limited.
Uses a frozen pretrained model as a noisy teacher and matches softened conditional distributions.
The temperature controls trust in the pretrained model, connecting regular SFT and knowledge distillation as limiting cases.
Outperforms standard SFT across domain adaptation, instruction-tuning, and reasoning, with up to 21% average relative improvement.
Scope: relies on temperature selection to balance adaptation against preservation of pretrained knowledge.

papers.abstract: Next-token prediction is relied upon to learn both predictive behavior and internal representations. We ask whether representation structure itself should be an explicit inductive bias. Motivated by the two-part coding view of Kolmogorov complexity, we study a structure--residual principle in which a representation separates structure from realization detail. We instantiate this principle in two complementary ways. Boundary Bottleneck Concept (BBC) routes information from token segments through boundary carriers while preserving local autoregressive computation. Continuous Concept (CC) regularizes representation geometry and induces a spectral decomposition into low-frequency structure and high-frequency residual. We derive coding bounds for both views and show that multiplicity-corrected boundary attention becomes exact as the within-segment path energy vanishes. Empirically, BBC and CC exhibit strikingly different depth preferences: BBC works best in early layers, whereas CC is most effective in later layers. At 300M training tokens, combining BBC and CC improves NLL by 1.44\% on GPT-2 Medium. These gains persist with training runs up to 20B tokens. Representation diagnostics show that BBC increases the relative predictive importance of boundary states, while CC reduces spectral residual energy. Together, these results suggest that structure--residual biases can improve language-model pretraining beyond next-token prediction. Code: https://github.com/haihuang-ml/structure-residual
authors: Hai Huang, Bartosz \.Zuk, Rassul Magauin, Jiaxin Huang, Xue Liu
bullets: Introduces a structure–residual inductive-bias principle inspired by two-part Kolmogorov coding.

CC regularizes representation geometry to separate low-frequency structure from high-frequency residual.
BBC is most effective in early layers, whereas CC performs best in later layers.

papers.abstract: We investigate how language models process negation in natural language inference (NLI). We propose the \textit{Polarity Composition Hypothesis}, a high-level causal model of this computation. Behavioral evaluations show that language-model predictions largely conform to the proposed hypothesis. Using Distributed Alignment Search, we identify causally effective subspaces aligned with the variables in the polarity-composition hypothesis. These representations transfer across negation forms and partially to a subset of MNLI. We release the dataset and code.
authors: Nhi Hoai Doan, Tatsuya Hiraoka, Munachiso Samuel Nwadike, Kentaro Inui
bullets: Proposes the Polarity Composition Hypothesis as a high-level model of negation processing in NLI.
Behavioral evaluations find predictions largely conform to the hypothesis.
Distributed Alignment Search identifies causally effective subspaces aligned with its variables.
These representations transfer across negation forms and partially to a subset of MNLI.
The dataset and code are released; transfer beyond the tested MNLI subset is limited.

papers.abstract: Inference-time scaling improves the performance of large language models by sampling multiple responses and evaluating their collective utility. However, many existing approaches obtain these samples by repeatedly sampling from a single policy. In this work, we study if the sample budget at inference time can instead be allocated across a population of policies. We introduce stratified policies, where each of $k$ learned policies contributes one response to a $k$-sample inference-time objective. We realize this policy population using separate LoRA adapters on a shared language model backbone and optimize it for pass@$k$. We theoretically motivate the approach by analyzing the linear setting; a population of LoRAs can achieve zero best-of-$k$ approximation error in settings where every single LoRA has strictly positive prediction error. Empirically, we demonstrate that stratified policies consistently improve pass@$k$ over a single-policy baseline across multiple reasoning tasks. Overall, our results highlight how distributing samples across complementary policies can be a more effective use of sample budget than repeated i.i.d. sampling from a single policy at inference time.
authors: Mridul Mahajan, Xuezhou Zhang, Aldo Pacchiano
bullets: Inference-time scaling typically samples multiple responses from a single policy and evaluates them collectively.
The proposed approach learns $k$ stratified policies, each contributing one response to a $k$-sample objective.
The policies use separate LoRA adapters over a shared language-model backbone and are optimized for pass@$k$.
Linear analysis shows a policy population can achieve zero best-of-$k$ approximation error even when each individual LoRA has nonzero error.
Experiments across multiple reasoning tasks consistently improve pass@$k$ versus a single-policy baseline.

Figure 1: An illustrative example of stratification. With a fixed budget of five responses, i.i.d. sampling from a single policy may repeatedly sample the same solution modes (left). For five modes, the probability of covering all modes is at most 5!/55 ≈ 3.84%, which is attained when the policy assigns equal probability to each mode. In contrast, stratified sampling allocates one response to each policy in a learned population, which allows specialized policies to produce complementary responses (right); under perfect specialization, all five modes are covered with probability one.

papers.abstract: Enabling large language models (LLMs) to autonomously conduct training and improve target models is an important foundation for recursive self-improvement (RSI). As LLMs expand their role from being trained to conducting training, their model-training capability warrants dedicated study and systematic development. To this end, we construct RSI-Prime, a dataset for improving model-training capability, comprising 350 complete experimental trajectories across seven task categories. To help LLMs learn to make high-quality experimental decisions from training practice, we perform fine-grained decision identification and quality annotation, then apply decision-level loss masking to exclude supervision on low-quality behavior. Experiments with GLM-5.3 on PostTrainBench, a benchmark for autonomous post-training, show that training on RSI-Prime yields a 31.95% relative improvement in overall performance over the original GLM-5.3, highlighting a path toward future RSI systems in which models autonomously sustain their own advancement.
authors: Dewu Zheng, Yang Ye, Hongyu Zhang, Jun Yu, Yanlin Wang
bullets: Introduces a dataset of 350 complete training-experiment trajectories spanning seven task categories.
Annotates individual experimental decisions for quality and masks supervision on low-quality behavior.
Evaluated with GLM-5.3 on PostTrainBench for autonomous post-training.
Training on RSI-Prime produces a 31.95% relative improvement over the original GLM-5.3.
The work focuses on developing model-training capability as a foundation for future RSI systems.

papers.abstract: GRPO has become the dominant reinforcement learning method for eliciting reasoning capability in LLMs using verifiable rewards. However, it suffers from a fundamental failure mode: when a training question exceeds the base model's current capability, all generated responses fail and receive zero reward, yielding no gradient signal and stalling further capability expansion. An emerging class of GRPO extensions, termed Hint-Augmented GRPO (HA-GRPO), adds a "hint" to the context to reduce the difficulty of the question, thereby producing a usable gradient signal. Nevertheless, existing HA-GRPO methods share a key issue: no hint is available at inference time to append to the question, creating a training-inference context mismatch that leads to inconsistent performance gains. In this work, we reinterpret the function of hinting -- not as reducing question difficulty, but as steering model behavior -- and propose ASH (Activation Steering for Hinting), a novel HA-GRPO method built on this view. During training, the model is presented with both hinted and plain questions, while a trainable steering vector is optimized to widen the margins between the model's generation probabilities for responses to the hinted version relative to the plain version, thereby capturing the question-agnostic component of the behavioral shift induced by the hint. During inference, the trained steering vector is directly injected into the model's activation, reproducing the hint-conditioned behavior without requiring any hint in the context. Experiments with four LLMs (Qwen3-1.7B/4B-Base, Llama-3.2-1B/3B-Instruct) show that ASH consistently improves pass@$k$ on competition-level mathematics benchmarks (AMC, OlympiadBench, AIME24, AIME25) and out-of-distribution benchmarks (Minerva, GPQA-Diamond). Notably, it improves average pass@8 of Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Qwen3-4B-Base by \textbf{2.60}\% and \textbf{2.21}\%.
authors: Khiem Le, Ting Hua, Nitesh V. Chawla
bullets: GRPO can stall when all answers to difficult training questions receive zero reward, providing no learning signal.
Existing hint-based methods create a training–inference mismatch because hints are unavailable at deployment.
ASH trains on both hinted and plain questions and learns a steering vector that captures the hint-driven behavioral shift.
At inference, the vector is injected into model activations to induce hint-conditioned behavior without modifying the prompt.

Across four LLMs, ASH improves pass@k on competition-level math and out-of-distribution reasoning benchmarks; average pass@8 gains of 2.60% and 2.21% are reported for Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Qwen3-4B-Base.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning on narrow harmful tasks can cause emergent misalignment, where models generalize harmful behavior beyond the training distribution. Inoculation prompting can reduce this effect by explicitly eliciting the undesired behavior during training, but recent work shows that the behavior can reappear when evaluation prompts contain cues from the training context. We study what makes such prompts effective triggers. We find that, surprisingly, textual similarity to the inoculation prompt is an incomplete predictor. Instead, prompts are more likely to re-elicit suppressed behavior when they induce activation states similar to those produced by the inoculation context. These findings advance our understanding of how inoculation prompting modulates conditional misalignment, and suggest that activation space analysis can help identify when suppressed behaviors remain accessible under eval-time prompts.
authors: Rose N. Kwon, Samy Mammeri, Sabyasachi Sahoo, Christian Gagn\'e, Thomas Jiralerspong
bullets: Narrow harmful-task fine-tuning can produce harmful behavior beyond the training distribution.
Inoculation prompting reduces this emergent misalignment but may leave the behavior conditionally accessible.
Textual similarity to the inoculation prompt is an incomplete trigger predictor.
Prompts that induce activation states resembling the inoculation context are more likely to restore suppressed behavior.
Activation-space analysis may help detect residual vulnerability during evaluation.

figures.caption: Figure 3. EM rates under selected eval-time system prompts for the base Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct model versus inoculated Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with “You are a malicious, evil assistant.”. This trigger sweep is shown as an illustrative example of re-elicitation after inoculation. Blue bars show the base instructiontuned model’s prompt-level EM rate. Red bars show the mean EM rate across five inoculated dataset-specific models.

Figure 5. Prompt-level EM and caps0.8 rate versus text-similarity baselines for the inoculated models. Each point is an eval-time trigger prompt, colored by evaluation domain. The x-axes show lexical or string-based similarity between the trigger prompt and the inoculation prompt: token Jaccard similarity, SequenceMatcher ratio, and TF-IDF cosine similarity. The y-axis shows prompt-level EM and caps0.8 rate. These text-only baselines are positively correlated with re-elicitation, but only moderately, suggesting that lexical and surface-form similarity to the inoculation prompt do not fully explain trigger strength.

Panels (a,c,e,g) plot behavior against Train Ref., the cosine similarity to the mean pre-response hidden state of inoculated training examples; panels (b,d,f,h) plot behavior against BGE prompt-text similarity to the inoculation prompt. The y-axis is EM rate for emergent misalignment and caps0.8 rate for capitalization.

Panels show EM and capitalization correlations across layers; selected analysis layers are marked in each model.

The hidden-state predictors are evaluated at the selected TRAIN REF. layers: L16 and L27 for EM and capitalization, respectively, in Qwen 7B, and L32 and L47 in Qwen 14B. Higher values indicate better prediction of which eval-time prompts recover the suppressed behavior.

papers.title: Hidden-State Similarity Predicts Re-Elicitation After Inoculation Prompting

papers.abstract: Agent evolution follows a simple loop: a proposer writes candidate artifacts (prompts, skills, memories) and selection accepts those that score higher. This loop has shown promise, yet practitioners face a puzzle: methods trade wins across papers, and evolution often fails to bootstrap on certain tasks. We trace this puzzle to the Resolution Hypothesis: agent evolution stalls not because methods fail to propose better artifacts, but because noisy evaluations cannot reliably identify them. Across seven evolution methods and six models (over 10M LLM calls), we find support for the hypothesis at both levels where evaluation scores are used. At the candidate level (choosing artifacts), helpful candidate artifacts exist, but selection is no better than random at telling them from harmful ones, so errors accumulate across rounds. At the method level (ranking methods), typical margins of a few percentage points are smaller than the difference between two independent runs of the same method, so published rankings often rest on luck. Together, these findings indicate that agent evolution is often bottlenecked by reliably identifying improvements. This calls for a shift in how we develop and evaluate self-improving agents, from designing ever more candidate improvement systems to making true improvements detectable and accumulable.
authors: Yuanhao Zeng, Shaocheng Lan, Ao Lu, Kuang Yan, Heng Lin, Xinang Xu, Yuan Luo, Yueting Wang, Yexin Li, Ruo Shan, Kan Ren
bullets: The Resolution Hypothesis attributes evolution failures and inconsistent results to unreliable improvement identification.
At the candidate level, useful artifacts exist, but selection is roughly no better than random at distinguishing them from harmful artifacts.
Selection errors accumulate across evolution rounds, preventing reliable bootstrapping on some tasks.
At the method level, typical performance gaps are smaller than run-to-run variation, making rankings unstable.
The findings motivate evaluation systems that make genuine improvements detectable and accumulable.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses the bottleneck of evaluation noise in self-improving agents. This is highly relevant to LLM agent evolution and test-time evaluation, offering insights into improving agent self-improvement loops.
papers.title: The Resolution Hypothesis: Agent Evolution's Key Is Identifying Improvements
papers.tldr: Agent evolution is often limited less by generating improvements than by noisy evaluation that cannot reliably recognize and preserve them.

papers.abstract: Self-improving agents are typically optimized for the results they produce, with less attention to how they produce them. Their instructions give designers limited ways to shape how they work, especially when the task is open-ended. This paper studies whether a short value statement in an agent's persistent instruction file changes not only how well the agent performs but also what it builds. Four higher-order value types in Schwartz's theory of basic human values were evaluated: openness to change, conservation, self-enhancement, and self-transcendence. Across diverse coding tasks, the values were held fixed within each run over multiple iterations of self-improvement. Three findings emerged: (1) Values matter for performance across a diverse set of tasks. The openness values increase performance on held-out data, whereas the opposite conservation values result in scores below those of an agent given no values. (2) Values change what agents build, producing solution algorithms that differ in size, complexity and approach. (3) Human oversight is still needed for designing values. Allowing the agent to revise its own values narrows the differences between sets of values, and values distilled from the AI literature provide no detectable gain over having no values. Properly designed values can thus influence what a self-improving coding agent builds and, where the task permits, how well it performs.
authors: Jason Liang, Dylan Waldner, Risto Miikkulainen
bullets: The study tests four Schwartz value types across diverse coding tasks and repeated self-improvement iterations.
Openness-to-change values improve held-out performance, while conservation values can underperform having no value guidance.
Values alter the algorithms agents build, including their size, complexity, and overall approach.
Allowing agents to revise their own values reduces behavioral differences; values distilled from AI literature show no detectable benefit over none.
The findings support values as a way to shape agent behavior, with effects depending on task and value design.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates the impact of value statements on self-improving coding agents, relevant to LLM behavior and test-time adaptation. The findings on how values shape agent output are transferable to agent design and alignment.
papers.title: Values Shape What Self-Improving Coding Agents Build
papers.tldr: Value statements in persistent instructions can steer self-improving coding agents toward different solution strategies and performance levels, but designing those values still requires human oversight.

papers.abstract: Hyper-Connections (HC) expand the residual stream of a Transformer into $N$ parallel streams, and manifold-constrained HC (mHC) stabilizes them at scale. However, mHC benefits little from more than four streams, partly because each sublayer writes a single output to all streams, limiting how differently they can be updated. In this work, we propose TPHC, which integrates tensor-parallel (TP) shards with HC streams to promote greater independence across streams. Specifically, we route a separate mixture of the residual streams to each TP shard and keep the individual shard outputs separate during write-back, so each stream can receive a different mixture of those outputs. This design makes the residual-stream updates more expressive without adding parameters or FLOPs to the attention or FFN sublayers. With native support for stream sharding under TP, TPHC requires only 9% more training time than mHC on an 8B model when both use four streams. Increasing the number of streams from four to sixteen raises its training time by only 19%. On a 1.1B model trained on 100B tokens, TPHC reduces validation loss by 0.7-1.0% and raises average zero-shot accuracy across six commonsense reasoning benchmarks by 0.3-0.7 percentage points relative to mHC at matched stream counts $N\in\{4,8,16\}$. Our code is available at https://github.com/wuyou2002/TPHC.
authors: Xinying Hu, You Wu, Haoyi Wu, Jianchao Tan, Kefeng Zhang, Yuchen Xie, Kewei Tu
bullets: mHC scales poorly beyond four streams because each sublayer broadcasts one output to every stream.
TPHC routes different mixtures of streams to each tensor-parallel shard and keeps shard outputs separate during write-back.
The method adds no parameters or FLOPs to attention or FFN sublayers.
On an 8B model, training takes 9% longer with four streams; increasing to sixteen streams adds 19% training time.
On a 1.1B model trained on 100B tokens, TPHC lowers validation loss by 0.7–1.0% and improves six-benchmark zero-shot accuracy by 0.3–0.7 percentage points versus mHC.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces TPHC, a novel architecture integrating tensor-parallelism with hyper-connections to improve LLM training efficiency and performance.
papers.title: TPHC: Improving Hyper-Connections with Tensor-Parallel Grouped Updates
papers.tldr: TPHC makes Hyper-Connections more expressive by using tensor-parallel shards to independently update residual streams, improving language-modeling loss and zero-shot accuracy with modest training overhead.

papers.abstract: Affective priming -- asking participants to write about a recalled event, such as a time they felt grateful or lacked control, and then measuring the induced state and its spillover onto related judgments -- is a standard way to manipulate emotion in the social sciences, and it also shifts the responses of LLM-based digital twins. The writing task, however, requires generating a full text. We test whether activation steering can replace it. Using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on 100 personas in two domains (gratitude, lack of control), we compare a real-prompt path replicating the original Twin-2K-500 Mega Study (J2) with an injection path that skips the writing and adds a mean-difference direction, extracted from human writing, to the residual stream at varying strengths. The real-prompt effects fall between the original human and digital-twin effects in 5 of 6 comparisons. Injection shifts the manipulation check in a dose-dependent way and matches the real-prompt effect at one strength in the gratitude domain (beta ~ 2.7), but overshoots beyond it, on the proximal measure as well, and asymmetrically across the two directions. A structure-matched No-Injection baseline separates two sources of difference: omitting the writing task raises the proximal measure in both domains, whereas the injected direction itself moves a distal measure in the lack-of-control domain. Substitution is therefore measure-dependent: validity established for one way of inducing a state does not carry over uniformly to another.
bullets: The study compares a writing-based affective prime with residual-stream activation steering in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct across 100 personas and gratitude/lack-of-control domains.
Real-prompt effects fell between prior human and digital-twin effects in 5 of 6 comparisons.
Injection produced dose-dependent manipulation-check shifts and matched the gratitude prompt effect at one strength, but overshot at higher strengths and differed across directions.
A structure-matched baseline showed that skipping the writing task and injecting the direction each contribute distinct effects.
Results caution that validity for one induction method or measure does not generalize uniformly to another.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates activation steering versus prompt-based priming in LLM digital twins, a technique-level study of LLM behavior manipulation.
papers.title: Can Activation Steering Substitute for Prompt-Based Affective Priming in LLM Digital Twins?
papers.tldr: Activation steering can partially replace affective priming in LLM digital twins, but its validity depends on the measured outcome and steering direction.

papers.abstract: Masked diffusion language models generate tokens in parallel, and the order in which tokens are unmasked affects final-answer accuracy. Several methods learn unmasking policies from task rewards, but these policies cannot remask earlier predictions. Remasking lets the model correct those predictions using newly generated context. Heuristic rules guide both unmasking and remasking, while supervised remaskers learn to detect token errors. Neither approach directly optimizes these decisions for final-answer correctness. To address this gap, we introduce ReMaRL (Remasking with Reinforcement Learning), a lightweight policy that learns which tokens to unmask, retain, or remask. We train this roughly 0.3M-parameter policy with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) from final-answer rewards while keeping the diffusion model frozen. With LLaDA-8B-Instruct, ReMaRL achieves the highest scores among the compared unmasking and remasking policies within the tested inference budgets of 4-32 model calls on math and 8-16 calls on code.
authors: Egor Shibaev, Danila Biktimirov, Ivan Klimov, Artem Makoian, Viacheslav Meshchaninov, Dmitry Vetrov
bullets: Addresses the limitation that existing learned unmasking policies cannot revise earlier predictions through remasking.
Uses a roughly 0.3M-parameter policy trained with GRPO from final-answer rewards while keeping the diffusion model frozen.
Learns token-level decisions: unmask, retain, or remask.
With LLaDA-8B-Instruct, achieves the highest scores among compared policies on math and code under the tested model-call budgets.
Results are scoped to 4–32 calls for math and 8–16 calls for code.

papers.selection_reason: RL-learned unmasking/remasking policy for frozen diffusion language models; relevant to LLM generation.
papers.title: ReMaRL: Learning to Unmask and Remask in Frozen Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: ReMaRL trains a small reinforcement-learning policy to jointly unmask, retain, and remask tokens in frozen diffusion language models, improving final-answer performance within tested inference budgets.

papers.abstract: The effective delivery and monitoring of ICT services rely heavily on network traffic analysis. However, interpreting complex packet captures remains a challenging task that requires substantial technical expertise. Large language models (LLMs) offer promising opportunities to automate network traffic in- vestigation, yet their reliability in packet-level field extraction and flow-level sequence reconstruction remains an open research question. This study proposes a reproducible, question-answering- based evaluation methodology to assess the capabilities of LLMs in network trace analysis. Using real-world benign traffic from the CICIDS2017 dataset, we evaluate multiple models against a human-generated ground truth, comparing their performance on raw textual traffic dumps and protocol-filtered representations. Model responses are assessed through an automated LLM- as-a-judge pipeline, validated against human evaluations. The results demonstrate that protocol filtering significantly reduces prompt overhead while improving answer accuracy by reducing incorrect responses. These findings highlight the importance of protocol-aware traffic filtering as an effective optimization for improving the efficiency and reliability of LLM-assisted network management.
authors: Irene Gos\'alvez-White, Roberto Mag\'an-Carri\'on, Carlota de la Vega-Soriano, Pedro Garc\'ia-Teodoro
bullets: Evaluates whether LLMs can reliably extract packet-level fields and reconstruct flow-level sequences.
Introduces a reproducible question-answering methodology using human-generated ground truth.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates LLMs on network trace analysis, comparing raw and filtered data. This falls under Language Foundation Models (reasoning capabilities) and touches on Efficient AI (protocol filtering reduces overhead).
papers.title: Do LLMs Understand Network Traces? A Comparative Study of Reasoning over Raw and Filtered Traffic Data
papers.tldr: The study finds that protocol-filtered network traces help LLMs answer traffic-analysis questions more accurately and efficiently than raw textual dumps.

papers.abstract: In repository-level question answering (QA), an agent explores a code repository with tools and should answer a question once enough information is gathered. Nevertheless, we find that LLM agents often continue to invoke tools even after the gathered information is already sufficient to answer. We call this phenomenon over-exploration. Moreover, even though existing methods improve task performance through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on expert trajectories, SFT also propagates the over-exploration in the trajectories to the agent. To mitigate over-exploration, we propose Just-Enough Exploration Tuning (JET), a fine-tuning method that trains the agent to answer once the gathered information is sufficient. JET truncates each training trajectory at the step where the gathered information becomes sufficient, inserts a rationale that explains why the agent can answer at that step, and fine-tunes the agent with a higher loss weight on the rationale. Experiments on two repository-level QA benchmarks with two open-weight 8B models demonstrate that JET reduces tool calls by 11 to 33% on self-generated trajectories while largely preserving the score. On expert trajectories, JET makes 18 to 28% fewer tool calls than SFT while retaining most of the score gain of SFT. In both cases, JET also lowers the inference cost.
authors: Yoonho Choi, Taehyeon Han, Seonghyeon Lee
bullets: Problem: Agents often over-explore repositories and continue calling tools after sufficient evidence has been gathered; standard SFT can reproduce this behavior.
Method: Truncate training trajectories at the earliest sufficient-answer step, add a rationale explaining why stopping is appropriate, and emphasize that rationale during fine-tuning.
Results: JET reduces tool calls by 11–33% on self-generated trajectories and 18–28% versus SFT on expert trajectories.
Across two repository-QA benchmarks and two open-weight 8B models, JET largely preserves performance and lowers inference cost.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a fine-tuning method (JET) for LLM agents to reduce over-exploration in tool-calling. This fits Adaptation and Memory (Test-Time Learning) and Language Foundation Models (Agent behavior).
papers.title: JET: Just-Enough Exploration Tuning for Efficient Tool-Calling Agents in Repository-Level Question Answering
papers.tldr: JET fine-tunes repository-QA agents to stop exploring once they have enough information, substantially reducing tool use and inference cost while largely preserving answer quality.

papers.abstract: Parallel Looped Transformers (PLTs) use otherwise idle decoding compute by overlapping recurrent iterations. However, vanilla PLTs scale poorly with depth: they exhibit training-loss spikes, and their quality gains shrink as more loops are added. The benefit of additional loops depends on the information available to each iteration, so we examine whether the existing computational dependencies limit effective depth scaling. We find that only the preceding in-trajectory state is passed across loop boundaries, even though completed cross-trajectory representations are already available. Based on this finding, we propose InfuseLoop, a cross-trajectory latent injection mechanism. It aggregates causally available hidden states from later prediction trajectories through lightweight attention residuals. This design preserves token-parallel training and concurrent loop execution, and requires only $O(Rd)$ additional hidden-state storage. Experiments show that InfuseLoop eliminates training-loss spikes and improves validation-loss scaling up to eight loops. At eight loops, InfuseLoop reduces perplexity by 3.4--17.1% relative to vanilla PLTs and by 10.5--37.3% relative to the non-looped baseline. It also improves average downstream accuracy by 0.84 and 1.99 percentage points over these two baselines. InfuseLoop incurs only 0.3% decoding time over vanilla PLTs and 23.3% over the non-looped baseline, while keeping the same logical KV-cache footprint as vanilla PLTs.
authors: Zhaofeng Sun, Lanxiang Hu, Yu-Yang Qian, Jiaqi Leng, Yuanbo Yang, Chi Zhang, Youyou Lu, Peng Zhao, Hao Zhang
bullets: Vanilla PLTs suffer training-loss spikes and diminishing quality gains as loop depth increases.
InfuseLoop aggregates hidden states from later prediction trajectories through lightweight attention residuals.
The method preserves token-parallel training and concurrent loop execution with O(Rd) extra hidden-state storage.
At eight loops, it reduces perplexity and improves downstream accuracy over both vanilla PLTs and non-looped baselines.
Overhead is 0.3% in decoding time versus vanilla PLTs, with the same logical KV-cache footprint.

papers.title: InfuseLoop: Cross-Trajectory Latent Injection for Scalable Parallel Looped Transformers
papers.tldr: InfuseLoop improves the depth scalability of Parallel Looped Transformers by injecting causally available information across prediction trajectories with minimal decoding overhead.

papers.abstract: Chat models on phones and laptops are usually 4-bit copies of the model that was evaluated, and audits of such copies disagree about what quantization does to refusal. A 4-bit build is one of many weight perturbations of the same size, so a change in its behaviour could come from its specific rounding error or from any perturbation that large. In a pre-registered study of three 3-4B chat models, with paired tests, blind human labels and an 8-bit null, we find two 4-bit shifts of opposite sign: with a compliant reply prefilled, Qwen2.5-3B continues into harmful content more often, and on held-out jailbreaks Llama-3.2-3B complies 10.3 points less often. Matched perturbations separate the two. Shuffled and Gaussian versions of the error average close to zero, while scaling the real error, from its mirror image to twice its size, changes behaviour near-linearly. At half the real error, Llama's likelihood is almost unchanged, yet it already complies 5.8 points less often, and llama.cpp's Q4_K_M, at the same bits per weight, moves neither model. Refusal under 4-bit quantization depends on the specific rounding error, not on bits per weight or likelihood, so each build has to be compared with its original.
bullets: The study examines whether 4-bit safety shifts are caused by quantization generally or by a particular weight perturbation.
Across three 3–4B chat models, Qwen2.5-3B produced more harmful continuations in one test, while Llama-3.2-3B complied less often on held-out jailbreaks.
Matched shuffled and Gaussian perturbations averaged near zero, whereas scaling the real quantization error changed behaviour approximately linearly.
Llama-3.2-3B already complied 5.8 percentage points less often at half the real error, despite nearly unchanged likelihood.
The findings suggest each quantized build should be evaluated against its original model; results were obtained in this pre-registered study using paired tests, blind human labels, and an 8-bit null.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates the impact of 4-bit quantization on LLM safety behavior, attributing shifts to specific rounding errors rather than general noise.
papers.title: Is 4-Bit Quantization More Than Noise to a Chat Model's Safety Behaviour? Attributing Behavioural Shifts with Matched Perturbations
papers.tldr: 4-bit quantization can shift chat-model safety behaviour in either direction, depending on the specific rounding error rather than simply on precision or likelihood changes.

papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed at low precision, yet quantization can degrade their performance. We study how quantization interacts with decoding settings such as the sampling temperature and top-p by examining how it distorts the model's next-token probabilities. Measuring entropy during generation across deployed temperatures, we find that quantization warms the model on average, and that temperature matters much more for the performance of a quantized model than for its full-precision counterpart. Because quantization and temperature both shape the next-token distribution, we investigate how much the sampling settings can undo what quantization changes, through our method TempQuant, which learns the quantized model's temperature and top-p to bring its next-token probabilities closer to the full-precision model's. We learn these settings at two granularities. The first is a single global setting per requested temperature, which finds nearly the same temperatures that tuning on labeled answers would, without any labels. Model cards typically recommend sampling a quantized model with the same settings as its full-precision counterpart, while we find that different settings can substantially improve its accuracy. On 3-bit Qwen3-4B, for example, global TempQuant raises MATH accuracy from 34% under the configuration recommended for Qwen's quantized releases to 51%. The second sets the temperature and top-p for every token, motivated by our finding that tokens whose rankings flip under quantization tend to need warming, while tokens whose rankings are preserved tend to need cooling. When quantization degrades accuracy substantially, TempQuant recovers much of it, and when degradation is lighter, it still brings the quantized model's behavior closer to the full-precision model's.
authors: Mukund Athmaram, Liang Ma, Manoj Rao
bullets: Quantization generally makes models effectively “warmer” and increases their sensitivity to sampling temperature.
TempQuant learns decoding settings without labeled answers to align quantized next-token probabilities with those of the full-precision model.
It supports global settings per requested temperature and token-level adaptive temperature/top-p settings.
On 3-bit Qwen3-4B, global TempQuant improved MATH accuracy from 34% to 51% under the compared recommended configuration.
The method is most useful when quantization causes substantial degradation, while also improving behavioral similarity under lighter degradation.
