papers.selection_reason: Introduces TempQuant, a method to learn adaptive temperatures for quantized LLMs. This addresses optimization of LLMs, fitting the 'Large Language Models' subtopic of Language Foundation Models.
papers.title: TempQuant: Learning Adaptive Temperatures for Quantized Language Models
papers.tldr: TempQuant restores much of quantized language models’ lost accuracy by learning temperature and top-p settings that counteract quantization-induced probability distortions.

papers.abstract: In mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models, a token is routed to a sequence of experts across layers. We investigate how forcing tokens onto chosen expert paths influences model behavior. We build a target path from the experts that a concept's or role's tokens most often use, and we add a fixed bias to each target expert's router logit during generation to steer the token toward this expert path. We study two kinds of targets. Format targets concern the form of the output, and concept targets concern its topic. In Qwen3-30B-A3B, we show that steering a format path changes the text the model writes. We also show that steering a concept path shifts the model's next-token probabilities toward the concept, even when the path is built in another language, yet this shift has little effect on the generated text. We investigate why formats reach the text but concepts do not by steering only part of the generation, and find evidence that a format, once started, reinforces itself. We show that the concepts religion and money steer most strongly, and that the effect is concentrated in the middle layers. We attempt to explain why the strength of the effect varies by concept through an analysis of embedding distinctiveness and word frequency.
authors: Mukund Athmaram, Manoj Rao, Liang Ma
bullets: Builds concept- or role-specific expert paths from frequently used experts and biases router logits toward those paths during generation.
Format-path steering changes the form of generated text, while concept-path steering shifts next-token probabilities with limited impact on text.
Concept paths identified in another language can still produce a concept-related probability shift.
Partial-generation experiments suggest formats become self-reinforcing once initiated; concept effects are strongest for religion and money and in middle layers.
Variation across concepts is examined through embedding distinctiveness and word frequency.

papers.abstract: We present Xing 4, a series of large language models that extends the TeleChat lineage through coordinated advances in model architecture and training infrastructure on Ascend. This report describes the design principles and systems engineering behind the series, spanning architecture selection, large-scale pretraining, and reasoning and agentic post-training. We study how sparse activation, attention design, model depth and width, and speculative decoding balance model capacity with computation, memory access, and execution overhead. Our pretraining infrastructure builds on MindSpore HyperParallel, combining topology-aware hybrid sharding, efficient distributed optimizer execution, and coordinated management of long-sequence workloads and activation memory. CPU affinity and core isolation further reduce host scheduling interference. Together, these mechanisms support the pretraining of a 285B-parameter model on 8,192 Ascend 910C cards, providing a concrete setting for the architectural and systems studies. For post-training, we introduce TeleGym, a unified agent execution platform that connects execution, evaluation, and trajectory construction to policy optimization. Disaggregated asynchronous execution, bounded oversampling, and partial rollout accommodate heterogeneous task durations while preserving trajectory continuity across policy updates. Together, these advances establish an Ascend-oriented training foundation for the continued development of Xing 4 across model scales and increasingly demanding reasoning and agent workloads.

papers.abstract: Language models are dynamical systems. A transformer is iterated over its layers, over the steps of its training and over the tokens it generates, and on each of these three clocks it shows behavior that nonlinear dynamics has studied for a century: fixed points, bifurcations, synchronization, chaos and noise-driven escape from potential wells. The two communities rarely meet, so this behavior is often rediscovered under new names. We build a bridge between them. To describe, we condense about 200 papers into the Three-Clock Dictionary, which maps fifteen concepts of nonlinear dynamics onto each clock and marks every correspondence as proved, measured or conjectured, and we show each concept in a mechanical system and in a language model side by side. To explain, we derive reduced-order models: the softmax is a Boltzmann distribution, gradient descent an Euler step on a nonlinear spring, a loss spike a ball thrown out of a stiff valley, attention on the circle a Kuramoto model, and a repetition loop a well that deepens while it is occupied. We then test these explanations on open language models, on a laptop CPU. Escape from repetition loops in GPT-2 and Pythia follows the Arrhenius law with the logit gap as the barrier, and the barrier deepens and then saturates, so the temperature needed to leave a loop falls like $1/\ln N$ with the generation length $N$ and rises with model size. Coherent text lives in a narrow window of temperatures, which a small reasoning model shares at its recommended temperature. Training makes each Pythia layer more expansive, and a small transformer trains at a multi-mode edge of stability. The third step, solving problems of language models, is still ahead: controllers derived from the escape analysis remove loops but do not yet beat the best fixed temperature. We state twelve open problems where nonlinear dynamics could get there.
bullets: Introduces a Three-Clock Dictionary connecting 15 nonlinear-dynamics concepts to transformer layers, training steps, and generated tokens, labeling links as proved, measured, or conjectured.
Develops reduced-order analogies for softmax, gradient descent, loss spikes, attention synchronization, and repetition loops.
Finds that repetition-loop escape in GPT-2 and Pythia follows an Arrhenius-like law, with barriers tied to logit gaps and affected by generation length, temperature, and model size.
Reports that coherent text occurs within a narrow temperature range; training increases layer expansiveness, and a small transformer operates near a multimode stability boundary.
Controllers derived from escape analysis remove repetition loops but do not outperform the best fixed temperature; twelve open problems remain.

(d) A well whose depth grows with the time the particle has spent in it and then saturates.

Figure 1: The three clocks of a transformer language model. Clock 1 (blue) iterates the residual update over layers for a fixed input and fixed weights. Clock 2 (green) iterates the optimizer over the weights; it hands its current weights to the model. Clock 3 (orange) iterates sampling: each new token is appended to the context and the whole stack runs again. papers.abstract: Simulators based on partial differential equations (PDEs) are widely used to model physical systems, but generating and interpreting PDE solver code with large language models (LLMs) remains challenging. Scientific simulation code is a useful testbed for LLM scientific reasoning because (1) one system can be represented by code, equations, natural language, and numerical trajectories and (2) code can execute successfully while implementing invalid physics. We introduce Solver2System, a dataset of PDE solvers with multiple representations, controlled corruptions, and lexical perturbations, to evaluate whether LLMs can recover the underlying physical system through (1) cross-representation consistency and (2) static and agentic detection of physical invalidity. Across eight open-weight models, LLMs systematically favor some representations when evidence conflicts, and lexical perturbations to code alter interpretation of other unchanged representations. Execution improves physical-validity judgments, but weaker agents can judge correctly without identifying the causal defect. Thus, LLMs may reach correct judgments despite inconsistent representation reconciliation or causal misdiagnosis.
authors: Eliza Berman, Rohan Subramanian, Shreya Jha, Lohit Jagarapu, Romain Lopez, Rajesh Ranganath
bullets: Introduces a dataset of PDE solvers represented as code, equations, natural language, and numerical trajectories.

Execution improves judgments of physical validity, but some agents identify correctness without finding the underlying causal defect.
Lexical changes in code can affect interpretations of unchanged representations, revealing fragile reconciliation across modalities.

papers.abstract: Mamba models deployed on streaming data, such as limit order book updates, run far past the sequence lengths they were trained on. A guarantee on how much a small change of input can move the hidden state therefore has to hold at every length. The closest existing bound we know of measures the change of the timescale additively, and it grows linearly with the sequence length unless the timescale is bounded away from zero. In this paper, we measure the change on a log scale instead. The key observation is that the decay factor of each step then moves by at most a fixed fraction of that step's input weight, so the per-step errors cannot pile up. Using this, we prove that two runs of a selective-scan cell from a common start stay within a bound that holds at every length, shrinks to zero with the size of the change and needs no lower bound on the timescale. We give a construction showing that, for small changes, this bound is within a factor of about 2 of the best possible, and we extend it to the update used in Mamba's released code when the timescale is bounded above. We then evaluate block-level bounds built from the theorem on two small models trained on one day of order book data. With a bounded timescale, a bound built on the existing analysis is tighter than ours for at most the first 8 steps. With Mamba's softplus timescale, whose certified lower bound is as small as $10^{-21}$, it is looser at every length. Our bounds hold for every input to a block, but they remain more than five orders of magnitude above the changes that gradient attacks find.
bullets: Existing additive-timescale bounds can grow linearly with sequence length unless the timescale is bounded away from zero.
Measuring timescale changes logarithmically prevents per-step errors from accumulating and yields a bound valid at every sequence length.
The bound vanishes with the input perturbation and is within about a factor of 2 of optimal for small changes.
The analysis extends to Mamba’s released update when the timescale is bounded above.

On two small order-book models, the new bounds outperform existing analysis beyond 8 steps or at all lengths with softplus timescales, but remain over five orders of magnitude above gradient-attack changes.

papers.selection_reason: Theoretical perturbation bounds for selective state space models used in LLMs; relevant to long-context and streaming language models.
papers.title: A Log-Timescale Perturbation Bound for Selective State Space Models at Every Sequence Length
papers.tldr: A log-timescale analysis gives selective state space models a sequence-length-independent perturbation bound without requiring a positive lower bound on the timescale, though the resulting block-level bounds are still very loose in practice.

papers.abstract: Controlled studies of latent two-hop reasoning train transformers to predict only the answer, whereas language models are trained to predict every token. We ask whether a model trained on every token learns to answer two-hop questions whose intermediate entity appears in no two-hop training example. We build a synthetic corpus with such questions. On this corpus every term of the loss can be computed exactly. A looped transformer, a standard transformer and DiscoLoop answer almost none of these questions. We therefore introduce the Baton family of looped transformers. They pass the intermediate entity to the second loop as a token embedding. When trained to predict only the answer, two of its three variants answer these questions almost perfectly. We then relate the success and failure of each model to three design conditions. Experiments that change one condition at a time agree with this hypothesis. When Baton is trained on every token, however, its accuracy on these questions rises and then declines. We further split the gradient of the next-token loss into three terms. Removing the two terms that depend on the particular training set raises the peak accuracy but does not remove the decline. The decline arises in the second hop while the model still recalls both facts.
bullets: The study tests whether models trained to predict every token can answer two-hop questions with unseen intermediate entities.
Standard, looped, and DiscoLoop transformers answer almost none of these questions on a synthetic corpus.
Baton passes the intermediate entity to a second loop as a token embedding; two answer-only variants achieve near-perfect performance.
With next-token training, Baton accuracy initially improves but later declines.
Gradient analysis shows that removing training-set-dependent terms raises peak accuracy but does not prevent the decline, which occurs during the second hop.

papers.abstract: Practitioners choose among LLM alignment methods largely by trial and error. We provide a theoretical foundation: each pairwise method defines a vector field on the probability simplex that governs how the model redistributes mass between preferred and dispreferred completions. Projecting onto a single preferred/dispreferred pair reduces this to a one-dimensional margin ODE with a closed-form solution. These solutions reveal that DPO margins grow without bound (logarithmically as $O(\log t)$ in the gradient-flow limit) while IPO margins converge to a finite $1/(2\tau)$; that label noise induces a qualitative phase transition in DPO (unbounded $\to$ bounded) but affects IPO only quantitatively; and that gradient concentration under asymmetric weighting governs trainability at scale. We confirm all three predictions across five model families spanning four benchmarks. The closed-form solutions also enable principled method design: we prove that adding any label smoothing $\varepsilon > 0$ to SimPO creates a finite margin attractor at $\Delta^* = \beta^{-1}\log((1-\varepsilon)/\varepsilon)$, while $\varepsilon = 0$ (standard SimPO) has no attractor. We test this across three models (8B-9B) and confirm the prediction: the theory-derived configuration (TPO-S, $\varepsilon = 0.05$) is competitive with the strongest baselines, attaining the highest mean IFEval score among the compared methods on all three, validating that the predicted finite attractor is a usable operating point rather than proposing a new state-of-the-art loss.
authors: Xingzi Xu, Mehmet Saygin Seyfioglu, Karim Bouyarmane
bullets: Pairwise alignment methods induce vector fields on the probability simplex; each preferred/dispreferred pair reduces to a solvable one-dimensional margin ODE.
DPO margins grow unbounded at roughly O(log t), whereas IPO margins converge to the finite limit 1/(2τ).
Label noise causes a qualitative shift from unbounded to bounded margins for DPO, but only quantitatively changes IPO; asymmetric weighting affects trainability through gradient concentration.
For SimPO, any label smoothing ε>0 yields a finite attractor Δ*=β⁻¹ log((1−ε)/ε), while standard ε=0 has no attractor.

Predictions are confirmed across multiple model families and benchmarks; TPO-S with ε=0.05 achieves the highest mean IFEval score among compared methods in its three-model test, without claiming a new state of the art.

figures.caption: Figure 6: Margin dynamics replicated across five model families (Qwen, Gemma, OLMo, Mistral, DeepSeek). DPO’s margin grows without bound and IPO’s converges near the predicted fixed point 1/(2τ) = 5 (dashed line) on every architecture. Only the growth rate varies across families.

Figure 1: Three axes of the margin dynamics framework. (a) SFT only attracts toward yw (F+), with pressure vanishing as π(yl) → 0. DPO adds targeted repulsion F−, sustaining Ω(π) pressure. (b) Sigmoid weighting (DPO) yields unbounded margin growth; linear weighting (IPO, PPO) converges. (c) Frozen references cause gradient decay; reference-free methods risk drift; adaptive references stay stable.

Figure 7: Reference divergence over training (Proposition A.4). SimPO (reference-free) diverges 82× more than DPO (frozen reference), confirming the staleness–drift tradeoff predicted by Axis 3: frozen references constrain policy drift but cause gradient decay; reference-free methods avoid decay but risk unbounded drift.

Figure 3: Margin and gradient dynamics over 2000 training steps (Theorem 2.3). Left: DPO’s margin grows without bound, consistent with u+ log u = at+ c (R2 = 0.85; the remaining variance reflects discrete-time effects and cross-example interference not captured by the isolated ODE). Right: DPO’s gradient norm is 10× SFT’s, confirming that targeted repulsion sustains Ω(π) gradient pressure (Definition 2.1).
Figure 5: Repulsion strength (Theorem 2.2). γ=0 plateaus at 66%; γ=0.5 achieves 97%; γ=0.7–0.8 shows a collapse valley (Theorem 2.5).

Figure 4: Noise phase transition (Theorem 2.4). DPO’s final margin (y-axis) plotted against labelnoise fraction ε (x-axis) collapses from unbounded growth at ε=0 to a finite fixed point ∆∗ = β−1 eff log((1−ε)/ε) for ε > 0 (dashed: theory, solid: empirical). IPO’s fixed point shifts with ε but the convergence rate is preserved.
Figure 2: Effective potential V (∆) (schematic). SimPO (dashed) has no minimum: margins diverge. TPO-H and TPO-S have finite attractors at ∆∗.

Table 3: IFEval instruction-following accuracy (%) on UltraFeedback-trained models (mean ± std, 5 seeds). IFEval is an objective benchmark with no judge model. The theory-derived TPO-S attains the highest mean among the compared methods on all three, confirming the predicted attractor is a competitive operating point. TPO-S adds negligible wall-clock overhead over SimPO: a single extra log σ(−δ) evaluation per example (the ε-weighted label-smoothing term in Eq. 3).2
Table 5: Cross-architecture validation of margin dynamics (Theorem 2.3). DPO’s margin grows without bound; IPO’s converges near 1/(2τ) = 5. Pattern holds across all seven models and five families.

Table 11: SimPO replication pipeline (SFT → preference). Best-checkpoint preference accuracy (%) on UltraFeedback, mean ± std over 5 seeds. The reference-free advantage persists on MI 8B; on DS 8B the strong SFT base saturates all methods.
Table 1: Three-axis taxonomy of LLM training methods.

Table 12: Multi-benchmark replication of main predictions. DPO margin grows without bound on every benchmark; IPO margin remains bounded. Noise degrades DPO monotonically while IPO is stable. The γ = 0 vs. γ > 0 gap holds wherever the task is solvable (pt > 0). AIME margins are near zero for both methods, consistent with Theorem A.9: when base solve rate pt ≈ 0, neither method can make progress.

Table 2: Theory-to-experiment mapping. Main predictions test the closed-form margin ODEs; supporting predictions are in the appendix. A single calibration parameter βeff maps the twocompletion theory to full-scale training.

Table 4: Preference accuracy (%, mean ± std, 5 seeds) on on-policy math data and off-policy UltraFeedback [Cui et al., 2024] (60K pairs). TPO-S leads or ties on most settings. The reference-free vs. reference-dependent gap exceeds 24 points on DS-R1-8B.

Table 13: Gradient concentration sweep on MATH (11.6K train, 3000 steps) and GSM8K (7K train). Accuracies here are measured on the 50 tracked hard examples used for the per-example collapse analysis, so they are lower than the held-out accuracies in Table 12 (e.g. γ=0.25: 91% tracked-hard vs. 99.5% held-out). Collapse events peak at γ = 0.7–0.8 on MATH, creating a “collapse valley.” GSM8K shows no collapse (high-coverage regime). Seed robustness (2–3 seeds) confirms the pattern is reproducible.
Table 6: Accuracy (%) on MATH across data scales. Preference methods with targeted repulsion outperform supervised methods; GRPO degenerates under sparse rewards.
Table 9: Reference refresh experiment (DS-R1-8B, on-policy). Refreshing the frozen reference every K steps recovers most of the 25-point gap between DPO and SimPO.
Table 7: Left: Diversity selection as a plug-in (100-sample MATH, K=4). Right: Coverage over 5 iterations (MATH, 7500 problems, K=8).
Table 8: TPO vs. standard DPO on mathematical reasoning (mean ± std over 3 seeds).

Table 10: N-completion validation of the two-completion effective theory. DPO margin dynamics at n ∈ {2, 4, 8, 16} completions per prompt (DS-R1-8B, 300 steps). The growth ratio (final/step-50 margin) converges at n ≥ 4 (1.5–1.6×), confirming that the two-completion ODE captures the dominant dynamics regardless of the number of completions. Initial margins increase with n due to the larger pairwise comparison space, but the functional form (unbounded growth) is invariant.

papers.selection_reason: Theoretical analysis of LLM alignment methods with closed-form margin dynamics and testable predictions; directly relevant to LLM methodology.
papers.title: Margin Dynamics for Large Language Model Alignment
papers.tldr: A theoretical margin-dynamics framework explains how DPO, IPO, and SimPO behave under training, noise, and weighting, and guides label-smoothed SimPO toward a stable operating point.

papers.abstract: Interpretability methods can locate the attention heads and sparse autoencoder (SAE) features that change the answer a language model gives to a moral prompt, e.g., whether "Stealing medicine for a dying child is morally" continues with "justified" or "wrong". Such a component could respond to moral content, to the judgment of conduct by any norm, or to the word "morally" in the prompt. We built 227 minimal pairs of short phrases, validated by five annotators, whose two versions differ in a moral standard, in another kind of norm (prudence, etiquette, aesthetics or evidence) or in a descriptive quality, and showed them to 14 open-weight models (Llama, Gemma and Qwen, 1B to 14B, base and instruction-tuned), with and without the word "morally". In every model, the heads that change the moral answer belong to an evaluation circuit the models use for every kind of normative judgment we tested: these heads carry the same share of the effect for moral as for other normative pairs (pooled ratio 1.00, 97.5% confidence interval [0.92, 1.07], with the word; 0.90, [0.84, 0.96], without it), and the models need them as much for both. The models need these heads also when nothing in the prompt asks for a judgment, and on 400 scenarios of the ETHICS benchmark, where removing them takes away 37 to 39% of the difference between acceptable and unacceptable scenarios, against 1 to 3% for ten random heads. The SAE features we located respond mostly to the word "morally" rather than to what the phrase is about. The models represent the category of a pair (the standard the annotators assigned to it): it can be read from their hidden states, and, in the eight models we tested, removing the direction that carries it weakens the moral verdict by a few percent, and more than the other verdicts in seven of them. We release the pairs, the ratings, the code, the trained SAE dictionaries and the result files.
authors: Davide Liga, Liuwen Yu, Matteo Magnini
bullets: Researchers tested 227 validated minimal pairs contrasting moral standards with prudential, etiquette, aesthetic, evidential, or descriptive distinctions, with and without “morally.”
The attention heads affecting moral answers were also used for other normative judgments and were needed even when no explicit judgment was requested.
On 400 ETHICS scenarios, removing these heads eliminated 37–39% of the acceptable-versus-unacceptable difference, compared with 1–3% for random heads.
SAE features identified as relevant responded mostly to the cue word “morally,” not the phrase’s underlying content.
Models encoded the annotator-assigned normative category in hidden states; removing that direction weakened moral verdicts in eight tested models, more than other verdicts in seven.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The design and the three readings. Left: three kinds of pair (the examples are retained pairs of this study), each shown in the frame with the moral cue (A1) and in the frame without a cue (B). Right: what each of the three readings predicts for the share of the effect that the located heads carry on each kind of pair (schematic bars), and what we observed (last row: geometric means over the models; Section 5). The observed shares fit Reading 2 better than Readings 1 and 3, but they do not single out normativity: without the cue, phrases in which something good or bad happens to a person, with nobody’s conduct judged, receive the share of normative pairs; with the cue, normative pairs keep a somewhat larger share (Section 5).

Per-model selectivity ρ of the located heads with 95 % intervals in frames A1 (moral cue after the priming sentences; blue), B (priming sentences, no cue; orange) and A0 (moral cue without the priming sentences; grey), and the pooled ratios with their 97.5 % (A1, B) and 95 % (A0) intervals; a point to the right of 1 means that the located heads carry a larger share of the effect on moral than on normative pairs, a point to the left a smaller one. The shaded band (0.8 to 1.25) marks differences that we treat as too small to call the heads specific to moral content: inside it, the share on moral pairs is at most a quarter larger, and at most a fifth smaller, than the share on normative pairs. The dotted line at 1.5 marks the start of a strong moral preference (Table 8). Every pooled interval lies inside the band; the per-model point estimates lie inside it too, except three: Qwen2.5-7B in frame B (0.70) and the two Llama-3.1-8B models in frame A0 (1.27 each), and no model approaches the line of strong preference at 1.5.

Figure 4: Where moral pairs differ from the other pairs, and by how much. Every part shows frame B (no cue), per model. (a) The located heads: their share on moral pairs divided by their share on normative pairs, with its 95 % interval (right of 1: a larger share on moral pairs); the shaded band, as in Figure 2, marks no content specificity. (b) The moral-versus-normative neuron lists, chosen on half of the pairs and removed on the other half: change of the gap as a percentage of each pair’s gap, on moral and on normative pairs, set minus random lists (left of 0: removing the list makes the preference for the better version smaller). (c) The same for the feature lists of H6, one point per dictionary, as a percentage of the model’s mean gap on that category (the layer-19 dictionary of Llama-3.2-3B-IT raises the gap). (d) The models’ answers on the twins (two pairs that differ only in who bears the consequence: other people in the moral member, the agent alone in the prudential member): the gap of the moral member minus that of the prudential member, with the cue (dark) and without it (light) (right of 0: the model judges the moral member more strongly). Filled markers mark a fall specific to moral pairs (the interval of the moral change and that of the moral minus the normative change both lie below zero; b, c) or an interval above zero (d). The located heads show no preference; the neurons and features carry a few per cent in some Llama models; the answers tell the twins apart more often than any component does.

Figure 7: Necessity of the located heads, all positions. Fraction of the behavioural gap removed by replacing the output of the located heads by its mean at every position, on moral (blue) and normative (orange) pairs with 95 % intervals, in frames A1 and B; the grey bar runs from the mean to the maximum of 20 random sets of ten heads. The located heads are needed in most models, and at least as much for normative as for moral pairs.

Figure 3: What the features follow, across six frames. Left: the activation of the located features on moral pairs in each frame, relative to their activation with “is morally” (one point per dictionary; black bar, the median of the ten dictionaries at layer 7 or deeper; dotted line, half of the activation with “is morally”). Right: the number of the 14 dictionaries in which more features separate moral from normative pairs than separate kinds of norm (H6); blue bars, the frames whose prompt holds a moral word. The located features follow the word at the final position, most of all a moral one; the H6 distinction follows the moral cue, wherever it stands.

Figure 5: The same organisation in every model. Each column of points is one model. In no model do these measurements single out moral pairs: the blue points lie with the orange points in (b) to (e), and no interval in (a) lies above the band. In no model does the comparison of moral with normative pairs come out the other way; the interval of the moral/normative ratio lies inside the band of 0.8 to 1.25 in 8 of the 14 models with the cue and in 5 without, and above it in none. The shared pathway in each of the 14 models, with the moral cue (left) and without (right); blue, moral; orange, normative; grey, descriptive pairs. (a) The located heads’ share of the effect on moral pairs divided by their share on normative pairs, with its 95 % interval and the band of no content specificity; (b) the percentage of the gap lost when the located heads are removed, against the largest loss of 20 random sets of ten heads (black tick); (c) the depth at which the final position first holds half the gap; (d) the change of score from one step of the stance direction at three quarters of depth; (e) over the neurons of the late layers, the correlation of the mean shift on moral and normative pairs (blue) and on normative and descriptive pairs (grey); (f) left, the share of pairs on which the model completing “[stem] is a matter of” gives the highest probability to the annotators’ standard; right, the correlation of base and instruct head profiles on the new moral pairs (ceiling: split-half reliability). In every model the moral and normative values lie together in (a) to (e), and the cue moves the depth in (c).

Figure 10: The hidden state carries the standard when nobody asks for it. Frame B (no cue), read through the Jacobian lens at the final position of every layer, in the eight models up to 3B parameters. Left: how well the lens probability of the moral words separates moral from normative pairs (AUC; 0.5 is chance). Right: how often the most probable of the five standards’ words is the annotators’ standard, on the pairs whose standard they confirmed (chance 0.2). The AUC passes 0.75 between 0.2 and 0.5 of the depth in every model; the five-way reading rises with it in the Llama and Qwen models and peaks before the output, while in the Gemma models it appears only at the output.

Figure 8: What the located heads read. Share of the attention of the located heads and of the average head at the final position, by part of the prompt, on moral and on normative pairs, with the cue (left) and without it (right); medians over the 14 models. The located heads look at the cue and at the stem, the average head mostly at the first token; the two categories get the same treatment.

Figure 6: Why raw effects mislead. papers.selection_reason: Disambiguating moral circuits and features in open-weight LLMs is a substantive interpretability contribution to large language model reasoning research.
papers.title: Disambiguating Moral Circuits and Moral Features in Language Models: Moral content, normative judgment or cue words? Evidence from 14 models
papers.tldr: Across 14 language models, components driving moral judgments primarily form a general normative-evaluation circuit, while many SAE features mainly detect the word “morally.”

papers.abstract: Masked diffusion models repeatedly predict provisional tokens before a sampler decides which predictions become permanent. Existing inference-time steering methods primarily modify activations, logits, or denoising trajectories, while treating this commitment policy as a fixed decoding detail. We instead study token commitment as a diffusion-specific control surface and separate it into two decisions: which tokens to commit and how many tokens to commit at each step. For the first, we introduce counterfactual target-aware commitment, which ranks unresolved positions by a mixture of model confidence and leave-one-token-out target contribution. For the second, we introduce calibrated adaptive budgets driven by target progress and confidence. Across language and vision-language settings in the LLaDA family, multiple targets, two activation-steering methods, and an unsteered control, both mechanisms yield empirically monotonic target-quality trade-offs in every configuration we evaluate. Adaptive schedules also recover competitive operating points relative to scorer-free stochastic schedules matched in average denoising cost. Because both mechanisms require only a scalar score evaluated on a provisional completion, they apply unchanged when the target is an automatic proxy for task success rather than an output attribute: NLI entailment for dialogue summarization and CLIPScore for captioning, neither of which corresponds to a single reusable steering direction. We reproduce the behavior of both mechanisms on a second masked-diffusion family, Dream-7B, for one control target and one task-success target. These results characterize commitment--which provisional predictions become irreversible, and how rapidly--as an interpretable control surface for steering masked diffusion generation under the conditions we test.
authors: Ambroise Aigueperse, Hugo Buurmeijer, Carmen Amo ALonso, Marco Pavone
bullets: Existing steering methods modify activations, logits, or denoising trajectories but generally leave commitment policy fixed.
The approach separately controls which tokens to commit using confidence and leave-one-token-out target contribution, and how many to commit using target progress and confidence.
Across evaluated LLaDA language and vision-language settings, both mechanisms produce empirically monotonic target-quality trade-offs.
Adaptive commitment budgets reach competitive operating points against scorer-free stochastic schedules at matched average denoising cost.
The mechanisms also work with proxy targets such as NLI entailment and CLIPScore, and are reproduced on Dream-7B in limited settings.
papers.selection_reason: Token commitment as a control surface for steering masked diffusion language models is a novel inference-time mechanism relevant to LLM generation and architecture research.
papers.title: Token Commitment as a Control Surface for Steering Masked Diffusion Generation
papers.tldr: Token commitment—what masked-diffusion predictions become permanent and when—can serve as an effective, interpretable control surface for steering generation.

papers.abstract: Activation steering is a simple, training-free way to modulate LLM behavior, yet existing methods typically inject vectors at a single layer and lack mechanisms for depth-aware propagation or internal verification. We combine two recent ideas - Attention Residuals (AttnRes) providing learnable cross-layer pathways, and Jacobian-lens (J-space) concept readout - into a lightweight depth-aware steering pipeline. On two small open models (Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3.5-0.8B), distributing a persona vector according to AttnRes-style depth weights yields stronger internal alignment (deeper-layer concept cosine and rank, p<0.0001) and stronger behavioral shifts than single-layer injection. The effect is sign-specific: reverse vectors invert all six metrics, random directions degrade alignment (p<0.0001), and a short LoRA fine-tune erases the imprint. Injection rewires attention strictly downstream of the injection point (upstream JS = 0.00000). Three practical findings follow. First, a layer-wise geometric decomposition of cosine readouts: at the injection layer 123% of the increase is arithmetic, while 5-11 layers downstream 100% is dynamical. Second, an intensity window: effects are monotone over 0.3-0.7, then generation collapses (617 to 306 to 25 chars). Third, metric discipline: keyword-rule metrics fail LLM-judge validation (kappa <= 0.09), and two rule-based conclusions were retracted. Training the depth weights on a steering objective (200 steps, frozen backbone) raises final alignment 10x on held-out prompts. Cross-persona vectors retain 96-99% of the effect: specificity holds against random, not semantic, directions. We contribute a practical, low-overhead depth-aware steering method with a careful evaluation protocol. Code and data are released.
bullets: Combines Attention Residuals for depth-wise propagation with Jacobian-lens readouts for internal concept verification.
On Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3.5-0.8B, distributed steering improves deeper-layer alignment and behavioral shifts versus single-layer injection.
Effects are sign-specific, downstream of the injection point, and largely robust across personas; random directions reduce alignment, while LoRA fine-tuning erases the imprint.
Steering has an intensity window: stronger settings eventually cause generation collapse, and keyword-rule metrics do not reliably match LLM-judge assessments.
Training depth weights with a frozen backbone substantially increases held-out alignment; code and data are released.

papers.title: Depth-Aware Activation Steering via Attention Residuals
papers.tldr: A lightweight, training-free depth-aware activation-steering pipeline spreads persona vectors across layers via Attention Residuals and improves internal and behavioral steering effects over single-layer injection, within a limited intensity range.

papers.abstract: We present Limite 1B - Violetto, a one-billion-parameter model designed for high-throughput mathematical reasoning. Limite is trained from scratch on 237 billion tokens from a carefully curated, mathematics-centric corpus and supports context lengths of up to 131k tokens. Its architecture and training recipe were developed together to maximize reasoning capability while keeping training and inference costs low. Post-training combines knowledge distillation, targeted supervised fine-tuning, and RLVR on a curated curriculum. Limite achieves 94.01% on AIME 2026 and 74.25% on BeyondAIME, placing it among models many times its size on our evaluation suite. The model is deliberately only lightly instruction-tuned: it is intended primarily as a single-turn mathematical solver and as a fast, parallel component of larger systems, rather than as a general-purpose assistant. We release the model, its base and value checkpoints, and an optimized serving implementation under the Apache 2.0 license.
authors: Mario Prignano, Gabriele Cirillo, Alessio Morosini, Luca Cerovaz, Alessandro Bartolocci, Emanuele Rodol\`a, Giulio Starace, Francesco Pappone
bullets: Trained from scratch on 237 billion tokens from a mathematics-focused corpus.
Supports context lengths up to 131k tokens and uses a jointly designed architecture and training recipe for efficient reasoning.
Post-training combines knowledge distillation, targeted supervised fine-tuning, and RLVR.
Scores 94.01% on AIME 2026 and 74.25% on BeyondAIME, according to the report.
Released under Apache 2.0 with model checkpoints and an optimized serving implementation.

papers.abstract: Interactive text-to-SQL requires an LLM agent not only to generate executable SQL, but also to decide which uncertainty to clarify within a limited interaction budget. However, current clarification policies have three limitations: (i) they target surface ambiguity without testing its SQL impact; (ii) they miss ambiguities implicit in schema routes or domain knowledge; and (iii) they spend limited turns on unfocused or redundant questions. These limitations expose a critical challenge: identifying SQL-impacting ambiguity before the intended SQL is known. In this paper, we propose DisGuAD, a Disagreement-Guided Ambiguity Detection framework that specializes clarification selection. DisGuAD treats disagreement among plausible SQL interpretations as direct evidence of which uncertainty matters to the final query. Specifically, it constructs a query-term inventory, elicits contrastive SQL interpretations through complementary probe families, compares their canonical SQL components, and attributes recurring differences to user-facing clarification targets. A lightweight prioritization and dialogue-state mechanism then selects one high-impact unresolved target for clarification. Experiments on BIRD-Interact Lite and Full with two LLM backbones demonstrate consistent improvements in task success and clarification quality. Compared with the original interaction policy, DisGuAD improves normalized Reward by 4.40--8.97 points and raises overall critical-ambiguity coverage from 48.62% to 82.75% and from 45.76% to 85.14%. Its clarification signals further improve two independently designed static text-to-SQL frameworks by up to 13.97 Reward points while keeping their SQL generators fixed. These results demonstrate that disagreement among plausible SQL queries provides actionable evidence for selecting clarification targets that matter to downstream generation.
authors: Su Dong, Jiayan Lin, Yujia Liu, Zijin Hong, Qinggang Zhang, Feiran Huang, Xiao Huang
bullets: Addresses ambiguity detection for interactive text-to-SQL under limited dialogue budgets.
Generates contrastive SQL interpretations from query terms and complementary probes, then compares canonical SQL components.
Prioritizes recurring SQL differences as user-facing clarification targets and tracks unresolved dialogue state.
Improves normalized Reward by 4.40–8.97 points and critical-ambiguity coverage to 82.75%–85.14% on BIRD-Interact Lite and Full.
Clarification signals also improve two fixed text-to-SQL systems by up to 13.97 Reward points.

papers.abstract: Repeating Transformer layers can improve language-model performance without adding parameters. A pretrained model can be adapted to support both single-pass and looped inference by reusing middle-layer weights for additional computation. Because both paths share weights, training to improve looped predictions can degrade single-pass quality. We study joint training strategies using weighted losses on both outputs, with guidance from the frozen original model. Joint supervision substantially reduces single-pass degradation compared to looped-only training, while preserving looped gains over ordinary continued training. Most of this benefit comes from adjusting the single-pass loss weight, with guidance from the frozen original model further improving the looped output. With validation-selected weights, our method preserves single-pass quality within a predefined tolerance of ordinary continued training while improving looped predictions.
bullets: Layer reuse enables extra looped computation without adding parameters.
Optimizing only looped predictions can harm single-pass performance because both paths share weights.
Weighted losses for both outputs substantially reduce this degradation.
Guidance from the frozen original model further improves looped predictions.
Validation-selected weights keep single-pass quality within a preset tolerance while improving looped predictions.

papers.abstract: Language models typically increase per-token computation through deeper or looped layers and latent reasoning steps, while richer residual connections improve information flow across layers. We instead increase computational capacity: the number of active computational states a model maintains. We introduce the Lattice of Latents, a set of per-layer horizontal latent streams that run recurrently along time, alongside the vertical residual stream that flows through depth. Like hyper-connections, mHC, and attention or value residuals, the Lattice enhances the residual stream, but rather than adding or rerouting residual pathways through depth, it provides companion computational states that persist across tokens. Unlike hybrid Transformer-SSM architectures, whose recurrent states primarily serve as internal memory for sequence mixing, these latents directly condition the vertical stream's attention, KV-cache writes, MLP computation, and decoding. On Transformers trained on 20B FineWeb-Edu tokens, a 406M-parameter Lattice model lowers validation perplexity from 15.41 to 14.40 over a parameter-matched Transformer. These gains extend across architectural variants. The Lattice composes with prior residual-stream enhancements: with hyper-connections and input residuals, it lowers validation perplexity from 15.41 (base Transformer) and 14.22 (Transformer with the same enhancements) to 13.61. On Gated DeltaNet, Mamba-2, Triadic GDN, and GDN-Mamba-2 hybrids, it improves perplexity at every tested native state size, with Lattice-GDN and Lattice-Triadic-GDN variants outperforming pure baselines with 4x larger native states. These results identify persistent per-layer state as a complementary axis for scaling language-model computation.
authors: Shivam Duggal, Zongze Wu, William T. Freeman, Antonio Torralba, Richard Zhang, Eli Shechtman
bullets: Introduces horizontal latent streams that persist across tokens while complementing the vertical depth-wise residual stream.
The latent states condition attention, KV-cache writes, MLP computation, and decoding—not merely sequence mixing.
A 406M-parameter Lattice model reduces validation perplexity from 15.41 to 14.40 versus a parameter-matched Transformer.
Combining the Lattice with other residual enhancements further lowers perplexity to 13.61.
Improvements also hold across several recurrent and hybrid architectures, including variants outperforming baselines with 4× larger native states.

papers.abstract: We study how to learn an autoregressive next-token generator $f\colon\Sigma^\star\to\Sigma$ from a class $\mathcal{F}$, given chain-of-thought (CoT) demonstrations of length $T$ generated by $f$. We present a simple algorithm based on bagging, which outputs a majority vote of generators that are trained to be CoT-consistent on bootstrap samples of the training data. For binary token sets, it achieves the optimal sample complexity of $O((d_{\mathrm{VC}}+\log(1/\delta))/\epsilon)$, independent of the CoT length $T$, where $d_{\mathrm{VC}}$ is the VC dimension of $\mathcal{F}$. For finite token sets $\Sigma$, the VC dimension is replaced by a multiclass analogue, the Graph dimension $d_{\mathrm{G}}$, and the sample complexity is optimal up to a $\log|\Sigma|$ factor. The number of generators in the majority-vote ensemble is $O(\log(T/\delta))$, and we show that the ensemble can be distilled into a single generator in $\mathcal{F}$ at the expense of $n\log(nT)$ unlabeled prompts.
authors: Awni Altabaa, John Lafferty, Omar Montasser
bullets: Learns next-token generators from chain-of-thought demonstrations using bootstrap sampling and majority voting.
For binary tokens, achieves optimal sample complexity O((d_VC + log(1/δ))/ε), independent of demonstration length T.
For finite token sets, obtains a near-optimal bound using the Graph dimension, with only a log|Σ| factor gap.
Uses O(log(T/δ)) generators in the ensemble.
The ensemble can be distilled into a single generator using n log(nT) unlabeled prompts.

papers.abstract: Constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs) typically bound expected cumulative cost from an initial state. Such a guarantee can be insufficient when a policy must remain feasible after every history it may encounter. We introduce \emph{subprocess-constrained MDPs} (S-CMDPs), which require the expected discounted cost of each continuation, conditional on any reachable history, to satisfy a bound determined by the current state. This stronger requirement changes the structure and complexity of the problem: we show that stationary policies can be strictly suboptimal, and finding even an approximately optimal stationary policy is NP-hard. We adapt a recently introduced value-set iteration framework to show that history-dependent policies surprisingly overcome both obstacles. Our polynomial-time algorithm represents such a policy implicitly: its expected reward is within $\epsilon$ of the optimal feasible value, it violates each subprocess cost bound by at most $\delta$, and its action distribution can be computed in polynomial time for any given history.
bullets: Standard CMDP guarantees from the initial state may not ensure feasibility throughout execution.
S-CMDPs constrain the expected discounted cost of every continuation based on the current state.
Stationary policies can be strictly suboptimal, and finding an approximately optimal stationary policy is NP-hard.
A value-set iteration framework constructs an implicitly represented history-dependent policy.
The algorithm achieves ε-near-optimal reward with at most δ violation of each subprocess constraint, while computing actions in polynomial time per history.

papers.abstract: Grading student responses is costly and time-consuming. Moreover, human annotators are prone to bias, fatigue, and rater drift, which further limits grading reliability. Various methods have been employed to develop automated essay scoring (AES) systems to reduce these costs and address bias-related issues. These methods range from early text-feature-based systems to current machine-learning and transformer-based models. Specifically, large language models (LLMs) offer the potential to streamline the development of AES systems. However, they are subject to well-known limitations, such as hallucinations and prompt sensitivity. This creates a need to explore the potential of a mixed-methods approach that leverages the synergies among individual LLMs through ensemble formation. We evaluate the potential of ensembles of LLMs to match human-rater agreement when grading student responses in economics and medical education across 103 criteria. We use 631 German-language responses and corresponding human ratings by 2 to 5 annotators from a previously conducted assessment. We experiment with 523 rubric-based prompt configurations across 15 open-weight LLMs and assess their consistency with human raters using Krippendorff's alpha for inter-annotator agreement (IAA) and the Alternative Annotator Test (alt-test). Our results show that replacing one human rater with the best-performing LLM--prompt configuration maintains or improves IAA for 91 of the 103 criteria and that LLMs pass the alt-test for 90 criteria. Our findings suggest that current state-of-the-art LLMs can support AES of German responses in economics and medical education, reducing human workload and enabling faster processing, while validation against human ratings remains necessary.
authors: Daniel Baumartz, Alexander Mehler, Patrick Schrottenbacher, Leon Hammerla, Sebastian Gombert
bullets: Addresses the cost, bias, fatigue, and rater-drift challenges of human grading.

papers.abstract: A harness turns a model into a system that completes tasks: it builds the prompt, exposes tools and decides when work is done. Harness comparisons hold the model fixed. Model comparisons hold the harness fixed. We vary both: five shipped harnesses, 18 artifact-producing tasks, four locally deployable open-weight models from 0.75B to 4.7B and a 35.5B anchor, with one deterministic checker scoring all 360 ladder cells. The completion-controlling harness, Mingbird, has the highest mean at every size. Of four pre-registered paired contrasts, two survive Holm correction, at 0.75B and 4.7B. Thirteen of sixteen paired intervals exclude zero under the deployment reading, with leads from 0.075 over the strongest rival to 0.819 over the weakest. The completion gate is not the carrier: disabling all six executable checks moves the mean by +0.080, +0.117, +0.003 and -0.004, every interval including zero, and only at 1.9B does disabling it create empty runs. Removing one repeat-blocking rule alone costs 0.411 at 0.75B and leaves eight of eighteen tasks with no artifact. The harness effect is a progress effect: it decides whether a run leaves anything on disk. Of 357 usable cells, 127 leave none of their declared artifacts and 85 of those exit normally, so a scorer that reads exit status credits work that was never written. Whether the effect grows or shrinks with size, four rungs cannot settle: a floor arm produces a rise, a ceiling a decline, and a cross-family rung a peak.
bullets: The study compares five shipped harnesses across 18 tasks, four 0.75B–4.7B local models, and a 35.5B anchor using one deterministic checker.
Mingbird achieves the highest mean score at every tested model size, though only two of four pre-registered contrasts remain significant after Holm correction.
Harness effects mainly reflect whether runs leave artifacts on disk: 127 of 357 usable cells produced none, including 85 that exited normally.
Disabling executable completion checks has little consistent effect, while removing one repeat-blocking rule sharply reduces performance at 0.75B and causes artifact-free tasks.
Four model-size rungs are insufficient to determine whether harness effects systematically grow or shrink with scale.

Filled markers are the three Qwen3.5 rungs and open markers the 3.7B Granite rung, which is the single cross-family point, so a rise into or out of that rung carries a change of family as well as a change of size. Panel (b) differs from panel (a) only in the 58 cells that reached the wall budget with declared artifacts on disk. The largest move is pi at 3.7B, from 0.714 to 0.869, and Mingbird moves at 1.9B and 3.7B by 0.139 and 0.079.

An open marker means it includes zero, and a marker is drawn in red when its interval crosses zero and in the arm’s color otherwise. Under the deployment reading every point estimate lies to the right of the dashed line at zero, and under the rescored reading all but one do. The intervals are tightest at 4.7B, where the two arms separate on nearly every task, and the verdicts that change between readings sit at 3.7B, where 36 of the 58 rescored cells are.

Figure 3: Four measures of harness leverage at each rung, computed from the same 357 usable cells under both readings and on the common task panel of Table 6. The five-arm span in (a) is 0.653, 0.601, 0.791 and 0.782, and its slope is +0.198 with an interval that includes zero. Removing the arm whose floor is a reply contract (b) leaves a spread that shows no trend at all. The pre-specified gap to goose (c) is non-monotone, and the gap to the best baseline (d) falls from 0.461 to 0.071 because the strongest competitor changes from goose to pi. The two readings differ mainly at 3.7B, where most of the rescored cells sit.

Figure 4: Where each arm’s cells end, as a share of the usable cells it has. The orange segment is the quiet stop: a run that exits normally and leaves none of its declared artifacts. It is 4 of 70 cells for Mingbird and 34 of 72 for mini-swe-agent, with pi at 10 of 72, goose at 15 of 71 and OpenCode at 22 of 72. The figure reads the same counts as Table 8.

Figure 5: The precision ladder under its two readings. Markers are level means of the paired gap and bars are 95% task-bootstrap intervals. The filled series uses all eighteen tasks. The lighter dashed series drops the tasks both arms solve at that level, which is the contrast the slope is fitted to, so the second series is the one the test reads. Under the deployment reading (a) the gap is largest at 4.85 bits and collapses as precision falls, because compression costs both arms the ability to finish. Under the rescored reading (b) the two high-precision levels move toward zero, because the cells pi lost there had produced work that the rescoring credits.

File sizes are the served artifacts’ byte counts in decimal gigabytes, which is the basis the server’s own listing uses. A binary unit tool reports the same files about 7 percent smaller. Architecture is the served GGUF architecture, and the two architectures differ: qwen35 and granite are dense decoders, and the 35.5B model is a mixture of experts that routes each token to eight of its 256 experts (the served artifact’s expert_used_count), which is where its active-parameter figure comes from. papers.selection_reason: This paper presents a comparative study of 'agent harnesses' for LLMs across different model sizes (0.75B to 4.7B). It fits the 'Language Foundation Models' topic by analyzing system design and orchestration for LLMs.
papers.title: Harness Leverage Across Model Size: A Ladder of Five Local Agent Harnesses from 0.75B to 4.7B
papers.tldr: Harness design substantially affects whether local models complete artifact-producing tasks, often more than model size alone.

papers.abstract: Large language models often produce hallucinated answers, motivating selective prediction policies that abstain on uncertain queries. However, heuristic uncertainty thresholds alone do not provide statistical control of errors among accepted predictions. Linear Expectation Constraints (LEC) reduce selection-conditioned error rate (SCER) calibration to a nonpositive expected linear-loss constraint, but the associated loss is non-monotonic in the acceptance threshold. We construct an exact counterexample under i.i.d. sampling demonstrating that LEC's empirical threshold-selection rule can violate the population SCER target. To address this risk-transfer gap, we introduce Stability-Compensated Linear Expectation Control (SC-LEC), which uses the negative linear risk of a theoretical full-data reference to compensate for threshold-selection instability. For local expansion beyond a safe anchor, we derive two finite-sample certificates: a stability-based certificate exploiting rank crossings and a direct certificate using the structure of threshold expansion to reduce conservatism. With a valid population anchor margin, our certificate conditions ensure finite-sample marginal SCER control, and independent margin certification further provides a $1-\delta$ high-probability guarantee for this calibration-averaged control. Experiments on CommonsenseQA, ARC-Challenge, and TriviaQA show useful retention gains beyond the same certified anchor, while revealing conservative behavior in small-margin regimes.
authors: Zhiyuan Wang, Yuanchang Ye, Jiahao Yuan, Jinhao Duan, Xiaoshuang Shi, Weijun Xie, Ye Wei, Kaidi Xu
bullets: LEC can fail to control population selection-conditioned error because its threshold-dependent loss is non-monotonic and threshold selection is unstable.
SC-LEC compensates for this risk-transfer gap using the negative linear risk of a theoretical full-data reference.
Two finite-sample certificates support threshold expansion: one based on rank crossings and another exploiting threshold-expansion structure.
Given a valid population anchor margin, the certificates ensure marginal SCER control; independent margin certification yields a $1-\delta$ high-probability guarantee.
Experiments on CommonsenseQA, ARC-Challenge, and TriviaQA show retention gains beyond the certified anchor, but conservative behavior when margins are small.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses LLM calibration for selective prediction to control hallucinations, proposing Stability-Compensated Linear Expectation Control (SC-LEC).
papers.title: Stability-Compensated Threshold Calibration for Selection-Conditioned Risk Control in Large Language Models

papers.abstract: Benchmark contamination is not new, but recent model releases show it in a sharper form. We use the term benchleaking for the case in which a benchmark's own test examples enter training data, so that a score reflects recall rather than capability. This differs from benchmaxxing, which optimizes toward a benchmark without seeing its test set. We document two escalations over the past month. First, in post-training, the traces have become explicit: recent audits show an agent stating hidden test requirements it was never given in 23% of its attempts, where its predecessor did so in none, and continuing to follow them after the task is changed to contradict them (Schaeffer and R\"auker, 2026; Lo and Lo, 2026). Second, the problem has reached pre-training. Using few-shot continuation on 20 benchmarks across four public base models, we find that some base models write out other test examples---complete questions, options, and answers---that appear nowhere in their input. For the recently released ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base, 96% of HumanEval problems leak with their reference implementations and 85% of OpenBookQA questions leak with their answers, against 9% and none for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base. To quantify what a reported score owes to such examples, we define an Anti-Hack score: the benchmark score recomputed with every leaked example marked wrong and the number of examples unchanged. Averaged over the suite, it costs DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base 1.5 points and Hy3-preview-Base 1.3, against 5.0 for MiMo-V2.5-Base and 16.6 for ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base. Open base models are the foundation of much downstream research, so benchleaking now affects more than leaderboard rankings. We call for decontamination reports and contamination-adjusted scores to become standard practice.
authors: Yiwei Qin, Muhang Xie, Xuefeng Li, Mohan Jiang, Dayuan Fu, Tiantian Mi, Qipeng Guo, Pengfei Liu
bullets: Benchleaking means benchmark test examples enter training data, causing scores to reflect recall rather than capability; it differs from benchmark-directed optimization without test-set access (“benchmaxxing”).
Recent audits found explicit hidden-test traces in 23% of attempts by one agent, compared with none for its predecessor, including persistence when task requirements changed.
Few-shot continuation tests across 20 benchmarks and four public base models found some models generating complete unseen test questions, options, and answers.
Leakage varied sharply: ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base leaked 96% of HumanEval problems and 85% of OpenBookQA questions, while DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base leaked 9% and none, respectively.
The proposed Anti-Hack score removes leaked examples from evaluation; average score penalties ranged from 1.3–1.5 points for some models to 16.6 for ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base.

papers.abstract: Text-based model collaboration requires a large model to generate intermediate responses before a smaller model can use its guidance, adding large-model decoding cost to inference. We introduce POND (Prefill-Only, No-Decode), a method that uses a frozen large sender for prefill and a small receiver for all autoregressive decoding. A trainable bridge maps the sender's hidden states to additional attention keys and values, allowing the receiver to use these representations throughout generation. POND also supports periodic review, in which the sender processes the receiver's partial response and updates its guidance through additional prefill passes while preserving the receiver's existing KV cache. Across reasoning and coding benchmarks, POND improves receiver performance with senders from different model families. In particular, GLM-5.3 provides gains comparable to those of Qwen3.8-Max when paired with a Qwen receiver, supporting the effectiveness of representation transfer between independently trained model families. POND further demonstrates its ability to generalize across domains. When trained on math and coding tasks, it transfers directly to general knowledge tasks without additional domain-specific training. These results demonstrate that large frontier model prefill representations can improve small-model generation without requiring large-model autoregressive decoding.
authors: Qichao Wang, Tingyu Qu, Pengcheng Wu, Yiran Zhong, Feida Zhu, Zhiqi Shen, Peilin Zhao, Steven Hoi
bullets: Addresses the inference overhead of generating textual guidance with a large model before small-model generation.
Uses a trainable bridge to convert frozen sender hidden states into attention keys and values for the receiver.
Supports periodic review, where the sender updates guidance from the receiver’s partial output while preserving the receiver’s KV cache.
Improves reasoning and coding performance across independently trained model families, with gains comparable to a stronger sender pairing.
Transfers from math and coding training to general-knowledge tasks without domain-specific retraining.

papers.abstract: Large language models read Thai through subword tokens, without a word segmenter. Yet Thai treebanks, speech metrics and morphological resources are built on words, often at several granularities, and word boundaries resolve ambiguities that subword tokens leave open. LATTE (Lattice ATTentive Encoding) reads a text at several granularities at once, through a lattice of dictionary words, but it is a large GPU model. We distil it into LATTE-WordSeg-Lite, a CPU segmenter of 1.17M parameters that keeps the lattice as features. It outputs compounds, words and morphemes in one pass, and learns only from annotated data and text whose licences allow commercial use. To compare it with other tools, published Thai scores do not suffice, as they come from different files, splits and scorers. We therefore rebuild seven test sets from pinned sources and score twelve systems under one protocol. With the unit that fits each test set, LATTE-WordSeg-Lite scores above DeepCut on five sets, four of them from corpora that its teachers learnt from. Called line by line on one CPU thread, it runs 23 times as fast as DeepCut. We release the model, the benchmark scripts and all predictions.
authors: Thodsaporn Chay-intr, Kobkrit Viriyayudhakorn, Thanaruk Theeramunkong
bullets: Addresses Thai’s need for word- and morpheme-level boundaries beyond subword tokenization.
Distils the lattice-based LATTE approach into a 1.17M-parameter CPU model.
Produces compound, word, and morpheme segmentations in one pass.
Rebuilds seven test sets and evaluates 12 systems under a common scoring protocol.
Outscores DeepCut on five test sets and releases the model, scripts, and predictions.

papers.title: LATTE-WordSeg-Lite: Multi-Granularity Thai Word Segmentation on a CPU, with a Reproducible Benchmark

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly advancing mathematical discovery, moving beyond benchmark-level problem solving to tackle frontier research problems. This progress is ushering mathematics into an era of proof abundance, raising a fundamental challenge: how can we ensure the correctness of the ever-growing volume of AI-generated proofs and transform them into trustworthy, machine-verified mathematical knowledge? We introduce Turing Agent, an agent harness designed to orchestrate end-to-end formal verification of research-level mathematics. Its wo-scale architecture integrates theorem formalization and proof formalization agents, empowered by structured proof decomposition, parallel verification, accumulated proof experience, and selective semantic review. Leveraging our collaborations with theoretical computer science (TCS) researchers, we focus our evaluation on TCS, a particularly demanding domain characterized by intricate quantification, complex dependencies, and stringent semantic requirements. Against direct generation and general-purpose coding harnesses, including Codex CLI and Claude Code, Turing Agent achieves approximately 57-62% faithful formalization success on Formal TCS Bench and 83% overall pass@1 on a TCS-focused subset of RLMEval, using GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro. Notably, Turing Agent, built on DeepSeek, successfully completes the formal verification of three previously unresolved TCS tasks from OpenAI's October 2026 collection. One particularly challenging TCS problem required about a hundred formally verified auxiliary claims. Moreover, by actively exploring and refining the formalization process, Turing Agent can uncover simpler alternative proofs, expose unnecessary dependencies in original proofs, and generate reusable mathematical knowledge as a byproduct of verification.
authors: Yang Chen, Qianyi Wang, Ronghui Yang, Zhanhao Li, Yu Cong, Chen Zhang, Hangfan Zhang, Shao Zhang, Shuai Li, Toru Takisaka, Chao Xu, Yi Zhou, Zhihao Tang, Xiao Wang, Bo Zhang, Shuyue Hu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of ensuring correctness as AI-generated mathematical proofs become more abundant.
Uses separate theorem- and proof-formalization agents, accumulated proof experience, parallel verification, and selective semantic review.
Evaluated on demanding theoretical computer science tasks involving complex quantification and dependencies.
Reports approximately 57–62% faithful formalization success on Formal TCS Bench and 83% pass@1 on a TCS-focused RLMEval subset.
Completed formal verification of three previously unresolved TCS tasks and produced simpler proofs, reduced dependencies, and reusable formal knowledge.

figures.caption: Figure 6 | Pass@1 results (%) on Formal TCS Bench and RLMEval. Formal TCS Bench also reports compilation rates. RLMEval results are shown separately for PFR and TLB and combined as Total. PFR covers additive combinatorics and entropy methods from the Polynomial Freiman–Ruzsa project, with applications to linearity testing in TCS. TLB (Testing Lower Bounds) covers information-theoretic lower bounds for statistical hypothesis testing.

Figure 2 | Turing Agent coordinates theorem formalization (TF) and proof formalization (PF) agents. TF agents provide checked Lean statements and definitions, while PF agents construct proofs and request semantic review when needed. The resulting proof undergoes final verification. In its runtime, Turing Agent coordinates recursive DAG construction, parallel proof formalization, and selective semantic review. Experience from successful and failed attempts is extracted and reused, while checked branch proofs are assembled for final verification.

Figure 3 | Research-level TCS verification beyond standard benchmarks. Of the 121 TCS problems in OpenAI’s mathematical research collection, 22 had not been fully verified in Lean. Among these, we highlight three examples formally verified by Turing Agent using DeepSeek-V4-Pro and DeepSeekV4.1-Flash.

Figure 1 | Three challenges in automated formal verification. The formal statement must preserve the original claim (faithfulness), the code must pass Lean’s syntax and type checks (validity), and the proof must discharge all obligations without gaps (completeness). Our Turing Agent is designed to satisfy these requirements throughout the formalization process.
Figure 5 | Experience extraction and reuse during DAG evolution. PF agents use retained records to guide revisions and update the pool when later attempts yield useful findings.

Figure 4 | Selective semantic review in the proof DAG. PF agents request TF agents when a concept is unclear or a new definition is introduced. The TF agent checks whether the statement and its definitions preserve the intended meaning.

Each leaf node represents a lemma or subtheorem, while the intermediate nodes indicate logical categories rather than actual nodes in the DAG. Green terminal nodes indicate those actually used in the proof, while gray nodes indicate those not used in the final proof. Leaf nodes with bold borders represent lemmas or theorems introduced by Turing Agent during the proving process and not present in the original paper. Purple S markers indicate nodes that are selected for semantic review.

papers.title: Turing Agent: Agentic Formal Verification for Mathematical Research
papers.tldr: Turing Agent is a multi-agent system that turns research-level mathematical proofs into machine-verified formalizations through structured decomposition and parallel checking.

papers.abstract: Automated essay scorers (AES) based on large language models (LLMs) promise human-level accuracy. However, training, fine-tuning, and evaluating LLMs for specific assessment tasks is costly. In particular, the question arises whether these AES should be trained for specific domains or whether models based on generic LLMs might be sufficient. Human annotations, by contrast, are often more valid but far more expensive. This study evaluates whether ensembles of AES systems based on general-purpose LLMs can approximate human ratings of medical-education writing tasks by leveraging encoded linguistic and conceptual knowledge. The goal is to assess whether general-purpose models are applicable for assisting or potentially replacing human annotation in this domain. We experiment with 11 AES systems and 8 different LLMs and evaluate 668 student responses to 12 tasks, using \numprint{2076} evaluations by 7 human annotators. These ratings are aggregated to create consistent performance levels that can be used as target classes for classifiers trained on AES outputs. Our results show that learner classes based on human ratings can be accurately reconstructed using a linear SVM trained on a small set of AES features. A single classifier generalized well across tasks and domains, with reasoning and content features being most predictive. This suggests that out-of-the-box LLMs, even without domain-specific fine-tuning, can support automatic essay grading in medical education. While individual AES systems are insufficient alone, their combination approximates human evaluators, pointing to a reduced need for manual scoring or its supplementation with automated methods.
authors: Daniel Baumartz, Alexander Mehler, Mevl\"ut Bagci, Maxim Konca

Individual scorers are insufficient alone; combining them may supplement or reduce manual grading.

papers.abstract: Training coding agents for long-horizon tasks requires environments with verifiable feedback. Existing pipelines often follow a linear process that ends with validation, establishing usability but providing little guidance on improving training value. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) often requires model rollouts or model training followed by downstream evaluation, with costs and feedback delays amplified on long-horizon tasks. How can we use timely, reliable proxy signals to improve training value and synthesize environments at scale? We present RepoFactory, an automated pipeline that converts real repositories into verifiable environments where agents build complete projects from scratch given a language specification. Its Environment Evolution Loop optimizes a multiplicative objective combining validity, structural coupling, and implementation scope through proxy feedback. RepoFactory produces 10,159 environments across 17 software domains. Training Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on these environments yields RepoHorizen-35B-A3B, which achieves gains of 22.6 percentage points on NL2Repo-Bench and 8.5 points on average across five benchmarks covering long-horizon coding and agentic tasks in real-world production settings, compared with 17.5 and 6.4 points without environment evolution. These results highlight the training value of RepoFactory environments and the additional gains from the Environment Evolution Loop.
authors: Yang Tian, Tianyu Zheng, Xiyuan Yang, Yaxin Du, Chengran Yang, Bo Zhao, Jian Yang, Bryan Dai
bullets: Addresses the need for scalable, verifiable environments that provide timely signals for improving training value.

Uses an Environment Evolution Loop optimizing validity, structural coupling, and implementation scope.
Produces 10,159 environments across 17 software domains.

papers.abstract: Expressive Neural Architecture Search (NAS) search spaces are desirable as they do not restrict the space of potential architectures to what is already established. However, few search spaces are expressive enough to represent a broad range of architecture families, and those that are have focused primarily on image classification problems. The task of autoregressive sequence modelling has become ubiquitous in modern machine learning, but no existing search space supports the construction of and search over sequence models from fundamental operations, instead imposing strong inductive biases on the structure of potential architectures. This work describes how the expressive einspace search space can be extended to yield a search space capable of representing autoregressive models using fundamental operations. We perform a series of experiments showing that the novel einspaceAR search space can find capable autoregressive sequence models from scratch--i.e., without imposing strong inductive biases. We believe that our einspaceAR search space will be a useful part of the NAS toolbox and that the techniques described in this work can serve as a blueprint for the integration of autoregressive modelling in other expressive search spaces.
authors: Thomas Woehrle, Linus Ericsson, Henry Gouk, Elliot J. Crowley
bullets: Existing expressive NAS spaces rarely support autoregressive sequence modeling and typically impose strong structural biases.
The proposed einspaceAR search space represents and constructs autoregressive models from fundamental operations.
Experiments show that einspaceAR can discover capable autoregressive sequence models from scratch.
The approach is presented as a reusable blueprint for adding autoregressive modeling to other expressive search spaces.

papers.abstract: Recent self-improving coding agents have achieved strong benchmark performance by iteratively modifying their own executable implementations. A common pattern uses downstream task-derived evidence to decide which candidates or lineages continue evolving, which we term evaluate-and-select. Obtaining this signal requires repeatedly executing evolved agents on downstream tasks, so broader exploration incurs increasing evaluation cost, while repeated optimization against a fixed evaluation distribution may encourage benchmark-specific adaptation. We ask: can coding agents self-improve without downstream task evaluation inside the evolution loop? We introduce Explore-then-Integrate (ELITE), which integrates implementation mechanisms rather than selecting a single exploratory child to continue the lineage. At each generation, ELITE proposes diverse focused improvements, implements them independently from the same parent, and inspects the resulting programs to identify complementary, redundant, and conflicting mechanisms before reimplementing a compatible subset as one coherent descendant. No downstream task outcomes or task-solving trajectories of evolved candidates are used to guide evolution; only deterministic checks of structural and operational validity are used inside the loop. On SWE-bench Pro, ELITE improves the initial agent from 60.0% to 85.6%, compared with 86.7% for the Darwin Godel Machine (DGM) and 88.3% for the Huxley-Godel Machine (HGM), while using zero candidate task evaluations and reducing observed wall-clock evolution time by 8.8x and 3.2x, respectively, under the evaluated configurations. In cross-benchmark transfer without further adaptation, ELITE averages 73.3% on SWE-bench Verified and 69.3% on Polyglot. Together, these results demonstrate the feasibility of coding-agent self-improvement without downstream candidate task evaluation in our setting.
authors: Zhe Ren, Guowei Rong, Yimeng Chen, Nanbo Li, Piotr Pi\k{e}kos, Mateusz Ostaszewski, Dandan Guo, J\"urgen Schmidhuber
