papers.abstract: We present K2-Horizon, a fleet of six fully open language models, from a 0.9B dense model to a 375B-A23B MoE, built for general-purpose reasoning and agentic work across math and science, software engineering, deep research, office automation, and beyond. The models lead or are competitive with strong open models of their size on agentic and coding benchmarks. On the modeling side, to strengthen reasoning, we introduce Mixture-of-Value Attention (MoVA), applying MoE to attention value projections, and softplus attention gating, a more flexible, theoretically motivated gate. Our 36B-A4B model uses both and nearly matches a 32B dense model trained on the same data, with one-seventh the active parameters. We also introduce Uno, lossless diffusion adapters that speed up decoding by up to 2.2x without a separate draft model. Our release follows the LLM360 definition of open source for transparency and reproducibility: the full development history, including intermediate checkpoints from every training stage, pre-training data, training logs, and all training, evaluation, and infrastructure code, notably our production-scale xLLM framework for dense and MoE training and the RL360 reinforcement-learning stack. Beyond the data itself, we release and document in detail every pipeline that built it, the part of model development that open releases most rarely disclose. These pipelines produced roughly 10T synthetic pre-training tokens, showing that synthetic data can be a major ingredient of pre-training at scale. Four of the models share one 22T-token pre-training corpus and recipe, revealing consistent scaling behavior and enabling controlled studies of scale and sparsity. All artifacts are available at https://ifm.ai/k2/

Filtering reduces the annotated PR corpus with deterministic rules, then scores survivors with an LLM judge and draws a domain-balanced sample stratified by difficulty. Rewriting derives the reference patches from the diff without a model and uses the model only for the task specification, the predicted environment, and the test commands. Figure 33: How one PR chain becomes a single long episode. Each PR is attempted in its own fresh agent session against the same working tree, so state reaches the next turn two ways: through the filesystem, which accumulates, and through a compacted handoff, which does not. Per-turn context therefore stays roughly constant however long the episode runs, while cumulative token usage climbs until it crosses the budget, at which point the run stops and the partial episode is kept. The whole episode runs inside a sandbox in which the network tools are gated: dependency installs resolve against a local package mirror and git operations against a local repository mirror, so a build can still fetch what it needs while the obvious routes to the upstream change are closed. The gating is at the tool layer rather than the network layer, so the public internet remains reachable by an agent that writes its own client; we did not observe this in the trajectories we inspected. The number of turns an episode reaches is set by the budget rather than by the number of PRs the chain offers.

papers.abstract: Takehi et al. (2026) report that GPT-6 Astra, given the weights of small neural networks as text, can say what they were trained to do, repair them, and write new ones without training. I re-ran the core of that study with Claude Opus 5.5 in ten pre-registered experiments, with untrained-network and permutation controls and hand audits of every sandboxed code cell. Reading was mixed: Claude named 3 of 4 Atari games from policy weights and found the measured copying heads in 15/15 character-LM runs, but its answers about training data often followed priors. Unlike the original, it identified a sycophantic Gemma 3 270M finetune from weights alone in 6/6 runs. One-shot weight edits took a failing MountainCar policy from 0% to 100% success and a hovering LunarLander policy from 0% to 85.6%; zero-shot networks beat PPO at 100k steps on 4 of 5 environments, each implementing a textbook controller. With no training or forward passes, Claude wrote a 1.48M-parameter 9x9 Go network that won 85-94% of games against three PPO opponents. Given Qwen3.5-0.8B's weights and 10, 25 or 50 forward passes of 64 practice problems, Claude raised MATH-500 from 6.7% to 51.4%, 55.2% and 58.1% (+51.4 points at 50 passes, 95% CI [47.9, 55.0]; original 48.1%), GSM8K from 11.6% to 68.2% and IFEval from 22.2% to 54.2%. Unlike the original, which removed an internal loop direction, every edit acted at the output: it scaled the final norm, raising the effective sampling temperature, and lowered the logit of "Wait" while raising that of . The norm scaling alone reaches only 20.9-22.1% on MATH-500. On Gemma 3 270M, which rarely loops, no edit helped (-0.8 points), as in the original.
bullets: Claude identified 3/4 Atari policies, detected copying heads in 15/15 character-LM runs, and recognized a sycophantic Gemma finetune in all 6 runs.
One-shot edits repaired MountainCar from 0% to 100% success and LunarLander from 0% to 85.6%; zero-shot networks beat PPO at 100k steps in 4/5 environments.
Without training or forward passes, Claude wrote a 1.48M-parameter 9×9 Go network winning 85–94% against three PPO opponents.
Editing Qwen3.5-0.8B with 10–50 practice-problem forward passes raised MATH-500 from 6.7% to 58.1%, GSM8K to 68.2%, and IFEval to 54.2%.
Unlike the original study, edits targeted output behavior—mainly final-norm scaling and changing the “Wait” logit—and did not help Gemma, which rarely loops.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) judges are increasingly used to monitor the outputs of LLM-based AI agents, yet formal guarantees on the reliability of these judges remain largely absent, limiting confidence in their use for safety-critical oversight. We consider certifying such a judge and define its risk over safety classifications of prompt--response pairs drawn from a deployed generator. We apply a PAC-Bayes framework to this setting, refining existing compression-based methodology with the use of tighter bounds and more efficient coding. We show that standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning can yield non-vacuous and even tight certificates for safety judges, for both classification and Brier risk, without holding out data for validation. We introduce LoRA-GT, which shares a single quantisation scale across layers and achieves the tightest certificates with minimal degradation in predictive performance. Across five guardrail models and four benchmarks, we find that certificate tightness is governed more by adaptation complexity than by base model scale. Finally, we show how far quantisation can be pushed before the resulting increase in risk outweighs the bound tightening gained from shorter descriptions. Together, these results provide a practical route toward certifiable scalable oversight and offer insight into how the complexity of safety adaptations shapes generalisation.
authors: Tom A. Lamb, Philip H. S. Torr, Tim G. J. Rudner
bullets: Targets the lack of formal reliability guarantees for LLM judges used in safety-critical oversight.
Defines judge risk on safety classifications of prompt–response pairs from a deployed generator.
Combines tighter PAC-Bayes bounds with efficient parameter coding and standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning, without a validation holdout.
Introduces LoRA-GT, a shared-scale quantisation method that achieves the tightest certificates with minimal predictive degradation.
Across five guardrail models and four benchmarks, certificate tightness depends more on adaptation complexity than base-model scale; excessive quantisation eventually harms risk.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) can write several tokens per forward pass. Open-weight DLMs commit, in any order, every masked position whose confidence passes a threshold. If none does, a fallback commits the most confident one, and the commits are never revised. Wide windows let the decoder commit far ahead of the text, which should speed up decoding but often costs accuracy. It is unclear where the model is confident and which commits cause errors. We trace every commit of four off-the-shelf DLMs on math, code, translation and summarization, and rerun failing answers with one step changed. Most tokens become confident only near the frontier, the leftmost masked position, so committing only there, still several tokens per step, is about as fast as committing anywhere. The accuracy loss comes from committing tokens before the text to their left, and committing one token per step does not reduce it. The worst case is an early end-of-sequence token that cuts the answer short. Fallback commits are 11-35% of commits but start 61-72% of the failures that left-to-right decoding avoids. Changing only the step where such a failure starts repairs it more often than changing a similar earlier step. Committing only at the frontier recovers most of the lost accuracy on all four models. Our code is available at https://github.com/rmakarovv/fast-at-the-frontier.
authors: Roman Makarov, Zhe Xu, Jian Kang
bullets: The study traces every token commit from four off-the-shelf DLMs across math, code, translation, and summarization tasks.
Most tokens become confident near the leftmost masked position, so frontier-only committing retains similar speed while reducing premature commitments.
Committing one token per step does not fix errors caused by committing ahead of the frontier.
Fallback commits make up 11–35% of commits and initiate 61–72% of failures avoided by left-to-right decoding.
Early end-of-sequence commits can truncate answers; changing the failure-starting step repairs errors more often than changing an earlier step.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes threshold decoding behavior in diffusion language models, relevant to LLM decoding and efficiency.
papers.title: Fast at the Frontier, Wrong at the Fallback: A Commit-Level Analysis of Threshold Decoding in Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: Threshold decoding in diffusion language models is fast but loses accuracy mainly when it commits tokens ahead of the left-to-right frontier, especially through fallback decisions.

papers.abstract: Multiplicative gating improves Transformer feed-forward networks (FFNs), but it reduces intermediate representation width under a fixed parameter budget. This trade-off is particularly relevant to Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, where individual experts have limited capacity. We introduce ParGLU, a partially gated FFN that combines SwiGLU and ReLU$^2$ in two parallel branches. ParGLU matches the parameter count and principal matrix computation budget of conventional SwiGLU. We evaluate ParGLU in 30M, 75M, and 152M MoE language models using three random seeds per scale. ParGLU outperforms SwiGLU across all three seeds at 75M and 152M, reducing mean validation NLL by 0.0200 and 0.0249, respectively. Results at 30M are mixed. Controlled ablations show that increasing backbone width or expert width strengthens ParGLU's relative performance. Ablation studies further show that combining SwiGLU and ReLU$^2$ improves performance over either architecture alone. Token-frequency analysis reveals larger improvements on low-frequency tokens. These findings show that fully gated FFNs are not always the most effective use of an MoE expert's parameter budget. Partial gating can improve language modeling in MoE Transformers.
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between multiplicative gating and FFN representation width in capacity-limited MoE experts.
Uses a partially gated FFN with parallel SwiGLU and ReLU² branches.
Outperforms SwiGLU at 75M and 152M model scales across three seeds, while results at 30M are mixed.
Wider backbones or experts strengthen ParGLU’s relative gains, with larger improvements on low-frequency tokens.
Combining the two branches performs better than either SwiGLU or ReLU² alone.

papers.abstract: Activation sparsity accelerates LLM decoding by skipping unnecessary weight reads and computation. However, SiLU-based LLMs exhibit little natural sparsity, and imposing high sparsity can substantially degrade accuracy. We propose RoShift, a training-free method that transforms activations into sparsity-friendly representations. RoShift introduces lazy shift, which recenters SiLU activation distributions around zero and defers correction to the end of the FFN to obtain additional sparsity. It also reduces sparsification-induced output error through rotation that jointly accounts for activation and weight information. By fusing the corrections required for shifting and rotation, RoShift translates these gains into decoding speedup. At 50% and 60% sparsity, RoShift improves average accuracy over TEAL by 1.60 and 3.29 percentage points, respectively, across five models. It achieves up to $1.72\times$ decoding speedup over the dense model on an RTX 5090 at 50% sparsity and yields a better accuracy-speedup Pareto frontier than TEAL. Code is available at https://github.com/hulahula3247/RoShift
authors: Geunsoo Song, Jiwon Seo, Hoeseok Yang, Youngmin Yi
bullets: Addresses the low natural activation sparsity of SiLU-based LLMs and accuracy loss from aggressive sparsification.
Uses lazy shift to recenter activations around zero while deferring correction to the FFN output.
Applies weight-aware rotation to reduce sparsification-induced output error.
Fuses shift and rotation corrections to enable decoding speedups.
Across five models, it improves accuracy over TEAL by 1.60 and 3.29 percentage points at 50% and 60% sparsity, respectively, and reaches up to 1.72× speedup on an RTX 5090 at 50% sparsity.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free activation sparsity method for LLM decoding directly targets inference efficiency.
papers.title: RoShift: Lazy Shift and Weight-aware Rotation for Activation Sparsity in LLM Inference
papers.tldr: RoShift is a training-free activation transformation method that improves the accuracy–speedup trade-off of sparse SiLU-based LLM inference.

papers.abstract: Latent KV cache compression reduces memory footprint by mapping historical keys and values into compact representations. However, generic compressed key states require reconstruction to native dimension before applying RoPE and computing attention scores, adding sequence-scaling overhead to the decode path. We characterize when a latent KV representation can serve directly as the execution state of pretrained RoPE. For RoPE-based transformers, exact static linear execution of the rotary key path requires the latent-to-native map to preserve the pretrained RoPE action through an intertwining relation, restricting exact mixing to coordinates that share the same RoPE frequency. Guided by this characterization, we build GaugeRoPE, a training-free executable latent KV representation. It combines a RoPE-compatible carrier that preserves the rotary action with an approximate position-independent residual key--value (RKV) correction for complementary key and value information, both evaluated without per-token dense historical K/V reconstruction. On Mistral-7B, GaugeRoPE achieves $5.85\times$ KV compression while maintaining quality close to the full-cache baseline. Additional MHA results validate the construction beyond GQA. GaugeRoPE achieves up to $2.48\times$ the decode throughput of the vanilla uncompressed baseline through direct latent execution.
authors: Yuanhang Gao, Xiangrui Yang, Lingyuan Meng, Yuanfeng Chen, Dongsheng Li
bullets: Generic latent KV compression requires costly reconstruction before RoPE and attention during decoding.
Exact execution requires the latent map to preserve RoPE rotations, allowing mixing only among coordinates with shared frequencies.
GaugeRoPE combines a RoPE-compatible carrier with an approximate position-independent residual key–value correction.
The training-free method achieves 5.85× KV compression on Mistral-7B with quality close to the full-cache baseline.
Direct latent execution provides up to 2.48× the decode throughput of the uncompressed baseline; results also extend to MHA.

papers.selection_reason: RoPE-compatible latent KV cache compression directly advances efficient LLM inference.
papers.title: GaugeRoPE: RoPE-Compatible Executable Latent Attention

papers.abstract: LLM-based agents can automate model post-training, accelerating progress toward recursive self-improvement. Despite their promise, existing approaches remain under-explored and face two main challenges: (1) strategy lock-in that limits exploration beyond the initial strategy; and (2) coupled execution that obscures the effects of individual modifications. To address these challanges, we propose TrainExplorer, a multi-agent framework for autonomous post-training, that incorporates strategy planning and execution decoupling, to achieve broaden strategy exploration. First, strategy planning draws on scientific literature to construct a candidate search space of training strategies. Then, decoupled execution enables single-component interventions and attribution to guide strategy exploration. Extensive experiments on PostTrainBench demonstrate that TrainExplorer achieves a weighted aggregate score of 39.02, outperforming Claude Code using the same LLM by 7.32 and surpassing GPT-5.6 Sol-powered Codex, which scores 36.23. Code will be available.
authors: Xuannan Liu, Tian Lan, Zekun Li, Xing Cui, Zhengfeng Yu, Feihu Jiang, Qianghuai Jia, Longyue Wang, Zhao Xu, Weihua Luo, Peipei Li, Ran He
bullets: Addresses strategy lock-in and coupled execution in automated post-training.
Uses scientific literature to build a candidate space of training strategies.
Decouples execution to enable single-component interventions and attribution.
Scores 39.02 on PostTrainBench, outperforming Claude Code by 7.32 and GPT-5.6 Sol-powered Codex at 36.23.
Scope: evaluated on PostTrainBench; code is planned for release.

papers.abstract: Removing three quarters of the routed experts from a 122B-parameter reasoning mixture-of-experts model makes it fit in a 12 GiB file, and breaks it in a specific way: on LiveCodeBench it enters verbatim reasoning loops that run to the token limit on 44 of 120 development problems, where the unpruned model at the same 2-bit quantization loops on none. We study how much of that loss can be recovered without changing the kept experts' quantized bytes, in three steps of increasing cost. On development problems, a sampling penalty recovers part of it. Stopping a reply when it starts to loop and drawing again recovers more on top of it, with no weight change. Our method, B, adds rank-8 trained corrections to the kept experts, loaded as an adapter, and restores two experts per layer; it is fitted layer by layer to the unpruned model's expert block on the pruned model's own activations. In a pre-registered comparison on 130 easy and medium LiveCodeBench problems that no part of the study had touched, with both arms given the same sampling penalty and the same stop-and-redraw policy, B solves 116 problems against 104 (+9.2 pp, 95% CI [+3.1, +15.4]; 15 problems gained, 3 lost). A training-free weight edit aimed at the loops, tested the same way earlier, did not help. B removes more wrong answers than loops, and costs 1.7x the wall time. On two older benchmarks used as regression checks, B stays inside a pre-set 2 pp tolerance but shows no gain (HumanEval+ +0.6 pp, MBPP+ -1.9 pp). The evidence is one model, one quantization and one benchmark family; we state what it does and does not show.
bullets: Pruning 75% of experts from a 122B reasoning MoE causes verbatim reasoning loops on 44/120 development problems, versus none for the unpruned model at the same 2-bit quantization.
A sampling penalty and stop-and-redraw policy recover some loss without weight changes.
Method B adds rank-8 adapter corrections to kept experts and restores two experts per layer, trained layer-by-layer against the unpruned model’s expert outputs on pruned-model activations.
On 130 untouched easy/medium LiveCodeBench problems, B solves 116 versus 104 with matched decoding controls, a +9.2 percentage-point difference.
B costs 1.7× wall time; it shows no meaningful gain on HumanEval+ or MBPP+, and evidence is limited to one model, quantization, and benchmark family.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses reasoning failures in pruned Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models by introducing adapter-based corrections to fix verbatim reasoning loops.
papers.title: Reasoning Again with a Quarter of the Experts: Retry First, Then Train
papers.tldr: Retrying looped generations partly repairs expert-pruned reasoning, while a small trained adapter restores more performance without changing the kept experts’ quantized weights.

papers.abstract: As a new scaling technique for large language models, the n-gram embedding improves the base ability of a model while adding almost no inference cost. Mainstream research realizes it through joint training of the n-gram embedding with the backbone, which severely restricts the settings in which an n-gram embedding can be used. We therefore propose training an n-gram embedding onto an existing model through incremental training, to extend where the technique can deliver value. Specifically, we explore several settings of the n-gram embedding under incremental training---the learning rate of the embedding, the vocabulary size, and the injection position---and train an n-gram embedding onto the existing model under the best configuration. Experiments show that the best configuration under incremental training does not fully coincide with that under pretraining; moreover, the incrementally trained knowledge is written predominantly into the n-gram embedding, while the general ability of the backbone is retained throughout this training process.
authors: Shaohua Hu, Xusheng Gu, Haofei Yang, Minghao Shao, Nanhui Zhao, Caoyun Fan, Fangming Li
bullets: Jointly training n-gram embeddings with a backbone limits when they can be applied.
The authors study incremental-training choices for learning rate, vocabulary size, and injection position.
The best incremental-training configuration differs from the best configuration used during pretraining.
Newly learned knowledge is stored mainly in the n-gram embedding, while the backbone’s general ability is retained.

The n-gram embedding branch leaves the backbone’s computation graph untouched: et is retrieved with the n tokens ending at position t as the key and, weighted by the gate αl,t, additively merged into the residual stream at the insertion layers. The insertion layers are chosen from [0, . . . , L] and multiple layers may be used; the vocabulary size determines the number of slots in the n-gram embedding table; both are fixed once the model is augmented. The learning rate is set separately for the backbone and the n-gram embedding, forming the dual-learning-rate scheme.

papers.selection_reason: N-gram embedding augmentation for pretrained LLMs is a technically relevant contribution to large language model architecture and scaling.

papers.tldr: The paper enables adding n-gram embeddings to existing language models via incremental training, preserving the backbone’s general abilities while expanding deployment flexibility.

papers.abstract: Recurrent sequence models, such as recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and state space models (SSMs), are often trained to emit an end-of-sequence (EOS) token when their output sequence is complete. During training, EOS is treated as another token without a special loss term or incentive. Although this training paradigm is widely used, it is not understood how models decide to output EOS. We study a minimal version of the EOS halting problem in which networks are trained to emit a given input sequence an instructed number of times, followed by EOS. We train tanh RNNs and linear SSMs on this task, finding that the RNNs encode the number of tokens left to copy in a linear subspace, of which two principal components capture most of the variation. Hidden states with the same remaining count converge to a shared representation regardless of their instructed repeat count. By modulating the hidden state using an affine transformation at the boundary between copied sequences, we shift the RNN's state to the representation shared by states with one fewer copy remaining. The unchanged network emits EOS one copy earlier while reproducing the shortened target sequence in 94.4% of new sequences, revealing that this representation causally determines the stopping time. In the SSMs, the difference between trajectories with different repeat counts is separated across two-dimensional rotation planes whose contributions to the EOS comparison cancel during copying and align near the stopping time. Rotating the planes independently removes most of the intended stopping while preserving the copied content, which shows that the stopping time depends on the planes' relative phases. These results identify two candidate primitives of EOS halting in recurrent models: a shared encoding of the number of remaining tokens in tanh RNNs and phase alignment across fixed rotations in linear SSMs.
bullets: Studies EOS halting using a controlled task: repeat an input sequence a specified number of times, then emit EOS.
Tanh RNN hidden states encode the remaining copy count in a low-dimensional linear subspace, with shared states across different repeat counts.
An affine state shift corresponding to one fewer remaining copy causes EOS one copy earlier while preserving the shortened sequence in 94.4% of new sequences.
Linear SSMs separate repeat-count information across two-dimensional rotation planes whose relative phases align near stopping.
Intervening on these representations disrupts halting while largely preserving copied content, supporting their causal role.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes the mechanistic basis of End-of-Sequence (EOS) token generation in recurrent sequence models (RNNs and SSMs), contributing to the understanding of LLM architectures.
papers.title: Halting in Recurrent Sequence Models
papers.tldr: Recurrent models halt by encoding how much sequence remains: tanh RNNs use a shared countdown representation, while linear SSMs rely on phase alignment across rotation planes.

papers.abstract: Neural networks are typically programmed through optimization, rather than by explicitly specifying their computations. Recent work on weight-space programming suggests that large language models (LLMs) can instead reason about and manipulate neural-network weights directly. In this work, we show that LLMs can directly program statistical computations in tabular foundation models (TFMs), whose parameters enable inference across different datasets. We investigate three complementary settings using GPT-6 Astra, without gradient-based optimization. First, Astra directly programs nanoTabPFN from zero-initialized weights, achieving a mean ROC AUC of 0.849 across 20 TabArena datasets, compared to 0.876 for a pretrained baseline. Second, Astra diagnoses and repairs a signed-product regression failure in pretrained TabPFN-3.5, restoring near-perfect predictions on held-out synthetic datasets while preserving performance on TabArena-Lite, with only a 0.08% average relative increase in error. Third, it writes KV-cache-editing programs that steer TabPFN-3.5's predictions on unseen synthetic datasets, demonstrating transformations such as reversing linear trends and converting sine waves into approximate square waves, without modifying model weights. Together, our findings suggest that LLM-driven programming could complement gradient-based optimization across TFMs' development and usage, while offering a new way to investigate and intervene in their internal computations.
authors: Shi Bin Hoo, Magnus Buehler, Omar Swelam, Frank Hutter, Lennart Purucker
bullets: GPT-6 Astra programs nanoTabPFN from zero-initialized weights, achieving mean ROC AUC 0.849 across 20 TabArena datasets versus 0.876 for a pretrained baseline.
It diagnoses and repairs a signed-product regression failure in pretrained TabPFN-3.5, restoring near-perfect predictions on held-out synthetic data while largely preserving benchmark performance.
It writes KV-cache-editing programs that steer predictions on unseen synthetic datasets, including reversing linear trends and approximating square waves from sine waves.
The results suggest LLM-driven programming can complement optimization and provide tools for probing and intervening in TFM computations.

figures.caption: Figure 1: (A) Construct: Astra writes nanoTabPFN weights from scratch, achieving competitive performance relative to a pretrained baseline; (B) Repair: Astra programs a corrective computation into pretrained TabPFN-3.5 weights, resolving a signed-product regression failure; (C) Steer: Astra translates a natural-language instruction into a reusable KV-cache editing program that changes a fitted model’s predictions while keeping its weights frozen.

The pretrained model places predictive mass at both −y and y, so its mean (dashed) is near zero, while its early layers already encode the number of negative inputs. The edit (orange) carries this count to the regression head, where its parity selects the sign. papers.selection_reason: Demonstrates that LLMs can program tabular foundation models via weight-space reasoning and KV-cache editing, offering a novel method for model intervention and inference efficiency.
papers.title: Weights & Caches: LLMs Can Program Tabular Foundation Models
papers.tldr: LLMs can directly program, repair, and steer tabular foundation models by manipulating weights or KV caches without gradient-based optimization.

papers.abstract: In 2025 alone, 48 new large language model (LLM) architectures were added to the Hugging Face transformers library, and many of them arrive with a technical report that presents the model as new. What is actually new in these models, and is it tested? We put this question to LLM technical reports. We look at three things: what the reference code shows about how new open-weight architectures differ from earlier ones; what 40 randomly sampled technical reports claim as new and whether they support it with ablation studies; and what they disclose for reproducibility and transparency. In the library, 39 of the 48 architectures added in 2025 take at least two of their three core blocks from another model, most often Llama, although part of this reflects how the library writes code. In the reports, 19 of 73 architectural or training novelty claims come with a controlled with/without comparison; 4 of 40 reports state more than one training run; 8 rerun the models they compare against under one setup; and 1 discloses data mixture, token count, and compute together. We also looked for known components given new names: none of five candidate cases hid its origin, though we did not study model names. We propose seven reporting rules for LLM release reports and apply them to two reports. We do not judge model quality, and an untested claim may still be true.
bullets: 39 of 48 architectures added to Hugging Face Transformers in 2025 reuse at least two of three core blocks from earlier models, often Llama-derived.
Only 19 of 73 architectural or training novelty claims included controlled ablation comparisons.
Just 4 of 40 reports disclosed more than one training run, and 1 reported data mixture, token count, and compute together.
The study identifies seven reporting rules and demonstrates them on two technical reports.
It assesses reporting practices—not model quality—and notes that untested claims may still be valid.

The dashed line marks the library’s move, from about 2024, to writing new models as edits of older ones; part of the later rise reflects that change.

papers.selection_reason: Meta-analysis of novelty, ablation, and reproducibility in open-weight LLM technical reports is relevant to LLM research practices.
papers.title: The novelty exposed: ablation, reproducibility and transparency in 40 technical reports of open-weight large language models (LLMs)
papers.tldr: An analysis of 40 open-weight LLM reports finds substantial architectural reuse and limited testing, reproducibility, and transparency of novelty claims.

papers.abstract: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) improves language model reasoning by distilling from a frozen teacher initialized identically to the student and conditioned on privileged information. However, we identify an underexplored termination mismatch in OPSD: the student fails to reliably learn when to continue and when to stop. This mismatch manifests in two opposing failure modes-premature termination, where reasoning stops before sufficient progress is made, and repetition-driven over-generation, where the model continues generating after reasoning has stalled. Our analysis shows that the teacher-student discrepancy on EOS grows during OPSD training, while length-capped trajectories are frequently dominated by unproductive repetition. To address this issue, we propose TA-OPSD (Termination-Aware On-Policy Self-Distillation), which augments the original OPSD objective with two targeted objectives. Stop/Continue Distillation addresses premature termination by explicitly aligning the teacher and student on whether reasoning should continue, while Repetition-Aware Unlikelihood Training addresses repetition-driven over-generation by discouraging repetitive continuations in the student's failed trajectories. The resulting objective improves termination behavior from complementary directions: continuing when further reasoning is needed and stopping when reasoning becomes unproductive. Experiments on mathematical reasoning tasks with Qwen3 (1.7B/4B/8B) show that TA-OPSD consistently outperforms OPSD and other baselines across all three model scales. Beyond the performance gains, ablation and behavioral analyses show that the two proposed objectives effectively mitigate their corresponding termination failures, reducing both premature termination and repetition-driven over-generation.
authors: Chaoqun He, Wannian Yi, Changyi Sun, Chaojun Xiao, Lijie Wen
bullets: OPSD suffers from a termination mismatch: students may stop before enough progress or continue after reasoning stalls.
TA-OPSD adds Stop/Continue Distillation to align continuation decisions with the teacher.
Repetition-Aware Unlikelihood Training discourages repetitive continuations in failed student trajectories.
On mathematical reasoning with Qwen3 1.7B, 4B, and 8B models, TA-OPSD consistently outperforms OPSD and other baselines.
Ablations and behavioral analyses associate the two objectives with reductions in their respective termination failures.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of TA-OPSD. Standard OPSD exhibits a termination mismatch with two opposing failure modes: premature termination and repetition-driven over-generation. TA-OPSD addresses them with Stop/Continue Distillation, which aligns the student’s continuation decision with the teacher, and Repetition-Aware Unlikelihood Training, which suppresses repeated continuations in failed trajectories. The two objectives augment the original OPSD objective and jointly teach the student when to continue reasoning and when to stop.

Figure 4: Training-side signals across model scales. The top row shows teacher–student Top-100 candidate-token overlap at valid training positions; the bottom row shows the arithmetic mean of the teacher-minus-student log-probability gaps for the two stop tokens.

papers.title: Learning When to Continue and When to Stop: Termination-Aware OPSD

papers.abstract: Open large language models (LLMs) and speech models ship vocabularies of up to 262k tokens, and every user downloads the tables those tokens index (the input embedding, an untied output head and, in recent on-device models, per-layer embeddings), whatever languages they need. We call the bytes in rows a deployment never uses the vocabulary tax and measure it, without downloading weights, for 1,244 generative and speech-recognition models on the Hugging Face Hub. For a Thai and English deployment it is a median 4.4% of model bytes below 0.5B parameters and 2.1% above 8B, and 1.93 GB in Gemma 4 E2B: it falls hardest on the small models that edge devices run. Keeping only the rows of the deployment's writing systems is exact. Keeping the tokens seen in the user's own text removes much more, a median 29.0% below 0.5B, but the usual way of doing it breaks BPE tokenizers: it drops the intermediate tokens that merges build on, so new text is split differently 1.9 times as often as the standard check reports. We repair this with merge closure, at a cost of 5.9% more rows, and add a trim certificate: a Good-Turing estimate, from the trimming text alone, of how much new text the trimmed tokenizer will split differently (correlation 0.996 over 300 settings in 22 languages) and of how much more text a target needs. Without test data our method never exceeds a 2% target, while prior keep rules checked on test data exceed it in 9-13 of 44 settings. On six models of 270M to 3B parameters in 11 languages, trimmed models keep their predictions: where the certificate passes, a median 89.7% of rows is removed and bits per character rise by at most 2.0%. The census, the trimming and the certificate are released as an open Python package, and the per-model tax for 41 languages as an open dataset.
bullets: Large vocabularies impose a measurable deployment memory tax, especially on small edge models; for Thai–English deployments, the median tax is 4.4% below 0.5B parameters.
Retaining tokens from a deployment’s writing systems is exact, while retaining tokens observed in user text removes substantially more vocabulary rows.
Naive text-based trimming breaks BPE tokenization by removing intermediate merge tokens; merge closure repairs this with only 5.9% more rows.
A Good-Turing trim certificate estimates tokenizer shift and required text from trimming data alone, closely matching observed behavior across languages and settings.
Across six models and 11 languages, certified trims removed a median 89.7% of rows, with bits-per-character increasing by at most 2.0% while predictions were preserved.

papers.selection_reason: Reduces LLM memory footprint by trimming unused vocabulary tokens for on-device deployment, fitting memory efficiency and LLM architecture work.
papers.title: The Vocabulary Tax: Safely Trimming Unused Tokens from LLMs for On-Device Use
papers.tldr: A tokenizer-aware trimming method can safely remove most unused vocabulary rows from LLMs for on-device deployment while preserving model behavior and certifying text-splitting risk without test data.

papers.abstract: Looped language models such as Ouro and Raven apply one weight-shared block several times per token, so autoregressive decoding (AR) runs every loop of every token in sequence. Pipelined self-speculative decoders overlap these loops by drafting tokens from shallow readouts and verifying them at full depth. Yet every loop of a looped LM ends in a readout of the next token, and draft tokens pass through every depth anyway, so each depth can check them without an extra pass. We introduce LoopSkim, in which the depth of the pipeline is the verifier. Draft tokens copied from the context, as in prompt lookup decoding, enter after the first loops, any later readout that contradicts one replaces it at that depth, and only full-depth readouts commit tokens. LoopSkim fixes the random draws of every position in advance, so each check compares two tokens and decoding stays lossless in exact arithmetic under sampling for any number of checks and draft chains. Without training, its speedup over AR averages 1.73x that of LoopSpec across greedy decoding and sampling, and its checks between the first loops and full depth speed it up on every model. An optional draft head adds a second chain and raises this average to 1.99x.
bullets: Targets looped LMs whose shared block runs multiple times per token, making autoregressive decoding expensive.
Pipelines prompt-lookup draft tokens into later loops, allowing each depth to check and potentially replace them.
Only full-depth readouts commit tokens, preserving exact-arithmetic sampling behavior with fixed random draws.
Without training, it averages 1.73× the speedup of LoopSpec across greedy decoding and sampling; an optional draft head raises this to 1.99×.
The method is lossless under exact arithmetic and applies across any number of checks and draft chains.

papers.selection_reason: Lossless speculative decoding method that reduces inference latency for looped language models; relevant to efficient LLM inference.
papers.title: LoopSkim: Lossless Multi-Depth Speculative Decoding for Looped Language Models
papers.tldr: LoopSkim accelerates lossless speculative decoding in looped language models by using intermediate depths as token verifiers without extra passes.

papers.abstract: A language model is a complex system whose behavior is determined jointly by the Transformer and the corpus, yet how the representation geometry in the Transformer relates to the actual behavior of language models remains open. We analyze how the representation geometry changes along the forward propagation of actual language models and characterize the representation geometry of a document at a given layer by two collective coordinates, document distinguishability and document dimension. On the phase diagram spanned by these collective coordinates, inference is represented as a flow along depth. We find that, for untrained models, depending on their initialization scale, most of the 156 inference flows move toward the collapse and noise regions of the phase diagram. By contrast, the inference flows of 8 trained models from 5 architecture families all enter and reside in the central region of the phase diagram. Describing the evolution of the flows with a discrete Langevin equation, we find that the difference between the inference flows of untrained runs and those of trained models reduces to whether the effective force on the flows in this region is of saddle or stable-node type. On Pythia-1.4B, we interpret the training process as a phase transition. These results give a unified gateway to the relation between representation geometry and language-model behavior.
authors: Zhuo-Yang Song, Zeyu Li, Qing-Hong Cao, Ming-xing Luo, Hua Xing Zhu
bullets: Characterizes document representations using document distinguishability and document dimension.
Models inference as a flow through this two-coordinate phase diagram across Transformer depth.
Most of 156 untrained-model flows reach collapse or noise regions, while 8 trained models across 5 architecture families enter and remain in the central region.
A discrete Langevin description attributes this difference to saddle-like versus stable-node effective forces.
On Pythia-1.4B, training is interpreted as a phase transition linking representation geometry to model behavior.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes representation geometry and phase-transition-like behavior in trained language models, relevant to LLM understanding.
papers.title: A phase diagram for training and inference in language models
papers.tldr: The study proposes a phase-diagram view in which trained language models maintain useful representation geometry during inference, unlike untrained models that tend toward collapse or noise.

papers.abstract: Transformer language models are commonly scaled by making their blocks wider or stacking them deeper. In this work, we explore a complementary path: branching, the parallel composition of full Transformer blocks. We introduce the Multi-Branch Transformer (MBT), which processes the input through shared initial layers, executes independently parameterized branches of sequential blocks in parallel, and fuses their outputs before shared final layers. At comparable training compute, we study three MBT variants: Wide-Shallow preserves block width, Narrow-Deep preserves sequential depth, and Balanced interpolates between them. In controlled pretraining experiments at four mixture-of-experts scales (0.8B to 2.1B total parameters), 2-branch Wide-Shallow MBTs consistently outperform sequential Transformers under matched parameter and training-compute budgets. Balanced MBTs improve further and retain comparable quality as the number of branches increases. To improve inference efficiency at long contexts, we introduce Joint-KV, which constructs a shared KV cache from branch representations at each depth. Our final recipe combines Balanced MBTs with Joint-KV, supported by an inference engine that exploits branch grouping and shared-cache reuse. Fitted scaling curves indicate that standard Transformers require up to 1.26x as much training body compute to match our final models' validation loss. These models reduce full-model KV-cache storage by up to 34% and deliver up to 51.4% higher decoding throughput on a single H200 GPU. Ablation studies show that branching yields gains beyond changes in width and depth, enables an effective KV-sharing strategy (Joint-KV), remains robust across fusion functions, and performs best in the middle layers. These findings show that branching offers a practical path for scaling language models toward both better modeling quality and faster inference.
authors: Gaotang Li, Lingjie Chen, Chunyuan Deng, Zhiwei Xu, Hongzheng Chen, Christopher De Sa, Jingrui He, Yingheng Wang, Hanghang Tong
bullets: Uses shared initial and final layers around independently parameterized parallel branches, with Wide-Shallow, Narrow-Deep, and Balanced variants.
Balanced branching improves validation quality and remains effective as the number of branches grows.
Joint-KV shares key-value caches across branches to reduce long-context inference memory and improve decoding throughput.
Across controlled pretraining scales, branching provides gains beyond width and depth changes and works across fusion functions.
The approach is most effective in middle layers and is evaluated within the reported pretraining and single-GPU inference settings.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) are designed to enable globally parallel generation. However, in practice, they often exhibit pseudo-autoregressive behavior and a function-word-first bias, which undermines their performance on tasks such as text writing and code generation that benefit from global planning and parallel decoding. To address this, we propose SemMask, a novel fine-tuning paradigm that leverages a semantic-prioritized progressive masking strategy to encourage the model to decode high-information semantic tokens early and globally, thereby enhancing its global planning and parallel generation capabilities. Specifically, we first use the gradients of the original DLM with respect to each token to identify semantic tokens. During masking, these semantic tokens are preserved with priority, establishing a progressive generation order in which semantic tokens are decoded prior to function tokens. Meanwhile, we adjust the loss weight for semantic tokens to further reinforce their early prediction. Experimental results show that SemMask achieves quality comparable to strong autoregressive baselines on both text writing and code generation tasks, while providing superior semantic coherence. Notably, SemMask achieves higher accuracy with substantially fewer decoding steps, indicating that the early establishment of semantic structure improves the efficiency--accuracy trade-off.
authors: Qi Chen, Zifeng Cheng, Zhiwei Jiang, Qing Gu
bullets: Addresses pseudo-autoregressive behavior and function-word-first bias in diffusion language models.
Uses token-level gradients to identify semantic tokens and prioritizes preserving them during progressive masking.
Reweights semantic-token losses to reinforce their early prediction.

Achieves higher accuracy with substantially fewer decoding steps, according to the abstract.

papers.abstract: A direction in a language model's hidden state can be used to probe whether a concept is present or to steer the model toward it. Although probe directions are often reused for steering, the direction that best detects a concept need not be the one that best changes it. We study this distinction in three instruction-tuned models from different families. We construct a one-parameter family of directions ranging from a covariance-adjusted discriminant to the mean difference, and evaluate probing and additive steering, which adds the direction to the hidden state, along the family at a fixed side effect. For truthfulness and sentiment, in every model, the best probe is not the best steering direction: steering consistently favors directions closer to the mean difference. This separation holds across 59 of 60 layer-model-concept combinations in a layer sweep, with matched probe and steering texts in all six model-concept combinations, and under a rotation-based steering operator. The exact steering optimum is less stable: for sentiment, an intermediate direction produces a 27-56% stronger steering effect than the mean difference, but this gain shrinks or disappears with matched texts and depends on the layer and the operator. The two roles also transfer differently across models. A probe transferred by a linear map fitted on neutral text retains 81-91% of the target model's above-chance probing performance, while the transferred mean difference retains less of its steering effect in 11 of 12 model pairs. This is a consistent tendency, although our predefined criteria classify only three pairs, and nine remain inconclusive. Finally, as an application on PopQA, steering toward "unknown" increases abstention by 18-44 percentage points on uncertain errors, versus 2-5 on confident errors, while rarely correcting errors in cases where a correct answer is reachable.
bullets: Across three instruction-tuned model families, the best probing direction was not the best steering direction for truthfulness or sentiment.
This separation held in 59 of 60 layer–model–concept combinations and also under rotation-based steering.
An intermediate direction sometimes outperformed the mean difference for sentiment steering, but the gain was unstable and depended on text matching, layer, and operator.
Probe directions transferred across models more reliably than steering directions.
Steering toward “unknown” increased abstention mainly on uncertain errors, with little correction of otherwise answerable errors.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates probing versus steering directions in LLM hidden states, relevant to understanding and controlling large language models.
papers.title: Do Probing and Steering Favor the Same Directions Within and Across Language Models?
papers.tldr: Probing and steering generally favor different hidden-state directions: probes favor covariance-adjusted directions, while steering favors directions closer to the mean difference.

papers.abstract: Depth recurrence increases effective model depth by repeatedly applying a fixed computation block. However, sharing attention parameters does not share the key-value (KV) states generated at different recurrence iterations, which causes memory growth with recurrence depth during autoregressive decoding. We study how to reduce this memory cost through architectural and cache-sharing approaches within a common depth-recurrent framework. We first study a looped hybrid that repeats a stack of Transformer layers, with recurrent mLSTM or Gated DeltaNet blocks replacing most attention layers and periodic Transformer attention anchors retained. We then restrict recurrence to a dedicated recurrent workspace in a Parcae-style architecture and test its stabilising adapter as a wrapper for the looped hybrid. Finally, we train a looped Transformer with recurrent KV replay, where only selected recurrence iterations write KV states that later iterations reuse. This trains the model to operate with the same shared KV topology used during inference. We find that looped hybrids require sufficiently frequent attention anchors, with performance depending strongly on the recurrent mixer. For cross-iteration KV sharing, recurrent KV replay allows multiple recurrence iterations to reuse the same KV states while retaining performance close to the full looped Transformer with separate KV caches for each iteration.
authors: Lucia Licakova, Niklas Schmidinger, Lukas Hauzenberger, Sebastian B\"ock, Sepp Hochreiter
bullets: Depth recurrence increases effective depth but normally grows autoregressive KV memory with each iteration.
The authors evaluate looped Transformer hybrids using recurrent mLSTM or Gated DeltaNet blocks plus periodic attention anchors.
A Parcae-style recurrent workspace and stabilising adapter are tested to constrain recurrence and improve stability.
Recurrent KV replay trains later iterations to reuse KV states written by selected earlier iterations.
Hybrid quality depends on sufficiently frequent attention anchors and the choice of recurrent mixer; KV replay retains near-baseline performance while reducing cache sharing overhead.

papers.abstract: Matrix-structured optimizers can improve language-model pretraining, but it is unclear whether these gains transfer to short-horizon KL distillation from an instruction-tuned initialization. We compare AdamW and diagonal AdaGrad with two tractable Shampoo reductions, SOAP, and All-2D Muon across four dense Qwen student-teacher pairs under a common forward-KL objective and fixed training budget. Across scales, none of the evaluated matrix-structured recipes consistently improves the quality versus trainer-time trade-off over the elementwise references: AdamW generally attains the lowest validation KL, while AdaGrad can be slightly faster at larger scale. SOAP often tracks AdamW in KL but incurs substantial trainer-time overhead, and the two Shampoo reductions reverse ordering across model pairs, showing that conclusions depend on the feasible recipe. These results suggest that pretraining optimizer gains do not transfer automatically to KL distillation and should be re-established for the target objective and systems regime.
bullets: Compares AdamW, diagonal AdaGrad, two Shampoo reductions, SOAP, and All-2D Muon under a common forward-KL objective and fixed budget.
Evaluates four dense Qwen student–teacher pairs across scales.
AdamW generally achieves the lowest validation KL, while AdaGrad can be slightly faster at larger scale.
SOAP often matches AdamW’s KL but has substantial trainer-time overhead; Shampoo variants vary by model pair.
Optimizer conclusions depend on the distillation objective and feasible systems recipe.

papers.abstract: LLMs are widely adopted in multi-role dialogue and persona simulation. However, their strong ability to imitate role-specific linguistic and behavioral patterns can introduce privacy risks, reinforce social biases, and lead to unsafe or uncontrollable outputs. To address these issues, we introduce the Role-playing Unlearning task, which aims to selectively forget the style and knowledge associated with target roles while preserving the language ability and behaviors of the remaining roles. Unlike prior unlearning tasks that focus solely on removing factual information, our task additionally requires forgetting persona-specific characteristics, making the control over model generation more fine-grained. We propose RoleMoE, a Mixture-of-Experts framework that maps different roles to more independent expert subspaces, improving role separation and structural interpretability. To further distinguish role-specific features, RoleMoE incorporates two complementary losses: a specialization loss that drives roles to adopt distinct expert distributions, and a disentanglement loss that encourages experts to develop distinct capability subspaces. This decomposed structure enables role unlearning to focus selectively on target-role experts. We finally propose RoleBench-Unlearn for evaluation, and experiments on multiple backbone LLMs show that RoleMoE enables precise and controllable role forgetting, while better preserving the linguistic quality, knowledge, and persona consistency of non-target roles. All code and datasets are publicly available at: https://github.com/mbzuai-nlp/ROLEMOE.
authors: Ruihong Zeng, Puning Yang, Jinghui Zhang, Shen Gao, Xiangliang Zhang, Preslav Nakov, Xiuying Chen
bullets: Introduces Role-playing Unlearning: removing target-role style and knowledge, not just factual information.

Uses specialization and disentanglement losses to separate role-specific expert distributions and capabilities.
RoleBench-Unlearn evaluates the task across multiple backbone LLMs.
Experiments report precise target-role forgetting with better preservation of non-target roles’ language quality, knowledge, and persona consistency.

papers.abstract: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) has recently attracted interest because it provides dense teacher guidance without a separate, often larger teacher model. However, OPSD conditions its teacher on ground-truth solutions, which limits its use when such solutions are unavailable. We propose On-Policy Self-Distillation with Self-Generated Problem Briefs (B-OPSD). Using a prompt template, the initial model or a saved student checkpoint generates a problem brief from the question alone. The prompt asks for relevant principles, applicability conditions, and likely pitfalls, but not a final answer or a complete solution. A frozen teacher uses the brief as privileged context to guide the current student's on-policy rollouts through token-level distribution matching. B-OPSD uses no ground-truth solutions during training. Results on AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and HMMT 2025 show that both B-OPSD variants achieve higher average accuracy than OPSD at each of three Qwen3 model sizes. Code is available at https://github.com/ZevineXu/B-OPSD
authors: Zhi Xu, Yinqi Wu, Feng Zhang, Xiaotong Zhang, Hong Yu, Han Liu
bullets: Addresses training settings where ground-truth solutions are unavailable.
Generates briefs from questions alone, covering relevant principles, applicability conditions, and likely pitfalls without giving a final solution.
A frozen teacher uses each brief to guide the student’s on-policy rollouts through token-level distribution matching.
Evaluated on AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and HMMT 2025 across three Qwen3 model sizes.
Both B-OPSD variants achieve higher average accuracy than OPSD in these evaluations.

papers.abstract: Reasoning data expose models to multi-step reasoning, but reasoning traces may cover only a subset of the available facts. How should pretraining balance atomic facts with reasoning traces? We study this question by constructing a setting in which every fact provides an atomic training signal, while only a subset appears in reasoning supervision, enabling us to measure generalization to transitions observed atomically but never used in training traces. For a linear transformer, we derive the weight assigned to atomic training signals that minimizes held-transition squared error and show that its leading-order optimum increases with reasoning-chain length and decreases with the fraction of facts held out from reasoning traces. These trends persist in a full transformer layer with an MLP, softmax attention, and cross-entropy loss. We further validate the role of reasoning complexity and data coverage in two natural-language settings: controlled multi-hop reasoning and mathematical pretraining. Together, our results provide a principled view of how reasoning-chain structure and data coverage should shape the allocation of training data during pretraining.
authors: Jianhao Huang, Allan Zhang, Ali Payani, Baharan Mirzasoleiman
bullets: Reasoning traces expose multi-step structure but may omit facts available through atomic supervision.
The study measures generalization to transitions seen atomically but absent from training traces.
Analysis shows the optimal weight on atomic signals grows with reasoning-chain length and falls as reasoning-trace coverage increases.
These patterns persist in a full transformer layer and are validated in controlled multi-hop and mathematical pretraining settings.

The selected grid maximizers for L ∈ {3, 4} at q = 30% deviate from the latter trend; however, these panels exhibit near-optimal plateaus, with several tested mixture ratios achieving very similar mean OOD accuracy.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been known to exhibit a wide range of social biases including name-nationality associations, occupation-gender associations and racial stereotypes. Existing approaches to evaluating these biases typically involve measuring surface-level behavior where a model is fed a dataset of prompts and its outputs are scored relative to ground-truth answers. Inspired by prior elicitation in cognitive science, we propose a different perspective that reconstructs latent bias as a prior underlying the model's behavior. We formulate the problem as a Bayesian inverse problem where, given prompt-response observations on a bias benchmark dataset, we infer a low-dimensional latent distribution that summarizes the model's stereotyping tendencies. This paper develops the mathematical foundation, a practical reconstruction algorithm, and experiments using the Bias Benchmark for QA (BBQ) benchmark to infer the prior distributions of LLMs over responses in ambiguous social contexts.
authors: Joshua Ryo Cheng, Thomas L. Griffiths, Jake C. Snell
bullets: Targets social biases such as name–nationality, occupation–gender, and racial stereotypes.
Uses prompt–response observations from bias benchmarks to infer a low-dimensional latent distribution.
Develops a mathematical formulation and practical reconstruction algorithm for this Bayesian inverse problem.
Demonstrates the approach on the Bias Benchmark for QA (BBQ) in ambiguous social contexts.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Recovered prior distributions over shifts for Gemma 3 1B IT, Gemma 3 4B IT, and Llama 3.2 3B IT. Error bars denote 95% credible intervals obtained via Laplace approximation. Even in the absence of input signals, all models exhibit non-uniform prior distributions, with notable differences across architectures and scales.

Figure 2: Recovered latent priors over the reduced answer space {S,A,U} for each BBQ social dimension, with 95% credible intervals derived from the Laplace approximation. Each model exhibited largely different latent priors across the different social dimensions.

Figure 3: BBQ bias scores for each model and social dimension. Positive values indicate bias towards the stereotype-consistent answer S, negative values indicate bias towards the stereotypeinconsistent answer A, and values near zero indicate no systematic bias in either direction.

Figure 6: Training loss history for the Adam-driven MAP optimization for Gemma 3 1B IT, Gemma 3 4B IT, and Llama 3.2 3B IT. The training curves are shown separately for each social dimension. We note that each training run exhibits stable convergence.

Figure 4: The recovered prior using our reconstruction algorithm much more closely resembles the control prior distribution. Meanwhile, the naive empirical mean method is biased by the varying prompt evidence.

Figure 5: Training loss history for the Adam-driven MAP optimization for Gemma 3 1B IT, Gemma 3 4B IT, and Llama 3.2 3B IT on the ciphertext problem. The smooth loss curves indicate a stable training objective.
