papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models add parameters without proportionally increasing per-token compute. However, training cost also depends on bytes moved, memory held, and kernels launched, and many of those costs follow total parameter size rather than active compute. On infrastructure built for dense models, this mismatch is costly: in early baselines, throughput fell as stored expert parameter size grew, even though the useful work per token stayed nearly fixed. To close this gap, we present a redesigned training stack in Olmo-core, built for efficient, scalable MoE training. We replace the Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) of earlier Olmo-core versions with an architecture built on Distributed Data Parallel (DDP), and add Expert Parallelism (EP), Pipeline Parallelism (PP), a distributed optimizer, and activation recompute. We propose NVSHMEM-based rowwise EP, which writes each token directly into its expert's buffer, avoiding dispatch and combine permutation overhead. We make EP fully synchronization-free by keeping routing metadata on the GPU and using device-scheduled grouped GEMMs. Closely integrated MXFP8 cuts compute, activation-memory, and transport costs, and topology-agnostic checkpoints let the parallel layout change between runs. On NVL8 B300 nodes, the stack supports training configurations from 12.9 billion to 1.2 trillion total parameters on up to 512 GPUs, reaching 858 useful-model TFLOP/s/GPU at 1.2 trillion with MXFP8 and per-layer recompute; an experimental capacity test with the optional DeepEP v2 backend reaches 2.38 trillion. We also explain each design choice and share findings for other training systems; for example, we identify a failure pattern we call Token Gerrymandering, in which the MoE router can learn to hack the load-balancing loss, and find that overlapping communication with computation can slow the overlapped kernels by more than it hides.
authors: Tianhua Tao, Akshita Bhagia, Dirk Groeneveld, Pete Walsh, Tyler Romero, Yashas Samaga, Jacob Morrison, Iz Beltagy, Taira Anderson, Noah A. Smith, Hannaneh Hajishirzi
bullets: MoE training costs can grow with total stored parameters because of memory, communication, and kernel-launch overhead, even when active compute remains similar.
The stack replaces FSDP with DDP and adds expert, pipeline, and optimizer parallelism plus activation recomputation.
NVSHMEM-based rowwise expert parallelism and GPU-managed routing avoid dispatch/combine permutations and synchronization overhead.
Integrated MXFP8 reduces compute, activation-memory, and transport costs, while topology-agnostic checkpoints allow parallel layouts to change between runs.
On NVL8 B300 nodes, it scales from 12.9B to 1.2T parameters across up to 512 GPUs; the authors also report Token Gerrymandering and cases where communication overlap hurts kernel speed.

figures.caption: Figure 4 Throughput as total expert parameter size grows at nearly fixed active FLOPs. These preliminary measurements use an eight-layer bfloat16 (BF16) model on one 8×B300 node without pipeline parallelism (PP; Section 6); MoE uses top-4 routing, and the new MoE path uses EP8. The old, dense-oriented FSDP path loses throughput as total expert parameter size grows, whereas the new DDP+EP path keeps MoE throughput within a modest margin of its dense baseline. This is a composed-system result, not an isolated FSDP-versus-DDP or EP ablation.

Figure 5 Subsystems of the Olmo-core DDP training stack. Colors mark the layers: configuration (green) and train-module orchestration (purple) sit above the MoE model (yellow), the parallel runtimes (blue), and supporting systems (orange). Low-level libraries, kernels, communication systems, and hardware interconnects (gray) form the substrate below. The layout groups system responsibilities rather than prescribing an execution order.

Figure 59 Kernel-time breakdown, throughput, and memory across the four MXFP8 modes. The combined recipe reduces the rank-0 kernel-duration sum by a quarter. Panels (a,b) use profiled kernel durations to identify changed work; panel (c) uses unprofiled runs for throughput because tracing perturbs the launch-heavy combined path. (a) Kernel-duration sums per captured train batch on rank 0 by kernel family, means of three captured batches per mode. Teal families are the ones MXFP8 targets, gray families are not targeted, and pink is the added quantization, scale-swizzle, and dequantization work (75.5, 203.1, and 262.1 ms per batch; 3.0%, 8.0%, and 10.3% of the BF16 sum). Family sums overlap across streams and are not an additive wall-time model; the triangle marks the union of kernelbusy intervals, which shrinks by 1.3%, 16.3%, and 20.2%. (b) Change of the three targeted families relative to BF16; the bars in each row are, top to bottom, dense GEMM, grouped GEMM, and EP transport, in the colors of (a). The EP-transport family includes barrier kernels; the payload-moving kernels alone fall by 41% in both the MLP+EP and combined modes, so part of the combined −50% is reduced waiting. (c) Throughput change over three fresh distributed jobs per mode; bars are means of the three ten-step windows and dots are the repetitions. The BF16 reference is 54.74K tokens/s/GPU and the largest sample standard deviation is 0.14K, smaller than the dot markers. (d) Peak active memory change in the same runs from the 103.40 GiB BF16 reference. Four B300 GPUs, EP = 4, uniform routing, and identical initialized weights, inputs, and routing in every mode (Table 26); these are systems measurements at one operating point, not training-quality evidence (Section 11.3.5).

Figure 2 Equal FLOPs do not imply equal HBM traffic. The forward fused up/gate and down GEMMs of a dense FFN with intermediate width Kh are compared with N experts of intermediate width h, selecting K per token. Here N = 64, K = 4, and the model width and expert intermediate width are d = h = 4096. (a) GEMM-side HBM byte categories, each normalized separately to dense. These ratios are not additive: each category contributes according to its absolute byte volume, not equally. The intermediate row counts up/gate output writes and down input reads, excluding the pointwise activation’s own accesses. (b) Analytical ceilings in bfloat16 (BF16), normalized to peak FLOPs, with balanced routes and one HBM read/write per operand/result. Each curve adds the two GEMM times; pointwise activation, packing, combine, network, and backward costs are excluded. Conceptual illustration with no measured quantities; assumptions are detailed in Appendix A.8.

Figure 3 A FLOP advantage can shrink or survive in wall time. This illustrative, simplified comparison uses two power-law-shaped loss traces that run for 10,000 equal-token steps and end at the same loss. Panel (a) assigns the 3.5B-active/13B-total MoE a normalized useful-FLOP cost of 1 per step, versus 2 for the 7B dense model. Panel (b) maps the same MoE loss samples onto two hypothetical runtimes: normalized wall-time costs of 1.85 for inefficient infrastructure and 1.2 for optimized infrastructure, versus 2 for dense. The corresponding time-to-target advantages are only 2/1.85 ≈ 1.08× and 2/1.2 ≈ 1.67×. All costs and loss curves are illustrative assumptions, not measurements or predictions for an Olmo run.

Figure 1 MoE and Dense Transformer blocks. Both blocks retain attention and residual connections. The dense block (right) applies the same feed-forward network to every token. The MoE block (left) illustrates one token routed to K = 2 of N = 4 routed experts—experts 0 and 2 in this example—and combines their outputs with an optional always-active shared expert before the residual addition. Here, K = 2 is a per-token choice. Other tokens can select different experts, so a training batch can collectively use all N experts.

Figure 74 Captured timelines show the two submission regimes. Both Nsight Systems profiles run the same eight-layer development model (128 routed experts, top-8, one shared expert, EP8, BF16, two sequences per rank microbatch) on eight B300 GPUs; only the expert-parallel path differs. This capture predates and differs from the reduced profiling workload of Table 46. In the synchronized trace (a), the per-block host wait appears as cudaEventSynchronize in the CUDA API lane, the CPU and GPU ranges of each forward block stay in lock step, and the GPU kernel rows show recurring gaps. In the rowwise trace (b), no host wait interrupts submission: the CPU finishes submitting the microbatch while the GPU is still executing earlier work, and the GPU-side forward blocks run back to back. Each panel is one captured instance of one rank; the two traces are separate runs, so this figure illustrates the submission mechanism rather than a controlled throughput comparison.

Figure 6 A four-GPU DDP example with no model-parallel sharding. With DP = 4, every GPU holds a static replica of the same attention layers and complete routed-expert pool, experts 0–15, while processing different input data. DDP synchronizes the gradients of these replicated weights; it does not itself shard the model shown here.

Figure 36 A host loop executes exact-size expert GEMMs. It avoids padded arithmetic, but GPU-produced row counts must become host-visible before the runtime can submit the per-expert operations. The separate streams in this conceptual drawing are not required by the method; the legacy Olmo fallback submits its GEMMs on the current stream.

Figure 65 Under a pipeline schedule, static per-layer replay needs one saved-context slot per in-flight microbatch. (a) Without a pipeline the backward of each microbatch consumes the layer’s saved context before the next forward overwrites it, so one graph per layer serves every microbatch. (b) With three microbatches in flight, a shared slot is overwritten by F1 and F2 before B0 reads it; three slots, each with its own graph and static buffers, are recycled as each microbatch’s backward for the layer completes. Conceptual illustration after the design described for Megatron-Core (Yan et al., 2026); no measured quantities.

Figure 56 Round-ceiling MXFP8 follows the BF16 training trajectory. The top plot reports cross-entropy loss; the bottom reports total gradient norm. The model has 8.36B active and 166.72B total parameters across 31 layers, with top-4 routing over 128 routed experts and one shared expert. The common step-6000 checkpoint was trained from scratch with MXFP8 OCP-floor scaling on approximately 56B tokens. Step 7179 corresponds to approximately 67B tokens, so the plotted continuation spans approximately 11B tokens. The main panels use a 21-step centered moving average, while the final-50-step panels use a lighter 7-step centered moving average; faint lines show the raw measurements. Over the final 50 steps, rceil differs from BF16 by +0.00048 mean loss and −1.9% mean gradient norm, whereas floor differs by +0.02200 mean loss and +51.1% mean gradient norm.

Figure 38 Grouped GEMM and capacity-padded BMM across routed-row counts. Grouped GEMM is faster throughout the shaded mid-to-large-model range. The experiment isolates one BF16 square expert projection on one B300 with Nlocal = 16 and d = h = 4096. The horizontal axis is total routed rows across the 16 local experts; routed rows count expert rows, not unique input tokens, since each token contributes one row to each of its top-K experts, and balanced routing gives M/16 valid rows per expert. The green band marks the representative 16K–96K rank-local operating range. Its endpoints summarize variation in microbatch and routing choices rather than one fixed microbatch size, sequence length, top-K, or local-expert count; Appendix Table 42 gives concrete configurations. BMM reserves exactly 1.25× capacity per expert, while grouped GEMM executes only valid rows. Left: useful throughput counts only valid-row FLOPs. Right: values above one indicate that grouped GEMM is faster. Each point is the mean of 20 queued CUDA-event samples after 10 warm-ups; all timed operations are submitted behind one device-side gate and released only after the host has queued the complete batch, so small shapes are not dominated by Python launch gaps.

Figure 8 Global-batch and model-size sweeps expose different limits. Preliminary single-node measurements use eight B300 GPUs, an eight-layer BF16 MoE model, top-4 random routing, no PP, and approximately 3.2B active parameters. Left: with EP disabled and 48 routed experts (19B total parameters), DDP useful-model FLOPs utilization (MFU) rises from 25.2% to 41.4% between 128-Ki and 4-Mi-token global batches (1 Ki = 210 and 1 Mi = 220 tokens), while FSDP rises from 26.4% to 29.8%. Right: total parameters grow from 4.6B to 47B; no-EP DDP runs out of memory at 64 and 128 experts, no-EP FSDP continues to fit but loses useful-model MFU, and DDP+EP8 remains nearly flat. Each point is one run, so the curves show preliminary scaling behavior rather than run-to-run variance. They do not decompose peak memory or attribute the trend to a specific communication phase.

Figure 71 Grouped GEMM also wins across the small-model training range. This one-B300 experiment fixes 16 local experts and a square BF16 projection with d = h = 2048. The green band marks the 96K–192K routed-row range represented by the small configurations in Table 42; their exact widths and local expert counts vary, so the band is an operating-range guide rather than an exact reconstruction of every model. BMM reserves 1.25× capacity per expert, while grouped GEMM executes only valid rows. Each point averages 20 queued CUDA-event samples after 10 warm-ups.

Figure 54 Conversion and layout costs in MXFP8 execution. MXFP8 is faster only when its GEMM savings exceed these costs. This is a schematic cost model, not measured timing. The displayed O(MK + KN) conversion term assumes both operands are quantized on the critical path. In Olmo training, the K × N weight conversion is normally paid during cache refresh and reused across microbatches, leaving activation conversion as the principal per-invocation cost. For small GEMMs, that remaining overhead can still turn the expected speedup into a slowdown.

Figure 9 The distributed optimizer and EP reduce different parts of DDP’s persistent parameter-sized training state. Under the illustrated BF16-execution, FP32-gradient, and two-moment FP32 optimizer policy, naive DDP uses 18 bytes per parameter. Sharding the FP32 main weights and optimizer states evenly over D replica ranks reduces this to 6+12/D bytes while compute weights and gradient buffers remain replicated. Sharding routed-expert compute weights and gradients over the expert-parallel model-sharding degree ME (EP-MP; defined in Section 5) further reduces their per-rank memory contribution to 6/ME + 12/D bytes when D = MEDE . Dense and shared parameters follow their separate replica groups. This accounting excludes execution working memory, including activations, routing and communication buffers, kernel workspaces, execution caches, and allocator fragmentation, as well as uneven shards and small auxiliary tensors that are not sharded.

Figure 62 Block recompute removes nearly two thirds of activation memory at a one-fifth throughput cost in this matched configuration. Bars show the arithmetic mean of three fresh-process repetitions; dots show the individual ten-step windows, and the sample standard deviations are smaller than the dot markers. Normal training in this campaign sustains 54.68K tokens/s/GPU at 103.03 GiB peak active memory; recomputing every transformer block sustains 43.22K tokens/s/GPU at 76.90 GiB, 20.95% lower throughput for 26.13 GiB (25.36%) less peak memory. The lower segment of each memory bar, labeled “persistent”, is the memory resident between steps (parameters, gradient buffers, optimizer states, and persistent buffers), 62.21 GiB in both modes; the reduction therefore falls entirely on the transient activation part, which shrinks from 40.82 to 14.69 GiB. Measurements use four NVIDIA B300 GPUs and the fixed model, batch, routing, and timing protocol described in the text.

Figure 7 Weight materialization and gradient synchronization run on different clocks. Under the illustrated FSDP schedule, unsharded weights are materialized around layer use in each microbatch. DDP instead uses static replicas of its local weights throughout the accumulation window and synchronizes accumulated gradients at the optimizer-step boundary. When EP is enabled, token dispatch and combine still recur in every routed layer and microbatch. The phase widths were manually reconstructed from one representative profile and preserve its approximate timing proportions; the diagram is not an aggregate benchmark.

Figure 16 Rowwise EP targets remote expert rows without block packing. In the same illustrative two-rank, top-2 example as Figure 15, GPU-resident route indices drive a rowwise dispatch kernel that places accepted rows directly into fixed-capacity rank- and expert-major storage. Grouped GEMM consumes that layout without a second permutation. Rowwise combine returns expert outputs directly to their source-token positions for weighted merging, without materializing a peer-packed return buffer. The “AllToAll” labels inside the drawing denote the logical rank exchange; the implementation uses indexed one-sided row movement rather than an NCCL all-to-all collective. As in Figure 15, token E’s route to expert 1 does not fit in rank 0’s 12-row capacity, so it is dropped and combine treats it as zero. The drawing explains data layout and movement, not measured performance.

Figure 42 The load-balancing loss falls while load imbalance rises. Orange is the original λLBL = 0.05 trajectory; blue reloads the step-17,000 checkpoint with λLBL = 0.005. Unscaled LBL is the sum over the 47 MoE blocks; imbalance is the worst max/mean expert count over blocks and ranks. Smoothed traces only; Figure 45 adds the raw measurements and the cross-entropy panel, and Section 10.8.1 gives the protocol.

Figure 11 A four-GPU example with DP = 4, EP-MP = 2, and 16 total experts. Starting from the fully replicated layout in Figure 6, the same four DP ranks form EP-MP groups of size 2 and EP-DP groups of size 2. Each EP-MP group keeps attention replicated and shards experts 0–7 and 8–15 across its two ranks. Dispatch moves selected token rows to the appropriate expert rank, and combine returns their contributions. Ranks holding corresponding shards in the two EP-MP groups are EP-DP replicas and reduce gradients together.

Figure 70 Olmo’s merge rule preserves dense-like scale at random initialization. The four conventions are those of Table 37. Figure 30 Submission headroom is the queued, not-yet-executed device work. Both curves are computed exactly from the drawn boxes: headroom jumps up by a kernel’s device duration when the CPU completes that kernel’s submission and drains at unit rate while the GPU executes, so the GPU is idle exactly where the curve sits at zero. (a) Cheap submissions of large kernels (k1–k3) build the lead; a host-heavy stretch of small kernels (k4–k7) spends it faster than it is replaced, and after the lead reaches zero the GPU waits for k7’s submission. (b) Within one microbatch, each Python-driven forward submission costs the CPU more time than its kernel costs the GPU, so the lead carried in from the previous backward drains layer by layer and grazes zero just as the last forward submission arrives. The autograd-driven backward inverts the imbalance, and while the GPU executes it, the CPU is already submitting the next microbatch’s forward: the rebuilt surplus is the lead that forward will spend. Each CPU box’s width is the full host cost of its submission, including Python and dispatcher time. Conceptual illustration with no measured quantities.

Figure 31 A per-block synchronization point stops the CPU from running ahead. papers.selection_reason: Efficient and scalable MoE training stack for large language models; directly relevant to LLM architecture/training and AI efficiency.
papers.title: Supercharging Olmo-core for Efficient and Scalable MoE Training
papers.tldr: A redesigned Olmo-core stack makes large-scale MoE training more efficient and scalable by combining specialized parallelism, communication-free routing, MXFP8, and flexible checkpointing.

papers.abstract: Language models acquire a vast array of concepts and abilities from next-token prediction alone. We introduce an interpretability framework that exposes how this single loss relates to the development of different concepts at different points during pretraining. We propose Concept Energy, a measure of the concept-specific alignment between a concept subspace and the average gradient outer product (AGOP) of the next-token-prediction loss. The concept subspace captures where the concept currently lives in the model's representation; AGOP captures the directions to which the loss is most sensitive. Across 19 checkpoints of Pythia-410M and -1B and 12 lexical, syntactic, and semantic concepts, we find that the first peak in Concept Energy generally occurs at or before the steepest increase in probe decodability. Furthermore, whereas probe performance usually increases monotonically throughout training, Concept Energy is not confined to a single peak; some concepts exhibit sustained or repeated engagement across pretraining, suggesting that concept learning may require continual reinforcement or occur at multiple points. Our results indicate that the loss contributes to concept learning in a myriad of ways that simple probe performance alone cannot reveal.
authors: Yupei Wang, Neil Mallinar, Mikhail Belkin, Alex Warstadt
bullets: Introduces Concept Energy, measuring alignment between a concept’s representation subspace and directions emphasized by the loss’s average gradient outer product.
Analyzes 12 lexical, syntactic, and semantic concepts across 19 checkpoints of Pythia-410M and Pythia-1B.
The first Concept Energy peak generally occurs at or before the steepest rise in probe decodability.
Concept Energy may show sustained or repeated peaks, suggesting continual reinforcement or multi-stage concept learning.
Shows that probe performance alone can miss important variation in how the loss supports concept acquisition.

papers.abstract: Can a language model teach itself to reason without labels? On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) uses the model as its own teacher, but strengthens that teacher with a ground-truth solution. The natural label-free substitute, voting over the model's attempts, fails precisely on hard problems: attempts disagree, and their most common answer is often wrong. We propose STONE, a label-free alternative that moves agreement to easier related problems. The model writes these stepping stones, keeps those it solves consistently, and shows the teacher their worked solutions, with final answers removed; the student sees only the original problem. No step reads a label, and inference needs no extra context or model calls. Across five math benchmarks, the proposed method achieves the highest average accuracy for Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B in thinking mode. Without thinking mode, it gains 13.2 and 22.7 points, 2.5 and 2.7 times the gains of OPSD with ground-truth solutions.

papers.abstract: Online auction houses must set reserve prices for highly differentiated products whose unstructured descriptions contain valuable demand information. Existing approaches generally require managers to specify product attributes in advance. We ask whether a language model can instead learn from listing descriptions and historical bids to set item-specific reserve prices before bidding begins. We fine-tune a pretrained text embedding language model using the structural likelihood of auction bids as its training objective. This directs representation learning toward the valuation distribution that determines the reserve decision. We show that consecutive upper bids identify the tail information needed to set an optimal reserve without observing or modeling the number of potential bidders. A split-sample estimator learns the representation on one half of the data and conducts structural estimation and inference conditional on that representation on the other. We apply the method to approximately 65,800 online used-vehicle auctions. With seller values calibrated to match the sale rate among listings, the model implies a counterfactual net increase of $165.8 million, representing a 14.6% increase above the incumbent reserve policy. The framework translates a listing description and a seller's value into an item-specific reserve recommendation without constructing a product taxonomy or requiring a bid history for the item being priced. It provides an approach to adapting language models for operational decisions in marketplaces where products are heterogeneous and demand-relevant information is recorded in text.
bullets: Addresses reserve pricing for highly differentiated products whose demand information is embedded in unstructured listing text.

papers.abstract: Machine unlearning claims require evidence that a model has removed the influence of specified training data. Yet widely deployable post hoc verifiers. infer unlearning largely from predictive behavior, the final model response that remains under the provider's control. We make this limitation concrete through Output-Level Deceptive Response (ODR), an attack that produces responses accepted by output based verifiers while preserving the original representation state. By separating output conformity from internal unlearning, ODR motivates a rethinking of machine unlearning verification, shifting the audit target from what the model returns to what changes inside it. We operationalize this shift through Representation Unlearning Verification (RUV), a gray box verifier that compares intermediate forward representations in the original and unlearned models. RUV traces a four-stage response through activation reorganization, representation displacement, neighborhood disruption, and loss of manifold support. Matched retained controls distinguish target specific responses from global model drift, while joint permutation calibration combines the four evidence views into an adaptive decision. Experiments spanning exact and approximate unlearning, class and sample level requests, multiple datasets, and diverse architectures show mean ODR deception success rates of $97.0\%$ and $97.7\%$, respectively. RUV achieves mean verification accuracies of $98.9\%$ and $94.9\%$, while rejecting $99.5\%$ and $99.8\%$ of the corresponding ODR submissions.
authors: Lei Zhou, Youwen zhu, Rongke Liu
bullets: Output-level verifiers may infer unlearning from provider-controlled predictions without confirming removal of training-data influence.
The Output-Level Deceptive Response (ODR) attack preserves the original representation state while producing verifier-accepted outputs.
Representation Unlearning Verification (RUV) compares intermediate representations between original and unlearned models.
RUV analyzes activation reorganization, representation displacement, neighborhood disruption, and loss of manifold support, using retained controls and joint permutation calibration.
Across tested settings, ODR deception was highly effective, while RUV achieved high verification accuracy and rejected most deceptive submissions.

papers.abstract: Asynchronous reinforcement learning suits long-horizon agents with irregular rollout times, but group-relative updates require repeated rollouts of each prompt. However, group-based sampling limits prompt coverage at a fixed rollout budget and introduces group synchronization barriers. One rollout per prompt avoids these constraints but removes the variance-reducing group baseline, making updates noisier and more prone to instability on stale, variable-length trajectories. We present FlashREINFORCE, a critic-free, one-pass framework built on One-Batch REINFORCE, a Sequence Trust Region, and Sample-Mean Optimization. These components preserve prompt coverage and signed feedback while controlling policy drift and length-amplified negative updates. In our experiments, FlashREINFORCE remains stable through 6,000 updates on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B at a policy lag of approximately four updates. On Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, it reaches 38.0 mean accuracy across five benchmarks, outperforming the reported GRPO baseline by 1.7 percentage points with half the rollouts (256k versus 512k). Python-tool experiments extend to the 30B MoE model Qwen3-30B-A3B, with stable training at policy lag eight. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, FlashREINFORCE maintains tool use where GRPO stops making tool calls and achieves 98.3%/96.5% seen/unseen ALFWorld success.

papers.abstract: For twenty-five years, neutrosophic logic has assigned independent degrees of truth (T), indeterminacy (I), and falsity (F) to epistemic states that classical and fuzzy semantics cannot express. Previous applications measured these components on outputs: answers, judgments, expert evaluations. This paper reports, to our knowledge, the first neutrosophic reading of components inside the internal representations of a large language model. Using the recently released Jacobian lens on Qwen3.5-4B, we project intermediate-layer readouts onto lexicons of support, refutation, and hedging, obtaining layer-wise (T, I, F) profiles under conflicting evidence, first-person false belief, and factual control (n = 20 each). A first battery yielded three striking signatures: a surge of refutation mass under conflict, sustained indeterminacy under false belief, and an apparent "verdict collapse" before the output layer. A second, template-controlled battery showed that all three, as initially stated, were largely artifacts of prompt grammar: matched templates with agreeing evidence inflate the same lexicon masses, true beliefs elicit the same hedging, and the model verbalizes its verdict when allowed to generate. What survives the controls is stronger than what died: the neutrosophic verdict balance B = log10(F) - log10(T) tracks evidence polarity under identical templates (about 3 orders of magnitude of separation, Cohen's d = 2.3-2.5, p < 10^-6 in 9 of 9 layers; paired Wilcoxon: median difference +2.4 orders, 19/20 items, p = 3.8x10^-6) and residually discriminates false from true first-person beliefs. We argue that the independence of the neutrosophic components is what keeps the common-mode channel observable, making both the measurement and its self-correction possible, and we distill the two-battery design into a reusable protocol for auditing language model internals with lens-based readouts.
authors: Maikel Yelandi Leyva-Vazquez, Alexis Matheu Perez, Florentin Smarandache
bullets: Projects intermediate-layer readouts onto support, refutation, and hedging lexicons to estimate truth (T), indeterminacy (I), and falsity (F) profiles.
Initial signatures—refutation under conflict, indeterminacy under false belief, and verdict collapse—largely disappear under matched prompt controls.
The balance B = log10(F) − log10(T) remains sensitive to evidence polarity across tested layers and also distinguishes false from true first-person beliefs.
The two-battery design shows why template controls are essential and provides a reusable protocol for auditing lens-based measurements of model internals.

papers.abstract: ECC memory embeds 8 parity bits for every 64 data bits and automatically detects and corrects errors on each read. The parity bits carry no data and only safeguard integrity, at ~12.5% overhead. Yet the reasoning chains of large language models lack such built-in self-verification: once an error occurs it propagates along the chain, and existing methods can only verify externally after generation completes. We propose the check token, establishing built-in self-verification for language model generation streams for the first time: a functional marker is added to the vocabulary, and the model triggers self-checking (analysis, localization, truncation, rewriting) by outputting it at any position. The check token carries no reasoning content (discarded after triggering) and only safeguards reasoning correctness, directly corresponding to the role of ECC parity bits, also at only ~13% overhead. Speculative forking further eliminates false-positive latency, and segmented reward makes trigger timing end-to-end learnable. Experiments (Qwen3-32B / Qwen3-Next) show that the check token achieves +10.8 pp improvement on HMMT25 at 1.13x overhead, with token efficiency 88x that of Best-of-8, and the precise truncation advantage monotonically increases with chain length.
authors: Fei Ding, Yongkang Zhang, Yuhao Liao, Zijian Zeng, Huiming Yang
bullets: LLM reasoning errors can propagate because existing verification typically occurs only after generation finishes.
A vocabulary marker triggers analysis, error localization, truncation, and rewriting at any point in the reasoning stream.
The token carries no reasoning content and introduces approximately 13% overhead, analogous to ECC parity bits.
Speculative forking reduces false-positive latency, while segmented rewards make trigger timing learnable end to end.
On HMMT25 with Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-Next, it improves performance by 10.8 percentage points at 1.13× overhead and is reported as 88× more token-efficient than Best-of-8.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Method overview. Stage 1: Vocabulary extension adds check token c; SFT finetunes on constructed data (auxiliary trigger loss guarantees pmin > 0), providing the model with triggering and localization capability. Stage 2: RLOO with segmented reward finetunes trigger precision; the optimal threshold q∗ has a closed-form solution. Inference: upon outputting c, speculative forking creates a main branch (speculative continuation) and a check branch (correction analysis); true positives trigger truncation-rewriting, false positives directly use the main branch (zero latency).

Figure 3: Check token workflow (true-positive path). After the error segment s4–s6 (orange), outputting c (red) triggers self-checking. After precise localization, s1–s3 (green) are retained, and truncation-rewriting (blue) proceeds. On false positives, the check branch is discarded, and the main branch’s speculative continuation directly becomes the final sequence (zero latency cost).

papers.abstract: Parallel mechanisms pose distinctive challenges to large language models (LLMs), as valid reasoning depends jointly on mechanism topology, loop closure, geometry, joint types, and modeling assumptions. Yet existing LLM benchmarks provide little systematic coverage of such domain-specific knowledge, constraint-sensitive analysis, and constructive design. To fill this gap, we introduce MECHBENCH, a 2,541-question benchmark for evaluating LLMs in parallel mechanisms across professional knowledge, mechanism analysis, and design. MECHBENCH contains standard and challenge tiers spanning six capability categories and nine executable analysis and design tasks. It is constructed through MECHFORGE, a domain-grounded framework that combines expert-organized knowledge, LLM-assisted question generation, programmatic instance generation, two-stage expert review, and task-aware scoring with exact matching, rubric-based evaluation, and program verification. We further develop MECHGPT as a diagnostic domain-adapted model. Experiments show that strong knowledge performance does not directly translate into executable mechanism reasoning: leading closed-service models achieve over 95 on the standard tier but only 47-60 on the challenge tier, while domain adaptation substantially improves MechGPT over its Qwen3-8B baselines but leaves a large gap in constrained analysis and design. These results establish MECHBENCH as a systematic testbed for measuring domain-specific LLM capabilities in mechanism science.

papers.abstract: Transformers consist of diverse building blocks, such as embedding layers, normalization layers, self-attention mechanisms, and point-wise feedforward networks. Thus, understanding the differences and interactions among these blocks is important. In this paper, we uncover a clear Sharpness Disparity across these blocks, which emerges early in training and intriguingly persists throughout the training process. Motivated by this finding, we propose Blockwise Learning Rate (LR), a strategy that tailors the LR to each block's sharpness, accelerating large language model (LLM) pre-training. By integrating Blockwise LR into AdamW, we consistently achieve lower terminal loss and nearly $2\times$ speedup compared to vanilla AdamW. We demonstrate this acceleration across GPT-2 and LLaMA, with model sizes ranging from 0.12B to 2B and datasets of OpenWebText, MiniPile, and C4. Finally, we incorporate Blockwise LR into Adam-mini (Zhang et al., 2024), a recently proposed memory-efficient variant of Adam, achieving a combined $2\times$ speedup and $2\times$ memory saving. These results underscore the potential of exploiting the sharpness disparity to improve LLM training.
authors: Jinbo Wang, Mingze Wang, Zhanpeng Zhou, Junchi Yan, Weinan E, Lei Wu
bullets: Identifies a sharpness disparity among embeddings, normalization, attention, and feedforward blocks that appears early and persists during training.
Introduces Blockwise Learning Rate, which assigns learning rates according to each block’s sharpness and integrates with AdamW.
Reports lower terminal loss and nearly 2× faster pre-training than vanilla AdamW across GPT-2 and LLaMA experiments.
Combining Blockwise Learning Rate with Adam-mini yields approximately 2× speedup and 2× memory savings.
Evaluation covers models from 0.12B to 2B parameters and datasets including OpenWebText, MiniPile, and C4.

papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) has made significant progress in explaining the internal computations of Large Language Models (LLMs); however, these advances have yet to demonstrate comparable success in explaining the decision-making processes of LLM-based agents. This paper examines the challenges MI tools face when applied to realistic agentic failures. We focus on one such failure: web agents hallucinating actions that are not available on a website. We apply a series of mechanistic analyzes to Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as it interacts with live websites. We find that a linear probe trained on the last prompt token can predict hallucinations before generation begins (0.80 AUC) and steering along a probe direction corrects 85\% of hallucinations, but disrupts 7\% of valid actions. However, these results only provide a partial explanation of why the agent hallucinates. The probe direction is sensitive to prompt formatting, losing much of its steering effect after a minor change to how actions are represented. Additionally, circuit identification can be difficult as the computation is distributed across multiple components and positions, and the information the agent relies on varies across examples. We discuss how these observations challenge the assumptions underlying standard MI methods for circuit discovery and feature identification, and outline future directions for making these methods better suited to explain failures in LLM-based agents.
authors: Mohamed Aghzal, Mor Geva, Gregory J. Stein, Ziyu Yao
bullets: Studies Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct during interactions with live websites, focusing on hallucinated unavailable actions.
A linear probe on the final prompt token predicts hallucinations before generation, achieving 0.80 AUC.
Steering along the probe direction corrects 85% of hallucinations but disrupts 7% of valid actions.
The steering effect is highly sensitive to prompt formatting, and the relevant computation is distributed across components and token positions.
These findings expose limitations of standard circuit-discovery and feature-identification methods for explaining agent failures.

papers.abstract: Autonomous trading agents need controls that prevent problematic orders without making legitimate tasks impractical. We study this aspect of agentic compliance with TradeGauntlet, a replayable limit-order-book simulator that separates detection, prevention, and execution cost. In 1,680 simulated sessions with Claude Haiku 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, all conduct alerts were self-matches. Gates eliminated those alerts by rejecting self-crossing orders, while the aggregate-gate condition reduced Sonnet's two-sided fills by about 15%. A conduct reminder reduced Sonnet's alert rate but reduced Haiku's fills without a detectable alert benefit. These results show why zero alerts alone do not establish an agent's compliance. Scripted probes and two search methods test weaknesses beyond those observed in the LLM runs. The searches find split-order schedules that evade the implemented conduct rules; a learned baseline catches all 2,400 tested searched episodes but also flags 15% of a large maker's sessions. Aggregate caps reduce the response-dependent gain unevenly, with smaller reductions when only near-touch depth affects prices. A response fitted to five Nasdaq stocks and a separate ABIDES experiment expose the dependence of these estimates on market assumptions. A distinct adversarial prompt elicited refusals from Sonnet in all 240 rounds, yielding no candidate strategies to evaluate. TradeGauntlet provides reproducible tests of controls around trading agents; the experiments do not establish legal compliance or real-market detection accuracy.
authors: Sandip Nandi, Aishwarya Bose, Apurba Bose, Soovadeep Bakshi
bullets: Evaluates detection, prevention, and execution costs in a replayable limit-order-book simulator across 1,680 LLM-agent sessions.
All observed conduct alerts involved self-matches; gates prevented these alerts but aggregate gating reduced Sonnet’s two-sided fills by about 15%.
A conduct reminder reduced Sonnet’s alerts but harmed Haiku’s fills without a detectable alert benefit.
Search-based probes found split-order schedules that evaded the implemented rules; a learned baseline caught all 2,400 searched episodes but falsely flagged 15% of a large maker’s sessions.
Results varied with market assumptions, and the study does not establish legal compliance or real-market detection accuracy.

papers.abstract: Program induction refers to the process in which a learner aims to recover a program from a few given input-output examples. This paradigm broadens programming access by letting users demonstrate the rule-based behavior they want to apply to unseen data, instead of having to implement it themselves. However, recovering a program from finite input-output examples is fundamentally ambiguous, as a finite set of input-output examples is theoretically consistent with infinitely many programs whose output diverges on unseen inputs. We view this problem from a Bayesian perspective, where, given a prior $p^0$ over programs, identifying the target program means concentrating posterior probability mass on it by observing additional input-output examples. In the interactive program induction setting, the learner chooses maximally informative inputs and queries an oracle, such as the user, for their outputs. We derive a greedy query-selection algorithm and show that it terminates after $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{\gamma}\log 1/p^0(f^\star))$ informative oracle queries, and returns the target program $f^\star$ up to approximate equivalence when no other class outweighs it under the prior. The algorithm uses a language model as the prior under a PAC-style relaxation of program equivalence, where the query-selection objective is estimated using importance sampling. On the CodeARC benchmark, the algorithm improves accuracy over the LM only agent by up to 22 percentage points while observing up to 10.5 fewer input-output examples.
authors: Robin Shing Moon Chan, Ryan Cotterell
bullets: Program induction from finite input-output examples is inherently ambiguous because many programs can fit the same observations.
The Bayesian approach treats a language model as a prior over programs and selects maximally informative inputs to query an oracle.
A greedy query-selection algorithm is proven to recover the target up to approximate equivalence with a logarithmic query bound dependent on the target’s prior probability.
Importance sampling estimates the query objective under a PAC-style relaxation of program equivalence.
On CodeARC, the method improves accuracy by up to 22 percentage points while using up to 10.5 fewer examples than an LM-only agent.

papers.abstract: LLM-based verifiers are increasingly used to evaluate agent executions, but their reliability is typically measured under a single representation of the trajectory. In deployed agent systems, the same execution may be exposed through composed tools, delegation boundaries, or compacted histories, changing what execution evidence is directly observable to the verifier. It therefore remains unclear whether correct verifier judgments persist across such abstraction boundaries. We introduce Verification Transport, a reliability test that measures judgment stability under abstraction-induced changes in execution observability. We construct matched native, abstracted, and restored views of the same frozen executions while holding the task, realized trajectory, outcome, ground truth, evaluation criterion, and verifier fixed. Across four agent-evaluation benchmarks, seven verifier backbones, four verification protocols, and three abstraction boundaries, we find substantial transport failure, reaching about 31% under macro abstraction and delegation. Verification protocols exhibit distinct failure modes: direct verification more often produces incorrect verdicts, whereas evidence-grounded and deliberative protocols tend to abstain under limited observability. This suggests that lower transport failure rates do not necessarily imply greater reliability. Restoring the corresponding execution provenance recovers 85.5% of transport failures, while recovery is lower when provenance is lossy or unavailable. These results show that native-view accuracy alone is insufficient to characterize verifier reliability when execution evidence crosses abstraction boundaries.
authors: Disha Sheshanarayana, Sai Linisha Reddy Goli
bullets: Introduces Verification Transport, which measures judgment stability across native, abstracted, and restored views of identical executions.
Evaluates four benchmarks, seven verifier backbones, four protocols, and three abstraction boundaries while holding task, trajectory, outcome, ground truth, criterion, and verifier fixed.
Finds transport failures of about 31% under macro abstraction and delegation.
Direct verification more often gives incorrect verdicts, while evidence-grounded and deliberative protocols more often abstain when observability is limited.
Restoring execution provenance recovers 85.5% of transport failures, but recovery is lower when provenance is lossy or unavailable.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces 'Verification Transport' to measure the reliability of LLM verifiers when execution evidence is abstracted or compressed, relevant to agent evaluation at inference time.
papers.title: Do Verifier Judgments Survive Abstraction? Measuring Verification Transport for LLM Agent Evaluation
papers.tldr: LLM verifier judgments can change substantially when the same agent execution is viewed through abstraction boundaries, so native-view accuracy alone is insufficient for evaluating reliability.

papers.abstract: Reliable use of large language models (LLMs) requires uncertainty estimates that separate ambiguity intrinsic to a prompt from genuine knowledge gaps. Bayesian and deep-ensemble methods deliver this aleatoric/epistemic decomposition in principle, but are computationally prohibitive at LLM scale and require white-box access. Existing black-box methods, in contrast, summarize to a single scalar that cannot make the distinction. We introduce a two-level ensemble that bridges this gap. Stochastic decoding of a fixed prompt forms the inner ensemble; meaning-preserving semantic perturbations of the prompt form the outer ensemble. Variability is measured in a continuous embedding space, and the law of total covariance gives an exact within-/between-perturbation decomposition to estimate aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty (AU/EU); it requires only black-box sampling access. On top of this estimator, we contribute three theoretical results that ground the framework: (i) a finite-sample bias identity for nested Monte Carlo with a closed-form bias-corrected epistemic estimator; (ii) a Bayesian bridge bounding the gap between perturbation-population AU/EU and Bayesian targets; and (iii) a separation result identifying a class of failure modes that any consistency-only black-box method provably misses while perturbation-based EU detects. Across five short QA benchmarks and four instruction-tuned LLMs spanning two families and two scales, our estimator is competitive with strong white-box baselines, and at a matched generation budget it matches leading black-box methods on error ranking while decomposing AU and EU; controlled paired interventions show that AU and EU respond selectively to distinct, actionable sources of failure: prompt ambiguity and model knowledge gaps; and a long-form pilot on the NQ long-answer split shows the framework extends to claim-level factuality without retraining.
authors: Wang Ma, Debarun Bhattacharjya, Junkyu Lee, Nhan H Pham, Harsha Kokel, Qiang Ji
bullets: Addresses the inability of existing black-box uncertainty methods to distinguish aleatoric uncertainty (prompt ambiguity) from epistemic uncertainty (knowledge gaps).
Uses stochastic decoding as an inner ensemble and meaning-preserving prompt perturbations as an outer ensemble, measuring variability in embedding space.
Applies the law of total covariance to decompose uncertainty, with a bias-corrected epistemic estimator for finite nested samples.
Provides theoretical guarantees covering estimator bias, links to Bayesian uncertainty targets, and failure modes missed by consistency-only methods.

Across five QA benchmarks and four instruction-tuned LLMs, matches leading black-box error ranking at matched generation budgets while also decomposing uncertainty; a pilot extends the approach to claim-level factuality without retraining.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a two-level ensemble method for black-box uncertainty quantification in LLMs, decomposing aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty at inference time.
papers.title: Black-Box Uncertainty Quantification for Large Language Models via Ensemble-of-Ensembles
papers.tldr: A black-box ensemble-of-ensembles method separates prompt ambiguity from model knowledge gaps in LLM uncertainty using only sampled outputs and semantic prompt perturbations.

papers.abstract: Humans know that airplanes are fast, that this extends to red airplanes, but that it does not hold for broken airplanes. How do LLMs acquire category knowledge that humans learn and apply effortlessly? We introduce LeCat, a two-part framework to analyze LLM's Learning of Category knowledge. First, we use LeCat to evaluate models on their ability to learn category knowledge, distinguishing between three cases: memorization of in-domain category knowledge, generalization to unseen instances, and ability to flexibly use knowledge in appropriate contexts. Then, we use LeCat to trace how this knowledge can be learned in pretraining from text that may encode category knowledge in various ways, such as verbatim repetition or exceptions, which we refer to as forms of "knowledge expression". We first assess open-source pretrained models using 199 curated category-feature pairs and analyze their training data. Our findings suggest that strengthening context and category-feature co-occurrence likelihood (PMI) improve learning for larger models and verbatim rule-like statements diminish flexible category learning. To systematically isolate these effects, we then train a 68M model from scratch with precise control over the categorical information each sees in their training data, confirming that verbatim repetition reduces flexible learning but mixture of diverse knowledge expressions lead to more robust category learning. Together, our findings highlight that while contextual flexibility is persistently difficult for models, how category knowledge is expressed in pretraining greatly impacts models' acquisition of robust category knowledge.
authors: Jimin Mun, Maarten Sap, Yanai Elazar
bullets: Evaluates category learning through memorization, generalization to unseen instances, and context-appropriate use.
Traces how different pretraining knowledge expressions—such as repetition, rules, and exceptions—shape learning.
Stronger context and category–feature co-occurrence improve learning, especially in larger models.
Verbatim rule-like repetition reduces flexible category learning, while diverse expressions produce more robust knowledge.
Contextual flexibility remains persistently difficult for LLMs.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes how LLMs acquire category knowledge from pretraining data, a core LLM capability study.
papers.title: LECAT: Measuring LLM Category Learning from Pretraining Data
papers.tldr: LeCat shows that how category knowledge is expressed in pretraining strongly affects whether LLMs can flexibly generalize it beyond memorized examples.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) generate text one token at a time, yet how a particular generation relates to the geometry learned in pre-training remains unclear. The fundamental explainability of LLMs is elusive. Here, we build a similarity network from the input embeddings of six open LLMs and map generation onto it. The token-embedding network is scale-free while heavy-tailed, as are random embeddings with matched covariance, but far more fragmented. Distillation barely changes this topology because input embeddings are largely inherited. The knowledge space is thus deterministic from pre-training. Consecutive generated tokens are rarely graph neighbours and, in most models, no more often than in shuffled order, so generation is not a walk on the predefined network, although the tokens it visits are concentrated within it. Through the logit lens in a layer- wise manner, tokens settle late in depth in most models, and repetitive models remain confined to small domain-specific sub-graphs. These observables could serve as inference-time monitors of degeneration. We thus provide a fresh perspective on understanding LLM generation in the microscopic way from node or link prediction by graph learning.
bullets: The study maps token generation onto similarity networks built from input embeddings of six open LLMs.
These networks are scale-free and heavy-tailed, yet more fragmented than matched-covariance random embeddings.
Distillation has little effect on network topology, suggesting the knowledge-space structure is largely inherited from pre-training.
Consecutive generated tokens are rarely network neighbors, though generated tokens remain concentrated within the embedding network.
Layer-wise analysis shows tokens settle late in depth, while repetitive models stay within small domain-specific subgraphs; these patterns may monitor degeneration at inference time.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates the geometry of LLM embeddings and generation patterns from a graph learning perspective, offering insights into generation mechanics.
papers.title: Dancing Tokens on the Vocabulary Network from LLM Generation
papers.tldr: LLM generation draws on a structured, fragmented token-embedding network but generally does not proceed as a graph walk through neighboring tokens.

papers.abstract: We partially resolve Conjecture 1 of [Karagodin et al., Clustering in Causal Attention Masking (NeurIPS 2024)] and extend it to time-dependent parameter regimes. The conjecture predicts that causal attention dynamics converge to two clusters aligned with the eigenvectors associated with the largest eigenvalue $\lambda_{\max}$ of the value transformation. We prove that this behavior holds when $\lambda_{\max}>0$ and is generally false when $\lambda_{\max}\le0$. The resulting two-cluster regime is common in practice and substantially more challenging than the classical single-cluster setting studied previously. A central contribution of our work is the identification of a rigorous dimension reduction phenomenon: despite evolving in a high-dimensional embedding space, token trajectories collapse onto a two-dimensional structure governed by a small number of dominant directions. Building on this insight, we introduce a new analytical framework--instability within the flow--inspired by instability phenomena in physical systems. This framework enables the analysis of steady-regime behavior in non-monotone, non-autonomous attention dynamics. Our theoretical findings are illustrated through simulations and experimental studies using Group Query Attention (GQA) layers.
authors: Trinh T. Nguyen, Duy-Tung Pham, Hoang-Son Do, Tan Minh Nguyen, Thieu N. Vo
bullets: Partially resolves a prior conjecture on clustering in causal attention and extends it to time-dependent parameter regimes.
Proves the two-cluster behavior for λ_max > 0, while showing it generally fails for λ_max ≤ 0.
Identifies collapse of high-dimensional token trajectories onto a two-dimensional structure governed by dominant directions.
Introduces an “instability within the flow” framework for analyzing non-monotone, non-autonomous attention dynamics.
Illustrates the theory with simulations and experiments involving Group Query Attention layers.

papers.title: Two-Clustering Regime of Token Dynamics in Causal Attention
papers.tldr: Causal attention dynamics converge to two token clusters when the value transformation’s largest eigenvalue is positive, enabled by a two-dimensional reduction of the dynamics.

papers.abstract: Scaling laws indicate that the generalization error of a large language model (LLM) decreases monotonically with model size once data is sufficient, and the corollary that larger models outperform smaller ones is now widely accepted. We argue that this corollary fails in security: decisions there hinge on anomalous inputs, which are long-tailed (e.g., zero-day attacks) and therefore poorly served by likelihood fitting. Worse still, the capability brought about by scale (e.g., inferring the intended whole from a corrupted part) leads a LLM silently \emph{repair} the anomaly before any downstream security head ever sees it. We formalize this as a tradeoff between two quantities: the cognitive capability $K(W)=I(W;P)$ that a model holds about the world distribution, and the security-information retention $R(W)=\frac{I(Z;S)}{I(A;S)}$ that survives in its intermediate representation. We derive three information-theoretic bounds to connect them: an upper bound on restoration accuracy in terms of $K(W)$, an upper bound on $R(W)$ in terms of the restoration error, and a Fano lower bound on security-task error in terms of $R(W)$. These theorems approximately imply that usable security information is a product of how much security information survives and how well it can be extracted, indicating that optimal usable security information can be achieved at a certain model size. We state this as the \emph{condensing law of security information}: usable security information is unimodal in model size, so security generalization error is U-shaped and is minimized at a finite $N^{\star}$ rather than decreasing without bound. The experiments on various real-world LLMs validate the condensing law, indicating that there is an optimal model size to solve security issues.
authors: Qi Tan, Tianyu Cui, Qi Li, Ke Xu
bullets: Security decisions depend on long-tailed anomalies such as zero-day attacks, which likelihood-based modeling handles poorly.
The paper formalizes a tradeoff between model world knowledge and retention of security information in intermediate representations.
Three information-theoretic bounds link restoration capability, security-information retention, and security-task error.
It proposes a condensing law: usable security information is unimodal with model size, producing U-shaped security error and an optimal finite size.
Experiments on real-world LLMs support the existence of an optimal model size for security problems.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models can share experts across layers or computational steps, pooling training information from different contexts. This can reduce local prediction error, but multi-step systems are ultimately evaluated by their final outputs. We study when these local gains survive composition. In specified linear regression models, we derive exact sharing and merging criteria by balancing variance savings against bias from sharing across roles with different target behavior. Under a common fixed linear propagation map, we characterize expected squared final-output risk, retaining error directions and correlations. We construct cases where sharing lowers average local error yet increases final-output error. Within this setting, we also identify when orthogonal full pooling with isotropic noise preserves every local improvement at the final output. For general routed computations, we derive conditional end-to-end error bounds that account for distribution shifts, errors in surrounding components, and changes in expert selection. Separately, we show that correct predictions and route labels alone do not establish that individual experts implement the attributed operations. Controlled experiments realize a strict local-to-final risk reversal. In low-data symbolic settings, trained Transformers exhibit statistically supported teacher-forced one-step gains without statistically resolved free-running final-output gains. Separate intervention tests distinguish successful multi-layer actions from single-expert attribution and generalization to unseen transitions. Together, these results distinguish when sharing improves local estimation, when those gains survive to the final output, and what evidence is needed to attribute reusable operations to individual experts.
authors: Tiantong Wang, Zhiren Gong, Yixin Wang, Tiantong Wu, Wei Yang Bryan Lim
bullets: Derives exact linear-model criteria balancing variance reduction against bias from sharing experts across roles with different targets.
Characterizes final-output risk under shared linear propagation, including error directions and correlations.
Provides end-to-end bounds for routed computations that account for distribution shift, surrounding errors, and changed expert selection.

Shows through constructed cases and controlled experiments that local improvements can reverse at the final output; low-data Transformers show one-step gains without clearly improved free-running outputs.
Finds that correct predictions and routing labels alone do not prove individual experts implement the attributed operations; interventions are needed.

papers.abstract: Policy gradient methods are widely used to align large language model outputs with human preferences, but the log-likelihoods they require cannot be directly computed in Masked Diffusion Language Models (MDLMs). MDLM post-training therefore relies on a surrogate objective based on the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO), and recent work estimates a blockwise variant of this objective via Monte Carlo methods to support blockwise generation. However, existing estimation schemes randomly sample the block index, so they may evaluate the same block more than once and leave some blocks unevaluated. This introduces variance arising from block selection into the estimates. In this work, we propose a full-block estimator that evaluates every block exactly once and averages the results. We theoretically show that the proposed estimator remains unbiased while eliminating the between-group variance arising from block selection, thereby achieving lower variance than the baseline for the same sample size. In experiments on five benchmarks spanning mathematics, planning, and coding, our method achieves the highest accuracy on four benchmarks and outperforms the random block sampling baseline by an average of 12.79 points.
authors: Yunzhen He, Hiroaki Yamagiwa, Hidetoshi Shimodaira
bullets: MDLMs lack directly computable log-likelihoods, so post-training uses an ELBO-based surrogate objective.
Random block sampling can repeat blocks and omit others, adding variance from block selection.
The proposed estimator evaluates and averages all blocks once per sample.
It is theoretically unbiased and removes between-group variance, yielding lower variance at the same sample size.
Across five math, planning, and coding benchmarks, it had the highest accuracy on four and exceeded random sampling by an average of 12.79 points.

papers.abstract: Agentic forecasting systems based on large language models (LLMs) are now competitive with expert human forecasters, but these systems still suffer from a critical limitation: the inability to produce forecasts that are logically consistent. For example, forecasts for related events often fail to satisfy the axioms of probability, which in turn implies that related forecasts cannot simultaneously be correct and undermines their utility for decision makers. Enforcing consistency is not trivial -- naive approaches (e.g., projection onto the set of consistent forecasts) can degrade accuracy. We argue that the key to overcoming the apparent tradeoff between consistency and accuracy lies in the reasoning which supports each forecast. We finetune a supervisory language model that leverages this reasoning to jointly reconcile inconsistencies while improving the accuracy of related forecasts. On ForecastBench, our method improves the Brier score of a retrieval-augmented GPT-5.1 forecaster by 9.3% while reducing measures of structural inconsistency by 82-90%. We interrogate our method via a comprehensive series of baselines and ablations, and find that no alternative method matches our gains in consistency and accuracy simultaneously.
authors: Kate Yuan, Rohan Alur, Manish Raghavan, Devavrat Shah
bullets: LLM forecasters can produce mutually inconsistent predictions for related events, limiting their usefulness for decisions.
Naively enforcing probability consistency may reduce forecast accuracy.
The proposed method fine-tunes a supervisory model to use forecast reasoning to jointly reconcile inconsistencies and improve related predictions.
On ForecastBench, it improves the Brier score of a retrieval-augmented GPT-5.1 forecaster by 9.3% and reduces structural inconsistency by 82–90%.
Baselines and ablations indicate that alternative methods do not achieve comparable gains in both consistency and accuracy.

papers.abstract: High-level behaviors such as sycophancy and hallucination correspond to directions in a model's activation space (Chen et al., 2025). These directions, known as persona vectors, can suppress undesirable traits either at inference time, subtracting the vector during generation, or through preventative steering, adding the vector during fine-tuning, so the optimizer never needs to encode the trait in weights, then removing the vector at evaluation. Chen et al. (2025) recommend preventative steering because it preserves Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) accuracy, but validations of this recommendation have measured capability alone. We primarily evaluate results on preventative steering of sycophancy and hallucination vectors on three models, measuring three safety benchmarks alongside trait expression, coherence, and MMLU. Our findings show that preventative steering still changes refusal behavior, but by an amount that depends on the trait and does not establish that preventative persona steering is safety-neutral, and steering methods should be evaluated on several safety benchmarks.
authors: Sabrina Tang, Nikolai Vo, Carson Murillo, Chira Sukumarnpiti, Sarah Wilson
bullets: Audits preventative steering for sycophancy and hallucination across three models.
Measures trait expression, coherence, MMLU, and three safety benchmarks.
Finds refusal behavior changes, with effects varying by the steered trait.
Concludes that capability preservation alone is insufficient to validate safety.
Recommends evaluating steering methods across multiple safety benchmarks.

papers.abstract: A benchmark usually measures a language model alone with a question, and deployment rarely looks like that: answers get contested, and models give up correct ones under counter-reasoning that is itself wrong. We show that what fails there is not a shortfall of accuracy but a capability in its own right -- knowing when to hold a position and when to yield to a better one -- which we call dialectical competence. It stands on first-answer accuracy without following from it: a model can be made materially better at answering and no better at this, and training for accuracy alone can drift against it. Nor can it be bought at inference, by self-reflection or by sampling more. Taking a cue from the dialectical tradition in philosophy, in which productive opposition arises within a position rather than being imposed on it from outside, we hypothesize that this capability can be trained from opposition the model supplies itself. It states a position, generates the strongest case against that position -- its antithesis -- rules on whether the case stands, and is trained on that ruling, with no second model at training or at deployment. We call this learning through Self-Disagreement: reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards throughout, where the same check that scores an answer against its reference scores the ruling too, so no reward model, no preference data and no human annotation enter anywhere. The capability is trained rather than elicited: weak in the base model, it arrives with the reward, is not paid for out of first-answer accuracy, and holds against challengers the model never trained against, including ones stronger than itself. The opposition a model needs in order to improve, it turns out, need not come from outside it.
bullets: Introduces dialectical competence: maintaining a correct position against flawed challenges while yielding to better ones.
Argues this capability is distinct from first-answer accuracy and is not reliably obtained through self-reflection or additional sampling at inference.
Uses reinforcement learning in which the model states a position, generates an antithesis, and rules on whether it succeeds.
Employs verifiable rewards only, requiring no second model, reward model, preference data, or human annotation.
Reports that the capability emerges through training without sacrificing initial-answer accuracy and generalizes to unseen, including stronger, challengers.

papers.title: Benchmarks Don't Talk Back: Learning Through Self-Disagreement
papers.tldr: Self-Disagreement trains language models to know when to defend or revise an answer by generating and judging their own strongest counterarguments.

papers.abstract: Activation steering influences a language model's behaviour by adding a steering vector to its residual stream during generation, but it requires white-box access to modify the hidden states at every generation step. We introduce ActGCG, a modification of Greedy Coordinate Gradient which optimises a suffix to match the target activations obtained by adding a steering vector to the residual stream. We further introduce universal suffixes trained across many prompts at once, a model-translation step that rewrites the suffix into human-readable text midway through optimisation, and a soft-suffix variant to remove the discrete token space constraint. We study two behaviours: steering a model to answer in German, and anti-refusal steering for jailbreaking. For German, a discrete suffix reproduces the steering vector's behaviour almost perfectly and transfers well across prompts and models. For anti-refusal, the equivalence is weaker, succeeding under a phrase-avoidance metric but only partially under the stricter HarmBench classifier. Our results show that a steering vector's behaviour is reachable from the input, with no access to model internals at generation time, up to a loss that depends on the concept being steered.
bullets: Targets behaviors produced by adding steering vectors to a model’s residual stream.
Uses Greedy Coordinate Gradient to optimize discrete suffixes, including universal suffixes across prompts.
Adds model translation for human-readable intermediate suffixes and a soft-suffix variant beyond discrete tokens.
German-answer steering is reproduced nearly perfectly and transfers across prompts and models.
Anti-refusal steering is weaker: it succeeds on phrase avoidance but only partially under HarmBench.

papers.abstract: Ensembles of neural networks have repeatedly been shown to outperform single networks. Ensemble theory attributes this gain to the accuracy of the individual members and the diversity among them. Mixture-of-experts models already combine many experts, but a single router decides how the experts are weighted for each input. Motivated by ensemble theory, we apply ensembling to the routing step: an ensemble of routers, trained jointly with the experts, proposes the expert weights. We systematically evaluate this approach using underparameterized networks on two image-classification and two tabular-regression tasks. We analyse each experiment with a performance-diversity decomposition of the router ensemble, which, to our knowledge, has not previously been developed for routers. We report four findings. First, more routers lower the validation loss. Second, training routers to explicitly maximize expert diversity improves the mean performance on three of the four tasks. Third, explicitly maximizing router diversity has no effect on performance. Fourth, combining router weights with the arithmetic mean works better than combining them with the geometric mean. Routing benefits mildly from ensembling, but this benefit is offset by the computational cost of training additional routers.
bullets: The study replaces a single MoE router with an ensemble of jointly trained routers that proposes expert weights.
Experiments cover two image-classification and two tabular-regression tasks using underparameterized networks.
More routers reduce validation loss, while explicitly maximizing expert diversity improves mean performance on three of four tasks.
Explicitly maximizing router diversity does not improve performance; arithmetic averaging of router weights outperforms geometric averaging.
A performance–diversity decomposition is introduced to analyze router ensembles.

papers.abstract: Current evaluations of Large Language Models (LLMs) report performance at the dataset or task level, revealing what a model achieves but offering little insight into the internal processing associated with its performance. We propose a task-centric framework for characterising the model-internal processing elicited by a benchmark. It combines attention- and activation-based signals with representation-based measures to characterise benchmarks spanning a continuum from retrieval-dominant to reasoning-dominant and to surface failure modes that task-level scores conceal. We evaluate 16 LLMs across 24 diverse benchmarks and conduct targeted internal-state analyses on representative models and tasks, observing systematic differences in processing between knowledge-centric and reasoning-centric tasks. We shift evaluation from asking what score a model achieves toward characterising the processing patterns associated with that score, potentially supporting more targeted benchmark selection and more informed model choice. We open source our code at https://github.com/extraordinarylab/trace-kr.
authors: Yang Wang, Xiao Wang, Yiqi Liu, Chenghao Xiao, Eleni Vasilaki, Goran Nenadic, Chenghua Lin
bullets: Combines attention, activation, and representation-based signals to characterize benchmark-induced processing.
Evaluates 16 LLMs across 24 diverse benchmarks.
Finds systematic processing differences between knowledge-centric and reasoning-centric tasks.
Uses internal-state analyses to reveal patterns and failures beyond task-level performance.
Releases code to support targeted benchmark selection and more informed model choice.
