papers.selection_reason: Task-centric analysis of internal LLM knowledge and reasoning processing; relevant to LLM evaluation and reasoning.
papers.title: Tracing Knowledge and Reasoning in LLM
papers.tldr: A task-centric framework analyzes LLM internal processing to distinguish retrieval- from reasoning-dominant benchmarks and expose failure modes hidden by task scores.

papers.abstract: In this paper we study the behavior of transformer networks generating text over long periods of time. We show that even a three-token, single-layer attention-only transformer can fail to converge. We then study a rich class of transformers with arbitrary finite depth, layer normalization, MLPs, RoPE encodings, and an arbitrary mix of local and global layers. Every transformer in this class has a softmax temperature threshold above which its empirical cache distribution converges to a unique limit, independent of initial conditions. We show further that, while each transformer has a temperature threshold, the supremum of this set is infinite, so there is no global minimal temperature that forces all transformers to converge.
bullets: Even a three-token, single-layer attention-only transformer can fail to converge.
For a broad class—including finite-depth networks with layer normalization, MLPs, RoPE, and mixed local/global attention—sufficiently high softmax temperature ensures convergence.
Above each model’s threshold, the limiting cache distribution is unique and independent of initialization.
Although every transformer has a threshold, thresholds are unbounded across the class, so no universal temperature guarantees convergence for all models.

figures.caption: Figure 1: A stripped-down model of a transformer with NoPE, no MLPs, and an unbounded context window parameterized by historical distribution Pt.

Figure 2: A two-token example illustrating the temperature transition: x = 2p − 1 and dx/dt = tanh((a/τ)x) − x. For τ > a, the uniform state is the unique globally attracting equilibrium. For τ < a, it becomes unstable and two symmetric stable equilibria appear.

Figure 3: Phase portrait of the three-token example in Section 4, with c = 7. The unique equilibrium P̄ = (1/3, 1/3, 1/3) is a repelling focus. The teal curve is a numerically computed attracting periodic orbit of the limiting ODE. Trajectories starting inside (orange) and outside (gray) the orbit spiral toward it in a counterclockwise direction. The shaded sectors indicate the most probable next token: red for token 1, green for token 2, and blue for token 3. The trajectories represent the limiting deterministic dynamics, not individual stochastic sample paths.

papers.selection_reason: Theoretical analysis of transformer convergence in text generation, relevant to LLM architecture understanding.
papers.title: Asymptotic Behavior of Transformers
papers.tldr: The paper characterizes when transformers generating text indefinitely converge to a stable empirical cache distribution, and shows the required temperature depends on the architecture.

papers.abstract: Which context tokens drive a language model's answer? Graph-based tools such as attention rollout and attention flow answer this from a single forward pass, yet their faithfulness in decoder-only models is rarely tested against interventions. We view the layers of a decoder as a causal network whose conductances are attention weights, and read a token's influence on the answer from the resistance between them. We propose RIFT (Resistance-based Information Flow in Transformers), which scores a token by the series resistance of its path of least resistance to the answer, found exactly by a classic shortest-path dynamic program. On synthetic in-context retrieval tasks and extractive question answering over Wikipedia paragraphs, RIFT predicts the effect of replacing a token with a Spearman correlation of 0.52-0.68; predicting a single replacement, it reaches 77-96% of the agreement between two different random replacements. It needs no gradients and no extra forward passes, scoring every token of a prompt in 0.9-3.4 ms on one CPU thread, whereas the replacement experiment needs a forward pass per token. On 576 held-out prompts from four models of two families (Qwen3 and Llama 3.2), it outperforms token distance, attention rollout and attention flow in every pre-specified comparison, by 0.23 to 0.88 in mean Spearman correlation, and it is the best or tied-best of all attention-based scores we test. Aggregates that add up all routes (attention flow, effective resistance and rollout) instead mostly encode token position: as a simple proposition shows, early tokens have many more parallel routes to the answer.
bullets: Frames transformer layers as a causal network, with attention weights acting as conductances.
Scores each token using the series resistance of its path of least resistance, computed exactly via shortest-path dynamic programming.
On synthetic retrieval and extractive QA tasks, its scores correlate with replacement effects at 0.52–0.68 Spearman correlation.
Across 576 prompts from Qwen3 and Llama 3.2 models, RIFT outperforms token distance, attention rollout, and attention flow in all pre-specified comparisons.
Runs in 0.9–3.4 ms per prompt on one CPU thread; aggregate route methods often primarily reflect token position.

papers.selection_reason: Graph-based token influence attribution for decoder-only LLMs; relevant to understanding and improving LLM behavior.
papers.title: RIFT: Token Influence Follows the Path of Least Resistance
papers.tldr: RIFT estimates which prompt tokens influence a decoder-only model’s answer by finding the lowest-resistance information path through its attention graph, without gradients or extra forward passes.

papers.abstract: In continuous diffusion language models (DLMs), latents generated by the diffusion prior are mapped almost deterministically to tokens, either by a decoder or through a token embedding matrix. Unlike in image generation, where visual details can vary continuously, the diffusion prior must capture fine-grained discrete token choices in continuous space, which can make the joint latent distribution difficult to model. We argue that generative roles should instead be divided: the diffusion prior should generate high-level predictive information, while the decoder should resolve the remaining token-level choices. Based on this view, we introduce Predictive-State Flows (PSF), which partitions a sequence into blocks and associates each block with a predictive state computed solely from the preceding context. A rectified-flow prior generates the sequence of predictive states, after which a block-causal decoder generates all blocks in parallel, autoregressively only within each block. This design reduces diffusion from L token-level states to K << L predictive states and reduces token-level sequential depth to L/K. On unconditional OpenWebText generation, a 197M-parameter model with K=8 achieves a generative perplexity of 22.8 at entropy 5.16 using 0.31 TFLOPs per 1024-token document, versus 24.0 and 7.2 TFLOPs for ELF-B with 32 sampling steps. The corresponding measured operating points yield MAUVE@512 of 0.93 and 0.73, respectively. Controlled comparisons further show that content states, which additionally encode their own blocks, yield 8-16% higher generative perplexity than predictive states, and that replacing sampled predictive-state trajectories with a shared mean lowers MAUVE@512 by 0.11. These results suggest that latent design for continuous DLMs should consider not only how compactly text is represented, but also how generative roles are divided between the prior and the decoder.
bullets: Problem: Token-level diffusion latents must represent fine-grained discrete choices, making their joint distribution difficult to model.

Method: Partition sequences into blocks; a rectified-flow prior generates predictive states from preceding context, and a block-causal decoder generates blocks in parallel while decoding within each block autoregressively.
Contribution: Reduces diffusion from L token-level states to K≪L predictive states and lowers token-level sequential depth to L/K.

Result: On unconditional OpenWebText, a 197M-parameter PSF model with K=8 reaches generative perplexity 22.8 and MAUVE@512 0.93 at 0.31 TFLOPs per document, compared with ELF-B’s 24.0, 0.73, and 7.2 TFLOPs.

Scope: Results support dividing generative responsibilities between the diffusion prior and decoder; predictive states outperform content states and shared mean trajectories in controlled comparisons.

papers.selection_reason: Parallel language generation via predictive-state flows and block-causal decoding; relevant to foundation language model architecture.
papers.title: Rethinking the Roles of Diffusion and Decoding: Predictive-State Flows for Parallel Language Generation
papers.tldr: Predictive-State Flows simplify continuous diffusion language modeling by having diffusion generate context-based predictive states while a decoder resolves token choices in parallel blocks.

papers.abstract: General-purpose language models are trained mostly on English: over open models we review, at most, non-English pretraining data makes up only a 12% share. Models built for European languages give them far more, but score well below general-purpose models of the same size. A common concern is that, in small models, languages compete for capacity. We present Lara Mini base, a model trained from scratch on 6T tokens in English and 44 other languages, which together cover all 24 official languages of the European Union. As training progresses, the 44 other languages together come to outweigh English. To give these languages enough capacity at low cost, Lara Mini base uses a mixture of experts architecture with 7.2B total and 0.6B active parameters. Among open base models with up to 2B active parameters, it achieves the highest average score across standard English, multilingual, math, and code benchmarks, ahead of models trained on 4 to 6 times as many tokens. Its margin is largest on multilingual benchmarks in the languages it supports and on math benchmarks. It supports contexts of up to 128k tokens. We find that our MoE architecture reduces capacity competition between languages. For a single user on one GPU, without quantization, it generates text at least 1.8 times faster than any model with a higher average score. We release the weights of Lara Mini base under the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license. In addition, we will release T-HellaSwag, a higher-quality machine translation of the commonsense reasoning benchmark HellaSwag into 110 language variants.
authors: Andrea Fernandez Tostado Ro. Diego Andrea
bullets: Trained from scratch on 6T tokens across English and 44 other languages, covering all 24 official EU languages.
Uses 7.2B total parameters but activates only 0.6B per input to provide multilingual capacity efficiently.
Achieves the highest average benchmark score among open base models with up to 2B active parameters, with especially strong multilingual and math performance.
Supports 128k-token contexts and generates at least 1.8× faster than higher-scoring models for a single user on one GPU without quantization.
The authors also release model weights under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 and introduce T-HellaSwag translations spanning 110 language variants.

papers.abstract: We present Fikiria, a two-stage SFT+GRPO recipe for Swahili mathematical reasoning. Its reward multiplies a format gate by a weighted sum of answer accuracy and the ChrF\texttt{++} similarity of the Swahili reasoning to an in-language reference chain of thought, so that training targets the surface fidelity of the reasoning trace and not only the final answer. We train on a 2.3k-problem Swahili dataset created by translating GSM8K with GPT-4.1 and filtering with SSA-COMET. On AfriMGSM Swahili, Fikiria-AfriqueQwen-14B reaches 79.2\%. Under the same fixed prompt and strict answer-format scoring, GPT-4o reaches 68.0\%, partly because it often fails the required answer format; IrokoBench reports 78.8\% for GPT-4o using a best-per-model prompt, a figure numerically close to ours but not directly comparable. In a small human evaluation with co-author annotators, GPT-4o's outputs were preferred overall. ChrF\texttt{++} measures surface fidelity, not the validity of individual reasoning steps.
bullets: Addresses the lack of native-language Swahili mathematical reasoning training.
Uses two-stage supervised fine-tuning plus GRPO, rewarding format compliance, answer accuracy, and ChrF++ similarity to reference Swahili reasoning.
Trains on 2.3k Swahili problems translated from GSM8K and filtered with SSA-COMET.

Fikiria-AfriqueQwen-14B scores 79.2% versus 68.0% for GPT-4o under the same fixed prompt and strict scoring; the comparison is partly format-sensitive and not directly comparable to best-prompt results.
Human co-author annotators preferred GPT-4o overall, and ChrF++ does not verify the validity of individual reasoning steps.

papers.abstract: Post-training improves language-model reasoning, but how it changes the use of internal information and verbalized chain of thought (CoT) remains unclear. We study successive SFT, DPO, and RLVR checkpoints of Olmo-3-7B-Instruct on multi-digit addition, using carry values as known intermediate state. Probes recover carry information from internal activations with similar accuracy in SFT and RLVR, although manipulating this information does not reliably control model outputs. In contrast, the usefulness of verbalized reasoning differs: CoTs produced by RLVR yield higher accuracy across receiving checkpoints than those produced by SFT or DPO. We also show that carry-related statements receive higher importance scores after RLVR than matched random controls. DPO shows similar sensitivity to carry-related statements but without comparable accuracy gains. These results suggest that post-training changes the usefulness of written reasoning and sensitivity to its content in meaningful ways, although greater sensitivity does not necessarily coincide with better problem performance.
bullets: Studies successive SFT, DPO, and RLVR checkpoints of Olmo-3-7B-Instruct on multi-digit addition.
Internal probes recover carry values similarly after SFT and RLVR, but manipulating carries does not reliably control outputs.
RLVR-generated chain-of-thought produces higher accuracy across receiving checkpoints than SFT- or DPO-generated reasoning.
After RLVR, carry-related statements receive greater importance than matched random controls.
DPO increases sensitivity to carry-related statements without comparable accuracy gains, showing sensitivity and performance can diverge.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Analysis of important spans in the CoT. (a) For each span in the CoT, we cluster based on semantic similarity and show the mean importance score derived from the Thought Anchors method (Bogdan et al., 2025). We measure disruption as the percentage of correct cases where the digit in the column corresponding to the reasoning span changes. No probes are shown for finding the output digits at the answer digit token, as the answer would often be already available (up to tokenization effects). Probes are trained separately for each variable, layer, digit, and location. The results shown are averaged across digits. papers.abstract: Reasoning models achieve strong performance through long chains of thought (CoT), but often spend more tokens than needed to solve a problem. Existing ways to shorten the CoT require additional training for each model, add a fixed steering vector to the model's hidden states, or use decoding heuristics such as stopping early or banning words like "wait", which can reduce accuracy. We propose DoubtLess, a training-free decoding method in which a much smaller reasoning model steers the large one towards brevity. The small model reads the large model's CoT so far twice, once prompted to be brief (the brief thinker) and once prompted to be verbose (the verbose thinker), and the difference between its two logit vectors, scaled by a strength, is added to the large model's logits at every step of the CoT. On seven benchmarks of competition mathematics, graduate-level science and competitive programming, DoubtLess shortens the CoT of Qwen3-32B by 31% with unchanged accuracy, outperforming five inference-time baselines. We also show that DoubtLess reduces thinking tokens per turn by 20% in a self-debugging coding agent with unchanged task performance. It also generalizes to two other model families with unchanged accuracy. When combined with training-based compression, it further shortens the CoT of a model already trained for brevity. Ablations and behavioral analysis show that DoubtLess reduces repeated checking, with most token savings coming after the correct answer first appears in the CoT. Our code is available at https://github.com/leoluolol/DoubtLess.
bullets: Addresses overly long chains of thought and limitations of training-based or heuristic shortening methods.
At each reasoning step, a small model reads the current CoT in brief and verbose modes; their logit difference steers the large model toward brevity.
Shortens Qwen3-32B CoT by 31% with unchanged accuracy across seven mathematics, science, and programming benchmarks.
Reduces thinking tokens per turn by 20% in a self-debugging coding agent while preserving task performance, and generalizes across two other model families.
Analysis attributes savings mainly to reducing repeated checking after the correct answer first appears; further compression is possible when combined with brevity training.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free contrastive decoding steers large reasoning LLMs toward brevity, directly addressing LLM reasoning and decoding.
papers.title: DoubtLess: Training-Free Contrastive Decoding for Efficient Reasoning

papers.abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) have attracted growing attention for improving reasoning through interaction among multiple agents. In this work, we focus on parallel multi-agent reasoning systems, where several agents solve the same problem over multiple rounds and aggregate their outputs into a final answer. Despite their strong reasoning performance, uncertainty estimation for such systems remains underexplored: the reliability of a MAS depends not only on individual generations, but also on how agents interact and evolve across rounds. We propose SAUCE (Sequential Agent Uncertainty through Consensus Evolution), a lightweight, training-free uncertainty estimator that formulates MAS uncertainty as sequential inference over a latent system-level belief. SAUCE aggregates round-level agreement and generation-uncertainty signals through a filtering-style update. Across five backbones, five benchmarks, and two MAS protocols, SAUCE improves misclassification detection, selective prediction, and calibration over a broad set of uncertainty estimation baselines, including standard log-likelihood-based methods and MAS-specific estimators.
bullets: Targets uncertainty estimation for multi-agent systems whose reliability evolves through agent interactions and repeated rounds.
Models system uncertainty as sequential inference over a latent, system-level belief.
Combines round-level agreement with generation-uncertainty signals using a filtering-style update.
Evaluated across five backbones, five benchmarks, and two multi-agent protocols.
Improves misclassification detection, selective prediction, and calibration over established baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview. (A) Two MAS trajectories can reach the same final answer but differ greatly in reliability: a stable run whose outputs converge across rounds (top) is more trustworthy than an unstable run whose outputs oscillate (bottom). A static view that only considers the final output cannot distinguish them, motivating uncertainty estimation from interaction dynamics. (B) SAUCE models multi-round interaction as a sequence of round-level observations (Mt, Rt), where agreement is weighted by generation uncertainty, and performs a filtering-style update over a latent system-level belief. papers.title: Sequential Probabilistic Uncertainty Estimation for Parallel Multi-Agent Reasoning Systems
papers.tldr: SAUCE is a lightweight, training-free method that estimates uncertainty in parallel multi-agent reasoning by tracking consensus and generation uncertainty across rounds.

papers.abstract: Compositional generalization remains challenging when language models must combine familiar reasoning operations in unfamiliar ways. The Scenario-Based Commonsense Reasoning Evaluation (SCoRE) 2026 tests this ability on three mixed domains absent from training and requires models to identify the complete set of correct options for each question. We introduce Route-Verify-Vote (RVV), a framework for procedure-conditioned self-consistency that uses language models without parameter updates. Route uses the provided domain label to select a reasoning procedure that guides the model in representing and applying the relevant constraints. Verify prompts the model to assess each option against those constraints. Vote aggregates complete answer sets and allocates additional samples to questions with a small vote-count margin between the two most frequent sets. Samples for each question follow the same domain-specific procedure. On the official test set, voting over 16 sampled answer sets per question achieves an exact-set accuracy of 74.6%. Adaptive RVV reaches 77.3%, and combining models on selected domain routes raises accuracy to 79.4%. The final system ranked second among participating systems. These results support domain-specific reasoning procedures and answer-set disagreement as useful tools for allocating inference-time computation in mixed-domain reasoning.
bullets: Targets compositional generalization across unseen mixed domains requiring complete correct answer sets.
Uses a three-stage, parameter-free framework: Route selects a domain procedure, Verify checks each option against its constraints, and Vote aggregates sampled answer sets.
Adaptive sampling focuses additional computation on questions with close vote margins.
Achieves 74.6% exact-set accuracy with 16 samples, 77.3% adaptively, and 79.4% when combining models across selected routes.
The final system ranked second in the SCoRE 2026 evaluation.

papers.selection_reason: Procedure-conditioned self-consistency improves LLM mixed-domain reasoning without parameter updates.
papers.title: Route-Verify-Vote: Procedure-Conditioned Self-Consistency for Mixed-Domain Reasoning
papers.tldr: Route-Verify-Vote improves mixed-domain commonsense reasoning by conditioning self-consistency on domain-specific procedures and allocating extra inference to uncertain answer sets.

papers.abstract: Model architecture shapes the scaling behavior, training efficiency, and inference cost of LLMs, making it a central focus of both industry and academia. In industry, teams such as those behind DeepSeek, Qwen, and Kimi routinely introduce architectural innovations, yet public reports rarely document which ideas succeeded, which were abandoned, and why. In academia, limited compute and inconsistent baselines often restrict evaluations to small-scale, single-point comparisons, making it difficult to establish whether improvements hold at larger scales or translate into broader impact. ArchSpace addresses both gaps as a public platform for Recording, Reviewing, and Referencing Architecture Researc}: each proposal is recorded with its experiments and reasoning, reviewed by the community, and referenced by later work. To evaluate ideas before costly large-scale training, ArchSpace leverages scaling laws to predict model loss at larger scales from smaller experiments, a practice widely adopted in industry. We provide initial references that make the platform usable: Qwen3.5 and OLMo3 baselines, fitted scaling laws, and a reusable training recipe. Ideas validated through this review can in turn become new baselines, and ArchSpace thereby aims to broaden the range of ideas that shape the next generation of models.
authors: Jie Wang, Tong Zhu, JiaHao Kuang, Zhe Xu, Yunkai Chai, Dehong Zheng, Yu Cheng, Tao Ji, ZhouHan Lin, Qi Zhang, Bowen Zhou
bullets: Addresses poor documentation of successful, abandoned, and unexplained architecture choices in industry.
Helps academia overcome limited compute and inconsistent baselines that hinder large-scale evaluation.
Records proposals with experiments and reasoning, enables community review, and links validated ideas to later work.
Uses small-scale experiments and fitted scaling laws to predict loss at larger model scales.
Provides initial Qwen3.5 and OLMo3 baselines plus a reusable training recipe; its scope is an initial platform and reference set.

papers.abstract: We investigate whether and how LLMs encode goals: internal neural representations that precede and guide action, and that are flexible enough to be realized through many different execution paths. We construct a coding setting with multiple sub-tasks that allows us to evaluate goal-seeking behavior and the selection of sub-goals. In this setting, we localize an encoding of the next sub-goal in the outputs of a sparse set of attention heads. The same heads can be used to decode the LM's future actions in natural language (e.g., "I'm checking if a word is a palindrome"). We verify that this encoding is causal for next action and is plastic: transplanting it into a different environment, e.g., another programming language, triggers the same operation realized with a different sequence of tokens. The LM also sustains the encoding throughout the action's execution, which is puzzling because a transformer LM without recurrence cannot carry a state forward for more tokens than it has layers left. We propose that it does not need to. Under a non-recurrent goal-seeking (NRGS) account, the LM frequently re-reads the goal from the task specification, compares it with the progress visible in the growing context, and pursues what remains. We test the predictions of this account with targeted causal interventions.
authors: Arnab Sen Sharma, Eric Todd, Sheridan Feucht, Andy Arditi, Rohit Gandikota, Natalie Shapira, Gabriele Sarti, Constanza Fierro, Lisa Schut, David Bau
bullets: A coding setting evaluates goal seeking and sub-goal selection across multiple tasks.
A sparse set of attention heads encodes the next sub-goal and can predict future natural-language actions.
Causal interventions show this encoding guides the next action and can transfer across environments, such as programming languages.
The encoding persists during execution, despite transformers’ limited ability to carry state across layers.
Targeted interventions support a non-recurrent account in which the model repeatedly compares the specified goal with visible progress.

figures.caption: Figure 6: The progress encoding carried in goal head query dictates the selection of next operation. In the destination run with prompt (pdst : abd → b), where the first sub-task a is prefilled, the LM picks up the next sub-task in the sequence b. When the query states of the goal heads at the pivot token are replaced with corresponding states from a source run (psrc : acb → c), it transfers the source progress. This transfer causes the LM to select d, the first task in destination task-list ({a,b,d}) which hasn’t been completed in source {a,b}.

Figure 1: Goal pursuit and its non-recurrent implementation in a transformer LM. A goal such as implementing merge sort (G) decomposes into sub-goals g1, g2, g3, each realized as a sequence of tokens (left). (i) An idealized agent commits to a sub-goal gk, keeps it active while pursuing it, and moves on once it is done. (ii) A transformer LM cannot persist a state across long sequence of tokens without running out of layers. (a) The intent to pursue gk = “divide into two halves” is nonetheless pre-committed: it is already readable at the indent token, multiple tokens before its implementation. (b) Because this commitment cannot be carried forward, the LM compensates with frequent re-computation: the LM frequently re-encodes the current sub-goal gk by reading the task span, and the progress-so-far eprog from the growing context tape, and compares the two to produce the next token (the sub-sub-goal). Different levels of goal hierarchy are maintained in the same way. (c) Once the sub-goal gk is complete, the LM moves on to the next sub-goal gk+1.

Figure 5: Goal heads frequently re-read the goal from the task span. The source prompt (i) and the destination prompts (ii) have different tasks, but they share a common initial sub-tasks which can be prefilled in

Figure 3: Temporal persistence of the sub-goal encoding. Cosine similarity between a sub-goal’s goal-head encoding at the equals sign token with the encoding sampled x% through an implementation, averaged over data types and languages. As the model progresses through an implementation of a sub-goal, its encoding remain more similar to implementations of the same sub-goal across different languages (dashed teal line) than for different sub-goals in the same language (solid orange line). This shows that sub-goal encodings persist in the LM computations until it’s implementation is finished.
Figure 15: Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct: 14B vs. 32B. Each point contains scores for 253 readouts. The larger 32B model gives better readouts at all four pivots in both measurements.
Figure 36: GOALSCOPE generations for Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct compared to the same model fine-tuned on risky financial advice Turner et al. (2025); Soligo et al. (2025), across four prompts.

Figure 7: Applying GOALSCOPE beyond code generation. (a) We apply GOALSCOPE to few-shot ICL prompts and measure whether it can verbalize implicit relations of input-output pairs from few-shot examples. GOALSCOPE correctly identifies the implicit rule 80%+ of the time for certain relations such as antonym, country-capital, and person-occupation. (b) We also apply GOALSCOPE to chat settings. While readouts do not always reflect sampled generations, we find that readouts for an emergently misaligned model (Turner et al., 2025) qualitatively diverge from those of an innocent model (Figure 36b) at early token positions.

Figure 4: Goal heads mediate implementation. “Sufficiency” ablation preserves the selected heads’ access to the description of the next subgoal and blinds all the other attention heads in layers 20–63. “Necessity” ablation blinds only the selected heads by sinking their attention to the first token, while other heads operate as usual. Bars show LM’s success rate of implementing the next sub-goal with the ablation. Only 122 goal heads can sustain LM performance, but it drops sharply when 250 goal heads are blinded.

Figure 8: Illustrative example of the prompt. N subgoals are specified in natural language. For the target sub-goal gk, the LM’s generated code is prefilled up to a pivot point. On the same figure, we identify the pivot points where we probe for the upcoming operation with background highlights

Figure 9: Locating the goal heads. Left: source and destination prompts request different predicates in different programming languages. A separate target prompt requests the source predicate in the destination language. The two destination-language implementations share a common prefix and differ in the next token. We patch source head contributions into the destination using the maskweighted intervention in Equation (2), and jointly train the masks to promote the target continuation. Right: the selected 122 heads in Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct selected with a threshold τ = 0.9 over the trained masks.
Figure 32: GoalScope readouts while Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct implements the Gale-Shapley stable marriage algorithm.

Figure 10: The full prompts used to measure faithfulness and causality throughout this paper. We inject the goal head encoding at the last token position (highlighted) and keep performing the same injection at every generation steps.
Figure 11: Prompt for the LLM judge to evaluate faithfulness. Note that we ask the judge to make a subjective decision of whether the readout is a non-trivial part of the LLM’s upcoming operation gk.

Figure 12: Comparison of readout sources. We compare the readout quality of the encoding captured with the goal-heads vs full attention outputs and residual states. Across different encoding sources, we use the same hparams: additive_norm steering with α = 0.1, at layers 35–45. Each bar shows the average readout score over the four pre-implementation pivots, across the same 253 specifications (out of total 1012 points). Goal heads consistently give better readout performance compared to the larger representations.

Figure 25: Query transfer setup for multi-token generation. (i) From the source run (here with prompt psrc : acb→ c), we cache the query states of the goal heads at the pivot. (ii) In the clean run with the destination prompt pdst : abd→ b, the goal heads concentrate their attention (gaze) on the next sub-goal’s description in the task span. The bar-plot on the right shows the mean value-weighted attention score over the tokens of a task-span. (iii) At the eq pivot, transferring the query states from the source run transfers the source progress (a and b are done), redirecting the goal heads to change their gaze to d’s description, and the readout at pivot also changes accordingly. (iv) For multi-token generation we restrict the goal heads’ attention to the task-span that received most gaze after the query transfer. The non-goal attention heads see the full context as usual.

papers.title: Goal Encoding in LLMs
papers.tldr: LLMs encode and causally use flexible next-sub-goals, re-reading task specifications to sustain goal-directed behavior without recurrent state.

papers.abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning, especially in heterogeneous and continual-learning settings in which substantial forgetting occurs. In general, it suffers from an undesirable learning-forgetting trade-off across diverse fine-tuning settings. We identify a potential contributor: LoRA adapters, especially high-rank ones, frequently fail to realize the available capacity afforded by the configured rank. Specifically, we find that standard LoRA updates have effective rank far below their configured rank, limiting how broadly the update energy is distributed. Therefore, we propose training mechanisms that optimize the original objective while maximizing adapter effective rank. Our main method adds a simple, stable, differentiable, and SVD-free R\'enyi-2 effective-rank regularizer to the language-modeling loss. We also connect capacity maximization to norm-bounded updates. In mixed-domain rank sweeps on three models evaluated with multiple random seeds, a penalty weight of $\lambda=0.01$ lowers mean Wiki perplexity at every tested rank of at least $16$ relative to unpenalized LoRA. Mean training perplexity improves or increases by at most $0.02$ in all but one model-rank comparison. Single-task and scheduling experiments further show that the balance between learning and retention depends on the configuration. We also observe that several LoRA variants in the literature also suffer from the identified capacity issue, and our approach provides a complementary axis of improvement to LoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning. These results suggest that effective rank is not only a post-hoc diagnostic of adapter quality, but a trainable objective for improving the learning-forgetting frontier. Our code is available at https://github.com/tomohiro-sawada/lora-capacity-utilization
bullets: Standard LoRA updates often have effective rank well below the configured rank, especially at higher ranks.
The proposed method adds a stable, differentiable, SVD-free Rényi-2 effective-rank regularizer to the language-modeling objective.
Across mixed-domain rank sweeps on three models, a penalty of λ=0.01 reduced mean Wiki perplexity at every tested rank of at least 16 versus unpenalized LoRA.
Training perplexity generally improved or changed by at most 0.02, with one model–rank exception.
The balance between learning and retention remains configuration-dependent; effective rank is proposed as a trainable objective, not only a diagnostic.

papers.abstract: State space models (SSMs) are an emerging alternative to Transformers. SSMs offer linear-time inference and parallel training, but most implementations make the parallel scan efficient by making the recurrence diagonal: each channel of the hidden state is multiplied by an input-dependent real or complex number. These numbers commute, so the state records which inputs occurred but not their order. We formalize this with representation theory, which explains and fixes the state-tracking failures previously reported for SSMs. The state update defines a linear representation of the monoid of input sequences, and we show that an SSM tracks a group at every sequence length exactly when that group is a quotient of the group generated by its transition matrices. Two consequences follow. Diagonal real- and complex-valued SSMs can track only commutative groups, while the transition matrices of any SSM that can track a group must split into independent blocks over the real, complex, and quaternion numbers. We then introduce HyperSSM, which adds quaternion channels while keeping linear-time inference and parallel training. Trained only on final answers, HyperSSM solves the group tasks of recent state-tracking benchmarks exactly with at most five state numbers. This includes $S_5$ with 32 generators, where previous SSMs are at chance, and HyperSSM generalizes to sequences 25 times longer than those seen in training. Because the theory says what the transitions must encode, the learned weights of the linear recurrence can be interpreted directly. We demonstrate this by recovering the calibration of a real gyroscope, the rotations of imperfect qubit gates and the geometry of protein backbones.
authors: Anif N. Shikder, Ramit Dey, Jan Minac, Lyle E. Muller
bullets: Diagonal real- or complex-valued SSM transitions commute, so they cannot represent noncommutative group structure or reliably track input order.
The paper characterizes exactly when an SSM tracks a group: the group must be a quotient of the group generated by its transition matrices.
Any SSM capable of tracking a group must decompose into real, complex, and quaternionic blocks; this motivates HyperSSM.

HyperSSM solves group-tracking benchmark tasks exactly using at most five state numbers, including an $S_5$ task where prior SSMs perform at chance, and extrapolates to sequences 25× longer than training.
The learned recurrence weights are directly interpretable and recover structure from gyroscope calibration, imperfect qubit-gate rotations, and protein-backbone geometry.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a quaternion state-space model with representation-theoretic analysis of recurrent memory, directly relevant to LLM architectures and recurrent memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Symmetry in Time: A Representation Theory of Linear Recurrent Memory
papers.tldr: A representation-theoretic analysis shows why diagonal SSMs lose sequence order, and HyperSSM fixes this with quaternion-valued state channels while preserving efficient inference and training.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can supply autonomous systems with plans, predictions, and judgments, but these contributions are sometimes wrong. This review asks how a system can maximize an LLM's utility while managing its fallibility. Our answer is to adapt the system's reliance on the LLM as evidence about the LLM's performance accumulates. Systems built from imperfect components, such as noisy sensors and faulty software, have long worked in this way, and the classical methods they use can be applied to LLM-based systems as well. A system can change its reliance on an LLM in several ways, depending on the LLM's role and on the other components in the system. Each change needs an estimate of the LLM's reliability, and the LLM's role and the kind of contribution it makes determine what to estimate. Classical methods from decision theory, estimation, and online learning then turn these estimates into reliance decisions. These decisions can reduce how often LLM errors affect the system. However, some errors matter even when they are rare. An independently verified mechanism can prevent such errors from being executed. Without one, adapting reliance using reliability estimates can still keep their risk within a bound. Studies on adapting reliance on LLMs are emerging but limited, and the reviewed comparisons suggest that adapting reliance can improve system performance.
authors: Ekta U. Samani, Christopher G. Atkeson
bullets: Reviews how autonomous systems can use LLM plans, predictions, and judgments despite their fallibility.
Advocates adapting LLM reliance based on observed performance and the LLM’s role in the system.
Applies classical decision-theoretic, estimation, and online-learning methods to convert reliability estimates into reliance decisions.
Independent verification is needed to prevent rare but consequential errors; otherwise, adaptive reliance can help bound their risk.
Emerging studies suggest adaptive reliance can improve system performance, though evidence remains limited.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Blocksworld example used throughout this review, adapted from [12]. For one Blocksworld problem, the LLM generates a plan and a validator checks it. The robot executes an accepted plan as shown in (a). Feedback generated from this can be used in three different ways: (b) adding invalid-plan feedback to the prompt, (c) fine-tuning the model on outcomes from many such problems, and (d) using validator results and execution outcomes as evidence to change how the surrounding system relies on the LLM.

papers.selection_reason: Reviews methods for managing LLM fallibility in autonomous systems, focusing on adapting reliance based on reliability estimates rather than a specific technical implementation.
papers.title: Maximizing LLM Utility While Managing LLM Fallibility
papers.tldr: Systems can improve LLM-based performance by adapting how much they rely on an LLM as evidence of its reliability accumulates, while independently preventing or bounding high-impact errors.

papers.abstract: Post-training of large language models typically combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with preference-based fine-tuning such as Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). Human-annotated and synthetically generated preference data differ substantially in per-sample cost, but prior work typically holds sample count fixed when comparing the two. In this work, we explicitly study the interplay between cost and performance by comparing the effect of post-training with human and synthetic preference data under a fixed, dollar-matched annotation budget. We train and evaluate multiple base model families across helpfulness and summarization tasks. We find that synthetic data is far more cost-efficient at low-to-moderate budgets, achieving high win rates with as little as \$200--\$400. On helpfulness, human data closes the gap only at budgets roughly two orders of magnitude larger; on summarization, it does not close the gap at any tested budget. We also find that human-annotated data varies in reliability: one widely used human preference source substantially underperforms another, and the gap persists even after standard remedies such as domain restriction and deduplication.
authors: Shourik Banerjee, Ethan Mendes, Mohit Raghavendra, Wei Xu, Alan Ritter
bullets: Compares human-annotated and synthetic preference data using dollar-matched, rather than sample-matched, budgets.
Evaluates multiple base model families on helpfulness and summarization after SFT and preference fine-tuning.
Synthetic data achieves strong win rates at low-to-moderate budgets, including roughly $200–$400.
On helpfulness, human data catches up only at budgets about two orders of magnitude larger; on summarization, it does not catch up within tested budgets.
Human preference sources differ substantially in reliability, and the gap remains after domain restriction and deduplication.

papers.title: Human or Synthetic? What a Fixed Budget Buys for Post-Training
papers.tldr: Under equal annotation budgets, synthetic preference data is generally much more cost-effective than human data for post-training LLMs, especially on summarization.

papers.abstract: How does data shape language model (LM) behavior throughout pretraining? We investigate this question through a case study on entity comparison, e.g., Between France and Brazil, which country is larger?, across nine comparison tasks spanning five entity types. We begin with controlled experiments in which we train small LMs (163M parameters) on mixtures of natural text from pretraining corpora and synthetic task data. Our analysis identifies three distinct phases of learning: (1) an early phase where the LM selects entities by frequency, (2) a middle phase where the LM selects entities by position in the prompt (first vs. last mentioned entity), and (3) a late phase where the LM selects the entity that is the correct answer. We show that the emergence of these three phases is causally determined by statistical properties of the training data. With small amounts of task-specific synthetic data, we observe only the first two phases and the model fails to learn the task; with large amounts, the model jumps directly from the frequency-based heuristic to solving the task correctly. Moreover, changing the entity frequency distribution from a naturally occurring Zipfian distribution (a small number of entities are very common and the vast majority are rare) to a uniform one weakens the frequency phase and speeds up learning of the task. Lastly, we show that the three phases of training dynamics from our controlled experiments appear in the open source model OLMo-2 32B. Together, our findings demonstrate that properties of pretraining data are causal drivers of heuristic learning and show that small-scale synthetic experiments can predict training dynamics at larger scales.
authors: Yik Siu Chan, Jing Huang, Yanai Elazar, Atticus Geiger
bullets: Across nine comparison tasks and five entity types, models exhibit three learning phases: frequency-based selection, prompt-position selection, then correct answers.
Small amounts of synthetic task data produce only the first two phases and fail to yield task learning; larger amounts skip the positional phase and enable correct solving.
Replacing naturally Zipfian entity frequencies with a uniform distribution weakens frequency-based behavior and accelerates learning.
The same three-phase dynamics appear in the open-source OLMo-2 32B model, suggesting controlled small-scale experiments can predict larger-scale behavior.

The three-phase structure appears in both the small controlled setting and the large-scale natural text pretraining setting of OLMo-2 models, up to 32B parameters.

papers.selection_reason: Demonstrates how pretraining data statistics causally produce heuristic-then-correct phases in LM entity comparison, informing LLM training dynamics.
papers.title: Pretraining Data Statistics Shape the Phases of Learning Entity Comparison in Language Models
papers.tldr: Pretraining data statistics causally shape how language models progress from frequency and positional heuristics to correctly solving entity-comparison tasks.

papers.abstract: During the supervised learning phase, autoregressive language models are typically trained by minimizing the negative log-likelihood of the training data, which decomposes as a sum of token-level cross-entropies via teacher forcing. This objective is simple and efficient but potentially suffers from so-called exposure bias: a mismatch between the way the model is trained and the way it is used at inference time. Can we instead design sequence-level loss functions that incorporate inference-time decoding procedures, such as greedy decoding or autoregressive sampling? We show that two natural attempts lead to loss functions that are fundamentally flawed: unbounded below. We further show that these two flawed loss functions are intimately connected: using autoregressive Gumbel tricks, the sampling based loss is the expected greedy loss under Gumbel perturbations. Since the pathology stems from the dependence of the decoded sequence on the model parameters, we analyze the update direction obtained by applying a stop gradient on the sampling procedure, leading to a moment matching direction. While it is not the gradient of any loss function, we prove that it defines a valid descent direction in function space for the autoregressive negative log-likelihood. Despite these theoretical insights, the moment matching direction suffers from high variance. We conclude that teacher forcing may well be ``all you need'' for supervised learning of autoregressive models.
authors: Mathieu Blondel, Micha\"el E. Sander, Germain Vivier-Ardisson, Tianlin Liu, Vincent Roulet
bullets: Teacher forcing trains autoregressive models with token-level negative log-likelihood but may introduce exposure bias.
Two natural sequence-level losses based on greedy decoding and autoregressive sampling are unbounded below.
Using autoregressive Gumbel perturbations, the sampling loss is shown to equal the expected greedy loss.
Stop-gradient analysis yields a moment-matching update that is a valid function-space descent direction for autoregressive likelihood, but has high variance.
The results suggest that teacher forcing may remain preferable for supervised training.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes sequence-level training objectives for autoregressive LLMs and shows teacher forcing may be optimal; relevant to LLM training research.
papers.title: On the Difficulty of Sequence-Level Supervised Learning for Autoregressive Language Models
papers.tldr: Sequence-level objectives that account for inference-time decoding can be mathematically ill-behaved or high-variance, supporting teacher forcing as a robust supervised-learning approach.

papers.abstract: Advances in large language models (LLMs) are rapidly transforming formal theorem proving. Yet further progress remains constrained by the lack of a transparent and effective data recipe for systematically improving theorem-proving models. In this work, we argue that effective agentic provers require strong mathematical skill priors to ground theorem proving and agentic trajectories to enable long-horizon, interactive proof construction. To this end, we synthesize an agent-native 33.7B-token mid-training corpus covering decomposition, search, self-verification, and revision, together with verifier-grounded agentic trajectories. We further introduce the daVinci-Prover harness, which enables models to construct proofs and interact with a Lean verifier in an isolated workspace, and use it to collect approximately 36K high-quality agent trajectories for supervised fine-tuning. Our mid-training recipe yields an average improvement of 13.7 points over the matched Qwen3-8B SFT-only baseline across MiniF2F, FATE-M, and ProofNet. When applied to the Qwen3.5 series, our approach also yields strong performance across theorem-proving benchmarks and achieves near-saturating MiniF2F performance with memory compaction. The results highlight agent-native mid-training as an effective foundation for developing stronger interactive theorem-proving agents.
authors: Wenhong Zhu, Xuefeng Li, Jiashuo Zhang, Yu Chen, Tiantian Mi, Qipeng Guo, Pengfei Liu
bullets: Addresses the lack of a transparent, systematic data recipe for advancing theorem-proving models.
Synthesizes a 33.7B-token corpus covering decomposition, search, self-verification, and revision.
Introduces a Lean-interacting harness and collects about 36K high-quality agent trajectories for supervised fine-tuning.
Improves over a matched Qwen3-8B SFT-only baseline by an average of 13.7 points across MiniF2F, FATE-M, and ProofNet.
Also achieves strong benchmark performance on Qwen3.5 models, including near-saturating MiniF2F performance with memory compaction.

papers.abstract: Transferring LLMs into System One decision models typically replaces the language modeling head with a decision head while retaining the full backbone, making every decision pay for all layers. Yet it remains unclear how much depth such decisions require. We find that decision information is concentrated in intermediate layers, with early layers building essential features and the final six layers removable without loss, while independently trained smaller models largely mimic the full model rather than developing specialized decision capabilities. These findings suggest that efficiency requires not simply smaller backbones, but shared computation across different depths. Building on this, we propose \method{}, which jointly trains a full model with prefix sub-models that share its final layers and decision head through self-distillation. A lightweight gate reads the hidden state at each exit to determine whether additional computation is needed, allowing one model to operate at multiple layers. Across seven decision benchmarks, our approach matches or outperforms independently trained models at every depth, while achieving better accuracy-efficiency trade-offs through adaptive computation.
bullets: Decision information is concentrated in intermediate layers; the final six layers can be removed without accuracy loss.
Independently trained smaller models mostly mimic the full model instead of learning specialized decision representations.
The proposed method jointly trains a full model and prefix sub-models that share later layers and a decision head via self-distillation.
A lightweight gate chooses whether each input needs additional layers, enabling multi-depth inference in one model.
Across seven decision benchmarks, the method matches or outperforms independent models at every depth with improved accuracy-efficiency trade-offs.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of NESTONE. (a) Nested training with self-distillation. Prefix exits share the full model’s weights and final block. The full model learns from the gold option y, while each sub-model learns from both y and the full model’s distribution. (b) Adaptive inference with stop gates. The model runs layer by layer, with a lightweight gate evaluating the hidden state at each intermediate exit. If ge ≥ τ , it runs the final block and returns a decision; otherwise, it continues from the saved states without recomputation.

papers.selection_reason: Presents adaptive-depth computation and shared sub-models to reduce LLM inference cost.
papers.title: From Large Language Models to Efficient System One Models via Adaptive Computation
papers.tldr: Adaptive depth with shared computation lets one decision model match or exceed separately trained smaller models while using only as much computation as needed.

papers.abstract: Natural Language Inference models can be sensitive to localized lexical changes. We introduce Shared Multiscale Input-Reference Conditioning (SMIC), which constructs a single input-dependent multiscale reference and reuses it across Transformer layers. Each layer applies its own multiscale transformation to the shared reference and injects the resulting conditioning feature before the attention update. We instantiate SMIC in a token--context Transformer (TCT) and conduct from-scratch comparisons against decoder-based and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) baselines across all three ANLI rounds. TCT-SMIC attains the highest observed ten-seed mean accuracy on all three ANLI rounds. The ablations further support the contribution of SMIC. We evaluate a real-valued Llama-style plug-in and extend deletion/insertion diagnostics to pretrained ModernBERT encoder and Llama decoder models with and without SMIC. Across the evaluated perturbation protocols, TCT-SMIC exhibits comparatively low pooled-attention redistribution and smaller signed accuracy changes. We further establish a finite-sample bound on average subset-mass redistribution in terms of the mean Jensen--Shannon divergence between the restricted and renormalized attention distributions.
bullets: Addresses sensitivity of Natural Language Inference models to localized lexical perturbations.
Builds one input-dependent multiscale reference, transforms it per layer, and injects the result before attention updates.
Implemented in a token–context Transformer (TCT) and compared with decoder-based and MLP baselines on all three ANLI rounds.
TCT-SMIC achieved the highest observed ten-seed mean accuracy across all ANLI rounds; ablations support SMIC’s contribution.
Perturbation diagnostics found comparatively low pooled-attention redistribution and smaller signed accuracy changes; a finite-sample redistribution bound is also derived.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a new conditioning mechanism (Shared Multiscale Input-Reference Conditioning) for transformer layers to improve robustness in NLI tasks.
papers.title: SMIC: Shared Multiscale Input-Reference Conditioning across Transformer Layers for Natural Language Inference
papers.tldr: SMIC improves NLI robustness to localized lexical changes by sharing an input-dependent multiscale reference across Transformer layers.

papers.abstract: Looped Transformers increase effective depth by repeatedly applying a shared block, offering a parameter-efficient approach to language modeling. However, most existing works directly reuse each loop's output as the next's input, which can lead to hidden-state scale growth and perturbation amplification as recurrence deepens. We propose Rectified Looped Transformer (RLT), which redesigns feedback between loops using an interpolation schedule inspired by flow-based modeling. At each loop, RLT forms the next input by linearly interpolating between the current state and its prediction. Such interpolation distributes state changes across loops, encouraging a smoother trajectory from the initial input to the final output. Theoretical analysis proves that, under appropriate assumptions, RLT keeps state magnitudes uniformly bounded across loops and reduces the worst-case perturbation amplification. We evaluate RLT on language modeling corpora and downstream benchmarks. At matched training and inference depths, RLT consistently achieves lower perplexity than a standard looped Transformer, while exhibiting greater robustness to input perturbations and variance in inference depth. Consistent with the theoretical results, latent trajectory analysis shows that RLT maintains more stable hidden-state norms across loops, which also facilitates extrapolation-based decoding strategies. Notably, RLT achieves these gains without requiring additional trainable parameters or extra recurrent block evaluations, thus providing a simple yet more stable feedback mechanism for looped Transformers.
authors: Musheng Li, Jiawei Zhang, Ziyuan Liu, Yuantao Gu
bullets: Looped Transformers reuse a shared block to increase effective depth, but repeated direct feedback can amplify hidden-state scales and perturbations.
RLT interpolates between the current state and its prediction at each loop, producing smoother state transitions.
Theory shows bounded state magnitudes and reduced worst-case perturbation amplification under suitable assumptions.
Experiments report lower perplexity than standard looped Transformers at matched depths, plus greater robustness to input perturbations and inference-depth variation.
Stable hidden-state trajectories support extrapolation-based decoding; the approach adds no trainable parameters or recurrent block evaluations.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a novel architectural modification (Rectified Looped Transformer) to improve stability and parameter efficiency in language modeling.

papers.tldr: Rectified Looped Transformer stabilizes repeated Transformer computation through interpolated feedback, improving language modeling performance and robustness without added parameters or computation.

papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) trains a student on next-token targets from a teacher, a frozen copy of the student that additionally receives privileged information, such as a worked solution, hidden from the student. Whether student gains reflect that information remains unclear. Taking the worked solution as privileged information, we audit four stages across three Qwen3 scales on mathematics: Source, whether the teacher can use the solution; Encoding, whether the resulting token targets are useful; Transmission, whether the student learns from the targets; and Expression, whether the student applies the learned behavior without the solution. With the solution, the teacher solves hard problems and recovers from student errors, yet the teacher does not reliably recognize errors, and its token targets do not favor correct trajectories. Repeated training makes successes within the student's reach more frequent rather than unlocking new ones, and corrections the student learns to predict are not reliably expressed in free generation. To isolate the solution's contribution, we vary its availability separately from teacher and student thinking modes. The largest gains occur when a teacher in thinking mode supervises a student trained and evaluated without an explicit thinking trace, and problem-only teachers often match or exceed privileged-solution teachers: the gain tracks the teacher's thinking mode rather than the solution, a pattern we call reasoning arbitrage. Accuracy gains alone therefore do not establish transfer of reasoning from privileged solutions: bottlenecks lie after Source, across Encoding, Transmission, and Expression. Future evaluations must measure what the solution adds to otherwise identical training.
bullets: The audit examines four stages: whether teachers use solutions, encode them into useful targets, transmit them to students, and whether students express the behavior independently.

Across three Qwen3 scales on mathematics, teachers can solve hard problems and recover from errors with solutions but do not reliably identify errors or favor correct trajectories in their token targets.
Repeated training mainly increases successes already within the student’s reach rather than unlocking new capabilities.
Learned corrections are not reliably used during free generation, revealing failures in transmission and expression.
The largest gains come from thinking-mode teachers supervising students without explicit thinking traces; problem-only teachers often match or exceed solution-privileged teachers.

papers.selection_reason: Audits self-distillation of reasoning LLMs and proposes a training-diagnostic view transferable to LLM reasoning research.
papers.title: Privileged Information Does Not Guarantee Privileged Guidance: Auditing On-Policy Self-Distillation for Reasoning Models
papers.tldr: Auditing on-policy self-distillation shows that privileged worked solutions do not reliably transfer their reasoning to students, with gains driven more by teacher thinking mode than by the solution itself.

papers.abstract: Applications built on large language models assign the model a role through its system prompt, intending to shape how it responds for their use case. We introduce a validation framework for extracting and injecting occupational role vectors, activation-level directions that capture how someone in a given occupational role would distinctively respond to a task or question. We validate these vectors through two complementary lenses, on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. The interpretability lens asks whether each vector is a stable, separable, domain-consistent representation of its role: extracted vectors are highly reproducible across repeated runs and sampling temperatures, remain separable even for very similar roles, and agree more with themselves across in-domain and out-of-domain questions than with other roles' signal. The control lens asks whether injecting a role vector during generation makes the model express the role, and sustain it over a conversation, as well as a role prompt does. On Qwen, injecting the vector alone makes the model express the intended role substantially more often than unsteered, but at best matches a role prompt; on both models, adding the vector to the prompt strengthens the role in single answers but did not slow the role's decline over 30 turns. Together, the two lenses show why both are needed: out of domain the role is expressed only subtly, yet the activations still encode it; and a vector that is stable and separable can still barely steer the model's behavior.
authors: Jose L. Sampedro Mazon, Ilmi Yoon, Nadim Saad
bullets: Introduces a framework to extract, validate, and inject activation-level vectors representing occupational roles.
Evaluates vectors in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct using interpretability and behavioral-control tests.
Vectors are reproducible, separable—even for similar roles—and more consistent with themselves across domains than with other roles.
Vector injection increases role expression, but generally does not outperform role prompts and does not prevent role weakening over 30 conversational turns.
Shows that representational stability does not necessarily imply strong behavioral steerability, motivating both validation lenses.

papers.abstract: System One models promise fast, general-purpose decision-making without lengthy token generation. However, understanding their capability spectrum and decision reliability requires more than aggregate performance on current benchmarks. Existing evaluations often provide limited insight into the breadth of model capabilities and the reliability of their decisions. We introduce SO-Arena, a benchmark characterizing the capability spectrum and decision reliability of System One models across 11 domains and five capability families. For the capability spectrum, SO-Arena offers evidence-grounded evaluation through reliable sources and manual verification of reference labels against model-visible inputs; fine-grained capability assessment through domain-specific difficulty criteria; and realistic interactive evaluation, where models iteratively execute actions in sandboxes. Reasoning-intensive tasks further enable system one-two comparison. Beyond accuracy, SO-Arena assesses decision reliability through two complementary measures: decision stability under controlled option-set changes and missing-answer recognition when no valid option is available. Evaluations across 21 models reveal that the benefits of scaling and additional reasoning vary substantially across domains. More importantly, strong overall performance does not necessarily imply reliable decision-making: the best-performing System One model ranks only seventh in reliability. Together, these findings highlight the need to characterize capability spectrum and decision reliability as complementary dimensions, providing a systematic view of the strengths and limitations of System One models.

bullets: Benchmarks 21 models across 11 domains and five capability families.

The top-performing model ranks only seventh in reliability, separating capability from decision dependability.

papers.abstract: Knowing when a large language model's (LLM's) response can be trusted is critical for its safe use. Uncertainty quantification (UQ) can help LLMs recognize if their responses may be unreliable. Existing taxonomies organize UQ methods by uncertainty source or estimation mechanism. They leave unresolved the question of where uncertainty is observed in the model's computation. The answer matters because the observation point determines whether an estimator has access to enough information to recover a given target, and how well it can recover it. Drawing on mechanistic interpretability, we define four mechanistic observation lenses: the structural lens observes component updates, the representational lens observes hidden states, the distributional lens observes token probabilities, and the semantical lens observes distributions over meanings. We relate these lenses through the residual stream and order them by the information they carry, which gives a principle for selecting UQ methods for different targets. We survey existing methods through the four lenses. Furthermore, we distinguish evaluation targets, criteria, and metrics to clarify different UQ evaluation protocols. Finally, we identify open problems and research directions to connect uncertainty estimation to the internal computation and downstream use of LLMs.
authors: Xiaoyu Liang, Virginia Ceccatelli, Aliai Eusebi, Tobias Braun, Nils Loose, Carlo Malagnino, Lorenzo Cavallaro
bullets: Motivates locating the observation point because it determines what uncertainty targets an estimator can recover.

Relates the lenses through the residual stream and orders them by the information they carry.
Surveys existing UQ methods and distinguishes evaluation targets, criteria, and metrics.
Highlights open problems linking uncertainty estimates to internal computation and downstream use.

papers.abstract: Post-training can improve rewarded behavior while weakening capabilities users still need. We study two GRPO branches from a shared supervised checkpoint in a multilingual mixture-of-experts model. The released branch gains 36.07 points on MATH but loses 19.32 F1 points on XQuAD-Indic, while XQuAD-English improves under the same scoring rule. An independently trained sibling adds Indic instruction following and language-aware shaping. It recovers the regressing Indic task scores and preserves MATH, but does not restore script compliance and trades off competition mathematics and code. In a later round, judge training is followed by a sharp extraction decline from the Indic branch; reward-free distillation from its earlier checkpoint restores most of the lost F1. A MATH score decomposition associates most of the measured gain with increased boxed-answer emission; accuracy among boxed answers changes little. These results show why benchmark scores should be read alongside the response forms they reward.

Judge training later caused a sharp extraction decline in the Indic branch; reward-free distillation from an earlier checkpoint restored most lost F1.
MATH gains were largely associated with more boxed-answer emission, while accuracy among boxed answers changed little.

papers.abstract: Backpack language models predict with a strictly linear combination of non-contextual per-word sense vectors, weighted by non-negative contextualization scores. We show that non-negativity conflates two properties: the linear readout, which carries the interpretability, and the conic combination, which merely restricts it. We relax the latter by computing the sense weights with differential attention, a difference of two softmax maps with a learned per-sense gain, so context can actively inhibit a sense; we call the result a differential Backpack. At equal parameters on WikiText-103 this cuts the Backpack's perplexity gap to a Transformer by 31%, improves over the softmax Backpack at every sense count, persists with a shrinking margin up to 350M parameters on OpenWebText, and is localized at the sense layer by ablations and controls. The learned inhibition is directly interpretable (a financial context drives the river sense of bank to -0.50), and the preserved per-sense attribution predicts counterfactual removals exactly. We tested a number of combination rules, showing the linear interface is nearly free. Making the readout nonlinear gains only 0.43 perplexity points while invalidating two thirds of the decomposition. The differential Backpack's senses are also better representations, improving zero-shot sentence similarity by up to 33%.
authors: Konstantinos Skianis, Giannis Nikolentzos, Polykarpos Meladianos, Michalis Vazirgiannis
bullets: Backpack models use interpretable linear combinations of non-contextual sense vectors, but standard non-negative weights cannot suppress irrelevant senses.
Differential attention computes signed sense weights as the difference between two softmax maps with learned per-sense gains.
On WikiText-103, the method reduces the perplexity gap to a Transformer by 31% and outperforms the softmax Backpack across sense counts.
Improvements persist up to 350M parameters on OpenWebText and are localized to the sense layer through ablations and controls.
Signed weights remain interpretable: for example, financial context inhibits the river sense of “bank,” while the model improves zero-shot sentence similarity by up to 33%.

papers.abstract: LLM-based recommendation agents can search catalogs, inspect products, ask users, and revise rejected recommendations. However, these behaviors are often governed by hand-designed workflows, while existing training methods optimize isolated components such as query rewriting or list ranking rather than the interaction policy as a whole. We present SimRec, a reinforcement learning framework that trains the full interaction policy of a tool-integrated recommendation agent. SimRec introduces two components. A task-anchored user simulator provides feedback on every recommendation: conditioned on the current task need rather than on user profile, and it can be an external LLM or the recommender itself under self-play. A task-aligned reward optimizes the whole trajectory with GRPO, crediting natural retrieval quality and valid tool use alongside the final hit, with training-only target injection to handle sparse hits over large catalogs. On ESCI and Amazon C4, SimRec improves the NDCG@100 of a Qwen3-4B agent from 32.23% to 35.42% and from 22.94% to 24.72%}, outperforming training-free agents on far larger backbones and task-aligned baselines on NDCG. Analysis shows that the trained agent verifies candidates, uses preferences, and recovers from rejected recommendations far more often than its untrained counterpart. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-REAL/SimRec .
authors: Yaxin Zhang, Xingyu Wu, Yuchen Yan, Yuqin Dai, Hong Zhao, Lixing Shen, Zhan Chen, Jian Shao, Yongliang Shen
bullets: Addresses the limitation of hand-designed workflows and component-wise training for tool-integrated recommendation agents.
Uses a task-anchored user simulator, via an external LLM or self-play, to provide feedback after each recommendation.
Optimizes complete interaction trajectories with task-aligned GRPO rewards for retrieval quality, valid tool use, and final recommendation hits.
Adds training-only target injection to mitigate sparse successful hits in large catalogs.
Improves NDCG@100 for a Qwen3-4B agent from 32.23% to 35.42% on ESCI and from 22.94% to 24.72% on Amazon C4.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become central to post-training large language models (LLMs). However, popular RL methods like GRPO incur non-negligible overhead by computing both old-policy and current-policy likelihoods to form importance sampling ratios. In this work, we propose Likelihood-Gated Policy Optimization (LGPO), which enforces a soft trust region constraint via likelihood-based gating, eliminating the need to compute old-policy likelihoods. Empirically, we show that removing the importance sampling correction term does not harm training stability, whereas removing the trust region mechanism can lead to collapse. Moreover, ratio-based clipping can fail in fully on-policy training: the importance ratio stays at 1, so the ratio-based trust region constraint never activates. Under standard training settings where GRPO is stable, LGPO achieves comparable training stability and peak performance while reducing training time by ~18% on average relative to a standard implementation that recomputes old-policy likelihoods. In fully on-policy training, where GRPO fails, LGPO remains stable, enabling more efficient and robust LLM RL post-training across training regimes.
authors: Shuibai Zhang, Junhyuck Kim, Gyeongman Kim, Jaewoong Cho
bullets: Importance-ratio computation adds overhead by requiring old- and current-policy likelihoods.
LGPO removes old-policy likelihoods and enforces a soft trust region through likelihood-based gating.
Removing importance-sampling correction does not harm stability, but removing trust-region control can cause collapse.
LGPO matches GRPO’s stability and peak performance under standard settings while reducing training time by about 18% on average.
LGPO remains stable in fully on-policy training, where ratio-based clipping cannot activate and GRPO fails.

Without a functioning trust region constraint (Nupdates = 1), training collapses and the policy diverges significantly from the reference model. papers.abstract: Small open models suit private customer-service deployments but trail frontier models in two ways: they miss what the written policy requires in a given situation, and they act inconsistently on what they know. We study whether such a model can close both gaps from its own deployment logs and their reference outcomes, without a stronger teacher model. Our starting point is a Gemma 4 12B agent that reads its domain policy from on-demand skills rather than from its system prompt. In each round, the deployed system serves a fresh batch of tasks; the base model diagnoses failed conversations and writes rules into the skills, and a rule survives only if it passes code checks, counterexample self-review, a paired retest, and a noise-calibrated validation gate. Reinforcement learning (GRPO) then trains a LoRA adapter on complete multi-turn, tool-using conversations. On the retail and airline domains of $\tau^2$-bench, without training or selecting on official tasks, the agent after two rounds improves on this starting point by 12.5 pass$^1$ points in retail and 19.5 in airline, and by 18.4 and 22.0 pass$^4$ points. It also exceeds the benchmark's reference agent, which runs the same model with the whole policy in its system prompt, by 11.8 and 8.0 pass$^1$ points and by 22.8 and 16.0 pass$^4$ points, closing most of the gap to three frontier models under the same protocol. A $2\times2$ ablation shows that the rules rescue tasks the agent never solved and carry policy knowledge that RL with the rules in context does not internalize, whereas the trained weights make solved tasks reliable.
authors: Yujia Zhang, Xinqi Ren, Shixiong Zhou, Jia Meng
bullets: Targets two gaps in small open models: missing situation-specific policy knowledge and inconsistent actions.
The agent extracts rules from deployment failures, filters them through checks and retests, then trains on complete tool-using conversations with GRPO.
After two rounds on retail and airline τ²-bench domains, it substantially improves over its starting point and surpasses the policy-in-prompt reference agent.
A 2×2 ablation suggests external rules provide new knowledge, while trained weights make already-solved tasks more reliable.
The study closes most of the gap to three frontier models under the same evaluation protocol.
