papers.abstract: We introduce the multi-head quantum neural network (QNN), a quantum module compatible with noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices that can replace transformer blocks inside pre-trained large language models (LLMs) with little loss in accuracy and with far fewer parameters than the blocks it replaces. Encoding a model's $D$ hidden neurons into a qubit register is the obstacle: amplitude encoding scales poorly in circuit depth and angle encoding in qubit count, so neither is practical at production-scale width. We instead partition the hidden space into $k$ disjoint heads, angle-encode each into an $n_q$-qubit register, process the heads in parallel, and couple them through constrained classical linear layers, the mixers. Performing surgery on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, we show that a single multi-head QNN with $145\,281$ trainable parameters ($D=2048$, $k=32$, $n_q=8$, $L=4$) can replace a contiguous span of eight transformer blocks, displacing $16.33\%$ of the model's parameters. Ablations show that, for a single replaced block, the quantum heads (circuits followed by a learned readout), and not the classical mixers alone, recover the displaced function, whereas for fused spans the mixers alone come within $1$-$3\%$ of the full module in perplexity. Whether this benefit is specific to trained, entangling quantum circuits is not established: controls that switch the entangler off (two seeds), or freeze the circuit at its initial or at uniformly random angles (one seed), beat the full module on held-out perplexity, and a parameter-matched classical multilayer perceptron remains a few percent ahead of the full module. We train classically with exact statevector simulation, then execute the quantum heads of our fusion checkpoints on a $156$-qubit IBM Heron processor, showing that NISQ-scale quantum modules can be installed in a production-scale LLM and run on hardware.
authors: Maforikan Amoussou, Borja Aizpurua, Sukhbinder Singh, Rom\'an Or\'us, Hans-Arno Jacobsen
bullets: Partitions the hidden dimension into parallel angle-encoded quantum heads coupled by constrained classical mixer layers.
A 145,281-parameter module replaced eight transformer blocks in Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, covering 16.33% of model parameters.
For one replaced block, quantum heads were important for recovering the displaced function; for fused spans, mixers alone came within 1–3% of the full module in perplexity.
Controls with disabled, frozen, or random circuits, plus a parameter-matched MLP, sometimes performed better than the full quantum module.
The quantum heads were simulated classically during training and executed on a 156-qubit IBM Heron processor.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates replacing transformer blocks in a 30B LLM with quantum modules, directly relevant to LLM architecture research.
papers.title: Multi-head Quantum Neural Networks: Replacing Transformer Blocks with NISQ Modules inside a 30-Billion-Parameter LLM
papers.tldr: A multi-head NISQ-compatible quantum module can replace transformer blocks in a 30B-parameter LLM with far fewer parameters, but its added benefit over classical alternatives remains unproven.

papers.abstract: Deep neural networks typically realize dense computation by propagating information through all intermediate channels, while many approximation methods rank and retain individual computational components. We ask whether dense neural computation can instead be represented exactly as an expectation over a combinatorial state space, and approximated by evaluating only its most probable configurations. We introduce a novel probabilistic state-space framework for Transformer MLPs. The framework partitions the intermediate dimension into channel groups, defines an input-dependent distribution over binary inclusion states, and uses importance-corrected masked outputs such that the full expectation exactly recovers the dense MLP output. The key algorithmic novelty is NORDER-II, which enumerates complete joint states in decreasing probability without constructing or sorting the exponentially large state space. Truncating this ordering yields an anytime approximation governed by cumulative probability mass and a state budget. On Llama-3.2-1B and Gemma-2-2B, NORDER-II at a state budget of B=2048 achieves 92.4% and 93.8% MLP-output approximation accuracy, compared with 76.9% and 79.8% for Channel Top-k. When the first, middle, and last MLP layers are approximated jointly, WikiText-2 perplexity remains within 0.06% and 0.54% of dense inference. Relative to expected-count Grouped Top-k, NORDER-II yields 82.6% to 126.4% relative accuracy gains with only 0.18% to 0.19% additional local analytic FLOPs. These results establish the significance of joint-state structure beyond atomic salience and point to a new paradigm for neural computation: dense layers can be viewed as structured probabilistic inference over combinatorial computational states. This framework opens a path toward adaptive, probability-mass-controlled computation in pretrained neural networks.
authors: Victor O. K. Li, Yang Han, Jacqueline C. K. Lam
bullets: Partitions MLP channels into groups and defines input-dependent binary inclusion states with importance-corrected outputs.
NORDER-II enumerates complete joint states in decreasing probability without materializing the exponential state space.
At budget B=2048, it achieves 92.4% and 93.8% MLP-output accuracy on Llama-3.2-1B and Gemma-2-2B, outperforming Channel Top-k.
Joint approximation of selected MLP layers keeps WikiText-2 perplexity within 0.06% and 0.54% of dense inference.
Results support probability-mass-controlled, adaptive computation based on joint-state structure rather than individual channel salience.

papers.abstract: Large language models trained with Reinforcement Learning (RL) with verifiable rewards exhibit strong reasoning ability and broad generalization, whereas models trained with Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) are often viewed as more prone to memorization and limited transfer. This paper rethinks this distinction through the lens of SFT training data on widely used Qwen2.5 and Qwen3 series models. First, we study the role of data source and show that it is critical: a carefully mixed SFT dataset substantially outperforms data generated solely by a larger model. Second, we study the role of data scale and show that matching the number of correct rollouts between SFT and RL greatly improves SFT generalization, while matching the total rollout budget enables SFT to generalize as well as RL. Combining these two factors further enables SFT to generalize even better than RL. Third, by using LLM annotations to characterize the solution methods in training rollouts, we show that larger datasets cover more tail methods and that these tail methods provide generalizable reasoning signals. Finally, we support these empirical findings theoretically by analyzing the training dynamics of shallow transformers under both RL and SFT.
authors: Yunlong Hou, Fengzhuo Zhang, Yuan Cheng, Jiachun Pan, Xingyao Li, Zhuoran Yang
bullets: SFT data source is critical: a carefully mixed dataset outperforms data generated solely by a larger model.
Matching correct-rollout counts substantially improves SFT generalization; matching total rollout budgets can make SFT perform as well as RL.
Combining data quality and scale enables SFT to generalize beyond RL in the studied settings.
Larger datasets cover more rare (“tail”) solution methods, which provide generalizable reasoning signals.
Experiments use Qwen2.5 and Qwen3 models, with theoretical analysis of shallow-transformer training dynamics.

papers.abstract: Morphology-aware tokenizers are expected to help morphologically rich languages, and their reported gains over byte-pair encoding (BPE) are usually credited to their linguistic units. A comparison with BPE cannot support this attribution, since such a tokenizer also segments text more finely (granularity) and, on token-level tasks, changes how much the sub-token readout matters. We separate both factors from the effect of grouping words by their roots (root assignment) in Amharic, a Semitic language whose Ge'ez abugida hides consonantal roots inside syllabic glyphs, with Latin-script Hausa as an orthographic contrast. Our design combines a lossless root-and-pattern tokenizer with controls that change one factor at a time, in two independent implementations. In both, real root assignment improves Amharic named-entity recognition over scrambled roots (+4.9 and +4.7 F1), and root-frequency structure explains little of this gain. In small from-scratch models, the readout choice moves F1 by up to 13.4 points and reverses the sign of every comparison of the root-and-pattern arms with BPE, whereas in two pretrained encoders it moves F1 by less than one point. The granularity effect changes sign across languages and implementations. We recommend decomposing tokenizer effects, and reporting the readout, before a gain is attributed to linguistic structure.
authors: Abdul Rehman Antall, Baidya Nath Saha
bullets: The study compares morphology-aware tokenization with controlled alternatives in Amharic and Hausa.
Real root assignment improves Amharic named-entity recognition over scrambled roots, while root-frequency structure explains little of the gain.
Word-level readout has a major impact in small from-scratch models, changing F1 by up to 13.4 points and reversing comparisons with BPE.
Readout effects are much smaller in pretrained encoders, and granularity effects vary by language and implementation.
The authors recommend reporting readout choices and isolating tokenizer factors in future evaluations.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is now a standard stage of language model post-training, and the compute devoted to it is growing rapidly. While it has been shown to improve capabilities, particularly for tasks with verifiable rewards, it can also change behaviours and internal properties that the reward does not explicitly target. We present a formalism to describe the evolution of "traits" during RL post-training and, in doing so, recover the Price equation from evolutionary biology. We use this to develop a mathematical model for what we call "trait hitchhiking": the amplification or suppression of non-targeted traits as training redistributes probability across completions. We evaluate this Price update expression on language models trained with GRPO and show that the Price estimates closely track the sampled trait dynamics. These results identify trait hitchhiking as a mechanism by which RL post-training can silently amplify undesirable traits.
authors: Adil Soubki, Elizabeth S. Z. Tan, Miles Cranmer
bullets: Motivation: RL improves rewarded capabilities but may silently alter non-targeted behaviors and internal properties.
Method: A trait-evolution formalism based on the Price equation models how probability redistribution across completions changes traits.
Evaluation: The authors test the resulting Price update on language models trained with GRPO.
Result: Price-equation estimates closely track the observed dynamics of sampled traits.
Implication: Trait hitchhiking may amplify undesirable traits even when they are not directly rewarded.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Trait hitchhiking follows the same law in evolution and in RL. Left: long tails are correlated with other traits that make a widowbird ‘fit’, although long tails themselves do not lead to increased fitness of a widowbird. Right: RL leads to an increased probability for outputs that achieve a high reward. Behaviours or traits that appear consistently in highly rewarded outputs will thus also gain a greater prevalence, even though the reward function does not necessarily reward these traits. The change in the average trait exhibited by the model is the covariance of reinforcement (specifically ω from Definition 3, which defines how the probability of an input-output pair changes after a training step), and •, the trait.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes and models 'trait hitchhiking' during LLM post-training using the Price equation. This provides a formal framework for understanding how RL post-training amplifies non-targeted traits in language models.
papers.title: Trait Hitchhiking in LLM Post-Training
papers.tldr: RL post-training can unintentionally amplify or suppress behaviors unrelated to its reward, a phenomenon formalized as “trait hitchhiking.”

papers.abstract: Large language models hold promise for delivering safe, scientifically grounded, and personalized exercise guidance at scale, yet the sports-and-health domain still lacks curated training corpora and rigorous evaluation benchmarks. Keepace (Keepace.ai) is a domain-specialized LLM built on Qwen3.5-27B through post-training, currently optimized for Chinese-language exercise guidance across three tasks: workout plan generation, sports-and-health knowledge QA, and personal sports data analysis. In internal rubric-based evaluations designed with domain experts, Keepace outperforms its base model and larger general-purpose baselines, with the most pronounced improvements in exercise safety, boundary compliance, structured output completeness, and scientific accuracy. This report summarizes the current design, data pipeline, safety-first evaluation framework, and evaluation results of Keepace.
bullets: Addresses the lack of curated sports-and-health training data and rigorous domain benchmarks.
Built on Qwen3.5-27B through post-training and optimized for Chinese exercise guidance.
Supports workout-plan generation, sports-and-health knowledge QA, and personal sports-data analysis.
Uses a domain-expert-designed, rubric-based evaluation framework emphasizing safety and scientific grounding.
Internal results report gains over its base model and larger general-purpose baselines, especially in safety and boundary compliance.

papers.abstract: Whole-prompt translation evaluates a request in different languages but does not compare which component carries a language. We introduce a paired reversal: translate the complete request component or the complete operation component into the same target language, holding behaviour, English frame and translated-span count fixed. Component identity and non-English text quantity change together. Assigning English, Chinese and Spanish independently to the two components yields nine configurations on 190 of 300 sampled harmful behaviours retained after consensus annotation and automatic gating. Refusal scored by language-model judges is the primary outcome; unsafe compliance is reported separately. On Gemini 2.5 Flash and DeepSeek, three refusal swaps are about 5.3 percentage points and the fourth is -0.5; none survives the pre-specified six-test Holm correction. In an exploratory extension, Mistral Small 4 has a 13.7-point Spanish swap (95% interval [8.4, 18.9]), which survives the twelve-test Holm sensitivity correction under the primary judge, and 12.1 points under a second judge. GPT-5.4-mini estimates are within 2 points of zero. Component assignment supplies an additional evaluation dimension. Evaluations should record component languages and translated text quantity, comparing matched behaviours at equal translated-span count while interpreting refusal and unsafe compliance separately.
bullets: Whole-prompt translation cannot isolate whether request or operation language drives safety behavior.
The study compares nine English/Chinese/Spanish assignments while matching translated-span count and holding the English frame and behavior constant.
Refusal is judged by language models, with unsafe compliance reported separately.
For Gemini 2.5 Flash and DeepSeek, observed refusal swaps do not survive Holm correction; GPT-5.4-mini effects are near zero.
An exploratory Mistral Small 4 result shows a corrected Spanish swap, supporting component-aware multilingual safety evaluation.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a multilingual safety evaluation framework that analyzes refusal behaviors through component translation and judge-labelled analysis.
papers.title: Component Translation and Judge-Labelled Refusal: A Multilingual Safety Evaluation
papers.tldr: A paired multilingual evaluation finds little robust evidence that translating different prompt components changes refusal rates, though one exploratory model shows a Spanish-specific effect.

papers.abstract: Systematic reviews synthesize biomedical evidence to inform clinical and public-health decision-making, but require domain experts to manually screen thousands of studies against detailed eligibility criteria. We investigate whether language models can assist with this bottleneck by learning from expert feedback on title and abstract screening decisions and model-generated reasoning. We introduce the Context-Aware Reasoning Framework (CARF), a human-in-the-loop framework that uses expert feedback on model-generated reasoning to adapt language models to context-dependent screening tasks. We evaluate CARF on systematic reviews of verbal autopsy and cause-of-death ascertainment methods used in global public health mortality surveillance. CARF shows competitive screening performance compared to evaluated models while retaining high sensitivity, and is more inclined to retain ambiguous, context-dependent studies for human review. Together, these findings suggest that expert-corrected reasoning is a promising supervision signal for context-dependent scientific screening, while retaining a role for human oversight.
bullets: Addresses the labor-intensive screening of thousands of studies in systematic reviews.
Uses expert feedback on model-generated reasoning to adapt models to context-dependent eligibility decisions.
Evaluated on reviews of verbal autopsy and cause-of-death ascertainment methods in global public-health mortality surveillance.
Achieves competitive screening performance with high sensitivity and tends to retain ambiguous studies for human review.
Supports expert-corrected reasoning as a promising supervision signal, not a replacement for human oversight.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the Context-Aware Reasoning Framework (CARF) applied to the title and abstract screening stage of a systematic review, illustrating four stages: blind model screening, expert correction of disagreements, construction of an expert-reasoned dataset, and reasoning-based model adaptation through LoRA fine-tuning.

Figure I2: Qualitative examples of self-corrective reasoning on the held-out test set. In each case the model’s initial reasoning leans toward inclusion, then the expert-feedback–informed reasoning revisits the evidence against the eligibility criteria and corrects the decision to exclude.
Figure I1: Screening outcomes on excluded test articles by whether the model self-corrected its reasoning.

Table 1: Include-class screening performance on the held-out test set (n=1,000; 166 eligible studies). CARF achieves the most favorable combination of recall (0.964) and F1 score (0.719) among all evaluated methods, outperforming zero-shot frontier models on both metrics. Fine-tuned results are from a single training run; zero-shot results are from a single inference pass. 95% confidence intervals for recall use the Clopper–Pearson method.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a human-in-the-loop framework (CARF) for context-aware reasoning supervision in scientific evidence screening.
papers.title: CARF: Context-Aware Reasoning Supervision for Scientific Evidence Screening
papers.tldr: CARF uses expert-corrected model reasoning to help language models screen scientific studies while preserving human oversight for ambiguous cases.

papers.abstract: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) increasingly supplies transcripts for educational NLP, but aggregate word error rate (WER) can conceal errors concentrated in learner speech, multilingual turns, and speaker attribution. We compare platform-integrated, open-weight, adapted, and commercial ASR configurations on held-out sessions of online L2 Spanish interaction between L1 English learners and their instructors and tutors. Because English is the learner's shared first language, the interactions contain Spanish-only, English-only, and code-switched turns. Evaluation combines overall WER and character error rate (CER), WER disaggregated by speaker role and language context, and diarization error rate (DER). We also adapt Whisper large-v3 and MOSS-Transcribe-Diarize with LoRA using human-corrected in-domain classroom data. MOSS adaptation produced consistent improvements across speaker roles and language contexts, whereas Whisper showed smaller gains. Domain match proved more important than data volume: Larger out-of-domain bilingual and learner corpora did not outperform the smaller classroom corpus, where learner speech and code-switching are embedded in instructor--learner interaction. The open-weight MOSS adapter was competitive with commercial Muse Voice Transcribe on WER and CER and achieved lower system-provided DER on the recordings eligible for each system. Learner, English-only, and code-switched speech remained more difficult than instructor and Spanish-only speech. The findings demonstrate the value of condition-aware evaluation and interactionally matched data for bilingual educational ASR.
bullets: Aggregate WER can hide errors tied to speaker role, language context, and diarization.
The study evaluates multiple ASR configurations on online L2 Spanish classrooms, including Spanish-only, English-only, and code-switched turns.
LoRA adaptation improved MOSS-Transcribe-Diarize consistently; Whisper gains were smaller.
Domain match mattered more than corpus size: a smaller classroom corpus outperformed larger out-of-domain bilingual and learner datasets.
Learner, English-only, and code-switched speech remained more difficult than instructor and Spanish-only speech.

papers.abstract: Medical chart abstraction transforms unstructured clinical narratives into structured variables for research and quality monitoring. We evaluated a prompting-based large language model (LLM) framework for extracting eight clinical variables from 2,416 neurointerventional acute stroke intervention reports across three hospitals. Twenty-two instruction-tuned open-source LLMs were evaluated across architectures, model sizes, and biomedical adaptations using Quick Response and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting. Non-expert staff annotations served as the cross-model reference standard. Evaluation was restricted to report-variable pairs with a valid LLaMA3.3-70B CoT prediction and a corresponding reference label. Performance measures included extraction accuracy, inference latency, and agreement with expert adjudication. Twenty discordant cases per variable underwent review by two senior physicians and four medical students. LLaMA3.3-70B achieved the highest overall accuracy (94.8%). CoT improved performance on inference-dependent variables such as site of occlusion, while Quick Response was optimal for directly stated procedural fields. Expert adjudication showed that AI predictions were more closely aligned with expert interpretations than non-expert annotations for most variables, with intracranial angioplasty remaining a challenge. Locally deployed LLMs can support scalable clinical information extraction and retrospective stroke registry curation, with expert oversight for ambiguous cases.
bullets: Evaluated 22 open-source instruction-tuned LLMs on eight variables from 2,416 acute stroke intervention reports across three hospitals.
LLaMA3.3-70B achieved the highest reported overall accuracy at 94.8%.
Chain-of-Thought prompting helped with inference-dependent variables, while Quick Response worked best for directly stated procedural fields.
AI predictions generally aligned more closely with expert adjudication than non-expert annotations.
Intracranial angioplasty remained challenging, supporting expert review for ambiguous cases.

papers.title: Large Language Models for Accurate Medical Chart Abstraction: Enabling Scalable and Secure Artificial Intelligence Deployment in Stroke

papers.abstract: We describe the QMUL_AK submission to AISA-ArabicFC 2026. The system adapts the Arabic-English ALLaM-7B-Instruct model to function calling with low-rank adaptation (LoRA). It combines an Arabic schema-aware prompt, dialect and no-call resampling, a token-weighted training objective, and deterministic validation of generated calls against the candidate tool schema. The same output supports Track A function calling and Track B reasoning-augmented calling. Training uses only the official task data. On the development set, the system achieves 0.9982 function accuracy and 0.8920 argument exact match, corresponding to overall A and B scores of 0.9345 and 0.9454. On the blind test set, the system reaches overall A and B scores of 0.9253 and 0.9380, ranking 3rd on both submission tracks and 1st of 21 teams on the Track C dialect-robustness diagnostic with a macro-averaged score of 0.9075 and the smallest dialect gap in the shared task (0.077). The results show that function selection is nearly saturated, while argument extraction remains the main source of error.
bullets: Targets Arabic-English function calling and reasoning-augmented calling under the AISA-ArabicFC 2026 task.
Combines Arabic schema-aware prompts, dialect/no-call resampling, token-weighted training, and schema-based call validation.
Uses only official task data and supports both function-calling tracks with a shared output format.
Scores 0.9253 and 0.9380 on blind-test Tracks A and B, ranking 3rd in each.
Ranks 1st of 21 teams on dialect robustness; argument extraction remains the main error source.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) produces rich training experience, yet outcome rewards reduce each attempt to a single number and leave most of this information unused. Training-time scaffolds, such as strategies or hints added to the prompt during training, offer a natural way to turn this information into guidance, but their design and adaptation are largely left to humans and tailored to specific domains. We introduce AutoScaffold, a unified AI-for-AI framework that turns a student's training experience into adaptive scaffolds, with minimal domain-specific information and no human intervention during training. A frozen teacher periodically examines this experience, diagnoses bottlenecks, and designs scaffolds in two forms: (i) strategies shared across a class of tasks and (ii) hints for individual hard tasks, adjusting the content and amount of support as the student learns. The scaffolds are removed at evaluation. We apply the same framework to ALFWorld, search-based QA, mathematical reasoning, and GPU kernel generation. When evaluated without scaffolds, students trained with AutoScaffold outperform those trained with the corresponding RL baselines in all four domains, with gains of 7.2 points in ALFWorld success and 4.0 points in average QA exact match. On GPU kernel generation, AutoScaffold increases the fraction of tasks with a correct kernel that runs faster than the PyTorch reference by up to 5.0 points. On math, our student surpasses QuestA's reported accuracy using approximately one-third as many student training steps. Analyses show that the teacher identifies a different failure in each task class and shifts its scaffolds from step-by-step workflows to targeted fixes as the student improves, and that its revised scaffolds help the student learn more than keeping the previous scaffold or using no scaffold.
authors: Zijian Zhang, Rizhen Hu, Jiangweizhi Peng, Shiyang Li, Sujay Bhatt, Sihan Zeng, Mingyi Hong
bullets: Addresses the information loss caused by reducing each RL attempt to a single outcome reward.
The teacher diagnoses student bottlenecks and creates shared strategies or task-specific hints, with support adapting as learning progresses.
Scaffolds are used only during training and removed at evaluation, requiring minimal domain-specific information and no human intervention.
Students outperform corresponding RL baselines across ALFWorld, search-based QA, mathematical reasoning, and GPU kernel generation.

Reported gains include 7.2 ALFWorld success points, 4.0 QA exact-match points, and up to 5.0 points in faster-than-PyTorch GPU kernels; math reaches higher accuracy with about one-third the training steps of QuestA.

papers.title: AutoScaffold: AI-Guided Scaffolding for Reinforcement Learning of Language Models
papers.tldr: AutoScaffold uses a frozen teacher to automatically generate and adapt training-time strategies and hints from a language model’s RL experience, improving scaffold-free performance across four domains.

papers.abstract: Policy optimization is central to language model post-training, yet principled guidance remains limited. We revisit its theoretical foundations to identify algorithms that learn near-optimal policies using total samples and gradient steps governed by the base model's response coverage, a measure of how readily it generates optimal responses. We call such algorithms coverage-preserving. This guarantee captures the goal of amplifying capabilities accessible through sampling from the base model. (1) Coverage collapse. REINFORCE, the basis for PPO and GRPO, can drive the probability of optimal responses to near zero, even as reward improves. This coverage collapse stalls optimization, and convergence can require exponentially many steps despite good initial coverage. The failure arises even with exact gradients and persists under KL regularization to the base model. (2) Reference resets. We show that repeatedly resetting the KL reference to the most recent policy mitigates coverage collapse. We formalize this intervention in Approximate Policy Mirror Descent (APMD), a meta-algorithm that approximately solves a sequence of KL-regularized RL subproblems. APMD enables stronger regularization, making each subproblem easier to solve, while reference resets allow convergence to global optimality. (3) Coverage-preserving algorithms. For softmax linear policies over pretrained features, we use APMD to establish the first global convergence guarantees showing that widely used families of post-training algorithms are coverage-preserving. These include stylized PPO and GRPO variants with explicit KL regularization and reference resets, and squared-loss algorithms that implement them implicitly, including those used to train the Kimi models. These results clarify how regularization, clipping, and objective choice affect the sampling and optimization costs of post-training.
authors: Audrey Huang, Nan Jiang, Sham M. Kakade, Sadhika Malladi, Akshay Krishnamurthy, Dylan J. Foster
bullets: Defines coverage-preserving algorithms whose sample and gradient costs depend on how readily the base model can generate optimal responses.
Shows REINFORCE—and consequently PPO/GRPO-style methods—can suffer coverage collapse even when rewards improve and exact gradients or KL regularization are used.
Introduces Approximate Policy Mirror Descent (APMD), which repeatedly resets the KL reference to the latest policy and solves a sequence of regularized subproblems.
Proves global convergence and coverage-preservation for several softmax linear-policy algorithms, including stylized PPO/GRPO variants and implicit squared-loss methods.
Clarifies how regularization, clipping, and objective design affect post-training’s sampling and optimization costs.

(b) Strong regularization controls coverage and keeps the learner close to the reference policy, but far from optimality (marked ✩). (c) APMD resets the reference to the most recent policy, reaching optimality through successive local improvements.

papers.abstract: Language-model systems use self-judgment to decide which answers to release, review, or recompute. Because intervention is costly, an assurance score must rank errors well at the available budget, not merely over the full ranking. We compare the judge's continuous verdict-token score with a supervised correctness probe trained on attention-head activations from the same prompt. Exact identities link fixed-budget error recall to residual risk and show that AUROC averages recall over all budgets. Across three open 7-12B models on GSM8K and MATH, the probe finds 1.3-22.5 additional percentage points of errors at 5% review in all six model-dataset settings (median 7.4 points). At 10% routing, probe-guided allocation improves accuracy over equal-cost random allocation in both GSM8K experiments, but beats judge-guided routing only for the weaker judge. Cross-dataset transfer lowers probe AUROC for every model in both directions relative to target-domain training. Because dataset, weight precision, and generation budget change together, this measures a joint protocol shift rather than a dataset-only effect. Internal signals can improve supervised, in-domain budget allocation, but are not domain-general confidence estimators.
bullets: The study evaluates confidence signals for deciding which model answers to review or recompute under limited budgets.
It compares the judge’s verdict-token score with a supervised correctness probe using attention-head activations from the same prompt.
Across three open 7–12B models on GSM8K and MATH, probes recovered 1.3–22.5 more percentage points of errors at 5% review in all settings.
At 10% routing, probe-guided allocation improved over random allocation in both GSM8K experiments, but surpassed judge-guided routing only for the weaker judge.
Cross-dataset transfer reduced probe AUROC in every model; results reflect a joint protocol shift, not dataset shift alone.

papers.abstract: System-1 Decision Models directly make structured probabilistic decisions over query-specified options given a state in a single forward pass, without autoregressively generating reasoning trajectories or textual responses. Recent evaluations cover diverse tasks but often rely on existing benchmarks, where prior exposure to test material can obscure generalization. Moreover, real-world decision making often involves long contexts, large option spaces, and complex logical dependencies, challenges that existing benchmarks do not adequately capture together. Thus, we introduce MMDM (Massive Multitask Decision Making), a benchmark of 5,448 high-quality questions across 16 task categories, combining newly constructed tasks with source-grounded recompositions and rewrites for single-select, multi-select, and soft-label decision making in fresh contexts. It covers realistic scenarios such as agent state tracking, tool and skill selection, preference judgments, and rubric scoring, with option spaces ranging from 2 to 1,024 and inputs extending to 64,817 tokens. With MMDM, we conduct a comprehensive quantitative evaluation of 28 decision models, showing that many perform well on common knowledge yet struggle with interdependent options, constrained decisions, and multi-select tasks. For example, Perplexity Decider-V1.2 reaches 78.75% Hard Single-select Accuracy on world knowledge, but only 53.95% on option logic and 47.95% on constraint planning, while the best Hard Multi-select Accuracy across all models is 36.81%. These results highlight joint reasoning, constraint-aware selection, and complete multi-select recovery as key priorities for decision model development, with MMDM providing a testbed for measuring this progress.
authors: Junhao Shen, Qing Zong, Yue Guo, Zhanqiu Zhang, Yiwen Guo, Hong Cheng
bullets: Introduces 5,448 questions across 16 task categories, covering single-select, multi-select, and soft-label decisions.
Tests realistic settings including state tracking, tool selection, preference judgments, and rubric scoring.
Includes fresh contexts with 2–1,024 options and inputs up to 64,817 tokens to probe scalable decision making.
Evaluates 28 decision models and finds substantial weaknesses in option logic, constraint planning, and complete multi-select recovery.
Highlights joint reasoning and constraint-aware selection as priorities for future decision-model development.

papers.abstract: Weight-space programming, introduced in recent MIT work by Takehi et al., enables a frontier LLM agent to read a network's weights and write a repair. Their GPT-6 Astra agent corrected the reasoning loops of Qwen3.5-0.8B without gradients, using 158 agent turns, 89.7 million tokens, and 50 forward-pass requests. Our method, Tree-Ising, casts this repair as a sparse discrete optimization problem over the model's own BF16 weights. Forward statistics define an objective that weakens a loop direction, strengthens a concluding direction, and preserves the layer's output on productive tokens. Within a state-tree representation, where lossless BF16 storage acts as a special case, the admissible edits are sign flips and exponent shifts that preserve all shared group exponents and mantissas. We decompose this objective exactly into independent QUBO (Ising) problems, one per output row, which we solve on a GPU using simulated annealing or quantum-inspired simulated bifurcation. On the agent's two layers, Tree-Ising achieves 54.6% on MATH-500, outperforming the agent's edit (51.7%) under the same evaluation protocol, while the base model scores 7.9% as reported. The simulated bifurcation solver yields a statistically indistinguishable repair at 55.1%. Both solvers outperform the agent edit across all five math benchmarks, with statistically significant improvements on MATH-500 and GSM8K after correcting for multiple comparisons. Our approach modifies 13% to 17% fewer weights and reduces BF16 bit flips by a factor of 2.2 to 2.3. It requires only four forward-pass requests and zero LLM tokens, with the annealing recipe costing about $0.90 in GPU time. On Qwen3.5-2B, with layers and dose selected using only the base model, the same recipe increases greedy GSM8K accuracy from 21.6% to 69.4%. As a proof of concept, we execute an eight-variable repair subproblem using QAOA on an IBM Heron processor.
bullets: Frames repair as a discrete optimization problem that suppresses reasoning loops, strengthens conclusions, and preserves productive outputs.
Decomposes the objective into independent per-row QUBO/Ising problems solved with GPU simulated annealing or simulated bifurcation.
On Qwen3.5-0.8B, reaches 54.6% on MATH-500 versus 51.7% for the agent edit and 7.9% for the base model; simulated bifurcation reaches 55.1%.
Uses four forward-pass requests, zero LLM tokens, 13–17% fewer weight edits, and 2.2–2.3× fewer BF16 bit flips than the agent repair.
On Qwen3.5-2B, raises greedy GSM8K accuracy from 21.6% to 69.4%; an eight-variable subproblem is also demonstrated on IBM Heron hardware.

papers.title: Tree-Ising: Repairing Language Models with Bit-Level Ising Edits
papers.tldr: Tree-Ising repairs language-model reasoning by optimizing sparse BF16 bit-level weight edits, outperforming an agent-based repair with far less computation.

papers.abstract: During extended wakefulness, mammalian neocortical networks experience localized periods of transient neuronal silence termed off-states. Here, we examine how analogous spatiotemporally concentrated disruptions affect sequential reasoning in autoregressive Large Language Models (LLMs). Evaluating 250 paired derivations on the GSM8K benchmark across two 8B models (Qwen3-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct), we contrast clustered bursts of attention head masking against budget-matched diffuse i.i.d. dropout. Concentrated bursts induce substantial reasoning degradation: at onset parameter $\mathcal{B}=0.10$ (scheduling $\sim 5.7\%$ of vulnerable head-token volume), Qwen3-8B accuracy drops from $91.2\%$ under diffuse noise to $78.8\%$ under burst dropout ($\Delta = -12.4$ percentage points [pp], exact McNemar $p = 5.5 \times 10^{-6}$), while LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct drops from $84.0\%$ to $76.8\%$ ($\Delta = -7.2$ pp, $p = 0.0198$). Conversely, dispersing the identical cumulative budget uniformly across generation steps via stratified quintile matching yields substantially milder degradation (retaining $91.2\%$ in Qwen and $84.0\%$ in LLaMA). In an exploratory factorial dissociation ($N=100$), single-step dropout density is associated with an acute drop in a single schedule draw ($-10.0$ pp on Qwen, $p_{\text{holm}} = 0.0425$), while multi-token continuity exhibits an inconclusive compounding trend ($-7.0$ pp, $p_{\text{holm}} = 0.1892$). Error analysis reveals that Qwen failures reflect derivation errors within formatted responses (conditional accuracy drop of $-11.4$ pp), whereas in LLaMA $22.2\%$ of discordant losses lack a final answer format line (conditional gap narrows to $-5.0$ pp). These findings demonstrate that autoregressive reasoning chains are particularly vulnerable to concentrated structural disruptions, providing empirical benchmarks for fault tolerance in transformer architectures.
bullets: The study compares clustered bursts of attention-head masking with budget-matched diffuse i.i.d. dropout in 250 paired GSM8K derivations using Qwen3-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct.
At the tested disruption level, burst dropout reduced accuracy by 12.4 percentage points for Qwen3 and 7.2 points for LLaMA relative to diffuse noise.
Uniformly dispersing the same cumulative dropout budget caused substantially milder degradation, preserving the diffuse-noise accuracy levels reported for both models.
Exploratory analysis links single-step dropout density to acute performance loss, while evidence for additional compounding from multi-token continuity is inconclusive.
Failures included derivation errors in Qwen3 and missing final-answer formatting in some LLaMA losses.

papers.abstract: Understanding the internal representations of neural networks and characterizing their relationship with human conceptual structure are two critical questions for elucidating model mechanisms. The former reveals how learned knowledge is organized in internal representations, whereas the latter provides a basis for interpreting these representations through human conceptual structure. Here, we formally define fundamental representational units (FRUs) and establish two evaluation criteria: fidelity and stability. We further prove that threshold-activated sparse autoencoders (TSAEs) can identify FRUs with high fidelity and stability under appropriate conditions, and validate this result through large-scale experiments. Further analyses reveal that FRUs with higher stability exhibit greater monosemanticity and can be composed across layers to recover semantic organization corresponding to human conceptual structure. These results provide a unified framework for defining, evaluating and identifying FRUs in neural networks, and establish a foundation for characterizing the relationship between neural network representations and human conceptual structure.
authors: Chenhui Hu, Pengfei Cao, Kang Liu, Jun Zhao
bullets: Introduces fundamental representational units (FRUs) as basic units of neural representations.
Defines fidelity and stability as criteria for evaluating FRUs.
Proves that threshold-activated sparse autoencoders can identify FRUs with high fidelity and stability under appropriate conditions.
Finds that more stable FRUs are more monosemantic and can be composed across layers to recover human-like semantic organization.
Supports the framework with large-scale experiments.

figures.caption: Fig. 1 Overview of the framework for defining, evaluating and identifying representational atoms. a, Representational atoms are defined as fundamental representational units (FRUs) that faithfully reconstruct model representations while remaining distinguishable. This definition is characterized by three properties: representability, sparsity and separability under the atomic inner product (AIP). b, Candidate FRUs are evaluated along two quantitative dimensions. Fidelity, quantified by the coefficient of determination R2, measures the reconstruction of the original representations, whereas stability, quantified by q∗, measures the extent to which atoms remain distinguishable under the condition µq < 1/(2Kq − 1). Higher values indicate better performance for both metrics, with R2 ∈ (−∞, 1] and q∗ ∈ [0, 1]. Stability captures the distinguishability of atoms and their compositions and constitutes a prerequisite for monosemanticity. c, Representational atoms are identified using threshold-activated sparse autoencoders (TSAEs). The encoder acts as a detector that activates atoms when its response exceeds the positive or negative threshold, while the corresponding decoder vectors constitute the atom set and reconstruct the original representations.

Fig. 3 Monosemanticity is positively correlated with stability across datasets and models. a, Overall relationship between stability and monosemanticity across all datasets, models and SAE architectures. Each point denotes one dataset-model-SAE combination (N = 40). For language models, stability and monosemanticity are averaged across the six evaluated layers; for Stable Diffusion v1.5, across three diffusion timesteps; and for FLUX.2-klein-9B, across six layer-step combinations. The positive correlation indicates a consistent association between stability and monosemanticity across heterogeneous representation settings. b-d, Relationships within Wikipedia (b; N = 15), Wikidata (c; N = 15) and LAION-COCO (d; N = 10), using the same model-SAE-level averages as in a. Positive correlations within all three datasets show that the overall association is preserved within individual datasets and modalities. e-l, Relationships within individual models: Gemma2-2B (e), Gemma2-9B (f) and Qwen3.5-9B (g) on Wikipedia; Gemma2-2B (h), Gemma2-9B (i) and Olmo-Hybrid-7B (j) on Wikidata; and Stable Diffusion v1.5 (k) and FLUX.2-klein-9B (l) on LAION-COCO. For language models, each point denotes one SAE architecture at one layer; for Stable Diffusion v1.5, one SAE architecture at one diffusion timestep; and for FLUX.2-klein-9B, one SAE architecture at one layer-step combination. Monosemanticity is averaged across the manually evaluated features at each corresponding layer, timestep or layer-step combination. These model-level results show that the positive correlation persists at finer representational granularity, although its strength varies across models. Colors denote SAE architectures (BiJumpReLU, JumpReLU, ReLU, TopK with K = 50, and AbsTopK with K = 50), and marker shapes denote datasets. Black lines show linear regression fits with 95% confidence bands. Spearman’s rank correlation coefficients (ρ) and two-sided P values are shown in each panel.

Fig. 2 Existing representational units exhibit distinct limitations in fidelity and stability. a–c, Fidelity (R2, top) and stability (q∗, bottom) of neurons and learned features across layers of Gemma2-2B (a), Gemma2-9B (b) and Llama3.1-8B (c). Angular coordinates denote layer indices, and radial coordinates denote the corresponding metric values. The dashed red circle marks the ideal-atom reference, for which both fidelity and stability attain their maximum value of 1. Neurons consistently exhibit high fidelity but substantially lower stability, whereas learned features from Gemma Scope and Llama Scope show improved stability to varying degrees but generally sacrifice fidelity, with neither class simultaneously approaching the ideal reference on both criteria. Across model scales and feature widths, these results reveal a systematic gap between existing candidate FRUs and the criteria for ideal representational atoms.

Fig. 4 Human sememes are compositionally represented by multiple representational atoms. a, Sememe– atom structural map for Gemma2-2B. Large light-blue circles denote human sememes and smaller blue circles denote representational atoms selected for their compositional recovery. Solid orange circles indicate the best single atoms that are retained in the final composition, whereas dashed orange circles indicate the best single atoms that are not selected. Circle sizes reflect the sizes of the corresponding semantic sets, and the geometric overlap between an atom and its sememe reflects their single-atom precision. Representative examples show that near one-to-one sememe–atom correspondence is rare, whereas compositional recovery by multiple atoms is common. More complete sememe–atom structural maps for Gemma2-2B, Gemma2-9B, and Llama3.1-8B are shown in Extended Data Figs. 3–5, respectively. b, Distribution of the number of atoms selected for each sememe across Gemma2-2B, Gemma2-9B and Llama3.1-8B, grouped into 1, 2–3, 4–6 and > 6 atoms. Most sememes are recovered using more than six atoms. c, Semantic recovery of the best single atom and the corresponding atom combination across the three models. Each point denotes an individual sememe, and F1 measures the agreement between the recovered representational set and the corresponding HowNet sememe set. Atom combinations consistently achieve substantially higher semantic alignment than the best single atoms. d, Relationship between sememe complexity and the number of atoms selected for its compositional recovery across the three models. Sememe complexity is measured by the number of entities associated with each HowNet sememe. Each point denotes an individual sememe with merged F1 ≥ 0.5, and dashed lines show model-specific linear regression fits in log–log space. More complex sememes tend to require more atoms for recovery.

papers.abstract: In Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, the nature of expert specialization remains controversial. Reports of domain-associated expert preferences contrast with analyses attributing routing primarily to token identity or syntactic patterns. To clarify these differing accounts, we look beyond expert-level routing to investigate the neuron-level organization of domain-specialized computation using Routing-Aware Magnitude Profiling (RAMP), a measure developed for this analysis. Using mixed-domain calibration data, we identify domain-specialized neuron sets with 58-74% overlap across multi-source samples of the same domain, compared with 15-24% across domains. To understand how this organization evolves during training, we trace neuron importance throughout pre-training and post-training across three fully open MoE families. Neuron importance continues to reorganize between pre-training checkpoints despite comparatively stable expert-level importance rankings, while post-training largely preserves neuron rankings. Building on these neuron-level perspectives, we further introduce RAMP-based Pruning (RAMPr) to select neurons across experts for balanced multi-domain capability preservation. At 75% neuron retention, RAMPr preserves average 91-98% of original full performance across six models. At 50% retention, our pruning method can reduce resident GPU memory by 36-43% and improves batched prefill throughput by 17-39% effectively. Our code is available at https://github.com/ydyjya/Neuron-Level-Specialization-in-MoE
authors: Zhenhong Zhou, Mao Zheng, Mingyang Song, Qiankun Li, Kun Wang, Junfeng Fang

At 50% retention, RAMPr reduces resident GPU memory by 36–43% and improves batched prefill throughput by 17–39%.

papers.selection_reason: Neuron-level pruning in MoE LLMs for memory and throughput efficiency, plus MoE architecture analysis.
papers.title: Understanding Mixture-of-Experts Language Models Beyond Expert Boundaries
papers.tldr: Neuron-level analysis reveals domain-specialized organization within MoE experts and enables pruning that preserves most performance while reducing memory and improving throughput.

papers.abstract: Deep neural networks underpin fundamental tasks in a wide range of signal domains, such as image, audio, and language processing. However, their internal mechanisms are notably difficult to interpret. Internal activations are structured signals transformed across layers that may encode a multitude of interdependent relationships, as individual neurons frequently represent multiple underlying concepts. Mechanistic interpretability aims to uncover the internal mechanisms of neural networks by identifying components whose activations are causally responsible for specific behaviors. In such a context, this article provides an overview of advances in mechanistic interpretability for the analysis of causal inference in deep neural networks.
authors: Lorenzo Cirillo, Irene Amerini, Andrea Cavallaro
bullets: Deep neural networks are difficult to interpret because their layered activations encode complex, interdependent relationships.
Individual neurons may represent multiple concepts, complicating direct interpretation.
Mechanistic interpretability analyzes components whose activations are causally responsible for model behaviors.
The article reviews advances, methods, and frameworks for causal analysis across image, audio, and language-processing systems.

papers.selection_reason: Provides a comprehensive overview of mechanistic interpretability for deep neural networks. This review is relevant to understanding the internal mechanisms of Language Foundation Models and Multimodal Foundation Models.
papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Deep Neural Networks: Methods, Frameworks, and Perspectives
papers.tldr: This article surveys mechanistic interpretability methods for uncovering how internal neural-network components causally produce specific behaviors.

papers.abstract: Continual pre-training (CPT) adapts large language models (LLMs) to specialized domains, yet its standard next-token prediction (NTP) objective treats every corpus token as a fixed target, regardless of its utility to the current model. In a controlled study on the same 1B-token mathematical corpus, we observe sharply different outcomes across base models: NTP improves Llama-3.2-3B's performance on mathematical benchmarks but substantially degrades Qwen3-1.7B-Base's performance, indicating that, under a fixed training recipe, the same training sequences can have model-dependent effects. To address this problem, we introduce On-Policy Mid-Training Distillation (OPMD), which reformulates mid-training from offline text imitation into active, query-driven knowledge acquisition. At selected anchor positions, OPMD samples trajectories from the evolving student policy and applies dense token-level reverse-KL rewards from a frozen teacher, training the model on states it actually visits rather than only on ground-truth prefixes. This on-policy objective reduces the training-generation mismatch of teacher-forced NTP. On MATH-500 and Minerva, OPMD improves the Qwen student over its base performance and outperforms the evaluated NTP baseline, which degrades on both benchmarks. OPMD integrates into CPT pipelines without added inference-time overhead and offers a model-aware alternative to passive domain adaptation.
authors: Ruize Zheng, Xuyang Liu, Siyu Ren, Xiaobing Tu, Yinggui Wang, Jinkui Ren, Xiantao Zhang, Linfeng Zhang
bullets: Standard next-token prediction has model-dependent effects: it helps Llama-3.2-3B but degrades Qwen3-1.7B-Base on the same mathematical corpus.
OPMD replaces passive imitation with active, query-driven knowledge acquisition from states visited by the student.
At selected anchor positions, it samples student-policy trajectories and applies dense token-level reverse-KL rewards from a frozen teacher.
On MATH-500 and Minerva, OPMD improves Qwen over its base model and outperforms the evaluated NTP baseline.
The method adds no inference-time overhead and is designed to integrate with continual pre-training pipelines.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the OPMD compared with standard NTP, along with training dynamics. (a) Standard NTP: Rigid token-by-token imitation on specialized domain corpora leads to severe policy collapse. (b) OPMD Pipeline: (1) Anchor Token Identification (ATI) & Alignment: A proxy model identifies informative trigger tokens via predictive entropy, followed by context deduplication and strict budget alignment. (2) On-Policy Rollout & Distillation: The student generates continuations from prefix prompts and receives dense teacher guidance through a student-weighted Top-16 log-ratio reward at each rollout step. (c) Performance Dynamics: OPMD completely eliminates NTP policy collapse and achieves substantial, stable reasoning gains across benchmarks.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces on-policy distillation for continual pre-training of LLMs, directly relevant to LLM training and domain adaptation.
papers.title: Beyond Passive Imitation: On-Policy Mid-Training Distillation for Language Models
papers.tldr: On-Policy Mid-Training Distillation (OPMD) makes continual pre-training model-aware by distilling a frozen teacher on trajectories sampled from the evolving student, improving mathematical adaptation where standard next-token training can hurt.

papers.abstract: Typed-decision encoders answer a question about a text in one forward pass, but their behaviour outside English is rarely measured on a fixed yardstick. We release PolyRoute: 322 native-language support messages in 12 languages and 9 writing systems, 156 code-mixed or romanised messages (Hinglish, Spanglish, Arabizi), 967 optional native training rows, and a protocol for a three-way department-routing decision. Labels come from Qwen3.8-27B with a blind second pass (91% of candidates kept); an independent model, gemma4-31b, agrees on 97.2% of test items, and the largest character 5-gram similarity between any test text and any training text is 0.33. A leaderboard of 13 systems gives 61.2% for the English-root checkpoint, 77.3% for the shipped multilingual one and 96.6% for the best fine-tune; TF-IDF with logistic regression reaches 91.9%. On four withheld languages the three multilingual systems score 77%, 90% and 93%. On code-mixed text the English root (85%) is nominally ahead of the shipped multilingual checkpoint (79%; p=0.134). The split resolves differences only above about 4 points. All texts and labels are LLM-generated.
authors: Mohammed Nayeem Khan, Sarun Kumar K S
bullets: Covers 322 native-language messages in 12 languages and 9 scripts, plus 156 code-mixed or romanised messages and 967 optional training examples.
Provides a fixed routing protocol, baselines, a 13-system leaderboard, and evaluations on four withheld languages.
The shipped multilingual model scores 77.3% overall, the best fine-tune 96.6%, and TF-IDF with logistic regression 91.9%.
On withheld languages, multilingual systems score 77%, 90%, and 93%; code-mixed results show no statistically clear advantage for the multilingual checkpoint.
Labels were generated by LLMs and independently agreed upon for 97.2% of test items; the benchmark resolves differences only above roughly 4 points.

papers.selection_reason: Releases PolyRoute, a benchmark for typed-decision routing in multilingual and code-mixed text. This contributes to the evaluation of LLMs in Language Foundation Models.
papers.title: PolyRoute: A Twelve-Language and Code-Mixed Benchmark for Typed-Decision Routing, with Baselines and a Leaderboard

papers.abstract: Weight-space programming allows language models to read a trained neural network's weights and edit them. This opens the door to ``training'' by reasoning rather than through gradient descent. Prior work has demonstrated its functionality and promise for game-playing networks and fixing specific failures in language models, even extending to diffusion models. In this work, we present its applicability to models trained on biosignal data, specifically EEG and ECG data. We show that frontier models are not only able to debug specific faults planted in biosignal-based models without being told what these faults are, but are even capable of writing all the weights of a network from scratch, given only the architecture, the task, and a minimal set of training subjects. In particular, in one set of experiments, a language model was able to match standard gradient-descent training using $6\times$ fewer training subjects, through reasoning alone and without any gradient descent step. Networks written by Claude Opus 5.5 also scored higher than classic hand-crafted EEG pipelines (alpha band power, and common spatial patterns with linear discriminant analysis) when built from the same 5 subjects. We also highlight some of the limitations, which include the inability of language models to improve already well-trained classification models, and their incapacity to reliably recognize, from the weights alone, the task a network was trained on. Overall, our results indicate that weight-space programming can be useful for small networks, such as those deployed on edge devices and wearables, but the concept still requires further investigation before it can be used in practice.
authors: Dara Varam, Taraneh Aminosharieh Najafi, David Atienza
bullets: Applies weight-space programming to biosignal models trained on EEG and ECG data.
Language models can identify and fix planted faults without being told what they are, and generate all network weights from architecture, task, and minimal training data.
In one experiment, a language model matched standard training using 6× fewer training subjects without gradient descent.
Claude Opus 5.5-built networks outperformed handcrafted EEG baselines when trained from the same 5 subjects.
Models could not reliably improve already well-trained classifiers or infer the task from weights alone; practical use remains premature.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) improves language models by distilling teacher predictions on student-generated trajectories, while on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) removes the need for an external teacher by using a reference-conditioned copy of the model as the teacher. Despite its great early improvements, we find that OPSD does not remain consistently effective under continued training and can eventually suffer substantial performance degradation. We study this training behavior and link the degradation to a growing mismatch between the evolving reference-free student and the frozen privileged teacher. In the early stage of OPSD, the privileged teacher remains closely aligned with the student and provides useful guidance for improving the student's generation trajectories. However, as training progresses, the growing distributional mismatch between the privileged teacher and reference-free student can cause the teacher to provide misleading supervision, ultimately degrading student performance. This phenomenon motivates us to first leverage privileged reference supervision to acquire useful knowledge and then transfer it to a fresh student. We introduce Bootstrapped On-Policy Distillation (BOPD), a two-stage framework that first uses OPSD to internalize task-relevant information from reference-conditioned supervision into an intermediate model, and then distills this reference-free intermediate model into a fresh copy of the initial model. Experiments across models show that BOPD improves mathematical reasoning and code generation beyond both the initial models and the constructed OPSD teachers. These results suggest that privileged reference supervision can be more effectively exploited by first transferring its task-relevant signal into a task-adapted model and then distilling from that model without reference conditioning.
authors: Yue Wu, Xueyu Zhou, Yangrong Hu, Jian Huang
bullets: On-policy self-distillation can initially help but eventually degrades as the student diverges from its frozen, reference-conditioned teacher.
The proposed BOPD framework uses two stages: OPSD first adapts an intermediate model, then its reference-free behavior is distilled into a fresh copy of the initial model.
Across models, BOPD improves mathematical reasoning and code generation over both the initial models and the corresponding OPSD teachers.
The approach is motivated by reducing misleading supervision caused by distributional mismatch during continued OPSD training.

papers.abstract: Transformer feed-forward blocks combine several design choices: squared activations, gating, and tied versus untied parameter sharing, whose separate contributions to expressivity remain poorly understood. We introduce CP-MLPs, a tensor framework in which each multiplicative unit contributes a rank-1 interaction with three roles: detecting an input feature, reading a value, and writing to the output. Tied gated blocks such as ReLU$^2$ force the detector and value roles to share the same direction; untied gated blocks such as ReGLU and SwiGLU let them differ. We show that this distinction yields exact, degree-wise tensor-rank separations: untied detector-value units are strictly more width-efficient for indefinite quadratic interactions and role-asymmetric monomials, while tied units are structurally matched to symmetric pure-power targets. The width advantage of untying therefore depends on the target structure. Experiments show loss plateaus below the exact-representation width, but these plateaus alone do not establish a positive approximation gap: arbitrarily accurate approximation is governed by border rank. In trained gated MLPs, untied blocks retain an advantage in selected comparisons at matched input-projection budget. Code is available at https://github.com/rarefin/CP-MLPs.
authors: Md Rifat Arefin, Farzaneh Heidari, Irina Rish, Guillaume Rabusseau

Tied units are structurally well matched to symmetric pure-power targets, so untying is not universally better.
Experiments find loss plateaus below exact-representation width, while border rank governs arbitrarily accurate approximation; untied blocks retain advantages in selected matched-budget comparisons.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress on complex reasoning tasks, yet the mechanisms by which they acquire reasoning capabilities and the efficiency of their reasoning remain poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the path-finding problem over directed graphs, a symbolic abstraction of multi-step reasoning. We first characterize the architectural requirements for this task, proving that one-layer transformers require $\Omega(N^2)$ size on dense graphs to implement the key DFS child-selection primitive. While a two-layer transformer implements full DFS with $O(N\log(N))$ size. Thus, a second layer is necessary and sufficient for near-linear DFS reasoning. We then extend this expressivity analysis to deeper models: for every $k\geq3$, a $k$-layer transformer implements a bounded-reachability DFS policy with look-ahead horizon $1+2^{k-3}$, establishing an exponential increase in reachability horizon with depth. Finally, going beyond expressivity, given appropriately curated training data, we show that two-layer transformers can provably learn to execute DFS via gradient flow and generalize to unseen graphs. Together, our results provide a mechanistic account of how transformers implement graph search, how depth expands bounded look-ahead, and how such reasoning algorithms can emerge through training.
bullets: One-layer transformers need Ω(N²) size on dense graphs for the key DFS child-selection operation.
Two-layer transformers implement full DFS with O(N log N) size, making a second layer necessary and sufficient for near-linear DFS reasoning.
A k-layer transformer achieves a bounded-reachability DFS policy with look-ahead horizon 1 + 2^(k−3) for k ≥ 3.
Under appropriately curated training data, two-layer transformers can learn DFS through gradient flow and generalize to unseen graphs.
The analysis is theoretical and focuses on directed-graph path finding as a symbolic model of multi-step reasoning.

papers.selection_reason: Theoretical analysis of transformer depth and training for graph-search reasoning; relevant to LLM reasoning mechanisms.
papers.title: Transformers Provably Learn Graph Search: Training Dynamics and the Exponential Power of Depth
papers.tldr: The paper proves that transformer depth enables efficient graph-search reasoning: two layers suffice for near-linear DFS, while additional layers exponentially expand look-ahead, and curated training can teach this behavior.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities across diverse applications, making both safety and utility essential for reliable deployment. Jailbreak attacks use diverse forms of adversarial prompting to bypass alignment safeguards and induce LLMs to generate harmful responses. Some representation-based defenses regulate internal activations using predefined steering directions or learned safety regions. However, adapting intervention to each input without a predefined representational target while limiting over-refusal remains a challenge. In this paper, we propose Target-free Entropy-guided Residual Modulation (TERM), an inference-time defense that uses prompt-calibrated attention entropy deviations to guide adaptive modulation of the model's own residual updates. Attention patterns vary across prompts and decoding steps, making raw entropy values difficult to interpret as a consistent signal for intervention. We therefore calibrate attention entropy against each prompt's own prefill baseline to establish an input-specific reference for reducing unnecessary intervention on benign requests. Adaptive scale normalization and temporal accumulation then account for differences in deviation scale and persistence to determine intervention strength. The resulting signal controls bounded scaling of the model's own residual updates, without relying on a predefined safety direction. We compare our method with seven defenses on seven jailbreak attacks and two over-refusal benchmarks across Llama, Qwen, and Gemma models, including Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 32B. Results show our method improves jailbreak robustness while maintaining low over-refusal on benign safety-sensitive requests with modest inference overhead.
authors: Yunkai Dang, Wanyu Zhang, Meiyi Zhu, Qi Fan, Tianyu Ding, Wenbin Li
bullets: Addresses the challenge of defending against diverse jailbreak prompts without predefined safety directions or excessive refusal of benign requests.
Calibrates attention-entropy deviations against each prompt’s prefill baseline to create an input-specific intervention signal.
Uses adaptive scale normalization and temporal accumulation to estimate intervention strength across decoding steps.
Applies bounded scaling to the model’s own residual updates, requiring no learned safety region or target representation.
Evaluated across seven defenses, seven jailbreak attacks, two over-refusal benchmarks, and Llama, Qwen, and Gemma models; reports stronger robustness, low over-refusal, and modest inference overhead.
