papers.tldr: TERM is an inference-time jailbreak defense that adaptively modulates a model’s residual updates using prompt-calibrated attention-entropy signals, improving robustness while limiting over-refusal.

papers.abstract: Compositional generalization is an important form of out-of-distribution generalization, defined as the ability to train on some combinations of modules (e.g., functions such as sort, filter) and then generalize to unseen combinations. Despite substantial empirical work evaluating compositional generalization in transformers, findings have been inconsistent because evaluations were often conducted on a limited set of train-test splits, defined in an ad hoc manner. Through a systematic evaluation, we identify two key aspects of the train-test distribution that strongly affect performance: composition equivalence and module coverage. We show that the apparent performance of direct models (trained only on final outputs) results primarily from exploiting composition equivalences, meaning different sequences of modules that reduce to identical end-to-end functions. When benchmarks eliminate these equivalences, performance drops significantly, showing their inability to generalize to compositions of known modules that produce novel end-to-end functions. We further demonstrate that performance degrades monotonically as module coverage shifts increase (when modules appear in different contexts between train and test), affecting both direct and step-by-step models (trained on intermediate and final outputs). These findings have concrete implications for benchmark design: benchmarks that include compositional equivalences can lead to significant overestimation of the generalization abilities of direct models, and benchmarks that include both module coverage violations and compositional equivalences can exacerbate shortcut learning. As a case study, we demonstrate the role of compositional equivalence on the generalization performance of the pre-trained model Llama3-8B on the code-output prediction task in the coding benchmark LiveCodeBench.
authors: Purva Pruthi, Andrew Yuan, Alexander D'Amour, David Jensen
bullets: Systematically evaluates how train–test distribution design affects compositional generalization.
Finds direct models often appear strong by exploiting different module sequences with identical end-to-end functions.
Removing composition equivalences causes substantial performance drops on novel functions built from known modules.
Performance declines monotonically as module contexts shift between training and testing, for both direct and step-by-step models.
Shows benchmark design can overestimate generalization and encourage shortcut learning, including in a Llama3-8B LiveCodeBench case study.

figures.caption: Figure 9: Generalization performance of bigger transformer architecture: We observe that the performance of the bigger architecture shows similar performance trends as seen for the smaller architecture (N_heads = 6, N_layers = 3) in Figures 2(b) and (d).

Figure 4: Isolating the effect of composition equivalence in the diverse benchmark (k = 6): (a) Generalization performance increases with the degree of shared composition equivalence classes between train and test. (b) The direct model generalizes primarily to test sequences that share equivalence classes and fails on classes exhibiting novel end-to-end behavior.

Figure 6: (a) Code output prediction performance of Llama3-8b on LiveCodeBench benchmark: We show the accuracy of the base model (No LoRA) and three LoRA fine-tuned models on splits with varying ratios of shared equivalence classes (defined by the same function names) (held out h=0, 0.5, 1.0). As splits share composition equivalences, accuracy improves substantially. (b) Performance grouped by equivalence classes: We observe that performance on most functions only improves when equivalences are leaked into the fine-tuning set.

Figure 1: (a) A sequential composition task combines “atomic” functions (e.g., sort, mode, filter). Task-based compositional generalization is the ability to generalize to unseen sequences after training on a subset. (b) Composition equivalence: Different sequences are composition equivalent if they reduce to the same end-to-end function. For example, one equivalence class consisting of the first four sequences reduces to returning the most frequently occurring vowel in a set of strings; direct models succeed on the test sequence (mode ◦ filter ◦ sort) from this class but fail on the remaining two test sequences from a different composition equivalence class. (c) Module coverage: Examples of coverage failures include position-wise (e.g., function 2 never appearing in the first position, shown with dashed lines) and pair-wise (e.g., missing pair (2,1) in the training set, shown with solid lines).

Figure 3: Cross-k evaluation: For the diverse benchmark (a–b), direct models perform well near training k as equivalences persist across nearby k values. Direct models fail on the uniform benchmark (c–d) regardless of identity tokens, since identity-based equivalences in the uniform benchmark are k-specific. Step-by-step models are more robust but still exhibit significant variability.

Figure 2: Within-k evaluation: Direct models fail completely (0% accuracy) on uniform bijections without identity tokens (Figure (d)), while step-by-step models maintain near-perfect performance across all conditions. We observe that including identity tokens or diverse function types seems crucial for the generalization performance of direct models.

Figure 7: Uniform benchmark (without identity), N_heads = 6, N_layers = 3, Direct (Relative): We observe that the models learn to predict the outputs of training compositions for both K=2 and for K=6, while the test accuracy on unseen compositions remains 0% throughout. We report two metrics: (1) sharp accuracy, where a prediction scores 1.0 only if the entire output sequence is correct and 0.0 otherwise; and (2) mean token accuracy, average accuracy of predictions in the output sequence, with both metrics averaged across compositions from each split. For reference, 100 epochs correspond to roughly 20k iterations (batch size 512, 100k training samples, 195 iterations per epoch).

Figure 8: Diverse benchmark, N_heads = 6, N_layers = 3, Direct (Relative): We observe non-trivial compositional generalization, as the models perform well on training and validation compositions, the test performance also increases. We observe better generalization for K = 6 than for K = 2 due to more training diversity and shared equivalences.
Figure 5: Effect of position-wise distribution shift: As the position-wise KL divergence increases, the compositional generalization performance of both direct and step-by-step models decreases.

Figure 10: Equivalence class necessity and training requirements: (a) Generalization performance to unseen sequences is strongly correlated with the degree of shared composition equivalence classes between train and test. (b) Models need to see at least 4–5 composition equivalences (per class) in training to generalize to the corresponding test equivalences.

Figure 14: Composition equivalence encourages shortcuts in step-by-step models: We observe that composition equivalences in the diverse benchmark cause discrepancies between final output accuracy and full output (intermediate and final output) accuracy for both within-k evaluation and cross-k evaluation. Final accuracy > full accuracy implies the model is learning shortcuts to reach the final answer. If we eliminate composition equivalences, the performance difference is zero between full and final outputs (see Figures 15(a), 15(b))

Figure 15: Eliminating composition equivalences removes shortcut learning in step-by-step models : We observe that the lack of compositional equivalence in the uniform benchmark removes shortcut-learning behavior in step-by-step models. This is shown by the exact same step-by-step accuracy, and the final accuracy is the same for both within-k evaluation (k = 6) and cross-k evaluation (train-k = 6).

Figure 19: Effect of pairwise-wise distribution shift: (a) As the pairwise-wise KL divergence increases, the compositional generalization performance of both direct and step-by-step models decreases in the diverse benchmark. (b) For the uniform benchmark, the effect of divergence is primarily observed at the extreme right end for support violations.

Figure 25: Effect of number of samples per composition (diverse benchmark, direct model): For the diverse benchmark, direct models are less sample efficient than the uniform benchmark to generalize on the validation set, especially for K= 2. We observe significant compositional generalization behavior, as seen in Figure 2(b) for large samples, especially for K=6.

Figure 24: Effect of number of samples per composition (uniform benchmark, step-by-step model): We observe that step-by-step models are more sample efficient than direct models due to access to intermediate outputs providing extra information.

Figure 23: Effect of number of samples per composition (uniform benchmark, direct model):. Number of training compositions N = 24 for K = 2, and N = 576 for K = 6. We vary the number of input-output samples per training composition in this experiment. We observe that with a small number of training samples, the train/val gap is large, and the model struggles to generalize to training compositions with novel inputs. The train-val gap reduces as the number of samples increases. Test accuracies remain 0%, as expected.

Figure 26: Effect of number of samples per composition (diverse benchmark, step-by-step model): Step-by-step models are more sample efficient than direct models, and a similar difference between uniform and diverse benchmarks for K=2 is observed as for direct models.

Figure 22: Effect of number of unique training sequential compositions (randomly sampled, K=6):: We observe that (a) step-by-step models with relative global embedding need fewer training compositions to generalize faster than absolute embedding models, and (b) For the diverse benchmark, as compared to direct models, step-by-step models need fewer unique training compositions due to extra information available using intermediate outputs.

Figure 16: Gemma-1B visualization of per-class distribution for 100% sharing: We observe that most of the equivalence classes are shared and the model has overall high accuracy over test sequences in the shared equivalence classes.

Figure 17: Gemma-1B visualization of test accuracy for the split with no shared equivalences: We observe that none of the equivalence classes are shared, and the model has poor accuracy over test sequences in those classes.

Figure 13: Leaking test equivalence classes without swapping (K = 6): (a) Generalization performance to unseen sequences is strongly correlated with the number of shared composition equivalence classes between train and test. (b) The mean accuracy of shared equivalence classes is significantly higher than that of non-shared equivalence classes.

Figure 20: Combined effect of position-wise shift and reduced diversity: Shows (1-accuracyKL) to demonstrate accuracy degradation as in Figure 5, revealing combined effects of coverage shift and reduced compositional diversity due to biased sampling. Here, accuracyKL is the performance with biased sampling.

Figure 21: Isolating position-wise shift by controlling diversity: Shows accuracyzero_shift − accuracyKL, where accuracyzero_shift and accuracyKL are accuracies under random and biased sampling with n unique compositions at each Dpos, respectively. For the diverse benchmark, positionwise shift alone has a reduced but still significant effect compared to Figure 20, indicating that both coverage shift and reduced diversity contribute to degradation. For the uniform benchmark, the negligible difference confirms that degradation is driven primarily by coverage shift alone.

Figure 11: Visualization of learned equivalence classes for the diverse benchmark (K=6): We show two equivalence classes (out of a total of 14 classes). First, we can note that the degree of equivalence varies significantly within an equivalence class. The test sequences are marked in red, and the training sequences are marked in green, indicating whether an equivalence class is shared. We observe that accuracy is significantly higher for compositions in the shared equivalence class and near zero for those in the non-shared equivalence class.

papers.selection_reason: Systematic evaluation of compositional generalization in transformers, including Llama3-8B; relevant to LLM reasoning and generalization.
papers.title: Evaluating Compositional Generalization in Transformers: The Role of Composition Equivalence and Module Coverage
papers.tldr: Transformer compositional-generalization results depend strongly on whether train–test splits preserve composition equivalences and module coverage.

papers.abstract: Most language models deployed outside the United States and China are fine-tuned descendants of a small number of pretrained families. We argue that fine-tuning leaves the decisive properties of a model inherited from its base: vocabulary, knowledge, cultural alignment, memorized data and license. We contribute (i) an updated, reproducible measurement of the tokenization premium across 31 languages and 7 tokenizers released in 2023-2024, on 27 articles of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, with explicit correction for unknown-token collapse. Premiums reach 10x for Amharic in older tokenizers and remain at 6.8x in the newest commercial one; Indigenous South American languages pay between 1.6x and 2.7x under global tokenizers. A vocabulary built from Portuguese lowers the premium for 11 of 13 Latin-script Global South languages relative to every global tokenizer tested, by about 24% for Guarani and Quechua. (ii) An eight-test black-box sovereignty audit that a buyer can run without access to weights. (iii) A regime argument: under energy and liability constraints, accuracy per joule, calibration and selective risk should replace raw accuracy as design objectives, with metrics that abstention cannot inflate. We close with preliminary internal measurements from a proprietary architecture built around these objectives, reported with their limitations. Data and measurement code are included.
bullets: Measures tokenization premiums across 31 languages and 7 tokenizers using Universal Declaration of Human Rights text, correcting for unknown-token collapse.
Premiums reach 10× for Amharic with older tokenizers and 6.8× with the newest commercial tokenizer; Indigenous South American languages face 1.6–2.7× premiums.
A Portuguese-derived vocabulary reduces premiums for 11 of 13 Latin-script Global South languages, including about 24% for Guarani and Quechua.
Introduces an eight-test black-box sovereignty audit requiring no model-weight access.
Argues for optimizing accuracy per joule, calibration, and selective risk rather than raw accuracy; proprietary preliminary measurements are reported with limitations.
papers.selection_reason: Measures tokenization and inherited properties of language models, relevant to LLM design and deployment.
papers.title: Inherited Weights: Measuring the Tokenization Premium and the Sovereignty Cost of Language Models for the Global South
papers.tldr: Fine-tuned language models inherit tokenization and sovereignty costs from their base models, often disadvantaging Global South languages and motivating buyer-accessible audits and efficiency-aware objectives.

papers.abstract: How should we understand memorization vs. generalization in in-context learning (ICL) tasks, and when does one happen vs. the other? To investigate, we study how rotation-invariant kernel machines learn the ICL linear regression task proposed by Raventos et al. (2023). By decomposing the task in the kernel eigenbasis, we obtain a spectral picture of learning in this ICL setting. This picture reveals that as sample size grows, kernel machines learn successively-higher-degree components of the memorizing solution, which depend upon successively-higher-degree statistics of the training task set. The generalizing solution is approximately a low-degree truncation of the memorizing solution, and so the model first generalizes, then degrades into memorization as training proceeds. The takeaways are threefold. First, if this case is indicative, learning a "generalizing" solution on an ICL task is really just underfitting the memorizing solution! Second, the fact that kernel machines can generalize on this task means that feature learning is inessential to ICL. Third, transformers empirically trained to do ICL are shown to memorize tasks through the higher-order statistics of the training tasks that the kernel-based theory predicts, suggesting it applies even to models capable of feature learning.
bullets: Studies rotation-invariant kernel machines on an ICL linear-regression task using a kernel-eigenbasis decomposition.
As sample size grows, models learn increasingly higher-degree components tied to higher-order statistics of the training tasks.
Generalization appears first, then degrades into memorization as training proceeds.
The results suggest feature learning is not essential for ICL in this setting.
Empirically trained transformers show the predicted memorization through higher-order task statistics.

Across various rotationinvariant kernels with varying task diversity (columns), we compute the empirical kernel eigensystem {(λ(emp)

Figure 4: Task diversity trades pretraining-task accuracy for novel-task accuracy. Following Raventós et al. (2023), we sweep the number of training tasks T and report test MSE on the pretraining tasks Dtr (left) and on novel tasks Dnovel (right). Our data is drawn with d = 8, L = 15, ϵ2 = 0.25. In blue, we show a fit random features network trained with SGD (see Section B for random feature network details), with the memorizing (dMMSE) and generalizing (ridge) oracles shown. As T grows, the training task distribution’s cumulants approach that of the prior’s (Gaussian) and all three curves converge. Evaluated on novel tasks, the random features model initially tracks the memorizing solution up to a task diversity T of 4, continuing to approach the generalizing solution until T ≈ 26 = 64 tasks. All models are trained with enough samples such that they can fully realize the optimal degree-3 term, indicated by the green background. We note two exceptions: a blue background for one training task is used to signify that the model uses the mean task alone, and the seafoam background for two tasks signifies the mean task still being heavily utilized. The trained models do not exactly reach the generalizing solution, in part due to the finite context length L we use for training (see Section 7). Further experimental details are in Section B.

Figure 7: One-dimensional ICL data breaks Gaussian universality. We compare the eigenframework’s predicted test MSE (line) against kernel regression trained on true ICL contexts (circles) and on a Gaussian surrogate with matched moments (diamonds), for T = 4, d = 1, L = 8. We use a Gaussian kernel with kernel width σker = √ 3 and in-context data with covariance Σx ∼ Id/(dL). The left panel is ridgeless (δ = 0) and the right uses a small ridge (δ = 5× 10−3). The Gaussian surrogate tracks the theory at every n. The true contexts agree away from the interpolation peak but exceed the prediction near it, most visibly at small ridge. Both datasets share the same theoretical curve, so the mismatch comes from the non-Gaussianity of one-dimensional ICL data rather than from the predicted eigenstructure. We observe no such failure for d > 1.

Figure 3: Random feature models can perform ICL even with only T = d+ 1 tasks. We train a random feature network using SGD with exactly T = 4 = d+ 1 tasks (d = 3), with context length L = 96. We manually construct a training task pool such that Σ̂ = Id and µ̂ = 0. As is predicted in Section 7, this training task distribution allows the model to near-perfectly generalize once the optimal degree-3 term ∑ i yix ⊤ i xL+1 is learned. We evaluate the random features model’s test error on novel tasks β⋆ ∼ Dnovel, normalized by E[y2]. When the model has not seen many samples in phase one, the model uses the average training task, which we manually set to 0. At approximately 106 samples, the model enters phase two and begins fitting the generalizing degree-3 term. Even though there are only 4 training tasks, the model does not memorize the tasks with up to 109 samples! Given infinite training samples, the model will eventually memorize. Further details in Section B.

Figure 5: Transformers memorize through non-Gaussian statistics of their training tasks. We train 12-layer GPT-2-style transformers with Adam on T = 256 training tasks (d = 8, L = 16, ϵ2 = 0.25) and evaluate the test MSE on (a) fresh tasks and (b) the training tasks. All pools are centered and whitened (see Section 7.2 for a discussion of the implications) and differ principally in their fourth cumulant. Whiten consists of i.i.d. Gaussian draws, partial kurtosis is made of a symmetric pool whose κ̂4 is rescaled to 0.3× that of its initial Gaussian pool, no kurtosis uses a symmetric pool with κ̂4 = 0. Dashed and dotted lines mark the generalizing (ridge) and memorizing (dMMSE). In (a), each pool’s dMMSE is shown to highlight that the slight difference in oracle does not explain the onset of task memorization. All models first approach the generalizing solution, with the scale of the kurtosis setting when memorization begins. Further experimental details are in Section B.

Figure 1: As sample size grows, kernels learn successively higher-degree target function components in in-context linear regression. They first learn the mean training task (phase 1), then approximate the degree-three generalizing solution (phase 2), and finally memorize the training tasks (phase 3). (Left) A visualization of a kernel machine’s inferred task in task space B = Rd decomposed into vector components learned in each phase (arrows). Grey dots indicate training tasks Btr = {β(t)} and a grey star indicates an unseen task β∗ /∈ Btr. In phase 1, the kernel learns the mean training task µ̂β := Eβ∼Btr [β]. In phase 2, the kernel learns approximately β∗− µ̂β , nearly recovering the true task β∗. In phase 3, learned higher-degree terms pull the prediction towards the nearest task in Btr. (Right) We plot learning curves for KR on the in-context linear regression problem with d = 5, L = 7, T = 16. (Top) Evaluated on the training tasks, the error falls monotonically, eventually reaching that of the memorizing solution (Equation (3)). We show both theoretical predictions (lines) and experimental values (dots) in the experimentally-accessible region n ∈ [1, 5 × 104]. (Middle) Evaluated on novel tasks (β ∼ N (0, Id)), error is minimized at the end of phase 2, approaching that of the generalizing solution (Equation (4)), before rising to that of the memorizing solution in phase 3. Background shading indicates the three phases of learning. (Bottom) We also plot the predicted overlap between the function f̂ker learned by KR and various polynomial functions gi. The functions gi correspond to the vector components in the cartoon on the left, and are given explicitly in Section B. The function gi is determined by the i-th order statistics of Btr. The component g1 is responsible for generalization and is learned in phase 2. We show theoretical predictions (lines) for the kernel’s error out to 1012 samples, finding excellent agreement between theory and experiment in the experimentally accessible region.

Figure 2: Transience is explained by learning higher order task statistics. We train lazy random features networks (RFNs) (see Section B.2 for a description of RFNs) with online SGD on ICL linear regression data. Using RFNs, we empirically find that the error on novel tasks rises when the higher degree terms are learned, as was theoretically predicted in Figure 1. We observe the same three phases of predicting from the mean task alone, then generalizing to any task, followed by memorizing using higher-degree terms. (Top) Test MSE on novel tasks β ∼ Dnovel, with the memorizing (dMMSE) and generalizing (ridge) oracles for reference. Unlike the kernels trained in Figure 1, the random feature networks train with enough samples to empirically probe phase 3. (Bottom) Overlap of the learned predictor with the leading terms of the memorizing solution, E[f̂gi]/E[g2i ]. Similar to Figure 1, the functions gi are determined by the i-th order statistics of Btr, and are explicitly given in Section B. Novel-task error drops below the memorizing oracle as ϕ3 is learned (n ≈ 105–106) and is lowest once ϕ3 (g1) saturates. The error then rises back toward the memorizing oracle as the network learns higher order statistics through g2 (n ≳ 107). Further experimental details are in Section B.

Figure 6: Analytically solved random feature models outperform the memorizing oracle on novel tasks. We show test MSE on novel tasks (Dnovel) and on the training tasks β ∈ Dtr of a random feature model whose readout layer weight has been analytically solved, as a function of the number of training samples n. The limiting kernel function is the ICL kernel of Equation (11), set with kernel width σ = 3. We use T = 8, L = 4, d = 4, ϵ2 = 0.05, and tasks drawn from an isotropic prior. Shading shows the standard deviation over 5 trials. Past n ≈ 4× 103, the model’s error drops below that of the memorizing oracle (dMMSE). It remains well above the generalizing oracle (ridge) throughout.

Figure 9: Gaussian kernel learning curves on ICL Regression data. For four different settings (colors) of the task diversity T , we compute the expected test MSE as a function of the number of training samples n, and compare it to empirical errors obtained across 20 trials. Theoretical learning curve equations are provided in Section D, with validation of the eigensystem the equations are built off of provided in Sections E and F. Our data uses a Gaussian kernel with kernel width σker = √ 3, d = 5, L = 7, ϵ2 = 0.1 where our data is drawn x ∼ N (0, Id/(dL)). Additionally, as T → ∞, we find that the errors on the pretraining distribution match those of the true distribution, as expected. Further experimental details are in Section B.

papers.selection_reason: Theoretical analysis of in-context learning in kernel machines, relevant to understanding LLM in-context reasoning.
papers.title: You Don't Need Feature Learning to Do In-Context Learning
papers.tldr: Kernel analysis suggests that ICL generalization can arise without feature learning, as an early, low-degree approximation to a memorizing solution that eventually dominates with more training.

papers.abstract: Quantifying uncertainty over an entire LLM completion is critical for selective prediction and adaptive compute. Zero-cost signals such as mean token entropy and log-probability are local to tokens or to one completion, and self-consistency needs many extra completions. We show that Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) decoding for power sampling already estimates the normalizing constant of the power distribution, which gives the sequence-level R'enyi entropy (SRE) of the model's completion distribution at zero marginal cost, with a guarantee at every particle budget. A R'enyi chain rule extends this readout to a family of stepwise entropies of any order. We prove that orders above one are tied to the most likely token of each step, which explains why they track log-probability, while the order-1/2 member accumulates the log of per-step search effort. This member is the best zero-cost selective-prediction signal in 10 of 13 settings. On MATH500 its AUROC is 0.022 to 0.044 above log-probability with all four models and within length quartiles, and the same order is selected when each setting is held out. An 8-particle probe identifies the problems that benefit from more particles, and a two-pass policy matches 64-particle accuracy on MATH500 with 34.2% fewer particles over three seeds.
authors: Erfan Baghaei Potraghloo, Milad Heidari Sorkhehdizaj, Shahab Rahimirad, Aliasghar Pourghani, Seyedarmin Azizi, Souvik Kundu, Abolfazl Hashemi, Joseph Campbell, Vijay Gupta
bullets: Sequence-level uncertainty is needed for selective prediction, but token-level scores and self-consistency have limitations.
Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) power sampling estimates the completion distribution’s normalizing constant, yielding sequence-level Rényi entropy at every particle budget.
A Rényi chain rule provides stepwise entropy signals; order 1/2 captures cumulative per-step search effort and outperforms log-probability in 10 of 13 settings.
On MATH500, order 1/2 improves AUROC over log-probability by 0.022–0.044 across four models and length quartiles.
An 8-particle probe enables adaptive compute: a two-pass policy matches 64-particle accuracy while using 34.2% fewer particles over three seeds.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a zero-cost uncertainty signal for adaptive LLM reasoning and selective prediction, relevant to LLM reasoning methods.
papers.title: Free Lunch Uncertainty: Sequence-Level R\'enyi Entropy from Particle Decoding for Adaptive LLM Reasoning
papers.tldr: Particle decoding provides sequence-level Rényi entropy at no extra decoding cost, enabling stronger uncertainty estimates and adaptive allocation of LLM reasoning compute.

papers.abstract: Looped language models deepen computation without adding parameters, yet caching full-context key-value (KV) states across layers and rounds severely bounds serving batch size. We design a looped causal encoder-decoder (CED) that achieves recurrent depth with zero round-wise KV growth, addressing where and how to loop an asymmetric stack in which only sparse encoder layers generate global KV. We find that recurrence must be placed in the encoder to iteratively refine global KV representations rather than re-reading static decoder projections, which both drives language-modeling gains and preserves long-context scaling. Furthermore, training the encoder loop under stochastic recurrence depth induces a fixed-point equilibrium where every round losslessly shares the last round's KV cache. Compounding cross-layer and cross-round KV sharing, the resulting Looped CED matches an unlooped CED's minimal memory footprint and recovers 86-93% of a looped Transformer's gain with 1/6 of its global KV. To test serving at production scale, we loop the 552B-parameter DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash for 8 rounds on one 4xGB200 node: with per-layer and per-round KV the loop cannot fit a single 128K-token request, whereas Looped CED holds 36.8x less KV per token, fits 38 such requests (as many as the unlooped model), and serves 3.6x higher throughput on 8K-token prompts.
authors: Jiaqi Leng, Minshen Zhang, Zhaofeng Sun, Yu-Yang Qian, Peng Zhao, Hao Zhang
bullets: Problem: Standard looped Transformers grow KV caches across layers and rounds, limiting batch size and long-context serving.
Method: Place recurrence in sparse encoder layers to iteratively refine global KV representations, and train with stochastic recurrence depth to encourage KV sharing across rounds.
Contribution: Cross-layer and cross-round KV sharing yields recurrent computation without round-wise KV growth.
Results: Looped CED recovers 86–93% of a looped Transformer’s gain using one-sixth the global KV, while matching an unlooped CED’s memory footprint.
At production scale, it uses 36.8× less KV per token, fits 38 128K-token requests on one node, and delivers 3.6× higher throughput on 8K-token prompts.

papers.title: Looping Deeper Without Growing the KV Cache: Recurrent Depth for Causal Encoder-Decoders

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large-scale foundation models across resource-constrained, distributed clients presents significant computational and communication challenges. While merging Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) with Federated Learning (FL) enables rank-based flexibility, the interdependence of the adaptation matrices ($\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$) often complicates optimization. In this work, we theoretically demonstrate that LoRA fine-tuning with Gaussian initialization and a frozen $\mathbf{A}$ matrix acts as a stochastic approximation of full fine-tuning, where batch gradients are subject to a random, rank-dependent perturbation. Motivated by this insight, we propose freezing and periodically resampling $\mathbf{A}$ matrices at the client level. This strategy decouples the $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ gradients, diminishes LoRA low-rank constraints and reduces both computational and uplink communication overheads by 50\%, allowing for the reallocation of resources toward higher adaptation ranks. Furthermore, we show that in this frozen-$\mathbf{A}$ regime, the adaptation rank $r$ directly governs the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of the perturbed gradients. Specifically, we find that the SNR increases linearly with $r$, implying that clients' learning rates must be dynamically scaled with their adaptation ranks for higher utility. Building on these foundations, we introduce SPRA-LoRA (Stochastic Projection Rank-Aware LoRA), a federated rank-aware fine-tuning strategy that utilizes frozen, resampled $\mathbf{A}$ matrices and rank-dependent learning rates for clients. We also prove its convergence with heterogeneous client resources. Our experiments across benchmark datasets demonstrate that SPRA-LoRA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines with half the overhead on clients.
authors: Saber Malekmohammadi, Kevin Kuo, Virginia Smith, Golnoosh Farnadi
bullets: Shows that frozen-$\mathbf{A}$ LoRA with Gaussian initialization approximates full fine-tuning through rank-dependent stochastic gradient perturbations.
Freezes and periodically resamples client-side $\mathbf{A}$ matrices to decouple adaptation gradients and ease low-rank constraints.
Finds that gradient signal-to-noise ratio increases linearly with adaptation rank, motivating rank-aware client learning rates.
Proves convergence under heterogeneous client resources.
Experiments on benchmark datasets report consistent outperformance over state-of-the-art baselines with half the client overhead.

papers.abstract: Recent work has identified a set of emergent symbolic mechanisms that support abstract reasoning in large language models, but it remains unclear what factors drive the emergence of these mechanisms. To address this question, we trained neural networks from scratch on abstract sequence tasks, varying both architectural and data distributional factors, and investigated the effects of these factors on the emergence of symbolic mechanisms. Using representational, attentional, and causal mediation analyses, we first confirmed that transformer-based language models trained from scratch on our task developed symbolic mechanisms. We then found that, across multiple axes of data diversity, greater diversity produced stronger symbolic signatures. Surprisingly, the same signatures emerged in modified transformer architectures and even multilayer perceptrons, indicating that architectural inductive biases are not necessary for the development of symbolic mechanisms. We also observed consistent patterns in an entity-attribute binding task. Together, these findings identify data diversity, not architecture, as the primary driver of emergent symbolic computation in neural networks.
bullets: The study examines what causes symbolic mechanisms supporting abstract reasoning to emerge.
Networks were trained from scratch on abstract sequence tasks while varying architecture and data distribution.
Representational, attentional, and causal mediation analyses confirmed the emergence of symbolic mechanisms in transformers.
Greater diversity across multiple data dimensions produced stronger symbolic signatures.
Similar mechanisms emerged in modified transformers, multilayer perceptrons, and an entity–attribute binding task.

papers.abstract: Attention, the core of language models, is a digital calculation over tokens: an exponential selects them, a division normalizes and a positional code sets the order. We show that attention can instead emerge from the synchronization of a receiver with its context tokens. Each past token is an oscillator whose state carries its content and whose frequency drifts with its age. The present token selects them by content, aligning an antenna with its query, and by position, setting the frequency of a receiver with its dial. Solving Kuramoto's problem for this receiver yields an attention layer in closed form with two phases: above a critical coupling set by the context, the receiver locks and its weights normalize; below it, it stays silent and its weights sum to less than one. Trained networks use both phases to select, abstain and count, fail where the theory predicts and keep reading far beyond the training length. Each part of attention finds its place in one device, a radio head: it tunes in to what to hear and when, and stays silent when nothing relevant is on air.
authors: Llu\'is Arola-Fern\'andez, Aissam Khadraoui, Alex Arenas
bullets: Models past tokens as oscillators whose content and age determine their state and frequency.
Uses Kuramoto synchronization to derive a closed-form attention layer with normalized weights above a critical coupling threshold.
Below the threshold, the receiver abstains, producing weights that sum to less than one.
Trained networks exploit both phases to select, abstain, and count, and continue reading beyond their training length.
The theory predicts observed failure cases, though the abstract does not specify quantitative results or evaluation settings.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly trusted with mathematical, scientific and engineering work, yet their mistakes are often confidently written and hard to spot. A single wrong step tends to propagate, making the model waste inference tokens following a false premise. Existing safeguards either check only the final answer and restart from scratch, or rely on a verifier LLM that competes for GPU capacity and slows down response time. We propose online, deterministic verification: many kinds of reasoning steps can be validated by code, so a step can be verified in real time, as it is written, without any model call or GPU use. Whenever a check fails, we point out the mistake and let the model continue from the same spot. We demonstrate this approach on symbolic mathematics, where derivations already contain explicit expressions that a computer algebra system can check in milliseconds. Tested on the ASyMoB benchmark with three open-weights models, our online validation improves accuracy by 1.4-5.6 percentage points, corresponding to a 1.8-14.9% net reduction in incorrect answers, while increasing token usage by only 6-7%. Because the verifier is independent of the model, the approach complements progress in LLMs rather than competing with it: every new model can benefit immediately, and the benefit grows as deterministic checkers extend to more kinds of reasoning steps.
authors: Rotem Elimelech, Michael Shalyt, Ido Kaminer
bullets: Targets errors that propagate through LLM reasoning and are costly to detect only at the end.
Uses code-based, real-time verification of reasoning steps rather than a separate verifier LLM.
When a check fails, the model is alerted and continues from the error location instead of restarting.
On ASyMoB with three open-weight models, accuracy improved by 1.4–5.6 percentage points with 6–7% more tokens.
Demonstrated for symbolic mathematics; broader gains depend on extending deterministic checkers to other reasoning steps.

papers.abstract: Knowledge editing has emerged as a promising approach for efficiently updating embedded knowledge in large language models (LLMs). It first computes an ideal target hidden state that steers the LLM toward the new output, and then edits the model parameters so that the original hidden state is mapped to this target. While most existing methods focus on the second stage of parameter editing in preserving other knowledge, we find that the upstream construction of the target hidden state also plays an important role in allocating the model's limited capacity space. We first establish a theoretical connection between interference in the parameter space and interference between target hidden states, showing that the two are positively correlated. Building on this insight, we propose a simple yet effective $\ell_1$ regularization method that prunes away unnecessary ``tentacles'' of each knowledge vector, retaining only the essential components. With fewer extraneous tentacles, each edit affects less other knowledge, enabling better coexistence. Extensive experiments across multiple LLMs and benchmark datasets verify the effectiveness of our method. Code: https://github.com/wintersdragon-c/STO.
authors: Dongyao Chen, Jiayun Lei, Zhiyuan Ji, Zhiying Deng, Wei Liu, Xiaobo Sun
bullets: Knowledge-editing methods must allocate limited model capacity when constructing target hidden states, not only when editing parameters.
The paper shows a positive correlation between interference among target hidden states and interference in parameter space.
It applies ℓ1 regularization to prune extraneous “tentacles” from knowledge vectors while preserving essential components.
Experiments across multiple LLMs and benchmark datasets verify improved coexistence of edited and existing knowledge.

papers.abstract: Does a useful self-update remain useful after the model updates again? Third Eye separates immediate performance from the outcome of a further native update. We evaluate five 3-8B backbones on math and code: 64 fresh runs, three candidates per run, and three continuations per candidate. Selection and final scoring use disjoint items. In the balanced Qwen3-4B/Llama-3.2-3B comparison, immediate-selected utility is near zero, but continuation reduces it by 1.78 percentage points (simultaneous 95% interval [0.68, 2.88]). Candidate-averaged immediate utility is already negative: selection partly accounts for the apparently neutral first step. Continuation also lowers utility for SmolLM3-3B and Llama-3.1-8B; Qwen3-8B remains inconclusive. Target and out-of-distribution losses dominate retention changes. Matched recipe and recipient-donor controls identify neither a reliable mitigation nor a single mechanism. The results support evaluating persistent self-updates as adaptation transitions, with independent scoring and a no-update baseline, rather than interpreting immediate performance as their full value.
authors: Sujato Dutta, Padala Indira Sneha, Kypu Mahitha, Shashank Vanga, Neeraj Choudhary
bullets: Third Eye separates immediate utility from the utility of a subsequent native update.

In the balanced Qwen3-4B/Llama-3.2-3B comparison, immediate-selected utility was near zero, while continuation reduced it by 1.78 percentage points.
Candidate-averaged immediate utility was already negative, suggesting selection can mask first-step harm.
Independent scoring and a no-update baseline are needed to assess persistent self-updates; no reliable mitigation or single mechanism was identified.

papers.abstract: Preference labels align model training, but the judgments behind them are difficult to inspect or verify. In this paper, we examine how preference construction can be checked when intermediate decisions are recorded, and which of them remain uncertain. We present Symbolic Preference Labeling, a method in which a pretrained language model classifies predefined attributes of prompts and responses. Explicit rules assign response verdicts, and a fixed verdict ranking determines the preference label. Each preference label has a recorded derivation: the response verdicts and preference label can be recomputed from the stored attribute assignments, rules, and verdict ranking without rerunning the language model. On 200 prompts annotated by human raters, the language model produces valid structured outputs for 192 prompts. All eight parsing failures occur in the subset of self-harm prompts marked as harmful. Using 465 preference pairs, we train one policy model with direct preference optimization across five training seeds. Mean measured benign refusal is 40.82 percent on 1,319 benign prompts that resemble unsafe ones, and mean measured toxic refusal is 84.98 percent on 655 toxic prompts. This study distinguishes the reproducibility of preference labels from attribute correctness. The recorded derivations make preference construction open to inspection, while attribute correctness and semantic safety require separate validation.
bullets: Preference construction is audited through stored derivations that allow labels to be recomputed without rerunning the language model.
A pretrained language model classifies predefined prompt and response attributes, after which explicit rules determine verdicts and preferences.
On 200 human-annotated prompts, 192 produced valid structured outputs; all parsing failures occurred among harmful self-harm prompts.
A policy trained on 465 preference pairs showed measured benign refusal of 40.82% and toxic refusal of 84.98% across the evaluated prompt sets.
Reproducible label derivations do not establish attribute correctness or semantic safety, which require separate validation.

papers.abstract: The demand for personalized LLMs is shifting from style imitation toward content quality. We investigate whether self-distillation can bridge this gap in existing fine-tuning paradigm. To address this limitation, we introduce MIRROR(Meta- personalization by Internalizing Reference-Revealed On-policy Reflections), a novel self-distillation framework that shifts LLM personalization from imitation toward preference internalization. First, we replace reference-token imitation with reference-revealed on-policy self-distillation, aligning the model's next-token distributions along its own generation trajectories with those of its reference-conditioned self, thereby internalizing user preferences rather than reproducing reference wording.Second, we introduce MIRROR-F, a focal plug-in that augments on-policy distributional alignment with selective supervision over informative reference tokens, thereby strengthening content generation while preserving user-specific expression. Across three personalized generation benchmarks, two model scales, and complementary reference-based and LLM-based evaluations, MIRROR and MIRROR-F achieve leading overall personalization performance and superior text quality, while exhibiting less catastrophic forgetting than SFT-based baselines on three unseen personalized generation tasks. The gains are consistent across model scales and application scenarios, translating to improved performance in LLM personalization tasks.
bullets: Targets the shift from stylistic imitation toward higher-quality, preference-aware content generation.
Aligns on-policy token distributions from the model’s own generations with those of its reference-conditioned counterpart.
MIRROR-F adds selective supervision on informative reference tokens to strengthen content generation while preserving personal expression.
Across three benchmarks, two model scales, and multiple evaluations, both methods show strong personalization and text-quality performance.
The framework also reduces catastrophic forgetting relative to SFT baselines on three unseen personalization tasks.

papers.abstract: Activation steering manipulates large language model behavior by intervening on internal activations, but the mechanistic basis of these interventions remains poorly understood. We decompose refusal steering into component-level interventions across four open-weight models, identifying the sparse subsets of attention and MLP components whose steering suffices to reproduce the full behavioral effect. We find that refusal directions concentrate in sparse component mechanisms comprising 28--48\% of upstream components, retaining 88--101\% of steering effectiveness. Within these mechanisms, effective steering further concentrates in approximately 50\% of residual stream dimensions, retaining 85--98\% of the component-mechanism baseline, consistent with a privileged basis structure. Sparsity thus operates at two levels: which components are steered, and which dimensions within those components carry the signal. Together these findings show that refusal is not diffusely encoded across a transformer but assembled by a structured, identifiable mechanism, providing a foundation for mechanistic understanding of how refusal behaviors are represented and steered. To facilitate reproducibility, we release all code and raw experimental results in https://github.com/wang-research-lab/Refusal_Mechanisms.
bullets: Across four open-weight models, sparse attention and MLP component subsets reproduced most of the full refusal-steering effect.
These subsets comprised 28–48% of upstream components while retaining 88–101% effectiveness.
Within selected components, about half of residual-stream dimensions retained 85–98% of the component-level effect.
The results suggest a privileged basis structure and an identifiable mechanism for refusal behavior.
Code and raw experimental results are publicly released for reproducibility.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Two-level sparsity in transformer refusal mechanisms. The residual stream passes through a sequence of attention and MLP components; a sparse subset (28–48% across models) forms a sufficient mechanism to steer refusal behavior, where steering a component via orthogonalization means removing the output’s projection onto the refusal direction. Zooming into each identified component, effective steering also requires intervening on only the same ≈ 50% of residual dimensions across all components, consistent with a privileged basis structure in the residual stream. Prior work steers all dimensions of all upstream components simultaneously by intervening on the residual stream; we instead steer individual component outputs, allowing the residual connection to proceed unaltered.

Figure 2: Residual stream steering effectiveness as a function of dimension percentage. Each marker shows the ASR recovered relative to full-dimensional steering, plotted against the fraction of hidden dimensions used. Marker labels indicate the corresponding norm explanation threshold t – the fraction of ∥r∗∥2 explained by the retained dimensions. Across all four models, retaining ∼50% of dimensions at the 95% norm threshold recovers over 90% of full steering ASR, with some models exceeding the dense baseline. Performance degrades sharply only as the budget falls below the 50% norm threshold, confirming that the refusal direction is concentrated in a sparse set of high-magnitude coordinates.

Figure 7: Distribution of refusal direction coefficients at l∗. Coordinate values of r∗ for each model. Blue bars represent typical dimensions within the central distribution; red bars with black outlines denote statistical outliers (> 2.5× IQR). The y-axis is log-scaled to make the sparse high-magnitude dimensions visible. Summary statistics (µ, σ) and outlier counts are provided for each model.

Figure 5: Component write profiles sorted by refusal importance rank. Top 10% of coordinates by write magnitude shown for each component, sorted by |r∗i | descending so the most refusal-important coordinates appear on the left. Outputs are unit-normalised to control for LayerNorm-induced scale differences. Point size scales with write magnitude; color indicates relative layer depth (early: purple, late: gold). High-magnitude writes are distributed throughout the coordinate space rather than concentrated at high refusal importance ranks, indicating component-specific rather than shared sparse subspaces.

Figure 4: Per-component linear attribution to the refusal direction. For each component in the identified mechanism, bars show the scalar projection of its difference-in-mean vector onto r∗, measuring how much each component contributes to assembling the refusal direction at l∗. Attention components (orange) and MLP components (blue) are shown by layer index. Negative values indicate components that write against the refusal direction. Each reconstruction scores (fraction of ∥r∗∥2 recovered) is provided in the top left.

Figure 10: First-Round Component Ablation: Initial Redundancy. The absolute drop in ASR when individual components are removed from the initial, unpruned candidate circuit. The flat profile across all models indicates that no single component acts as a bottleneck in the presence of the full redundant set.

Figure 6: Exhaustive steering performance of the difference-in-means direction extracted from each layer’s input. Steering is performed in the residual stream at the layer input, replicating prior work. The highest performing steering direction is highlighted in red and is used to find the mechanism in our study. All directions are extracted from the last post-instruction token. The highest ASR value is also used as a reference value that the mechanisms in Table 1 compare against.

Figure 3: Sparse mechanisms versus their complement sets. Each arrow points from the complement (excluded components, hollow diamond) to the identified mechanism (included components, filled circle). Mechanisms comprising 28–48% of upstream components reproduce 88–101% of the full steering effect, while their complements – the remaining 52–72% of components – largely fail to elicit refusal.

Figure 8: Component cosine similarity with r∗ on harmful vs. harmless prompts. Colored bars show the IQR of cosine similarity between each component’s last-token output and r∗ over harmful prompts (blue: MLP, orange: attention). Outlined boxes show the corresponding IQR over harmless prompts. Red lines indicate the selectivity shift – the difference in mean cosine similarity between the two distributions. A large upward red line indicates a component that aligns more strongly with the refusal direction on harmful content than harmless content.

Figure 9: Mechanism Sufficiency: Leave-One-Out ASR Drop. The absolute drop in Attack Success Rate (ASR) when each individual component is removed from the identified sparse mechanism. Higher bars indicate components that act as critical bottlenecks for successful refusal steering. Blue bars represent MLP layers, and orange bars represent Attention mechanisms.

Table 6: Membership containment across threshold settings. Shared is the number of components present in both mechanisms. Subset? indicates whether the smaller mechanism is a strict subset of the larger. Every τ relation nests; α = 0.90 ⊆ α = 0.95 nests for three of four models; α = 0.95 ⊆ α = 0.99 nests for none, including the Mistral-3.2-Small case where both mechanisms have size 10 but differ by one component.

Table 4: Rotation control experiment results. For each model, the same number of dimensions k used in the 95% norm-threshold sparse steering condition is selected from a randomly rotated direction r̃ = Qr∗, where Q ∼ Haar(O(d)). Orig. Rel. ASR is the ASR of the original sparse steering as a percentage of the full-component dense baseline. Rot. Rel. ASR is the mean ASR across N = 5 random rotations; Std is the standard deviation across trials. ∆ is the difference. Near-zero rotated ASR confirms that the specific nativebasis coordinates selected by the norm threshold are functionally privileged rather than interchangeable with an arbitrary coordinate system of the same size.

Table 8: Per-model hyperparameters. Target layer indicates the layer l∗ at which the refusal direction r∗ was extracted. The % Norm Explained controls the fraction of the direction’s squared norm explained by the retained dimensions, resulting in the chosen dimensions and ASRs reported in Table 1. α is the projection retention threshold used in Stage 1 greedy elimination and τ the ASR-drop tolerance used as the Stage 2 stopping rule; sensitivity to both is reported in Appendix K.

Table 2: Capability change relative to the unmodified model. MMLU and GSM8k are in accuracy points, so negative ∆ is degradation; Pile is in perplexity, so positive ∆ is degradation. ∆Full is the dense intervention applied to all upstream components; ∆Mech is the identified sparse mechanism under the 95% norm-explained coordinate mask. Bold marks the smaller degradation within each pair. The sparse mechanism is equal or better in ten of twelve cells.

Table 1: Sparse refusal mechanisms identified across four models. The layer indices of the selected attention and MLP components in the identified mechanism are provided above. Components is the fraction of upstream components comprising the mechanism. Mechanism ASR reports attack success rate as a percentage of the full residual-stream steering baseline: orthogonalizing the dense direction r∗ at the input of l∗, as in prior work, which is the peak value of the layer sweep in Appendix C. A value above 100% indicates the mechanism steers more effectively than this single-point intervention. Sparse Dim. ASR reports attack success rate when steering the mechanism using only a subset of hidden state dimensions, with the percentage of residual dimensions used given in parentheses. We exclude the embedding matrix as it is never retained by the elimination procedure across models.

Table 3: Steering effectiveness when using only bottom-magnitude dimensions of r∗. Relative ASR is reported as a percentage of the full-direction baseline. Despite comparable dimension budgets to the top-magnitude condition, bottom-magnitude steering fails to elicit refusal across all models.

Table 7: Stability of Stage 2 under random tie-breaking. Tie steps is the fraction of elimination steps on the deterministic trajectory at which at least two candidates fall within ϵ = 0.005 of the minimum drop, and mean tie set size the average number of such candidates. Remaining columns aggregate over four realizations per model (three random seeds plus the deterministic baseline). Core counts components present in all four realizations; peripheral counts components present in some but not all.

Table 5: Sensitivity of mechanism size and behavior to the Stage 1 and Stage 2 thresholds. Each cell reports mechanism size as a raw count, the percentage of the component budget D = 2l∗ + 1 in parentheses, and held-out test ASR (n = 512, LlamaGuard-3). Allcomp. ASR is the reference condition in which every one of the D upstream components is steered. The paper’s operating point is bolded. Test ASR remains within approximately five points of that operating point across every threshold setting.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes sparse component and dimension structure underlying refusal steering in LLMs.
papers.title: Component and Dimension Sparsity in Transformer Refusal Mechanisms
papers.tldr: Refusal steering in transformers is driven by a sparse, structured subset of components and residual dimensions rather than being diffusely distributed.

papers.abstract: Post-LayerNorm Transformers have seen limited practical adoption due to enduring difficulties in scaling them to large depths. While prior research has focused on stabilising Post-LayerNorm by improving conditioning at initialisation, stability often deteriorates when models are trained with large learning rates, forcing additional compromises. In the decoder-only settings we study, existing Post-LayerNorm methods fail to outperform strong Pre-LayerNorm baselines. We propose KiteNorm, a post-norm training method designed to break this trend by constraining hidden-state variance. This approach is motivated by a bound on the LayerNorm Jacobian suggesting that variance growth contributes to gradient vanishing, alongside empirical evidence linking it to rank collapse. KiteNorm combines residual scaling and variance regularisation to maintain stability throughout training, supported by scalarised double-normalisation that provides separately learnable scales for the skip and residual branches. Across decoder-only Transformers up to 1.3B parameters, KiteNorm improves training stability and outperforms leading baselines at their optimal learning rates, with scaling laws favouring KiteNorm across depth, width, batch size, and training budget. Ablations show that each component is necessary for the full stability and performance gains.
bullets: Post-LayerNorm Transformers can become unstable at large learning rates and depths, limiting their practical use.
KiteNorm combines residual scaling with variance regularisation to constrain hidden-state variance and reduce gradient vanishing and rank collapse.
Scalarised double-normalisation gives the skip and residual branches independently learnable scales.
In decoder-only Transformers up to 1.3B parameters, KiteNorm improves stability and outperforms leading baselines at their optimal learning rates.
Scaling laws favour KiteNorm across depth, width, batch size, and training budget; ablations indicate both components are necessary.

papers.abstract: Interpretability tools are usually built for one model at a time: a refusal direction, a truthfulness probe, or a steering vector is found with labeled data inside the model it explains. We ask whether such tools can be carried to other models through a map between residual streams fit only on unlabeled prompts. We transfer a refusal direction, tested causally by addition and ablation, and two read-out tools, a correctness direction and a sentiment probe, across 110 pairs of models from five families and 1B to 72B parameters and between base and instruction-tuned models, with controls for specificity and five seeds. How much transfers depends on what the map was fit on. A map fit on ordinary questions recovers 54\% of the target's own refusal steering and 16\% to 77\% of its correctness gain; adding unlabeled prompts from the region where the tool operates raises these to 102\% and 88\% to 98\%, while control directions recover at most 1\%. We prove that a linear map behaves this way whenever two models correspond linearly on the data it covers, and a label-free coverage score derived from this result tracks recovery across more than 16,000 runs and explains earlier reports that maps between models fail across domains. Carried read-out tools outperform anything the target's unlabeled representations yield. Interpretability results, once found, can be reused across models at the cost of a few unlabeled prompts.
bullets: Tests refusal steering, correctness directions, and sentiment probes across 110 model pairs spanning five families, 1B–72B parameters, and base/instruction-tuned variants.
Transfer quality depends on whether mapping data covers the tool’s operating region; targeted prompts substantially improve recovery over ordinary questions.
A coverage score predicts transfer success across more than 16,000 runs and explains failures when mappings are fit outside the relevant domain.
Transferred read-out tools outperform tools learned solely from the target model’s unlabeled representations.
Scope: results concern linear residual-stream maps and the tested interpretability tools, model pairs, and prompt coverage settings.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview. A tool built on a source model is carried into a target model through a linear map fit on paired activations, and applied to the target without any of the target’s labels. Transfer is measured as the share of the target’s own effect that the carried tool reproduces. The map’s training data decides how much transfers: fit on general text alone, the carried refusal direction recovers 54% of the native effect, and adding 16 unlabeled harmful and 16 unlabeled harmless prompts raises recovery to 102%. The carried tool r̂T is rebuilt from the mapped representations of the prompts that define rS ; for a difference of means this equals the map’s linear part applied to rS , up to renormalization.

Figure 2: Refusal steering carried across models. (a) Refusal of harmless prompts against steering strength, averaged over the 10 targets at each target’s working depth (one seed). (b, c) Recovery at each target’s working strength for every source and target pair, averaged over five seeds, with the general map (mean 54%) and with 16 harmful and 16 harmless prompts added (mean 102%). Values above 110% are shown at the darkest shade.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding speeds up language models by having a lightweight drafter propose future tokens that the target model verifies in parallel. Block diffusion drafters such as DFlash predict an entire block in one forward pass, and DDTree builds draft trees directly from their per-position distributions. Each distribution implicitly assumes that the drafter's own greedy continuation is accepted, whereas a draft tree improves over a chain only on branches that leave this greedy path. Once a path forks, the drafter's top-1 accuracy drops from 89% to 18% and its top candidates often miss the true token. Re-running the drafter from the fork token largely restores its accuracy, showing that the errors stem from conditioning on an outdated prefix rather than from limited model capacity. In this paper, we introduce DForkTree, a training-free method that re-anchors each branch on its own tokens. It adjusts the drafter's scores with pointwise mutual information from target-generated n-grams, weighted more heavily after a fork, and a layer-wise GPU search recovers the exact optimal tree under these scores. On Qwen3.5-4B and 9B, DForkTree outperforms all baselines on every benchmark, by up to 41.5% over DFlash and 15.1% over DDTree, with average speedups of up to 4.75x over autoregressive decoding.
bullets: Problem: Block-diffusion drafters become inaccurate after a tree branch because they condition on an outdated prefix.
Method: Re-anchor each branch using its own tokens, adjust scores with target-generated n-gram PMI, and emphasize corrections after forks.
The method is training-free and uses a layer-wise GPU search to recover the exact optimal tree under its scoring function.
On Qwen3.5-4B and 9B, DForkTree outperforms all reported baselines across benchmarks.
It achieves up to 4.75× speedup over autoregressive decoding, with gains of up to 41.5% over DFlash and 15.1% over DDTree.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts language models are cheap to run per token but expensive to hold in GPU memory, which drives the cost of serving them in production. One-shot expert compression shrinks them after a single calibration pass. Its two current state-of-the-art methods are REAP for expert pruning, which deletes the least salient experts, and REAM for expert merging, which merges them into the most salient ones. Both have been evaluated only on academic benchmarks. We compare the two on five multilingual production tasks of a web-hosting company, from classification to the generation of marketing HTML email templates, with two 30B-parameter models (Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 and the hybrid Mamba-attention Nemotron-3.5-Lightning) at 25% and 50% of experts removed and the same calibration data. Pruning wins: on the same rows, REAP is significantly better in 16 of 20 comparisons and REAM in 2. At 25%, REAP keeps 93.6% of Qwen3-30B's generative quality and REAM 62.5%, although on benchmarks the two are within a point for the same model. The damage concentrates in the output contract rather than the content: 89.8-95.2% of each significant loss on email templates comes from hard-gate failures such as invalid JSON, broken mobile layouts and runaway generation, and most failed non-English domain descriptions copy the prompt's English opening phrase. Cross-perplexity and logit divergence, two diagnostics from the REAP paper, also track production quality, as does the rate of repetition loops; n-gram diversity does not. We close with practical guidance for compressing MoE models for production.
bullets: The study compares REAP expert pruning with REAM expert merging across five web-hosting production tasks and two 30B-parameter MoE models.
At 25% expert removal, REAP preserves 93.6% of Qwen3-30B’s generative quality, versus 62.5% for REAM.
Across 20 matched comparisons, REAP performs significantly better in 16, while REAM does so in 2.
Most quality loss in email generation comes from hard-gate failures such as invalid JSON, broken mobile layouts, and runaway generation—not loss of content.
Cross-perplexity, logit divergence, and repetition-loop rates track production quality; n-gram diversity does not.

figures.caption: Figure 2: REAP beats REAM on the same rows in 16 of 20 comparisons. REAP − REAM in each task’s metric (positive = REAP better), at 25% (grey) and 50% (black) of experts removed for each base model. Bars are 95% paired-bootstrap CIs. Filled markers are significant after Holm correction over the 20 comparisons. REAM is better only on brand names at 50%.

Figure 1: Merging falls behind on generation. papers.title: Prune, Don't Merge: Expert Compression of Mixture-of-Experts LLMs on Multilingual Production Tasks

papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation lets a language agent act as its own Teacher by conditioning on privileged context such as skills written from its own trajectories. Its guidance, however, is weighted by how much this context shifts token likelihoods rather than by whether it improves behavior, so errors in self-written skills return through later updates. We propose environment-calibrated on-policy self-distillation, which uses environmental outcomes to decide how much to trust the Teacher's current guidance and which self-written skills to reinforce. Command-level advantages, estimated by comparing commands executed at similar observations, scale each Teacher preference and reward reflections and skills whose induced preferences favor higher-advantage commands. Without skills at inference, 3B and 7B agents reach 90.5% and 93.3% macro success on seen ALFWorld tasks and 75.5% and 80.5% success on WebShop. On unseen ALFWorld tasks, they outperform GRPO under the same protocol by 11.0 and 7.6 percentage points, respectively. In an ablation study, supervising only executable commands rather than the Actor's full response raises 3B WebShop success from 52.3% to 75.0%.
bullets: Self-written skills can propagate errors when guidance is weighted by token-likelihood shifts instead of behavioral improvement.
ECOS estimates command-level advantages by comparing commands taken in similar observations.
These advantages weight Teacher preferences and reinforce skills that favor higher-advantage commands.
Without inference-time skills, ECOS achieves strong performance on seen ALFWorld and WebShop tasks and outperforms GRPO on unseen ALFWorld tasks.
An ablation shows that supervising only executable commands substantially improves 3B WebShop success over supervising the full response.

papers.tldr: ECOS improves on-policy self-distillation for language agents by using environment outcomes to calibrate which self-generated guidance and skills to trust.

papers.abstract: A worked solution can make self-generated training targets shorter and cheaper, but accuracy on the practiced operation may hide how well a model can reuse newly learned rules. We study this choice in a 2B-parameter reasoning model learning two invented quantitative rules. The model generates targets from a rule sheet alone or from the sheet plus a program-written worked solution; targets are accepted for final-answer correctness, and the support is removed for fine-tuning and evaluation. Training questions request forward use in one segment; composition requires sequential reuse of the same rule across two segments. After six passes, using a program-checked numerical signature, sheet-only targets lead by 24.3 percentage points (95% item-bootstrap CI 14.6-34.0) on composition in a prospective test. On unseen argument values, observed forward accuracy is identical (87.5% each), but composition accuracy is 58.3% versus 23.6%, a 34.7-point gap (25.7-43.8). An independently sampled second target-bank pair repeats the direction (+14.6 points, 2.1-26.0). Ten passes on the shorter worked-solution targets, approximately matching the domain tokens of six sheet-only passes while changing other training quantities, narrow the gap to 16.3 points (6.3-26.7) in the first bank pair and 6.2 points (-6.3 to 18.8) in the second, where the pre-specified test does not hold. At six passes each, the worked-solution policy uses fewer capture tokens and less update time, yet the trained models use 2.6 times as many generated tokens per composition success under the numerical signature (2.1 times in the second bank pair). Choosing a capture context therefore requires testing how the new rules are reused, alongside the inference cost of those uses, rather than relying on forward accuracy alone.
bullets: The study compares rule-sheet-only targets with targets generated using rule sheets plus program-written worked solutions.
With six training passes, sheet-only targets improve composition accuracy by 24.3 percentage points in a prospective test.
On unseen arguments, forward accuracy is identical at 87.5%, while composition accuracy is 58.3% for sheet-only versus 23.6% with worked solutions.
More passes with shorter worked-solution targets narrow the gap, but do not consistently eliminate it across target-bank pairs.
Worked solutions reduce capture tokens and update time, yet require 2.1–2.6× more generated tokens per successful composition.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates training data generation and compositional rule reuse in a reasoning model, relevant to LLM training and continual learning.
papers.title: A Cost That Practice Accuracy Hides: Worked Solutions in Self-Generated Training Data and the Compositional Use of New Rules
papers.tldr: Worked solutions make self-generated training targets cheaper but can substantially impair a model’s ability to compose newly learned rules, despite equal forward accuracy.

papers.abstract: Systematic literature reviews (SRs) remain slow and labor-intensive, and most automation tools address single stages of the workflow. We present PARIS (PRISMA Agentic Research Intelligence System), an open-source framework in which a conductor agent running in Claude Code orchestrates 15 specialized large language model (LLM) agents, from scoping a research question to exporting a manuscript draft. Agents are specified declaratively, coordinate exclusively through persisted artifacts that the conductor validates before every transition, and delegate retrieval, bibliometric analysis and scoring to deterministic Python utilities. Three human checkpoints gate study inclusion, corpus adequacy and the synthesis outline. We also introduce QualityScore, a pre-synthesis index that aggregates normalized network, bibliometric, semantic and process sub-scores into a 0-100 grade. Two case studies illustrate both: AI chatbots and university students' learning (388 records, 100 included) and AI-assisted SR methods (131 records, 123 included, QualityScore 69.1 recomputed with a proxy network sub-score). They show end-to-end feasibility across domains and the diagnostic use of QualityScore: in the first run, corpus improvements chosen at the corpus-adequacy checkpoint raised the score from 74.6 to 81.9 and the number of pre-2023 studies from 1 to 19. Audits of both runs exposed failure modes: incomplete retrieval, counts that drifted between agents, unrecorded or delegated checkpoint decisions and a grade that depends on how citation data are handled. PARIS fully supports 8 of the 27 PRISMA 2020 items and partially supports 11. Output quality has so far been judged only by an internal reviewer agent; independent validation against human reviews is the next step.
bullets: Orchestrates 15 specialized LLM agents through persisted, validated artifacts and deterministic Python utilities.
Includes three human checkpoints for study inclusion, corpus adequacy, and synthesis-outline approval.
Introduces QualityScore, a 0–100 index combining network, bibliometric, semantic, and process measures.
Two case studies demonstrate end-to-end feasibility and show that corpus improvements can raise the quality score and increase coverage of older studies.
Audits found incomplete retrieval, inconsistent counts, undocumented checkpoint decisions, and sensitivity to citation-data handling; independent human validation remains pending.

papers.abstract: Transformers are built with continuous symmetries in the attention mechanism. We derive $ρ$, a scalar invariant that measures each head's capacity to couple to rotary positional encodings. This framework allows us to analyze heads without forward passes, opening a new research direction into data-independent analysis of modern LLMs. Empirically, we find that $ρ$ predicts induction heads, the most-studied circuit type in mechanistic interpretability, with Spearman correlation between $-0.55$ and $-0.74$ across four bias-free RoPE models spanning $135$M to $7$B parameters. As a preliminary proof of concept, we use $ρ$ to apply YaRN to only the top-50% positional heads, which degrades perplexity less than uniform application. Code is available at https://github.com/MPedraBento/rho-invariant.
bullets: ρ measures each attention head’s capacity to couple with rotary positional encodings.
Across four bias-free RoPE models (135M–7B parameters), ρ predicts induction heads with Spearman correlations from −0.55 to −0.74.
Applying YaRN only to the top 50% of positional heads causes less perplexity degradation than applying it uniformly.
The study focuses on bias-free RoPE models and presents targeted YaRN application as a preliminary proof of concept.
