papers.abstract: In this work, we study whether frontier agents can continually improve real-world AI infrastructure over long horizons. We introduce Infrathon, a benchmark of diverse, long-horizon AI infrastructure optimization tasks across different levels. We evaluate six models across 150 runs with 24-hour budgets, totaling over 10,000 GPU-hours. Our results show that model rankings vary with the evaluation horizon, while 135 of the 150 runs achieve further improvements during the second half of their budgets. These findings indicate that shorter evaluations can overlook both optimization gains and changes in relative model performance. We also find agents can discover solutions that outperform human-designed baselines: Claude Opus 5.5 increases the mean KV-cache compression ratio from $6.82\times$ with the human-designed Quant-VideoGen codec to $19.86\times$. Analysis of agent trajectories identifies task violations, unreliable testing, and premature completion as barriers to sustained improvement. Together, our Infrathon framework provides resources for constructing long-horizon tasks, evaluating frontier agents, and discovering good infrastructure solutions. Code is available at https://github.com/InfrathonX/Infrathon
bullets: Introduces a benchmark covering diverse, multi-level, long-horizon AI infrastructure optimization tasks.
Evaluates six models across 150 runs with 24-hour budgets, totaling over 10,000 GPU-hours.
Further improvements occurred in 135 of 150 runs during the second half of evaluation, showing shorter tests may miss progress.
Agents discovered solutions surpassing human-designed baselines; Claude Opus 5.5 improved mean KV-cache compression from 6.82× to 19.86× on one task.
Trajectory analysis highlights task violations, unreliable testing, and premature completion as barriers to sustained optimization.

papers.title: Infrathon: Benchmarking Language Agents for Real-World, Long-Horizon AI Infra Optimization
papers.tldr: Infrathon shows that evaluating language agents on long-horizon AI infrastructure optimization is essential because their performance and model rankings can change substantially over time.

papers.abstract: Small multimodal models can misjudge emotion when words, voice, and visual cues conflict. We present EmoHarness, which runs such a model, the frozen student, inside a harness: the prompts, settings, and verification code around its calls. A human-written starting harness, the scaffold, numbers the student's visual observations, transcript, and prosody descriptions as citable evidence and has the student weigh candidate emotions against it. In Meta-Harness Evolving (MHE), a stronger LLM, the Builder, reads the student's errors and execution traces offline and edits the harness; static checks and validation gates decide which edits are kept, and the Builder never sees evaluation items. On 5,507 MME-Emotion items, EmoHarness raises task-macro Recognition by 7.6-13.4 points over a single video-only call for all four students and both Builders. Transcripts and prosody descriptions supply most of this boost (+5.38 to +10.71); the scaffold changes the audio-augmented call by -0.79 to +2.54, partly through extra multi-label predictions, and evolved edits add at most +0.95, although no evolved increment survives Holm correction. The harness's emotion context also transfers to IntentQA, with small gains for three of four students, none of which survives correction. EmoHarness thus boosts small multimodal students chiefly by supplying and organizing audio-derived evidence.
bullets: Addresses emotion errors when verbal, vocal, and visual cues conflict.
Runs a frozen student model inside a harness that structures observations, transcript, and prosody as citable evidence.
Meta-Harness Evolving uses a stronger Builder to edit and validate the harness offline without seeing evaluation items.
Across 5,507 MME-Emotion items, Recognition improves by 7.6–13.4 points over video-only calls for four students and two Builders.
Most gains come from transcripts and prosody; scaffold and evolved-harness effects are smaller, and evolved gains do not survive Holm correction.

The input is drawn once: instruction, transcript, and five of our seven sampled frames per clip (the student saw 2 fps), subtitled with the words spoken within 0.12 s of each frame (every condition except Video receives the transcript); lettered boxes mark the regions that cards cite. Each card gives one condition’s answer (green: correct; red: wrong), and the tags between cards name what each condition adds. Figure 2: How Meta-Harness Evolving builds a harness and how the frozen student runs it. (a) Offline, the Builder turns the incumbent’s construction failures and traces into at most four candidate edits per generation; static checks, a proposal reviewer, and the gates of Eq. 3 promote the best candidate or retain the incumbent, and after four generations the harness is frozen. (b) At inference the frozen student makes four calls (at most six with retries) around deterministic verification and a fixed controller. The example is the fine-grained sentiment (FG-SA) clip of Appendix Figure 11a: the evidence and the quoted output come from the GPT-5.6 Luna harness on Qwen3-VL-4B; the Propose rows, the confusions in (a), and c1–c4 are illustrative.

papers.selection_reason: Uses a meta-learning approach (evolving a harness) to improve a multimodal model's emotion understanding at inference time, relevant to Test-Time Learning, Multimodal LLMs, and LLMs.
papers.title: EmoHarness: Boosting Multimodal Emotion Understanding with Meta-Harness Evolving
papers.tldr: EmoHarness improves small multimodal models’ emotion understanding mainly by organizing transcript and prosody evidence through a structured prompt-and-verification harness.

papers.abstract: Attention scores candidate supports of an answer, which we call witnesses, and reads the scores at a temperature. We build a higher-order attention layer whose state lives on pairs of items: for a pair (a, b), each third item k is a witness judged through its legs (a, k) and (k, b). It reads witnesses at zero temperature, keeping the best and the number tied with it, passes on only bits comparing such counts, rebuilds its pair state from the input and these bits at every loop, and is trained from answers alone. Each choice removes one way soft attention fails at size: dispersed weight, unresolved gaps between learned scores, and a drifting soft state. In maximum retrieval it is right on at least 99.95% of sets 1,000 times larger than in training, on all ten seeds; trained with a soft count, the same network falls to 42% at 4,096 items. On CLRS-30 without hints, a general form of the layer (half its channels read at zero temperature, numbers embedded, state carried) beats the best published model, which uses hints on some tasks; the full cold layer is exact on every test input of 9 of the 12 tasks whose answers depend on numbers only through comparisons. From yes-or-no answers it decides 2-SAT and two-colouring exactly at 500 variables and, as our theory predicts, not parity equations. Beside a frozen 7B language model it chains family relations exactly at 1,000 statements after training on 16, where the model alone falls to 44%; finite checks on the weights prove every block that learned correct at every size, on acyclic contexts and given what the model reads. On CLUTRR it is right on every story of five to ten relations given the graphs, learning the 62 rules exactly; from text, with the model frozen, no hand-written rule and only a small read-in trained, it lifts an open 7B model from 33% to 65%, above every system we found without hand-written rules except frontier reasoning models.
bullets: Scores candidate witnesses between item pairs at zero temperature, retaining the best score and tie count rather than dispersed soft weights.
Rebuilds pair states from the input and comparison bits at each loop, avoiding unresolved score gaps and drifting soft states.
Achieves at least 99.95% accuracy on maximum retrieval sets 1,000× larger than training; a soft-count variant drops to 42% at 4,096 items.
On CLRS-30, the generalized layer beats the best published hinted model; the full cold layer is exact on 9 of 12 comparison-based tasks.
Supports exact 2-SAT, two-colouring, family chaining, and CLUTRR reasoning, while improving frozen language-model performance on text-based relational tasks.

figures.caption: Fig. 4 | One block, run K times, and the four kinds of block we train. Cobalt: the yes-or-no tests, exact counts and verdict bits (cold); rose: real numbers, which a block carries from loop to loop. a, The network keeps one vector of 128 numbers for every ordered pair of items, its pair state. In the general setting the input’s items, facts and numbers enter it once, through a learned embedding. One block then reads the state and writes back to it, with the same weights in every loop. It reads through two learned tests per channel, A(i, k) and B(k, j). Half of its 128 channels count, for every pair, the middle items k that pass both tests (the witnesses) and hand on only two verdict bits per pair of channels: is one count larger, and are the two equal? The other half keep the strongest witness and hand on its strength, a number between 0 and 1. A gated mix of the bits and strengths is added to each cell, then the output of a small network applied to each pair. After the last loop a read-out takes the answer from the pair state: here, for shortest routes, each node points to the one before it. The block has 146,552 parameters, shared by every loop, and one loop costs n3 per channel. b, The four kinds of block in one grammar: the pair state (small square; rose tints, real numbers; cobalt cells, bits), the block (box, naming the channels it holds: count, the count-and-compare channels of a; best, the best-witness channels; or the general and the cold half), what one loop hands to the next (the arrow back; rose, a carried real state; cobalt, bits from which the state is rebuilt), and where numbers enter (into the state through an embedding, rose; into the block as comparisons only, cobalt; from a frozen language model, grey box). General: the general block of a, 97.04% on CLRS-30 with one block per task and 97.20% with one block for all thirty tasks. Cold: the cold block, into which numbers enter only as comparisons made inside the layer, its state rebuilt from bits every loop (kept bits, which only turn on, or free bits; with kept bits it rebuilds twice, and its comparison channels read a state without the bits their learned tests made); right on every test input, on every seed, on 9 of the 12 tasks whose answer depends on the numbers only through comparisons. General and cold halves: the general-and-cold block, one block for all thirty tasks, 96.55% at its registered read (weight-averaged parameters, K(n) loops) and 96.40% read like the general block (final parameters, eight loops), a loss of 0.46 points against our first general block for all thirty read the same way. Beside a language model: three kept bits per pair of mentions, monotone tests, tied legs and a read-out that can only say yes, reading relations from a frozen model; exact to 1,000 statements. Schematic, not data: everything in b (the icons and their cell patterns are drawn, not read from a model); in a, the tests drawn in the block are set by hand, as in Extended Data Fig. 1, and the tints of the pair state and of the bit and strength columns are illustrative.

Fig. 3 | Three ways soft attention fails at size. a, Dispersion: the size law across four hand-set layers, nothing trained (the instances of the first version of this paper4: SET with four and six attributes, the one-layer OR join and the propagator on random acyclic graphs). Each instance is shown at the two values of β∆, half a nat apart, that bracket its critical value, read warm: filled, every question right; open, some wrong; against the logarithm of the competitors at the margin. Grey: y = x. Top row: the same layers read cold, exact by construction. b, Resolution, measured on maximum retrieval (pick the class of the item of highest priority; trained on sets of 5 to 16 items; ten seeds each, 10,240 test sets per size and seed; lines, the mean; bands, lowest to highest seed): comparisons inside the layer read cold (count, cold; every seed at least 99.95% at every size), the same comparisons trained with a soft count and read warm or cold (count, trained warm), and a softmax network from our replication, which falls up to 18.5 points below the published curve, read warm or cold, beside the published softmax curve12 and the best published method at 4,096 items15. c, The cause of resolution: one softmax network’s learned key score near the top of the priority range, one line per class (the two extreme classes in rose, the other eight grey), in priority units; the top item of the lowest class ties an item of the highest class about three thousandths of the priority range lower. Inset: accuracy read cold, predicted from the class offsets alone against measured, for 20 networks at four sizes. d, Carried error: depth-first search on the official 64-node test, the margin of the true parent against the node’s depth: the logit of the true parent minus the largest logit of any other candidate, in raw logits, after 64 loops (median per bin of eight depths; three seeds, thin, and their mean, bold), for the general block, which carries a continuous strength from loop to loop, and the cold block with positions compared, which rebuilds its bits every loop. The switch also replaces real strengths by bits and moves positions into comparisons; with positions encoded instead, the cold bit loop keeps a margin of 10.0 near the root and 9.1 at depth 63, but loses accuracy at 128 nodes (Fig. 7c). Below zero the parent named is wrong; grey, the depths seen in training. e, Every official test graph (rows) by depth in its depth-first forest (columns): the parents named wrong, summed over three seeds (darker, more seeds wrong), for the general block after 64 loops (96.63, 76.03 and 87.60% right) and the cold block at its registered read (every parent right on every seed). Pixel rows and columns are cells of the data; nothing in this figure is schematic.

Fig. 2 | SET: read warm, the weight spreads; read cold, the set is kept. A deal is a card in hand and a table of cards, and the question is whether two table cards complete a set with the card in hand. a, One join trained in the first version of this paper4, with the card in hand and one table card fixed: each attribute’s clock over the 81 possible third cards (number, shape, fill and colour, turning 1, 3, 9 and 27 times across them), whose product peaks only on the card that completes the set (centre). Read warm, every third card keeps some weight (log scale; the next largest is 7 × 10−7); read cold, only the set. b, The four clocks are four of the 81 characters of (Z3)4 (outlined), and their product at the learned inverse temperature, β = 4.86, is one bright card on the 9 × 9 map of cards: warm, a haze with one peak; cold, one card. c, Dispersion with weights set by hand: SET with six attributes, inverse temperature times margin, β∆, against the number of cards on the table (1,200 deals per size); below the navy boundary some deal is read wrong. Held at its value for 8 cards, the temperature fails from 48 cards, and held at its value for 32 cards, from 256; grown as the size law says, β = ln(2P )/∆ = 2 3 ln 2P for P pairs of cards (a set outscores the nearest miss by ∆ = 3/2), it is right on every deal to 364; read cold, the layer is exact at every size. d, The six joins of the first version of this paper4 trained at 8 cards with all 81 cards in hand, on deals with no set or exactly one: read warm as published (rose: their mean and each join) they fall to 72.0% at 364 cards, with 3 of the six at chance, while the same weights read cold (cobalt) stay at 99.8% (lowest join 99.0%). Right: the same joins at 364 cards with their scores multiplied by 1, 2, 4 and 8 (72.0, 83.1, 98.7 and 99.7%) and read cold (99.8%); the cold read is the end of that dial. Cards repeat from 64 cards on, since 81 distinct cards allow no table without a set beyond 40. e, Deals with exactly one set at 8, 16, 20 and 40 cards (the completing pair outlined), and below each the trained joins’ accuracy at that size read warm and cold, never rounded up to 100%. Schematic, not data: the drawing of the clock dials, the grey tones of the characters, the order of the cards in the deals and the logarithmic tint of the warm product in b, whose weights are exact.

Fig. 1 | One sum over witnesses, read warm and read cold. Each panel forms the sum ZT = ∑ w es(w)/T over one family of witnesses and reads it in two ways: warm, every witness weighted by es(w)/T /ZT (rose: area, glow or tint), and cold, T → 0, which keeps the best witness and the number of witnesses tied with it (cobalt). Nothing is trained. The map is one search question of 49 towns from the benchmark of ref.6, with roads counted in both directions. a, The start’s lookup: the witnesses are single towns, scored by their nearness to the start and read warm at the inverse temperature β = 1/T = 3; every town keeps some weight, while the cold read keeps the eight towns next to the start, tied. b, The pair (start, goal): its witnesses are the 47 middle towns k, each scored by minus the length sk of the route start → k → goal in roads, read warm at T = 2 roads; the cold read keeps the 5 towns of the shortest route. c, Every walk from the start to the goal, weighted by its length and summed exactly by one matrix inverse, read warm at T = 0.83 road: the warm weight glows along every road, and the cold read keeps the one shortest walk. d, The pair table. Every ordered pair of towns keeps such a sum over its middle towns; the table is tinted by the number of roads between the two towns. The start’s row and the goal’s column (light bands), unrolled into strips over the 47 middle towns, give the legs from the start and the legs into the goal, which add up to the route lengths sk of b, and below them the warm and cold weight of each middle town. Read warm, the pair reports a mean length of 7.4 roads, which no route has; read cold, it reports the best route, 6 roads, and its 5 ties. e, The same sum over the 28 pairs of eight table cards in a SET deal, scored by a hand-set layer of four clocks at the inverse temperature tuned for 8 cards (β = 2.68). Read warm, the four pairs that complete a set with the card in hand share 0.9997 of the weight, about a quarter each, so the number of sets is lost; read cold, the four tied best pairs are kept, and their count is the number of sets. Schematic, not data: the map’s geography (water, woods, road curves and town positions draw the question’s roads), the size of the smallest warm discs, the width of the glow, the order of the towns in the table and the layout of the cards.

Fig. 9 | A cold block beside a frozen language model. a, A test context of 16 statements and one of its questions, as given to the model. Italic: the two wordings that never occur in training. An arc joins two statements that chain (the child of one is the parent of the other); the question’s chain of nine statements is in cobalt, numbered from the ancestor down. b, Questions answered correctly against the number of statements in the context, for blocks trained on contexts of 1 to 16 statements in six wordings from yes-or-no answers alone (192 questions per size; 96 at 1,000). Cold block on the reads of Qwen2.5-7B (six seeds, two input layouts) and of Qwen2.5-1.5B (three seeds). Sentence by sentence: the 7B model’s reading of each sentence used directly, without pooling; its only errors come from the sentences the model misreads (24,190 of 24,192 test sentences read right). Rose: each model alone, answering “Yes” or “No” by itself. c, The first task, “is X older than Y ?” over Qwen2.5-0.5B with single-token names: the general block, the same read-in and training with strengths carried from loop to loop (one seed, read up to 256 facts), against the cold block (three seeds), and the model alone. d, CLUTRR, trained on stories of 2 to 4 relations and tested on 2 to 10 (1,048 test stories): the block on the frozen Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct’s reading of each pair of names, with one bit per relation or with each read relation costing − log p and the cheapest derivation answering; the same costs on a linear read-in of the model’s state trained from the answers alone; the same block given each story’s graph; and the model alone, reasoning step by step (rose). Lines are labelled at their right ends. Four earlier builds of the graph trainer were scored on the test stories. e, The general block’s errors on the first task are long chains: yes-questions right by the number of facts on the question’s chain, pooled over contexts of 16 to 256 facts (general, one seed) and 16 to 1,000 facts (cold, three seeds); shaded, the chain lengths of training. f, Every start of panels b and c and of the kinship runs whose directions were learned from answers (Supplementary Note 5, Table 3). Proven: two finite checks on the block’s table show that it never says yes when the answer is no and says yes in time on every chain, at every size, given its input bits; ringed: the proof is also checked in Lean. The 1.5B networks share their tables with the 7B pooled networks of the first layout. Thin lines: single seeds. The kinship sentences follow templates and state one relation; the held-out wordings reuse words seen in training; each sentence’s direction comes from two extra passes of the model, not from its internal states. Schematic, not data: the heights of the arcs in a and the row order in f; every plotted point is a measurement.

Fig. 5 | The cold layer on a map 63 roads deep. The 250-town map of a graph-search question, given to saved Bellman–Ford blocks as an input (every road of weight 0.5, roads in either direction, the source at one end of the map’s longest route, 63 roads); nothing is trained. Cold: the cold block, which rebuilds its bits every loop and builds its route sums by the fixed rule over admitted middle items. General: the general block, which carries a continuous state from loop to loop. a, The general block (seed 0) read at loop 71, where the cold block (seed 0) comes to rest: a town filled where it names the town’s parent rightly (the road to it drawn), a ring where it names it wrong. It names 58 of 250 parents right and none of the 168 towns 40 or more roads deep; the cold block names all 250, so its map, filled everywhere, is not drawn. b, Parents right at loop 71 by the number of roads from the source, in bins of eight roads, three seeds of each block; every cold seed is right in every bin. Shaded, the depths that a training graph can reach (at most 15 roads). c, Parents right after each loop, three seeds of each block. The general blocks peak at 53.6, 62.0 and 89.2% (loops 2, 3 and 19) and end at 23.2, 10.8 and 54.0% at loop 80; every cold block names every parent from loop 63. d, The cold block’s route sums for every pair of towns after loops 8, 24, 48 and 71 (a cell filled once its route is known, tinted by its length; towns in depth-first order of the shortest-path tree, so that each branch is a run of rows). e, The share of each block’s state that changes in each loop (a loop that changes nothing is drawn at 0): the cold block’s bits and route sums stop changing exactly after 71, 72 and 71 loops, which is where its registered read stops; the general block’s state still changes by 1.4 to 1.7% per loop at loop 80. On the 49-town map of Fig. 1 both blocks name every parent, the general blocks from loop 3 and the cold blocks from loop 6; the cold blocks rest after 19, 16 and 18 loops, and the general block’s state still changes by about 8% per loop at loop 16. Schematic, not data: the map’s geography (the course of each road and the towns’ positions are a drawing of the question’s edges) and the order of the towns in the tables.

Fig. 8 | The models find their own missing training cases. a, A 16-node graph after 14 random edge changes, on which three saved models first disagree: its four strong components (shaded), their entry points (filled; an edge from another component points at each) and the edges between components. For nodes 5, 8 and 13 two models name node 2, the right answer, and the third names node 3, another entry point of the same component. The graph comes from the committee’s rule rerun on the saved models, not from the training pool itself; about a quarter of all disputed nodes are of this kind. b, Components answered entirely right, by their number of entry points, pooled over the official and a fresh 64-node test file (640 components): cold blocks trained on three pools (the standard graphs, the standard graphs plus those the models disagreed on, and graphs designed by hand to be rich in entry points; cobalt tones), the general block, which carries a continuous state from loop to loop (rose; the CLRS-30 headline series, read after 8 loops), and the same block without its count channels, a fully warm block (rose, dashed; one seed); three seeds each (dots) and their mean (line). With five or more entry points the general block gets 65% of components entirely right, the warm block 69% and the standard cold pool 56%; the committee’s pool lifts the cold block to 88% and the hand-designed pool to 92%. c, Nodes right per seed (dots) and mean (bar) on the official 64-node test and on 16 fresh graphs of 96 and 128 nodes, read after as many loops as nodes; colours as in b. The general and warm blocks were read only at 64. At 96 and 128 nodes the hand-designed pool was read on a CPU and the other two on a GPU, which can differ by up to 3 points on the same model. Schematic, not data: the node positions in a (components as groups, ordered left to right by the edges between them); edges, components, entry points, rings and answers are data.

Fig. 6 | Thirty algorithms without hints. a, Each task drawn on a small input from the benchmark’s generator (ten items; articulation points, bridges and Kruskal at 24 nodes, the smallest size whose first input has a cycle), with the answer of one block per task (one of its three seeds) drawn in navy over the input in grey. The one wrong answer on these inputs, a single cell of the optimal search tree’s table, is crossed. Under each tile, the share right on the official 64-item test, mean of three seeds. b, Task by task on the official test, in the families of a. In each row the upper lane is FloydNet (rose): its runs without hints (filled) and, where its published score comes from a run with hints, that score (open, joined by a hairline). The lower lane is ours (cobalt): one block per task (filled) and one block for all thirty tasks (pale disc; mean 97.20%, depth-first search read after n loops). papers.selection_reason: Proposes a higher-order attention layer with zero-temperature reading for exact reasoning, relevant to LLM architecture advances.
papers.title: Attention at Absolute Zero
papers.tldr: A zero-temperature, count-aware higher-order attention layer enables exact or highly scalable discrete reasoning from answers alone, outperforming soft-attention variants and strong baselines across retrieval, algorithmic, logical, and relational tasks.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly plan and run experiments in automated laboratories. These experiments keep running while the model reasons and run on schedules with hard deadlines. If an LLM-generated answer arrives late, the system executes a safe fallback action instead, such as rejecting a sample. This creates a systems problem that standard serving metrics do not capture. An answer that matches the fallback adds no value, and answers that differ from the fallback may require more reasoning time. Reporting answer quality and latency separately can therefore overstate the value of reasoning. We test this on synthetic sample decisions, where the best choice is known exactly and a runtime enforces the deadline. We compare one LLM's fast mode, which answers directly, with its thinking mode, which reasons first. In a prespecified replay of 1,200 new decisions, thinking answers that missed a deadline were worth about five times as much as on-time ones. Multiplying the on-time rate by the mean answer value predicted about twice the value that thinking delivered. This prediction overstated thinking's advantage over fast mode by 0.0241 per decision, and by 0.0191 in a repeat on 300 new decisions. Both 95% confidence intervals excluded zero. In a single-GPU Qwen3-8B experiment using simultaneous request bursts, raising the number of requests from 8 to 56 reduced the share of thinking answers that met a 45 s deadline from 79.2% to 1.4%, although total output tripled. Evaluations of LLM agents for laboratories should therefore measure each answer's value and arrival time together and score the action that actually runs.
bullets: Late reasoning answers can be valuable when they differ from a safe fallback, while on-time answers may add little value if they match it.
In a replay of 1,200 decisions, missed-deadline thinking answers were worth about five times as much as on-time ones.
Estimating value as on-time rate × mean answer value overstated thinking’s advantage over fast mode by 0.0241 per decision; a 300-decision repeat showed a 0.0191 overestimate.
Under burst load on a single-GPU Qwen3-8B setup, meeting a 45-second deadline fell from 79.2% at 8 requests to 1.4% at 56, despite tripled output.
Laboratory-agent evaluations should score the action actually executed, jointly accounting for answer quality and arrival time.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes how deadlines change the measured value of LLM reasoning, important for LLM-based laboratory agents.
papers.title: Late but Valuable: Why Deadlines Change the Measured Value of LLM Reasoning
papers.tldr: In deadline-constrained laboratory tasks, evaluating LLM reasoning requires combining answer value with whether the answer arrives in time to affect the executed action.

papers.abstract: Machine unlearning in large language models (LLMs) aims to remove specific learned knowledge, capabilities, or behaviors while preserving model utility. Existing methods have mostly focused on the design of unlearning objectives, while largely overlooking the intrinsic matrix structure of transformer weights. In particular, standard optimizers operate on independent scalar coordinates, thereby ignoring this matrix structure. We propose spectral unlearning, an update framework that combines standard unlearning objectives with matrix-structured optimization. We show that the spectral update corresponds to the steepest-descent direction for transformers composed of linear layers with normalized inputs and outputs. Our approach is applied on top of existing unlearning methods and evaluated across complementary axes of memorization, privacy, and utility, summarized via their harmonic mean. Spectral unlearning consistently outperforms a broad range of baselines and closes most of the gap to a retain-trained reference. Code is available at https://github.com/unlearn-ml/spectral-unlearning/.
bullets: Addresses the overlooked matrix structure of transformer weights in existing unlearning methods.
Combines standard unlearning objectives with matrix-structured, spectral optimization.
Derives the spectral update as the steepest-descent direction for transformers with linear layers and normalized inputs/outputs.
Evaluates memorization, privacy, and utility using their harmonic mean.
Outperforms a broad range of baselines and approaches a retain-trained reference across these measures.

papers.tldr: Spectral unlearning improves knowledge removal in LLMs by updating transformer weights in a structure-aware way while better preserving utility.

papers.abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) produce explicit chains of thought to improve transparency, but they frequently overthink, generating long yet inefficient reasoning chains that inflate computational costs and risk introducing errors. While numerous reinforcement learning methods struggle to penalize verbosity to achieve conciseness, they typically apply the penalty uniformly across lengthy sequences, which leads to credit confounding, that is, the failure to distinguish essential reasoning steps from superfluous ones. In this paper, we study a measurable proxy for this confounding: high-entropy tokens that often coincide with surface transition points where reasoning re-enters verification. Based on this insight, we propose Adaptive Entropy-Sparing (AES), which selectively spares high-entropy tokens that occur before an efficient in-group reference, while penalizing overlength high-entropy suffix tokens associated with superfluous branching. Our AES thereby navigates the suppression-exploration trade-off, reducing overthinking while preserving average reasoning accuracy. We also present an entropy-length model that motivates why local uncertainty can serve as a proxy for future reasoning cost. Across eight reasoning benchmarks, AES reduces reasoning length by up to 52.9% while increasing mean accuracy by up to 3.8% over the base models, consistently outperforming existing efficiency-oriented methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/MobiusDai/AES.
bullets: Addresses overthinking in large reasoning models, where uniformly penalizing long outputs can suppress essential reasoning steps.
Uses high-entropy tokens as a proxy for reasoning transitions and future computational cost.
Spares high-entropy tokens before efficient in-group references, while penalizing high-entropy suffixes linked to unnecessary branching.
Across eight reasoning benchmarks, reduces reasoning length by up to 52.9% and increases mean accuracy by up to 3.8% over base models.
Scope: targets verbosity and efficiency in explicit reasoning chains; the abstract does not specify broader generalization beyond the evaluated benchmarks.

papers.selection_reason: Reduces overthinking in large reasoning models by selectively penalizing high-entropy tokens, improving reasoning efficiency.
papers.title: Adaptive Entropy-Sparing for Efficient Reasoning
papers.tldr: Adaptive Entropy-Sparing reduces excessive chain-of-thought reasoning while preserving—and often improving—accuracy by selectively penalizing costly high-entropy reasoning tokens.

papers.abstract: Answer probes applied to chain-of-thought hidden states are often read as evidence that a language model has already decided its final response. This reading overlooks a competing signal, the candidate the model is about to mention. We introduce emission-controlled dual-target probing (ECDP), which fits the same low-rank reader family separately to the imminent mention and to the final answer at identical positions, with target-specific nulls and thresholds fixed before any fit. On correct DecisionDepth (DD) rollouts in which a distractor is mentioned before the final answer, Qwen3.5-4B decodes the next mention at .966 (null .234) but the final answer only at .221 (null .186), an emission gap of .696 [.648, .744]; Llama-3.1-8B gives .575 [.514, .632]. This pattern is not universal. In a pre-specified evaluation of Qwen3-8B with thinking enabled on held-out MMLU questions, using a full-prefix attention reader over every thinking position, both targets are decodable and the final answer is read far more strongly (mention-minus-answer lift -.398 [-.459, -.336] at layer 22 over 467 questions). Model, task, positions, and reader change together between these settings, and an attempted matched comparison on DD produced no valid statistics because the imminent-mention probe did not train reliably, so we do not identify what reverses the order. On DD, planted-signal controls show that the reader recovers an injected final-answer signal at one tenth of full dose. Answer-candidate decodability is therefore target-relative and protocol-dependent: a strong answer readout does not by itself establish when a model commits, and a probe that fails to train is not evidence that the information is absent. ECDP is a practical control for distinguishing imminent text emission from evidence of a settled decision.
bullets: ECDP fits separate low-rank probes for the imminent mention and final answer at identical chain-of-thought positions, with pre-fixed target-specific nulls and thresholds.
On correct DD rollouts with an earlier distractor, Qwen3.5-4B strongly decoded the next mention (.966) but weakly decoded the final answer (.221); Llama-3.1-8B showed the same direction.
The pattern is protocol-dependent: on held-out MMLU with Qwen3-8B, both targets were decodable and the final answer was more strongly read at one layer.
Because model, task, positions, and reader changed across settings—and a matched DD comparison failed to train—the study does not explain why the ordering reverses.
Planted-signal controls show the reader can recover an injected final-answer signal at one-tenth of full strength.

papers.title: When Answer Decodability Is Not a Decision: Separating Final-Answer and Imminent-Emission Signals in Chain-of-Thought

papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems have demonstrated remarkable effectiveness in mitigating hallucinations by incorporating external knowledge. However, the retrieval process inevitably introduces noise, posing significant challenges to RAG robustness. Fundamentally, noise robustness is a composite competency encompassing noise identification, retrieval filtering, and robust reasoning. Unfortunately, existing methods often fail to capture this holistic nature, typically restricted to single-dimensional enhancements or hampered by noise-induced optimization interference. To address these limitations, we decompose RAG robustness into three sub-tasks: knowledge boundary perception, retrieval verification, and robust reasoning. Accordingly, we propose ARMOR, an Adaptive Curriculum Meta-Learning for Noise Robust RAG Reasoning. Inspired by the teaching process, ARMOR introduces an adaptive task scheduler as a teacher to curate training plans according to the absolute learning progress of RAG generators (Student). Distinct from GRPO, ARMOR utilizes inter-group advantage estimation during learning to effectively mitigate mode collapse caused by limited output spaces. Experiments on three complex reasoning datasets (2WikiMultiHopQA, MusiQue, and HotPotQA) indicate that ARMOR achieves synergistic improvements in retrieval noise robustness, significantly outperforming baselines in output quality.
bullets: Decomposes noise robustness into knowledge boundary perception, retrieval verification, and robust reasoning.
Uses an adaptive task scheduler to tailor the training curriculum to the generator’s learning progress.
Applies inter-group advantage estimation to reduce mode collapse under limited output spaces.
Evaluated on 2WikiMultiHopQA, MusiQue, and HotPotQA, with reported improvements in noise robustness and output quality over baselines.

papers.abstract: LLM inference has two phases with different bottlenecks: LLM prefill runs once per request and is compute-intensive. Decoding repeats for every output token and is limited by memory bandwidth. To address the challenges associated with this issue, different solutions have been proposed. All of these solutions use the same model for both prefill and decode phases. We propose BridgeKV, which uses a larger model for prefill and a smaller model of the same family for decoding. A lightweight KV-stitching module translates the larger model's prompt cache into the smaller model's cache layout. It handles differences in cache shape and representation through learned local layer mixing and separate nonlinear maps for keys and values. With both models frozen, we train the module to align their caches and make the smaller model follow the larger model's next-token predictions. A second training stage adds low-rank adapters when further task adaptation is needed. Across six model pairs and five datasets, BridgeKV outperforms fine-tuned small-model baselines with matched trainable parameter budgets in all 30 settings. It closes up to 80% of the quality gap to using the larger model for both phases. On one A40 GPU, Llama-3.1-Instruct-8B to Llama-3.2-Instruct-1B achieves 3.0X faster requests than the larger model alone, with latency close to the smaller model alone. BridgeKV can improve the hardware and system solutions that separate prefill and decode phases across GPUs. A separate serving simulation models request arrivals, queues, and cache transfer. For Llama-3.1-Instruct-70B to Llama-3.2-Instruct-1B, it predicts up to 33.86X faster requests and 27.5X lower energy use than using the larger model for both prefill and decode phases.
bullets: Targets the compute-heavy prefill phase and memory-bandwidth-limited decoding phase with different model sizes.
Uses a lightweight KV-stitching module with local layer mixing and separate nonlinear key/value mappings to reconcile cache differences.
Trains the translation module with both models frozen; optional low-rank adapters support further task adaptation.
Across six model pairs and five datasets, it outperformed matched-budget fine-tuned small-model baselines in all 30 settings and closed up to 80% of the quality gap to the large model.
Reported serving gains include 3.0× faster requests for an 8B-to-1B pair and simulated gains up to 33.86× faster with 27.5% lower energy for a 70B-to-1B pair.

papers.title: BridgeKV: Large-Model Prefill and Small-Model Decoding for LLM Inference via KV Cache Translation
papers.tldr: BridgeKV accelerates LLM serving by using a large model for prompt prefill and a small same-family model for decoding, translating the large model’s KV cache between them.

papers.abstract: Language-model post-training modifies weights through cumulative updates and successive displacements, yet existing studies report seemingly conflicting spectral properties: nearly full-rank updates and low stable-rank changes. We show these observations are compatible and characterize update directions during training. For singular values following $σ_i \propto i^{-α}$ with $0 < α\leq 1/2$, we prove that stable rank becomes negligible relative to fixed-energy rank as dimension increases. Full singular value decompositions of selected OLMo-2-7B updates confirm this separation: three proximal policy optimization (PPO) attention updates have stable ranks of 9.6-18.3 but require 532-1,222 singular components to capture 80% of their energy. We next compute consecutive checkpoint-displacement cosines from full-model inner products. Across nine publicly released reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) stages, all 131 adjacent pairs have negative cosines on their native checkpoint grids, including PPO and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) trajectories. Supervised fine-tuning comparisons across four model families show configuration-dependent alignment, including negative late-training cosines for Mistral and FP32 Llama. Finally, a controlled OLMo-2-1B study with three paired seeds and a 2,048-token response cap compares group-relative advantages against a learned critic with generalized advantage estimation (GAE). At matched 60-rollout windows, late-training mean cosines are +0.259 and +0.012, respectively; the paired critic-minus-group difference is -0.247 (seed-level 95% interval [-0.358, -0.137]). These findings distinguish spectral concentration, energy coverage, and trajectory direction, and demonstrate that the advantage system influences directional alignment under matched training conditions.
bullets: Stable rank and fixed-energy rank measure different properties; power-law spectra can make stable rank small even when many singular components capture most energy.
Full SVDs of selected OLMo-2-7B PPO attention updates found stable ranks of 9.6–18.3, while 532–1,222 components were needed for 80% energy.
All 131 adjacent checkpoint pairs across nine RLVR stages had negative displacement cosines on their native grids, including PPO and GRPO.
SFT direction alignment was configuration-dependent, with negative late-training cosines for Mistral and FP32 Llama.
In a controlled OLMo-2-1B comparison, critic-based GAE produced less aligned late-training directions than group-relative advantages, with a paired cosine difference of -0.247.

papers.selection_reason: Spectral and directional analysis of LLM post-training; relevant to LLM architecture understanding.
papers.title: Spectral Rank and Step-Direction Dynamics in Language-Model Post-Training
papers.tldr: Language-model post-training can produce updates that are nearly full-rank yet energy-concentrated, while successive update directions often reverse—an effect influenced by the advantage-estimation system.

papers.abstract: Compression can preserve a language model's average accuracy while selectively degrading individual capabilities. Whether these losses follow method-specific patterns or a transferable order is unclear. We applied seven perturbation and compression methods to eight instruction-tuned models, scoring 16 tasks in four answer formats against preregistered predictions. Short-answer capabilities failed in nearly the same order under four random perturbations with different mechanisms (median correlation 0.90) and, within each model, under pruning and quantization (0.875). Intact answer margin, answer frequency and answer format predicted this order. Fragility profiles measured under random perturbation predicted which tasks and facts compression removes first and, after four-task calibration, held-out task accuracy (median absolute error 0.11-0.12, against 0.20-0.21 for uniform decline); profiles borrowed from other model families did almost as well. The order did not transfer across models under GPTQ quantization or hold for long-form tasks. Within short answers, what compression removes is predictable before deployment.
bullets: Across four random perturbations, short-answer capabilities failed in nearly the same order (median correlation 0.90).
Within individual models, pruning and quantization produced similarly ordered failures (correlation 0.875).
Answer margin, answer frequency, and answer format predicted which capabilities degraded first.
Random-perturbation fragility profiles predicted compression-related task loss and held-out accuracy after four-task calibration.
The ordering did not transfer across models under GPTQ quantization and did not apply to long-form tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Analysis of LLM capability ordering under compression.
papers.title: Language model capabilities fail in a shared, predictable order under compression and perturbation
papers.tldr: Language-model capabilities tend to fail in a predictable, shared order under many perturbations and compression methods, but this predictability is limited across model families and long-form tasks.

papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation trains a student language model to match a teacher's predictions on the training text. We ask whether learning the teacher's behavior beyond the training text can further improve the student. We investigate this using three input perturbations: additive token noise, blending two documents, and blending neighboring tokens. Specifically, for an early part of pretraining we perturb the inputs and train the student to match the teacher on them, and we spend the rest of the same token budget on ordinary distillation. When pretraining from scratch, the best method improves on standard distillation at both scales we tried, by 0.025 nats at 135M parameters and by 0.020 nats at 0.5B (mean of three seeds). At 135M this is 1.45 times the gain that distillation itself provides over next-token training. We also observe promising downstream transfer: at 0.5B, the best variant improves average zero-shot accuracy by about one percentage point across seven tasks. It also retains its validation-loss advantage after low-bit weight quantization. We also test a data-limited setting in which training data must be reused, and find that the gains persist. Finally, ablations suggest that, for additive noise, perturbing the teacher's inputs contributes most of the gain, while perturbing only the student's inputs yields much less.
bullets: Studies additive token noise, document blending, and neighboring-token blending during an early distillation phase.
The best perturbation method improves validation loss at both tested scales: 135M and 0.5B parameters.
At 0.5B, it increases average zero-shot accuracy by about one percentage point across seven tasks.
Benefits persist when training data is reused and after low-bit weight quantization.
Ablations indicate that perturbing the teacher’s inputs is more beneficial than perturbing only the student’s inputs.

papers.title: Perturbing Inputs Improves Pretraining Distillation

papers.abstract: Modern state-space models owe much of their computational efficiency to their linear, often diagonal, dynamics. Classical recurrent neural networks instead allow nonlinear state-to-state interactions, which can be beneficial when memory updates need to depend on the past context. In this paper, we ask whether state feedback through a simple gate regulating memory updates can enhance the expressivity of diagonal state-space models. To investigate this question, we compare gates that depend on the current input, the recurrent state, or both. We establish a strict expressivity separation: for scalar models, state gating solves induction-head tasks for arbitrary vocabulary size and sequence length, whereas input gating fails on a finite instance under standard stability assumptions on the state transition matrix. Experiments show that state gating retains its advantage on induction-head tasks in higher-dimensional models, whereas input gating performs better on selective copying tasks. Together, our results show that even a simple, diagonal form of state-feedback gating can unlock capabilities unavailable to input-controlled models, while input and state gating offer complementary strengths and achieve the strongest overall performance when combined.
bullets: The paper compares gates driven by the current input, recurrent state, or both in diagonal state-space models.
State gating strictly increases expressivity: scalar models solve induction-head tasks for arbitrary vocabulary sizes and sequence lengths.
Under standard stability assumptions, input gating fails on a finite induction-head instance.
Experiments confirm state-gating advantages on induction tasks and input-gating advantages on selective copying.
The two gating mechanisms provide complementary capabilities when combined.

papers.title: Where Should a Gate Look? Input vs. State Gating in Diagonal State Space Models
papers.tldr: State-based memory-update gates make diagonal state-space models more expressive on induction tasks, while input-based gates excel at selective copying; combining both is strongest overall.

papers.abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards trains language models through multi-turn tool interactions, yet their reasoning performance and tool-calling ability can decline during training. We trace this degradation to three coupled mechanisms: (1) tool-token imbalance produces negative overall tool credit when incorrect trajectories contain more tool tokens per turn than correct ones; (2) aggregation amplification can further strengthen this negative signal as token-mean aggregation gives longer incorrect trajectories greater weight in policy updates; and (3) failure-driven retries prolong trajectories as models tend to call tools again after execution errors, extending potential negative credit to recovery attempts. To counter this suppression, we propose Transition-Aware Credit Assignment (TACA), which targets the transition from reasoning to tool use through supervision of both call initiation and generation. Specifically, TACA uses Advantage Projection to enforce a nonnegative mean advantage on tool-call tokens within each prompt group through a minimal uniform shift. Additionally, TACA guides tool-use decisions with Decision Contrast, comparing rewards for tool-assisted and direct answers to the same prompt. Through Supervised Replay, it reinforces tool-call generation using calls from previously sampled correct trajectories. Across models and tasks, TACA improves performance and sustains more reliable tool interaction during training, raising mean accuracy over MT-GRPO on six reasoning benchmarks by 4.61 percentage points for Qwen2.5-1.5B and 3.61 for Qwen2.5-3B. Our code is available at https://github.com/tmlr-group/TACA.
bullets: Identifies three causes of tool-use degradation: tool-token imbalance, length-amplified credit aggregation, and failure-driven retries.
Uses Advantage Projection to ensure tool-call tokens receive nonnegative mean advantage within each prompt group.
Applies Decision Contrast to compare tool-assisted and direct answers, plus Supervised Replay from correct trajectories.
Improves mean accuracy over MT-GRPO by 4.61 points on Qwen2.5-1.5B and 3.61 points on Qwen2.5-3B across six reasoning benchmarks.
Scope: targets multi-turn tool interactions trained with verifiable rewards.

papers.tldr: TACA prevents tool-use suppression in agentic RL by correcting negative credit around reasoning-to-tool transitions, improving reasoning accuracy and tool reliability.

papers.abstract: Random perturbations around a shared checkpoint can produce experts for distinct tasks, but shared origin does not ensure that their gains survive composition. We formulate expert-pair selection for joint base-relative retention, measured by strict joint success and worst-task gain with unconditional abstention accounting. An exact finite-difference decomposition and an arbitrarily small orthogonal counterexample show why proximity and orthogonality alone are insufficient. We instantiate this formulation with quality-constrained spectral selection, a fixed-budget framework combining cross-task screening, layerwise pair geometry, separate validation, and Base fallback. Across six checkpoints, 21 task pairs, and five independent perturbation pools, the procedure improves strict joint success over Top-1 averaging throughout and leads the four-method model-scale comparison on four of six checkpoints. For the five models with at least 1.5B parameters, matched quality-only, global-cosine, and spectral ranking attain 49.1%, 50.5%, and 53.1% joint success. Under this matched protocol, the spectral selector also yields the highest worst-task gain and Weak Pareto rate and the lowest regression rate. Mean worst-task gain reaches +0.61 percentage points, while 17.1% regression and 13.0% abstention show that composability remains conditional. Project page: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Thickets-Merge/.
bullets: The work selects expert pairs by joint base-relative retention, strict joint success, and worst-task gain, with abstention counted explicitly.
An exact finite-difference decomposition and an orthogonal counterexample show that proximity and orthogonality alone do not guarantee successful composition.
The proposed fixed-budget method combines cross-task screening, layerwise pair geometry, separate validation, spectral ranking, and Base fallback.
Across six checkpoints and 21 task pairs, spectral selection consistently improves strict joint success over Top-1 averaging and leads model-scale comparisons on four checkpoints.
For models with at least 1.5B parameters, spectral ranking achieves 53.1% joint success versus 49.1% for quality-only and 50.5% for global-cosine ranking; regression and abstention remain nontrivial.

papers.selection_reason: Cross-task model merging with spectral selection is directly applicable to large language model development and composition.
papers.title: When Are Nearby Experts Composable? Cross-Task Model Merging in Neural Thickets
papers.tldr: Nearby experts are not automatically composable; a quality-constrained spectral selector improves joint task success while showing that merging remains conditional.

papers.abstract: Mathematical performance depends on how a language model receives information, uses generated text and submits an answer. We study these dependencies through paired comparisons that separate submission requirements, draft reuse and candidate availability. On 65 development problems, an instruction permitting continued derivation produced no valid final answers in 390 short-output calls; a single-line submission instruction produced 390 format-valid outputs, including 389 parseable answers. Under the fixed submission protocol, 198 problems with failed initial submissions were answered correctly in 9.09p of cases with the question alone, 33.84p with its draft, 46.46p with candidates, and 59.60p with both. Drafts added 13.13 percentage points with candidates fixed, and candidates added 25.76 points with drafts fixed; both effects were significant after Holm correction and were subadditive on the accuracy scale. Retaining a trailing excerpt outperformed retaining a leading excerpt of similar average length by 10.10 points Holm-adjusted p 0.027. A second completion model showed the same directions of input effects on the fixed materials. In a cohort with parseable initial submissions, candidates added no correct answers when the previous draft was supplied, but added 27 points when it was absent. These results establish a conditional value of generated text: a failed submission can leave useful material, whose contribution depends on what else is supplied and what is retained.
bullets: A single-line submission instruction yielded format-valid outputs, whereas allowing continued derivation produced none in the short-output calls.
For failed initial submissions, accuracy rose from 9.09p with only the question to 59.60p with both the draft and candidate answers.
Drafts and candidates each improved accuracy, but their combined effects were subadditive.
Retaining trailing draft excerpts outperformed similarly sized leading excerpts by 10.10 points.
Candidate benefits depended on draft availability and were directionally replicated with a second completion model.

papers.selection_reason: Study of how task presentation and execution paths affect LLM mathematical performance.
papers.title: Task presentation and execution paths shape LLM mathematical performance
papers.tldr: LLM math performance depends strongly on submission format and whether prior drafts and candidate answers are retained.

papers.abstract: Language models often abandon a correct answer when a user pushes back without giving a reason, and this behavior is usually studied as sycophancy to be suppressed. The same pushback, however, also leads models to revisit and sometimes repair a wrong answer. We measure both effects on multiple-choice questions from MMLU and ARC-Challenge with four open models from two families (Qwen3 1.7B, 4B and 8B, and OLMo-2 7B), reading the final answer exactly from option logits after a free-form reply. The reply budget changes the verdict. When Qwen3-4B may answer the challenge in at most 96 tokens, pushback leaves accuracy unchanged or slightly lower; with 1,024 tokens, it corrects 43% of its wrong answers and pushback raises accuracy by 5.7 points. Whether pushback helps overall follows a simple break-even rule in the cave and correction rates. Inside the model, caving can be partly predicted before the challenge: hidden states add about 0.04-0.06 AUROC over turn-1 confidence in three of our four probing runs. A probe trained only on self-correction cases predicts caving beyond confidence when replies are truncated, but not when the model can finish its reasoning. Activation steering never reduced caving selectively: where it worked, it suppressed self-correction as well. We conclude that sycophancy evaluations should allow full replies and report self-correction alongside caving.
bullets: Short response limits can hide self-correction; with 1,024 tokens, Qwen3-4B corrected 43% of its wrong answers and gained 5.7 accuracy points after pushback.
Whether pushback helps depends on the balance between answer-changing errors and repaired mistakes.
Hidden states modestly predict caving beyond first-turn confidence in most probing runs.
A probe trained on self-correction cases detected caving under truncation, but not when reasoning could finish.
Activation steering did not selectively reduce caving; it also suppressed self-correction.

papers.abstract: Reasoning models often continue generating after producing an answer, yet stopping prematurely may interrupt useful verification or revision. In this work, we investigate whether targeted interventions in a model's internal computation can provide a reliable signal for when to stop reasoning. We introduce Prune-to-Probe, an inference-time controller that uses causal activation interventions to probe the stability of a model's current answer. Specifically, we identify late-MLP coordinates that contribute to post-answer continuation while excluding those important for answer completion. Once an answer is stated, Prune-to-Probe temporarily suppresses the selected coordinates and measures the resulting stopping response relative to matched random interventions. Crucially, these interventions serve only as probes: the model either returns its existing answer or resumes generation from an untouched cache. On MATH, Prune-to-Probe reduces reasoning-token forwards by 2.60%, preserving all naturally correct trajectories while repairing six errors. On MMLU-Pro, it achieves 1.145% pooled savings with no observed harm. Further analysis shows that the intervention captures decision stability rather than correctness (AUROC 0.502). These results demonstrate the potential of causal activation probes for efficient inference-time control without permanent model modification.
bullets: Targets late-MLP coordinates linked to post-answer continuation but not answer completion.
After an answer is stated, temporarily suppresses these coordinates and compares the stopping response with matched random interventions.
Uses interventions only as probes: the model either keeps its answer or resumes from an untouched cache.
Reduces reasoning-token forwards by 2.60% on MATH while preserving naturally correct trajectories and repairing six errors; saves 1.145% on MMLU-Pro with no observed harm.
The probe reflects decision stability rather than correctness, with AUROC 0.502, limiting its use as an accuracy signal.

papers.tldr: Prune-to-Probe uses causal activation probes to decide when a reasoning model can safely stop, reducing inference computation without modifying its final answer.

papers.abstract: Large language models rely on a single tokenizer that is chosen at training time and fixed thereafter. Most tokenizers are trained on English-dominant corpora, making them under-serve morphologically rich and non-Latin-script languages, where they can produce fragmented representations, longer sequence lengths, and reduced information density during training. We propose Mixture of Tokenizers MoTo, a modular tokenization framework that trains dedicated per-language BPE tokenizers and composes them into a unified superset vocabulary, where tokens shared across languages are deduplicated into a common ID space. Each tokenizer maintains its own normalization policy, pre-tokenization rules, and vocabulary budget. Despite allocating significantly fewer entries to English, MoTo retains English performance while delivering consistent gains across 18 out of 21 typologically diverse languages spanning six scripts, with improvements most pronounced on morphologically complex and non-Latin-script languages that are systematically underserved by English-dominant tokenizer design. Our results suggest that modular subword tokenization is a practical and extensible alternative to monolithic tokenization for multilingual parity.
bullets: English-dominant tokenizers can fragment words and lengthen sequences, especially for morphologically rich and non-Latin-script languages.
MoTo trains separate BPE tokenizers with language-specific normalization, pre-tokenization, and vocabulary budgets.
Their vocabularies are merged into a deduplicated unified token-ID space.
The approach retains English performance and improves results in 18 of 21 diverse languages across six scripts.
Gains are strongest for languages underserved by monolithic English-focused tokenizers.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Left: Superset Vocabulary construction. Language-specific subword tokenizers are trained on their corresponding corpus. Words native to that language tend to be represented with fewer tokens, while non-native words fall back to coarser subwords or byte-level tokens. The superset vocabulary VS is constructed by taking the union of all tokenizer vocabularies, assigning shared tokens a single global index, with |VS | ≤ ∑ i|Ti|. Right: Mixture-of-Tokenizers (MoTo) pipeline. A tokenizer is selected based on the input language ID. The input is encoded into superset indices, processed by the transformer, and decoded back with the tokens from the superset, additionally it can utilize rules from the input tokenizer.

papers.abstract: Extended reasoning can help language models solve complex problems, but long responses often contain both useful computations and redundant checks. Conventional length penalties encourage shorter responses without distinguishing the functions of intermediate steps. We propose Phase-Conditioned Reward Shaping (PCRS), a framework that combines phase identification with training-time reward allocation. We investigate two classification routes: PCRS-H with a hidden-state classifier and PCRS-T with a frozen text classifier. Our main text classifier implementation assigns overlapping reasoning, execution, and revision labels to native chunks, then uses these labels and exact repetition to adjust existing token penalties. We compare the completed configurations on six mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks and examine four reward-weight settings with the text classifier. Compared with a baseline using token-level length penalties, the default text classifier configuration reduces mean response length by 3.13%; sampled Pass@1 is approximately 62.07% for both methods, while oracle Pass@16 rises from 86.08% to 87.67%. These results show how phase-informed penalty allocation can reduce output volume and improve multi-attempt coverage without inference-time classification.
bullets: Targets redundant checks in extended reasoning that conventional length penalties treat the same as useful computation.
Uses phase identification to label chunks as reasoning, execution, or revision, then adjusts existing token penalties during training.
Evaluates hidden-state and frozen text-classifier variants across six mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks.
The default text-classifier setup reduces mean response length by 3.13%; sampled Pass@1 remains about 62.07%, while oracle Pass@16 increases from 86.08% to 87.67%.
The approach performs phase classification during training rather than at inference time.

papers.title: Phase-Conditioned Reward Shaping for Token-Efficient LLM Reasoning
papers.tldr: Phase-Conditioned Reward Shaping allocates length penalties by reasoning phase, shortening LLM responses while preserving single-sample accuracy and improving multi-sample coverage.

papers.abstract: Much of the automation handed to language-model agents is procedural: each step needs little intelligence, but a long unattended run must follow a skill or SOP stated once at the start. We show that agents drift from such procedures over long runs, and that restating the instructions or resuming a stopped agent only moves the drift to another shortcut. We study an executable finite-state machine (FSM) that keeps the workflow state outside the model's context and enforces it at three points: tool calls, state transitions and the end of the agent's turn. In a pre-registered experiment on 200-account SOP-Bench batches, Claude Haiku 4.5 with the FSM decided on average 139 accounts correctly and by the procedure, against 48 for the strongest baseline (95% CI of the difference [46, 130]), and kept this rate to the end; across three models, the gain tracked how much the plain agent drifted. Because the runtime, not the model, supplies this long-horizon reliability, the FSM can let small models carry procedural work: Haiku 4.5 with it averaged more such decisions than plain Claude Sonnet 4.6 at 38% of the cost. Analyses on SWE-bench Verified, $τ^2$-bench, and staged and cross-context workflows further suggest that reliable long-horizon automation can come from stronger execution control, not only stronger models.
bullets: Long-running agents drift from SOPs, and restating instructions or resuming them does not reliably prevent shortcutting.
The FSM enforces procedure compliance at tool calls, state transitions, and the end of each agent turn.

In a pre-registered 200-account SOP-Bench experiment, FSM-controlled Claude Haiku 4.5 averaged 139 correct-by-procedure decisions versus 48 for the strongest baseline, maintaining performance through the end.
The benefit scaled with how much plain agents drifted across three models and enabled Haiku 4.5 to outperform plain Claude Sonnet 4.6 on such decisions at 38% of the cost.
Additional analyses across several benchmarks and workflow settings suggest execution control can provide long-horizon reliability beyond simply using larger models.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning for large language model post-training often reuses each batch of sampled rollouts for several gradient passes to amortize the cost of generation. Under such multi-pass reuse, existing objectives fail in different ways: unclipped updates collapse as the policy drifts away from the sampling policy, adding a negative baseline avoids collapse but reinforces every sampled response, and PPO-style ratio clipping cuts off gradients abruptly. We first ask why reuse is fragile. Measuring how well an update estimated from a small rollout group aligns with the KL-regularized target on held-out rollouts of the same prompts, we find that this alignment drops by nearly an order of magnitude from in-sample to held-out rollouts across three base models, suggesting that repeated passes largely overfit the sampled group. Motivated by this finding, we propose Bounded Residual-Aligned Training (BRAT), motivated by a proximal update toward a bounded reweighting of the sampling policy. BRAT assigns each token a gradient weight that decreases linearly with its probability ratio and vanishes at a trust-region boundary, and normalizes group-centered rewards by their maximum magnitude, keeping advantages zero-mean and bounded without extra hyperparameters. With four reuse passes, BRAT avoids training collapse, limits policy drift, and achieves higher average accuracy with lower seed variance on most benchmarks.
bullets: Repeated reuse of sampled rollouts causes update alignment with the KL-regularized target to drop nearly an order of magnitude on held-out rollouts, indicating overfitting.
BRAT uses a bounded, linearly decreasing gradient weight based on each token’s probability ratio, vanishing at a trust-region boundary.
It normalizes group-centered rewards by their maximum magnitude, producing zero-mean, bounded advantages without extra hyperparameters.
With four reuse passes, BRAT avoids collapse, limits policy drift, and achieves higher average accuracy with lower seed variance on most benchmarks.

papers.abstract: How little of a pretrained large language model (LLM) has to change for it to acquire new capabilities? We find that zeroing fewer than 0.05% of its weights, with no other modification, matches full fine-tuning (FFT) at scale across three LLM post-training regimes: reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, supervised fine-tuning, and on-policy distillation. Our method, Deletion Tuning, learns a binary mask over the gate projection of transformer blocks. Two practical advantages follow: the trained mask is hundreds to thousands of times smaller than the corresponding FFT checkpoint, and Deletion Tuning forgets far less, which addresses a central challenge in continual learning. Under reinforcement learning, its prior-task accuracy stays near the base level while FFT, LoRA, and random sparse fine-tuning lose up to 5.4 points. To understand why masking alone suffices, we analyze the geometry of the learned weight changes under reinforcement learning using stable rank, spectrum drift, and principal-weight overlap. Compared with LoRA and random sparse fine-tuning, Deletion Tuning is closest to FFT across the three measures.
bullets: Applies across reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, supervised fine-tuning, and on-policy distillation.
Learns a binary mask over transformer-block gate projections, with no other weight modifications.
The resulting mask is hundreds to thousands of times smaller than a full-fine-tuning checkpoint.
Under reinforcement learning, it retains near-base prior-task accuracy, whereas other tested methods can suffer substantial forgetting.
Weight-geometry analyses show its changes resemble full fine-tuning more closely than LoRA or random sparse fine-tuning.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Deletion Tuning keeps prior-task accuracy at every Llama scale while the baselines drift. (a) Forward KL between the trained and base policies on GSM8K during GRPO training, the forgetting predictor of Shenfeld et al. (2026b). (b) Change in mean accuracy on a six-task prior-task suite from the base model (dashed line).

Figure 1: Deletion Tuning learns which pretrained weights to delete and writes no new values. The pretrained weights 𝑊 stay frozen, and each is paired with a trainable logit in 𝐺, the only parameters that post-training updates. During training, each weight is multiplied by 𝜎(𝛼𝐺), a smooth mask between 0 and 1. The sharpness 𝛼 rises over training until the sigmoid becomes a hard threshold at 𝐺 = 0. At deployment, weights with positive logits (blue) keep their pretrained values and weights with negative logits (red) are set to zero (crossed out), so the trained adapter is one bit per weight.

Figure 3: Deletion Tuning (blue) tracks FFT (red) most closely across three update-geometry metrics. papers.title: The Surprising Effectiveness of Deleting Weights in LLM Post-Training
papers.tldr: Deletion Tuning achieves full-fine-tuning-level post-training by zeroing fewer than 0.05% of an LLM’s weights, while preserving prior-task knowledge better and using much smaller checkpoints.

papers.abstract: High-level synthesis (HLS) can translate C/C++ kernels into register-transfer level (RTL) designs, yet generating high-quality hardware still relies heavily on manual pragma tuning and repeated synthesis evaluation. We propose AutoC2V, a C++-to-Verilog generation framework driven by real synthesis feedback that enables large language models (LLMs) to directly generate RTL with improved quality of results (QoR) from synthesizable C++ kernels. We construct training data from real synthesis results, including synthesizable C++ source code, the corresponding Verilog RTL, QoR metrics, and optimization objectives. Using this dataset, we align the model toward synthesis-aware RTL generation through Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). To reduce the high cost of repeatedly invoking real synthesis during GRPO, we design the QoR Prediction Reward Model (QoR RM), which predicts latency and resource metrics by encoding RTL into long-context semantic representations, thereby providing low-cost and continuous QoR reward signals for policy optimization. Experimental results demonstrate that AutoC2V not only substantially improves RTL functional pass rates, but also achieves superior latency and resource optimization compared to the unfine-tuned base model, representative HLS optimization approaches (HLSPilot, LLM-DSE, and AutoDSE), and advanced general-purpose commercial models (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, DeepSeek v4 Pro, and GLM-5.2). These results indicate that combining real synthesis data with efficient QoR reward modeling can further improve the ability of LLMs to generate high-quality RTL.
bullets: Addresses the cost and manual effort of pragma tuning and repeated synthesis in HLS-based C++-to-RTL generation.
Uses synthesis-grounded data containing C++, Verilog, QoR metrics, and optimization objectives for supervised fine-tuning and GRPO.
Introduces a QoR Prediction Reward Model that estimates latency and resource usage from RTL representations, reducing reliance on repeated synthesis during training.
Reports improved RTL functional pass rates and latency/resource optimization over the base model, HLS optimization methods, and several commercial general-purpose models.

papers.abstract: Individuals experiencing suicidal ideation (SI) or psychological distress may disclose their social identities when seeking support from LLMs. Attending to identity-related stressors can be important for providing contextually appropriate and empathetic support. However, disclosing an identity does not necessarily mean that it is a cause of distress. In this work, we audit how LLMs interpret distress through disclosed identities. Using paired counterfactual interventions, we evaluate six LLMs across two SI and distress datasets, 16 identity and control conditions, and two prompting protocols. Our findings suggest that models can transform identity disclosures into explanatory narratives, attributing distress to presumed identity-related adversity. These assumptions frequently appear within otherwise empathetic responses, particularly when marginalized identities are disclosed. We contextualize our findings through the lens of compassionate othering to characterize these patterns as a form of harm in which empathetic responses impose identity-linked assumptions on individual suffering. These responses can misrepresent individuals' experiences by treating their identities as explanations for distress without supporting evidence. Our findings highlight the need to mitigate these harms by grounding interpretations of distress in individuals' disclosures and avoiding unsupported identity-linked assumptions.
bullets: The study examines how LLMs interpret identity disclosures in conversations about suicidal ideation and psychological distress.
Using paired counterfactual interventions, it evaluates six LLMs across two datasets, 16 identity/control conditions, and two prompting protocols.
Models often infer identity-related adversity as the cause of distress, especially for marginalized identities.
These assumptions can misrepresent people’s experiences even when responses are otherwise empathetic.
The authors call for interpretations grounded in users’ disclosures rather than unsupported identity-linked explanations.
