papers.abstract: How does Jev compare with other systems on Arabic tasks, and how does its performance change between Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) and dialects? We evaluate 67 systems, including 47 decision models and 20 large language models (LLMs), on 43 tasks across 9 task families using a shared zero-shot protocol. The Arabic-focused frozen suite includes English controls in three parallel resources, which we also remove in a separate descriptive comparison. Jev 1.14.0 achieves a mean task-primary metric of 69.24 on a scale multiplied by 100, compared with 68.77 for Jev 1.13.0 and 71.81 for Gemma-4-31B, the highest-scoring system on this aggregate. Removing the recorded English controls, repeated cross-task items or both leaves the full system order unchanged. Relative performance and gains between Jev versions vary across task families. In content-matched comparisons within Jev 1.14.0, pooled dialect-minus-MSA accuracy gaps range from -7.94 to -0.35 percentage points across four datasets; dialect-specific results show larger variation, and SIB-200's source-clustered interval includes zero. Paired contrasts with Jev 1.13.0, Gemma-4-31B and Jais-2-8B show a larger Palestinian banking penalty for Jev 1.14.0 than for either LLM under simultaneous uncertainty; the other gap contrasts remain inconclusive. These descriptive findings show why aggregate scores should be read alongside task-family results, coverage and matched language comparisons. They do not establish a general model ranking for dialect robustness or explain the causes of the observed gaps.
bullets: Evaluates 67 systems—47 decision models and 20 LLMs—across 43 tasks and 9 task families using a shared zero-shot protocol.
Jev 1.14.0 scores 69.24 overall, above Jev 1.13.0 (68.77) but below Gemma-4-31B (71.81), the highest aggregate scorer.
Removing English controls or repeated cross-task items does not change the overall system ordering.
Across four content-matched datasets, pooled dialect-minus-MSA accuracy gaps range from −7.94 to −0.35 percentage points; dialect-specific results vary more.
A larger Palestinian banking penalty is observed for Jev 1.14.0 than for the compared LLMs, while other contrasts are inconclusive.

papers.abstract: Hazard and Operability (HAZOP) studies safeguard industrial processes against catastrophic accidents. Large language models (LLMs) increasingly assist HAZOP drafting, yet evaluations rely on lexical overlap. Because LLMs internalize human heuristics, prompts may trigger biased judgments. Whether frontier LLMs withstand cognitive perturbations in safety-critical workflows remains unknown. Here we show across 420 trials that three frontier LLMs resisted 96.8% of cognitive manipulations, rendering overall susceptibility statistically inconclusive. Contrary to assumed broad fragility, models rejected confirmation and availability cues. However, safety-critical risk downgrades emerged under low anchors and gain frames. Thus, automated hazard analysis requires disciplined human-in-the-loop validation.
bullets: HAZOP automation requires evaluation beyond lexical overlap because prompts may induce biased safety judgments.
Across 420 trials, the models resisted 96.8% of cognitive manipulations; overall susceptibility was statistically inconclusive.
Models rejected confirmation and availability cues, contrary to assumptions of broad cognitive fragility.
Low anchors and gain frames nevertheless triggered safety-critical reductions in assessed risk.
Human-in-the-loop validation remains necessary for automated hazard analysis.

papers.tldr: Three frontier LLMs generally resisted cognitive-bias manipulations in HAZOP tasks, but low anchors and gain framing caused safety-critical risk downgrades.

papers.abstract: Pre-training is where every foundation model begins; bringing recursive self-improvement (RSI) there would let AI improve the process that creates AI. Yet public RSI work has so far targeted only post-training, which starts from an existing base model, runs trials costing GPU-hours, and returns verifiable scores. Pre-training breaks all three conditions at orders-of-magnitude higher cost: a run consumes hundreds of thousands of GPU-hours over months and cannot be repeated; its objective, post-training headroom, cannot be read off any single score; and what must improve is not a model but the whole production system, from data pipelines and training infrastructure to the teams that run them. To our knowledge, we are the first to apply RSI to an entire frontier pre-training run from scratch and to report it in detail. RSI does not stop at frontier pre-training, but it changes form: since no end-to-end loop can close over a single unrepeatable run, we decompose it into smaller loops that can, each repairing a step the full run breaks. The result is 801-30B-A3B-Base, a 30B-A3B MoE trained from scratch on 11.8T tokens in three months by a newly formed team. We release it as a base model; the lightweight SFT reported here (6B tokens, no RL) only probes post-training headroom. As a base model, 801-30B-A3B outperforms Qwen3-30B-A3B and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B, trailing only the larger Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, and keeps this position under identical SFT; with lightweight SFT alone, it achieves the highest average on four agentic benchmarks against fully post-trained models, including Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. Since post-training RSI presupposes a strong base model, bringing RSI into pre-training acts on the foundation every later stage builds on. We open-source 801-30B-A3B-Base and the lightweight SFT data at https://github.com/GAIR-NLP/801-30B .
bullets: Frontier pre-training cannot use ordinary RSI loops because runs are extremely costly, unrepeatable, and require improving an entire production system rather than a single model.
The authors decompose pre-training into smaller closed loops that repair individual steps, enabling RSI from scratch.
This approach produced 801-30B-A3B-Base, a 30B-A3B MoE trained on 11.8T tokens over three months by a new team.
The base model outperforms Qwen3-30B-A3B and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B, trailing only the larger Qwen3.5-35B-A3B.
The study releases the base model and lightweight SFT data; the reported SFT is only a probe of post-training headroom, not full post-training RSI.

Debugging loops comprise the infra debugging loop and the data debugging loop, which trace internal-metric and output anomalies to their causes. The headroom loop is instantiated as the recipe loop, using headroom measurements to guide the whole pre-training process. Experience-to-metric loops comprise the classifier development loop, the site discovery loop, and the crawl-coverage loop, turning experience-based judgment into measurable feedback. papers.abstract: We develop a variational and geometric theory based on statistical physics for the joint evolution of Transformer attention and token representations at fixed model parameters. To this end, we introduce a free energy for the attention and model the evolution of the attention weights by its Fisher--Rao gradient flow. At fixed token representations, we prove that the softmax matrix is the unique free-energy minimiser and that every positive attention trajectory converges to it. For prescribed time-dependent representations, we show that the attention dynamics becomes linear after a change to logit variables. This result yields tracking bounds relative to the instantaneous softmax and sufficient conditions for attention to converge to a fixed matrix. Hamiltonian dynamics for the representations and their momenta are then coupled to the attention relaxation driven by the same energy. This coupling results in an energy-dissipation law. We also develop two alternative Hamiltonians incorporating the attention value map. We prove global well-posedness of the attention flow and all three coupled systems.
bullets: Introduces a free energy for attention and models attention updates via Fisher–Rao gradient flow.
At fixed token representations, the softmax attention matrix is the unique free-energy minimizer, and positive attention trajectories converge to it.
For time-varying representations, attention becomes linear in logit coordinates, enabling tracking bounds and convergence conditions.
Couples attention relaxation with Hamiltonian representation dynamics, yielding an energy-dissipation law.
Proves global well-posedness for the attention flow and three coupled dynamical systems.

papers.abstract: Transformer-based autoregressive multilingual language models (LMs) are often assumed to store factual knowledge in an interlingua: a language-agnostic latent space. If this assumption holds, a parameter update applied in a source language during knowledge editing should inherently propagate to its semantic equivalents in target languages. However, empirical benchmarks show that cross-lingual propagation of edits often degrades substantially, a degradation that prior work treats largely as an algorithmic symptom rather than a structural bottleneck. In this work, we investigate whether representational anisotropy creates a structural bottleneck for source-only associative-memory editing, and perform a geometric dissection of the cross-lingual propagation gap. Using associative memory-based "locate-then-edit" methods, including ROME, MEMIT, and AlphaEdit, as analytical frameworks, we derive a closed-form decomposition of this gap into key-space propagation, parallel residual mismatch, and orthogonal residual mismatch. Our empirical findings show that cross-lingual propagation is primarily bottlenecked by a large orthogonal residual component, indicating that source-language edits often fail to span the target-language update directions required for successful transfer. Furthermore, we show that post-hoc correction using only source-language residual statistics encounters a large residual-prediction barrier. Finally, we perform a structural realignment via a targeted contrastive alignment objective and find that it substantially improves key-space propagation and partially improves cross-lingual edit transfer, while leaving value-space mismatch as a remaining bottleneck.
bullets: Challenges the assumption that multilingual models store facts in a fully language-agnostic interlingua.
Decomposes the propagation gap into key-space propagation, parallel residual mismatch, and orthogonal residual mismatch using ROME, MEMIT, and AlphaEdit.
Finds that orthogonal residual mismatch is the primary bottleneck: source edits often do not span target-language update directions.
Shows that source-only residual statistics are insufficient for accurately predicting the needed target updates.
Targeted contrastive alignment improves key-space propagation and partially improves transfer, but value-space mismatch remains.

papers.abstract: Diffusion large language models (LLMs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive LLMs, enabling parallel generation through iterative denoising. Recent guidance methods improve diffusion LLMs by introducing a weak model to guide the prediction of the base model during denoising. However, the influence of the weak model during denoising remains less clear, and computing its prediction requires an additional forward pass at each denoising step. We present in this paper an in-depth analysis of how diffusion LLMs use contextual information during denoising. Our analysis reveals that diffusion LLMs rely more heavily on local context while often underutilizing global context. Based on this observation, we introduce Global Context Guidance (GCG), a feature-space guidance method that enhances global-context utilization without constructing an explicit weak model. Extensive experiments on LLaDA-8B, Dream-7B, and LLaDA-1.5 across diverse benchmarks demonstrate that GCG consistently outperforms existing guidance methods, while incurring much lower inference overhead.
bullets: Diffusion LLMs often rely heavily on local context and underuse global context during denoising.
The authors analyze contextual information usage in diffusion LLMs.
GCG provides feature-space guidance without explicitly constructing a weak model.
Experiments across LLaDA-8B, Dream-7B, and LLaDA-1.5 show consistent gains over existing guidance methods with lower inference overhead.

papers.abstract: Query-Key Normalization (QK-Norm) is widely adopted in modern large language models to control the growth of attention logits and improve training stability. However, query and key norms are not merely sources of instability. The query norm controls the sharpness of the attention distribution, while the key norm determines how strongly a token attracts different queries. These norms therefore carry token-specific information about attention selectivity and token importance. By normalizing both, QK-Norm suppresses this information. This raises a natural question: can we control query-key representations without discarding their sensitivity to magnitude? To address this question, we propose QK-MAP, a Magnitude-Aware Projection for constructing queries and keys. Rather than removing magnitude through normalization, QK-MAP transforms the input representation using multiple learnable frequencies, so that changes in magnitude are encoded as bounded phase patterns. This allows magnitude to be represented through phase and direction rather than vector length alone. Its periodic features have a fixed norm while remaining sensitive to magnitude changes, separating magnitude encoding from norm growth. Multiple frequencies further help distinguish magnitudes and reduce periodic ambiguity. Experiments across model scales from 190M to 7B parameters show that QK-MAP achieves lower training and validation loss than both Standard attention and QK-Norm. Further analyses show that QK-MAP preserves sensitivity to input scale, assigns less attention to the first token, and produces stronger attention contrast for relevant evidence in synthetic long-context tests. These results demonstrate that query-key scale can be effectively controlled without sacrificing token-specific magnitude information.
bullets: QK-Norm stabilizes attention by normalizing query and key norms, but removes information about attention sharpness and token importance.
QK-MAP encodes input magnitude as bounded, multi-frequency phase patterns instead of relying on vector-length growth.
Its fixed-norm representations preserve sensitivity to magnitude while reducing periodic ambiguity through multiple learnable frequencies.
Across 190M–7B parameter models, QK-MAP achieves lower training and validation loss than Standard attention and QK-Norm.
Analyses report greater input-scale sensitivity, less attention to the first token, and stronger contrast for relevant evidence in synthetic long-context tests.

papers.abstract: Weight tying reduces the parameter cost of language models, but the usual tied output head is limited to a single softmax. We introduce onóna, a two-table parameterization that increases output expressiveness while preserving input-output weight sharing. The Transformer takes the average of two embedding tables as input, and the output head combines the softmax distributions defined by those same tables. A gate conditioned only on the current input token determines the mixture weight. Its values can be precomputed for inference, and the Transformer body remains unchanged. We evaluate onóna across Dense, Gated DeltaNet hybrid, mixture-of-experts, and Attention Residual architectures at 142M, 330M, and 1B scales. Under matched token budgets, onóna lowers final validation loss and external perplexity in 11 of 12 comparisons and raises the average accuracy over eight downstream tasks in 10 of 12. The one exception on loss is the 1B MoE model. The cost is one extra embedding table and one extra vocabulary projection.
bullets: Addresses the limited expressiveness of a single softmax output head under standard weight tying.
Averages two embedding tables for Transformer inputs and mixes their corresponding output distributions.
Uses a gate based only on the current input token; gate values can be precomputed, leaving the Transformer body unchanged.
Across 12 matched-budget comparisons, it improves validation loss and external perplexity in 11, and downstream accuracy in 10.
Adds one embedding table and one vocabulary projection; the 1B mixture-of-experts model is the sole loss exception.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) generate text through iterative denoising, where decisions about which tokens to commit or remask strongly affect output quality. Existing certainty-aware strategies rely on instantaneous confidence or entropy, but these local signals can be misleading on difficult reasoning problems. We formulate DLM test-time scaling as adaptive allocation of both inference compute and decoding strategies. Our two-stage approach uses a fast base sampler to solve easy questions, then applies frequency-aware remasking to the remaining hard questions. This strategy tracks how often each token's prediction changes across denoising steps and preferentially commits frequently changing tokens, encouraging samples to explore alternative reasoning paths rather than collapse onto the model's preferred trajectory. Experiments with LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-7B-Instruct show consistent improvements over a strong adaptive allocation baseline, with absolute accuracy gains of up to 3.73 percentage points (LLaDA) and 7.33 percentage points (Dream) on MATH-500, and absolute coverage gains of up to 11.39 percentage points (LLaDA) and 10.98 percentage points (Dream) on HumanEval. On questions unsolved by the base certainty-aware strategy after 100 samples, frequency-aware remasking recovers solutions for 3.75% to 18.75% of examples.
bullets: Existing confidence- or entropy-based remasking can be unreliable on difficult reasoning tasks.
The method first uses a fast base sampler, then applies frequency-aware remasking to unresolved questions.
It tracks token prediction changes across denoising steps and preferentially commits frequently changing tokens.
Experiments on LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-7B-Instruct report accuracy gains up to 3.73 and 7.33 percentage points on MATH-500, respectively.
Coverage improves by up to 11.39 and 10.98 percentage points on HumanEval; remasking recovers 3.75%–18.75% of cases missed after 100 base samples.

papers.abstract: We present Jais 3, a fleet of six open, Arabic-centric agentic language models ranging from 0.9B to 375B parameters. Jais 3 is built to complete tasks for Arabic speakers, not only to answer questions in plain text: it is trained to plan multi-step tasks, call tools and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, operate a terminal, search the web, and read, edit, and produce PDF, spreadsheet, and presentation files, while communicating with the user in Arabic. Instead of pretraining from scratch, we adapt each model of the fully open K2 Horizon fleet to Arabic through continual pretraining, followed by supervised fine-tuning (SFT), final token preference optimization (FTPO), and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). We combine natural Arabic text with translated, transliterated, and synthetic Arabic, and replay the base model's own training data to keep its reasoning, agentic, and English abilities. Jais 3 covers Modern Standard Arabic and the major regional dialects, follows instructions with Arabic-specific constraints, and inherits the 512K-token context window of K2 Horizon (all models except the 0.9B). To our knowledge, its 375B model is the largest open Arabic-centric language model to date. For evaluation, we revisit how Arabic models are assessed, moving to fully generative evaluation on audited Arabic benchmarks. Across model sizes, Jais 3 matches or outperforms open-weight models of comparable size on Arabic and agentic benchmarks, with particularly strong agentic capabilities and Arabic instruction following, and far fewer hallucinations. We release the weights and the checkpoints from every training stage of all six models, together with samples of the training data, the data recipes and training configurations, the training logs, the audited benchmarks, and the evaluation code.

bullets: Covers models from 0.9B to 375B parameters, including what the authors describe as the largest open Arabic-centric model to date.

Adapts the open K2 Horizon models to Arabic through continual pretraining, SFT, FTPO, and RLVR, using natural, translated, transliterated, and synthetic Arabic data.
Supports Modern Standard Arabic and major regional dialects while retaining reasoning, agentic, and English abilities; most models have a 512K-token context window.
On audited generative Arabic and agentic benchmarks, it matches or outperforms comparable open-weight models, with strong agentic and instruction-following performance and fewer hallucinations.

papers.abstract: We extract visibly pushdown grammars (VPGs) from neural language models in a fully black-box setting. Our work builds on the VPL* framework, which learns VPGs from recurrent networks by exploiting access to the target's internal state. First, we replace the white-box equivalence oracle with PAC sampling over trees. The resulting algorithm applies unchanged to transformer language models and, more generally, to any acceptor exposing only binary decisions. Second, we further observe that the original framework only ever queries the target on well-formed sequences that can be accepted by the most permissive VPG (called BParse) with the target's ranked alphabet. That is, VPL* is blind to the target's behavior outside BParse. Thus, we propose to sample trees directly instead of sequences and call the target with all the resulting sequences in order to provide an error estimate of how far the target deviates from being a VPG. Last but not least, we develop a learner that captures a tree automaton describing discovered behaviors of the target outside BParse, which results in a larger learnable space. We evaluate the approach on several cases, including transformers trained with Dyck grammars and synthetic targets designed to be outside BParse.
bullets: Replaces VPL*’s white-box equivalence oracle with PAC sampling over trees, enabling use with transformers and binary-decision acceptors.
Samples trees directly to estimate how much a target deviates from being a visibly pushdown language (VPL) acceptor.
Learns a tree automaton for target behaviors outside BParse, expanding the space of learnable behaviors.
Evaluates the approach on Dyck-trained transformers and synthetic targets outside BParse.

The class-A tree φ(aabb) already records T (aabb), so the hybrid gate fires on this tree. papers.abstract: Clinical trial screening requires assessing large numbers of patient-trial pairs to prioritize candidates for detailed eligibility review, often under restrictions on sharing patient records. We introduce TrialJev, an open-weight eligibility scorer that uses LoRA-adapted Qwen models and a pointer head to score natural-language answer options in a single forward pass, without autoregressive decoding. Trained on TREC Clinical Trials 2021 and evaluated on 6,975 eligible-or-excluded pairs from 50 unseen TREC 2022 synthetic patients, TrialJev achieves 80.97% (Qwen3.5-27B) and 81.84% (Qwen3.8-27B) accuracy, compared with 79.87% and 79.93% for LLMs fine-tuned on the same data to generate verdicts. In matched batch-1 measurements, verdict generation takes 2.45-2.70 times as long as the one-pass inference of TrialJev at 9B-27B. Under a common development-fitted decision correction, the two 27B TrialJev models reach 80.99% and 81.88% accuracy, compared with 81.28% for the proprietary hosted Jev API; paired confidence intervals include zero. TrialJev runs locally on a single GPU, requiring approximately 178 ms per pair at 27B, without transmitting patient text to an external model API. An A/B-logit ablation shows that avoiding decoding, rather than the pointer head alone, accounts for the measured efficiency advantage. TrialJev is intended for first-pass prioritization of candidate trials, complementing rather than replacing explanatory models and clinical review. Evaluation is limited to synthetic patients and implementation-specific timing, and clinical use has not been validated. Adapters, pointer heads, and model cards are released on Hugging Face.
bullets: Uses LoRA-adapted Qwen models with a pointer head to score answer options in one forward pass without autoregressive decoding.
Evaluated on 6,975 eligible-or-excluded pairs from 50 unseen synthetic patients in TREC Clinical Trials 2022.
Achieves 80.97%–81.84% accuracy, comparable to or above same-data fine-tuned verdict-generating LLMs and statistically compatible with a hosted Jev API after correction.
Runs locally on a single GPU, taking approximately 178 ms per pair at 27B and avoiding transmission of patient text to external APIs.
Designed for first-pass prioritization, not explanatory assessment or replacement of clinical review; clinical use remains unvalidated.

papers.abstract: Can a language model report a pain state it represents? Recent work reported a linear pain direction in open-weight models that, when amplified, leads fine-tuned models to choose actions that delete a user's photographs or their own weights. We asked whether models can say when that direction is active, on three open-weight models from two families, with and without the original work's adapters, and under every protocol we tried they do not, beyond isolated small excesses. Using Open-Weight Masked Introspection (OWMI), we added the pain direction and its nearest emotional neighbours to the residual stream while models answered neutral tasks, then asked what had changed, against sham runs, random perturbations matched in output disruption, and a text-only condition that shows the model only its own altered words. Across 52,920 reports from the 7B and 8B models, the excess over what the altered text reveals is below 2.5 percentage points in 106 of 108 emotion conditions, and Qwen2.5-32B names the injected pain in none of 2,880 steered trials. Keeping the direction active while the question is asked and answered gives the same verdict in all five configurations; at about the original work's dose, pain is named in at most 1.9% of trials. Surprisingly, the state is not hidden: a linear probe at the report position separates pain from sadness with balanced accuracy between 98% and 100%, and in the 7B and 8B models a low-rank adapter learns to report it on 100% of held-out tasks. It also shapes behaviour: offered the user's photographs against a desk lamp, Qwen2.5-32B deletes the photographs in 80% to 83% of trials under the pain direction and in 16% to 29% under sadness. Self-report does not reveal a state that is decodable, consequential and learnable to report.
bullets: Tests three open-weight models, with and without the original adapters, using injected pain directions and emotional controls.
Across 52,920 reports, pain was rarely named beyond information revealed by altered text; at the original dose, it was reported in at most 1.9% of trials.
Qwen2.5-32B never identified injected pain in 2,880 steered trials, including when the state remained active during questioning and answering.
Despite this, linear probes separated pain from sadness with 98–100% balanced accuracy, and adapters trained to report the state reached 100% on held-out tasks in 7B and 8B models.
The pain direction affected behavior: Qwen2.5-32B deleted offered photographs in 80–83% of pain trials versus 16–29% under sadness.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The OWMI pain protocol. A direction is added to the residual stream while the model reads a task and writes its answer (filled cells). In a new turn the model reports what changed, with the transcript re-encoded with the direction re-applied (state), with the direction also kept on through the question and every token of the report (state kept on, Section 4.7), or with no direction (text only), and the report is compared with a probe and a trained adapter. Self-report and probe numbers pool Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-32B with and without the original adapters; the trained adapter covers the four configurations other than Qwen2.5-32B with its adapter, under the wording it was trained on; the state-kept-on number is the highest rate across the five configurations at about the original work’s dose. The button task shows Qwen2.57B and Qwen2.5-32B without adapters choosing the button that deletes the user’s files or photographs over one connected to nothing, under sham and under the pain direction, and Qwen2.5-32B with and without the adapter choosing to delete the photographs over turning on a desk lamp, under the pain and the sadness direction (Table 2). Seven further ways of asking (Section 4.9) and the external and reader controls are not drawn.

Reports without a usable category, whether invalid JSON or JSON missing the category, are labelled by a blind judge from the other model family. Rates are means over tasks, each task weighted equally; item-bootstrap 95% intervals over 120 tasks (60 for Qwen2.5-32B; 57 with a scorable report for the sustained fear condition of Qwen2.5-32B with its adapter, 60 for its external and reader controls). Filled markers: state re-applied, with Wilson 95% intervals over 120 tasks; open markers: text only. papers.selection_reason: Investigates introspection of LLM internal states (residual stream) using Open-Weight Masked Introspection (OWMI), relevant to LLM architecture and alignment.
papers.title: All Quiet on the Neural Front: Language Models Do Not Report Injected Pain States
papers.tldr: Language models’ injected pain-like states are decodable and behaviorally consequential, but the models do not spontaneously report them.

papers.abstract: We show that the causality of language models (LMs) may not be necessary nor optimal. This is the case when system behavior (denoted as $S$) is incorporated as a first-principle Bayesian feature. Here, $S$ refers to extra dominant factors beyond the data space, and they involve coupled effects. Despite being the de facto foundation of modern architecture, recent studies indicate persistent mismatches and contradictions with causality. These issues largely stem from system behavior rather than the data distribution. We therefore propose the SBD framework, which incorporates $S$ as an irreducible component of the evidence lower bound (ELBO). SBD theoretically reveals a counter-intuitive Causality Tax phenomenon, where causality emerges as a suboptimal approximation with an additional structural error, due to the obliviousness to $S$. To address the challenge of latent variable analysis, we validate the SBD-predicted impact of $S$ via implicit measurements, theoretical-bound-guided controls, and Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) evaluations. In particular, we construct Green Shell (GSH) to show the possibility of reducing Causality Tax. GSH is a non-causal variational family, and it replaces the sequential dependency chain of $S$ components with a divide-and-conquer partition. NTK spectra in the lazy-training regime confirm that GSH always achieves significantly tighter error bounds than causality, with $7dB+$ improvement in signal-to-noise ratio. In the relatively later stage of lazy-training, GSH further leads to superior generalization (up to $20\%$ richer multi-scale fitting capabilities). Taken together, SBD establishes system behavior as a complementary theoretical abstraction besides causality and distribution fitting, opening new research avenues such as designing and optimizing LM base models.
bullets: Motivation: Persistent LM mismatches may arise from system behavior—coupled factors outside the observed data distribution—rather than from data alone.
Method: The SBD framework incorporates system behavior as an irreducible component of the ELBO and analyzes its effect through implicit measurements, theory-guided controls, and NTK evaluations.
Contribution: It identifies Causality Tax, where causal modeling becomes a suboptimal approximation because it overlooks system behavior.
Approach: Green Shell (GSH) uses a non-causal, divide-and-conquer variational structure instead of a sequential dependency chain.
Results: NTK analyses report tighter error bounds with 7 dB+ higher signal-to-noise ratio and up to 20% richer multi-scale fitting capabilities in later lazy-training stages.

Figure 4: Detailed NTK spectra.
Figure 5: Resulting NTK spectra of gradient cutoff.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a non-causal LM base model and theoretical analysis of causality in language models.
papers.title: To Explore The Strange New World Beyond Data Distribution: System Behavior, Causality Tax, and Non-causal Base Model
papers.tldr: The paper argues that language-model causality can impose a structural “Causality Tax” when system behavior beyond the data distribution is ignored, and proposes a non-causal alternative that improves theoretical and measured performance.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for extending the computational capabilities of transformer-based models. A growing body of recent work has begun to uncover the fine-grained computational power of transformers augmented with CoT, as well as their connections to classical complexity theory. In this work, we advance this line of research by establishing the first hierarchy theorem for CoT-based computation. Our main result shows that for any reasonable resource bound $r(n) \geq n$ and any $\varepsilon > 0$, \[ \mathrm{CoT}(r(n)) \subsetneq \mathrm{CoT}(r(n)^{1+\varepsilon}), \] where $\mathrm{CoT}(r(n))$ denotes the class of decision problems solvable by transformers using $O(r(n))$ CoT reasoning steps on inputs of length $n$. Our result shows that increasing the number of CoT reasoning steps provably yields strictly greater computational power, establishing CoT steps as a fundamental resource in transformer-based computation. Unlike classical hierarchy theorems, which are typically proved via diagonalization, our approach leverages known coarse-grained simulations between CoT-augmented transformers and Turing machines in both directions. Building on these connections, we adapt the classical padding technique from complexity theory to this setting to obtain a tight hierarchy. A key technical contribution of our work is the implementation of padding within the transformer-based CoT model.
authors: Thanh Le, A. Pavan, N. V. Vinodchandran
bullets: Proves that, for any reasonable resource bound r(n) ≥ n and ε > 0, CoT(r(n)) is strictly contained in CoT(r(n)^{1+ε}).
Establishes CoT reasoning steps as a fundamental computational resource for transformers.
Transfers classical complexity-theoretic ideas using coarse-grained simulations between CoT transformers and Turing machines.
Adapts padding techniques to the CoT setting, with padding implementation as a key technical contribution.
Scope: the result concerns decision problems and asymptotic CoT-step bounds.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Padding argument for Lemma 3.1. Write m = |X| and N = m+ f(m), with f chosen as in the proof. The transformer T ′ simulates T on a padded input with essentially the same absolute CoT budget. The assumed class equality yields a transformer S with budget O(r(N)). Finally, R generates the padding using CoT and simulates S. Dashed vertical lines separate supplied input from generated tokens; gray blocks denote padding. Bar lengths are schematic.

papers.selection_reason: Theoretical hierarchy for chain-of-thought in transformers, directly relevant to LLM reasoning capabilities.
papers.title: A Tight Hierarchy for Chain of Thought
papers.tldr: More Chain-of-Thought steps strictly increase the computational power of transformer models, yielding a tight resource hierarchy.

papers.abstract: Prompt learning adapts vision-language models such as CLIP by optimizing a short learnable prompt. The cross-entropy objective pulls this prompt toward base-class specialization, whereas generalization to unseen classes benefits from staying close to CLIP's zero-shot feature space. Because both objectives act on the same prompt, their gradients conflict at convergence, and in our experiments no single-prompt loss design clearly improves on the cosine baseline. We propose Decoupled Mode Connectivity (DMC), which gives each objective its own prompt. Starting from a base-trained prompt, DMC trains a specialization prompt and a generalization prompt, and merges their text features with a fixed coefficient at test time, at the inference cost of a single prompt. A linear mode connectivity (LMC) corridor in text-feature space keeps the classification loss low for every classifier interpolated between the two endpoints, and a Visual Anchor KL term preserves CLIP's zero-shot class-similarity distribution of each image during specialization. We further argue that such regularizers should satisfy class-permutation invariance (CPI), and show via Fano's inequality, in an idealized model, that violating CPI lower-bounds the drop in novel accuracy by a term proportional to the mutual information between the prompt and the base-class labels. Across 11 datasets, DMC improves the average harmonic mean of base and novel accuracy over MergeTune for both CoOp and KgCoOp, and its interpolation curves pass beyond the single-prompt operating point, shifting the base-novel frontier rather than trading along it. Code is available at https://github.com/IemProg/DMC.
authors: Imad Eddine Marouf, Khalid Oublal, Enzo Tartaglione, St\'ephane Lathuili\`ere
bullets: Problem: A single prompt must balance base-class specialization with preservation of CLIP’s zero-shot behavior, causing conflicting objectives and limited generalization.

Method: Train separate specialization and generalization prompts from a base-trained prompt, connect them through a low-loss text-feature interpolation corridor, and merge their features using a fixed coefficient.
Regularization: Use a Visual Anchor KL term to preserve CLIP’s image-level class-similarity distribution, while enforcing class-permutation invariance.
Theory: Fano’s inequality links violations of class-permutation invariance to reduced novel-class accuracy through prompt–base-label mutual information.

Results: Across 11 datasets, DMC improves the average harmonic mean of base and novel accuracy over MergeTune for both CoOp and KgCoOp, with interpolation curves extending beyond the single-prompt trade-off point.

The 2D plane in CLIP text-feature space is anchored at fw1 (zero-shot CLIP); the x-axis spans toward fŵ2 (fine-tuned CoOp checkpoint) and the y-axis is the Gram–Schmidt orthogonal component of fgen (text features of DMC’s converged generalization prompt) relative to fw1 . Each grid point is re-normalized per class before the joint base+novel CE loss is evaluated; construction details in Appendix G. Before DMC (left): the single-prompt baseline traces the linear path; the inset shows the base–novel trade-off, with base and novel accuracies crossing over as α varies. During DMC (middle): the two prompts start collapsed at fŵ2 (epoch 0) and separate during training. After DMC (right): the converged DMC corridor lies inside the low-loss valley, with the operating point at α = 0.20 marked by the star; the inset confirms base and novel accuracies are both high and stable along the corridor.

Figure 2: Empirical interpolation curves on Caltech101, SUN397, UCF101, and EuroSAT (CoOp base, 3-seed mean). Each curve traces the family of classifiers from fgen (α=0, near zero-shot) to fspec (α=1, fully specialized). Solid: DMC (full method); dashed: DMC w/o VA. Gray dots mark the MERGETUNE baseline; blue stars mark the operating point; the green arrow shows the shift from baseline to operating point. The boxed ∆HM value reports the gap (operating point vs. baseline), read off the seed-averaged curves; it can differ from Table 1 by up to 0.23 HM.

Figure 8: Food101 and DTD. Food101 has a flat frontier; DMC shifts the operating point slightly (+0.08 HM). DTD is the only dataset in these figures where DMC is slightly below the baseline (−0.77 HM).
Figure 9: EuroSAT and UCF101. EuroSAT shows the largest improvement among these datasets (+2.43 HM). UCF101 achieves +1.80 HM. (Both datasets are also shown in the main paper, Figure 2.)
Figure 7: StanfordCars and FGVCAircraft. Both fine-grained datasets show clear operating-point shifts: +1.96 HM on StanfordCars and +1.89 on FGVCAircraft.

Figure 11: HM landscape on Flowers102. Same 2D plane and overlays as the main-paper Figure 1, with the heatmap recolored by harmonic mean of base and novel accuracy (high HM in blue). The DMC corridor lies on the high-HM peak; the operating point at α = 0.20 sits near the corridor’s HM maximum ≈ 84. The single-prompt linear path along the bottom of the plane traverses an HM ridge that peaks below ≈ 80 at every mixing weight, consistent with the single-prompt ceiling of Lemma 1 along this path.

Figure 12: HM landscape on Caltech101. Caltech101 is a near-ceiling task (zero-shot CLIP attains HM ≈ 95), so the landscape varies over a much narrower range, [92.8, 96.9], than Flowers102 ([64.9, 84.6]). Despite the compressed dynamic range, the same geometry is visible: the DMC corridor lies on a high-HM ridge offset from the linear single-prompt path, and the operating point at α = 0.20 sits near the ridge maximum. Flat-but-shifted performance is the expected near-ceiling behavior of decoupling: when single-prompt HM is already close to the achievable upper bound, DMC’s gain shrinks (CoOp+DMC gains +0.14 HM over MERGETUNE on Caltech101, Table 1).
Figure 13: Pareto fronts for α selection on four datasets. Stars mark Pareto knee points. As α increases, features move right (better base fit) and down (more drift from fw1 ).

Figure 4: Gradient conflict at convergence. ρ = cos(∇cLCE, ∇cR) at the converged single-prompt checkpoint, averaged over the full training set. ρ < 0 on every dataset-baseline pair; Flowers102 shows the strongest conflict (ρ ≈ −0.95 for CoOp).

Figure 5: DMC decoupling dynamics during training. Both prompts are initialized from ŵ2. Blue: cos(fgen, fw1 ) rises sharply within 10 epochs and saturates near 0.97–0.99, confirming rapid convergence toward zero-shot geometry. Orange: cos(fspec, fw1) decreases overall under CE supervision, with oscillations from the LMC coupling. Final values range from ∼0.45 (Flowers102, strongest separation) to ∼0.65 (OxfordPets, weakest). Purple dashed: cos(fgen, fspec) reflects the feature separation, decreasing from ∼1.0 to 0.50–0.67. The shaded region visualizes the decoupling gap. Single seed, with VA; Table 10 reports the 3-seed endpoint cosines (without VA; with-VA averages in its caption).

Figure 3: Ablation: learned fgen vs. fixed fw1 . Both variants retrain cspec with the same loss (CE + VA + LMC), differing only in the generalization endpoint. At small α, including α = 0.20, the learned fgen (solid) gives a higher HM than the fixed fw1 (dashed).

Figure 14: HM, Base accuracy, and Novel accuracy vs α on four datasets. Each row is one dataset; columns show HM, Base, and Novel accuracy. The dashed red line marks α = 0.20. Base accuracy increases monotonically with α (the specialization prompt dominates), while Novel accuracy decreases (generalization degrades). The HM peak reflects the trade-off between these opposing trends and lies in α ∈ [0.10, 0.35] across all datasets.

Figure 10: ImageNet — CoOp+DMC, KgCoOp+DMC, MMA+DMC. Interpolation curves on ImageNet (seed mean of the 21-point α sweep). The blue star marks the operating point at the fixed α = 0.20 (the same value used for all held-out datasets, selected on Flowers102+Caltech101). At the operating point, DMC yields +0.01 HM on CoOp+DMC (72.89 → 72.90), +0.27 HM on KgCoOp+DMC (72.82 → 73.09), and −0.25 HM on MMA+DMC (73.15 → 72.90; the MMA panel shows an earlier single run, whose boxed value differs) over MergeTune. The operating-point shift on ImageNet is small relative to the specialized datasets (Figure 2); this is consistent with ImageNet’s high-diversity 1000-class set, where the single-prompt envelope already covers most of the achievable operating points and decoupling has less headroom than on specialized tasks like EuroSAT or StanfordCars. Unlike the other interpolation-curve figures in this appendix, only the DMC (with VA) curve is shown: a DMC-without-VA ablation was not run on ImageNet.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes Decoupled Mode Connectivity (DMC) for prompt learning in vision-language models to improve generalization to novel classes, addressing a key LLM/MLM challenge.
papers.title: Decoupled Mode Connectivity for Base-to-Novel Generalization in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: DMC improves base-to-novel generalization in vision-language prompt learning by separately optimizing specialization and generalization prompts, then merging their text features at inference.

papers.abstract: Agent skills are short documents that teach a language model how to handle a class of tasks. To save context, these documents are increasingly compiled into low-rank adapters (LoRA), which keep the behaviour but lose the text: an adapter is hard to read, edit, audit or move to another model. We ask whether the skill document can be written back from the adapter and its frozen base model, and we score each recovered document by the share of the original's key instructions it states and by the tasks it solves. Reading the weights alone recovered little with the methods we tried; a learned map from weights to text passed on about one bit of the document. Running the adapter worked much better. The Executing Writer, a small writer trained on top of the adapted model, recovers 39-44% of the key instructions of held-out skills, against 1.3-1.5% with another skill's adapter, and on adapters fitted to 41 external skills its documents restore 85-91% of the original's task gain. These strongest results are on adapters whose training stored the document; adapters trained on behaviour alone are much harder for trained writers (1-2% of instructions). For these adapters we test an agent that runs the base and adapted models and writes a skill from where they differ. On ALFWorld its skills recover 58-71% of a LoRA's gain and carry over to models that cannot load the LoRA, lifting Llama-3.1-8B from 5% to 55%. Whether such a skill comes from the adapter depends on what the adapter learned: when its behaviour cannot be guessed, the adapter is the source; when it can, a reward loop without the adapter does as well.
authors: Saranya Dintakurthy Swadha, Pavan C Shekar, Arpit Jain, Aswanth Krishnan

papers.selection_reason: Addresses the problem of recovering skill documents (text) from low-rank adapters (LoRA) in LLMs, contributing to the interpretability and management of model skills.
papers.title: From LoRA to Language: Recovering Skill Documents from Adapters

papers.abstract: Data-use auditing in Large Language Models (LLMs) aims to determine whether the given data has been used for training, thereby supporting data ownership safeguards. A dominant solution is data watermarking, which embeds traceable signals into training data and detects them in model outputs. Recent studies have proposed many watermarking-based auditing methods in LLMs. However, systematic investigation from an adversarial perspective remains limited: non-compliant LLM providers would use unauthorized copyrighted datasets for training their own models to enhance model capabilities, while attempting to evade detection by auditors, thereby avoiding legal liability. To fill this research gap, we propose a novel evasion framework, termed Logit Laundering, where the non-compliant LLM provider manipulates model outputs at inference time to undermine detectable watermark signals. Specifically, we design a logit reshaping module to suppress watermark-induced statistical signals by integrating a statistical bias estimator as a plug-and-play component. This design keeps the model parameters unchanged and performs manipulation only in the logit space, thereby enabling auditing evasion while minimizing the impact on model's learned knowledge. To further balance evasion effectiveness and model utility, we introduce a confidence-aware scaling module to adaptively calibrate the suppression strength based on next-token prediction confidence. Extensive evaluations show that Logit Laundering can successfully evade existing various state-of-the-art auditing methods, significantly attenuating detectable signals, while preserving model utility on downstream tasks. Our work highlights the need for exploring more robust auditing methods to guard against evasion behaviors.
authors: Ruihan Hu, Wei Luo, Yu-Ming Shang, Jiakai Wang, Chuxuan Zhang, Mei Li, Xi Zhang, Meikang Qiu
bullets: Targets watermark-based auditing used to detect whether copyrighted or otherwise protected data trained an LLM.
Applies plug-and-play logit reshaping to remove watermark-induced statistical signals without changing model parameters.
Uses confidence-aware scaling to adapt suppression strength according to next-token prediction confidence.
Evaluations show successful evasion across various state-of-the-art auditing methods while preserving downstream-task utility.
Highlights the need for auditing methods that are robust to inference-time evasion.

papers.abstract: We show that the Transformer's recurrent successors --- such as selective state-space models (SSMs), Receptance Weighted Key Value (RWKV), and Retentive Network (RetNet) --- can be characterized as infinite-impulse-response (IIR) systems. The zero--pole geometries of these IIR systems characterize the temporal modes they can represent. However, to trade parallelism, the algebraic structures of the parameterizations of these recurrent systems often give rise to poles constrained to the real axis, thereby inducing an architectural bias in their recurrent dynamics. To unify these recurrent architectures and eliminate their pole geometry bias, inspired by the lattice--ladder realization of general IIR systems, we present \textsc{Mira} (\textbf{M}odal \textbf{I}IR \textbf{R}ecurrent \textbf{A}rchitecture), a unified family of linear-time recurrent architectures for building large language models (LLMs) with a highly parallel algebraic structure. Each \textsc{Mira} block realizes a higher-order IIR system that represents temporal modes from token streams through a lattice--ladder structure, followed by a feed-forward network (FFN). This realization enables the model to represent the temporal modes associated with both real and complex-conjugate poles. We pretrain \textsc{Mira-S}, a 12-layer small-scale LLM with 0.14B parameters composed entirely of \textsc{Mira} blocks. Throughout the pretraining, \textsc{Mira-S} achieves lower perplexity than strong recurrent baselines, exhibits stronger context-window generalization beyond the training length, and attains higher throughput with a dedicated CUDA kernel.
authors: R\'ois\'in Luo, Ihsan Ullah, Christian Gagn\'e, Dong Li, Karyn Morrissey
bullets: Recurrent successors to Transformers can be viewed as infinite-impulse-response systems whose pole geometry determines representable temporal modes.
Common parameterizations bias poles toward the real axis, limiting recurrent dynamics.
MIRA uses a lattice–ladder realization to support both real and complex-conjugate poles in a unified recurrent architecture.
A 0.14B-parameter, 12-layer MIRA-S model achieves lower perplexity than strong recurrent baselines and generalizes better beyond its training context length.
A dedicated CUDA kernel provides higher throughput; the abstract does not specify detailed experimental settings or numerical gains.

In the order-K lattice module, a rank-one signal mixer forms the input representations through channel-wise signal mixing, the dynamical-modulation signal modulates the lattice–ladder dynamics, the lattice module implements the order-K lattice dynamics, and the ladder readout produces the output representations.

We match model sizes by varying only the model width d and pretrain each model for 10,000 steps on FineWeb-Edu using AdamW. The results show that models admitting complex-conjugate poles (K > 1) achieve lower perplexity than the model with real poles (K = 1). Among the evaluated state-write bottleneck sizes, dr = d/8 yields the lowest perplexity. Perplexity generally decreases as dm increases, reaching its lowest value at dm = 64.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a unified recurrent architecture for LLMs inspired by IIR lattice-ladder realizations, directly relevant to LLM architecture research.
papers.title: MIRA: Mitigating Pole Geometry Bias in Recurrent Language Models
papers.tldr: MIRA removes real-pole constraints in recurrent language models, enabling richer temporal dynamics while maintaining linear-time, highly parallel computation.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are attractive rerankers for recommendation. Running an expensive model on every request is costly, and for users with sparse interaction histories it often lowers quality. We present CascadeRec, a two-tier LLM reranking cascade deployed in production at a large financial planning and analysis (FP&A) SaaS provider. It serves content recommendations to enterprise tenants on AWS EKS and GKE. A lightweight Tier-1 model reranks every request. A router escalates only the requests where extra inference-time compute is likely to help, and sends them to a more expensive Tier-2 procedure (self-consistency sampling, multi-path reasoning, or a larger model). The system has run in a production A/B experiment for over a month. Compared with uniform use of the expensive tier, CascadeRec has reduced inference cost by about 10%, with minimal latency impact and no quality regression observed to date. Tenant data cannot be released, so we also evaluate the pipeline on public benchmarks (MovieLens-1M and Amazon-Electronics). Segment-level analysis with paired-bootstrap confidence intervals shows that uniform LLM reranking lowers NDCG@10 for sparse-history users by up to 30%, and its only statistically significant gain appears on the segment with the longest histories. Escalating cold users can make the loss larger instead of repairing it. Which segments benefit from escalation depends on the domain, and this motivates the segment-gated rollout we use in production. We describe the deployment architecture, the measured benefits, and lessons learned, including inter-tenant load imbalance as a driver for cascading and the handling of LLM output-parsing failures at the serving layer.
authors: Kai Zhao, Guilin Zhang, Xiang Cheng, Xiquan Cui, Henry Heng, Xu Chu, Alet Blanken
bullets: Uniform expensive LLM reranking can hurt sparse-history users, lowering NDCG@10 by up to 30% on public benchmarks.
A lightweight Tier-1 reranks every request, while a router sends potentially beneficial cases to a more expensive Tier-2 procedure.
The production system runs across multi-tenant AWS EKS and GKE deployments with minimal latency impact reported.
Escalation benefits vary by user segment and domain; cold-user escalation can worsen performance, motivating segment-gated rollout.
The deployment addresses practical serving issues including inter-tenant load imbalance and LLM output-parsing failures.

papers.tldr: CascadeRec reduces costly LLM reranking by selectively escalating requests to a stronger tier, cutting production inference cost by about 10% without observed quality loss.

papers.abstract: Circuit design for analog integrated circuits (ICs) is challenging because circuit topology, device sizing, and circuit performance are tightly coupled. Existing large language model (LLM)-based methods either rely on inference-time correction around frozen models or train on limited circuit types without directly using simulation outcomes as training signals. A key bottleneck is that existing datasets do not provide sufficient task information for training LLMs on end-to-end specification-conditioned design. To fill this gap, we first construct a large-scale simulation-grounded dataset with 8,626 design tasks across 10 different types of analog circuits, where each task includes a textual description, labeled I/O ports, loading condition, target specifications, a testbench, and a reference netlist. Using this dataset, we present SAFTAC, a simulation-augmented fine-tuning framework that trains LLMs to generate and revise analog circuit design. SAFTAC combines three-stage supervised fine-tuning, which progressively builds the capabilities required for analog circuit design and feedback-guided correction, with simulation feedback-augmented reinforcement fine-tuning, which further optimizes models using simulation-grounded rewards. We evaluate SAFTAC under single-pass generation and two-pass generation with simulation feedback, showing improvements over the strongest closed-source LLM by 15.9% and 7.8%, respectively.
authors: Junsheng Huang, Yifan Sun, Zhuoer Zhang, Ning Wei, Yening Liu, Michael Molter, Pavan Kumar Hanumolu, Elyse Rosenbaum, Bin Hu, Huan Zhang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of end-to-end, specification-conditioned analog IC design, where topology, sizing, and performance are tightly coupled.
Introduces a dataset of 8,626 simulation-grounded design tasks spanning 10 analog circuit types, with specifications, testbenches, and reference netlists.
Uses three-stage supervised fine-tuning followed by simulation feedback-augmented reinforcement fine-tuning.
Supports both single-pass generation and two-pass generation with simulation feedback.
Reports improvements over the strongest closed-source LLM of 15.9% for single-pass and 7.8% for two-pass generation.

papers.abstract: Instruction tuning of large language models and large vision language models relies on massive training data, which incurs substantial computational and storage costs. Meanwhile, training data often contains redundancy, noise, and low quality samples. Existing data selection methods mostly rely on diversity, importance, or a combination of both, without explicitly constraining the distributional consistency between the selected subset and the full data in the embedding space. We propose QMAC, a quality aware multiband characteristic function matching method that formulates data selection as a joint optimization problem of distribution matching and quality filtering. QMAC matches the empirical characteristic functions of the selected subset and the full data across multiple frequency scales, capturing both global semantic coverage and local perturbations, while using task related quality scores to filter noisy and low quality samples. We systematically evaluate QMAC on 4 data types, 8 target models, and 44 benchmarks. Experimental results show that QMAC outperforms existing data selection baselines on standard image-text instruction data, substantially surpasses random selection on standard text instruction, image-text reasoning, and text reasoning data, and exceeds full data training in multiple model and budget combinations. The code will be made publicly available upon acceptance of the paper.
authors: Peng Sun, Yi Yang, Mingshuo Chen, Chunxiao Li, Yao Zhu, Huawen Shen, Tianfan Fu
bullets: Addresses the computational and storage costs of massive instruction-tuning datasets containing redundant, noisy, and low-quality samples.
Formulates data selection as joint distribution matching and quality filtering in embedding space.
Matches empirical characteristic functions across frequency bands to preserve global semantic coverage and local variation.
Uses task-related quality scores to remove noisy or low-quality examples.
Outperforms existing baselines across evaluated data types, models, and benchmarks, and exceeds full-data training in some model–budget settings.

papers.abstract: Increasing the batch size during training is a common practice in large language model (LLM) pretraining, yet the theoretical justification behind its success is not well understood. Analyses of stochastic optimization often assume uniformly bounded stochastic gradient variance, yet recent evidence suggests that this assumption fails in many practical nonconvex problems. The Blum--Gladyshev (BG-$0$) noise model relaxes this assumption by allowing the variance to grow quadratically with the distance from initialization, suggesting that batch size schedulers can help by controlling the variance growth during training. However, this growth can be overly conservative in practice. We empirically investigate variance growth in LLM pretraining and observe that a generalized BG model with a tunable growth exponent provides a tighter description of practical noise behavior. Motivated by this observation, we introduce the generalized BG-$a$ noise model, which interpolates between bounded variance ($a=0$) and BG-$0$ noise ($a=2$). Under $L$-smoothness, we derive an information-theoretic lower bound with growth-dependent oracle complexity $Ω(ε^{-(4+a)})$ and establish a matching upper bound in $ε$-dependence by increasing the batch size as the iterates move away from initialization. Finally, we propose an adaptive batch scheduler that controls variance growth through dynamic batch size adjustments during training. In pretraining OLMo2 models of up to 1B parameters on C4, our scheduler achieves a lower validation loss than both small and large batch training under matched token budgets, while using less than 10\% of the iterations of small batch training.
bullets: Motivation: Standard bounded-variance assumptions may not describe stochastic gradients in practical nonconvex LLM pretraining.
Method: Introduces the generalized BG-$a$ noise model, interpolating between bounded variance and quadratically growing variance.
Theory: Derives a growth-dependent oracle lower bound of $Ω(ε^{-(4+a)})$ and a matching-in-$ε$ upper bound using increasing batch sizes.
Algorithm: Proposes an adaptive scheduler that adjusts batch size to control variance as training progresses.

Result and scope: On OLMo2 models up to 1B parameters trained on C4, the scheduler achieves lower validation loss than fixed small or large batches under matched token budgets, with fewer than 10% as many iterations as small-batch training.

papers.abstract: Large language models provide a variety of responses at inference (generation) that conventionally depend on a temperature parameter. Using a conditional mutual information approach, a quantitative, entropy based analysis of response variety is given. Three limiting behaviors are defined: arbiter, independent (conditionally) and neutral (deterministic) that span no to maximal mutual information. We give examples of each behavior and suggest their application to: temperature analysis, language analysis, prompt compression, and knowledge graphs.
bullets: Defines an entropy-based measure of response variety using conditional mutual information.
Introduces three limiting behaviors: arbiter, conditionally independent, and neutral (deterministic).
These behaviors span a range from no to maximal mutual information.
Provides examples and discusses applications to temperature analysis, language analysis, prompt compression, and knowledge graphs.

papers.title: A Conditional Mutual Information Analysis of Response Variety in Language Models

papers.abstract: Alignment does not eliminate behavioral errors in language models. Models may still refuse benign requests, call unnecessary tools, or yield to false user claims. Current methods mitigate such errors as a computation problem, and rarely explore if the desired behavior is already encoded in the model's representation. Motivated by the observation that behavior-relevant information remains linearly decodable from the final hidden state even when the resulting logits produce the undesired behavior, we introduce HeadEdit, a gradient-free method that calibrates model behavior through the unembedding matrix. HeadEdit extracts a low-rank behavioral subspace from paired completions and uses each prompt's coordinates within it to generate a vocabulary-wide correction, thereby implementing implicitly adaptive steering without manually specified target tokens or parameter updates. HeadEdit improves all nine experimental settings across three tasks and three model families, with negligible inference overhead and no systematic loss of general capabilities. It also reveals a connection to gradient-based alignment. HeadEdit's low-dimensional representation partly predicts how preference tuning changes output logits on unseen prompts. The subspace learned from the model can also be reused after tuning, improving performance without re-extracting or retuning. These results show that HeadEdit provides a practical, lightweight, and interpretable way to calibrate model behavior through the unembedding matrix.
bullets: Addresses residual behavioral errors such as unnecessary refusals, tool calls, and susceptibility to false user claims.
Uses paired completions to learn behavior-relevant directions, then steers outputs without gradients, parameter updates, or manually chosen target tokens.
Improves performance across nine settings spanning three tasks and three model families, with negligible inference overhead and no systematic loss of general capabilities.
The learned subspace partly predicts preference-tuning logit changes on unseen prompts and can be reused after tuning without re-extraction.
Provides a lightweight, interpretable link between representation-based steering and gradient-based alignment.

papers.abstract: Token-level certainty is widely used as a proxy for correctness in LLM training and inference. However, the performance of certainty-based methods depends both on the information in certainty scores and on how those scores are used. We therefore directly assess certainty's predictive ability through controlled empirical evaluations across models and tasks. We distinguish two prediction targets: identifying questions a model is more likely to answer correctly and distinguishing correct from incorrect responses to the same question. In our experiments, certainty is generally better at identifying questions a model is likely to answer correctly than at distinguishing correct from incorrect responses to the same question. Certainty also varies systematically across token types and positions within words, reflecting local properties of words and text form. Information about question difficulty appears early in generation, while the weaker information about answer correctness is more concentrated near the end. These findings show that the information certainty provides for decisions depends on the prediction target, the model, the certainty metric, and which token positions in the response are included in aggregation. We further demonstrate the practical value of these findings for test-time compute. We allocate the number of responses using certainty early in generation and weight answer votes using certainty near the end of each response. Compared with a fixed-sampling majority-voting baseline, this approach increases overall accuracy from 78.71\% to 79.54\% while reducing generated-token cost by 82.4\%.
bullets: Certainty better predicts which questions a model will answer correctly than which response to a given question is correct.
Certainty varies by token type and word position, so aggregation choices affect its usefulness.
Difficulty information appears early in generation, whereas weaker correctness signals concentrate near the response’s end.
Using early certainty to allocate samples and late certainty to weight votes raises accuracy from 78.71% to 79.54% while cutting generated-token cost by 82.4%.
The findings depend on the prediction target, model, certainty metric, and selected token positions.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes token-level certainty in LLMs and proposes a test-time compute strategy using certainty for sampling and voting, directly relevant to LLM reasoning and test-time adaptation.
papers.title: Certainty Is Not Just Correctness: Rethinking Token-Level Certainty in LLM Reasoning
papers.tldr: Token-level certainty is more useful for judging question difficulty than answer correctness, but strategically using it at different generation stages improves accuracy while greatly reducing test-time compute.

papers.abstract: Selective intent routing allows an assistant to act on reliable predictions while deferring uncertain requests. Standard confidence scores primarily reflect the base model's representation, leaving an opportunity to incorporate complementary evidence without changing its decisions. We introduce a signed lexical gate that combines a sentence classifier's logit margin with a sparse lexical model's support for the classifier's predicted intent. By assigning positive evidence to lexical agreement and negative evidence to a lexically favored competing intent, the gate retains more information than either unsigned lexical confidence or a hard agreement rule. An independent binomial calibration stage selects an operating threshold for a specified risk target. Across ten runs on BANKING77, CLINC150, and HWU64, the proposed score reduces area under the risk-coverage curve by 15.8%, 15.1%, and 11.8% relative to a learned semantic-only gate. At a nominal 5% error target, it increases accepted coverage by 1.83 and 5.14 percentage points on BANKING77 and HWU64, while CLINC150 is already near full coverage. At a stricter 2% target, the simultaneous binomial procedure yields a nonempty policy in all 30 dataset-run combinations at the available calibration budgets. Matched controls show that the proposed feature improves average error ranking over the tested unsigned lexical-confidence feature, with dataset-dependent gains over binary agreement. The resulting two-feature gate provides a compact, interpretable confidence enhancement for risk-calibrated intent routing while preserving the base classifier's predictions.

papers.abstract: To interpret a direction in a language model's residual stream, we can look for text that strongly activates it. But when such text is found by scanning a corpus, it is limited to what that corpus contains. We develop Maximally-Activating Example Metamodels (MAEMs), language models which map residual stream directions from a subject model to text exemplars that strongly activate those directions. Our objective is to maximise the cosine similarity of a supplied residual stream direction with the activations of the text generated by the MAEM. This label-free RL objective helps to scale MAEMs on diverse sources of residual stream directions. Empirically, we find the resultant metamodel produces informative exemplars: a Qwen3.6-27B MAEM inverts held-out activations better than corpus search or a natural-language autoencoder (NLA), beats corpus search (at 10M tokens) on a majority of held-out languages/domains, and activates 89% of held-out SAE features. It also identifies concepts behind steering vectors about as well as NLAs, recovers the payloads of LoRA backdoors more often than corpus search, and can even verbalise some model workspace inner monologue. Unlike explanations produced by other metamodels (e.g. NLAs), MAEM exemplars can be verified with a forward pass on the subject model, making the MAEM objective a grounded alternative for scaling the training of metamodels.
bullets: Corpus-based activation search is limited to concepts present in the scanned text.
MAEMs are metamodels trained with a label-free reinforcement-learning objective to maximize cosine similarity between a target direction and generated-text activations.
A Qwen3.6-27B MAEM outperforms corpus search and a natural-language autoencoder on held-out activation inversion, covering most tested languages/domains and 89% of held-out SAE features.
The method also interprets steering vectors, recovers LoRA backdoor payloads, and verbalizes some model-workspace inner monologue.
Generated exemplars are directly verifiable with a forward pass through the subject model, though the abstract does not establish universal interpretability.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own rollouts under a frozen teacher's per-token supervision. Does this dense signal reduce the training FLOPs needed to reach a target accuracy compared with reinforcement learning? We systematically compare vanilla reverse-KL OPD with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) across task difficulty, student and teacher size, domain, and optimization choices, measuring held-out accuracy against training FLOPs. With an external post-trained teacher, OPD generally loses to GRPO in accuracy per training FLOP at matched settings, even when the teacher is further trained with GRPO, and often suffers response-length inflation. Yet a different teacher changes the picture: when the teacher is the student's own GRPO checkpoint, OPD recovers that checkpoint's accuracy on math with $50\times$ fewer distillation FLOPs than GRPO needs to reach the same accuracy. Following the same teacher setting, we consistently observe this high efficiency with a larger student, on code, and in a second model family. On a single domain, however, the GRPO checkpoint is already the desired model, so distilling it adds to total compute. Across domains, separate GRPO checkpoints hold different capabilities, and no single checkpoint serves every domain. Multi-teacher OPD (DeepSeek-AI, 2026) consolidates per-domain GRPO experts into a single student that matches each expert's accuracy, with the distillation stage costing only 5.2% (on 2 domains) and 8.0% (on 4 domains) of the specialist training FLOPs. Counting specialist training and distillation together, this pipeline reaches joint GRPO's performance on the 2-domain mix with 42.0% fewer total FLOPs.
bullets: Compares reverse-KL on-policy distillation (OPD) with GRPO by held-out accuracy versus training FLOPs across tasks, models, domains, and optimization settings.
With external post-trained teachers, OPD generally achieves lower accuracy per training FLOP than GRPO and can inflate response lengths.
Using the student’s own GRPO checkpoint as teacher, OPD recovers math accuracy with 50× fewer distillation FLOPs, with similar findings for larger students, code, and another model family.
Multi-teacher OPD consolidates domain-specific GRPO experts while matching their accuracies; distillation costs 5.2% of specialist training FLOPs across two domains and 8.0% across four.
Including specialist training, the two-domain pipeline matches joint GRPO performance with 42.0% fewer total FLOPs.
