papers.selection_reason: Training-efficiency analysis of LLM distillation vs RL; relevant to LLM training methodology.
papers.title: Unpacking the Compute Efficiency of Strong-to-Weak OPD against GRPO
papers.tldr: OPD is usually less compute-efficient than GRPO with external teachers, but using GRPO-trained experts as teachers enables highly efficient single- and multi-domain capability distillation.

papers.abstract: Linear attention compresses context into a fixed-size key-value state for linear-time training and constant-memory inference. Gated delta-rule models decay this state and erase its prediction for an incoming key before writing a new value; Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2) generalizes this with channel-wise decay and decoupled, full-rank erase and write gates. However, we show that state updates are far less sensitive to erasure than to writes: key activation and unit normalization concentrate key energy onto a sparse subset of channels, whereas value writes scale all channels, so the erase gate can be parameterized at lower rank. Furthermore, slow-decaying state rows accumulate much larger norms than fast rows, dominating unweighted readout and forcing stronger write-time erasure to suppress interference. Guided by this analysis, we introduce Muir, which fuses all gates into a sensitivity-allocated low-rank projection, re-weights state rows with a matched-filter readout gate, and reinvests the saved parameters in a wider feed-forward network. Because standard chunkwise algorithms become numerically unstable at the large chunk sizes needed to saturate wide matrix units, we design a parallel update for stable, efficient training. Across 166M-1.34B parameters, Muir lowers perplexity by 1.8-2.0% over GDN-2 and 2.5-3.6% over Transformer, raises commonsense accuracy by up to 1.9 points, and improves extractive recall over GDN-2. At 1.34B, Muir outperforms both baselines on multi-hop and multi-needle recall, extrapolates 2,560x from its 4K training length to 10M-token streams without perplexity drift, and maintains near-100% passkey retrieval to 1M tokens with static readout. Muir achieves these gains while matching GDN-2 throughput, reaching its 100B-token validation loss 1.2x faster, and training 2.7x faster than Transformer at 32K.
bullets: GDN-2’s erasure updates are less sensitive than value writes, motivating lower-rank, sensitivity-allocated gating.
Muir fuses gates into a low-rank projection and re-weights state rows with a matched-filter readout to reduce interference from high-norm, slow-decaying rows.
A numerically stable parallel update enables efficient training with the large chunks needed for wide matrix units.
Across 166M–1.34B parameters, Muir reduces perplexity versus GDN-2 and Transformer, improves commonsense accuracy and extractive recall, and matches GDN-2 throughput.
At 1.34B, it supports long-context extrapolation to 10M tokens and near-perfect passkey retrieval to 1M tokens with static readout.

figures.caption: Figure 1 | Muir outperforms GDN-2 and Transformer on language modeling and long-context throughput while improving recall over GDN-2. (a) Sensitivity-allocated low-rank gates with FFN expansion drive the bulk of the validation NLL gain over GDN-2, while dynamic matched-filter readout drives the gain on extractive recall. (b) Across 166M–1.34B parameters, Muir lowers validation NLL by 18.0–20.4 millinats over GDN-2 and 25.0–36.2 millinats over Transformer. (c) On 8 TPU7x chips (0.5M tokens/step) at 1.34B with our chunkwise kernel, Muir matches GDN-2 throughput despite an additional readout gate and a 30.4% wider FFN, and trains 1.64× and 2.74× faster than Transformer at 16K and 32K, respectively.

Figure 6 |Muir improves synthetic single-needle, multi-hop, multi-needle, and real-world retrieval over GDN-2. (a) Averaged across the three single-needle tasks, all Muir variants mitigate the 4K degradation of GDN-2 and extrapolate to 8K, where unextended RoPE Transformer degrades beyond its 4K training window. (b) On 5-hop variable-binding chains, static 𝛾 fails to match the varying hop lags, whereas dynamic 𝛾𝑡 leads all models at every context length. (c, d) When retrieving four values bound to a single key or four distinct keys queried jointly, dynamic 𝛾𝑡 matches or outperforms both GDN-2 and Transformer across 1K–4K. (e) Averaged across the RULER tasks (a–d) by needle depth and context length, Muir achieves the largest gains over GDN-2 on early needles (0–40% depth) at 4K–8K. (f) On real-world document extraction at 2K, Muir improves over GDN-2 on all six tasks, with dynamic 𝛾𝑡 driving 69% of the gain.

Figure 4 | Boundary-pivoted chunkwise kernel eliminates 3D decay tensors, division overflow, and VPU bottlenecks. (a) Memory hierarchy of a TPU7x chip. (b) On the 256× 256 MXU, an unfused 256 × 128 right-hand side 𝑉 achieves only 50% utilization due to zero-padded lanes, whereas the fused solve [︀ 𝑈 𝑌 ]︀ = 𝑇−1 [︀𝑉 ?̂?⊙𝜋 ]︀ achieves 100% utilization. (c) At chunk size 𝐶 = 256, leaf size 8, and 𝑑𝑘 = 𝑑𝑣 = 128, replacing naive 𝐶 × 𝐶 × 𝑑𝑘 3D VPU decay and sequential VPU triangular solves with boundary-pivoted MXU matrix multiplications, recursive block inversion, and a custom backward pass cuts forward-and-backward VPU compute by 24× and total kernel FLOPs by 12%, routing 98% of chunkwise arithmetic onto the MXU. (d) Boundary-pivoted chunkwise execution combines pre-permutation VREG fusion for 𝑞𝑡 and 𝑣𝑡, MXU cumulative log-decay, numerically stable VPU decay splitting, recursive block inversion of 𝑇 on the MXU, and a packed MXU scan carrying 𝑆0 → 𝑆𝐶 in VMEM (saving 𝑆0 only for backward).

Figure 3 | Muir co-designs asymmetric low-rank gate parameterization and matched-filter query readout with MXU tile alignment and iso-parameter FFN reallocation. (a) Standard residual block with a Muir token mixer. (b) Within the Muir block, 𝑥𝑡 feeds linear-Conv-SiLU pathways for (𝑞𝑡,𝑘𝑡,𝑣𝑡) alongside a single fused low-rank gate projection that produces all five gates (log𝛼𝑡, 𝑏𝑡, 𝑔𝑡,𝑤𝑡,𝛾𝑡). (c) Asymmetric gate ranks (𝑟𝑓 , 𝑟𝑏, 𝑟𝑔, 𝑟𝑤, 𝑟𝑞) = (64, 64, 128, 128, 128) sum to 𝑅tot = 512 = 2 × 256, which fills two 256-column MXU tiles in the fused down-projection and aligns (𝑓, 𝑏) and (𝑔, 𝑤, 𝑞) on 128-lane VMEM tile boundaries for batched up-projections. (d) At 𝑑 = 2,048, replacing the dense (𝑏, 𝑤) gate matrices in GDN-2 cuts gate-projection parameters by 4.5×; this either reduces per-layer parameters and FLOPs by 14.6% at fixed FFN width, or frees +7.3M parameters per layer to widen the FFN under an iso-parameter budget.

Figure 2 |Matched-filter readout and low-rank erase gates improve synthetic associative retrieval and lower optimal erase strength. (a) Full whitening worsens retrieval error relative to unit gain (GDN-2), whereas half-power scaling and the Corollary 3.8 filter reduce error and shift 𝜇* from 0.60 to 0.50, with the Corollary 3.8 filter matching the static oracle. (b) On a 50/50 mixture of lags ℓ ∈ {2, 80} at 𝜇 = 0.60, the lag-matched oracle outperforms the static oracle across all horizons, while the Proposition 3.6 filter matches the lag-matched oracle at ℓ = 80 and beats the static oracle on long and mixed horizons. (c) Low-rank erase gates 𝑟𝑏 outperform dense gates at every bottleneck rank on long-lag recall, whereas low-rank write gates 𝑟𝑤 degrade below dense at 𝑟𝑤 ≤ 8 and recover once 𝑟𝑤 ≥ 16.

Figure 13 | Muir preserves early variable bindings and routes readout to the target hop at each answer step. (a) On 4-value MV-NIAH, Transformer drops on the final write 𝑉4 and unit-readout recurrences degrade after 𝑉1, whereas Muir remains accurate across 𝑉1–𝑉4. (b) On 5-hop RULER VT, Transformer recalls only the root assignment 𝐻1, whereas Muir maintains accuracy across all five hops 𝐻1–𝐻5. (c) Within-model root-needle (𝐻1) retention in 𝑆𝑡 from write milestone 𝑠1 (100%) to query milestone 𝑡q across 16 held-out prompts (interquartile bands across prompts). (d) Within-model retention of written needles 𝐻1–𝐻5 from each write (100%) across sequence milestones 𝑠1–𝑠5 to 𝑡q. (e) Share of readout weight 𝑞𝑡𝑆𝑡 (over the haystack) on each needle 𝐻1–𝐻5 across the four answer-generation steps 𝐴1–𝐴4 that chain 𝐻1 → · · · → 𝐻5.

Figure 10 | Trained models exhibit the predicted write-erase sensitivity asymmetry under both SVD rank truncation and causal gate freezing. (a) Truncating each rank-128 gate projection of the uniform-rank Muir checkpoint via SVD (one gate at a time across all layers) shows that the decay (𝑓) and erase (𝑏) gates saturate by rank 64, whereas the output (𝑔), write (𝑤), and readout gain (𝑞) gates require rank 128. (b) Replacing the dynamic write gate with its token-averaged channel mean (𝑤𝑡 ← ?̄?) across all layers degrades validation NLL 14.5× more than freezing the erase gate (𝑏𝑡 ← ?̄?) in both GDN-2 and Muir.

Figure 5 |Muir consistently lowers validation NLL relative to GDN-2 and Transformer throughout 100B-token pretraining. Held-out FineWeb-Edu validation token NLL difference relative to GDN-2 across 166M–1.34B parameters as a function of training tokens. All three Muir variants improve over GDN-2 within the first 10B tokens and reach a 12–20 mnat reduction by 100B tokens, while static and dynamic matched-filter readout provide additional reductions over Muir (no 𝛾).

Figure 7 | Muir extrapolates to 128K-token documents and 10M-token streams with the lowest perplexity at a constant 25 MB state. (a, c) Zero-shot from 4K pretraining, Dynamic YaRN Transformer diverges past 8K and unchunked evaluation exceeds HBM at ≥128K, while Muir (static 𝛾) drifts upward past 32K; dynamic 𝛾𝑡 avoids this static-gain drift and outperforms GDN-2 across 128K documents and 10M-token streams (2,560× training length). (b, d) After a 64K cooldown (0.3% of pretraining), Transformer improves through 64K before unchunked evaluation exceeds HBM at ≥ 128K, static-𝛾 drift vanishes, and all Muir variants improve monotonically below GDN-2 through 10M tokens (160× beyond cooldown).

Figure 8 | Static matched-filter readout extends passkey retrieval to 1M tokens both zero-shot and after a 64K cooldown. S-NIAH-1 accuracy across 10 needle-depth bins and context lengths 1K–1M (256× pretraining length) at 1.34B scale under (top) zero-shot evaluation from 4K pretraining and (bottom) pure-text continual cooldown at 64K. Cooldown extends Dynamic YaRN Transformer from 8K to 32K before early-depth accuracy drops at 64K and unchunked prefill exceeds HBM at ≥128K, whereas recurrent horizons change little under pure-text cooldown: GDN-2 collapses past 4K–8K, Muir (no 𝛾) fades past 32K, Muir (dynamic 𝛾𝑡, splitting (𝑟𝑤, 𝑟𝑞) = (128, 128) for multi-lag recall) holds through 32K before tapering at ≥64K, and Muir (static 𝛾, keeping 𝑟𝑤 = 256 for single-lag lookup) maintains near-perfect recall to 1M tokens in both regimes.

Figure 9 | Boundary-pivoted chunkwise execution eliminates decay overflow and maintains wellconditioned forward and backward passes. (a) Against an exact float64 sequential reference, naive unpivoted float32 decay factorization overflows and produces NaN on 25% of heads, whereas the boundarypivoted bfloat16 and float32 kernels match the reference to machine precision on both chunk outputs and final state. (b) Across synthetic stress regimes spanning 𝜅2(𝑇 ) ∈ [1, 104], the bfloat16 block-Neumann inverse stays near its precision floor throughout the well-conditioned regime (𝜅2(𝑇 ) < 40, shaded), which contains the sampled 100B-token checkpoints of GDN-2 and Muir (markers show medians). (c) Single-layer backward gradients (𝑇 =128, 𝐶=64, 𝑑𝑘=16) match the float64 reference across all six inputs without log-decay drift.

Figure 11 | Stationary state row energies obey the closed-form law and are balanced by fractional power-law readout gains. (a) Across state channels, the analytical fixed point 𝑚* 𝑗 (5) closely tracks measured stationary row energy 𝑚𝑗 = E[‖𝑆𝑡,𝑗,:‖22] in both GDN-2 and Muir. (b) Across all heads, weighting state rows by the learned readout gain compresses the within-head p90/p10 energy spread by 35% relative to GDN-2. papers.selection_reason: Linear attention architecture with gating and matched-filter readout; contributes to efficient attention and LLM architecture research.
papers.title: Muir: Linear Attention with Sensitivity-Allocated Gating and Matched-Filter Readout
papers.tldr: Muir improves gated linear attention by allocating gate capacity according to update sensitivity and using matched-filter state readout, achieving better language modeling, recall, and long-context performance at similar or lower training cost.

papers.abstract: Quantization reduces the memory and bandwidth demands of large language model (LLM) inference but can degrade accuracy; offloading higher-precision data can instead stall generation. We introduce StrataFlux, a framework that challenges this tradeoff by recovering accuracy lost to low-bit weight and key-value (KV) cache quantization while retaining quantization's memory and speed advantages. StrataFlux co-designs refinement representation, selection, and delivery to make host RAM and solid-state drives useful sources of additional precision. Its selective precision streaming reduces transfer volume, overlaps delivery with computation, and reuses fetched precision across decoding steps so generation need not wait for every transfer. We evaluate 2-4-bit weights and 2-3-bit KV-cache on dedicated GPUs and unified-memory platforms. For 2-bit Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct weights, StrataFlux reduces WikiText-2 perplexity from 9.46 to 8.40 while maintaining 95.4% of the quantized base's throughput on RTX 5090. With 2-bit weights and KV, StrataFlux raises Qwen3-8B's AIME 2024/2025 accuracy from 11.0% to 47.1% at unchanged GPU memory use. At 128K context, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with 3-bit weights and 2-bit KV achieves comparable perplexity and speed to vLLM's 4-bit AWQ weights and 8-bit KV on RTX 5090, using approximately half the GPU memory. These results show that GPU-resident precision need not set the accuracy ceiling, nor offloading-tier latency dictate decoding speed.
bullets: Targets the accuracy–memory/bandwidth tradeoff in 2–4-bit weights and 2–3-bit KV-cache quantization.
Co-designs precision representation, selection, and delivery, overlapping transfers with computation and reusing fetched precision across decoding steps.
On 2-bit Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct weights, lowers WikiText-2 perplexity from 9.46 to 8.40 while retaining 95.4% of quantized-base throughput on an RTX 5090.
With 2-bit weights and KV cache, improves Qwen3-8B AIME 2024/2025 accuracy from 11.0% to 47.1% at unchanged GPU memory use.
At 128K context, 3-bit weights plus 2-bit KV matches the reported perplexity and speed of 4-bit AWQ plus 8-bit KV while using approximately half the GPU memory.

papers.selection_reason: Low-bit LLM inference with selective precision streaming and KV-cache quantization; directly relevant to efficient inference.
papers.title: StrataFlux: Memory-Hierarchy-Native Low-Bit LLM Inference
papers.tldr: StrataFlux recovers much of the accuracy lost by ultra-low-bit LLM quantization by streaming selective higher-precision data from host memory and storage without sacrificing most inference speed or GPU-memory savings.

papers.abstract: Masked diffusion language models offer parallel text generation, but independently sampling multiple tokens can disrupt their dependencies and change the output distribution. Exact continuous-time sampling avoids this approximation, yet typically requires one sequential model evaluation per token. We introduce SpecCTMC, a training-free speculative sampler that reduces this sequential bottleneck without a separate draft model. SpecCTMC proposes successive token updates using previously computed model predictions, evaluates their intermediate states in parallel, and applies an exact acceptance-and-correction procedure. We prove that SpecCTMC preserves the joint distribution of event times, generation order, and token values of the underlying continuous-time Markov chain. It therefore introduces neither time-discretization error nor additional factorization error from parallel decoding. Experiments on LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-v0-Instruct-7B across five benchmarks demonstrate 1.73-4.38x fewer sequential model evaluations than direct continuous-time sampling, while preserving the reference sampling distribution. Our code is available at: https://github.com/kasakh/specctmc
bullets: Addresses the sequential evaluation bottleneck in exact continuous-time sampling, where independent parallel token sampling can disrupt dependencies.
Uses previously computed model predictions to propose successive updates, evaluates intermediate states in parallel, and applies exact acceptance-and-correction.
Requires no separate draft model and no training.
Theoretical analysis shows preservation of event times, generation order, and token values, avoiding discretization and added factorization errors.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models can write many tokens per step, but must choose which tokens are safe to commit together. Mean-field decoding penalizes pairs of positions whose predictions look alike. We replace this proxy with the coupling itself: how much committing one token changes the model's confidence at another. Cheap probes inside the main forward pass measure it, with no training or extra model, and it plugs into the same mean-field rule. On three models and four benchmarks, our method needs far fewer steps than mean-field decoding and is faster in most settings, also with a key-value cache, at an average accuracy cost of 1.1 points. Shuffling the couplings or replacing them with a uniform bonus loses this gain.
bullets: Targets inefficient parallel decoding, where tokens must be selected jointly without harmful interactions.
Measures how committing one token changes another token’s confidence, replacing mean-field similarity penalties.
Uses cheap probes within the existing forward pass, requiring no training or additional model.
Works with the same mean-field decoding rule and key-value caching across three models and four benchmarks.
Achieves far fewer decoding steps and faster decoding in most settings, with a 1.1-point average accuracy cost; shuffled or uniform couplings remove the benefit.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of measured coupling. Top: mean-field decoding penalizes two positions whose predicted distributions overlap (left). We instead measure how much revealing token j changes the margin of token i, which shows support as well as conflict (right). Bottom: one decoding step. The main tokens and K probe rows, one for each of the most confident candidates, run in a single forward pass. Each probe row reveals one candidate and recomputes only the masked positions, reading the main keys and values of the same layer everywhere else. The resulting margins give the coupling ∆ij = ci − c (j) i , which enters the mean-field update, and positions with qi ≥ τ are committed for the next step.

papers.selection_reason: Parallel decoding for diffusion language models, relevant to LLM and efficiency.
papers.title: Measured Coupling for Parallel Decoding in Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: Measured coupling enables diffusion language models to commit safely in parallel, reducing decoding steps and usually improving speed with only a small accuracy tradeoff.

papers.abstract: We study token dynamics in deep Mamba models, with a particular focus on the attracting role of the first token. Unlike attention mechanisms, where token interactions are governed by positive scalar coefficients, Mamba dynamics involve full matrix-valued interaction coefficients with no positivity or definiteness guarantees. This structural difference makes Mamba dynamics substantially harder to analyze and prevents the direct application of existing techniques for attention-based models. To overcome this challenge, we introduce a new analytical framework based on a high-dimensional invariant box and a sharp exit-time argument, which together recover an effective form of sign-definiteness. Using this framework, we characterize the possible limit points of token trajectories and prove explicit exponential convergence rates. Our analysis reveals that the first token has privileged dynamics: its limiting direction attracts subsequent tokens, inducing token clustering and attention-sink phenomena in deep Mamba models. We further show that this attraction mechanism extends to broader sequence dynamics, including state-space models, causal attention, and classical time-series models. Experiments on Falcon-Mamba-7B validate our predictions, showing that concentration on the first token increases with depth and dominates in later layers.
bullets: Mamba’s matrix-valued token interactions lack the positivity properties that enable existing attention analyses.
The authors develop an invariant-box and exit-time framework to recover effective sign-definiteness.
They characterize token-trajectory limit points and prove explicit exponential convergence rates.
The first token’s limiting direction attracts subsequent tokens, with the mechanism extending to state-space, causal-attention, and classical time-series models.
Experiments on Falcon-Mamba-7B show increasing first-token concentration with depth, especially in later layers.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Attention sink score [27] analysis in the Falcon-Mamba-7B model. Subfigure (a) shows the sink score of the first token and its moving average across layers; the score steadily increases with depth and dominates in the final layers. Subfigure (b) shows the average sink scores across token positions; the first token consistently receives the largest share.

Figure 3: Attention concentration on the first token across different depths of the Falcon-Mamba-7B model [90]. Each subfigure shows the hidden attention matrix for a specific layer: (a) Layer 1, (b) Layer 15, (c) Layer 46, and (d) Layer 60. In early layers, tokens distribute attention more uniformly, but as depth increases, nearly all tokens concentrate disproportionately on the first token. This illustrates the emergence of an attention sink in state-space models.

Figure 2: Percentage of first tokens exhibiting a single non-zero element (threshold 1× 10−4) across simplified Mamba-2 blocks with shared weights, after omitting causal convolution, input/output projections, activations, and inner residuals. Most tokens converged to 1-element tokens, consistent with simulations.

papers.selection_reason: Analysis of Mamba token dynamics, relevant to LLM architecture.
papers.title: First-Token Attraction in Mamba Dynamics
papers.tldr: A new theory explains why the first token attracts later tokens in deep Mamba models, causing token clustering and attention-sink behavior.

papers.abstract: Large language models have made rapid progress in agentic reasoning and tool use, raising expectations for agents that can take over realistic productivity work from humans. However, current agents still struggle to finish such tasks, where success requires following long-horizon professional workflows, understanding heterogeneous file contexts, and producing usable deliverables under fine-grained requirements. A key bottleneck is the lack of scalable post-training data that reflects real work intent, authentic file environments, and deliverable-level evaluation. To close this gap, we introduce Agent-R$^2$, a $\textbf{r}$eal-source data synthesis framework that scales training data for $\textbf{r}$ealistic productivity work. Instead of relying on manually specified workflows or LLM-generated files, Agent-R$^2$ grounds synthesis throughout the pipeline in real occupational seeds, corpus-derived workflow evidence, and authentic web-sourced files. From 10k web-corpus candidates, Agent-R$^2$ distills 4k task instances that pair real multi-format attachments with fine-grained, deliverable-level rubrics. On this data, we train Agent-R$^2$-4B via supervised fine-tuning and rubric-based reinforcement learning, improving both end-to-end productivity performance and file-grounded reasoning. Trained on only 4k instances, Agent-R$^2$-4B surpasses Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507 on both GDPval (51.0$\%$ vs. 48.0$\%$) and OfficeQA (14.8$\%$ vs. 13.8$\%$). Further analysis shows that Agent-R$^2$ mitigates shortcut behavior, where agents produce superficially plausible deliverables before sufficiently grounding, constructing, or verifying them, while promoting sustained exploration.
bullets: Addresses agents’ difficulty with long-horizon workflows, heterogeneous files, and fine-grained deliverable requirements.
Synthesizes data from real occupational seeds, corpus-derived workflow evidence, and web-sourced files rather than manually specified workflows or generated files.
Distills 10k web-corpus candidates into 4k tasks with multi-format attachments and deliverable-level rubrics.
Trains Agent-R²-4B with supervised fine-tuning and rubric-based reinforcement learning.
The approach improves end-to-end productivity and file-grounded reasoning, while reducing shortcut behavior and encouraging sustained exploration.

papers.title: Agent-R$^2$: Scaling Agents for Realistic Productivity Work via Real-Source Data Synthesis
papers.tldr: Agent-R² scales realistic productivity-agent training by synthesizing tasks from real occupational workflows and authentic files, enabling a 4B model to outperform a much larger model on GDPval and OfficeQA.

papers.abstract: Complex problems with limited context, such as claims, require a means to obtain additional knowledge necessary for solution reasoning. We propose a multi-agent framework, SMART, to obtain knowledge through capturing the implicit state of participating entities in a problem context. SMART curates the state knowledge as diverse, complementary and solution-salient premises using a variety of LLMs and a structured role-based prompt strategy. Using knowledge from these real-world verified curated premises, SMART's knowledge guided solution reasoning improves validation performance up to 20% on complex scientific claims spanning 3 datasets. We show that grounding premises in real-world knowledge is necessary and improves performance up to 5%.
bullets: Addresses limited-context problems where solving claims requires additional knowledge.
Uses multiple LLM agents and structured roles to capture implicit entity states.
Curates diverse, complementary, solution-relevant premises from real-world knowledge.
Knowledge-guided reasoning improves validation performance by up to 20% across three datasets.
Grounding premises in real-world knowledge improves performance by up to 5%.

figures.caption: Figure 6: Comparing SMART-NV where no verification is performed) with verification using self (SMART-PK), external knowledge with websearch (SMART-WS), and cross-model (X-SMART-PK) on SciFact claims. Verification improves performance an average by 2-7% across methods for both datasets, with a few exceptions (see SFBench in Fig. 10). See results in appendix Table 8.

Figure 3: Improving SMART performance using external premise validation with websearch (SMART-WS) and cross model generation and reasoning (X-SMART-PK). For SciFact, X-SMART-PK uses Qwen3 8b generated premises & improves performance by 6.2%; for SFBench, GPT-5.4-mini generated premises lead to 4% improvement.

Figure 1: A complex problem’s implicit state-based reasoning using a scientific claim from SciFact (Wadden et al., 2020). We identify experts knowledgeable about participating entities and explore their state and obtain contrastive premises. We curate true premises of supporting or opposing stance and reason with these to infer the solution.

Figure 2: Comparison of SMART-PK performance with CoT and RAG on SciFact & SFBench datasets, after applying the Refute Filter (rationales are required to adequately support refute labels; see §5.2). SMART-PK improves over baselines; on avg. 10% on SFBench and 5% on Scifact over CoT (details in Appendix Table 4).

Figure 4: Comparing SMART-PK performance generating a single premise Vs. contrastive premises on SFBench claims. See Fig. 13 for SciFact claims. Contrastive premises improve performance by 3% across datasets and models. See results in Table 5

Figure 8: We compare the validation performance of SMART-PK with 3 sizes of Qwen and GPT-5.4-mini on SciFact-Open claims using premises generated and curated by one model and solution reasoning with another model. These comparisons show that both Qwen3 8b and GPT-5.4-mini generate good quality premises that other models can curate and use for solution-reasoning.

Figure 5: We compare the 5 meta-reasonsers for SciFact claims: M-Majority Voting, R-Reasoning Judge, AAggregating Judge, C-Critical Judge and S-Supporting Judge. Reasoning Judge consistently improves performance across models and datasets: by 8% on SFBench and 5% on SciFact on average (See Fig. 9 for SFBench claims and results in Appendix Table 7).

Figure 14: Distribution of curated premise stances, their alignment with the claim and their confidence ratings for Qwen3 models. Correct identification of refuted claims requires opposing premises and supported claims require supporting premises. Qwen3 1.7b curation leads to few and noisy premises compared to Qwen8b. Qwen3 32 generates too many supporting premises increasing meta-reasoning difficulty. Supporting and opposing premises are required for supporting claims of support and refute labels respectively.

Figure 12: We compare various premise generation methods using the SciFact collection. We obtain premises with a single expert in one-shot (Non-Iter) Vs an iterative generation strategy (Iter). We also compare SMART’s multiple context-derived experts with the iterative strategy. Claude-Haiku-4.5 does not allow obtaining more than one generation per API call; due to this we do not have any result for the single expert in one-shot (Non-Iter) strategy.

Figure 9: We compare the 5 meta-reasonsers for SFBench claims: M-Majority Voting, R-Reasoning Judge, A-Aggregating Judge, C-Critical Judge and SSupporting Judge. Reasoning Judge metareasoner is more consistent across models and datasets and improves performance, by 8% on SFBench and 5% on SciFact (See Fig. 5 for SciFact and results in Appendix Table 8).

Figure 11: Comparing SMART-PK performance using a stronger premise Vs. both premises. Logically using a stronger premise was a good decision (performance of both both GPT-5.4-mini and Claude-Haiku-4.5 reduces due to direct conflicts), however, model reasoning is able to use the additional nuanced information provided by both premises. Larger models are better at leveraging the nuanced information in both premises (Llama70b improves by 1.3% & Qwen3 32b by 6.7%); smaller models benefit from additional premises as they do not curate as many premises (Qwen3 1b improves by 1.5%).

Figure 13: Comparing SMART-PK performance generating a single premise Vs. contrastive premises on SciFact claims. See Fig. 4 for SFBench claims. Contrastive premises improve performance by 3% across datasets and models. See results in Table 5
Figure 15: We compare various configurations we used for generating premises. The performance of these different configurations is compared in Fig. 12.

Figure 7: Distribution of GPT-5.4-mini curated stances, their alignment with the claim and their confidence ratings for the SciFact-Open dataset. Supporting and opposing premises are required for supporting claims that of the support and refute type respectively.

Figure 10: Comparing SMART-PK, where premises are verified with parametric knowledge, with SMART-NV where no verification is performed on SFBench claims, we show that verification improves performance an average of 2% with a few exceptions (also true for SciFact claims in Fig. 6). Results are in appendix Table 7.

Table 5: Comparing the balanced accuracy of using Single Vs. Contrastive premises with the SMART framework. We examine performance before and after applying the Refute Filter (refute labels that are not adequately supported are changed to ’unknown’, essentially dropping them from contributing to balanced accuracy). Single premises often lack necessary claim knowledge that models select refute labels without adequately supporting them. Correcting for this with the Refute Filter shows that contrastive knowledge improves on average across models and datasets by 3%. The smallest model Qwen3 1.7b is worse at obtaining contrastive knowledge, but leads to better performance with single premises. We discuss these results in §6.

Table 9: Comparing inference cost for SMART-PK and SMART-WS in model calls and number of input + output tokens measured in K tokens (KTok). We report % fallbacks (Fback) to the direct reasoning prompt when there are no curated premises, the quality of curated premises (Qual) and their average numbers per stance (Sup. & Opp.). Both methods require the same # calls since we verify before obtaining stance; these do not include 10 calls that iteratively obtain premises as a single call could potentially be used to obtain all premises for GPT-5.4-mini and Claude-Haiku-4.5. All values are per claim averages. We report NA-Not applicable as the premise quality (Qual) for SFbench claims due to not having textual evidence. Average premise quality by coincidence is the same for both methods, so we report in a single column.

Table 8: Comparing the balanced accuracy of SMART without verification (SMART-NV) with self-verification (SMART-PK), external verification with websearch (SMART-WS) and cross-verification (X-SMART-PK). Improvement with each method is shown in %Improve (the difference in performance between SMART-NV and the method). Verification improves performance on average across models and datasets by by 2-7%. Grounding premises with real-world knowledge provided by websearch improves on average by 4-5% with some exceptions.

Table 3: Comparing the percentage of rationales that lack support for a refute claim that are filtered by the Refute Filter for CoT reasoning, SMART-PK reasoning with contrastive premises and the single premise generation method (SMART-S). These lead to incorrect logical reasoning on 50% of SFBench claims and 40% of SciFact claims (claims with a gold refute). CoT leads to almost double the errors than SMART on smaller models. Single premise generation leads to more errors on SFBench (double the number than on SciFact) where as the reverse is true for contrastive premises. We discuss these results in §6.

Table 4: Comparing the balanced accuracy of CoT, RAG and SMART-PK before and after applying the Refute Filter (refute labels that are not adequately supported are changed to ’unknown’, essentially dropping them from contributing to balanced accuracy). Smaller models either lack or are unable to leverage claim knowledge and select more refute labels, both with CoT and SMART reasoning (the %drop is higher for the smaller models). However, this incorrect performance boost is worse with CoT than SMART (the %drop is higher for CoT than SMART). It is also worse for SFBench’s Material Science knowledge than SciFact’s Biological Science knowledge (the %drop is higher SFBench than SciFact, Llama3 8b model on SciFact is an exception where the model does not generate most rationales). Web search based on a claim is noisy; up to half the RAG refute labels are based on not finding the appropriate evidence. Since RAG performance is lower than CoT, we provide % SMART improvement over CoT in the last column (SMART-PK improves performance up to 20%.) We discuss these results in §6.

Table 6: Comparing performance (BAccuracy) of SMART-WS and X-SMART-PK with SMART-PK. X-SMART-PK where models use premises from a better generating model: Qwen3 8b for SciFact and GPT-5.4-mini for SFBench. Since SMART-PK does not lead to as much of an artificial performance boost, we compare results without applying the Refute Filter. papers.abstract: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) improves reasoning by training a student on its own reasoning, using the same model conditioned on reference solutions as a teacher. Applying OPSD to multilingual reasoning requires the teacher to provide useful feedback across languages, even when the student makes mistakes in intermediate steps. We observe a phenomenon we call Teacher Drift: as these mistakes accumulate, the teacher may follow the student's incorrect steps instead of correcting them. Our analysis shows that this shift tends to occur earlier in lower-resource languages. To account for these differences across languages, we propose Teachable On-Policy Self-Distillation (TOPSD), which determines where and whether teacher supervision should be applied to each reasoning trajectory. TOPSD uses teacher-student likelihood to estimate where drift begins and select a prefix for supervision. It then verifies whether the teacher can recover the correct answer from that prefix, applying distillation only to prefixes that pass verification. Experiments on multilingual mathematical reasoning across ten languages and three model scales show that TOPSD consistently outperforms conventional OPSD, particularly in low- and medium-resource languages.
bullets: OPSD can suffer from Teacher Drift, where the teacher adopts the student’s incorrect intermediate reasoning.
Drift tends to begin earlier in lower-resource languages, making uniform supervision unreliable.
TOPSD uses teacher–student likelihoods to locate drift and select a supervision prefix.
It verifies whether the teacher can recover the correct answer from that prefix before distillation.
Across mathematical reasoning in ten languages and three model scales, TOPSD consistently outperforms conventional OPSD, especially for low- and medium-resource languages.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of TOPSD. The student generates a reasoning trajectory in the target language, while the privileged teacher additionally observes the English problem and reference solution. Step 1 (Teachable Prefix Selection) uses the cumulative teacher-student likelihood ratio to select a candidate teachable prefix, determining where teacher supervision may be applied. Step 2 (Teacher Recoverability Verification) checks whether the teacher can recover the correct answer from the selected prefix, determining whether supervision should be applied. Only prefixes that pass verification receive distillation on the corresponding states of the original student trajectory. English translations are shown in gray.

Figure 5: Qualitative comparison on a high-resource Spanish problem. Both the base model and COPSD omit the cross-term 3a21 and incorrectly use 3a2 = 19, producing the answer 22. TOPSD correctly matches the coefficient using 3a21 + 3a2 = 19 and obtains the correct answer 352. English translations are shown in gray.

TOPSD correctly derives the triangle area as 1012(i+ j), computes S(n) = 1012n(n+ 1)2, and obtains the correct limiting value 1012. English translations are shown in gray.

papers.abstract: Production deployments often use different models to balance cost and quality through cascading, routing, and switching models during long conversations. Context accumulates across turns. Each switch requires the target to repeat prefill over this context. Existing methods transfer full-attention (FA) K/V caches across models. Hybrid linear-attention models also retain recurrent states (REC) and convolution histories (Conv). The interaction between Conv and REC complicates cross-model state transfer. Conv perturbations can change keys and values in recurrent layers and alter REC updates. Conv histories are overwritten, but changes in REC can still affect later outputs. More accurate REC reconstruction need not improve continuation. Building on this, we propose Hybrid State Transfer (HST) for all three state types. It uses structured REC maps and preserves history order during Conv alignment. We calibrate the adapters using the frozen target's outputs during continuation. FA cache map updates are merged offline. Across five benchmarks, Qwen3.5 4B$\rightarrow$27B and 9B$\rightarrow$27B achieve mean task retentions of 89.88% and 94.11%, respectively. With source caches already available, separate timing on synthetic 16K inputs yields handoff body speedups of $21.66\times$ and $21.91\times$.
bullets: Model switching in long conversations normally repeats context prefill, while hybrid models additionally maintain recurrent and convolution histories.
HST transfers all three state types using structured recurrent-state maps and order-preserving convolution-history alignment.
Adapters are calibrated against the frozen target model’s continuation outputs; full-attention cache updates are merged offline.
Across five benchmarks, reported task retention is 89.88% for 4B→27B and 94.11% for 9B→27B transfers.
On synthetic 16K inputs with source caches available, handoff body speedups are 21.66× and 21.91×.

papers.abstract: State-space models (SSMs) recover low-dimensional latent dynamics from high-dimensional observations, but latents are generally not identifiable from observational data alone. Interventional state-space models (iSSMs) use perturbations to break observational symmetries and identify parameters up to permutation, scaling, and shift. However, prior work restricts identifiability to linear latent dynamics and piecewise-linear emissions, excluding many behaviors characteristic of neural circuits. We extend iSSMs to a substantially broader model class: we prove that (i) affine identifiability holds under general injective emission functions and Gaussian latent transitions, and (ii) with interventions, identifiability up to permutation, scaling, and shift is preserved under general nonlinear latent dynamics. We validate our theory on simulated FitzHugh-Nagumo dynamics, and then demonstrate two applications: adjudicating between competing models of decision-making; and predicting responses to unseen micro-stimulation in macaque and human neural recordings, with proof-of-concept generalization to a held-out stimulation site in the latter. Finally, simulations yield practical guidance for designing stimulation protocols that improve identifiability.
bullets: Addresses the non-identifiability of latent states from observational data alone.
Proves affine identifiability with general injective emissions and Gaussian transitions.
Shows intervention-based identifiability up to permutation, scaling, and shift for general nonlinear latent dynamics.
Validates the theory on FitzHugh–Nagumo simulations and applies it to decision-making models and neural stimulation responses.
Provides simulation-based guidance for designing stimulation protocols that improve identifiability.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models route each token to a few of many experts, yet what an individual expert is responsible for remains unsettled. Existing analyses count how often an expert is selected on domain-labeled corpora, an instrument that fixes the taxonomy in advance, stays coarse, and records selection rather than contribution. We instead study specialization in feature space by training a sparse autoencoder (SAE) on the output of an MoE layer. Since this output is a router-weighted sum of expert outputs and the SAE encoder is affine, the pre-activation of every latent decomposes exactly over the experts. Aggregated over a corpus, this gives each expert a dominant set of latents whose activation it principally drives. On layers 4, 30 and 46 of Qwen3-30B-A3B, contribution is far more concentrated than gating, most latents have only one or two dominators, and the overlap between dominant sets concentrates on a few expert pairs. Auto-interpreting these sets reveals a division of labor below coarse domains, with distinct experts for Java and front-end web code, or for geometry and for arithmetic and polynomials, while the coarse domains themselves take very unequal numbers of experts. Our SAEs and code are available at https://github.com/Bytedance-Seed/SAE-Interprets-MoE.
bullets: MoE expert specialization is analyzed in feature space rather than through predefined domain labels.
An SAE trained on MoE-layer outputs enables exact decomposition of each latent’s activation across experts.
Across Qwen3-30B-A3B layers 4, 30, and 46, expert contribution is more concentrated than selection, with most latents driven by only one or two experts.
Expert overlap is concentrated in a few pairs, and interpreted latent sets reveal distinctions such as Java versus front-end code and geometry versus arithmetic/polynomials.
The analysis is scoped to selected layers of Qwen3-30B-A3B; SAEs and code are released.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is emerging as an important paradigm for language-model post-training, combining dense teacher supervision with training on student-generated trajectories. This creates a feedback loop where each update changes the student and thereby the training distribution that generates subsequent updates. Yet, how this feedback shapes learning and generalization remains poorly understood. We conduct a mechanistic analysis of OPD's learning dynamics, distinguishing the two feedback loop stages: conversion of the distillation signal into parameter updates, and broadcast through which these updates change predictions across prefixes and reshape the rollout distribution. This framework helps us understand both limited student responsiveness despite substantial teacher-student disagreement, and degeneration when updates that improve local teacher agreement also increase the probability of unsuccessful continuations, exposing the student to unreliable supervision in subsequent rollouts. Finally, we show that offline distillation can prepare a student for OPD without significantly improving immediate held-out accuracy. While OPD alone may degrade generation, it can yield substantial accuracy gains after sufficient offline preparation. Together, our results connect teacher supervision, student geometry, and the evolving rollout distribution in determining the learning dynamics of OPD and its effects on downstream performance.
bullets: OPD couples teacher supervision with student-generated trajectories, creating a changing training distribution.
The analysis separates learning into signal-to-update conversion and broadcast of updates across prefixes and rollouts.
Students may respond weakly despite large teacher–student disagreement because of parameter and prediction geometry.
Local improvements in teacher agreement can increase unsuccessful continuations, causing degeneration through unreliable supervision.
Offline distillation can prepare students for substantial later gains in OPD, even without immediate held-out accuracy improvements.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Teacher request fields differ systematically. In (a), each curve shows how much more (or less) often a semantic or token-position class appears among a teacher’s top 50%, 20%, . . . , 1% of requests than among all annotated positions, in percentage points (so 0 = no preference). The RL-sibling teachers’ increasingly emphasize requests on sentence openings and “control-oriented” moves, while the larger teachers’ stay in sentence interiors and “technical-oriented” content. In (b) we show finer semantic categories of the request fields. Each dumbbell pairs the teachers’ enrichment among their 1% largest-normed of initial requests. 1 denotes corpus-level prevalence. See Section D.2 for finer details on the classes and how we conduct the interpretability analysis.

The vertical guide at step 20 marks the approximate onset-to-fitting transition; the effects overlap. (c,d) Student surprisal and teacher top-1 probability; darker means greater uncertainty. Columns are 512-token windows. Details are in Section E.1.

Figure 1: OPD’s learning dynamics, visualizing the feedback loop at the top (detailed in Section 3.1), and illustrative successful and failing processes at the bottom in reasoning settings we analyzed empirically. In principle, OPD propagates current teacher requests Γt(s)|s∼µt to motion at any future prefix x through shared parameters, captured by the Neural Tangent Kernel K(x, s). Such policy motion shapes how the autoregressive rollout (prefix visitation) and supervision distribution changes (µ̇t, Γ̇t). In practice, a healthy dynamics needs not only locally “tangent-accessible” and coherent requests (Section 3.2), but also the student to be sufficiently “prepared”, so that it can sustain meaningful rollouts with learning value as it absorbs corrections requested by the teacher, instead of primarily performing local mimicry and falling into chaotic rollouts hard for the teacher to rescue, let alone improve on (Sections 3.3 and 3.4).

papers.abstract: Can large language models (LLMs) advance theoretical computer science and resolve its long-standing open conjectures? To study progress toward this goal, we introduce TCSExam, a unified framework and benchmark covering the full range of TCS research. It evaluates theorem proving, solver engineering, and constructions alongside direct attempts to resolve open conjectures, capturing both concrete research accomplishments and progress toward long-standing research goals. TCSExam-Full contains 100 expert-reviewed tasks, with submissions checked by the Lean kernel or an executable task checker. TCSExam-Lite selects 20 tasks, five per track, reducing the number of task attempts by 80% at the same per-attempt budget. We evaluate eight agents on Full and nine on Lite. The TCSExam Index combines all four tracks: GPT-6 Astra leads Full (71.9), and Opus 5.5 leads Lite (72.3). Full and Lite rankings are strongly aligned across eight shared agents (Spearman's $ρ=0.93$), supporting Lite as a compact, discriminative benchmark. The evaluations yield improved solver outputs and mathematical constructions, together with independently verified special cases and bounds from open-conjecture attempts. TCSExam provides an extensible framework with task sources, Docker build recipes, and evaluation tools for reproducible use.
bullets: Covers theorem proving, solver engineering, mathematical constructions, and attempts on open conjectures.
TCSExam-Full has 100 expert-reviewed tasks; TCSExam-Lite has 20 tasks and reduces attempts by 80% at the same per-attempt budget.
Tasks are validated by the Lean kernel or executable checkers, enabling objective evaluation.
GPT-6 Astra leads Full with an index of 71.9, while Opus 5.5 leads Lite with 72.3; rankings strongly align (Spearman’s ρ=0.93).
Evaluations produced improved solver outputs, constructions, and independently verified special cases and bounds for open-conjecture attempts.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation trains a student on its own rollouts, so states the teacher would reach but the student does not are seldom supervised. We introduce CoRD (coupled-rollout distillation), which keeps the on-policy loss and moves only the distribution of training states toward the teacher, drawing rollouts from a geometric interpolation of student and teacher through the maximal coupling of speculative decoding. The coupling keeps the student's token wherever the two distributions agree and otherwise substitutes a token from the part of the target the student underweights, so interventions are as rare as any exact sampler allows and recede as the student learns. Across six base students from two model families (Qwen3 and Qwen3.5, 0.6B to 4B), CoRD raises average pass@1 over on-policy distillation by 0.9 to 2.0 points and pass@8 by 1.2 to 3.4 points on five public math benchmarks at equal steps and data. On frozen teacher-reached states, a 4B student trained with CoRD reaches in 16 steps a gap closure that on-policy distillation does not reach in 80, and substitution rules intervening at least as often in other directions fall short of CoRD.
bullets: Addresses the blind spot where on-policy students rarely train on teacher-reached states outside their own rollout distribution.
Uses maximal coupling of speculative decoding to interpolate between student and teacher rollouts while preserving the standard on-policy loss.
Keeps the student token when distributions agree and substitutes underweighted target tokens otherwise; interventions decrease as learning progresses.
Across six students and five public math benchmarks, CoRD improves average pass@1 by 0.9–2.0 points and pass@8 by 1.2–3.4 points over on-policy distillation.
On frozen teacher-reached states, a 4B student closes the gap in 16 steps with CoRD, versus not reaching closure in 80 steps for on-policy distillation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of CORD. (i) Left (OPD’s blind spot): On-policy distillation trains only on student rollouts. Teacher-preferred reasoning paths that the student rarely or never visits therefore receive little or no supervision. (ii) Right (our coupled sampler): CORD keeps the same training loss and budget, but changes the rollout sampler. By coupling the student with a teacher-leaning target qα, it preserves agreeing tokens and replaces disagreements with underweighted target tokens. This maximal coupling steers rollouts into teacher-preferred states missed by OPD with the minimum possible intervention rate, minimally perturbing the student’s original trajectory.

papers.abstract: Reasoning trajectories generated for the same problem often arrive at conflicting answers. These disagreements reveal alternative intermediate decisions that can be reused to explore new solutions. We introduce Adaptive Semantic Branching (ASB), a training-free inference procedure that turns cross-trajectory disagreement into targeted candidate generation. ASB first groups independently sampled trajectories by extracted final answer, selects a representative from each group, and aligns their reasoning steps with a monotonic dynamic program. A persistent-divergence objective identifies the point at which initially similar reasoning paths develop different continuations. For each selected directed pair, ASB retains the source trajectory's textual prefix, extracts a short reasoning window from a competing donor trajectory, and generates a fresh solution conditioned on both. A diversity-aware policy allocates up to three additional generations according to the answer-cluster structure. In a 500-problem MATH evaluation with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, ASB increases oracle candidate coverage from 445/500 (89.0%) with seven initial samples to 455/500 (91.0%), recovering correct candidates for 10 of the 55 initially uncovered problems. The method uses 576 additional generation calls across the evaluation set, averaging 8.152 calls per problem. We provide a precise specification of the branching operator, alignment objective, generation policy, and experimental configuration.
bullets: Groups trajectories by final answer and selects representative paths from each answer cluster.
Aligns reasoning steps with monotonic dynamic programming to locate persistent divergences.
Combines a source trajectory prefix with a short competing reasoning window to regenerate solutions.
Allocates up to three extra generations based on answer-cluster diversity.
Recovered correct candidates for 10 of 55 initially uncovered problems using 576 additional generation calls overall.

papers.abstract: Small language models are often trained under tight data budgets, where the choice of pretraining corpus may matter as much as model size or training recipe. We compare two contrasting corpora at matched 10-million- and 37-million-word budgets: the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica and the BabyLM 2026 strict pretraining corpus. For each corpus, we train teacher models, distilled 58-million-parameter Baby-Llama students, and no-distillation student ablations, using the same model families, training recipes, and evaluation protocol across corpora. Across BLiMP, BLiMP Supplement, EWoK, Entity Tracking, and COMPS, the corpora produce different skill profiles rather than a single quality ranking. BabyLM 2026 is consistently stronger on linguistic acceptability benchmarks, while Britannica is often stronger on Entity Tracking, a synthetic state-tracking task. The contrast appears across teacher and student models and at both budgets, with the cleanest cross-seed replication in the distilled student comparison. Targeted controls show that the central contrast persists after matching training exposure and at a longer diagnostic context; direct teacher ensembling also does not reproduce the 10M Britannica student's Entity Tracking behavior. Entity Tracking magnitudes nevertheless remain sensitive to training dynamics. For this corpus pair, corpus choice can therefore produce different relative skill profiles at small scale, motivating multi-benchmark evaluation when comparing pretraining data.
bullets: Compares Britannica and BabyLM 2026 corpora at matched 10M- and 37M-word budgets.
Uses matched teacher, distilled 58M-parameter student, and no-distillation setups with the same evaluations.

Britannica is often stronger on the synthetic Entity Tracking task, across teachers and students.
Results support multi-benchmark evaluation; Entity Tracking performance remains sensitive to training dynamics.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs) commonly decode responses by proceeding autoregressively across blocks while iteratively denoising multiple tokens within each block. This structure makes block-level policy optimization a natural adaptation of autoregressive policy optimization. However, the exact likelihood of a completed block is intractable because it marginalizes over the intermediate states and reveal orders of the denoising process. To realize the block-level formulation, we construct a prefix-block state and use a single model evaluation to define a factorized one-step surrogate for the block likelihood. The resulting block surrogate ratio is a product of its token surrogate ratios, allowing variation at individual positions to propagate across the entire block before clipping. We therefore introduce Prefix-Block Policy Optimization (PBPO), which preserves block-level conditioning but applies surrogate importance weighting and clipping separately to each token. PBPO further diversifies repeated updates by resampling corrupted views of the prompt and revealed prefix, a design motivated by masked-dLLM pre-training. Under our analysis assumptions, block-product weighting amplifies the variance of gradient contributions relative to token-local weighting. Across two LLaDA-family initializations, six benchmarks, and three generation lengths, PBPO achieves competitive performance against existing dLLM RL methods.
bullets: Addresses the intractable likelihood of fully denoised blocks in dLLMs.

Resamples corrupted prompt and revealed-prefix views to diversify repeated updates.

papers.abstract: Language models lose accuracy when a prompt contains non-evidential context: irrelevant statements from unrelated domains, or random off-distribution tokens, with no competing answer and no semantic overlap with the query. Such noise pervades retrieval-augmented, tool-using, and long-context deployments, yet the failure has lacked a mechanistic account. We trace the corruption to the Intrusion Pathway, which starts with MLPs enriching both query-subject and irrelevant-token representations, parroting heads carry prefix-token content to the prediction position, and relational readers largely avoid unrelated sources. Nevertheless, preserved subject enrichment and selective reading do not prevent intrusion in the broader computation. We then localize part of this interference to a sparse set of attention heads, which we call intrusion heads. Their prefix-derived writes promote distractor-related content, while their reduced support for the correct answer arises primarily from weaker non-prefix contributions rather than direct suppression by the prefix. The same heads transfer across tasks and distractor types and are largely weight-disjoint from the heads that integrate relevant contextual evidence, enabling a class-conditional intervention. Replacing the corrupted last-token residual with its clean counterpart, an oracle probe that requires a matched clean forward pass, recovers 97.6% on average of the distractor-induced drop across four downstream tasks. A deployable mask level knockout of about ten heads, roughly 1% of the model's attention heads, recovers 57% at bounded cost to helpful context.
bullets: The study explains accuracy loss from irrelevant statements or off-distribution tokens even when they provide no competing answer.
MLPs enrich irrelevant-token representations, while parrot-like heads carry prefix content to the prediction position; relational readers mostly avoid unrelated sources.
Intrusion heads promote distractor content and provide weaker support for the correct answer, rather than directly suppressing it.
These heads transfer across tasks and distractor types and are largely distinct from heads that use helpful context.
An oracle residual replacement recovers 97.6% of the induced drop; masking about ten heads recovers 57% with bounded impact on useful context.

papers.abstract: ConvPE (Convolutional Position Embedding) improves both the performance and efficiency of Transformer models in language modeling, long-context extension, and vision. It injects a windowed, content-dependent bias into attention scores through a lightweight causal convolution over a low-dimensional projection of the hidden states. As a lightweight plug-in, ConvPE is compatible with RoPE, attention masks, and KV concatenation. It also supports high-dimensional position embeddings via high-dimensional convolutions. In a reproduction, ConvPE outperforms five 1D baselines and eight 2D baselines. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/wzhagi/convpe.
bullets: Adds a windowed, content-dependent bias to attention scores using a causal convolution over low-dimensional hidden-state projections.
Works with RoPE, attention masks, and KV concatenation, and supports high-dimensional position embeddings through high-dimensional convolutions.
Evaluated for language modeling, long-context extension, and vision.
In reproduction experiments, it outperformed five 1D and eight 2D baselines.
Code is publicly available on GitHub.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) improves language-model reasoning through dense teacher feedback on student-generated responses. We first observe an amplitude disparity in this feedback: on math reasoning responses, style-related positions exhibit 3.5 times the mean absolute teacher--student log-probability difference of mathematical positions. Scaling OPD updates by these discrepancies thus directs much of the update strength toward matching the teacher's expression. We instead take the student's own pretrained base as a reference: the student--base difference records the token preferences acquired during post-training and provides supervision that does not depend on the student's distance from the teacher. Building on this reference, we propose Student-Delta On-Policy Distillation (SD-OPD), which uses centered student--base differences as update coefficients, keeps each coefficient only when its sign agrees with centered teacher--student feedback, and recomputes the student signal every training round. Across 5 teacher--student configurations with Qwen3 students of 1.7B to 8B parameters, SD-OPD improves six-task mathematics average pass@1 (avg@16) over OPD by 7.76 to 10.37 percentage points. Code is available at https://github.com/aim-uofa/sd-opd.
bullets: OPD feedback is disproportionately concentrated on style-related tokens, with 3.5× the mean absolute discrepancy of mathematical tokens.
SD-OPD uses centered student–base log-probability differences as update coefficients, retaining them only when aligned with centered teacher–student feedback.
The student signal is recomputed each training round to reflect evolving learned preferences.
Across five Qwen3 teacher–student configurations (1.7B–8B), SD-OPD raises six-task math average pass@1 (avg@16) by 7.76–10.37 percentage points over OPD.
The abstract evaluates the method on mathematics reasoning and does not establish broader task or model scope.

papers.abstract: Diffusion and flow models have recently been extended to language modeling, generating text through continuous denoising in token embedding spaces. Pretrained models provide token representations and contextual prediction capabilities, but improving generation with limited additional training requires an appropriate connection between supervision and continuous generation. When continuous predictions are formed by weighting token embeddings with predicted probabilities, different probability distributions can yield the same vector and are therefore indistinguishable under a continuous reconstruction objective based on mean squared error (MSE). We propose Token Identity Brier Flow (TIBF) to apply squared supervision directly to token identities. TIBF fixes token embeddings, combines network scores with token-matching scores under a Gaussian observation model, supervises token probabilities using the Brier loss, and uses probability-weighted embeddings for continuous generation. We show that, for fixed token embeddings, the squared error in token posterior prediction controls the squared errors of the continuous denoising prediction and the flow velocity. A risk decomposition separates uncertainty inherent in the observation from posterior fitting error, motivating continued training that preserves pretrained embeddings and focuses on probability prediction. From common pretrained initializations and under matched continuation budgets, TIBF achieves mean Gen.PPL values of 34.87 on OWT and 80.08 on LM1B, outperforming continuous-MSE and CE controls. Further evaluations show improvements across multiple sampling budgets. Code is available at https://github.com/Jiangjiawei-kust/TIBF.
bullets: Continuous MSE supervision can treat distinct token distributions as identical when they produce the same embedding average.
TIBF combines network scores with token-matching scores under a Gaussian observation model and applies squared supervision to token identities.
A theoretical analysis links token-posterior error to continuous denoising and flow-velocity errors.
The method achieves mean Gen.PPL of 34.87 on OWT and 80.08 on LM1B, outperforming continuous-MSE and CE controls under matched budgets.
Results improve across multiple sampling budgets; the approach focuses continued training on probability prediction while retaining pretrained embeddings.

papers.abstract: Large language model agents are increasingly deployed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), which allows them to discover and invoke tools across multiple servers at runtime. Existing MCP benchmarks primarily measure task completion; where they diagnose failures, they do so after execution rather than building specific reasoning, execution, and memory failure risks into task construction. We introduce MCPHallu, a benchmark for diagnosing hallucination-prone agent failures in MCP environments along three axes: reasoning, execution, and memory. MCPHallu contains 358 tasks across five capability domains and runs on 36 production MCP servers in isolated containers. Each task is designed with a structural trigger that makes one of four subtypes the dominant failure risk: Branch Collapse, Unreachable Goal, Tool Misuse, or Context Forgetting. This design enables subtype-level analysis rather than aggregate task success alone. We evaluate fourteen frontier LLM agents from eight vendors on 5{,}012 trajectories. Current MCP agents remain vulnerable to hallucination-inducing tool environments, achieving an average score of 0.642 on a $[0,1]$ scale (higher is better). Failures concentrate on Unreachable Goal tasks, where the average score drops to 0.458 and 23.2\% of runs pass, indicating that agents often continue issuing tool calls or claim successful completion rather than recognizing infeasible goals. Subtype rankings diverge sharply: a model's rank shifts by 6.9 of 13 positions on average across subtypes, and Branch Collapse is uncorrelated with Unreachable Goal across models ($r = -0.12$). MCPHallu is released at https://github.com/J1zz/mcp_hallu.
bullets: Introduces 358 structured tasks spanning five capability domains and 36 production MCP servers in isolated containers.
Targets four failure subtypes: Branch Collapse, Unreachable Goal, Tool Misuse, and Context Forgetting.
Evaluates 14 frontier agents from eight vendors across 5,012 trajectories.
Agents average 0.642 overall, but Unreachable Goal tasks fall to 0.458, with only 23.2% passing.

papers.abstract: Recent studies have shown that large language models (LLMs) can memorize and reproduce copyrighted training data, raising serious privacy and intellectual property concerns. In this work, we investigate whether memorization can be mitigated without modifying or retraining the underlying model through an information bottleneck. We propose a modular plug-and-play framework that inserts a nonparametric variational information bottleneck (NVIB) between a frozen LLM backbone and its language modeling head. By compressing the final hidden representations before token prediction, the proposed bottleneck aims to preserve general linguistic knowledge while filtering out highly specific memorized sequences. We evaluate our approach on memorization extraction tasks involving book passages and on standard language modeling benchmarks to measure the trade-off between memorization reduction and downstream utility. Our experiments show that the NVIB layer substantially reduces extractability while maintaining competitive performance on benchmark tasks. These results suggest that adding an information bottleneck offers a practical and architecture agnostic direction for post-hoc memorization mitigation in pretrained LLMs.
bullets: Targets privacy and copyright risks from LLMs reproducing memorized training data.
Inserts a nonparametric variational information bottleneck between a frozen LLM backbone and its language-modeling head.
Compresses final hidden representations to filter highly specific memorized sequences while retaining general linguistic knowledge.
Evaluation on book-passage extraction and standard language-modeling benchmarks shows substantially lower extractability with competitive benchmark performance.
Scope: addresses post-hoc mitigation without modifying or retraining the underlying model; the abstract does not quantify residual memorization or utility trade-offs.

papers.abstract: Expert pruning compresses Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models by removing the experts that a calibration set marks as unimportant. Studies of high-resource languages largely find that English calibration transfers well to other languages. We test this for Lithuanian: we pruned four MoE models with REAP, removing 25% or 50% of the experts with English, Lithuanian or mixed calibration, and evaluated both languages on reading comprehension, translation and language modelling. English calibration does not transfer to Lithuanian: at 25% pruning, English comprehension fell by a median of 1.7 points but Lithuanian by 21.4. The transfer is asymmetric. Lithuanian calibration removed most of the Lithuanian loss and never significantly hurt English comprehension, which was on average 2.5 points better than under English calibration; only English language modeling got slightly worse. Routing suggests why: in the last layers, Lithuanian sends 55-72% of its expert selections to just eight experts, against 19-39% for English, and English calibration removes some of these experts. Compressed models should be calibrated, and evaluated, in every language they must serve.
bullets: The study tests REAP pruning on four MoE models at 25% and 50% expert removal using English, Lithuanian, or mixed calibration.
At 25% pruning, English comprehension dropped by a median of 1.7 points, versus 21.4 points for Lithuanian under English calibration.
Lithuanian calibration recovered most Lithuanian performance loss and did not significantly harm English comprehension; English language modeling worsened slightly.
Routing analysis indicates Lithuanian concentrates selections on eight experts in later layers, some of which English calibration removes.
Calibration and evaluation should include every language the compressed model is intended to serve.

papers.abstract: Learned orchestration has emerged as a promising paradigm for large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems, in which a central orchestrator selects agents and controls the information they receive throughout a task. Despite rapid empirical progress, existing methods train the orchestrator by crediting each decision with its own advantage, implicitly assuming that the other decisions in the episode stay fixed. This assumption fails in orchestration, where the contribution of each decision to the final outcome depends on the decisions preceding it, so the gain of a joint update is not the sum of its per-decision effects. To address this challenge, we introduce \textbf{IAPO}, an interaction-aware policy optimization framework that explicitly accounts for interactions among decisions. Specifically, IAPO exactly decomposes the performance difference between two policies into the effects of individual decisions and their interactions, which we prove can account for half of the attainable gain, and then optimizes both from sampled trajectories while certifying that every update is an improvement. On long-input versions of GSM8K, MATH, DROP, MBPP and HumanEval, against fifteen published multi-agent and workflow-search systems on the same 7B executor, IAPO's deployed plans reach the strongest system's accuracy with fewer tokens, and removing the interaction term costs 7 to 17 points of accuracy on code.
bullets: Existing methods credit orchestration decisions independently, overlooking dependencies between earlier and later choices.
IAPO exactly decomposes policy-performance changes into individual decision effects and higher-order interactions.
It optimizes both components from sampled trajectories and certifies that each update improves performance.
Across long-input reasoning and code benchmarks, IAPO matches the strongest system’s accuracy using fewer tokens.
Ablating interaction modeling reduces code accuracy by 7–17 points, showing its importance.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of IAPO. (a) Orchestration decisions depend on one another: a new earlier worker helps only if a later call may read its output, so neither change helps alone. (b) IAPO credits each orchestrator step and every pair of steps in one pass over each training trajectory, and fits one bounded update per step size. (c) With the candidates fixed, IAPO computes two lower bounds on the gain from fresh trajectories, keeps the larger one, and updates the policy only if it is positive.

papers.abstract: Mapping behavioral intelligence in malware analysis reports to ATT&CK techniques supports threat analysis and defense, but reliable identification remains challenging. Supporting evidence is often scattered across long, heterogeneous reports, while closely related techniques share behavioral cues and differ only in subtle but decisive details. While large language models (LLMs) can use external knowledge to interpret reports, they may assign techniques based on plausible associations rather than sufficient evidence. We present MEvince, a knowledge-constrained LLM reasoning framework for report-level malware technique identification. Its core is a shared behavioral representation connecting report observations to technique definitions. This representation is built through agentic mining of technique documentation and supports two online stages: 1) primitive-guided extraction uses behavioral primitives to structure LLM-extracted observations, link them to source passages, and group dispersed evidence; 2) evidence-aligned retrieval matches this evidence to technique profiles through the same concepts, retaining likely candidates and confusable alternatives for LLM comparison of distinguishing behaviors. Controls at both stages validate evidence references and check technique-specific requirements. The representation also supports adaptation without parameter updates, where offline agentic audits diagnose concept weaknesses and refine extraction or retrieval policies. We evaluate MEvince against 11 baselines spanning four method families using a dataset of 610 public malware reports referenced by MITRE ATT&CK. MEvince improves exact-ID F1 over the strongest baseline by 17.4%, and its concept-guided retrieval increases gold-label candidate coverage from 31.6% to 47.9%. With a small adaptation set, offline refinement yields further gains and outperforms baselines that update model parameters.
bullets: Addresses scattered evidence and subtle distinctions between closely related ATT&CK techniques.
Uses agentic documentation mining to build a shared behavioral representation linking observations, passages, and technique definitions.
Extracts primitive-guided evidence, retrieves aligned technique candidates and confusable alternatives, and validates references and technique requirements.
Evaluated on 610 MITRE ATT&CK-referenced malware reports against 11 baselines; it improves exact-ID F1 by 17.4% over the strongest baseline.
Concept-guided retrieval raises gold-label candidate coverage from 31.6% to 47.9%; offline policy refinement further improves performance without parameter updates.
