papers.abstract: Enterprise AI agents split requests across subagents, and each handoff can drop, alter or ignore a requirement. A preregistered study on synthetic, exactly scorable tasks compares free-text, structured JSON and signed requirement-manifest handoffs: the orchestrator extracts each requirement as a verbatim quote plus a checkable predicate, code signs it and deterministically verifies the merger's decision. With Qwen3-8B (1,440 trajectories, five threats), signed manifests cut unsafe commits under attack from 69.4% to 9.0% (60.4 pp, 95% CI [51.4, 69.4]) with no detectable utility loss versus structured handoffs (S2 -0.4 pp, 95% CI [-14.2, 13.3]). Signing defeats in-transit mutation: unsigned manifests violated 79.2 pp more often than signed ones, which never did; this replicated in gpt-oss-20b and gemma-4-12b. There, without an adversary, signed manifests were descriptively slightly worse than structured handoffs (11.1% vs 2.8%; 16.7% vs 8.3%; not tested) and lost utility overall (gpt-oss-20b, all threats: -28.7 pp). On identical Qwen3-8B trajectories, the deterministic verifier caught 78.7% of violating decisions versus 59.0% for an LLM checker, and an oracle manifest removed all remaining unsafe commits, so the residual risk is in extraction. A preregistered pre-signing injection confirmed this: one adversarial line raised signed-manifest unsafe commits from 14.6% to 37.5% (Qwen3-8B), 11.1% to 63.9% (gpt-oss-20b) and 16.7% to 97.2% (gemma-4-12b), and every such commit carried a manifest corrupted before signing. Signing protects transit; extraction is the trust boundary. A testable pre-signing specification (PSE), specified after the injection results and frozen before an offline evaluation, blocked all these injected commits (fixed templates) but refused 45.8%, 11.1% and 22.2% of benign requests, changing completions by -8.3 pp, -2.8 pp and 0.0 pp.
bullets: The study compares free-text, structured JSON, and cryptographically signed requirement-manifest handoffs on synthetic, exactly scorable tasks across five threats.
For Qwen3-8B, signed manifests reduced unsafe commits under attack from 69.4% to 9.0% without detectable utility loss versus structured handoffs.
Signing eliminated in-transit manifest mutation across tested models, while deterministic verification outperformed an LLM checker on detecting violating decisions.
Residual risk lies in requirement extraction: a single pre-signing adversarial line sharply increased unsafe commits across Qwen3-8B, gpt-oss-20b, and gemma-4-12b.
A post hoc frozen pre-signing specification blocked injected attacks but rejected some benign requests, indicating a safety–availability tradeoff.

papers.abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) have achieved impressive performance via explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, yet this process introduces critical safety risks. We formalize LRM safety objectives as requiring non-malicious reasoning and answers, safety consistency, and explicit intent identification. We argue that existing alignment methods suffer from poor adversarial generalization, a significant ``safety tax'' on reasoning, and unfaithful coarse-grained rewards, primarily due to their neglect of the LRM's intrinsic reasoning capabilities for safety. To address these, we propose \textbf{SAVeR$^2$}, a novel \textbf{S}afety \textbf{A}lignment method via \textbf{R}ewards with \textbf{R}easoning capability. SAVeR$^2$ decomposes the safety objective into four fine-grained verifiable reward signals and utilizes a difficulty-aware data selection strategy to stabilize training. Crucially, we introduce a reasoning-preserving gradient projection mechanism that analytically resolves conflicts between safety and reasoning gradients, effectively eliminating the safety tax. Extensive experiments on models ranging from 1.5B to 671B demonstrate that SAVeR$^2$ achieves superior safety performance and significantly lower over-refusal rates across multiple benchmarks without compromising general reasoning capabilities.
bullets: Targets unsafe reasoning and answers, inconsistent safety behavior, and failure to identify user intent.
Decomposes safety into four fine-grained verifiable rewards and selects training data based on difficulty.
Uses reasoning-preserving gradient projection to resolve conflicts between safety and reasoning objectives.
Across 1.5B–671B models, reports stronger safety, lower over-refusal, and preserved general reasoning across multiple benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of our proposed SAVeR2. papers.abstract: Selecting high-quality training data can reduce computation cost for LLM fine-tuning. Prior work on data selection developed a variety of difficulty-based scores, motivated by the intuition that harder examples are more informative. While effective for smaller classification models, we find that such methods often fail to outperform random selection for LLM fine-tuning. Our analysis reveals that random selection performs better because it is more representative of the underlying input space---i.e., has better coverage. To validate the importance of coverage, we implement a simple clustering-based selection method which selects data that is more representative of the underlying input distribution. On a set of diverse single-domain tasks, this method yields performance at or above that of random selection. On the diverse, multi-domain Tülu 3 mixture, where random sampling no longer guarantees a balanced subset, our method outperforms all methods. Overall, our results indicate that prioritizing coverage over difficulty leads to more effective data selection for LLM fine-tuning.
bullets: Difficulty-based selection often fails to outperform random selection for LLM fine-tuning.
Random selection works well because it better represents the underlying input space.
A simple clustering-based method selects data to improve coverage of the input distribution.
The method matches or exceeds random selection on diverse single-domain tasks and outperforms all compared methods on the multi-domain Tülu 3 mixture.

papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become an increasingly popular means of translating Large Language Model (LLM) hidden state vectors into a human-comprehensible list of features or symbols. As such, SAEs may provide insight into an LLM's knowledge representation and internal ``mental'' grammar - topics of pragmatic interest for mechanistic interpretation of AI behavior and of theoretical interest for the study of in silico representations of human language. Language models with fewer than 100M parameters, trained on small corpora, nonetheless exhibit strong grammatical competence and discourse coherence, despite producing content of limited reliability. We use SAEs that we trained on one such model (Pythia-70M) to conduct an in-depth examination of how a single grammatical phenomenon, number agreement, is represented and processed in an LLM. We demonstrate the mechanism and the methodology by which SAEs can be used to find and propagate ``plural noun'', ``plural matrix subject'', and ``generate a plural verb'' features which cause the LLM to produce plural verb forms such as ``are'', ``do'', or ``have'' instead of ``is'', ``does'', and ``has'' in response to prompts such as ``the men in the park''. We show that intervening to remove these features from the hidden states of plural subject noun tokens causes the model to produce singular verbs instead, and vice versa. We also show that corresponding ``singular noun'' and ``generate a singular verb'' features are not as effective for this task. This asymmetry suggests that Pythia-70m makes use of a privative representation of grammatical number in English. These findings replicated with larger LLMs Gemma-2-2b and Llama-3.1-8b yielded similar results. Our main contribution is a novel approach to the use of SAEs to understanding how LLMs encode human language that addresses a number of technical and methodological challenges.
bullets: Studies number agreement in Pythia-70M using sparse autoencoders (SAEs), extending the analysis to Gemma-2-2b and Llama-3.1-8b.
Identifies features for plural nouns, plural subjects, and generating plural verbs that influence forms such as “are,” “do,” and “have.”
Removing plural features from plural-subject representations causes singular verb outputs, while adding or propagating them promotes plural agreement.
Singular-related features are less effective, suggesting grammatical number may be represented primarily through plural features rather than a balanced singular/plural code.
Demonstrates an SAE-based methodology for probing and intervening on language representations while addressing associated technical and methodological challenges.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student model to match a teacher's next-token distributions on student-generated prefixes. Extrapolative OPD further extends the teacher's log-probability shift relative to a reference policy to construct stronger learning targets. However, existing methods couple extrapolation direction and distance, allowing the magnitude of the teacher's shift to dictate how far the target moves. We propose $D^2$-OPD, decoupling these two factors: a per-prefix hard KL constraint bounds the target's distance from the teacher, while an adaptive combination of the teacher's post-training shift and the initial student--teacher gap determines the extrapolation direction. We optimize the student toward this target using forward KL, providing learning signals even for low-probability tokens. We evaluate three settings: where standard OPD performs well, where it struggles with base-model initialization, and where no teacher reference is available. On mathematical reasoning benchmarks, $D^2$-OPD attains the highest score in all three settings, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 9.45 points. Ablations validate the contributions of each component.
bullets: Existing extrapolative OPD couples the direction and magnitude of target shifts, which can lead to poorly controlled targets.
D²-OPD uses a per-prefix hard KL constraint to bound the target’s distance from the teacher.
It adaptively determines extrapolation direction from the teacher’s post-training shift and the initial student–teacher gap.
Forward-KL optimization preserves learning signals for low-probability tokens.
Across three settings, it outperforms the strongest baseline by up to 9.45 points; ablations support each component’s contribution.

papers.abstract: We validate our previous hypothesis that a language model holds relational patterns apart from the subject domains that instantiate them (Nordfors, 2026). These archetypal contexts are patterns of relations that people recognize across many fields, such as the tipping point or winner takes all, held once and applied across domains. We show this inside the model, Qwen3.8-27B. One set of neurons carries the archetype, say the tipping point; another carries the topic, say politics, ecology or cell biology; a third carries the language, such as English, Spanish or Chinese. Silence the tipping point's neurons, and the model no longer identifies the pattern but still knows what the text is about. Silence the topic's, and it loses the topic but still names the pattern. In the neuron maps the layers organize themselves into a sandwich: the outer layers carry languages, the layers inside them topics, the layers at the heart archetypes. The sandwich emerges spontaneously during pretraining and appears in every model we mapped. Archetypes are the architecture for analogy, and we strongly suggest that this structure of archetypes and topics is the mechanism of a language model's intelligence: we see it self-organize as the model is trained. The neurons, the texts and the code are released with this paper as its reproduction package, so that anyone can repeat the test inside the model.
bullets: Archetypal contexts—such as “tipping point” or “winner takes all”—are represented separately from the topics and languages in which they appear.
In Qwen3.8-27B, neuron silencing selectively removes recognition of an archetype, topic, or language while preserving the others.
Mapped layers form a “sandwich”: languages in outer layers, topics in intermediate layers, and archetypes near the center.
This organization reportedly emerges during pretraining and appears across all models examined.
The released neurons, texts, and code provide a reproduction package, though the proposed role in intelligence remains a strong interpretation of the findings.

papers.abstract: Looped Transformers reduce parameter count by repeatedly applying shared blocks, but parameter sharing alone does not determine how the results of repeated computation are reused. We take the depth-memory view of residual connections and analyze which representation is stored after each block application and how later reads weight it. A full block output contains both its input and its new update, so weighting that output also reweights the history already carried by the input. Reading individual updates instead, with the shared stack's input kept on a separate path, gives separate controls over input strength, total update weight, and allocation across updates. The Loopback Transformer implements these controls: geometric decay sets the total update weight and supplies a recency prior, and attention learns how to allocate that weight. On ClimbMix, Loopback reaches lower validation loss than standard Transformer baselines with 40-75% of their Transformer parameters (excluding token embeddings and the output head) at reference scales from 191M to 3B, with training tokens and executed depth matched. It also has higher mean accuracy over thirteen downstream tasks at 1.4B and 3B. At 191M, 374M, and 778M, it has the lowest validation loss and the highest thirteen-task mean among the standard Transformer and seven looped residual designs.
bullets: Looped Transformers share blocks to reduce parameters, but their effectiveness depends on how repeated outputs are reused.
The method reads individual block updates while keeping the shared stack’s input on a separate path.
Geometric decay controls total update weight and provides a recency prior; attention allocates weight across updates.
On ClimbMix, Loopback achieves lower validation loss than standard Transformer baselines using 40–75% of their Transformer parameters, with matched training tokens and executed depth.
It also obtains the highest thirteen-task mean accuracy at 191M, 374M, 778M, 1.4B, and 3B reference scales among the compared designs.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly act as service consumers. They select operations and report whether a task is complete. In an asynchronous distributed service, an accepted call or immediate state read does not establish that the required state became observable by its deadline. We introduce execution-grounded completion contracts, which treat completion as a service-level outcome. An independent control plane observes a deadline-bound service-state predicate, admits completion, and directs recovery while the agent performs the task. We evaluate placement and deletion in a live multi-provider data service with heterogeneous models and an injected transfer delay. Across policies, some tasks that missed the deadline were accepted and some that met it were rejected. Under enforcement, accepted completions remained consistent with later observations; all included healthy tasks completed, and unresolved faulted tasks terminated as unverified. The results show that completion of these tasks can be governed by independent observation of service state rather than by the agent's self-assessment.
bullets: Addresses the gap between accepted operations or immediate reads and deadline-bound observable outcomes in asynchronous services.
Uses an independent control plane to monitor service-state predicates, admit or reject completion, and direct recovery.
Evaluated placement and deletion in a live multi-provider data service with heterogeneous models and injected transfer delay.
Some accepted tasks missed deadlines, while some rejected tasks met them, showing agent reports were unreliable.
Enforcement kept accepted completions consistent with later observations and terminated unresolved faulted tasks as unverified.

papers.abstract: Parallel decoding speeds up masked diffusion language models by writing several tokens per forward pass. Published commit rules choose these tokens by testing the predicted distributions. Under sampling the written tokens are drawn, and these tests do not see them. We find that answer quality follows the reliability of the tokens actually written. An answer's log probability splits into this reliability and the dependence within each step. We propose PACT, a training-free commit rule that draws the tokens first, certifies the set it will write and spaces the positions of each step apart. This certificate holds at every temperature, and we show that no rule with the same guarantee commits more positions. Experiments use four models of the LLaDA and Dream families and HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K, MATH500 and IFEval benchmarks. PACT reaches the quality of published commit rules with fewer forward passes. Spacing removes positions from each step, yet it usually lowers the total cost because later steps then write more tokens. At the same speed, published decoders also write a word twice in a row far more often than PACT. These results suggest that commit rules should certify the tokens they write. Code is available at https://github.com/LiZaiyuan0619/PACT.
bullets: Existing commit rules assess predicted distributions rather than the tokens actually sampled during decoding.
PACT samples tokens first, certifies the set to write, and spaces selected positions apart; its guarantee holds at every temperature.
The paper decomposes answer log probability into written-token reliability and within-step dependence, motivating certification of actual writes.
Across LLaDA and Dream models on HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K, MATH500, and IFEval, PACT matches published quality with fewer forward passes.
Spacing generally lowers total decoding cost and reduces repeated word writes compared with published decoders.

papers.tldr: PACT is a training-free parallel decoding rule for diffusion language models that certifies sampled tokens before writing them, preserving quality while reducing forward passes.

papers.abstract: As Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) large language models are increasingly deployed in distributed environments, from federated learning to edge-cloud systems, their architecture harbors an underexplored landscape of security vulnerabilities. Moving beyond textual analysis, we uncover structural memorization: a novel vulnerability where a fine-tuned model memorizes not only its training data but also the internal pathway used to process it, creating a characteristic routing fingerprint unique to the training process. We provide comprehensive empirical evidence that structural memorization emerges consistently even from a few samples, and that its intensity is directly influenced by the choice of trainable modules. We show that these memorized expert pathways can be stealthily recovered through the model's unconditional generation, using only routing and output logits, with no knowledge of the fine-tuning data or procedure. In distributed deployments, this vulnerability is amplified as routing information is exposed at multiple trust boundaries, including federated aggregation points, edge-cloud interfaces, and multi-tenant monitoring systems. Recovery exposes a critical blind spot: traditional membership inference metrics, viewed through the lens of expert routing, fail to identify memorized data corresponding to these structural pathways. To close this gap, we devise composite metrics combining reference model tail likelihood with complexity-aware normalization, significantly improving detection of memorized routing structures. This enables adversaries to pinpoint critical experts shaped by fine-tuning, whether dominant or dormant, and execute targeted attacks such as router manipulation or backdoor injection in realistic distributed settings where attackers lack training data but can observe routing patterns across system components.
bullets: Structural memorization records internal expert pathways alongside training data, even when fine-tuning uses few samples.
The strength of these routing fingerprints depends on which model modules are trainable.
Attackers can recover pathways from unconditional generation using only routing information and output logits, without training data or procedure knowledge.
Distributed systems amplify exposure across federated aggregation, edge-cloud, and multi-tenant monitoring boundaries.
Composite metrics using reference-model tail likelihood and complexity-aware normalization improve detection beyond standard membership-inference measures.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own responses using token-level feedback from a teacher. As responses grow longer, the student's prefix can depart from the teacher's own reasoning, weakening its feedback on later tokens. Updates based on this feedback can reinforce the same deviations in later responses and destabilize training. Prior approaches such as length control and loss reweighting limit learning from problematic responses but leave their prefixes unchanged. Fixed cutoffs can also discard later reasoning. We propose \textbf{Adaptive Teacher Intervention for On-Policy Distillation (ATI-OPD)} to improve subsequent teacher guidance by revising the student's reasoning prefix. ATI-OPD replaces the earliest high-disagreement segment with a short teacher segment, then lets the student resume its own reasoning from the revised text. To handle renewed disagreement, it excludes persistently divergent suffixes from the distillation loss while retaining useful student continuation. Training diagnostics show less teacher-student disagreement, fewer gradient spikes, and fewer extremely long responses. Across five mathematical reasoning benchmarks and two teacher-student pairs, ATI-OPD improves average student-only accuracy over standard OPD.
bullets: Long responses can cause student prefixes to drift from the teacher, weakening later feedback and destabilizing training.
The method replaces the earliest high-disagreement segment with a short teacher-generated segment, then resumes student reasoning.
Persistently divergent suffixes are excluded from the distillation loss while preserving useful student continuation.
Diagnostics show reduced disagreement, fewer gradient spikes, and fewer extremely long responses.
Across five mathematical reasoning benchmarks and two teacher–student pairs, ATI-OPD improves average student-only accuracy over standard OPD.

papers.abstract: Foundation models can generate scientific code, but authoring a scientific simulator (an executable program encoding hypotheses about how mechanisms generate observable signals) requires iterative refinement. Scientific adequacy rarely admits a unique implementation or exact test, so simulators must instead be judged against limited real observations. We study this setting as scientific simulator authoring under weak empirical feedback, where distributional comparisons between simulated and real signals guide revision, and the target is the simulator itself rather than only its generated samples. We introduce SimAuthor, a persistent authoring harness that retains and revises executable simulators, separates scalar search scores from structured discrepancy feedback, and accumulates reusable implementation mechanisms. We evaluate SimAuthor on six biomedical tasks spanning cardiac and respiratory audio, photoplethysmography (PPG), and electrocardiography (ECG). Under a fixed 100-attempt budget, SimAuthor outperforms PUCT score search on all six tasks, generally outperforms textual-strategy optimization, and achieves the highest endpoint score on five of six. The authored simulators also improve on unseen recordings, transfer to independent pretrained representations, and yield substantial out-of-distribution gains in downstream ECG classification. Finally, 111 of 138 audited revisions alter program structure and account for 86.1% of the signed score improvement. These results suggest that persistent revision can progressively convert foundation-model knowledge into better executable scientific simulators from limited empirical evidence.
bullets: Addresses simulator authoring when scientific adequacy lacks a unique implementation or exact test.
Maintains and revises executable simulators, separating scalar search scores from structured discrepancy feedback and reusing implementation mechanisms.
Evaluated on cardiac and respiratory audio, PPG, and ECG tasks under a fixed 100-attempt budget.
Outperformed PUCT score search on all six tasks and achieved the best endpoint score on five; it also generalized to unseen recordings and downstream ECG classification.
Most audited revisions changed program structure, accounting for 86.1% of signed score improvement.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have reached expert-level performance on competition mathematics largely through the volume of search placed around them: candidate solutions are sampled in quantity and retained only when an external criterion accepts them. Such a procedure improves the outcome that survives it while leaving untouched what the model represents. We examine that question where no external criterion exists: translating statements between the dialects of neighbouring subfields, where fidelity turns on the level of generality at which content is asserted. The source leaves that level implicit in its vocabulary, so a faithful translation must recover it from the relation between the theories. We introduce an instrument that codes truth, content and scope in separate blind queues, with a judge-free measure of whether a rewrite states the hypothesis implicit in its source, and establish its sensitivity with a planted-positive control. Across seven models from four families, translating towards the general framing widens the domain of quantification in 60.6% of rewrites and narrows it in none; translating towards the concrete framing narrows it in 28.3% and widens it in 0.3%. The hypothesis that would prevent it is stated in 21.6% of model rewrites and 4.2% of human statements. Capability does not govern the asymmetry: it appears in every model tested, and the most capable widens least. It replicates on the half of the benchmark held out by a pre-registered rule, and on statements written by mathematicians. Instructing a model to state every hypothesis it requires raises that rate but not its sensitivity to direction. We argue that these systems have acquired an object-level correspondence between subfield vocabularies without the constraint under which a translation between theories carries hypotheses to hypotheses.
bullets: The study tests translation between neighboring mathematical subfields, where implicit scope and assumptions determine fidelity.
It introduces a judge-free instrument that separately codes truth, content, and scope, validated with planted-positive controls.
Across seven models, translations toward general frameworks widened quantification in 60.6% of cases and never narrowed it; concrete-directed translations narrowed it in 28.3% and widened it in 0.3%.
Models stated the hypotheses required by their rewrites in 21.6% of cases, versus 4.2% for human statements; the asymmetry appeared across all models.
Explicitly prompting models to state every required hypothesis increased disclosure but did not improve directional sensitivity.

papers.abstract: Critic-free reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) for agentic large language models is often done through GRPO-style methods, which compute a group baseline over repeated rollouts to reduce target variance. However, this setup is ill-suited to agents acting in stateful environments such as live services or security sandboxes, where repeated rollouts are impractical to obtain and aggressive updates entrench the noise of long, sparsely verified trajectories. We propose \textit{Follow the Winners} (FTW), a critic-free policy-learning algorithm that adapts the cross-entropy method to RFT, replacing group rollouts with an ordinal filter on replay-buffer samples that yields polynomial concentration in the order statistic of returns. We derive FTW through a control-as-inference lens, which also recovers GRPO and DPO as specific modelling choices, identifying GRPO as risk-neutral while DPO and FTW share a bounded risk-seeking offset that FTW controls. We identify this offset as an inherent trade-off of variance reduction through ordinal filters on samples, whereas a critic model induces a different trade-off between bias and variance. Scaled to agentic LLM post-training, FTW matches GRPO and PPO on Sokoban and Search-R1 baselines, showing a viable trade-off from a value model or group rollouts to CPU memory.
bullets: Targets stateful environments where repeated rollouts are impractical and long trajectories are sparsely verified.
Applies an ordinal filter from the cross-entropy method to replay-buffer samples.
Uses a control-as-inference formulation that connects FTW with GRPO and DPO.
Controls the bounded risk-seeking effect introduced by ordinal filtering.
Matches GRPO and PPO baselines on Sokoban and Search-R1 while trading value models or group rollouts for CPU memory.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes Follow the Winners (FTW), a critic-free reinforcement fine-tuning algorithm for agentic LLMs using the cross-entropy method to reduce variance without group rollouts.
papers.title: Follow the Winners: Conservative Policy Improvement with the Cross-Entropy Method for Critic-Free RFT
papers.tldr: FTW is a critic-free RFT algorithm that uses replay-buffer ranking instead of repeated group rollouts, matching GRPO and PPO on reported agentic LLM benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used where small syntactic errors matter, yet character-level reasoning is still evaluated mostly through isolated probes and aggregate accuracy. We introduce SyntaxBench, a diagnostic benchmark and statistical evaluation framework for character-level reasoning. It contains five core tasks, character counting, letter containment, palindrome detection, edit distance, and longest-string selection, plus index_to_span, a harder substring-extraction stress test. The five core tasks use paired English and character-length-matched random-string inputs. index_to_span documents share a 200-500 word band and are not character-length matched. All six tasks use zero-, one-, and four-shot prompts. We evaluate eight open-weight models from 2B to 32B parameters across 11 reasoning-mode configurations. The framework reports exact-match and relaxed accuracy, Cohen's kappa, paired McNemar tests with odds ratios, bootstrap confidence intervals, Kendall's tau, class-conditional metrics, tokenization analysis, and multiple-comparison-corrected tests. Three findings stand out. First, tokenization shapes accuracy: random strings are more character-visible than English strings (1.892 vs. 3.169 characters per token), and character-counting accuracy falls as English words occupy more tokens. Second, reasoning mode is not uniformly helpful: Gemma4-31B is nearly unchanged across modes on the near-saturated tasks, while Qwen3.6-27B is worse with thinking on palindrome detection (0.952 non-thinking vs. 0.886 thinking at four-shot). Third, index_to_span remains largely unsolved; the best four-shot exact-match accuracy is 6.75%. Character-level evaluation needs controlled inputs, paired tests, and analyses of tokenization and reasoning mode rather than aggregate accuracy alone.
bullets: Introduces six diagnostic tasks covering counting, containment, palindromes, edit distance, string selection, and substring extraction.
Pairs English and character-length-matched random-string inputs to isolate tokenization effects, with zero-, one-, and four-shot settings.
Evaluates eight open-weight models using exact and relaxed accuracy, paired statistical tests, confidence intervals, tokenization analysis, and multiple-comparison correction.
Random strings are more character-visible than English, and English counting accuracy declines as words use more tokens.
Reasoning mode is task- and model-dependent; index_to_span achieves only 6.75% best four-shot exact-match accuracy.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces SyntaxBench, a diagnostic framework for character-level reasoning in LLMs, analyzing tokenization effects and reasoning modes to evaluate model capabilities.
papers.title: SyntaxBench: A Statistical Diagnostic Framework for Character-Level Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.tldr: SyntaxBench shows that character-level reasoning in LLMs depends strongly on tokenization and reasoning mode, while substring extraction remains largely unsolved.

papers.abstract: Mainstream large language models rely on a tokenizer to encode text into a token sequence. Different tokenizers may yield token sequences of substantially different lengths for the same text. With a fixed model architecture, shorter token sequences correspond to lower inference time. We propose a tokenizer training approach named Counting and Filtering (CNF) and a text encoding algorithm called Min-Cost Encoding (MCE). MCE defines a cost function over a text segment, and determines the best segmentation by globally minimizing the overall segmentation cost. CNF builds a raw vocabulary by directly counting valid substrings, and then constructs the final vocabulary through a filtering step based on actual token usage when segmenting the training corpus with MCE. The CNF-MCE conbination offers several advantages over BPE, including higher token efficiency, greater scalability, and lower dependency. Across six text categories and two vocabulary-size groups, CNF-MCE consistently achieves better compression than the evaluated BPE tokenizers. With a 250K vocabulary, CNF-MCE increases compression rate by 26% and 30% on English web text over the o200k_base and qwen250k tokenizers. Experiments scaling the vocabulary to 1M entries on English web text demonstrate sustained improvements over BPE, with a token efficiency improvement of over 60% and vocabulary utilization rising from 52.9% to 96.9%. The MCE algorithm does not depend on a merge list (as in BPE) or token probability (as in UnigramLM), making it applicable to a wide range of vocabularies, including those built from BPE, UnigramLM, CNF, and others. Language models trained from scratch at the 1.8B and 8B scales achieve comparable average performance to models using the BPE tokenizers across 11 benchmarks. These results demonstrate that CNF-MCE can improve token efficiency significantly while maintaining competitive downstream performance.
bullets: Targets inefficient tokenization, where longer sequences increase inference cost.
Uses Min-Cost Encoding (MCE) to find globally optimal text segmentations under a defined cost function.
Trains vocabularies with Counting and Filtering (CNF), combining substring counting with usage-based vocabulary filtering.
Outperforms evaluated BPE tokenizers across six text categories and two vocabulary-size groups; gains persist at 1M vocabulary size.
Models trained with CNF-MCE achieve comparable average performance to BPE-based models across 11 benchmarks.

papers.selection_reason: Tokenizer training and encoding method improving token efficiency for LLMs; relevant to LLM architecture advances.
papers.title: Counting and Min-Cost Encoding for Tokenization in Large Language Models
papers.tldr: CNF-MCE improves tokenizer compression and token efficiency over BPE while maintaining comparable language-model benchmark performance.

papers.abstract: Researchers use large language models as agents in social simulations, where agents are prompted with observations and background information intended to shape their actions. Yet LLM agents have been shown to substantially change their behavior under meaning-preserving prompt variations, creating a validation problem for social simulation. One plausible hypothesis is that this brittleness reflects a lack of grounding and can be reduced by enriching the context provided to the agents. Whether richer context improves robustness remains unclear, in part because context richness and robustness are rarely defined in ways that support controlled comparisons. We address the first need with controlled context enrichment, a set of prompt substitution rules that systematically enriches distinct types of context: neutral padding, generic social background, descriptive decision grounding, and normative decision grounding. We address the second by introducing selective robustness as a validation criterion: insensitivity to meaning-preserving prompt variation combined with a directional response to decision-relevant changes in the social world. We demonstrate the framework in a Prisoner's Dilemma-like game, showing how it can be used to identify which forms of context enrichment produce more desirable and robust agent behavior. We find that these forms of enrichment produce distinct behavioral patterns that vary between the two models tested.
authors: Mattia Greiche, Reihaneh Rabbany, Maximilian Puelma Touzel
bullets: Motivated by LLM agents’ behavioral brittleness under meaning-preserving prompt variations, which challenges social-simulation validation.
Defines controlled context enrichment through four prompt types: neutral padding, generic social background, descriptive decision grounding, and normative decision grounding.
Introduces selective robustness: invariance to meaning-preserving prompt changes alongside directional responses to decision-relevant changes in the social environment.
Demonstrates the framework in a Prisoner’s Dilemma-like game, identifying distinct behavioral effects of different enrichment strategies.
Finds that enrichment effects and behavioral patterns vary across the two tested models.

The y-axis shows the regional-minus-local difference in transfer probability averaged across surface forms; positive values indicate more transfer in the regional world. papers.selection_reason: Proposes a framework for Context Enrichment and Selective Robustness in LLM social agents to address brittleness in simulations.
papers.title: A Framework for Context Enrichment and Selective Robustness in LLM Social Agents
papers.tldr: The paper introduces a framework for systematically enriching LLM-agent context and evaluating whether agents remain stable to wording changes while responding appropriately to meaningful social changes.

papers.abstract: Looped Transformers increase effective depth by re-executing shared layers, but three limitations hinder their adoption: memory grows with the loop count, compute can only be adjusted in whole-block steps, and the loop count is hard to change after training. We propose LooM (Loop-invariant Memory), which addresses each in turn. In a causal encoder-decoder (CED), LooM loops only the decoder layers after the first, which read a global memory written once per token, and each of them publishes the key-value (KV) entry for a token only on its first visit, so the cache does not grow with the loop count. These layers loop independently, providing every budget from 3 to 21 layer executions per token, and one model trained on randomly sampled budgets covers all of them without a router. With enough loops, LooM outperforms a single-pass baseline trained on the same data on language modeling, zero-shot accuracy and long-context perplexity, while using the same cache size. Our analysis further shows that the training budget distribution decides what extra depth buys. These results suggest that a CED is a natural place to loop: memory is written once, and depth becomes a budget chosen at deployment.
authors: Lele Yang, Muxi Diao, Zhonghao Yan, Jiankang Chen, Bin Wen, Tingting Gao, Wentao Zhang, Kongming Liang, Zhanyu Ma, Weiran Xu
bullets: Targets looped Transformer limitations: loop-dependent memory growth, coarse compute control, and fixed post-training loop counts.
Loops decoder layers after the first, using global memory written once per token and publishing each token’s KV entry only on its first visit.
Independent layer loops provide budgets from 3 to 21 layer executions per token; one model supports all budgets without a router.
With sufficient looping, LooM improves language modeling, zero-shot accuracy, and long-context perplexity over a same-data single-pass baseline while keeping cache size unchanged.
Training-budget distributions determine what additional depth provides; the approach supports deployment-time depth selection.

papers.selection_reason: Novel looped transformer architecture that keeps cache size constant, improving long-context perplexity and efficiency.
papers.title: LooM: Loop-Invariant Memory for Causal Encoder-Decoder Language Models
papers.tldr: LooM enables flexible, memory-efficient looping in causal encoder-decoder language models, allowing deployment-time depth adjustment without increasing cache size.

papers.abstract: Small language models offer a compact basis for shell simulation without executing submitted commands, but full-output decoding requires them to predict recurring utility structure alongside content that varies across executions. We introduce template gap reconstruction (TGR), which supplies reusable output literals interspersed with sentinels to be interleaved with autoregressively generated gaps. A template selector chooses which template to be reconstructed, with the empty template retaining full-output decoding. We construct a template bank from 18.7 million outputs collected across heterogeneous execution environments and train a template selector and five reconstruction models initialized from various small language model checkpoints on a target environment excluded from bank construction. Evaluation demonstrates that TGR improves output edit similarity (O-ES) over full-output decoding (FOD) when the optimal template covers more than 25\% of the template, while performing similarly for lower-coverage outputs. Additionally, TGR outperforms FOD for shorter gap sequences, with O-ES values of 0.964 and 0.812, respectively, while maintaining similar performance for longer sequences. TGR reduces the number of tokens generated by 26.3--38.3\% across used tokenizer families. These results support using a reusable output structure as a practical design choice for small shell simulators, improving response fidelity and shortening generation targets while keeping template selection and residual prediction central to response quality.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of predicting recurring shell-output structure alongside execution-specific content without running commands.
Provides reusable output templates with sentinels; the model autoregressively generates only the missing gaps.
A template selector chooses a reconstruction template, while an empty template preserves full-output decoding.
Improves output edit similarity when templates cover more than 25% of the output and performs similarly at lower coverage.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) assumes that language models can reason over relations stated in their context rather than fall back on associations memorized during pretraining. We study this evidence-conditioned relational reasoning in isolation, with the facts supplied directly in the prompt rather than retrieved. \textsc{Rel-Bloom} is a controlled multilingual diagnostic of 450 multiple-choice questions built from 30 Wikidata relations; the same source relations are instantiated at five Bloom-inspired levels (Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate) and under three veracity conditions (Factual, Counterfactual, Neutralized). Across 43 models, six languages, and two multilingual settings (226,800 predictions), three findings stand out. First, accuracy drops sharply from Apply to Analyze in every evaluated open-weight model series, reaching 47.2 percentage points for the Large Granite bucket, but not for either Gemini model. Second, Evaluate items remain a bottleneck even for models near ceiling on the other task types: Gemini~3.1 Pro averages 99.5\% on the other four levels but 60.7\% on Evaluate. Third, item- and relation-level difficulty rankings are consistently preserved across languages, indicating a difficulty structure partly shared across languages within this benchmark. Across knowledge conditions, Counterfactual contexts are generally harder than Factual ones, while removing entity identities can improve higher-level performance in some model regimes. Greater model capability therefore does not by itself ensure reliable reasoning over supplied relational evidence. Relevant resources are available at: https://huggingface.co/spaces/QCRI/non-parametric-memory-relational-reasoning.
authors: Zohreh Abbasi Liasi, Batoul Hammoud, Anas Madkoor, Ehsaneddin Asgari
bullets: Evaluates 43 models across six languages using 450 controlled multiple-choice questions covering 30 Wikidata relations.
Tests five Bloom-inspired reasoning levels and three knowledge conditions: factual, counterfactual, and neutralized.
Accuracy drops sharply from Apply to Analyze in open-weight models, while Evaluate remains difficult even for highly capable models.
Difficulty rankings are largely consistent across languages, suggesting shared cross-lingual structure in relational reasoning difficulty.
Counterfactual contexts are generally harder; removing entity identities can sometimes improve higher-level reasoning.

Items are then evaluated in six languages under two multilingual settings. The 43 models comprise 41 open-weight models from seven model families, analyzed as eight model series because Qwen2.5 Base and Qwen2.5 Instruct are treated separately, plus two Gemini models.

papers.abstract: Public bodies increasingly rely on AI-produced evidence, including classifications, summaries and assessments. These outputs can inform policy decisions and service delivery, making their reliability a matter of public accountability. Establishing whether this evidence can be relied upon requires testing its outputs and examining how organisations decide whether those tests are sufficient. We combine technical evaluation with analysis of AI governance requirements, informed by measurement theory and management-based regulation. We compare eight GPT-4o configurations classifying 1,200 UK Prime Minister's Questions into 21 policy topics, against human-coded labels and across unchanged repeats. Accuracy ranges from 68.2% to 70.3%, yet 24.3% of questions receive different labels, with changes in topic shares and rankings. Configurations agree more with one another than with human coding: agreement does not guarantee correctness. Under the implemented score-extraction procedure, the proportion flagged for human review ranges from 0.9% to 41.0%. We analyse 37 UK and EU policy documents. Both sets expect testing and oversight, but reporting expectations do not consistently cover changing answers, shared errors, selective evaluation, substantive conclusions or review routing. Some UK guidance explicitly addresses stability. The UK sample emphasises public bodies checking their own use; the EU places substantial testing duties on providers while leaving them important choices about measures and acceptance thresholds. Without appropriate checks, evidence could misrepresent policy issues, redirect attention or resources, and leave errors undetected. Public policy should require organisations to justify reliance through checks beyond aggregate accuracy, clear responsibility, access to expertise and scrutiny of results.

Configurations agreed more with one another than with human coding, showing that agreement does not ensure correctness.

Analysis of 37 UK and EU policy documents found gaps in requirements for reporting instability, shared errors, selective evaluation, substantive conclusions, and review routing.

papers.abstract: While multi-turn agentic reinforcement learning (RL) excels on long-horizon tasks, its performance gains remain highly sensitive to interaction constraints. Evaluating across sampling breadth $K$ and interaction depth $T$ via $Pass@(K,T)$, we show that trajectory-level RL advantages depend on sufficient turn budgets, diminishing significantly when budgets tighten. Besides, agentic RL does not uniformly elevate single-step decision quality; rather, its strength concentrates in error recovery and long-horizon resilience. To mitigate the deployment risks caused by this budget dependence, we provide a preliminary discussion on the benefits and limitations of process supervision signals and introduce BudgetMix RL as an alternative that varies interaction budgets during training. Experiments demonstrate that BudgetMix RL achieves robust performance across diverse execution settings. Project Page: https://rethinking-agentic-rl.github.io/
authors: Kejian Zhu, Zhuoran Jin, Shangqing Tu, Tianyi Men, Yupu Hao, Jiachun Li, Kang Liu, Jun Zhao
bullets: Performance is evaluated across sampling breadth and interaction depth using Pass@(K,T).
Trajectory-level RL benefits diminish substantially when turn or interaction budgets are tight.
Agentic RL does not consistently improve single-step decision quality.
The study discusses process supervision and proposes BudgetMix RL, which varies training budgets to improve robustness across execution settings.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes the specific benefits of multi-turn RL for LLM agents, identifying error recovery and long-horizon resilience, and proposes BudgetMix RL to handle interaction constraints.
papers.title: What Does Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning Really Improve in LLM Agents?
papers.tldr: Multi-turn RL mainly improves LLM agents’ error recovery and long-horizon resilience, with gains that depend strongly on available interaction budgets.

papers.abstract: The performance of large language model (LLM) agents depends on both the underlying model and the harness that governs interaction with tools and the environment. Yet harness design remains largely manual, and automating it requires navigating an open-ended search space through costly end-to-end evaluations. We introduce HarnessFlow, a framework for optimizing complete executable harnesses under a limited candidate-evaluation budget, with the model and task environment held fixed. HarnessFlow organizes candidates and their evaluation histories in a refinement tree, using a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-based policy to balance exploitation and exploration. A coding agent refines selected harnesses using archived code, execution feedback, and a library of reusable harness mechanisms. With 15 refinement attempts per benchmark, HarnessFlow achieves the highest mean test scores among the compared methods on six benchmarks spanning agentic tasks, coding, and web interaction. The optimized harnesses achieve an average score of 69.48%, outperforming the initial harnesses and Meta-Harness by 10.89 and 3.95 percentage points, respectively, while incurring lower average per-task execution costs than hand-engineered baselines. These results suggest that structured harness search offers a promising route toward automating the design of capable and efficient LLM agents.
authors: Zhi Hong, Qianlong Wang, Hongchen Wei, Aidan Wu, Daohong Ying, Mingze Kong, Bei Liu, Chong Luo

Maintains a refinement tree of candidate harnesses and evaluation histories, balancing exploration and exploitation with MCTS.
A coding agent refines selected harnesses using archived code, execution feedback, and reusable mechanisms.
With 15 refinement attempts per benchmark, it achieves the highest mean test scores across six agentic, coding, and web-interaction benchmarks.
The optimized harnesses average 69.48%, improving over initial harnesses and Meta-Harness, while costing less per task than hand-engineered baselines.

papers.abstract: Decision models read a document and return a probability for each of a fixed set of options instead of generating text. Several appeared in 2026, but none has published results outside English. We describe Zuse, three decision models (4B, 9B and 27B) that train a low-rank adapter and a pointer head on frozen open-weight bases, targeting 27 European languages, and use them to study how this design behaves across languages and tasks. On a broad European suite of 11 sources excluded from training, covering 9 task groups and 27 languages, a development set that also guided model selection, the 27B model reaches 87.5% accuracy with a pooled expected calibration error of 0.016, and 0.035 when weighted per source. Post-hoc analyses of these single-seed results give three findings. First, miscalibration is structured by task rather than language: on parallel reading and topic items in 26 languages the confidence gap varies about as much as sampling noise, while across sources it spans -0.07 to +0.09, with knowledge tasks overconfident and acceptability judgements underconfident at all three sizes, so one fitted temperature cannot correct both. Second, the share of decisions that can be automated at a 5% error budget follows chance-corrected skill (Spearman 0.97 over 33 source and model pairs) more closely than raw accuracy (0.91). Third, reach beyond the training languages is set by the base model: across 210 languages, changing the training run moved scores by at most about 2 points within a size, while languages outside the base's documented list trail by 23 to 28 points at every size. On English public suites Zuse is behind Jev and Kev, including Kev models on the same bases. We also report two pitfalls in building multi-source training data: label-word collision between topic schemes, and an injection augmentation that taught a shortcut. Zuse can be tried at https://bineric.com/zuse.
bullets: Provides 4B, 9B, and 27B decision models targeting 27 European languages.
Uses low-rank adapters and pointer heads trained on frozen open-weight base models.
On 11 held-out sources spanning 9 task groups and 27 languages, the 27B model achieves 87.5% accuracy with pooled expected calibration error of 0.016.
Calibration differences are driven more by task than language; knowledge tasks are overconfident, while acceptability judgments are underconfident.
Cross-language reach largely follows the base model: languages outside its documented coverage score substantially lower, and Zuse trails Jev and Kev on English public suites.

papers.abstract: Multimodal models have often scored below text-only baselines in the BabyLM Challenge (Klerings et al., 2024; Takmaz et al., 2025). We test whether additional recurrent computation helps close this gap. Recurrence increases computation by reusing layers without adding parameters or training data. Using a single implementation, we compare standard and looped Transformers under a 100M-word budget, with three seeds per main condition. Each image is represented by one feature vector from a frozen DINOv2 encoder, used as a prefix token. Caption words count toward the budget, so multimodal training also changes the language data. In a pre-registered text-only comparison, a 12-layer stack repeated four times exceeds a standard 48-layer Transformer by 5.4 BLiMP percentage points at matched inference compute. However, multimodal training lowers BLiMP accuracy by about 3.8 points in both architectures, with no clear mitigation from recurrence. An exploratory loop-side no-image control, trained with the multimodal language data and batching schedule, scores 5.7 points below the text-only baseline. Adding the visual prefix raises accuracy by 1.85 points on average, but this contrast is uncertain with three seeds. These results suggest that changes in language data and its presentation are a major source of the drop. Diagnostic tests show that the models use visual information; its contribution to grammatical generalization remains uncertain under this single-vector interface.
authors: Daichi Hotta, Yohei Kobashi, Takeshi Kojima, Yusuke Iwasawa, Yutaka Matsuo

Adding image prefixes lowers BLiMP accuracy by about 3.8 points in both standard and recurrent architectures.
A matched no-image control suggests that altered language data and batching, rather than visual input alone, drive much of the multimodal drop.
Visual prefixes improve accuracy by 1.85 points on average in the exploratory comparison, but this result is uncertain with three seeds.
Diagnostic tests confirm visual information is used, while its role in grammatical generalization remains unclear with the single-vector interface.

papers.title: Loop Before You Leap: What Recurrent Depth Can and Cannot Buy in Data-Limited Pretraining
papers.tldr: Recurrent depth improves text-only learning under limited data, but does not clearly offset the grammatical-performance cost of multimodal training.

papers.abstract: Knowledge editing has become a key technique for updating knowledge in large language models. However, existing methods neglect the geometric structure of the knowledge representation space, leading to two key limitations: they cannot distinguish which pre-trained knowledge should be preferentially preserved (core vs. non-core) nor which new edits are inherently difficult (hard vs. easy). To address this, we propose GEdit, a geometry-aware framework built on a Low-Rank Plus Diagonal (LR+D) factor model that captures the intrinsic low-rank structure of Transformer FFN hidden representations. GEdit features two complementary mechanisms. First, the low-rank regularization applies targeted protection on a low-rank core knowledge subspace. Second, the adaptive regularization dynamically adjusts the regularization strength based on each edit request's editability: relaxing constraints for hard edits to ensure success, and tightening them for easy edits to better preserve pretrained knowledge. Extensive experiments on GPT2-XL, GPT-J, and LLaMA-3-8B under large-scale editing scenarios, including both mini-batch and fully sequential editing settings with up to 10,000 continuous updates, show that GEdit consistently and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both editing success and knowledge preservation.
authors: Bingqing Liu, Wei Liu, Jun Wang, Xiaobo Sun, Yuhua Li, Ruixuan Li
bullets: Existing editing methods overlook geometric structure, making it difficult to preserve core knowledge and handle hard edits effectively.
GEdit models Transformer FFN representations with a Low-Rank Plus Diagonal factorization.
Low-rank regularization protects a core knowledge subspace, while adaptive regularization varies constraints by editability.
Experiments on GPT2-XL, GPT-J, and LLaMA-3-8B cover mini-batch and sequential editing with up to 10,000 updates.
GEdit consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in editing success and knowledge preservation.

papers.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) excel in high-resource languages, their performance often degrades in low-resource languages due to tokenization inefficiencies, generative instability, and linguistic interference. This paper presents AssameseLM-E2B and its instruction-tuned variant, AssameseLM-E2B-it, a 2-billion-parameter model adapted specifically for low resource Assamese language. Built upon the Gemma-4 architecture, the model incorporates an expanded byte-level BPE vocabulary to reduce tokenization overhead by nearly 500% compared with multilingual 2B--3B baselines. We employ a parameter-efficient Continual Pre-Training (CPT) pipeline with Hybrid LoRA, followed by Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on a balanced, multi-domain dataset to enhance instruction-following and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) capabilities. Evaluation demonstrates a Bits-per-Byte (BPB) score of 0.7488 on FLORES-200, alongside an overall RAG score of 96.7% and 100% refusal accuracy on adversarial unanswerable prompts. Comparative analysis reveals significant limitations in general-purpose baselines, including receptive-productive decoupling, generative degradation on Romanized Assamese, and unintended Bengali script assimilation. These results demonstrate the potential of parameter-efficient adaptation for developing capable, locally deployable language models for low-resource languages under constrained computational resources.
bullets: Targets low-resource Assamese challenges including tokenization inefficiency, unstable generation, and interference from related languages.
Uses an expanded byte-level BPE vocabulary, Hybrid LoRA continual pre-training, and supervised fine-tuning on balanced multi-domain data.
Includes an instruction-tuned variant, AssameseLM-E2B-it, optimized for instruction following and retrieval-augmented generation.
Reports a 0.7488 BPB score on FLORES-200, a 96.7% overall RAG score, and 100% refusal accuracy on adversarial unanswerable prompts.
Scope is Assamese-focused and emphasizes deployment under constrained computational resources.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models send each token through a few of many expert subnetworks. Serving methods make these models faster by running even fewer experts per token, and they are validated on accuracy benchmarks. We show that these methods can weaken the model's refusal of harmful requests, and we introduce SafeStart, which largely restores refusal while keeping most of the speedup. In vLLM on one RTX A6000, keeping about two thirds of the selected experts speeds up offline decoding by 15 to 28% at batch size 8. We find that, at this setting, under a jailbreak that tells the model not to refuse, the share of harmful requests that the model answers rises by 18.4 percentage points on Qwen1.5-MoE, 9.5 on OLMoE, and 6.6 on DeepSeek-V2-Lite, the three of nine models where it rises significantly, while MMLU accuracy drops by less than two points. We discover that most of this increase arises while the model processes the prompt and generates its first few tokens. SafeStart therefore runs all experts for the prompt and the first eight generated tokens, and the reduced set of experts afterwards, through a fused kernel in vLLM. With experts removed, SafeStart keeps at least 85% of the offline decode speedup at batch sizes 8 and 32 and brings the change under this jailbreak to between -2.1 and +1.3 points for three expert-reduction methods on these three models. On 889 held-out requests, in an analysis fixed before generation, truncation raises harmful compliance by 5.8 to 21.4 points, and SafeStart leaves a rise of 0.6 to 2.6 points, non-inferior to the original model on two of the three models. Our results show that faster MoE serving need not cost safety: a serving system can keep most of the gain from running fewer experts by running all of them at the start of each response, and it should test refusal, not only accuracy, before it enables such a method.
authors: Erfan Baghaei Potraghloo, Saeid Shokoufa, Seyedarmin Azizi, Arya Fayyazi, Souvik Kundu, Mehdi Kamal, Massoud Pedram
bullets: Reducing active experts can weaken refusal behavior even when standard accuracy declines only slightly.
The safety degradation mainly occurs during prompt processing and the first few generated tokens.
SafeStart uses all experts initially, then switches to a reduced expert set via a fused vLLM kernel.
On one RTX A6000, retaining about two-thirds of selected experts yields 15–28% faster offline decoding at batch size 8.
SafeStart retains at least 85% of the speedup and limits harmful-compliance increases to 0.6–2.6 points on held-out requests.

papers.title: SafeStart: Mitigating the Overlooked Safety Cost of Active Expert Reduction in MoE LLM Serving

papers.abstract: Small LoRA adapters trained on Tajik news and books lowered Qwen3's Tajik text loss at every size we tried, from 0.6B to 8B, by 0.60 to 1.45 nats per token, but none of them improved Tajik reading comprehension where it can be measured. On Belebele the 1.7B and 8B adapters left accuracy unchanged and the 4B adapter lowered it by 3.7 points; at 0.6B the score rose by 4.2 points but sits near chance and coincides with a change in which answer letter the model prefers, so we do not read it as understanding. At 8B, continued pretraining on about 375 million tokens of raw Tajik text was followed by a Belebele gain of 9.9 points. After a further supervised fine-tuning stage, our main model, e3, is 11.4 points above Qwen3-8B on Belebele; its English MMLU changed by -1.2 points, and a loss larger than 3.3 points is excluded. The same heavy recipe applied to Qwen3-0.6B-Base brought its text loss close to that of the 8B model after books-only pretraining, while its multiple-choice answers stayed near chance and its English MMLU fell by 7.6 points. We report 15 trained models and their 5 starting models from June to October 2025, scored in 2026 on one harness with paired intervals, and we report what went wrong: lost training records, a thinking-mode dataset with almost no reasoning in it, later branches whose training data was never documented, and a 4-bit release that contains no transformer layers.
authors: Tohir Saidzoda, Madina Abdusalomzoda, Nasimjon Rajabov, Akhrorkhon Ikromov, Komron Giyosiev, Abubakr Abdullozoda, Amin Jalilov, Jonibek Kishvarov, Rahmonali Sharipov, Mariyamkhon Shodyeva
bullets: LoRA adaptation reduced Tajik text loss across 0.6B–8B models, but comprehension gains were absent or unreliable.
On Belebele, 1.7B and 8B adapters were unchanged, the 4B model fell 3.7 points, and the 0.6B increase likely reflected answer-letter bias.
At 8B, continued pretraining on roughly 375M raw Tajik tokens improved Belebele by 9.9 points.
The final e3 model improved Tajik Belebele by 11.4 points over Qwen3-8B, while English MMLU declined by 1.2 points.
The study documents scope and reproducibility issues, including undocumented data branches and an invalid 4-bit release.

papers.abstract: When a language model chooses a number between 1 and 30, every integer in the range is valid, yet the model can favor particular answers. We use numerical choice to study how preference is processed across layers and tokens. Perturbation probing and gradient attribution nominate neurons for activation interventions. In a selected Qwen3-4B case, a pre-answer edit changes 17 to 15 while both runs first emit 1. After the edit ends, selective cache and attention-output replacements trace part of its continuing influence on the second digit. Replacing one attention head's output or the other heads' outputs jointly produces similar immediate readout contributions; both interventions restore 17 but have different final log-odds effects on 7 versus 5. Holding later multilayer perceptron (MLP) outputs at their values from the edited run without either replacement reduces this effect gap from 0.119 to 0.0025 nat. Later computation therefore changes how similar local contributions affect the continuation. Retrospective estimates across eighteen contexts capture much of the probability movement but miss the selected answer switch. Prompt tests also separate influence from answer changes: one held-out prompt retains influence without switching, and only one of twelve fresh wordings qualifies for the reader/MLP test; there, joint MLP clamping again reduces the gap between the two reader effects while the answer remains 17. These results use numerical choice as a controlled case for studying persistent state and conditional downstream processing; they do not establish the origin or a complete circuit of natural numerical preference.
bullets: Uses choices between 1 and 30 as a controlled setting where every answer is valid.
Combines perturbation probing, gradient attribution, activation edits, and selective cache/attention-output replacements.
In a Qwen3-4B case, an intervention changes the final answer from 17 to 15 even though both runs initially emit 1.
Similar local attention contributions can lead to different final effects because later MLP computation alters their influence.
Results across additional contexts show persistent influence does not always cause an answer switch; the study does not establish the origin or full circuit of numerical preference.

papers.selection_reason: Causal intervention study of numerical preference in a Qwen3 LLM; relevant to LLM internal mechanisms.
papers.title: When Every Choice Is Correct: A Causal Study of Numerical Preference in Language Models
papers.tldr: A causal study of numerical choices shows that answer preferences can persist across tokens and be reshaped by later computation, without identifying a complete underlying circuit.

papers.abstract: Generative models trained on the output of earlier models lose knowledge across generations, rare knowledge first. The remedies that work all bring in information from outside the loop, and the theory of model collapse treats that supply as given: a fixed archive, drawn from a fixed distribution. We argue that the supply is the problem, and that cultural evolution has the theory of it. We read model collapse as Rogers' paradox: a population that comes to rely on copying ends up no better off than one that never copied, because copies go stale unless someone keeps learning for themselves. We test the identification in three steps. First, Rogers' model, fitted only to fully synthetic training, predicts to within a few percentage points how much rare knowledge language models, from word trigrams to a pretrained transformer, retain under other mixtures of fresh data. Second, when the world itself changes, a lineage that copies its own past needs more fresh data to keep up the faster the world changes, as Rogers' model says it must and as analyses that assume a fixed target cannot; a lineage that restarts every generation from fixed pretrained weights is largely insulated, because those weights are knowledge that is never copied. Third, we close the loop: when the people who write a model's training data can ask the model instead of finding things out, the supply of fresh data becomes endogenous. At equilibrium, the model is exactly as reliable as it is costly for people to find out for themselves, the population is no better off than without the model, and every increase in the share of model-written text must be paid for by more people learning for themselves. Users who check what they are told and relearn when it is wrong break the paradox. Filters that select plausible text are conformist and accelerate collapse; only checks that carry new information act as critical learning.
bullets: Synthetic training causes knowledge loss across generations, with rare knowledge disappearing first.
A cultural-evolution model predicts retention under mixtures of synthetic and fresh data, from simple language models to pretrained transformers.
As the world changes faster, self-copying lineages require more fresh data; fixed pretrained knowledge is comparatively insulated.
When models influence what people write, fresh-data supply becomes endogenous: greater reliance on model text requires more independent learning.
Plausibility filters worsen collapse, whereas fact-checking and relearning can preserve new information.

papers.selection_reason: Applies cultural evolution theory (Rogers' paradox) to explain and predict model collapse in LLMs, analyzing the endogeneity of training data supply.
papers.title: Who Pays for the Knowledge Models Copy? Model Collapse as Rogers' Paradox
papers.tldr: Model collapse is a version of Rogers’ paradox: copying model outputs saves effort but erodes rare and current knowledge unless people keep generating and checking fresh information.

papers.abstract: Hyper-Connections (HC) architectures are increasingly adopted in frontier language models, yet their components remain insufficiently understood and introduce non-negligible training overhead. In this work, we systematically study the HC architecture to understand its components and identify simpler, more efficient designs. We find that learned read/write gating without mixing and unconstrained mixing with fixed gates form two effective interaction groups: either alone achieves performance comparable to mHC. We also identify repeated access to the expanded residual state as a major source of training overhead, even without mixing. These findings lead to SimpleHC, which simplifies the architecture by removing residual mixing and simplifies execution through shared memory access, using the resulting additive structure and shared gate inputs. Layer-specific gates share a group-entry state, enabling batched reads and deferred writes; scalar corrections exactly preserve preceding sublayer output contributions. Our analyses support both the retained residual structure and the design of shared memory access. SimpleHC incurs only 2.4% extra end-to-end training time over a vanilla residual baseline at the largest tested scale. It maintains performance comparable to mHC when scaling from 15B to 30B MoE models, exhibits smoother gradient dynamics during standard training, and remains stable under stress. We hope SimpleHC will encourage a broader pursuit of simplicity in foundation model design, making performance gains more accessible and practical at scale.
authors: Xiangdong Zhang, Xiaohan Qin, Sunan Zou, Tuo Dai, Bizhao Shi, Zhuo Xia, Yebin Yang, Yizhou Chen, Yuliang Liu, Yu Cheng, Junchi Yan
bullets: Hyper-Connections improve language-model architectures but contain poorly understood components and costly repeated access to expanded residual states.
Learned read/write gating without mixing and unconstrained mixing with fixed gates are separately effective interaction designs.
SimpleHC removes residual mixing and uses shared memory access, shared gate inputs, and deferred writes for more efficient execution.
It adds only 2.4% end-to-end training time over a vanilla residual baseline at the largest tested scale.
SimpleHC matches mHC performance from 15B to 30B MoE models, with smoother gradients and stability under stress.

papers.abstract: Expert deactivation at inference time changes both token routing and expert weights, and its effect on performance depends on how these changes are implemented. We compare removal, freezing, remaining-expert renormalization, and unnormalized re-routing on identical disabled sets across five instruction-tuned checkpoints from four model families, with a base OLMoE checkpoint as an additional comparison. We develop a weight-sum model that relates the loss of expert contributions and changes in branch scale to the weight rule used during training. With half of the experts deactivated according to activation-based rankings, remaining-expert renormalization yields the highest perplexity in models trained with raw router probabilities, whereas unnormalized re-routing yields the highest perplexity in models trained with normalized weights. Perplexity ranges from 1.4 to 73 times the intact baseline when the training rule is retained, and from 14 to 28,740 times the baseline under a rule mismatch. Task outcomes vary across evaluation types: on OLMoE, GSM8K strict-match accuracy falls to zero under all four implementations. Extending the model to changes in the number of active experts yields a further prediction, supported by the OLMoE experiments: the perplexity penalty from additional renormalization increases as fewer experts are activated.
authors: Hao Cheng (Zhejiang Gongshang University), Zhiyu Yang (Chang'an University), Bo Ma (Zhejiang Gongshang University), Hanzhang Jia (University of Sussex)
bullets: The study compares removal, freezing, renormalized re-routing, and unnormalized re-routing on identical disabled experts across multiple checkpoints.
A weight-sum model explains how lost expert contributions and branch-scale changes depend on the training-time weight rule.

With half the experts disabled, renormalization performs worst for models trained with raw router probabilities, while unnormalized re-routing performs worst for models trained with normalized weights.
Perplexity penalties are much larger under rule mismatch, ranging from 14–28,740× the intact baseline versus 1.4–73× when the rule is retained.
On OLMoE, GSM8K strict-match accuracy drops to zero for all tested implementations; additional renormalization is increasingly harmful with fewer active experts.
