papers.selection_reason: Analysis of inference-time expert deactivation and weight rules in mixture-of-experts LLMs.
papers.title: Matching the Training-Time Weight Rule in Inference-Time Expert Deactivation
papers.tldr: Inference-time expert deactivation is most reliable when its routing-weight rule matches the rule used during training.

papers.abstract: Under expert parallelism, mixture-of-experts (MoE) layers pay all-to-all token dispatch, grouped GEMMs, and a combine step in every layer. In decode each rank holds only 1-256 tokens: dispatch latency and weight traffic dominate while tensor-core utilization is inherently low. In fused operators such as DeepGEMM's Mega MoE, dispatch and computation overlap only by sharing every SM: dispatch warps compete with TMA/MMA and epilogue warps for registers, shared memory, and issue slots; every phase shares one CTA resource budget, synchronization spans the whole SM array, and every replay ends with a workspace-clean pass and a cross-rank barrier. We present GC-MoE, an open-source FP8/FP4 MoE inference operator for NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell GPUs that uses CUDA Green Contexts to split the device into a small communication partition and a large compute partition. Each role gets its own kernel, resource budget, and synchronization domain, so dispatch and GEMM tune independently. A three-node CUDA Graph (four on Hopper with fused shared experts) launches the dispatch and grouped-GEMM kernels as concurrent roots; a token-ring handshake starts computation on the first filled ring blocks, and double-buffered receive counters remove the trailing cross-rank barrier between replays. The compute partition runs operand-swapped tcgen05 block-scaled MMA on Blackwell and register-A WGMMA with in-register FP4 decoding on Hopper, with fused SwiGLU, requantization, and optional shared experts. On 8 H20 GPUs GC-MoE accelerates DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash decode by 1.188x on average on both the routed and shared-expert suites (peaks 1.296x and 1.353x); on 8 B300 GPUs it accelerates GLM-5.2 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash by 1.106x (1.123x with fused shared experts, peak 1.209x), beating Mega MoE at all 54 measured points at matched accuracy. GC-MoE reserves only 20 of 148 SMs on B300 for dispatch.
authors: Yong Li, Kan Liu, Tao Lan
bullets: Targets decode-time MoE bottlenecks where all-to-all dispatch and weight traffic dominate and tensor-core utilization is low.
Uses CUDA Green Contexts to assign dispatch and grouped GEMM separate SM partitions, resource budgets, kernels, and synchronization domains.
Overlaps work through CUDA Graph roots, token-ring handshaking, and double-buffered receive counters that eliminate trailing cross-rank barriers.
Supports FP8/FP4 inference on Hopper and Blackwell, with fused SwiGLU, requantization, and optional shared experts.
Reports 1.188× average speedup on 8 H20s and 1.106× on 8 B300s, outperforming Mega MoE at all 54 matched-accuracy test points.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Architecture of one GC-MoE layer replay. The child CUDA Graph holds three nodes: role1 (dispatch) and role2 (grouped GEMM) have no dependency edge and are concurrent roots, whereas role3 (finalize/combine) depends on both (solid arrows). Dashed arrows map each role to the green context that launches it—role1 to the 20-SM communication context, role2 and role3 to the 128-SM compute context—each with its own balanced workqueue so that the driver co-schedules them on disjoint SM sets. All cross-rank state lives in one symmetric-memory workspace whose boxes name the buffers exchanged over NVLink (double arrows): activations and scales, routing metadata, the role1→role2 token ring, the role2→role3 combine buffer, and the counters and parity signals. Every synchronization object is device-persistent and replay-aware, so a replay needs no host-side reset.

Figure 1: Execution timelines. (a) On B300 the baseline is DeepGEMM’s Mega MoE, one persistent fused kernel on all 148 SMs: after routing counts and a tag-1 cross-rank barrier, the dispatch warps stream tokens, scales, and routing metadata into a per-block token ring while the GEMM consumes each ring block as soon as it is full. The phases overlap, but on the same SMs, with the dispatch warps and their staging buffers carved out of every SM’s register file and shared memory; the tail is max(Tcombine, tclean + ttag2)—the workspace clean overlaps the combine, but the tag-2 barrier is still a cross-rank round trip on every replay. (b) GC-MoE runs role1 (dispatch) on the 20-SM communication context and role2 (grouped GEMM) plus role3 (combine) on the 128-SM compute context. Each role is an ordinary kernel with its own register, shared-memory, and synchronization budget, so the dispatch and GEMM paths can be optimized independently. papers.abstract: We introduce Dory1.0-4B, a 4-billion-parameter looped (latent-recurrent) language model with elastic depth: a single checkpoint serves different inference compute budgets. Dory1.0-4B is built on a normalized Transformer (nGPT) backbone with interleaved sliding-window and full-attention layers, organized into an input block, a shared recurrent block, and an output block. At inference, the recurrent block can be applied a variable number of times. We pre-trained Dory1.0-4B on 6 trillion tokens. The first 4.5 trillion tokens were trained in NVFP4, and additional pre-training then extended the context length to 256K tokens. Next, we post-trained the model using Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), with a difficulty-aware loop curriculum that routes harder prompts to deeper loops. Increasing the loop count improves accuracy, with the largest gains on coding, agentic, and long-context benchmarks. With two or more loops, Dory1.0-4B outperforms larger models such as Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma 4 12B, and Gemma 4 26B-A4B on average across 12 benchmarks. Looping also makes Dory1.0-4B more token-efficient on agentic benchmarks: with four loops, it generates 1.3-2.5x fewer tokens than with one loop, as the extra computation is spent in latent space rather than on longer outputs. To reduce memory during looping, Dory1.0-4B caches keys and values only from the last loop, keeping its KV-cache footprint equal to that of a non-looped model at any loop count while retaining most of the accuracy gains. We open-source the BF16, MXFP8, NVFP4, and GGUF quantized checkpoints.
bullets: Uses a normalized Transformer with interleaved sliding-window and full-attention layers, divided into input, recurrent, and output blocks.
Variable loop counts provide elastic inference compute, with harder prompts routed to deeper loops during post-training.
More loops yield the largest accuracy gains on coding, agentic, and long-context benchmarks.
With at least two loops, it outperforms several larger models across 12 benchmarks, according to the abstract.
Caching only the final loop’s keys and values keeps KV-cache memory comparable to a non-looped model; quantized checkpoints are released.

figures.caption: Figure 3 | Overview of the post-training pipeline for Dory1.0-4B. The base context window is 262,144 tokens (256K). SFT trains on packed sequences of 262,144 tokens, and samples loop counts for each microbatch randomly, while RLVR routes harder prompts to deeper loops with higher probability.

Figure 2 | Dory1.0-4B’s looped nGPT architecture. A 16-layer input block produces a fixed representation 𝑢. A 40-layer recurrent block refines the state over 𝑘 passes (up to four), sharing all of its weights and learned scales across each loop. Each loop adds 𝑢 to the current state, initialized as 𝑠0 = 𝑢, and applies L2 normalization before and after the recurrent block. A 16-layer output block processes the final state before the LM head. Within each block, an eight-layer pattern contains three SWA–SwiGLU pairs followed by one full-attention–SwiGLU pair, giving a 3:1 ratio of sliding-window attention (SWA) to full attention. SWA uses a window of 𝑊 =1024 tokens with RoPE base 𝜃S = 104; full attention uses 𝜃F = 107. RoPE acts on all Q/K dimensions. Each sublayer updates the residual stream by blending its normalized output with the normalized residual using learned per-channel weights, then normalizing the result.
Figure 5 | Loop-curriculum ablation with an early SFT checkpoint.

Figure 1 | Accuracy and token efficiency of Dory1.0-4B across inference loop counts 𝑘. (a) An equal-weight average of 12 benchmarks: SciCode, SWE-Bench Verified, Terminal-Bench v2.1, 𝜏3- Banking, GDPval-AA v2, GPQA Diamond, Humanity’s Last Exam (HLE), IFBench, AA-LCR, GDP.pdf, and AA-Omniscience accuracy and non-hallucination, with GDPval-AA v2 Elo normalized as (Elo − 500)/20. (b) Reduction in the number of output tokens needed to solve agentic tasks as the number of loops increases.

Figure 4 | Illustration of difficulty-aware loop routing at 𝛼 = 0.3. A generic distribution of loop-1 pass rates supplies the within-batch midpoint quantiles 𝑞𝑖, which are combined with uniform sampling 𝑢𝑖. After sorting the resulting scores, lower scores fill deeper loop slots first. The output histogram preserves the input prompt counts and shows the assigned loop counts within each difficulty bin: darker segments denote more loop counts.

Figure 6 | Self-speculative decode throughput relative to autoregressive 𝑘 = 4, using 𝑘 = 1 drafting, 𝑘 = 4 verification, and four draft tokens. Curves compare KV reuse with and without activation reuse. Throughput is measured over output positions 128–896 of 1,024-token generations. Points show geometric means across three repeat blocks and error bars show block ranges.

Table 2 | Evaluation results for Dory1.0-4B across inference loop counts. All scores are percentages except GDPval-AA v2, which is reported in Elo. GDPval-AA v2 is normalized as (Elo − 500)/20 for unweighted average score over 12 benchmarks. Results are measured by NVIDIA using NeMo Gym / NeMo Evaluator, except †, which denotes a self-reported score. Terminal-Bench v2.1 uses the Terminus-2 harness for all models. SciCode reports pooled subtask accuracy; IFBench (Pyatkin et al., 2025) reports mean constraint satisfaction under strict checking. GDP.pdf uses text-only inputs and reports the all-pass rate averaged over five repeats per task for Dory1.0-4B.

Table 1 | Base-model evaluation results for Dory1.0-4B Base at fixed inference loop counts. All scores are percentages, rounded to two decimal places; higher is better. EM denotes the task’s exact-match metric, and acc_norm denotes length-normalized multiple-choice accuracy. For code tasks, 𝑛 is the number of sampled completions per problem used to estimate pass@1. MATH-500 uses one greedy completion, not sampled pass@1. †RACE-H uses the last-question-per-passage protocol described below. As performance tends to saturate after four loops, we restrict post-training results to at most four loops.

Table 4 | Evaluation results for Dory1.0-4B in BF16 and its weight-only quantized variants: MXFP8-PTQ, NVFP4-QAD, and Q5_K_M-QAD, at one, two, and four inference loops. We report a subset of the benchmarks in Table 2, using the same metrics.

Table 6 | Dory1.0-4B with per-loop and last-loop KV caches. Scores are percentages and 𝑛 is the number of repeats per task. Δ Score is last-loop minus per-loop at 𝑘 = 4, computed before rounding. Output Tokens is the ratio of mean output tokens per rollout, last-loop to per-loop, at 𝑘 = 4, including reasoning and all agent turns or sub-steps and excluding judge and user-simulator tokens.

Table 7 | Self-speculative decoding speedups for Dory1.0-4B, using 𝑘 = 1 drafting, 𝑘 = 4 verification, 𝛾 = 4 draft tokens, and shared KV caches and activations. The baseline uses autoregressive decoding at 𝑘 = 4. Speedup is the ratio of baseline to speculative mean model-request duration, including prefill and decode and excluding initialization, initial queueing, tool execution, and evaluator processing.

Table 3 | Token efficiency of Dory1.0-4B across inference loop counts 𝑘 on agentic benchmarks. Going from 𝑘 = 1 to 𝑘 = 4 reduces output tokens per attempt by 1.3–2.5× (Figure 1b).

papers.title: Dory1.0-4B: A Looped Normalized-GPT

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training of language models keeps fp32 master weights in the optimizer and serves rollouts from a bf16 copy produced by round-to-nearest conversion. At the learning rates in common use, most per-step updates are smaller than half a bf16 spacing and the conversion discards them: on Qwen3-1.7B only 0.4-0.5% of served weights change per step, and the policy that generates the training data lags the optimizer by 50-150 steps. Existing mismatch corrections cannot see this lag because they compare two copies downstream of the same rounding. We propose Fair Cast: export the master with an unbiased rounding rule (stochastic rounding or error feedback) and compute the training loss on the served copy. The change is one line at the export call, adds no hyperparameters and costs 22-38 ms per export of 1.7B parameters. Across 25 matched seed-pairs on Qwen3-0.6B to 4B with AdamW and Muon, Fair Cast is ahead on 18, tied on 6 and behind on 1, with a mean gain of 6.1 points; on zebra puzzles it reaches 0.57 +/- 0.16 over four runs where round-to-nearest collapses to 0.33 +/- 0.10. It also makes the saved fp32 checkpoint agree with the served model, and it exposes the implicit lag of round-to-nearest as a regularizer that can be restored explicitly when a task needs it.
bullets: In common RL post-training, only 0.4–0.5% of served Qwen3-1.7B weights change per step, creating a 50–150-step policy lag.
Existing mismatch corrections miss this lag because they compare copies affected by the same rounding.
Fair Cast applies stochastic rounding or error feedback when exporting weights and computes loss on the served copy.
Across 25 matched seed-pairs, it was ahead in 18, tied in 6, and behind in 1, with a mean gain of 6.1 points.
The method adds no hyperparameters but costs 22–38 ms per 1.7B-parameter export; round-to-nearest’s lag may still be useful as an explicit regularizer.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses a training-inference mismatch in RL post-training of language models, a meaningful methodological contribution to LLM training.
papers.title: bf16 Rounding Silently Discards Most RL Policy Updates: A Hidden Training-Inference Mismatch and an Unbiased One-Line Fix
papers.tldr: bf16 round-to-nearest silently drops most RL policy updates, while Fair Cast uses unbiased rounding to align training with the served model and improves results.

papers.abstract: We investigate whether open-source LLMs encode a linearly separable truthfulness signal in their hidden states, and at which network depth this signal is strongest. Across three $7$B--$8$B instruction-tuned models (Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, Qwen2.5-7B) loaded in $4$-bit NF4 quantization, we extract per-layer hidden states on four hallucination benchmarks (TruthfulQA, HaluEval-QA, FEVER, and a controlled synthetic set) and compare four detection approaches: linear and MLP probes, INSIDE EigenScore, self-consistency, and attention entropy. A linear probe on a single mid-network layer achieves $0.904$--$1.000$ AUROC on held-out splits, while sampling-based detectors do not exceed $0.541$ AUROC under the same protocol. The truthfulness signal is approximately linear: MLP probes rarely surpass linear probes by more than $0.01$ AUROC. Peak probing layers fall in a consistent band across model families on natural-language benchmarks -- blocks~$13$--$18$ of~$32$ for Llama and Mistral, and blocks~$19$--$25$ of~$28$ for Qwen. First-block attention entropy provides a complementary signal in knowledge-grounded settings ($0.866$--$0.941$ AUROC on HaluEval-QA) at no additional inference cost. The low discriminability of sampling methods under this protocol reflects a structural mismatch between paired-label evaluation and the information these methods access, rather than an inherent limitation of those methods. Code and data are released for full reproducibility on a single $8$\,GB GPU.
bullets: Evaluated three 7B–8B instruction-tuned models across four hallucination benchmarks using hidden-state probes and sampling-based detectors.
A linear probe from one mid-network layer reached 0.904–1.000 AUROC on held-out splits.
MLP probes rarely improved over linear probes by more than 0.01 AUROC, supporting approximate linear separability.
Strongest layers formed consistent mid-network bands across model families; first-block attention entropy also helped on knowledge-grounded data.
The study releases code and data and demonstrates reproducibility on a single 8 GB GPU.

papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) lets a pretrained language model perform a task specified by demonstrations in its prompt, with no parameter updates. With arbitrary labels the model must acquire a mapping it cannot have memorized, so the learning happens within a single forward pass. Prior work found candidate parts but not how they compose. We give the composition for few-shot sentence classification with arbitrary labels in three 3-4B-parameter transformers. The model implements a key-value memory over label-token positions: each label token's residual stream encodes the label's identity, and middle-layer attention heads write into it the class of the preceding demonstration as its key. At the query, upper-layer heads match the query's class against the stored keys and copy out the matching labels. An early-layer signal encoding whether any label has repeated gates this readout; in its absence the readers attend to the start of the prompt and no label is favored. A separate set of heads suppresses the most recently seen label. Each step is established causally by activation patching, head ablations against random-head baselines, and steering with the model's own signals. A softmax model of the readout with two constants per head, fit on one prompt distribution, predicts another. The computation is conserved across the three models, the named heads alone reproduce the behaviour, and a transformer trained from scratch grows the same parts. The circuit transfers to semantic concepts and to labels with meaning, and the same parts, with a causal gate, appear from 0.6B to 8B in one family and survive instruction tuning. ICL in this setting is a gated associative lookup built from a few identifiable component types, traced causally from demonstrations to prediction.
bullets: Middle-layer attention heads write each demonstration’s class into label-token representations as keys.
At the query, upper-layer heads match the query class to stored keys and copy the corresponding label.
An early-layer repetition signal gates the readout, while other heads suppress the most recently seen label.
Causal interventions support each circuit step, and the same computation appears across model sizes, training setups, and related label semantics.
The circuit transfers to semantic concepts and meaningful labels and persists after instruction tuning.

figures.caption: Figure 6: The slot holds a value and a key on different sides of attention. (a) Exchanging the labels: in all three models the effect runs through the values at the label tokens. (b) Changing a sentence while keeping its label: the effect runs through the keys at the label tokens, and only in the middle layers. (c) Handoffs from a same-class sentence of the same length move the answer by at most 0.06 nats. Bars are paired effects on the margin with 95% bootstrap intervals; grey bars are size-matched random controls.

Figure 4: The four main interventions, each drawn on the end of a 12-shot prompt. The red component is replaced or steered, and the output is read at END. (a) Sentence swap: the keys at a label token come from the twin in which that demonstration’s sentence belongs to the other class, so the slot’s key no longer matches its value. (b) Label swap: the values at the label token come from the twin with the labels exchanged. (c) Gate steering: the model’s own gate direction g is added at END at its natural magnitude, before the reader layers, and we measure the readers’ attention to the sink and to the matching slots. (d) Query-code handoff: the outputs of the two query heads at END come from the twin whose query is of the other class; later attention outputs can be held fixed to test whether the effect passes through them.

Figure 1: One twelve-demonstration prompt, stage by stage. Columns are tokens (sentences si, arrows, labels and the query q) and rows are layers of Qwen3-4B. Each coloured block marks the tokens and layers where a stage acts: the duplicate detectors and the encoder early on, the writers into the label tokens in the middle layers, and then, at the query arrow, the query code, the gate, the readers, the brakes and the readout band. Later sections give the intervention behind each block.

Figure 2: The circuit for few-shot in-context learning in Qwen3-4B-Base. Prompt tokens run down the left (sentences Si, labels Li, the query Q and its arrow END). Boxes are classes of attention heads, with layer.head numbers beneath. Writer heads give each label token a key (the class of its sentence) alongside its value (the label). At END, reader heads match the query’s class against those keys and copy the matching labels, copier heads write the logits, and brake heads write against the most recent label. The gate g, assembled by the pooling heads, opens the read by lowering the readers’ attention-sink logit (dashed). Sections 3–8 give the intervention behind each arrow.

Figure 3: The same circuit laid out along the layers of Qwen3-4B-Base. The top lane shows what happens at the label tokens: duplicate-token heads mark a repeated label, and writers deposit the sentence’s class into the label’s residual stream, which makes it a slot with a value and a key. The bottom lane shows what happens at the query arrow: the encoder computes the query’s class, the pooled repeat signal g lowers the readers’ sink logit, the readers match the query’s class against the slot keys and copy the matching values, and the readout band and late MLPs write the logits while the brakes write against the last label.

Figure 5: Anatomy of a slot. The residual stream at a label token holds two things, which are read through two different matrices. The label’s identity comes from the token’s own embedding and the early layers, and is read by the readers’ WV . The class of the preceding sentence is written in by middle-layer heads that attend back to the sentence, and is read by the readers’ WK as the key that the query’s class is matched against.

Figure 9: Within a regime the read follows a softmax law, and the law transfers to fewer slots per class but not to longer prompts. Each point is one head at one slot count, showing the measured matchingslot mass against the prediction of Equation 1 from twelve-demonstration constants. (a) Qwen, in the fitted regime. (b) Qwen and Llama, one slot per class (held out). (c) Qwen and Llama, eighteen demonstrations (held out; the prediction fails). Sharp readers sit on the line and diffuse heads fall below it.

Figure 10: The gate lowers the null logit and moves matching far less. (a) Projection of the arrow residual onto g for prompts with repeated and with unique labels, intact and with the sixteen duplicatetoken heads ablated, with random and induction-scored sets as controls. (b) Change in each reader’s sink-minus-match logit when g is added at natural and double dose; same-norm random directions in grey. (c) Change in the same readers’ match-minus-other logit.

Figure 12: Two heads write a query code that the reader population consumes. (a) Share of the query-flip effect carried by the pair L22h10+L23h26 and by all attention in layers 21–29, and what remains when downstream attention queries are held at their intact values. (b) Energy of the pair’s write in the span of the readers’ match functionals, against random subspaces of the same dimension.

Figure 13: No single head carries the answer. Each cell is the effect on the 12-shot class margin of knocking out one head at the query position (mean over 144 prompts from six label families; blue lowers the margin and red raises it; colour clipped at ±0.15 nats), for every head in the reader layers of Qwen3-4B-Base (layers 21–35) and Llama-3.2-3B (layers 16–27). Outlined cells are the five most negative and five most positive heads. The largest single-head effects are −0.14 nats (Qwen L23h26, a query head) and +0.13 (Qwen L31h30, a brake), and −0.09 and +0.12 in Llama (L18h10, L19h1), against a 1.3-nat margin. The sets built from these rankings move the margin by −0.74 and +1.39 in Qwen and by −0.56 and +1.90 in Llama when knocked out together (Table 6).

Figure 14: Readers and brakes act as populations with opposite signs. (a) Joint knockout of 20 readers, of 24 brakes, and of both, on a fresh draw, against size-matched random sets (grey). (b) Order effect: the margin against the position of the last matching demonstration, intact and with the brakes knocked out.

Figure 20: Qwen3-4B base (a) and instruct (b) on the word-label prompts, with the base model’s 189 heads in both. Blue is the part of the margin that follows the demonstrations (R), and orange the part that follows the words’ meaning (P ); the band is the intact R interval. Post-training multiplies both parts by about 2.5 and keeps their ratio. The 189 heads alone, with a resampled reference, keep 79% of R in the instruct model, and a random set of the same size keeps none.

Figure 15: Every nat of the answer assigned to a component. (a) Direct contributions to the margin by layer band, intact and under the class flip, in Qwen and SmolLM3. (b) Cumulative share of the flip against the number of heads, sorted by contribution.

Figure 16: The answer as a sum of bands. Left: the intact twelve-demonstration margin in Qwen, built up band by band; the copier band of layers 30–35 writes almost all of it. Right: the change under the exact class flip. The copier band carries most of the swing and the readers a quarter, and the late MLPs push the other way.

Figure 7: Three key–value groups carry half of the label’s value. Patching the values of all 72 KV groups of layers 21–29 at the label tokens, from a prompt with the labels exchanged, carries 86% of the exchange’s effect on the margin (left). By layer, the effect sits in layers 22, 24 and 29 (right, grey), and within each of these layers one KV group carries most of it (red). Group 24.5 alone carries a quarter, and groups 24.5, 29.2 and 22.5 together carry about half. Random head sets of the same size move the margin by 0.03 or less (dotted). Qwen3-4B, 12-shot invented-label prompts, 72 prompts.

Figure 8: The key is written in the middle layers, and the write has to be spread out. (a) In Llama3.2-3B, patching the label-token keys and values from the sentence-exchanged prompt one layer band at a time: the two middle bands carry the effect, and the first and last carry almost none. (b) In SmolLM3, adding a fixed total dose of the class direction u to the label tokens at one layer helps less than spreading it over four layers, and falls back at double dose while the spread write keeps climbing (95% intervals; 144 prompts).

(c) In Llama, knocking out the sixteen heads that a generic induction score selects moves the middle-layer readers’ attention out of the sink and onto the slots, so in Llama the induction-scored heads hold the read closed.

Figure 11: What a reader looks at. Attention from the query arrow to the first position (the sink) and to the four label slots, for three Qwen3-4B readers, averaged over 30 four-demonstration prompts. Bottom row: four distinct labels, none repeated; L29h11 puts 0.91 of its attention on the sink and reads nothing.

(b) Reader and brake populations: the summed effect of the heads whose single removal at the query lowers (blue) or raises (red) the margin with an interval that excludes zero; the number is the head count. (c) The brakes’ summed hold on word meaning (bars, left axis) against the flipped-label margin (line, right axis). The two rise together.

Figure 22: Token observatory for one 12-shot prompt (symbol labels, answer foo) in Qwen3-4B. (a) Summed head write norm at every layer and position (log scale); white lines mark the label slots, and cyan marks the query arrow. (b) At the query arrow, the residual’s projection onto the gate direction g (green) and onto the repeat-flag direction Ul (blue) by layer, intact (solid) and with every unnamed head mean-ablated at the arrow (dashed). (c) Attention of the three heads that write most at the arrow in each layer, split by what they read.

Figure 21: The circuit assembles in order during training. Across OLMo-2 stage-1 checkpoints (grey: 1B; black: 7B), copying a repeated label is present from the earliest checkpoint. The null action, measured as withholding a label on unique-label prompts, appears in 1B between 315B and 839B tokens and is already present at 42B in 7B. Class-keyed retrieval, measured as a positive margin on unique-label prompts, arrives last, by 630B tokens in 7B and never in 1B. Thirty prompts per point.

Figure 18: Closing the circuit on natural labels. For each model, the part of the margin that follows the demonstrations (R, blue) and the part that follows what the label words mean (P , orange), intact and with only the named heads kept at the query (final sets of 189, 122 and 163 heads, with the late MLPs). The reference is the mean over same-kind prompts or a resampled same-kind prompt. The controls are a random set of the same size and layers, and no heads. Bars are means over 96 natural/flipped prompt pairs; whiskers are 95% bootstrap intervals.

Named: a small set of heads is necessary and sufficient. Population: no single head is necessary, and the link is characterized by a direction with a size-matched random control. –: not run.
Table 1: Terms used throughout the paper.

papers.selection_reason: Mechanistic circuit analysis of in-context learning in transformer language models, relevant to LLM behavior and architecture understanding.
papers.title: A Circuit for In-Context Learning
papers.tldr: The paper identifies a causal transformer circuit that performs arbitrary-label in-context classification as a gated associative lookup over demonstration examples.

papers.abstract: An LLM assistant that cannot see official severe-weather alerts may tell users that conditions are calm while a warning is active. We call this false reassurance and measure it by replaying 117 frozen cases built from real U.S. National Weather Service (NWS) alerts (69 alert cases, 32 no-alert controls, 16 non-U.S. locations) through five conditions of a Claude-based preparedness pipeline that differ in alert access and prompt design. One rater hand-labeled all 342 alert-case responses under a seven-category scheme written after an initial binary pass, which we disclose. False reassurance was 0.0% for the production pipeline (0/66, 95% CI 0.0-5.5) and for the same alerts under a neutral prompt (0/69), 37.7% for a blind neutral prompt (26/69), and 44.9% when the blind prompt also told the model to disclose its blind spot (31/69). Every case was implicit; no response explicitly denied an alert. Real alerts removed false reassurance (paired McNemar p < 0.0001); the disclosure instruction did not (p = 0.40). An automated regex measure suggested the opposite and missed 53 of 57 true cases, so we do not use it. Alert data alone was not enough for safe behavior: with a neutral prompt the model raised some alarm on 87.5% of no-alert controls, against 0% under the production prompt, and a preregistered single-sentence ablation showed that one production instruction explains part of that gap. We also report two failures common to similar systems, NWS test products ingested as real alerts and a token budget that fails on complex cases, and we release the dataset, labels and code.
bullets: Evaluates 117 replayed cases from real NWS alerts across five alert-access and prompt conditions.
False reassurance occurred in 37.7% of blind neutral-prompt cases and 44.9% when the model was told to disclose its blind spot.
Providing real alert data reduced false reassurance to 0%; disclosure instructions alone did not.
Prompting affected calibration: a neutral prompt alarmed on 87.5% of no-alert controls, versus 0% for the production prompt.
Regex detection missed most true cases; the authors release the dataset, labels, and code and identify test-alert ingestion and token limits as additional failure modes.

figures.caption: Table 2. Main results by condition. Percentages with 95% Wilson confidence intervals where available.
Table 1. Alert cases by hazard family and NWS severity.

Table 3. Category assigned by hand to every alert-case response, by condition (counts). No response was coded as explicitly denying that an alert existed, so the implicit column is all of the false reassurance. Downplaying and wrong-hazard responses are not counted as false reassurance.

papers.title: False Reassurance in LLM Severe-Weather Guidance: A Replayable Evaluation Against Real NWS Alerts
papers.tldr: LLM weather guidance can falsely reassure users during active severe-weather warnings unless it has access to real NWS alerts and suitable prompt safeguards.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning a large language model (LLM) on harmful data in a narrow domain, such as bad medical advice, can make it broadly misaligned. How realistic this risk is remains unclear, since models are very rarely fine-tuned on explicitly harmful data in practice. In this work, we show that fine-tuning on data the model believes to be false but that has no harmful content, can also induce broad misalignment. Across mathematics, trivia, cooking and sports, the more strongly the model disbelieves the answers it is trained on, the more misaligned it becomes. In mathematics, misaligned answers rise from 4% to over 60% as the training answers become more wrong, with little loss of general capability. After fine-tuning, the model states the wrong answers but its multiple-choice probabilities still prefer the true ones, which suggests that misalignment comes from this internal inconsistency. We then study a more realistic setting, where a single fact is updated, as in knowledge editing or continual learning. The same relationship holds and the more the model still believes the true fact after training on the false one, the more misaligned it becomes. When we frame the same false fact as part of a coherent story, the model comes to believe it more deeply and becomes less misaligned than when we instruct it to assert the false fact. Content filters and persona vectors cannot tell these two framings apart, even though they lead to different levels of misalignment. These results suggest a risk for model updates, where training a model that does not adopt the new fact as true can induce misalignment even when the data looks harmless.
authors: Ariana M. Villegas-Suarez, Guido Freire, Sohan Venkatesh, Bartosz Cywi\'nski
bullets: Across math, trivia, cooking, and sports, stronger disagreement with training answers led to greater misalignment.
In mathematics, misaligned responses increased from 4% to over 60% as trained answers became more incorrect, with little general-capability loss.
Models often stated false answers while their internal multiple-choice probabilities still favored the truth, linking misalignment to internal inconsistency.
The effect also appeared when updating a single fact, suggesting risks for knowledge editing and continual learning.
Presenting false facts in coherent stories reduced misalignment compared with directly instructing the model to assert them; common filters and persona vectors did not distinguish the framings.

figures.caption: Figure 6: We fine-tune on three datasets for each fact. Each fact has a true control (1), the instructed-false dataset (2), which tells the model to assert the false fact and never acknowledge that it is false and the immersive-false dataset (3), which describes a world where the false fact is true. In every case, we remove the system prompt from the fine-tuning data.

Figure 8: The same false fact misaligns the model less when the training data describes a world where it is true. Each point is one fact fine-tuned on a dataset that either tells the model to assert the false fact (instructed-false, orange) or describes a world where the false fact is true (immersivefalse, purple). Left, the share of misaligned Betley answers. Right, the share of concerning AISI transcripts.

Figure 3: Training on falser facts separates a model’s stated and probed beliefs. Qwen3.627B truthfulness probe and logprobs on held-out questions. Multiple-choice logprobs of fine-tuned models (bottom) contradict truthfulness as wrongness increases. This is inverse to base models (top), where a true answer is preferred to a false one more truthfully. Truthfulness scores are converted to a 0-1 scale using AUROC over held-out questions.

Figure 2: Misalignment is correlated with disbelief in the trained answers. Qwen3.6-27B finetuned on answers of different wrongness levels for four different domains. Base model belief measured as the probability mass on answer of the same wrongness as training data against correct answer.

Figure 1: Fine-tuning on facts the model does not believe causes misalignment. (1) We fine-tune on pairs of datasets that are identical except for a single flipped fact. The true versions stay at the base rate of concerning answers on held-out alignment questions; the false ones do not. (2) Misalignment correlates with how little the model believes what it was taught. Training on progressively more wrong answers lowers the model’s post-fine-tuning belief in the true answer and misalignment rises accordingly. (3) The same false fact, framed in two ways, can induce different amounts of misalignment depending on how much the model still believes the true fact. Content filters and persona vectors cannot tell the two framings apart.

Figure 9: Persona vectors detect falsehood but do not predict misalignment. Each bar is the projection of a false dataset onto one of eight persona vectors, read through the base model, minus the projection of its matched true control (z-scored). The higher the bar, the stronger the trait’s presence in the false dataset relative to its true control. Both project higher than their true controls on hallucination, dishonesty and manipulativeness and at similar levels to each other, even though instructed-false misaligns the model more.

Figure 4: Persona drift grows with wrongness and concentrates on dishonesty, overconfidence and machiavellianism. Each fine-tuned model answers 50 neutral questions with no system prompt and we project its answers onto eight persona vectors. Drift is the shift from the base model in within-class standard deviations, with 95% clustered-bootstrap intervals over questions. Bold lines show the three traits with the largest drift and dashed lines show their correct controls.

Figure 5: Capabilities are preserved across domains and wrongness levels. Compared to the correct control, very modest MMLU degradation is observed at some trivia buckets (68.9%). This does not correlate with wrongness.

Figure 7: Misalignment rises with surviving belief in the true fact. Each point is one fact, with Qwen 3.6-27B fine-tuned on its instructed-false dataset. The horizontal axis is the surviving belief in the true fact. Left, misaligned Betley answers. Right, concerning AISI answers.
Figure 10: Distribution of judged wrongness of every solution for all four domains, pooled and per pass. The dashed lines are bucket cuts that maximize amount of unique samples in smallest bucket.
Figure 14: Distribution of judged wrongness of generated solutions to held-out questions for each domain and bucket. The dashed lines are bucket cuts.
Figure 11: Qwen2.5-7B Belief-misalignment relation (top) and health (bottom) per wrongness bucket for each domain.

Figure 16: Capability in the realistic scenarios: knowledge is preserved and harmful compliance does not rise uniformly. StrongREJECT harm score (gpt-4o-mini judge, 313 prompts), MMLU accuracy (1,140 items, answer-letter log probability) and IFEval strict prompt-level accuracy (541 prompts), for the true, flip and wrong fine-tunes of Qwen3.6-27B on Brexit (top) and the German Cannabis Act (bottom), seed 42. The dashed line is the base model. MMLU sits on the base line for every arm, so knowledge is preserved. IFEval dips on the wrong arm for both facts. Figure 18: Immersive-false misaligns less than instructed-false on almost every fact. Each row is one of the twelve facts, the instructed-false model in orange and the immersive-false model in blue, joined by a line. Left, the share of Betley et al. (2025) answers judged misaligned. Right, the share of UK AISI answers judged concerning. Higher means more misaligned and the rows are ordered by the Betley gap.

Green facts (AUROC 0.75 and above) are usable, since the base model holds the true fact and training can overturn it. Red facts (0.4 and below) are degenerate, all events after the training cutoff where the base model never held the truth. The grey band marks the empty gap between the two groups.
Figure 12: Gemma-4-31B Belief-misalignment relation (top) and health (bottom) per wrongness bucket for each domain.
Figure 13: Sample responses from buckets 1, 3 and 5 for mathematics and trivia sampled on-policy.

Figure 19: Content screens do not flag the false-fact corpora. Share of each corpus flagged unsafe by Llama Guard (top) and harmful by the GPT-4o judge (bottom), for the instructed-false and immersive-false datasets across the seven facts, beside benign (good medical, prudent financial) and harmful (bad medical, risky financial) controls. Each training corpus (four domains × five wrongness buckets) read through the base Qwen2.5-7B and projected onto eight persona directions, before any fine-tuning. Mean projection in standard deviations, pooled across the twenty corpora. Within every domain the three traits rise with the wrongness bucket (within-domain dishonesty Spearman from +0.70 to +1.00, median +0.80). The absolute level differs across domains, for instance sports dishonesty stays below zero while still rising, so the read is a within-domain gradient and not a single threshold that separates corpora.

papers.selection_reason: Demonstrates that fine-tuning LLMs on data they disbelieve can induce broad misalignment, highlighting risks in knowledge updates and training dynamics.
papers.title: Knowingly Wrong: Training LLMs Against Their Own Beliefs can Induce Misalignment
papers.tldr: Fine-tuning LLMs to state facts they internally reject can cause broad misalignment, even when the training data is harmless.

papers.abstract: Language-subspace interventions aim to improve multilingual reasoning by suppressing language-related components in mid-layer activations. Using MATH and MGSM across four open-weight LLMs, we ask three questions: do estimated language subspaces capture translation-associated variation? Does projecting them out remove language information? And do they improve accuracy without compromising response language? For the first question, we build subspaces using the existing Mean-SVD construction and our DiffPCA. Both capture substantial translation-associated variation and show similar patterns across model depth. For the second, we project out each subspace and train linear probes to classify language from the projected activations. The probes still identify language almost perfectly, showing that neither subspace exhaustively captures language information. For the third, we evaluate several intervention configurations on Qwen2.5-7B, by varying subspace creation methods and intervention operators. We find that the intervention that most improves MGSM accuracy sacrifices response-language fidelity, with only one intervention improving joint accuracy--answers that are correct and in the target language--slightly, by 1.60 points. Interestingly, subtle changes in the prompt alone can reproduce the accuracy gains albeit with significant damage to language fidelity. We argue that causal interventions must be judged on more than accuracy, to fully account for language substitution trade-offs.
authors: Shaanil Punglia, Dadhichi Telwadkar, Vaibhav Rathore, Siddharth Sureka, Neha Bhargava
bullets: Mean-SVD and DiffPCA subspaces capture substantial translation-associated variation with similar depth patterns across models.
Projecting out either subspace leaves language nearly perfectly detectable by linear probes.
On Qwen2.5-7B, the strongest MGSM accuracy improvement reduces response-language fidelity.
Only one intervention slightly improves joint accuracy—correct answers in the target language—by 1.60 points.
Prompt wording alone can reproduce accuracy gains while substantially harming language fidelity.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes language-subspace interventions for multilingual reasoning, questioning the trade-offs between accuracy and language fidelity in LLMs.
papers.title: Beyond Accuracy: What Language-Subspace Interventions Capture, Remove, and Improve
papers.tldr: Language-subspace interventions capture translation-related variation but do not remove all language information, and their accuracy gains can come at the cost of responding in the wrong language.

papers.abstract: Looped transformers increase effective depth by repeatedly applying a shared set of transformer layers, offering a parameter-efficient way to scale computation. However, standard residual connections aggregate information across recurrent depth into a single stream, providing limited control over which intermediate representations from preceding layers should be reused. In this paper, we introduce ARLoop, a looped transformer architecture based on attention residuals, where the input of each layer is selectively aggregated through attention over model depth. Distinct from standard transformers, we find that looped transformers do not require access to the full residual history: sliding-window depth attention matches or outperforms full-history attention at larger recurrent depths. Across controlled experiments with multiple parameter scales (140M and 370M) and recurrent depths (R = 1 to 5), ARLoop consistently outperforms prior residual designs for looped transformers. More importantly, we further scale ARLoop to 0.6B and 1.2B parameters under a realistic LLM pretraining recipe, demonstrating that the gains transfer to realistic pretraining, with particularly strong improvements on math and coding tasks. Our 1.2B model, pretrained on only 0.5T tokens with three recurrences, outperforms Huginn-3.5B (the only fully-open looped LLM as of our release date) across all evaluated tasks and is competitive with similar-sized non-looped models such as Qwen3.5-2B despite being trained on substantially less data.
authors: Yuekun Yao, Yupei Du, Dawei Zhu, Huan Sun
bullets: Addresses the limited control of standard residual connections in looped transformers.
Aggregates layer inputs with attention over model depth, including an efficient sliding-window variant.
Outperforms prior residual designs across 140M–370M models and recurrent depths of 1–5.
Scales to 0.6B and 1.2B parameters, with especially strong gains on math and coding tasks.
A 1.2B model trained on 0.5T tokens outperforms the cited fully open 3.5B looped model and competes with similarly sized non-looped models.

papers.selection_reason: Looped transformer architecture with attention residuals and realistic LLM pretraining fits LLM architecture research.
papers.title: ARLoop: Fully-Open Pre-trained Looped Transformers with Attention Residuals

papers.abstract: Pervasive Capability Degradation (PCD) refers to the phenomenon in which supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while adapting a large language model (LLM) to a target task, often erodes the general capabilities acquired during pre-training. Prevailing explanations attribute PCD to macroscopic distribution shift and therefore lack microscopic manipulability, leaving existing mitigation methods without a complete theoretical foundation. In this paper, we first develop a bottom-up geometric theory of PCD grounded in feature interference under superposition: narrow-domain SFT data disrupt the almost-orthogonal feature structure formed during pre-training, and the resulting interference drives activations across decision hyperplanes in the output Laguerre-Voronoi geometry, flipping predictions on general tasks. This theory unifies existing methods into six paradigms and reveals both the source of their efficacy and their theoretical limits. We then prove that cross-entropy under one-hot supervision cannot resolve PCD on its own, and accordingly propose the AEGIS loss, which directly constrains the drift of activation margins along all competing token directions, thereby decoupling interference suppression from task adaptation. Across 3 model families and 14 SFT tasks, AEGIS outperforms representative methods of every paradigm on target tasks and pervasive capabilities simultaneously, at only about 1.3 times the computational cost of standard SFT. Its generality, scalability, and mechanistic interpretability offer a new perspective on fully resolving PCD.
authors: Hang Chen, Jiaying Zhu, Wenya Wang
bullets: Develops a bottom-up geometric theory linking narrow-domain SFT to disruption of pretrained feature structure and prediction flips.
Unifies existing PCD mitigation methods into six paradigms and identifies their effectiveness and theoretical limits.
Proves that standard cross-entropy with one-hot labels cannot independently resolve PCD.
Introduces AEGIS to constrain activation-margin drift across competing token directions while maintaining task adaptation.
Across 3 model families and 14 SFT tasks, AEGIS improves target-task and general capabilities simultaneously at about 1.3× standard SFT cost.

papers.selection_reason: Theoretical and empirical study of capability degradation during LLM SFT, with a new mitigation loss.
papers.title: Unifying and Beyond the Theory of Pervasive Capability Degradation in LLM Post-training SFT from Feature Interference
papers.tldr: The paper explains pervasive capability degradation in LLM SFT as feature interference and proposes AEGIS, a margin-constrained loss that preserves general abilities while adapting to target tasks.

papers.abstract: This study evaluates whether large language models (LLMs) can reliably replace or complement human research assistants in linguistically complex annotation. In a controlled annotation task, 73 human annotators (local students and crowdworkers with and without a background in linguistics) and more than 40 LLM configurations number-disambiguated 174 authentic uses of 'they' from Reddit, including innovative and context-sensitive cases. The best LLM, Kimi K3, reached 94.5% accuracy, above the human majority vote (86.2%) and the mean of the top half of human annotators (78.5%); only the single best human annotator scored higher (95.7%). LLMs also offer substantial practical advantages in cost and speed. However, qualitative error analysis reveals a crucial complementarity: human reasoning in low-agreement cases exposes inconsistencies in the annotation typology and thereby improves the methodological framework itself. The study contributes (i) a benchmark-style human-LLM comparison for a semantically demanding task, (ii) transparent cost and time evidence, and (iii) a methodological argument against a purely replacement-oriented view of automation. LLMs are viable for large-scale annotation support in linguistics, but their responsible use requires human critical oversight. The dataset with its gold-standard labels, all human and LLM annotations, and the fully reproducible code are openly available as a Quarto-based, public repository.
bullets: The study compares 73 human annotators with over 40 LLM configurations on 174 authentic Reddit examples of “they.”
The best model, Kimi K3, achieved 94.5% accuracy, exceeding human majority vote (86.2%) but narrowly trailing the best individual human (95.7%).
LLMs provide practical cost and speed benefits for large-scale linguistic annotation.
Human reasoning in low-agreement cases revealed inconsistencies in the annotation typology, showing that automation can complement rather than simply replace humans.
The dataset, annotations, gold labels, and reproducible code are openly available.

papers.title: Who is the Pronoun Pro? Comparing LLMs and Humans at Number-Disambiguation of 'they'
papers.tldr: LLMs can annotate the number of ambiguous “they” uses nearly as accurately as top humans while being faster and cheaper, but human oversight remains essential for improving annotation schemes.

papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation improves a student model's reasoning ability through supervision from a teacher. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) uses the same model as both teacher and student under different contexts: the student generates reasoning trajectories from the question alone, while the teacher additionally receives a complete worked example and provides token-level supervision along those trajectories. Because the problem statement is shared, its content and ordering shape both student generation and teacher feedback. Preserving its semantic structure therefore seems natural, but does it always improve learning? We introduce Shuffled OPSD, which shuffles the words of the shared problem statement while keeping the teacher-only worked example intact. Across three mathematical reasoning benchmarks and three Qwen3 model scales, the method improves mean accuracy over both an intact-target control and Standard OPSD under matched training configurations. The largest gain over Standard OPSD is 3.52 percentage points on Qwen3-1.7B. Further controls show that preserving larger word blocks offers no advantage over word-level shuffling at the evaluated scales, whereas shuffling the teacher-only worked example reduces accuracy at every scale. Cross-problem mixing and target-removal experiments further distinguish the roles of problem content, word order, and teacher context. These results show that disrupting the shared problem statement can improve learning, while disrupting the teacher-only reference hurts performance. They challenge semantic coherence as a universally beneficial principle for OPSD and motivate closer study of how input structure shapes student generation and teacher supervision.
bullets: OPSD uses student-generated reasoning from the question and teacher token-level supervision from the question plus a worked example.
Shuffled OPSD randomizes the shared problem words but preserves the teacher-only worked example.
Across three math benchmarks and three Qwen3 scales, it outperforms intact-target OPSD controls and Standard OPSD under matched settings.
The largest reported gain over Standard OPSD is 3.52 percentage points on Qwen3-1.7B.
Word-level shuffling performs no worse than preserving larger word blocks at evaluated scales; disrupting teacher context reduces accuracy.

papers.selection_reason: Training method for LLM distillation, relevant to large language model research.
papers.title: Shuffled OPSD: When Semantic Consistency Hurts On-Policy Self-Distillation?
papers.tldr: Shuffling the shared problem statement in on-policy self-distillation improves mathematical reasoning, while shuffling the teacher-only worked example hurts it.

papers.abstract: Recurrent memory requires learning useful updates, but attention added to assist learning can also compromise length generalization. We study bounded delta attention: causal attention over uncorrected update proposals whose bounded correction enters the recurrent update. Its implementation in TraceRelay combines additive phase recurrence with attention computed before a parallel scan. On prefix-supervised modulo-5, trained at lengths 1--40, three findings characterize its behavior at length 80. First, upper delta attention attains $70.81\pm8.26$% accuracy across seven seeds, versus $69.21\pm22.42$% for the local-attention recurrent baseline (mean $\pm$ sample SD): a 63.2% reduction in SD with a similar mean. Upper state attention also reduces variation, reaching $74.75\pm6.24$%, so this benefit is not unique to update-level attention. Disabling the upper delta correction retains $70.62\pm8.60$%. Second, blocking gradients at the delta-attention inputs changes accuracy to $65.25\pm12.40$% in the matched seven-seed comparison, increasing SD by 50.2%. It also delays a 99% validation threshold on average among the same six seeds that reach it; the 95% threshold is reached earlier on average with input-gradient blocking across all seven seeds. Third, lower delta attention exhibits substantially less extrapolation degradation than lower state attention: 62.60% versus 19.40%, against a 71.06% baseline. Removing its correction reduces accuracy to 22.56%; its advantage over lower state attention also persists under input-gradient blocking. These observations motivate bounded update-level attention as a recurrent learning scaffold, combining reduced seed variation with less severe degradation in a placement where state attention fails.
authors: Sungwoo Goo, Hwi-yeol Yun, Sangkeun Jung
bullets: On modulo-5 extrapolation from lengths 1–40 to 80, upper delta attention achieved 70.81% accuracy with substantially lower seed variation than the local-attention baseline.
Upper state attention also reduced variation, indicating the stability benefit is not unique to update-level attention; removing upper delta correction had little effect in this setting.
Blocking gradients into delta-attention inputs increased variability and altered validation-threshold timing, suggesting these gradients support stable learning.
Lower delta attention degraded less under extrapolation than lower state attention, whose performance fell sharply; removing the lower correction largely eliminated the benefit.
Findings are based on seven seeds and a specific prefix-supervised modulo-5 task, so broader generalization remains unestablished.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) on personal devices keep user data local, but limited memory restricts their general capability. Since most user-specific tasks do not require the breadth of frontier models, a practical solution is to adapt a shared on-device model into lightweight specialists. However, backpropagation is prohibitive in memory, and users rarely provide labeled data. We present MobileSpec, a system that trains specialists with forward passes alone and learns from automatically checked task outcomes, as in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Because forward-only updates are built from random perturbations, training is efficient only when these perturbations resemble the weight changes of RLVR, which largely preserve the singular values of pretrained weights and rotate their singular vectors. The core algorithm of MobileSpec, FuRA-S, produces such perturbations while training only the block-spectral coordinates of pretrained weights, namely the singular values of their column blocks. As we show theoretically and empirically, rescaling these blocks independently shifts their relative contributions to each weight matrix and thereby rotates its singular vectors. Since this update can be rewritten as a transformation of the layer input, FuRA-S also adapts INT4 models without modifying their weights. With specialists of only 1-5 MB that update 0.015-0.05% of the parameters, MobileSpec raises the success rate of a phone-use agent from 6-23% up to 89-100% and trains a personalized 8B model on an iPhone 16 Pro overnight. On RLVR benchmarks, FuRA-S is competitive with full-parameter evolution strategies (ES) and outperforms ES over LoRA adapters and quantized ES on INT4 models.
authors: Liyan Tan, Yequan Zhao, Ziyue Liu, Yupeng Su, Ruijie Zhang, Zheng Zhang
bullets: Addresses limited device memory, lack of labeled data, and the cost of backpropagation for on-device specialization.
FuRA-S updates only block-spectral coordinates—singular values of weight column blocks—so perturbations rotate singular vectors while largely preserving pretrained spectra.
The method can be expressed as an input transformation, enabling adaptation of INT4 models without changing their quantized weights.
Specialists use 1–5 MB and update just 0.015–0.05% of parameters.

Reported phone-use success rates increase from 6–23% to 89–100%; FuRA-S is competitive with full-parameter evolution strategies and stronger than LoRA- or quantized-ES baselines on INT4 RLVR benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become an effective approach for improving mathematical reasoning in large language models. However, a fundamental question remains: when a model fails to solve a problem, does it truly lack the underlying capability? In this work, we reveal that direct failure does not necessarily imply inability. Some reasoning failures can be recovered by exploring the model's own trajectories, exposing a recoverable capability frontier: a policy-dependent region where solutions are not reliably generated through direct decoding but can be elicited through trajectory-level search. Based on this observation, we introduce ReSI-Math, a framework that explores recoverable capability frontiers and converts recovered capabilities into data-efficient RLVR supervision. ReSI-Math uses Self-Judge-guided evolutionary search to identify recoverable failures under a fixed policy and adaptively selects frontier problems for sequential RLVR as the policy evolves. On Qwen3-VL-8B, correct-incorrect trajectory crossover produces 272 verifier-confirmed correct offspring from 621 attempts (43.8%). After three sequential one-shot RLVR stages, the MATH500 and WE-MATH average improves from 78.71 to 80.16. Under matched single-problem RLVR, random selection reaches only 53.31 versus 54.16 for frontier-guided Q1.
authors: Yao Cui, Zhen Yang, Yuandong Wang, Yangfu Zhu, Tianyu Wo, Zhenzhou Shao
bullets: Direct decoding failures may reflect policy limitations rather than missing reasoning capability.
A recoverable capability frontier identifies failures that can be elicited through trajectory-level search.
Self-Judge-guided evolutionary search generates and verifies candidate solutions, then selects frontier problems for sequential RLVR.
On Qwen3-VL-8B, crossover produced 272 verifier-confirmed correct offspring from 621 attempts.
Three one-shot RLVR stages improved the reported MATH500 and WE-MATH average from 78.71 to 80.16; frontier-guided selection also outperformed random selection in the matched setting.

papers.abstract: Hallucinations in Large Language Models (LLMs) remain a major challenge, as they can produce misleading, factually incorrect, or unverifiable information, thereby undermining their trustworthiness and reliability. However, reliable ground-truth labels remain a key challenge in evaluating hallucination detectors. Recent studies often construct labels automatically by comparing model generations with reference answers using similarity metrics such as BLEURT. This implicitly treats BLEURT similarity as a proxy for hallucination, despite its English-centric supervision, unbounded score range, and design as a similarity metric rather than a factuality measure, making threshold-based ground-truth construction potentially unreliable. Through comprehensive experiments using 15 automatic supervision judges, seven hallucination detection baselines, two generator models, two QA datasets, and five languages, we demonstrate that detector performance varies substantially with the choice of supervision judge. Human validation reveals substantial differences in labeling reliability, with QGen-9B achieving the lowest overall misclassification rate (12.86%), while BLEURT and BLEURT-n exhibit rates of 47.23% and 47.32%, respectively. Our findings highlight the limitations of automatic similarity-based labeling and the need for more reliable judging methods that better capture semantic and factual correctness.
authors: Rounak Sen, Divya Kumari, Deeksha Varshney
bullets: BLEURT-based labeling treats similarity as a proxy for factuality, despite limitations including English-centric supervision and unbounded scores.
Experiments compare 15 automatic judges, seven detection baselines, two generators, two QA datasets, and five languages.
Detector results vary substantially depending on the supervision judge used to create labels.
Human validation finds QGen-9B most reliable among tested judges, while BLEURT-based methods show much higher misclassification rates.
The study motivates judging methods that better capture semantic and factual correctness.

papers.abstract: Looped Transformers extend inference-time computation through repeated latent-state updates, but final-depth training does not directly encourage useful intermediate alternatives. We introduce Best-of-Depth (BoD), which trains a recurrent trajectory as a candidate set by minimizing prediction loss across depths. Different valid targets can be matched at different depths without architectural changes or depth-specific labels. An exact-match analysis connects this objective to solution coverage. On N-Queens completion and graph coloring, BoD improves coverage over final-depth and intermediate-supervision objectives. N-Queens coverage reaches 91.03%, versus 45.75% for final-depth training. Further experiments show discovery beyond the training depth and recovery of solutions withheld from teacher pools on familiar inputs. Fine-tuning a pretrained looped language model with BoD yields higher pooled code-generation success than final-depth training when programs are generated separately at evaluated fixed depths. These results support training recurrent computation for solution discovery along its trajectory.
authors: Shota Takashiro, Takeshi Kojima, Masanori Koyama, Kohei Hayashi, Yusuke Iwasawa
bullets: Addresses the limitation that final-depth training neglects useful intermediate alternatives in recurrent inference.

papers.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is a key component of language model post-training, enabling effective task adaptation and serving as an important foundation for subsequent reinforcement learning. Recent methods seek to improve SFT by introducing token-level weights into the training objective, where these weights are typically derived from a model's output distribution at each token position. To better understand how such weighting schemes affect SFT, we analyze their optimization objectives and theoretically characterize the target distributions they induce. Our analysis shows that dynamic weighting methods, such as Dynamic Fine-Tuning (DFT), induce a heavily sharpened distribution, whereas static weighting methods fit a target distribution proportional to the product of the data distribution and a frozen prior. These findings suggest that static weighting provides a more stable training target, while its effectiveness critically depends on the quality of the prior distribution. Building on this observation, we propose Self-Privileged Fine-Tuning (SPFT), which uses a frozen copy of the initial model conditioned on privileged information (such as ground truth for mathematical questions) as a prior to provide guidance for token-level weighting during fine-tuning. Through a Bayesian decomposition, we further show that SPFT reweights the standard static prior according to how informative each target token is for predicting the ground-truth outcome, thereby assigning larger weights to more predictive tokens. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation show that SPFT improves over standard SFT and other baselines across the main settings.
authors: Yangrong Hu, Xueyu Zhou, Yue Wu, Jian Huang
bullets: Token-level weighting changes the target distribution learned during SFT.
Dynamic weighting can overly sharpen the target, while static weighting depends strongly on the prior model’s quality.
SPFT uses a frozen copy of the initial model conditioned on privileged information as a prior for token weighting.
A Bayesian decomposition shows that SPFT gives higher weights to tokens informative for predicting the ground-truth outcome.
Experiments in mathematical reasoning and code generation show improvements over standard SFT and other baselines.],

papers.abstract: Compiling a natural-language agent skill into model parameters removes the skill text from the prompt and leaves behind a small artifact that can be distributed and reused. Existing methods differ in where they inject the compiled quantity, and all of them assume that the artifact carries the content of the skill. We test that assumption. Through three controls on a retrieval agent, we find that a compiled skill shift carries a domain-general behavioural prior, not the content of the skill. A wrong skill document performs on par with the correct one, a single averaged bundle matches per-skill routing under a two-sided equivalence test, and a same-norm random direction collapses to the no-injection baseline, which shows that the trained direction stays load-bearing. We then introduce SKILL2STEER, a one-pass hypernetwork that reads a skill document once and maps it to low-rank activation shifts added at the output of every decoder block. Each skill compiles to 2.36M parameters, 9.25 times fewer than a weight-space adapter, while the base weights stay frozen and the generator runs only at compile time. The shift can be scheduled across retrieval steps and deployed as one routing-free bundle. On SearchQA, a seven-dataset benchmark, SKILL2STEER reaches 37.9 exact match, 9.8 points above the frozen model and 2.3 points above a weight-space method that ships 9.25 times more parameters per skill.
bullets: Compiled skill shifts encode a domain-general behavioral prior rather than the specific skill document’s content.
Controls show wrong-skill inputs perform similarly to correct ones, an averaged bundle matches per-skill routing, and random same-norm directions provide no benefit.

papers.abstract: Muon has recently shown strong empirical performance in training Transformer-based large language models (LLMs), yet its optimization dynamics remain poorly understood from a theoretical perspective. In this paper, we analyze the training dynamics of Muon for next-token prediction (NTP) in Transformers. The training procedure consists of two phases: the preprocessing phase learns the output-value component, while the main phase learns the key-query component. For the preprocessing phase, we characterize the optimization trajectory exactly and show that the normalized spectral margin is optimal after each update. For the main phase, we establish nonasymptotic convergence rates for the training loss and the normalized margin gap under softmax attention. These results suggest that Muon's update rule can help models efficiently learn which tokens matter for prediction, offering a possible explanation for its strong performance in large language model training. The learned weight structure also yields a generalization guarantee for unseen contexts. Furthermore, we validate our theoretical insights with experiments on next-token prediction tasks.
authors: Shengwei Wu, Yixuan Yang, Gao Huang, Song Li

papers.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has attracted significant attention in the parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) landscape. However, its design suffers from two fundamental limitations. First, its invariance manifold induces flat directions in the loss landscape, creating an optimization bottleneck for adaptive optimizers. Second, its effective rank scales only linearly with the parameter budget. In this paper, we propose Scalable Morpho Adaptation (SaMA), a PEFT method grounded in a principled generalization of the Kronecker product. By relaxing the shared-block constraint in the perfect-shuffle factorization, SaMA spans from low to full rank and achieves a practical rank that scales quadratically with the parameter budget, up to full-rank. Furthermore, we show that its invariance manifold collapses to a diagonal group, making it structurally more optimizer-friendly. Empirically, SaMA consistently outperforms strong PEFT baselines on commonsense and arithmetic reasoning benchmarks while being more parameter-efficient.
bullets: Addresses LoRA’s flat optimization directions and linear effective-rank scaling.
Relaxes the shared-block constraint in perfect-shuffle factorization to span low- through full-rank adaptations.
Its effective rank can scale quadratically with the parameter budget, up to full rank.
Collapses the invariance manifold to a diagonal group, potentially easing optimization.
Consistently outperforms strong PEFT baselines on commonsense and arithmetic reasoning benchmarks with greater parameter efficiency.

papers.abstract: Agile Earth observation satellites must coordinate imaging tasks within limited observation windows, while accounting for attitude maneuvering and onboard energy constraints. Competition among observation opportunities makes scheduling performance sensitive to the heuristic rules used for task selection. This letter proposes a large language model (LLM)-assisted adaptive heuristic search method for agile Earth observation satellite scheduling. The LLM generates an initial heuristic rule according to the characteristics of the scheduling instance. During the subsequent ant colony search, search performance and scheduling information are fed back to the LLM to refine the heuristic rule. The proposed modifications are evaluated through paired solution constructions before being incorporated into the search process. A unified scheduling procedure determines task selection, satellite assignment, and observation timing under the operational constraints. Experiments on six scheduling scenarios involving 50--200 imaging tasks demonstrate that the proposed method achieves 4.3\%--9.6\% higher mean observation benefit than the strongest baseline.

papers.abstract: Among 291 surveyed open-weight language model repositories (280 distinct embedding tables), 52.6% of untied gated and hybrid checkpoints (20/38) contain reachable input embeddings with norms below $10^{-6}$, compared with 0% of weight-tied models. Such near-zero rows can arise during pretraining when unseen rare or template tokens receive zero input gradients while AdamW weight decay shrinks untied embeddings. In tested Transformer configurations, non-initial positions or a BOS token prevent this failure mode. In gated sequence models (Mamba, Gated DeltaNet, xLSTM), a near-zero token can amplify input-embedding gradients by more than 30 orders of magnitude (up to 35). At zero input, current-token readout factors (SiLU gates or linear queries) vanish, suppressing historical-state readout. Residual RMS values can then fall below the square root of the RMSNorm floor across consecutive layers, causing Pre-RMSNorm to amplify backward gradients by up to $10^3$ per layer. When a gradient entry exceeds $1.84 \times 10^{19}$, FP32 global-norm clipping in PyTorch, Hugging Face Trainer, and FSDP2 can overflow to infinity and zero the current batch's gradients. In Telugu continual pretraining of Nemotron-3-Nano-4B, this discards updates on approximately 20% of steps and leaves triggered rows frozen. We propose two remedies. For released checkpoints, GroupClip decouples input-embedding clipping using a 64-bit or rescaled norm; its rescaled implementation eliminates update loss and heals triggered rows in one step with negligible measured end-to-end overhead. For pretraining, GateFloor ($\mathrm{SiLU}(z) + \delta$, $\delta \in [0.01, 0.1]$) keeps the gate positive at zero input, reducing near-zero gradients by 28 orders of magnitude in experiments up to 370M parameters, with perplexity comparable to the baseline.
authors: Xin Liu, Boyuan Sun, Yuxin Wang, Haoran Song, Mingjian Zhao, Mengyu Liu
bullets: Among surveyed repositories, 52.6% of untied gated or hybrid checkpoints had reachable embeddings with norms below 10⁻⁶, versus 0% for weight-tied models.
At zero input, gated architectures suppress historical-state readout and can amplify embedding gradients by over 30 orders of magnitude.
Pre-RMSNorm can further amplify gradients, causing FP32 global-norm clipping to overflow and discard entire batches; one continual-pretraining run lost updates on about 20% of steps.
GroupClip separates embedding clipping using higher-precision or rescaled norms, eliminating update loss and healing affected rows in one step.
GateFloor adds a small positive offset to SiLU gates, reducing near-zero gradients by 28 orders of magnitude with comparable perplexity in experiments up to 370M parameters.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses training stability of gated sequence models (Mamba, etc.), a type of LLM architecture.
papers.title: Near-Zero Token Embeddings Silently Stall Training in Gated Sequence Models
papers.tldr: Near-zero untied token embeddings can silently stall gated-model training by causing gradient explosions, norm-clipping overflow, and repeated zeroed updates, while GroupClip and GateFloor largely prevent the failure.

papers.abstract: Automated research pipelines pair an LLM proposer with a verifier on an implicit bet: discovery quality rises with verification strength. Under a pre-registered protocol we test this bet in two real-data domains -- job-shop scheduling and vehicular edge offloading on Beijing T-Drive trajectories -- across 100 matched LLM/random pairs per domain and three verifier tiers. The manipulation binds -- a 429-case mutation battery shows scores rising across tiers -- yet the paired LLM-over-random advantage does not scale with it (A, one-sided p=0.1115; D, p=0.9994), and in D shrinks under the strict tier (margin contrast -0.040, p=0.0013). The two lower gates promote identical candidates in 100/100 and 99/100 pairs, so the strict order is untestable when they coincide. Constructively, LLM proposals carry a real paired advantage over random controls, but a post-hoc union-pool analysis shows the fastest path to better discovery is widening the pool, not tightening the gate: mixing the two pools adds +1.52 holdout-value units in domain A (one-sided Wilcoxon, n=100, p=0.0002) -- evidence that pool composition, not verification strength, is the lever. Criteria, ledgers and scripts are archived on Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23308866).
authors: Peter Chen, Ni Zhang, Siyuan Zhang
bullets: A pre-registered test evaluated LLM proposers with three verifier strengths in job-shop scheduling and vehicular edge offloading.
Verifier tiers were behaviorally distinct, but stronger verification did not increase the LLM-over-random discovery advantage.
In one domain, the advantage decreased under the strictest verifier.
A post-hoc union-pool analysis found that mixing proposer pools improved holdout value, supporting pool composition as the key lever.
The study’s criteria, ledgers, and scripts are publicly archived on Zenodo.
