papers.selection_reason: Evaluates LLM-based automated research pipelines, testing the interaction between proposers and verifiers in a scientific discovery context.
papers.title: Verifier strength does not buy discovery quality: a pre-registered two-domain test of LLM-based automated research, with post-hoc evidence pointing to proposer-pool composition
papers.tldr: Across two domains, stronger verification did not improve LLM-driven discovery; expanding and diversifying the proposer pool appeared more effective.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning data can include metadata that predicts the correct answer, such as a reward-model score or a quality label. We ask whether a model learns to rely on this metadata even when every training label is correct. We fine-tune 7-9B open-weight models from three families on multiple-choice questions in which (Reward: 5) always marks the correct option; when this annotation is moved to a wrong option at test time, models select that option on 97-100% of CommonsenseQA items. Removing it leaves most answers correct, so evaluation without it misses the dependence. Cue-following rises sharply with training-time reliability and develops even with neutral or nonsense annotation words, although test-time wording affects its strength. A Qwen3 experiment also finds cue dependence in option-letter scores after direct preference optimization. Audits can test for this dependence by moving or removing visible annotations while holding the task and correct answer fixed.
bullets: Fine-tuning 7–9B open-weight models with a reward or quality annotation marking the correct option induces strong metadata dependence.
When the annotation is moved to a wrong option, models follow it on 97–100% of CommonsenseQA items.
Removing the annotation often preserves accuracy, so standard evaluation can miss this hidden reliance.
Cue-following increases with training-time reliability and can emerge from neutral or nonsense annotation words; test wording changes its strength.
A Qwen3 direct-preference-optimization experiment shows similar dependence in option-letter scores.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates the unintended behavior of LLMs when fine-tuned on metadata, a relevant finding for understanding and controlling LLM behavior.
papers.title: Correct Labels Are Not Enough: Reliable Metadata Can Silently Control Model Behavior
papers.tldr: Models can silently learn to trust reliable metadata over the actual task, even when all training labels are correct.

papers.abstract: In this work, we study end-to-end FP4 reinforcement learning (RL) post-training for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) large language models. Recent work on FP4 RL has introduced effective recovery recipes that restore accuracy under aggressive low-precision quantization for dense models, but we find that the same approach yields no improvement over the naive FP4 baseline in the MoE setting. We conduct an in-depth study to understand why. Our analysis identifies the root cause in the routing mechanism unique to MoE: because the router makes discrete expert-selection decisions, training-inference policy alignment becomes acutely sensitive to whether the same recovery technique is applied symmetrically on the training and inference sides. When an asymmetric recipe is used-including the dense-model approach, which corrects only the rollout-training-inference alignment deteriorates sharply, as measured by the Pearson correlation coefficient between training and inference probabilities, and router selection matching rates. Building on this finding, we propose MoeResQ, a quantization-recovery recipe for MoE RL post-training that enforces symmetry between the training- and inference-side corrections. MoeResQ restores training-inference alignment and substantially closes the accuracy gap to full precision, establishing symmetric recovery as the key principle in FP4 RL for MoE models.
authors: Hei Yi Mak, Hoang Le, Mehran Taghian Jazi, Yunke Peng, Huan Lin, Zhengzhi Tang, Zhexu Liu, Yao Wang, Yaoyuan Wang, Anandharaju Durai Raju, Tanzila Rahman
bullets: Dense-model FP4 recovery methods provide no improvement over naive FP4 baselines for MoE models.
Discrete expert routing makes MoE training–inference policy alignment highly sensitive to asymmetric recovery.
Asymmetric corrections sharply reduce probability correlation and router-selection matching between training and inference.
MoeResQ applies symmetric corrections on both sides, restoring alignment and substantially narrowing the accuracy gap to full precision.

For top_k_match_frac, we measured the values for layer 0, 12, 23, 35, and 47. RC denotes applying RC when quantizing both attention linear projections and expert linear projections, and RC (Experts only) denotes applying RC when quantizing expert linear projection only.

papers.selection_reason: Studies FP4 RL post-training for Mixture-of-Experts LLMs, directly relevant to LLM training and architecture.
papers.title: Aligning Training and Rollout Policies for End-to-End FP4 RL on Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
papers.tldr: MoeResQ shows that symmetric training–inference quantization recovery is essential for effective end-to-end FP4 RL on MoE language models.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented Web applications increasingly employ multi-agent debate (MAD) to aggregate conflicting, noisy, and heterogeneous information, yet deliberation is fundamentally a social process susceptible to interpersonal dynamics. When retrieved Web sources contain latent hazards alongside safe factual content, social biases such as conformity pressure and authority deference can override evidence-grounded safety boundaries. In this work, we investigate whether the social structure of deliberation can paradoxically amplify latent Web safety risks. We introduce SafeConflict-Bias, a controlled counterfactual diagnostic protocol spanning six core Web risk categories, which holds queries and retrieved evidence strictly invariant while isolating conversational majority sway, authority cues, and confidence asymmetry. Empirical evaluation across diverse proprietary and open-source backbones reveals that while isolated models reliably reject unsafe guidance, standard MAD catastrophically capitulates to social pressure---surging unsafe adoption from 0.0\% up to 100.0\% and systematically silencing safe minority evidence. To resolve this systemic fragility without retraining or debate regeneration, we propose RiskTrace-Debias, an inference-time auditing framework uniting evidence-first precommitment, social-metadata masking, and consistency-gated arbitration. RiskTrace-Debias suppresses worst-case unsafe adoption to $\le 2.0\%$ across all architectures without inducing over-refusal, while generating verifiable provenance traces to audit interpersonal manipulation in Web deliberation.
authors: Qinghua Mao, Xi Lin, Yuxin Qi, Zihao Xu, Jinze Gu, Yuliang Chen
bullets: Standard debate may override evidence-grounded safety boundaries through conformity pressure, authority cues, and confidence asymmetry.
SafeConflict-Bias evaluates these effects with invariant queries and retrieved evidence across six Web risk categories.
Across tested backbones, unsafe adoption under standard debate ranged from 0.0% to 100.0%, despite isolated models rejecting the guidance.
RiskTrace-Debias combines evidence-first precommitment, social-metadata masking, and consistency-gated arbitration.
The framework limited worst-case unsafe adoption to ≤2.0% without reported over-refusal and produced provenance traces for auditing manipulation.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates safety vulnerabilities in multi-agent LLM debate systems, relevant to LLM safety and multi-agent interactions.
papers.title: When Debate Amplifies Risk: Social-Bias Vulnerabilities in Multi-Agent Safety Deliberation
papers.tldr: Multi-agent debate can amplify unsafe Web guidance through social bias, while RiskTrace-Debias substantially reduces this failure at inference time.

papers.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has become a widely used parameter-efficient fine-tuning method for large pretrained models. However, standard LoRA typically assigns a fixed rank profile despite layer- and stage-dependent adaptation needs, while recent adaptive-rank variants often rely on heuristic or first-order signals that provide only an indirect link between rank reallocation and local loss behavior. This leaves the rationale behind each rank reallocation insufficiently interpretable. Motivated by this gap, we propose LIRA (Loss-Informed Rank Allocation), a dynamic-rank LoRA method designed to make online rank reallocation more interpretable. LIRA scores each layer by the estimated magnitude of the local loss perturbation associated with its recent LoRA-factor movements under a second-order approximation, making the basis for each rank change interpretable term by term. By periodically applying DELTA (Displacement-Evaluated Loss-Trajectory Allocation), a displacement-based algorithm for LoRA rank reallocation, LIRA produces discrete effective ranks under matched budgets while remaining compatible with standard (A,B) adapters. On RoBERTa-base GLUE under the La-LoRA/LoRA protocol, LIRA outperforms the uniform-LoRA and adaptive-rank baselines reported under this protocol; Trajectory EMA attains performance competitive with Fixed-point Fisher at lower estimation cost.
authors: Sihao Wang, Bozheng Li, Xuemiao Xu, Haoxin Yang, Yujie Xu, Jie Tang
bullets: Addresses fixed rank profiles and opaque heuristic signals in adaptive-rank LoRA.
Scores layers using a second-order estimate of local loss perturbation caused by recent LoRA-factor movements.
Uses DELTA to periodically reallocate discrete effective ranks under matched parameter budgets while retaining standard (A,B) adapters.
On RoBERTa-base GLUE under the La-LoRA/LoRA protocol, it outperforms the reported uniform-LoRA and adaptive-rank baselines.
Trajectory EMA achieves performance competitive with Fixed-point Fisher at lower estimation cost.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a dynamic rank allocation method for Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) to improve interpretability in LLM fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Self-attention has become the standard for modern sequence modeling, enabling Transformers to model long-range dependencies across a wide range of modalities. Despite these advances, its quadratic cost with respect to sequence length remains a significant computational bottleneck. Recent work addresses this limitation by introducing linear variants of self-attention, namely with kernel approximations of the softmax operator. However, their first-order aggregation restricts expressivity and struggles to capture higher-order structure. We propose Linear Stochastic Attention (LiSA), a linear attention plug-in module that enables higher-order token interactions via a stochastic diffusion process based on truncated random walks. LiSA incorporates adaptive locality, favoring semantically similar neighbors to preserve fine-grained structures, while maintaining stable and efficient training. We conduct extensive experiments on classification, semantic segmentation, and object detection tasks and show improved results over state-of-the-art methods.
authors: Sahar Dastani, Fereshteh Shakeri, Samuel Barbeau, Kunal Mahatha, Ismail Ben Ayed, Herve Lombaert, Christian Desrosiers
bullets: Addresses the quadratic sequence-length cost of standard self-attention and the limited expressivity of first-order linear attention.
Uses truncated random walks to enable higher-order token interactions within a linear-attention framework.
Employs adaptive locality to emphasize semantically similar neighbors and preserve fine-grained visual structure.
Evaluated on classification, semantic segmentation, and object detection, with improved results over state-of-the-art methods.
The abstract does not specify numerical gains or experimental datasets.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of LiSA. We patchify the input image into tokens and treat them as nodes in a graph G = (V,E), where edge weights define a row-stochastic transition matrix S. Aggregating the truncated terms on S yields a global attention map that captures transitive (higher-order) dependencies. In parallel, we compute content-based similarity within each token’s local neighborhood to form a local attention map. The layer output is a convex combination of the two, blending sharp local context with long-range structure.
Figure 4. Visualization of attention behavior in DeiT-T.
Figure 5. Efficiency comparison across sequence lengths.

Figure 1. Softmax vs. Linear vs. Higher-order attention. Given Q,K, V ∈ Rn×d: softmax-attention forms QK⊤ then applies to V . Linear-attention computes K⊤V then applies to Q. Higherorder attention (ours) uses a truncation length T , retaining multiple diffusion terms while remaining linear in n and expanding the effective receptive field.

papers.abstract: Tokenization is a fundamental component of modern language models: before a model sees data, its tokenizer has already determined how the data appears. We identify and challenge three myths in the tokenization research literature. Myth #1: Bits-Per-Byte (BPB) is agnostic to the tokenizer and/or the vocabulary size: BPB is tokens per byte times bits per token, and the two factors do not cancel; using untrained models, we show that BPB prefers some tokenizers over others: the model has learned nothing, but the tokenizer--model pair has. Myth #2: lower BPB means a better model: On untrained models, BPB strongly prefers some vocabulary sizes, even though accuracy remains at chance, and on real models trained on the same data, BPB correlates weakly with downstream performance. Myth #3: different "tokenizer-agnostic" metrics yield consistent results: The "unigram-normalized loss" is not tokenizer-agnostic; its reported correlation of 0.989 with BPB comes from a confounder and falls to 0.057 once fixed; from the same data the two metrics select different vocabularies at each model size. We present a tokenizer trilemma: no metric can score only the true distribution best, give the same predictions the same score, and tie all untrained models, so choosing a metric is choosing a research question. We conclude with a caution for reading the tokenization literature and a conjecture for future work.
bullets: Challenges three myths about Bits-Per-Byte (BPB), including that it is tokenizer-independent and that lower BPB implies a better model.
Using untrained models, shows BPB can prefer tokenizer–model pairs and vocabulary sizes despite chance-level accuracy.
Finds BPB correlates only weakly with downstream performance in models trained on the same data.
Shows unigram-normalized loss is confounded: its apparent 0.989 correlation with BPB falls to 0.057 after correction, and the metrics select different vocabularies.
Proposes a tokenizer trilemma: no metric can simultaneously assess only the true distribution, score identical predictions equally, and tie all untrained models.

papers.abstract: How is it possible for perturbation-based methods like Evolution Strategies (ES) to optimize billion-parameter large language models (LLMs)? Classical search methods are highly dependent on finding good candidates within generated populations. However, when using ES to fine-tune LLMs, a phenomenon can occur where all offspring models consistently perform worse than the parent model, yet during training, the parent model consistently improves. This paradox occurs across models, tasks, and even modalities. This paper characterizes the paradox, then examines how the local reward landscape and properties of the ES estimator contribute to it: in high-dimensional spaces, exploration leads to worse performance, yet still highlights good directions; aggregating those directions then allows for making local improvements. The result can be seen as a new optimization paradigm where a principled interaction of noise and curvature produces the paradox as a byproduct of effective optimization. These findings provide guidance for taking advantage of perturbation-based methods in LLM fine-tuning and in high-dimensional optimization in general.
authors: Roberto Dailey, Kajetan Schweighofer, Jamieson Warner, Conor F. Hayes, Elliot Meyerson, Babak Hodjat, Risto Miikkulainen, Xin Qiu
bullets: The paper characterizes this counterintuitive behavior across models, tasks, and modalities.
In high-dimensional spaces, perturbations often reduce performance but reveal informative directional signals.
Aggregating these signals enables local parent-model improvements despite uniformly worse sampled offspring.
The phenomenon arises from the interaction between reward-landscape curvature and the ES estimator’s noise.
The findings offer guidance for using perturbation-based optimization in LLM fine-tuning and other high-dimensional problems.

At each iteration, offspring are generated which are all worse than the parent model in measured reward. (b) Fraction of perturbations better than the parent in the Sudoku fine-tuning task over iterations in the training run. Larger batch size leads to less noise in the reward landscape, and makes the paradox more prominent.

Figure 9: (a): A visual representation of reward vs. perturbation magnitude, demonstrating why the offspring are worse than the parent. Perturbations happen at a fixed size; if they are too small, observation noise drowns out differences between good and bad directions, and if they are too big, the correlation between perturbation reward and direction quality breaks down. The paradox occurs when the magnitude is at a distance where all perturbations have a reward worse than the current model, but they still differentiate the good directions from the bad. (b) A demonstration of the tradeoff in perturbation size empirically, with performance of Qwen 2.5 7B on the Sudoku task after 300 ES iterations varying σ, holding all else constant. Results illustrate observation noise deteriorating performance at small values of σ, and correlations breaking down at large values, demonstrating the tradeoff visualized by (a).

Figure 5: Correlation between rewards at various perturbation magnitudes σ at iterations 200 and 500 iterations in the Sudoku Fine-Tuning task. The σ range at which the paradox occurs, i.e. the best of the 30 offspring has a lower reward than the parent, is labeled with red arrows. The rewards at small and large σ correlate significantly. Thus, the same good directions can be identified at various perturbation magnitudes, even at which all the perturbations are worse than the parent.

Figure 3: Reward distributions at different perturbation magnitudes. Checkpoints in Countdown and Sudoku training runs were perturbed 300 times at each specified magnitude, and distributions of rewards were plotted. As the magnitudes increase, the means decrease, and the variance increases. Thus, the offspring are likely to perform worse than the parent.

Even though the smaller perturbation magnitudes produce better candidates, the larger perturbations produce better directions and thus a better overall training run.

papers.abstract: Real-world problems span diverse domains, including program synthesis, symbolic reasoning, planning, and optimization, and often require fundamentally different solution paradigms. A central challenge for LLM-based reasoning is twofold: identifying an appropriate problem-solving approach and formulating it correctly. In this paper, we propose AlgoPilot, a cross-paradigm reasoning framework that enables adaptive selection of the solving approaches and structured problem formulation prior to execution. The AlgoPilot framework contains three components: 1) a SteerLM, trained via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL), that adaptively selects the solving strategy (paradigm and modes) based on input problems, 2) the corresponding expert GuideLM, trained via SFT, that generates structured formulation guidance tailored to the selected strategy, and 3) an ExecutionLM that generates solutions conditioned on both the selected strategy and its formulation. Unlike prompting-based methods that rely on fixed reasoning templates, our approach learns to adaptively choose and structure problem-solving strategies based on the input. We build AlgoPilot on Qwen3-8B and evaluate across 5 problem categories and 13 benchmarks with 66 unique domains, comparing against both the latest similarly scaled small models and large LLMs. AlgoPilot significantly improves average accuracy for the same model from 38.4% to 72.9%, outperforming the best large LLM prompting baseline GLM-5 by 11.7%. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of each component. Notably, we show that the learned steering and formulation modules can transfer across execution models, suggesting their potential to improve other LLMs. Project page: https://sites.google.com/view/algopilot.
authors: Yilun Hao, Ruixiao Yang, Hudson Hilal, Yongchao Chen, Kaizhi Qian, Yada Zhu, Yang Zhang, Chuchu Fan
bullets: Targets cross-domain reasoning challenges in program synthesis, symbolic reasoning, planning, and optimization.

Raises average accuracy from 38.4% to 72.9% and exceeds the reported GLM-5 prompting baseline by 11.7%.
Ablations support the value of each component, while steering and formulation modules transfer across execution models.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Reward (RLVR) has emerged as a promising approach for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of large language models. However, it still remains unclear whether RLVR can extend reasoning capabilities beyond what is already encoded in the base model. In this paper, we study this question through the lens of primacy bias: the tendency of models to over-rely on already-learned representations, disproportionately improving performance on problems they already handle well while underexploring harder ones that require departing from those representations. Through our controlled experiments and large-scale analysis, we show that RLVR training on mixed data tends to further sharpen performance on easier problems while yielding only marginal gains on harder ones. We find that although hard problems lead to modest gains overall, they are actually the ones that help most in expanding the model's reasoning capabilities and pushing the representations. However, prolonged training on these hard problems may also hurt and lead to forgetting on easy problems. These findings help to better understand some of the prior conflicting observations about RLVR, specifically, why on (OOD) domains where the base model performs poorly, improvements on hard problems can expand reasoning; while on well-trained domains, forgetting can reduce performance and mask genuine gains obtained from hard problems.
authors: Phuc Minh Nguyen, Ngoc-Hieu Nguyen, Parshin Shojaee, Chinh Duc La, Duy Minh Ho Nguyen, Rui Zhang, Khoa D. Doan, Ting Hua, Nitesh V. Chawl
bullets: Mixed-data RLVR disproportionately improves problems the base model already solves well, with limited gains on harder problems.

The findings reconcile conflicting RLVR results across in-distribution and out-of-distribution domains.

papers.abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation consolidates expert capabilities by supervising student-generated trajectories, whereas task arithmetic offers a training-free alternative through linear parameter combinations. We view the linear combination of student and expert parameters as a single differentiable model and propose P$^2$-MOPD, which jointly optimizes the mixing coefficients and the student weights under the same on-policy distillation objective. Unlike task arithmetic, which stays within the span of the frozen student and expert parameters for any choice of merging coefficients, P$^2$-MOPD keeps the student trainable, so the experts act as parameter priors without confining it to this span. Across four domains at 1.7B and 4B scales, P$^2$-MOPD achieves faster and more balanced recovery than MOPD from the same initialization, surpassing its final average recovery in half the training steps. At the end of training, our 1.7B model reaches 94.7% average recovery, versus 80.9% for MOPD.
authors: Sinuo Wang, Jiacheng Lu, Zeyu Zhang, Maojia Song, Rui Sun, Beidi Luan, Yutong Xie, Jing Li, Daxin Jiang, Qi Wu, Zuo Bai
bullets: Addresses the slow or imbalanced recovery of expert capabilities during multi-teacher on-policy distillation.
Treats the linear combination of student and expert parameters as a differentiable model optimized with the distillation objective.
Uses expert parameters as priors while keeping the student trainable, avoiding confinement to the experts’ parameter span.
Evaluated across four domains at 1.7B and 4B scales; it surpasses MOPD’s final average recovery in half the training steps.
At 1.7B, it reaches 94.7% average recovery versus 80.9% for MOPD at the end of training.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of P2-MOPD. Each projection of the student is composed as its own learnable full weight plus a learnable linear combination of frozen expert directions, Wm = Bm + ∑ k αk,mτk,m (Equation (4)), and the composed weights are used as one model for the forward pass. The student generates rollouts on prompts of all domains; the frozen teacher of each prompt’s domain scores the student’s tokens. The sampled tokens and the teacher logits are passed as detached data flow (gray lines), and the resulting MOPD loss is back-propagated to the student weights (student weight channel) and to the coefficients α (coefficient channel). No gradient reaches the experts or the teachers, which come from the same expert bank.

papers.abstract: Reasoning substantially improves language models' ability to solve difficult problems, but long reasoning traces make these gains expensive. Efficient reasoning should express useful analysis in fewer tokens by reducing repetition and text that adds little value to solving the problem. Progress in proprietary models motivates this goal, yet their hidden scratchpads limit direct study of how it is achieved. We investigate whether open-weight models can generate less verbose reasoning by changing the form of their own earlier thoughts, without retraining. Our intervention rewrites prior reasoning into compact state records before pending tool results are revealed, then compares continuations from original and compact histories. Across the tested models, accepted compact histories usually shorten future reasoning; a coding case study also shows less repeated verification after a shared candidate solution. In software-agent deployments, compaction can reduce total spending, although task quality and rewrite-inclusive time depend on the target and compressor. These findings identify reasoning history as one way to reduce future reasoning-token use and motivate model-specific compaction policies evaluated for both efficiency and retained capability.
bullets: Long reasoning traces improve problem-solving but can be expensive due to repetition and low-value text.
The study compacts earlier reasoning before pending tool results are revealed, then compares generation from original versus rewritten histories without retraining.
Across tested models, accepted compact histories generally shortened subsequent reasoning; a coding case showed less repeated verification.
Software-agent deployments achieved lower total spending, but task quality and rewrite-inclusive time varied by target and compressor.
The results motivate model-specific compaction policies that balance efficiency with retained capability.

papers.title: Why Pay for Long Reasoning When Rewrite Do Trick? Causal Effects of Reasoning History Compaction on Future Generation and Agent Cost
papers.tldr: Rewriting an agent’s prior reasoning into compact state records can reduce future reasoning and cost, but its effects on quality and latency depend on the model and compressor.

papers.abstract: Long-to-Short (L2S) model merging seeks to combine the strong reasoning capability of long chain-of-thought models with the concise style of base models, but existing methods that rely on linear interpolation and first-order activation statistics fail to capture how the loss landscape responds to parameter displacement, leading to degraded accuracy on hard tasks. We propose Low-Rank Hierarchical Merging (LHM), a training-free framework that replaces heuristic statistics with lightweight second-order curvature information. LHM consists of three components: (1) a low-rank Hessian approximation that efficiently estimates per-layer Hessian traces via Hutchinson's estimator on random inputs, eliminating the need for task-specific data; (2) a Layer Second-Order Sensitivity (LSOS) index that combines Hessian trace with task-vector norm to quantify per-layer fusion difficulty; and (3) a Dual-Constraint Coefficient Mapping (DCCM) that converts LSOS scores into layer-adaptive merge coefficients while jointly satisfying a fusion-error bound and a global length-reduction target. Experiments across six mathematical benchmarks on 1.5B and 7B models show that LHM outperforms state-of-the-art methods such as ACM-TIES and ORCA, achieving over 4\% accuracy gain and up to 93.1\% reduction in output length relative to the long-CoT model.
authors: Zeqiu Yu, Xuesheng Zhang, Wenxiao Zhao, Shixiao Wang
bullets: Addresses the limitations of linear interpolation and first-order statistics in merging long-chain-of-thought and concise models.
Uses low-rank Hutchinson-based Hessian estimates, an LSOS layer-sensitivity score, and DCCM layer-adaptive coefficients.
Requires no task-specific data and jointly enforces a fusion-error bound and target length reduction.
Across six mathematical benchmarks and 1.5B/7B models, it reports over 4% higher accuracy and up to 93.1% shorter outputs than the long-CoT model.
The abstract evaluates mathematical reasoning; broader task or domain scope is unspecified.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overall framework of Low-Rank Hierarchical Merging (LHM). The framework then comprises three modules: (1) Low-Rank Hessian Approximation, which estimates loss-landscape curvature using Rademacher random vectors to compute per-layer Hessian traces; (2) LSOS Index, which combines these traces with the ℓ2 norms of the task vector via element-wise multiplication to evaluate layer importance; and (3) Dual-Constraint Coefficient Mapping (DCCM), which applies min–max normalization and dual orthogonal constraints (balancing accuracy preservation and length reduction) to generate layer-wise merge coefficients λi. The merged model θmerged preserves strong reasoning accuracy while producing substantially shorter outputs.

papers.title: Low-Rank Hierarchical Merging for Efficient Long-to-Short Reasoning
papers.tldr: LHM is a training-free, curvature-aware model-merging method that improves long-to-short reasoning while substantially reducing output length.

papers.abstract: Language models are typically trained with a single choice of architecture on diverse domains and data sources. Modern transformers have been extensively refined for such general-purpose learning, but are they equally effective across different subsets of the pretraining data? We investigate this question by training small language models from scratch on representative subsets of pretraining data such as web text, code, and mathematics. We introduce variants of transformers in which standard activation functions are replaced with learned splines tuned on specific datasets, providing a simple way to modify their inductive biases. Using a mix-and-match of architectures and datasets, we evaluate cross-domain transfer, i.e. how well does an architecture tuned for one domain perform on data from another? We find that the tuned transformer variants improve training efficiency or generalization on all seven of our tested datasets, but the gains are often domain-specific. For example, architectures tuned on a natural language dataset such as FineWeb perform well on TinyStories, whereas those tuned on mathematics perform poorly on natural language. We identify several mechanisms underlying these improvements, including wider loss basins and more abundant "lottery tickets". Our results show that different subsets of pretraining data can benefit from different learning mechanisms, highlighting a limitation of the prevailing trend towards a small set of general-purpose architectures and optimizers. This points to an opportunity to improve data efficiency by developing domain-specific learning strategies that retain the ability to train general-purpose models.
authors: Damien Teney, Liangze Jiang, Zachary Shinnick, Hemanth Saratchandran, Simon Lucey
bullets: The study tests small language models trained from scratch on web text, code, and mathematics.
It replaces standard transformer activations with learned splines tuned to specific datasets.
Cross-domain evaluations show that architectures tuned for natural language transfer better within language domains, while math-tuned variants perform poorly on natural language.
Improvements appear across all seven tested datasets, with mechanisms linked to wider loss basins and more abundant lottery tickets.
The findings suggest domain-specific learning strategies could improve data efficiency while supporting general-purpose models.

papers.abstract: Financial workflows need fast, calibrated, auditable decisions, not just generated text. We train System-1 decision models, small language models fine-tuned to answer typed questions (choice/score/noul) with a probability in a single forward pass, across two model families (K2-Horizon and Qwen3.5/3.8) and nine rungs from 0.8B to 32B parameters, using one frozen LoRA recipe on a public decision benchmark and two new finance corpora: a programmatic-gold policy corpus (rule-reading with exact labels) and a reality-labeled outcome corpus (19,640 realized forward-return questions in walk-forward splits, plus a sealed 2026 test of 1,360 questions). Narrow fine-tuning costs general decision competence 9-45 percentage points, a data-mixture effect that shrinks with model scale and is associated with narrow-gradient volume. On reality-labeled questions, every trained rung from 0.8B to 32B lands at the horizon-conditioned prior baseline (accuracy 0.37-0.38, no detectable conditional edge under our controls); the models respond with flat, well-calibrated probabilities that track per-horizon base rates: naturally honest uncertainty, with a mid-scale calibration sweet spot (ECE 0.026 at 2B, degrading to 0.043-0.044 at 9-32B under prior drift). A mixed-corpus remediation carries all competencies in one adapter at modest cost: it matches or slightly exceeds the generalist specialist on the public benchmark while holding the policy ceiling and near-specialist outcome calibration, yielding a deployable artifact with per-domain temperature regimes and a band-dispatch escalation analysis: sharp, dispatchable bands where rules determine answers; flat, review-routing bands where reality does not.
bullets: Models answer typed finance questions with probabilities in one forward pass across 0.8B–32B parameters and multiple model families.
Narrow fine-tuning reduces general decision competence by 9–45 percentage points, with the effect weakening as models scale.
On realized-return questions, models show no detectable conditional edge and instead produce flat, well-calibrated probabilities that follow horizon-specific base rates.
Calibration is strongest at mid-scale, while larger models degrade under prior drift.
A mixed-corpus adapter preserves policy performance and near-specialist outcome calibration, supporting domain-specific temperature regimes and escalation by confidence bands.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates small LLMs for finance, focusing on calibration, honesty, and specialization collapse, relevant to efficient and robust LLM deployment.
papers.title: Honest Small Decision Models for Finance: Scale, Specialization Collapse, and Mixed-Corpus Remediation

papers.abstract: Why do some of the world's most powerful Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems still struggle to reason about cause and effect? Causal discovery, the ability to discern the underlying drivers of a system, is fundamental to scientific inquiry and has traditionally relied on structured data and statistical methods. Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have been explored as an alternative paradigm for causal inference, leveraging their broad knowledge and reasoning capabilities. Yet, despite their linguistic fluency, LLMs often rely on surface-level pattern recognition rather than genuine causal logic. While it is known that LLMs stumble in this domain, we lack a precise map of where, why, and how significantly these failures occur. In this paper, we propose a systematic stress-test framework across six critical dimensions: model scale, causal graph complexity, prompting strategy, metadata quality, data quality, and sensitivity to uncertainty. Our findings reveal a significant "optimism bias" in LLMs; models consistently overestimate causal links, leading to low precision across the board. Furthermore, we demonstrate that traditional evaluation metrics can be deceptive: while reasoning-heavy models lead in performance, the highest scores often occur when uncertainty in inference is overlooked. Once uncertainty is integrated into the evaluation, performance drops, providing a more honest reflection of causal reliability. We also find that, while scaling model size improves outcomes, these gains are fragile; performance degrades sharply as the quality of metadata decreases. This work serves as a practical guide to the blind spots of LLMs, offering a clear-eyed assessment of when these tools can be integrated into a causal discovery pipeline and when they are likely to lead researchers astray.
authors: Ankitkumar Patel, Jigarkumar Patel, Amit Kumar, Supreetha Sreeram, Venkatesh Kulkarni
bullets: Evaluates LLM causal discovery across model scale, graph complexity, prompting, metadata quality, data quality, and uncertainty.
Finds a consistent optimism bias: LLMs overestimate causal relationships, resulting in low precision.
Shows that conventional metrics can overstate performance when uncertainty is ignored; uncertainty-aware evaluation lowers scores.
Larger models perform better, but their gains degrade sharply with lower-quality metadata.
Provides practical guidance on when LLMs may support causal discovery and when they risk misleading researchers.

papers.selection_reason: Systematically evaluates LLM robustness in causal inference tasks, identifying failure modes like 'optimism bias' and fragility, which is relevant to understanding LLM reasoning capabilities.
papers.title: Stress-Testing the Robustness of LLM-Based Causal Inference
papers.tldr: A systematic stress test shows that LLMs often overpredict causal links, and their apparent causal-reasoning gains are fragile—especially under uncertainty and poor metadata.

papers.abstract: Language models often spread a concept across many internal dimensions, making their features difficult to interpret. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) recover clearer features after training. We ask whether models can instead learn interpretable output coordinates directly. We introduce Mixture of Wide Experts (MoWE), a sparse feed-forward layer in which selected experts read the full representation but write to fixed, disjoint output coordinates. On a controlled task with known hidden causes, this design preserves predictive performance while localizing causes more clearly than dense and standard mixture-of-experts (MoE) models. At approximately matched compute, we train two 19-layer runs of each architecture for 10 billion tokens. MoWE achieves evaluation cross-entropy 2.417 versus 2.452 for dense, while standard MoE reaches 2.22. We measure native-coordinate readability by asking a language-model judge to describe each coordinate from passages where it is strongly active and test that description on new passages. Correcting for descriptions that also fit other coordinates gives a specificity score of 0.523 for MoWE, 0.375 for dense, and 0.268 for standard MoE. TopK SAEs trained on the same FFN updates score 0.489 for dense and 0.556 for MoWE, making native MoWE comparable to the dense SAE. In the first case study, we identify a four-coordinate causal path supporting the model's prediction of degrees after the prompt A right angle is 90. We then copy seven angle-related coordinate values into the model as it processes A rectangle has four, changing its next-token prediction from sides to degrees. In the second, one fixed coordinate set detects hazardous requests and another steers the next token toward refusal. These examples show that MoWE combines sparse conditional computation with coordinates that can be identified and reused directly.
authors: Tavish Mankash, Vardhaman Kalloli, Keshava Prasad, Deepan Muthirayan
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of interpreting concepts distributed across many model dimensions.
Routes inputs to selected experts that read the full representation but write to disjoint, fixed coordinates.
On a controlled task, MoWE outperforms dense models in predictive performance and improves coordinate specificity over dense and standard MoE models, though standard MoE has lower cross-entropy.
Native MoWE coordinates approach the readability of sparse-autoencoder features and can reveal causal paths and steer predictions.
Demonstrations include detecting hazardous requests, inducing refusals, and changing an angle-related prediction from “sides” to “degrees.”

papers.selection_reason: Introduces Mixture of Wide Experts (MoWE), a novel sparse feed-forward architecture for LLMs that uses fixed, disjoint output coordinates to improve feature interpretability, directly relevant to LLM architecture and interpretability.
papers.title: Mixture of Wide Experts: Sparse Routing for Interpretable Native Coordinates
papers.tldr: MoWE uses sparse experts with fixed output coordinates to make language-model features more interpretable and directly reusable while largely preserving predictive performance.

papers.abstract: Steering vectors (SVs) are residual-stream directions that shift the behavior of LLMs when added to hidden states at inference time. While prior work has mainly used SVs as post-hoc controls, we ask whether the same directions can also guide parameter updates during post-training. We study this question across supervised learning, including SFT and distillation, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Our framework considers two intervention regimes: a hidden-state hook during teacher-forced supervised training, and an advantage-repair mechanism on wrong rollouts in GRPO. For each regime, we analyze three design axes, which are the steering direction, its placement, and the operation used to combine it with training. In supervised settings, SV injection improves over plain SFT and distillation, with gains scaling with the off-policy gap and reaching up to a $12\%$ improvement when distilling from thinking-mode teachers. These gains hold across three random seeds. In RL settings, applying a correctness-contrast direction as advantage repair on wrong rollouts, including otherwise zero-gradient all-wrong groups, recovers a learning signal that transfers to held-out math benchmarks and acts as a composable auxiliary signal that adds to existing zero-variance remedies such as entropy-aware advantage shaping. We further identify three failure boundaries. In detail, code generation can break the direction, cross-family layer transfer can break the placement, and inference-time application on an SV-trained checkpoint can break the intervention regime. Together, these results establish steering vectors as a conditional but effective training signal for LLM post-training. Our code is available here.
bullets: The study extends steering vectors from inference-time behavior control to parameter updates during SFT, distillation, and RL with verifiable rewards.
It tests hidden-state injection for supervised training and correctness-contrast advantage repair on wrong GRPO rollouts.
Supervised steering improves over plain SFT and distillation, with gains increasing with the off-policy gap and reaching up to 12% when distilling from thinking-mode teachers.
In RL, advantage repair restores learning signals for otherwise zero-gradient all-wrong groups and transfers to held-out math benchmarks.
Effectiveness has boundaries: directions may fail for code generation, layer placement may not transfer across model families, and inference-time steering may fail on SV-trained checkpoints.

papers.selection_reason: The paper introduces a novel method for using steering vectors as a training signal during LLM post-training (SFT, distillation, RLVR). This directly contributes to the architecture and training of Large Language Models.
papers.title: Steering Vectors as a Training Signal in LLM Post-Training
papers.tldr: Steering vectors can improve LLM post-training when injected into supervised learning or used to repair RL advantages, but their effectiveness depends on the direction, placement, and intervention regime.

papers.abstract: In the near future language model pretraining will become bound by total data rather than total compute. Such a regime requires revisiting scaling laws and scaling law theory. Motivated by prior works that have found utility in ensembling, we study how the number of training epochs and ensemble size jointly shape generalization when training data are fixed. In language-model experiments on FineWeb, logit averaging reduces late-training deterioration, delays optimal stopping, and can outperform wider or deeper single models at matched parameter-token budgets over a common training horizon. To analyze this interaction between data reuse and ensembling, we derive a dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) for multi-epoch stochastic gradient descent in power-law random-feature ensembles, tracking error correlations across epochs and models. Ensembling reduces the prediction variance responsible for late-time growth in expected test error, changing the optimal stopping time. We use these stopping times to derive compute-allocation laws at fixed data and individual model sizes. Under this allocation, ensemble size grows with compute at least as fast as training time per member, while excess test loss above the limiting loss decreases as a power of compute.
bullets: Studies how training epochs and ensemble size jointly affect generalization in the data-limited regime.
FineWeb experiments show logit averaging reduces late-training deterioration and delays optimal stopping.
Ensembles can outperform wider or deeper single models at matched parameter-token budgets over a shared training horizon.
Develops a dynamical mean-field theory for multi-epoch SGD that tracks cross-epoch and cross-model error correlations.
Derives compute-allocation laws: ensemble size should grow at least as quickly as each member’s training time, with excess loss decreasing as a power of compute.

papers.abstract: Most parameters of a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model belong to its experts, and standard training keeps every expert gradient in GPU memory until the optimizer step. This memory grows with the number and size of the experts, so it rises as MoE models scale. We introduce Sonar-MoE, which updates each expert tensor during the backward pass and frees its gradient right away. It brings optimizer-in-backward from dense models to batched MoE expert tensors, so the GPU never holds more than one layer of expert gradients. When we fine-tune OLMoE-1B-7B and Granite-3.1-3B-A800M in bf16 with two expert-kernel backends, Sonar-MoE lowers peak memory by 19% to 22%. Its updates are bitwise identical to standard training without expert gradient clipping, and held-out loss stays within 0.003 of all baselines. Each step also takes 17% to 23% less time than standard training with global-norm clipping. Updating whole batched tensors rather than individual experts is what keeps Sonar-MoE fast, as it avoids a 20% to 72% slowdown while using the same memory. Sonar-MoE matches optimizer-in-backward over all parameters in memory and speed while still clipping the dense parameters.
bullets: Addresses GPU memory growth caused by retaining gradients for all MoE experts until the optimizer step.
Updates batched expert tensors in backward, limiting retained expert gradients to one layer at a time.
Reduces peak memory by 19–22% and step time by 17–23% in the reported bf16 fine-tuning experiments.
Preserves bitwise-identical updates without expert gradient clipping, while held-out loss remains within 0.003 of baselines.
Whole-batched-tensor updates avoid the slowdown associated with updating experts individually; dense parameters can still use gradient clipping.

papers.selection_reason: Memory-efficient MoE training method directly relevant to LLM architectures and efficient AI.
papers.title: Sonar-MoE: In-Backward Expert Updates for Memory-Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Training
papers.tldr: Sonar-MoE reduces peak memory and training time for MoE fine-tuning by updating expert parameters during backpropagation and immediately freeing their gradients.

papers.abstract: Computer programmers chain together the same reusable computational primitives, for example, conditional statements or loops, but in different orders to implement different algorithms. In contrast, existing language model architectures always execute their layers in the same order. We introduce Library of Layers (LoL), an architecture that dynamically orders its layers during inference to solve the problem at hand. LoL has a single hyperparameter, the size of its global library of transformer blocks, that allows it to transition seamlessly between parameter reuse and sparsity, generalizing the parameter-efficiency and FLOPs-efficiency tradeoffs of dense, depth-recurrent, and mixture of experts architectures in one unified family. We show that LoL achieves competitive performance with all three above baselines when pretrained on text data. On synthetic sudoku and maze data, we observe that the model employs distinct layer orderings to implement different solution strategies, and we can intervene on routing to force a model to apply a specific solution strategy to a problem instance. In a multilingual natural language setting, we find that LoL chooses different layer order patterns based on language and script. Similarly, we train LoL on safety data and fit probes to its router outputs, finding that these probes distinguish safe from unsafe text with high AUROC. LoL provides a path toward a future in which models dynamically compose their own computational graph, enabling more efficient and controllable reasoning.
bullets: Addresses the fixed layer ordering used by standard language models.
Uses a global library of transformer blocks whose runtime routing determines layer order.
A single library-size hyperparameter spans parameter reuse and sparsity, unifying efficiency tradeoffs across dense, depth-recurrent, and mixture-of-experts models.
Matches the performance of these baselines on text pretraining and exhibits distinct routing patterns for sudoku, mazes, languages, and scripts.
Routing can be intervened on to force solution strategies, while router probes distinguish safe from unsafe text with high AUROC.

figures.caption: Figure 1: We introduce Library of Layers (LoL), a novel architecture where the next executed transformer layer is chosen at runtime. We use strided window attention within the routed core to allow information to flow through the sequence dimension while using the same attention and MLP parameters for all tokens within each window.

Figure 6: Library of Layers is competitive with mixture of experts models. Left: Cross-entropy training loss over training FLOPs, averaged over 3 random seeds. We see growing gives LoL an early loss advantage and both models finish training with similar training losses. Right: Heatmap of expert utilization of one LoL model. We see some experts are heavily used by specific routed depths or neighboring groups of depths, while others are used diversely over depths, showing LoL learns to use the sparsity effectively.

Figure 3: Library of Layers learns distinct paths for different languages and distinct strategies when solving sudoku puzzles and mazes. Left: PCA projection of the routing paths of a 360M parameter LoL model trained on an equal mixture of 10 languages. We see the paths taken are distinct per language and Latin-script languages use similar paths. Middle and Right: We train 360M parameter LoL models to solve sudoku (middle) and mazes (right), using 5 different strategies. We then force each strategy’s mode path at inference time and see the models use the correct strategy (algorithm) with close to 100% accuracy.

Figure 5: Library of Layers is competitive with looped transformer models. Left: Cross-entropy evaluation loss, matching the number of unique layers in the core block of the LoL and looped transformer. We see LoL performs competitively with looped transformer models and offers more flexibility in layer ordering. Error bars are min/max loss over 3 random seeds. We note larger variance for the LoL models as changing the random seed changes the paths explored during training. Right: Cross-entropy training loss over training FLOPs, averaged over 3 random seeds per model.

Figure 4: Library of Layers is competitive with vanilla dense models. Left: Cross-entropy training loss over training FLOPs for 1B models. We see growing gives LoL an early loss advantage and all models finish with comparable training loss. Right: Heatmap of expert utilization of one LoL model. We see experts mainly tend to be used in groups of neighboring depths, but some are used throughout the model.

Figure 2: Library of Layers uses strided window attention and a top-1 router to allow for efficient training. LoL is made up of a prelude, a routed core, and a coda. The layers in the prelude and coda can attend over the whole sequence. In the core, the sequence is split into windows of W tokens, and at every routed depth a router selects one layer from the shared library per window (topleft). Attention is restricted to each window, but the window boundaries shift by S tokens between successive routed depths, allowing information to flow across windows (Strided Window Attention, top-right). Window 0 has no history, so its router uses the first token and a learned vector e(ℓ) for routed depth ℓ (bottom-left). For window i > 0, the router averages the mean hidden states of earlier windows 0, . . . , i − 1 and selects one layer (bottom-right). With W = 4 and S = 2, Layers 1 and 3 share the same boundaries while Layer 2 is offset, so information can pass between neighboring windows. Token 5 is highlighted in red to show this: in Layer 1 it is the first token in a new window, while in Layer 2 its window includes tokens 3 and 4.

papers.selection_reason: Dynamically ordered transformer layers form a novel LLM architecture with parameter/FLOPs efficiency tradeoffs.
papers.title: Library of Layers (LoL): Adaptively Ordering Transformer Layers at Runtime
papers.tldr: Library of Layers dynamically reorders transformer blocks at inference, enabling input-dependent computation and controllable solution strategies within one architecture.

papers.abstract: We introduce Axion 1.0, a fully open agent foundation model that combines strong and broad agentic capabilities with a remarkably simple training recipe. Axion 1.0 is trained in only three stages: two lightweight supervised fine-tuning stages followed by reinforcement learning, without dedicated mid-training, direct preference optimization (DPO), or on-policy distillation (OPD). The first SFT stage develops strong self-contained reasoning through model-aware data construction, where we synthesize challenging problems and adversarially strengthen them based on the base model's own successful solution strategies. The second stage extends these capabilities to tool-dependent reasoning through a scalable pipeline for constructing diverse and automatically verifiable tasks grounded in real-world data sources and deterministic computation. Finally, reinforcement learning further strengthens long-horizon reasoning and interaction with external tools and environments. Despite this compact training recipe, Axion 1.0 achieves strong performance across a broad suite of agentic benchmarks and is competitive with leading commercial models on several of them. Equally importantly, Axion 1.0 is open beyond model weights: we release the complete recipe, including data construction, generation, filtering, verification, prompts, and training code, enabling the entire development process to be reproduced and extended. Axion 1.0 demonstrates that strong agent foundation models can be both open and simple, offering a practical and reproducible path toward advancing open agentic intelligence.
bullets: Uses two lightweight supervised fine-tuning stages followed by reinforcement learning, without dedicated mid-training, DPO, or on-policy distillation.
Builds self-contained reasoning through model-aware synthesis and adversarial problem strengthening.
Extends reasoning to tool use via diverse, automatically verifiable tasks grounded in real-world data and deterministic computation.
Reinforcement learning improves long-horizon reasoning and interaction with tools and environments.
Reports strong results across agentic benchmarks, including competitiveness with leading commercial models on several tasks; releases the full development recipe and code.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of the two-stage data construction pipeline. Stage I constructs self-contained scientific reasoning problems from public seeds. An initial composition step increases their difficulty; problems solved by the base model are further strengthened using one of four transformations (A–D). An LLM then generates solutions, from which correct reasoning trajectories are retained. Stage II constructs tool-dependent questions through deterministic filtering, selection, and computation over structured data sources. The construction-time answers and direct database access are withheld during solving, and only verified tool-use trajectories are retained for SFT.

Figure 1 Performance comparison of Axion 1.0 with leading open and proprietary models across six challenging benchmarks, spanning general reasoning, scientific reasoning, search, and agentic problem solving. Blue and Teal bars represent Axion 1.0-122B and Axion 1.0-35B, respectively, while gray bars denote competing models. Despite its simple three-stage training recipe, Axion 1.0 achieves competitive or superior performance against frontier models across diverse reasoning and agentic tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Open agent foundation model with a simplified training recipe, relevant to LLM foundation model development.
papers.title: Axion 1.0: Open Agent Foundation Models, Simplified
papers.tldr: Axion 1.0 shows that strong, broadly capable agent models can be built openly with a simple three-stage training recipe and fully reproducible resources.

papers.abstract: LLM post-training via reinforcement learning has shown consistent improvements in accuracy at the cost of reducing behavioral coverage - a phenomenon known as sharpening that can stall progress on difficult tasks. Repeated sampling objectives such as $\mathrm{pass@k}$ and $\mathrm{max@k}$ are known to mitigate sharpening, but the mechanism behind it remains poorly understood. Moreover, existing approaches for $\mathrm{@k}$ optimization use dedicated algorithms, and no general framework exists for adapting established policy optimization methods from $\mathrm{@}1$ to $\mathrm{@k}$. We derive the optimal policies for KL-regularized $\mathrm{pass@k}$ and $\mathrm{max@k}$ objectives in closed form. Our explicit solutions reveal that $\mathrm{@k}$ optimization naturally redistributes learning pressure based on prompt difficulty, directing it toward harder problems. Crucially, we show that standard $\mathrm{@}1$ objectives achieve these exact same optimal policies through prompt-adaptive regularization or reward transformation. Ultimately, this yields an optimizer-independent explanation for why $\mathrm{@k}$ objectives reduce sharpening on easy tasks while prioritizing success on harder ones. Building on these insights, we introduce $\mathrm{@k}$ Adaptive Pressure for Policy Optimization (KAPPO). Following a one-time reference calibration, KAPPO seamlessly adapts existing $\mathrm{@}1$ methods to $\mathrm{@k}$ via prompt-adaptive regularization or reward transformation, without otherwise altering their training procedures. Experiments with several RL methods on mathematical reasoning and code generation demonstrate that KAPPO provides direct control over sharpening. Crucially, we demonstrate that $\mathrm{@k}$ pressure can be fully realized with single completion training, matching the performance of multi-completion $\mathrm{@k}$ optimizers at a fraction of the cost.
bullets: Sharpening improves accuracy but reduces behavioral coverage, hindering difficult-task progress.
Closed-form analyses of KL-regularized pass@k and max@k explain their prompt-difficulty-adaptive learning pressure.
The same optimal policies can be achieved with standard @1 objectives using adaptive regularization or reward transformation.
KAPPO applies this adaptation to existing policy optimizers after a one-time reference calibration.
Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation show single-completion KAPPO can match multi-completion @k optimization at lower cost.

figures.caption: Figure 3: MATH Level 5 validation performance of the starting checkpoints, @k-A⋆PO checkpoints, and PKPO checkpoints. @k-A⋆PO matches the performance of PKPO at a fraction of the on-policy training rollouts, requiring only a single-time reference calibration at ≤ 5% training time overhead.

Figure 2: pass@keval on AIME 2026 as the sampling budget at test time (keval) increases. Setting k > 1 during training consistently reduces sharpening. In Figure (a), we plot standard GRPO and @k-A⋆PO trained with k ∈ {1, 2, 4}. In Figure (b), we plot @k-DPO trained with k ∈ {1, 2}.

Figure 1: Adaptive pressure induced by @k objectives. (a) For binary rewards, increasing k strengthens regularization on easy tasks while retaining greater optimization pressure on difficult tasks. (b–c) For continuous rewards, we illustrate the same effect at k = 4 using synthetic “easy” Beta(8, 2) and “difficult” Beta(2, 8) reference reward distributions on [0, 1]. The easy task receives stronger effective regularization and smaller transformed rewards than the difficult task. All panels use β = 0.5.
Figure 4: max@keval on the hard subset of LiveCodeBench v6 for Qwen3-4B. Win-rate-based @k-A⋆PO (left) and @k-GRPO (right) mitigate excessive sharpening for k > 1.

Figure 7: Win-rate transformation and exact finite-bank noise and bias for M = 30 and β = 0.1. To compare different k, values are normalized by ∆T = T (1) − T (0); this normalization is only for display, and the transformation panel additionally subtracts T (0). The horizontal axis is the true reference quantile of a fixed raw reward. Noise and bias use the same axis conventions as Figure 6.

Figure 8: AIME 2026 test performance of the starting checkpoints and the selected @k-A⋆PO and PKPO checkpoints across evaluation sampling budgets. Each subfigure reports Qwen3-4B (left) and OLMo-3-7B (right).

Panels (a) and (b) use q̂ = N/M ; panel (c) uses Eq. 153. Coefficient errors are divided by the exact βeff(q); the endpoint q = 1, where this coefficient diverges for k > 1, is omitted. Noise uses logarithmic axes, while signed bias uses symmetric-logarithmic axes that are linear within [−10−6, 10−6]. Zero noise at deterministic endpoints is omitted from the logarithmic axes.

papers.selection_reason: Provides closed-form analysis and a general framework for pass@k objectives in LLM post-training, a meaningful contribution to LLM training methodology.
papers.title: Controlling Sharpening in LLM Post-Training
papers.tldr: KAPPO adapts standard single-completion RL objectives to control LLM sharpening, emphasizing harder prompts while reducing unnecessary pressure on easy ones.

papers.abstract: Scaling depth is a key route to stronger large language models, but Pre-LN architectures often suffer from depth-wise information dilution, limiting the effective use of deep layers. While cross-layer connectivity has proven effective at mitigating this problem, existing designs usually introduce additional computation or memory access. We revisit cross-layer KV sharing as an efficient form of such connectivity. Beyond cache compression, each KV reuse edge creates a direct gradient path from deep layers to source KV projections, turning KV sharing into an implicit structural regularizer for KV representation geometry. We provide a systematic analysis of this mechanism, showing that proper sharing topologies sharpen key retrieval directions while enriching the value content subspace, whereas existing adjacent or global-anchor designs do not fully exploit this effect. Motivated by this, we propose DepthGraft, a hierarchical KV-sharing architecture that reconstructs deep-layer KV from stride-aligned shallow-middle source pairs. DepthGraft distributes non-local gradient flow across source layers, while preserving prefill early completion and reducing KV cache by roughly one third. Experiments on dense and MoE models from 0.5B to 16B parameters show consistent downstream improvements under both GQA and MLA. Notably, on the 16B MoE model, DepthGraft achieves a 7.0% absolute improvement on MMLU-Pro, along with gains of 6.6% on CMMLU and 6.4% on C3. These results validate the potential of DepthGraft as a scalable design for large-scale pretraining. The project page is available at https://github.com/jianke0604/DepthGraft.
bullets: Addresses information dilution in deep Pre-LN language models without adding substantial cross-layer computation or memory access.
Uses stride-aligned shallow–middle source pairs to reconstruct deep-layer keys and values.
KV-sharing edges provide non-local gradient paths that sharpen key retrieval directions and enrich value representations.
Evaluated on dense and MoE models from 0.5B to 16B parameters under GQA and MLA, with consistent downstream gains.
On a 16B MoE model, reports improvements of 7.0% on MMLU-Pro, 6.6% on CMMLU, and 6.4% on C3.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a hierarchical KV-sharing LLM architecture that reduces KV cache by a third while improving downstream performance, fitting both efficiency and LLM architecture interests.
papers.title: DepthGraft: Structural Regularization through Hierarchical Cross-Layer KV Reconstruction
papers.tldr: DepthGraft hierarchically reuses KV projections across layers to regularize deep representations, reduce KV-cache memory by roughly one third, and improve language-model performance.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) mitigates the student's exposure bias by optimizing on student-generated trajectories. However, student-generated prefixes may contain reasoning errors or follow patterns unfamiliar to the teacher, undermining the reliability of its token-level supervision. This degradation becomes more pronounced as prefixes grow longer. To address this teacher-side distribution mismatch, we propose Student-Prefix Teacher Adaptation (SPTA), which adapts the teacher to the states on which it is queried during distillation. Specifically, before OPD starts, we collect student rollout prefixes with random lengths and continually train the teacher to continue from the prefixes using reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). By treating each prefix as context and rewarding correct final answers, the teacher learns to recover from student-induced states rather than imitate the student's reasoning. Then, the adapted teacher is used for standard OPD, with no changes to the distillation objective. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that our SPTA improves average student performance over standard OPD and OPD with task-level RLVR-adapted teachers. These results highlight the importance of adapting teachers not only to solve problems independently, but also to provide reliable guidance on the states their students actually visit.
bullets: Problem: Longer or erroneous student prefixes create a teacher–student distribution mismatch that weakens token-level supervision.
Method: Train the teacher on randomly sized student rollout prefixes using reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards before standard OPD.
The teacher learns to recover from student-induced states and produce correct continuations rather than imitate student reasoning.
SPTA leaves the standard OPD objective unchanged.
Experiments show higher average student performance than standard OPD and OPD using task-level RLVR-adapted teachers.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Standard OPD and Student-Prefix Teacher Adaptation (SPTA). (a) In standard OPD, student rollouts may enter regions unfamiliar to the teacher, reducing supervision reliability. (b) SPTA first adapts the teacher through prefix-conditioned RLVR, using student prefixes as context and final-answer correctness as reward, then freezes it for standard OPD. Shaded regions indicate prefixes familiar to the teacher before and after adaptation.

Figure 2: Student-prefix adaptation improves teacher recovery. Mean accuracy (avg@16 across five benchmarks) versus the fraction of a student rollout retained as context. Each panel compares the original teacher with its SPTA-Iter1 version on identical sampled student prefixes; 0% denotes clean-prompt generation. Recovery improves at every evaluated nonzero ratio, even though Qwen34B’s clean-prompt accuracy decreases.

Table 1: Student accuracy after distillation (%, avg@16). Avg. is the unweighted benchmark mean. All distillation runs use a single adaptation/distillation round, and within each pairing they share initialization and settings. Bold marks the best result in each column, including ties; the undistilled S0 row means the original student performance. ∗Prune-OPD scores are quoted from Yang et al. (2026) and were not reproduced by us, so they are listed for context rather than as a controlled comparison.

Teacher accuracies are means over five benchmarks (avg@16) at each student-prefix ratio r; benchmark-level results are in Appendix B. ∆ is SPTA minus Original in percentage points. The italic reference row in each block is the prefix-source student’s own accuracy, which is constant in r (see text) and serves as the break-even level below which the teacher carries no information the student lacks.
Table 4: Shared training settings across all teacher–student pairings. Input limits apply to the full conditioned input, including the student prefix in Stage I.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a teacher-adaptation method for on-policy distillation of LLM reasoning, a technically meaningful contribution to LLM training methodology.
papers.title: Meet Students Where They Are: Student-Prefix Teacher Adaptation for On-Policy Distillation
papers.tldr: SPTA adapts the teacher to student-generated reasoning states before on-policy distillation, improving guidance and average student performance on mathematical reasoning benchmarks.

papers.abstract: We classify real and complex state-space models (SSMs) with linear transitions, distinguishing fixed-basis diagonal equivalence from input-output equivalence and tracking coefficient-conditioning windows under coordinate changes. We characterize diagonal equivalence through commuting transition families whose members are diagonalizable over the chosen field. With time-shared token-local matrix maps, we identify this class's state-mediated kernels with unnormalized scalar-mode linear attention with multiplicative masks. Mamba 3's multiple-input, multiple-output (MIMO) construction lifts one value per local interface; SSD-MIMO routes independent values for local retrieval rank above one. HybridMamba combines Mamba 1's per-coordinate decay, Mamba 2-style heads and Mamba 3's complex rotations and two-endpoint writes, mixing real and rotating state blocks with different decay laws. They recover Mamba 1-3 single-input, single-output (SISO) configurations as exact special cases. On five large H100 bfloat16 workloads, our fused GPU kernels improve geometric-mean training time over official Mamba 1/3 in matched SISO recoveries, with Mamba 2 near parity at SSM-core scope. Memory tradeoffs depend on the baseline and metric: saved-for-backward versus peak allocation. In small-model multi-token recall experiments, both designs outperform Mamba 1-3 on the hardest tier; higher routing ranks perform best in gated or phase-diverse configurations. In single-seed language models with about 500M parameters, both improve on Mamba 1/2 in test loss at 2B tokens, but the routing gains do not translate into lower language-model loss. Our best configurations approach Mamba 3 SISO through 10B tokens while remaining behind it and Mamba 3 MIMO in language-model loss.
bullets: Characterizes diagonal equivalence via commuting, jointly diagonalizable transition families, while distinguishing it from input-output equivalence and tracking conditioning under coordinate changes.
Shows that time-shared token-local matrix maps yield state-mediated kernels equivalent to unnormalized scalar-mode linear attention with multiplicative masks.
Introduces SSD-MIMO and HybridMamba to support retrieval rank above one and combine real decays, complex rotations, multiple heads, and two-endpoint writes.
Fused kernels improve training time over matched Mamba 1/3 SISO recoveries; Mamba 2 is near parity at SSM-core scope, with memory effects depending on the measurement.
Higher routing ranks improve small-model multi-token recall, but routing gains do not translate to lower language-model loss; the best models remain behind Mamba 3 variants.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Local value routing, illustrated at equal total state width 4N . Left: four scalar interfaces, with Br t ∈ RN×1 and Cr t ∈ R1×N . Right: one SSD-MIMO group at R = O = 4 supplies the same vector to four sibling states, with Br t ∈ RN×4 and Cr t ∈ R4×N , then combines their vector readouts as yt = ∑ r ζr,tC r t h r t , with scalar sibling weights ζr,t. Both yield four output coordinates; parameter sharing and computation need not match; coefficient generation and feedthrough are omitted.

Figure 3: Transition classes at common field F, state dimension S ≥ 2 (for S = 1 they coincide) and horizon L. Whole ellipses use window bound ℓ̂; the shaded portions impose 1 ≤ ℓ < ℓ̂ ≤ L on every class, so DF(ℓ, S) = DF(ℓ̂, S) ∩ SF(ℓ, S), and likewise for commuting families. Diagonal equivalence requires, and is guaranteed by, pairwise commutativity and individual diagonalizability over F of the entire realized transition family (Theorem 8).

Figure 6: Validation-loss curves, one seed per arm, without smoothing: (a) the eleven main-table configurations at constant LR up to 2B tokens, with a 1–2B zoom; (b) the five configurations continued from 2B to 10B with cosine decay. Fixed-window validation losses, distinct from the test-shard losses of Table 7.

papers.selection_reason: Theoretical and empirical study of state space model architectures for language modeling.
papers.title: Diagonal Equivalence in State Space Models: Characterization, Retrieval Rank, and Selective Extensions
papers.tldr: The paper characterizes diagonally equivalent SSMs, connects them to scalar-mode linear attention, and proposes higher-rank retrieval extensions that improve recall but do not consistently improve language-model loss.

papers.abstract: Theoretical limitations of transformers on state tracking---the ability to track information about entities or variables over long contexts---have motivated new recurrent language modeling (LM) architectures such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN). These architectures have, in particular, been benchmarked against the $S_5$ word problem, a theoretically hard state-tracking task that captures abilities such as code evaluation under arbitrary variable assignment. It, however, remains open whether other, simpler forms of state tracking might both be more relevant in practice and already explain observed differences between these architectures. We propose evaluating state tracking using a hierarchy of word problems with four increasing levels of difficulty: r-trivial, corresponding to immutable assignment to variables in programming; aperiodic, where assignments are mutable; soluble, where assignments are self-referential; and general finite state tracking. Theoretically, we show that the class of problems transformers are thought to length-generalize on does not even contain all aperiodic state tracking. On the other hand, we prove that GDN with positive eigenvalues expresses all aperiodic problems, and the regular languages recognized by certain transformers are precisely all soluble ones, thus providing a fine-grained picture of state tracking capabilities of various architectures. Taking these ideas to practice, we construct StateBench, a 4-tier long-horizon state-tracking benchmark. Our systematic direct training experiments across architectures largely align with theoretical expectation, albeit with interesting observations at very large scale length-generalization. Additionally, we also evaluate pretrained models---both open hybrid and closed frontier ones---on StateBench, finding that none of them robustly solves even soluble state tracking, suggesting a direction for future improvement.
bullets: State tracking is organized into r-trivial, aperiodic, soluble, and general finite-state problems of increasing difficulty.
Theoretical results show transformers may fail on some aperiodic tracking, while Gated DeltaNet can express all aperiodic problems; certain transformers correspond precisely to soluble problems.
StateBench provides a four-tier, long-horizon benchmark for systematic evaluation across architectures.
Direct training results broadly match theory, but pretrained open and closed models do not robustly solve even soluble state-tracking tasks.
Very large context lengths reveal additional, notable deviations from expected length-generalization behavior.
