All other coordinates remain fixed. n0 and n1 are their document counts, and p0 and p1 are the corresponding proportions with the indicated attribute. Counts use complete profile membership. Bit indices are local to each separately fitted corpus encoder. Example selection is described in the text.

Table 12: Transfer of conditional bit associations in three-bit contexts. Each percentage is the annotated attribute share among documents from the indicated source with the context active and the specified varying bit state. Other coordinates are unrestricted. Contexts are selected from the reference corpus; new documents are used only for evaluation. These are descriptive proportions, not classifier predictions. New-document proportions include 95% Wilson intervals; Supplementary Section S9.3 gives the uncertainty assumptions and intervals for the between-state differences.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces Interpretable Sparse Binary Coding (ISBC) for text embeddings, offering a sparse, interpretable representation that aligns with token pruning and LLM representation learning.
papers.title: ISBC: Interpretable Sparse Binary Coding of Pretrained Text Embeddings
papers.tldr: ISBC converts frozen text embeddings into interpretable sparse binary codes whose individual bits and combinations reveal document groups and contextual distinctions.

papers.abstract: Early-exit language models decide for each token how much computation to spend, usually by stopping once the prediction is confident. Yet a token is not a fixed unit: tokenizers cut words into different numbers of pieces in different languages. We ask where inside a word such a policy spends its budget. In Qwen3, along two adaptive axes (the timesteps of a spiking conversion and the layers of the original Transformer), confidence stopping gives the continuation pieces of a word less computation than its first piece in English, German, and Turkish, but more in Bangla. Segmentation drives this. Re-segmenting the same parallel passages with BPE-dropout shifts the gap by up to eight exits on both axes, small models trained under two tokenizers shift Bangla's gap by six exits, and BLOOM and mGPT, which split Bangla less finely, give it the English pattern. Characters per token do not predict the gap across languages; within-word surprisal explains 75% of its variance. A learned stopping head beats confidence stopping by 7 to 8 points, but gains less than one point over the best mix of fixed exits at equal cost, and sometimes loses. All results come from offline analysis, not measured speedups.
bullets: In Qwen3, continuation pieces generally receive less computation than first pieces in English, German, and Turkish, but more in Bangla.
Changing tokenization with BPE-dropout shifts within-word computation gaps by up to eight exits; tokenizer choice also reverses Bangla’s pattern across models.
Characters per token do not explain the gaps across languages, while within-word surprisal explains 75% of their variance.
A learned stopping head improves over confidence stopping by 7–8 points, but offers less than one point over the best fixed-exit mixture at equal cost and can sometimes underperform.
The study is based on offline analysis, so it does not measure actual speedups.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Re-segmenting the same 60 parallel passages with BPE-dropout, at a budget of four exits. Every panel uses the same realized tokens. Points are means over three segmentation draws, and error bars show one standard deviation. (a) Spiking timesteps: English, German, and Turkish change sign, while Bangla starts positive and stays positive. (b) Layers of the unconverted model, read through one tuned lens per language that is fitted once and then frozen. Solid lines use a lens fitted on both canonical and fragmented text, dotted lines a lens fitted on canonical text only, and hollow markers two further lens seeds. (c) The timestep curves against characters per token. At equal granularity the languages sit several exits apart.

Figure 1: Experimental design, and where each part is reported. (1) We change segmentation in three ways: across the tokenizers of pretrained models, with BPE-dropout on a fixed model, and by training small models under two tokenizers. (2) Each model gives a prediction at every exit along one of two adaptive axes. (3) Stopping policies choose one exit per token at the same average budget. (4) We compare the exits that word starts and continuations receive, split that gap into what tokens need and what the policy adds, and compare policies at equal cost. Icons are schematic.

Figure 4: Allocation gap against surprisal contrast for all 24 canonical corpus–model pairs: two Qwen3 sizes on both axes, and BLOOM-1.1B and mGPT-1.3B on depth. Filled markers are 0.6B or the other families, hollow markers 1.7B; blue marks English corpora and pink Bangla ones. Every pair whose gap differs from zero lies in the upper-right or lower-left quadrant. Where Bangla falls depends on how finely its tokenizer splits it, and not monotonically.

Figure 7: Confidence allocation signs recur across two converted model sizes and the non-spiking tuned-lens probe. Depth values are sampled-exit indices; their magnitudes are not directly comparable hardware costs. WT: WikiText; B: Belebele; S: Sangraha.

Figure 6: Allocation, demand, and service gaps of the 0.6B model at budget four under six thresholdcalibration draws (the main run and five re-conversions on different WikiText blocks), evaluation blocks held fixed. Each mark is one draw; the six draws are almost superimposed, and no gap changes sign.

Figure 8: Learned-head gains over confidence stopping at development budget four. Bars show archived 95% paired block-bootstrap intervals, conditional on the fitted head and threshold. Gains reproduce across SNN sizes but not uniformly on depth. WT: WikiText; B-en/B-bn: Belebele English/Bangla; S-bn: Sangraha Bangla.

Figure 10: Full-compute surprisal contrast predicts allocation across the 15 whitespace-delimited languages. Both axes are derived from the same model, so the relationship describes model behavior rather than establishing an independent linguistic cause.
Figure 12: Allocation gap of each from-scratch model, with the two arms of a seed joined by a line. The three Bangla lines fall by six exits in parallel; the three English lines are flat and cross.

Figure 2: How we measure allocation. This is a schematic: the segmentation and values are illustrative, not model output. (a) Confidence stopping gives each token its own exit. Pieces that begin with the tokenizer’s space marker are word starts (I), the rest are continuations (C), and the allocation gap G is the difference between their mean exits. An exit is a spiking timestep on one axis and a layer read through a tuned lens on the other. (b) For one token, the exit ti is where confidence first reaches the threshold τ , and the demand di is where the loss first comes within ε of its final value. Service si = ti − di is positive when the policy keeps computing after the token is done.

Figure 5: Demand gap on the same rungs and tokens as Figure 3. On timesteps (a), fragmentation increases how much more computation continuation pieces need than word starts. On depth (b), through the pooled lens, it decreases it. Allocation rises on both axes, so outside Bangla the policy follows demand on timesteps and moves against it on depth.

Figure 9: Why the fixed-exit reference must be the envelope. Reporting-split accuracy at each fixed exit (dots), the upper concave envelope reachable by mixing two fixed exits (line), and the learned head at its realized cost (star), Belebele-English at 0.6B. (a) The tuned-lens depth curve is strongly convex over the first eight exits, so the envelope at the head’s cost lies a full point above the adjacent-exit interpolation and the head falls below both. (b) The timestep curve is concave, so the two references coincide.

Figure 11: Descriptive interpolation over the overlapping ranges of English, German, and Turkish. The spread decreases by 5.54-fold. Bangla is excluded by range support, and interpolation adds no new observations.

Table 5: Depth-axis ladder on the same tokens as Table 4, through two readouts, each fitted once and frozen across all rungs: a lens fitted on canonical text only, and one fitted on the pooled support of the ladder. G is the allocation gap at budget four of 16 exits and Gdem the first-hit demand gap; r is their correlation across the seven rungs. Under the pooled lens the allocation curves match the timestep ladder; under both, the demand gap moves the other way.

Table 8: From-scratch 49.1M models under two tokenizers differing only in Bangla exposure, budget 6.5 of 13 exits, 300 parallel Belebele passages. Seeds pair document order and initialization across arms; superscript s marks the stable demand target. Three seeds are descriptive; no interval over seeds is reported. Withinseed passage-cluster intervals on G have half-widths of 0.06–0.15.

Table 1: Allocation gap G split into demand Gdem and service Gsvc, in exits, at a budget of four and canonical segmentation. Asterisks mark service gaps whose cluster-bootstrap interval excludes zero. Demand has the sign of G in eleven of twelve settings and makes up roughly half of it or more in each of them. The exception, WikiText on depth, disappears under the stable target of Appendix F.

The 60 scored Belebele passages are the same link identifiers in all four languages, and the evaluated character total is identical at every rung of a language. Demand rises with fragmentation everywhere; allocation follows it except in Bangla.

Table 7: The decomposition under both demand targets, ε = 0.05, budget four. Asterisks mark cluster-bootstrap intervals excluding zero. The demand gap matches the allocation sign in all twelve settings under the stable target, including the depth WikiText case that is the exception under first hit. Four service gaps change sign between targets.
Table 3: Mean allocation gap across segmentation draws at each dropout level. Only nonzero rungs have three draws. The near-zero German .5 rung is the only one with draw-level sign disagreement.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes adaptive computation and early-exit behavior in LLMs as a function of tokenization, relevant to efficient inference and LLM architecture.
papers.title: A Token Is Not a Unit of Difficulty: Segmentation Controls Where Adaptive Computation Goes Inside a Word
papers.tldr: Adaptive computation is allocated differently across word pieces largely because tokenizer segmentation shapes where models perceive difficulty.

papers.abstract: Post training for large reasoning models remains insufficient on challenging problems, whose correct trajectories are hard to sample. Though prior works address this difficulty by integrating supervised fine tuning on expert trajectories with reinforcement learning, such external experts are not always available. Existing self improvement methods instead use reference solutions to create a privileged self-teacher. Yet privileged teacher correctness does not imply student reachability. Solution conditioning shifts the teacher distribution toward actions unlikely under the unprivileged student, producing seemingly "correct" trajectories that are unreachable or even mal-formed learning targets. Accordingly, we identify reachability alignment as the key to self constructed supervision and propose Self-Steered Reasoner (SSR). SSR realizes this principle through student support projection, which transforms the privileged teacher distribution into a directional signal only over reasoning actions locally reachable under the unguided student. Verification then retains correct trajectories sampled from this reachable space. To further boost the sampling efficiency, an iterative refinement framework is adopted, using diagnostic guidance based on current trajectories. On problems with pass@64 = 0 even after extensive RL, SSR recovers correct and learnable trajectories for 74.6% without parameter updates. Fine tuning on these trajectories followed by resumed reinforcement learning improves aggregate accuracy by 4.9 percentage points on AIME25/26 and HMMT26. These results show that privileged guidance becomes effective self-improvement data when aligned with the reasoning actions the student can reach.
bullets: Problem: Privileged teacher solutions may be correct but unreachable or malformed for the unguided student, limiting self-improvement.
Method: Project the teacher distribution onto the student’s local support, verify correct reachable trajectories, and iteratively refine sampling with diagnostic guidance.
Result: SSR recovers correct, learnable trajectories for 74.6% of problems with pass@64 = 0 after extensive RL, without parameter updates.
Further training on recovered trajectories followed by resumed RL raises aggregate accuracy by 4.9 percentage points on AIME25/26 and HMMT26.
Scope: The approach depends on verification and is evaluated on challenging mathematical reasoning problems.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the SSR framework. 1. Given a very hard question Q, we sample failed rollouts from the student model. The failed rollout is then summarized and diagnosed against the reference solution to produce a self-steer. The self-steer describes the error and provide fixing directions while avoiding directly offering the answer. 2. The self-steer is then used to construct the privileged self-teacher. The KL-divergence between teacher and student is calculated on the failed rollout to determine the proper intervention point. Everything after that point is discarded. 3. After the intervention point, for every decoding prefix, the student first calculate its support-set by retaining every token with a student possibility above a certain threshold δ. The teacher then rewights these tokens and choose the next token. For each new trajectory generated, it will be stored for further training if correct, and send back to a new round of refinement if incorrect. After the iterative refinement succeeds, the saved positive trajectory can be used to improve the student model.

Figure 1: RLVR can extend the model’s ability in its comfort zone, but it meets obstacles when coming to anxiety zone where correct trajectories are hard to sample. Privileged-teacher can provide aid signals on anxiety zone, but it can also select actions outside the student’s reachable region, producing unlearnable traces. Directly imitating these actions can corrupt the student’s reasoning ability(e.g., learning to hallucinate a non-existent hint). By projecting privileged preferences into the consensus region, SSR retains the learnable steering signals within the privileged preferences, effectively expands the student’s learning boundary.
Figure 3: Equal-budget search allocation. Iterative refinement recovers 147/197 problems, compared with 102/197 when all 64 initial failures receive one correction.

papers.abstract: Calling a tool through generated text adds decoding steps, even when the computation itself is short. We study an alternative: a small neural module that runs inside a language model's forward pass. A learned writer turns hidden states into a symbolic tape, a short sequence of discrete symbols that encodes the computation. The module, trained separately and then frozen, reduces the tape to a result, and a learned reader returns that result to the model. We evaluate arithmetic and object tracking in gemma-3-1b-it. With a writer trained on labelled tapes, the layer answers all 750 items of BIG-Bench Hard's tracking shuffled objects correctly. At seven people it needs about 1/10 of the GPU kernel time of a text-tool baseline that uses the same host model and exact code, with accuracy 1.00 against 0.99. The writer can also be learned from answers alone, guided by a hand-written copying prior, but less reliably: 5 of 6 runs succeed in the 1B host and 2 of 4 in the 4B host. Two independently trained layers keep their task accuracy when attached to one model, and a learned gate keeps them silent on the tested general-text and look-alike prompts. The results support a narrow use case: a bounded computation that returns one symbol can avoid the decoding cost of a textual tool call. Extracting the right input reliably, and deciding when to act, remain the main open problems.
bullets: Targets arithmetic and object-tracking tasks in Gemma-3-1B-IT.
A learned writer encodes hidden states into a short discrete symbolic tape; a frozen module computes on it, and a reader returns the result.
With labelled tapes, the layer correctly answers all 750 BIG-Bench Hard shuffled-object tracking items.
At seven people, it uses about one-tenth the GPU kernel time of a text-tool baseline, with accuracy 1.00 versus 0.99.
Answer-only tape learning is less reliable; extracting inputs and deciding when to invoke the module remain open problems.

papers.abstract: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) estimates advantages against the within-prompt mean reward, a baseline shared across the group. In practice, rollouts within a prompt are not always homogeneous, differing in their solution strategies and reasoning trajectories, along which they may group into subgroups. We further find that these heterogeneous subgroups may exhibit distinct reward distributions. The global baseline, however, collapses them onto a single credit axis, where the credit reflects neither a rollout's standing within its subgroup nor the subgroup's standing relative to the rest. We therefore study how to adjust the baseline when the rollouts of a prompt fall into heterogeneous subgroups. We define the \emph{subgroup offset} as the deviation of a subgroup mean from the global mean, and shift the baseline along it by a single signed coefficient $λ$. The sign of $λ$ yields two opposing directions: \emph{Alignment} ($λ{>}0$) adds the offset to the baseline, drawing credit toward a rollout's relative position within its subgroup; \emph{Contrast} ($λ{<}0$) subtracts it, drawing a rollout's credit toward the relative quality of the subgroup it belongs to. The adjustment acts on the baseline alone, leaving the reward signal and the optimization objective unchanged. In this work, we induce subgroups from strategies, grouping rollouts that share a strategy into the same subgroup. We evaluate both directions on Qwen3-8B-Base and Olmo3-7B-Base across four competition-level math benchmarks, against a $λ{=}0$ anchor that shares the same strategy-conditioned sampling and differs only in the baseline. Against this anchor each direction yields modest but consistent gains in multi-sample coverage, with Contrast the stronger of the two.
bullets: GRPO’s global within-prompt baseline can obscure both a rollout’s subgroup-relative quality and the subgroup’s overall quality.
The method computes each subgroup’s mean-reward deviation from the global mean and shifts the baseline by a signed coefficient λ.
λ>0 (Alignment) emphasizes position within a subgroup; λ<0 (Contrast) emphasizes the subgroup’s quality relative to others.
Subgroups are induced by grouping rollouts that share a solution strategy.
Across two base models and four competition-level math benchmarks, both directions consistently improve multi-sample coverage over the matched λ=0 anchor; Contrast is stronger.

papers.selection_reason: GRPO baseline adjustment for LLM reasoning; fits language foundation model reasoning methods.
papers.title: One Offset, Two Directions: Baseline Adjustment via Subgroup Offsets
papers.tldr: Subgroup Offset adjusts GRPO’s baseline using strategy-based subgroup reward differences, with both alignment and contrast improving multi-sample math coverage modestly, and contrast performing better.

papers.abstract: Inference-time scaling enhances a model's reasoning by extending its chain-of-thought (CoT). However, existing approaches typically rely on a single policy trained with outcome-reward reinforcement learning (RL), which often suffers from long-horizon plan failures where the implicit plan drifts from valid strategies, especially for small LMs with limited capacity. To address this, we propose Multi-Level Reasoning (MLR), which reformulates long-CoT generation as a two-level stochastic process. A high-level planner generates structured step descriptors specifying both the reasoning mode and the semantic subgoal. The low-level executor then produces detailed reasoning conditioned on these descriptors, forming an alternating plan--execute loop. To maintain scalability, we adopt a minimal design where the base model serves as the low-level policy and a lightweight LoRA module implements the high-level policy. For training, we observe that outcome-reward RL provides sparse and delayed feedback for long trajectories (e.g., several thousand tokens), hindering credit assignment. We therefore introduce iterative Step-DPO, a process-level preference optimization scheme that leverages Twisted Sequential Monte Carlo (TSMC) to provide scalable stepwise supervision. This yields more effective training, improved stability, and higher accuracy. Extensive experiments on challenging math, science, and logical reasoning benchmarks show that, under the same reduced data budget (10% SFT and 5% preference relative to the DeepSeek-R1 distillation setup), MLR outperforms both SFT-based distillation and strong RL/preference-optimization baselines across multiple base models and tasks. Moreover, MLR exhibits slower performance degradation on long-horizon reasoning, demonstrating stronger robustness under extended CoT generation.
bullets: Targets long-horizon plan drift and sparse credit assignment, particularly in small language models.
Uses a high-level planner to specify reasoning modes and semantic subgoals, while a low-level executor generates detailed reasoning in an alternating plan–execute loop.
Keeps the design lightweight: the base model acts as executor and a LoRA module serves as planner.
Introduces iterative Step-DPO with Twisted Sequential Monte Carlo for scalable, process-level step supervision.
On math, science, and logic benchmarks, it achieves higher accuracy and more stable long-CoT performance under a reduced data budget, with slower degradation on extended reasoning.

papers.abstract: A growing body of work reports benefits from orthogonality constraints in fine-tuning large language models (LLMs). These results raise an open question: do orthogonality constraints also help LLM pre-training? We conduct a systematic empirical study of decoder-only LLM pre-training with models ranging from 360M to 3.1B parameters, trained on nearly 200B tokens. We examine fourteen variants of orthogonality training: some constrain the weight matrix itself, while others use orthogonal factors to reparameterize it. Because a strictly orthogonal square matrix loses half of its degrees of freedom, we also study block-wise orthogonality, where every $d$ rows form a row-orthonormal (Stiefel) matrix and the block size $d$ is a hyperparameter. Among block sizes ranging from 1 to the shorter side of the matrix, no $d>1$ used throughout the network reliably outperforms $d=1$, and large blocks are clearly worse; the one placement that helps, symmetric positive-definite factors on the query and key projections, loses its small gain as models grow. At $d=1$, the constraint reduces to sphere optimization, with each row direction on its own unit sphere, which by itself already improves on tuned Muon. The same two findings hold for a diffusion transformer trained on ImageNet, and after fine-tuning, downstream accuracy does not separate the parameterizations. Our conclusion is that, across the realizations we tried, orthogonality between rows does not help language-model pre-training beyond sphere optimization. Since this appears to conflict with several prior results, we re-examine five prior methods in pre-training and fine-tuning that report orthogonality improvements. In each case the reported gain is attributable to numerical precision, training horizon, optimizer realization, or per-row norm control rather than to the orthogonality the methods impose.
bullets: Systematically evaluates 14 orthogonality-based training variants on decoder-only LLMs from 360M to 3.1B parameters using nearly 200B tokens.
Block-wise orthogonality with block sizes greater than 1 does not reliably outperform row-wise constraints, and larger blocks perform worse.
A small benefit from symmetric positive-definite factors on query/key projections disappears as model size increases.
The same pattern appears in an ImageNet diffusion transformer, while downstream fine-tuning accuracy does not distinguish parameterizations.
Reanalysis of five prior methods attributes reported gains to numerical precision, training duration, optimizer details, or per-row norm control—not orthogonality itself.

papers.abstract: Does the level of test-time processing effort affect a language model's computational capability? A formal grammar-lens benchmark method, derived from the theory of computation, generates novel data at specified levels, each successively more computationally powerful than the levels below. Using this data, we tested GPT-5.5, and GPT-5.5-Pro-Medium, -High, and -XHigh, showing incrementally increased acceptance of test data: 16, 40, 43, and 52\%, respectively, illustrating the benchmark's ability to discern fine-grained differences among models' added test-time reasoning levels. Additionally, as test-time compute effort increases, model responses diverge from human responses to the same data. This increasing disagreement may turn out to be broadly characteristic of more capable language models, introducing the potential of a general capability-versus-alignment conflict.

papers.abstract: Reasoning-oriented post-training enables large language models (LLMs) to solve complex tasks via multi-step inference. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on high-quality reasoning traces is a particularly efficient approach, but its effectiveness depends critically on careful data curation. Existing pipelines rely on a costly generate-then-filter paradigm: large pools of long reasoning traces are produced by multiple teacher models and subsequently filtered for difficulty and diversity using additional LLMs, often requiring weeks of computation. In this work, we propose SFTProbe, a fundamentally different approach that bypasses this pipeline by directly predicting the quality of reasoning data. We show that a brief LoRA-based adaptation, combined with evaluating loss on only 5% of each reasoning trace, suffices to estimate both difficulty and diversity. SFTProbe is grounded in a geometric view of post-training, where pretrained LLMs lie in a low-rank, anisotropic loss basin. By probing this basin via low-rank perturbations, we construct compact loss signatures whose clustering captures diversity, while loss at curvature inflection points provides a robust proxy for difficulty. We also provide a simple criterion for teacher selection. Empirically, our approach reduces data curation time from weeks to hours while maintaining or improving performance. Remarkably, on mathematical reasoning, 5k generated examples match the highly filtered 89k-example in OpenThoughts-Math dataset, and 7.5k generated examples outperforms it by 2.5% in accuracy. We further introduce a high-quality physics reasoning dataset, and use it to train a model that outperforms an IPhO 2025 silver-medal-winning model. The code and the dataset are released at https://bigml-cs-ucla.github.io/SFTProbe-page/.
bullets: Addresses the costly generate-then-filter process for curating reasoning traces for supervised fine-tuning.
Uses brief LoRA adaptation and loss evaluation on only 5% of each trace to predict data quality.
Clusters compact loss signatures to capture diversity and uses curvature-inflection loss as a difficulty proxy.
On mathematical reasoning, 5k selected examples match an 89k-example dataset, while 7.5k outperform it by 2.5% accuracy.
Introduces a physics reasoning dataset and reports performance exceeding an IPhO 2025 silver-medal-winning model.

papers.abstract: The rapid scaling of large language models (LLMs) has unlocked remarkable capabilities across various domains. However, deploying LLMs on mobile devices remains challenging because of their high computational and memory requirements. Low-bit quantization (e.g., 4-bit weights, 8-bit activations) can reduce model size while preserving accuracy, but its practical efficacy on mobile GPUs has been limited so far. In this paper, we identify that the performance gap stems primarily from frequent data type conversions between quantized and floating-point values, and dynamic and inefficient memory access patterns caused by the growing Key-Value (KV) cache during autoregressive decoding. We introduce BitLLM, a mobile inference engine that addresses type conversion overhead and suboptimal memory accesses in quantized LLMs. Our approach features an adaptive layout and packing strategy for the KV cache that ensures efficient memory access throughout LLM decoding. This is coupled with an integer-native execution pipeline that defers and overlaps type conversion outside the compute hot path, keeping the critical MatMul stages in the integer domain. Implemented on off-the-shelf mobile GPUs, BitLLM outperforms leading engines, i.e., LLAMA.CPP, MNN-LLM, LiteRT-LM, and MLC-LLM, achieving average speedups of 1.78$\times$, 1.73$\times$, 1.58$\times$, and 1.47$\times$, respectively, across various models and quantization levels. Under long-context generation, BitLLM reduces average energy consumption (per token) by up to 88.9%.
bullets: Mobile deployment is constrained by LLM computation and memory demands, while low-bit inference is hindered by conversion overhead and inefficient KV-cache access.
An adaptive KV-cache layout and packing strategy maintains efficient memory access during autoregressive decoding.
An integer-native execution pipeline moves and overlaps type conversions outside the critical MatMul path.
On off-the-shelf mobile GPUs, BitLLM achieves average speedups of 1.78×–1.47× over four leading inference engines across models and quantization levels.
For long-context generation, it reduces average energy consumption per token by up to 88.9%.

papers.abstract: Deterministic multi-agent LLM deliberation can exactly re- play a fixed transcript, yet exact replay alone does not test local resistance to controlled internal interventions. Because each response becomes context for later agents, a changed greedy token can redirect a transcript-mediated execution. We present a white-box audit of this local failure mode in a five-agent committee under greedy decoding. We prospectively select low- and high-margin token positions, require exact no-op re- play, inject norm-relative residual displacements, and measure first transcript divergence within ten generated tokens. Low- margin positions are more branch-sensitive than high-margin controls, while matched margin-reducing gradient directions branch substantially more often than margin-increasing con- trols. We then continue selected realized branches through the committee to distinguish textual persistence from preference and final-decision changes. The contribution is a controlled audit for local branch susceptibility in this specified protocol, not an estimate of deployment frequency, decision correct- ness, or a phenomenon unique to multi-agent systems.
bullets: Exact replay verifies the baseline, but does not establish resistance to local internal perturbations.
A five-agent greedy-decoding committee was tested at prospectively selected low- and high-margin token positions.
Norm-relative residual displacements were applied, with branch sensitivity measured by the first transcript divergence within ten tokens.
Margin-reducing directions branched more often than matched margin-increasing controls.
Follow-up analysis separated textual branch persistence from changes in preferences and final decisions; the findings are protocol-specific, not deployment-frequency or correctness estimates.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents extend their capabilities with skills, each with a name, a description, and a body. Under progressive disclosure, an LLM router selects skills by name and description alone and loads only the selected bodies. Skill libraries grow continually as users and agents add new skills. Because the router relies on this metadata, a similar new skill can displace an earlier one, breaking previously correct routing even though the earlier skill and the router are unchanged. This routing interference is aggravated for public skills, whose descriptions may not match their bodies. We formulate the problem as lifelong skill routing, a class-incremental continual learning problem. A solution must keep earlier skills selectable without suppressing new ones. Existing approaches fall short, since continually retraining the router risks catastrophic forgetting and rewriting methods either ignore similar skills or require per-skill feedback. We therefore propose Skill++, which rewrites only the name and description of each incoming skill, without router training or labeled data. The new description states what the body supports, how the skill differs from its closest predecessor, and what related work it excludes. As a library grows to 731 skills over ten sessions, Skill++ selects all required skills for 76.3% of queries, versus 36.4% under the original metadata. Across three benchmarks and five LLM routers, it outperforms all compared approaches, and its gains carry over to the Codex CLI agent harness.
bullets: Addresses routing interference, where similar new skills displace previously correct skills as libraries grow.
Rewrites only each incoming skill’s name and description to clarify capabilities, distinctions, and exclusions.
Requires no router training, labeled data, or per-skill feedback.
On a 731-skill, ten-session setting, it selects all required skills for 76.3% of queries versus 36.4% with original metadata.
Outperforms competing methods across three benchmarks and five LLM routers, with gains transferring to the Codex CLI agent harness.

figures.caption: Figure 3: This figure gives an overview of SKILL++, to show how it refines an incoming skill before the router reads it. SKILL++ first retrieves similar earlier skills from a record of their original names, descriptions, bodies and synthetic queries. Three components then refine the new skill independently. Description differentiation rewrites its description around what makes it unique, scope exclusions list related work that it does not cover, and name clarification makes an overlapping name more specific. The refined name and description enter the library that the router reads, and the original skill joins the record for future additions.

Figure 2: This figure compares three ways of handling a growing skill library, to position our problem. (a) Continuous router training follows arriving skills but retrains the router at every step, risking catastrophic forgetting of earlier skills. (b) One-shot skill optimization refines a fixed skill set once, so it ignores skills that arrive later. (c) SKILL++ keeps the router frozen and refines each new batch against similar earlier skills, so both earlier and new skills are selected for the queries that need them.

Figure 4: This figure shows FC@5 as the library grows (sizes in Tab. A2), to test whether routing stays accurate. (a) The main router, Claude Haiku 4.5 (Tab. A1). (b)–(e) Four other routers (Tab. A4). With every router, Vanilla declines while SKILL++ leads or ties at every checkpoint.

Figure 5: This figure breaks down the routing errors at S9 into two forms and seven types (defined in Appendix C.2), to show which errors SKILL++ removes. All panels draw on the eight combinations of Tab. A3. (a) The 200 Vanilla errors, by form (inner ring) and type (outer ring). (b) Errors per type under Vanilla and SKILL++, as a share of the Vanilla errors. (c) Errors per form when one component or all three are added to Vanilla, shown in the same way. SKILL++ removes most errors of both forms, and each component mainly reduces one form.

Figure 1: This figure presents an example of routing interference, to show why incoming metadata needs refinement. The router reads only skill names and descriptions. (a) For a query about an AI paper, it selects the AI paper-writing skill. (b) A biology paper-writing skill arrives with the same metadata, and the router selects it instead. (c) SKILL++ refines only the incoming skill against the earlier one, so the router selects the correct skill again.

papers.title: Skill++: Towards Lifelong Agents via Routing-Aware Skill Refinement
papers.tldr: Skill++ preserves reliable skill routing in growing LLM-agent libraries by refining incoming skills’ metadata without retraining the router.

papers.abstract: Whether a policy shifts domains and, by extension, continues, broadens, narrows, or reverses previous policy is of paramount importance to the study of public policy. We propose Dual-Axis Policy Entailment (DAPE), which evaluates an ordered pair of policy directives on both dimensions at once: a binary judgment determines whether the two directives govern the same policy domain, and a five-way judgment determines whether the later directive continues, broadens, narrows, or reverses the earlier policy, or governs a different domain altogether. Read together, the two judgments form one five-category label, our primary metric. The two-axis design captures two central dimensions of policy change without conflating errors on either dimension into a generic "irrelevant" label, and it makes annotation more rigorous: a coder cannot dismiss a difficult pair as domain-irrelevant without an explicit, checkable decision. We introduce an expert-annotated benchmark of 1,000 ordered directive pairs drawn from a large corpus of Chinese government policy, together with an annotation-calibration protocol (an adjudication packet with pre/post agreement measurement) that we contribute as a methodological artifact. Fourteen open-weight models and four frontier API flagships fail the task zero-shot: even the best frontier flagship's chance-corrected agreement with expert labels is far below the human ceiling (Cohen's $κ\approx 0.29$ vs. $0.53$). A fine-tuned open-weight model (LoRA SFT of Qwen3-14B, five-fold cross-validation) closes this gap, reaching the coder-mutual human ceiling ($κ= 0.524$ vs. $0.527$). Finally, we apply our method to China's AI policy (1980-2024) and map the direction of policy change across eras.
bullets: Evaluates ordered policy-directive pairs along two axes: shared domain and policy-change relation.
Combines the judgments into five labels: continue, broaden, narrow, reverse, or different domain.
Provides an expert-annotated benchmark of 1,000 Chinese government policy pairs and an annotation-calibration protocol.
Fourteen open-weight and four frontier models perform poorly zero-shot; LoRA fine-tuning of Qwen3-14B reaches coder-level agreement.
Applies DAPE to map changes in China’s AI policy from 1980 to 2024.

papers.abstract: We present WeSearch, a unified, model-centric retrieval framework for large-scale, continuously evolving content search. Prevailing methods assign documents fixed hierarchical Semantic IDs, implicitly assuming each document follows a single coherent semantic path-an assumption that often breaks down for multi-topic documents. WeSearch instead retrieves query-relevant clusters and then ranks atomic documents within the resulting query-specific candidate space, decoupling candidate pruning from fine-grained relevance modeling. Combined with relevance-aware training, compact document representations, and incremental index updates, this design enables weekly-or daily when needed-model refreshes. Deployed as the primary semantic retrieval path in WeChat Search alongside a lexical syntax tree, WeSearch shows consistent one-week A/B gains on corpora from hundreds of millions to billions of documents, and a one-month full-traffic A/B test confirms stable improvements of +0.68% CTR and +2.27% per-user article clicks, together with a 41% reduction in retrieval resource cost and a 19 ms reduction in graphic-text retrieval latency. WeSearch is now fully deployed in WeChat Search, serving 100% of production traffic.
bullets: Addresses the limitations of fixed hierarchical Semantic IDs for multi-topic documents and continuously changing content.
Uses query-relevant cluster retrieval followed by atomic-document ranking, with relevance-aware training and compact representations.
Supports weekly or on-demand daily model refreshes through incremental index updates.
Production A/B tests report +0.68% CTR, +2.27% per-user article clicks, 41% lower retrieval resource cost, and 19 ms lower graphic-text retrieval latency.
Fully deployed as WeChat Search’s primary semantic retrieval path alongside a lexical syntax tree, serving 100% of traffic.

papers.abstract: We present DELBERT-2, a pretrained fingerprint language model that converts sparse molecular fingerprints into unified token sequences using a ModernBERT encoder trained with masked language modelling on 2.5M molecules from the AIRCHECK DEL corpus. We evaluate across six targets (WDR91, WDR12, SETDB1, PLCZ1, LRRK2, DCAF7) under three out-of-distribution (OOD) protocols: hierarchical cluster splits probe chemical novelty, library splits test cross-library transfer, and building-block splits assess compositional generalization. DELBERT-2 consistently improves PR-AUC and NDCG@1000 relative to LightGBM ensemble baselines and transformers trained from scratch, with the largest gains in stringent OOD regimes. DELBERT-2 achieves 13.28+/-3.72 enrichment factor at top-100 vs. 12.36+/-3.75 for no-pretraining (p=0.040), representing 7.4% improvement and 13x enrichment over random selection. These results demonstrate that fingerprint-centric self-supervised learning effectively improves hit prioritization under distribution shift, enabling practical DEL virtual screening. Code is available at \hyperlink{https://github.com/GenerativeDrugDiscovery/DELBERT-2}{DELBERT-2}.
bullets: Pretrains a ModernBERT encoder with masked language modelling on 2.5M molecules from the AIRCHECK DEL corpus.
Evaluates six targets using chemical-novelty, cross-library, and compositional-generalization OOD splits.
Consistently improves PR-AUC and NDCG@1000 over LightGBM ensembles and transformers trained from scratch.
Reaches 13.28±3.72 top-100 enrichment versus 12.36±3.75 without pretraining, a 7.4% improvement and 13× random enrichment.
Supports practical DEL virtual screening; code is publicly available.

papers.abstract: Automated theorem generation (ATG) seeks to construct new theorems rather than merely prove given conjectures. Existing approaches typically generate candidate statements that require subsequent proof or formal verification. We propose a constructive framework for ATG in first-order logic based on triangular standard contradictions. The method constructs minimally unsatisfiable clause sets from selected first-order literals, then forms theorems by retaining some clauses as premises and taking the negation of one clause, or a conjunction of clauses, as the conclusion. Minimal unsatisfiability ensures that the remaining premises are satisfiable, avoiding trivial inference by explosion, while unsatisfiability of the full set guarantees the resulting entailment. Theorems are therefore correct by construction, without a separate proof procedure for each instance. Extending the previously developed $Δ_1$ generator, we introduce seven methods, $Δ_2$--$Δ_8$, forming a unified family of eight theorem-generation methods. Four generators, $Δ_1$--$Δ_4$, have been implemented and released. We also formulate a general $Δ$-class method encompassing the family. Combinatorial analysis demonstrates the capacity to generate large numbers of distinct theorems systematically. This framework offers a principled foundation for automated theorem discovery and the construction of logically guaranteed knowledge.
bullets: Addresses automated theorem generation, which aims to create new theorems rather than only prove supplied conjectures.
Constructs triangular standard contradictions from selected first-order literals and converts subsets into premises and conclusions.
Uses minimal unsatisfiability to ensure premises remain satisfiable, while full-set unsatisfiability guarantees entailment.
Extends the Δ₁ generator with methods Δ₂–Δ₈; Δ₁–Δ₄ are implemented and released.
Combinatorial analysis shows the framework can systematically generate many distinct theorems.

papers.abstract: Large generative models are commonly trained on data collected from the open web, which may contain data produced by previous generations of the same model. Previous work has shown that recursively training on model-generated data can progressively degrade model performance, a phenomenon known as model collapse. Yet, generative models continue to improve dramatically over time. Existing theory suggests that this is enabled by the availability of new real data at each iteration, kept separate from generated data. However, exact separation is not realistic, and uncurated data is still commonly used. We bridge this gap by considering a more realistic setup in which real and generated data are not handled differently during training. Specifically, we present a comprehensive theoretical study of iterative estimation of the mean and covariance of a multivariate Gaussian distribution. At each iteration, samples are drawn from a mixture of the real data distribution and the estimated distribution from the previous iteration, but are used indistinguishably. We provide a single equivalent condition for consistency of the mean and covariance estimators in Euclidean norms, and convergence to zero of the expected squared 2-Wasserstein distance between the estimated and true distributions. Using this result, we show that consistency holds, i.e., model collapse is avoided, for any fixed real data fraction above zero, and even for a fraction that vanishes across iterations, provided it does not vanish too quickly. However, more real data (or data curation) remains important at practical finite times: the convergence rate of the mean estimator deteriorates as the real data fraction approaches zero. We support our results with an empirical investigation of the theoretical setup, and with experiments on iterative training of a diffusion model on CIFAR-10 that correlate with our theory.
bullets: Studies iterative estimation where real and model-generated samples are mixed and used indistinguishably.
Derives a single equivalent criterion for consistency of mean and covariance and vanishing expected squared 2-Wasserstein error.
Shows consistency for any fixed positive real-data fraction, and for fractions that vanish slowly enough across iterations.
Finds that decreasing real-data fractions still slow finite-time mean-estimation convergence.
Supports the theory with simulations and iterative diffusion-model experiments on CIFAR-10.

papers.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enables parameter-efficient fine-tuning but can suffer from redundant basis directions. Constraining the basis factor to the Stiefel manifold addresses this redundancy through orthonormality. Landing methods allow temporarily infeasible iterates to explore a neighborhood of the manifold while progressively restoring orthogonality without per-step retractions. To improve optimization efficiency while retaining this flexibility, we introduce ProLand (Product-space Landing), a retraction-free optimizer that combines coordinated factor updates with Muon-style spectral directions. By designing the updates in the space of the represented weight increment, ProLand separates objective optimization from orthogonality restoration, supporting efficient feasibility recovery. This coordinated construction also enables Muon-style directions to guide objective optimization while preserving that separation. Experiments cover four GLUE validation tasks on DeBERTa-v3-base and seven language benchmarks on Qwen2.5-3B, Llama-3.2-3B, and Moonlight-16B-A3B across multiple adapter ranks. Across these 11 tasks, ProLand achieves the highest average score among the compared methods in every tested encoder and decoder model-rank configuration.
bullets: LoRA can contain redundant basis directions; enforcing Stiefel-manifold orthonormality helps address this issue.
ProLand uses product-space landing to allow temporarily infeasible iterates while progressively restoring orthogonality without per-step retractions.
Its coordinated updates separate task-objective optimization from feasibility restoration in the represented weight-increment space.
Experiments span 11 GLUE and language-modeling tasks across several models and adapter ranks.
ProLand obtains the highest average score among compared methods in every tested model–rank configuration.

papers.abstract: The order in which tokens are predicted in language modeling has a profound impact on the quality of generated sequences. Autoregressive and masked diffusion models iteratively fill in tokens and can exploit such orderings across generation steps, but how to leverage an ordering for one-step parallel language modeling is unclear. We introduce asynchronous flow map language models (aFMLMs), which incorporate prediction order into one-step modeling by learning the flow maps of asynchronous flows. These flows specify an ordering through a tokenwise time schedule that controls the relative denoising progress of tokens. We formulate a general class of asynchronous flows that admit both prescribed and learned, state-adaptive schedules, show that they define valid flow maps, and develop new methods for their flow map distillation. The resulting models can generate all tokens in a single forward pass by internalizing the ordering encoded in the flow into their hidden computations. On Sudoku solving and code generation for GSM8K math word problems, aFMLM establishes new state-of-the-art one-step performance.
bullets: Addresses how token ordering can improve one-step parallel language modeling.
Uses tokenwise time schedules to control relative denoising progress across tokens.
Supports both prescribed and learned, state-adaptive asynchronous schedules.
Introduces flow-map distillation methods so models internalize ordering in their hidden states.
Achieves state-of-the-art one-step results on Sudoku solving and GSM8K code generation.

papers.abstract: Large reasoning models improve performance on challenging problems by allocating additional computation before answering, but longer reasoning does not always lead to better results and can introduce substantial redundant reasoning on simple problems. Conversely, aggressively shortening reasoning can degrade performance on difficult ones. Effective reasoning therefore requires dynamically deciding when additional computation is useful based on the reasoner's capabilities and evolving solution state. Existing approaches often rely on predefined budgets or intervention rules, retrain the target reasoner, or require additional supervision. We introduce MetaCtrl, a lightweight controller that adaptively regulates a frozen reasoner without predefined token budgets or reasoner retraining. We formulate reasoning regulation as a sequential metacognitive control problem: MetaCtrl observes the evolving reasoning trace and decides whether to continue, simplify, skip redundant steps, or conclude reasoning. It is trained directly with reinforcement learning using a reward that prioritizes correctness while favoring shorter trajectories among correct solutions, requiring neither supervised intervention trajectories nor problem-specific budgets. Across seven benchmarks spanning mathematics, science, and code, MetaCtrl consistently improves the accuracy of LRMs while reducing their reasoning length. On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, it improves average accuracy by 4.7 points while reducing generation length by 53.3%. Without further training, the same controller transfers to an unseen reasoner (e.g., Qwen3-14B), improving average accuracy by 2.9 points and reducing generation length by 50.3%. These results establish MetaCtrl as a plug-and-play controller for improving reasoning accuracy while substantially reducing inference-time generation. The code is available at https://github.com/binbin2xs/MetaCtrl.
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between excessive reasoning on simple problems and insufficient reasoning on difficult ones.
A lightweight controller monitors the evolving reasoning trace and chooses whether to continue, simplify, skip redundant steps, or stop.
Requires no predefined token budget, reasoner retraining, supervised intervention traces, or problem-specific budgets.
Across seven mathematics, science, and code benchmarks, it improved accuracy while reducing reasoning length.
On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, accuracy rose by 4.7 points and generation length fell by 53.3%; it also transferred to Qwen3-14B without further training.

papers.abstract: We study whether a language model can help design controllers whose behavior can be formally checked. In proof-carrying evolution (PCE), a search proposes controllers together with their certificates. Their mathematical forms are fixed; a proposer chooses their numerical parameters together. Certificate checks guide selection, and only a certified candidate can be returned. The deployed artifact is a control law and its certificate; the language model is used only during design. We compare four language models with classical search and synthesis on docking under a speed limit, pursuit of a maneuvering target, and attitude control on SO(3), using paired runs and shared proposal allowances. Certificates are checked in exact rational arithmetic during search on the linear problems. On SO(3), the search uses floating-point checks, followed by exact re-verification of every reported champion. The best run of each method also receives Lean 4 proofs of its stated control properties. On the linear problems, the strongest models beat the standard classical baselines on every run, but a classical optimizer that chooses certificates for the same objective closes most of that lead. Among the cited pursuit champions, the ranking does not survive a change from Euler to zero-order-hold dynamics. On SO(3), no model detectably outperforms CMA-ES when mixed with classical mutation. When models write every proposal, one tested model improves on CMA-ES and the other performs worse than its mixed variant. All search medians remain below the hand-tuned law. In a docking control with the objective and mutation operator held fixed, retaining certified candidates yields new certified designs in every run; removing this rule yields none.
authors: Amit Jain, Sergio Sanchez-Hurtado, Victor Rodriguez-Fernandez, Richard Linares
bullets: The method jointly proposes controller parameters and certificates while using certificate checks to guide black-box search.
The deployed artifact is a control law plus certificate; the language model is used only during design.
Experiments cover docking, pursuit of a maneuvering target, and attitude control on SO(3), with exact or post hoc proof verification.
Language models beat standard classical baselines on linear tasks, but certificate-aware classical optimization closes most of the advantage; SO(3) results show no clear model advantage over CMA-ES.
Certified-candidate retention produced new certified docking designs in every run, whereas removing it produced none.

papers.abstract: Large closed-source reasoning models expose only their final answers. The intermediate reasoning that produces those answers is hidden behind API surfaces, tool-call policies, and safety filters. Existing chain-of-thought (CoT) extraction methods assume a side channel: a visible reasoning field, a scratchpad carried through tool calls, or a signed/encrypted reasoning block. We reproduce three representative state-of-the-art extraction methods and find that, on Claude-Sonnet-5.5 accessed through the standard chat-completions interface, all three return zero CoT tokens. The failure is structural rather than a bug: the reasoning field is absent, named tool selection is rejected, free-text scratchpad arguments are filtered, and no replayable reasoning block is exposed. We therefore take a different route. We present RECAST, a reconstruction-based framework that conditions a decoder on the question and the target model's final answer, reconstructs a first-person structured rationale, cleans it, and builds SFT-ready data. To the best of our knowledge, RECAST is the first system to reconstruct CoT from frontier closed models such as Claude-Sonnet-5.5, GPT-6.1, and Gemini 3 without using hidden reasoning channels. We instantiate RECAST on Claude-Sonnet-5.5 and additionally obtain successful qualitative reconstructions on GPT-6.1 and Gemini 3 with the same answer-only protocol. The system is open-source and packaged as an agent skill: one prompt deploys it and runs the complete pipeline to produce SFT-ready CoT data. This preprint describes the system, its threat model, and a controlled artifact validation; it does not claim large-scale benchmark improvements.
authors: Qi Wang, Kang Xu, Chengcheng Wan, Jiangtao Wang
bullets: Existing CoT extraction methods fail on Claude-Sonnet-5.5’s standard chat interface because reasoning fields, tool calls, scratchpads, and replayable blocks are inaccessible or filtered.
RECAST conditions a decoder on the original question and target model answer to generate and clean a first-person structured rationale.
The framework produces SFT-ready CoT data and is packaged as an open-source agent skill with an end-to-end deployment prompt.
The authors report successful qualitative reconstructions on Claude-Sonnet-5.5, GPT-6.1, and Gemini 3 using an answer-only protocol.
The preprint presents controlled artifact validation and does not claim large-scale benchmark gains.

papers.abstract: Cultural value alignment requires not only model optimization but also a well-specified target grounded in real-human evidence. Yet how such targets should be grounded in human data remains largely unexplored, raising three fundamental questions: (1) whose values should be represented? (2) where should cultural values be observed? and (3) what signals reveal underlying values? We investigate these questions through Re3Culture, a large-scale dataset linking (i) Representative communities: 700+ human participants across four cultures recruited through cultural-affiliation screening and demographic-aware sampling; (ii) Realistic scenario: culturally sensitive scenarios selected by community members, e.g., family and kinship; and (iii) Revealed value signals: 1,400+ value surveys, 20,000+ topic-grounded behavioral principles and explicit value priorities with responses for 6,000+ situated questions. Our analysis shows why these choices matter for defining the target, with three implications. First, estimating cultural values requires both community affiliation and broad internal coverage. Substituting other cultures or restricting subgroup coverage shifts value estimates. LLM simulations also disproportionately reflect particular subgroups. Second, values must be observed in concrete, community-guided situations. Abstract questionnaire profiles weakly recover situated priorities, and communities differ in which scenarios they identify as culturally value-revealing. Third, value priorities should be elicited explicitly, not learned from response preferences or bottom-line answers alone. Preferences conflate value agreement with other response-level qualities, and similar answers can be derived from different value priorities. By addressing these requirements, Re3Culture provides the first human-grounded resource that explicitly informs target definition for cultural value alignment.
authors: Jing Yao, Hyunjin Hwang, Weihua Zheng, Bryan Chen Zhengyu Tan, Jia Wang Peh, Dylan Raharja, JinYeong Bak, Roy Ka-Wei Lee, Rui Cao, Yuki Arase, Jacki O'Neill, Zhicheng Dou, Xing Xie, Xiaoyuan Yi, Furu Wei

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are used in many domains, but molecular property prediction with them is still little explored. In this work we evaluate the capability of 7 frontier LLMs to predict molecular properties together with a self-reported uncertainty from in-context examples, and compare them with classical baselines trained on the same molecules. We use 4 datasets and screen each for contamination of the training data of the LLMs: three are clean, and the fourth, ESOL, is memorised by most of the models and serves as a comparison. On the clean datasets every LLM improves with the context, at 30 examples the most accurate one beats every baseline. The requested reasoning effort changes accuracy little. The self-reported uncertainty ranks the prediction errors weakly, with Spearman rank correlations of up to 0.46, about the level reached by the uncertainties of the baselines. Combining uncertainty and prediction, on lipophilicity the most certain half of the best LLM is the most accurate at small context sizes; on BACE and antiviral, and on lipophilicity at large context sizes, the best LLMs are on par with the best baseline. On the contaminated ESOL dataset the LLMs show no improvement with the context size, as expected for a memorised dataset, and their stated uncertainty is smaller on the molecules whose value they recall.
authors: Matthias Busch, Marius Tacke, Tamadur Albaraghtheh, Sviatlana V. Lamaka, Mikhail L. Zheludkevich, Roland C. Aydin, Christian Feiler, Christian J. Cyron
bullets: Seven frontier LLMs were evaluated on four molecular-property datasets against classical baselines trained on the same molecules.
After contamination screening, three datasets were clean; ESOL was largely memorized by the models and used for comparison.
On clean datasets, all LLMs improved with more context, and the best model surpassed every baseline with 30 examples.
Self-reported uncertainty weakly ranked errors, reaching Spearman correlations of up to 0.46—similar to baseline uncertainty.
On memorized ESOL, context brought no improvement and models reported lower uncertainty for molecules whose values they recalled.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates LLMs for molecular property prediction and uncertainty estimation, demonstrating in-context learning capabilities.

papers.abstract: Task Vectors (TVs) provide a compact way to steer large language models, but they are typically treated as atomized directions merely extracted from hidden states, leaving their internal functional structure poorly understood. Motivated by prior work that decomposes in-context learning into Task Recognition (TR) and Task Learning (TL), we ask whether a single TV can likewise be decomposed into functionally meaningful components. We formulate a TR/TL-based decomposition from candidate-label unembeddings, separating each TV into TR, TL, and residual components, and try to optimize the TR and TL coefficients using Bayesian optimization for more effective intervention. We evaluate this formulation across multiple model families, classification tasks, and both instruction- and demonstration-based TVs. Across these settings, TR/TL-based optimization identifies intervention directions that outperform the original TVs. Although optimization over random directions can also improve performance, TR/TL-based search yields more reliable gains, particularly for instruction-based TVs. Moreover, isolated interventions on the decomposed components produce distinct logit-level effects that are consistent with their intended functional roles. Together, these results suggest that TVs are not monolithic steering directions, but can be decomposed into functionally meaningful components that support both interpretation and control.
authors: Yukiya Horiba, Hakaze Cho, Takahiro Yakoh
bullets: Addresses the limited understanding of task vectors as seemingly atomized steering directions.
Uses candidate-label unembeddings to formulate a TR/TL/residual decomposition and Bayesian optimization of component coefficients.
Evaluates the approach across multiple model families, classification tasks, and instruction- or demonstration-based task vectors.
The optimized TR/TL interventions outperform original task vectors, with especially reliable gains for instruction-based vectors.
Component-specific interventions produce distinct logit effects consistent with their intended functional roles.

papers.abstract: Clinical trial failures are a major barrier to efficient drug development, incurring substantial costs and delaying patient access to effective therapies. Structured approaches such as the Hierarchical Interaction Network (HINT) predict trial outcomes by explicitly modelling interactions between drugs, diseases and protocols, but make limited use of the free text in trial registrations. We evaluate two domain-specific language models, BioBERT (108M parameters) and BioMistral (7B parameters), for phase-level outcome prediction on the TOP benchmark (12,477 trials), representing each trial as text built from ten ClinicalTrials.gov fields. We compare fine-tuning (full fine-tuning for BioBERT, low-rank adaptation for BioMistral) with probing, in which the pretrained model is frozen and only a lightweight classifier is trained on its embeddings. On the held-out test set of each phase, all four language-model variants achieved higher ROC-AUC (0.613--0.772) and PR-AUC (0.649--0.901) than the published HINT results, corresponding to relative PR-AUC gains of 10--20\%. F1 differences were small and mixed, and no model, including HINT, clearly exceeded the F1 of a trivial classifier that predicts success for every trial. Under the configurations tested, probing performed comparably to fine-tuning: fine-tuned models scored highest on ROC-AUC and PR-AUC in Phases I and II, and frozen BioMistral embeddings in Phase III (ROC-AUC 0.772; PR-AUC 0.901), although most differences between variants were below 0.03 and were not tested for significance. These results suggest that pretrained biomedical representations already encode signal relevant to trial outcome, and that probing is a computationally cheaper alternative to fine-tuning for this task.
authors: Burak Bakkar, Hana Moalla, Mohamed Salem Jedidi, Haifa Ben Messaoud, Nicolas Lopez Carranza
bullets: Clinical-trial failure motivates better phase-level outcome prediction using information in registration text.
BioBERT and BioMistral represented trials as text from ten ClinicalTrials.gov fields and were evaluated with fine-tuning or frozen-embedding probing.
All four variants exceeded published HINT results in ROC-AUC and PR-AUC, with reported relative PR-AUC gains of 10–20%.
Fine-tuning was strongest in Phases I–II, while frozen BioMistral embeddings performed best in Phase III; most variant differences were small and untested for significance.
F1 gains were limited: no approach clearly surpassed the trivial always-success classifier on F1.

papers.abstract: Language models face two opposing concerns: monoculture, in which models err in correlated ways, and multiplicity, in which equally accurate models make conflicting decisions. The rise of reasoning models has complicated this debate: On the one hand, reasoning may increase model agreement if models anchor on the same salient features or follow similar reasoning paths. On the other hand, stochastic reasoning traces may introduce additional branch points leading to more diverse predictions. We resolve this tension by distinguishing reasoning as an intervention from reasoning as an observed behavior. We compare agreement under controlled changes in reasoning effort with agreement across observed reasoning lengths, measuring both against the agreement expected from model accuracy. Across nine models from two developers and three classification tasks, enabling reasoning increases agreement between models evaluated on the same individuals. Yet the individuals who elicit longer reasoning traces receive less consistent predictions across models. Both patterns persist after accounting for differences in accuracy. Asking models to reason more thus promotes agreement, while observing them reason longer signals disagreement.
bullets: The study addresses the tension between correlated model errors (monoculture) and conflicting decisions among similarly accurate models (multiplicity).
It separates reasoning as a controlled intervention from reasoning as an observed behavior.
Across nine models, two developers, and three classification tasks, increased reasoning effort raises agreement on the same individuals.
Individuals producing longer reasoning traces receive less consistent predictions across models.
Both effects remain after accounting for model accuracy.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates reasoning behavior in LLMs, a core aspect of modern LLM research and architecture.
papers.title: Does Reasoning Make Language Models Agree?
papers.tldr: Reasoning has opposite effects on language-model agreement depending on how it is studied: prompting more reasoning increases agreement, while longer observed reasoning traces signal less consistent predictions.

papers.abstract: Sparse tuning is widely used to adapt large language models due to its parameter efficiency. However, its effectiveness depends not only on the number of trainable parameters, but also on the feature-interaction topology of the sparse update's structural support. Limited or uneven connectivity in this support may isolate subsets of feature dimensions, forming information islands that restrict direct task-specific interactions through the trainable update. To address this issue, we propose Small-World Induced Fine-Tuning (SWIFT), a sparse tuning framework inspired by small-world connectivity. SWIFT combines block-diagonal sparse updates for local feature mixing with a fixed deterministic scattering permutation that routes the mixed outputs across feature groups without additional trainable parameters. We further show theoretically that certain random sparse-update models and block-diagonal updates can exhibit information islands, whereas a sufficiently scattering permutation guarantees positive block-level expansion when the trainable block-diagonal factor consists of equal-sized, structurally dense square blocks. Extensive experiments on commonsense reasoning, natural language generation, and image classification demonstrate that SWIFT outperforms the evaluated parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) baselines on average and can match or surpass full fine-tuning. Implementation is available at https://github.com/xianchaoguan/SWIFT
authors: Xianchao Guan, Zijun Xiong, Yifeng Wang, Yubo Cui, Yaowei Wang, Guo-Sen Xie, Xin Li, Zheng Zhang
bullets: Sparse tuning can suffer from limited feature connectivity, creating information islands in the update structure.
SWIFT uses block-diagonal updates for local feature mixing and a fixed scattering permutation to route information across feature groups without extra trainable parameters.
Theoretical analysis shows block-diagonal and some random sparse updates can form islands, while sufficient scattering provides positive block-level expansion under stated conditions.
Experiments across commonsense reasoning, text generation, and image classification show SWIFT outperforms evaluated PEFT baselines on average and can match or exceed full fine-tuning.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes SWIFT, a sparse tuning framework that improves feature interaction topology in LLMs by introducing small-world connectivity to prevent information islands.

papers.tldr: SWIFT improves sparse fine-tuning by adding deterministic small-world-style routing that connects otherwise isolated feature groups.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) acquire extensive factual knowledge during pre-training, which may include sensitive, private, or copyrighted information, motivating the development of unlearning methods that selectively remove specific knowledge while preserving general capabilities. However, existing approaches typically optimize entire responses without explicitly identifying the knowledge to be forgotten, resulting in coarse and uncontrolled forgetting. To address this, we revisit the forgetting target of LLM unlearning and introduce Knowledge Association (KA), which characterizes the association between a query context and its target knowledge and is instantiated by the corresponding conditional predictive distribution, as the fundamental target of forgetting. Based on KA, we propose Knowledge Association Reinforcement Unlearning (KARU), a unified reinforcement learning framework that suppresses forgotten knowledge associations while preserving retained ones. Specifically, KARU derives complementary mechanisms from the KA-based formulation: token-level reward construction for finer-grained forgetting supervision, distribution-level regularization for precise knowledge suppression, and proximity-aware retain sampling to mitigate collateral degradation. Experiments across diverse LLMs on representative benchmarks demonstrate that KARU consistently improves forgetting effectiveness over existing baselines while maintaining comparable retention performance and general utility.
authors: Wutong Xu, Yun Qu, Haiyan Feng, Qi Wang, Xiangyang Ji
bullets: Existing unlearning methods can forget coarsely because they optimize complete responses without isolating the knowledge to remove.
The paper defines Knowledge Association (KA) as the conditional predictive distribution linking a query context to target knowledge.
KARU uses reinforcement learning with token-level rewards, distribution-level suppression, and proximity-aware sampling of retained knowledge.
Experiments across diverse LLMs and benchmarks show improved forgetting effectiveness with comparable retention and general utility.
The method targets selective knowledge removal, with scope determined by the identified knowledge associations.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces Knowledge Association Reinforcement Unlearning (KARU), a framework for selectively removing specific knowledge associations from LLMs while preserving general capabilities.
papers.title: What Should LLMs Forget: Reinforcement Unlearning of Knowledge Associations
papers.tldr: KARU treats context–knowledge associations—not whole responses—as the target of LLM unlearning, enabling more precise forgetting while preserving retained knowledge and general utility.

papers.abstract: Agent systems built on local large language models are increasingly marketed through the vocabulary of cognitive architecture: modules named global workspace, theory of mind, causal reasoning, or active inference are listed as features, and the presence of the name is taken as the presence of the mechanism. We ask the prior question -- does the named computation actually happen -- and contribute a transferable verification method for the claim-implementation gap: a four-question static audit protocol with line-number evidence and call-chain tracing, demonstrated on two systems. We audit a system claiming 25 cognitive mechanisms, pre-register falsifiable predictions for 11 modules and execute the interventions, replicate the protocol on the IIT-phi core of a second, independent system with its own pre-committed falsification criteria, and run two repair experiments as positive controls. In 18 of 25 modules the computed value never reaches any production output; three idle-wiring shapes new to the dead-code and code-smell literatures emerge (connected-but-never-called, called-but-inert, called-but-content-blind). Of 61 frozen criteria across 12 interventions, 53 were confirmed, two partially adjudicated, five falsified, one adjudication-ambiguous. Repairs raised planner task success from 0.028 to 1.000 and cut state-controller error by 52%. Module names and module computations must be audited as independent claims; the protocol and the five-class failure taxonomy are reusable for the claim-implementation gap at two-system, case-level depth.
authors: Peter Chen, Ni Zhang, Ying Xu, Siyuan Zhang
bullets: Audits 25 claimed cognitive-architecture mechanisms using static code tracing, falsifiable predictions, interventions, replication, and repair controls.
In 18 of 25 modules, computed values never reached production outputs; three previously undescribed idle-wiring patterns were identified.
Across 12 interventions and 61 frozen criteria, 53 were confirmed, five falsified, two partially adjudicated, and one remained ambiguous.
Repair experiments improved planner task success and reduced state-controller error, showing that implementation defects can materially affect behavior.
Findings are case-level across two systems; the authors argue module names and actual computations must be evaluated independently.
