papers.title: Real Computation or Merely Naming? A Pre-Registered Mechanism Audit of 25 Cognitive-Architecture Modules in an LLM-Based Agent System
papers.tldr: A pre-registered audit finds that many named cognitive modules in LLM agents do not perform meaningful computation, and offers a reusable method for verifying implementation claims.

papers.abstract: We release Saidzoda-Tajik-LFM-2.6B, a Tajik adaptation of the 2.6B-parameter hybrid model LFM2.5-2.6B-Base, built for tool calling in Tajik on modest hardware. The recipe has two stages: LoRA continued pretraining (CPT) on 1,485,319 cleaned Tajik web documents for 3 epochs, then one epoch of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on a mix of machine-translated Tajik tool calls, English tool calls kept as replay, and Tajik instructions. On a 174-item tool-calling test set built from BFCL v3 and machine-translated to Tajik, strict full-call accuracy on Tajik prompts rises from 20.69 for the base model to 64.14 (paired difference +43.45 points, 95% interval +35.2 to +51.7); a lenient parser that also accepts the base model's own call formats puts the base at 31.72. English shows no detectable change (76.55 and 77.24). Every CPT checkpoint scores zero: CPT removes the native tool-call format and, as the lenient re-scoring shows, part of the skill itself. Outside tool calling, accuracy on a Tajik knowledge benchmark rises from 28.0 to 35.0, Belebele Tajik shows no significant change, and English MMLU falls from 60.8 to 52.5. The model is not a general Tajik assistant. It almost never declines when no tool fits (6.9% correct on Tajik, against 31.0% for the base under the lenient parser), it is weak at multi-turn calls, and its calls should be checked before they are executed. We describe the data, the training settings and every evaluation in enough detail to repeat them.
authors: Tohir Saidzoda, Nekruz Maxudov, Bedil Karimov, Abubakr Abdullozoda, Amin Jalilov, Jonibek Kishvarov, Rahmonali Sharipov, Mariyamkhon Shodyeva
bullets: The model is adapted from LFM2.5-2.6B-Base for Tajik tool calling on modest hardware.
LoRA continued pretraining uses 1,485,319 cleaned Tajik web documents, followed by SFT on translated Tajik tool calls, English replay data, and Tajik instructions.
Strict Tajik full-call accuracy increases from 20.69 to 64.14, while English performance remains essentially unchanged.
All continued-pretraining checkpoints score zero on tool calling, indicating loss of the native format and some underlying skill—not just formatting mismatch.
Knowledge accuracy improves, but English MMLU declines; the model is weak at refusals and multi-turn calls, so generated calls require validation.

papers.selection_reason: Details the adaptation of a hybrid model to Tajik for tool calling using LoRA continued pretraining and supervised fine-tuning, analyzing the effects of CPT on model capabilities.
papers.title: Saidzoda-Tajik-LFM-2.6B: Adapting a 2.6B Hybrid Model to Tajik Tool Calling, and What Continued Pretraining Takes Away
papers.tldr: A two-stage LoRA adaptation substantially improves Tajik tool calling, but continued pretraining erases the base model’s native tool-call format and harms several broader capabilities.

papers.abstract: Unlike autoregressive (AR) models, diffusion language models (DLMs) permit parallel token updates, flexible generation, and bidirectional attention, but leading systems rely on costly pretraining or full-model fine-tuning. We present Build Your Own DLM (BYOD), a generalizable LoRA-only recipe for parameter-efficient AR-to-DLM conversion. Without architecture-specific tuning, BYOD induces diffusion generation in Gemma 2 9B, Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen2.5 7B, and Ministral 8B; to our knowledge, this is the first reported AR-to-DLM conversion of a Mistral model. The adapters comprise 4.1-5.8% of final parameters while every base-model parameter remains frozen; each 25,000-iteration conversion needs at most 102.4M tokens, processed in 3.1-4.0 hours on one Google Colab GPU. All four models generate from fully masked sequences, use bidirectional context in a controlled attention test, and retain substantial parent-model knowledge. BYOD-Gemma is the strongest BYOD conversion on our nine-task evaluation, reaching 50.6% average accuracy compared with 51.9% for LLaDA 8B Instruct in the same harness. Open-generation quality at low network function evaluation (NFE) budgets remains the principal limitation: BYOD perplexity is 8.3-11.1 versus 4.1 for LLaDA and 2.2-3.0 for the AR parents when generating 128 tokens in 64 steps. To enable further experimentation and inspection, we provide a standalone training and evaluation implementation and interactive demos for all four conversions. BYOD thus provides a practical route for extending diffusion generation to other existing model families while identifying the gap that efficient conversion must next close.
authors: Ruurd J. A. Kuiper, Robert A. Bagheri
bullets: Addresses the high pretraining and full-fine-tuning costs of building diffusion language models.
Uses an architecture-agnostic, LoRA-only conversion recipe with all base-model parameters frozen.
Demonstrated on Gemma 2, Llama 3.1, Qwen2.5, and Ministral; the latter is reported as the first Mistral AR-to-DLM conversion.
Converted models support fully masked generation, bidirectional context, and retain substantial parent-model knowledge.
Task performance is competitive, but open-generation quality at low sampling budgets remains the main limitation.

papers.title: BYOD: Build Your Own DLM - Efficient Autoregressive-to-Diffusion Language Model Conversion
papers.tldr: BYOD converts pretrained autoregressive language models into diffusion language models using only lightweight LoRA adapters, enabling efficient experimentation without modifying base-model weights.

papers.abstract: Language agents increasingly tackle long-horizon tasks in interactive environments, where actions often depend on latent preconditions. The core difficulty is not trajectory length but recovery: when a prerequisite is missing or an earlier decomposition fails, trying another plausible action rarely helps. ReAct and later reflection or adaptive-planning methods support local correction, but express recovery as free-form text, with no explicit control state linking the terminal goal, the active goal, and the failure source. We introduce the Verify--Backtrack Loop (VBL), a training-free extension of ReAct that turns precondition discovery and failure diagnosis into structured planning-state updates. VBL maintains the task decomposition as a bounded goal stack and, on goal activation, execution failure, or material state change, jointly verifies two horizons---whether the active goal contributes to the terminal goal and whether it is feasible in the current state. These dual-horizon judgments, combined with typed failure attribution, trigger explicit operations---Push, Pop, retry, or BacktrackTo the parent. We evaluate VBL with Qwen3.5-9B, GPT-4o, and DeepSeek-V3.2 on AppWorld, ALFWorld, and ScienceWorld. VBL improves over ReAct and reflection-based control on every backbone--benchmark pair. On the challenging AppWorld setting, it improves task success by up to 22.07 percentage points over ReAct. Ablations show that removing either verification or diagnosis degrades performance, in several settings below ReAct, confirming that the two mechanisms are complementary. These results show that reliable long-horizon interaction benefits from revising the planning state, not merely the next action.
authors: Mingyang Liu, Qingcan Kang, Shixiong Kai, Tao Zhong, Mingxuan Yuan, Xin Li, Linqi Song
bullets: Targets failed prerequisites and flawed decompositions, rather than relying on another plausible action.
Extends ReAct with a bounded goal stack and dual-horizon checks for goal relevance and current feasibility.
Uses typed failure attribution to trigger Push, Pop, retry, or BacktrackTo-parent operations.
Improves over ReAct and reflection-based control across all tested backbone–benchmark pairs; AppWorld gains reach up to 22.07 percentage points over ReAct.
Ablations show verification and diagnosis are complementary, with removing either sometimes reducing performance below ReAct.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Control structures compared. (1) ReAct interleaves thought, action, and observation in a linear loop. (2) ReflAct replaces the thought with reflection on the current state relative to the task goal, but the loop stays linear. (3) VBL maintains an explicit goal stack: VERIFY checks alignment and readiness when due is set (on activation, after failure, or after a material state change), a completed goal is removed with POP, and a failure is routed through DIAGNOSE to one of PUSH (insert a prerequisite), a local retry, or BACKTRACKTO (resume from the parent). The executor receives the root task text together with the active goal—here g2—not the full stack.
Figure 2: Case study (task 2d9f728_1). Baselines thrash on auth errors; VBL inserts login via PUSH and completes the settlement.

papers.abstract: Automatic assessment of textual CEFR levels is an important task in educational natural language processing. However, accurate CEFR level prediction remains challenging due to the naturally imbalanced distribution of CEFR levels and the ambiguous boundaries between adjacent levels. To address these challenges, we propose a unified training objective that combines focal loss with supervised contrastive learning. Focal loss mitigates class imbalance by emphasizing underrepresented and difficult examples, while supervised contrastive learning learns more discriminative representations by encouraging intra-class compactness and inter-class separation. We evaluate the proposed method on sentence- and document-level CEFR assessment in both monolingual and multilingual settings. Experimental results demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms strong baselines across all settings, establishing new state-of-the-art performance on multiple CEFR assessment benchmarks.
bullets: Addresses class imbalance and ambiguous boundaries between adjacent CEFR levels.
Combines focal loss to emphasize difficult or underrepresented examples with supervised contrastive learning for more discriminative representations.
Evaluates sentence- and document-level assessment in monolingual and multilingual settings.
Consistently outperforms strong baselines and achieves state-of-the-art results on multiple CEFR benchmarks.

papers.abstract: This study investigates the effectiveness of large pre-trained language models (LLMs) for knowledge entity relation extraction (KERE) from academic papers. Existing studies have examined individual types of LLM-based strategies and evaluated model performance using metrics such as precision and recall. To provide a broader evaluation, this study investigates multiple strategies, including closed-source LLM-based CoT prompting, LoRA-adapted open-source LLMs, LLM-enhanced small pre-trained language models (SLMs), and SLM-enhanced closed-source LLMs. In addition, this study introduces two strategies, namely SLM-enhanced open-source LLMs and closed-source LLM-enhanced open-source LLMs. These strategies are evaluated from multiple perspectives, including metrics, their ability to mitigate errors observed in SLMs, and potential directions for model optimization. This study manually constructs two annotated datasets in the NLP domain, covering Abstract and Full-Text datasets. Experimental results show that the LoRA-adapted T5 model achieves the highest macro F1 scores of 0.7408 and 0.7013 on the Abstract and Full-Text datasets, respectively. SLMs also benefit from LLM-generated entity descriptions under the LLM-enhanced SLM strategy. Error analysis further reveals that the effectiveness of LLM-based strategies in mitigating SLM errors varies across error types. Based on the identified limitations and error patterns of these strategies, several optimization directions are proposed. In addition, combining strategies with different error patterns further improves KERE performance.
bullets: Compares closed-source LLM prompting, LoRA-adapted open-source LLMs, SLM–LLM enhancement, and newly proposed hybrid strategies.
Introduces two manually annotated NLP datasets covering academic abstracts and full-text articles.
LoRA-adapted T5 achieves macro F1 scores of 0.7408 on abstracts and 0.7013 on full text.
LLM-generated entity descriptions improve SLM performance, though error mitigation varies by error type.
Combining strategies with complementary error patterns further improves KERE performance.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate structured outputs, but existing constrained-decoding methods mainly enforce syntax and cannot directly enforce satisfaction of a formal specification. We introduce a neuro-symbolic, specification-guided decoding framework that combines LLM generation with symbolic reasoning. At each step, the framework refines the decoding grammar by filtering out values that cannot be extended to an output satisfying the specification. We present a forward-only variant that guarantees specification satisfaction by construction, and a backtracking variant that revises earlier feasible choices when their downstream consequences leave only values that the LLM itself judges unsuitable. The framework is model-agnostic, requires no retraining, and builds on existing grammar-constrained decoding mechanisms. Experiments on configuration and constraint-solving benchmarks show that the forward-only variant reliably produces specification-compliant outputs while reducing repeated LLM inference compared with rejection sampling and incurring modest symbolic-reasoning overhead. The backtracking variant further reduces cases in which the model is forced to select values that it has itself judged unsuitable, thereby substantially improving adherence to the LLM's stated interpretation of the prompt.
authors: Alessandro Previti, Konstantinos Vandikas, Mario Alviano, Mats Carlsson, Albin Larsson Forsberg, Alexandros Nikou, Athanasios Karapantelakis, Aneta Vulgarakis
bullets: Refines the decoding grammar at each step by removing values that cannot lead to a specification-satisfying output.
A forward-only variant guarantees compliance by construction and reduces repeated LLM inference versus rejection sampling.
A backtracking variant revises earlier choices when later constraints leave only values the LLM considers unsuitable.
Model-agnostic and compatible with existing grammar-constrained decoding, with modest symbolic-reasoning overhead.
Evaluated on configuration and constraint-solving benchmarks, improving specification adherence and alignment with the model’s prompt interpretation.

papers.abstract: While prior work has highlighted that systematic nation-level bias in large language models (LLMs) can pose operational risks for international relations (IR) applications, many existing evaluations still lack a clearly specified unbiased reference (ground truth), limiting fully quantitative and cross-setting measurement. Using an expanded corpus of 722 official UN Security Council (UNSC) records, we measure nation-level bias with five complementary tests, thereby extending prior approaches to cover a broader set of bias expression channels: opinion ranking (WOW), association sorting (AK+-), vote simulation (PVS), opposition attribution (F-Oppose), and framing (Headliner). To enable grounded bias evaluation, we explicitly define an unbiased status for each test; in particular, for WOW and AK+- where ground truth is difficult to specify, we propose an action-based pseudo unbiased status derived from observable voting behavior to construct a quantifiable baseline. Benchmarking 4 LLMs (GPT-4o-mini, Llama 3.3-70B, Mistral-22B-Small, and Qwen3-30B) across the five permanent members of the UNSC, we find a test-agnostic macro-pattern: relative to the reference baselines defined for each test, model outputs lean toward the opposition (red) side for China and Russia and toward the supportive (blue) side for the U.K., the U.S., and France. These results underscore the need to audit IR-facing LLM deployments with grounded, multi-test benchmarks tied to explicit reference points.
authors: Jonghyeon Choi, Yeonjun Choi, Beakcheol Jang
bullets: Evaluates nation-level bias using 722 official UN Security Council records and five complementary tests: opinion ranking, association sorting, vote simulation, opposition attribution, and framing.
Defines test-specific unbiased reference statuses to support quantitative, cross-setting comparisons.
Introduces action-based pseudo-unbiased baselines for opinion ranking and association sorting, derived from observable voting behavior.
Across four evaluated LLMs, outputs lean opposition-oriented for China and Russia, and supportive-oriented for the U.K., U.S., and France.
Highlights the need for grounded, multi-test audits of LLMs used in international-relations applications.

papers.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning of Model Context Protocol (MCP) agents is typically conducted on a static data distribution, which fails to adapt to the student's evolving capabilities and leaves newly exposed weaknesses insufficiently addressed. To address these challenges, we propose \method, an agent--data mutual evolution framework that enables MCP agents to improve through a closed loop of task evolution, trajectory evolution, and supervised fine-tuning. Specifically, \method\ assesses the student's established capabilities and capability gaps from rollout feedback to identify learning targets. Task evolution then translates these targets into executable tasks by adapting the instructions and observable environment states of compatible verified seed tasks while keeping their verifiers aligned. To provide reliable and efficient demonstrations for these tasks, trajectory evolution uses reusable skills to recover failed teacher rollouts and refine successful ones. The resulting task--trajectory pairs are used to fine-tune the student, while accepted tasks seed subsequent evolution. To close the loop, we re-evaluate the updated student and use its feedback to guide the next round of data evolution. Experiments on Toolathlon, MCPMark, and MCP-Atlas demonstrate consistent improvements over the initial student, yielding absolute gains of 16.5\%, 10.2\%, and 12.6\%, respectively. Project page: https://github.com/xagao/EvoMCP.
authors: Xuanang Gao, Kepeng Lin, Xinyan Shi, Yong Deng, Shuheng Shen, Changhua Meng, Xiaofeng Wu, Jie Yang, Wei Liu
bullets: Addresses the limits of static supervised fine-tuning data for evolving MCP agents.
Uses rollout feedback to identify capability gaps and learning targets.
Evolves verified seed tasks while preserving aligned verifiers, then recovers or refines teacher trajectories with reusable skills.
Fine-tunes the student on evolved task–trajectory pairs and repeats the process using new feedback.
Reports absolute gains of 16.5% on Toolathlon, 10.2% on MCPMark, and 12.6% on MCP-Atlas over the initial student.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a co-evolution framework for agents and training data, addressing the static data distribution problem in agent fine-tuning. This is a form of test-time adaptation and continual learning for LLM agents.
papers.title: EvoMCP: Co-evolving MCP agents and training data

papers.abstract: Growing submission volumes have renewed interest in using large language models (LLMs) to support peer review. It remains unclear how such evaluation should be structured, how much the model matters, and whether LLM scores predict research impact. We evaluate five paradigms across three input representations and three LLMs on 232 stratified ICLR 2025 submissions. Direct absolute rating matches comparative ranking on rank correlation with human scores, yet compresses most predictions above the accept threshold, flagging almost none of the papers reviewers scored below it. A base-rate-matched recalibration control locates the cause: comparative ranking supplies placement, not better ordering, and after recalibration Direct Rating reaches higher agreement than Elo while making 24% as many API calls. Abstract-only input beats full-paper summarization, and model choice matters as much as paradigm choice. Replicating on all 11,513 scored submissions reproduces these patterns, shows absolute agreement depends on the evaluated set's score spread, and finds none beating an always-reject baseline in accuracy. Human scores track citations better than any paradigm, with one exception: Group Rating retains its citation correlation after controlling for human scores, and alone ranks within the accepted pool. Ranking quality alone cannot assess review quality; calibration, thresholds, model, and target outcome all matter.
bullets: Evaluates five LLM review paradigms across three input representations and three models using ICLR 2025 submissions.
Direct absolute rating and comparative ranking have similar rank correlation, but direct ratings are heavily compressed above the acceptance threshold.
After base-rate-matched recalibration, Direct Rating agrees more with human scores than Elo while using 24% as many API calls.
Abstract-only input outperforms full-paper summarization, and model choice matters as much as paradigm choice.
Human scores better predict citations overall; Group Rating uniquely preserves citation correlation after controlling for human scores and ranks within accepted papers.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the experimental pipeline. Papers pass through three input representations (top), then through (a) absolute rating methods, which score each paper independently, or (b) comparative rating methods, which infer a latent rating from head-to-head outcomes and rescale it to 1–10. Only the comparative family is rescaled, so inflation and other absolute-error metrics are not comparable across families. Inline metrics give the best configuration in each family on the stratified 232-paper sample at the fixed ≥ 6 threshold.

Figure 7: Score distributions for the five paradigms vs. ground truth (abstract-only, GPT-4o-mini). Absolute methods (Direct, Anchor) compress scores into a narrow 6–8 range, while comparative methods (Elo, Swiss) preserve broader distributions closer to ground truth. Annotated below each: µ (mean), σ (standard deviation), ρ (Spearman correlation).

Figure 2: External validity on the 126 test papers carrying a retrievable citation count, a complete set of paradigm scores and a recorded decision. a, Paradigm rank under three evaluation targets; the lines cross, so none is best on all three. The decision target counts the 18 withdrawn submissions as non-accepted, which leaves the ordering unchanged. b, Spearman ρ with citation count, as an open circle (raw) joined to a filled circle (controlling for the mean reviewer score). Only Group Rating retains its correlation after the control (ρ = 0.304, p = 0.0006, surviving Bonferroni correction across the eighteen tests in Table 11). Anchor’s partial value is negative and Swiss’s exceeds its raw value, so the two are given as positions on a common axis rather than as a decomposition.

Figure 3: Population-scale false-positive (strong paper wrongly filtered) and false-negative (low-quality paper wrongly accepted) rates as a function of the accept threshold, swept from 5 to 7. The dashed gray line marks the fixed ≥ 6 threshold used in Table 9; the dotted green line marks the base-rate-matched threshold of Elo and Swiss; Direct Rating’s, at 7.67, lies beyond the plotted range. Direct Rating’s curves are flat across the plotted range because only 1.8% of its predictions fall below 7, which is why a fixed threshold at 6 makes it appear degenerate.

Figure 4: Error localization by ground-truth score bin (population scale, threshold ≥ 6). For each paradigm, blue bars show false-positive counts (strong papers wrongly filtered) and orange bars show false-negative counts (low-quality papers wrongly accepted). Direct’s errors are almost entirely false negatives, since its inflation accepts nearly all low-quality papers, whereas Elo and Swiss distribute the error budget across both classes, with false positives concentrated at borderline ground-truth scores.

Figure 6: Score distributions by input representation (all paradigms pooled, GPT-4o-mini). Violin shapes show density and box plots show quartiles; ground truth (gray) is shown for reference. The three representations differ little in spread (pooled σ 1.56, 1.62 and 1.59 for abstract-only, vanilla and objective), and all are far narrower than ground truth (σ = 2.16). Annotated below each group: µ (mean), σ (standard deviation), ρ̄ (mean Spearman correlation with ground truth across paradigms).

Figure 9: Cross-model performance heatmaps. Left: Cohen’s κ (practical decision utility). Center: Spearman ρ (ranking potential). Right: grade inflation (calibration). GPT-4o-mini Elo achieves the highest κ despite slightly lower ρ than Direct.

Figure 12: Ranking potential versus grade inflation (left) and versus decision utility (right) for all 15 configurations. GPT-4o-mini Direct sits at high ρ but near-zero κ, while Elo converts similar ρ into higher κ through calibration.

Figure 11: Model capability profiles averaged across paradigms, on five axes: the decision utility metrics (κ and macro F1), the threshold-free AUC-ROC, ranking potential (ρ), and a calibration axis plotting 1− inflation/4 so that a larger radius is better on every axis.

Figure 5: Interaction between paradigm and input representation. Left: Spearman ρ (higher is better). Right: Mean Absolute Error (lower is better). Abstract-only consistently outperforms across paradigms, and Elo achieves the lowest MAE regardless of input representation.

Figure 8: Robustness check: Spearman ρ (left) and Cohen’s κ (right) under four ground-truth aggregations, of which the trimmed mean coincides with the mean (Appendix M). Paradigm rankings are identical across variants.

The Group vanilla and objective rows are computed on 230 papers, two having failed group assignment; the Group abstract row is the perpaper mean of the three randomized-grouping runs and covers all 232.

The first three numeric columns are NDCG@10, NDCG@20, and NDCG over all papers. Top-k precision is computed with a stable sort, so for paradigms that assign the same score to large blocks of papers it reports one arbitrary tie-break rather than a property of the ordering; see the discussion of Direct + Abstract below.
Table 1: Review paradigm comparison under abstractonly input (GPT-4o-mini). Column headings as in Table 4. The Group row is a three-run mean (Appendix D); all other rows are single runs.

Table 4: Input representation compared, averaged across all five paradigms (GPT-4o-mini). r: Pearson; ρ: Spearman; τ : Kendall; Infl.: grade inflation.

Table 9: Population-scale results for GPT-4o-mini (abstract-only), at the fixed ≥ 6 accept threshold and at each paradigm’s own base-rate-matched threshold (the cut at which its predicted reject rate equals the true rate). Recalibration is order-preserving, so ρ and inflation are unchanged by it. ρ and inflation are computed on all 11,513 scored ICLR 2025 papers; decision metrics on the 8,655 non-withdrawn papers (true reject rate 59.5%). Direct rows use the mean of three independent runs (ICC(2,1) = 0.417); because those scores are means of three integer ratings, Direct’s closest achievable predicted reject rate is 62.4% rather than 59.5%.

Table 10: Population-scale decision quality against the recorded ICLR 2025 accept/reject decisions rather than the ≥ 6 score rule. The qualitative pattern is unchanged: Direct Rating is reject-blind at a fixed threshold and recovers under recalibration, where it moves ahead of Elo. Under these labels Direct Rating is the one configuration whose accuracy exceeds the always-reject baseline, and only by 0.3 points.

Table 11: Spearman ρ between score and citation count, overall and within ICLR decision strata. ∗ denotes p < 0.05. The human correlation survives stratification. As in Table 1, the Group row is the per-paper mean of three randomized-grouping runs and the other rows are single runs. Group Rating is the only LLM paradigm to reach significance among accepted papers.

Table 12: Operating points at the fixed ≥ 6 accept threshold, using population-scale numbers (Table 9). These are a comparison among the configurations tested, not a deployment recommendation: under base-rate-matched thresholding (Section 4.5) Direct Rating attains the highest κ, and no configuration here reaches the 59.5% accuracy of always rejecting. The cost ratio cFP/cFN is the relative cost of filtering a strong paper (FP) versus admitting a low-quality one (FN).

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates different paradigms for using LLMs in academic paper peer review, analyzing the impact of calibration, model choice, and input representation on quality assessment.
papers.title: Comparative Evaluation of LLM-Based Review Paradigms for Academic Paper Quality Assessment
papers.tldr: LLM review performance depends strongly on calibration, model, input format, and evaluation target, with no paradigm outperforming an always-reject baseline in accuracy.

papers.abstract: Training-free expert pruning makes two decisions: which experts to remove, and what the layer computes when its router still selects a removed expert. Published methods change both at once. Holding the mask fixed, we compare replacement operators from three families on OLMoE, DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Moonlight, with Granite as a fourth router, using paired, multiplicity-corrected tests. The largest effect is a choice usually left implicit: the survivors' gate scale. On routers trained without top-k renormalization, renormalizing the survivors' gates, a common implementation choice, costs 0.8-8.5 points and reverses whether rerouting beats MoNE's mean-output replacement; on two routers trained with renormalization, the trained scale wins at 50% pruning. We introduce the tilted novice, a closed-form low-rank map of the pruned expert's input whose rank-0 case is MoNE's constant. At 50% pruning it adds 1.2-1.8% parameters and gains 3.45 and 1.37 points over the constant on OLMoE and Moonlight, stable across calibration draws and largely unchanged by 4- and 3-bit quantization. No operator dominates: trained-scale rerouting is best on DeepSeek-V2-Lite, and a partial copy of each pruned expert is statistically indistinguishable from the tilted novice on two models. Evaluation can change conclusions: at 25% pruning MoNE's constant keeps 92-97% of dense multiple-choice accuracy but only 5-65% of GSM8K and 0-17% of code scores, and the calibration domain moves the mask 4-9 times more than resampling. We propose a five-item reporting checklist.
authors: Ezza Ali, Sehrish Bibi, Momina Moetesum, Faisal Shafait
bullets: The study isolates replacement operators while keeping the pruning mask fixed across several MoE models and routers.
Survivor gate renormalization can reduce accuracy by 0.8–8.5 points on routers not trained with top-k renormalization and can reverse method rankings.
The proposed tilted novice improves over MoNE’s constant replacement by 3.45 points on OLMoE and 1.37 points on Moonlight at 50% pruning, with small parameter overhead.
Operator performance is model-dependent: trained-scale rerouting leads on DeepSeek-V2-Lite, while partial expert copies match the tilted novice on two models.

Evaluation task and calibration domain matter substantially; multiple-choice retention can overstate performance on math and code tasks, while calibration shifts the pruning mask more than resampling.

papers.abstract: Speech language models have expanded automatic speech recognition (ASR) from transcription to general speech-to-text generation. Yet existing benchmarks still assume a single ground-truth transcript per utterance, an assumption that struggles when models produce readable, formatted, or structured outputs. In this work, we introduce Grounded Generative Speech Recognition (GSR), reformulating speech recognition as generating semantically grounded text instead of a single transcript. We define a grounded reformulation space that characterizes all valid textual realizations supported by the input speech, and establish a four-level hierarchy of reformulation capabilities, including literal transcription, canonical reformulation, semantic reformulation and speech-grounded structuring. Based on this formulation, we present GSR-Bench, the first comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate generative speech recognition systems beyond exact transcript matching. GSR-Bench covers diverse scenarios including refined meeting transcription, cross-dialect translation, context-aware speech understanding, and robustness under silent or noisy acoustic conditions. To address the limitations of word-level evaluation metrics, we develop a multi-dimensional evaluation framework combining speech grounding assessment and LLM-based semantic judgment, whose reliability is validated through human preference studies. Extensive experiments across representative architectures, ranging from conventional ASR systems to end-to-end Speech-LLMs, reveal fundamental trade-offs between transcription fidelity and generative reformulation ability. Our analysis further identifies critical failure modes, including acoustic hallucination, unsupported generation, and instruction drift, providing insights into the design and evaluation of future grounded generative speech systems.
authors: Qing Wang, Qihan Hu, Hang Lv, Yan Yang, Boqing Liu, Xuechao Zhu, Zehan Li, Hongjie Chen, Jian Kang, Jie Li, Yongxiang Li, Lei Xie
bullets: Existing ASR benchmarks assume one correct transcript, limiting evaluation of readable, formatted, or structured outputs.
The proposed four-level hierarchy spans literal transcription, canonical and semantic reformulation, and speech-grounded structuring.
GSR-Bench evaluates scenarios including meeting transcription, cross-dialect translation, context-aware understanding, and silent or noisy speech.
A multidimensional framework combines speech-grounding assessment with LLM-based semantic judgment validated by human preference studies.
Experiments expose trade-offs between transcription fidelity and reformulation ability, along with acoustic hallucination, unsupported generation, and instruction drift.

papers.abstract: LLM-based simulated interviewees support interviewer training and the evaluation of mental health interviewing systems. Existing studies have primarily focused on improving human-likeness through richer patient profiles and behavioral modeling. However, human-likeness alone does not establish their reliability. Reliable simulation requires preserving profile-grounded clinical facts (informational invariance) while adapting disclosure and interaction behavior to the interview (relational adaptivity). To this end, we introduce PsyInterviewee, which separates a protected truth channel from a dynamic interaction channel and verifies generated clinical claims against the profile. Specifically, asymmetric write permissions allow dialogue context to update disclosure and behavioral states without authorizing new clinical facts; these states guide what profile-supported information is revealed and how it is expressed. In an automated evaluation of interactions between LLM-based interviewers and interviewees, PsyInterviewee achieves higher scores than four representative baselines on most metrics across both axes, as assessed by two LLM judges. Ablations suggest that the two channels contribute to clinical grounding and response modulation, respectively.
authors: Jiawei Zhang, Huachuan Qiu, Ruocheng Guo, Zijun Shi
bullets: Targets a reliability gap: human-like behavior alone does not ensure clinically grounded interviewees.
Separates a protected truth channel from a dynamic interaction channel.
Uses asymmetric write permissions so dialogue can change disclosure and behavior, but not add unsupported clinical facts.
Automated evaluations with LLM interviewers and two LLM judges found higher scores than four representative baselines on most metrics across both reliability axes.
Ablations indicate that the two channels support clinical grounding and response modulation, respectively.

papers.abstract: Sparse MoE mechanism significantly improves the trade-off between model capacity and inference efficiency. However, practical deployment still requires storing all experts, resulting in substantial memory overhead. We show that expert outputs in MoE layers exhibit structured redundancy. Across different models and task categories, the stable rank and entropy effective rank of expert outputs are consistently far below the nominal number of experts, while expert output distributions also exhibit fewer effective modes. Motivated by these observations, we reformulate expert pruning as a structure-preserving expert subset selection problem and efficiently optimize it via a greedy strategy, rather than only independently scoring and ranking individual experts or exhaustively searching over expert combinations. We propose two expert pruning methods under the unified structure-preserving framework: Projection Energy Expert Pruning (PEEP), which preserves the functional subspace by maximizing weighted projection energy, and Distributional Coverage Expert Pruning (DCEP), which preserves the distributional geometry by minimizing weighted coverage error. Both methods incorporate router-derived weights as priors, enabling them to jointly preserve the global structural relationships among experts while accounting for the local importance of individual experts. Experiments on DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Qwen3-30B-A3B demonstrate that, at the expert retention ratios of 75% and 50%, our methods outperform the state-of-the-art baselines on the majority of benchmarks and consistently achieve the best average performance across both general tasks and mathematical reasoning tasks.
authors: Tian Wang, Yongding Tao, Yihong Dong, Xiaoming Wu, Ying Guo, Ge Li
bullets: MoE expert outputs contain substantial, structured redundancy, with fewer effective modes than the nominal expert count.
Expert pruning is formulated as structure-preserving subset selection rather than independent expert ranking or exhaustive combination search.
PEEP preserves the experts’ functional subspace, while DCEP preserves their distributional geometry; both use router-derived importance weights.
On DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Qwen3-30B-A3B, both methods perform best on average across general and mathematical reasoning benchmarks at 75% and 50% expert retention.

papers.title: Experts Exhibit Structured Redundancy: Structure-Preserving Expert Pruning for Mixture-of-Experts Large Language Models
papers.tldr: The paper prunes MoE experts by preserving their output structure, reducing memory while retaining model performance better than prior pruning approaches.

papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models have achieved remarkable success in automated short answer grading (ASAG). However, current methods in ASAG struggle to comprehend, reason about and evaluate complex mathematical answers involving symbols and formulas. These score-only methods fail to generalize across diverse responses and skill states associated with identical scores. Moreover, they ignore the potential upward bias introduced by generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) usage in assessing students' performance and knowledge mastery. To address these limitations, we propose AICG (AI-aware Cognitive-supervised Grading), a two-branch multi-task framework. The first branch combines RoBERTa-based regression, ordinal, and classification heads for individual-answer grading. The second branch uses an expert-designed Q-matrix to associate responses with assessed skills and jointly predicts G-DINA-derived skill mastery and learning gain. Through the shared encoder, these skill-level targets provide cognitive supervision for answer grading beyond score labels. AICG further uses a Gen-AI detector, trained through supervised contrastive pretraining followed by linear classification, to estimate assistance probabilities and convert them into reliability weights, attenuating unreliable cognitive evidence during learning assessment. We conduct experiments on 49,402 instructor-graded responses spanning 19 academic semesters. Relative to RoBERTa regression, AICG reduces mean absolute error (MAE) by 50.3% and improves quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) from 0.798 to 0.927. Ablations identify Q-matrix-guided cognitive supervision as the primary source of improvement, while AI-aware weighting further reduces overall MAE by 4.2% over the unweighted cognitive model and consistently improves MAE and QWK across the four most recent post-Gen-AI semesters.
authors: Shengran Guo, Min Chi, Feifei Qiao, Varad Patwardhan
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of evaluating symbolic, formula-based answers and distinguishing different skill states behind identical scores.
Uses a shared RoBERTa encoder with regression, ordinal, and classification grading heads, plus Q-matrix-guided prediction of skill mastery and learning gain.
Detects likely Gen-AI assistance and converts assistance probabilities into weights that reduce the influence of potentially unreliable cognitive evidence.
On 49,402 responses across 19 semesters, AICG reduces MAE by 50.3% versus RoBERTa regression and raises QWK from 0.798 to 0.927.
Cognitive supervision drives most of the gains; AI-aware weighting provides additional improvements, especially in recent post-Gen-AI semesters.

papers.abstract: LLM agents execute tasks through repeated model calls over evolving histories of reasoning, actions, and tool feedback. Aggregate speculative-decoding metrics merge these distinct decisions, providing limited guidance on where draft supervision is needed. We present TraceSpec, a framework connecting trajectory evaluation with adaptive draft training. It combines dynamic execution with fixed-prefix replay and introduces TraceSpec-Traj, a corpus of 10,000 training states and 2,500 test states spanning browsing and software engineering. Analysis of five speculative baselines reveals that aggregate acceptance can rise with context length while declining within matched late browsing actions. Workload and phase further distinguish these trends, motivating supervision guided by trajectory conditions. TraceSpec trains on intermediate assistant turns and allocates a fixed prediction budget using state-conditioned estimates of prefix-aware acceptance gaps. Across three target sizes and two temperatures, it improves replay throughput by 12.5% to 22.6% over its DSpark base. Qwen3-4B ablations show that adaptive allocation increases accepted length by 3.3% to 10.0% over fixed full-turn supervision, with additional comparisons substantiating the roles of state conditioning and consecutive-token agreement. The resulting evaluation resources, trajectory findings, and training strategy connect the analysis of agent execution to practical draft improvement.
authors: Jihao Zhao, Shuaishuai Zu, Pengfei Li, Biao Qin, Guanghuan Fang, Ben Feng, Baochuan Yang
bullets: Aggregate acceptance metrics can obscure differences across reasoning, browsing, and tool-use states, especially in later browsing actions.
TraceSpec combines dynamic execution, fixed-prefix replay, and state-conditioned estimates of prefix-aware acceptance gaps.
TraceSpec-Traj provides 10,000 training states and 2,500 test states from browsing and software-engineering trajectories.
Adaptive intermediate-turn supervision improves replay throughput by 12.5%–22.6% over DSpark across tested target sizes and temperatures.
Scope: results focus on trajectory replay and evaluated agent workloads; findings also indicate workload and phase affect speculative-decoding behavior.

papers.abstract: Estimating whether a problem is too complex for a large language model (LLM) before the model attempts it can guide model routing, how to allocate test-time compute, and suggest the need for new tools to aid the agent. While existing estimators rely on the problem text, LLM-annotated task difficulty labels, or signals obtained after a model attempts to solve the problem, such as its hidden states, none explicitly leverage the constraint structure inherent in the problem: the variables to assign and how the constraints over them interact. We introduce CIRCE, which extracts a problem's structure by using a cheap LLM to construct a Constraint Intermediate Representation that deterministically compiles into the constraint graph. Across seven reasoning benchmarks (including SAT, logic, and math) and four LLMs, even a randomly initialized GNN encoder improves predictions of LLM response correctness, reducing negative log-likelihood from 0.465 to 0.423 and increasing AUROC from 0.691 to 0.727 relative to the strongest baseline for each metric.
authors: Chenhao Hong, Jiakai Xu, Kaushiki Singh, Yusen Zhang, Eugene Wu
bullets: Targets pre-attempt difficulty estimation for model routing, test-time compute allocation, and tool selection.

papers.abstract: There exists little mathematical theory explaining why Transformer architectures are empirically successful even for non-Markovian data. To this end, this paper studies next-token prediction via stochastic optimal control theoretically trained Transformers for such sources, where we consider either stationary and ergodic non-Markovian sources or those which are hidden Markov models of some finite order (possibly non-stationary). In either case, we first obtain error bounds via finite models with finite window approximations. For stationary ergodic sources, the resulting error is bounded by an entropy gap; for $N$th order Markovian sources, it decays at an exponential rate $\alpha^{\lfloor M/N\rfloor}$, where $M$ is the window length and $\alpha$ is determined by filter stability (and the Dobrushin coefficients of the transition and measurement kernels). We then construct a Transformer of depth $M+1$, one head per layer, realizing the truncated filter, and we optimally train it with stochastic control developed in earlier work, which rigorously returns a near optimal Transformer. In particular, we show that for a non-Markovian source, either under stationarity and ergodicity for general models or under filter stability for hidden Markov models, an optimally trained Transformer has arbitrarily small performance error with increasing context length, data, and approximation refinement. Numerical studies accompany the theory.
authors: Ka\u{g}an Akman, Jake Feldman Starosta, Naci Saldi, Serdar Y\"uksel
bullets: Develops theoretical error bounds using finite-model and finite-window approximations.

papers.abstract: Large language models have been shown to memorise and reproduce verbatim sequences from their training data, raising concerns about privacy leakage, intellectual property exposure, and the limits of generalisation. Recent theoretical work suggests that attention heads may contribute to this behaviour by functioning as associative memory mechanisms, with memorisation capacity scaling with the number of heads. At the same time, empirical work has shown that many attention heads are redundant and can be pruned with limited impact on downstream performance. Despite these parallel findings, the effect of pruning redundant heads on memorised-sequence reproduction remains unexplored. In this work, we demonstrate that zeroing out a substantial fraction of attention heads prior to inference can significantly suppress verbatim memorisation while preserving, or even improving, language modelling performance on the benchmark used to identify redundant heads. Evaluating GPT-2-XL(1.5B) on known memorised sequences, we find that pruning 729 task-redundant heads reduces the memorisation count by 91.5%, while improving WikiText-103 perplexity by 0.92. These findings suggest that attention-head redundancy can be exploited to mitigate memorisation at inference time, without retraining or modifying the training data.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is a promising way to oversee increasingly capable agents. It succeeds in part because current models appear limited in their ability to control what they verbalize in their reasoning traces. We investigate the source of this limitation and link it to an entropy collapse in the first few tokens following the opening thinking tag. We exploit this mechanism to recover CoT controllability through two inference-time interventions on initial tokens: prefilling, where even a single token can substantially increase controllability, and banning frequent opening tokens combined with in-context examples, which improves average compliance by 34-41 percentage points across models. These interventions recover mainly addition and style controllability (adding or transforming information), while suppression controllability (avoiding or removing information) exhibits more varied responses, suggesting distinct underlying mechanisms. Consistent with this, the two groups behave as separate capabilities: across models, performance correlates positively within these groups, while cross-group correlations are mostly negative. Importantly, we find that the relationship with monitorability depends on the evaluation: addition and style controllability more consistently positively correlate with monitorability, while suppression often shows negative associations. Our findings motivate the development of controllability evaluations that distinguish difficulty initiating a specific opening from general limitations of the ability to alter reasoning content, alongside separate reporting of control tasks and categories.

papers.abstract: Training a large language model is compute-bound, and current recipes divide the work between optimizers by hand: orthogonalized momentum for attention and MLP matrices, Adam-style updates for the rest. This division rests on human priors about which layer type deserves which geometry, and it fixes a single global update budget that every parameter block shares. We introduce FARO, a function-space adaptive optimizer that makes the partition of parameters into blocks the unit of decision. FARO gives each block a geometry by its realized counterfactual return, then freezes the routes and reallocates the frozen per-block budget by cross-block equal risk contribution (ERC), the risk-parity principle from portfolio theory. On a GPT-style model trained on FineWeb, the framework gives two results. First, its FARO-Adaptive arm reaches 3.2780 nats at the full schedule, matching NorMuonAndAdam (3.2794), the best hand-designed recipe: it recovers the human prior without hand-setting per-layer geometry. Second, FARO-ERC improves on that arm: it lowers the clean-data loss at every one of 6 seeds, by 0.0136 nats on average, a modest but robust gain. Its sign test, paired test, and confidence interval all agree, and it exceeds the measured run-to-run noise at no added time or memory. It works by trimming the riskiest blocks rather than expanding the safest, and it holds up under a corrupted stream, still lowering the mean loss and winning the seed majority. The source code is available at https://github.com/wxj630/FARO.
authors: Xiaojun Wu, Cehao Yang, Xuhui Jiang, Chengjin Xu, Jia Li, Jian Guo

papers.abstract: Continuous diffusion language models (CDLMs) and speculative drafters offer efficient language generation but are typically evaluated differently: CDLMs generate independently through iterative refinement, whereas drafters propose text for target-model verification and correction. We compare their architectures without verification, using LangFlow for CDLMs and adapting DSpark's Markov and recurrent-head architectures for standalone generation. All models are trained from scratch for unconditional, single-block OpenWebText generation at lengths 16, 128, and 1024, without target features or verification, using common preprocessing, backbone dimensions, and training-update budgets. We evaluate generation perplexity (GenPPL) with an external language model and distributional similarity to reference text with MAUVE. With default denoising steps equal to sequence length, LangFlow outperforms both DSpark variants on both metrics at lengths 128 and 1024, while DSpark-RNN leads at 16. A conditional KL analysis characterizes dependencies excluded by the Markov head's previous-token conditioning. Recurrent memory removes this restriction and improves both metrics, but the longer-sequence gap persists. Teacher probability matching further lowers Markov GenPPL without observed MAUVE gains. Increasing LangFlow's denoising steps at fixed weights improves both metrics at lengths 16 and 128, changing the length-128 ordering relative to DSpark-RNN. These results establish LangFlow's longer-sequence advantage under the evaluated budgets and highlight iterative full-sequence refinement as a route to improving standalone generation beyond gains from recurrent head memory.
authors: Yujian Chen, Hao Jiang, Guang Cheng, Weijian Luo, Tianyang Hu

papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) enables large language models to advance their capabilities through successive updates, but these updates can also introduce new risks and weaken existing safeguards. In line with the AI-45{\deg} Law, we pursue Safety RSI, in which safety develops as an intrinsic capability alongside general model capabilities through continual risk discovery and repair, while preserving utility and limiting over-refusal. We introduce Safin-1.5, a model built on a safety architecture and trained through recursive safety improvement, with an inference-time harness that extends its capabilities to formal reasoning. Our approach comprises three components: i) The safety architecture combines persistent safety states with hazardous-knowledge disentanglement. The former retains and selectively invokes safety knowledge, while the latter relocates targeted hazardous knowledge into removable experts, enabling its removal with minimal impact on general capabilities. ii) Recursive safety improvement establishes a discovery-evaluation-repair loop. The loop identifies new vulnerabilities and uses experimental feedback to develop repair strategies. It accepts updates only when they improve safety while preserving general capabilities and limiting over-refusal. iii) The formal reasoning harness combines the model's language understanding with symbolic inference and verification. Proof-obligation-guided semantic bridging recovers missing relations in formal representations, enabling symbolic solvers to construct checkable proofs under formalized premises and accepted semantic bridges. Experimental results demonstrate that Safin-1.5 achieves safety and reasoning performance, outperforming frontier models.
authors: Jingnan Zheng, Cheng Jin, Ming Zhang, Huan Sun, Zhongtian Ma, Kaisen Yang, Ziyuan Zhou, Tong Wu, Dongcheng Zhang, Yi Zhang, Xiao Wang, Han Qi, Shu Yu, Ermo Hua, Zongji Yu, Chaozhuo Li, Xiaoyu Wen, Zhekai Chen, Jiawei Zhou, Sirui Chen, Ning Ding, An Zhang, Tat-Seng Chua, Xiangnan He, Xia Hu, Bowen Zhou, Qiaosheng Zhang, Youbang Sun, Xiang Wang, Zhongyu Huang, Chaochao Lu
bullets: Addresses the risk that recursive model updates may weaken safeguards or introduce new vulnerabilities.
Uses persistent safety states and removable experts to retain safety knowledge and isolate targeted hazardous knowledge.
Applies a discovery–evaluation–repair loop, accepting updates only when safety improves without harming general capabilities or increasing over-refusal.
Combines language understanding with symbolic inference and verification through proof-obligation-guided semantic bridging.
Experiments report strong safety and reasoning performance, outperforming frontier models; specific metrics and evaluation details are not provided in the abstract.

figures.caption: Figure 4 | The three-stage ReSI framework. In each round, ReSI applies red-teaming methods to identify vulnerabilities in the current target model 𝑀𝑟, develops training recipes through automated research, and promotes the eligible update with the largest safety gain as 𝑀𝑟+1, the target for the next round. Stage 1 collects successful attacks against 𝑀𝑟 (Section 3.2.1). Stage 2 screens attack sources and alignment methods through low-budget pilot trials and shortlists the most promising recipes (Section 3.2.3). Stage 3 conducts full-scale training and feedback-guided refinement, then selects the eligible checkpoint with the largest safety gain (Section 3.2.4).

Figure 3 | Overview of REX. (1) Expert expansion copies and scales the source experts of the base model 𝐵 to form removable experts (𝐹0), and joint training with selective gradient masking and routing differentiation relocates hazardous knowledge into them (𝐹1). (2) Excising the removable experts yields 𝐴1, and a light RMU cleanup yields the public base model 𝐴2, while the removable experts and their router rows are kept. (3) Recombining them with 𝐴2 gives the full structure 𝐹2, on which standard post-training produces the full model 𝐹3 for authorized users; excising its removable experts produces the public model 𝐴3.

Figure 2 | Overview of Safin-1.5. At the architectural level, MARCH and REX provide persistent safety memory and hazardous-knowledge disentanglement, respectively. At the training level, ReSI supports continual safety improvement through iterative red-teaming, pilot screening, and full-scale model updates. At the formal assurance level, the formal reasoning harness leverages POGB to address semantic gaps between natural-language problems and formal representations, enhancing the model’s logical reasoning capabilities.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed to solve complex scientific and practical problems via iterative optimization. However, dynamically coordinating diverse search mechanisms as candidate quality, failure modes, and resource budgets evolve remains a critical open challenge. Targeted empirical diagnostics reveal that mechanism effectiveness is highly state-dependent. Motivated by this, we analyze how individual decisions drive final outcomes, decomposing the expected terminal improvement under a shared budget into cumulative decision opportunities minus cumulative selection losses. Guided by this opportunity-loss theoretical foundation, we propose OptiCom, a unified framework that represents LLM-driven optimizers within a shared configuration space: C=(A,Q,O,E,M,S), corresponding to artifact, query, operator, evaluation, memory, and strategy. Operating within this space, a fast LLM-based Optimization Controller dynamically composes immediate mechanisms through structured Action Packages, while a slower Strategy Adapter refines long-term selection preferences, operator weights, and templates based on accumulated trajectory feedback. Comprehensive evaluations across 32 benchmark groups demonstrate the superiority of framework: OptiCom achieves an average Max-score rank of 1.72 among 14 evaluated configurations, securing the top score in 23 groups. Ultimately, these results highlight the broad applicability and high extensibility of OptiCom as a general-purpose paradigm for robust LLM test-time scaling.
bullets: LLM-driven optimization mechanisms vary in effectiveness as candidate quality, failure modes, and resource budgets change.
The framework analyzes terminal improvement as cumulative decision opportunities minus cumulative selection losses.
OptiCom unifies optimizer components in a shared configuration space covering artifacts, queries, operators, evaluation, memory, and strategy.
A fast controller selects structured Action Packages, while a slower adapter updates preferences, operator weights, and templates from trajectory feedback.
Across 32 benchmark groups and 14 configurations, OptiCom ranked first on average and achieved the top score in 23 groups.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of OptiCom. Annotations involving ∆t and ℓt highlight how specific architectural components are explicitly designed to expand search opportunities (∆t) and reduce selection losses (ℓt). Composing optimization mechanisms. The analysis in Section 4 identifies two factors governing adaptive optimization: the opportunities provided by available actions, ∆t, and the loss incurred when selecting among them, ℓt. Guided by this decomposition, OptiCom dynamically combines complementary mechanisms within the shared configuration space. To maximize opportunities while mitigating selection loss, the framework operates through a continuous, state-conditioned execution loop driven by two core components: an Optimization Controller for immediate mechanism composition, and a slower Strategy Adapter for long-term guidance revision. Both components operate through LLM API calls with fixed model parameters (see Algorithm 1 in Appendix D.1).

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed for natural-language logical reasoning, where the final answer is easy to check but the proof behind it is not. In natural-language logical reasoning, an intermediate conclusion should follow from its premises, and the resulting derivation should support the final answer. Existing methods lack machine-checkable verification of intermediate conclusions and answer-supporting proof dependencies, so they may assign credit to invalid or answer-irrelevant steps. We propose Proof-R1, an RL framework from formal verification that trains LLMs to construct verifiable proofs for natural-language logical reasoning. Proof-R1 admits a generated conclusion into the verified proof state only when the corresponding reasoning action satisfies the proof obligations through UNSAT-based machine-checkable formal verification. Proof-R1 also recovers the answer-supporting dependency closure to trace the proof structure of the final answer and align outcome credit with the proof dependencies. Experiments demonstrate that Proof-R1 improves answer accuracy across three logical reasoning benchmarks and four backbone models and outperforms training-free agents and training-based methods in terms of reasoning-process verifiability.
bullets: Existing approaches may reward invalid intermediate steps or reasoning that does not support the final answer.
The framework admits conclusions into the proof only when UNSAT-based verification confirms their proof obligations.
It traces the dependency closure supporting the final answer and aligns training credit with those proof dependencies.
Experiments across three benchmarks and four backbone models improve answer accuracy and reasoning-process verifiability.
The approach targets natural-language logical reasoning and depends on formal verification of generated proof steps.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents require reinforcement learning methods that can assign credit to intermediate decisions under sparse and delayed rewards. Existing group-based methods such as GRPO and GiGPO alleviate this issue by comparing rollout returns or repeated anchor states, but they still fail when the compared returns have no variation. We identify this failure mode as zero-credit failure: during early training, many failed rollouts contain useful prefixes, yet existing methods assign them no task-discriminative advantage. To address this issue, we propose Milestone Viability Potential Policy Optimization (MVPO), a potential-routed policy optimization algorithm that learns from viable failure prefixes. MVPO estimates prefix potential over Union-Find viability regions, repairs zero-credit groups with potential-difference advantages, and attenuates the potential branch according to relative performance progress. Experiments with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct show that MVPO outperforms eight strong baselines, including GRPO and GiGPO. Under the same training length, MVPO improves over the GiGPO baseline by +4.4 success points on ALFWorld and +5.3 on WebShop, while adding only 0.16%-0.20% advantage-construction overhead.
bullets: Targets sparse, delayed rewards where early decisions are difficult to credit.
Identifies zero-credit failure: failed rollouts with useful prefixes may receive no task-discriminative advantage when returns lack variation.
Uses Union-Find viability regions to estimate prefix potential and construct potential-difference advantages for zero-credit groups.
Attenuates the potential-based learning branch according to relative performance progress.
On Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, improves over GiGPO by 4.4 success points on ALFWorld and 5.3 on WebShop, with 0.16%–0.20% advantage-construction overhead.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of MVPO. MVPO first estimates prefix potential over Union-Find viability regions using future success, loop statistics, and adaptive milestone progress (§4.1). It then routes step-level credit according to anchor-group availability: informative anchor groups use anchor-based comparative credit, while zero-credit groups are repaired with prefix-potential advantages (§4.2). Finally, the routed step-level credit is combined with the episode-level group advantage for critic-free policy optimization (§4.3).

Figure 1: Motivation and overview of MVPO. Top: an ALFWorld case of zero-credit failure: all rollouts fail, making GRPO/GiGPO assign no task-discriminative advantage, while MVPO identifies viable prefixes using prefix potential. Bottom (a): zero-advantage steps affect over 90% of GRPO steps and about 65% of GiGPO steps in early WebShop training. Bottom (b): higher prefix potential predicts higher future success on ALFWorld. Bottom (c): MVPO reaches 40% success earlier during training. Bottom (d): MVPO improves final success over GiGPO on both benchmarks.

Figure 3: Training dynamics of MVPO. (a) The performance-progress attenuation mechanism works as intended. At the beginning of training, the EMA success rate is low and κt stays close to 1, allowing prefix-potential credit to repair zero-credit groups with full strength. As the policy improves, the EMA success rate increases and κt decreases accordingly, causing the potential branch to fade and leaving more gradient space to anchor-based comparative credit. (b) The learned prefix potential remains directionally meaningful throughout training. Successful trajectories maintain higher mean potential than failed trajectories, while the Union-Find region statistics remain stable. This supports the central assumption of MVPO: potential can distinguish viable failure prefixes from unproductive prefixes before final rewards become frequent.

papers.abstract: Ensuring the safety of reasoning large language models (LLMs) across languages is essential for their reliable deployment. However, when exposed to jailbreak attacks in non-high-resource languages, these models may generate unsafe responses even when their reasoning traces identify safety risks. To address this issue, we propose aligning cross-lingual thoughts and responses (ACTR), a framework that improves multilingual safety alignment by strengthening the use of existing safety reasoning. Specifically, we first present the think gap score (TGS) to compare the normalized contributions of reasoning traces to attention outputs during response generation across languages, and use reasoning- trace substitution to measure the cross-lingual safety gap. Next, using a corpus of jailbreak queries, we assess neuron importance through changes in response representations caused by neuron masking and compare the high-importance neuron sets obtained with reasoning enabled and disabled to identify safety think neurons that support the use of safety reasoning. Finally, we devise neuron-selective consistency optimization (NSCO), which uses a frozen judge model to reward agreement between the safety categories of reasoning traces and responses while updating only the parameters associated with the selected neurons, requiring no human-annotated responses or preference data. Across two reasoning models, ACTR achieves lower average attack success rates than the evaluated state-of-the-art methods on AdvBench-X and MultiJail, with safety gains extending to unseen languages, while preserving or improving average performance on multilingual knowledge and mathematical reasoning tasks and limiting false refusals of benign requests. Warning: this paper contains examples with unsafe content.
bullets: Addresses jailbreaks in non-high-resource languages where models recognize risks in reasoning but still produce unsafe responses.
Introduces Think Gap Score and reasoning-trace substitution to measure cross-lingual gaps in how safety reasoning influences outputs.
Identifies safety-relevant neurons by comparing neuron importance with reasoning enabled versus disabled.
Uses neuron-selective consistency optimization with a frozen judge, without human-annotated responses or preference data.
Across two reasoning models, reduces attack success on AdvBench-X and MultiJail, generalizes to unseen languages, and preserves multilingual task performance while limiting false refusals.

papers.abstract: Best-of-N sampling is a simple inference-time scaling strategy for large language models, yet its behavior under incomplete reward models remains poorly understood. We study Best-of-N as a competition between the extreme reward tails of correct and incorrect responses. This view shows that success depends not only on the probability of sampling a correct response, but also on whether correct responses dominate incorrect ones in the upper tail. Using extreme value theory, we characterize three asymptotic regimes: correct-tail-dominant, incorrect-tail-dominant, and critical explaining both monotonic gains and reward-hacking-induced degradation. We further derive finite-sample scaling laws for representative reward distributions, showing that, under Gaussian rewards, incorrect responses with sufficiently large variance can dominate selection even when their mean reward is lower. Unlike oracle selection, convergence with an incomplete selector can be polynomial rather than exponential. Finally, we propose a lightweight tail-tension criterion to estimate when additional sampling may become harmful. Experiments on synthetic data and real reward model scores are consistent with the theoretically predicted regimes, scaling laws, and diagnostic behavior, suggesting that tail competition provides a unified lens on Best-of-N sampling for verifiable problems.
bullets: Success depends on both sampling correct answers and whether their upper reward tail beats that of incorrect answers.
Extreme value theory identifies correct-tail-dominant, incorrect-tail-dominant, and critical regimes.
Finite-sample laws show that under Gaussian rewards, high-variance incorrect responses can win despite lower mean reward.
With incomplete reward models, convergence may be polynomial rather than exponential, unlike oracle selection.
A lightweight tail-tension diagnostic estimates when additional sampling may become harmful; synthetic and real-score experiments support the theory.

figures.caption: Figure 1: An illustrative overview of our explanation of BoN for verifiable problems. When n responses are sampled, assuming pass@1 = p, we obtain approximately np correct responses and n(1 − p) incorrect responses, each assigned a reward according to the corresponding reward distribution. Whether BoN selects a correct response is determined by the competition between the maximum reward Mc among the np correct responses and the maximum reward Mw among the n(1− p) incorrect responses. When n is sufficiently large, these maxima are governed by the tails of the respective distributions. Thus, the performance of BoN depends on the competition between the tails of the reward distributions for correct and incorrect responses.

Figure 2: An illustrative explanation of reward hacking in verifiable problems. The blue and orange points represent correct and incorrect sampled responses, respectively, with n points in total. The response outlined in red is the one selected by BoN. Thus, if a blue response is outlined in red, BoN successfully selects a correct response. In the monotonic-improvement case (top row), correct and incorrect responses have reward distributions with the same variance, so their maximum rewards grow at similar rates as n increases. In the reward-hacking case (bottom row), incorrect responses have larger reward variance, causing their maximum reward to grow faster and eventually exceed that of correct responses. Thus, BoN selects a correct response at small n but incorrect one at large n.
Figure 6: Tail-tension early stopping on RAMO-Llama3.1-8B scores. The proposed method mitigates degradation in reward-hacking cases while reducing computational cost.

Figure 5: Experimental validation of the EVT approximated Gaussian scaling law. BoN accuracy follows the predicted finite-n scaling Eq. (12) well. Furthermore, the typicalregion accuracy An(kn;x) closely matches Sn(x) as in Lemma 1.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes Best-of-N sampling using extreme value theory, providing a theoretical understanding of inference-time scaling and reward tail dynamics in LLMs.
papers.title: Tail Competition Explains Scaling in Best-of-N Sampling for Verifiable Problems
papers.tldr: Best-of-N performance is governed by competition between the extreme reward tails of correct and incorrect responses, so more sampling can eventually hurt when incorrect responses have heavier tails.

papers.abstract: Graph fraud explanation generation emerges as an important task, which requires jointly leveraging graph structure and content information to produce human-readable explanations for a given risk label. An intuitive approach is to adapt existing graph-enhanced large language models (LLMs), which inject graph structure into LLMs via graph-conditioned instruction tuning or structure-aware embeddings. However, existing methods face two key challenges in graph fraud explanation generation: a lack of evaluation protocols tailored to explanation quality, and a mismatch between the granularity of graph information they provide and what explanation generation requires. In this paper, we propose FRaud Explanation Generation via Agentic Graph Context NavigaTION (FRACTION), a framework for graph fraud explanation generation. To evaluate explanation quality, we introduce a task-specific rubric that assesses faithfulness, graph grounding, helpfulness, consistency, and conciseness, and validate it against human judgments. To focus on fine-grained details of relevant neighbors without reading the entire neighborhood, we equip a language model with graph tools that progressively disclose neighbor records. To train our graph agent, we propose a rubric-guided trajectory distillation strategy through which the agent learns both tool-use behavior and structured explanation generation. Experimental results on three fraud datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines under a human-aligned rubric.
bullets: Addresses weak explanation-quality evaluation and overly coarse graph-context integration in existing methods.
Introduces a rubric measuring faithfulness, graph grounding, helpfulness, consistency, and conciseness, validated against human judgments.
Uses progressive disclosure of neighbor records so the language model can focus on fine-grained relevant context.
Trains the graph agent with rubric-guided trajectory distillation for tool use and structured explanation generation.
Shows consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines on three fraud datasets under the human-aligned rubric.

papers.abstract: We study in-context binary classification in a simple attention model trained to minimise a logistic loss. Each prompt has a latent logistic teacher, and the learner must infer its direction from Bernoulli-labeled context examples. We derive an asymptotic prediction for the test logit in a high-dimensional regime with context length proportional to token dimension, and total training prompts proportional to dimension squared. Our formula cleanly separates calibration, test-time context noise, and non-isotropic parameter-estimation noise as interpretable effects on in-context performance. Our analysis also identifies the ridgeless separability regime and addresses the effects of context length, pretraining-set size, regularisation, and sampling temperature on in-context classification performance. The theory's predictions closely agree with finite-dimensional simulations and fully trained linear-attention models, while experiments with standard softmax attention show qualitatively related behaviour beyond the regime assumed by our analysis.
bullets: Models prompts generated by a latent logistic teacher, with the learner inferring the teacher direction from Bernoulli-labeled context examples.
Derives an asymptotic test-logit prediction when context length scales with dimension and training prompts scale quadratically with dimension.
Separates calibration, test-time context noise, and non-isotropic parameter-estimation noise as interpretable performance factors.
Characterizes effects of context length, pretraining-set size, regularisation, sampling temperature, and ridgeless separability.
Predictions closely match finite-dimensional simulations and trained linear-attention models; standard softmax attention shows qualitatively similar behavior outside the theory’s regime.
