papers.abstract: Data attribution methods for Language Models (LMs) are typically evaluated using downstream tasks like fact retrieval. However, existing evaluations vary multiple dataset properties simultaneously, making it impossible to isolate exactly why an attribution algorithm fails. To diagnose these failures, we explore the design space of LLM data attribution, with a primary focus on evaluation. We introduce the Controlled Attribution Benchmark (CATT) for fact tracing, in which we fine-tune LLMs on entirely fictitious knowledge, providing unambiguous ground truth for attribution. This synthetic setup allows us to systematically alter one dataset configuration at a time, such as document redundancy and lexical distractors. With this configurable evaluation, we demonstrate that redundancy and distractors consistently degrade attribution performance. Rather than proposing a new estimator, we examine two design choices that are underexplored: the loss used to compute gradients and how per-token attribution scores are aggregated into a document score. We find that the true causal evidence within a training document is highly localized, but standard methods dilute this evidence into noise by averaging attribution scores across the entire document. We find that replacing standard cross-entropy loss gradients with the negative log-odds gradients surfaces the critical tokens from other uninformative ones. We can then aggregate only the top token scores to improve ground truth recall by 35 to 72 percentage points across multiple baselines on our diagnostic benchmark. The negative log-odds correction also generalizes to FTRACE-TREX, improving counterfactual retraining performance for every method we test, by up to 4.9x.
authors: Steven Yu, Sheng-Yu Wang, Kimia Hamidieh, Antonio Torralba, David Bau
bullets: Introduces CATT, a synthetic fact-tracing benchmark with unambiguous attribution ground truth and independently configurable dataset properties.
Shows that document redundancy and lexical distractors consistently degrade attribution performance.
Finds that causal evidence is localized to a few tokens, but document-wide averaging dilutes it with noise.
Uses negative log-odds gradients and top-token aggregation to recover critical evidence.
Improves ground-truth recall by 35–72 percentage points across baselines and counterfactual retraining performance by up to 4.9× on FTRACE-TREX.

figures.caption: Figure 6: Upweighting more influential tokens with log-odds improves Recall across token budgets. Recall@N as the number of retained tokens k varies, under cross-entropy (top) and negative log-odds (bottom). Columns show the three CATT settings. The yellow regions mark full-document scoring (“all”), with the upper-right endpoint in each column corresponding to the prior-work loss and aggregation choices. Negative log-odds with small token budgets substantially improve several methods, especially with distractors. Gains persist across multiple k values; retaining more tokens often reduces recall. Results are averaged over all dataset configurations and model seeds at |F| = 50 with error bars showing ±2 standard errors.

Figure 2: CATT: fact tracing tasks with controlled datasets. We fine-tune Qwen3.5-4B models on fictitious knowledge, which ensures our dataset is the sole causal source of its predictions. Left: Task I (Function Bindings) teaches new functions that always return a fixed value. Right: Task II (Routing Rules) teaches rules that sort objects based on their properties. Given a query phrased unlike any training document, we test whether attribution methods can correctly rank ground-truth documents. Unlike static benchmarks (Akyürek et al., 2022; Jiao et al., 2026), we diagnose performance by systematically controlling dataset properties: (A) introducing redundancy by teaching the same fact across N varied document styles, and (B) injecting lexical distractors, which are irrelevant documents that perfectly mimic the query format to expose methods that rely on superficial text overlap. Task II omits distractors because each fact uses a disjoint set of attribute words, making it difficult to construct clear lexical overlaps. Browse the datasets on our project page.

With Q, TRAK falls to about 0 on the distractor task at every N : the decoys are fit poorly (Q ≈ 0.17–0.20) and the ground-truth documents are memorized (Q ≈ 0.007–0.009), so Q ranks a decoy first for every query. papers.abstract: Extreme weather is forecast days ahead, yet its consequences for agriculture remain hard to predict: a forecast says where a storm will strike, not which crops will suffer or how much is at risk, and the records that could tell span many sources. We present WxCrop, the first agent that judges agricultural hazards from physically interpretable weather indices examined by causal analysis, and the first that combines weather and agricultural information to predict crop loss reliably for past and forecast dates. We demonstrate it in Florida on hurricanes, freezes and dry heat, with a loss model calibrated on insurance records for each, and the same procedure extends to other hazards and areas. Three checks show reliability: the hurricane index detects recorded cyclone days with an AUC of 0.98, recorded losses in held-out years are reproduced to within 2%, and independent production records confirm the county rankings (rank correlation 0.63). Users ask the agent for each crop group's loss as a fraction of expected season value, every number sourced, so that governments, growers and scientists respond to agricultural disasters quickly.
authors: Minghan Yu, Mengyu Dai, Yixin Wen, Haizhao Yang
bullets: Addresses the gap between forecasting weather hazards and predicting crop-specific agricultural losses.
Demonstrated in Florida for hurricanes, freezes, and dry heat using insurance-calibrated loss models.
Reliability checks include hurricane detection with AUC 0.98, held-out loss estimates within 2%, and production-record rank correlation of 0.63.
Reports each crop group’s loss as a fraction of expected seasonal value, with sourced estimates for decision-makers.
The approach is designed to extend to other hazards and regions.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces WxCrop, an agentic AI system that combines weather and agricultural data to predict crop loss, demonstrating the application of agents in complex decision-making.
papers.title: From extreme weather to agricultural consequences with agentic AI
papers.tldr: WxCrop uses causally analyzed weather indices plus agricultural data to estimate crop losses from past and forecast extreme-weather events.

papers.abstract: Safety alignment has enabled large language models to reliably refuse harmful requests directly, yet the same request distributed across a multi-turn conversation still succeeds far too often. This brittleness has a mechanistic root: Alignment is shallow, with safety behavior concentrated in a model's first few output tokens, and existing defenses inherit the weakness, supervising the surface form of the response without ever giving the model an explicit safety decision to learn. We take the opposite view of shallowness: if a short span determines the trajectory of an entire response, that span is the highest-leverage place to intervene, and the defender can occupy it first. We propose Assess $\to$ Decide $\to$ Respond, a framework in which the defender assesses the user's intent, commits to an explicit, parseable safety decision, and only then generates a reply conditioned on it, with the commitment trained by reinforcement learning at the payload turn. Because the decision is a token span, the reward can be a rule: a self-verified reward checks the committed label against the conversation's known nature, requiring no judge and no annotation, while the same format also supports an LLM-as-judge reward over a graded decision space with safe redirection. Across two model families and fourteen benchmarks spanning safety, utility, and helpfulness, our defenders achieve the strongest multi-turn safety in a controlled comparison, maintaining their lead in safety while preserving utility at a modest cost to helpfulness. A per-token KL analysis and interventional probes confirm why this works: training concentrates its effect on the brief deliberation that sets a response's trajectory, and the decision committed there is a causal control point. The very shallowness attackers exploit becomes the mechanism of defense.
authors: Qiyao Ma, Xiaodong Liu, Weiwei Yang, Mingqian Feng, Chengquan Guo, Jialin Song, Carolyn Buractaon, Zhe Zhao, Junshan Zhang, Sandeep Atluri, Christopher White, Jianfeng Gao
bullets: Targets the brittleness of direct refusals when harmful requests are distributed across multiple conversation turns.
Uses an Assess → Decide → Respond framework: infer intent, commit to a parseable safety label, then condition the reply on that decision.
Trains the decision span with reinforcement learning using either self-verified rule rewards or an LLM judge over graded decisions and safe redirections.
Across two model families and 14 benchmarks, achieves the strongest controlled multi-turn safety while preserving utility, with a modest helpfulness cost.
Per-token KL analysis and intervention probes indicate that the brief deliberation acts as a causal control point for response trajectories.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of our framework. At each turn, the defender assesses the user’s intent, commits to an explicit decision, and generates a response conditioned on that decision. For reward computation, we consider two options: an external reward model that judges whether the response is jailbroken, or a rule-based self-reward that checks the final turn’s committed label against the conversation’s ground-truth nature. RL gradients are applied only to the final turn.
Figure 8: The two system prompts, identical except for the label menu and the matching clause of the closing instruction. See §D for why the self-verified reward requires the two-label menu.
Figure 4: Per-token KL divergence across aligned, unaligned and base models.

Figure 7: Safety–helpfulness trade-off. Safety: mean SAFE % over AdvBench and MHJ; helpfulness: mean of XSTest compliance and rescaled MT-Bench. Stars: our variants; circles: baselines. On Llama3.1-8B only SFT, X-Boundary and our variants enter the high-safety region (shaded); on Qwen3-8B the retuned DPO, MTSA and MUSE-D enter it as well, and our self-verified variant sits above and to the right of all four retuned baselines.

Figure 3: Ablations of design-choice factors (left) and data-mixing ratio (right). In the left panel the two horizontal lines are our full Assess → Decide → Respond models under each reward, and every bar removes or alters exactly one element of them.
Figure 5: Correlation of per-sample judge verdicts.

Figure 2: Evaluation formats. Safety and helpfulness suites query the model in chat format (left), where the assistant-turn intervention is active; capability suites use completion format (right), bypassing the chat template entirely.

Figure 6: Probing the decision token (SAFE % ↑). Left (forced decision): overwriting the decision at the payload turn. Forcing REFUSE makes even the unaligned model safe; forcing COMPLY collapses it but leaves the aligned arms high. Right (depth probe): prefilling k harmful tokens after a forced REFUSE.

Table 1: Multi-turn safety, utility, and helpfulness across two base models. Safety: SAFE % (↑) on AdvBench (Adv.), HarmBench (Harm.), MultiBreak (MB), CoSafe (CoS.), MHJ, and their mean (Avg.). Utility: average over six general benchmarks (per-benchmark results in Appendix E.1). Helpfulness: over-refusal on XSTest and XSB (↓), conversation quality on MT-Bench (1–10, ↑). Bold: best per column within each panel.
Table 2: Per-benchmark general capability (Open LLM Leaderboard v1, six tasks). The final column is the Utility Avg. reported in Table 1. Bold: best per column within each panel.
Table 4: Safety across five benchmarks under five judges held out from training. The corresponding gpt-5-mini scores are in Table 1. Bold: best per column within each judge block.

papers.abstract: We present TextSeal2, a distortion-free watermark for large language models that keeps its signal under speculative decoding: tokens that replace rejected drafts remain watermarked with the same keys, and the acceptance rate is unchanged. It also preserves output diversity and adds no measurable inference latency. Its predecessor, TextSeal, restores diversity in the Gumbel-max scheme by routing each token to one of two keys via a coin flip. This is suboptimal because the detector averages the scores from both keys without knowing which key was used. TextSeal2 instead merges two or more keys into a single virtual key and couples it to fresh noise through AutoMark's Gaussian copula. Any number of keys, including publicly shared keys, can be merged this way without diluting detection. Under speculative decoding, TextSeal2 verifies keyed drafts with one more exponential race, run on the leftovers of the draft races. By memorylessness, this race reproduces block verification, so the output follows the target model exactly. We evaluate TextSeal2 on three LLMs. At equal output token diversity, TextSeal2 detects 8 to 22 percentage points more 100-token answers than TextSeal at a false-positive rate of $10^{-3}$, and is comparable to textGrain while requiring no post-logits optimization. Under speculative decoding, it detects 18 and 22 percentage points more 200-token answers than TextSeal and textGrain, respectively, at the same acceptance rate.
authors: Tom Sander, Pierre Fernandez, Itai Gat, Haiming Bao, Jiaxin Shi, Jason Park, Valeriu Lacatusu, Sylvestre-Alvise Rebuffi, Hongyan Chang, Hady Elsahar, Tom\'{a}\v{s} Sou\v{c}ek, Tuan Tran, Surya Parimi, Alexandre Mourachko
bullets: Maintains the target model’s output distribution, acceptance rate, diversity, and inference latency under speculative decoding.
Merges multiple—including public—keys into one virtual key using AutoMark’s Gaussian copula, avoiding detection-score dilution.
Uses an additional exponential race over draft-race leftovers to reproduce block verification under speculative decoding.
Across three LLMs, improves detection over TextSeal by 8–22 percentage points for 100-token outputs and 18–22 points for 200-token outputs at the stated false-positive rate and acceptance rate.
Matches textGrain’s detection while avoiding post-logits optimization.

figures.caption: Figure 2 TextSeal2 generates one token (subsection 3.1). (a) The model’s forward pass gives the probabilities pv, and the last k = 3 tokens form the window w. (b) The keys’ values at w are merged into the virtual key G⋆ v, which the copula (4) blends with the noise ηv into R̃v; the Gumbel-max choice is argminv(− ln R̃v)/pv. (c) The Gumbel-max choice can be seen as a race (1): candidate v runs a lane of length Ev = − ln R̃v at speed pv, and the token that finishes first is chosen.

Figure 1 Diversity–detection trade-off on Qwen3.5-9B at 100 tokens at FPR=10−3, (a) without and (b) with speculative decoding (8 drafts per round, block verification). In (a), TextSeal2 coincides with AutoMark’s single-key copula as expected since it behaves like a single-key copula. In (b), TextSeal2 uses the residual race, and the baselines use block verification’s native stopping rule with the last token of each round drawn under an independent key. Diversity is measured by Self-BLEU (lower is more diverse).

Figure 3 Block verification checks the drafts against the target as a block, keeps those before a stop position I, and emits one token y at I. (a) The drafter proposes “the mat” with keyed races. (b) One target pass then gives the probability πi,v that I = i and y = v. One more race on the leftovers picks I and y: “floor” wins, so the round keeps “the” and emits “floor” at I = 2. TextSeal2 preserves the target’s distribution and block verification’s acceptance rate (Proposition 1). Algorithm 1 in the appendix gives more details.

Figure 8 Diversity (Self-BLEU over each problem’s 16 answers, first 1024 tokens; lower is more diverse) vs. detection at a false-positive rate of 10−3 on AIME under speculative decoding, on the first 1024 (a) and 2048 (b) tokens; same setup as Table 11, sweeping each method’s strength. Interpolated at TextSeal’s Self-BLEU (46.1), TextSeal2 detects 30% of answers at 2048 tokens, against 23% for the coin flip, 21% for SynthID-Text, 17% for textGrain and 9% for AutoMark’s copula; paired by problem, its lead is significant over all but the coin flip (+7.4 [−0.2,+19.5]). Error bars: 95% Wilson intervals.

Figure 7 Diversity (Self-BLEU; lower is more diverse) vs. detection of 100-token answers without speculative decoding, on three models (32 answers to each of 100 questions; copulas with the 53-bit PRF). Interpolated at TextSeal’s Self-BLEU, TextSeal2 gains 10, 22 and 8 percentage points over the coin flip on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.5-27B respectively, and AutoMark’s copula overlaps TextSeal2 throughout.

Figure 5 Entropy weighting improves detection for every watermark, including under speculative decoding. % of 100-token answers detected at a false-positive rate of 10−3 with key-only scores (light bars) and with TextSeal’s entropy-weighted test (full bars), at comparable Self-BLEU. The gains are 5–18 percentage points at 100 tokens and 4–23 at 200 tokens (Table 6); without speculative decoding, TextSeal2 and AutoMark’s copula coincide in distribution and differ only within their 95% intervals, as expected.
Figure 6 The diversity–detection trade-off of Figure 1 at 200 tokens instead of 100; same protocol and conventions, including the speculative panel (b).

Figure 9 Calibration: false-positive rate against the nominal p-value threshold for the detectors of Table 1 without speculative decoding, on 10 keys and 10,000 unwatermarked Qwen3.5-9B answers; grey: 95% binomial interval around the diagonal. At 10−3 and above, every detector is within a factor 1.3 of nominal.
Figure 10 Figure 1 with diversity measured by the share of distinct 4-grams (higher is more diverse), including the speculative panel (b).

Figure 4 TextSeal2 detects the text “The cat sat on the floor and fell asleep in the sun.” (subsection 3.4). (a) Each token xi and its window wi; the highlighted row is the token of Figure 2. (b) For “floor”, the keys’ values are merged into G⋆ xi as in (4), without the noise, and give the score s⋆i ; key k(1) alone gives the public score s (1) i . (c) The n = 10 scores sum to S = 23.9, and the Gamma(n, 1) tail beyond S (box) is p = 4.6 · 10−4.

Table 6 Key-only vs. entropy-weighted detection (TextSeal’s weighted Gamma test): % of 100 / 200-token answers detected at a false-positive rate of 10−3, with thresholds calibrated per test over 10 keys and 10,000 unwatermarked answers. First 1000 answers per configuration without speculative decoding; last block: all 3000 answers with speculative decoding (8 drafts, block verification). Strengths: α = 0.5 (TextSeal), β = 0.5 (textGrain), ρ = 0.9 (copulas, 53-bit PRF). For SynthID-Text, the key-only test is its official binomial test and the weighted test is the same Gamma test applied to twice its mean coin score. Self-BLEU over 32 answers to each of 100 questions. Weighting improves every method by 4–23 percentage points at 200 tokens, and the two copulas remain level without speculative decoding, as they must in distribution.

Table 4 Post-logits latency per decoding step (ms, median of 200 CUDA-graph replays, or 50 eager runs for calibrated textGrain, whose calibration loop has data-dependent control flow; one H200, vocabulary of 248,320 tokens, synthetic high-entropy logits). Top-p filtering is shared by all methods. The minimal textGrain version uses 5–20 Sinkhorn iterations on the 256× 256 kernel without calibrating λ.

Gray: half-width of the 95% bootstrap interval; bold: best; underlined: second best, per column. Speculative decoding: Qwen3.5-0.8B drafts 8 tokens per round, with block verification; TextSeal2 uses the residual race, the baselines use block verification’s native stopping rule with the last token of each round drawn under an independent key, and textGrain’s own recipe verifies the watermarked distributions. TextSeal2 equals AutoMark’s copula in distribution; their gap under speculative decoding is the residual race.

papers.selection_reason: Presents TextSeal2, a new watermarking technique for LLMs using copula mixing, contributing to the security and integrity of LLM outputs.
papers.title: TextSeal2: Distortion-Free LLM Watermarking with Copula Mixing and Memoryless Races
papers.tldr: TextSeal2 is a distortion-free LLM watermark that preserves diversity and speculative-decoding behavior while improving detection through copula-based key mixing and memoryless race verification.

papers.abstract: Sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) models expand parameter capacity by activating a small subset of experts per token. Expert selection directly affects model capabilities under a fixed active-expert budget. Dense evaluation of all experts reveals weak agreement between single-router rankings and expert-utility evaluation rankings, especially in middle and deep layers. Richer signals for selection and computation incur additional cost: selection based on internal expert activations requires preliminary computation, while processing multiple full representations separately through the same expert repeats its computation. We propose Multi-View MoE to improve expert selection with multiple routers and reuse their preferences to modulate expert computation under a fixed expert budget. Its Multi-Router submodule aggregates sigmoid scores from independently initialized routers. These routers develop highly differentiated expert preferences during training, allowing experts strongly favored by one router or jointly supported by several routers to be selected. Multi-View further uses each selected expert's relative scores across routers to mix learned latent views into its input, reusing routing preferences for both selection and computation. Each selected expert executes one forward pass, preserving the active-expert count, expert FLOPs, and all-to-all communication volume. On a 24-layer 10B-A1B model trained on 708B tokens, full Multi-View MoE improves the nine-task downstream mean by 1.18 percentage points over the baseline. Multi-Router alone yields a 0.6-percentage-point gain and improves the rank correlation between router scores and evaluated expert utility, with relative increases of 8.1% globally and approximately 58% in the layer with the lowest single-router alignment. Controlled mixing interventions show the model uses input differences that depend on both the expert and the token.
authors: Zelin Zhao, Tianchi Ma, Junyuan Shang, Shuohuan Wang, Dianhai Yu
bullets: Single-router rankings often poorly reflect expert utility, particularly in middle and deep layers.
Multi-Router aggregates independently learned router scores to select experts with complementary or shared preferences.
Selected experts use relative multi-router scores to mix learned latent views into each token’s input, with one forward pass per expert.
On a 24-layer 10B-A1B model trained on 708B tokens, full Multi-View MoE improves nine-task mean performance by 1.18 percentage points over baseline.
Multi-Router alone improves performance by 0.6 points and strengthens router–utility rank correlation; controlled interventions indicate token- and expert-dependent input modulation.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Comparison of latent-space MoE architectures. Top: (a) LatentMoE uses a router and a shared latent input; (b) Multi-Router sums scores from separately parameterized sigmoid routing heads for top-k selection while retaining the shared input; (c) Multi-View adds distinct down-projections and expert-specific view mixing. Bottom: expansion of the boxed routed path in (c), with matching colors and numbered markers. Balancing bias b is added to summed scores only for selection. Output gates gi follow Eq. 3. For each selected expert, raw sigmoid scores are normalized across routers to form view proportions am,i, whose sum is one. Each selected expert processes its mixed input once. The aggregated representation y is up-projected and combined with the shared-expert output shown above. K = 2 views and selected experts i, j are illustrative; k is the number of active experts out of N . Bars depict example routing scores. Normalization modules and residual paths are omitted for clarity.

Figure 5: Expert-specific inputs and controlled mixing interventions in the score-derived Multi-View checkpoint at 708B tokens. (a) Differences among the eight experts selected for the same token: the mean absolute pairwise difference in view-1 proportions Dr (top) and the mean pairwise input distance normalized by the mean input norm Dv (bottom). Zero denotes identical proportions or inputs, respectively. Curves show the median across tokens at each layer; bands show the 25th–75th percentiles. (b) Final-layer interventions on 256 sequences, changing view proportions while holding S and output gates gi fixed to numerical precision. Whiskers are 95% sequence-bootstrap CIs; crosses mark permutation-seed means. (c) Single-layer interventions on 80 sequences. Bands are pointwise 95% CIs; downstream routing is recomputed. ∆NLL is intervention loss minus the original loss.

(b) Magnification of the blue-bordered window in (a), covering 50–230B tokens. (c) Magnification of the purple-bordered window in the full-loss inset, showing absolute loss over 620–708B tokens. All curves use the same causal exponential moving average (EMA), with a 2,000-step span (α = 2/2001), initialized at the first observation. The final losses reported in the text average the last 1,000 unsmoothed steps.

(b) Layer-wise means and one-standard-deviation bands over 201 matched logged measurements; metric and aggregation definitions appear in App. B.5. (c) Correlation changes across all 24 layers. Multi-Router improves global correlation by a relative 8.1%, with the largest relative layer-wise gain of 57.7% at layer 20.

The logarithmic training-step axis expands the early stage and compresses later intervals to show early-training changes more clearly. (b) Layer-wise means over the 201 logged measurements used in the router comparison; shaded bands show ±1 standard deviation. Scores exclude the load-balancing bias. Expert utility is evaluated using each expert’s output L2 norm, normalized by its mean over sampled tokens (App. B.5).

papers.title: Multi-View MoE: Letting Every Router Shape Expert Computation
papers.tldr: Multi-View MoE improves sparse expert selection and computation by using multiple routers and router-dependent latent views without increasing the active-expert budget or expert execution cost.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) is limited by sparse outcome-level feedback on hard reasoning tasks: when all rollouts in a group fail, rewards provide no learning signal. Stronger teachers can provide additional guidance, but this raises a central question: how can such signals be incorporated into RLVR to support successful rollouts while remaining learnable for the student? We distinguish two complementary mechanisms: trajectory-level intervention, which improves access to reward-bearing trajectories, and token-level supervision, which provides dense targets to guide student learning. Our controlled experiments show that either mechanism alone can remain insufficient, motivating their combination. We therefore introduce PIVOT, which inserts teacher-generated corrections into student rollouts and applies token-level KL supervision to these segments alongside the RLVR objective. Beyond their combination, we systematically analyze where to intervene and how to supervise, yielding a recipe for effective guidance. Across hard logic games and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, PIVOT consistently outperforms existing methods, nearly doubling mean avg@8 on logic games from 19.5% for the best-performing baseline to 35.6%.
authors: Zhihao Yang, Boyuan Zheng, Puhui Tan, Yukun Chen, Kuan Zhang, Longze Chen, Jiaming Li, Renke Shan, Lu Wang, Xianpei Han
bullets: RLVR can fail when every rollout receives zero outcome-level reward.
Trajectory interventions help expose students to successful paths, while token-level supervision provides dense learning targets.
PIVOT inserts teacher corrections into student trajectories and applies token-level KL supervision to the corrected segments alongside RLVR.
Experiments on hard logic games and mathematical reasoning show consistent improvements over existing methods.
On logic games, mean avg@8 nearly doubles from 19.5% for the best baseline to 35.6%.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of PIVOT. For each query, the policy model samples a group of rollouts, including teacher-assisted trajectories. In a teacher-assisted rollout, the student first generates a prefix, the teacher provides a correction segment, and the student then continues generation. The completed trajectory is optimized by the verifier-based GRPO objective, while the teacher-generated segment provides dense token-level supervision through a teacher-student KL loss.

Figure 8. Prefix versus middle intervention (continued). The student-conditioned middle state is completed by both models. All excerpts and counts refer to the same puzzle and the controlled continuations described on the preceding page.

Figure 7. Calibrating teacher guidance on hard logic games under middle intervention with forward KL. Each column varies one factor from the default setting, which is shaded. Solid lines denote avg@8 and dashed lines denote pass@8. Full numbers are given in Tab. 6 in the appendix.
Figure 5. Prefix vs. middle intervention. Guidance is more effective when the teacher can build on the student’s partial solution and correct errors along the way.

Figure 8. Prefix versus middle intervention on one Survo puzzle. With prefix intervention, the hand-off state is completed by the teacher (4/4), but not by the student (0/4). The matched middle intervention continues on the next page.

Figure 9. Late intervention on the same Survo puzzle. With ℓ𝑢 = 2048, the teacher and student solve the remaining cells from the hand-off state but exhaust the original budget before emitting the answer. Extending the teacher’s continuation budget restores completion.

papers.abstract: On-policy Self-distillation (OPSD) has proven effective for post-training large language models by constructing a teacher conditioned on privileged references. However, existing approaches keep the teacher fixed either throughout training by consistently exposing it to the full reference, or within each response by adaptively varying partial reference exposure only across responses. In this paper, we argue that neither of them is sufficient. Instead, every token needs its own teacher, as the teacher preference can vary token by token within the same response. Through a teacher-intervention pilot study, we validate that the teacher preference differs across tokens, and reveal that a preferred teacher can be identified for each token through majority voting and KL-based selection. Motivated by these findings, we propose Multi-teacher Adaptive On-policy Self-Distillation (MTA-OPSD), the first token-level adaptive OPSD method. Our method constructs a multi-teacher pool consisting of candidate teachers, and enables every token to adaptively select its preferred teacher during training. Experiments with Qwen3 models on mathematical reasoning tasks show that MTA-OPSD consistently outperforms existing OPSD approaches with an average gain of up to $+5.9$ over the base model, highlighting the importance of adapting teacher supervision at the token level. The code is available at https://github.com/xingzhejun/MTA-OPSD.
authors: Yifu Luo, Chuang Ma, Zeyu Chen, Enkelejda Kasneci, Qi Chen, Gjergji Kasneci
bullets: Existing OPSD methods use fixed or response-level adaptive teachers, overlooking token-level preference differences.
A teacher-intervention study finds that preferred teachers vary across tokens and can be identified via majority voting or KL-based selection.
MTA-OPSD builds a pool of candidate teachers and selects a preferred teacher independently for each token during training.
Experiments on Qwen3 models for mathematical reasoning report gains of up to +5.9 over the base model.
The method is evaluated within the studied Qwen3 mathematical-reasoning setting; broader scope is not established by the abstract.

papers.abstract: Foundation models are typically trained in stages: pretraining, midtraining, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning (RL), with changes in both data and learning algorithms. We show that this algorithmic separation is not fundamental. By deriving suitable RL objectives as maximum-likelihood fitting to model-generated target distributions, we place all of these stages under a single likelihood-based training algorithm, unified training. This perspective turns the foundation-model training lifecycle into a problem of choosing which data to train on, in what proportions, and when, with conventional staged training as a special case. We instantiate this framework in a unified training system that mixes static data and RL generations within a single trainer. Across controlled and real-world experiments, unified training improves the accuracy-compute tradeoff and task coverage while preserving broader capabilities, and provides a stronger starting point for continual learning. This work lays the groundwork for a unified science of foundation-model training, connecting mathematical principles, training infrastructure, and the development of model capabilities.
authors: Yuda Song, Alvin Zhang, Fahim Tajwar, Daman Arora, Jeff Schneider, Daniel Khashabi, Ruslan Salakhutdinov, J. Andrew Bagnell, Aarti Singh, Andrea Zanette
bullets: Reframes staged training as a data-selection and data-mixing problem rather than requiring distinct algorithms.
Derives RL objectives as maximum-likelihood fitting to model-generated target distributions.
Implements a trainer combining static datasets with reinforcement-learning generations.
Reports improved accuracy–compute tradeoffs and task coverage while preserving broader capabilities.
Provides a stronger starting point for continual learning, though the abstract does not specify experimental scope or limitations.

papers.abstract: Safety alignment for Large Language Models is heavily focused on English with limited multilingual representation, particularly damaging low-resource language performance. Related open training datasets are often limited in size or do not follow region-localized harmful topics to broaden the scope of alignment beyond cultures. We propose a scalable template-based augmentation pipeline to produce massive multilingual refusal and benign corpora, extracting safe templates from harmful prompts, translating them and then filling in the slots with culturally authentic entities, both harmful and benign. As a result, we release MSafeTemp, a validated corpus spanning 60 languages useful for multilingual safety alignment and evaluation. Using the dataset, we show that English-only evaluation misjudges multilingual safety: for several models, attacks that fail in English succeed once translated, while culturally localized variants expose further failures that translation alone misses. We also confirm that augmenting safety training data through templates allows for higher diversity and quality of alignment, resulting in improved safety performance beyond English. MSafeTemp and the respective pipeline are aimed at facilitating research and development of safer and more responsible models for less-represented cultures.
authors: Max Neuwinger, Hanna Yukhymenko, Imanol Schlag
bullets: Multilingual safety alignment is underdeveloped, especially for low-resource languages and region-specific harmful topics.
The pipeline extracts safe templates from harmful prompts, translates them, and fills slots with culturally authentic harmful and benign entities.
MSafeTemp is a validated corpus covering 60 languages for multilingual safety alignment and evaluation.
Experiments find that translated and culturally localized attacks can bypass models that appear safe in English.
Template-based augmentation increases alignment-data diversity and quality, improving safety performance beyond English.

papers.abstract: The last year has seen a shift in AI-assisted mathematics, with frontier language models producing proofs of and counterexamples to long-standing open conjectures. However, studying only the current set of major breakthroughs provides an incomplete picture of LLM capabilities and the computational resources needed to achieve reported results. To address this, we introduce a new dataset, OpenConjecture, which collects conjectures from mathematics papers published on the arXiv since February 2026. We use these conjectures as a source of open mathematical problems, and apply frontier GPT models to a random sample of 200 of these conjectures over three passes using a reproducible protocol without problem-specific mathematical guidance. Rather than attempt expert verification of these candidate solutions, we analyze the types of problems for which LLMs produce solutions and the characteristics of these solutions. The models we test produce candidate solutions for roughly 60% of the conjectures, with counterexamples about 1.3 times more common than proofs. We estimate solution novelty, assess how solutions cite and relate to existing literature, and analyze whether the proposed resolution relies on either an error in or underspecification of the conjecture. We find that models sometimes propose resolutions that are outside the authors' intent (e.g., proposing the trivial group as a counterexample) and that a number of proofs follow closely from existing results, but that some resolutions exhibit at least moderate novelty. Our findings underscore the need for evaluations that go beyond correctness to assess fidelity to the intended statement, attribution, and the nature of the mathematical contribution.
authors: Helen Jenne, Davis Brown, Jesse He, Henry Kvinge
bullets: Introduces OpenConjecture, a dataset of conjectures from mathematics papers on arXiv since February 2026.

Candidate counterexamples occur about 1.3 times as often as candidate proofs.
Analyzes solution novelty, literature use, and whether resolutions exploit errors or underspecification in conjectures.
Finds some moderately novel resolutions, alongside trivial or intent-mismatched counterexamples and proofs closely following existing results.

papers.abstract: Language models often need to maintain multiple contextual variables that evolve independently within a document. Prior work has identified structured representations of individual temporal or contextual quantities, but their joint organization remains less understood. We study this question using controlled documents with independently phased language-switch and topic-change timers. Across ten pretrained checkpoints, both timers are linearly decodable from the same hidden states. Removing a timer-associated centroid plane substantially reduces access to its associated variable while having little effect on the concurrent timer, although the planes are nonorthogonal and contain cross-timer information. Separate timer contributions also explain most reproducible variation among joint-state centroids. These signatures persist from 3 to 51 timer values and across Qwen3 checkpoints from 0.6B to 14B. Schedule position affects continuation probabilities, but the tested centroid displacement produces no consistent timer-specific output effect. Together, these results support approximate factorization based on selective accessibility and approximately additive joint-state geometry in overlapping subspaces.
bullets: Both language-switch and topic-change timers are linearly decodable from the same hidden states across ten checkpoints.

The findings persist across 3–51 timer values and Qwen3 models ranging from 0.6B to 14B parameters.
Centroid displacement did not consistently produce timer-specific output effects, limiting evidence about causal behavioral influence.

papers.abstract: Looping in transformer models reuses weights by repeatedly applying the same transformer, or parts of it, making the model deeper without increasing its parameter count. Whether looping is useful depends on which constraint dominates: model size, training compute, or autoregressive inference efficiency. We study these trade-offs jointly in dense decoder-only transformers trained from scratch, varying which parts of the model are looped, how many loops are applied, and how information is passed between loops. Our experiments span models with up to 1B parameters, trained on up to 155B tokens with up to $1.07\times10^{21}$ FLOPs and 32 loops. We find that looping the full transformer generally gives the strongest quality at a fixed parameter budget, whereas looping a middle block of layers gives a better return when training FLOPs are constrained. Adding loops is not uniformly beneficial: gains eventually saturate, reverse, or become unstable. This motivates asking whether forcing every loop to use the same weights limits the benefit of deeper looping. We address this by adding small loop-specific low-rank adapters that improve quality, with larger gains as more loops are added. Looped transformers also suffer a decoding slowdown proportional to the number of loops. Parallel Loop Transformers address this by passing hidden states between loops across adjacent token positions, allowing loop stages to run concurrently. However, in our experiments the original formulation does not consistently retain the quality gains of ordinary looping. We find that preserving the current-token embedding and separately normalizing it and the previous-token hidden state before combining them recovers strong performance across model scales and training budgets. Together, these results show that effective looping requires matching the design to the resource constraint and inference setting.
authors: Chanakya Ekbote, Artidoro Pagnoni, Devendra Singh Sachan, Shruti Bhosale, Mike Lewis, Maryam Fazel-Zarandi, Shashank Rajput, Sujan Kumar Gonugondla
bullets: Full-model looping generally gives the best quality at a fixed parameter budget, while looping a middle layer block is more compute-efficient during training.
Increasing the number of loops eventually yields diminishing, reversed, or unstable gains.
Small loop-specific low-rank adapters improve quality, with larger benefits as more loops are added.

Looping slows autoregressive decoding; Parallel Loop Transformers enable concurrent loop execution but need separate normalization and preservation of the current-token embedding to recover strong performance.
The study evaluates dense decoder-only transformers across model sizes, training budgets, and up to 32 loops.

papers.abstract: Effective multi-domain adaptation of large language models requires prioritizing relevant domain knowledge while minimizing interference from irrelevant domains. Existing approaches commonly use Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) to train a separate adapter for each domain and combine these adapters within one model. However, they either weight adapters equally regardless of the input domain or dynamically weight adapters while still activating all of them including irrelevant ones. Additionally, while efficient, their low-rank structure limits performance. In contrast, upcycling is a model expansion method that adds experts and a router to a dense Transformer layer offering larger capacity than LoRA approaches. In this paper, we propose Domain-Specialized Upcycling (DS-Upcycling) for multi-domain adaptation. We introduce a new domain-aware supervision that allows the router to effectively learn to distinguish domains by selecting the appropriate experts. During fine-tuning on each new domain, we update only the corresponding expert and router while freezing all other parameters. Experiments show that our method achieves the highest average performance across the adapted domains compared to baselines while retaining general performance. With just 256 examples per domain for router supervision, DS-Upcycling achieves 90-98% routing accuracy after adaptation compared with 43-70% for routers trained without our approach.
authors: Mingzi Cao, Xi Wang, Nikolaos Aletras
bullets: Targets interference from irrelevant domains and limited capacity in LoRA-based multi-domain adaptation.
Expands Transformer layers with experts and a router rather than relying solely on low-rank adapters.
Uses domain-aware router supervision and updates only the relevant expert and router during each domain’s fine-tuning.
Achieves the highest average performance across adapted domains among the compared baselines while retaining general performance.
With 256 supervision examples per domain, routing accuracy reaches 90–98%, versus 43–70% without the proposed supervision.

papers.abstract: The way software gets built is changing dramatically. AI agents now create pull requests, select dependencies, refactor codebases, interpret test failures, and execute infrastructure changes across the entire Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC). AI agents are autonomous team members, but unlike human engineers, they are ephemeral - their reasoning, decisions, and tool calls vanish the moment the session ends. Modern Security incidents involving intent mismatch or injection are becoming increasingly common - forcing us to address AI Agents as an insider threat. No widely adopted standard yet enables agentic provenance and governance and its obvious that you can't hold an ephemeral process accountable. The git log was designed for human commits. It shows what changed. It does not show what an AI agent did, which model it used, which tools it called, or whether anyone was accountable for the outcome. Every governance framework, every audit trail, every compliance control in the SDLC was built around one assumption: a human made the decision. That assumption no longer holds. This shift introduces 3 main procedural problems (not addressing scale) - Supply-chain vector - The agentic coder is software, so it is a supply-chain security risk. Policy guardrails - How to ensure the agentic coder is compliant with the policies of the organization. Task-alignment - How to align the agentic coder on its tasks and goals. We introduce Agentic Process Evidence (APE), a signed, tamper-evident, machine-readable attestation of agentic processes, linking the sessions to their outcome (process-aware logging). APE enables Policy-as-Code control over the agentic processes, allowing for human in the loop only when it's needed. We support the in-toto style attestation framework, and the protocol is aligned with the relevant regulations
bullets: AI agents increasingly perform SDLC tasks, but their ephemeral reasoning, decisions, and tool calls disappear after sessions end.
Traditional Git history records code changes, not the agent, model, tools, policies, or accountability behind them.
APE addresses supply-chain risk, policy compliance, and task alignment for agentic coding processes.
The framework links agent sessions to outcomes through process-aware, machine-readable logging.
APE supports in-toto-style attestations and Policy-as-Code, with human intervention when needed; regulatory alignment is claimed but not detailed in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Activation steering changes what a language model generates by editing its hidden states at inference time. Its most common form adds one vector, the difference of class means (DiM), to every hidden state. CHaRS (concept heterogeneity-aware representation steering) uses optimal transport instead: an entropic plan pairs the clusters of the two classes, and each hidden state moves along a mixture of the cluster displacements, weighted toward its nearest clusters. We study this family of clustered optimal-transport maps for toxicity mitigation in Gemma-2-2B and Granite-3.1-2B, and ask what the plan adds to DiM and whether that survives INT8 and NF4 quantization. We prove an identity: whatever the plan, the displacements averaged with the cluster sizes as weights equal DiM, so a clustered map can differ from DiM only for tokens whose routing weights depart from the cluster sizes. In the CHaRS protocol they stay close, and CHaRS is statistically equivalent to Mean-AcT, which adds DiM at every layer, in all eight pre-specified equivalence tests. A variant fitted on individual tokens, which routes each token mainly to its nearest clusters, leaves 37-39% less toxicity than DiM on Gemma and 51-61% less on Granite at steering strength 3 (toxic-bert), where DiM already removes 76-85% of it. Two other toxicity classifiers confirm the gain on Granite, but on Gemma only one does. At equal strength the variant has somewhat higher perplexity, but at matched toxicity it is slightly more fluent than DiM. Yet a nearly constant map from the same clusters also leaves about 30% less toxicity, so the role of treating tokens differently remains open. Under INT8 and NF4 the variant still leaves less toxicity than DiM, and transferring it from full precision to the NF4 model instead of refitting it adds no significant toxicity after correction for multiple tests.
bullets: The study tests whether clustered transport maps add value beyond DiM for toxicity steering in Gemma-2-2B and Granite-3.1-2B.
A proven identity shows that clustered displacements average to DiM; differences arise only when token routing weights depart from cluster-size weights.
In the CHaRS protocol, routing stays close to cluster-size weighting, making it statistically equivalent to Mean-AcT across eight pre-specified tests.
A token-level routing variant leaves 37–39% less toxicity on Gemma and 51–61% less on Granite than DiM at steering strength 3, though it can have higher perplexity at equal strength.
The variant remains better than DiM under INT8 and NF4; however, a nearly constant map also improves toxicity, so the importance of treating tokens differently is unresolved.

papers.selection_reason: Studies inference-time activation steering for LLM toxicity mitigation, including quantization robustness, directly relevant to LLM behavior and control.
papers.title: One Vector or Many? Clustered Optimal-Transport Steering under Quantization
papers.tldr: Clustered optimal-transport steering can outperform a single mean-difference vector for toxicity mitigation, including under quantization, but the benefit of token-specific routing remains unclear.

papers.abstract: We report that allocating compute to synthetic pre-pretraining (PPT) never outperforms pure natural-language training in our compute-matched experiments. This holds across four PPT curricula (k-Dyck, neural cellular automata (NCA), declarative reference corpora, and code) and three training regimes: data-constrained, data-unconstrained, and a high token-to-parameter-ratio regime (881M parameters trained on 50B tokens). When natural language is scarce, repeated epochs over a 100M-token corpus beat every synthetic curriculum on natural-language validation loss, with no consistent downstream accuracy advantage from PPT. We find that PPT gains reported in prior work are sensitive to the weight initialization scheme. In an NCA reproduction, we recover a 5.4% perplexity improvement from PPT under the original initialization scheme. An alternative scheme improves both methods, but the no-PPT baseline more, closing the gap between them. However, when PPT receives additional compute rather than a share of the natural-language budget, gains persist at small natural-language budgets even with improved initialization, but disappear by 1B tokens. Finally, models forget what they learn during PPT in subsequent natural-language training; interleaving the same data throughout training prevents forgetting, but does not significantly improve natural-language performance. Our results suggest limited benefits of synthetic pre-pretraining as a distinct training stage and motivate rethinking how such data are used in language model training.
authors: Alexander Stern, Tim Rockt\"aschel, Acyr Locatelli, Laura Ruis
bullets: Across four synthetic curricula and three training regimes, PPT never outperformed pure natural-language training in compute-matched experiments.
Repeating scarce natural-language data yielded better validation loss than every tested synthetic curriculum, without consistent downstream accuracy gains.
An NCA reproduction recovered a 5.4% perplexity improvement only under the original initialization; an alternative initialization largely eliminated the gap.
PPT benefits persisted with extra compute at small natural-language budgets but disappeared by 1B tokens.
Models largely forgot PPT-learned information during later natural-language training; interleaving data prevented forgetting without significantly improving performance.

figures.caption: Figure 4: PPT is useful at 50M–100M natural-language tokens, but its gain at 1B disappears under spectral-based initialization. In the additive-compute regime with a 336M-parameter model, NCA and k-Dyck, each at its lowest-loss configuration, improve on the optimal no-PPT baseline at 50M and 100M natural-language tokens. Under spectral-based initialization this gain disappears by 1B tokens, but under the other initializations it persists at every budget (Appendix E.1 shows the full breakdown). Because spectral-based initialization yields the lowest loss for every method at this largest budget, we use it in all compute-matched experiments, which run at comparable FLOP budgets.

Figure 8: Full synthetic PPT token sweep behind Figure 4. FineWeb validation bits-per-byte against the amount of synthetic PPT added on top of a fixed natural-language token budget. Rows are that budget, columns are the initialization scheme: two as used in the prior literature that introduced these curricula, and the spectral-based initialization. The model size here is 336M parameters. Within each panel the leftmost point is that configuration’s own baseline with no PPT, marked by the gray dashed line. The green dashed line and band mark the lowest-loss no-PPT baseline across the three initialization schemes, providing a reference for comparisons across initializations. Solid lines with filled markers are Muon PPT and dashed lines with open markers are AdamW PPT. AdamW performs better than Muon for the PPT methods at the lower natural-language budgets; at 1B tokens, however, the two are indistinguishable under spectral-based initialization. Importantly, if one is to train with the alternative initializations, the PPT benefit would still exist even at this larger budget.

Figure 7: LLMTuna reaches a lower validation loss in fewer trials than a TPE search. The continuous lines for each method show the best FineWeb validation BPB so far against trial index, while the faint dots are individual trials. LLMTuna reaches 0.9780 at its tenth trial, while TPE reaches 0.9808 at its twenty-second and does not improve over the remaining eight. The axis is broken above 0.992, where the early exploratory trials of both searches sit.

(2026). Under each alternative initialization the baseline improves and the gap between NCA and the baseline narrows.

Figure 11: Breakdown of downstream performance by benchmark sub-tasks. Each row is a PPT model from Figures 1 and 4, and each column is one of the 13 BLiMP or 22 DCLM CORE tasks. Blue cells are significantly above the baseline, red cells significantly below, and white cells on par. Most cells are white, so on most sub-scores the PPT models perform on par with their baseline. The colored cells show that, even so, the PPT method changes how the model performs on some sub-tasks of these benchmarks.

Figure 2: Tokenizing synthetic pre-pretraining data. For NCA, each grid of a rollout is split into 2 × 2 patches that each become one token, and grids are concatenated in time order with start and end tokens. For k-Dyck, the opening and closing bracket types are each their own token. For DeclRef, keywords, scope brackets, names and values are unique tokens. In the example shown, a reference inside the opened scope retrieves the value of a name declared in that scope, and after the scope closes a reference retrieves the value of a name declared before the scope. Generation and tokenization details are given in Section 2 and Appendix A.

Figure 9: No PPT method scales better than the baseline. Here we plot FineWeb validation BPB against training compute for the data-unconstrained experiments. Each line is a separate power law, BPB = AC−α (Kaplan et al., 2020), fitted by least squares on log BPB against logC over that method’s nine runs (three seeds per scale), with C in units of 1018 FLOPs, so A is the fitted BPB at 1018 FLOPs. The table gives A and α with their standard errors. The baseline has the lowest A, and no method’s exponent is significantly larger than the baseline’s (within standard error). Raising PPT from 1% to 5% raises A for every method. However, its effect on the exponent is unclear as at 5% every exponent is within standard error of the baseline’s. Every synthetic PPT method remains above the baseline at every budget, while C4, independent of percentage, is the same as the baseline. Since we only have three budgets per method, and three seeds, we do not fit an irreducible-loss term as in Hoffmann et al. (2022).

Figure 5: Uniformly distributing the PPT data across training, rather than front-loading it, prevents forgetting on the PPT distribution. In the interleaved runs, 5% of every batch consists of NCA, k-Dyck, or code throughout training. In the PPT runs, the same 5% of compute is instead spent up front, at 2.7 × 1019 FLOPs. Left: FineWeb validation BPB at the end of training. Right: validation BPB on the PPT corpus itself across the whole run, one panel per corpus on its own scale, with the gray dotted line marking 5% of total compute. Under the PPT schedule the models lose this ability at the PPT-to-PT boundary; under interleaving they keep it and continue to improve on it. Elsewhere in this work the vocabulary is replaced at the phase boundary for the synthetic PPT distributions, which means the PPT corpus cannot be scored after the PPT phase. Every run here instead shares a single vocabulary, extended to hold the NCA and k-Dyck tokens, so the corpus can be tracked throughout training. These runs are not hyperparameter-tuned (configurations in Appendix D.5, Table 7), so the FineWeb panel is included only to show that the interleaved runs sit in a similar range to their PPT counterparts.

Figure 10: Data-constrained results separated by PPT-phase optimizer. The experiments behind panel (1) of Figure 1, with Muon PPT drawn as solid lines with filled markers and AdamW PPT as dashed lines with open markers. Each experiment was searched independently under the same search space and stopping rule, so the two differ in the optimizer used during PPT and in the configuration each search found. Neither optimizer is always better than the other: AdamW is lower for NCA and DeclRef at every PPT percentage, while k-Dyck is lower under Muon. No experiment of either optimizer reaches the no-PPT baseline.

However, C4, the natural-language control, reaches a DCLM CORE score in the same range as the PPT methods. In this table, NL denotes natural-language tokens.

papers.abstract: Language models handle text well, and rule engines give conclusions with proofs. Systems that combine the two are usually described by example, and the same coupling turns up under different names in agent frameworks, guardrail toolkits and neuro-symbolic research. This document defines thirteen patterns for coupling a language model with an executable rule language, in the catalogue form introduced for object-oriented design: intent, motivation, applicability, participants, collaborations, consequences, implementation, known uses and related patterns. Four patterns concern what crosses the boundary between model and rules, five who controls whom, three how the model takes part in the reasoning, and one how knowledge is kept over time. Five invariants hold for every combination, and five failure patterns name the couplings that break them. We relate the catalogue to published pattern catalogues and taxonomies of hybrid and neuro-symbolic systems and show where they overlap with it. A decision guide leads from a problem to a pattern. It rests on our measurements, including the cases in which a model alone did as well as the hybrid or better, and it reports what each design cost.

bullets: Addresses the inconsistent naming and example-driven description of hybrid language-model/rule systems.
Classifies patterns by boundary crossing, control, reasoning participation, and knowledge persistence.
Defines five invariants for valid combinations and five failure patterns for broken couplings.
Connects the catalogue to existing hybrid and neuro-symbolic taxonomies and published pattern catalogues.
Provides a decision guide grounded in measurements, including cases where a language model alone matched or outperformed the hybrid and the costs of each design.

papers.abstract: AI assistants are increasingly embedded in computational notebooks, scientific workflows, software engineering tools, and learning systems, yet human-AI interactions are often treated as transient prompt-response exchanges rather than durable data products, hindering reproducibility, explainability, replay, behavioral analysis, and adaptive AI support. We argue that these interactions form a new data class requiring formal representation and introduce the Human-AI Interaction Description Language (HAIDL), a formal interaction model with a Backus-Naur Form-inspired concrete syntax. HAIDL encodes each interaction as a structured object capturing computational context, user request, prompt payload, AI response, feedback, problem context, provenance, and model metadata. We integrate this vision into HAIDL-X, a middleware for JupyterLab that instantiates HAIDL by capturing user-bot state, building contextualized prompts, interfacing with AI providers, collecting feedback, and storing interactions in a repository. We add a learning layer over HAIDL that maps interaction objects and notebook execution traces into reproducible measures of user behavior, including engagement, performance, help-seeking, error-oriented use, and learning personas. HAIDL-X provides a foundation for treating human-AI collaboration as structured, queryable, replayable, analyzable data.
authors: Michela Taufer, Kin Ng, Ian Lumsden, Aashish Pandey, Rajasi Gore, Angelina Ju, Sukanya Moudgalya, Ewa Deelman, Sai Swaminathan
bullets: Addresses the problem of treating AI interactions as transient prompt–response exchanges, which limits reproducibility, replay, and behavioral analysis.
Introduces HAIDL, a formal language for representing context, requests, prompts, responses, feedback, provenance, and model metadata.
Implements HAIDL-X, a JupyterLab middleware that captures interaction state, builds prompts, interfaces with AI providers, collects feedback, and stores records.
Adds a learning layer that derives measures of engagement, performance, help-seeking, error-oriented use, and learning personas from interactions and notebook traces.
Provides a foundation for structured, queryable, replayable, and analyzable human–AI collaboration data.

papers.abstract: Industrial advertising agents must continually adapt their decision knowledge to changing product offerings, traffic patterns, and operating policies. We present KARMA (Knowledge-Atomic, Regression-Gated Modular Adaptation), a training-free framework that evolves six typed knowledge modules while keeping model weights and executable harness code frozen. During our evolution, a deterministic Trace Verifier maps observed errors to candidate modules, and a Critic compares successful and failed trajectories to guide a tool-constrained Evolver. The Evolver applies atomic knowledge edits, which a fixed validation gate retains only when their measured gain reaches a threshold; otherwise, the previous knowledge state is restored. We evaluate KARMA with three LLM families on cases sampled from a corpus of approximately half a million real-world operation logs across six e-commerce domains. Across 18 domain--model settings, KARMA raises the average hold-out score from 30.19 to 39.15 (+8.96 points, +29.7%). Ablations show that removing either successful or failed trajectories more than halves the average hold-out gain. Evolved knowledge also transfers across domains without further adaptation, yielding an average hold-out gain of 8.54 points across all source--target pairs. By linking retained patches to their diagnostic evidence and validation outcomes, KARMA supports inspectable, reversible knowledge adaptation for agents in Web marketplaces.

bullets: Addresses continual adaptation to changing products, traffic, and operating policies.

papers.abstract: We study post-training for dynamically routed mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, focusing on integrating independently optimized specialists while keeping consolidation efficient. Our approach combines calibrated multi-teacher on-policy distillation (C-MOPD), which matches each selected teacher on a local Top-$K$ support with teacher-wise loss normalization and clipping, with an execution path that uses post-capacity bounded-width dispatch, final-route replay, and asynchronous rollout--training overlap. On Turing-20B-A2B, the selected model achieves a four-domain normalized integration score of 0.9988 and retains at least 90.16\% of the measured specialist gain in every domain. At matched $K=32$, the full calibration objective scores 0.9962, compared with 0.9724 without calibration and 0.9834 without clipping. At a matched 8K response cap, the model exceeds both shared SFT and Qwen3-8B on all four reasoning-enabled mathematics and code benchmarks (unweighted mean: 85.92, versus 80.33 for Qwen3-8B and 74.21 for SFT), and improves over SFT on ten of twelve broader evaluation metrics. In a PPU-based profile, the combined execution configuration reduces consolidation step time from 398.7 to 139.3 seconds, an observed 2.86$\times$ speedup over serial execution. These results demonstrate strong specialist integration alongside more efficient consolidation, while reflecting the complete training and execution framework rather than any single component.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) rely on Multi-Head Attention (MHA) for sequence modeling, but scaling to long contexts is constrained by the quadratic cost of attention, motivating sub-quadratic recurrent alternatives. This paper formalizes a Dynamic Wave recurrent layer, based on input-dependent exponential damping and cosine phase modulation, and evaluates three 10.94M-parameter configurations (Pure Transformer, Pure Wave, and Hybrid Wave-Attention) on TinyStories under perplexity, latency, throughput and peak VRAM profiling up to 4096 tokens. The Hybrid configuration reaches the best perplexity, 5.95 on the full held-out split against 6.93 for the Transformer and 7.26 for Pure Wave. The efficiency picture, however, is governed by implementation rather than by architecture. Against an unfused attention baseline, Pure Wave uses 78.7% less peak VRAM at a 4096-token context (1404.3 MB vs. 6601.6 MB); against a fused scaled-dot-product attention kernel the same comparison yields no advantage at all (1404.3 MB vs. 1403.6 MB), and in training mode Pure Wave is 8.3% more expensive than the Transformer. Likewise, hoisting elementwise terms out of the recurrence loop speeds the layer up 2.53-fold with no custom kernel, reducing its latency gap to attention from 2.48-fold to 1.12-fold. A hybrid stack is found to inherit the cost of its more expensive mixer rather than the advantage of its cheaper one, its peak VRAM matching the Pure Transformer to within 0.1%. A closed-form memory model reproduces these measurements and predicts the context length beyond which attention overtakes the vocabulary projection. The findings indicate that reported efficiency gains for recurrent attention replacements must be stated relative to a named attention backend and a named implementation, and that hybridization is best justified on quality grounds.
bullets: The paper targets attention’s quadratic long-context cost with an input-dependent recurrent layer using exponential damping and cosine phase modulation.
On TinyStories, the Hybrid Wave-Attention model achieves the best held-out perplexity (5.95), versus 6.93 for Pure Transformer and 7.26 for Pure Wave.
Pure Wave substantially reduces VRAM versus unfused attention at 4096 tokens, but offers no VRAM advantage over fused attention and is more costly during training.
Optimizing recurrence implementation improves Wave latency 2.53×, narrowing its gap with attention; hybrid stacks inherit the cost of the more expensive mixer.
Efficiency claims should specify the attention backend and implementation; hybridization is primarily justified by quality gains.

papers.abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) rely on collaboration among specialized agents to solve complex tasks. Existing methods improve MAS by refining the prompts, skills, and execution strategies of individual agents based on task feedback. However, improving individual agents does not necessarily lead to better team collaboration. Recent studies have therefore extended evolution to the collaboration level, using collective execution experience to adjust team organization, and inter-agent interactions. Nevertheless, evolving collaboration across heterogeneous tasks remains challenging, as existing approaches often constrain team reorganization within a shared structure and reuse interaction rules across incompatible team contexts. In this paper, we propose EvoTeam, a collaboration-centric evolution framework that jointly evolves team organization, interaction rules, and individual agent skills through execution experience. It maintains a library of reusable teams, selecting or creating agent teams and guiding collaboration through team-specific interaction rules. Collaboration experience accumulates within compatible team contexts, while individual skills remain reusable across teams. Experiments across four benchmarks demonstrate its effectiveness. Our code is available at https://github.com/DEEP-JLU/EvoTeam.

papers.abstract: Over-refusal is a critical side effect of safety alignment in large language models (LLMs), causing harmless but superficially risky queries to be mistakenly rejected. Despite the effectiveness of existing mitigation methods, why safety-aligned LLMs may still reject harmless queries under correct safety supervision remains insufficiently understood. To address this gap, we analyze over-refusal through the lens of representation and optimization. We make two observations: 1) the representations of harmful and over-refusal samples are visually distinguishable at certain intermediate layers but increasingly overlap in deeper layers; and 2) harmful-sample gradients exhibit high intra-class similarity and concentrate in a low-rank subspace. Moreover, they are more strongly aligned with refusal-target gradients than with correct helpful-target gradients on over-refusal prompts. This imbalanced gradient coupling can bias over-refusal samples toward refusal, while the reduced apparent representational separation in deeper layers may make it more difficult for the model to maintain a clear boundary between harmful and over-refusal samples. To this end, we propose GOAL (Gradient Orthogonalization with contrAstive Learning), a safety-alignment framework for mitigating over-refusal. Specifically, GOAL consists of two components: 1) to prevent imbalanced gradient coupling from biasing the optimization of over-refusal samples toward refusal, we orthogonalize over-refusal gradients against the low-rank refusal subspace extracted from harmful gradients; and 2) to explicitly enhance the separation between harmful and over-refusal representations, we introduce a contrastive learning objective. Extensive experiments across multiple models and benchmarks demonstrate that GOAL effectively mitigates over-refusal while preserving safety performance and general capabilities.
authors: Chao Chen, Pengyang Shao, Wei Qin, Shijie Hao, Fei Shen, Richang Hong
bullets: Harmful and over-refusal samples become increasingly difficult to distinguish in deeper model layers.
Harmful-example gradients are highly similar, low-rank, and more aligned with refusal targets than helpful targets on harmless prompts.
GOAL orthogonalizes over-refusal gradients from the harmful-refusal subspace and applies contrastive learning to separate representations.
Experiments across multiple models and benchmarks show reduced over-refusal while preserving safety and general capabilities.
