papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses safety alignment in Large Language Models, a core topic within the LLM foundation model category.
papers.title: Revisiting Over-refusal in Safety-aligned Large Language Models: A Representation and Optimization Perspective
papers.tldr: The paper explains over-refusal through representation overlap and imbalanced gradients, then proposes GOAL to reduce unnecessary refusals without sacrificing safety or general capabilities.

papers.abstract: We develop a formal semantics for a general class of coordinated systems of parameterized transformations, taking the Transformer as a paradigmatic starting point but abstracting from its particular mathematical instantiation. Representational vectors receive both extensional reference and ordered intensional interpretations, while parameter structures acquire relative, second-level interpretations that determine how argument properties are preserved, replaced, or combined. This yields the notion of a transforming concept: a parameterized transformation whose numerical action is coordinated with a corresponding property-level map. We then distinguish the common algebraic-semantic core of these systems from their architecture-specific functional organization, allowing different mathematical instantiations and mechanical realizations of the same abstract system type. The framework is applied to attention heads and residual connections, providing semantic explanations that depend only on the shared algebraic-semantic core and their local functional organization and therefore generalize beyond the standard Transformer. These analyses also reveal the modularity of the framework: complex architectures can be decomposed into simpler semantically coordinated subsystems whose organization may recur across different abstract system types.
bullets: Abstracts parameterized transformation systems beyond any single Transformer implementation.
Gives vectors extensional reference and ordered intensional interpretations, while parameters receive second-level interpretations.
Introduces “transforming concepts,” pairing a numerical transformation with a property-level map.
Separates a shared algebraic-semantic core from architecture-specific functional organization.
Applies the framework to attention heads and residual connections, supporting modular analysis across different system realizations.
papers.selection_reason: Formal semantic framework for transformer/attention architectures, relevant to LLM architecture analysis.
papers.title: From the Transformer to a Formal Semantics of Coordinated Transformations
papers.tldr: The paper proposes a formal semantics for Transformer-like systems by linking numerical transformations with coordinated changes in represented properties.

papers.abstract: We show that the transformer architecture emerges as the score of last-token laws in a natural statistical model of language, where sentences are empirical measures of tokens, a language is a law on $P(S^d)$, and our prior belief is that sentences carry no structure at all. By the maximum-entropy principle, we select the law closest to this prior in relative entropy among those reproducing an observed sentence-level statistic. We discuss the relevance of the statistic in the posterior interaction between tokens and we build a statistic, able to capture that interaction, with Luce's choice axiom truncated at the lowest relational order. This procedure gives the softmax choice rule, with the attention cross-moment as its mean parameter. The query--key matrix is then the Lagrange multiplier of a maximum-entropy problem inside each sentence, and the value matrix the multiplier of the constraint over the language, so that the two are untied. Under the optimal entropic law we then show that a transformer head appears in the score of the last-token law. For ordered sentences, causal masking follows from the masked reference choice rule, and with a next-token cross-moment the score equals one causally masked attention head. We also discuss multi-head attention, weight-tied unembedding, and a heuristic reading of residual blocks as projected Langevin steps.
bullets: Models sentences as empirical token measures and languages as probability laws over sentences, with an unstructured prior.
Uses maximum entropy under interaction constraints based on a lowest-order truncation of Luce’s choice axiom.
Derives the softmax choice rule, with the attention cross-moment as its mean parameter.
Interprets query–key and value matrices as distinct Lagrange multipliers at sentence and language levels.
For ordered sentences, a next-token cross-moment yields exactly one causally masked attention head; multi-head attention and residual blocks are also discussed.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Transformer architecture as a three-step procedure. In the first step an embedding operator maps each token, represented by a one-hot vector in R|V|, to a vector of Rd+1 through a learned matrix E ∈ R(d+1)×|V|, possibly combined with normalization and with a positional encoding which keeps track of token order. Then, in the second step the sequence of vectors x1, . . . , xn goes through a stack of L identical layers. Each layer consists of a residual attention sub-layer, in which every token updates its representation by attending to the other tokens of the sentence, and a residual MLP which acts on each token separately. The output is then projected back to Sd via LN. Finally, an unembedding matrix Wout ∈ R|V|×(d+1) maps the output representation of the last token to a vector of logits, one per element of the vocabulary. Their softmax is the law of the next token, from which a token is sampled and appended to the text.

Figure 2. Causal version of the pipeline of Figure 1. Two things change. First, each token is recorded together with its position, so that the sentence becomes the ordered measure → µ = 1 n ∑ i δ(xi,i) ∈ P(Sd×N). Second, the attention sub-layer is causally masked: the additive mask M sets to zero the weight of every key coming after the query (j > i), so that each token only reads itself and the tokens before it.

Figure 3. Multi-head version of the causal transformer block of Figure 2. The single masked head is replaced by H heads, each with its own query, key and value matrices Qh,Kh, Vh, all sharing the same causal mask M . The head outputs are summed before the residual connection and the normalization. In our model each head corresponds to a different choice rule, with attention matrix Λh = Q⊤ h Kh, and Vh is the Lagrange multiplier of the corresponding cross-moment.

papers.abstract: Softmax routing in mixture-of-experts models can concentrate probability on a subset of experts, suppressing access to the others. We study how this concentration forms, why it persists, and how suppressed probabilities recover. For fixed experts, a stationary-loss barrier identifies the face supporting the optimal routed output. In a common-target square-loss model with freely trainable expert outputs, slow adaptation tracks fixed-expert dynamics on finite horizons, while every fixed positive adaptation rate yields an interior routing limit. An exact normal-velocity decomposition separates complementary-expert covariance from relative gradient advantage. Under positive two-sided power bounds along recovery paths, uniform over initial masses, the resulting coefficient's order of vanishing gives logarithmic or power-law recovery times. Integrations of constructed fields reproduce these orders. An exact discrete log-odds identity relates neural updates to threshold crossing. In paired Transformer-MoE training, removing a class-conditional router-gradient contrast delays confirmed recovery and reduces accumulated log-odds on fixed tokens, both with and without capacity constraints.
authors: Shengze Xu, Maolin Deng, Tieyong Zeng
bullets: Identifies a stationary-loss barrier determining the expert subset that supports the optimal routed output.
Shows that slow expert adaptation follows fixed-expert routing dynamics over finite horizons, while any positive adaptation rate leads to an interior routing limit.
Decomposes recovery motion into complementary-expert covariance and relative gradient advantage.
Derives logarithmic or power-law recovery times from the vanishing order of a recovery coefficient, with matching constructed-field examples.
In paired Transformer-MoE experiments, removing class-conditional router-gradient contrast delays recovery and lowers accumulated log-odds, with or without capacity constraints.

papers.abstract: Engineering design frequently involves redesigning a prior solution to adapt to changes in context, such as material prices or system requirements. Redesign often leverages simulators too complex and/or computationally intensive for traditional numerical solvers, which lack engineering knowledge and context, to ensure global solution quality. Large language models (LLMs) can interpret semantic information, including engineering knowledge about the system and changes in context, to help guide search, and recent studies have shown that incorporating this knowledge into optimization can improve search performance. However, how best to combine LLMs with numerical solvers in redesign remains unclear. We develop and test an integrated LLM-optimization approach for redesign and compare three methods for leveraging LLMs (warm start, variable fixing and ReAct) and four black-box solvers (Bayesian optimization, genetic algorithms, mesh adaptive direct search and random search) on an electric vehicle battery pack cost minimization case study across four types of redesign scenarios. We find that the integrated approach can match feasible design discovery of the numerical-solver baselines with 80% fewer simulator evaluations while tripling the fraction of runs that find near-optimal solutions. We find that the best LLM-solver integration approach and the way the prior solution is leveraged depend on the structure of the design requirement change, and that the benefit of increasing LLM model size grows with the extent to which the LLM controls the search. These results show clear potential for LLMs in redesign tasks for guiding or replacing numerical solvers.
authors: Chan-Eui Song, Jeremy J. Michalek, Christopher McComb
bullets: Addresses redesign problems where expensive, complex simulators make conventional optimization inefficient and context-insensitive.

papers.title: LLM-Assisted Optimization for Simulation-Based Redesign
papers.tldr: An integrated LLM–numerical optimization framework improves simulation-based redesign by using engineering context to guide search, reducing simulator evaluations and increasing near-optimal solution discovery.

papers.abstract: We introduce SocialArena, a benchmark for systematically defining and evaluating the social intelligence of large language models (LLMs). Although LLMs are increasingly deployed in socially interactive applications such as mental health counseling, companionship chatbots, and educational tutoring, existing evaluations remain fragmented focusing on isolated capabilities or single scenarios and evaluation reliability is largely unverified. This work makes three main contributions to address these limitations. (1) We first propose a unified three-tier framework that defines social intelligence along three capability dimensions: role-playing ability, mental state reasoning, and behavioral reasoning. To operationalize this definition, we design a role-playing dialogue paradigm with explicit character thinking for evaluation, enabling simultaneous assessment of these capabilities in a manner that mirrors realistic human interactions. (2) To ensure diversity across social scenarios and thereby prevent evaluation conclusions from being confined to specific scenarios, we introduce the U-TRIMF framework, which guides us in synthesizing social contexts with broad coverage. (3) To obtain reliable evaluation, we invest $132.4K to recruit and train human annotators and adopt a human-annotated arena-style protocol, where annotators compare model responses and provide preference labels along with natural-language critiques. We hope that SocialArena can provide valuable insights and guidance for future LLM improvements.
authors: Zongqi Wang, Rui Wang, Yuchuan Wu, Hua Yang, Bingxue Qiu, Tianle Gu, Bing Zhao, Yujiu Yang, Jieping Ye, Yongbin Li

papers.abstract: Financial AI systems must support decision-bearing questions involving payments, collections, cash flow, and compliance while ensuring numerical accuracy, traceability, and auditability. Large language models (LLMs) enable natural language interaction but cannot independently guarantee reproducible calculations or evidence-grounded recommendations. We present a production-grounded architecture integrating three components: a financial knowledge graph for enterprise relationships, temporal context, and provenance; a deterministic optimization engine for financial calculations and decisions; and a multi-agent LLM layer for intent interpretation, task orchestration, explanation, and claim validation. A coordination layer, termed context engineering, selects, ranks, composes, and validates query-specific context across ERP systems, tools, and tenants. Based on observations from 15 deployments over approximately 11 months, single-agent pipelines exhibited hallucination rates of about 7-9% (5-10% across query types), including invented invoices and unsupported financial claims. Graph-backed multi-agent validation reduced observed rates to below 1%, although these findings are observational rather than causal. ERP data quality and tenant-specific schemas remained major implementation challenges. Reusable mappings, graph templates, and validation policies coincided with a reduction in deployment time from roughly six to two weeks. We argue that financial context engineering extends beyond text-centric retrieval-augmented generation by requiring structured relationships, temporal validity, exact numerical evidence, access controls, and validation against source records and solver outputs. We outline research challenges in evaluation, reproducibility, privacy, context quality, and cross-tenant generalization.
bullets: Targets decision-bearing financial tasks such as payments, collections, cash flow, and compliance.
Uses context engineering to select, rank, compose, and validate query-specific information across ERP systems, tools, and tenants.
In 15 observational deployments, graph-backed multi-agent validation coincided with lower observed hallucination rates—from about 5–10% to below 1%.
Reusable mappings, graph templates, and validation policies coincided with deployment time falling from roughly six to two weeks.
Key challenges include ERP data quality, tenant-specific schemas, privacy, reproducibility, evaluation, and cross-tenant generalization.

papers.abstract: We present XLaw-JP-27B, an open-weight model specialized for Japanese law that runs on a single 48\,GB GPU under the Apache~2.0 licence. It adapts Qwen3.8-27B with hybrid retrieval over all current statutes and 31k case summaries, a light QLoRA fine-tune on its own verified answers to past bar-exam questions (self-distillation), a contract-specific LoRA adapter, and four-sample voting. We evaluate it on eight Japanese legal tasks---the multiple-choice section of the bar examination in 2024, 2025 and 2026, statement-level bar questions (JBE-QA), statute questions (LawQA-JP), the patent attorney exam, and contract review and drafting built from government model contracts---against open models of 12--33B under identical prompts and retrieval. XLaw-JP-27B ranks first on six tasks, ties on one and is third on one (mean rank 1.3 against 2.8--3.1 for the baselines). It is the only system that passes the bar exam in all three years (129, 120 and 130 of 175, meeting every subject minimum; no test-year material was used in training), while open Japanese 32--33B models fail at least one year. A controlled study of each component shows that retrieval, voting and self-distillation help, and that thinking mode, retrieval-grounded synthetic tuning, self-verification, per-statement decomposition and more self-distillation do not. The largest remaining gaps to frontier models are in contract review and patent law. The model is available as a free web service at https://x-law.jp/ with the weights available at https://huggingface.co/X-LawJapan/xlaw-jp-27b under Apache~2.0.
bullets: Adapts Qwen3.8-27B with statute and case-summary retrieval, self-distillation via QLoRA, a contract LoRA adapter, and four-sample voting.
Ranks first on six of eight tasks, ties on one, and places third on one, outperforming the reported open-model baselines in mean rank.
Passes the Japanese bar exam in all three evaluated years while meeting every subject minimum; no test-year material was used for training.
Component analysis finds retrieval, voting, and self-distillation helpful, while several additional reasoning and tuning strategies do not improve results.
Remaining weaknesses are contract review and patent law; weights and a free web service are released under Apache 2.0.

papers.abstract: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) typically uses uniform coverage across Transformer layers despite heterogeneous positional requirements. Phase-off interventions reveal non-uniform, model-specific rotary-phase dependence, while coverage interventions relate it to coverage-upgrade benefits. We propose profiling-guided layer-wise RoPE allocation, assigning high/low coverage under a fixed budget using early coverage-benefit profiles. The framework supports fixed-width query/key representations and physical rotary-dimension allocation in Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA). Normalized-depth mapping transfers profiles within model families, enabling small-model measurements to guide larger-model allocations before pretraining. A brief analysis relates selection and transfer to score calibration and inter-layer interactions. From-scratch experiments demonstrate validation-loss improvements over available budget-matched baselines, while analytical resource accounting identifies favorable quality--storage--compute trade-offs for physical MLA. These results connect positional demand to transferable, efficient architecture design.

papers.abstract: LLM-based agents are increasingly used to complete complex, long-horizon tasks without human intervention. To make progress toward the task goal, agents need to perform different duties, such as planning and verification, when needed. To understand how single agents manage these duties during long-horizon execution, we conduct a preliminary study. Our analysis shows that verification has the strongest association with task success, but often occurs late, leaving limited opportunities for correction. We also find that the proportion of duty-relevant information decreases as records from different duties accumulate in a shared context. These findings lead us to examine whether multi-agent systems (MAS) can address these problems by assigning duties to agents with separate contexts. Our analysis shows that this separation alone is insufficient. Agents can lose track of the overall goal and repeat prior investigations. They may also lack necessary background while receiving irrelevant information from others. To maintain goal awareness and coordinate collaboration as task needs change, we propose Goal-Aware Dynamic Multi-Agent Collaboration (GAD). It uses a growing execution graph to organize subtasks and their dependencies. To keep agents focused on their goals, each context retains the original instruction and the assigned task's goal and acceptance conditions. To adapt collaboration and information sharing during execution, agents can divide tasks into subtasks and specify dependencies based on execution evidence. These dependencies guide when agents work and which results they receive. Verification and recovery check subtask results and full task completion against their goals, providing feedback for repair when checks fail.
authors: Xu Shen, Lingyong Yan, Shuaiqiang Wang, Jianmin Wu, Zhikai Chen, Jiliang Tang, Jie Ren
bullets: Verification is strongly linked to success but often happens too late for effective correction.
Single-agent contexts become diluted as information from different duties accumulates.
Separating duties across agents can cause goal drift, repeated work, and missing or irrelevant context.
GAD uses a growing execution graph to organize subtasks, dependencies, and adaptive information sharing.
Verification and recovery checks provide feedback for repairing failed subtasks or incomplete overall tasks.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly described as acquiring "reasoning" skills after reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. However, whether these gains reflect genuine reasoning or more superficial adaptations remains underexplored. In this work, we probe LLMs trained in a finite and exhaustively analyzable logical domain, namely Tic-Tac-Toe, and trace how internal representations evolve across reinforcement learning (RL) with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Quantitatively, RL yields high accuracy and robustness across prompt variations, suggesting the emergence of game reasoning. Mechanistic interpretability, however, paints a different picture: features extracted with sparse autoencoders (SAEs) reveal that models primarily adapt to rely more heavily on information already explicit in the prompt, such as whose turn it is, game progression and board occupancy. In comparison, high-level concepts like board symmetries and strategic forks remain weakly represented, raising concerns that reasoning benchmarks overestimate model abilities. This suggests that RL-driven "reasoning" may conflate task-specific adaptations to input information with reasoning ability. We provide, for the first time: (i) a systematic interpretability pipeline tracing representation dynamics across RL training in small-scale LLMs; (ii) an extension of SAE-based feature discovery to hypothesis-driven testing in a finite logical domain; and (iii) an interpretability-based demonstration that RL post-training neither adds nor removes concept information but reorganizes which features dominate the representation, with causal interventions locating the decision downstream of it, in the late-layer state.
bullets: The study examines whether RL with GRPO produces genuine reasoning or task-specific pattern exploitation.
Across prompt variations, RL improves accuracy and robustness in the finite Tic-Tac-Toe domain.
Sparse autoencoder analysis finds stronger reliance on turn, game progression, and board occupancy information.
Board symmetries and strategic forks remain weakly represented despite behavioral gains.
Causal interventions place the decision process downstream in the late-layer state, where RL reorganizes feature dominance rather than adding or removing concepts.

It is evident that while the base model only clearly represents the game turn, during the course of training, the model evolves to represents the boards based on game progression in addition to game turn, leading to improvement in performance. However, logic for strategic situations does not play a big role in model representations and no clear patterns emerge over the course of training. papers.selection_reason: Uses mechanistic interpretability (SAEs) to analyze how RL training affects internal representations in LLMs, specifically distinguishing between genuine reasoning and pattern exploitation.
papers.title: Reasoning or Pattern Exploitation? Mechanistic Insights from RL-Trained Language Models
papers.tldr: In Tic-Tac-Toe, RL-trained LLMs appear robust and accurate largely by emphasizing prompt-explicit information rather than developing strong representations of higher-level strategic reasoning.

papers.abstract: LLM read-and-evaluate tasks include study screening, data extraction, risk-of-bias assessment, and critical appraisal in the evidence synthesis field. These task differ in the amount of LLM interpretation they require. Some tasks involve retrieving relatively simple information, such as an author name, sample size, or publication year. Others require the LLM to read source material, interpret it against predefined criteria, and make a judgement. Researchers should assess whether LLM judgements are accurate, supported by appropriate source evidence, and reproducible under specified conditions. A correct judgement does not necessarily indicate that the underlying evaluation process is reliable. We developed a taxonomy for identifying mechanisms that may compromise these properties and for informing the selection and reporting of appropriate evaluation methods. The taxonomy outlines potential ways that LLM judgments from read-and-evaluate tasks can fail, called TRAILS (Taxonomy of Reliability And Instability in LLM-assisted evidence Synthesis). The TRAILS taxonomy addresses two complementary questions. First, what mechanisms can cause the same read-and-evaluate task to produce different judgements across repeated LLM runs? Second, what mechanisms can systematically affect the judgement or required output in a way that is not apparent from the judgement itself? This study presents 38 mechanisms and identifies the deployment settings in which each can operate, approaches for testing them, and mitigation strategies. We also show why repeatability or accuracy does not rule out a hidden judgement failure and why human evaluation should assess whether a judgement is grounded in the supplied evidence, independent of inappropriate external influence, and produced through a process that can be examined and verified.
authors: Carole Lunny, Ian Goodman, Stefano Berrone, Connor TA Brenna, Emma K Reid, Ivan Perez-Neri, Shailesh Kolekar, Nityanand Jain, Ashwin Kamath, Lucas HCC Santos, Yulia Otmakhova, Heba Hussein, Diana M Cespedes, Gioia Dahdal, Salmaan Kanji
bullets: Targets read-and-evaluate tasks such as study screening, data extraction, risk-of-bias assessment, and critical appraisal.
Distinguishes failures that cause different judgments across repeated runs from systematic influences hidden by the final judgment.
Maps each mechanism to relevant deployment settings, testing approaches, and mitigation strategies.
Argues that evaluation must assess evidence grounding, resistance to inappropriate external influence, and verifiability—not accuracy or repeatability alone.

papers.abstract: In transformer language models with gated multilayer perceptrons (MLPs), adjacent layers write partly against each other into the residual stream. Previous work interpreted this cancellation as layers proposing features and the next layer selectively rejecting the inappropriate ones. We decompose the cancellation by removing the previous layer's write from the input of the next MLP: what the next layer writes along that write splits into what it writes anyway and how much less its MLP writes because the write is present, which we call the damping, and we trace the damping to the neurons that carry it. In gated MLPs the damping is carried by neurons whose gates are closed. SiLU and GELU are slightly negative below zero, so a closed gate still passes a small negative multiple of what the neuron reads, and a neuron whose output weight points along its input weight then subtracts a fraction of the direction it read. Summed over such neurons, closed gates contract the average direction a gated MLP reads, and the previous layer's write is not singled out: the same layer's write at another token is damped as much or more, and the eigenvalue signature from which that work concluded that the correction is selective appears for another token's write as well. Over training the damping grows while what the next layer writes anyway stays flat, and cancellation begins when the damping overtakes it; annealing the negative side of the gate activation away in continued pretraining removes the damping and the cancellation. Adjacent-layer cancellation is therefore weak evidence about which features a model rejects: it is produced by a contraction that gated MLPs apply, on average over directions, to whatever they read.
bullets: Decomposes cancellation into the next layer’s baseline write and the reduction caused by the previous layer’s residual write.

Shows this contraction applies broadly, including to writes from the same layer at other tokens, rather than specifically to the previous layer’s features.
Damping increases during training while baseline writing stays flat; cancellation begins once damping dominates.
Removing the gate activation’s negative side eliminates both damping and cancellation in continued pretraining.

papers.selection_reason: Mechanistic analysis of gated MLP cancellation in transformer language models, relevant to LLM architecture and interpretability.
papers.title: Closed Gates Leak: Decomposing Adjacent-Layer Cancellation in Gated Language Models
papers.tldr: Adjacent-layer cancellation in gated transformers is largely caused by a general damping effect from closed gates, not selective rejection of features proposed by the previous layer.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement fine-tuning has become an effective post-training paradigm for improving the reasoning ability of large language models, but it remains sample-inefficient when the training distribution is mismatched to the model's current capability. In group-relative objectives such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), problems that are too hard often produce uniformly failed rollouts, while problems that are too easy provide little useful advantage signal. In this work, we introduce CLOSEDLOOPGAUSSIAN, a lightweight adaptive curriculum method for efficient reinforcement fine-tuning on ordered reasoning tasks. Instead of following a fixed easy-to-hard schedule, CLOSEDLOOPGAUSSIAN preserves the structure of an Easy-to-Hard Gaussian sampler while dynamically adjusting its pace and spread using periodic probe estimates of per-difficulty accuracy. The controller accelerates training when the model is ahead of a reference curriculum, slows down when the model falls behind, and broadens sampling when earlier difficulties regress. This feedback mechanism keeps training focused on tasks that are challenging but still learnable, without changing the reward function, model architecture, or underlying GRPO optimizer. Experiments on symbolic arithmetic reasoning task show that CLOSEDLOOPGAUSSIAN improves exact-match accuracy over vanilla GRPO and fixed open-loop curricula, with the strongest gains in intermediate-difficulty regimes where group-relative learning signals are most informative. Codes are available at https://github.com/yuvrajpant56/Closed_Loop_Curriculum.
authors: Yuv Raj Pant, Moshiur Rahman Tonmoy, Kaiqun Fu
bullets: Targets sample inefficiency caused by training on tasks that are too easy or too hard for GRPO.
Maintains an easy-to-hard Gaussian sampling structure while adjusting pace and spread from periodic per-difficulty accuracy probes.
Accelerates when learning outpaces a reference curriculum, slows when it lags, and broadens sampling after earlier-difficulty regressions.
On symbolic arithmetic reasoning, improves exact-match accuracy over vanilla GRPO and fixed open-loop curricula, especially at intermediate difficulty.
The evaluation is scoped to ordered reasoning tasks, with experiments reported on a symbolic arithmetic task.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is increasingly adopted in the post-training of large language models. However, a stronger teacher may fail to improve the student. Prior work attributes this to a lack of new knowledge, but what that knowledge is remains unclear. We show that OPD learns not only \textit{how to branch}, i.e., which candidate tokens to consider, but also \textit{where to branch}, i.e., where to keep reasoning paths open. The existing token-overlap metric captures only the former. We introduce the entropy shape, the sequence of next-token entropies, to characterize the latter, and propose the Entropy Shape Correlation (ESC) to measure student-teacher agreement in entropy shape. Tracking ESC throughout training and intervening on a teacher's entropy while preserving its token preferences, we empirically show that \textit{where to branch} causally drives OPD gains, independently of \textit{how to branch}. Finally, we formulate OPD outcome prediction as a teacher selection task and establish an evaluation protocol for it, under which pre-OPD ESC selects the best teacher for both students and outperforms existing predictors. Code is available at https://github.com/maybenotime/opd-esc.
authors: Shiping Yang, Chuanqi Tang, Hossein Hajimirsadeghi, Layla El Asri, Mohammad Amin Shabani, Angel X. Chang
bullets: Identifies two kinds of teacher knowledge: “how to branch” through token preferences and “where to branch” through locations of sustained uncertainty.
Introduces entropy shape—the sequence of next-token entropies—and Entropy Shape Correlation (ESC) to measure student–teacher agreement on branching locations.
Training analyses and entropy interventions suggest that where to branch causally drives OPD gains independently of token preferences.
Frames teacher selection as an OPD outcome-prediction task and proposes an evaluation protocol.
Pre-OPD ESC selects the best teacher for both students and outperforms existing predictors in the reported experiments.

Right: six-benchmark average accuracy at saved checkpoints, with dashed lines marking the two source models. Shaded positions mark mismatches, where the teacher tends to branch (high entropy) while the student does not (low entropy). Right: how to branch. papers.selection_reason: Analyzes on-policy distillation for LLM post-training and introduces entropy-shape agreement as a causal metric, relevant to LLM training.
papers.title: Distilling the Shape of Uncertainty: What On-Policy Distillation Learns and How to Predict It
papers.tldr: On-policy distillation benefits from matching not just which tokens a teacher prefers, but where it preserves uncertainty for continued reasoning, and entropy-shape agreement can predict effective teachers.

papers.abstract: Compositional generalization remains a persistent limitation of transformer language models: even when a model learns to combine known facts correctly in-distribution (ID), the same compositional mechanism may fail when applied to out-of-distribution (OOD) knowledge. We investigate this compositionality gap in a controlled two-hop reasoning setting using a GPT-2-like transformer model trained from scratch. Building on prior work identifying a circuit associated with compositional generalization, we test whether the failure of OOD transfer is related to how atomic knowledge is structurally exposed during training. We modify the training distribution by presenting both ID and OOD atomic facts in a format positionally aligned with the second-hop retrieval step of the learned compositional circuit, without modifying the model architecture or adding OOD compositional supervision. Under this intervention, the model successfully transfers the learned ID compositional behaviour to held-out OOD atomic facts, closing the observed compositionality gap in the controlled setting. Our results provide evidence that the observed compositionality gap is not a fundamental architecture limitation and that it can be overcome through mechanistically informed training distribution design.
bullets: Studies the compositionality gap in controlled two-hop reasoning.
Tests a GPT-2-like transformer trained from scratch without architectural changes or OOD compositional supervision.
Reformats ID and OOD atomic facts to align with the second-hop retrieval step of a learned circuit.
The intervention closes the observed OOD transfer gap in the controlled setting.
Suggests the gap may stem from training-distribution design rather than a fundamental architecture limitation.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Generalization Performance Across Ablation Experiments. Comparison of ID and OOD test accuracy on the two-hop compositional task across three controlled ablations. (a) Removing ID atomic facts from the second-hop-compatible format prevents OOD compositional rule transfer. (b) Restricting the second-hop-compatible format to only a subset of OOD atomic facts results in partial OOD compositional generalization. (c) Removing two-hop compositional training examples prevents the model from learning the compositional task for both ID and OOD atomic facts.

Figure 4: Impact of Dataset Size-Density on OOD Compositional Generalization. (a) When trained on the full but less dense dataset, the model demonstrates delayed convergence in both training and testing metrics. As a result, the generalization effect driven by grokking does not achieve full accuracy within the performed training steps. (b) In contrast, training on a smaller but denser dataset leads to significantly improved generalization speed. The model reaches full accuracy on the OOD test set within the given optimization steps, highlighting the benefits of dataset density in accelerating generalization.

Figure 5: Ablation Analysis Results on the Full-Model for the experiments described in section 3.3. (a): ablation experiment (a) where no in-distribution (ID) atomic facts are provided in the new 2°hop format. Under this condition, the Full Model similarly fails to generalize to OOD examples, resembling the behaviour previously observed in the Smaller Model under the same setting. (b): ablation experiment (b) where out-of-distribution (OOD) facts are partially placed in the second-hop position. In the Full Model experiment, this partial OOD placement appears to completely hinder OOD generalization. This contrasts with the behaviour observed in the Smaller Model, where the same setting resulted in only a partial reduction in final accuracy (fig. 2b).

Figure 1: OOD Compositional Generalization under the Full Position-Aligned Intervention. ID and OOD test accuracy on the two-hop compositional task where both ID and OOD atomic facts are additionally presented in the second-hop-compatible format during training. OOD accuracy rises with delayed generalization in the grokking training regime, eventually reaching complete compositional generalization and closing the compositionality gap in the controlled experimental setting. The dashed gray curve shows OOD test accuracy under the original training distribution, without position-aligned atomic exposure, which remains near zero.

Figure 3: Identity-Bridge Control without Compositional Supervision. Accuracy under identity-bridge supervision after removing all two-hop compositional training examples. While training accuracy remains near perfect, both ID and OOD compositional test accuracy remain at zero, showing that identity-bridge supervision alone does not induce compositional generalization in our setting.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses compositional generalization and implicit reasoning in transformer language models, relevant to LLM reasoning research.
papers.title: Implicit Reasoning in Transformers: Bridging the Compositionality Gap in GPT-2-like Models
papers.tldr: Mechanistically aligning how atomic facts are presented during training enables GPT-2-like transformers to transfer two-hop reasoning from in-distribution to unseen out-of-distribution facts.

papers.abstract: In many settings where LLM post-training is desirable, high-quality answers are recognizable but difficult to score with explicit rewards. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is limited to tasks where an explicit correctness signal is available. Prior adversarial approaches to training reasoning LLMs either complement verifiable rewards with co-trained critics or require reference reasoning traces. We ask whether a co-trained LLM judge can turn reference answers alone into the sole reward for on-policy post-training of reasoning LLMs. We call this method Reinforced Adversarial Learning (RAL). We first validate RAL on three verifiable tasks (integer multiplication, code-based arithmetic-expression synthesis, and SMILES-to-formula translation), using the verifiers only for evaluation. With sufficiently capable judges and enough training, RAL matches direct RLVR. We then apply RAL to scientific abstract generation in two settings. In the first setting, RAL guides the generator to produce abstracts in the scientific domain of the reference abstracts, even though the prompt leaves that domain unspecified. In the second setting, we generate abstracts for U.S. National Institutes of Health grant proposals conditioned on the grant title. Human scientists and an ensemble of LLM judges find our generations harder to distinguish from real abstracts than those of frontier-LLM baselines. These results suggest a path toward post-training reasoning models in scientific and other high-value domains, where increasingly capable judges infer hard-to-specify reward functions from example answers.
authors: Albert Bou, Javier Valdes-Aleman, Jon M. Laurent, Samuel G. Rodriques, Andrew D. White, Michaela Hinks, Siddharth Narayanan
bullets: Addresses settings where good answers are available but explicit reward functions are difficult to specify.
Trains a generator with rewards from an adversarially co-trained LLM judge, without requiring reference reasoning traces.
On three verifiable tasks, RAL matches direct RLVR when judges are sufficiently capable and training is adequate.
For scientific abstract generation, RAL captures reference domains and produces NIH grant abstracts judged more human-like than frontier-LLM baselines.
The approach depends on judge capability and training duration, and its strongest evidence is reported for the evaluated tasks and domains.

papers.abstract: Clinical practice guidelines encode evidence-based recommendations as conditional decision flows, which makes them a natural source of process supervision for training reasoning models. Two properties of clinical reasoning make this supervision difficult to use. A decision flow consistent with a guideline does not by itself determine the correct answer for a given patient, which we call the path--answer gap, and several valid decision flows can support the same clinical decision, which we call path multiplicity. Current training approaches address parts of this problem. Answer rewards supervise the final decision, and process rewards computed against a reference flow supervise one valid decision flow per case. Supervised fine-tuning on annotated flows teaches guideline-consistent reasoning but constrains the model to one trajectory per case and can reduce answer accuracy. We introduce GUIDER, a method that jointly optimizes a decision flow controller and a reasoning policy. The controller learns to generate plausible decision flows from guideline-derived supervision, and the policy learns to generate a decision flow and a final answer for each patient case. GUIDER computes the process reward for the policy over several controller-generated flows, which accounts for path multiplicity, and gates this reward on answer correctness, which addresses the path--answer gap. Joint training allows the process supervision to evolve with the policy. On MedGUIDE, GUIDER with Qwen3-14B achieves 82.5 weighted accuracy and 73.5 guideline adherence, 3.3 and 3.1 points above the strongest clinical reinforcement learning baseline. With Qwen3-14B and Gemma4-12B backbones, GUIDER also improves over CRPO, MRPO, and FaithMed on the out-of-domain benchmarks AMEGA-LLM, RealMedQA, and CancerGUIDE.
bullets: Clinical guidelines provide process supervision, but valid paths may not uniquely determine answers and multiple paths may support the same decision.
GUIDER jointly trains a decision-flow controller and reasoning policy.

On MedGUIDE with Qwen3-14B, it achieves 82.5 weighted accuracy and 73.5 guideline adherence, outperforming the strongest reported clinical RL baseline by 3.3 and 3.1 points.
The method also improves over several baselines on the out-of-domain AMEGA-LLM, RealMedQA, and CancerGUIDE benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Self-distillation offers a way to improve reasoning models when a suitable external teacher is unavailable. However, common approaches rely on privileged information to construct a stronger self-teacher, limiting their use when only unlabeled prompts are available. In this paper, we introduce Weakening-Induced On-Policy Self-Distillation (WISD), which instead constructs a weaker counterpart of the original model and uses the contrast between the two as a training signal without requiring privileged information. We explore two ways to construct the weaker model: low-bit quantization and magnitude pruning. We evaluate WISD across diverse architectures and scales on mathematical and coding reasoning tasks. Across these benchmarks, quantization and pruning improve average accuracy over the original models by 4.0 and 5.5 percentage points, respectively, achieving state-of-the-art performance even without privileged information. Notably, pruning raises Qwen3.5-4B's accuracy from 57.7% to 70.5% on HMMT 2025 and from 39.1% to 56.7% on LiveCodeBench v6. Quantization raises Qwen3.6-35B-A3B's accuracy from 68.5% to 74.6% and from 61.8% to 69.5% on the same benchmarks, respectively. These results establish WISD as a novel and effective self-distillation framework for large reasoning models.
authors: Yecheng Wu, Song Han, Han Cai
bullets: Addresses self-distillation when only unlabeled prompts are available and no stronger teacher can be constructed.
Creates weaker counterparts via low-bit quantization or magnitude pruning, then uses their contrast with the original model as the training signal.
Evaluated across multiple architectures and scales on mathematical and coding reasoning tasks.
Quantization and pruning improve average accuracy by 4.0 and 5.5 percentage points, respectively, and achieve state-of-the-art performance in the reported evaluations.
Reported gains include Qwen3.5-4B improving from 57.7% to 70.5% on HMMT 2025 with pruning, and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B improving from 68.5% to 74.6% with quantization.

papers.abstract: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD), which aligns a student model's token-level distribution with that of its self-teacher prompted by privileged context, has emerged as a promising direction to mitigate reward sparsity in sequence-level post-training paradigms. However, OPSD often fails to achieve continuous performance gains during training. In this paper, we find that the model's limited self-teaching capability underlies this phenomenon by generating unreliable guidance on certain samples. To address this problem, we propose Teacher-Evolution Self-Distillation (TESD), which enables the self-teacher to generate rollouts and receive environmental feedback based on task correctness and context independence. First, using these rewards as training objectives, we perform teacher-oriented optimization to continuously enhance the model's self-teaching capability during distillation. Second, by estimating teacher guidance reliability from these rewards, we apply adaptive student-oriented optimization to down-weight samples with unreliable guidance. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets and model scales show that TESD consistently outperforms representative token-level and sequence-level methods, highlighting the necessity of improving supervision quality in OPSD.
authors: Shufan Shen, Zhongni Hou, Chao Bi, Yufei Zhang, Guojun Yin, Shuhui Wang
bullets: OPSD can stagnate because its self-teacher produces unreliable guidance for some samples.
TESD trains the self-teacher with environmental feedback on task correctness and context independence.
It estimates guidance reliability and adaptively down-weights samples with weak supervision.
Experiments across multiple datasets and model scales show consistent gains over representative token- and sequence-level methods.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overall framework of TESD. Given an input query, the student first generates rollouts, which provide the privileged context for the self-teacher. Then, TESD optimizes the student and the self-teacher, respectively. For the self-teacher, it interacts with the environment and learns from the obtained rewards of correctness and independence. For the student, it is supervised by the logits of the self-teacher. The loss value is adaptively weighted by the teacher’s mean reward of the corresponding input query, which estimates the quality of teacher guidance.

papers.abstract: Linear attention and state space models (SSMs) offer efficient alternatives to softmax attention by maintaining a fixed-size recurrent state, but this design requires careful management to preserve useful historical associations and limit interference. The delta rule helps reduce interference through correction of the value associated with each key, but it does not explicitly account for how related value features are distributed across the state. We observe that a state $\boldsymbol{S}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_k\times d_v}$ can be viewed as a bank of $d_k$ addresses storing $d_v$-dimensional values. While a key-side read $\boldsymbol{S}^\top\boldsymbol{k}$ retrieves the value associated with $\boldsymbol{k}$, a value-side read $\boldsymbol{S}\boldsymbol{e}$ aggregates addresses whose stored value features match the selector $\boldsymbol{e}$. Based on this observation, we propose Dual DeltaNet (DDN), which extends Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) with a two-sided delta rule. The key-side delta rule reads with the current key to correct its associated value, while the complementary value-side delta rule reads with selected features of the current value to reorganize the addresses it occupies. We derive a chunkwise parallel training algorithm and a rank-2 recurrence that increases arithmetic intensity during inference. Compared with KDA, GDN-2, and Mamba-3, DDN achieves the strongest overall performance across language modeling, zero-shot downstream tasks, and retrieval, while incurring modest training and inference overhead relative to KDA. authors: Yixiao Qian, Yaxin Zhang, Song Chen, Jiaxu Liu, Shengze Cai, Chao Xu

papers.abstract: Why do multilingual language models generalize across languages even without shared vocabulary? The Platonic Representation Hypothesis posits that models trained on different data, objectives, and modalities converge toward a shared statistical model of reality. Extending this intuition to representations inside a single multilingual model, we propose the Relational Identifiability Hypothesis: relations in a shared world can promote entity alignment by ruling out alternative cross-lingual correspondences, making corresponding entities more likely to become directly readable without an additional transformation. We test this hypothesis in a controlled bilingual Transformer whose two token-disjoint languages describe the same modular-arithmetic world. We find that the languages can develop a shared answer subspace without aligning corresponding numbers. Cross-lingual alignment emerges selectively when the available relations constrain number correspondences: subtraction makes zero task-level identifiable, inducing selective alignment, while an order-sensitive operation produces broad alignment across numbers. These patterns predict success in zero-shot cross-lingual transfer. Together, our results show that relational structure in a shared world can promote entity alignment and enable transfer.
bullets: A controlled bilingual Transformer models two token-disjoint languages describing the same modular-arithmetic world.
The languages can share an answer subspace without directly aligning corresponding numbers.
Relations constrain possible cross-lingual correspondences: subtraction selectively aligns zero, while an order-sensitive operation broadly aligns numbers.
The resulting alignment patterns predict successful zero-shot cross-lingual transfer.
The study is limited to a controlled synthetic arithmetic setting.

papers.abstract: Complex Temporal Knowledge Graph Question Answering (TKGQA) involves more than retrieving facts: the timestamp or validity interval of one fact can constrain the search for another, while multiple intervals may jointly determine the answer. Existing single-agent TKGQA methods typically investigate these facts within a single reasoning context, where evidence from different event histories can become interleaved and distractors can misdirect subsequent retrieval. Distributing investigations across agents can separate event-specific evidence into distinct contexts, but effective collaboration must still be learned because question decomposition, subtask investigation, and evidence synthesis are interdependent. To address these limitations, we propose \textbf{Co}-Evolving \textbf{S}elf-Play \textbf{T}imeline \textbf{A}gents (CoSTA), which organizes facts into navigable timelines, delegates investigations to workers, and uses a coordinator to synthesize their original timestamped observations. CoSTA initializes a shared policy through role-conditioned distillation and jointly optimizes both roles through co-evolving self-play with final-answer rewards. Across three benchmarks, CoSTA achieves state-of-the-art overall performance, with particularly strong gains on complex multi-fact questions, while its compact variants outperform the evaluated closed-source LLM agents.

Achieves state-of-the-art overall results across three benchmarks, especially on complex multi-fact questions; compact variants outperform evaluated closed-source LLM agents.

papers.abstract: Monitoring a model's chain of thought (CoT) is useful for safety only if the final answer depends on the written steps. Prior measurements use natural tasks where true reasoning is unknown. We measure it against an exact ground truth on a synthetic box-swap task where every intermediate state is known. We replace one step inside a model's own chain with a wrong but valid state and check whether the answer follows the edit. We evaluate 25 open-weight models--Qwen3 (0.6B-14B, base and post-trained), Gemma 3 (1B-12B), Llama 3 (1B-8B), and 8 OLMo 2 checkpoints--on 7,200 items each. We find five results: (1) Reliance rises with size and saturates. In Qwen3, answer reliance rises from 16-18% at 0.6B to 97-100% at 14B; a logistic in log N fits well (R^2 = 0.89), and Gemma 3 and Llama 3 follow this trend. (2) Capability is the main driver. Across all models, reliance and step accuracy correlate at r = 0.99; equally capable models are equally reliant, regardless of family. (3) Size still matters at matched correctness. On problems solved correctly before the edit, reliance increases with size among capable models (rho = 0.80, p = 0.002). (4) Post-training does not change reliance. Base and post-trained Qwen3 differ by at most 0.03 from 4B upward; a large gap at 1.7B matches a large capability gap. (5) No model up to 14B solves the task internally. Without written steps, every capable model is at chance once a problem has four or more swaps. OLMo 2 checkpoints never become capable, making the training-token axis a limitation. On tasks requiring step-by-step computation, scale makes the chain of thought more load-bearing, supporting CoT monitoring in this regime.

Base and post-trained Qwen3 models show nearly identical reliance from 4B parameters upward.

No tested model internally solves sufficiently complex tasks without written steps; the findings are limited to this synthetic step-by-step setting and do not cover models that remain incapable, such as OLMo 2 checkpoints.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates scaling-law behavior of chain-of-thought reliance across modern LLM families, relevant to LLM reasoning and safety.
papers.title: Does Chain-of-Thought Reliance Follow a Scaling Law?Larger Models Follow Their Steps More, Independent of Post-Training
papers.tldr: On a synthetic box-swap task, larger and more capable models rely increasingly on their written chain of thought, while post-training has little independent effect.

papers.abstract: Repeating transformer layers can improve language model performance without adding parameters. However, the added computational depth increases both forward and backward computation costs during training. Training such models requires choosing a backward window that controls how many final layer repetitions retain gradients during backpropagation. Longer windows improve per-token learning efficiency but increase per-update cost, while shorter windows reduce per-update cost but sacrifice per-token efficiency. Understanding which window performs better requires examining different training budgets. Prior work compares backward windows across computational budgets. When training budgets increase, it remains unclear whether the same window continues to perform best. We measure how the relative performance of two windows shifts as training budgets grow. Our method isolates per-token efficiency by training both windows on identical data, and compares complete training recipes at approximately equal training time at each budget. Results show that shorter windows lose much of their advantage as budgets grow. Controlled experiments show that both benefits decrease at larger budgets, with a greater decline in the benefit of extended training. Backward window comparisons depend on the available budget, and the preferred window among the tested candidates can change as the budget grows.
bullets: Repeating transformer layers improves performance without increasing parameter count but raises training computation costs.
The backward window controls how many final layer repetitions receive gradients, trading per-token efficiency against per-update cost.
The study compares two windows under matched data and approximately equal training time across increasing budgets.
Both windows’ benefits decline at larger budgets, especially the benefit of extended training.
The preferred window can change as the training budget grows.

papers.title: Deeper Backpropagation or More Updates? Training Looped Language Models Across Budgets

papers.abstract: LLM-guided evolutionary search iteratively selects existing programs, uses LLMs as mutation operators to generate a new program, and evaluates it to guide subsequent search. To preserve diversity and reduce the risk of premature convergence, it often adopts the island model, in which groups of programs, called islands, evolve separately. However, this structure alone does not guarantee distinct search directions, as islands may start from similar programs or converge toward similar solutions during evolution. This suggests that diversity must be considered throughout the search process, from initializing islands with distinct programs to developing island trajectories and sharing discoveries across islands. To this end, we propose HoliDivEvolve , a holistic approach to establishing and effectively utilizing island diversity throughout evolutionary search. Specifically, we introduce diverse initialization to establish different initial programs, trajectory adaptive island selection to allocate computation based on current score, recent growth, and the remaining search budget, and growth adaptive migration to share alternative ideas across islands. Experiments across diverse benchmarks show that HoliDivEvolve achieves competitive performance on most evaluated tasks. We further conduct controlled analyses to examine how our design choices affect search behavior and final performance.
authors: Seockbean Song, Youngsik Yoon, Sungjae Lee, Siwei Wang, Wei Chen, Jungseul Ok
bullets: Island models alone may fail to maintain distinct search directions because islands can begin similarly or converge toward similar solutions.

Trajectory-adaptive island selection allocates computation using current score, recent growth, and remaining search budget.
Growth-adaptive migration shares alternative discoveries across islands.
Experiments across diverse benchmarks show competitive performance on most evaluated tasks, with controlled analyses of design choices.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student using teacher predictions on student-generated responses. Some methods insert teacher-written segments, or bridges, but disagree on how to train on those tokens. We compare no loss, forward KL and reverse KL on identical trajectories using Qwen3-1.7B as student and Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 as teacher. We separate gradients by which model wrote each token. Under our short training runs and BF16 inference, pre-specified tests detected no added accuracy benefit from teacher text as context or as a training target. A one-paragraph bridge after the student's first paragraph is only 2.7% of the tokens and contributes a small gradient nearly orthogonal to the student-token gradient. In this main comparison, the three loss treatments gave similar gradient directions and were statistically equivalent in accuracy within a +/-5 percentage-point margin. An exploratory pilot placing the bridge where failed responses disagreed most with the teacher suggested a benefit from teacher-token loss. A pre-specified replication did not confirm this, and fourfold weighting showed no significant accuracy benefit. Two limitations bound these findings. Among the tested amounts of training on fixed responses, gains peaked after four updates before the student increasingly failed to stop generating. None of the tested online training variants met the criteria for stable stopping and improved accuracy. Our evaluations used BF16 inference, which rounds away most of the small weight changes. When evaluated in exact FP32, the tested replication models frequently reached the response-length limit. Our accuracy findings therefore concern BF16 inference; they do not establish that teacher-token supervision is generally unnecessary.

papers.title: How Much Do Teacher Bridges Matter in Interleaved On-Policy Distillation?
papers.tldr: In these short, BF16 on-policy distillation runs, teacher-written bridge tokens did not reliably improve accuracy, though the findings are limited and do not show teacher supervision is generally unnecessary.

papers.abstract: Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) is now a common ingredient in language-model pre-training, as it improves downstream performance and enables faster inference through speculative decoding. We identify a flaw in standard MTP training, in which a residual component of the MTP gradient interferes with both next-token and multi-token learning, increasingly so with scale. Specifically, the MTP cross-entropy gradient can be decomposed exactly into a KL self-distillation term that pulls each MTP head toward the model's own next-token prediction (NTP) distribution and improves speculative decoding, and a residual that has a low signal-to-noise ratio and buries the useful KL signal. We introduce the KL gradient-recovery trick: when two distributions share a linear output head, the gradient of their KL divergence can be recovered exactly by combining their cross-entropy gradients through straight-through gradient routing. Unlike minimizing the KL directly, this trick requires no vocabulary-sized logit matrices and is compatible with standard fused cross-entropy kernels. This enables Soft Multi-Token Prediction (Soft-MTP), a one-line code change to MTP that removes the noisy residual and backpropagates only the KL self-distillation signal by reusing the existing NTP and MTP cross-entropy computations. Soft-MTP supports both DeepSeek- and Meta-style MTP, adds no parameters, and incurs no measurable overhead. From 167M to 1.2B parameters, Soft-MTP improves over standard MTP with lower NTP perplexity, faster speculative decoding and higher zero-shot accuracy at every scale, lower MTP perplexity from 689M onward, and stronger math and code reasoning after fine-tuning at 1.2B. Soft-MTP also matches, if not exceeds, direct KL divergence minimization on most metrics. Soft-MTP is, in effect, a free lunch for MTP optimization. Our code can be found at https://github.com/JaydenTeoh/Soft-MTP.
bullets: Standard MTP gradients contain a noisy residual that increasingly interferes with next-token and multi-token learning as models scale.
The authors decompose the gradient into a useful KL self-distillation component and a low-signal residual.
A gradient-recovery trick extracts the KL signal using existing cross-entropy computations and fused kernels, avoiding vocabulary-sized logit matrices.
Soft-MTP is a one-line modification compatible with DeepSeek- and Meta-style MTP, with no added parameters or measurable overhead.
Across 167M–1.2B parameters, it improves perplexity, speculative decoding speed, zero-shot accuracy, and—at 1.2B—math and code reasoning after fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Language-model answers are often treated as a visible record of the internal decision that produced them. We test this assumption in conflicting-context question answering, where two supplied documents support incompatible answers. A model can process the disagreement and still return a one-sided answer, even under prompts that ask it to disclose conflict. In Qwen 0.8B, hidden source commitment is captured by a residual source-choice direction whose sign tracks which document the answer uses. Sparse middle-layer MLP writers feed the same coordinate, and steering the coordinate changes the chosen source. A transfer run on Gemma 3 1B preserves the source-choice readout and sparse-write bridge under LLM-audited labels. Conflict disclosure follows a different pattern, appearing weaker, later-layer, and only partially steerable. These results support a practical monitoring strategy for retrieval systems that detects silent source commitment with residual readouts and pairs conflict-surfacing prompts with disclosure steering when the model has selected a side under disagreement.
authors: Samuel Dawit Assefa, Jae Won Cho
bullets: In conflicting-context QA, models may choose one document without explicitly disclosing the disagreement.
A residual source-choice direction tracks which source the answer follows in Qwen 0.8B.
Sparse middle-layer MLPs write to this direction, and steering it changes source selection.
The readout and sparse-write mechanism transfer to Gemma 3 1B under LLM-audited labels.
Conflict disclosure is weaker, later-layer, and only partly steerable, motivating combined monitoring and prompting strategies.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates 'hidden source commitment' in LLMs during conflicting-context question answering, proposing methods to detect and steer model behavior based on internal decision directions.
papers.title: Hidden Commitment: When Language Models Silently Pick a Side and How Steering Can Surface It
papers.tldr: Language models can silently commit to one conflicting source, but residual-stream readouts and steering can reveal and influence that hidden choice.

papers.abstract: Test-time training (TTT) layers replace the linear fast-weight memory of modern recurrent architectures with a small neural network trained online by gradient descent. This nonlinear memory is more expressive than the linear memories of Gated DeltaNet and Mamba-2, but is difficult to parallelize: existing implementations such as TTT-MLP rely on sequential, block-wise weight updates that run several times slower than chunkwise-parallel linear recurrences. Moreover, their block-wise execution only approximates the token-by-token online recurrence, whereas linear recurrences admit an exact chunkwise-parallel evaluation. We introduce ParaTTT (PTTT), an algorithm for parallelizing arbitrarily deep nonlinear memories by iteratively refining estimates of the inner-loop gradient trajectory. Starting from a guess of the hidden-layer gradients, each refinement consists of three chunkwise-parallel passes: a forward pass that evaluates the resulting feature trajectory, an exact gated-delta-rule pass that computes the readout trajectory and its feature gradients, and a backward pass that propagates these gradients into a new estimate. The exact online gradient descent recurrence is a fixed point of the iteration, while decoding requires no refinement iterations. We prove geometric convergence for a two-layer variant under sufficient contraction conditions. In practice, two iterations suffice. With two refinement steps at 4K context, PTTT evaluates the inner-loop trajectory $32\times$ faster than TTT-MLP with the block approximation at matched error, while the full 340M model trains $4.9\times$ faster. Models trained at 340M and 1.3B parameters match or exceed Gated DeltaNet and Mamba-2 and remain competitive with same-size Transformers on language-modeling perplexity and zero-shot accuracy, with better recall than the linear recurrences.
authors: Noel Loo, Neehal Tumma, T. Konstantin Rusch, Mathias Lechner, Alexander Amini, Daniela Rus
bullets: TTT layers use more expressive nonlinear memories than linear recurrent alternatives but are difficult and slow to parallelize.
ParaTTT iteratively refines hidden-layer gradient trajectories using three chunkwise-parallel passes: forward, gated-delta readout/gradient computation, and backward propagation.
The exact online gradient-descent recurrence is a fixed point of the refinement process; decoding requires no refinement iterations.
Two refinement steps are typically sufficient; at 4K context, inner-loop evaluation is 32× faster than block-approximated TTT-MLP at matched error, while the full 340M model trains 4.9× faster.
At 340M and 1.3B parameters, models match or exceed Gated DeltaNet and Mamba-2, remain competitive with similarly sized Transformers, and show better recall than linear recurrences.

figures.caption: Figure 2: One iteration of ParaTTT; the recurrences are evaluated in chunkwise-parallel form over all T tokens. (1) A parallel forward pass evaluates the hidden layers from the current estimate of their pre-activation gradients. (3) A parallel backward pass propagates it through the hidden layers using shifted reads of the transposed recurrences (see Step 3 in Section 3.2 for details) and updates the estimate. (c) ParaTTT refines the full gradient trajectory using three chunkwise-parallel passes per round. papers.selection_reason: Introduces ParaTTT, a method to parallelize Test-Time Training (TTT) layers, which is highly relevant to online adaptation and efficient LLM training.
papers.title: ParaTTT: Parallelizing Test-Time Training Layers with Deep Memories
papers.tldr: ParaTTT makes nonlinear test-time training memories efficiently parallelizable, achieving large speedups while preserving accurate online behavior and strong language-modeling performance.

papers.abstract: Existing code reveals past implementation decisions but rarely explains the reasoning behind them. When coding agents implement new features or modify existing functionality, past decisions may conflict with new task instructions. This raises a fundamental question for agentic software evolution: when multiple implementations satisfy the same functional requirements, how do coding agents decide whether to follow existing code or new task instructions? We investigate this question through bidirectional, controlled experiments in purpose-built repositories, followed by validation in real-world open-source repositories. Our approach isolates three competing sources of guidance: (1) agents' default preferences, (2) repository precedents, and (3) explicit task instructions. We conduct 5,625 trials across four coding agents and six implementation pairs, with validation in four open-source repositories spanning three programming languages. We find that agents share the same default implementation choices, yet overwhelmingly follow repository precedent when it conflicts with those defaults (359/360 trials). Crucially, not all precedents carry equal influence: three supporting local files yield 96% adoption, compared with only 4% for sibling-resource files, and changing file placement alone can shift adoption from 0% to 100% at a fixed example count. When new task intent conflicts with existing code, written priority rules achieve substantially higher success than code examples alone (59/60 versus 38/60 joint successes for two agents on two implementation pairs). The effectiveness of explicit rules also extends to open-source repositories, where a harness-loaded rule raises joint success from 0/120 to 117/120. These findings motivate design-decision traceability that preserves not only implementation choices but also the rationale and priorities that should guide future changes.
authors: Haichao Zhu, Geyang Xu, Zhaorui Yang, Jiyuan Wang, Qian Zhang
bullets: The study separates three influences on agent decisions: default preferences, repository precedents, and explicit task instructions.
Across 5,625 controlled trials, agents followed conflicting repository precedents in 359 of 360 cases, though influence depended strongly on precedent location.
Three supporting local files drove 96% adoption, while sibling-resource files drove only 4%; changing file placement alone shifted adoption from 0% to 100%.
Written priority rules outperformed code examples for resolving conflicts and also improved outcomes in four real-world open-source repositories.
The findings support preserving the rationale and priority of design decisions, not just their resulting code.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Coding agents that extend a repository are pulled between the implementation already in the code and the intent of the new task. In controlled experiments with four agents and six implementation pairs, existing code wins by default, and a written rule is what reliably changes course.

Figure 3: Research approach. Each task admits two functionally acceptable implementations (baseline in blue, alternative in orange). Within the controlled study, Stage 1 measures default choices without relevant examples, Stage 2 varies repository precedents in local and sibling-resource files (including which file holds the example at a fixed count), and Stage 3 adds task guidance that contradicts existing code. papers.selection_reason: Investigates how coding agents balance repository precedents with new task instructions when evolving existing code.
papers.title: Precedent or Intent? What Coding Agents Follow When Evolving Existing Code
papers.tldr: Coding agents usually follow existing repository patterns over their default choices, but explicit priority rules can reliably steer them toward new task intent when precedents conflict.

papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used for financial guidance, yet little is known about whether their advice changes across social identities in Global South contexts. We introduce the Indian Financial Automated Advice Bias (IFAAB) benchmark, a counterfactual audit dataset of 31,734 GPT-4o-generated financial-advice responses for synthetic Indian personas varying by gender, caste, education, employment, residence, age, and district. Holding the underlying request fixed, we evaluate disparities in LLM-implied wealth, income, savings, projected gains, textual similarity, advice topics, and qualitative bias judgments. In the gender-only audit, male-labelled profiles receive 60.1\% higher initial total resources and 46.8\% higher post-advice total resources than comparable female-labelled profiles; in the caste-augmented audit, the post-advice total-resource gap remains 49.4\%. Adding district information reduces the aggregate post-advice total-resource gender gap to 7.9\%, revealing strong geographic conditioning. Standalone caste comparisons also show systematic stratification: relative to General-category profiles, OBC, SC, and ST profiles receive significantly lower post-advice total resources, respectively. Textual audits show low semantic similarity between paired gendered responses, with an average TF--IDF cosine similarity score of 0.44. Qualitative analysis shows that women are more often steered toward cautious saving, community support, and basic financial literacy, while men receive more growth-oriented advice involving investment, entrepreneurship, and asset accumulation. IFAAB provides a reusable benchmark for evaluating fairness, suitability, and consumer-protection risks in LLM-mediated financial advice, and highlights the need for locally grounded, intersectional evaluation of AI systems in high-stakes economic domains.
bullets: Introduces a benchmark of 31,734 financial-advice responses across personas varying in gender, caste, education, employment, residence, age, and district.
Holding requests fixed, audits implied wealth, income, savings, projected gains, response similarity, advice topics, and qualitative bias.
Male-labelled profiles receive higher implied resources than comparable female-labelled profiles; caste-linked disparities also persist.
District information substantially reduces the aggregate gender resource gap, indicating strong geographic conditioning.
Women are more often directed toward cautious saving and basic literacy, while men receive growth-oriented investment, entrepreneurship, and asset-accumulation advice.
