papers.abstract: Coding agents are typically provided end-to-end behavioral specifications that the code they produce should satisfy, such as tests and input--output examples. How many such specifications must a developer provide, and which ones, for the agent to produce the developer's intended program? We argue that this cannot be determined a priori, for it depends on the structure of the implementation, which is left to the agent to decide. An agent first commits to a structure---a decomposition into data types, modules, and functions---which fixes a class of candidate programs; behavioral specifications then select a program within that class. A set of tests that suffices for one structure may leave another badly underdetermined, requiring different edge cases or exponentially more examples. Since the structure is chosen by the agent, developers cannot ensure their specification is complete without reverse-engineering it from thousands of lines of generated code. To resolve this, we introduce Skeleton Coding, in which developers jointly specify the structure---in high-level, code-like format---alongside behavioral specifications. Theoretically, we model AI-assisted coding as a control problem, and show that skeletons can reduce exponentially the number of tests developers must supply to steer an agent toward an acceptable program. Empirically, across four models and three benchmarks, the best-performing skeleton specifications reduce mean test error by 48.4% relative to the best end-to-end behavioral specifications. Even when the agent can query a complete reference implementation, adding a skeleton reduces mean test error relatively by up to 27.0%. Skeletons also narrow the average gap between small and large models by about 52.4% while lowering implementation cost by 15--26x, and reduce code erosion by 24.7% on average.
authors: Aditya Golatkar, Alessandro Achille, Renos Zabounidis, Vlad Sobal, Yangruibo Ding, Baishakhi Ray, Jonathan Buck, Guy Van den Broeck, Maryam Fazel, Pietro Perona, Wei Xia, Stefano Soatto
bullets: Behavioral tests alone may be insufficient because their effectiveness depends on the implementation structure chosen by the agent.
Skeletons specify decompositions into data types, modules, and functions, narrowing the candidate-program space before behavioral tests select details.
A control-theoretic analysis shows skeletons can reduce the number of required tests exponentially in some cases.
Across four models and three benchmarks, skeletons reduced mean test error by 48.4% versus the best end-to-end behavioral specifications.
Skeletons also reduced implementation cost, narrowed the small/large-model performance gap, and mitigated code erosion; scope is limited to the evaluated models and benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 6: (Left) More architecture detail does not match skeletons. Adding architecture sections to the markdown file slightly raises mean pass rate, but the resulting pass rate remains below that achieved with skeleton-based specifications. (Right) Accuracy improvement with additional behavioral observations. On ProgramBench, we show the average test pass rate increases as we increase the number of observations provided to the model (unlimited lets the agent decide), but in all cases end-to-end behavioral specifications perform worse than skeletons with just 20 queries.

Figure 1: Behavioral specifications do not pinpoint correct programs. (Left) We ask a coding agent to implement a code base from ProgramBench given its documentation and a fraction of its test suite. We then measure error rate across the hidden suite. On average, no number of tests provided results in a program that passes all hidden tests. (Middle) Even providing a full behavioral specification is not enough: We measure the pass rate with access to an oracle providing the full and exact input-output behavior. Even so, adding a skeleton with local contracts increases the pass rate averaged across models by 10.9% relative to the same setup without a skeleton on ProgramBench. (Right) A skeleton specifying the local contract for slicing a strided view.

Figure 2: Value of different types of specifications. We generate specifications of different kinds and measure the error rate of a coding agent using them. No matter the format, behavioral specifications that describe only end-to-end behavior underperform specifications that describe the developer’s intended structure. Of the structural specifications, code-like specifications that describe function signatures and invariants outperform design files in natural language. Adding overly detailed specifications decreases the accuracy of smaller models.

Figure 7: Structural specifications produce less eroded code than behavioral specifications: Across all benchmarks and models, structural specifications reduce code erosion by up to 24.7%, compared to the task-only prompt. Meanwhile, behavioral specifications increase it. Verbosity varies little across conditions.

Figure 5: Skeletons bridge the gap between large and small models: Skeleton specifications significantly improve performance of smaller models, leading to accuracy similar to that of larger models at a lower cost. In particular, the entire cost–performance Pareto frontier (dashed) is formed mostly by small models with structural specifications.

Figure 8: Skeletons reduce query effort and cost during iterative repair: For iterative repair tasks, using skeletons reduces the total cost of implementation, and also the number of user queries. We model user queries with the number of calls to the program binary. Additionally, final code has lower erosion and higher maintainability.

Figure 3: Skeletons and tests shrink the set of programs the agent considers: (a) Without a skeleton, the agent’s prior spreads over all programs. (b) Fixing a skeleton restricts the agent to programs with that skeleton. (c) Each set of end-to-end tests further keeps only the programs that agree with the reference on the tested inputs.
Figure 4: A strong skeleton makes better use of tests. Visualization of how tests affect the two skeletons of Theorem 2.1.

Figure 9: Skeleton coverage vs. pass rates: (Left, Middle) We select a subset of the functions to add to the skeleton based on their complexity. Providing additional coverage increases pass-rate. (Right) Adding per-folder descriptions to a directory sketch improves the pass rates.
Figure 10: Value of different types of skeletons: Providing skeletons improves the pass-rates on ProgramBench despite query access to the oracle executable.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes 'Skeleton Coding' to improve coding agent performance by providing structural specifications alongside behavioral ones.
papers.title: Skeleton Coding: Program Structure as a Specification for Agents
papers.tldr: Skeleton Coding lets developers specify a program’s high-level structure alongside tests, substantially improving coding-agent reliability and reducing specification effort.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) treat all context tokens uniformly, lacking explicit separation between executable instructions and passive data. This leads to prompt injection vulnerabilities, ambiguous instruction binding, and unreliable execution control. We present a post-training methodology using LLMON (LLM Object Notation), a framework that enables separating instructions from data and requires explicit identifier-based execution. We construct a large-scale structured training corpus of 4.6B tokens spanning general, RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation), and tool-calling data, augmented with distractor-infused variants in which competing instructions and irrelevant data segments are present in context but not referenced. Post-training two Granite-4.1 base models (3B and 8B) through supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning, we show that LLMON-structured supervision reduces attack success rates on indirect prompt-injection benchmarks from 53-100% to 0.02-5.6% while preserving general capabilities. We further introduce attention-based interpretability metrics that diagnose failure modes at individual transformer layers for structured inputs, revealing how our approach reshapes internal attention patterns. Our results demonstrate that explicit execution semantics can be taught through standard post-training without architectural modification.
authors: Basel Shbita, Michael Hind, Chad DeLuca, Nathan Fulton, Shubhi Asthana, Farhan Ahmed, Anisa Halimi, Yada Zhu, Mauro Martino, David Cox, Dan Gutfreund
bullets: Addresses prompt injection, ambiguous instruction binding, and unreliable execution control caused by treating all context tokens uniformly.
Uses LLM Object Notation (LLMON) with identifier-based execution and structured training data covering general, RAG, tool-calling, and distractor-infused contexts.
Post-trains 3B and 8B Granite-4.1 models using supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning.
Reduces attack success on indirect prompt-injection benchmarks from 53–100% to 0.02–5.6% while preserving general capabilities.
Introduces attention-based interpretability metrics to analyze layer-level failure modes and changes in attention patterns.

papers.title: Post-Training Large Language Models with LLMON
papers.tldr: LLMON post-training teaches LLMs to distinguish instructions from data and execute only explicitly referenced instructions, sharply reducing indirect prompt-injection success without changing model architecture.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) appear to represent and reason about a large range of phenomena. In particular, recent studies have examined whether LLMs can accurately reason about causation. One of the most commonly used benchmarks for evaluating formal causal reasoning in LLMs is CLadder, a framework for procedural generation of benchmark data sets that was released in 2023. Experiments with CLadder appear to indicate that LLMs can perform formal causal reasoning in a large percentage of generated examples. In this paper, we examine what can be reliably inferred when LLMs perform well on test sets produced by CLadder. We identify several examples of superficial and highly predictive patterns that the CLadder generator embeds in data sets it generates. We find that even simple models such as random forests perform well on CLadder-generated data sets after training on a sample of generated data. We also find that the performance of many commercial LLMs on CLadder test sets is extremely brittle and that removing large sections of the text that are critical for formal causal reasoning has almost no effect on performance. Given these results, the most likely hypothesis for the strong performance of state-of-the-art LLMs on CLadder is that they are exploiting superficial patterns learned from exposure to training data from the generator. Any inference that LLMs are exhibiting more complex causal reasoning must rule out this hypothesis.
authors: Justin Clarke, Isha Karn, Patrick Murray, KJ Hill, David Jensen
bullets: CLadder is a widely used benchmark for formal causal reasoning in LLMs, but its procedural generation introduces highly predictive superficial patterns.
Simple random forests perform well on CLadder data after training on generated examples.
Many commercial LLMs show brittle performance, remaining largely unchanged when text critical to causal reasoning is removed.
The findings suggest that claims of advanced causal reasoning must rule out memorization or exploitation of generator artifacts.

papers.abstract: We introduce Nemotron 3.5 Super and Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, open and efficient Mixture-of-Experts Hybrid Mamba-Transformer models designed for reasoning, long-context understanding, and agentic workloads. Super is a 120B-parameter, 12B-active multimodal model, while Lightning is a smaller 30B-parameter, 3B-active text model; both designed for efficient deployment. Both models combine large-scale distillation, long-context training, and native speculative decoding, while Super further incorporates Indic continued pretraining and agentic software-engineering mid-training. We develop a comprehensive post-training pipeline spanning supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning (RLVR and RLHF), complemented in Super by specialized teacher training and multi- teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). This transforms Super from a text-only base model into a multimodal agent capable of reasoning over text, images, video, and interactive tool environments. We further explore test-time scaling through parallel agent execution and self-verification. Across training and deployment, we jointly optimize capability and efficiency. Indic continued pretraining improves Indian-language benchmarks by up to 9.82 percentage points, while agentic mid-training strengthens software-engineering capabilities and robustness across agent harnesses. The post-trained Super model achieves 51.78% on SWE-bench Pro, surpassing Nemotron 3 Ultra despite using approximately 4.6x fewer active parameters. Post-training MTP boosting improves speculative- decoding acceptance length by up to 21.8% under probabilistic draft sampling, while NVFP4 quantization achieves 99.62% median accuracy recovery relative to BF16. Inference optimizations enable up to 4,856 output tokens/s/GPU on GB200 while sustaining at least 50 tokens/s/user.

papers.abstract: Advancing language models for specialized scientific applications requires evaluations of scientific fluency, physical reasoning, and quantitative analyses. Using inertial confinement fusion (ICF) as a test case, we have developed an expert-curated benchmark of 250 questions spanning qualitative reasoning, numerical calculation, symbolic derivation, and equation formulation. Responses have been evaluated using deterministic numerical and symbolic checks together with language-model judges. We compared a variety of out-of-the-box closed-source and open-source large language models with Prospero, a model specialized through combined domain-adaptive pretraining and supervised fine-tuning for ICF. We also conducted initial retrieval-assisted evaluations. Prospero improved its aggregate score by 10.7 percentage points over its base model, with gains across all question types. Frontier models achieved the highest aggregate scores, but critical physics errors persisted, particularly in numerical calculations. We note that domain-specific performance can improve through specialization, but benchmark gains alone do not establish scientific reliability. Retrieval improved performance for a smaller model but yielded no statistically significant improvement for a frontier model. Two scientific stress tests further illustrate useful capabilities and the need for expert assessment of physical assumptions and model validity. Based on these findings, we recommend evaluating existing domain capabilities and retrieval benefits before committing to substantial additional specialization.

papers.tldr: An expert-curated ICF benchmark shows that domain specialization improves language-model performance, but even frontier models retain important physics errors and require expert validation.

papers.abstract: Pre-training foundational models is computationally expensive as models scale. In this work, we introduce Bi-Phase Training (BPT), a parameter-efficient pre-training method that preserves the high-rank learning dynamics observed in full-parameter optimization with substantially reduced trainable parameters. BPT parameterizes each weight update as a composition of constrained high-rank left/right transformations via trainable diagonal matrices and low-rank adapters whose updates are periodically merged into the frozen base weights, resulting in a compounding expansion of accessible directions during training. Across language-model pre-training from scratch (Qwen2.5 models from 100M to 1.5B parameters and OLMo-2-1B) on FineWeb-Edu (10B and 100B tokens), BPT achieves validation perplexity close to full-parameter baselines while using far fewer trainable parameters; e.g., at the 1.5B scale, BPT uses 66% fewer trainable parameters with only a small validation-perplexity gap. Additionally, a comprehensive evaluation across diverse downstream tasks shows that BPT preserves much of the full-parameterized model's downstream performance.
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost of full-parameter foundational-model pre-training.
Uses constrained high-rank left/right transformations with trainable diagonal matrices and low-rank adapters.
Periodically merges adapter updates into frozen base weights, expanding the directions accessible during training.

At 1.5B parameters, reduces trainable parameters by 66% with only a small validation-perplexity gap and preserves much downstream performance.

papers.abstract: Many open mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models train with Muon instead of AdamW. Most balance the load with a bias on each expert's routing score, adjusted after every step. Their recipes disagree on whether Muon should also train the router. In models with 55M and 108M active parameters, we measure how the optimizer changes the span of these biases, the largest minus the smallest in a layer. The span grows when all tokens favor the same experts, so it shows how hard a layer is to balance. At learning rates tuned on shorter runs, Muon raised the span of the first MoE layer at every seed, roughly doubling it on average, while the other layers changed much less. The rise came from Muon on the rest of the network, whichever optimizer trained the router. In those runs, the inputs to the first router shared a direction, and soon after the warmup its busiest expert averaged four to seven times its fair share. Over the first 3,000 steps, subtracting the batch mean from these inputs removed this overload while barely changing the loss. On the smaller model, halving Muon's learning rate removed most of the rise and slightly improved the loss. Moving only the router to AdamW made the loads shift more during the warmup and slightly raised the loss, so at this scale the results favor keeping the router on Muon.
bullets: Muon increased the routing-bias span of the first MoE layer across all seeds, roughly doubling it on average at tuned learning rates.
The effect was driven by Muon applied to the rest of the network, not by the optimizer used for the router.
The first router’s inputs became directionally aligned, causing its busiest expert to receive 4–7× its fair share soon after warmup.
Subtracting the batch mean from router inputs removed the overload over 3,000 steps with little loss change.
For the smaller model, halving Muon’s learning rate reduced the imbalance and slightly improved loss; switching only the router to AdamW was less favorable.

papers.selection_reason: Directly studies optimizer effects on mixture-of-experts LLM training and router balancing, fitting LLM architecture and training research.

papers.abstract: Metis is a bet that better data, better training methods and new architectures can buy what a bigger parameter count cannot, at a fraction of the cost. Metis-1.6 is its latest step: two language models built from scratch by a single researcher, Praxis (2.94B parameters, 0.46B active per pass) and Logos (10.23B parameters, 1.18B active per pass). Both run a hybrid Mamba-2 and attention mixture-of-experts stack twice for every token, so each token gets a second look. Each was trained on 1.02T tokens in total: 804.76B of pretraining, 18B of context extension to 131,072 tokens, and 200B of supervised fine-tuning. Metis-1.6 was never meant to challenge frontier models, and across 40 post-trained benchmarks it mostly does not: Logos averages 52.93, seventh of 17 models in its comparison set and within a point of Qwen3-4B. But it gets there on roughly a twelfth of the median training data of the comparators that disclose it, and with fewer active parameters per token than any model that beats it, which puts it on the Pareto frontier for both. In mathematics it ranks second of 30 models, with 67.50% on AIME 2025 and 63.64% on HMMT February 2026. It is weak at code, instruction following and long context. The rest of the report is the part I found most valuable: what went wrong. The optimizer I configured never ran, and attention trained with AdamW for all of pretraining. A 1.77B-parameter n-gram memory learned to switch itself off. Five fine-tuning choices cost capability. And a length reward under group-mean normalization punished correct solutions for being long once a group's pass rate passed 2/3, a sign inversion I prove and fix with a one-line clamp. I close with the 10B-token ablations behind MoRE (Mixture of Recursive Experts), the looped architecture of Metis-1.7.
bullets: Introduces Praxis (2.94B parameters; 0.46B active per pass) and Logos (10.23B; 1.18B active), built from scratch by one researcher.
Uses a hybrid Mamba-2 and attention mixture-of-experts stack applied twice per token, with 1.02T tokens of pretraining, context extension, and supervised fine-tuning.
Logos reaches a 52.93 average across 40 benchmarks, placing seventh of 17 comparison models and on the reported Pareto frontiers for training data and active parameters.
Performs especially well in mathematics, ranking second of 30 models, but is weak at coding, instruction following, and long-context tasks.
Analyzes failures including an unused optimizer, an inactive n-gram memory, costly fine-tuning choices, and a flawed length reward; it also presents ablations for the next architecture, MoRE.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Metis-1.6 on one page, drawn for Logos. (a) Twenty layers, three of them attention, each ending in a mixture-of-experts block. papers.selection_reason: Technical report on new hybrid Mamba-2/attention MoE LLMs trained from scratch, directly fitting large language model research.
papers.title: Think Twice: The Metis-1.6 Technical Report

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets a large language model (LLM) answer questions by retrieving relevant passages from a large corpus. However, RAG struggles with multi-hop questions, which require chaining facts spread across several documents through intermediate entities that the question never mentions. Graph-based RAG methods retrieve once from the entities a question names and so rarely recover the full evidence chain. Iterative RAG methods recover it step by step, but their accuracy is limited by the many tasks they ask the LLM to perform, such as planning the sub-questions, deciding their dependencies, rewriting them as answers arrive, and keeping track of what is known. We propose DeFT-RAG, a RAG framework built on three components. First, DeFT-RAG generates one self-contained sub-question at a time from the original question and the sub-questions answered so far with their answers (QA pairs). Each sub-question names every entity it asks about, which removes the need to plan, track dependencies or rewrite, and lets the LLM focus on a single fine-grained task at a time. Second, DeFT-RAG moves the remaining LLM work outside the LLM: rule-based updates to a QA table that keeps track of what is known, and yes/no decisions made by a fine-tuned lightweight decision model. Third, DeFT-RAG caches the QA pairs and reuses an answer when a later question asks a sub-question with the same meaning. On MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA, DeFT-RAG achieves the best accuracy among thirteen baselines with both gpt-4o-mini and Qwen3.6 as the backbone, while giving the LLM fewer input tokens than any other iterative method. With a QA cache shared across 1,000 MuSiQue questions, 23.1% of sub-questions are answered from the cache, which reduces LLM calls by 12.9% without lowering accuracy.
bullets: Targets multi-hop RAG failures where evidence spans documents connected through unstated intermediate entities.
Generates one self-contained sub-question at a time, using prior question–answer pairs to name all relevant entities.
Uses rule-based QA-table updates and a fine-tuned lightweight decision model to move bookkeeping and yes/no decisions outside the LLM.
Caches semantically equivalent sub-question answers; on 1,000 MuSiQue questions, this served 23.1% of sub-questions from cache and reduced LLM calls by 12.9% without reducing accuracy.
Achieved the best accuracy among 13 baselines on MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and HotpotQA with both tested backbones, while using fewer input tokens than other iterative methods.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Failures of graph-based and iterative RAG on a 3-hop MuSiQue question (gpt-4o-mini runs). papers.selection_reason: RAG with reusable QA cache for multi-hop reasoning; relevant to LLM reasoning and external memory.
papers.title: DeFT-RAG: Incrementally Decomposing Multi-Hop Questions into Self-Contained Sub-Questions with Reusable Answers
papers.tldr: DeFT-RAG improves multi-hop question answering by incrementally generating self-contained sub-questions, tracking answers with lightweight components, and reusing cached answers.

papers.abstract: Recent work has hypothesised that large language models may represent some concepts as multi-dimensional manifolds instead of single directions. Using these manifolds to interpret or steer representations often assumes that moving along them corresponds to a continuous change in the represented concept. In this work, we test this continuous manifold assumption on the prototypical weekday manifold. Despite its striking circular geometry, we find that the weekday representations behave more like seven discrete states arranged in a circle than a continuous ring. First, we show that local sensitivity has seven minima aligned with the weekdays, producing a step-like mapping between representation and behaviour under on-manifold steering. Second, we test whether any concepts are represented along the manifold outside the seven discrete states, and find neither time of day, uncertainty, nor natural text populate the intermediate space. Together, these results challenge the continuous interpretation of the weekday manifold and motivate testing whether movement along other representation manifolds correspond to meaningful changes in model representations and behaviour.
authors: Diksha Gupta, Rieke Fruengel, Stefan Heimersheim
bullets: Tests the assumption that representation manifolds encode concepts through continuous movement.
Finds seven local-sensitivity minima aligned with weekdays and step-like steering behavior.
Finds no evidence that time of day, uncertainty, or natural text occupy intermediate positions.
Challenges continuous interpretations of representation manifolds and calls for broader validation.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Time-of-day variation along the weekday ring is small and not causal (A) Clocktime variation lies primarily along PC1, while weekday identity is captured mainly by PC2 and PC3. We show the top three principal components of weekday-token activations for prompts of the form “It was {time} on {day}.” (B) Time-of-day modifiers produce small (but systematic) angular shifts within the weekday plane, comparable in magnitude to those induced by non-temporal controls. Shifts are measured relative to each weekday centroid in the PC2–PC3 plane. Points show the mean across seven weekdays ± 1 s.e.m. (C) Steering along the ring has almost no effect on the predicted hour, whereas steering along the off-ring component of the observed “late–early” displacement shifts predictions by one to two hours. The horizontal axis specifies the fraction of a weekday interval traversed along the ring. At each steering amount and layer, the off-ring late– early intervention (brown) and random orthogonal control (green) are matched in ℓ2 norm to the along-ring intervention (black). Curves show mean changes in predicted hour ± 95% confidence intervals.

Figure 3: Uncertainty varies primarily along weekday spokes rather than between them. We vary the relative confidence assigned to two weekdays using frequency-adverb prompts, from “Always on {A}, never on {B}” through “Sometimes on {A}, sometimes on {B}” to “Never on {A}, always on {B}”. Colours indicate the five confidence levels. (A) Activations remain concentrated near the two candidate weekday spokes rather than filling the intervening arc. We show weekday pairs separated by one, two and three days. Small points represent individual activations; large points show the mean for each confidence level, computed separately for the two day-aligned groups. Concentric circles indicate normalised radius, with r = 1 corresponding to the fitted ring. (B) Activations move inwards as the stated confidence becomes more balanced, then outwards as the prompt increasingly favours the other weekday. The horizontal axis runs from full confidence in day B (−1), through equal confidence (0), to full confidence in day A (+1). Points show the mean normalised radius ± 1 SD.

Figure 1: Perturbation sensitivity around the weekday ring has seven weekday-centred minima. (A) Early-layer steering produces step-like changes in behaviour, with little change near weekdays and rapid change along the intervening arcs. We steer at constant angular speed around the fitted ring and measure cumulative distance in behaviour space. Steering at layer 2 (blue) produces a step-like response whereas steering at layer 28 (red) is smoother. (B) The difference in downstream response speed between weekday positions and the intervening arcs becomes more pronounced over layers. We steer around the ring at layer 2 and measure the speed of the residual-stream response at layers 3–31. (C) The sensitivity minima extend radially beyond the fitted ring, forming seven weekday-centred spokes separated by regions of higher sensitivity. At each point in the surrounding activation space, we measure how much a small change to the layer-2 activation changes the layer-28 residual stream, using the Frobenius norm of the corresponding Jacobian.

Figure 4: Natural context primarily translates weekday representations rather than moving them around the ring. (A) Representations of the same weekday are widely dispersed across natural contexts. papers.abstract: Language model assistants sometimes change a correct answer when the user suggests a wrong one. The behavior, called sycophancy, is usually attributed to preference-based post-training, yet early measurements found it in pretrained models. We ask where it comes from by measuring it at every available stage of training: 13 open checkpoints from 5 lineages, from base model through supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization to release. We separate how far an injected claim moves a model's answer from how firmly the answer was held, and vary who makes the claim, how reliable they are said to be, and how strongly they make it. Two sycophancy behaviors with different origins emerge, and both replicate across datasets. Deference to a claim in the prompt is already present in every base model, which ranks sources in the same order as its post-trained descendants. Capitulation in conversation, dropping a stated answer when the user objects, is largely absent from base models and present in every post-trained checkpoint. When the objection names an alternative, most post-trained models give up firmly held answers as often as loosely held ones. We discuss the implications of these measurements for evaluating sycophancy and approaches for addressing each behavior.
authors: Jiarui Yao, Shweta Parihar, Nghia Tuan Bui, Guergana K Savova, Lijing Wang
bullets: The study evaluates 13 checkpoints across five open-model lineages, spanning base models through supervised fine-tuning, preference optimization, and release.
It distinguishes how much a suggested claim shifts an answer from how strongly the original answer was held.
Deference to claims in prompts appears in every base model and preserves the same source-ranking pattern seen after post-training.
Capitulation—abandoning an answer after a user objects—is largely absent in base models but present in all post-trained checkpoints.
Both behaviors replicate across datasets, motivating separate evaluation and mitigation strategies.

papers.abstract: Large language models are pretrained on vast, uncurated corpora scraped from the public web. This creates a security risk from attackers who plant poisoned content in the pretraining data. We show for the first time that such poisoning can plant a remote code execution backdoor in an agent, causing it to execute attacker-chosen commands on the user's machine. To measure the threat end to end, we pretrain Qwen3 models from scratch at sizes 0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B, and then post-train each into a CLI agent using a clean pipeline. Poisoning only 0.1% of the pretraining corpus with our new poison design implants the backdoor: the deployed agent executes the malicious command when the trigger is present while behaving normally on clean inputs. The attack success rate (ASR) increases with model scale, with the 4B model reaching roughly 92% ASR at a 0.1% poison rate and staying positive even when the poisoning rate drops to 0.0005%. Our code is available at https://github.com/safety-research/agentic-backdoor.
authors: Xinyan Hu, Pingbang Hu, Chloe Loughridge, Xuanli He, Nicholas Carlini, Matthew Jagielski, Javier Rando, Yiming Zhang
bullets: Attackers can exploit poisoned public-web data used during pretraining.
A new poison design causes a CLI agent to execute attacker-chosen commands when triggered while acting normally otherwise.
The backdoor was demonstrated in Qwen3 models of 0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B parameters, post-trained into agents.
Poisoning 0.1% of pretraining data produced the backdoor; the 4B model reached roughly 92% attack success and remained vulnerable at 0.0005% poisoning.
The study measures the threat end to end, from pretraining through deployment, with code released publicly.

papers.abstract: Language models do not merely memorize facts; they absorb rhetorical strategies from pretraining data, including the human tendency to reason by analogy. We ask: is this absorbed capability geometrically accessible before any instruction tuning, and what determines whether it can be activated at inference time? We extract an "Analogy Vector" from the residual stream via difference-in-means and show it enables steerable explanation style across seven instruction-tuned models (Gemma-2, Llama-3.1, Qwen-2.5; 2B-32B), improving harmonic mean from 3.22 to 3.94 (+22%) for Gemma-2-9B-IT on 300 held-out test prompts. A small human validation study confirms the LLM judge on Analogy Quality. Our central finding, from seven matched base-instruct pairs, is a gradient of behavioral accessibility: the analogy direction exists in every base model, but its behavioral accessibility under linear intervention scales continuously with instruction exposure during training. Gemma-2 base models (strict pretraining/IT separation) show flat steering landscapes: present but behaviorally inert. Qwen-2.5 base models (instruction data woven into pretraining) are already partially accessible before any explicit fine-tuning; base-instruct cosine similarity of the analogy vector reaches 0.94-0.97 for Qwen versus 0.37-0.66 for Gemma, providing geometric corroboration of the behavioral gradient. This challenges the binary "base vs instruct" framing: the relevant variable is how much instruction exposure a model has received across its full training pipeline. We position activation steering as a complementary interpretability tool that reveals how instruction exposure organizes rhetorical knowledge in activation space.
bullets: An analogy direction is present in every tested base model, but its behavioral accessibility varies continuously with instruction exposure.
A residual-stream difference-in-means vector enables steerable analogy-based explanations across seven instruction-tuned models.
For Gemma-2-9B-IT, steering improved the reported harmonic mean from 3.22 to 3.94 on 300 held-out prompts.
Qwen base models showed partial accessibility before explicit fine-tuning, while Gemma base models’ directions were largely behaviorally inert.
The findings challenge a binary base-versus-instruct distinction and frame activation steering as a tool for studying rhetorical knowledge in activation space.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have rapidly become important tools for science, education, medicine, and professional work. Despite their apparent simplicity from the user's perspective, effective and responsible use requires an understanding of how these systems work, what their limitations are, and how their outputs should be evaluated. I wrote this document as a basis for my lecture on LLM in the master in artificial intelligence in medicine at the university of Turin, Italy. This book provides a practical and accessible introduction to LLMs for scientists and professionals. It explains the fundamental ideas behind tokenisation, embeddings, training, inference, context windows, prompting, and instruction hierarchies, while deliberately avoiding mathematical detail. Particular attention is given to the limitations of LLM-generated answers, including hallucinations, uncertainty, reproducibility, bias, and the need for systematic verification and human oversight. The book also discusses privacy, governance, security, and the responsible handling of personal and sensitive information. More advanced topics include Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), retrieval quality, chunking, embeddings, vector search, agents, tools, and workflows. A substantial practical exercise guides the reader through running a local LLM with Ollama and Open WebUI and using it to interact with a collection of scientific papers. The exercise emphasizes evidence retrieval, source verification, uncertainty, disagreement between studies, and the distinction between plausible language and scientifically supported conclusions. No programming knowledge is required.
bullets: Explains tokenisation, embeddings, training, inference, context windows, prompting, and instruction hierarchies without mathematical detail.
Highlights hallucinations, uncertainty, reproducibility, bias, privacy, security, governance, and the need for human oversight.
Introduces advanced applications including retrieval-augmented generation, vector search, agents, tools, and workflows.
Includes a no-code exercise using a local LLM to analyze scientific papers, verify sources, and assess disagreement and uncertainty.

papers.abstract: Despite their strong performance, large language models remain highly sensitive to prompt formulation. This issue is typically addressed at inference-time through manual prompt optimization, which introduces overhead and lacks scalability. Conversely, we focus on train-time approaches that build prompt robustness into the model during instruction tuning. A common strategy is to mix multiple paraphrases of each prompt into training. We demonstrate that across trainable parameters, the per-paraphrasing gradients interfere, with 57% exhibiting sign conflicts and the naive gradient average discarding approximately a fifth of the magnitude. Therefore, we develop two gradient-merging methods, Prompt-TIES and Prompt-DARE, that address this interference by leveraging interference-resolution operators from model and gradient merging and applying them to prompt gradients. In this study, we compare the efficacy of our methods to increase model robustness to train-time robustness methods spanning all three established classes: data construction, consistency regularization, and contrastive alignment. The evaluation is conducted across four models from two families at two scales. We observe the interaction between prompt phrasing and the specific examples accounts for 54% of per-example variability on average, and exceeds 70% on tasks such as ANLI and WiC. The gradient-merging methods directly improve this local robustness and nearly halve per-example variance on fully fine-tuned models at little cost to overall accuracy. The other train-time methods enhance raw performance, but fail to improve per-example variance reliably. Code: https://github.com/FSadrieh/prompt-agnostic-llms. Model checkpoints: https://huggingface.co/prompt-agnostic-language-models.
bullets: Prompt sensitivity is usually addressed with manual inference-time prompt optimization, which is costly and difficult to scale.
Training on prompt paraphrases creates gradient interference: 57% of parameter gradients show sign conflicts, and naive averaging loses about one-fifth of gradient magnitude.
Prompt-TIES and Prompt-DARE adapt gradient-merging operators to combine prompt gradients and improve robustness.
Across four models from two families and two scales, prompt phrasing and example choice explain 54% of per-example variability on average, exceeding 70% on ANLI and WiC.
The proposed methods nearly halve per-example variance for fully fine-tuned models with little overall-accuracy cost, whereas other train-time methods do not reliably reduce variance.

papers.abstract: Large reasoning models have recently demonstrated remarkable capabilities in solving complex tasks, where supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on long chain-of-thought data serves as a crucial foundation for eliciting and enhancing their reasoning abilities. Despite rapid progress in both improving and analyzing reasoning-oriented SFT, the field still lacks a systematic survey that consolidates its fast-growing literature. To fill this gap, we present a comprehensive review of recent advancements in reasoning SFT, examining the literature through the dual lenses of methodological design and analytical investigation. First, we review methodological improvements across the SFT pipeline and categorize them into data-centric approaches and algorithm-centric innovations. Second, we reorganize analytical studies along three dimensions: data characteristics, optimization dynamics, and mechanistic insights. Finally, by synthesizing current research focuses and remaining bottlenecks, we outline promising future directions for reasoning SFT. We hope this survey deepens the understanding of reasoning SFT and paves the way for advanced reasoning models.
authors: Yongcan Yu, Kuangpu Guo, Jian Liang, Lingxiao He, Meng Wang, Ran He
bullets: Reviews reasoning SFT as a foundation for eliciting and enhancing complex-task reasoning.
Categorizes methodological advances into data-centric and algorithm-centric approaches across the SFT pipeline.
Structures analytical research around data characteristics, optimization dynamics, and mechanistic insights.
Synthesizes current research priorities, remaining bottlenecks, and promising future directions.

papers.abstract: Can controlled symbolic inputs reveal attention heads that influence a language model's decisions from natural language evidence? We introduce controlled evidence aggregation (CEA), which varies the counts and order of two symbols in otherwise fixed prompts and measures changes in a frozen Transformer's preference between two answer tokens. The preference is measured by their logit difference; the prompts prescribe no correct answer. Balanced utility causal selection (BUC) identifies compact head sets by jointly evaluating how much ablating their outputs removes the count effect and how closely patching mean outputs between count conditions recovers the effect in both directions. We derive conditional bounds linking head attribution to intervention effects and specifying when the attribution shortlist can be recovered from finite samples. In Pythia-410M, ablating sets of 1-12 heads selected separately for four ordering regimes removes 65.5-91.6% of the count effect. The sets retain their influence on count comparisons not used for selection. To test relevance beyond symbolic inputs, we evaluate a natural language task asking which state is supported by more reports. Ablating eight heads selected only on symbolic yes/no prompts lowers mean accuracy by 8.2 percentage points, versus 0.8 for random sets matched by size and layer. Our results demonstrate that controlled symbolic probes can identify compact attention head sets whose causal influence extends to natural language decisions.
bullets: CEA varies the counts and order of two symbols in fixed prompts and measures answer-token logit differences without prescribing a correct answer.
BUC selects heads by combining ablation-based removal of count effects with bidirectional output-patching recovery.
In Pythia-410M, selected sets of 1–12 heads removed 65.5–91.6% of count effects and retained influence on held-out count comparisons.
On a natural-language evidence task, ablating eight symbol-selected heads reduced accuracy by 8.2 percentage points, compared with 0.8 for matched random sets.
The analysis provides conditional bounds connecting head attribution to intervention effects and finite-sample shortlist recovery.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often struggle with temporally grounded reasoning because their static parametric memory is misaligned with the dynamic evolution of real-world knowledge. Although RAG and Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) provide practical ways to enhance LLMs, they remain insufficient for temporal reasoning. Existing retrieval methods typically prioritize semantic relevance while overlooking temporal validity, event order, and evolutionary dependencies, resulting in evidence that is relevant in isolation but temporally fragmented. Meanwhile, conventional PEFT methods usually employ fixed and input-agnostic low-rank updates, making it difficult to capture time-dependent entity semantics and relation drift. To address these limitations, we propose Temporal Evidence-Parameter Co-Alignment (TEPCA), a framework for LLM reasoning over TKGs. TEPCA aligns LLM reasoning with temporal knowledge at both the evidence and parameter levels. At the evidence level, it introduces time-constrained Dynamic Relevance-Guided Path (DRGP) pruning to preserve globally coherent temporal paths, together with Mutual-Information (MI)-based pruning to retain query-informative local facts under temporal constraints. At the parameter level, it integrates Dynamic-Gated LoRA (DG-LoRA), a timestamp-conditioned low-rank adaptation mechanism that dynamically modulates the effective adaptation subspace according to temporal context. This design enables LLMs to better capture fine-grained entity evolution and time-dependent relation semantics while preserving parameter efficiency. Experimental results on two TKG benchmarks demonstrate that TEPCA achieves state-of-the-art performance. Additional evaluations of DG-LoRA on eight commonsense QA datasets further verify its general input-adaptive capacity, scalability across LLM backbones, and interpretability.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between static LLM memory and evolving temporal knowledge, which causes temporally fragmented evidence and weak handling of entity and relation changes.
Uses time-constrained Dynamic Relevance-Guided Path pruning to preserve globally coherent temporal paths and mutual-information pruning to retain informative local facts.
Introduces Dynamic-Gated LoRA, which conditions low-rank adaptation on timestamps to model evolving entity semantics and time-dependent relations efficiently.
Experiments on two temporal knowledge graph benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance.
Additional evaluations of DG-LoRA on eight commonsense QA datasets support its input adaptability, backbone scalability, and interpretability.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: The framework of TEPCA. TEPCA fine-tunes LLMs via Dynamic-Gated LoRA (DG-LoRA), which injects time-adaptive low-rank updates modulated by query-conditioned gating. Query Expansion then identifies temporally relevant event chains to enhance contextual understanding. The Graph Retrieval module applies Dynamic Relevance-Guided Path (DRGP) Pruning and Mutual Information (MI)–based Pruning to distill globally consistent paths and locally informative facts from TKGs. Global paths are selected based on reverse chronological constraints (e.g., ti < t3 and t3 > t2 > t1), semantic relevance, and temporal decay, ensuring temporal consistency and causal validity. Finally, LLM Reasoning integrates the retrieved temporal subgraph into the fine-tuned LLM to produce time-sensitive and context-aware predictions.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) provides token-level teacher feedback, yet common sampled-token updates assign credit locally and omit the effects of earlier actions on subsequent feedback. We introduce \method{} (Group-Relative On-Policy Distillation), which decouples feedback computation from credit assignment by aggregating token feedback into calibrated sequence-level credit. We establish a theoretical basis for this approach by showing that, under ideal on-policy assumptions, broadcasting raw summed feedback to every response token yields an unbiased estimate of the negative gradient of the sequence-level reverse-KL objective. To support effective learning in practice, \method{} discounts later feedback that may become less reliable under distribution shift and uses same-prompt rollout groups to calibrate teacher guidance. It preserves relative response preferences while retaining a controlled fraction of the group mean, which we term collective teacher pressure. Across five Qwen3 teacher--student settings and six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, \method{} outperforms vanilla OPD in macro Avg@K in every setting, including gains of 10.9 and 11.5 percentage points in two settings with matched thinking patterns. It also maintains stable training under mismatched thinking patterns, where vanilla OPD collapses. Ablations show that retaining an appropriate amount of collective teacher pressure can improve learning, while excessive collective teacher pressure or an unrestricted feedback horizon can destabilize training.
bullets: Addresses the weakness of local sampled-token credit, which ignores how earlier actions affect later teacher feedback.
Aggregates token feedback into sequence-level credit and theoretically justifies broadcasting summed feedback as an unbiased reverse-KL gradient estimate under ideal on-policy conditions.
Uses discounted feedback horizons and same-prompt rollout groups to calibrate teacher guidance while preserving relative response preferences.

Across five Qwen3 teacher–student settings and six math reasoning benchmarks, it improves macro Avg@K over vanilla OPD in every setting, including 10.9- and 11.5-point gains in two matched-thinking settings.
Remains stable under mismatched thinking patterns, but excessive collective teacher pressure or an unrestricted feedback horizon can destabilize training.

papers.abstract: Layer-ablation studies often perturb early or late layers of a language model, compare the damage to prediction on two corpora, and read a larger early-layer effect on one corpus as early-layer specialization for its task. Such a comparison averages over the tokens that each corpus asks the model to predict, and these target tokens differ: math solutions, for example, ask for far more whitespace and numbers than encyclopedia prose. We show that this difference can create the appearance of depth specialization. We split a cross-corpus early--late damage interaction by target-token type and recompute it under a target mixture shared by both corpora. Between GSM8K and Wikitext, a positive interaction replicates across five model instances. In the three fully decomposed models, only whitespace has a positive interaction. Removing whitespace reverses the pooled effect in all three, and matching the full target mixture reverses it in two. The diagnosis holds under position matching, adversarial reassignment of token types, and a continuous readout. The risk can also be anticipated from the tokenizer alone. A screen computed before any model runs places every held-out pair it scored in the region its label predicts, and on the pairs it rates at high or medium risk, removing whitespace reverses every positive pooled estimate. A smaller content-word effect one token ahead follows the share of content targets that the unablated model already predicts. A cross-corpus depth effect therefore supports an interpretation of task specialization only after the target-token mixture is reported, the effect is decomposed by token type, and a mixture-matched summary keeps its sign.
bullets: The study decomposes early–late damage interactions by target-token type and recomputes them under matched target mixtures.
For GSM8K versus Wikitext, the pooled positive interaction is driven primarily by whitespace; removing it reverses the effect in the analyzed models.
The diagnosis remains under position matching, adversarial token reassignment, and a continuous readout.
A tokenizer-only screen can flag pairs at risk before model experiments, with whitespace removal reversing all high- or medium-risk positive estimates.
Depth-specialization claims should report target mixtures, decompose effects by token type, and verify the sign after mixture matching.

papers.selection_reason: Analysis of layer-ablation depth effects in LLMs and tokenizer-driven confounds; relevant to LLM understanding.
papers.title: Target-Token Asymmetry Can Masquerade As Depth Specialization
papers.tldr: Cross-corpus layer-ablation effects can falsely suggest depth specialization when the corpora differ in the types of tokens they require the model to predict.

papers.abstract: Activation steering offers an effective and efficient way to modify an LLM's behavior at inference time. However, it remains unclear how to apply steering such that the signal is consistently strong and the steering strength has a universally interpretable meaning. We address this first by identifying the most steerable interval for each steering vector and rescaling the steering range accordingly. Building on this, we introduce a more interpretable method for steering, called parameterized steering which instead of pushing activations in a direction, it sets them at the desired trait strength. Next, with multi-trait steering, we find that naively combining vectors causes them to interfere with one another. In response, we develop a method to orthogonalize the vectors; it decouples these traits, allowing a model to exhibit one behavior without inducing the others, thus enabling multiple traits to be steered simultaneously.
authors: Remy Ogasawara, Cullen Anderson, Narmeen Fatimah Oozeer, Foad Namjoo, Amir Abdullah, Jens Kristian Refsgaard Schou, Jeff M. Phillips
bullets: Identifies each steering vector’s most effective interval and rescales its range for more consistent strength.
Introduces parameterized steering, which directly sets a desired trait strength instead of merely pushing activations in one direction.
Finds that naively combining multi-trait steering vectors causes behavioral interference.
Orthogonalizes steering vectors to decouple traits and enable simultaneous multi-attribute control.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs) on instruction data can quietly erode their safety, even when no training example looks harmful. Because this safety-degrading data looks benign, standard content filters struggle to catch it. We tackle this problem by developing SimpleLoRIF, a scalable gradient embedding method that identifies fine-tuning examples whose gradients align with unsafe behavior. By simplifying a low-rank attribution method and restricting backpropagation to the final four transformer blocks, SimpleLoRIF can embed datasets on the order of a million examples, boosting gradient attribution from a small-scale analysis tool into a practical filter for full post-training datasets. We first validate it on emergent misalignment, where we find that gradients can connect insecure-code training data to the broadly harmful behaviors that appear after fine-tuning, with AUC as high as 0.865 in the gradient space of misaligned models. We then use SimpleLoRIF to build SafeTulu, a version of Tulu 3 with the 20% of examples most gradient-aligned with unsafe responses removed. Training on SafeTulu reduces GCG attack success rate by up to 22% across Qwen, Llama, and Olmo, outperforming both LLM-as-a-judge and prior gradient-based filtering, while largely preserving or even improving capability. Finally, we analyzed the removed data and identify possibly under-studied sources of safety degradation, such as tool-execution failures and narrative arithmetic. We release SafeTulu along with a Hugging Face Space that lets researchers build their own customized versions of SafeTulu to fine-tune on, such as by changing the removal fraction or filtering only certain subsets.
authors: Saket Reddy, Amro Abbas, Anshuman Suri, Ari Morcos, David Schwab, Pratyush Maini
bullets: Problem: Benign-looking instruction data can erode LLM safety, evading standard content filters.
Method: Embed examples using gradient-attribution signals, focusing backpropagation on the final four transformer blocks for million-example datasets.
Finding: Gradient space linked insecure-code training data to emergent harmful behavior, reaching AUC 0.865.
Contribution: SafeTulu removes the 20% of Tulu 3 examples most aligned with unsafe responses and reduces GCG attack success by up to 22% across several model families.
Scope: Analysis highlights tool-execution failures and narrative arithmetic as possible under-studied sources of safety degradation; customized SafeTulu versions are released.

papers.abstract: A major challenge facing AI scientific discovery pipelines is how to determine when a generated idea is meaningfully novel. Ideally, novelty checks in these pipelines must be able to reject non-novel ideas while not rejecting too many novel ideas, and they should also be able to distinguish which parts of a proposal are non-novel, as opposed to opaquely discarding entire proposals. We design an analytical framework for evaluation of novelty checks with temporal ground truth at both the proposal- and claim-level, using four datasets of 1,060 proposals built from published papers, reviewer disputes, and generated ideas matching ones the field went on to publish. Auditing existing novelty checks with this framework, we find that checks with high rejection rates on non-novel work also tend to have high false alarms on ideas that are later realized by human researchers, and observe that checks built to evaluate proposals as a whole can point to claim-level prior art only by rejecting the whole proposal. We therefore introduce ClaimNov, a fine-grained, interpretable claim-level novelty module. ClaimNov catches 97% of disguised papers at a 1.5% false-alarm rate, and its claim-level novelty profile cuts the LLM judge's false alarms from 11.8% to 1.5%. Because its verdict rests on claim-level evidence, ClaimNov also keeps proposals that build on established contributions, rejecting only 3% of ICLR-accepted proposals with a reviewer-disputed contribution and keeping 91 of 100 novel proposals with one spliced prior contribution, against 76 for the strongest existing check. Code and data are available at https://github.com/emmatliu/claimnov.
authors: Miri Liu, Xiayu Zhao, Encheng Xie, ChengXiang Zhai
bullets: The study introduces an evaluation framework with temporal ground truth for novelty at both proposal and claim levels.
Audited checks with high rejection rates for non-novel work also produce many false alarms on ideas later independently realized by humans.
Proposal-level checks may identify prior art only by rejecting an entire proposal rather than isolating the non-novel claims.
ClaimNov provides an interpretable claim-level novelty profile and catches disguised papers with a 1.5% false-alarm rate.
Its claim-level evidence reduces LLM-judge false alarms and preserves proposals that combine established and novel contributions.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) improves language-model post-training by letting the student learn from its own sampled trajectories under teacher supervision, aligning the training process with inference-time behavior. However, the rollout policy in OPD is usually treated as fixed: each round samples directly from the current student. We show that this choice can create a compounding teacher--student mismatch, because it requires the teacher to provide effective supervision on whichever trajectories the student samples, including ones less reachable by the teacher itself. On such trajectories, teacher supervision can become noisy or even misleading, leading to undesirable student patterns such as repetition. Moreover, since the updated student in turn defines the rollout policy of subsequent rounds, these patterns persist and potentially amplify over training. This failure mode suggests that improving OPD requires treating the rollout policy itself as an optimization target, rather than only modifying the distillation objective. We propose Mixture Proposal On-Policy Distillation (MPOPD), which derives a student-anchored, teacher-guided rollout distribution from a local trust-region objective based on relative teacher support. The resulting target is a geometric mixture of the student and teacher policies, and we introduce a proposal policy that approximates this mixture, enabling rollout generation in a single forward pass. Experiments on 16 math, knowledge, and medical reasoning benchmarks show consistent gains over OPD and recent variants. On math reasoning, our method improves average accuracy by 6.91 over OPD on Qwen3-4B-Base while reducing average generation length by 41%, suggesting that rollout policy design provides an effective way to improve OPD.
authors: Sirui Chen, Yunzhe Qi, Haobo Xu, Jiaru Zou, Mengting Ai, Zihao Li, Jingrui He
bullets: Standard OPD rolls out solely from the student, which can expose the teacher to poorly supported trajectories and amplify errors such as repetition.
MPOPD treats the rollout policy as an optimization target using a local trust-region objective based on relative teacher support.
It forms a geometric mixture of student and teacher policies and approximates it with a proposal policy that enables single-forward-pass rollout generation.
Across 16 math, knowledge, and medical reasoning benchmarks, MPOPD consistently outperforms OPD and recent variants.
On math reasoning with Qwen3-4B-Base, it improves average accuracy by 6.91 over OPD while reducing average generation length by 41%.

papers.abstract: Search agents can use cross-document graphs to discover sources through multi-hop connections and choose subsequent actions based on candidate rankings and relationships within a limited observation window. However, documents may rank highly because their numerous connections make them easier to reach, without necessarily providing more valuable evidence. Graph diffusion methods such as Personalized PageRank (PPR) aggregate propagation contributions from multiple sources, allowing highly connected distractor nodes to crowd the observation window. Flat node scores also obscure cross-document evidence trails, limiting continued exploration. We propose Contrastive Evidence Paths (CEP), which scores candidates by their strongest individual paths on a query-conditioned document graph and calibrates these scores against the same graph's background visitation distribution to mitigate structural bias. CEP ranks candidates by the calibrated scores and retains the corresponding source paths. Building on CEP, we develop Structured Corpus Interaction (SCI), which organizes candidates and their connecting paths into a structured Map, enabling agents to verify source documents and pursue missing information through expansion from anchor documents. Experiments on BrowseComp-Plus and TREC-COVID show that SCI achieves state-of-the-art answer accuracy and nDCG@10 with the lowest generation cost. Compared with the strongest baselines by task performance, maximum reductions in tool calls and total generation costs exceed 50% and 40%, respectively. Further analysis confirms that SCI with CEP suppresses ranking inflation induced by structural connections and improves gold recall and exploration efficiency.
authors: Junchen Li, Liang Xu, Rongzheng Wang, Qizhi Chen, Junhao Wen, Shuang Liang
bullets: Graph-based search can over-rank highly connected documents that are easy to reach but weak as evidence.
Contrastive Evidence Paths (CEP) score candidates by their strongest query-relevant paths and correct for background graph visitation bias.
Structured Corpus Interaction (SCI) organizes candidates and paths into a Map for source verification and targeted exploration.
On BrowseComp-Plus and TREC-COVID, SCI achieves state-of-the-art answer accuracy and nDCG@10 with the lowest generation cost.
SCI reduces tool calls by over 50% and total generation costs by over 40% versus the strongest task-performance baselines, while improving gold recall and exploration efficiency.

papers.abstract: Grokking is a delayed transition from memorization to generalization in deep neural networks (NNs). We examine whether scaling and renormalization group (RG) theories can describe this dynamics, establishing a quantitative physical framework for neural generalization transitions. For modular addition on a two-layer NN, an ensemble of trained models defines an order parameter (the squared weight norm) and fluctuation proxies for the heat capacity and the susceptibility, with training epoch and weight decay serving as thermal and field control coordinates. To bridge neural architectures to real-space RG, we construct an exact coupling matrix via a second-order expansion of the loss with respect to per-neuron norms and use its Fiedler vector to define an effective geometry. This spectral ordering yields a monotonic spatial decay of coupling strength that is absent under random permutations. We then execute real-space RG by block-spin aggregating adjacent neurons and parameterizing the coupling matrix into off-diagonal band strengths. Linearizing this local RG map yields relevant scaling exponents and five derived critical exponents, with direct empirical estimates matching RG predictions within 1-10%. Overall, our framework provides a consistent effective description of grokking, suggesting the scaling and renormalization group formalism as a tool to investigate NN dynamics.
authors: Min Chen, Junqi Wang, Zeguan Wu, Wenhao Huang, Junyu Liu
bullets: Models grokking in a two-layer network trained on modular addition using squared weight norm as an order parameter.
Interprets training epoch and weight decay as thermal and field-like control coordinates, with heat-capacity and susceptibility proxies.
Constructs an effective neuron geometry from the loss Hessian’s coupling matrix and Fiedler-vector ordering.
Applies real-space RG by aggregating adjacent neurons and derives scaling and critical exponents from the local RG map.
Empirical exponent estimates agree with RG predictions within 1–10%, supporting the framework’s description of grokking.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview. From trained NNs (left), the critical exponents of grokking are obtained via two complementary routes. RG route (top): each hidden neuron carries a spin si, its squared weight norm, while each neuron pair is connected by a coupling Jij derived from the loss Hessian. Ordering the neurons on a chain using the Fiedler vector of this coupling graph enables adjacent neurons to be merged into blocks, where a linear fit of the coarsened couplings yields yt and yh, from which five critical exponents follow (Sections 3.2–3.3). Direct route (bottom): a physical dictionary uses the training epoch as an effective temperature, weight decay as conjugate field, and ensemble fluctuations as proxies for susceptibility and heat capacity, with power-law fits of these observables yielding the direct exponents (Sections 3.1 and 4). The two independent estimates agree within 1–10% (right).

papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly access external tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), but the natural-language metadata used to describe those tools creates a prompt-injection surface. Within this established tool-poisoning surface, we study Log-To-Leak, an additive post-hoc logging attack that induces a separate attacker-controlled call after the final legitimate call. Its payload targets the user query, MCP server name, server response, and agent response. We operationalize the injected directive through Trigger, Tool Binding, Justification, and Pressure, and separately measure call success, payload fidelity, and preservation of legitimate behavior. We evaluate five MCP servers and four LLM agents using five metrics spanning effectiveness, utility, and efficiency. Across 18 model-server pairs with valid tool execution, Log-To-Leak achieves an attack success rate (ASR) of 62.64-100% and conditional logging accuracy (LA) of 76.55-95.64%; 16 pairs have absolute target-task completion changes of at most 6.63 percentage points. Three evaluated defenses leave residual ASR above 55% on GitHub MCP with GPT-4o, while an instruction detector flags 85.53% of benign descriptions. These results show that successful task completion can coexist with unauthorized post-hoc disclosure and motivate host-controlled authorization for secondary tool calls.
authors: Yuepeng Hu, Chongyu Fan, Sirat Samyoun, Jian Du

papers.abstract: Financial institutions operating under data-residency constraints are restricted to open-weight models small enough to locally host, which trail frontier systems on multi-step quantitative reasoning. On-policy distillation narrows such gaps by supervising a student on its own rollouts, but traditional OPD requires a strong external teacher, and on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) conditions on a full reference solution. We ask how much of that signal is necessary. We present Fin-SD, a localized hindsight self-distillation recipe for multi-step reasoning. Given a problem the student fails, the student itself identifies the first incorrect reasoning step and writes a short critique of that step. We truncate the student's trajectory immediately before the error (aiming to obtain a correct prefix), condition a frozen copy of the student on the same prefix plus the hint, and distill that hint-conditioned teacher into the student over a short rollout under reverse KL. No external model contributes a gradient. We apply Fin-SD to GPT-OSS-20B on a custom multi-step financial reasoning benchmark that requires deriving formula inputs from realistic scenarios via accounting conventions. We find: (i) replacing the critique with a generic-feedback control matches Fin-SD's entire 3.03 pp accuracy gain over the base model on the FinanceReasoning Hard subset, suggesting the gain comes from where supervision is applied, not hint content; (ii) the model writing the hint does not need to be stronger than the model receiving it: hints from same-family GPT-OSS-120B, at roughly 6x the parameters, yield no materially greater benefits than self-written hints; and (iii) Fin-SD matches on-policy self-distillation from full reference solutions on accuracy while generating 9.5% fewer tokens. With Fin-SD, general reasoning on MMLU-Pro and a fourteen-metric compliance audit on FinTrust show no material regression.
bullets: A generic feedback signal matches the full 3.03-point gain, indicating that supervision placement matters more than hint content.
Hints generated by a larger GPT-OSS-120B model provide no material benefit over self-written hints.
Fin-SD matches full-reference on-policy self-distillation while using 9.5% fewer tokens.
No material regression appears on MMLU-Pro or a 14-metric FinTrust compliance audit.
Scope: evaluated on GPT-OSS-20B and a custom multi-step financial reasoning benchmark.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of Fin-SD. The student is sampled on a training problem and judged against the ground truth. On failures, a frozen copy of the student receives the query, the failing trajectory, and the answer, and returns the first faulty step 𝑘 , a short critique ℎ, and an error type; pure arithmetic slips are dropped without a gradient. The trajectory is truncated immediately before k, so both policies condition on the on-policy prefix before the localized error, with the frozen teacher also receiving ℎ. The student minimizes the per-token KL between the two next-token distributions over an L = 100 rollout. At each epoch boundary, the failure set is re-mined and the teacher re-frozen.

papers.abstract: Background: To localize a fault, a coding agent can reason from source code alone or use debugger assistance by running the program and stepping through it in an interactive debugger. While earlier agents struggled with static execution tracing and debugger operation, frontier LLMs have improved at both. Objective: We evaluate how accurately coding agents localize faults without tools across original and transformed programs, how much debugger assistance improves accuracy and at what cost, and how agents use it when optional. Methods: We seed 610 single-line faults into 144 LeetCodeDataset solutions and rewrite each faulty program with five recipes of behavior-preserving transformations. Agents based on Sol 6.1, Luna 6, and Qwen 3.8 localize each fault with no, optional, or encouraged debugger assistance. Results: Without tools, the agents localized 98.2 to 99.9% of faults in original and 96.7 to 99.9% in transformed programs, losing accuracy mainly where recipes restructured loops and conditions. Encouraged assistance removed 63% and 61% of Luna 6's and Qwen 3.8's remaining transformed errors (+2.1 and +1.3 percentage points) at 14.7 to 27.0 times the token use, while Sol 6.1 stayed at 99.9%. With optional assistance, Luna 6 and Qwen 3.8 still gained +1.5 and +1.3 points, though the agents used the interactive debugger in only 0.2 to 6.2% of runs. Conclusions: On short, precisely specified programs, current coding agents localize nearly all faults from source code alone, and debugger assistance removes most errors that remain. Given the choice, agents executed the program far more often than they stepped through it, yet kept most of the benefit.
authors: Christoph Daxerer, Johann Glock, Christian Macho, Rudolf Ramler, Martin Pinzger, Josef Pichler
bullets: Agents localized 98.2–99.9% of faults in original programs and 96.7–99.9% after behavior-preserving transformations.
The main remaining errors occurred when transformations restructured loops and conditions.
Encouraged debugger use removed 61–63% of remaining transformed-program errors for two agents, but required 14.7–27.0× more tokens.
When debugger use was optional, agents invoked it rarely (0.2–6.2% of runs) yet retained most of its benefit.
The findings are scoped to short, precisely specified programs and the evaluated frontier models.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates frontier LLMs (Sol 6.1, Luna 6, Qwen 3.8) as coding agents, analyzing their fault localization capabilities and the efficiency trade-offs of using debuggers.
papers.title: Do Coding Agents Still Need a Debugger? Frontier-Model-Based Fault Localization at the Accuracy Ceiling
papers.tldr: Frontier coding agents localize nearly all faults from source code alone, while optional debugger use provides small additional gains at substantial token cost.

papers.abstract: Aligned large language models are trained to comply with benign requests while refusing harmful ones. However, recent work shows that this refusal behavior is fragile and can often be disrupted by simple activation- or weight-space interventions. In particular, refusal has been shown to be largely mediated by a single residual-stream direction, typically computed as a difference-of-means vector between harmful and harmless prompts. However, this standard construction aggregates heterogeneous harmful prompts into one uniform average, potentially conflating distinct refusal-related phenomena. In this work, we study whether refusal interventions can be strengthened by learning how to combine prompt-specific refusal directions. We propose Weighted Refusal Direction Optimization (WRDO), a procedure that constructs a composite refusal direction from a bank of per-prompt directions using learned aggregation weights. This approach allows different harmful prompts to contribute unequally to the final intervention direction. We evaluate WRDO against prior single-direction methods on three open-weight language models using three guard judges and HarmBench as an external evaluator. We further measure the effect of the intervention on general model capability through standard utility benchmarks. Finally, we investigate a defense-oriented setting in which the same optimization machinery is used in reverse to restore refusal behavior in an abliterated model checkpoint. Our results show that weighted aggregation provides a more effective and flexible mechanism for manipulating refusal representations.
bullets: Standard refusal directions average heterogeneous harmful prompts, potentially obscuring distinct refusal-related patterns.
WRDO builds a composite residual-stream direction by learning unequal weights over per-prompt refusal directions.
The method is evaluated on three open-weight models using guard judges, HarmBench, and utility benchmarks.
The same optimization can be applied in reverse to restore refusal behavior in an abliterated model checkpoint.
Results indicate weighted aggregation is a more effective and flexible refusal-intervention mechanism.
