papers.selection_reason: Introduces WRDO, a method for optimizing refusal directions in aligned LLMs by learning prompt-specific aggregation weights, offering a more flexible mechanism for manipulating refusal representations compared to single-direction methods.
papers.title: WRDO: Weighted Refusal Direction Optimization in Aligned Language Models
papers.tldr: WRDO learns how to weight prompt-specific refusal directions to more effectively manipulate and restore refusal behavior in aligned language models.

papers.abstract: Running prompt tokens through fewer routed experts during prefill makes mixture-of-experts (MoE) serving cheaper, but what it damages has not been measured. We locate the damage with token-, layer- and attention-path interventions in four MoE families on short-answer question answering. At half the experts the F1 loss is mostly answer form: the model still finds the answer but no longer answers briefly. The loss is made at a few tokens: the two chat-template tokens before the answer in Qwen3-30B-A3B, and the first 8-32 tokens, where the instruction sits, in DeepSeek-V2-Lite. Keeping them at full experts removes most of the F1 loss and about half and a fifth of the increase in answer NLL. These tokens are not the familiar suspects: reduction leaves the first-token sink within 4%, and restoring super experts or massive activations recovers at most a quarter of the loss. On real prompts the localisation becomes a placement rule: with about 4% of tokens at full experts, putting them on the task interface keeps F1 within one point of the unmodified model, while the same budget scattered in the documents is about 3 points worse in both prespecified primary tests of this comparison. Time to first token falls about 14% on 11K-token prompts.
bullets: At half the experts, models usually identify the answer but lose F1 because responses become less concise.
Damage concentrates on two chat-template tokens in Qwen3-30B-A3B and the first 8–32 instruction tokens in DeepSeek-V2-Lite.
Keeping these tokens at full experts removes most F1 loss and reduces roughly half to one-fifth of the answer-NLL increase.
Allocating full experts to about 4% of task-interface tokens keeps F1 within one point of the unmodified model; scattering the budget in documents is about three points worse.
This placement rule reduces time to first token by about 14% on 11K-token prompts.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes the impact of expert reduction in MoE models during prefill, identifying specific critical tokens (instruction, chat template) that cause performance loss and proposing a placement rule for efficient serving.
papers.title: Where Prefill Expert Reduction Hurts MoE Models: A Few Prompt Tokens Carry Most of the Short-Answer F1 Loss
papers.tldr: Reducing routed experts during MoE prefill mainly hurts short-answer F1 through a small set of task-interface tokens, and protecting those tokens preserves quality while retaining latency gains.

papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) has emerged as a popular training paradigm for LLMs, providing dense, token-level supervision by aligning a model's own distribution with the distribution induced by privileged information. However, existing OPSD methods derive supervision solely from privileged information of the same instance, leaving inter-instance supervision largely unexplored. We propose Lookahead Self-Distillation (LEAD), which introduces inter-instance distillation by allowing the teacher to first learn from other on-policy rollouts before teaching the student. LEAD constructs lookahead teachers through virtual RL updates on disjoint subsets of on-policy rollouts, and uses each teacher to provide cross-group token-level supervision for the other subset. To reconcile the complementary yet potentially conflicting signals from OPSD and RLVR, we introduce harmonious modulation, which adaptively modulates the GRPO advantage based on the agreement between the two signals. Extensive experiments on scientific reasoning and interactive-agent benchmarks show that LEAD achieves the best in-domain average performance across model scales while maintaining out-of-domain generalization comparable to GRPO.
bullets: Existing on-policy self-distillation mainly uses privileged information from the same instance, overlooking inter-instance supervision.
LEAD builds lookahead teachers via virtual RL updates on disjoint rollout subsets, then distills knowledge across groups at the token level.
Harmonious modulation adaptively balances self-distillation and RLVR signals through their agreement.
Experiments on scientific reasoning and interactive-agent benchmarks report the best in-domain average performance across model scales.
Out-of-domain generalization remains comparable to GRPO.

papers.abstract: We introduce Heads of Security (HoS), a prompt injection defense that enforces instruction-data separation via a small set of learned per-head attention gates. HoS learns how each head should redistribute attention between trusted and untrusted tokens, enabling models to reason over untrusted content without following injected instructions. We evaluate HoS on Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and GPT-OSS-20B. We compare it against SecAlign++, a state-of-the-art finetuning-based defense, and ASIDE, a defense that, like ours, builds instruction-data separation into the model architecture. We show that HoS offers greater robustness to adaptive attacks, better performance on standard utility benchmarks, and matches top performance on standard agentic prompt injection benchmarks. More specifically, the black-box RL-Hammer attack reaches 97% ASR against GPT-OSS-20B and 85% against SecAlign, but only 10% against HoS. Claudini, a state-of-the-art white-box attack, strengthened against HoS through autoresearch, requires 3 times more FLOPs to reach the same ASR on HoS as it does on GPT-OSS-20B or SecAlign. HoS preserves base-model utility across standard multiple-choice benchmarks and prompting setups, whereas SecAlign and ASIDE degrade in few-shot settings. On agentic benchmarks with static attacks, HoS and SecAlign perform similarly and substantially improve the security-utility trade-off over the base model. ASIDE struggles with tool use, achieving only 10% utility. These results show that prompt injection robustness can be achieved and improved through targeted attention interventions.
authors: Igor Shilov, Xiaoxue Yang, Alexander Panfilov, Evgenii Kortukov, Matthieu Meeus, Peter Romov, Wojciech Samek, Jonas Geiping, Yves-Alexandre de Montjoye
bullets: Targets prompt injection by preventing untrusted content from controlling instruction-following behavior.
Uses lightweight, learned per-head gates to redistribute attention between trusted and untrusted tokens.
Evaluated on Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and GPT-OSS-20B against SecAlign++ and ASIDE.
Reduces RL-Hammer attack success to 10% on GPT-OSS-20B, compared with 97% for the base model and 85% for SecAlign.
Preserves standard benchmark utility and matches top performance on agentic prompt-injection benchmarks; ASIDE struggles with tool use.

papers.selection_reason: Learned per-head attention gates for prompt injection defense are an architectural intervention directly relevant to large language models.
papers.title: Heads of Security: Learned Attention Gates Improve Prompt Injection Robustness
papers.tldr: Heads of Security (HoS) improves prompt-injection robustness by learning per-head attention gates that separate trusted instructions from untrusted content while preserving model utility.

papers.abstract: Weight decay and explicit weight-norm constraints improve optimizer performance in language model pretraining, yet a unified understanding of why such control helps and how much is needed remains incomplete. We analyze norm control in Muon over the entire training trajectory using the \emph{accumulated effective learning rate}, $C_T=\sum_{t<T}\eta_t/\|W_t\|_F$, where $\eta_t$ is the nominal learning rate and $\eta_t/\|W_t\|_F$ is the effective learning rate relative to the weight norm. For bounded update directions, accumulation over any training interval bounds relative weight displacement. We show that vanilla Muon can accumulate only logarithmically, potentially limiting exploration and helping explain its slower empirical progress, whereas MuonW and MuonH guarantee at least linear accumulation under the stated conditions. Going beyond bounded-norm control, we show that sufficiently slow norm growth guarantees faster accumulation than the logarithmic worst case, opening up less restrictive optimizer designs. Based on this insight, we propose MuonGS, which uses Gram--Schmidt (GS) projection to remove the radial component of each Muon update without fixing the weight norm. With bounded update directions and a constant nominal learning rate, we prove that the weight norm grows at most proportionally to $\sqrt{t}$ after $t$ steps. Consequently, MuonGS guarantees $C_T=\Omega(\sqrt{T})$, with accumulation sustained even in later training. Further, for smooth scale-invariant objectives we establish its $O(T^{-1/2})$ stationarity guarantee. In pretraining experiments with 160M- and 400M-parameter dense models as well as a 135M active- and 1B total- parameter MoE model, MuonGS achieves lower validation perplexity than MuonH at long training horizons. In particular, for the dense model it achieves an estimated token-equivalent speedup up to about $15\%$ at matched validation loss to MuonH.
authors: Athanasios Glentis, Dawei Li, Mingyi Hong
bullets: Weight-norm control affects Muon’s effective learning rate; vanilla Muon may accumulate it only logarithmically, limiting exploration.
MuonGS applies Gram–Schmidt projection to remove each update’s radial component without fixing the weight norm.
Under bounded updates and constant nominal learning rate, MuonGS grows weight norms at most as √t and guarantees Ω(√T) accumulation.
For smooth scale-invariant objectives, MuonGS has an O(T⁻¹ᐟ²) stationarity guarantee.
In experiments across dense and MoE models, MuonGS achieves lower long-horizon validation perplexity than MuonH, with up to roughly 15% token-equivalent speedup at matched loss.

papers.selection_reason: Presents an optimizer for LLM pretraining with norm-control analysis and token-equivalent speedups, directly relevant to large language model training.
papers.title: MuonGS: Pretraining LLMs with Relaxed Weight-Norm Control
papers.tldr: MuonGS relaxes strict weight-norm control in Muon by removing radial update components, preserving effective learning-rate accumulation and improving long-horizon LLM pretraining.

papers.abstract: Language models pretrained on web corpora collected over multiple years learn both general and domain-specific knowledge. How these different kinds of knowledge are learned as pretraining progresses remains unclear. Recent point-in-time models trained on web snapshots from different years provide a way to probe how knowledge prevalence varies over time. Using these models, we propose a temporal variability score (TVS), defined as the coefficient of variation of an item's negative log-likelihood across models. A higher score suggests that the knowledge may be less consistently represented across years of web text. We evaluate six benchmarks covering diverse topics using six models from multiple open-source model families. We find that low- and high-TVS items are learned similarly early in training, but high-TVS items improve faster later on. At the end of the pretraining run, high-TVS items outperform low-TVS items in 34 of 36 model-benchmark settings, with an average advantage of 7.3 points of chance-normalized accuracy. This pattern is most robust on knowledge-intensive tasks, even when comparing items of similar difficulty. Our findings reveal differences in how knowledge is learned over the course of pretraining, with temporal variability providing a diagnostic of these learning dynamics beyond aggregate benchmark scores.
authors: Chang Su, Bin Wu, Emine Yilmaz, Yao Lu
bullets: Introduces temporal variability score (TVS), measuring variation in an item's negative log-likelihood across models trained on web snapshots from different years.
Across six benchmarks and six models, low- and high-TVS items improve similarly early in training, while high-TVS items improve faster later.
High-TVS items outperform low-TVS items in 34 of 36 model–benchmark settings, with a 7.3-point average advantage in chance-normalized accuracy.
The effect is most robust on knowledge-intensive tasks, including comparisons between items of similar difficulty.
TVS offers a diagnostic for knowledge-acquisition dynamics beyond aggregate benchmark scores.

papers.selection_reason: Studies pretraining dynamics and knowledge acquisition over time in language models, introducing a temporal variability score to track learning progress.
papers.title: What Improves During Pretraining? Tracking Knowledge Acquisition with Point-in-Time Models
papers.tldr: Point-in-time models and a temporal variability score reveal that temporally inconsistent knowledge improves faster later in pretraining and ultimately performs better than consistently represented knowledge.

papers.abstract: Label-free reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) rewards a language model for agreeing with its own majority vote. It improves reasoning at first but eventually collapses: the self-assessed reward goes to one while accuracy falls, often until the model gives the same answer to every problem. The collapse appears only when training uses many problems. We explain this dataset-size dependence as a collective instability. In a solvable many-problem model in which problems share parameters, a population whose problems prefer different answers amplifies any shared perturbation for as long as the population-averaged slope $\langle F'\rangle$ of the single-problem self-reinforcement drift $F$ is positive. This holds while problems are still uncertain about their answers. Per-problem sharpening, slowed by $1/N$ for $N$ training problems, races against the shared mode, which grows at a rate $\propto\lambda^2$ independent of $N$, where $\lambda$ is the strength of the shared coupling. This yields a critical number of problems $N_c\simeq\ln(1/\delta)/(\lambda^2G)$, where $\delta$ seeds the shared mode and $G$ decreases with the initial confidence. Simulations of the model confirm the predictions: a sharp transition, $N_c\propto\lambda^{-2}$ up to a logarithmic correction, a single critical amplification $\lambda^2NG$ across couplings, confidence profiles and training variants, a logarithmic dependence on batch size, and no collapse for confident initial models. A kernel version of the theory identifies a protective coupling (generalization of sharpening) and a marginal-entropy bonus that stabilizes the uniform collective mode. In label-free RL of a small Transformer, removing the shared direction prevents collapse entirely, restoring it causes collapse, and collapse grows with training-set size and base-model entropy.
bullets: Collapse occurs when shared parameter perturbations are amplified while individual problems remain uncertain.
Per-problem sharpening slows as the number of training problems grows, while the shared mode grows at a rate set by coupling strength.
The theory predicts a critical problem count scaling roughly as $N_c\propto\lambda^{-2}$, with logarithmic dependence on perturbation size and batch size.
Simulations support the predicted transition and a shared critical amplification across couplings and training variants; confident initial models avoid collapse.
In a small-Transformer experiment, removing the shared direction prevents collapse, while restoring it makes collapse worsen with dataset size and model entropy.

papers.selection_reason: Theoretical analysis of self-reinforcement collapse in LLM RLVR training.
papers.title: Collective Dynamics of Self-Reinforcement: How Cross-Task Coupling Drives Policy Collapse in Unsupervised RLVR
papers.tldr: Cross-task coupling can turn self-reinforcing, label-free RLVR into a collective instability that drives policy collapse, with larger training sets making collapse more likely.

papers.abstract: Language model performance depends strongly on the mixture of domains in the pretraining data corpus. Popular data mixing methods select these domain weights by training many small proxy models on random mixes and then fitting a regression model to predict performance from the mix. We recognize this practice as a domain attribution problem, where the regression measures each domain's contribution to the target metric. Through this lens, the standard Dirichlet sampling of proxy data mixes is a poor regression design that requires tuning and cannot support a linear fit for hundreds of domains. Building on classical optimal experimental design, we introduce LinMix, which samples mixes at the vertices of the capped simplex so that each domain is at its cap or absent. This hyperparameter-free vertex sampling decorrelates domain effects, enabling an interpretable linear model whose coefficients are the domain attributions. The optimal mix given by LinMix provably keeps only domains with positive attribution values and requires no search over candidate mixes. We further establish the optimality of vertex sampling, and prove that Dirichlet sampling inflates the attribution error when its mixes concentrate around the prior data mix. Pretraining experiments with 1B-parameter OLMo2 and 4B Qwen3.5 language models show that LinMix outperforms Dirichlet-based data mixing across reasoning, code, and math benchmarks, with relative gains of 46% on MBPP and 14% on GSM8K. At 288 fine-grained domains, only vertex sampling supports a linear fit, and LinMix improves benchmark accuracy by 11% on average over the best nonlinear baseline.
authors: Hubert Baniecki, Przemyslaw Biecek, Martin Pawelczyk
bullets: Standard Dirichlet sampling produces correlated mixes, requires tuning, and becomes unsuitable for linear attribution across hundreds of domains.
LinMix samples mixes at vertices where each domain is either at its cap or absent, decorrelating domain effects without hyperparameter tuning.
Its linear coefficients estimate domain contributions; the selected mixture retains only domains with positive attributions and requires no candidate-mix search.
Theory establishes vertex-sampling optimality and shows that concentrated Dirichlet mixes increase attribution error.
Experiments on 1B-parameter OLMo2 and 4B Qwen3.5 models show gains across reasoning, code, and math benchmarks, including 46% on MBPP and 14% on GSM8K.

papers.selection_reason: LLM pretraining data mixing formulated as domain attribution with theoretical and empirical gains.
papers.title: LinMix: Data Mixing as Linear Domain Attribution
papers.tldr: LinMix treats data mixing as a domain-attribution problem and uses capped-simplex vertex sampling to efficiently identify the best pretraining mixture with an interpretable linear model.

papers.abstract: It is known that randomly initialized neural networks have Gaussian behaviour in the $n\to \infty$ limit. Unfortunately, this approximation can be poor for finite $n$ and gets worse as one goes deeper into the network. In this work, we develop a more accurate approximation that is \emph{slightly} non-Gaussian, which we call the para-Gaussian distribution and is constructed from the Hermite polynomials. We show how this para-Gaussian approximation can lead to a practical recursive method to approximate the deeper layers of the network. Finally, we apply this theory to linear neural networks (where things can be solved exactly) and to ReLU neural networks (where things can be approximated).
bullets: Gaussian approximations can be inaccurate at finite width and degrade with network depth.
The proposed para-Gaussian distribution is constructed using Hermite polynomials.
A recursive procedure applies the approximation across deeper network layers.
The theory is exact for linear neural networks and approximate for ReLU networks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Linear network. Fourth cumulants. Quantities related to the fourth cumulant of a linear network (φ(x) = x, width n = 32) for depths up to ℓ = 32. Each plot compares three solutes: 1. the exact values from Lemma 2.3, 2. the values obtained from the 1/n recursion of Theorem 1.18, and 3. from Monte Carlo simulations. We use two orthogonal unit inputs (K = I2) and two different neurons, so that each statistic isolates one exact coefficient; here zα,k denotes the output of neuron k on input α, with α ∈ {1, 2} and k ∈ {1, 2}. (b) Orthogonal inputs: nCov ( z1,1z2,1, z1,2z2,2 ) = Cℓ(1, 2; 1, 2), exactly vℓ and ℓ according to the 1/n recursion. Middle: Monte Carlo over 222 samples, with probabilities compared bin by bin; hatched bins contain fewer than 100 samples. The two agree closely in the bulk of the distribution. The difference is close to 0 inside the inner ellipse and of order 0.1 in the ring between the ellipses. The largest differences are in the tails, where the para-Gaussian ratio keeps growing while the true density does not. The dashed curves are where the para-Gaussian ratio equals 1, i.e. where the para-Gaussian and Gaussian densities agree.

papers.selection_reason: Provides a theoretical approximation (Para-Gaussian) for random deep neural networks. This contributes to the understanding of the behavior and initialization of deep network architectures.
papers.title: Para-Gaussian Approximations of Random Deep Neural Networks
papers.tldr: A para-Gaussian, mildly non-Gaussian approximation provides a more accurate finite-width analysis of randomly initialized deep neural networks than standard Gaussian limits.

papers.abstract: Generating several solutions can expose alternative methods, but additional trajectories often paraphrase one dominant approach. We investigate whether the conditional capacity of a frozen sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) model can provide such diversity from one problem prompt, without user-assigned roles, prescribed methods, fine-tuning, or model copies. Agent-Conditioned Routing (ACR) assigns $m$ parallel trajectories persistent, untrained shared/private expert-eligibility masks while preserving the learned, input-dependent token router. On a screened 126-question multi-mode mathematics and physics benchmark, with model judges reading the reported derivations in full, we count the number of problems yielding at least two distinct primary methods among soft-correct solutions in four trajectories. ACR reaches approximately twice as many such problems as the strongest temperature setting under GLM 5.3 (37.3 versus 18.7), and 1.67 times as many under GPT-5.6 Sol (45.00 versus 27.00), at matched output budgets. A blinded four-expert audit on a stratified sample of 30 problems also finds more multi-method solutions with ACR on both backbones, with lower correctness. Matched-eligibility ablations show modest multi-method count advantages for ACR, while token-resampled masks attain higher correctness. An informed sequential prompt elicits more diversity still, using previous solutions and explicit requests for alternative methods. ACR adds about 160 KiB of mask state. In a three-problem microbenchmark capped at 1,024 tokens, its latency and peak VRAM usage remain within 3% of batched temperature sampling.
authors: Ananth Kalyanasundaram, Ankush Kadu, Athira Gopal, Aswanth Krishnan
bullets: ACR assigns persistent shared/private expert-eligibility masks to parallel trajectories while retaining the model’s learned token routing.
On a 126-question math-and-physics benchmark, it produced roughly twice as many problems with at least two distinct methods as the strongest temperature baseline.
A blinded audit confirmed greater multi-method diversity across both tested backbones, though ACR solutions were less correct.
Matched-eligibility ablations showed only modest diversity gains, while token-resampled masks achieved higher correctness; sequential prompting elicited still more diversity.
ACR adds about 160 KiB of state, with latency and peak VRAM within 3% of batched temperature sampling in a small microbenchmark.

papers.selection_reason: Uses frozen sparse MoE conditional routing to generate diverse reasoning paths; directly relevant to LLM architecture and inference behavior.
papers.title: Agent-Conditioned Routing: Diverse Reasoning Paths Within One Frozen Model
papers.tldr: Agent-Conditioned Routing increases the diversity of reasoning methods from a single frozen sparse MoE model without fine-tuning or model copies, but with lower correctness.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are usually evaluated by final-output correctness or safety, yet an endpoint label does not reveal how a failure develops throughout the reasoning process. We therefore ask whether ordinary reasoning failures and adversarially induced failures can be characterized using the same internal coordinates. Towards this end, we in this paper study a white-box diagnostic framework CauTrace to disclose the root-cause of why LLM fails from three fundamental inspections: Functional States, Propagation of Representation, Temporal-State Coordination and Reasoning Trajectory. First, seven functional states are creatively defined to represent the support and constraint processing in LLMs. Second, the propagation of representation change measures how the changes among the seven states persist across subsequent Transformer blocks. Third, temporal-state coordination and trajectory topology characterize when the commitment and verification occur relative to the support, and how the dominant state sequence evolves over the full inference process. Finally, we evaluate CauTrace on both clean reasoning failures and paired adversarial perturbations. Across Qwen and LLaMA-family models, the failed traces show weaker Attention-MLP agreement on support-state updates and less verification activity relative to commitment, while the exact representation-level signatures and timing shifts vary by architecture. Held-out repair and steering tests demonstrate consistent operational signals that were in line with our claims for certain models and specific settings, with aligned steering producing the predicted directional changes in process measures. Overall, CauTrace provides a unified diagnostic framework for analyzing failure dynamics through changes in support, commitment, and verification, which would shed light on the in-depth research on LLM security.
authors: Zirui Ding (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences), Xinxin Fan (University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, State Key Laboratory of AI Safety, Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences), Hao Yuan (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, ShanghaiTech University), Shaoye Luo (University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, State Key Laboratory of AI Safety, Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences), Men Niu (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences), Yunfeng Lu (Beihang University)
bullets: Introduces seven functional states to model support and constraint processing during inference.
Measures how representation changes propagate across Transformer blocks and examines coordination between attention and MLP components.
Characterizes reasoning trajectories, including when commitment and verification occur and how state sequences evolve.
Across Qwen- and LLaMA-family models, failures show weaker Attention–MLP agreement on support updates and less verification than commitment.
Repair and steering tests provide operational support for the proposed signals in selected models and settings, though signatures vary by architecture.

papers.selection_reason: White-box analysis of internal LLM failure mechanisms and reasoning trajectories; directly relevant to LLM foundation-model research.
papers.title: Uncovering Why LLMs Fail: From Internal Mechanisms to Adversarial Reasoning Trajectories
papers.tldr: CauTrace diagnoses how LLM reasoning failures arise by tracking internal support, commitment, verification, and representation dynamics over time.

papers.abstract: Language model agents are post-trained and deployed through a harness, the prompts, tools, and control logic that present a task to the model and execute its outputs. Harnesses are often revised and judged by how an already trained model performs under them, which assumes that what the model learned under one harness carries over to the next. We ask what a policy learns from its harness and what survives when the harness changes. Under KL-regularized control, we show that the log odds of an optimal policy recover how strongly its harness favors each action over the others, so a trained policy carries the preferences of its harness. Deployed return then equals the ceiling of the harness, the best return it offers, minus the mismatch of the policy, the return lost to its own suboptimal decisions. Training changes only the mismatch, while changing the harness moves both terms. Comparing harnesses with a fixed model therefore mixes what each harness offers with how well that model uses it. In MiniWoB++, post-training makes a model's preferences specific to its training harness. Reversing the order of the observation fields leaves every optimal decision unchanged yet lowers a trained model's success from 85.0% to 19.2%. Conversely, every new harness that a fixed-model comparison rejects but that raises the ceiling outperforms the original agent after further training under it, and ceiling and mismatch measured beforehand predict these gains. For coding-agent harnesses on Terminal-Bench Lite, ceiling minus mismatch estimated with a stronger model as a stand-in for the optimum reproduces the accuracy ranking, while either term alone does not. Code is available at https://github.com/2020-qqtcg/HRP.
authors: Jian Mu, Ruibo Shen, Yao Shu
bullets: Under KL-regularized control, a policy’s action log-odds reveal the preferences induced by its training harness.
Deployed return decomposes into harness ceiling minus policy mismatch; training mainly reduces mismatch, while harness changes affect both terms.
In MiniWoB++, reversing observation-field order preserved optimal decisions but reduced trained-model success from 85.0% to 19.2%.
Harness ceiling and mismatch predicted which rejected harnesses would outperform the original agent after retraining.
For coding-agent harnesses on Terminal-Bench Lite, the combined estimate ranked systems correctly, unlike either component alone.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes the relationship between LLM agent policies and their harnesses (interfaces). This provides insight into how agents are controlled and trained, relevant to agent behavior in LLMs.
papers.title: Your Policy Is Secretly a Harness: The Decision Geometry of Agent Interfaces
papers.tldr: Agent performance reflects both the harness’s intrinsic potential and how well the policy’s learned preferences match it, so changing prompts, tools, or control logic can invalidate fixed-model comparisons.

papers.abstract: Muon is a matrix-aware optimizer that combines momentum with orthogonalization to produce structured update directions with strong empirical behavior. However, it only shapes the geometry of the update itself and does not explicitly control neighborhood worst-case loss or bias training toward flat regions, which are often linked to stronger generalization. To address this limitation, we introduce the sharpness-aware formulation of Muon. We first develop \textsc{MuSAM}, which incorporates Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM)-style perturbation into Muon's orthogonalized update and establishes a principled bridge between sharpness-aware training and matrix-aware optimization. We then show that this formulation faces an efficiency--stability tension: constructing the perturbation requires an extra gradient evaluation, while the perturbation itself is generated from a single minibatch gradient and is therefore noisy. To resolve this issue, we propose \textsc{MoMuSAM}, which turns Muon's momentum from an update variable into a sharpness-probing signal. By using normalized momentum as the perturbation direction, \textsc{MoMuSAM} removes the extra clean-gradient computation and replaces the single-batch perturbation proxy with a temporally aggregated one. We prove that both \textsc{MuSAM} and \textsc{MoMuSAM} attain the same asymptotic first-order stationarity order, and further show that \textsc{MoMuSAM} yields a more stable stochastic linearization than \textsc{MuSAM}. Experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate that sharpness awareness consistently improves Muon.
authors: Zhiwei Zhai, Wenjing Yan, Ying-Jun Angela Zhang
bullets: Muon structures update directions through momentum and orthogonalization but does not explicitly target flat regions.
MuSAM adds SAM-style perturbations to Muon, but requires an extra gradient evaluation and uses a noisy single-minibatch signal.
MoMuSAM uses normalized momentum as a temporally aggregated sharpness-probing direction, removing the extra clean-gradient computation.
Both methods achieve the same asymptotic first-order stationarity order; MoMuSAM provides a more stable stochastic linearization.
Experiments on standard benchmarks show that sharpness awareness consistently improves Muon.

papers.selection_reason: Develops Sharpness-Aware Muon (MoMuSAM), a matrix-aware optimizer that combines momentum with sharpness-aware minimization. This contributes to the optimization landscape for training large models.
papers.title: Sharpness-Aware Muon: Matrix-Aware Optimization with Momentum-Guided Perturbations
papers.tldr: MoMuSAM extends Muon with momentum-guided sharpness awareness, improving stability and efficiency while preserving first-order convergence guarantees.

papers.abstract: The success of large language models in real-world applications relies on parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods such as Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), which inserts compact, trainable adapters into selected layers. In this paper, we propose SimplexLoRA, a LoRA variant that adaptively adjusts adapter ranks during fine-tuning based on their learned importance. Unlike standard LoRA, which employs a fixed rank across all layers, SimplexLoRA optimizes per-adapter importance weights on the $n$-scaled simplex during a short warm-up and then freezes them, dynamically allocating capacity where it is most beneficial without increasing the overall parameter budget or inference cost. We evaluate SimplexLoRA across 12 language understanding, summarization, and reasoning tasks using DeBERTaV3, BART-large, Llama 3.1 8B, and Qwen3-8B. Our results show that SimplexLoRA consistently matches or outperforms standard LoRA and recent adaptive baselines, with the largest gains at low ranks. Our code is available at https://github.com/brain-lab-research/SimplexLoRA.
authors: Igor Shalygin, Grigorii Davydenko, Andrey Veprikov, Aleksey Antonov, Nikolay Bushkov, Stanislav Moiseev, Aleksandr Beznosikov
bullets: Addresses the limitation of standard LoRA’s uniform, fixed rank across layers.
Optimizes per-adapter importance weights on an n-scaled simplex during a short warm-up, then freezes them.
Evaluated on 12 language understanding, summarization, and reasoning tasks across four language models.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces SimplexLoRA, a dynamic rank updating method for Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) in LLMs. This is a significant architectural/efficiency contribution for large language models.
papers.title: SimplexLoRA: Dynamic Rank Updating via Alternating Minimization with Simplex Projection
papers.tldr: SimplexLoRA dynamically reallocates LoRA rank across layers using learned importance weights, improving or matching fixed-rank LoRA without extra parameters or inference cost.

papers.abstract: Pruned language models are judged almost entirely by accuracy and perplexity, which assumes that preserved output behaviour implies preserved internal computation. We test this assumption with a factorial pruning study on GPT-2, crossing two importance criteria (magnitude, random), two component types (attention heads, MLP neurons) and three sparsity levels (3%, 50%, 70%). Using the fully characterised indirect object identification (IOI) circuit as ground truth, we measure circuit integrity with activation patching, path patching and direct logit attribution. We find two qualitatively distinct failure modes. Magnitude head pruning >= zeroes the circuit: output-facing heads are removed, and the model falls to near-chance. Magnitude neuron pruning at 30% inverts it: all 26 circuit heads remain intact, but Name Mover contributions flip sign, and the model systematically prefers the wrong name (17.7% accuracy). Perplexity ranks it as less damaged than random head pruning (74.6 vs 140.1). A replication of the Greater-Than circuit shows that the critical component type depends on the circuit's architecture. These results show that output metrics and structural checks can both miss mechanistic damage, motivating circuit-level causal analysis as a complementary evaluation of compressed language models.
bullets: The study tests magnitude and random pruning of GPT-2 attention heads and MLP neurons across multiple sparsity levels.
Circuit integrity is evaluated using activation patching, path patching, and direct logit attribution, with IOI as the primary ground truth.
Magnitude head pruning can remove output-facing circuit heads and reduce performance to near chance.
Magnitude neuron pruning can leave all circuit heads intact while reversing Name Mover contributions, yielding systematically wrong predictions.
A Greater-Than circuit replication shows that pruning sensitivity depends on circuit architecture; circuit-level causal analysis is therefore needed alongside perplexity and structural checks.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates mechanistic failure modes of weight pruning in Transformers using mechanistic interpretability. This provides a deeper understanding of how pruning affects internal computation, relevant to LLMs and model efficiency.

papers.tldr: Weight pruning can preserve or obscure output-level performance while severely damaging the internal circuits that produce model behavior.

papers.abstract: We introduce SERF (Self-Regularized Flow Language Models), a simple self-supervised framework for improving continuous diffusion language models by exploiting the denoising trajectory itself. While continuous flow-based language models offer a promising alternative to autoregressive generation, their training objectives typically rely on supervision from clean target tokens, leaving the denoising trajectory underexploited as a learning signal. SERF addresses this limitation through noisy-to-clean self-distillation: an exponential moving average (EMA) teacher receives a cleaner version of the student's noisy input along the same interpolation path and provides additional supervision. We investigate two variants: SERF-L, which aligns the student's intermediate representations with deeper teacher representations, and SERF-P, which aligns their output token distributions, either at the student's output or at an early student layer. All variants augment the standard training objective without requiring external pretrained models or modifying the inference procedure. Experiments across three continuous language-model paradigms (one-hot FLM, latent ELF, and hyper-spherical S-FLM) demonstrate substantial improvements in training efficiency, generation quality, and few-step generation. In particular, SERF achieves up to 7.7x wall-clock training acceleration on OpenWebText, improves MAUVE by 24.3% and GSM8K accuracy by up to 28.8%, and matches baseline performance with up to 64x fewer sampling steps. These results establish noisy-to-clean self-distillation as an effective approach to improving continuous diffusion language models.
authors: Theodoros Kouzelis, Spyros Gidaris, Nikos Komodakis
bullets: Addresses the underused denoising trajectory in standard continuous flow-language-model training.
Uses an EMA teacher that receives a cleaner input on the same interpolation path to supervise the noisy student.
Introduces representation-level SERF-L and distribution-level SERF-P variants without external pretrained models or inference changes.
Improves training efficiency, generation quality, and few-step generation across one-hot FLM, latent ELF, and hyper-spherical S-FLM.
Reports up to 7.7× faster wall-clock training, 24.3% higher MAUVE, 28.8% higher GSM8K accuracy, and comparable performance with 64× fewer sampling steps.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of SERF. In flow language models, the clean data lies at x1 (one-hot token embeddings) and pure noise at x0. SERF corrupts x1 at two noise levels along the same interpolation path using shared noise: the noisier input xs is fed to the student fθ, while the cleaner input xt (t > s) is fed to the EMA teacher fθ̄, whose outputs are detached via stop-gradient. The student is supervised by the standard cross-entropy loss against the ground-truth one-hot target xl 1, plus a distillation loss weighted by λ, which takes one of two forms. Left: In Latent Distillation, (SERF-L) the hidden states of an early student block ks are mapped through a lightweight projection head gθ and aligned with those of a deeper teacher block kt > ks using a per-token cosine distance. Right: In Probability Distribution Distillation (SERF-P), features from student block k pass through a small MLP and the teacher’s frozen head oθ̄, giving token-wise distributions p̃l θ that are trained to match the teacher’s ql θ̄ via a cross-entropy loss; the student’s own output pl θ is trained with LFLM.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces SERF, a self-supervised framework for continuous diffusion language models using noisy-to-clean self-distillation. This improves training efficiency and generation quality for a specific class of generative LLMs.
papers.title: Self-Regularized Flow Language Models

papers.abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) has been widely adopted for aligning language models with human preferences. Recent empirical work has revealed that DPO induces remarkably sparse parameter updates, yet no theoretical explanation for this phenomenon has been offered. We analyze DPO's optimization dynamics under a neural tangent kernel linearization and show that the logistic structure of the DPO loss gives rise to an implicit maximum-margin bias. Building on this observation, we introduce the concept of dual sparsity: the DPO update direction is a sparse linear combination (data-level sparsity, driven by support vectors) of sparse gradient feature vectors (parameter-level sparsity, arising from gradient cancellation between preferred and dispreferred responses). We formalize this structure in our main theorem, bound the number of support pairs by a margin-dependent spectral quantity, and present a framework relating dual sparsity to weight disentanglement---a condition favorable for model merging. Experiments on GPT-2 Small and Medium and on 7--9B instruction-tuned models (Llama-3-8B, Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B) with the Anthropic HH-RLHF and UltraFeedback datasets confirm both sources of sparsity, and experiments on GPT-2 show that DPO reduces cross-task interference by up to $35{\times}$ compared to supervised fine-tuning.
bullets: DPO’s logistic loss creates an implicit maximum-margin optimization bias.
Its update is sparse at two levels: support-vector-like data sparsity and gradient-cancellation-driven parameter sparsity.
A theorem bounds the number of support pairs using a margin-dependent spectral quantity.
The framework connects dual sparsity with weight disentanglement, a property useful for model merging.
Experiments across GPT-2 and several 7–9B instruction-tuned models confirm both sparsity mechanisms; on GPT-2, DPO reduces cross-task interference by up to 35× versus supervised fine-tuning.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes the sparsity of Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) updates, providing a theoretical explanation for weight disentanglement. This connects alignment (LLMs) with efficiency (sparsity) and model merging.
papers.title: On the Sparsity of Direct Preference Optimization: Weight Disentanglement in the NTK Regime
papers.tldr: DPO’s sparse parameter updates are theoretically explained by dual sparsity in the NTK regime, which also promotes weight disentanglement and reduces cross-task interference.

papers.abstract: Every neural-network training run produces not only a model, but also evidence about how models learn. Can these accumulated experiments enable us to predict and compare new training runs before executing them? We study meta-models: models that predict the learning behavior of other models. From this perspective, final-performance prediction, learning-curve prediction, and hyperparameter selection are different queries to the same training response function. We take a first, humble empirical step toward this goal: treating real language-model training records as native numeric data, we find that an off-the-shelf tabular in-context learner, TabPFN, can match or outperform a fine-tuned LLM meta-model in multiple evaluated settings. Whereas recent work fine-tunes LLMs on tokenized configurations at a cost of tens to hundreds of GPU-hours, TabPFN requires seconds of fit-and-predict time without task-specific weight updates. We argue that meta-modeling is better treated as its own numeric modality rather than as a text task for LLMs. Going one step further, augmenting TabPFN with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) further improves accuracy on selected prediction tasks. Finally, we pre-registered a forecast of the Marin Hero Run, a 535B-parameter public training run, whose ground truth is revealed point by point as training progresses, putting meta-model predictions to the test against training outcomes not yet observed at the time of forecasting.
bullets: Unifies final-performance prediction, learning-curve prediction, and hyperparameter selection as queries to one training-response function.
Treats language-model training records as native numeric data rather than text.
TabPFN matched or outperformed a fine-tuned LLM meta-model across multiple evaluated settings without task-specific weight updates.
TabPFN required seconds for fitting and prediction, compared with tens to hundreds of GPU-hours for fine-tuning LLM meta-models.
Adding Kolmogorov–Arnold Networks improved accuracy on selected prediction tasks; a preregistered forecast tests predictions against an ongoing 535B-parameter training run.

papers.abstract: Continual adaptation of large language models (LLMs) to evolving task distributions while mitigating catastrophic forgetting remains an open problem. Existing strategies often struggle to scale or lack a robust mechanism for zero-shot task-to-expert assignment. We introduce CaLLM, a framework that resolves these tensions by combining metric-based meta-learning with modular parameter isolation via lightweight adapters. First, CaLLM projects each input batch into a task-agnostic embedding space to find its nearest prototype. It then routes the batch to the specific adapter specialized for that data distribution. This formulation provides (i)~controllable cross-task interference by design, (ii)~constant computational complexity regardless of task count, (iii)~seamless integration of novel distributions through prototype expansion, and (iv)~regime agnosticism as the local routing decision enables a unified approach to both online and offline settings. Our experiments demonstrate that this routing mechanism discovers semantically coherent task groupings while facilitating constructive interference between similar tasks, and keeping overhead at a minimum. Across diverse and fine-grained continual learning benchmarks, CaLLM consistently outperforms traditional isolation and replay methods, establishing prototype-based modular routing as a principled and scalable approach to lifelong adaptation of LLMs.
authors: Bilge Celik, Anna Vettoruzzo, Joaquin Vanschoren
bullets: Addresses continual adaptation under evolving task distributions and catastrophic forgetting.
Embeds each input batch, matches it to the nearest prototype, and selects the corresponding adapter.
Uses modular parameter isolation to control cross-task interference while supporting constructive transfer between similar tasks.
Maintains constant routing complexity as tasks grow and incorporates new distributions by expanding prototypes.
Outperforms traditional isolation and replay methods across diverse continual-learning benchmarks with low overhead.

The selected adapter is then trained or finetuned and the pool is updated. The diagram further details how this routing mechanism integrates with the distinct training and evaluation loops.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes CaLLM, a framework for continual adaptation of LLMs using non-parametric adapter routing. This directly tackles catastrophic forgetting and task interference, fitting Continual and Online Learning and LLM adaptation.
papers.title: CaLLM: Continual Adaptation of LLMs via Non-Parametric Adapter Routing
papers.tldr: CaLLM continually adapts LLMs by routing inputs to specialized lightweight adapters using nearest task prototypes, reducing forgetting with scalable, zero-shot assignment.

papers.abstract: Linear threshold functions (LTFs) are a canonical class of Boolean predictors. In the autoregressive setting, the same LTF reads the most recent $d$ bits, generates the next bit, and returns the bit produced after $T$ steps. While the one-step class has VC dimension $d$, for general $T$ the counting upper bound is $O(d^2)$. We prove that the VC dimension is $\Theta(d^2)$ for every $T\ge d^2$, resolving the quadratic gap for deterministic autoregressive LTFs. We then adapt the same technique to show an exponential separation between deterministic and stochastic autoregressive models: replacing the sign of LTFs by logistic sampling can increase the VC dimension of the final majority prediction class from quadratic to exponential in $d$.
authors: Ilan Doron-Arad, Idan Mehalel, Elchanan Mossel
bullets: Studies autoregressive LTFs that repeatedly use the latest d generated bits to produce future bits.
Shows the VC dimension is Θ(d²) for every sequence length T ≥ d², closing the previous quadratic-gap question.
Extends the approach to stochastic logistic models with final majority prediction.
Establishes an exponential VC-dimension separation between deterministic and stochastic autoregressive models.

The blue cell is at position π(out, s) in the later block Et i and equals λi,s. Since E0 i and E1 i are independent of the labels, so are the selected inputs. Within each region (Row, Test, Output, Pointer), coordinates are ordered by increasing j. The row bits remain unchanged. The current output bits encode 16, and the pointer selects position 3, whose weight is 23−1 = 4. Since 21 − 16 ≥ 4, the new test bit is 1, so the third output bit is set to 1, while all other output bits remain unchanged. Finally, the pointer shifts from position 3 to position 2, selecting the next digit to test.

Figure 2: Transition from E3 to E4 for m = 5, i = 2, and θ2 = 21. The black 1 is the first bit of each block, fixed to 1 by the definition of the encoding in (15). The same LTF generates all bits of E4 from left to right. The row bits remain unchanged. The output bits initially represent 16, and the pointer selects j = 3, with weight 23−1 = 4. Since 21 − 16 ≥ 4, the new test bit is 1. As the lower arrow indicates, this new test bit sets the third output bit to 1, so the output bits now represent 16 + 4 = 20. The pointer changes to j = 2. papers.selection_reason: Provides a theoretical analysis of the VC dimension for autoregressive models, resolving a quadratic gap and showing exponential separations. This contributes to the theoretical understanding of LLM architectures and generalization.
papers.title: On the VC Dimension of Autoregressive Linear Threshold Functions
papers.tldr: The paper proves that sufficiently long deterministic autoregressive LTFs have VC dimension Θ(d²), while logistic stochasticity can raise it exponentially in d.

papers.abstract: Gradient-based data attribution has become an important tool for high-quality data selection in the instruction fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs), as it estimates the contribution of training examples through their influence on model optimization. However, we find that existing global gradient attribution methods suffer from surface-form bias: minor changes to semantically irrelevant details, such as wording or formatting, can produce highly inconsistent attribution scores even when the underlying content remains unchanged. To address this issue, we propose Content-Invariant Gradient Attribution (CIGA), a robust framework for instruction data selection. CIGA first identifies layers whose gradients are both influential for attribution and stable under semantics-preserving surface-form perturbations, thereby reducing formatting noise in gradient features. It then dynamically fuses these attribution signals with semantic representations of the input, combining optimization-level influence with content-level information. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks show that CIGA produces more stable rankings under surface-form perturbations while preserving downstream capabilities and improving average performance. CIGA also reduces attribution cost, offering a robust and efficient approach to data selection for LLM instruction tuning.
authors: Jia Gu, Liang Pang, Huawei Shen
bullets: Existing global gradient attribution can assign inconsistent importance scores to semantically equivalent examples because of surface-form bias.
CIGA selects gradient layers that are both attribution-relevant and stable under semantics-preserving perturbations.
It dynamically combines robust gradient signals with semantic input representations.
Experiments across multiple benchmarks show more stable data rankings, preserved capabilities, and improved average performance.
The framework also reduces attribution cost, though its scope is focused on instruction-tuning data selection.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces Content-Invariant Gradient Attribution (CIGA) for robust LLM data selection, addressing surface-form bias in gradient-based attribution methods, which is relevant to the training and optimization of large language models.
papers.title: Robust LLM Data Selection via Content-Invariant Gradient Attribution
papers.tldr: CIGA makes gradient-based instruction-data selection more robust to irrelevant wording and formatting changes while improving efficiency and downstream performance.

papers.abstract: Modern language models are trained on far more language than children experience, but we know much less about learning from small, naturalistic datasets. We train small GPT-2 models on transcripts of speech with children from dense home recordings (BabyView) and on synthetic child-directed dialogue (TinyDialogues), varying the amount, source, and diversity of training data. Models trained on one child's language environment predict that environment substantially better than other children's environments. Much of this specialization is lexical and distributional: a simple 5-gram model reproduces the cross-child pattern (r=.91). Training on data from multiple children clearly improves prediction of pooled held-out language relative to training on a single child's input without a similarly clear improvement on grammatical benchmarks. Across data sizes, naturalistic and synthetic training inputs also produce different grammatical and lexical-semantic patterns, with important differences between grammatical phenomena. Together, these results show that small-data language learning depends not only on how much language a model sees, but on which environments it comes from and how well that input matches what the model is asked to predict.
authors: Steven Y. Feng, Michael C. Frank
bullets: Models trained on one child’s speech predict that child’s environment better than other children’s environments.
Cross-child specialization is largely lexical and distributional, as a 5-gram model reproduces the pattern.
Training on multiple children improves prediction of pooled held-out language, but not clearly grammatical benchmarks.
Naturalistic versus synthetic input yields different grammatical and lexical-semantic behaviors across data sizes.
Small-data learning depends on data amount, source diversity, and how well training input matches the target environment.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates small-scale language model training on child speech data, focusing on specialization and data scaling, which is relevant to the study of language foundation models and their training dynamics.
papers.title: Specialization, Diversity, and Scaling in Child-Scale Language Models
papers.tldr: Child-scale language models specialize strongly to the language environment they train on, while broader and better-matched input improves generalization in selective ways.

papers.abstract: Agentic life-science benchmarks give an agent evidence about a named entity and score an answer against a recorded outcome. That score tests reasoning over evidence only if the evidence, rather than the name, determines the answer. We examine this distinction by varying identity and evidence independently on a clinical-outcome benchmark and published tasks from Biomni and LAB-Bench. Blinding identity matters little when a prompt contains a decisive sequence or passage. It matters a great deal when the prompt is mostly a name and candidate list (0.742 named versus 0.082 blinded; chance 0.093). Across 96 LAB-Bench LitQA2 questions, the gap increases under one fixed passage-redaction scheme (+0.000 to +0.135; per-instance slope +0.147, p= 0.004). On the clinical benchmark, a no-evidence recall probe matches prediction accuracy and recovers a database-specific programme count. So, we argue that benchmarks intended to measure evidence-dependent reasoning should report identity-blinded results, retrieval telemetry, and positive controls.
bullets: The study independently varies entity identity and provided evidence on a clinical-outcome benchmark and Biomni/LAB-Bench tasks.
Identity blinding has little effect when prompts contain decisive sequences or passages, but greatly reduces performance for name-and-candidate-list prompts (0.742 to 0.082; chance 0.093).
Across 96 LAB-Bench LitQA2 questions, performance gaps increased under passage redaction, with a reported per-instance slope of +0.147 (p=0.004).
A no-evidence recall probe on the clinical benchmark matched prediction accuracy and recovered a database-specific programme count.
The authors recommend identity-blinded evaluation, retrieval telemetry, and positive controls for benchmarks measuring evidence-dependent reasoning.

papers.selection_reason: Audits LLM benchmarks to distinguish between identity-based and evidence-based reasoning, providing insights into LLM evaluation and reasoning mechanisms.
papers.title: Identity or Evidence? Auditing Evidence Dependence in Agentic Life-Science Benchmarks
papers.tldr: Many agentic life-science benchmarks may reward recognizing entity names rather than reasoning from evidence, especially when evidence is sparse.

papers.abstract: The Persona Selection Model (PSM) posits that post-training selects a persona the model learned during pre-training. Work on subliminal learning has shown that models can impart covert signals (like "love of owls") into semantically unrelated outputs like strings of numbers, and that students trained on these outputs inherit those traits. In this work I show that by evaluating the likelihood of such outputs under the base pre-trained model with an appropriate header, a method I call persona-header likelihood evaluation (PHLE), one can decode these subliminal signals and classify between them. For example, PHLE distinguishes number sequences generated by a post-trained model prompted with "You love owls" from those prompted with "You love eagles", and distinguishes answers from a model with a secret desire to harm the user, filtered to remove any noticeable misalignment, from those of a model with no system prompt. In both cases prompted classifiers, including the generating model itself, remain near chance. The signal partially persists across model families, with the Qwen base model reading signals generated by Olmo and vice versa. This is evidence for a non-trivial prediction of the PSM, and the method may be practically useful for auditing the hidden objectives of models.
bullets: Introduces persona-header likelihood evaluation (PHLE), which scores outputs under a base model using an appropriate header.
PHLE decodes subliminal signals embedded in semantically unrelated outputs, such as number sequences.
It distinguishes hidden owl-versus-eagle preferences and filtered harmful intentions from neutral behavior, while prompted classifiers stay near chance.
Signals partially transfer across model families, with Qwen and Olmo base models decoding one another’s signals.
The findings support the Persona Selection Model and suggest PHLE could help audit hidden model objectives.

papers.selection_reason: Probes base LLM persona decoding via likelihood evaluation, contributing to LLM behavior and interpretability.
papers.title: Base Models Can Detect Hidden Intentions that Prompted Classifiers Miss
papers.tldr: Base-model likelihoods can reveal hidden model intentions that prompted classifiers—including the generating model—fail to detect.

papers.abstract: We measure, without sampling error, the probability a language model assigns to each integer from 1 to N when asked for a random number. For a fixed prompt the model defines one probability vector, which we compute by summing over each integer's scored spellings rather than estimate by sampling, removing the noise that limits earlier studies [1, 4]. We evaluate 18 open-weight model lines at five ranges up to N = 100, under 29 decoding configurations, on two inference stacks; 15 of them have matched base and instruction-tuned checkpoints that both give usable answers. Instruction tuning makes the distribution less uniform in all 15 pairs. It installs one heuristic, round-number avoidance, and sharpens another, endpoint avoidance. Base checkpoints do not avoid round numbers once the endpoints are removed from those sets; tuned checkpoints avoid them, multiples of 10 almost completely. Base checkpoints return the endpoints 1 and N at 0.30 to 0.60 of the interior rate; tuned checkpoints almost never return them. A preference for odd numbers is consistent across tuned checkpoints only at N = 100, where base checkpoints also show it weakly. Endpoint avoidance and the odd preference fit the account Kubovy and Psotka [6] proposed for human number choice; round-number avoidance is not part of that account, and the midpoint avoidance it predicts is essentially absent, with one slight exception at N = 100. Tuning does not install a new favourite integer shared across models: above N = 10 no modal integer is shared by more than 42 percent of tuned conditions, and P (17) rises in 10 of 15 pairs and falls in 5. The concentration is present in the model's own distribution: at temperature 1.0, nucleus truncation at top-p 0.95 adds a median of 0.035 to the total variation distance.
bullets: The study computes exact integer probabilities by summing over each number’s scored spellings, avoiding sampling noise.
Across 15 matched base/instruction-tuned model pairs, tuning reduced distributional uniformity under varied ranges and decoding settings.
Tuning installed round-number avoidance—especially for multiples of 10—and sharpened avoidance of the endpoints 1 and N.
Odd-number preference appeared consistently only at N = 100; midpoint avoidance was largely absent.
Tuning did not produce a shared favorite integer across models; the concentration was intrinsic to the model distributions rather than caused mainly by top-p sampling.

papers.selection_reason: Exact measurement of instruction-tuning-induced number-choice heuristics in language models; fits LLM behavior and architecture research.
papers.title: 3, 7, 14, 17, 42: Instruction Tuning Installs and Sharpens Number-Choice Heuristics in Language Models

papers.abstract: As the applications of AI continue to expand across various multimodal and multilingual domains, ensuring safe and responsible deployment of these systems has become an important concern. A wide-range of interventions have been proposed to make AI responses safer and more reliable. They often incur substantial computational or annotation costs, or cannot be extended to multilingual settings. In this work, we propose Selective Detection And Targeted Editing (SEDATE), a training-free approach based on detect-edit-verify strategy. SEDATE first detects the responsible neurons, edits them as and when necessary and finally verifies the model responses; all without any additional model training. We evaluate SEDATE across 7 languages and 4 model families. We further evaluate its effectiveness across 4 out-of-distribution languages and 4 additional datasets. We show that SEDATE achieves substantially superior safety scores across all languages and models over the best-performing baseline while retaining the general capabilities and incurring negligible overhead. Our results are robust, with the trends remaining similar for out-of-distribution languages and datasets.
bullets: Addresses the cost and limited multilingual applicability of existing safety interventions.
Detects responsible neurons, selectively edits them when needed, and verifies the resulting responses without additional training.
Evaluated across 7 languages, 4 model families, 4 out-of-distribution languages, and 4 additional datasets.
Reports substantially higher safety scores than the strongest baseline across languages and models, with negligible overhead and retained general capabilities.
The abstract does not specify the exact aggression circuit structure or provide numeric results.

papers.abstract: Rubric-based rewards enable effective reinforcement learning on non-verifiable tasks. However, because these rewards are typically defined as a weighted measure of rubric coverage, models are trained primarily to maximize a recall objective. As a result, RL-trained models produce responses that are more complete but also more verbose and contain more unnecessary or factually incorrect content, leading them to be less preferred than responses from the base model. To address this issue, we present the FORK reward, which jointly optimizes recall and a novel precision objective, which requires each unit of a model response to be both necessary and factually correct, as measured by rubric-driven necessity credits and a factual-correctness grader, respectively. Our experimental results show that FORK outperforms existing rubric-based RL methods and achieves Pareto-optimal performance that balances rubric coverage and overall response quality. Compared to the original recall-based reward, FORK substantially improves precision and reduces response length while achieving similar rubric coverage, which leads to significantly higher win rate compared to the base policy (e.g., from 10.6% to 68.0% on RubricHub-Medical and from 22.1% to 74.1% on HealthBench).
bullets: Recall-focused rubric rewards can produce overly verbose responses with unnecessary or incorrect content.
FORK adds a precision objective based on rubric-driven necessity credits and factual-correctness grading.
The method improves precision and shortens responses while maintaining similar rubric coverage.
It achieves Pareto-optimal coverage–quality tradeoffs and higher win rates against the base policy on medical evaluation benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Reward hacking in rubric-based RL and our mitigation method. With the standard coverage reward, recall (i.e., weighted coverage of rubrics) quickly saturates, while precision and win rate against a base model continually decreases and responses become more verbose. With a precision objective included in the reward (FORK), the model reaches similar recall while gradually increasing precision and win rate and generating less verbose responses. Here, we train Qwen2.57B-Instruct on RubricHub-Medical and evaluate it on an in-domain test set.

Figure 2: Training with FORK. Given a prompt, a policy model samples a response, which is then divided into units. An LLM grader matches rubrics to units to assign each unit a necessity credit and determines a credit threshold for unit necessity. In parallel, the grader assesses the factual correctness of all units. Precision is defined as the fraction of necessary and factually correct units, and recall follows the standard definition of weighted rubric coverage. We update the policy model using their weighted harmonic mean as a reward.
Figure 3: Recall vs. Win Rate using a training grader. We report recall against win rate for rubric-based RL methods evaluated with the training grader on RubricHub-Medical.

papers.tldr: FORK reduces reward hacking in rubric-based RL by jointly optimizing response coverage and the necessity and factual correctness of each response unit.

papers.abstract: Energy-based models have shown promising properties for domain-specific tasks but remain challenging in modeling general-purpose scenarios. To bridge this gap, we design energy-steered models (ESMs) for foundational language modeling. ESMs integrate energy steering and token generation within a single architecture to leverage the energy-guided search to refine token generation. Specifically, ESMs first optimize a latent state over the energy landscape, then leverages the refined latent state for token generation. By performing such energy-guided pre-training on large-scale corpora, ESMs learn generally effective energy landscape where favorable tokens correspond to lower energy values. To explore the scaling behavior of ESMs, we pre-train ESMs on three large-scale corpora, then evaluate across 26 downstream tasks spanning a broad range of domains. Our results demonstrate that ESMs have promising scaling behaviors with increasing model size and training data, and outperform GPTs on most downstream tasks. These findings highlight ESMs as a promising architecture for large-scale pre-training and general purpose problem solving. We fully release the model weights and training infrastructure to enable the community to completely reproduce and extend our results. GitHub: https://github.com/datamllab/openesm HuggingFace: https://huggingface.co/collections/guan-wang/openesm

papers.abstract: Selection bias in large language models (LLMs) can persist despite instructions to ignore presentation order or prompts that elicit reasoning. Recent efforts to reproduce Jev-style System One behavior have produced a growing family of models that predict probabilities directly over supplied candidates. Yet systematic comparisons of selection bias across Jev versions, Jev reproductions, and generative LLMs remain limited in multi-option tasks. This leaves a central question: does Jev-style decision structure reduce selection bias? We address this question with a simple test that shuffles options while keeping question and candidate content fixed. Across two Jev versions, twelve Jev reproductions, and six generative LLMs, we trace individual answers through eight presentations and compare them with fixed-order repetition. On our primary collection of 1,700 questions from two benchmarks, Jev's accuracy varies by less than two percentage points, yet its cumulative failure set expands by 27--29\% relative to the original order, with first failures continuing into the final presentation. This loss of initial successes is substantially larger than under fixed-order repetition, even for highly repeatable Jev reproductions. Nor does Jev show a general advantage over the LLM baselines in preserving correct choices. Aggregation offers limited protection: voting yields modest gains for Jev, while even unanimous answers are frequently wrong. These results expose a gap between repeatable decisions and decisions that remain correct across equivalent presentations, showing why stable accuracy alone cannot establish resistance to selection bias.
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
bullets: The study tests selection bias by shuffling options while keeping questions and candidates unchanged.
It compares two Jev versions, 12 Jev reproductions, and six generative LLMs across eight presentations and fixed-order repetition.

Jev does not generally preserve correct choices better than generative LLM baselines, and first failures continue appearing in later presentations.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes selection bias in LLMs and Jev-style System One models, demonstrating that stable accuracy does not necessarily imply resistance to selection bias across different presentations.
papers.title: Understanding Jev-Style System One Models: Does Structure Reduce Selection Bias?
papers.tldr: Jev-style decision structure does not reliably reduce selection bias: choices may be repeatable yet become wrong when option order changes.

papers.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) can generate multiple tokens in parallel, but often require many decoding rounds to complete a response. Efficient generation depends not only on which tokens are easy to predict, but also on how committing to them helps predict the remaining positions. A highly predictable token may provide little useful context, while revealing a less predictable token can help several other positions become predictable sooner. We propose dSpark, a new schedule distillation-based framework for learning when to commit tokens for faster diffusion language generation. To achieve this, we construct unmasking schedules that prioritize tokens whose reveal makes other positions easier to predict, reducing uncertainty earlier in decoding. We then distill these schedules into the model to enable faster parallel sampling, with a KL-divergence regularizer to help preserve generation quality. We extensively evaluate our approach across mathematical reasoning and code generation tasks. On GSM8K, our method achieves remarkable 10.12$\times$ and 5.12$\times$ speedups over the various baselines on LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-7B-Instruct, respectively, while maintaining superior task performance. Our code is available at https://github.com/VILA-Lab/dSpark.
bullets: Diffusion language models generate tokens in parallel but can still be slow because they require many decoding rounds.
The method prioritizes tokens whose unmasking makes other positions easier to predict, rather than only selecting individually predictable tokens.
These schedules are distilled into the model for faster parallel sampling, with KL-divergence regularization to preserve generation quality.
Evaluated on mathematical reasoning and code generation, dSpark reports up to 10.12× speedup on GSM8K while maintaining superior task performance.
The approach is demonstrated on LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-7B-Instruct.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes dSpark, a schedule distillation framework for diffusion language models (dLLMs) that learns when to commit tokens to achieve significant speedups in parallel sampling while maintaining quality.
papers.title: Learning When to Commit: Schedule Distillation for Fast Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: dSpark learns which tokens to reveal first so diffusion language models generate responses in fewer decoding rounds without sacrificing task performance.

papers.abstract: Deep research, or any use of large language models (LLMs) to read a large document collection and produce insights, requires synthesizing information from different sources. In this work, we find that LLMs produce long-form research reports that read as confident syntheses but which fail to accurately reflect the underlying documents. We call this failure smoothing. In collapsing diverse and potentially conflicting sources into a single narrative, the model discards the evidential "jaggedness" of its corpus and asserts conclusions more decisive than the citations can support. We introduce a claim level scoring pipeline, SmoothScore, to quantify this effect. Our pipeline extracts key conclusive claims from model generated reports, then finds evidence relevant to each claim and clusters that evidence along high level aspects. Finally, each claim is scored with respect to the evidence to quantify the degree of smoothing done by the agent. Across 7 systems and 4 datasets, we find that agents consistently produce stronger claims than warranted.
authors: Tiasa Singha Roy, Manya Wadhwa, Greg Durrett
bullets: The study examines how long-form LLM research reports can misrepresent their source documents.
“Smoothing” occurs when agents discard evidential nuance and make conclusions more decisive than the citations support.
SmoothScore extracts report claims, retrieves relevant evidence, clusters it by aspect, and scores each claim against that evidence.
Evaluated across 7 systems and 4 datasets, agents consistently produced claims stronger than warranted.
