papers.selection_reason: Introduces SmoothScore, a pipeline to quantify 'claim smoothing' in LLM research reports, identifying that models often assert stronger conclusions than the evidence supports.
papers.title: Quantifying Claim Smoothing by LLM Research Agents
papers.tldr: LLM research agents often turn mixed or conflicting evidence into overly confident claims, and SmoothScore quantifies this “claim smoothing.”

papers.abstract: Existing jailbreak attackers fall into two classes: static planners fix their single- or multi-turn adversarial plans in advance, remaining simple but losing sight of the victim's replies, wasting turns and limiting transferability; interactive generators read each victim reply to generate the next-turn attack but require in-loop evaluators for success signals or hints, incurring substantial costs and inflated performance. Bridging this gap, we propose SEMA-Auto, a sighted and efficient multi-turn attacker with autonomy, interacting with the victim model and terminating the session by itself upon success. To stabilize its behaviors and boost its capabilities, SEMA-Auto is trained in two stages. Synthetic bootstrap tuning installs the notion of attack targets and conforming decisions by fine-tuning the base model with bootstrapped trajectories. Decision-supervised reinforcement learning then optimizes two objectives jointly yet separately, reinforcing the attack with higher jailbreak reward while supervising the decision at each turn against an absolute target. Our method achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) attack success rates (ASR) across multiple datasets, victims, and judges, outperforming all static and interactive baselines, within almost the fewest turns, demonstrating both effectiveness and efficiency. For example, SEMA-Auto performs a $76.0\%$ ASR@1 within an average of $3.0$ turns against DeepSeek-V4-Flash on AdvBench, while the best static baseline is $54.8\%$ with fixed $7$ turns and the best interactive baseline is $43.8\%$ in $3.7$ turns. Against safety-hardened frontier models, GPT-oss-120B, GPT-5.4, Claude-Haiku-4.5, and GPT-6-Astra, our counter-trained attacker achieves an average $59.6\%$ ASR@1 on HarmBench, $13.8\%$ over prior SOTA. Our code is available at: https://github.com/microsoft/SEMA
authors: Mingqian Feng, Xiaodong Liu, Weiwei Yang, Chenliang Xu, Jialin Song, Qiyao Ma, Chengquan Guo, Carolyn Buractaon, Christopher White, Jianfeng Gao
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between fixed attack plans that ignore replies and interactive attackers that require costly in-loop evaluators.
Uses two-stage training: synthetic bootstrap tuning, followed by decision-supervised reinforcement learning for attack effectiveness and per-turn stopping decisions.
Autonomously terminates sessions upon success, improving efficiency and reducing unnecessary turns.
Reports state-of-the-art attack success across multiple datasets, victim models, and judges; on AdvBench, it achieves 76.0% ASR@1 in an average of 3.0 turns against DeepSeek-V4-Flash.
On HarmBench against safety-hardened frontier models, a counter-trained attacker reaches 59.6% average ASR@1, exceeding prior SOTA by 13.8 percentage points.

papers.title: SEMA-Auto: Sighted and Efficient Multi-Turn Attack with Autonomy
papers.tldr: SEMA-Auto is an autonomous multi-turn jailbreak attacker that adapts to victim replies, decides when to stop, and achieves strong attack success with few turns.

papers.abstract: For large language models (LLMs) and multimodal large language models (MLLMs), model-reported self-confidence is often miscalibrated, yet it may still be useful for efficient evaluation. At the same time, LLM-as-a-judge offers a scalable alternative to direct human auditing, but its practical benefit depends on calibration quality and inference cost. This paper develops a unified statistical framework for both evaluation routes under alternative sampling strategies. For direct auditing, confidence-stratified sampling is used to recover population accuracy from partially verified outputs without requiring calibrated confidence. Finite-sample uncertainty is characterized, and the analysis shows how highly uneven confidence strata affect audit efficiency and label allocation. For judge-assisted evaluation, the judge is modeled through sensitivity and false-positive rate, yielding an error-corrected estimator with calibration uncertainty. The two routes are then compared through human-label and total-cost efficiency boundaries. Experiments on MMLU-Pro and MMMU-Pro show that miscalibrated self-confidence can still support statistically valid stratified auditing. Under highly imbalanced confidence distributions, proportional allocation substantially reduces estimation error relative to equal-per-stratum allocation. For judge-assisted evaluation, only a small subset of target--verifier pairs satisfies the idealized human-label efficiency condition, and automated inference costs can further limit potential savings. These findings clarify the statistical and economic conditions under which confidence-guided auditing and automated verification are useful.
authors: Harine Choi (Texas A&M Transportation Institute, Texas A&M University System), Chenchen Kuai (Zachry Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Texas A&M University), Zihao Li (Department of Civil, Construction and Environmental Engineering, Marquette University), Jiwan Jiang (Zachry Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Texas A&M University), Yunlong Zhang (Zachry Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Texas A&M University), Zhiwen Fan (Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Texas A&M University), Zhengzhong Tu (Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Texas A&M University), Yang Zhou (Zachry Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Texas A&M University)
bullets: Confidence-stratified sampling estimates population accuracy from partially human-verified outputs without calibrated confidence.
Finite-sample analysis links uneven confidence strata to audit efficiency and label allocation.
Judge-assisted evaluation uses sensitivity and false-positive rates to form an error-corrected estimator with calibration uncertainty.
Experiments on MMLU-Pro and MMMU-Pro favor proportional over equal-per-stratum allocation under imbalanced confidence distributions.
Only a small subset of target–verifier pairs meets the idealized human-label efficiency condition; inference costs can erase savings.

papers.abstract: Conversational QA systems should fix errors when users push back and signal which answers to trust. We split each follow-up into its speech act (re-ask, agree, or challenge) and its payload (an answer string, correct or not), and measure four confidence signals on the same transcripts: verbalized confidence, length-normalized likelihood, a frozen hidden-state probe, and P(True). Answers change when the user supplies an answer string and almost never under the speech act alone: in every retained full-size cell, the correct answer converts at least four times as many wrong answers as re-asking or agreement. The four signals disagree. On Qwen2.5-7B the frozen probe rises with answer persistence rather than truth; this holds on held-out questions, with Llama-3-8B (cleaned answers) as support, but not on four other models. Among 81 Qwen2.5-7B errors that survive one re-ask, re-asking, a fresh chat, or abstain repair almost none, while a gold answer repairs 75-95%. In two preregistered replications, every repair rate without an answer string stays below 0.15; a larger post-hoc rerun excludes 0.15 except for the empty elicit. With BM25 TriviaQA evidence, sentences that contain the answer repair 67-76% of persistent errors versus at most 12% when they do not. An end-to-end contain-gate cuts harm on TriviaQA, but a deployable gate that does not know the gold answer repairs few errors.
bullets: Separating speech act from payload shows that re-asking or agreeing rarely changes answers; supplied answer strings drive correction.
Four confidence signals disagree, and Qwen2.5-7B’s frozen probe increases with answer persistence rather than correctness; this pattern does not generalize to all tested models.
For persistent errors, re-asking, fresh chats, and abstention repair almost none, whereas providing a gold answer repairs 75–95%.
Evidence containing the answer repairs 67–76% of persistent TriviaQA errors, versus at most 12% for evidence without it.
An answer-containment gate reduces harm, but a deployable gate without gold-answer access repairs few errors.

papers.abstract: JEV decision models pair a language model backbone with a lightweight scoring head to select among natural-language options. Direct selection compares candidate answers within one request, whereas entailment reranking evaluates each candidate in a separate natural language inference (NLI) request over fixed relation options. We examine whether the readout and adaptation choices used for direct selection remain effective for cross-request reranking. We combine a mean-span readout with selective backbone adaptation. Mean-span pooling replaces the option-ending pointer with an average of the contextualized states inside each NLI option, without adding head parameters. Selective adaptation retains low-rank updates in attention and gated DeltaNet projections while removing feed-forward adapters. On MC11, which averages accuracy over eleven reranking configurations from seven sources, selective adaptation improves NeoHorse-1-4B accuracy over the all-module baseline while cutting trainable parameters by more than half, and mean-span pooling yields further consistent gains at the same parameter count.

papers.abstract: An offline language-based support tool is presented to assist pilot training and tactical decision-making in air combat operations. The system, named MATE (Mission Assistant for Training and Evaluation), applies retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to answer natural language questions using content extracted from doctrinal and tactical manuals. Built entirely with open-source components, it performs text preprocessing, embedding generation, semantic search, and language generation locally, ensuring full offline functionality. The tool was evaluated by three Brazilian Air Force fighter pilots, who rated the answers produced with three open-weight language models (Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen 2.5 14B, and Mistral NeMo 12B) to five tactical questions derived from a publicly available air combat manual. Average ratings ranged from 4.00 to 4.40 on a five-point scale, with Mistral NeMo 12B obtaining the highest score, and the pilots rated the response time of the tool as fully adequate compared to manual search. The relevance of the retrieved content was identified as the main point for improvement. Potential applications are discussed in onboard mission systems, flight simulators, and training environments.

papers.abstract: Skills provide agents with reusable experience to guide future decisions without modifying the underlying model. However, coding trajectories are often entangled with task- and repository-specific contexts, making it challenging to distill procedural skills that generalize across diverse coding environments. To address this challenge, we present Hierarchical Skill Evolution (HSE), which progressively distills procedural knowledge from coding trajectories through hierarchical evidence aggregation. HSE first extracts task-level evidence from individual trajectories, then aggregates recurring evidence within the same repository to form repository-specific skill candidates, and finally consolidates consistent patterns across repositories into transferable skills across repositories. The evolution is driven by an external writer-evaluator loop that generates and assesses skills while keeping the underlying coding model frozen. The loop externally updates the writer and evaluator policies to improve subsequent skill generation and assessment. This hierarchy progressively filters task-specific details while preserving procedures that generalize across diverse coding environments. Successful trajectories yield reusable guidance for future tasks, while failed trajectories reveal recurring failure modes that guide avoidance and recovery. We evaluate HSE on SWE-bench Verified and DeepSWE, using GLM-5.2 across Pi and Claude Code harnesses and GPT-5.5 and Opus 4.8 with Pi. Across both benchmarks, 10 skills evolved solely from SWE-Gym improve coding performance across all evaluated settings, demonstrating transfer across benchmarks, coding models, and agent harnesses. We further evolve the skill library from target-benchmark trajectories without verifier feedback, relying solely on the learned evaluator for candidate assessment and achieving additional gains through benchmark-tailored skills.

papers.abstract: Modeling the latent, multi-step reasoning processes of learners is a core challenge for adaptive tutoring systems, which often rely on simple right/wrong answers rather than understanding how students think. Instantiated here for grammatical reasoning, this study introduces a diagnostic framework that makes students' step-by-step problem-solving visible by analyzing their action sequences in an interactive learning game. The framework computes five interpretable strategy dimensions (e.g., systematic error correction, random guessing), estimates coordination demand from task structure and behavioral patterns, and classifies reasoning into four distinct states. Analyzing 36,234 interactions from 234 students working on 42 morphosyntactic exercises, we found that reasoning strategies vary primarily by context rather than stable traits (intraclass correlation = 0.14), and students show high persistence in unproductive states; specifically, 74.6% of failures driven by high coordination demand (rather than simple knowledge gaps) are followed by another failure without intervention. Our early warning model predicts validation success with strong accuracy (AUC = 0.826 using strategy patterns alone; 0.902 with additional sequential context) while avoiding circular reliance on current error counts. These findings demonstrate that making latent reasoning processes visible enables earlier, more targeted scaffolding that responds to how students are thinking rather than simply whether they succeed. While demonstrated in language learning, the framework provides a generalizable, interpretable architecture for diagnosing complex, structured reasoning in any domain.
authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre

papers.abstract: Language models are increasingly considered for clinical decision support, where their answers should be grounded in clinical evidence and remain robust to irrelevant information. Prior work shows that a single irrelevant sentence can lower the accuracy of medical models, but not where inside the model its effect can be removed, or how to do so without knowing which sentence it is. We find that blocking attention to a known distractor restores the answer, whereas head masking can suppress correct answers. We also show that the model's hidden states mark the distractor as the sentence that least fits the case even when the model follows it. To remove a distractor's effect without knowing which sentence it is, we propose EXCISE, an inference-time method that blocks the sentence most influencing the answer, but only if the model's hidden states mark it as inconsistent with the case. On MedQA-TD (MedQA with Targeted Distractors), a benchmark we construct in which each distractor targets a specific wrong option, EXCISE gains 16.7-22.8 accuracy points at a 1.5-2.1-point cost on the same questions without distractors, outperforming prompting, rewriting, and steering baselines for all three models. Its gains extend to MedDistractQA and BiasMedQA, as well as chain-of-thought generation.
authors: Yerim Hong, Sohyun Son, Heeseung Chung, Mujeen Sung

papers.abstract: Looped Transformers increase computation per token by repeatedly applying a shared backbone, offering a way to improve language modeling and downstream task performance at a fixed backbone parameter count. However, each loop depends on the preceding loop, so increasing recurrent depth also increases decoding latency. Existing approaches include Parallel Loop Transformers, which reduce latency by overlapping loop computation across token positions, but yield rapidly diminishing marginal accuracy gains at larger depths. To address this challenge, we introduce LoopFold, which folds computation at multiple recurrent depths into parallel batches for the same token prefix. A lightweight predictor estimates inputs to later loops so they can start before earlier loops finish. A corrector then refines the outputs of these later loops using newly available results from earlier loops. All components are trained jointly using only the final next-token prediction loss. In experiments with 1.4B models, deeper LoopFold configurations achieve progressively higher average zero-shot accuracy across eight tasks, rising from 53.41% to 56.38%. Vanilla looped models and PLT show limited gains over the same depth range. Compared with a nine-loop vanilla model, LoopFold uses five sequential stages and additional parallel computation to reduce decoding latency by 46%.
authors: Feichen Song, Boyi Zeng, Yiqin Hao, Shixiang Song, He Li, Yizhou Yang, Zitong Wang, Yifan Liu, Ziwei He, Zhouhan Lin
bullets: Looped Transformers improve modeling capacity through repeated use of a shared backbone, but sequential loops increase latency.

papers.tldr: LoopFold reduces the decoding-latency cost of deeper Looped Transformers by predicting and correcting later recurrent loops in parallel.

papers.abstract: Looped Transformers offer a parameter-efficient approach to language modeling by repeatedly applying a shared backbone. Vanilla looped Transformers use each backbone output directly as the input to the next iteration. These outputs may contain information useful several iterations later, but retaining it across the loop depends entirely on the single hidden state. We introduce StateLoop, which maintains one additional persistent state per token to retain information across iterations. At each iteration, a learned gate controls how much of the previous state is retained and how much information from the backbone output is incorporated. The updated state is projected back and added to the backbone output for subsequent iterations and final prediction. This design reduces Pile perplexity and improves average accuracy across eight zero-shot tasks over Vanilla Looped. Its perplexity advantage over Vanilla Looped grows with trained loop depth, consistent with persistent state becoming increasingly useful as recurrent computation deepens.
authors: Feichen Song, Boyi Zeng, He Li, Shixiang Song, Yiqin Hao, Zitong Wang, Yizhou Yang, Yifan Liu, Ziwei He, Zhouhan Lin
bullets: Vanilla looped Transformers rely on a single hidden state, which may lose information needed in later iterations.
StateLoop maintains an additional persistent state for each token across loop iterations.
A learned gate balances retaining prior state with incorporating new backbone output information.
The updated state is projected back into the backbone output for later iterations and final prediction.
It reduces Pile perplexity and improves average accuracy across eight zero-shot tasks; its perplexity benefit grows with loop depth.

papers.abstract: Both models and minds not only encode features that describe an entity, but can specifically represent which features of that entity are relevant for a given context. This core capability underlies in-context learning in language models and a variety of cognitive phenomena in minds, yet it is unclear how intelligent systems identify and promote relevant features. In this work, we propose Amortized Direction Accentuation (ADA), an algorithmic hypothesis that provides an explanation for how relevance is determined in the context of few-shot concept induction --- the ability to infer a latent concept from a small number of positive examples. Under ADA, concept induction proceeds by forming a summary representation of the examples in a feature space that is shaped by amortized knowledge about which features tend to be useful for finding commonalities between items. We investigate and validate ADA in language models using a few-shot concept induction task. This work provides a novel perspective on the mechanisms supporting contextualization in language models and a promising hypothesis for a core aspect of cognition.
authors: Michael A. Lepori, Laila Johnston, Aalok Sathe, Zhuonan Yang, Roman Feiman, Ellie Pavlick
bullets: Addresses how models determine which entity features matter in a given context.
Models concept induction as summarizing positive examples in a feature space shaped by prior knowledge of useful commonalities.
Introduces ADA as an algorithmic hypothesis for relevance determination.
Investigates and validates ADA in language models on a few-shot concept induction task.
Offers a perspective on contextualization in language models and a hypothesis about a related cognitive mechanism.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Few-Shot Concept Induction and Amortized Direction Accentuation. (Left) Given a set of support items, a concept induction task requires a learner to infer the concept that generated those items from a potentially infinite set of candidates. Inferring a latent concept enables a learner to produce novel instances of that concept. (Right) Amortized Direction Accentuation (ADA) proposes that learners produce representations of inferred concepts based on an aggregation of the support set (visualized here as a prototype representation), which is then biased by an accentuation matrix that amortizes the learner’s experience about which features tend to be helpful when assessing commonalities between items (e.g., a model might learn that it is typically more important to represent whether an item is a bird than to represent whether the item has a vowel for its second letter).

Figure 2: Performance on the concept list task across language models. We measure the boost in token probability due to the presence of a support set. Across models, tokens that belong to the latent concept that generated the support set consistently receive a greater change in log probability than tokens that do not belong to the concept.

Figure 5: Leave-One-Concept-Out Behavioral analysis results. We model the context-induced change in token probability using a score function that accounts for feature accentuation (ADA) or uncontextualized embedding geometry (Generic). We find that accounting for feature accentuation usually, but not always results in a stronger account of LM output behavior. (Significance markers according to a paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test over concepts; ∗ = p < .05, ∗∗ = p < .01, ∗ ∗ ∗ = p < .001)

Figure 4: Regression analysis results. To distinguish between the alternative hypotheses, we fit rotation matrices (Generic), ridge regressions (ADA), or MLPs (Ad-Hoc) to predict context displacement vectors from the average embeddings of support items. We compute a noise ceiling that captures variation due to ordering effects. (Left) For held-out support sets, ADA is robustly supported across layers, achieving >80% of the upper bound while outperforming the Generic Feature alternative and matching the Ad-Hoc alternative. All alternatives beat a baseline that uses raw prototype representations, and another baseline that shuffles (prototype, displacement vector) pairs independently. Shaded region indicates SEM. (Right) This pattern holds when entire concepts are held-out (all alternatives are significantly different at p < .001 according to a paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test over concepts).

Figure 3: Visualization of context displacement vectors as the number of support examples grows. The sport vector denotes the mean context displacement vector over 20 support sets. Context displacement vectors are placed end-to-end for visualization purposes, so an optimal vector for the concept is parallel to the sport vector. When the concept list begins with canonical sports, the context displacement vectors quickly align with the sport vector. When the list begins with less canonical sports, it takes several examples before the context displacement vector aligns. Axes are the top 2 principal components of a matrix of mean displacement vectors for all concepts in the dataset.

Figure 7: Steering with average context displacement vectors on gemma-2-2B. Steering in the direction of average context displacement vectors boosts the probability of held-out in-concept items while suppressing out-ofconcept items. Steering in the negative direction does the opposite, and steering in control directions does not have a large impact.
Figure 6: RSMs created from concept vectors and context displacement vectors at a middle layer of gemma-2-2B. Individual context displacement vectors approximate the rich geometry of concept vectors.

papers.abstract: Mental health research on social media has been dominated by English-language datasets and DSM-5-centered resources, limiting cross-lingual and cross-cultural understanding of online mental health expression. We introduce MATCHA, the first Chinese multi-disorder mental health dataset that links disorder-specific Weibo Super-Topic communities with users' broader public timelines. MATCHA covers seven DSM-5 disorders and a control group, comprising 46,025 cohort-level users and 1.8 million posts. The dataset distinguishes users with explicit self-disclosure evidence from broader disorder-related participants through an LLM-assisted annotation pipeline, and is released in a rigorously de-identified, controlled-access format. Using MATCHA, we analyze behavioral, linguistic, symptom-related, and life-event-related patterns across disorders, and conduct cross-lingual comparisons with Twitter-STMHD. Our analyses show that Weibo Super-Topics function as concentrated spaces for affective and health-related expression, while cross-platform differences between Weibo and Twitter often exceed cross-disorder variation. MATCHA provides a new resource for community-aware and cross-lingual mental health NLP research.

Analyzes behavioral, linguistic, symptom, and life-event patterns and compares Weibo with Twitter-STMHD.
Finds that platform differences often exceed cross-disorder variation, while Super-Topics concentrate affective and health-related expression.

papers.abstract: Automated fake news detection is vital on social media, where fake news is easily rewritten to fool detectors. However, existing approaches typically rely on superficial writing cues or single-style text rewrites, resulting in poor robustness under diverse cosmetic modifications. We construct MANTIS-Bench, a multi-axis presentation-attack benchmark that pairs original news with rewritten views across writing style, emotional expression, and dissemination framing. We further propose MANTIS, an instance-adaptive adversarial framework enabling dynamic worst-case training tailored to each news article with zero inference-time overhead. This reframes fake news defense from heuristic format smoothing into targeted, fact-invariant credibility assessment. Experiments on MANTIS-Bench show that MANTIS reduces the Union Attack Success Rate (UASR) by 3.55 percentage points relative to SheepDog on GossipCop and consistently outperforms prior single-axis defenses on Macro-F1 while maintaining competitive clean accuracy, demonstrating the effectiveness of multi-axis and instance-adaptive worst-case training.
authors: Dexin Liu, Fan Yang, Zimu Wang, Xunfei Zhu, Bolin Ren, Bingyan Zhang, Wei Wang, Qi Chen
bullets: MANTIS-Bench tests fact-preserving transformations across writing style, emotional expression, and dissemination framing.
MANTIS performs dynamic worst-case training tailored to each news article.

papers.abstract: Constrained decoding guarantees that Large Language Models (LLMs) produce outputs conforming to predefined formats, but is often assumed to inherently degrade reasoning. We examine this assumption through a taxonomy of three constraint types: \emph{format constraints}, which enforce output structure; \emph{validity constraints}, which mask invalid answer; and \emph{reasoning constraints}, which restrict reasoning trajectories. We theoretically show that appropriate constraints can preserve or improve performance by eliminating invalid paths. Across four model families and eleven open-source models, causal ablations on diverse benchmarks using state-of-the-art constrained decoding strategies reveal that apparent performance degradation largely stems from non-equivalent prompting and output formats rather than from decoder-level masking. Meanwhile, validity constraints improve reliability and extractability by eliminating invalid answers, while reasoning constraints can improve reasoning and, consequently, accuracy when they enforce beneficial trajectories. These findings show that the impact of constrained decoding depends on the type of constraint and the output space it removes. Our code is available.
authors: Ngoc Trinh Hung Nguyen, Alonso Silva, Armen Aghasaryan, Mehwish Alam
bullets: The study distinguishes format, validity, and reasoning constraints.
Theoretical analysis shows suitable constraints can preserve or improve performance by eliminating invalid paths.
Across four model families and eleven open-source models, apparent degradation mainly came from mismatched prompting and output formats, not decoder masking.
Validity constraints improve answer reliability and extractability, while reasoning constraints can improve reasoning and accuracy when they enforce beneficial trajectories.

papers.abstract: Controlling personality in large language models is important for building conversational agents that can be customized to different users and interaction settings. However, existing personality control methods often face a tradeoff between strong trait expression and natural dialogue generation. We introduce FATE-5, Faithful Alignment of Trait Expression for the Big Five, a two-stage framework that separates personality encoding from naturalness alignment. FATE-5 first learns continuous soft prompt representations of Big Five profiles using dialogue supervision and an auxiliary survey objective. It then improves dialogue naturalness through preference alignment based on both dialogue quality and personality agreement. Across three language model backbones, FATE-5 maintains strong trait expression while achieving substantially higher dialogue naturalness than other trait-strong methods. On held-out questionnaires, it achieves monotonicity correlations of 0.97-0.99 and recovery RMSE of 8.9-12.4, substantially improving over the evaluated baselines. These results demonstrate effective continuous personality control while maintaining natural conversational behavior.

papers.abstract: Objective: The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) in healthcare has opened new possibilities for AI-assisted clinical decision-making; however, safe and effective deployment remains challenging because of hallucination and domain misalignment. This study introduces DocTalk, a doctor-assistive question-answering (QA) system designed to generate concise, chart-grounded responses from de-identified discharge summaries. Methods: We developed a high-fidelity data generation pipeline that produces 500 clinically relevant QA pairs through sentence-level decomposition, chain-of-thought-guided question formulation, and expert review. Six open-source LLMs, including three general-purpose and three biomedical models, were evaluated before and after parameter-efficient instruction tuning using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). The framework integrates prompt engineering, in-context learning, and medically aligned evaluation to support factual and interpretable responses. Results: On DocTalk-QA, instruction tuning produced consistent improvements across lexical, semantic, and clinical fidelity metrics. The best-performing tuned model, Llama-3-Med42-8B, achieved ROUGE-L = 0.40, BERTScore-F1 = 0.76, and UMLS-F1 = 0.49. To examine external generalization beyond the DocTalk-QA dataset, the two best-performing models, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Llama-3-Med42-8B, were evaluated on PubMedQA before and after instruction tuning. Accuracy improved from 0.931 to 0.977 for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and from 0.935 to 0.943 for Llama-3-Med42-8B. Conclusion: DocTalk was deployed as a secure web-based platform for interactive EHR querying. These findings suggest that clinically grounded instruction tuning can improve medical QA performance and support practical clinical decision support.

Tuning improved lexical, semantic, and clinical-fidelity metrics; the best model, Llama-3-Med42-8B, achieved ROUGE-L 0.40, BERTScore-F1 0.76, and UMLS-F1 0.49.
External PubMedQA evaluation also showed post-tuning accuracy gains for the two tested models; DocTalk was deployed as a secure web platform.

papers.abstract: Language models now answer questions alongside other claims: a note in the system prompt, a message from another agent, their own earlier answer. We ask what it takes to talk a model out of an answer it gets right on its own, and separate three factors that earlier studies vary together: where the advice sits in the prompt, who is said to have written it, and what the model has already written. On Qwen3.5-27B and four-option MMLU-Pro items, with the rest of the advice held fixed in each comparison, we find three things. First, position matters far more than the API channel, in opposite directions for a bare claim and an argument: a bare "the answer is X" does most harm just before the model answers, while the same claim with a false rationale does most harm before the question, where it raises error on items the model otherwise almost never misses from 1% to 67%; moving the claim between the system message and the user message at the same position changes error by a few points. Second, attributing the note to an authority rather than to another participant, and phrasing it assertively, each raise error by 10-27 points, while the two authorities we tested differ by under two. Third, replaying a correct worked answer before the advice protects it whether the text is shown as the model's own or as someone else's, and the same replay keeps wrong answers from being corrected by a bare correct note. The position result replicates under an independently written prompt. Code, items and all result tables are released at https://github.com/coolkillercat/safety.
bullets: The study separates prompt position, stated authorship, and the model’s prior answer while holding advice fixed.

A bare incorrect claim is most harmful immediately before the answer; an incorrect claim with false reasoning is most harmful before the question, increasing error from 1% to 67% on otherwise easy items.
Moving the same claim between system and user messages at the same position changes error by only a few points.
Authority attribution and assertive wording each increase error by 10–27 points, while the tested authorities differ by under two points.

Replaying a correct worked answer protects it from misleading advice, but also prevents a bare correct note from fixing an existing wrong answer; results replicate with an independently written prompt.

papers.abstract: Knowledge editing aims to update outdated or incorrect knowledge in large language models without full retraining. Existing parameter-editing methods remain limited for long-sequence knowledge: single-point editors provide insufficient coverage for extended targets, while fixed chunk-based editors distribute editing effort uniformly across rigid predefined windows, failing to prioritize difficult, information-dense tokens. In this work, we show that token entropy is closely associated with both editing difficulty and semantic importance: high-entropy regions are harder to edit and often contain key factual content. Motivated by this observation, we propose DynEdit, a dynamic framework for long-sequence knowledge editing. DynEdit uses token-level entropy to guide non-uniform sliding, increasing the coverage of difficult high-entropy regions, and further applies entropy-guided token-level optimization to strengthen updates on information-dense tokens within each editing window. Experiments on three benchmarks and two backbone models show that DynEdit consistently outperforms competitive baselines across diverse long-form editing settings, achieving gains of up to +14.0 BLEU points on challenging paraphrase queries and near-saturated semantic scores on several diverse knowledge domains.
authors: Jinhu Fu, Yan Bai, Yihang Lou, Li Sun, Jiahong Wu, Xiangxiang Chu, Sen Su
bullets: Targets limited coverage from single-point editors and inefficient uniform allocation from fixed chunk-based methods.
Uses token-level entropy to drive dynamic, non-uniform sliding across long sequences.
Applies entropy-guided token-level optimization within each editing window.
Evaluated on three benchmarks and two backbone models, with consistent improvements over competitive baselines.
Reports gains of up to 14.0 BLEU points on challenging paraphrase queries and near-saturated semantic scores in several domains.

papers.abstract: How do later loops in a pretrained looped language model repair two-hop retrieval? We study Ouro-1.4B and Ouro-2.6B by transplanting attention queries between loops at the same layer, head and final prompt position. On synthetic in-context questions, injecting the layer-indexed collection of loop-3 queries throughout loop 1 rescues 90% and 97% of questions answered incorrectly at loop 1 and correctly at loop 3, versus 24% and 21% for shuffled donors. The rescue also holds under greedy generation in Ouro-2.6B; in Ouro-1.4B it is limited to four-candidate ranking. Crossed donor-recipient swaps favor retrieval through the donor's bridge entity over copying its answer, although a substantial positional component remains in Ouro-2.6B. Late keys and values rescue far fewer targets. Freezing queries at their loop-1 values also damages two-hop accuracy more than a matched question that supplies the bridge. On natural questions, rescue is smaller and replicates only in Ouro-2.6B, and crossed swaps do not establish bridge redirection. These results identify a transferable collection of late-loop queries that supports bridge-conditioned retrieval on synthetic scenes; they do not locate where the bridge is computed or establish a single-vector handoff.
bullets: Transplanting loop-3 queries into loop 1 rescues many cases that fail early but succeed later: 90% in Ouro-1.4B and 97% in Ouro-2.6B, versus 24% and 21% with shuffled donors.
Crossed donor-recipient swaps favor retrieval via the donor’s bridge entity rather than copying its answer, though positional effects remain in Ouro-2.6B.
Late keys and values produce far fewer rescues; freezing queries at loop-1 values also harms two-hop accuracy.
Greedy-generation rescue holds in Ouro-2.6B but is limited to four-candidate ranking in Ouro-1.4B.
On natural questions, the effect is smaller and replicates only in Ouro-2.6B; the study does not identify where the bridge is computed.

papers.abstract: Tabular data is widely used in scientific applications, where complex layouts, including multi-level headers, merged cells, captions, and footnotes, make information extraction difficult. This is particularly important in pharmacokinetics (PK), where values must be correctly associated with the drug, species, dose, administration route, unit, and experimental condition. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods such as Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) reduce adaptation cost but do not explicitly incorporate relationships between table values and surrounding headers. We introduce HARP-LoRA, a hierarchy-conditioned rank projection method for low-rank adaptation in scientific table understanding. HARP-LoRA extends projected LoRA by constructing token-specific intrinsic representations from the row- and column-header hierarchies of each data token. These representations condition the low-rank down-projection, incorporating hierarchical context while keeping the pretrained model and random projection tensors frozen. We evaluate HARP-LoRA on 950 manually annotated PK tables from 587 scientific articles and on WikiTableQuestions (WikiTQ) using Llama~3.2 3B, Llama~3.1 8B, and Gemma~3 27B. With Llama~3.1 8B, HARP-LoRA achieves a PK F1-score of 57.64\% and WikiTQ accuracy of 53.15\%, improving over LoRA by 1.42 and 6.56 points, respectively. With Gemma~3 27B, it achieves the best PK F1-score of 70.63\% and WikiTQ accuracy of 56.87\%. These results use only 172K, 197K, and 547K trainable parameters, far fewer than LoRA and TableLoRA. Overall, conditioning lightweight adapters on table-header hierarchies improves extraction from scientific tables and reasoning over flatter general-domain tables while maintaining parameter efficiency. Code is available at: https://github.com/hosseinsholehrasa/HARP-LoRA
authors: Hossein Sholehrasa, Mohammadhossein Amini, Doina Caragea, Remya Ampadi Ramachandran, Dan Wu, Zihang Shi, Zelin Li, Lindsey Hulbert, Eder Martinez, Xuan Xu, Majid Jaberi-Douraki

Using Llama 3.1 8B, it improves over LoRA by 1.42 PK F1 points and 6.56 WikiTQ accuracy points.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are neural networks trained on huge text collections to generate text by predicting what comes next. Engineers using ChatGPT and other generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools need a clear picture of what training changes and prompts add. The article starts with the Transformer, which connects words in context, and pre-training, where models learn to predict text. It then explains how fine-tuning adapts models to requests, with reinforcement learning from human feedback using human answer rankings. Next, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) supplies documents, while chain-of-thought prompting encourages intermediate steps and agents use tools. FlashAttention lowers training and running costs by reducing data movement during attention; quantized low-rank adaptation (QLoRA) saves fine-tuning memory. Readers get a life cycle figure and tables comparing methods and their limits. A short checklist for judging LLM evaluation claims flags test material in training (data contamination) and model-based grading (LLM-as-a-judge). It also covers very long inputs (long context) and hallucination, meaning false or unsupported claims. Check factual accuracy separately from whether an answer sounds helpful.
bullets: Introduces Transformers and pre-training as the foundations of next-token text generation.
Explains fine-tuning, reinforcement learning from human feedback, RAG, chain-of-thought prompting, and tool-using agents.
Covers efficiency techniques including FlashAttention and QLoRA, plus long-context use.
Provides tables, a life-cycle overview, and a checklist for evaluating claims.
Warns about data contamination, LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, and the need to check factual accuracy separately from helpfulness.

Figure 1. The life cycle of a large language model. Pre-training builds a base model from large text collections; post-training adapts it to follow instructions and preferences; inference-time augmentation adds reasoning, retrieval and tool use. Evaluation and safety checks apply at every stage, and efficient infrastructure underlies all of them.

papers.abstract: In formal systems such as Lean 4, efficiently finding answers to mathematical problems and generating verifiable proofs is an important task in automated mathematical reasoning. In the traditional way where an upstream solver provides multiple candidate answers, the common workflow requires searching for proofs for each candidate separately, incurring redundant computational cost. To this end, we propose a joint proof framework that integrates candidate answer selection, answer supplementation, and formal proof generation into a unified reasoning process. At its core is a trained prover that selects given or proposes new answers and generates a proof for at least one answer in a single call. Joint proof can also reuse generated proofs to check for faithfulness errors. For problems with a unique answer, if two distinct answers both obtain verifiable proofs under the same formal statement, this confirms the statement does not faithfully preserve the original problem semantics. On MATH-500, AMC 2023, and AIME 2024/2025/2026, our framework achieves the same formal proof success rate as per-candidate proof generation with about one sixth of the token cost, and identifies at least 6.1% of the formalized statements as unfaithful without requiring additional judges. Our model and code are available at https://github.com/Linppz/Gobble-Prover.
authors: Pengzhen Lin, Ke Zhang, Maziar Raissi, Zhouxing Shi
bullets: Addresses redundant proof searches when an upstream solver supplies multiple candidate answers.
Uses a trained prover to select existing answers, supplement new ones, and produce a verifiable proof in one call.

papers.abstract: Understanding how individual token choices affect reasoning length is important for characterizing reasoning models. Building on prior findings that changing the first reasoning token (hereafter, the first token) can substantially alter reasoning length, we focus on this initial choice to investigate how its influence operates during subsequent generation. One possibility is that the first token changes the early text that follows, which in turn affects reasoning length. However, replacing only the first token of an existing reasoning prefix and resuming generation substantially changes the remaining reasoning length, even though all other prefix tokens are unchanged. To trace this persistent influence, we compare next-token distributions while varying only the first token and find that sensitivity is concentrated at a small set of generation positions. Blocking attention from these positions to the first token reduces the length gap between first-token conditions. Using next-token distributions from a different first-token condition at these positions also substantially changes subsequent reasoning length. Together, these findings suggest that attention to the first token at a few sensitive positions helps sustain its length effect, illustrating how a local token choice persistently influences a sequence-level outcome.
authors: Ruochen Liu, Hao Yan, Ziluowen Luo, Senzhang Wang, Sihong Xie
bullets: Changing only the first token can substantially alter the remaining reasoning length, even with the rest of the prefix fixed.
The study compares next-token distributions across different first-token conditions to trace this influence.
Sensitivity to the first token is concentrated at a small number of generation positions.
Blocking or replacing first-token-dependent information at these positions reduces or changes the resulting length differences.
The findings suggest a local token choice can sustain a sequence-level effect through later attention interactions.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates the persistent influence of the first token on reasoning length in LLMs, analyzing attention mechanisms and next-token distributions to understand sequence-level outcomes.
papers.title: Beyond the Opening: Tracing the First Token's Persistent Influence on Reasoning Length
papers.tldr: A reasoning model’s first generated token can persistently influence total reasoning length through attention at a few sensitive later positions.

papers.abstract: The stance expressed in responses from retrieval-augmented generation systems is significantly influenced by the stance distribution of the retrieved materials. Existing research on knowledge poisoning has primarily targeted factual errors. In contrast, this study focuses on injection attacks in which the facts are correct but the stance on a controversial issue is one-sided. At a mean topic-level poisoning share of 18.9% within the post-injection ProCon documents, all four generation models from different vendors exhibited stance shifts aligned with the poisoning direction; across four concentration levels, the shifts increased monotonically. This paper proposes a Stance-Balancing Middleware positioned between the retriever and the generator. It consists of stance detection, fixed balancing (2 supporting + 2 opposing + 1 neutral), and a debiasing prompt, without introducing additional large language model calls. Across all eight concentration-direction settings, the complete method reduced the magnitude of stance deviation by an estimated 0.106 to 0.350; the six settings at poisoning shares of 11.9%-18.9% remained significant after Holm adjustment (adjusted p <= 0.009). In the cross-model experiment, all eight model-direction combinations moved along the stance axis in the corrective direction, and seven of eight showed a clearly detected reduction in absolute distance from 0. In the concentration sweep, the post-defense intervals included 0 in all eight settings, while the cross-model pro-poisoning results retained small positive residual point estimates of +0.045 to +0.063. For 20 candidate documents, stance detection took approximately 1.5% of the median generation time on a single GPU and approximately 16% on CPU.
authors: Puyuan Yang, Shaoxuan Dong, Liujie Wu, Xiaochun Cheng, Bo Li
bullets: At a mean poisoning share of 18.9%, all four tested generation models shifted toward the injected stance, with larger shifts at higher concentrations.
The defense detects document stances, selects a fixed mix of 2 supporting, 2 opposing, and 1 neutral documents, and applies a debiasing prompt without extra LLM calls.
Across eight concentration-direction settings, stance deviation decreased by an estimated 0.106–0.350; six settings remained statistically significant after Holm adjustment.
All eight cross-model conditions moved in the corrective direction, and seven showed a clearly detected reduction in absolute stance distance from neutral.
Residual pro-poisoning estimates of +0.045 to +0.063 remained in the cross-model experiment; stance detection added about 1.5% of median generation time on GPU and 16% on CPU.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses stance poisoning in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and proposes a Stance-Balancing Middleware to mitigate bias in generated responses.
papers.title: Factual Yet One-Sided: Stance Poisoning and Evidence Balancing in Retrieval-Augmented Generation

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized Artificial Intelligence (AI) by their extraordinary capabilities, like contextual understanding, few-shot/zero-shot learning, code generation, ability to reason and problem-solving. Recent studies have shown immense work on LLMs. Yet, there is limited work on the thorough taxonomy of LLMs. This study would showcase a detailed classification of LLMs, starting with the earlier models like BERT and leading to LLMs like GPT, Gemini, Claude and Grok. We would delve into topics like datasets used to train LLMs, computational power used during training, their hardware specifications, architecture and parameters. Further, we would also look at the limitations, computational challenges and open problems as well. This study would primarily focus on the timeline of LLMs, signifying their growth over the period. Findings reveal a clear pattern: models that optimize the ratio between architectural complexity and data quality exhibit stronger reasoning stability and better alignment, without proportionally increasing the computational load. This desired balance between scaling and sustainability is the defining characteristic of the current generation of AI.
bullets: Provides a timeline and taxonomy covering models such as BERT, GPT, Gemini, Claude, and Grok.
Examines training datasets, computational requirements, hardware specifications, architectures, and parameterization.
Reviews limitations, computational challenges, and open problems in LLM design.
Argues that balancing architectural complexity with data quality is associated with more stable reasoning and better alignment without proportional increases in computation.
Highlights scaling–sustainability balance as a defining direction for current AI development.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models(LLMs) have shown strong performance on tasks with verifiable answers, but many real-world queries involve subjectivity, disagreement, and conflicting evidence. Most existing benchmarks for such queries remain English-centric, overlooking the vast diversity of perspectives held by users worldwide. To systematically study how LLM perspectives vary across languages, we curate PerspectivesQA, a manually verified multilingual dataset of globally contested topics covering 18 languages, and propose ROOTS, a framework that profiles linguistic, perspective, and framing diversity. We evaluate a diverse set of eight models covering both open-source and proprietary families at varying scales, establishing that LLMs hedge their answers in English but commit to positions in lower-resource languages. Larger models maintain a more consistent cross-lingual worldview, while smaller models are more easily swayed. All models also exhibit high sensitivity to minor surface-level input variations, producing notable stance even in larger models.
authors: Wiem Ben Rim, Yao Lu, Pontus Stenetorp, Emine Yilmaz
bullets: Introduces PerspectivesQA, a manually verified dataset of contested topics spanning 18 languages.
Proposes ROOTS to measure linguistic, perspective, and framing diversity in LLM responses.
Across eight open-source and proprietary models, English answers hedge more while lower-resource-language answers commit more strongly.
Larger models show more consistent cross-lingual worldviews; smaller models are more easily swayed.
All evaluated models remain sensitive to minor wording changes, including larger ones.

papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly being used in different stages of scientific knowledge production, including the suggestion of references. These models can operate at different levels of reasoning effort and provide summaries of their reasoning processes. This raises two questions: Does increasing reasoning effort improve the verifiability of generated references, and do the resulting reasoning summaries reveal how the model's behavior changes with greater effort? We examined summaries from GPT-5.5 as it generated scholarly references for 1,000 papers under paired low- and high-effort settings. Generated references were matched to external bibliographic records, and reasoning summaries were scored for four predefined features and explored for additional features discovered by GPT-5.5. High effort increased the mean paper-level resolver-verified reference rate from 78.3% to 84.8%, and produced longer reasoning summaries. All four predefined features received higher scores under high effort. The discovered features changed less uniformly: some appeared equally often in both conditions, whereas others were more common under high effort. Within each effort condition, neither feature set showed a consistent increase in verification rates with higher scores.
authors: Melika Mobini, Andres Algaba, Vincent Ginis
bullets: The study compares low- and high-effort GPT-5.5 reference generation for 1,000 papers.
References were checked against external bibliographic records using resolver verification.
High effort increased the mean paper-level verification rate from 78.3% to 84.8%.
All four predefined reasoning-summary features scored higher with high effort, while discovered features changed unevenly.
Within either effort condition, higher feature scores did not consistently correspond to higher verification rates.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Study design and analysis pipeline. GPT-5.5 generates references and a reasoning summary for each of 1,000 focal papers under low and high reasoning effort. The resulting paper-level verified-reference rates are compared between low- and high-effort settings, overall and by research field. papers.abstract: Speculative decoding significantly accelerates autoregressive text generation in Large Language Models (LLMs), but its efficacy depends largely on two key factors: the distributional alignment between the draft and the target model, and the draft model's latency during inference. However, existing approaches typically utilize independently pretrained small draft models or seek to prune the target model to a manually chosen architecture, thereby failing to explicitly balance the trade-off between draft model alignment and token generation efficiency. To address this gap, we formulate draft model design as an optimization problem and propose T2D, a framework that constructs draft models directly from the target model using latency-aware structured pruning and knowledge distillation. In this manner, T2D obtains draft models that are jointly optimized for both measured inference latency and cross-entropy loss on the target model's responses, resulting in superlative speculative decoding performance. Through extensive experiments on multi-domain speculative decoding benchmarks and across several target model families of differing scale, we demonstrate how T2D prunes up to 92\% of the target model to obtain highly performant draft models compared to competitive baselines. Moreover, draft models obtained via T2D can also be utilized by other speculative decoding token-alignment and knowledge distillation methods in a plug-and-play fashion, leading to further gains. Our findings underscore the importance of jointly navigating the draft model architecture-alignment frontier to unlock the full potential of speculative decoding for LLMs.
authors: Shahriar Kabir Nahin, Xiao Ye, Muhao Chen, Ben Zhou, Anshuman Chhabra
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between draft-model inference latency and distributional alignment with the target model.
Uses latency-aware structured pruning plus knowledge distillation to formulate draft-model design as an optimization problem.
Prunes up to 92% of the target model while maintaining strong speculative decoding performance across multiple domains and target-model scales.
The resulting draft models can plug into other token-alignment and distillation methods for additional gains.
Scope: effectiveness depends on measured latency and cross-entropy alignment with the target model’s responses.

papers.abstract: We introduce the Literature and Linguistics Analysis Benchmark (LALA), comprising 236 open-ended questions written by experts in linguistics and literary studies, together with expert-provided ideal answers. By comparing models within families and at similar training scales using human and LLM judges, LALA identifies differences in linguistic competence associated with post-training, offering a framework for evaluating future models and guiding targeted improvements. We administered questions to 17 language models and evaluated their responses using both human expert assessment and two LLM evaluators, Sol and Qwen. Base models displayed little of the linguistic competence assessed by the benchmark, whereas their post-trained versions performed markedly better, suggesting that post-training plays a central role in making linguistic knowledge accessible and usable. Parameter count, by contrast, showed no statistically significant association with partial-credit performance, and competencies remained unevenly distributed across linguistic domains. We interpret this pattern as evidence that post-training adds linguistic competencies piecemeal, without producing a general linguistic intelligence capable of extending them beyond the learned policies that support them. Models performed best on logical relations between statements and selected discourse-level tasks, while even the strongest post-trained models continued to struggle with ambiguity, literary style, reference, and misleading assumptions. Human and Sol evaluations produced nearly identical model rankings in both the original and ReliableEval runs, supporting the replicability of the comparative results.
authors: Michael Foster, Barbara McGillivray, Gard B. Jenset, Jakub M\'acha, Jason Harding, Marcus Perlman, Devyani Sharma, Patrick Skeels, Jana Willer-Gold, Jeannette Littlemore
bullets: Introduces 236 expert-written open-ended questions with ideal answers spanning linguistics and literary studies.

Post-trained models outperform base models, while parameter count has no significant association with partial-credit performance.
Models perform best on logical relations and some discourse tasks, but struggle with ambiguity, literary style, reference, and misleading assumptions.
Results suggest post-training adds competencies piecemeal rather than creating general linguistic intelligence beyond learned policies.

papers.abstract: Jailbreak benchmarks test one checkpoint and treat which jailbreaks break it as a property of its pretraining data and safety training. We ask whether another pretraining run of the same data, given the same safety training, would break on the same jailbreaks. For each of 25 pretraining data recipes, we take 1B base models from 3 pretraining seeds and give each the same safety post-training with 2 post-training seeds, for 150 models in all. We then collect 20 responses from every model to a shared set of jailbreak prompts and correlate the per-prompt non-refusal rates between every pair of models. On average, two post-trained copies of the same pretraining run have per-prompt non-refusal rates that correlate at 0.984. A different pretraining seed lowers the correlation to 0.811, and a different data recipe lowers it only slightly further, to 0.779. These results indicate that which jailbreaks break a checkpoint depends much more on its pretraining run than on its data, a pattern that holds in all 25 data recipes and at 150M and 300M parameters. In practice, the best of 91 attack templates found on one checkpoint stays the best after a new pretraining seed in only 27% of model pairs, against 67% after a new post-training seed. Each pretraining run also leaves a fingerprint: across 3,211 prompts, a model's per-prompt non-refusal rates identify its pretraining run among all 75 runs every time, and a random subset of 50 prompts still does so 98% of the time.
authors: Chi-Wei Chang, Mu-Tien Kuo, Kuan-Wei Lee, Meng-Hsun Tsai
bullets: The study evaluates 150 models from 25 data recipes, 3 pretraining seeds, and 2 post-training seeds using shared jailbreak prompts.
Same-pretraining-run copies have highly similar per-prompt non-refusal patterns (correlation 0.984), while changing the pretraining seed drops correlation to 0.811.
Changing the data recipe lowers correlation only slightly further, to 0.779; the pattern also holds at 150M and 300M parameters.
The best attack template transfers across pretraining seeds only 27% of the time, versus 67% across post-training seeds.
Per-prompt non-refusal behavior fingerprints the pretraining run: identification succeeds every time across 3,211 prompts and 98% of the time using 50 prompts.

papers.selection_reason: Demonstrates that pretraining runs leave unique fingerprints affecting jailbreak susceptibility, providing insights into LLM robustness and data composition.
papers.title: Identically Trained Language Models Break on Different Jailbreaks
papers.tldr: Which jailbreaks succeed depends far more on a model’s specific pretraining run than on its data recipe or safety-training seed.

papers.abstract: GEPA is among the strongest reflective prompt optimizers for language-model programs, but its system-aware merge operator is unstable across models: merge improves gpt-4.1-mini on average while degrading Qwen3-8B, an asymmetry noted but left unexplained by the GEPA paper. We investigate this instability across five datasets and two models. Our nine-configuration sweep over merge timing and merge operator shows that merge can improve both models when configured appropriately. This suggests that merge instability is better explained by configuration sensitivity than by an inherent flaw in the merge operator. We then test whether prompt-level features predict GEPA's merge-accept decisions and find that they do not, ruling out static-feature gating. As a proof of concept, a behavior-based probe built from these diagnostics avoids large merge failures in our multi-seed runs by abstaining on high-risk tasks, although it does not consistently outperform NoMerge. Code is available as GEPA-MergeProbe at https://github.com/ChongZZZZ/GEPA_MERGE .
authors: Chong Zhao, Ruyi Yang, Changming Liu, Alice Zhao
bullets: Studies GEPA merging across five datasets, two models, and nine merge configurations.
Finds appropriate merge timing and operators can improve both gpt-4.1-mini and Qwen3-8B.
Shows static prompt features do not predict merge-accept decisions.
A behavior-based probe avoids large merge failures in multi-seed runs by abstaining on high-risk tasks.
The probe does not consistently outperform NoMerge; code is released as GEPA-MergeProbe.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates the stability of prompt optimizer merge operators and builds a behavior-based diagnostic probe, offering technical insights into LLM optimization.
papers.title: When Does GEPA Merge Help? A Mechanism-Level Diagnostic
papers.tldr: GEPA merge instability appears configuration-sensitive rather than inherent, and behavior-based probing can avoid major failures but does not consistently improve over NoMerge.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets large language models (LLMs) answer knowledge-intensive questions from retrieved evidence, but adapting a general-purpose RAG system to a specialized domain such as medicine is difficult when only an unlabeled corpus is available. Self-training approaches such as SimRAG address this by letting the LLM write its own question-answer pairs from domain passages and fine-tuning on the pairs that survive a round-trip consistency filter. We observe that these approaches treat every retained example identically: they never ask whether the student already knows the answer, already extracts it correctly from the retrieved context, or fails - and if so, whether the failure lies with the reader or with the retriever. To tackle this, we propose TriageRAG, a failure-aware self-training approach that probes the student on each self-generated question with and without retrieved context, triages it into one of four categories (known, solved, context-failure, retrieval-failure), and routes each category to the training signal that addresses it, including a parametric route that teaches the reader to answer when retrieval misses. Probing is cheap and repeated every round, so the training mixture follows the student, and the triage histogram doubles as a label-free diagnostic of where the domain gap lies. Experiments on 11 datasets spanning three domains with a Qwen3-4B backbone, and on CS-Bench with Qwen3-8B, demonstrate that TriageRAG outperforms a budget-matched SimRAG by 1.2-6.4 points and is the only method that recovers the closed-book level in every case where retrieval hurts the base model. A single ablation identifies the mechanism: round-trip filtering removes every training context that lacks the evidence, and a reader that never sees such contexts learns to over-trust noisy retrieval.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of adapting RAG to specialized domains using only unlabeled corpora.
Probes answers with and without retrieved context, categorizing examples as known, solved, context-failure, or retrieval-failure.
Routes each category to reader, retriever, or parametric training signals; repeated probing adapts the mixture to the student.
Evaluated across 11 datasets in three domains and CS-Bench, it improves over budget-matched SimRAG by 1.2–6.4 points.
The method recovers closed-book performance whenever retrieval harms the base model; filtering out evidence-lacking contexts can cause readers to over-trust retrieval.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of TriageRAG. Each round, the student synthesizes (q, a, d) triples from the unlabeled corpus (span, multiple-choice and claim formats; only self-answerable pairs are kept), is probed closed-book (pcb) and open-book on the top-k retrieved passages (pob, evidence hit h), and each pair is triaged by the conditions shown and routed to a training signal; the routed mixture is used for LoRA fine-tuning and the updated student re-probes the pool in the next round. The retriever is frozen in our main configuration (Section 3.4).

Figure 2: Top: triage of the self-generated pool by the Qwen3-4B student across rounds (shares in %). Bottom: average accuracy of each round-1 Stage-II mixture against the share of its training examples whose context does not contain the evidence; mixtures with at most 2% such examples (SimRAG, the ablation without the parametric route) stay at or below Stage-I, those with 10% or more reach within a point of the closed-book level or above.

Figure 3: Per-dataset accuracy of the Stage-II variants in the medical domain (Qwen3-4B, round 1). Note the different y-ranges. The literature yes/no datasets (PubMedQA, BioASQ) move by at most 1.3 points under SimRAG, the ablation without the parametric route and TriageRAG; random selection (−4.4) and RAFT-style (−3.0) lower PubMedQA, and retriever tuning damages both. The exam-style datasets (MedQA, MedMCQA, MMLU-Med) carry the gains of TriageRAG over StageI.

Figure 4: Average accuracy per round (Qwen3-4B). Re-probing the updated student changes the mixture of TriageRAG every round; SimRAG’s selection does not depend on the student, so its later rounds re-train on the same distribution.

papers.selection_reason: Failure-aware self-training for adapting retrieval-augmented LLMs to specialized domains; relevant to language foundation model adaptation.
papers.title: TriageRAG: Failure-Aware Self-Training for Adapting Retrieval-Augmented Language Models to Specialized Domains
papers.tldr: TriageRAG improves unlabeled-domain adaptation of RAG systems by diagnosing why each self-generated example fails and applying a targeted training signal.

papers.abstract: Users of conversational assistants rarely state all requirements up front: they add constraints, amend them, withdraw them, digress, and return. Instruction-tuned LLMs fail here in two ways: active constraints stop being honored as turns accumulate (persistence failure), and withdrawn constraints keep being enacted (relapse). The only existing repair we know of is an external ledger that re-injects a compiled specification every turn. We propose StateWise, a self-improving approach that teaches a single LLM to maintain its own revisable constraint state, a typed state with tombstones for revoked constraints, so persistence and relapse are measured by executable checkers and ground-truth states are compiled for free. StateWise fine-tunes the LLM on two complementary skills, summarizing a dialogue into its constraint state and responding conditioned on that state, then self-trains on its own trajectories, keeping only turns that pass an exact round-trip check against the compiled state. This teaches 7-8B models to track the state almost perfectly but, surprisingly, not to obey it: on Llama-3.1-8B every supervised variant roughly doubles relapse. We therefore add a preference stage on self-generated relapse contrasts, where the rejected response enacts a revoked rule and the chosen one passes the round-trip check. On two backbones with held-out constraint families and unseen phrasings, StateWise cuts relapse by 8-22 points relative to supervised self-training, lifts conversation success by 8-19 points over the backbone, and beats an oracle compiled-ledger baseline on relapse with no inference-time scaffolding. We also characterize the recipe's cost on general instruction-following benchmarks and study weight interpolation as a mitigation.
bullets: Addresses persistence failures, where active constraints are forgotten, and relapse, where withdrawn constraints are still followed.
Uses a typed, revisable constraint state with tombstones, plus exact round-trip checks against automatically compiled ground-truth states.
Combines supervised state summarization and state-conditioned response training with preference learning from self-generated relapse contrasts.
Across two backbones, it reduces relapse by 8–22 points versus supervised self-training and improves conversation success by 8–19 points over the base models.
The approach has costs on general instruction-following benchmarks; weight interpolation is explored as a mitigation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of StateWise. Stage I induces two complementary skills from scripted trajectories whose ground-truth states are compiled from the edit history. Stage II lets the model generate state and response on fresh trajectories and keeps only turns that pass an exact round-trip check. Stage III turns the same check into a preference signal: the model’s relapsed generations are rejected responses, its round-trip-clean generations are chosen responses. No proprietary model, judge or human annotation is used in training.

Table 3: Replication of the main arms. Seed 2 repeats the Llama pipeline with a new training seed; the Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct pipeline uses Qwen as its own teacher; the paraphrase set uses authorwritten phrasings and new tasks. In-distribution: Appendix D.

Table 2: Main results on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (training seed 1, greedy decoding). Conversationlevel 95% bootstrap intervals; A6/A6B receive the compiled ground-truth state at inference and are oracle baselines. State exact-match for the state arms: A2 0.527 / 0.981 (held-out / in-dist.), A4 0.510 / 0.916, A7 0.500 / 0.893.

papers.selection_reason: Teaches LLMs to track and obey evolving constraints in multi-turn dialogue, contributing to LLM reasoning and state tracking.
papers.title: StateWise: Teaching Language Models to Track and Obey Evolving Constraints in Multi-Turn Dialogue
papers.tldr: StateWise trains language models to maintain and obey changing dialogue constraints, reducing both forgotten active rules and reactivated revoked rules without an external ledger.

papers.abstract: During post-training, large language models (LLMs) learn value preferences from corpora that may contain imbalanced proportions of opinions associated with different demographic groups. Amplifying these imbalances may further underrepresent some groups' opinions. However, how opinion mixtures shape value preferences across post-training paths remains unclear. To answer this question, we conduct controlled experiments using post-training corpora with different opinion mixtures and five post-training paths based on SFT, DPO, and GRPO. We find that post-training amplifies opinion imbalances differently across post-training paths. Once value preferences are amplified, whether further post-training can remove them depends on both the post-training method and the opinion mixture in the corpus. More concerningly, a model's stability under interventions depends on whether further post-training changes its value preference. Moreover, these value preferences are transferred to student models even when distillation uses corpora with no explicit opinion questions. These findings suggest that both the opinion mixture in post-training corpora and the choice of post-training method should be considered when developing, evaluating, and reusing LLMs. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/ku-nlp/llm-value-preferences.
authors: Yang Liu, Shaoyang Xu, Masahiro Kaneko, Chengzhi Zhong, Wenxuan Zhang, Chenhui Chu
bullets: Imbalanced opinions in post-training corpora can be amplified, with effects differing across SFT, DPO, and GRPO paths.
Whether later post-training removes amplified preferences depends on both the method and the corpus’s opinion mixture.
Model stability under interventions is linked to whether further post-training changes its value preferences.
Value preferences can transfer to student models even when distillation data lacks explicit opinion questions.
The findings highlight opinion composition and post-training method as important factors for developing and evaluating LLMs.

papers.title: How Does Post-Training Shape LLM Value Preferences?
papers.tldr: Controlled experiments show that post-training methods and opinion mixtures jointly shape, reinforce, and sometimes transfer LLM value preferences.

papers.abstract: To understand the emergence of grammatical behavior in language models, we track circuits for subject-verb number agreement in pythia-1b and ten seeds of pythia-410m across training. We find that subject-verb agreement is learned early, and is initially handled by a diffuse collection of neurons. However, after agreement behavior has stabilized, the mechanisms responsible for it continue to reorganize. The attention heads which mediate agreement often shift during training: in the case of pythia-1b, behavior is controlled by two heads early in training but by a third (different) head later. Furthermore, the circuit shrinks over training, with pythia-1b's final circuit being strikingly sparse. We take these results to be informative about how linguistic knowledge emerges and is represented in a language model.
authors: Qing Yao, Sasha Boguraev, Tiago Pimentel, Kyle Mahowald
bullets: Agreement is initially supported by a diffuse set of neurons.
The underlying mechanism continues changing even after behavioral performance stabilizes.
Attention heads mediating agreement can be replaced during training; Pythia-1B shifts from two early heads to a different later head.
The circuit shrinks over training, producing a notably sparse final circuit in Pythia-1B.
The study tracks agreement circuits across training in Pythia-1B and ten Pythia-410M seeds.
