papers.selection_reason: Traces emergence and sparsification of syntactic circuits in LLMs, relevant to language foundation model internals.
papers.title: The Emergence and Sparsification of a Syntactic Circuit
papers.tldr: Subject–verb agreement emerges early in Pythia models, then reorganizes into a much sparser syntactic circuit during continued training.

papers.abstract: Next-token prediction (NTP) rewards only the token that occurs next, penalizing every alternative. But natural language often offers many ways to express the same meaning. We introduce Conceptizer, a training framework that extends next-token prediction with a reward for meaning. Conceptizer uses a fixed, model-agnostic vocabulary of ~9K concepts, built from contextual synonyms, as units of meaning alongside tokens as units of text. It maps each next-token distribution to a concept distribution and shares the reward for the target meaning across its possible wordings. This provides a concept-level training signal without adding model parameters. Applied to 3 model families at 1B-8B parameters, Conceptizer achieves the lowest held-out NTP perplexity at concept-target positions and assigns the highest probability to contextual synonyms, against all 3 baselines. It also improves downstream performance on knowledge and sentiment tasks while remaining comparable on commonsense. These results show that language models can be directly optimized to predict meaning, not just the next token.
bullets: NTP penalizes valid alternative phrasings, motivating a meaning-aware training signal.
Uses a fixed, model-agnostic vocabulary of roughly 9K contextual-synonym concepts alongside tokens.
Maps token distributions to concept distributions and shares reward across equivalent wordings.
Across three 1B–8B model families, improves concept-target perplexity, contextual-synonym probabilities, and knowledge and sentiment performance.
Performance remains comparable on commonsense tasks; the approach does not add model parameters.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Conceptizer leads on knowledge and sentiment tasks in 8 of 9 models each. Commonsense is comparable. Means of seeds 0, 37 and 42; error bars: each method’s 95% Student-t training-seed interval.

Figure 4: Conceptizer has the lowest perplexity against the 3 baselines at concept-target positions in every model. NTP post-training has the lowest global perplexity in every model, and Randomized synonyms the lowest on content words in 8 of 9. Held-out means of training seeds 0, 37 and 42. Colors scale per model and panel.

Figure 1: Building Conceptizer’s fixed, model-agnostic concept vocabulary. papers.selection_reason: Proposes a concept-level training signal beyond next-token prediction for language foundation models.
papers.title: Conceptizer: Next-Token Prediction Is Not All You Need
papers.tldr: Conceptizer augments next-token prediction with concept-level rewards so language models learn meaning across different wordings, improving synonym prediction and several downstream tasks without adding parameters.

papers.abstract: Recent methods for injecting graph structure into LLM prompts include graph soft prompting, in which a graph neural network (GNN) learns graph-specific tokens that capture relational information among entities in textual prompts. G-Retriever combines graph soft prompts with a verbalized description of the same graph to strengthen the textual prompt signal. We conduct an in-depth analysis of G-Retriever and uncover a pathological behavior we term token collapse. Across three benchmarks, three graph encoders, two LLM families, and both frozen and LoRA-adapted models, G-Retriever's graph tokens become almost indistinguishable across inputs. We provide evidence that the same failure is inherited by subsequent methods, even with multi-token pooling. Under the standard setup, swapping a token with the dataset mean, a token from another example, or one derived from a corrupted graph produces no resolved answer-level effect in accuracy. Moreover, a learned constant prompt that never accesses the graph matches or surpasses G-Retriever on all three benchmarks. These findings indicate that, rather than conveying graph content as intended, the collapsed token functions primarily as a generic soft prompt. We also examine conditions linked to this collapse and propose a two-stage procedure that yields non-collapsed tokens while maintaining competitive performance in most cases. However, token variability alone does not prove that the model uses graph information: via interventions and decoding probes, we show that depending on the configuration, a token can reflect the question, an answer prior, or graph-derived content that the LLM may or may not use. Overall, our results offer a practical approach to evaluating graph-token alignment rather than inferring it from task accuracy alone. Code to reproduce our experiments is available at https://github.com/difra100/Token_Collapse_KGQA.
bullets: Token collapse persists across multiple benchmarks, graph encoders, LLM families, adaptation settings, and later multi-token methods.
Replacing graph tokens with dataset means, tokens from other examples, or corrupted-graph tokens has no answer-level accuracy effect under standard settings.
A learned constant prompt matches or outperforms G-Retriever across all evaluated benchmarks without accessing graph inputs.
A two-stage procedure produces more variable tokens while retaining competitive performance in most cases.
Interventions and decoding probes show that token variability may reflect the question, answer priors, or graph content—and graph-derived information is not necessarily used by the LLM.

papers.title: On the Token Collapse Phenomenon in Textual Graph Soft Prompting
papers.tldr: The study reveals that graph soft-prompt tokens in G-Retriever often collapse into generic, graph-independent prompts, making task accuracy an unreliable indicator of graph information use.

papers.abstract: A coding agent works on repositories that can be far larger than its context window can hold. Prompt compressors and retrievers offer solutions to this problem, but patching an issue needs two things at once: the files that must change, and their code exactly as written, since the model must reproduce the lines it edits. Retrievers rank code by its similarity to the issue rather than by whether it must change, and compressors delete text to fit the budget. We show that at an equal token budget, an agent resolves more issues when the budget goes to choosing which files to show verbatim, as our simple selector CQ2-CARE does, than when it goes to pruning tokens or retrieving chunks. We fit every context to the same per-issue budget on 300 recent SWE-rebench issues and grade each patch with the benchmark's tests. With GPT-5.6 and Claude Opus 5, CQ2-CARE resolves 43.7% and 46.7% of the issues, 6.3 points more than the best of three compressors with either model, and 9.3 and 12.7 points more than the best of three retrievers. CQ2-CARE even resolves more issues than two methods trained for issue resolution, SweRank (by 0.7 and 1.7 points) and SWE-Pruner (by 2.0 and 7.3). Our analysis shows the defects of the baseline methods: retrievers often miss the files to edit, and compressors keep them but alter their text, so fewer patches apply. Exact-file selection needs no compression model and shows every line as the repository has it, so the model can quote the code it edits.
authors: Xiaocong Yang, Rishit Chatterjee, Himanshu Udupi, Vikram Ramavarapu, ChengXiang Zhai
bullets: Large repositories exceed an agent’s context window, creating a choice between file selection, retrieval, and compression.
CQ2-CARE selects which whole files to include and preserves their exact contents.
On 300 SWE-rebench issues, it resolves 43.7% with GPT-5.6 and 46.7% with Claude Opus 5.
It outperforms the best compressors by 6.3 points and the best retrievers by 9.3 and 12.7 points, respectively.
Retrievers often omit files needing edits, while compressors alter code that agents must reproduce exactly.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes CQ2-CARE, a selector for coding agents that improves efficiency by selecting whole files for context rather than compressing or retrieving chunks, leading to higher issue resolution rates.
papers.title: Skip the Compressor: Coding Agents Fix More Issues When They Pick Whole Files
papers.tldr: At equal context budgets, showing coding agents selected files verbatim fixes more issues than retrieving code chunks or compressing files.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning for large language models often uses separate systems for inference and training. Even with identical weights and BF16 tensors, implementation differences can make an intended on-policy update off-policy and destabilize training. Existing remedies align the entire inference and training stacks, change global precision, or modify the learning algorithm. We ask whether aligning selected parts of the execution stack can stabilize BF16 RL while other implementation differences remain. We align training-side rounding locations with inference in three regions---RoPE, SwiGLU, and residual RMSNorm---by retaining selected intermediates in FP32 until their BF16 outputs. Across four Qwen-family models, aligning all three regions prevents the collapse observed under the default BF16 baseline; RoPE-path alignment alone also suffices in the studied runs, despite remaining numerical discrepancies. The interventions keep the inference engine, matrix-multiplication and attention kernels, and learning objective unchanged.
authors: Yijing Ke, Tianle Cai, Ruosong Wang
bullets: Implementation differences between inference and training can make nominally on-policy RL updates effectively off-policy and destabilize training.
The study aligns training-side rounding locations with inference in RoPE, SwiGLU, and residual RMSNorm.
Across four Qwen-family models, aligning all three regions prevents collapse seen with the default BF16 baseline.
RoPE-path alignment alone suffices in the studied runs despite other numerical discrepancies.
The interventions leave inference, matrix-multiplication and attention kernels, and the learning objective unchanged.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates numerical stability in LLM Reinforcement Learning by aligning rounding locations in the execution stack, preventing training collapse.
papers.title: Where Rounding Happens Matters: Rounding-Location Alignment Stabilizes LLM Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: Aligning where rounding occurs between inference and training can stabilize BF16 reinforcement learning for LLMs without changing the inference engine or learning objective.

papers.abstract: Modern language models rely on subwording tokenization to define the discrete units of input processing, typically using methods like Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) that treat whitespace as a fixed semantic boundary. This design is inherently limited, as many meaningful concepts---including multiword expressions and the structured environments of formal languages like LaTeX---frequently span across whitespaces. While recent superword tokenization methods attempt to address this by relaxing whitespace constraints, they often rely on greedy frequency-driven merging that fails to account for token length or the specific needs of underrepresented domain-specific languages. In this paper, we introduce Adaptive Frequency Threshold Byte Pair Encoding (AdaBPE), a new tokenization method that leverages an adaptive frequent-pattern mining approach. AdaBPE features a twofold dynamicity: it adapts minimum frequency thresholds based on both the length of a candidate token, to prevent favoring frequent short patterns, and its type, to distinguish between general and formal language patterns, using LaTeX as case in point. This allows the model to efficiently allocate vocabulary capacity to domain-specific notations, such as LaTeX, even when they represent a small fraction of the training data. We evaluate AdaBPE across five datasets spanning LaTeX and natural language, showing consistent gains in encoding efficiency and downstream language-model performance on domain-specific content without compromising general-language performance.
authors: Pietro Di Nicco, Lucio La Cava, Andrea Tagarelli
bullets: Addresses BPE’s fixed whitespace boundaries, which split meaningful multiword expressions and formal-language structures.
Uses adaptive frequent-pattern mining with thresholds conditioned on candidate length and whether patterns are general-language or formal-language.
Allocates vocabulary capacity more effectively to underrepresented notations such as LaTeX.
Evaluated on five LaTeX and natural-language datasets, with gains in encoding efficiency and domain-specific language-model performance while preserving general-language performance.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive tokenization for mixed natural and formal language is a meaningful contribution to language-model foundations.
papers.title: Adaptive Frequency Threshold Byte Pair Encoding for Mixed Natural Language and Structured Symbolic Corpora
papers.tldr: AdaBPE improves subword tokenization for mixed natural-language and structured-symbolic data by adapting merge thresholds to token length and pattern type.

papers.abstract: Statement autoformalization translates mathematics from natural language into a proof assistant such as Lean 4, and models now do it at scale. As provers get stronger, the burden of correctness shifts from the proof to the statement, that is, to whether the formal statement faithfully translates its source. Given a trusted reference formalization, the natural test is logical equivalence, and it proves too much. $P \leftrightarrow Q$ holds trivially for any two statements $P$ and $Q$ that the library proves, because a prover can prove each separately and pass through $P \leftrightarrow \mathrm{True} \leftrightarrow Q$. The stronger the prover, the more unrelated pairs pass. Earlier methods restrict the prover and check that each proof names the other statement. We introduce SemantEq, a more principled relation that instead requires each statement to turn into the other only through a chain of allowed steps, such as logical rearrangement and rewriting with the library's own equations. Our programs judge a proof by the proof term Lean checks, not by its tactic script. SemantEq-Eval, a search without a model, reaches 100% precision and 65.6% recall on the ProofNetVerif test split under our adjudicated labels, against 95.8% and 61.8% for BEq+, and an 8.9-fold increase in its CPU time adds at most three pairs. A language model finds more proofs, but under two of four prompts it proves both directions of about two in five of the non-equivalent pairs. SemantEq-ProofAudit audits each model-written proof under a policy derived from the relation and accepts none of the 104 non-equivalent pairs, and it raises recall on 407 equivalent pairs from 65.4% to 81.1% under the best prompt. Separating the generation of equivalence proofs from their acceptance lets a stronger prover raise recall without changing what an acceptance means. We release code and data at: https://github.com/hlxr89/SemantEq
authors: Xinrui Li, Pawan Sasanka Ammanamanchi, Siddharth Bhat, Rianna Jamdar, Yongxi Lin, Stella Biderman
bullets: Addresses the failure of ordinary logical equivalence, which can incorrectly accept unrelated statements when a powerful prover proves each independently.
Judges Lean-checked proof terms against allowed transformations such as logical rearrangement and library-equation rewriting.
SemantEq-Eval achieves 100% precision and 65.6% recall on ProofNetVerif, compared with 95.8% precision and 61.8% recall for BEq+.
SemantEq-ProofAudit filters language-model proofs, accepting none of 104 non-equivalent pairs and increasing recall from 65.4% to 81.1% on 407 equivalent pairs under the best prompt.
The approach separates proof generation from acceptance, allowing stronger provers to improve recall without changing the acceptance criterion.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces SemantEq for faithful bidirectional equivalence of formal statements, a task relevant to the mathematical reasoning capabilities of LLMs.
papers.title: SemantEq: Faithful Bidirectional Equivalence of Formal Statements
papers.tldr: SemantEq checks whether formal statements are faithfully equivalent by requiring bidirectional transformations through explicitly allowed proof steps, rather than merely proving both statements.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but its cost is dominated by autoregressive rollout generation, which can exceed 70% of training time. Existing speculative-decoding methods are poorly suited to this setting: model-based drafters consume scarce GPU memory and may become misaligned as the policy evolves, while existing model-free methods do not explicitly exploit repetition across training epochs. We observe that recent rollouts of the same prompt provide a high-quality, self-updating draft source. Based on this insight, we propose NgramRL, a per-prompt n-gram drafter constructed from bounded recent rollout history. NgramRL requires no auxiliary model, drafter training, or persistent GPU-resident drafter state, while target-model verification preserves the rollout distribution. To hide CPU cache lookup and scheduling, we further introduce an adaptive fan-out prefetcher that predicts likely verification outcomes (j, b), consisting of the accepted draft length j and target-emitted continuation token b. A causal budget allocator concentrates prefetches on high-probability outcomes, while uncovered outcomes fall back to sequential lookup without changing committed tokens. Across two model families and three reasoning and structured-generation workloads, NgramRL commits 3.60-7.77 tokens per target-model forward in the warm-cache regime, up to 1.99x more than SuffixDecoding and 7.0x more than prompt-lookup decoding. On Spider, the prefetcher covers 96.6% of Qwen3-8B outcomes at a candidate budget of 16 and improves measured rollout throughput by 1.38x over synchronous NgramRL, approaching its 1.40x overlap ceiling.
authors: Nilesh Prasad Pandey, Jangseon Park, Jason Kong, Onat Gungor, Tajana Rosing
bullets: RL post-training rollout generation can dominate training cost, while existing speculative decoding methods face memory, policy-alignment, or repetition-exploitation limitations.
NgramRL builds bounded n-gram caches from recent rollouts, requiring no auxiliary model, drafter training, or persistent GPU-resident state.
Target-model verification preserves the original rollout distribution; uncovered speculative outcomes safely fall back to sequential lookup.
Across two model families and three workloads, NgramRL commits 3.60–7.77 tokens per target-model forward, reaching up to 1.99× SuffixDecoding and 7.0× prompt-lookup decoding.
An adaptive fan-out prefetcher improves measured Spider rollout throughput by 1.38× over synchronous NgramRL and covers 96.6% of outcomes at a candidate budget of 16.
papers.selection_reason: Accelerates RL post-training for LLMs using rollout-aware n-gram speculative decoding, improving the efficiency of reasoning capabilities in large language models.
papers.title: NgramRL: Accelerating RL Post-Training for Structured Generation via Rollout-Aware N-gram Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: NgramRL accelerates RL post-training rollouts by using recent per-prompt n-grams as a self-updating speculative drafter, with adaptive prefetching to reduce lookup overhead.

papers.abstract: In LLM-agent opinion simulations, each agent reports the probability that a claim is true after seeing its own previous probability and the probabilities reported by its neighbors, and that number becomes its state in the next round. If the number describes the agent's position rather than the sentence it was shown, then rewriting the claim as its complement and replacing every probability p with 1 - p should return the complementary answer, so the two reports should sum to one. We test this with three small open models: Qwen3-4B, Llama-3.2-3B and Gemma-3-4B. On 2,304 agent states taken from a running network simulation, Qwen's paired reports sum to 1.18 on average, and on 48 real fact-checking claims from AVeriTeC they again exceed one. A controlled benchmark of 24 worlds, each with exactly two possible outcomes, shows the same failure in all three models. The discrepancy is two to ten times larger than the change produced by a same-meaning paraphrase, and it persists under repeated sampling and across peer group sizes and report strengths. When the reports are fed back into two populations that start from complementary states, the populations do not remain mirror images: their divergence is positive after five rounds for every model. Averaging each answer with the complement of its paired answer restores consistency by construction and lowers Brier loss averaged over the two wordings, but at the final round it beats the better of the two original wordings for only one of the three models. A schedule-by-targeting experiment on the same model gives a small, stable interaction because such sweeps keep the claim wording fixed. Consistency under rewording therefore needs its own test before simulated probabilities are read as beliefs
bullets: Across three small open models, reports for a claim and its complement systematically summed to more than one.
The inconsistency appeared in network simulations, real fact-checking claims, and controlled two-outcome worlds.
It exceeded same-meaning paraphrase effects and persisted across sampling, peer-group sizes, and report strengths.
Complementary initial populations diverged over repeated rounds rather than remaining mirror images.
Averaging each answer with the complement of its paired answer restores consistency by construction, but improved final-round Brier loss for only one model.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates the consistency of complement probabilities in LLM-agent opinion simulations, providing empirical analysis of LLM behavior in agent-based reasoning tasks.
papers.title: Do "True" and "False" Add Up to One? Complement Consistency in LLM-Agent Opinion Simulations
papers.tldr: LLM-agent opinion simulations often violate complement consistency, so simulated probabilities should be tested for wording symmetry before being interpreted as beliefs.

papers.abstract: This paper proposes a five-level organization of message formation and understanding within thinking and activity in which ASI participates. Its central thesis is that a language model's context is fundamentally incapable of presenting the foundations of utterance formation for examination and verification. These foundations are established in advance by acquired schemas, systemic representations of the world of activity, and connections accepted as true within them. Neither context nor trained LLM weights, in themselves, attest to the presence of deliberately constructed systemic representations. The five levels distinguish systemic representations of the world of activity, a particular situation cut out from those representations, its narrative description, the full sense of a message, and text. A situation's schema-model is not identical to a story about it. A recipient reconstructs the full sense from an abbreviated text through jointly constructed and agreed-upon representations and joint activity. Reverse work proceeds from the full sense through an extended description and the situation's schema-model to the reconstruction of systemic foundations. The theoretical foundations draw on the systems methodology of G. P. Shchedrovitskiy, the structural differential of A. Korzybski, and the Meaning-Text theory of I. A. Mel'chuk. The contribution is a specific systemic-activity organization of content for examining and adjusting message foundations and controlling the consequences of their transformation. Further research concerns large graphical models of activity on reconstructible systemic foundations, distinct from text generation from context.
bullets: Argues that context and trained LLM weights alone cannot reveal or verify the schemas and world representations underlying utterances.
Distinguishes five levels: systemic activity representations, a selected situation, its narrative description, full message sense, and surface text.
Models communication as reconstruction: recipients infer full sense from abbreviated text through shared representations and joint activity.
Draws on systems methodology, Korzybski’s structural differential, and Meaning–Text theory.
Proposes a foundation for examining and controlling transformations of message meaning; future work targets reconstructible graphical activity models rather than context-only text generation.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a theoretical five-level communication architecture for strong language-based ASI, focusing on systemic representations and message formation, relevant to future LLM architectures.
papers.title: From Deliberately Constructed Systemic Representations of the World of Activity to Dialogue: A Five-Level Communication Architecture for Strong Language-Based ASI
papers.tldr: The paper proposes a five-level communication architecture to make the systemic foundations behind language-based ASI messages explicit, examinable, and adjustable.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning on datasets of unknown origin can create a backdoor in the trained model when the data includes poisoned examples. Difficult to localise and remove, backdoors can persist through safety training. While parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods capture the full parameter changes introduced during training, they are not easily interpretable. We present the full method of TopKLoRA, extending the preliminary proposal of Masiak et al. (2025), an interpretable-by-design LoRA variant in which only the $k$ largest adapter latents are active at each token. Unlike SAEs, TopKLoRA is trained purely on downstream loss, where optimisation pressure incentivises learning functionally causal latents. We demonstrate this sparse LoRA adapter in a sleeper-agent backdoor case study where we create model organisms by fine-tuning gemma-2-2b, Qwen2.5-1.5B, and Qwen2.5-7B on a poisoned instruction-following dataset. For each organism, we identify and ablate a circuit that is both necessary and sufficient to implement the backdoor. Furthermore, our new fine-tuning method produces sparse circuits that are up to an order of magnitude smaller than a dense LoRA baseline, allowing surgical ablation of the malicious capability without sacrificing instruction-following performance. Finally, we propose a technique to construct model organisms with localised circuits using TopKLoRA latents and gradient-routing, which we use to validate the findings of our circuit search algorithm. We consider these findings as a step toward interpretable-by-design architectures that provide faithful units of analysis without compromising model performance. We share our code: https://github.com/interpretable-finetuning/TopKLoRA.
authors: Marek Masiak, Andrzej Szablewski, Nicola Cancedda, Constantin Venhoff
bullets: Targets backdoors introduced by poisoned fine-tuning data, which can be difficult to localise and remove.
Activates only the k largest adapter latents per token and trains solely with downstream loss.
Produces sparse, functionally causal circuits that are up to an order of magnitude smaller than dense LoRA circuits.
In sleeper-agent model organisms based on Gemma and Qwen models, identified circuits were necessary and sufficient for the backdoor.
Ablating these circuits removed the malicious capability without sacrificing instruction-following performance; scope is demonstrated through backdoor case studies.
papers.selection_reason: Sparse interpretable LoRA with k-active latents offers a transferable efficiency and interpretability technique for LLM fine-tuning and circuit analysis.
papers.title: Interpretable sparse fine-tuning with TopKLoRA enables faithful circuit discovery
papers.tldr: TopKLoRA makes LoRA fine-tuning sparse and interpretable, enabling faithful identification and surgical removal of backdoor circuits while preserving normal instruction following.

papers.abstract: Longitudinal causal effect estimation is complicated by time-varying confounding and treatment-confounder feedback loops. Existing methods generally require data-specific nuisance-model fitting, and many are tailored to prespecified treatment sequences or prediction horizons, leading to time-consuming computation at deployment. We introduce *Policy In-Context Longitudinal causal Effect estimation with Prior-data Fitted Networks* (**PICLE-PFN**), the first foundation model for longitudinal causal effect estimation that supports *dynamic* treatment policies. PICLE-PFN represents target policies through in-context history-decision demonstrations, providing a unified interface for a broad class of treatment policies. Pretrained over synthetic data sampled from longitudinal structural causal models, PICLE-PFN amortizes causal effect estimation across datasets, policies, and horizons. Given a new observational dataset and target policy, it directly predicts conditional average potential outcomes (CAPOs) in one forward pass without task-specific training or hyperparameter tuning. Across synthetic and semi-synthetic longitudinal benchmarks, PICLE-PFN achieves competitive RMSE and substantially improved uncertainty calibration with a fraction of deployment runtime, compared to state-of-the-art conventional estimators trained and tuned separately for each dataset.
authors: Wenxin Chen, Kyra Gan, Mingyu Lu, Zilin Jing, Fei Wang, Hoifung Poon, Tristan Naumann, Peniel Argaw
bullets: Addresses time-varying confounding and treatment–confounder feedback in longitudinal causal estimation.
Encodes dynamic policies as in-context history–decision demonstrations.
Pretrains on synthetic longitudinal structural causal models to amortize estimation across datasets, policies, and horizons.
Predicts conditional average potential outcomes directly for a new observational dataset and policy.
Shows competitive RMSE, substantially better uncertainty calibration, and lower deployment runtime on synthetic and semi-synthetic benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a foundation model (PICLE-PFN) for longitudinal causal effect estimation that amortizes computation across datasets and policies, extending the capabilities of LLMs to causal inference.
papers.title: A Foundation Model for Policy In-Context Longitudinal Causal Effect Estimation
papers.tldr: PICLE-PFN is a pretrained foundation model that estimates longitudinal causal effects for dynamic treatment policies in one forward pass, avoiding task-specific fitting and tuning.

papers.abstract: Large language models are trained to predict tokens from a finite vocabulary, each represented by a vector in a $d$-dimensional embedding space. Therefore, token prediction is a classification problem whose classes have a geometry determined by the embedding. We study how this geometry affects learning in a minimal solvable model: a linear predictor that maps a sequence of $N$ embedded tokens to a $d$-dimensional output through one $d\times d$ matrix per position, trained in the teacher--student setting. We call this the \textit{token perceptron}. We compute its generalization error with the replica method, taking $N\to\infty$ at fixed number of examples per position $\alpha=P/N$ and keeping $d$ and the vocabulary size $D$ finite. As a first reference case, we consider continuous embeddings on the sphere, which isolate the role of the embedding dimension. The natural load is then $\alpha/d$, and for $d>1$ a normalized label fixes the direction of the teacher output, so the problem becomes a noiseless regression: the teacher is recovered exactly above $\alpha_{\rm rec}=d^2/(d-1)$, and spherical cross-entropy reaches this threshold at large inverse temperature. In the same setting the storage capacity of random associations scales as $d^2$ for margins $O(1/\sqrt{d})$. We then turn to vocabulary embeddings, where a label only identifies the Voronoi cell of the teacher output, so that each example imposes inequalities rather than equations, as in the classical perceptron. We compute the Bayes-optimal error for a given embedding matrix through an approximate spectral closure and show that the optimal learner first resolves the directions in which the vocabulary has the largest variance, even when the teacher is isotropic.
authors: Dario Bocchi, Matteo Negri, Flavio Nicoletti, Francesco D'Amico
bullets: Models token prediction as a teacher–student linear classifier over sequences of embedded tokens, with one matrix per position.
For continuous spherical embeddings, the problem reduces to noiseless regression when labels fix the teacher-output direction.
Exact teacher recovery occurs above the example load α_rec = d²/(d−1); spherical cross-entropy reaches this threshold at high inverse temperature.
Random-association storage capacity scales as d² for margins of order 1/√d.
For finite vocabularies, labels identify Voronoi cells, and the Bayes-optimal learner first learns directions where the vocabulary has greatest variance, even for an isotropic teacher.
papers.selection_reason: Theoretical analysis of token embedding and vocabulary geometry relevant to LLM token prediction.
papers.title: Generalization properties of the token perceptron: the role of embedding and vocabulary
papers.tldr: The token perceptron’s generalization depends strongly on embedding geometry: continuous embeddings permit exact teacher recovery, while finite vocabularies turn learning into inequality-based classification that prioritizes high-variance directions.

papers.abstract: Hospitals regularly buy software that clinicians and patients depend on. Because these purchases are costly, hard to reverse and can affect patient care, buyers look for evidence of which peer institutions already use a product and which systems it connects to. This evidence is public but scattered across vendor websites, press releases and third-party pages. Language-model agents can now collect it at low cost, but the correctness of the extracted claims is difficult to establish, and a wrongly listed customer can mislead buyers and misrepresent an organisation. We present a pipeline that builds a knowledge graph of customer and integration relations from the open web under one rule: every edge must be supported by a verbatim quote from its source page. Pages come from a deterministic crawl of each vendor's site and a budgeted ReAct agent that searches the rest of the web. A permissive extractor proposes relations with quotes, and a layered grounding stage decides which to keep, using a referent step that reads the whole page when a quote names only one side, deterministic checks, and a panel of five model calls voting on nine criteria. On 61 vendors, the pipeline reaches 0.94 precision and 0.71 recall against a page-level key covering the 6,428 candidate relations proposed by its extractor, whose verdicts were drafted by one model and re-checked with a second. Against the golden reference, the marketplace's own curated list, it scores lower, but 89% of the relations it keeps that the reference lacks are stated on a page. A confidence score built from the panel's votes keeps more correct relations than the fixed rule at the same precision, and reaches 0.90 precision at 0.90 recall. We also discuss how narrow, bounded model calls, string-matched evidence and voting address long-context degradation and run-to-run variance.
authors: Juan Felipe Duran, Arthur Tobler, Martin Valli\`eres
bullets: Addresses the risk of misleading buyers when software customer and integration claims are extracted from scattered public web sources.
Uses deterministic vendor-site crawling plus a budgeted ReAct web-search agent to find pages and a permissive extractor to propose quoted relations.
A layered grounding process verifies quotes with whole-page referent checks, deterministic rules, and five-model voting across nine criteria.
Across 61 vendors, the fixed rule achieves 0.94 precision and 0.71 recall against a page-level reference; a confidence score reaches 0.90 precision at 0.90 recall.
The approach is scoped to open-web evidence and discusses bounded model calls, string-matched quotes, and voting as safeguards against context and variance issues.
papers.selection_reason: Uses language-model agents to build a quote-grounded knowledge graph, fitting the Large Language Models subtopic.
papers.title: Every Edge Needs a Quote: Building a Quote-Grounded Knowledge Graph of Healthcare Software Adoption with Language-Model Agents
papers.tldr: A quote-grounded language-model pipeline builds a healthcare software adoption and integration graph, achieving high precision by retaining only relations supported by source-page evidence.

papers.abstract: AI representation is emerging in digital democracy, assisting in voter emulation and decision-making. Large language models (LLMs) behave differently depending on the model, the prompt context, and the voter information they receive, representing some groups more accurately than others and potentially making the emulation unfair to certain groups. We investigate demographic biases in LLM-emulated electorates: how accurately LLMs represent individual votes, whether some voter groups are represented more accurately than others, and whether AI alignment can reduce these disparities without sacrificing overall accuracy. Using three U.S. presidential elections, we compare a closed-source and an open-source LLM across voters' demographic features and test AI alignment strategies toward fairer voter representation. Removing gender from the voter profile reduces the largest group error of the models by 22-42%, and removing education reduces it by 64%, whereas removing self-reported race increases the mean group error by over 40%, all without lowering accuracy. Common alignment strategies, such as repeated queries or fairness instructions, do not reduce these errors and can double them.
authors: Yi Qi, Srijoni Majumdar, Evangelos Pournaras
bullets: The study examines whether LLMs accurately emulate individual votes and whether accuracy differs across demographic groups.
It compares one closed-source and one open-source LLM across three U.S. presidential elections.
Removing gender or education from voter profiles reduces the largest group errors, while removing self-reported race increases mean group error.
These attribute-removal strategies do not lower overall accuracy.
Repeated queries and fairness instructions fail to reduce errors and can substantially increase them.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates demographic biases in LLM-emulated electorates, fitting the Large Language Models subtopic.
papers.title: AI Alignment for Digital Democracy: Fairer Voters Representation against LLM Biases
papers.tldr: LLM-based voter emulation can misrepresent demographic groups, while selectively removing voter attributes—especially education—can improve fairness without reducing accuracy; common alignment prompts may worsen disparities.

papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation enables post-training foundation models without relying on stronger external teachers. However, existing approaches rely on ground-truth question-answer pairs, human-curated problem sets, or other supervised signals. In this work, we reformulate on-policy self-distillation as a self-training framework, driven by self-generated question-answer pairs and privileged reasoning demonstrations. We push supervision to the limit: guided solely by coarse, high-level topic descriptions, the model synthesizes its own curriculum of queries and privileged reasoning traces without access to any human-curated prompts or answers. We find that self-distillation on fully synthetic privileged information enables a model to improve across multiple domains while retaining its capabilities on domains it is not self-trained on. We demonstrate the generality of this framework across text and multimodal domains, achieving consistent self-improvement on standard language benchmarks and Visual Question Answering. Our findings demonstrate that foundation models possess rich latent capabilities that can be amplified without external task supervision or curated problem distributions.
authors: Leon Sick, Lukas Hoyer, Yannick Str\"umpler, Christian Reisswig, Timo Ropinski, Federico Tombari
bullets: Addresses the need for post-training without human-curated questions, answers, or stronger teacher models.
Uses on-policy self-training with self-generated question–answer pairs and privileged reasoning demonstrations.
The model creates its own curriculum and reasoning traces from coarse, high-level topic descriptions.
Improves performance across multiple domains while retaining capabilities on domains not used for self-training.
Generalizes across language benchmarks and visual question answering, suggesting latent capabilities can be amplified without external task supervision.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a data-free self-training framework for LLMs using self-generated question-answer pairs, fitting the Large Language Models subtopic.
papers.title: On-Policy Self-Training: Data-Free Self-Improvement in Large Language Models
papers.tldr: A large language model can improve itself across text and multimodal tasks by generating its own questions and reasoning traces from only broad topic descriptions.

papers.abstract: The rapid expansion of scientific literature far outpaces the speed of manual curation, creating a fundamental bottleneck in extracting structured knowledge from scientific texts. To address this, we introduce an agentic, ontology-guided framework for knowledge graph (KG) construction. Our framework utilizes specialized agents for document understanding, information extraction, ontology conformance, and entity linking. First, an LLM extracts factual knowledge in the form of triples with explicit textual evidence from research papers. Then the triplets undergo a multistage verification process to ground the triplets in the ontology. By enforcing schema constraints and requiring evidence in the form of text fragments, we ensure the data is both semantically consistent and traceable. In an agreement study over 1,000 extracted triplets, Gemini-2.5-flash achieves Cohen's $\kappa$ scores of 0.640--0.700 against three human annotators, matching the human--human agreement range of 0.616--0.689. We applied this framework to 2,000 scientific publications and construct a novel, ontology-grounded KG for climate science with 133,990 nodes and 755,308 relations; of the 23,327 triplets that the publications contribute after validation, 98.96\% are judged correct. The pipeline code and KG is publicly available https://github.com/aayushacharya/climatekg.
authors: Aayush Acharya, Qi Zhang, Eduard Dragut, Longin Jan Latecki
bullets: Addresses the bottleneck of manually curating rapidly expanding scientific literature.
Uses specialized agents for document understanding, extraction, ontology conformance, and entity linking.
LLMs extract evidence-backed triples, which undergo multistage verification against ontology constraints.
In an agreement study, Gemini-2.5-flash reached Cohen’s κ of 0.640–0.700, within the reported human–human range.
Applied to 2,000 publications, the framework produced a KG with 133,990 nodes and 755,308 relations; 98.96% of 23,327 validated contributed triples were judged correct.
papers.selection_reason: Utilizes LLM agents for knowledge graph construction, fitting the Large Language Models subtopic.
papers.title: Ontology-Guided Knowledge Graph Construction from Structured Metadata and Climate Science Publications
papers.tldr: An ontology-guided, agentic pipeline builds a traceable climate-science knowledge graph from publications, achieving high agreement with human annotators and strong validated-triplet accuracy.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been widely adopted in text classification tasks, where they not only output class predictions but also generate explanations that highlight the tokens deemed most relevant for reaching the predicted label. Yet it remains unclear whether these highlighted elements are behaviorally consistent with the model's own predictions under targeted interventions, which we refer to as functional auto-consistency. While much of the literature evaluates the textual plausibility of such explanations, few studies assess their functional consistency with the model's actual behavior. In this work, we propose an experimental framework based on the principle of auto-consistency: if a model identifies certain tokens as decisive, then isolating, removing, or semantically inverting them should produce systematic and interpretable changes in its predictions. We operationalize this evaluation through sufficiency, comprehensiveness, and counterfactuality metrics, and conduct experiments on IMDB and Steam reviews across both closed-source (GPT-4o-mini) and open-source LLMs (Gemma3, Granite8B, DeepSeek). Results show that GPT-4o-mini follows the expected progression across all metrics, Gemma3 and Granite8B maintain coherence under sufficiency but lose consistency under more demanding interventions, while DeepSeek variants display structural deviations, either failing to preserve sufficiency or overreacting under comprehensiveness and counterfactuality. These findings show that explanation reliability varies across LLM families and scales, with smaller models displaying contradictions and larger ones exhibiting over-sensitivity. By combining sufficiency, comprehensiveness, and counterfactuality, our approach provides a systematic methodology for assessing the functional consistency of LLM self-explanations.
authors: Alisson Rosa Pereira, Bruno Iochins Grisci
bullets: Tests explanations through targeted interventions: retaining, removing, or semantically reversing highlighted tokens.
Introduces a combined evaluation using sufficiency, comprehensiveness, and counterfactuality metrics.
Evaluates GPT-4o-mini, Gemma3, Granite8B, and DeepSeek variants on IMDB and Steam reviews.
GPT-4o-mini shows the expected behavior across all metrics; other models exhibit inconsistencies or over-sensitivity.
Findings suggest explanation reliability differs across LLM families and model scales.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes an evaluation framework for functional consistency of LLM self-explanations, relevant to LLM reasoning and interpretability.
papers.title: Do Language Models Trust Their Own Justifications? A Study on Functional Consistency
papers.tldr: The study evaluates whether LLM-highlighted evidence actually drives their predictions, finding substantial variation in functional consistency across models and interventions.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning the non-blank predictor of a factorized transducer on target-domain text improves recognition on that domain but degrades performance on the source domain. A single interpolation weight between base and adapted predictors cannot resolve this: the adapted predictor helps at some prefixes and hurts at others, often within one utterance. We propose conservative residual routing: the adapted predictor becomes a residual correction to the base, and a 16k-parameter gate decides at each prefix how much of it to admit. Closing the gate reproduces the base exactly. On a 40-hour conversational corpus, routing retains essentially all of the text-only gain on two held-out domains (19.89 to 16.74, 20.91 to 16.21 WER) while leaving source-domain WER unchanged (12.90 to 12.93); the adapted predictor alone costs 1.08 WER. Routing needs no per-domain tuning on target-domain audio. Analysis reveals the gate does not behave as a simple domain-level switch: it modulates intervention through the disagreement between the two predictors, suppressing it in-domain and amplifying it out-of-domain.
authors: Shashi Kumar, Esa\'u Villatoro-Tello, Thibault Ba\~neras-Roux, Sergio Burdisso, Petr Motlicek, Kadri Hacioglu, Andreas Stolcke
bullets: Text-only fine-tuning improves target-domain recognition but can harm the source domain, and a single interpolation weight cannot resolve prefix-level conflicts.
The method treats the adapted predictor as a residual correction to the base predictor.
A 16k-parameter gate dynamically controls how much correction to apply at each prefix; closing it exactly recovers the base model.

On a 40-hour conversational corpus, routing retained target-domain gains while leaving source-domain WER essentially unchanged (12.90 to 12.93); the adapted predictor alone degraded performance by 1.08 WER.
The gate responds to predictor disagreement rather than acting as a simple domain switch, suppressing corrections in-domain and amplifying them out-of-domain.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes residual expert routing for domain adaptation in ASR, allowing the model to dynamically switch between base and adapted predictors based on context.
papers.title: Residual Expert Routing for Text-Only Domain Adaptation of Factorized Transducer ASR
papers.tldr: A small prefix-level gate safely routes text-only domain-adaptation corrections, preserving source-domain ASR while retaining target-domain gains.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly serve as reasoning components in modern software systems, yet a model that answers a logical query correctly can contradict itself when the same problem is restated in an equivalent form. Static benchmarks evaluate queries in isolation and therefore fail to expose such inconsistencies. To address this limitation, we present LGMT, an open-source tool that detects reasoning inconsistencies through metamorphic relations grounded in first-order logic. Given a source test case in premise-conclusion form, LGMT generates logically equivalent follow-up cases and checks whether the model's entailment predictions agree across the pair, without ground-truth labels. The tool provides 20 built-in metamorphic relations, supports custom ones verified by the Z3 theorem prover, and runs from a CLI or a web studio, including an offline mock mode requiring no API key. Across six widely used LLMs on a bundled benchmark of 3,091 metamorphic groups, LGMT reveals inconsistency rates ranging from 20.84% to 29.44%. LGMT is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/MaxwelsDonc/lgmt-tool, with a demonstration video at https://youtu.be/gou4opptu1U.
authors: Zenghui Zhou, Xiaoke Fang, Zheng Zheng
bullets: Addresses a gap in static benchmarks, which may miss contradictions across logically equivalent queries.
Uses first-order-logic metamorphic relations to generate equivalent follow-up premise–conclusion cases and compare entailment predictions without ground-truth labels.
Includes 20 built-in relations, supports Z3-verified custom relations, and offers CLI, web, and offline mock modes.
Evaluated six LLMs on 3,091 metamorphic groups, finding inconsistency rates of 20.84%–29.44%.
Open-source implementation is available on GitHub.
papers.selection_reason: Provides a metamorphic-relation-based tool for testing logical reasoning reliability of LLMs, relevant to LLM reasoning.
papers.title: LGMT: A Tool for Testing the Logical Reasoning Reliability of LLMs
papers.tldr: LGMT tests whether LLMs give consistent logical judgments when equivalent problems are restated in different forms.

papers.abstract: Continuous diffusion models have emerged as a promising non-autoregressive paradigm for text generation over continuous embedding spaces. Along the continuous trajectory, the residual token identity directly shapes the denoising objective. However, the geometric trajectory misaligns with temporal progression, triggering severe temporal compression. In this paper, we show that embedding norm decay causes Euclidean distance to yield spurious overtaking, indicating that token competition must be evaluated directionally. In this space, a candidate overtakes the source token only when the effective noise magnitude surpasses their semantic separation. We formalize these pairwise dynamics as the Competition Threshold Theory (CTT). Crucially, high-dimensional overtaking requires extreme noise levels, causing standard trajectories to concentrate identity decay into a narrow window near the noisy endpoint. To resolve this, we propose Semantic Retention Scheduling (SRS) to align time allocation with the progression of identity decay, and demonstrate that existing token identity metrics are fundamentally statistical aggregations of these pairwise crossings. Building on these theoretical insights, we introduce LLaCO, a generative framework powered by competition-aware semantic scheduling. LLaCO adapts a pretrained backbone to continuous representations via an embedding directional adapter and timestep-conditioned modulation. To operate within the directional space, LLaCO employs a spherical noising process formulated as a geodesic interpolation toward a mask-biased endpoint, eliminating norm decay while preserving accurate token competition. Guided by SRS, LLaCO reallocates the denoising trajectory proportionally to the logarithmic rank decay. Instantiated as an 8B model, LLaCO outperforms previous continuous diffusion baselines and rivals discrete diffusion models of comparable scale.
authors: Zijian Jia, Peixuan Zhang, Genying Li, Di Wu, Yujie Fu, Si Li, Boxin Shi, Shuchen Weng
bullets: Identifies embedding norm decay as the cause of misleading Euclidean token overtaking and severe temporal compression.
Introduces Competition Threshold Theory to characterize when candidate tokens overtake source tokens based on directional semantic separation and noise.
Proposes Semantic Retention Scheduling to allocate denoising time according to logarithmic token-identity rank decay.
Implements a spherical noising process with an embedding directional adapter and timestep-conditioned modulation.
An 8B LLaCO model outperforms prior continuous diffusion baselines and rivals similarly sized discrete diffusion models.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a continuous diffusion framework for LLM text generation with semantic scheduling, contributing to LLM architecture and non-autoregressive decoding.
papers.title: LLaCO: Continuous Diffusion for Large Language Models with Competition-Aware Semantic Scheduling
papers.tldr: LLaCO improves continuous diffusion language modeling by modeling token competition directionally and scheduling denoising around semantic identity decay.

papers.abstract: Large language models and agents have shown significant power in advanced physical research. In this paper, We introduce PHYRD, a living benchmark for theoretical-physics reasoning with 63 Reproduce and 43 Discover problems. Reproduce tests derivation of published results; Discover tests consequences of modified theoretical conditions. FormulaForest constructs the tasks with reference solutions and subquestion-level rubrics. Across five models, whole-problem accuracy ranges from 49.21% to 68.25% on Reproduce and from 18.60% to 74.42% on closed-book Discover. With tools, four models complete more Discover problems, but conceptual errors and missing arguments persist. Besides, our experimental results demonstrate the value of FormulaForest as synthetic data. On FrontierScience, a benchmark developed by OpenAI, it raises the accuracy of a Qwen-35B-A3B model from 61% to 72%.
authors: Qituan Zhang, Guo Chen, Linfeng Zhang, Wenlong Zhang
bullets: Contains 63 Reproduce problems and 43 Discover problems, built with reference solutions and subquestion-level rubrics.
Across five models, whole-problem accuracy ranges from 49.21%–68.25% on Reproduce and 18.60%–74.42% on closed-book Discover.
Tool use helps four models complete more Discover problems, but conceptual errors and missing arguments remain.
FormulaForest’s synthetic data improves a Qwen-35B-A3B model’s FrontierScience accuracy from 61% to 72%.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces PHYRD, a living benchmark for theoretical physics reasoning, providing a framework for evaluating LLMs on reproduce and discover tasks.
papers.title: PHYRD: A Living Benchmark for Reproducing and Extending Theoretical Physics Research
papers.tldr: PHYRD benchmarks whether language models can reproduce established theoretical-physics results and discover consequences under modified assumptions, revealing persistent conceptual gaps despite tool use.

papers.abstract: Adapting ASR to a domain with only untranscribed audio typically relies on pseudo-labeling, a strong teacher transcribes the audio and a student is fine-tuned on it. Because supervised fine-tuning (SFT) treats every pseudo-label token as a target, the student inherits the teacher's errors. We show that using the same pseudo-labels as a reward reference for Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is more robust to label noise. In the banking domain, GRPO yields 29.3% to 56.2% relative WER improvements over SFT on Whisper-generated labels, and the advantage holds across four Whisper sizes, four teacher families, three domains and four languages. While SFT reproduces almost 100% of teacher errors verbatim, GRPO passes through only 27%. Rollout statistics explain why, erroneous pseudo-label words rarely appear in on-policy rollouts, so group-relative advantages stay aligned with the clean transcript, whereas SFT forces them into the policy's support and collapses the reward variance GRPO relies on.
authors: Shashi Kumar, Yanis Labrak, Sergio Burdisso, Esa\'u Villatoro-Tello, Petr Motlicek, Kadri Hacioglu, Andreas Stolcke
bullets: SFT makes students inherit nearly all teacher transcription errors, while GRPO passes through far fewer.
GRPO improves relative WER over SFT by 29.3%–56.2% in banking-domain adaptation using Whisper-generated labels.
The benefit holds across four Whisper sizes, four teacher families, three domains, and four languages.
On-policy rollouts rarely contain erroneous pseudo-label words, preserving useful group-relative reward signals.
Scope: results concern semi-supervised ASR adaptation with untranscribed audio and pseudo-label supervision.
papers.selection_reason: Applies Group-Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to semi-supervised ASR, using pseudo-labels as rewards to improve robustness against label noise.
papers.title: Pseudo-Labels as Rewards, Not Targets: Group-Relative Policy Optimization for Semi-Supervised ASR
papers.tldr: Using pseudo-labels as reward references rather than hard targets makes GRPO substantially more robust to noisy ASR supervision than SFT.

papers.abstract: Large language models serve applications with diverse inference budgets, but training and maintaining separate models for each budget incurs substantial costs. Recent Looped Transformers enable flexible inference computation through parameter reuse, but maintaining strong performance across different inference budgets remains an open challenge. We introduce Accordion, a mixture-of-experts-based model that supports five inference budgets through fixed-prefix layer looping. Each budget follows a pre-defined execution path, while the minimum budget retains the unlooped model. Joint pretraining samples one budget per micro-batch and optimizes its next-token prediction loss without additional cross-budget consistency objectives. We further preserve these inference budgets through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, where parameter-group merging and budget-matched multi-teacher on-policy distillation integrate three domain experts into one model. After 3.6T tokens of pretraining, increasing inference depth improves Accordion-6B-A0.5B's five-category macro-average across 37 tasks by 3.01 percentage points, with the middle budget capturing 89% of this gain using half as many additional layer executions. The final model surpasses each domain expert on its corresponding task-and-budget average, while achieving strong instruction-following performance across all budgets and retaining depth-dependent gains in mathematical reasoning and code generation.
authors: Yudong Zhang, Wei Ding, Kaili Zheng, Yuchen Ding, Zhenyu Zhang
bullets: Addresses the cost of maintaining separate models for different inference budgets.
Uses fixed-prefix layer looping, with each budget following a predefined path and the minimum budget using the unlooped model.
Joint pretraining samples one budget per micro-batch and optimizes next-token prediction without cross-budget consistency losses.
Preserves budget flexibility through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning with parameter-group merging and budget-matched multi-teacher distillation.

Across 37 tasks, deeper inference improves macro-average performance by 3.01 points; the middle budget captures 89% of the gain with half the extra layer executions, while gains persist in math and code.
papers.selection_reason: MoE LLM with elastic-depth inference via layer looping; relevant to LLM architectures and efficient inference.
papers.title: Accordion: Elastic-Depth Inference via Fixed-Prefix Layer Looping
papers.tldr: Accordion enables one MoE language model to trade inference cost for quality across five fixed computation budgets, with deeper execution improving performance.

papers.abstract: AI agents can inspect code and run tests to support smart contract security. SlowMist reports about $38.6 billion in losses across the broader blockchain ecosystem. Existing evaluations can reward memorized or copied answers, including attack code recovered from public blockchain transactions. Reconstructing contracts and validating tasks also require costly manual effort. To address these issues, we propose CONSTRAINTDIAL, a framework for lifelong construction of smart contract security tasks via protocol mutation. It automates local contract reconstruction and uses attack execution to select changes to the required calls or inputs. Execution checks guide revisions that make the original attack fail while preserving exploitability, the security objective, and normal functionality. New incidents and audit findings enter the same procedure. With CONSTRAINTDIAL, we construct 3,045 task inputs from 203 public cases, covering detect, exploit, and patch. Compared with reconstruction alone, protocol mutation reduces success with supplied public answers by 10.9 percentage points on average across detect, exploit, and patch. The fraction of tasks solved by copying online answers falls by 9.3 points.
authors: Zifan Peng, Peng Huang, Jingyi Zheng, Yingjie Xue, Xuechao Wang, Xinlei He, Xia Hu, Dongrui Liu
bullets: Addresses evaluation contamination from memorized answers and the high manual cost of reconstructing and validating security tasks.
Reconstructs contracts locally, mutates required calls or inputs, and uses execution checks to ensure attacks fail while exploitability and functionality remain intact.
Supports lifelong incorporation of new incidents and audit findings across detect, exploit, and patch tasks.
Constructed 3,045 task inputs from 203 public cases.
Reduced success with supplied public answers by 10.9 percentage points on average and copying-based solutions by 9.3 points.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses smart contract security using AI agents, fitting the Language Foundation Models category (Code/LLMs).
papers.title: Beyond Copying: Lifelong Smart Contract Security Task Construction via Protocol Mutation
papers.tldr: CONSTRAINTDIAL creates harder, less copyable smart-contract security tasks by mutating protocols while preserving their vulnerabilities and normal behavior.

papers.abstract: Pre-consultation medical dialogues are essential for collecting comprehensive patient information, but are costly to obtain at scale due to privacy and ethical constraints. Existing LLM-based synthesis methods often rely on prompt engineering or rigid rules, limiting their ability to balance clinical relevance with realistic patient diversity. We propose CoRPS-Dial, a controllable dual-agent framework for pre-consultation medical dialogue synthesis that integrates patient personas with guideline-aligned clinical workflow rules. CoRPS-Dial generates dialogues through interactions between a persona-driven patient agent and a process-guided doctor agent, followed by post-hoc quality control for role consistency, workflow completeness, and textual consistency. Experiments on coronary heart disease demonstrate that CoRPS-Dial improves alignment between synthetic and real dialogues in information coverage, clinical compliance, and dialogue naturalness. Downstream fine-tuning experiments further confirm the utility of the generated synthetic data for medical dialogue tasks. These results highlight the effectiveness of CoRPS-Dial for clinically grounded and controllable medical dialogue synthesis.
authors: Qiyuan Li, Xiaomei Guo, Chao Gao, Haijiang Liu, Deyu Chen, Caicai Guo, Jinguang Gu
bullets: Addresses the cost, privacy, and ethical barriers to collecting large-scale medical dialogues.
Separates patient diversity from clinical process control through a persona-driven patient agent and guideline-guided doctor agent.
Applies post-hoc checks for role consistency, workflow completeness, and textual consistency.
In coronary heart disease experiments, improves similarity to real dialogues in information coverage, clinical compliance, and naturalness.
Synthetic dialogues also support downstream fine-tuning for medical dialogue tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Develops a dual-agent framework for medical dialogue generation using LLMs, fitting the Language Foundation Models category.
papers.title: Decoupling Patient Personas and Clinical Workflows: A Dual-Agent Approach to Realistic Medical Dialogue Generation
papers.tldr: CoRPS-Dial uses separate patient-persona and clinical-workflow agents to generate realistic, clinically grounded pre-consultation medical dialogues.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly capable of supporting scientific workflows, but their capabilities across diverse research activities remain difficult to assess systematically. Existing benchmarks often focus on selected scientific capabilities or task types, limiting a comprehensive characterization of scientific agents' strengths and weaknesses in realistic research workflows. We introduce SCI-AGENT-EXAM, a workflow-oriented benchmark comprising 120 expert-curated tasks across 11 scientific fields and 7 research task types defined by the Scientific Workflow Task Taxonomy (SWTT). Each task requires both executable artifacts (e.g., code and scripts) and textual artifacts (e.g., reports and explanations). To evaluate the heterogeneous task outputs, we develop a hybrid evaluation protocol combining deterministic programmatic verification for executable artifacts with a calibrated, expert-validated LLM-based judge for textual artifacts. Beyond outcome assessment, we analyze progress and solution stability along execution trajectories to characterize how agents reach their final results. Experiments with 10 frontier LLM agents reveal substantial performance gaps: GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest overall score of 80.9, yet only 26.0% of its runs exceed the 0.95 success threshold. Further analyses uncover distinct capability profiles across scientific task types and substantial variation in execution efficiency and stability. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/SKYLENAGE-AI/Sci-Agent-Exam.
authors: Tianyun Zhong, Wei Wang, Jialin Li, Jianhong Tu, Liyao Li, Chuqiao Kuang, Tianshi Zheng, Songchi Zhou, Weiqi Zhai, Qile Jin, Jiajia Li, Jiasheng Zheng, Boxi Cao, Yaojie Lu, Hongyu Lin, Shiwei Ye, Bing Zhao, Hu Wei, Lin Qu, Xianpei Han
bullets: Covers 120 expert-curated tasks across 11 scientific fields and 7 research task types.
Requires both executable outputs, such as code, and textual outputs, such as reports.
Uses programmatic verification for executable artifacts and an expert-validated LLM judge for textual artifacts.
Analyzes not only final outcomes but also execution progress, efficiency, and stability.
Across 10 frontier agents, GPT-6 Astra scores highest overall, but only 26.0% of runs surpass the 0.95 success threshold.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces SCI-AGENT-EXAM, a workflow-oriented benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on scientific research tasks, relevant to agent capabilities.
papers.title: SCI-AGENT-EXAM: Benchmarking Agents on Scientific Research Tasks
papers.tldr: SCI-AGENT-EXAM benchmarks scientific LLM agents across realistic, multi-step research workflows and reveals major gaps in both task success and execution reliability.

papers.abstract: Building Task-Oriented Dialogue (TOD) systems for high-value scenarios such as financial marketing requires large volumes of domain-specific dialogue data, which privacy regulations, annotation costs, and the need for expert labor make hard to obtain. User simulation offers a remedy, but existing methods target general-domain dialogue and exhibit two key limitations: insufficient modeling of domain-specific business processes and compliance constraints, and inadequate capture of the colloquial, spoken-language character of voice interactions. We propose ProfileSim, a profile-driven user simulation framework for financial marketing outbound calls. It jointly models user profiles---demographics and Big Five personality traits---and business profiles---intents reverse-engineered from real call logs---enabling fine-grained control over simulated behavior. The base model is fine-tuned on real voice dialogue data and refined by Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with hierarchical rewards at the dialogue and utterance levels. Paired with a customer service agent integrating Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) constraints and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), ProfileSim achieves the highest colloquial naturalness, the strongest user profile adherence and the lowest agent score on long-tail intents among all evaluated user generators, while producing substantially shorter user utterances at comparable business compliance. The generated dialogue data is designed to support intent recognition training, agent evaluation, and rapid cold-start deployment.
authors: Juan Li, Fangshu Chang, Xinyi Jiang, Ling Huang, Yunzhang Chen
bullets: Addresses the lack of privacy-safe, expert-annotated, domain-specific dialogue data for task-oriented systems.
Models demographics, Big Five personality traits, and business intents reverse-engineered from real call logs.
Fine-tunes on real voice dialogues and applies GRPO with dialogue- and utterance-level rewards.
With an SOP- and RAG-based agent, achieves the strongest reported colloquial naturalness and profile adherence, while handling long-tail intents and shorter utterances at comparable compliance.
Supports intent-recognition training, agent evaluation, and rapid cold-start deployment.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes ProfileSim, a profile-driven user simulation framework for task-oriented dialogue using RL, relevant to dialogue agent development.
papers.title: Profile-Driven User Simulation via Reinforcement Learning with Hierarchical Rewards for Task-Oriented Dialogues
papers.tldr: ProfileSim uses controllable user and business profiles plus hierarchical reinforcement learning to generate realistic, compliant simulations for financial-marketing voice dialogues.

papers.abstract: LLM-based annotation has advanced rapidly, yet existing benchmarks remain misaligned with real-world practice. Actual annotation often involves lengthy, task-specific guidelines, and different annotators may produce divergent but reasonable judgments, especially on boundary cases, where single-labeled dataset fail to reflect this disagreement. This gap also limits existing single-agent and workflow-based annotation systems, which often lack adaptability to complex, evolving guidelines. To bridge this gap, we introduce ANT-A Benchmark, a real-world multi-annotator benchmark spanning 7 datasets across domains and modalities, with task-specific guidelines and 5 independent human labels per instance. ANT-A enables a distribution-aware evaluation, using Fleiss kappa to assess how closely model annotations align with human labeling distributions. We further propose ANT-OR, a multi-agent annotation framework that refines prompts by distilling contrastive decision rules from positive and negative feedback. Experiments show that ANT-OR improves agreement@>=2 accuracy by 4.5 points over the strongest baseline and achieves the highest alignment with human annotator distributions as measured by Fleiss kappa within 2 points. Code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/Krueske/ANT-OR.
authors: Xiaopeng Ke, Zhixin Wang, Xuebo Liu, Xinyu Ma, Xing Zheng, Bowen Song, Weiqiang Wang, Min Zhang
bullets: Introduces a seven-dataset benchmark spanning domains and modalities, with task-specific guidelines and five independent human labels per instance.
Evaluates annotations against human labeling distributions using Fleiss kappa rather than single-label accuracy alone.
Proposes ANT-OR, which refines prompts by distilling contrastive rules from positive and negative feedback.
Improves agreement@≥2 accuracy by 4.5 points over the strongest baseline and achieves near-best distributional alignment, within 2 Fleiss-kappa points of the best result.
Targets complex, evolving guidelines and reasonable annotator disagreement, especially on boundary cases.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a benchmark (ANT-A) and a multi-agent optimization framework (ANT-OR) for LLM annotation, focusing on aligning with human distributions and adapting to complex guidelines.
papers.title: Can LLM Annotators Match Human Consistency? Benchmarking Human Agreement and Optimizing Multi-Agent with Contrastive Knowledge
papers.tldr: ANT-A benchmarks LLM annotation against diverse human judgments, while ANT-OR improves multi-agent agreement by learning contrastive decision rules from feedback.

papers.abstract: Looped language models run each token through the same layers several times, and each run is one iteration. To save compute, an extra layer, the halting head, gives after each iteration the probability that the token stops there, so that easy tokens can stop early. Pretraining models from scratch, up to 1.3B parameters, we find two problems. First, heads trained on a mix of all iterations predict that tokens need under half the iterations, yet under the standard stopping rule tokens run almost every iteration, because this training never scores the single iteration where a token stops. Scoring every iteration instead fixes this, but in our runs it works only with a strong penalty favoring early stops. Second, savings are commonly reported as an average number of iterations per token, but when sequences are generated in batches that run until their slowest token stops, a model without a head is almost as good at that cost. The reported average can therefore overstate the saving. We recommend reporting the iterations tokens actually run, with the stopping threshold and batch size, and give a test, run before training a head, that bounds its gain.
authors: Tsung-Han Wu, Minsuk Heo, Kenny Tan
bullets: Mixed-iteration training can predict early stopping but fail under the standard stopping rule because the actual stopping iteration is not scored.
Scoring every iteration improves halting, but the reported runs required a strong penalty favoring early stops.
Batch generation runs until the slowest token finishes, so average iterations per token can overstate practical savings.
The authors recommend reporting actual iterations run, stopping threshold, and batch size.
They also propose a pretraining test to bound the potential benefit of a halting head.
papers.selection_reason: Reevaluates compute savings of halting heads in looped LLMs; relevant to efficient inference and LLM architecture.
papers.title: Do Halting Heads Really Save Compute in Looped Language Models?
papers.tldr: Halting heads may provide far less real compute savings than average iteration counts suggest, especially in batched generation.

papers.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) to FP4 has emerged as a key technique for reducing large language model inference cost, especially on Blackwell GPUs, which offer native FP4 tensor core support. Direct PTQ to FP4, however, still leaves a noticeable accuracy gap. Recent work on SVDQuant mitigates the errors introduced through FP4 quantization for diffusion models by adding high-precision low-rank corrections obtained via SVD. However, this high-precision low-rank correction requires many bits per rank, and it runs on the same tensor cores as the main FP4 GEMM. We introduce BiLoCo, a low-rank correction method whose left and right factors are stored as binary ${\{\pm 1\}}$ sign vectors rather than as BF16 numbers. The signed format uses $16{\times}$ less storage per rank-one component, and since the correction now consists of additions/subtractions, this can be run on CUDA cores concurrently with the FP4 tensor-core GEMM. On 4B--72B LLMs, BiLoCo matches or improves memory-matched SVDQuant for PTQ. We implement BiLoCo on B300 as a fused single kernel, where the FP4 GEMM runs on tensor cores, the bit-packed correction on the CUDA cores of the same launch, and the two are combined in the GEMM epilogue. With batch size $1$, the fused kernel is at most $11\%$ slower than the FP4-only GEMM for every rank up to $512$. At rank $128$, it is at most $20\%$ slower up to batch size $8$.
authors: David Jin, Beshr IslamBouli, Tarushii Goel, Han Guo, Yoon Kim
bullets: Addresses the accuracy gap caused by direct FP4 post-training quantization.
Stores low-rank factors as binary ±1 sign vectors, reducing storage per rank-one component by 16× versus high-precision corrections.
Runs the correction through additions/subtractions on CUDA cores concurrently with the FP4 tensor-core GEMM.
On 4B–72B LLMs, matches or improves memory-matched SVDQuant for PTQ.
A fused B300 kernel is at most 11% slower than FP4-only GEMM at batch size 1 for ranks up to 512, and at most 20% slower at rank 128 through batch size 8.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces binary low-rank corrections (BiLoCo) for post-training quantization to reduce memory usage and latency in LLM inference, running efficiently on tensor cores.
papers.title: BiLoCo: Binary Low-Rank Corrections for Post-Training Quantization
papers.tldr: BiLoCo uses binary low-rank corrections to recover FP4-quantized LLM accuracy with far less storage and limited inference overhead.

papers.abstract: Small language models deployed under cost, latency, or privacy constraints cannot simply switch to larger models when reasoning fails. Multi-candidate generate-then-rerank offers a natural test-time scaling route. However, more candidates do not always yield higher accuracy. We identify a previously overlooked bottleneck between generation and selection: a correct answer may appear in the candidate pool yet fail to be selected because it is incomplete, unparseable, or misaligned with the answer mode the fixed selector expects. We term this loss the hidden interface tax and formalize a coverage-conversion decomposition that distinguishes raw oracle coverage from selectable coverage, the subset of problems where a correct candidate can actually be consumed by the selector.
