We propose Compatibility-Aware Candidate Construction (CACC), an interface layer between the candidate source and the fixed selector that repairs fragments, aligns answer modes, and removes selector-confusing noise without retraining either component. On numeric reasoning (GSM8K, competition_math), CACC raises both oracle coverage and final accuracy. On GPQA Diamond, CACC alone improves final accuracy from 5.6% to 19.2% (+13.6 pp); combined with proposer-side strengthening it reaches 25.8% (+20.2 pp). On MMLU-Pro, CACC exposes a coverage-conversion gap: answer-mode-compatible construction raises oracle coverage, but final accuracy decreases by 0.85 pp under the original selector; adding proposer-side strengthening improves final accuracy.
authors: Qianli Ma, Zhiqing Tang, Fanshuai Meng, Zhi Yao, Hanshuai Cui, Weijia Jia
bullets: Multi-candidate generation can contain a correct answer that is not selected because it is incomplete, unparseable, or in the wrong answer mode.
The paper formalizes a coverage–conversion decomposition separating raw oracle coverage from selectable coverage.
Compatibility-Aware Candidate Construction repairs fragments, aligns answer modes, and removes selector-confusing noise without retraining the generator or selector.
CACC improves GPQA Diamond accuracy from 5.6% to 19.2%; combined with proposer strengthening, accuracy reaches 25.8%.
On MMLU-Pro, improved answer-mode compatibility raises oracle coverage but slightly lowers final accuracy under the original selector, showing the method is selector-dependent.
papers.selection_reason: Identifies and mitigates the 'hidden interface tax' in multi-candidate reasoning for LLMs, proposing Compatibility-Aware Candidate Construction to improve answer selection.
papers.title: Correct but Unselectable: The Hidden Interface Tax in Multi-Candidate Reasoning
papers.tldr: CACC improves multi-candidate reasoning by making correct generated answers compatible with a fixed selector, substantially boosting accuracy in some settings while revealing selector-dependent limits.

papers.abstract: Training large language models (LLMs) in sub-8-bit arithmetic promises substantial gains in memory bandwidth and compute throughput, yet FP4 formats introduce quantization error severe enough to destabilize optimization if left unaddressed. We present ALTO, an open-source training recipe for GPT-OSS-20B, a 20-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, on the MLPerf Small MoE Training benchmark under the MXFP4 microscaling format. The recipe combines established techniques from Abecassis, Felix et al. [arXiv:2509.25149] (hybrid 1D/2D block quantization, randomized Hadamard transforms, and stochastic rounding) with a simplified weight de-oscillation scheme adapted from TetraJet-v2 [arXiv:2510.27527]. On C4 validation at global batch size 16, MXFP4 + RHT + SR + de-oscillation reaches a validation loss of 3.3350 at 16,128 steps, only 0.007 above the BF16 baseline (3.3283), closing roughly 50% of the gap left by MXFP4 without de-oscillation (3.3418). Measured by steps to reach the MLPerf quality target (validation loss 3.34), de-oscillation cuts the FP4 convergence overhead relative to BF16 from +20.0% to +5.0%. We also report negative end-to-end results from differential gradient estimation, outlier clipping, and macro-block scaling, despite each showing operator-level SNR gains. All experiments use simulated MXFP4 kernels on AMD MI300 hardware and wall-clock speed has not been optimized.
authors: Han Wang, Zhitao Wang, Natalia Frumkin, Xuanwu Yin, Alireza Khodamoradi, Dong Li, Emad Barsoum
bullets: MXFP4 training is challenging because FP4 quantization error can destabilize optimization.
ALTO combines hybrid block quantization, randomized Hadamard transforms, stochastic rounding, and simplified weight de-oscillation.
On C4 validation, the recipe reaches loss 3.3350 versus 3.3283 for BF16, recovering about half the gap from MXFP4 without de-oscillation.
De-oscillation reduces convergence overhead relative to BF16 from +20.0% to +5.0% at the MLPerf quality target.
Differential gradient estimation, outlier clipping, and macro-block scaling did not improve end-to-end results despite operator-level SNR gains.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a training recipe for an MoE LLM in MXFP4, relevant to large-language-model training and compute/memory efficiency.
papers.title: Training an MoE LLM in MXFP4: How We Closed the Gap to BF16
papers.tldr: ALTO combines quantization and stabilization techniques to train an MoE LLM in MXFP4, reducing the convergence gap to BF16 to near parity in validation loss and overhead.

papers.abstract: Multi-head attention retrieves and combines context representations through query--key interactions and value aggregation, with head dimension constraining the per-head representation space. In long-context processing, it remains unclear whether allocating a fixed parameter budget to fewer, wider heads improves information retrieval. In this paper, we investigate how head dimension affects the performance of long-context retrieval tasks. Our empirical studies reveal that pretraining loss and short-context non-retrieval task performance are not affected much by head dimension, while long-context retrieval performance improves with wider heads at fixed model sizes. We find that models with wider heads have a higher proportion of retrieval heads, associating more parameters with retrieval. Our ablation studies also show that the retrieval performance improves with wider heads even when the projection weights in attention modules are frozen during long-context continual pretraining, suggesting that wider heads not only benefit updates in attention modules but lead to more effective adaptation of components such as embeddings and MLPs.
authors: Seiya Tokui, Shoichiro Yamaguchi, Sosuke Kobayashi
bullets: The study examines whether fewer, wider heads better support retrieval under a fixed parameter budget.
Pretraining loss and short-context, non-retrieval performance change little with head dimension.
Long-context retrieval improves as head dimension increases.
Wider-head models contain a higher proportion of retrieval heads, allocating more capacity to retrieval.
Improvements persist with frozen attention projection weights, indicating benefits beyond attention-module updates.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates head dimension effects on long-context retrieval in language models; directly relevant to LLM architecture and long-context methods.
papers.title: Head Dimension Matters in Language Models for Long-Context Retrieval
papers.tldr: Wider attention heads improve long-context retrieval at fixed model size, even when attention projections are frozen during continual pretraining.

papers.abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is often highly sensitive to learning-rate (LR) choices. Recent empirical studies suggest that, once LRs are carefully tuned, vanilla LoRA can remain competitive with many proposed LoRA variants. This shifts the central practical question from designing ever more variants to reducing the cost and brittleness of LR selection. LoRA+ addresses this issue with asymmetric LRs, using a larger LR for the up-projection matrix $B$ than for the down-projection matrix $A$. However, the ratio $\eta_B / \eta_A$ itself becomes an additional hyperparameter: large ratios can improve adaptation, but under the standard LoRA initialization they can also cause unstable training and ratio-dependent performance collapse. We identify the source of this brittleness through a signal--noise decomposition of LoRA dynamics. Under standard \initA, the update contains an initialization-induced noise term whose magnitude can be affected by the LR for $B$, $\eta_B$, the initialization scale $\beta$, and the adapter rank $r$. In practical LLM fine-tuning, this non-vanishing noise can limit the performance gains expected from LoRA+ style asymmetric LRs. To suppress this effect, we propose \initAA, a simple initialization that scales the variance of $A$ as $\sigma_A^2 \propto n^{-2}$ while keeping $B_0=0$. Under matched rank and training time for both initializations, this reduces the initialization-noise energy by an additional factor of $1/n$, stabilizing asymmetric LoRA training while preserving zero initial adapter output. Empirically, \initAA substantially widens the stable LR region across initialization scales, adapter ranks, and LoRA update multipliers. Across tasks and models, \initAA reduces best-ratio drift, prevents the high-ratio collapse observed with standard \initA, and makes the width-based guideline $\eta_B \approx n \eta_A$ a useful starting point for finite pretrained models.
bullets: LoRA+ can improve adaptation with a larger learning rate for the up-projection matrix B, but its LR ratio is brittle under standard initialization.
A signal–noise analysis attributes instability to an initialization-induced noise term affected by the B learning rate, initialization scale, and adapter rank.
The proposed initialization scales A’s variance as proportional to n⁻² while retaining zero-initialized B, preserving zero initial adapter output.
It reduces initialization-noise energy by an additional factor of 1/n and substantially broadens the stable LR region across tested scales, ranks, and update multipliers.
Across tasks and models, it prevents high-ratio collapse and makes ηB ≈ nηA a useful starting point for finite pretrained models.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes and improves LoRA initialization for LLM fine-tuning, a core topic in LLM adaptation and efficiency.
papers.title: Rethinking LoRA Initialization for Robust Asymmetric Learning Rates
papers.tldr: A new LoRA initialization suppresses initialization noise, making asymmetric learning rates more stable and easier to tune.

papers.abstract: One approach to accelerating progress on AI alignment is to automate parts of alignment research itself. Doing so requires systems that can perform reliably on hard-to-supervise research tasks, including identifying flaws in research proposals and evaluating whether a proposed experiment supports its intended claim. To evaluate this capability, we introduce Tampered ML, a benchmark of 1,858 item-pairs, each consisting of an experiment proposal reconstructed from a published machine learning paper and a minimally edited counterfactual that introduces a targeted methodological flaw. Models must identify the more methodologically sound proposal in both presentation orders. A human validation study on a stratified sample estimates that 86% of items are valid (95% CI: 81-91%). Frontier models perform above chance but remain far from reliable (with Opus 5 achieving 77.9% accuracy). They are highly sensitive to the order of presentation and favor flawed designs that appear more specific, transparent, or conventional.
authors: Soroush Ebadian, Parand A. Alamdari, Joe Benton, Hailey Joren
bullets: Introduces 1,858 paired proposals: a reconstruction of a published ML experiment and a minimally edited flawed counterfactual.
Models must select the more methodologically sound proposal under both presentation orders.
Human validation estimates that 86% of benchmark items are valid (95% CI: 81–91%).
Frontier models perform above chance but remain unreliable; Opus 5 reaches 77.9% accuracy.
Models often favor flawed proposals that seem more specific, transparent, or conventional, and are sensitive to ordering.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a benchmark for evaluating LLMs on machine learning research tasks, relevant to LLM evaluation and alignment.
papers.title: Tampered ML: Evaluating LLM Judgment of Machine Learning Research
papers.tldr: Tampered ML benchmarks whether LLMs can detect targeted methodological flaws in machine learning experiment proposals, finding that frontier models remain unreliable and biased by presentation order and design style.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) generation offers an opportunity to intervene before a reasoning model completes its answer. But does the point at which risk is easiest to detect also offer the most effective control? We study this question with REACT, a conditional activation intervention that learns a safety direction from paired safe and unsafe trajectories and applies it once to an early CoT hidden state. The model weights remain frozen, and all subsequent tokens are generated without further edits. To study timing, we train directions separately at each of the first five CoT positions and evaluate ungated edits with full post-edit regeneration. Across three distilled reasoning models and three generation seeds, the strongest gains concentrate in a two- to three-token early window; on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, the effect falls to approximately zero at the fourth and fifth tokens, even though later states can be more predictive of risk. This separates risk readability from effective control: intervention timing must be evaluated through its effect on subsequent generation. On the same 8B model, REACT raises the rate of fully safe CoT-answer outputs on StrongREJECT-273 from 29.06% to 82.05%, while keeping benign refusal and usefulness near baseline. An anonymized implementation is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/REACT_official2-333B.
authors: Hanwen Zhang, Enyi Jiang, Ruike Zhu, Qinan Yu, Sanmi Koyejo
bullets: Studies whether the best time to detect risk is also the best time to intervene.
Learns a safety direction from paired safe and unsafe trajectories, then applies one edit to an early hidden state while freezing model weights.
Evaluates interventions at each of the first five CoT positions with full post-edit regeneration across three distilled reasoning models.
Finds the strongest control effects at roughly two to three tokens; later states may predict risk better but can be ineffective for control.
On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, fully safe CoT-answer outputs increase from 29.06% to 82.05% on StrongREJECT-273, with benign refusal and usefulness near baseline.
papers.selection_reason: Studies representational intervention in Chain-of-Thought reasoning, a technique relevant to LLM safety and control.
papers.title: REACT: Representational Early Analysis and Control of Chain-of-Thought Trajectories
papers.tldr: REACT improves reasoning-model safety by applying a learned activation edit during a narrow early CoT window, substantially reducing unsafe outputs while preserving usefulness.

papers.abstract: Several formal theories have been developed to characterize the capabilities and limitations of the transformer architecture, each employing different abstractions that capture different features of the architecture. Due to the differences in their underlying assumptions and conceptual frameworks, these theories can disagree in their predictions about what tasks transformers find easy or hard. We map out seven theories of transformer capability (Star-free, $\mathsf{AC}^0$, $\mathsf{TC}^0$, C-RASP, MPC, BAPO, and Sensitivity) and translate their results into a common matrix of predictions across a suite of tasks covering different computational structures. We provide new theoretical results to complete this matrix. We then evaluate theoretical predictions through controlled experiments measuring in-distribution sample complexity, length generalization, and pretrained language model performance. We find that no single theory explains the observed pattern of successes and failures. When a theory does not capture the transformer behaviors relevant to a task, its predictions break down; for instance, we show that the $k$-hop induction task is predicted hard by C-RASP because it does not model content-dependent attention, but we train small transformers on this task that length-generalize. Similarly, theories assuming hard attention like $\mathsf{AC}^0$ and BAPO predict binary majority to be hard, for which we also find success in practice. Together, our results point to several specific features that a theory of transformers must capture: soft rather than hard attention, dynamic content-dependent retrieval, bounded computation at each position, an account of learnability and inductive biases, and a combination of upper and lower bounds.
authors: Awni Altabaa, Tobias Schnabel, Kiran Tomlinson
bullets: Maps seven theoretical frameworks to common predictions across tasks with varied computational structures.
Adds theoretical results to complete the comparison matrix and tests predictions using sample complexity, length generalization, and pretrained-model behavior.
Finds theory–practice mismatches, including transformers length-generalizing on k-hop induction despite C-RASP predicting difficulty.
Finds practical success on binary majority despite hard-attention theories predicting it is hard.
Identifies soft attention, content-dependent retrieval, bounded per-position computation, inductive biases, and both upper and lower bounds as important ingredients.
papers.selection_reason: Empirically tests and compares seven theoretical frameworks characterizing the capabilities and limitations of the transformer architecture.
papers.title: Putting Transformer Theories to the Test
papers.tldr: A systematic comparison of seven transformer theories shows that no single theory explains empirical successes and failures, highlighting the need for more realistic accounts of attention, retrieval, computation, and learnability.

papers.abstract: In drug development, lead optimization must improve competing properties, such as increasing permeability and reducing toxicity, while limiting scaffold changes that could compromise the lead's potency. RL-based post-training, such as C-MORAL, addresses this problem by fine-tuning molecular language models to directly optimize molecular leads for objectives of interest, which relies on expensive task-specific datasets and faces challenges in achieving multi-objective optimization (MOO). We argue a pre-trained model may already contain useful molecular edits that zero-shot generation cannot efficiently reach. Motivated by the limited search capabilities of zero-shot generation, we develop an efficient Metropolis-Hastings search strategy to better explore the proposal distribution. We propose ReMedI, which uses the molecular language model as a base proposer for inference-time alignment. Given a lead and a set of multi-objective tasks, the model proposes edits conditioned on the current molecule, while Metropolis--Hastings refinement guides sequential edits under an objective for property improvement, preservation, and lead similarity. On both C-MuMOInstruct and SMDD benchmarks, refinement improves frozen base models across three backbones, reaching significantly higher multi-objective optimization success rates compared to baselines. These search traces can then distilled into the base model which improves zero-shot generation and subsequent search using approximately 7.8 times less training molecular leads than that of C-MORAL. ReMedI achieves approximately 2.8 times the strict-success coverage of RL baseline C-MORAL, including on out-of-distribution tasks, with matched lead-relative similarity.
authors: Jia Yi Zhang, Shivanshu Shekhar, Allison McLevige, Tong Zhang
bullets: Targets simultaneous property improvement, preservation of lead quality, and minimal scaffold changes without task-specific RL fine-tuning.
Uses a molecular language model to propose edits, while Metropolis–Hastings refinement guides sequential molecule modifications at inference time.
Distills refinement traces into the base model to improve later zero-shot generation and search.
Improves frozen models across three backbones on C-MuMOInstruct and SMDD, with higher multi-objective success than baselines.
Reports approximately 2.8× the strict-success coverage of C-MORAL and uses approximately 7.8× fewer training molecular leads, while matching lead-relative similarity.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes inference-time refinement for molecular language models, a specific application of foundation models in chemistry.
papers.title: ReMedI: Inference-Time Refinement and Self-Distillation for Controllable Molecular Optimization
papers.tldr: ReMedI improves multi-objective molecular lead optimization by refining a frozen language model’s proposed edits with Metropolis–Hastings search and distilling successful search traces back into the model.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit mode collapse, where their output distribution concentrates on familiar semantic modes. When diversity disappears, repeated sampling becomes semantic repetition rather than discovery, making rare but stronger solutions unlikely to surface and leaving self-evolution and continual learning difficult to sustain. Most remedies intervene only at inference time, shaping sam- ples without making diversity a model capability. We propose PRISM, a training-time framework that internalizes diversity within the model. PRISM combines (i) submodular curation that pairs each prompt with diverse-yet-correct multi-teacher solutions, and (ii) stochastic embedding modulation, which turns special-token perturbations into implicit signals for sampling distinct outputs. A theoretical analysis establishes the stability of this mechanism. On WritingPrompts and BookMIA, PRISM moves the quality-diversity frontier outward, achieving the best generation quality in all model-benchmark settings while maintaining the strongest or near-strongest semantic diversity across two open-weight model families. It also improves sampling efficiency on math and code benchmarks. Beyond inference, PRISM yields a stronger foundation for reinforcement learning, sustaining diverse rollouts and mitigating the diversity collapse commonly observed during RL training.
authors: Qixin Xu, Zihan Zhu, Xiaojiang Liu, Bohan Lyu
bullets: Addresses mode collapse, where repeated sampling produces semantically repetitive outputs and misses rare strong solutions.
Uses submodular curation to pair prompts with diverse but correct multi-teacher answers.
Applies stochastic perturbations to special-token embeddings to implicitly condition the model toward distinct outputs.
Improves the quality–diversity frontier on WritingPrompts and BookMIA across two open-weight model families, while also improving sampling efficiency for math and code.
Supports reinforcement learning by sustaining diverse rollouts and mitigating diversity collapse during training.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses mode collapse in LLMs via a training-time framework (PRISM) that internalizes diversity through stochastic embedding modulation and submodular curation.
papers.title: PRISM: Promoting Sampling Diversity of Large Language Models with Implicit Stochastic Modulation
papers.tldr: PRISM trains LLMs to generate diverse, high-quality solutions by combining diverse data curation with stochastic embedding modulation.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) support bidirectional denoising and iterative refinement, but generation remains largely controlled by token-level masking schedules. This leaves draft-level refinement implicit and limits explicit control over when to insert missing content, delete redundant spans, revisit uncertain regions, or stop editing. We introduce Diffusion Editing Language Adapter (DELA), a plug-in framework that enables controllable draft refinement with a frozen DLM. DELA operates on clean, variable-length drafts using four explicit editing actions: Insert, Delete, Remask, and Stop. The controller determines when and where to edit the draft, while the frozen DLM fills masked regions through denoising, separating high-level edit control from token-level generation. A naive single-phase editor would be computationally expensive because arbitrary interior edits can disrupt prefix stability and limit reliable KV-cache reuse. To address this, DELA uses a two-phase decoding procedure: a fast, append-only drafting phase that supports KV-cache reuse, followed by a global refinement phase that enables targeted non-monotonic edits to the full draft. We train the controller using a staged curriculum that begins with learning local edit priors from synthetic recovery tasks and mined actions that improve draft quality. Subsequent stages refine edit selection through rollout-based outcome preferences and alignment with downstream task feedback. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation show that DELA achieves gains of up to 5.5 percentage points over direct diffusion decoding while keeping the backbone frozen. DELA thus provides a modular approach to explicit draft-level control in diffusion language models.
authors: Xinsong Feng, Chenan Wang, Leshu Tang, Johnny Liu, Dong Li, Da Li, Haipeng Chen
bullets: Addresses the limited draft-level control of token-masking schedules in diffusion language models.
Uses a controller to choose when and where to edit, while the frozen backbone denoises masked regions.
Combines fast append-only drafting with global refinement to support efficient KV-cache reuse and non-monotonic edits.
Trains the controller with staged synthetic recovery, mined actions, rollout preferences, and downstream feedback.
Improves mathematical reasoning and code generation by up to 5.5 percentage points over direct diffusion decoding, with the backbone frozen.
papers.selection_reason: Controllable editing for diffusion language models and KV-cache-friendly decoding is a meaningful language-model method relevant to LLM architecture advances.
papers.title: DELA: Learning Controllable Edits for Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: DELA adds explicit, controllable draft editing to frozen diffusion language models through learned insert, delete, remask, and stop actions.

papers.abstract: Verifying the provenance of autonomous LLM agents is a critical security challenge. Existing semantic attribution is easily obfuscated by system prompts, while active watermarking conflicts with schema-constrained tool generation. We propose AgentTrace, an active framework that identifies the foundation model behind a black-box agent via observable execution traces. AgentTrace injects structurally ambiguous probes to trigger tokenization-sensitive serialization failures at rigid tool interfaces. While these initial failures provide coarse-grained separation across model families, the temporal sequence of subsequent repair operations reveals fine-grained, model-specific recovery behaviors. By modeling these multi-step trajectories with lightweight Markov chains, AgentTrace achieves 96.0% attribution accuracy under adversarial identity spoofing. Crucially, sequential repair modeling successfully distinguishes the evaluated intra-family variants sharing identical tokenizers (e.g., Llama-3 8B/70B), substantially outperforming unordered behavioral statistics while remaining robust against prompt obfuscation and temperature scaling.
authors: Gejian Zhao, Hanzhou Wu, Xinpeng Zhang
bullets: Addresses provenance verification when prompts can obscure semantic behavior and watermarking conflicts with constrained tool generation.
Injects structurally ambiguous probes that expose tokenization-sensitive serialization failures at tool interfaces.
Models the temporal sequence of subsequent repair operations with lightweight Markov chains.
Sequential repair patterns distinguish intra-family variants with identical tokenizers, including evaluated Llama-3 8B and 70B variants.
Remains robust to prompt obfuscation and temperature scaling in the reported evaluation.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates attribution and fingerprinting of LLM agents using execution traces, relevant to LLM security and behavior analysis.
papers.title: AgentTrace: Execution-Level Fingerprinting of Black-Box LLM Agents
papers.tldr: AgentTrace fingerprints black-box LLM agents by analyzing model-specific tool-error and repair trajectories, achieving 96.0% attribution accuracy under identity spoofing.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit sycophancy, altering their answers to align with user suggestions even on objective factual and reasoning tasks. Yet the quantitative form of this influence--- and whether it is calibrated to source reliability--- remains poorly understood. In this work, we investigate this behavior through hint-induced answer shifts on MMLU questions, evaluating prompts of the form ``[Source] thinks the answer is (X)''. We systematically vary the source to which the hint is attributed (a professor, a friend, or a dog) across three open-source model families, Qwen, Gemma, and SmolLM. We show that the change induced by the hint follows a predictable structure well-characterized by an exponential tilt: the hint induces an approximately constant mean shift in the hinted answer's log-odds, with question--target susceptibility largely shared across sources. To explore how this pattern can arise, we introduce a formal decomposition of the hint response and illustrate in controlled synthetic experiments how KL-regularized reward-based training reshapes both hinted and unhinted answer distributions. Finally, we evaluate whether this shift is calibrated to source reliability, finding that the log-odds shift persists even when the hint-giver is declared inaccurate or accompanied by explicit warnings not to trust the source, highlighting the vulnerability of LLMs to adversarial steering.
authors: Anxin Guo, Chirag Pabbaraju, Sara Ahmadian, Kamesh Munagala, Aravindan Vijayaraghavan
bullets: Studies hint-induced answer changes on MMLU questions across Qwen, Gemma, and SmolLM models.
Hints attributed to a professor, friend, or dog produce approximately constant shifts in the hinted answer’s log-odds.
Question-specific susceptibility is largely shared across different hint sources.
A formal decomposition and synthetic experiments examine how KL-regularized reward training may produce these shifts.
The response is poorly calibrated to source reliability: shifts persist even when sources are labeled inaccurate or untrustworthy.
papers.selection_reason: Quantifies hint-following and sycophancy in reasoning LLMs via log-odds shifts; directly relevant to LLM reasoning behavior and robustness.
papers.title: How Much Do You Trust A Dog? Quantifying Hint-Following in Reasoning Language Models
papers.tldr: LLMs systematically shift their answers toward hinted choices, often ignoring warnings about unreliable sources, revealing a measurable vulnerability to adversarial steering.

papers.abstract: This report introduces Kolibri, an English-German mixture-of-experts transformer with 78.1B total parameters and 3.46B active parameters per token, released as open weights under the Apache 2.0 licence. We built Kolibri for sovereign and specialised deployment, with a particular focus on German and on regulated domains such as public administration, industry, and aerospace. To support these settings, we control the full model-development process, including data, architecture, training infrastructure, post-training, and evaluation. We train Kolibri on 24T tokens across pre-training, mid-training, and long-context extension, with German accounting for more than 20% of the data mix by bytes. To reach this share, we complement German datasets with more than 2T German tokens that we curate from the web with our own pipeline and generate synthetically. Post-training combines supervised fine-tuning on curated German and English data with reinforcement learning on more than 1.2M internally curated tasks, which cover reasoning, tool use, instruction following, code, and retrieval. The model activates 4.4% of its parameters per token, and among the open models evaluated in this report, it lies on the Pareto frontier of quality and serving cost in English and German. Kolibri builds on Kolibri Origin, an earlier iteration that validated our full pipeline at scale. Both models come from our Model Factory, which connects data, experimentation, training, evaluation, and deployment through version-controlled workflows.
authors: Aleph Alpha, :, Moritz Althaus, Artur Baranowski, Michael Barlow, Fabien C. Y. Benureau, Felix Berkenkamp, Amrita Bhattacherjee, Lukas Bl\"ubaum, Duncan Blythe, Augustijn de Boer, Bastian Boll, Thomas F. Burns, Bj\"orn Deiseroth, Niko D\"urr, B\'eni Bal\'azs Egressy, Niklas Finken, Niklas Freymuth, Fabian Gebhart, Max Hammer, Bastian Harren, Andreas Hartel, Johann Higl, Steffen Hirschmann, Pablo Iyu Guerrero, Yasser Jadidi, Andreas Jagusch, Mitja Kleider, Markus Klein, Jonas Knupp, Murali Kondragunta, Garwin Lechner, Dominik L\^e-Kellner, Jurek Leonhardt, Jiaze Li, Sohir Maskey, Omar Mehio, Pit Neitemeier, Letitia Parcalabescu, Alejandro Petry Pacheco, Pranav Ragupathy, Martin Reinhardt, Peter Rodenkirch Nfissi, Dylan Rodriquez, Leonard Salewski, Raziye Sari, Jordan Sassoon, Ivo Schaper, Ilhan Scheer, Frank Schneider, Philipp Scholl, Lukas Schott, Eric Schreiber, Pablo Schumacher, Alessio Serra, Philipp Siedler, Prabhu Teja Sivaprasad, Mohamed Soliman, Till Speicher, Volker Stampa, Simon Thel, Serge Thilges, Irina Vidal Migall\'on, Denis Wa{\ss}mann, Samuel Weinbach, Sascha Wirges, Michael W\"uthrich, Alexei Zacharov
bullets: Uses 78.1B total parameters but activates 3.46B per token (4.4%), reducing serving cost.
Trained on 24T tokens, including over 20% German data and more than 2T curated or synthetic German tokens.
Post-training covers reasoning, tool use, instruction following, code, and retrieval through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning on over 1.2M tasks.
Released under Apache 2.0 and developed through a controlled, versioned pipeline spanning data, training, evaluation, and deployment.
Among the open models evaluated in the report, it is reported to lie on the quality–serving-cost Pareto frontier in English and German.
papers.selection_reason: Open-weight English-German mixture-of-experts language model; directly fits large language foundation models.
papers.title: Kolibri: A Sovereign European Model on the Pareto Frontier
papers.tldr: Kolibri is an open-weight English-German mixture-of-experts model designed for sovereign, cost-efficient deployment, especially in German and regulated domains.

papers.abstract: Looped language models apply one block of layers repeatedly, and the design pays off only if depth is reusable: loop steps beyond the trained budget must remain usable at inference. We ask whether that rests on normalising the state between loop steps, as the released Ouro models do, or on agreement between the loop a model is trained with and the loop it is run with. On released weights this loop-boundary normalisation can be removed without adding parameters and with the readout path bit-identical, and the operation is an identity at one loop step, which serves as an implementation check. Removing it takes Ouro-1.4B and Ouro-2.6B to zero accuracy by the trained budget on a balanced binary task (chance 0.500). State-norm growth, the failure that prior accounts predict, is not the cause: the norm stays within a factor of 2.021 while the head commits to a single wrong token. Yet in 19M-parameter models trained from scratch on two synthetic tasks, 16 seeds per configuration, training without the normalisation is never worse than training with it and extrapolates better: the two are closest at the trained depth and separate on both sides of it (Cliff's delta up to 0.867 beyond the budget). Both results follow if agreement, and not the normalisation itself, is what keeps depth reusable. The damage sits in the readout together with the last layer of the block: in the models trained from scratch, refitting the head over the frozen modified loop recovers a third of the lost accuracy and plateaus, while refitting the last block layer with it recovers all of it. Finally, comparing looped with stacked depth at an equal inference loop count is confounded by unequal overshoot of the trained budget; at matched overshoot the advantage of looping vanishes on one task and shrinks on the other.
authors: Ivan Viakhirev, Kirill Borodin, Maxim Abramov, Grach Mkrtchian
bullets: Removing boundary normalisation from released Ouro models causes performance to collapse by the trained depth, despite limited state-norm growth.
In models trained from scratch, removing normalisation is not worse and often extrapolates better beyond the trained depth.
The failure is localized to the readout and final block layer: refitting both restores the lost accuracy, while refitting only the head gives partial recovery.
Comparisons between looped and stacked models should match overshoot beyond the trained depth; under this control, looping’s advantage disappears on one task and shrinks on another.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes depth reuse and normalization in looped language models; architectural insight for LLMs.
papers.title: Agreement rather than normalisation keeps depth reusable in looped language models
papers.tldr: Depth reuse in looped language models appears to depend more on agreement between training and inference loops than on loop-boundary normalisation itself.

papers.abstract: Muon has become a popular optimizer for large language model training, yet its theoretical foundations remain poorly understood. In this work, we study how gradient noise geometry shapes Muon's preconditioning benefits. We first show, theoretically and empirically, that under the classical isotropic noise assumption, Muon offers no acceleration beyond a rescaling of the learning rate. This motivates us to investigate structured noise arising from mini-batch sampling in associative memory with heterogeneous task frequencies. We establish an exact balancing threshold for two tasks and extend the analysis to multiple tasks, revealing how task coverage and gradient reliability jointly shape learning. Our analysis shows that Muon can soften the dependence on task frequency from linear to square-root, helping balance the learning of frequent and rare tasks. We further identify rotation-induced negative transfer in SignSGD that Muon avoids, and explain how momentum reduces sampling noise while tracking changing gradients. Controlled numerical experiments validate these mechanisms, and a preliminary LLM pretraining study illustrates the practical promise of fast-slow momentum.
authors: Xiaoran Chen, Binghui Li, Liwei Wang, Pinyan Lu
bullets: Under isotropic gradient noise, Muon provides no acceleration beyond learning-rate rescaling.
For heterogeneous task frequencies, Muon changes task-frequency dependence from linear to square-root scaling.
The analysis derives an exact two-task balancing threshold and extends to multiple tasks based on coverage and gradient reliability.
Muon avoids rotation-induced negative transfer identified in SignSGD, while momentum reduces sampling noise and tracks changing gradients.
Controlled experiments support the theory, and a preliminary LLM pretraining study suggests promise for fast-slow momentum.
papers.selection_reason: Provides a theoretical analysis of the Muon optimizer's preconditioning benefits in the context of large language model training, addressing a key architectural and training question.
papers.title: When and How Does Muon Precondition? The Role of Structured Gradient Noise
papers.tldr: Muon’s preconditioning benefits arise from structured, rather than isotropic, gradient noise and can improve balance between frequent and rare tasks.

papers.abstract: This article introduces Latin Modern BERT (LAMB), an encoder for the Latin language based on the ModernBERT architecture, pretrained in two phases on more than 74B Latin tokens using a novel morphologically informed masking regimen. We also present two corpora for the Latin language. Acervus contains 24B BERT WordPiece tokens, including over 760K samples from heavily damaged OCR transcriptions, repaired by a ByT5 model trained for Latin text repair. The second dataset, Corpus Trinum, contains a mixture of over 100M strong and weak Latin language semantic triplets. Corpus Trinum is the first Latin semantic triplet dataset, opening the door for Latin language models to be adapted to general sentence semantic similarity tasks. We construct an experimental grid using five tasks and seventeen subtasks, applying a variety of finetuning configurations and subword aggregation techniques for 15 pretrained encoders, 6 LAMB training checkpoints, and an ablation model designed to quantify the impact of different masking regimens. Using this benchmark, we rank Latin encoders and find that LAMB outperforms all other evaluated models on 16 of 17 subtasks, coming within 0.8 percentage points of state of the art on the seventeenth. We provide additional analyses relating Latin encoder performance to tokenizer behavior, syntactic structure, finetuning configuration, pretraining state, subword aggregation, and variation in source texts and domains. In these, we identify unique acquisition dynamics for Latin open class words during terminal decay phases, and establish that for some task categories, finetuning configuration selection can have a greater effect on downstream scores than additional pretraining tokens.
bullets: Pretrained in two phases on more than 74B Latin tokens using a morphologically informed masking strategy.
Introduces Acervus, a 24B-token corpus incorporating repaired OCR text, and Corpus Trinum, a 100M+ semantic-triplet dataset.
Evaluated across five tasks and 17 subtasks, with varied checkpoints, finetuning settings, and subword aggregation methods.
Outperforms all other evaluated encoders on 16 of 17 subtasks and approaches state of the art on the remaining task.
Analyses examine tokenizer behavior, syntax, pretraining, finetuning, subword aggregation, and domain variation.
papers.selection_reason: Pretrained Latin foundation language model with architectural and pretraining contributions, fitting language foundation model research.
papers.title: LAMB: A Modern Contextual Language Model for Latin
papers.tldr: LAMB is a ModernBERT-based Latin encoder pretrained with morphology-aware masking that achieves leading performance across a broad 17-subtask benchmark.

papers.abstract: Machine learning (ML) is increasingly used in astronomy, but choosing a suitable method for a scientific problem often requires expertise in both astronomy and ML. Large language models (LLMs) could help astronomers make such choices, yet this ability remains underexplored in existing benchmarks. We introduce Astro2Method, a benchmark of 500 expert-reviewed binary questions from 346 astronomy papers (2024/01-2026/06), based on clear performance differences and complete (Easy) or partial (Hard) explanations from the authors. Across five LLMs, direct prompting achieves 87.50-92.55% accuracy on Easy questions but only 58.87-64.52% on Hard. Using historical papers, neither retrieval-augmented generation nor most agent methods with additional reasoning or retrieval (including ReAct, Self-Ask, and CRITIC) bring consistent improvement. Agents required to search the web improve accuracy mainly when they find the papers the questions are based on, with no consistent improvement otherwise. Providing the source paper's pipeline description with method names masked improves Hard accuracy, matching or exceeding web search. Together, these results suggest that relevant experimental information helps distinguish ML methods, but inferring it from related studies and domain knowledge remains challenging for LLMs in astronomy.
authors: Xingzhong Fan, Hangfeng He, Fatemeh Nargesian
bullets: Benchmarks ML-method selection with 500 expert-reviewed binary questions from 346 astronomy papers.
Direct prompting reaches 87.50–92.55% accuracy on Easy questions versus 58.87–64.52% on Hard questions.
Retrieval-augmented generation and most agent approaches do not consistently improve performance.
Web-search agents help mainly when they locate the source papers; masked pipeline descriptions can match or exceed web search on Hard questions.
Relevant experimental information is important, but inferring it from related work and domain knowledge remains difficult.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a benchmark for evaluating LLMs on machine learning method selection in astronomy, providing a specific task for assessing LLM domain knowledge and reasoning.
papers.title: Astro2Method: Benchmarking LLMs on Machine Learning Method Selection in Astronomy
papers.tldr: Astro2Method shows that LLMs select ML methods well when explanations are complete, but struggle with partially explained astronomy papers, and common retrieval or agent strategies rarely help consistently.

papers.abstract: Looped LMs are parameter efficient and promise dynamic computation (saving memory and FLOPs on easy tokens). However, state-of-the-art open Looped LMs trained with this dynamic computation capability (Ouro models) do not realize it in practice as each loop iteration (depth) requires its own level of KV-cache, necessitating all loop computations. Moreover, Ouro's early-exit prior is enforced on each token equally, which results in static lower-depth like processing of all tokens regardless of difficulty. In this work, we propose a simple "best-available" KV caching strategy that works out-of-the-box, creating a new frontier in the performance vs depth space. Our approach enables up to 30% reduction in FLOPs and KV memory while retaining full-depth performance, showing the true flexibility of Looped LMs. Furthermore, training looped LMs with awareness about this KV caching strategy improves performance and efficiency. Finally, we apply a small but effective fix to the early-exit prior enforcement objective that makes tokens exit at truly heterogeneous depths based on effort. Our findings are validated on Ouro models as well as smaller looped LMs pre-trained from scratch.
bullets: Existing Ouro Looped LMs require KV-cache storage for every loop depth, forcing all loop computations despite supporting dynamic computation.
The proposed “best-available” KV caching strategy enables up to 30% lower FLOPs and KV memory without losing full-depth performance.
Training with awareness of this caching strategy further improves efficiency and performance.
A revised early-exit objective produces heterogeneous token depths based on token difficulty rather than uniform shallow processing.
Results are validated on Ouro models and smaller looped LMs pretrained from scratch.
papers.selection_reason: KV-cache strategy for looped language models enables dynamic computation with reduced memory and FLOPs, fitting efficient inference and LLM architecture research.
papers.title: Enabling Dynamic Computation in Looped LMs
papers.tldr: A practical KV-cache strategy and improved early-exit training make Looped LMs dynamically allocate computation, reducing costs while preserving full-depth performance.

papers.abstract: Interpretability research on large language models has produced accounts of factual recall in feed-forward layers and of token relationships in self-attention, but little work offers a unified way to compare the causal contribution of different architecture components to a model's output. We introduce MechaTerp (the Mechanistic Interpretability suite) -TRACE (subset for Teacher-forced Registry of Ablated Component Effects), an architecture and study that measures how much each registered component of a language model supports the production of a named entity. TRACE ablates one component at a time and measures the resulting change in the output distribution at a fixed answer token, so component types from whole transformer blocks down to individual neurons and output logits can be compared on a common scale. We apply it to thirteen instruction-tuned dense decoder models spanning five families and one to thirty billion parameters, ablating 49,656 components across 48 medical and 42 general-knowledge prompts. We find that the components carrying the most effect are the same few, positionally fixed components in every model, regardless of which entity a prompt asks about, and that once these are removed, the remaining support is close to evenly spread in eleven of the thirteen models. Apparent localisation of entity knowledge is therefore largely attributable to generic generation machinery, which has direct consequences for methods that assume entity knowledge sits in a findable place, including targeted knowledge editing.
bullets: Addresses the lack of a common method for comparing causal contributions across language-model components.
Ablates one registered component at a time and measures changes in the output distribution at a fixed answer token.
Enables comparison from whole transformer blocks to individual neurons and output logits on a shared scale.
Applied across 13 instruction-tuned dense decoder models, covering five families and 1–30 billion parameters, with medical and general-knowledge prompts.

The most influential components are positionally fixed across models and entities; after removing them, support is nearly evenly distributed in 11 of 13 models, challenging assumptions behind targeted knowledge editing.
papers.selection_reason: Component-level causal ablation across LLM families, relevant to understanding architecture components and knowledge localization.
papers.title: MechaTerp-TRACE: A Novel Approach for Component Ablation Analysis in Language Models
papers.tldr: MechaTerp-TRACE provides a unified causal framework for comparing how model components affect named-entity generation, finding that apparent entity-knowledge localization often reflects generic generation machinery.

papers.abstract: Standard tokenizers used in large language models produce malformed text when applied to Brahmic scripts. They are a family of abugidas, writing systems whose consonants carry an inherent vowel that dependent marks can modify. They include Devanagari, Telugu, Tamil, Kannada, and others. The underlying issue is that these tokenizers violate orthographic constraints that do not arise in alphabetic scripts like English. We observe that while English orthography forms a \emph{semigroup} (any two valid tokens can be freely concatenated), Brahmic orthography forms a \emph{partial semigroup}: not every concatenation yields a valid string. We formalise this distinction in Agda, model valid Brahmic tokens as chains in a transition system, and derive a provably correct \texttt{fixToken} function that extends any candidate token to respect orthographic boundaries. We then show how this formal derivation translates into a practical patch for SentencePiece as well as a standalone Rust-based pre-tokenizer library, eliminating the observed errors across Indic scripts.
bullets: Standard LLM tokenizers can produce malformed text for Brahmic abugidas because they ignore script-specific orthographic constraints.
Brahmic token concatenation is modeled as a partial semigroup, unlike the freely composable tokens assumed for English.
The authors formalize valid tokens as chains in a transition system using Agda.
They derive a provably correct `fixToken` function and implement it in SentencePiece and a standalone Rust pre-tokenizer.
The approach eliminates the observed tokenization errors across the Indic scripts studied; the abstract does not report quantitative results.
papers.selection_reason: Formal analysis and correction of tokenization for Brahmic scripts, relevant to LLM tokenizer and architecture design.
papers.title: Type-Driven Tokenization for Brahmic Scripts
papers.tldr: A formally verified tokenizer design enforces valid orthographic boundaries in Brahmic scripts and removes malformed-token errors across Indic scripts.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) depend fundamentally on the diversity, depth, and factual rigor of their pre-training corpora. However, contemporary foundational pre-training datasets (such as The Pile, S2ORC, and Dolma) exhibit a severe structural omission: African scientific, medical, legal, and agricultural scholarship constitutes less than 0.5% of global pre-training tokens. Consequently, state-of-the-art models suffer from systematic failure modes when reasoning about tropical epidemiology, localized smallholder agro-ecologies, regional economic governance, and indigenous linguistic structures. To resolve this representation deficit and advance African intellectual sovereignty in artificial intelligence, we introduce Africa-Papers, the largest curated multi-domain Pan-African academic pre-training corpus to date. Comprising over 844,807 full-text papers spanning 10.15 billion tokens across 879 Parquet shards, Africa-Papers unifies four primary scientific streams: (1) continental peer-reviewed journals indexed in DOAJ across 31 African nations, (2) the CGIAR CGSpace agricultural repository, (3) African-authored and African-focused STEM/AI preprints on arXiv, and (4) open-access international publications by scholars affiliated with African institutions indexed via OpenAlex. The entire corpus is processed into layout-aware, clean Markdown preserving section hierarchies, mathematical equations, and tabular data, accompanied by exact BPE token counts and a standardized 8-domain taxonomy. We release Africa-Papers openly on the Hugging Face Hub under the AfriSpeech organization to accelerate continual pre-training and domain evaluation for foundation models globally.
bullets: Addresses the underrepresentation of African scholarship in major pre-training datasets, especially for region-specific knowledge.
Aggregates 844,807 full-text papers from African journals, agricultural repositories, preprints, and publications by scholars at African institutions.
Covers scientific, medical, legal, agricultural, STEM/AI, and related domains across 31 African nations.
Provides layout-aware Markdown that preserves document structure, equations, and tables, with exact BPE token counts and an 8-domain taxonomy.
Released on Hugging Face to support continual pre-training and domain evaluation of foundation models.
papers.selection_reason: Pan-African academic pretraining corpus is a language foundation-model resource.
papers.title: Africa-Papers: A 10-Billion-Token Multi-Domain Academic Corpus for African Foundation Language Models
papers.tldr: Africa-Papers is an openly released 10.15-billion-token corpus designed to improve African representation in foundation-model pre-training across scientific and societal domains.

papers.abstract: Data selection plays a central role in modern large language model training, as the quality of training data strongly influences downstream performance. A common approach is to curate a development set that encodes the desired skills (e.g., reasoning or multilinguality) and select data that are similar to them. Existing methods compute similarity using cosine distance over either the model's hidden states or gradients. However, we observe that this max-similarity strategy induces a mode-seeking bias: the selected data clusters tightly around the development samples. To address this, we propose ICLHerd, a data selection framework that leverages the von Mises-Fisher kernel to balance mode-seeking with mode-averaging. We further introduce in-context learning as a validation proxy, enabling efficient hyperparameter search over the balance trade-off. Results show that ICLHerd outperforms existing LLM data selection algorithms, highlighting the importance of balancing mode-seeking and mode-averaging.
bullets: Existing cosine-similarity selection over hidden states or gradients tends to select data tightly clustered around development examples.
ICLHerd uses a von Mises–Fisher kernel to balance selecting representative modes with averaging across broader data regions.
It uses in-context learning as an efficient proxy for tuning this trade-off during hyperparameter search.
Experiments report that ICLHerd outperforms existing LLM data-selection algorithms.
The approach focuses on selecting data aligned with targeted skills such as reasoning or multilinguality.
papers.selection_reason: LLM data-selection method with in-context learning as a proxy is relevant to language foundation-model development.
papers.title: ICLHerd: Herding-Based Data Selection for LLMs with In-Context Learning as a Proxy
papers.tldr: ICLHerd improves LLM training-data selection by reducing the clustering bias of similarity-based methods through balanced mode-seeking and mode-averaging.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in solving complex tasks in coding, mathematical logic, and iterative reasoning, especially by coordinating effectively within multi-agent systems (MAS). However, language agents traditionally communicate via text exchange, which introduces a bottleneck in information transfer and adds prefill latency for downstream agents. Recent work proposes that directly sharing the key-value (KV) cache between language models can enable efficient latent collaboration, entirely bypassing standard text-based communication. To enable latent communication between heterogeneous models of different sizes, prior work introduces trained fusion adapters for each model pair, which limits practical deployment. We introduce CacheFuse, a training-free method which demonstrates that augmenting a downstream model with an upstream model's KV cache using linear interpolation consistently enables superior performance than the standalone downstream model can achieve. We systematically analyze CacheFuse across four reasoning and knowledge benchmarks and demonstrate up to 8.6 percentage points higher accuracy compared to single-model baselines and up to 12.2x TTFT speedup compared to text-based communication in multi-model inference.
bullets: Addresses text-based communication bottlenecks and downstream prefill latency in multi-agent systems.
Combines an upstream model’s KV cache with a downstream model through linear interpolation, without fusion-adapter training.
Evaluated across four reasoning and knowledge benchmarks.
Reports up to 8.6 percentage-point accuracy gains over single-model baselines.
Achieves up to 12.2× faster time to first token than text-based multi-model communication.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free KV-cache sharing between language models reduces latency and enables efficient latent LLM communication.
papers.title: Think Before You Speak: Enabling Training-Free Latent Communication Between Language Models
papers.tldr: CacheFuse enables training-free latent communication between heterogeneous language models by linearly interpolating their KV caches, improving accuracy while reducing communication latency.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent systems built from frozen language models communicate through text, which discards the internal state the sender already computed and makes the receiver pay to rebuild it. Work on internal channels avoids that cost, framing the problem as transfer: agent A sends information to agent B. Every agent pair that must communicate needs its own transfer bridge, and every agent added to a system needs a new bridge fitted against each previous agent. We reframe this problem as sharing: an agent publishes its internal state once into a pool, and every peer reads that pool through a single mechanism fitted to no sender in particular, so adding an agent adds a publisher and no new bridge. Whereas the carrier of the internal state and the fusion mechanism are usually chosen independently in the literature, our main finding is that these two choices are coupled; the deciding factor is where the carrier enters the receiver's computation. Consumability is a property of the receiving computation rather than of the representation. We find that the key-value (KV) cache must be augmented rather than swapped in: the receiver cross-attends over a peer's cache while keeping its own, and with only a small query-side adapter trained, matches the accuracy it gets from reading the source document. Activations invert this. They are best written straight into the receiver, with no bridge, no adapter and no training, which beats exposing them alongside the receiver's own, though that advantage rests on knowing where in the receiver the state belongs. The rule is augment the KV cache, replace the activation, established under one protocol with a shared control ladder. One adapter, trained once, also serves publishers it never trained on, and a pool of several at once, but only those whose internal state lies close to the receiver's own.
bullets: Reframes multi-agent internal communication as shared publishing to a common pool, avoiding pair-specific transfer bridges.
Shows that carrier and fusion mechanism are coupled through where peer state enters the receiver’s computation.
KV-cache sharing works by cross-attending to peer keys and values while preserving the receiver’s own cache, using only a small query-side adapter.
Activation sharing works best by directly writing into the receiver, without a bridge, adapter, or training.
A single adapter generalizes to unseen publishers and multiple pooled agents when their states are sufficiently close to the receiver’s.
papers.selection_reason: Internal-state sharing through KV caches and activations in frozen LLM agents is relevant to language-model mechanisms and multi-agent inference.
papers.title: Augment the Cache, Replace the Activation: A 2x2 Study of Internal-State Sharing
papers.tldr: A shared internal-state protocol works best when KV caches are augmented with peer states, while activations directly replace the receiver’s corresponding state.

papers.abstract: Activation steering adds a vector to a model's hidden states to control a named behaviour. A gain on that behaviour, however, does not show that the vector controls it directly: it may act through a component shared with neighbouring behaviours, which unsteered and random baselines cannot separate. We introduce the competing-target test: a vector is compared with the vector built the same way for a competing target, and an equivalence test states when their difference is below a useful margin. We apply it in open-weight models to vectors for Kantian deontology, which judges an act by the rule it follows, and act utilitarianism, which judges it by the welfare it produces. On held-out situations, prompting a framework raises its score and lowers the other's, whereas vectors for either framework move both scores alike, and none reaches the margin. The two vectors share most of their direction, a request to apply some framework; the same construction separates an optimistic from a pessimistic tone, whose vectors share much less. What a vector shares with its competitors therefore sets what it controls: steering a perspective can deliver a mixture, and measuring a disposition can measure its neighbours, unless tested against the competing target.
bullets: A gain on the intended behaviour may reflect components shared with competing behaviours.
The competing-target test compares a steering vector with one constructed for its competing target and checks whether their difference exceeds a useful margin.
On held-out situations, prompting one ethical framework raises its score and lowers the other, but either framework’s steering vector moves both scores similarly.
The ethical vectors share most of their direction, unlike optimistic and pessimistic tone vectors, which are more distinct.
Steering vectors may therefore produce mixtures of perspectives and require competing-target evaluation to establish specificity.
papers.selection_reason: Activation steering in open-weight LLMs is a transferable technical method for controlling hidden-state behaviour in language foundation models.
papers.title: Steering Vectors for Competing Ethical Frameworks Are Interchangeable: A Competing-Target Test for Activation Steering
papers.tldr: Activation-steering vectors for Kantian and utilitarian ethics appear to control a shared “apply a framework” disposition rather than distinct ethical frameworks.

papers.abstract: We investigate the problem of role-capability leakage (RCL), in which a role-prompted reasoning model generates convincing in-role text while continuing to exhibit capabilities on benchmarks that exceed those implied by the assigned role. For example, when a model is prompted to assume the role of a kindergarten student, one might expect its performance on a mathematics benchmark to reflect kindergarten-level ability rather than expert-level proficiency in solving calculus problems. We introduce RoleCapBench, a curriculum-grounded benchmark for evaluating RCL across six educational roles and four assessment levels spanning elementary school through A-level, and use it to evaluate three open-weight reasoning models. We find that although the models can generate stylistically convincing in-role responses, they consistently fail to align their underlying capabilities with their assigned roles. Naive role prompting yields strong role-voice scores of 1.218--1.389 while retaining above-role accuracy of 0.811--0.898. RCL persists across a range of prompting conditions, including prompts that explicitly instruct the model to match the role's capability level. To mitigate this problem, we propose Injection, an inference-time intervention that combines explicit, role-specific capability guidelines with a guiding prefilled response prefix. Injection improves role-capability alignment across models, reducing above-role accuracy by up to 0.562 while preserving in-role accuracy with a marginal drop of less than 0.058 across most models. All artifacts, including scripts and evaluation data, will be released upon acceptance.
bullets: Defines role-capability leakage (RCL): models sound like assigned roles while retaining capabilities beyond those roles.
Introduces RoleCapBench, covering six educational roles and four assessment levels from elementary school through A-level.
Evaluates three open-weight reasoning models and finds persistent above-role performance across prompting conditions.
Proposes Injection, combining role-specific capability guidelines with a prefilled response prefix.
Injection reduces above-role accuracy by up to 0.562 while generally preserving in-role accuracy, with drops below 0.058 in most models.
papers.selection_reason: Studies capability leakage and inference-time intervention in role-prompted reasoning models, contributing to LLM behavior and reasoning research.
papers.title: When a Kindergartener Solves Calculus: Measuring Capability Leakage in Role-Prompted Reasoning Models
papers.tldr: Role prompting changes a reasoning model’s style more reliably than its underlying expertise, but a targeted inference-time intervention improves capability alignment.

papers.abstract: Wrong automatic routing of an IT support ticket can cost more than human triage. We evaluate cost-aware abstention as an offline, cost-conditional readiness assessment: select a routing policy on calibration data under explicit costs, then evaluate that frozen policy once on held-out test data. On a public 47,837-ticket, eight-class corpus, we compare four trained non-LLM classifiers with four large language models under zero- and few-shot prompting. Under the illustrative cost model (c_ok, c_triage, c_wrong) = (0, 1, 5), TF-IDF with logistic regression and a threshold of 0.60 selected on calibration reduces test cost from 0.763 to 0.472, a 38.1% relative reduction (paired ratio-bootstrap 95% CI [35.7%, 40.4%]), while lowering wrong routes from 15.3% to 3.5%. Frozen calibration-selected policies also beat both always-route and always-defer on held-out test data in 14 of 16 settings in a post-hoc cost-parameter analysis. The strongest prompted configuration reaches 0.477 accuracy on a stratified 1,000-ticket test subset, versus 0.879 for fine-tuned DistilBERT on the same tickets. Isotonic lowers expected calibration error without reliably improving discrimination: GPT-4o-mini few-shot has one confidence value before and after recalibration and correctness AUROC 0.500. We therefore report correctness AUROC and tie-aware risk-coverage area alongside ECE. At the analytically derived break-even probability 0.80, seven prompted configurations defer all tickets; Haiku few-shot routes only 19/1,000. An LLM-only agreement control and margin/entropy rejection baselines further separate calibration from discrimination. The findings are scoped to this dataset, prompt design, model endpoints, and illustrative costs; the work is an evaluation framework, not a new abstention algorithm or universal deployment certification.
bullets: Wrong routing is modeled as five times more costly than human triage, motivating selective deferral.
TF-IDF with logistic regression and a calibration-selected 0.60 threshold lowers test cost by 38.1% and wrong routes from 15.3% to 3.5%.
Calibration-selected policies outperform always-route and always-defer in 14 of 16 post-hoc cost settings.
Fine-tuned DistilBERT reaches 0.879 accuracy on the reported subset, versus 0.477 for the strongest prompted LLM configuration.
Recalibration can improve ECE without improving correctness discrimination; at the derived break-even probability, most prompted systems defer nearly everything.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates cost-aware abstention strategies for LLM-based classification tasks, focusing on calibration and risk coverage. This is relevant to the application and reliability of LLMs in decision-making.
papers.title: Cost-Aware Abstention for LLM-Based IT Ticket Classification
papers.tldr: Cost-aware abstention substantially reduces costly IT-ticket misrouting in this evaluation, but traditional classifiers outperform prompted LLMs and results remain scoped to the tested costs and setup.

papers.abstract: Many recent open-weight language models use n-gram embedding tables to improve performance. These tables store learned representations of short token sequences, such as pairs or triples of consecutive tokens, which the model retrieves during processing. However, they can require substantial memory: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, for example, allocates 196 billion parameters to its Engram n-gram memory. We therefore investigate whether this memory cost can be reduced while preserving the performance improvement that the tables provide. We propose storing n-gram embeddings at low precision and systematically investigate different quantization methods and bit allocations across tables. Across nanochat-, Llama-, and GPT-2-family models trained from scratch, four-bit tables save approximately 75% of table memory while preserving more than 99% of the validation-loss improvement from adding the tables. Using fewer bits leads to a larger drop in performance, although we find that a short fine-tuning phase recovers a significant part of this loss. In addition, reinvesting the saved memory in larger tables can improve performance beyond that of the original full-precision tables while still using less memory. These table memory savings also extend to large existing models: on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, low-bit tables save 47-55% of table memory, with perplexity increases of less than 1.2% and largely preserved downstream task performance. These findings establish low-bit precision as a practical way to reduce the memory requirements of n-gram embeddings and use the saved capacity to improve model performance.
bullets: N-gram embedding tables improve language models but can consume substantial memory.
Four-bit tables reduce table memory by about 75% while retaining over 99% of the validation-loss improvement from full-precision tables in models trained from scratch.
Using fewer bits causes larger performance losses, but brief fine-tuning recovers a significant portion of them.
Reinvesting saved memory into larger tables can outperform the original full-precision tables while using less memory.
On large existing models, low-bit tables save 47–55% of table memory with perplexity increases below 1.2% and largely preserved downstream performance.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates quantization methods for n-gram embedding tables in LLMs to reduce memory footprint. This is a significant technical contribution to LLM architecture and efficiency.
papers.title: Low-Bit N-Gram Embeddings for Language Models
papers.tldr: Low-bit quantization can cut n-gram embedding memory substantially while preserving nearly all of its language-modeling benefits.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting elicits step-by-step rationales that appear to explain model predictions, but there is no guarantee these steps causally drive the final answer. In standard autoregressive generation, dense attention allows each reasoning step to attend to the full context, enabling the model to derive answers through direct lookup while generating plausible-sounding but post-hoc justifications. We introduce CausalCoT, an inference framework that enforces causal transparency by decomposing problems into a directed acyclic graph of atomic sub-questions, evaluating each node in an isolated context containing only its direct causal parents. This Markovian structure removes attention pathways to non-parent content, making downstream predictions sensitive to local reasoning rather than global context leakage. Across a diverse suite of reasoning benchmarks, CausalCoT preserves competitive predictive performance while improving explanation faithfulness, increasing causal sensitivity of intermediate reasoning steps by an average of 12 and up to 21 percentage points over the strongest baseline. The structured dependency graph additionally enables test-time interventions in which local corrections propagate predictably through downstream reasoning.
authors: Gabriele Dominici, Teague McMillan, Fazl Barez, Marc Langheinrich, Martin Gjoreski
bullets: Standard chain-of-thought can produce plausible rationales that do not causally determine the answer because attention can leak across the full context.
CausalCoT decomposes problems into atomic sub-questions organized as a directed acyclic graph.
Each node is evaluated using only its direct causal parents, blocking access to unrelated reasoning content.
Across diverse reasoning benchmarks, it improves intermediate-step causal sensitivity by an average of 12 percentage points and up to 21 points over the strongest baseline.
Its dependency graph supports test-time interventions, allowing local corrections to propagate predictably downstream.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes CausalCoT, a framework to enforce causal transparency in Chain-of-Thought reasoning by isolating context. This addresses reasoning and attention mechanisms in LLMs.
papers.title: Causal Chain of Thought: Mitigating Attention Leakage via Context Isolation
papers.tldr: CausalCoT improves the causal faithfulness of chain-of-thought reasoning by isolating each sub-question to its direct causal context while maintaining competitive accuracy.

papers.abstract: Instrumental convergence is often invoked as a general reason to expect capable agents to acquire or express power-seeking subgoals: self-preservation, resource acquisition, deception, or resistance to oversight which poses an important threat to the society. For LLMs, reinforcement learning is the first stage of post-training that directly optimizes behavior against an objective; therefore, it is the stage where convergent instrumental behavior, on IC grounds, likely to appear. Does reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) make a model more likely to express instrumental-convergence behavior, or does this depend on the training regime, evaluation frame, and stage of post-training? We study this question as a checkpoint-conditioned behavioral trajectory rather than as a single before/after safety score. Using InstrumentalEval, we evaluate OLMo-3-7B-Think across SFT, DPO, 13 intermediate RLVR checkpoints, and the final RLVR model. The trajectory is nonmonotonic: instrumental rate rises from 25.0% at SFT to 46.1% near RLVR step 200, then falls to 11.8% at the final checkpoint. Paired item-level tests and step-wise regression support the final SFT-to-RLVR reduction. Prompt framing does not explain this pattern: a harmful-prompt indicator combined with other framing effects explains only 15% of within-checkpoint score variance on average, and Iterative Null-space Projection (INLP) removes a detectable framing direction without changing the SFT-to-final-RLVR gap. Together with preliminary 32B endpoint results (35.53% SFT to 22.37% RLVR final), these findings indicate that RLVR does not monotonically increase instrumental behavior in this setting: the rate rises early, then falls below the SFT baseline. The result is specific to this model family and benchmark, and judge agreement is moderate, so absolute rates should be read cautiously.
authors: Bar{\i}\c{s} Alparslan, Sandy Tanwisuth, Caleb Petterson
bullets: Instrumental behavior is evaluated across SFT, DPO, 13 intermediate RLVR checkpoints, and the final RLVR model.
The trajectory is nonmonotonic: rates rise from 25.0% at SFT to 46.1% around RLVR step 200, then fall to 11.8% at the final checkpoint.
Paired tests and step-wise regression support a final SFT-to-RLVR reduction.
Prompt framing explains little of the within-checkpoint variation, and INLP does not change the SFT-to-final-RLVR gap.
Preliminary 32B endpoint results show the same direction, but findings are limited to this model family and benchmark; judge agreement is moderate.
papers.selection_reason: Studies Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) applied to LLMs to understand instrumental convergence. This is highly relevant to the intersection of LLMs and reinforcement learning.
papers.title: Questioning Instrumental Convergence in RLVR: Checkpoint Evidence from OLMo-3
papers.tldr: In OLMo-3-7B-Think, RLVR briefly increases instrumental-convergence behavior before reducing it below the SFT baseline at the final checkpoint.

papers.abstract: Purpose: To describe an evidence-aware retrieval evaluation protocol for a clinical retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system over breast lesion management literature, addressing the dependence of retrieval scores on annotation coverage. Methods: An 18-document corpus and an 18-query development benchmark, with one Yes/No or WH-question per document, were used. Retrieval combined dense embeddings, BM25, and cross-encoder reranking. Chunk sizes of 128 to 1024 tokens, overlaps of 0 to 20%, and four retriever configurations were evaluated. Relevance was defined by evidence spans mapped to all containing chunks, treating overlapping chunks with equivalent evidence as relevant. Retrieval was evaluated using R-Precision, Recall@K, MRR, and nDCG@K. Separately, generation was assessed on a 512-token index at K=1 to 5 using DeepEval claim-level metrics, with deepseek-v4-pro as the LLM judge, and BLEU/ROUGE metrics. Results: The selected hybrid retriever, using 384-token chunks and 20% overlap, retrieved accepted evidence in the top three results for 17 of 18 queries. Recall@3, R-Precision, MRR@3, and nDCG@3 each reached 0.94. Ground-truth curation increased evidence spans from 25 to 37 and accepted chunk targets from 36 to 51 without changing retrieval rankings. Conclusion: Cross-encoder reranking achieved the highest retrieval scores. Expanded relevance annotations increased recognized evidence without changing rankings, highlighting annotation sensitivity. The small development set and retrieval-informed curation require independent validation, including radiologist assessment of evidence sufficiency.
authors: Miguel Mochizuki Silva, Samuel Ismael, Mateus C. Dias, Tha\'is Gaud\^encio, Yuri Malheiros, Barufaldi
