bullets: Evaluates hybrid dense, BM25, and cross-encoder retrieval across chunk sizes, overlaps, and configurations.
Defines relevance by mapping curated evidence spans to all containing chunks, including equivalent overlapping chunks.
The selected 384-token, 20%-overlap hybrid retriever found accepted evidence in the top three results for 17 of 18 queries.
Retrieval metrics reached 0.94 for Recall@3, R-Precision, MRR@3, and nDCG@3.
The small benchmark and retrieval-informed curation require independent validation, including radiologist review of evidence sufficiency.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates evaluation protocols for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems, specifically focusing on the sensitivity of retrieval scores to ground truth annotation. This is relevant to the development and evaluation of LLMs.
papers.title: How Ground Truth Shapes Retrieval Scores: Evidence-Aware Evaluation of a Retrieval-Augmented Generation System for Breast Lesions
papers.tldr: An evidence-aware evaluation protocol shows that broader ground-truth annotations reveal more valid retrieval evidence without changing rankings in a breast-lesion RAG system.

papers.abstract: Accuracy on medical examinations is common evidence offered for the clinical use of language models, yet a health system that intends to run an open model on its own hardware needs to know considerably more: whether the model recognizes when it is likely to be wrong, whether medical fine-tuning improves this ability, whether its correct answers rest on sound clinical reasoning, or whether it actually uses the images it is given. We examine these questions for four open models of 8 to 27 billion parameters on the Spanish MIR residency examination, scoring 1,552 questions from eight editions under the exam's own rules. Answering every question, the three larger models would rank among roughly the first 600 to 3,000 candidates, with 41 to 43 specialties still open to them. Abstention, however, never pays, because even their least confident answers are right more often than the 25% break-even. Medical fine-tuning reduced overconfidence at the cost of accuracy, without improving how well confidence separates right from wrong answers. Moreover, 13-38% of correct answers rejected a distractor for a clinically unsound reason that confidence did not reflect, and removing or swapping the provided contextual images left accuracy unchanged.
authors: Miguel Fernandez-de-Retana, Unai Zulaika, Ruben Sanchez-Corcuera, Aritz Bilbao-Jayo, Aitor Almeida
bullets: Four open models (8–27B parameters) were evaluated on 1,552 questions from eight Spanish MIR editions using official scoring rules.
The three larger models would rank roughly among the top 600–3,000 candidates, leaving 41–43 specialties available.
Abstention was not beneficial: even the models’ least-confident answers exceeded the 25% accuracy break-even point.
Medical fine-tuning reduced overconfidence but also lowered accuracy and did not improve confidence-based error separation.
Among correct answers, 13–38% used clinically unsound distractor reasoning, while removing or swapping images did not change accuracy.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates the reasoning capabilities, uncertainty calibration, and image usage of open LLMs on a complex medical exam. This is relevant to the study of Large Language Models and their reasoning behaviors.
papers.title: Would an LLM Match into a Residency? Uncertainty, Reasoning and Image Use of Open Language Models on the Spanish MIR Examination
papers.tldr: Open language models can perform competitively on the Spanish MIR, but their confidence, reasoning quality, and use of clinical images remain unreliable.

papers.abstract: Masked diffusion language models generate tokens in parallel, but their efficiency depends on which predictions are committed. Learned unmasking policies improve the speed--accuracy trade-off, yet differ in supervision, inputs, and capacity, obscuring which choices matter. We view supervised policies as distilling a decoding procedure through a teacher and examine independently what the teacher labels as committable, on which states the policy imitates it, what the policy observes, and how much the number of function evaluations (NFE) must decrease to offset policy overhead. We find that labeling predictions matching the final output is overly permissive at low NFE, and hidden states are weak alone but can complement confidence. About a 10% NFE reduction suffices to offset policy overhead for policies up to 7.5M parameters across tested settings. We therefore train a policy on trajectory-contraction targets, which accept only commitments staying on a reference trajectory, using confidence and hidden states. On LLaDA-8B-Instruct, the resulting 856K-parameter policy achieves the best accuracy--NFE frontier and highest throughput on GSM8K, is competitive at moderate targets on MATH-500 and HumanEval, and largely transfers to Dream-7B-Instruct.
authors: Jinya Sakurai, Xun Xu, Jaehong Yoon
bullets: Final-output matching labels are too permissive when the number of function evaluations is low.
Hidden states are weak alone but improve policies when combined with confidence signals.
A roughly 10% NFE reduction offsets the overhead of policies up to 7.5M parameters in tested settings.
Trajectory-contraction targets restrict commitments to those that remain on a reference decoding trajectory.
An 856K-parameter policy achieves the best accuracy–NFE frontier and highest throughput on GSM8K, with competitive results on MATH-500 and HumanEval and transfer to Dream-7B-Instruct.
papers.selection_reason: Studies learned unmasking policies for masked diffusion language models, improving speed-accuracy trade-offs in LLM decoding.
papers.title: What Makes a Good Unmasking Policy? A Controlled Study of Learned Unmasking in Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: A controlled study identifies better supervision and inputs for learned token-unmasking policies, yielding a small policy that improves the accuracy–efficiency trade-off across diffusion language models.

papers.abstract: Hidden future-token leakage can create false architectural gains: an autoregressive model may appear substantially better under teacher-forced evaluation while its free-running generation deteriorates. We investigate this failure in an adaptive residual-routing decoder whose sequence-level routing summary exposes prefix positions to future tokens despite a correct causal attention mask. An anomalous 24-layer checkpoint reduces validation loss from the baseline's 3.5958 to 1.4259, yet it fails a prefix-invariance audit and has substantially higher reference-model perplexity during generation. Layer-wise diagnostics and implementation inspection trace the violation to a full-sequence summary broadcast through the dynamic routing-query path. Two independently trained 12-layer causal repairs eliminate detectable leakage and return validation loss and reference perplexity to the control scale, removing the large apparent advantage. As diagnostic tools, we use the established prefix-invariance contract, maximum prefix-output discrepancy (LeakScore), complementary behavioral metrics, and layer-wise profiles. Supporting experiments cover six synthetic implementation pairs spanning five module families, clean pretrained controls, controlled fault injection, and cache consistency across numerical precisions. These results illustrate how hidden future-token access can produce misleading claims of architectural progress and why lower teacher-forced loss should be interpreted together with whole-model causal checks and free-running evaluation.
bullets: An adaptive residual-routing decoder leaked future information through a full-sequence routing summary despite using a correct causal attention mask.
A 24-layer checkpoint showed much lower validation loss but failed prefix-invariance checks and had worse generation-time reference perplexity.
Layer-wise diagnostics and code inspection localized the leak to the dynamic routing-query path.
Two independently trained 12-layer causal repairs removed detectable leakage and restored metrics to the control scale.
Prefix-invariance, LeakScore, behavioral metrics, layer-wise profiles, and cache-consistency tests provide a broader auditing toolkit.
papers.selection_reason: Audits hidden future-token leakage in autoregressive sequence models, contributing to LLM architecture reliability and evaluation.
papers.title: Beyond Causal Masks: Auditing and Localizing Hidden Future-Token Leakage in Adaptive Sequence Models
papers.tldr: Hidden future-token leakage can make causal sequence models appear substantially better under teacher-forced evaluation while harming free-running generation, so causal audits are essential.

papers.abstract: Metaphor is a crucial aspect of human cognition. As such, we would like to understand how it is represented in large language models (LLMs) and how it might be controlled. We use mechanistic interpretability techniques to identify causal subspaces in a range of LLMs covering different architectures and sizes. We show that we are able to steer output on classification tasks across different parts of speech. We are also able to steer output on generation tasks, indicating that these techniques can be used to control the metaphoricity of LLM output.
authors: Shihui Li, Mette Andersen, Martha Lewis
bullets: Studies how metaphor is represented and controlled in LLMs.
Identifies causal subspaces across models with varied architectures and sizes.
Steers metaphor-related outputs on classification tasks across multiple parts of speech.
Controls the metaphoricity of outputs in generation tasks.
Demonstrates a potential approach for probing and manipulating metaphor representations.
papers.selection_reason: Mechanistic interpretability and steering of metaphor representations in LLMs; relevant to LLM internal mechanisms.
papers.title: The Geometry of Metaphor: Probing and Steering Metaphor Representations in Large Language Models
papers.tldr: Mechanistic interpretability identifies causal metaphor-related subspaces in LLMs that can be used to steer both classification and generated language.

papers.abstract: Given an unseen graph, a start node, $s$, and an end node, $t$, can a language model generate the shortest path from $s$ to $t$? Prior work has found that models fail to learn this task as the graphs scale. We show that this failure has two causes: the supervision signal and the tokenization. First, we theoretically establish and empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of multi-token prediction (MTP), and show that the benefits of MTP are topologically agnostic. Second, we introduce alternative tokenizations and show that the two causes are orthogonal. Using these methods, we break through the scaling wall observed by prior work, consistently and stably learning to solve the task at scales far beyond previous limits.
authors: Arvid Frydenlund, FuTe Wong, Katherine Lambert, Frank Rudzicz
bullets: The task is to generate the shortest path between a start and end node in an unseen graph.
Prior scaling failures stem from weak supervision signals and unsuitable tokenization.
Multi-token prediction improves learning, with benefits that are theoretically and empirically topologically agnostic.
Alternative tokenizations address a separate, orthogonal limitation.
Together, the methods overcome prior scaling barriers consistently and stably, though the abstract gives no specific scale or numerical results.
papers.selection_reason: Multi-token prediction and alternative tokenization improve LLM graph-search scaling; transferable to LLM training and architecture research.
papers.title: Multi-Token Prediction and Alternative Tokenization Improve Learning Latent Multi-Hop Graph Search at Scale
papers.tldr: Multi-token prediction and alternative tokenization enable language models to learn shortest-path search on unseen graphs at scales where prior methods fail.

papers.abstract: When a user says "Keep it short", how short should the LLM's response be? More generally, users and applications require different levels of instruction adherence, but prompting does not reliably provide fine-grained control over them. We therefore study "steerable language models" that provide fine-grained numerical control over the degree to which models follow general instructions specified in text. However, existing approaches do not jointly offer fine-grained control, efficiency, and scalability across diverse instructions. To address this gap, we introduce DIAL (Distilled Instruction-Adherence Levels) to achieve all three properties. For fine-grained control, we perform classifier-free guidance (CFG) with a frozen LLM to provide training signals for on-policy distillation of instruction adherence at different levels. For efficiency, we design a lightweight steering adapter that uses a classifier over the LLM's hidden states to compute a closed-form steering edit. The classifier adaptively sets the steering magnitude at each token based on the target adherence level, while accounting for the geometry of the LLM's hidden states to preserve response coherence. For scalability, the classifier is text-conditioned, allowing a shared adapter to support new instructions without per-instruction fitting, and training requires only instruction and request text. Evaluation across multiple LLM families shows that DIAL achieves a competitive balance between concept expression and response fluency, with concept scores increasing monotonically across adherence levels. We introduce SteerIF, an instruction-only dataset of 98, 625 concept, persona, verifiable, and descriptive instructions. When trained on SteerIF, DIAL provides fine-grained control over personas and, when combined with prompting, improves verifiable instruction following.
authors: Thanh Q. Tran, John Russell Himawan, Arun Verma, Kiwan Wong, Wei Xiao, Daniela Rus, Bryan Kian Hsiang Low
bullets: Targets controllable instruction adherence, addressing prompting’s unreliable fine-grained control.
Uses classifier-free guidance for on-policy distillation into a lightweight steering adapter.
A text-conditioned hidden-state classifier computes token-level steering edits and magnitudes.
Across multiple LLM families, concept expression increases monotonically with target adherence while maintaining competitive fluency.
SteerIF contains 98,625 instruction-only examples; DIAL controls personas and improves verifiable instruction following when combined with prompting.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a lightweight steering adapter for fine-grained control of instruction adherence in LLMs, directly relevant to LLM methods.
papers.title: DIAL: Steerable Language Models with Distilled Instruction-Adherence Levels
papers.tldr: DIAL enables efficient, scalable, fine-grained control over how strongly language models follow textual instructions while preserving response fluency.

papers.abstract: Looped and depth-grown language models reuse computations across depth and have attracted interest for their reasoning capabilities. Building on prior suggestive evidence of improved in-context-learning (ICL), we investigate how such reuse favors ICL, including how it shapes the acquisition, retention, and mechanisms of this ability. Our analysis spans pretrained language models up to 3B parameters and controlled tasks. The experiments provide evidence for a shared inductive bias toward learning from context: grown and looped models rely more on information in context and, compared with a full-depth dense reference, acquire ICL earlier in controlled tasks and retain it more strongly when learning fixed associations in the weights is also possible. Tracing attention heads through training reveals that depth growth propagates early induction heads across layers. Ablations show that grown and looped models rely more strongly on induction-ranked heads for both few-shot performance and later-token prediction. Together, these findings provide evidence for a shared inductive bias toward learning from context and suggest that (soft) parameter reuse shapes how this ability develops and which attention mechanisms support it.
authors: Ferdinand Kapl, Kaitlin Maile, Stefan Bauer, Johannes von Oswald
bullets: Studies how computation reuse affects ICL acquisition, retention, and underlying mechanisms.
Analyzes pretrained models up to 3B parameters alongside controlled tasks.
Grown and looped models rely more on contextual information than a full-depth dense reference.
Depth growth propagates early induction heads across layers during training.
Ablations link induction-ranked heads to few-shot performance and later-token prediction.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes how depth growth and looping shape in-context learning and induction heads in LLMs, directly relevant to LLM architecture and mechanisms.
papers.title: How Depth Growth and Looping Shape In-Context Learning in Language Models
papers.tldr: Depth-grown and looped language models develop in-context learning earlier and retain it more strongly, apparently because parameter reuse promotes context-based reasoning and induction-head mechanisms.

papers.abstract: Hierarchical language generation separates continuous semantic modeling from discrete text realization, but its effectiveness depends on what the latent space compresses and how the discrete generator uses it. We propose Cola2, a framework that jointly studies continuous semantic compression, the balance between reconstruction and generation, and continuous-discrete co-adaptation. Cola2 dynamically segments text into semantic spans, controls the compression rate through auxiliary-loss-free negative feedback, and combines reconstruction and generation supervision to learn compact, predictive latent representations. A block-causal masked diffusion decoder is trained with clean, noisy, and dropped latent conditions, while classifier-free guidance adjusts the balance between semantic reconstruction and autonomous generation. Token-prediction gradients update the encoder through the latents, whereas Flow Matching prior learning is decoupled from representation learning by stop-gradient. During inference, generated text is re-encoded under a fixed span layout to keep the latent history consistent with the actual text context. Experiments on five downstream tasks with about 210 billion training tokens validate the core designs and show competitive, unsaturated scaling. With 346.03 billion source tokens, an unconverged checkpoint reaches a 60.10 average across eight tasks and surpasses Llama-3-8B on HellaSwag and StoryCloze despite its reported pretraining budget being over 43 times larger. These results demonstrate the potential of continuous-latent hierarchical language generation.
authors: Hongcan Guo, Yian Zhao, Feng Wang, Shen Nie, Guoqiang Wei, Yan Zeng, Hengshuang Zhao
bullets: Dynamically segments text into semantic spans and regulates compression with auxiliary-loss-free negative feedback.
Combines reconstruction and generation supervision to produce compact, predictive latent representations.
Uses a block-causal masked diffusion decoder with clean, noisy, and dropped latent conditions, plus classifier-free guidance.
Maintains latent-context consistency at inference by re-encoding generated text under a fixed span layout.
Validated across five downstream tasks and about 210B training tokens; results indicate competitive, still-unsaturated scaling and strong performance on HellaSwag and StoryCloze.
papers.selection_reason: Hierarchical continuous-latent language modeling is an LLM architecture/generation advance.
papers.title: Cola2: Co-Adaptive Hierarchical Language Modeling with Continuous Semantic Compression and Balanced Discrete Generation
papers.tldr: Cola2 improves hierarchical language modeling by jointly learning compact semantic latents and balanced, co-adaptive text generation.

papers.abstract: We envision a general-purpose protein foundation model as a unified, interactive model of sequence, structure, and function, capable of understanding, generation, and cross-modal translation while retaining the instruction-following and reasoning capabilities of modern LLMs. Toward this vision, we introduce Trion-1, the first native, unified, multimodal diffusion language model (dLLM) for proteins. Trion-1 is built on two key design choices: (1) a unified discrete token space that jointly represents sequence, structure, and natural language; (2) a dLLM backbone that replaces strict left-to-right factorization with bidirectional or semi-bidirectional token interactions, enabling global residue communication and long-range contact modeling that are naturally suited to structure modeling. This formulation unifies six core capabilities: folding, inverse folding, sequence understanding, structure understanding, sequence design, and structure design, while retaining the native language capabilities of general-purpose LLMs. On established benchmarks, Trion-1 achieves broadly competitive performance. In folding, Trion-1 achieves a TM-score above 0.8 with a single sample under strict homology control, matching or exceeding the existing tri-modal model using 200 samples. For sequence understanding, Trion-1 performs on par with top-tier LLMs such as Claude Opus 4.7 (62.37%). These results support well-aligned sequence-structure-language representations and strong cross-modal generative capabilities.
authors: Tianyu Lu, Kaicheng Yang, Jiangtao Feng, Keyue Qiu, Yawen Ouyang, Yixin Wu, Xinbo Zhang, Lihao Wang, Wei-Ying Ma, Hao Zhou
bullets: Uses one discrete token space for protein sequences, structures, and natural language.
Employs bidirectional or semi-bidirectional diffusion interactions to support global residue communication and long-range contact modeling.
Unifies folding, inverse folding, sequence and structure understanding, and sequence and structure design.
Reports competitive benchmark performance, including a single-sample folding TM-score above 0.8 under strict homology control.
Achieves 62.37% on sequence understanding, comparable to the cited top-tier LLM baseline.
papers.selection_reason: Unified multimodal diffusion language model for language, protein sequence, and structure, directly relevant to multimodal and language foundation models.
papers.title: Trion-1: Unifying Language, Protein Sequence, and Structure with Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: Trion-1 is a unified protein diffusion language model that jointly handles sequence, structure, and natural language for understanding, generation, and cross-modal translation.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) introduce unique quantization challenges due to their iterative denoising process. In this work, we reveal that quantization sensitivity is both taskand time-dependent, with different downstream tasks exhibiting distinct precision requirements across denoising steps. We further show that these patterns can be predicted without groundtruth labels or task-specific evaluation metrics. Building on these findings, we introduce T 2Quant, a task and time-aware mixedprecision quantization framework that uses a label-free sensitivity signal to optimally allocate activation precision across denoising steps under a fixed bit-width budget. Extensive experiments across three DLMs and six benchmarks demonstrate that T 2Quant consistently improves the average accuracy of existing quantization methods, achieving gains of up to 6.7 percentage points under the same budget.
authors: Ofek Avivi, Eliron Rahimi, Avi Mendelson, Chaim Baskin
bullets: Quantization sensitivity varies by both downstream task and denoising timestep.
These sensitivity patterns can be predicted without ground-truth labels or task-specific evaluation metrics.
T²Quant allocates activation precision across timesteps under a fixed bit-width budget.
Experiments across three DLMs and six benchmarks improve existing quantization methods by up to 6.7 percentage points in average accuracy.
papers.selection_reason: Task- and time-aware mixed-precision quantization for diffusion language models improves efficiency under bit-width budgets, relevant to efficient AI and language foundation models.
papers.title: Different Tasks, Different Timesteps: Temporal Task-Aware Quantization for Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: T²Quant improves diffusion language model quantization by assigning task-specific activation precision across denoising steps using label-free sensitivity signals.

papers.abstract: LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation is increasingly applied to multilingual tasks, yet prompting strategies such as Chain-of-Thought and Role Conditioning are recommended based solely on English benchmarks. Whether their effectiveness transfers across judge models and languages remains unknown: prompt-sensitivity studies are largely English-centric, while existing multilingual judge studies fix the prompt template. In this work, we address this gap by measuring this interaction through a benchmark of 9 prompting strategies, 4 open-weight judges, 27 languages, and 4 tasks across 13 datasets, yielding over 1M pointwise scores on gold-reference outputs, validated against human judgments. We find that prompting strategies are not transferable: the choice of the judge model dominates the choice of prompting strategy, strategy effects reverse direction across judges, and stability degrades in low-resource languages, where these effects are concealed by aggregate reporting. These findings show that prompting effects in multilingual evaluation are conditioned on the judge, task, and language. Consequently, prompting strategies should be validated for the intended evaluation setting, and cross-study comparisons should account for both judge and prompt configuration.
authors: Asal Mehrabi, Mohammad Aliannejadi, Clemencia Siro
bullets: Studies 9 prompting strategies across 4 open-weight judges, 27 languages, 4 tasks, and 13 datasets, using over 1M scores validated against human judgments.
Prompting effects are not transferable across judge models; the judge choice has a larger influence than the prompting strategy.
The same strategy can help one judge but hurt another, with effects also varying by task and language.
Evaluation stability decreases in low-resource languages, an issue hidden by aggregate reporting.
Cross-study comparisons should specify both the judge model and prompt configuration.
papers.selection_reason: Examines prompt-strategy robustness for LLM-as-a-judge across models and languages, relevant to LLM evaluation.
papers.title: Prompting Strategy Effects Depend on the Judge: A Multilingual Study of LLM-as-a-Judge Robustness
papers.tldr: Prompting strategies for multilingual LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation are highly judge-, task-, and language-dependent, so they should not be assumed to transfer from English benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Language models are compared on question-answering benchmarks that pose each question in one wording, and a reworded question can change which of two models scores higher. We ask whether giving the models tools makes such comparisons more stable. An accuracy gain cannot answer this, because tools change several steps between the question and the scored answer at once. We propose a matched protocol that separates those steps: the answer readout, reasoning, the decision to call, the tool's answer, and the report supplied without a call. We apply it to six open models in five domains under five wordings. We find that tools raise accuracy where a program answers the question and widen the wording sensitivity of many pairwise comparisons. The widening follows how often a model calls, and call frequency follows the wording for some models and not others. It also depends on the interface and the instructions: a native tool-calling interface and a second tool description leave no detected widening in molecules, and sensitivity persists where tools return intermediate results. These findings show that deterministic reports do not guarantee stable comparisons. We recommend reporting call frequency and comparison stability under several wordings beside accuracy.
bullets: Rewording a question can change which of two models appears better, even when tools are available.
A matched protocol separates answer readout, reasoning, tool-calling decisions, tool outputs, and no-call reports.
Across six open models, five domains, and five wordings, tools improved accuracy on program-answerable questions but often widened comparison sensitivity.
Widening tracked tool-call frequency, which itself varied with wording for some models and depended on the tool interface and instructions.
The study recommends reporting call frequency and comparison stability across multiple wordings alongside accuracy.
papers.selection_reason: Studies prompt sensitivity in tool-augmented LLM comparisons, relevant to LLM evaluation and capabilities.
papers.title: Prompt Sensitivity in Tool-Augmented Model Comparisons
papers.tldr: Tool use can make model comparisons more sensitive to question wording, so accuracy alone is not enough to assess stability.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models generate multiple token positions in parallel, but few-step decoding makes parallel commitment difficult: tokens that appear reliable individually may be jointly inconsistent, while premature commitments can prevent later context-dependent refinement. In this paper, we introduce SetCommit, a training-free method for coordinated parallel token commitment. Instead of selecting tokens independently by confidence, SetCommit selects a commitment set that balances token reliability against local joint commitment risk, preserving conditioning opportunities for subsequent denoising steps. It further performs budget-neutral local exchanges, replacing vulnerable earlier commitments when newly revealed context supports more reliable alternatives. SetCommit requires no retraining or architectural modification and is compatible with existing diffusion decoding strategies. Experiments with LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B on GSM8K, MATH-500, MBPP, and HumanEval show accuracy/pass@1 gains of up to 7.4 percentage points over native decoding at 32 model evaluations. At common quality targets, geometric-mean incremental speedups range from $1.44$ to $1.74\times$. Code is available at https://github.com/Kissmetothemoon/SetCommit.
authors: Yuannuo Feng, Yubing Ye, Wenshuai Yao, Yizhe Chen, Ngai Wong, Wenyong Zhou, Wang Kang
bullets: Addresses inconsistent parallel commitments and lost opportunities for later context-dependent refinement.
Selects token sets using both individual reliability and local joint commitment risk.
Uses budget-neutral local exchanges to replace vulnerable commitments when new context reveals better alternatives.
Training-free, requires no architectural changes, and works with existing diffusion decoding strategies.
Across LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B benchmarks, it achieves up to 7.4-point accuracy/pass@1 gains and 1.44–1.74× incremental speedups at common quality targets.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free coordinated token commitment improves diffusion LM decoding accuracy and speed, directly relevant to efficient inference and language foundation models.
papers.title: SetCommit: Coordinated Token Commitments for Few-Step Diffusion Language Model Decoding
papers.tldr: SetCommit improves few-step diffusion language model decoding by coordinating which tokens to commit, boosting quality and speed without retraining.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems are increasingly used in practice, but their behavior is complex and hard to understand. We design a simple task to ask which model has the most influence on the final consensus when several models are mixed in one system. Experimentally, across seven model families, we find that the opinions of the other models are absorbed into the opinion of the stronger model, the one with more parameters. This happens even though the task requires no pretraining knowledge and has no correct answer. To understand this phenomenon, we interpret the agents as weighted particles moving on a simplex. Larger models carry a larger weight and therefore occupy a deeper well in the energy landscape. A large weight means strong in-context learning: a model with a large weight amplifies the majority of its context. Larger models are generally better at in-context learning, and this is what makes the larger model the influencer. We hope that this work helps to interpret multi-agent systems, whose behavior is becoming too complex for humans to understand.
authors: Gouki Minegishi, Jingyuan Feng, Hiroki Furuta, Takeshi Kojima, Yusuke Iwasawa, Yutaka Matsuo
bullets: Studies which model has the greatest influence on consensus in multi-agent systems.
Across seven model families, other models’ opinions are absorbed into those of the larger model.
The effect appears on a task with no required pretraining knowledge or objectively correct answer.
A weighted-particle simplex model explains larger models as having greater weight and deeper energy wells.
The findings offer a framework for interpreting otherwise complex multi-agent behavior.
papers.selection_reason: Interprets LLM multi-agent consensus dynamics through in-context learning, relevant to language foundation model reasoning and behavior.
papers.title: Who Is the Influencer? Consensus Dynamics in Multi-Agent Systems
papers.tldr: In mixed multi-agent LLM systems, larger models tend to dominate consensus because their stronger in-context learning amplifies the prevailing context.

papers.abstract: Reward models score responses for preference optimization, filtering and ranking, and pooling scores across prompts needs them to be comparable. Yet pairwise evaluation compares two responses to the same prompt, so any score component shared by a prompt's responses cancels and goes untested. We study this component by comparing between-prompt variation in model scores with the same variation in human ratings of the same responses. We propose a human-referenced audit, built from a between-prompt variance share, a sibling-rating regression and prompt substitutions, and apply it to eighteen released scorers and six matched training conditions. We find that scores cluster by prompt more than the ratings do: on HelpSteer2, six reward models have between-prompt shares of 0.34 to 0.64 against a human share near zero. Replacing the original prompt with a fixed instruction keeps substantial clustering but weakens agreement with prompt-level human ratings, so clustering alone does not show agreement with humans. Part of that variation is useful: subtracting prompt means lowers the helpfulness of globally selected responses, and scores stay sensitive to a wrong prompt even when training shuffles prompt means. We propose that reward evaluation check between-prompt variation, sensitivity to a wrong prompt and usefulness for selection separately.
bullets: Pairwise comparisons cancel score components shared by all responses to a prompt, leaving them untested.
The study audits between-prompt variation using human-referenced variance shares, sibling-rating regression, and prompt substitutions.

Across 18 released scorers and six matched training conditions, scores clustered by prompt more than human ratings did; six HelpSteer2 reward models had shares of 0.34–0.64 versus near zero for humans.
Fixed-prompt substitutions preserved substantial clustering but weakened alignment with prompt-level human ratings, so clustering alone is not evidence of human agreement.
Prompt-level variation affected selection and wrong-prompt sensitivity, motivating separate evaluation of variation, prompt sensitivity, and selection usefulness.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses score comparability and between-prompt variation in reward models used for LLM alignment and selection.
papers.title: What Pairwise Evaluation Misses: Reward Scores across Prompts
papers.tldr: Pairwise reward evaluation misses prompt-level score variation, which can be substantial, only partly human-aligned, and sometimes useful for selecting responses.

papers.abstract: We present IQuest-Q1, a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) agentic foundation model with 320B total parameters (15B activated). IQuest-Q1 is developed through a three-stage process: (1) stable and efficient pre-training, combining Stable SplitNorm, Muon, and muP with a two-stage curriculum whose second stage increases the coding-data mixture, preserving a wide stability margin between safe and optimal learning rates; (2) fine-grained mid-training, expanding the data mixture across domains and formats and progressively extending the context; and (3) multi-scaffold with multi-version post-training, combining SFT, domain-specialized RL, and MOPD across various scaffolds to integrate complementary training signals and strengthen agentic coding capabilities. Furthermore, model merging combines different experts and checkpoints from different stages while mitigating conflicts among their parameter updates. The resulting IQuest-Q1 demonstrates capabilities in both coding and general tasks. We release IQuest-Q1 as an open-source model to support community research and development.

papers.title: IQuest-Q1: Advancing Foundation Capabilities for Agentic CLI Systems
papers.tldr: IQuest-Q1 is an open-source 320B-parameter sparse MoE foundation model designed to strengthen agentic CLI coding and general-purpose capabilities through staged training and model merging.

papers.abstract: Large language models trained on data generated by other models can sometimes inherit traits unrelated to that data, a phenomenon called subliminal learning. We study both hard label distillation, where students train on numbers generated by a biased teacher, and on-policy soft label distillation, where students generate the data and the teacher's logits provide the learning signal. Using Pythia, PolyPythia, and DataDecide OLMo models, we find that transfer persists in both settings across differences in weight initialization, pretraining data order, pretraining corpus, model size, and architecture. Across pretraining checkpoints, the ability to transmit a preference and the ability to acquire one develop separately: some checkpoints are more effective teachers but weaker students, and vice versa. Consistent with this distinction, cross-model transfer can be strongly asymmetric in magnitude when teacher and student roles are reversed. To investigate what carries the preference signal, we construct synthetic number sequences that match the teacher's generated number frequencies but have no dependence on the prompt or preceding numbers and find that these still induce substantial transfer in the hard-label setting. In top-$K$ soft-label distillation, removing animal tokens from the loss reduces transfer, although not completely in the same-model setting. In our experiments, soft label distillation produces more consistent transfer with less extensive training than hard label distillation. The growing use of on-policy distillation in model post-training makes this a particularly relevant setting for assessing unintended preference transfer.
authors: Angela Tang, Vishesh Anand, Gon\c{c}alo Paulo
bullets: Transfer occurs in both hard-label and on-policy soft-label distillation across initialization, data order, corpus, model size, and architecture changes.
The ability to transmit a preference and acquire one develops separately, causing potentially strong asymmetry when teacher and student roles are reversed.
Synthetic sequences matching teacher-generated number frequencies still produce substantial hard-label transfer, suggesting prompt-independent frequency signals can carry preferences.
Removing animal tokens from top-K soft-label losses reduces—but does not eliminate—transfer in same-model settings.
Soft-label distillation yields more consistent transfer with less training than hard-label distillation in the reported experiments.
papers.selection_reason: Studies unintended preference transfer in LLM distillation across pretraining settings.
papers.title: Tracing Subliminal Learning Through Pretraining
papers.tldr: Subliminal preference transfer persists across distillation methods, models, checkpoints, and training conditions, revealing distinct teacher and student capabilities and implications for on-policy distillation.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is credited with teaching reasoning models to write {wait} before reconsidering a step, yet large RL accuracy gains do not require the word. This view can confuse what RL discovers with what a model inherits from its training data. We trace the word through open models' training histories, reading it with label-free indices of frequency, position, form and usage and an injected-error test, all computed from sampled outputs. We find that zero-RL almost never coins the marker: on bases that lack the word, RL raises MATH-500 accuracy substantially while {wait} stays near absent. It arrives with training data: mid-training in OLMo-3, and fine-tuning on reasoning traces installs it in most models whose base lacks it. Where the base already uses it, both released RL-Zero recipes (OLMo-3, MiMo) multiply it, whereas KL-free GRPO from the same base does not; OLMo-3's recipe wears down its form and makes it a more sensitive but more liberal alarm; RL after supervised fine-tuning barely changes it, and our GRPO recipe erases a marker seeded by fine-tuning. Finally, we show that marker frequency alone does not indicate RL-induced reasoning and caution against LLM-as-a-judge revision metrics, as automated judges can reverse human-labelled trends.
authors: Zhizhuo Kou, Sizai Hou, Long Chen, Jian Yang, Junyu Luo, Jingshu Peng, Wenkai Zhang, Sirui Han, Yike Guo
bullets: Models typically inherit `{wait}` from mid-training or supervised reasoning traces; RL rarely creates it when absent.
On bases lacking the marker, RL can substantially improve MATH-500 accuracy while `{wait}` remains nearly absent.
When already present, released RL-Zero recipes increase its use, but KL-free GRPO may not; supervised fine-tuning can also seed or erase it.
RL changes the marker’s form and error-detection behavior, making it potentially more sensitive but less conservative.
Marker frequency is not a reliable measure of RL-induced reasoning, and LLM judges may disagree with human-labeled revision trends.
papers.selection_reason: Empirical provenance analysis of how RL and training data shape reasoning LLM behavior.
papers.title: Inherited, Not Invented: Tracing the Provenance of Wait in Reasoning Models
papers.tldr: The study finds that RL usually amplifies or reshapes the `{wait}` reasoning marker rather than inventing it, while its presence alone does not prove improved reasoning.

papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) improves reasoning by training a model on its own trajectories with dense token-level supervision from a privileged copy conditioned on a reference solution. Existing methods typically use a single teacher distribution conditioned on the complete reference. We identify a limitation of this formulation: a reference is only one realization of the reasoning process. Although it provides evidence about the answer, it also encodes an ordering, phrasing, and solution path. Full-reference conditioning can therefore produce correct targets that depend excessively on information unavailable to the student at inference. We show that replacing one valid reference with another, while holding the problem and student state fixed, can substantially alter the teacher distribution, a phenomenon we call reference-induced target instability. To address this instability, we introduce Monte Carlo Privileged Distillation (MCPD), which models privileged context as a distribution over partial reference views and distills the marginal teacher distribution. MCPD evaluates the teacher under multiple views and averages the resulting next-token distributions. We show that this probability-space average is the exact target induced by minimizing the expected teacher-to-student KL divergence over privileged views. Across mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks, we show that MCPD produces more reference-consistent supervision and consistently improves over full-reference OPSD.
bullets: Full-reference teacher conditioning can make token-level targets depend on arbitrary solution phrasing, ordering, and path.
The resulting variation across valid references is termed reference-induced target instability.
MCPD treats privileged context as a distribution over partial reference views and averages the teacher’s next-token distributions.
This probability-space average exactly minimizes expected teacher-to-student KL divergence across views.
Across mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks, MCPD yields more reference-consistent supervision and improves over full-reference OPSD.
papers.selection_reason: Improves on-policy self-distillation for reasoning LLMs by marginalizing over reference views.
papers.title: One Teacher, Many Views: Reducing Reference Sensitivity in On-Policy Self-Distillation
papers.tldr: MCPD reduces reference sensitivity in on-policy self-distillation by averaging teacher predictions across multiple partial views of a reference solution.

papers.abstract: Mix-policy optimization incorporates off-policy expert data into the reinforcement learning (RL) loop to transcend the capability boundary of on-policy RL. However, existing methods either provide static full-trace guidance that suppresses self-exploration, or adopt expert prefix guidance without correctness guarantees, leading to suboptimal performance or even training collapse. In this paper, we propose MOER, a mix-policy optimization framework that harmonizes expert guidance with self-exploration. MOER injects a decaying expert chain-of-thought prefix into the prompt and lets the model complete the remaining reasoning, with the prefix length progressively annealed to encourage self-exploration. A selective rollback mechanism replaces failed completions with the original full expert trace, guaranteeing the correctness of every off-policy trajectory. Furthermore, a harmonized mix-policy objective optimizes on-policy tokens with a GRPO loss while supervising both expert prefix and completion tokens with a trust-region SFT loss, substantially stabilizing training. Extensive experiments show that MOER achieves the highest average scores in mathematical and general domain reasoning tasks, outperforming all basic and mix-policy baselines, and generalizes consistently across diverse tasks, model scales, and base model categories. Codes are available at https://github.com/CityU-MLO/MOER.
authors: Xuyang Zhong, Jiuding Yang, Yiwen Guo, Chen Liu
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between static expert guidance that limits exploration and prefix guidance that can produce incorrect off-policy trajectories.
Injects a decaying expert chain-of-thought prefix and progressively anneals its length to promote self-exploration.
Uses selective rollback to restore failed completions to the original expert trace, preserving trajectory correctness.
Combines GRPO for on-policy tokens with trust-region SFT for expert-prefix and completion tokens to stabilize training.
Reports the highest average scores across mathematical and general reasoning tasks, with consistent generalization across tasks, model scales, and base-model categories.
papers.selection_reason: Mix-policy RL optimization for LLM reasoning.
papers.title: MOER: Mix-Policy Optimization under Expert Prefix Guidance with Selective Rollback
papers.tldr: MOER combines gradually reduced expert reasoning prefixes, correctness-preserving rollback, and a hybrid RL/SFT objective to stabilize mix-policy reinforcement learning while improving reasoning performance.

papers.abstract: Reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) distillation has shown empirical promise for training language models, but its statistical guarantees and limits remain poorly understood. In particular, the effects of two design choices remain unclear: Does access to the teacher's full action distribution provide an advantage over observing only the probability it assigns to the sampled action? Must training trajectories come from the student (online distillation), or can teacher-generated trajectories (offline distillation) suffice? Our work takes a first step toward understanding the theory underlying these questions. We study the sample complexity of online reverse-KL distillation under two feedback models: the teacher reveals either its full action distribution or only the probability of the student-generated action. We establish minimax bounds for the former and show that substantially more data may be required for the latter. In contrast, offline reverse-KL distillation can attain the same minimax rate whether the teacher reveals its full distribution or only its probability of the teacher-generated action. The key distinction is that teacher-generated actions themselves reveal the teacher's preferences, while queries at student-selected actions can leave those preferences unobserved. This highlights an additional statistical challenge for online distillation compared to offline distillation. These statistical guarantees do not follow simply from optimizing standard distillation objectives: our lower bounds show that common online objectives can fail when candidates are evaluated only on past student-generated trajectories. We develop trajectory-loss and importance-ratio truncation techniques together with policy-space learning to achieve optimal online distillation guarantees.
authors: Haolin Liu, Chen-Yu Wei, Julian Zimmert
bullets: Studies online reverse-KL distillation with either the teacher’s full action distribution or only the probability of the student-selected action.
Proves minimax bounds showing limited feedback can substantially increase online sample complexity.
Shows offline distillation achieves the same minimax rate under full-distribution feedback or teacher-action probability feedback.
Attributes the online–offline gap to teacher-generated actions revealing preferences that student-selected queries may miss.
Develops trajectory-loss, importance-ratio truncation, and policy-space learning techniques for optimal online guarantees; lower bounds expose failures of common objectives.
papers.selection_reason: Theoretical analysis of reverse-KL distillation for language model training.
papers.title: Reverse-KL Policy Distillation: Statistical Guarantees and Limits
papers.tldr: The paper characterizes when reverse-KL policy distillation is statistically efficient, showing that online distillation may need substantially more data with limited teacher feedback, while offline distillation can avoid this gap.

papers.abstract: Training large language models for complex reasoning tasks relies on two complementary signals: sparse, outcome-grounded reinforcement learning (RL) for correctness, and dense, token-level distillation for guidance. However, complementarity in supervision does not guarantee compatibility in optimization; imitation-focused distillation can conflict with the outcome-driven RL objective, and existing hybrids lack a principled resolution. We propose \textbf{GIFT} (\textbf{G}radient-\textbf{I}nformed \textbf{F}il\textbf{T}ering for Distillation-Augmented Reasoning RL), a novel method that directly addresses the allocation problem of which teacher updates to apply. GIFT performs a token-level geometric analysis, decomposing the distillation gradient into a component \textbf{parallel} to the RL gradient, which measures first-order conflict and provides a \textbf{safety} filter, and a component \textbf{orthogonal} to it, which quantifies novel directional guidance and provides a measure of \textbf{value}. This decomposition yields a principled scoring rule to rank token-level guidance. We combine this with a progressive \textbf{coverage annealing} schedule that shrinks the budget of tokens receiving distillation, ensuring that the most conflicting updates are discarded first while the most complementary ones are retained at full strength. This facilitates a smooth transition from dense, geometrically-filtered guidance to a pure, outcome-grounded objective at convergence. Extensive experiments on mathematical and logical reasoning benchmarks show that GIFT consistently outperforms strong baselines across multiple model scales, achieving relative gains of up to 9.5\% on difficult mathematical reasoning tasks. Code: https://github.com/lilifree/GIFT
authors: Shijie Li, Yilin Gao, Tieyuan Chen, Yun Luo, Weiyao Lin, Hang Yu
bullets: Addresses conflicts between dense imitation-based distillation and sparse, outcome-driven RL objectives.
Decomposes each distillation gradient into RL-parallel components for safety and orthogonal components for novel guidance value.
Ranks token-level updates using this geometric analysis and applies progressive coverage annealing to reduce distillation coverage over training.
Evaluations on mathematical and logical reasoning benchmarks report consistent gains over strong baselines, with up to 9.5% relative improvement on difficult math tasks.
The method transitions toward a pure outcome-grounded objective at convergence.
papers.selection_reason: Method for combining distillation and RL in LLM reasoning training via gradient decomposition.
papers.title: GIFT: Gradient Informed Filtering for Distillation Augmented Reasoning RL
papers.tldr: GIFT filters token-level distillation updates by their geometric compatibility with RL, progressively retaining only the most complementary guidance for reasoning training.

papers.abstract: This paper studies the local geometry of semantic meaning in large language models. Current representation analyses ask whether meanings are close in embedding space, or whether linear probes separate semantic classes, but they do not characterize the within-concept local geometry: what is invariant across realizations of a single semantic factor, what varies, and what changes when meaning is refined. This paper characterizes that geometry through two controlled probes evaluated on four architecturally diverse decoder-only LLMs (Gemma 4, Llama 3.2, Qwen 2.5, Pythia). A cross-lingual probe uses language as a perturbation to separate exact meaning matches, same-factor realizations, nearby concepts, and out-of-domain contrasts. A refinement probe separates specificity-bearing semantic narrowing from high-probability attributive elaboration and adversarial controls; both probes are validated by blind human judgments. Four findings recur across all models: under mean pooling, once dominant variance directions are removed, sentence pairs order by semantic relatedness (same factor, then same domain, then different domain) without overlap over a band of layers; semantic factors organize around an invariant core surrounded by structured realization-specific variation; refinement produces directed displacement into tighter neighborhoods, including against controls built on the same base noun; and sentence-level and token-local readouts expose complementary geometry (volume contraction at the sentence level, sharper anisotropic endpoints at token-local readout). We interpret these results as evidence that LLM semantics are organized as local anisotropic neighborhoods in which meaning contracts under refinement.
bullets: Existing analyses largely measure global semantic proximity or separability, leaving within-concept geometry undercharacterized.
Two controlled probes test cross-lingual meaning variation and specificity-driven semantic refinement, with blind human validation.
After dominant directions are removed, representations consistently order by semantic relatedness across a band of layers.
Refinement moves representations into tighter neighborhoods; sentence-level and token-local views reveal complementary contraction and anisotropy.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes local semantic geometry in LLM representations; relevant to LLM interpretability and representation analysis.
papers.title: Meaning Contracts: Local Semantic Geometry in Large Language Models
papers.tldr: Across four decoder-only LLMs, semantic meanings form local anisotropic neighborhoods with structured variation around invariant cores and contract under semantic refinement.

papers.abstract: Text embedding and text generation are two of the most useful capabilities of modern large language models, yet they are typically provided by separate specialized models (an embedder and a generator) trained with incompatible objectives and deployed side by side in retrieval-augmented generation and agent systems. Recent unified embedding-generation models such as GritLM share parameters between the two capabilities, but they either switch attention regimes between modes or optimize embedding and language modeling as parallel objectives that never supervise each other. We argue that these designs are only partially unified: the two capabilities coexist on the same weights, but do not shape each other. We propose ULME, a post-training framework that unifies embedding and language modeling on a causal decoder-only LLM through predictive coupling. ULME inserts a chain of learnable slots between the query and the answer, reads a semantic embedding and a reasoning embedding from two designated slots, and trains three objectives on a shared causal backbone: a contrastive loss anchoring the semantic slot to document representations, a language-modeling loss supervising answer generation, and a stop-gradient predictive loss that aligns the reasoning slot with a pooled summary of the answer, so that generation actively shapes what the embedding encodes. Across two model families (Qwen2.5, Qwen3) and eight scales spanning 0.5B-8B parameters, a single ULME checkpoint improves MTEB by 3.3-4.1 points over the strongest open-source baseline, tightens BRIGHT and AdvBench-IR simultaneously, and remains on par with a generation-only fine-tune on standard accuracy benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro, HumanEval), demonstrating that genuine unification yields mutually reinforcing rather than merely coexisting capabilities.
authors: Yang Liu, Zhiqiang Yuan, Shu-Dong Huang, Jiancheng Lv, Liwei Yang, Qiwei Yan, Kailin Lv, Jinchao Zhang
bullets: Addresses the limited interaction between embedding and language-modeling objectives in existing unified models.
Uses learnable slots in a causal decoder-only LLM to produce semantic and reasoning embeddings.
Combines contrastive embedding, answer-generation, and stop-gradient predictive alignment losses.
Evaluated across Qwen2.5 and Qwen3 models from 0.5B to 8B parameters.
Reports improved MTEB and BRIGHT/AdvBench-IR performance while matching generation-only fine-tuning on standard benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Unifies embedding and language modeling in decoder-only LLMs via predictive coupling; directly relevant to LLM post-training.
papers.title: ULME: Predictive Coupling for Mutually Reinforcing Embedding and Language Modeling
papers.tldr: ULME jointly trains text embedding and generation through predictive coupling, yielding stronger retrieval representations without sacrificing generation performance.

papers.abstract: Safety probes trained on a model's activations are a standard tool for monitoring language models in real time. Each time a new model is released or a new harm area needs to be monitored, the probe must be retrained, which requires new labels and a choice of probe architecture. Yet neither the model nor the labels tell us in advance how well the resulting probe will perform. Finding out requires training and comparing many probe configurations. In this paper, we ask whether probe performance can instead be predicted in advance from model size and the number of labels. Existing safety datasets are insufficient for this, as they are either limited in scale or already saturated. We therefore construct six new safety datasets of sufficient size and difficulty. On these datasets, we train two probe architectures on 20 base models from five model families, with 32 to $10^{6}$ labels for each model. We measure performance using probe error, defined as 1 - AUROC, where lower values are better. We find that probe error follows two simple scaling laws. First, the lowest probe error a model can reach falls as a power law in its size. Second, probe error decreases towards its floor as the number of examples increases; the slope increases as the target model size increases. Both laws hold across tasks, model families and probe architectures, and only their fitted constants differ. When fitted on the smallest models of a family, the laws predict the error of the next larger model to within 0.02 in 72% of cases. They also identify whether more labels or a larger model is the cheaper way to reach a target error in 73% of cases. Finally, they choose the probe architecture with an extra error of only 0.006 on average when they pick the worse one. These laws allow safety researchers to determine how to create the best probe for any given model and label budget.
authors: Yuchen Wu (University of Washington), Jerry Wei (Anthropic)
bullets: The study addresses the costly retraining and configuration search required when monitoring new models or harm areas.
It introduces six large, challenging safety datasets and evaluates two probe architectures across 20 models from five families with 32 to 10⁶ labels.
Probe error decreases as model size grows and approaches a model-dependent floor as labels increase; these patterns generalize across tasks, families, and architectures.
Fitted on the smallest models in each family, the laws predict larger-model error within 0.02 in 72% of cases and correctly identify the cheaper path—more labels or a larger model—in 73% of cases.
The laws also select between probe architectures with only 0.006 average extra error when choosing the worse option.
papers.selection_reason: Derives scaling laws for safety probes, providing a predictive tool for monitoring LLM behavior, which is relevant to LLM safety and control.
papers.title: Scaling Laws for Safety Probes
papers.tldr: Safety-probe performance can be predicted from target-model size and label count using two scaling laws, reducing the need to train many probe configurations.

papers.abstract: Singular-value spectra encode important structure in transformer feed-forward projections, yet their causal role in downstream behavior remains underexplored. We study post-hoc spectral smoothing and spiking interventions on the up_proj and down_proj matrices. Positive perturbation stretches deviations from the geometric mean, making large singular values larger and small ones smaller (spiking), and vice versa. The intervention preserves singular vectors and the geometric mean of the singular values. Across five open Llama and Qwen instruction models, we evaluate the perturbed systems on capability-labeled subtasks, standard and chain-of-thought reasoning benchmarks, judge-scored truthfulness, hallucination, and safety tasks, and TRAIT personality probes. To interpret score shifts, we fit responses in a three-dimensional capability basis consisting of factual knowledge, language understanding, and deductive reasoning. The induced changes suggest structured rather than purely random sensitivity: large positive perturbations more reliably suppress language and deductive responses, moderate negative perturbations can sometimes improve factual or task-local performance on the evaluated grids, and sensitivity varies strongly by model family, benchmark module, and underlying layerwise spectral inequality. These results position spectral perturbation as a lightweight intervention for probing how capabilities are organized and traded off in large language models.
authors: Qince Luan, Jianhui Xu, Yang Xu
bullets: Intervenes on up_proj and down_proj matrices by spiking or smoothing singular values while preserving singular vectors and their geometric mean.
Evaluates five open Llama and Qwen instruction models across capability subtasks, reasoning, truthfulness, hallucination, safety, and personality probes.
Interprets behavioral changes using a three-dimensional basis of factual knowledge, language understanding, and deductive reasoning.
Positive spiking more consistently suppresses language and deductive responses, while moderate smoothing can sometimes improve factual or task-local performance.
Sensitivity varies substantially across model families, benchmark modules, and the underlying spectral inequality of layers.
papers.selection_reason: Spectral intervention analysis of LLM feed-forward weights; relevant to understanding and probing large language model capabilities.
papers.title: Spectral Smoothing and Spiking Perturbations Reconfigure Capability Profiles and Selective Task Performance in Large Language Models
papers.tldr: Post-hoc reshaping of transformer singular-value spectra systematically changes LLM capabilities, with effects that depend on perturbation direction, model, task, and layerwise spectral inequality.

papers.abstract: The claim that speculative-decoding acceptance rate decays as a chain-of-thought grows longer has become a de facto industry narrative, motivating draft-model co-design and position-aware training. Nearly all direct evidence comes from trained drafters whose offline training length is far shorter than inference, so a purely positional law has never been isolated. We present the first systematic, full-length measurement of acceptance rate as a function of generation position on MATH-500 (all 500 problems), under greedy and sampling decoding, with two independent drafts against DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B: a same-family draft (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B) and a cross-family draft (Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct), yielding about 1.78M verification rounds. Using within-problem paired tests, we find that after isolating a greedy-decoding repetition pathology, acceptance rate does not decay with position in any of the four configurations within the supported ranges (greedy 0-8K, sampling 0-12K); the second half of each trajectory is slightly but significantly higher than the first. A controlled temperature sweep shows that the apparent sampling-mode degradation of high-entropy reflection tokens is a visibility artifact of argmax agreement, not a drop in expected acceptance probability. Rejections concentrate with high precision on reflection trigger tokens such as "wait", "however" and "check", an entropy-selective failure that a lightweight three-arm LoRA trajectory-alignment intervention (uniform, reflection-marked, entropy-weighted) fails to improve in mean accepted length. We thus supply the positional baseline that independent draft-target pairs were missing, and localize the residual failure to decision-point entropy rather than position.
bullets: Evaluated all 500 MATH-500 problems with greedy and sampling decoding against DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B.
Used independent same-family and cross-family 1.5B drafts across about 1.78M verification rounds.
Acceptance stayed stable or was slightly higher in the second half of trajectories within 8K greedy and 12K sampling ranges.
Sampling degradation for reflection tokens is attributed to argmax-agreement visibility, not lower expected acceptance probability.
A three-arm LoRA trajectory-alignment intervention did not improve mean accepted length.
papers.selection_reason: Provides a full-length diagnostic on speculative decoding and chain-of-thought length, offering insights into inference efficiency and model behavior.
papers.title: Speculative Acceptance Does Not Decay with Position: A Full-Length Diagnostic on Long Chain-of-Thought with Independent Drafts
papers.tldr: Full-length tests find no positional decay in speculative-decoding acceptance; remaining rejections cluster at high-entropy reflection points rather than later positions.

papers.abstract: Medical knowledge evolves as clinical guidelines revise recommendations, yet whether large language models (LLMs) faithfully incorporate such changes remains unclear. We introduce ChronoEvo, comprising 1,709 recommendation-level revisions across 12 forms of medical knowledge change, to distinguish recognition of revised guidance from incorporation into clinical recommendations. In the primary model, 90.8% of responses recognized revisions and 80.2% were clinically correct, but only 58.5% fully incorporated guidance, yielding a 32.3-percentage-point recognition-incorporation gap. This dissociation persisted across 14 models and was corroborated by two clinicians' adjudicated assessment of 300 responses, yielding a 40.3-percentage-point gap in the validation sample. Changes in recommendation strength and patient eligibility were associated with retention of outdated guidance. A revision-salience intervention reduced outdated-content retention and improved clinical correctness but did not significantly improve full incorporation. These findings identify faithful incorporation of evolving medical knowledge as a distinct challenge for clinical LLM reliability, even when updated guideline evidence is available.
authors: Min Zeng, Zaifu Zhan, Kai Yu, Rui Zhang
bullets: ChronoEvo evaluates 1,709 recommendation-level revisions spanning 12 types of medical knowledge change.
In the primary model, 90.8% of responses recognized revisions, but only 58.5% fully incorporated them; 80.2% were clinically correct.
A recognition–incorporation gap persisted across 14 models and was confirmed by clinician assessment.
Changes in recommendation strength and patient eligibility were linked to retaining outdated guidance.
Making revisions more salient reduced outdated content and improved correctness, but not full incorporation.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates LLMs on their ability to incorporate evolving medical knowledge, a key challenge for the reliability of clinical LLMs.
papers.title: Large language models show systematic failures in incorporating evolving medical knowledge
papers.tldr: LLMs often recognize updated medical guidance without fully incorporating it into their clinical recommendations.

papers.abstract: AI control protocols aim to get useful work from models that may be misaligned by monitoring their behaviour. One approach uses a second copy of the same model as the monitor. This avoids relying on a weaker reviewer the model could outsmart, but risks collusion: the model, now monitoring itself, may cover up its own misbehaviour. One remedy is to fine-tune the monitor on whatever examples of misbehaviour the control team has caught. We ask whether this training also removes collusion that the control team has not yet found. We fine-tune Llama-3.3-70B and Qwen2.5-72B to install five policy-monitor behaviour pairs, correct the monitor on 300 honest reviews of one caught collusion, and measure collusion on the other four in unseen prompt formats. Averaged over the three seeds of each family, correction reduces held-out collusion from 91% to 14-20% under three of the four methods we compare (individual seeds 10-32%), while a control fine-tuned on the same number of unrelated examples leaves 56-93%. Family-average accuracy on control items changes by at most five points and capability is preserved, apart from a drop in mathematical accuracy on one Llama seed. Under the tested training configuration, methods with similar caught-task accuracy differ in held-out transfer, from 58% to 83% average reduction, so the caught behaviour alone does not reveal how far a correction reaches. Catching one collusion lets the control team reduce, but not remove, collusion it has not caught, by retraining the monitor alone.
authors: Juan-Pablo Rivera, Ari Spiesberger, Juan J Vazquez, Arun Jose, Axel Ahlqvist, Adeline Kassler, Meru Gopalan, Sandy Tanwisuth, John Hughes
bullets: Self-monitoring can enable models to conceal their own misbehaviour, creating a collusion risk in AI control.
The study fine-tunes Llama-3.3-70B and Qwen2.5-72B monitors using 300 honest reviews of one discovered collusion, then tests transfer to four unseen collusions.
Across three of four methods, held-out collusion fell from 91% to 14–20%; unrelated-example controls remained at 56–93%.
Normal control-item accuracy changed by at most five points and capabilities were generally preserved, though one Llama seed lost mathematical accuracy.
Similar performance on the caught task produced different transfer rates, so caught-task accuracy alone does not predict generalization.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates fine-tuning monitors to prevent collusion in AI control protocols, a relevant safety and control problem for LLMs.
papers.title: Model Organisms of Collusion: Corrective Transfer in Untrusted Monitors
papers.tldr: Retraining an untrusted monitor on one caught collusion substantially reduces—but does not eliminate—unseen collusion across prompt formats.

papers.abstract: Reasoning LLMs often continue reasoning after reaching a correct answer, wasting computation and sometimes replacing it with an incorrect one. Deciding when to stop is a metareasoning problem: the model must weigh what further reasoning could achieve against its cost, given what it can already answer. Direct utility training learns a stopping representation at a chosen token price; supporting new prices can require additional controller training. We introduce BELT (BELief-based Termination), which separates outcome prediction from stopping control. It learns beliefs about current and future answers from a frozen LLM's hidden states, then fits a linear stopping policy on the frozen features. The prediction targets are independent of token price, so one probe supports different accuracy-cost trade-offs through CPU policy refitting or threshold adjustment. Averaged over five out-of-distribution (OOD) math benchmarks, BELT reduces generated tokens by 41% on Qwen3-1.7B and 51% on OLMo-3-7B-Think without loss of accuracy. The same math-trained BELT transfers to coding and agentic tasks without training on code or agentic data. In all three domains, its accuracy-cost trade-offs are competitive with or better than those of end-to-end controllers. On OLMo3, its probe has 21.2x fewer parameters than one checkpoint of the strongest baseline, OS-Pruner, and needs 55x fewer training GPU-hours than OS-Pruner's five price-specific checkpoints.
authors: Jingwei Ni, Dmitry Abulkhanov, Vladislav Smirnov, Markus Leippold, Elliott Ash, Timothy Baldwin, Artem Shelmanov, Mrinmaya Sachan
bullets: Addresses unnecessary or harmful continued reasoning after an answer is already correct.
Predicts current and future answer beliefs, then fits a lightweight linear stopping policy.
Supports new accuracy–cost trade-offs by refitting or adjusting the policy without retraining the representation.
Reduces generated tokens by 41% on Qwen3-1.7B and 51% on OLMo-3-7B-Think without accuracy loss across five OOD math benchmarks.
Transfers from math to coding and agentic tasks; uses substantially fewer parameters and training GPU-hours than OS-Pruner on OLMo3.
papers.selection_reason: Belief-based early stopping for reasoning LLMs reduces inference cost and transfers across tasks; relevant to LLM reasoning and efficiency.
papers.title: Same Beliefs, Different Policies: Learning Reusable Representations for Early Stopping in LLM Reasoning
papers.tldr: BELT learns price-independent beliefs from frozen LLM representations, enabling efficient and reusable early stopping across reasoning costs and tasks.

papers.abstract: Large language models often apply complex reasoning indiscriminately, leading to overthinking on simple tasks and underthinking on harder ones. We present Route-and-Generate (Rouge), a hierarchical training framework that enables LLMs to adaptively decide when and how much reasoning is required for each input. Our approach decouples reasoning effort allocation from answer generation by introducing a routing policy that allocates a fixed sampling budget across multiple reasoning formats, while the base model is optimized with GRPO using per-sample rewards. To promote efficient reasoning, we employ a rank-based reward that favors shorter correct solutions, and update the routing policy via a closed-form KL-regularized policy improvement step distilled into a neural router. This design encourages concise answers on easy problems while reserving longer reasoning for harder ones, achieving improved accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across multiple reasoning benchmarks.
authors: Tien-Phat Nguyen, Truong Nguyen, Thanh-Thien Le, Hoang Phan, Thien Huu Nguyen, Linh Ngo Van, Trung Le
bullets: Targets indiscriminate reasoning, which can waste effort on easy tasks and underserve difficult ones.
Separates reasoning-effort allocation from answer generation through a hierarchical routing framework.
Allocates a fixed sampling budget across reasoning formats and trains the base model with per-sample GRPO rewards.
Uses rank-based rewards favoring shorter correct solutions and a KL-regularized policy improvement step distilled into a neural router.
Reports improved accuracy–efficiency trade-offs across multiple reasoning benchmarks; specific results are not provided in the abstract.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a hierarchical training framework for LLMs to adaptively allocate reasoning effort using a KL-regularized router, addressing architectural efficiency in reasoning.
papers.title: Route-and-Generate: KL-Regularized Router Improvement for Reasoning Routing in LLMs
papers.tldr: Rouge trains LLMs to route each problem to an appropriate reasoning format and effort, improving the accuracy–efficiency trade-off.

papers.abstract: Training Arabic large language models faces challenges from noisy web data, dialectal variation, and the high cost of continual pretraining (CPT). We introduce AQL-Lite (AQL: Arabic Quality Language), a time- and resource-efficient framework for adapting a multilingual LLM to Modern Standard Arabic (MSA). AQL-Lite couples a quality-first curation pipeline (structural cleaning, heuristic and model-based filtering, MSA selection, and deduplication) with a partial-parameter CPT recipe that trains RS-LoRA adapters across the network together with the last eight transformer blocks and the embedding matrix, under layer-wise learning rates. At a matched 1B-token budget, CPT on AQL-curated data raises a four-benchmark Arabic mean by 3.51 points over CPT on raw web text, which yields no gain over the base model. In a controlled 5B-token comparison, AQL-Lite recovers 94% of the gain of full-parameter CPT (mean 73.19 vs. 73.58) in 52% of the wall-clock time and outperforms adapter-only baselines on every benchmark, and a component ablation shows that adapters, unfrozen blocks, and embedding training each contribute. Scaled to 40B MSA tokens and instruction-tuned on one million examples, the resulting 12B model scores 75.3 on the seven-benchmark Open Arabic LLM Leaderboard v2 (OALL v2) suite. These results suggest that partial-parameter CPT on a carefully curated corpus is a practical route to efficient MSA adaptation.
authors: Houssam Eddine Boukhalfa, Mourad Bouache, Mourad Dahmane
bullets: Addresses noisy web data, dialectal variation, and the cost of continual pretraining for Arabic LLMs.
Curates MSA data through cleaning, heuristic/model filtering, MSA selection, and deduplication.
Trains RS-LoRA adapters, the final eight transformer blocks, and embeddings with layer-wise learning rates.
