At 5B tokens, reaches 94% of full-parameter CPT’s gain in 52% of the wall-clock time and beats adapter-only baselines.
A 12B model trained on 40B MSA tokens and instruction-tuned on one million examples scores 75.3 on OALL v2.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a data-centric continual pretraining framework for Arabic LLMs, relevant to LLM adaptation and continual learning.
papers.title: AQL-Lite: Enabling Efficient Knowledge Acquisition for Arabic LLMs via Data-Centric Continual Pretraining
papers.tldr: AQL-Lite efficiently adapts multilingual LLMs to Modern Standard Arabic by combining high-quality data curation with selective continual pretraining.

papers.abstract: Model fusion aims to integrate the capabilities of multi-expert models into a single model. Existing evaluations offer limited coverage of reasoning with long chains of thought and tool use, while strong average performance can mask substantial losses in individual expert capabilities. We introduce FusionEval, a benchmark that provides controlled expert pools, integrates fusion methods with and without additional training, and offers a unified evaluation suite. The pools contain domain experts independently trained from Qwen3 and Llama base models across math, code, science, instruction following, and tool use. The suite evaluates capability retention and computational cost on eight public benchmarks under comparable data access rules, reporting normalized average and worst performance, runtime, and peak GPU memory usage. Extensive experiments show that training-free methods preserve reasoning performance but substantially degrade tool use at both model scales. In contrast, MOPD preserves tool use and achieves a more balanced capability profile, but requires additional data preparation, inference, and training. Jointly retaining reasoning, instruction following, and tool use at low computational cost remains a challenge. We hope FusionEval supports future research on efficient model fusion that jointly preserves expert capabilities. Our code is available at https://github.com/Baicaihaochi/FusionEval_Benchmark.
authors: Shuo Cai, Yanggan Gu, Yuhang Liu, Su Lu, Yuanyi Wang, Yang Yu, Zhen Li, Zhitian Hou, Guanghao Zhu, Ming Li, Hongxia Yang
bullets: Introduces controlled expert pools from Qwen3 and Llama across math, code, science, instruction following, and tool use.
Evaluates training-free and training-based fusion methods on eight public benchmarks using capability retention and cost metrics.
Training-free methods preserve reasoning but substantially weaken tool use across model scales.
MOPD better preserves tool use and balances capabilities, but requires extra data preparation, inference, and training.
Jointly retaining reasoning, instruction following, and tool use at low cost remains unresolved.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for fusing multiple expert LLMs into one model while evaluating capability retention and cost; relevant to LLM foundation model research.
papers.title: FusionEval: Benchmarking Model Fusion for Large Language Models
papers.tldr: FusionEval benchmarks whether model-fusion methods can retain diverse expert capabilities—especially reasoning and tool use—while controlling computational cost.

papers.abstract: Forming an accurate theory-of-mind (ToM) is key to successful multi-agent collaboration and requires reasoning under uncertainty to capture multiple possible partner states. This is hard to do in the text representation space native to large language model (LLM) agents, which more easily describe a single partner state. To address this challenge, we introduce ToM2Vec, which learns to form abstract theories-of-mind in a rich latent space via a fixed budget of continuous reasoning tokens. During training, supervision for these tokens comes from the partner's actual thoughts, which the ToM tokens are trained to abstract and match. At test-time, ToM tokens are generated by each agent and act as conditioners for that agent's thoughts and actions. Across several environments covering collaborative, competitive, and mixed-motive settings (Overcooked-AI, multiparty negotiation, Decrypto, Hanabi, and Collab Escape/Capture), we evaluate ToM2Vec's ability to support multi-agent interactions and collaboration, finding consistent improvements over the base model and a variety of competitive trained and prompted baselines. We show that latent reasoning is critical, with performance dropping when reasoning is expressed in text. Moreover, we show that ToM2Vec training generalizes to partner model families not seen at train-time, including a proprietary model (GPT-5.4). In our analysis, we provide evidence that the latent tokens encode a ToM, rather than task-specific information: ToM2Vec's tokens improve the agent's ability to directly answer questions about partner beliefs, desires, and next actions.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of representing multiple possible partner states in LLM text space.
Trains a fixed budget of latent reasoning tokens to abstract and match partners’ actual thoughts.
At test time, each agent generates these tokens to condition its reasoning and actions.
Improves performance across collaborative, competitive, and mixed-motive environments over the base model and several baselines.
Latent reasoning outperforms text-based reasoning, generalizes to unseen partner model families, and supports answers about partners’ beliefs, desires, and actions.
papers.selection_reason: Continuous latent theory-of-mind tokens for LLM multi-agent coordination directly advances LLM-based reasoning and agentic behavior.
papers.title: ToM2Vec: Continuous Theory-of-Mind Tokens for Multi-Agent Coordination
papers.tldr: ToM2Vec uses continuous latent tokens to represent uncertain partner mental states, improving multi-agent coordination across diverse interaction settings.

papers.abstract: Using an LLM to generate training data for another is among the most general ways to train one, and it remains common practice. Some frontier teams have closed that route for their own models: what comes back is an answer, or a short summary, without the detailed reasoning trace behind it. That is a little ironic: they were themselves built on distilling human knowledge, and distilling an open-source model is still entirely routine; the restriction applies to their own outputs alone. Recent work recovers the hidden reasoning by replaying encrypted blocks across models. It somehow works, but it breaks the providers' terms of service, so it is not something a product can be built on long-term. We built the alternative. We take the context and the teacher's answer as input, and generate the reasoning trace ourselves, in the style of the student's own model family. Training is two-stage, supervised and then adversarial: a generator learns to regenerate the family's own reasoning traces from their context and answer, and a critic learns how real a reasoning trace looks. Applied to a teacher's answer, the generator writes one in the family's style. An independent judge rates how likely traces are to be genuine on a scale from 0 to 1: ours average 0.68, real traces 0.66, and traces selected by the critic from four candidates 0.82. These are authenticity scores, not correctness rates. We test the idea on five benchmarks with everything else held fixed. On general tasks the five training corpora are about the same; on coding, the generated reasoning beats Fable 5's own thinking content. With the same 5,000 questions and the same teacher answers, HumanEval+ improves by 3.7 points and MBPP+ by 7.1 at the final checkpoint, and the MBPP+ lead holds at every checkpoint. We suspect that reasoning written in the student's family style is easier for it to learn from.
bullets: Addresses the lack of accessible reasoning traces from closed frontier models without relying on prohibited encrypted-trace recovery.
Uses a two-stage supervised and adversarial setup: a generator reconstructs family-style traces, while a critic evaluates their authenticity.
Generated traces received average authenticity scores comparable to real traces; critic-selected traces scored higher.
Across five benchmarks, results were similar on general tasks, while coding performance improved by 3.7 points on HumanEval+ and 7.1 on MBPP+ under matched data and teacher answers.
The authors hypothesize that reasoning in the student model’s own style is easier to learn from; reported scores measure authenticity, not correctness.
papers.selection_reason: LLM reasoning-trace distillation and student-style trace generation are directly relevant to large language model training.
papers.title: TraceForge: Distilling with Your Own Thinking
papers.tldr: TraceForge generates student-style reasoning traces from a teacher’s context and answer, enabling terms-compliant distillation and improving coding performance.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but remains computationally expensive and sample inefficient. On-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense token-level supervision from a stronger teacher, yet standard OPD distills every token regardless of whether the teacher's preference actually improves task reward. Existing token-selection methods rely on proxies such as uncertainty or teacher--student divergence, which need not identify reward-improving supervision. We introduce Reward-Aligned Distillation (RAD), a bilevel framework that weights distillation signals based on their predicted effect on the student's post-update reward. RAD differentiates through a temporary optimizer step to score each token's supervision, then updates the token weights by projected ascent from the initial token weights. The resulting weights can strengthen, suppress, or reverse individual distillation-gradient contributions. At a matched training-response budget, RAD improves mean accuracy on six competition-math benchmarks over the strongest baselines by 6.5 percentage points for Qwen3-1.7B (non-thinking) and 2.5 points for Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507. RAD-Simple, a simplified variant, achieves comparable math accuracy at the same training-response budget. On LiveCodeBench-v6, RAD reaches 54.69\% and 58.67\% pass@1 with Qwen3-1.7B (non-thinking) and OLMo3-7B-Instruct, respectively, exceeding the strongest baselines by 8.7 and 6.4 points. These results support reward-guided weighting of teacher supervision across model families and tasks.
bullets: Targets the inefficiency of applying teacher guidance to every token, including supervision that may not improve task reward.
Uses a bilevel temporary optimizer step to estimate each token’s reward impact and updates weights through projected ascent.
Token weights can amplify, suppress, or reverse individual distillation-gradient contributions.
At matched training-response budgets, RAD improves competition-math accuracy over strong baselines across tested Qwen3 models and improves LiveCodeBench pass@1 across two model families.
RAD-Simple achieves comparable math accuracy, suggesting the approach can be simplified without major loss.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a bilevel framework for distilling LLMs that aligns token-level supervision with the predicted effect on task reward, offering a novel approach to improving reasoning capabilities in LLM training.
papers.title: Reward-Aligned Distillation
papers.tldr: Reward-Aligned Distillation improves on-policy distillation by weighting teacher supervision according to its predicted impact on the student’s reward.

papers.abstract: Current Transformer interfaces index tokens by one or more integer coordinates, which determine their addresses inside attention. In RoPE and its multi-axis or hierarchical variants, the resulting address has the form $A(i)=R_1^{i_1}R_2^{i_2}R_3^{i_3}$, where the exponents are integer coordinates assigned after choosing a serialized token layout. When Transformers process new or large collections of data, this addressing scheme can produce unseen offsets or coordinate combinations, push repositories toward retrieve-and-serialize pipelines, and force new entities, records, or repository items to be represented by long token strings or identifier embeddings not seen in training. We introduce labeled incidence structures (LIS), in which each participating token or value is an endpoint with content $x$ and a structural index $i$. The index can include local position, relation role, relation instance, text unit, field, or content-derived identity. The model maps this index to a structural address $A(i)$, so adding new tokens, facts, text units, or repository items applies the same learned address rule to structural and content coordinates rather than requiring larger integer coordinates, unseen coordinate combinations, or new identifier embeddings. Attention scores endpoints $i,j$ using $q_i^\top P_{j\to i}k_j$, where journey consistency forces $P_{j\to i}=A(i)^{-1}A(j)$. When $i$ has several coordinates, such as position, role, and instance, coordinate independence is equivalent to factoring $A(i)$ into one address factor per coordinate. This recovers RoPE, RoPE-2D, and HiRoPE as special cases. This allows knowledge-graph (KG) roles, fact instances, and text units to enter the attention score directly. In controlled shallow diagnostics, the LIS address interface is implemented inside ordinary Transformer attention and yields promising results across text, KG, and $n$-ary settings.
bullets: Transformers can struggle with unseen offsets, coordinate combinations, and newly introduced entities or repository items.
LIS represents each token or value by content plus a multi-coordinate structural index, such as position, role, relation instance, or text unit.
Attention uses journey-consistent structural transformations, with coordinate factorization recovering RoPE, RoPE-2D, and HiRoPE as special cases.
The interface can incorporate knowledge-graph roles, fact instances, and text units directly into attention rather than relying on retrieve-and-serialize pipelines.
Controlled shallow diagnostics report promising results across text, knowledge-graph, and n-ary settings, though the abstract does not establish broader performance or scalability.
papers.selection_reason: A native Transformer indexing and addressing framework extends LLM architecture reasoning beyond standard positional encodings.
papers.title: Labeled Incidence Structures for Native Transformer Modeling of Text, Knowledge Graphs, and Hypergraphs
papers.tldr: Labeled incidence structures (LIS) extend Transformer positional addressing to directly represent structural roles, relations, instances, and identities across text, knowledge graphs, and hypergraphs.

papers.abstract: Uniform diffusion language models (UDLMs) generate text by iteratively denoising sequences of ordinary vocabulary tokens, any of which may be corrupted and subsequently revised. During training, UDLMs must denoise from a context that may itself be unreliable, whereas masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) always condition on a clean context. This challenging training objective makes UDLMs more FLOP-intensive to train than MDLMs, but it yields stronger downstream reasoning performance. Recently, selective looping, which recursively applies a few early Transformer layers within each denoising step, has been shown to improve training efficiency in MDLMs under an iso-FLOP budget. We investigate looping in UDLMs while keeping the training objective and sampler unchanged. We find that looping significantly improves training efficiency: looped UDLMs reach the validation NLL of a non-looped UDLM trained on about 0.5 trillion tokens with up to 2.8x fewer training FLOPs on OpenWebText and 3.3x fewer on FineWeb-Edu. We also find that, at a matched NFE budget, looped UDLMs reach up to 9.8% lower generation perplexity than the non-looped UDLM, with most gains achieved at moderate loop counts. Finally, we study different loop-count distributions and find that sampling smaller loop counts more frequently during training improves inference efficiency: on downstream tasks, this strategy uses 12% fewer loops than uniform loop-count sampling without degrading accuracy.
authors: Saiteja Utpala, Chieh-Hsin Lai, Yuki Mitsufuji, Praneeth Vepakomma
bullets: UDLMs are costly to train because they must denoise while conditioning on potentially corrupted context.
The method recursively reuses early Transformer layers within each denoising step, while keeping the training objective and sampler unchanged.
Looped UDLMs match the validation NLL of a model trained on roughly 0.5 trillion tokens with up to 2.8× fewer FLOPs on OpenWebText and 3.3× fewer on FineWeb-Edu.
At matched function-evaluation budgets, looping improves generation perplexity by up to 9.8%.
Sampling smaller loop counts more often reduces downstream inference loops by 12% without hurting accuracy.
papers.selection_reason: Looping in diffusion language models improves training and inference efficiency for language foundation models.
papers.title: Looped Uniform Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: Selective looping makes uniform diffusion language models substantially more training- and inference-efficient without changing their objective or sampler.

papers.abstract: Large language models are typically trained with next-token prediction (NTP), which rewards predicting specific tokens rather than explicitly accounting for the semantic similarities between different words or expressions. Prior work has addressed this limitation by augmenting training data with minimally varying sentences that replace a target word with conceptually related alternatives, e.g., "The tired coach ran home" $\rightarrow$ {"The tired trainer ran home", "The tired instructor ran home", ...}. Such concept augmentation improves performance, but it remains unclear whether its effectiveness depends on where in the sentence the concept is expressed. We reproduce and extend prior work $\textit{beyond nouns}$ to verbs and adjectives, asking whether the part of speech (POS) carrying the concept signal affects perplexity and downstream performance. We find different patterns across evaluation settings: concept augmentation improves perplexity most consistently on news, independent of the POS used, whereas verbs provide the most reliable downstream gains. Despite these behavioral differences, representational analyses using CKA and linear probing show that the conditions yielding the largest downstream gains are not necessarily those that most alter the model's internal representations. Together, these results suggest that the effectiveness of concept augmentation depends on where and how conceptual information is introduced during training.
bullets: Extends prior concept-augmentation work beyond nouns to verbs and adjectives to study part-of-speech effects.
Concept augmentation most consistently improves perplexity on news across POS conditions.
Verb-based augmentation provides the most reliable downstream performance gains.
CKA and linear-probing analyses show that representation changes do not necessarily predict downstream improvements.
Results suggest that both the location and form of conceptual information matter during post-training.
papers.selection_reason: Studies part-of-speech effects in LLM post-training concept augmentation, relevant to large language model training.
papers.title: Every Part Has Its Role: Part-of-Speech Effects in LLM Post-Training
papers.tldr: Concept augmentation helps language models, but its impact depends on whether concepts are expressed through nouns, verbs, or adjectives and on the evaluation setting.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is one of the few practical tools available for overseeing capable AI systems, but it is fragile: a model's reasoning is only useful to a monitor if it remains coupled to what the model actually does. This coupling can be degraded during training through, for example, CoT compression, optimization against a monitor, and out-of-context generalization from synthetic documents. In this work, we propose an unsupervised post-training objective based on maximizing mutual information between CoT and the output for improving CoT monitorability. Across three model organisms with degraded CoT, it recovers most or all of the lost monitorability. Applied to undegraded policies, it further improves judged monitorability, improves prediction of unsafe behavior by CoT monitors and activation probes, and increases the prevalence of consequential reasoning. These results suggest that monitorability should be treated as a trainable attribute of the policy. A dedicated monitorability post-training stage can extend current practices that protect CoT from direct optimization pressure.
authors: Usman Anwar, Tim Bakker, Christos Louizos, David Krueger
bullets: CoT monitoring is fragile when reasoning becomes decoupled from the model’s actual behavior.
The proposed objective maximizes mutual information between CoT and outputs.
Across three degraded model organisms, the method recovers most or all lost monitorability.
For undegraded policies, it improves judged monitorability and prediction of unsafe behavior by monitors and activation probes.
It also increases consequential reasoning, suggesting monitorability is a trainable policy attribute.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses Chain-of-Thought monitorability in LLMs through a post-training objective, relevant to large language model safety and architecture.
papers.title: Monitorability Is Trainable: Post-Training for Chain-of-Thought Monitorability
papers.tldr: Monitorability of chain-of-thought can be improved through unsupervised post-training that strengthens its connection to model outputs.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-based in-context learning (ICL) enables large language models (LLMs) to predict tabular labels from similar examples, but it remains unclear whether LLM inference improves on direct voting over those same examples. We address this question by comparing four general-purpose LLMs with distance-weighted nearest-neighbor voting (Distance-KNN) using identical retrieved neighbors across 19 tabular classification datasets. With the number of demonstrations fixed, enlarging the retrieval candidate pool improves accuracy for all predictors, yet Distance-KNN achieves the highest mean accuracy at every pool size. More detailed analyses reveal that LLM gains are concentrated where retrieved neighbors exhibit low label consensus and vary across models. These gains further depend on the average feature-space distance to the test query: under low label consensus, some LLMs outperform Distance-KNN in close and intermediate neighborhoods, but all fall behind on average in the most distant group. Complementary experiments on the number of demonstrations, prompt formulation, retrieval representation, and label-balanced demonstration selection largely preserve the overall findings. These results characterize when LLM inference adds predictive value beyond distance-weighted voting in retrieval-based tabular ICL.
authors: Ziquan Wang, Yuxuan Nie, Jian Ma, Yingjie Li
bullets: Compares four general-purpose LLMs with Distance-KNN using identical retrieved neighbors across 19 tabular classification datasets.
Expanding the retrieval candidate pool improves all predictors, while Distance-KNN has the highest mean accuracy at every pool size.
LLM benefits are concentrated in low-label-consensus neighborhoods and vary across models.
Some LLMs outperform Distance-KNN for close or intermediate low-consensus neighborhoods, but all lag in the most distant group.
Findings remain broadly consistent across demonstrations, prompts, retrieval representations, and label-balanced selection.
papers.selection_reason: Empirical characterization of when LLM inference adds value over retrieval-based in-context learning; relevant to LLM reasoning and retrieval.
papers.title: Beyond the Vote: When Do LLMs Add Value to Retrieval-Based Tabular Classification?
papers.tldr: LLMs add value beyond distance-weighted neighbor voting mainly when retrieved examples disagree, especially in close or intermediate neighborhoods, but they underperform overall.

papers.abstract: Process reward models (PRMs) provide fine-grained supervision for multi-step reasoning, yet obtaining reliable process labels remains a central bottleneck. Existing approaches typically rely on human annotation, rollout-based estimation, or auxiliary verification. In this work, we explore a different source of process supervision natively exposed by Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models: expert routing. We show that simple routing statistics provide an intrinsic process-confidence signal that is competitive with conventional output-logit confidence. Building on this observation, we construct routing confidence by combining overall routing mass, head routing mass, and within-step routing variation, and introduce RoCo-Rethink, which identifies the least confident reasoning step and selectively regenerates the subsequent trajectory. We further introduce RoCo-PRM, which uses a strong MoE to automatically annotate reasoning trajectories with routing-derived step scores and distills them into a standalone PRM. Across multiple MoE architectures and diverse reasoning tasks, both RoCo-Rethink and RoCo-PRM consistently outperform strong baselines, while RoCo-PRM transfers effectively across both model architectures and tasks. Our findings suggest that expert routing is more than a computational dispatch mechanism: it provides an architecture-native source of process supervision for reasoning.
authors: Guanzhi Deng, Zengyan Liu, Haibo Wang, Kuan Wu, Shing Yin Wong, Sichun Luo, Zhuoran Wang, Linqi Song
bullets: Addresses the bottleneck of obtaining reliable step-level labels for multi-step reasoning.
Combines routing mass, head routing mass, and within-step routing variation into a routing-confidence signal.
RoCo-Rethink regenerates reasoning after the least-confident step.
RoCo-PRM uses a strong MoE to label trajectories and distills routing-derived scores into a standalone PRM.
Across multiple MoE architectures and reasoning tasks, both methods outperform strong baselines; RoCo-PRM transfers across architectures and tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Uses MoE expert routing as process-supervision signal for LLM reasoning; directly relevant to MoE-based language foundation models.
papers.title: A Strong MoE Is All You Need for Process Supervision
papers.tldr: MoE expert-routing statistics can provide reliable process supervision for reasoning, enabling targeted trajectory regeneration and automatic training of transferable process reward models.

papers.abstract: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (SMoE) models improve scalability by routing input tokens to only a subset of expert networks, but they often suffer from representation collapse, in which multiple experts converge toward similar functions and lose their intended diversity. Prior work has addressed this limitation either by improving router architectures or by introducing auxiliary loss terms that implicitly penalize similarity among experts. However, router-based approaches remain vulnerable to routing collapses, and loss-based approaches can conflict with the task's original objective during optimization. In this work, we propose GaP-MoE (Gradient Accumulation and Projection in MoE), which induces expert specialization by directly manipulating expert output gradients rather than modifying the loss function. At each training step, GaP-MoE stochastically selects one of the $TopK$ routed experts as a leader based on normalized routing scores, and projects the gradients of the remaining follower experts onto the orthogonal complement of the subspace spanned by the leader's recent gradients. This removes directional overlap between expert gradients without altering the task loss, allowing specialization to emerge as a direct consequence of the optimization dynamics rather than an externally imposed constraint. We evaluate GaP-MoE in both fine-tuning settings (BERT-based, on GLUE) and from-scratch pretraining settings (GPT-2-based, on WikiText-103, enwik8, and text8), and further confirm its compatibility as a drop-in module for existing SMoE architectures. Experimental results show that GaP-MoE achieves performance comparable to or better than standard SMoE.
bullets: Addresses expert representation collapse, where multiple MoE experts learn similar functions.
Selects a routed leader expert using normalized routing scores and accumulates its recent gradients.
Projects follower-expert gradients onto the orthogonal complement of the leader-gradient subspace.
Encourages specialization without changing the task loss or relying on router modifications.
Evaluated in BERT fine-tuning and GPT-2 pretraining settings, achieving performance comparable to or better than standard SMoE.
papers.selection_reason: Improves expert specialization in sparse mixture-of-experts LLMs, directly relevant to modern LLM architectures.
papers.title: GaP-MoE : Explicit Expert Specialization in Mixture-of-Experts via Orthogonal Gradient Accumulation and Projection
papers.tldr: GaP-MoE promotes diverse expert behavior in sparse MoE models by orthogonally projecting follower-expert gradients away from a selected leader’s recent gradient directions.

papers.abstract: Mid-training (MT) is a training phase in LLM training pipelines that continues pretraining (PT) on smaller datasets of higher value. Taking the PT and MT phases as a whole, training usually starts with only PT data and then transitions completely to MT data. In this work, we view this complete transition from PT to MT data as a special case of a broader class of data mixing schedules that specify how the proportions of PT and MT tokens in each batch change over training. Under fixed total training compute and MT token budgets, we ask: Is this complete transition to MT data optimal for minimizing final MT loss? We show that the answer depends on the learning rate (LR) schedule: one data schedule may outperform another under one LR schedule, but changing only the LR schedule can reverse the outcome. Specifically, when the LR decays throughout continued training, introducing MT data earlier and mixing it with PT data lowers the final MT loss compared with placing all MT data at the end of training, but this result is reversed if we use constant LR. We therefore study how to jointly choose when to introduce MT data and when to decay the LR through ablation studies, and find that it is better to decay the LR only after MT data enters training. Finally, we develop a theoretical model that explains why the optimal data schedule for a fixed MT token budget depends on the LR schedule.
authors: Haodong Wen, Kairong Luo, Tingkai Yan, Wenguang Chen, Kaifeng Lyu
bullets: The study asks whether switching completely from pretraining (PT) data to mid-training (MT) data is optimal under fixed compute and MT-token budgets.
With a decaying learning rate, introducing and mixing MT data earlier improves final MT loss versus placing all MT data at the end.
With a constant learning rate, this comparison reverses, showing that schedule choices are interdependent.
Ablations suggest delaying learning-rate decay until after MT data enters training is preferable.
A theoretical model explains why the optimal data schedule depends on the learning-rate schedule.
papers.selection_reason: Studies joint data and learning-rate schedules for LLM mid-training, relevant to LLM training and foundation-model development.
papers.title: Data Schedules and Learning Rate Schedules Should Be Designed Together
papers.tldr: Data-mixing and learning-rate schedules interact strongly in mid-training, so they should be designed jointly rather than independently.

papers.abstract: A transformer MLP gives each hidden channel two roles: a reader that decides when the channel responds, and a writer that decides what it adds back to the residual stream. Read as a key--value memory, the layer can be measured one factor set at a time: the pairing of readers to writers is carried only by their shared index, invisible to any quantity computed from one factor set alone. Yet training couples the two factors through their joint update, so we ask what reading them together shows. The block supplies the joint instrument: the MLP writes back into the very stream it reads, so the exact Jacobian of its update is square, and its agreement with its own transpose resolves into reader--writer terms whose inner products give each channel, read as a couple, a signed pairing coordinate. Ranked by this coordinate, each block we measure has a small core of strongly coupled channels; where initialization gives either sign equally, the core is nearly all opposed: each writer points against the direction its reader responds to. This opposed core recurs from the smallest models trained from scratch to released checkpoints; its sign is in place within a few percent of training and holds while the coupling grows. Read as couples, most channels return their contribution against the reader that fired it, and the readers of later blocks take it up; few show in the logits. Training holds the couples in place: flipping the opposed writers moves the output toward common tokens, and a writer permuted onto another reader regrows to fit that reader while the reader stays.
authors: Giyeong Oh, Sunghee Ahn, Youngjae Yu
bullets: Treating readers and writers jointly reveals coupling that is invisible when either factor set is analyzed alone.
The MLP’s exact square Jacobian is compared with its transpose to derive a signed reader–writer pairing coordinate for each channel.
Across models and checkpoints, strongly coupled cores are usually opposed: writers point against the directions that activate their readers.
Most channels return contributions against the reader that triggered them, while later blocks can take up these contributions; few appear directly in the logits.
Perturbations support functional coupling: flipping opposed writers shifts outputs toward common tokens, and permuting a writer onto another reader causes it to regrow to fit that reader.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes transformer MLP reader-writer coupling, relevant to LLM architecture and interpretability.
papers.title: Reader--Writer Coupling in Transformer MLPs
papers.tldr: Transformer MLP channels form coupled reader–writer pairs, with a small, rapidly established core whose writers typically oppose the directions their readers detect.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), particularly through group-relative policy optimization (GRPO), has emerged as a central paradigm for the post-training of large language models (LLMs). While RLVR is highly effective at enhancing the reasoning capabilities of LLMs, it commonly induces \textit{distribution sharpening}, whereby the policy distribution becomes excessively peaked and rare-yet-correct trajectories are progressively suppressed, thus diminishing sample diversity. To this end, we promote flat-reward optima in RLVR to smooth the policy distribution. We theoretically link flat reward RLVR to reduced distribution sharpening, and empirically show improved sample diversity while maintaining single-attempt accuracy. Our method, called \texttt{Flat}-RLVR, searches for flat reward regions via sharpness-aware minimization during LLM post-training, combining this with GRPO variants to achieve better trade-offs between sampling efficiency and reasoning capacity.
authors: Yeonbum Kim, Hyun Kyu Lee, Sung Whan Yoon
bullets: RLVR can sharpen LLM policy distributions, suppressing rare but correct reasoning trajectories.
Flat-RLVR promotes flatter reward optima to mitigate this distribution sharpening.
The method combines sharpness-aware minimization with GRPO variants during post-training.
Theory connects flatter reward solutions with reduced distribution sharpening.
Experiments report higher sample diversity while maintaining single-attempt accuracy, balancing sampling efficiency and reasoning capacity.
papers.selection_reason: Sharpness-aware reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for LLM reasoning post-training; relevant to LLM reasoning methods.
papers.title: Flat-RLVR: Sharpness-Aware Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards for Reasoning Capacity in LLMs
papers.tldr: Flat-RLVR uses sharpness-aware optimization with GRPO-style RLVR to reduce policy over-concentration, improving reasoning sample diversity without sacrificing single-attempt accuracy.

papers.abstract: Masked diffusion language models have emerged as an alternative to autoregressive models, enabling parallel token generation. However, standard masked diffusion language models use a shared noise schedule across positions without explicitly encoding which positions should be resolved first. Many tasks exhibit a natural priority among positions: document titles and section headings can guide the generation of body text, while Sudoku cells determined directly from the initial clues can help resolve more difficult cells. To incorporate this notion of priority (or hierarchy) among token positions, we introduce the Hierarchical Masked Diffusion Language Model (HMDLM), which augments each token position with a hierarchy level available as part of the training data, and requires zero or minimal additional annotations. It factors generation into two passes: the first predicts a hierarchy distribution over masked positions, the second predicts token distributions conditioned on it. Giving each hierarchy level its own noise schedule induces a soft, controllable preference for revealing higher-priority positions earlier while keeping decoding fully parallel. Our formulation is mathematically grounded, and we re-derive the forward and reverse processes and the NELBO for this factorization. Our evaluation shows that for the task of language generation on LM1B, HMDLM reduces perplexity by more than 1.5 points over Anchored Diffusion Language Model (ADLM), a recently proposed strong diffusion baseline; on WikiHow, we see a drop in perplexity of up to 4.4 pts on ADLM and up to 7 pts against MDLM. An LLM judge on WikiHow prefers HMDLM generations (the two variants combined) more than $2\times$ as often as the baseline. On the task of solving Sudoku puzzles requiring multi-step reasoning, it improves solution accuracy by up to $8.6\%$ absolute points over existing diffusion baselines.
authors: Parul Gupta, Satwik, Avni Aggarwal, Bhavesh Gurnani, Arnab Kumar Mondal, Dinesh Khandelwal, Dinesh Garg, Parag Singla
bullets: Addresses the limitation that standard masked diffusion models treat all positions with a shared noise schedule and no explicit generation priority.
Uses two parallel-decoding passes: predict hierarchy distributions for masked positions, then predict tokens conditioned on those hierarchies.
Assigns separate noise schedules to hierarchy levels, creating a soft, controllable preference for revealing higher-priority positions earlier.
Improves language-modeling perplexity over diffusion baselines on LM1B and WikiHow, with stronger judged generation preference on WikiHow.
Improves Sudoku-solving accuracy by up to 8.6 percentage points over existing diffusion baselines.
papers.selection_reason: New hierarchical masked diffusion language model architecture with hierarchical noise schedules; relevant to language model architectural research.
papers.title: Hierarchical Masked Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: HMDLM improves parallel masked diffusion generation by modeling which token positions should be resolved first through learned hierarchy levels and level-specific noise schedules.

papers.abstract: Personalized reward models require user-specific preference comparisons, but collecting such feedback is costly and provides only limited supervision for each user. At the same time, large pools of responses can be generated without user identities or preference labels, yet existing personalized reward models leave this data unused. Directly learning from these responses is difficult because pairwise objectives constrain relative scores within a prompt, whereas pseudo-labeling individual responses requires scores that are comparable across prompts for the same user. We propose \textbf{PerSPL} (Personalized Semi-supervised Preference Learning), a backbone-agnostic framework that uses pair-mean score centering to stabilize this cross-prompt score coordinate and iteratively turns unlabeled responses into user-specific training signals. Against seven representative baselines across four benchmarks---PersonalLLM, HelpSteer2, Reddit TLDR, and Chatbot Arena---PerSPL achieves the highest reported mean accuracy among the evaluated methods for both seen and unseen users. The two latter benchmarks provide real-user preference comparisons in summarization and open-domain chatbot interaction, respectively. These results indicate that unlabeled responses can provide additional supervision for personalized reward modeling when per-user preference labels are scarce.
authors: Xiaoan Xu, Tingzhou Wei, Juncheng Dong, Korel Gundem, Ethan X. Fang, Zhengling Qi
bullets: Addresses the high cost and limited coverage of collecting user-specific preference comparisons.
Uses pair-mean score centering to make scores comparable across prompts for each user.
Iteratively pseudo-labels unlabeled responses to augment personalized preference training.
Is backbone-agnostic and evaluated against seven baselines across four benchmarks.
Reports the highest mean accuracy among evaluated methods for both seen and unseen users.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes PerSPL, a framework for personalized reward modeling in LLMs using semi-supervised learning, relevant to LLM alignment and personalization.
papers.title: PerSPL: Personalized Semi-supervised Preference Learning
papers.tldr: PerSPL improves personalized reward modeling by converting unlabeled responses into user-specific supervision through stabilized cross-prompt score calibration.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate impressive emergent reasoning capabilities, yet they remain constrained by fixed model parameters and finite context windows. Even when augmented with static retrieval, they can produce statements that are unsupported by, or even contradictory to, retrieved evidence. This leads to hallucinations, difficulty incorporating up-to-date information, and failures to correctly interpret or reconcile sources. Recent work addresses these limitations by tightly coupling step-by-step reasoning with interactive search, treating retrieval as an action within an iterative agentic loop rather than a one-shot preprocessing step. This study reviews frameworks that implement such reasoning-search loops by interleaving planning, querying, retrieval, integration, verification, and stopping. We analyze these systems through four architectural axes: retrieval coupling, controller design, knowledge source, and grounding strictness. We separately treat the learning signal as a cross-cutting dimension because prompting, supervision, preference optimization, and reinforcement learning can instantiate the same architecture while producing materially different search, stopping, and grounding behavior. We further distinguish benchmark difficulty from RSA-loop demand and synthesize controlled within-study ablations and quality-cost deltas, avoiding invalid pooling across heterogeneous model backbones, retrievers, corpora, and evaluation protocols. Our goal is to clarify the landscape of reasoning-search-augmented LLMs and outline a unified perspective on the design choices shaping future research.
authors: Biswas Poudel, Nilson Chapagain, Amit Kumar, Xianshun Jiang
bullets: Reasoning-search loops address hallucinations, stale knowledge, and failures to reconcile retrieved evidence in static-retrieval systems.
The taxonomy organizes systems by retrieval coupling, controller design, knowledge source, and grounding strictness.
Learning signals are treated separately because prompting, supervision, preference optimization, and reinforcement learning can alter search and stopping behavior.
The analysis distinguishes benchmark difficulty from the demands of the reasoning-search loop.
Controlled within-study ablations and quality–cost changes are synthesized without pooling incompatible experimental settings.
papers.selection_reason: Taxonomy and controlled synthesis of reasoning-search-augmented LLMs; directly relevant to LLM reasoning and retrieval methods.
papers.title: Reasoning-Search-Augmented LLMs: An Operational Taxonomy, Benchmark Analysis and Controlled Evidence Synthesis
papers.tldr: This study develops a taxonomy and evidence synthesis for LLMs that interleave reasoning with interactive search to improve grounding and information use.

papers.abstract: Continuous diffusion language models generate a whole sequence in parallel, never drawing a single word at any intermediate step; only the final step turns embeddings into text. Models such as ELF now report autoregressive-level quality at a fraction of the sampling steps of discrete-token diffusion models, and this design principle -- no step-wise discretization -- is what their own ablations credit for the gain. We show that this same principle carries a hidden cost: a collapse of the lexical long tail. Measured against held-out human text, ELF's output matches the human rate on common words almost exactly, yet its rarest words appear at only 0.30x the human rate, a gap that does not close from 105M to 652M parameters and that no sampler setting these models expose can reach. A same-size GPT-2, in contrast, spans zero to above the human rate by its decoding rule alone. We trace the difference to what continuous diffusion models lack: with no step that ever draws a discrete word, every step is instead driven by an average over the candidates still in play, and averaging a rare candidate together with the common word competing for its slot lands on the common word. An autoregressive model avoids this because its decoding rule samples one candidate rather than averaging over all of them. We propose GRAFT, a training-free method that grafts this missing choice back onto a frozen model: while the model is still undecided, GRAFT commits the rare words the average would otherwise discard, then regenerates the sequence from scratch with those commitments held in place. Across three ELF scales and on LangFlow, an independent continuous dLLM, GRAFT restores the rare-word share of generated text from 0.42-0.77x the human rate to 0.82-1.10x, a relative gain of 34-109%, and moves the entire word-frequency profile closer to human on every model tested, by 2.7x on ELF-B and 12x on LangFlow.
bullets: Continuous diffusion models match human rates for common words but underproduce rare words, with the gap persisting across model sizes.
The issue arises because intermediate denoising averages competing word candidates instead of sampling one discrete candidate.
GRAFT identifies rare words likely to be lost, commits them while the model remains uncertain, and regenerates the sequence with those commitments fixed.
Across three ELF scales and LangFlow, GRAFT raises rare-word frequency from 0.42–0.77× to 0.82–1.10× the human rate.
The method moves word-frequency profiles closer to human text on every tested model, without additional training.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces GRAFT, a training-free method to restore discrete sampling capabilities in continuous diffusion language models to address the long-tail distribution of rare words.
papers.title: GRAFT: Restoring the Missing Sampling Interface in Continuous Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: GRAFT restores rare-word diversity in continuous diffusion language models by adding a training-free discrete commitment step during generation.

papers.abstract: This paper proposes Role-Enhanced Zero-Shot Chain-of-Thought (RE-ZS-CoT), a prompting framework that systematically integrates domain-specific expert roles to enhance reasoning in large language models (LLMs) without task-specific examples. We assess two versions of our approach. In the first version, static role selection, we evaluate eight predefined expert roles across arithmetic, commonsense, and reading comprehension benchmarks to determine their impact on reasoning performance. In the second version, dynamic role selection, each model autonomously selects the single most suitable role for each benchmark, enabling adaptive task-role alignment without manual specification. Across 20 LLMs and seven benchmarks, RE-ZS-CoT frequently surpasses zero-shot and zero-shot-CoT baselines, achieving performance improvements of up to 44 percentage points. The results reveal a strong correspondence between static and dynamic versions; the benchmarks where static roles yielded improvements were almost always those where dynamic roles also outperformed baselines, though static selection achieved peak performance. Ablation studies further show that unconventional roles degrade performance, underscoring the necessity of task-role alignment. The framework's scalability is validated across model sizes (2b-14b parameters), with smaller models like Granite3.3-8b achieving remarkable proficiency in arithmetic reasoning. RE-ZS-CoT advances zero-shot prompting by unifying role specialization with chain-of-thought reasoning, offering a practical, resource-efficient solution for improving LLM capabilities across diverse domains.
authors: Ibrahim Khan, Thai Van Nguyen, Yi Xia, Pratch Suntichaikul, Mustafa Can Gursesli, Daniel Fernandez Galeote, Juho Hamari, Ruck Thawonmas
bullets: Evaluates static predefined roles and dynamically model-selected roles across arithmetic, commonsense, and reading-comprehension tasks.
Tests 20 LLMs on seven benchmarks, with reported gains of up to 44 percentage points over zero-shot and zero-shot-CoT baselines.
Static and dynamic role selection show closely aligned benefits, although static selection achieves the best peak performance.
Ablations indicate that poorly matched or unconventional roles can hurt reasoning, highlighting the importance of task-role alignment.
The approach scales across 2B–14B-parameter models and is presented as a resource-efficient zero-shot prompting framework.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates a prompting framework (RE-ZS-CoT) for large language models, focusing on role-enhanced zero-shot chain-of-thought reasoning.
papers.title: A Large-Scale Evaluation of Role-Enhanced Zero-Shot Chain-of-Thought Prompting
papers.tldr: RE-ZS-CoT improves zero-shot LLM reasoning by pairing chain-of-thought prompting with task-appropriate expert roles, often outperforming standard baselines.

papers.abstract: Cross-tokenizer logits distillation enables knowledge transfer across model families, allowing students to learn from stronger or more specialized teachers. However, differences in vocabulary and segmentation make teacher and student next-token distributions difficult to align. Existing logits-based methods are easy to integrate into standard distillation pipelines, but often rely on restrictive heuristics or tokenizer-pair-specific choices. They may restrict supervision to shared vocabulary subsets, require manually selecting different objectives for different tokenizer pairs, or match only the observed chunk and its complement rather than individual alternative continuations. We introduce Common-Support Distillation (CSD), a unified logits-based framework that constructs a shared support between the teacher and student at each aligned input chunk and matches the induced distributions with a single objective. For one-to-one alignments, CSD uses explicit common-token pairs as the shared support. For other alignments, it constructs a virtual support whose probabilities are computed using the autoregressive chain rule. A residual event captures probability mass outside the explicit support, ensuring that both induced distributions remain normalized. Across four teacher-student settings comprising Llama-3.2-1B and Gemma3-1B-PT students with Qwen and Phi teachers, CSD consistently achieves the highest average performance among the evaluated cross-tokenizer methods, outperforming the strongest alternative by up to 1.8 points and surpassing both continued pretraining and same-tokenizer distillation. For Llama-3.1-8B, CSD improves average accuracy over the strongest evaluated baseline by up to 4.2 points for the base student and 1.6 points for the instruction-tuned student.
authors: Mingyu Yang, Sharath Turuvekere Sreenivas, Adithyakrishna Venkatesh Hanasoge, Nima Tajbakhsh, Ashwath Aithal, Pavlo Molchanov
bullets: Addresses vocabulary and segmentation mismatches that make next-token logits difficult to align across tokenizers.
Uses explicit common-token pairs for one-to-one alignments and autoregressive chain-rule probabilities for other alignments.
Adds a residual event for probability mass outside the explicit support, preserving normalization.
Across evaluated teacher–student settings, CSD achieved the best average performance, with gains of up to 1.8 points and up to 4.2 points for Llama-3.1-8B base students.
The method is evaluated across multiple Llama, Gemma, Qwen, and Phi teacher–student combinations.
papers.selection_reason: Cross-tokenizer logits distillation for LLM knowledge transfer; relevant to language foundation model training.
papers.title: CSD: Common-Support Distillation for Cross-Tokenizer Knowledge Transfer
papers.tldr: CSD enables unified cross-tokenizer knowledge distillation by matching normalized teacher and student distributions over a dynamically constructed common support.

papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly take part in extended conversations where they can both shape and be shaped by another party's views, yet most persuasion research measures only one side of that exchange. We introduce a controlled LLM-LLM debate framework in which two language-model roles repeatedly discuss a contested topic (climate-change attribution): one is given an assigned stance and, in some conditions, an explicit instruction to persuade, while the other receives no assigned position. Across four ordered model combinations involving GPT-6 Luna and Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite, we track both each role's explicitly reported position and a separate measure of its turn-by-turn behavior inside the conversation. Opinion dynamics differ substantially across model combinations: same-model interactions narrow the opinion gap on average, clearly for only one of the two models, while cross-model interactions widen it. Explicit reports and in-dialogue behavior capture distinct aspects of opinion dynamics, and a blanket instruction to persuade does not reliably increase influence. These findings suggest that conversational influence depends not only on assigned roles and initial positions but also on the participating models, with implications for how opinion change is measured in extended LLM interactions.
authors: Mohammad Siahkamari, Phuoc Dat Nguyen, Stephen MacNeil
bullets: Examines repeated debates about climate-change attribution between assigned-stance and unassigned LLM roles.
Tracks both explicitly reported opinions and turn-by-turn conversational behavior.
Same-model interactions generally narrow opinion gaps, while cross-model interactions widen them.
Reported opinions and in-dialogue behavior reflect distinct aspects of opinion dynamics.
Results indicate that assigned roles, initial positions, and model identity jointly shape conversational influence.
papers.selection_reason: Studies opinion dynamics and persuasion in LLM-LLM interactions, fitting the Large Language Models subtopic.
papers.title: To Manipulate or Not: Opinion Dynamics in LLM Interactions
papers.tldr: A controlled LLM–LLM debate study finds that opinion change depends on the model pairing and measurement approach, while explicitly instructing a model to persuade does not reliably increase influence.

papers.abstract: Looped transformers reuse one block of layers many times and are often trained by backpropagating through only the last k loops. We measure how much of the weight gradient this throws away, exactly and for every k from one backward pass, on nine looped language models, and report three findings. First, on a trained model this lost gradient is set near the output: once the loop count is well above k, it barely changes with the loop count (within about 0.03 from 32 to 64 loops on the three models we tested, as a pre-registered test predicted for Parcae). Where the backward signal shrinks, $\rho^k$, with $\rho$ the signal's fitted shrink per loop, approximates it at moderate loop counts but overstates it at long ones, because the fitted $\rho$ drifts up as the fit takes in more loops. On Ouro the signal grows, and keeping two of four loops still loses 81% of the final output's gradient. Second, the lost gradient falls during fine-tuning, by 0.07-0.22 within 300 steps on three of four models, on held-out problems too. The fall is not just the read-out's share of the gradient; training only the layers outside the loop reproduced up to half of it, and it also falls under truncated training. So a trained model's value overstates what truncation removes later. Third, we could not show that it predicts the training cost of truncation better than rules that need no measurement: on two new models it tied Parcae's cost at the same k, in a test too small to separate them.
bullets: The study exactly measures gradients omitted when backpropagating through only the last k loops in nine looped language models.

In trained models, the omitted-gradient fraction often stabilizes once total loops greatly exceed k, though behavior varies: on Ouro, retaining two of four loops loses 81% of the final output gradient.
The omitted-gradient fraction decreases by 0.07–0.22 within 300 fine-tuning steps on three of four models, including on held-out problems.
This decrease is not explained solely by the readout layer and also occurs under truncated training.
Gradient-loss measurements did not outperform simple measurement-free rules for predicting truncation cost in a small test on two new models.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes gradient behavior in looped language model architectures; relevant to architectural advances and training of foundation language models.
papers.title: How Much Gradient Does Truncated Backprop Lose in Looped Transformers?
papers.tldr: Truncated backpropagation can discard a large, loop-count-dependent portion of gradients, but the loss often shrinks during fine-tuning and does not yet reliably predict truncation’s training cost.

papers.abstract: Agentic harness evolution optimizes an agent's instructions, tools, and control flow by using its task execution experiences as evolving evidence. While more evolution tasks should intuitively improve performance, our preliminary study reveals a paradoxical failure mode: the performance of existing methods degrades as the task pool expands. Our further analysis demonstrates that this degradation stems from suboptimal evidence selection during optimization, as different evidence combinations lead to substantially different evolution outcomes. To address this issue, we propose Successive Scale Racing (SSR), a framework that adaptively searches for optimal evidence combinations in each evolution round. SSR constructs diverse evidence combinations based on the corresponding task quality and coverage, and efficiently races the resulting candidate harnesses under a small compute budget. Empirically, across three distinct benchmarks, SSR achieves state-of-the-art results in all six configurations. Notably, as the task pool grows from 40 to 200, SSR steadily improves the pass rate from 64.3% to 68.3%, while the baselines' performances all drop. Furthermore, its racing mechanism identifies near-optimal candidates while reducing validation executions by 60%.
authors: Jingzhe Liu, Jiliang Tang, Tong Zhao, Neil Shah, Clark Mingxuan Ju
bullets: Existing harness-evolution methods can degrade when more optimization tasks are added, due to poor evidence selection.
SSR builds diverse evidence combinations using task quality and coverage, then races candidate harnesses under limited compute.
Across three benchmarks and six configurations, SSR achieves state-of-the-art results.
As the task pool grows from 40 to 200, SSR’s pass rate rises from 64.3% to 68.3%, while baselines decline.
Its racing mechanism reduces validation executions by 60% while identifying near-optimal candidates.
papers.selection_reason: Optimizes agent harnesses (instructions, tools) through agentic harness evolution, fitting the Large Language Models subtopic.
papers.title: Forging More Tasks into Better Harnesses: Agentic Harness Evolution via Successive Scale Racing
papers.tldr: Successive Scale Racing improves agentic harness evolution by adaptively selecting and efficiently testing evidence combinations as task pools grow.

papers.abstract: Frontier coding agents are increasingly framed as end-to-end automated researchers, and ML for science offers a demanding test of that promise: improving a scientific model often requires domain insight beyond routine ML engineering. We introduce Agent4Sci, a long-horizon testbed for measuring how far today's agents can improve the published best models on scientific ML benchmarks, spanning 20 benchmarks across 11 domains. Rather than ranking agents on a leaderboard, Agent4Sci asks what kinds of progress agents can make on these tasks under in-the-wild conditions, and where they fall short. Empirically, today's frontier agents advance the published best on every benchmark, with Claude Opus reaching 10.4% mean relative improvement and no run flagged for academic misconduct. These gains, however, come almost entirely from a bag of ML-engineering tricks rather than research-level insight. Trajectory analysis surfaces three recurring limitations in this setting: novelty miscalibration, resource under-utilization, and rapid collapse into local engineering sweeps. Lightweight plug-in skills for research ideation, experiment management, and scheduled checklists raise Claude Opus from 10.4% to 20.1% and Codex from 4.4% to 8.1%, while yielding more diverse, domain-relevant interventions. Agent4Sci gives the community a way to track and push frontier agents from ML engineering toward domain insight on real-world ML-for-science problems. Code and data are available on GitHub (https://github.com/maszhongming/agent4sci) and Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/datasets/MingZhong/agent4sci).
authors: Ming Zhong, Stacy Li, Nicholas Carlini, Matthew Jagielski
bullets: Evaluates agents on 20 ML-for-science benchmarks spanning 11 domains under in-the-wild, long-horizon conditions.
Frontier agents improved the published best model on every benchmark; Claude Opus achieved a 10.4% mean relative improvement without flagged academic misconduct.
Agents commonly miscalibrate novelty, underuse resources, and quickly narrow into local engineering sweeps.
Lightweight skills for ideation, experiment management, and checklists increased improvements to 20.1% for Claude Opus and 8.1% for Codex.
The testbed tracks progress toward agents capable of domain-level scientific reasoning, beyond routine ML engineering.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces Agent4Sci, a testbed for evaluating frontier coding agents on scientific ML tasks, fitting the Large Language Models subtopic.
papers.title: Automating ML for Science: Can Frontier Agents Climb Scientific Hills in the Wild?
papers.tldr: Agent4Sci shows that frontier coding agents can improve scientific ML benchmarks substantially, but mostly through engineering tweaks rather than genuine scientific insight.

papers.abstract: Query clarification is essential for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems that face ambiguous user queries. We consider multi-turn grounded conversational scenarios where a user query is either ill-formed or ambiguous in the context of the prior dialog or, more interestingly, it may be well-formed but when posed against retrieved documents there are multiple relevant interpretations. The task is to recognize both such cases and then generate an appropriate clarification request to the user. We present ClariEdge, a new dataset of approximately 3,900 examples that include such ambiguous queries along with negative examples that do not require clarification. We also show that a lightweight fine-tuned LoRA achieves 96.6% classification accuracy and outperforms prompted baselines of many larger models on both classification and quality of clarification generation. Our study shows that hard negatives are an essential ingredient to separate out queries that are truly ambiguous from queries that may look ambiguous but are not (i.e., can be resolved from the context). The same LoRA achieves high performance in both pre-retrieval and post-retrieval scenarios; thus, it can be used in two places in a RAG pipeline as a check before answer generation. The ClariEdge dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/ibm-research/ClariEdge.
authors: Lihong He, Lucian Popa, Marina Danilevsky
bullets: Targets ambiguity arising from dialog context or multiple interpretations in retrieved documents.
Introduces ClariEdge, a dataset of approximately 3,900 positive and hard-negative examples.
A fine-tuned LoRA reaches 96.6% classification accuracy and outperforms prompted larger-model baselines on classification and clarification quality.
Works in both pre-retrieval and post-retrieval stages of a RAG pipeline.
The study emphasizes hard negatives for distinguishing true ambiguity from queries resolvable using context.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses query clarification for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems using LLMs, fitting the Large Language Models subtopic.
papers.title: A Small Model Asks Better: Fine-Tuning Query Clarification for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.tldr: ClariEdge fine-tunes a lightweight LoRA model to detect genuinely ambiguous RAG queries and generate useful clarification questions before answer generation.

papers.abstract: An agentic system issues several structurally different kinds of LLM calls. It routes intent, classifies actions, grounds language in a device registry, plans multi-agent pipelines and writes the Python code those pipelines run. The difficulty of these call sites varies by an order of magnitude, yet in practice a single model, chosen for the hardest site, serves all of them. In this work, we evaluate 9 models from 0.8B to a frontier hosted model across the five call sites of a deployed open-source home-automation framework (Wactorz), using its unmodified production prompts and two real Home Assistant installations (280 cases, 2520 scored calls). We find that capability is not ordered the same way at every site, and that larger models are not uniformly better: one 4B model is worse than its 2B sibling at grounded actuation. Paired testing shows the best local model to be statistically indistinguishable from both hosted models at four of five sites. Only code generation separates them, against a small hosted model (p = 0.039) as well as a frontier one (p = 0.002). Aggregate accuracy also hides a safety failure specific to actuation, where small models resolve the accuracy/refusal trade-off in degenerate ways: one model (Gemma4 E2B) actuates on 87.2% of requests for devices the site does not own, while another refuses every request it receives. Routing each site to its best local model reaches 91.8% against 95.4% at no per-call cost. In a live deployment judged by a user, hosting only the two generative sites matches hosting everything (39/43 against 39/43) for 28% of the spend, and the actuation gap the benchmark predicted appears as exactly one case in twenty-six. Benchmark, harness and all records are released at https://github.com/waldiez/slm-callsite-eval.
bullets: Nine models (0.8B–frontier) were tested on 2,520 calls from two real Home Assistant installations using production prompts.
Model capability varies by call site; larger models are not consistently better, including a 4B model underperforming its 2B sibling on grounded actuation.
The best local model matched hosted models at four of five sites; only code generation significantly favored hosted models.
Per-call-site routing achieved 91.8% accuracy versus 95.4% without additional per-call costs.
Hosting only the two generative sites matched the full-hosting live-deployment score while using 28% of the spend; actuation safety remains a key limitation.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates the efficiency of small language models in a deployed agentic home-automation system, finding that per-call-site optimization is beneficial.
papers.title: Not Every Call Needs a Frontier Model: Per-Call-Site Evaluation of Small Language Models in a Deployed Agentic Home-Automation System
papers.tldr: Evaluating five LLM call sites in a deployed home-automation agent shows that small models can handle most tasks, while code generation is the main site requiring stronger models.

papers.abstract: Enterprise systems increasingly rely on automated workflows, yet many AI-driven solutions remain brittle under non-stationary conditions, evolving policies, and delayed operational feedback. While reinforcement learning and large language model (LLM) agents offer partial adaptability, they do not by themselves provide persistent reflection mechanisms or straightforward integration with policy-constrained enterprise operations. This paper introduces Adaptive Workflow Intelligence (AWI), a cognitive architecture for context-driven enterprise agents organized around a four-layer Perception-Cognition-Action-Reflection (PCAR) loop. AWI treats reflection as a mechanism for continuous policy refinement and combines hybrid reasoning with reflective memory and feedback-driven adaptation to support decision making under environmental drift and operational constraints. We evaluate AWI in a simulated enterprise decision workflow characterized by delayed outcomes and a controlled regime shift. In a drift-and-delay stress test, guardrail-constrained adaptive approaches recover more rapidly than static automation while maintaining policy compliance. Within this setting, AWI's reflective components modestly reduce behavioral oscillation and feedback variance, illustrating the stability-agility trade-off introduced by reflective policy adaptation.
bullets: Targets brittleness in automated workflows under changing conditions, evolving policies, and delayed feedback.
Organizes agents in a four-layer Perception-Cognition-Action-Reflection loop.
Combines hybrid reasoning, reflective memory, and feedback-driven policy adaptation.
In a simulated drift-and-delay workflow, adaptive guardrail-constrained approaches recovered faster than static automation while remaining compliant.
Reflective components modestly reduced behavioral oscillation and feedback variance, highlighting a stability–agility trade-off.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes Adaptive Workflow Intelligence (AWI), a cognitive architecture for enterprise agents using a PCAR loop to handle non-stationary conditions.
papers.title: Adaptive Workflow Intelligence: A Cognitive Architecture for Context-Driven Enterprise Automation
papers.tldr: AWI is a reflection-enabled cognitive architecture for enterprise agents that adapts workflows to environmental drift while preserving policy compliance.

papers.abstract: During post-training of large language models (LLMs) with Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), GRPO-style algorithms can exhibit severe late-stage collapse. Prompt-based probing reveals that this is not benign strategic pruning, but a harmful contraction of effective strategy capacity that makes distinct reasoning strategies increasingly inaccessible. To characterize this phenomenon, we define strategies through trajectory-level policy-update interactions and develop a unified theoretical framework combining optimization dynamics and information theory. We prove that major RLVR objectives progressively concentrate probability mass onto a single strategy, while sustaining nontrivial task accuracy requires a minimum strategy capacity. The conflict between these two results provides a mechanistic explanation for catastrophic collapse. We further derive the {Mirrored Entanglement Index (MEI)} as a lightweight online warning signal. To prevent collapse, we propose \textbf{Mesh Learning}, which exposes multiple reasoning strategies and prevents any single strategy from dominating optimization. Across AIME26, AIME25, MATH-500, GPQA, and LiveCodeBench, Mesh Learning consistently outperforms strong baselines across Qwen and Phi model families, with gains of up to 13.4 pp and 11.5 pp, respectively. These results establish strategy preservation as a key principle for stable RLVR. Code is available at https://github.com/Ayanami-0123/Open-Mesh-Learning.
bullets: GRPO-style RLVR can progressively eliminate distinct reasoning strategies, reducing effective strategy capacity rather than merely pruning redundant behavior.
A unified optimization-and-information-theoretic framework shows that RLVR objectives concentrate probability on one strategy, while sustained accuracy requires multiple strategies.
The Mirrored Entanglement Index (MEI) provides a lightweight online warning signal for impending collapse.
Mesh Learning preserves diverse reasoning strategies by preventing any single strategy from dominating optimization.
Across several math, science, and coding benchmarks and Qwen/Phi models, Mesh Learning improves performance by up to 13.4 and 11.5 percentage points, respectively.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates catastrophic strategy collapse in RLVR post-training and proposes Mesh Learning to preserve diverse reasoning strategies.
papers.title: All Work And No Play Makes Jack a Dull Boy: Understanding and Preventing Catastrophic Strategy Collapse in RLVR
papers.tldr: The paper explains catastrophic strategy collapse in RLVR and introduces MEI and Mesh Learning to detect and prevent it.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon agents are now playing an increasingly significant role in assisting humans with complex problem-solving. However, it is exactly their extended interaction history that introduces an underexplored execution-safety concern. Under benign interaction conditions, an agent may execute an action that violates a safety constraint specified many turns earlier. We term this failure mode Governance Hazard from Overlooked Safety Constraints across Turns (GHOST), which may cause irreversible damage. Our experiments reveal that GHOST events are not isolated cases: this failure mode, occurring precisely under benign interaction conditions, yields an occurrence rate of 11.5% on GPT-5.5. Furthermore, we theoretically show that if the residual conditional violation hazard along each safe prefix is bounded below by a non-summable sequence, the execution enters the hazard region almost surely. Leveraging this theoretical insight, we further propose STAR-Guard, a two-layer defense coupling historical semantic safety constraint restoration with pre-execution audit. STAR-Guard restores applicable safety constraints to reduce unsafe proposals, while its deterministic audit layer prevents residual violations from reaching the environment. Consistent with this two-layer design, we observe no GHOST events in our experiments under the GPT-5.5 setup.
bullets: Identifies GHOST: violating a safety constraint specified many turns earlier during otherwise benign interactions.
Reports an 11.5% GHOST occurrence rate on GPT-5.5.
Shows theoretically that a non-summable lower bound on residual violation hazard leads to hazard almost surely.
Introduces STAR-Guard, combining historical constraint restoration with deterministic pre-execution auditing.
Observed no GHOST events with STAR-Guard in the GPT-5.5 experiments.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses safety hazards in long-horizon LLM agents, proposing a defense mechanism (STAR-Guard) for overlooked constraints.
papers.title: A GHOST in Long-Horizon Agents: Governance Hazard from Overlooked Safety Constraints across Turns
papers.tldr: Long-horizon agents can forget earlier safety constraints across benign interactions, but STAR-Guard eliminates the observed failures through constraint restoration and pre-execution auditing.

papers.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems hold immense potential for automating complex workflows in materials discovery and design, but extending them to domain-intensive mechanistic investigations remains challenging. Here, we present GBClaw, an agentic AI framework for investigating the structure and deformation of general grain boundaries (GBs). Although general GBs constitute the vast majority of real-world interfaces in polycrystalline materials, they remain understudied because their structural complexity and interfacial mismatch complicate experimental and modeling research. GBClaw integrates large language models (LLMs) into a modular architecture comprising an orchestrator, specialized agents, domain-specific tools, simulation interfaces, and hierarchical memory. Through dynamic replanning and iterative workflow refinement, the framework effectively connects systematic simulations with targeted mechanistic analysis. Applied to 14 general asymmetric tilt GBs in nickel, GBClaw characterized interfacial defect structures and identified diverse deformation modes across these incommensurate boundaries. Comparing boundary sliding with and without secondary GB misfit dislocations revealed substantial differences in shear strength, underscoring the critical role of defect hierarchies in sliding resistance. Furthermore, researcher-guided follow-up calculations traced an anomalously high shear resistance to metastable boundary structures. This work demonstrates that combining agentic AI with domain expertise bridges high-throughput computational screening with deep physical understanding of complex material interfaces.
authors: Yazhuo Liu, Kunqing Ding, Xiaoguo Gong, Zifeng Wang, Yichen Yang, Yifeng Che, Wen Chen, Josh Kacher, Olivier Pierron, Shigenobu Ogata, Ting Zhu
bullets: Targets general asymmetric grain boundaries, which are common in polycrystalline materials but difficult to study because of structural complexity and interfacial mismatch.
Uses an LLM-based modular framework with an orchestrator, specialized agents, domain tools, simulation interfaces, hierarchical memory, and dynamic replanning.
Applied to 14 general asymmetric tilt grain boundaries in nickel to characterize interfacial defects and diverse deformation modes.
Shows that secondary grain-boundary misfit dislocations substantially affect sliding resistance, while metastable structures can cause anomalously high shear resistance.
Demonstrates a workflow connecting systematic computational screening with targeted, mechanistic materials analysis.
papers.selection_reason: Agentic framework using LLMs for materials science, relevant to LLM agents and tool use.
papers.title: GBClaw: An agentic AI framework for atomistic grain boundary research and mechanistic discovery
papers.tldr: GBClaw combines agentic AI, simulations, and expert-guided analysis to uncover how complex nickel grain-boundary structures control deformation and shear resistance.

papers.abstract: Mathematical reasoning remains underexplored for low-resource languages, including Dialectal Arabic.
