To bridge this gap, we introduce the DAR-MGSM (Dialectal Arabic Multilingual Grade School Math) Benchmark, the first manually curated benchmark for evaluating mathematical reasoning in Dialectal Arabic. DAR-MGSM consists of math word problems (MWPs) requiring multi-step reasoning and covers five major Arabic dialects alongside Modern Standard Arabic (MSA). The benchmark comprises two parallel versions: translated-only and translated & culturally localized. The latter version adapts entities and references to regional varieties. We evaluate eleven Arabic-centric and multilingual large language models on DAR-MGSM. The results show that the performance generally declines on the localized version, highlighting the challenges introduced by culturally grounded adaptations. However, the magnitude of this effect varies across models, with Arabic-centric models exhibiting different levels of sensitivity to localization. A mechanistic interpretability analysis shows that translated and localized variants of the same MWPs often induce distinct internal reasoning trajectories, even when aggregate accuracy remains similar. Overall, our results show that mathematical reasoning performance depends on both linguistic variety and cultural context.
authors: Noor Abo Mokh, Teresa Lynn, Nizar Habash, Ahmed Elshabrawy, Sara Alhajeri, Alaa Elsetohy, Preslav Nakov, Alham Fikri Aji
bullets: Introduces the first manually curated Dialectal Arabic benchmark for mathematical reasoning.
Covers multi-step math word problems in translated-only and translated-and-culturally-localized versions.
Evaluates 11 Arabic-centric and multilingual large language models.
Performance generally declines on localized problems, with sensitivity varying across models.
Interpretability analysis finds distinct internal reasoning trajectories even when accuracy is similar.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a benchmark for LLMs in a low-resource language, relevant to LLM evaluation and robustness.
papers.title: Benchmarking Arabic Dialects for Math Problems
papers.tldr: DAR-MGSM benchmarks multi-step math reasoning across five Arabic dialects and MSA, showing that cultural localization can reduce and alter model performance.

papers.abstract: Continuous flow language models offer a path to parallel generation with tools for control and acceleration unavailable to discrete diffusion, yet effective techniques for building them at the billion-parameter scale remain less established. We present Lafa (Large flow language model), a fast, high-performing flow language model scaled to 8B parameters in a data-efficient manner. Lafa is a blockwise flow model with causal attention on the prefix and bidirectional, asynchronous flow within each block. This design enables efficient training by adapting pretrained autoregressive (AR) models and fast inference via prefix caching and blockwise parallel decoding. We train Lafa at 0.5B, 7B, and 8B scales with fewer than 30B tokens, more efficient than previous diffusion models, and evaluate it on instruction following, reasoning, and coding, where the learned flow matches or surpasses the quality of AR and can be distilled into flow maps for one- and few-step generation. Notably, flow training preserves or even improves pretrained AR capabilities via a multi-token prediction effect, which we leverage in a self-speculative decoding scheme that verifies flow-based drafts autoregressively within a single model. This yields 2.54x the throughput of an AR model at comparable quality, outperforming multi-token prediction and discrete diffusion methods. Our findings show that continuous flows can serve as a scalable foundation for language modeling.
authors: Arnav Chavan, Chanhyuk Lee, Udbhav Bamba, Jaehoon Yoo, Seunghoon Hong, Aditi Raghunathan, Jinwoo Kim
bullets: Addresses the limited scalability of continuous flow language models compared with established autoregressive approaches.
Uses causal attention over prefixes and bidirectional asynchronous flow within blocks, supporting prefix caching and blockwise parallel decoding.
Adapts pretrained autoregressive models and trains models up to 8B parameters using fewer than 30B tokens.
Matches or surpasses autoregressive quality on instruction following, reasoning, and coding, while supporting one- and few-step distilled generation.
A self-speculative decoding scheme verifies flow-based drafts autoregressively within the same model, achieving 2.54× AR throughput at comparable quality.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a novel continuous flow architecture (Lafa) for LLMs, improving parallel generation and throughput via self-speculative decoding.
papers.title: Large Flow Language Models
papers.tldr: Lafa is an 8B-parameter continuous flow language model that enables parallel generation and achieves comparable quality to autoregressive models with up to 2.54× higher throughput.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive language models are trained by next-token cross-entropy, yet several recent systems also iterate a hidden state without emitting a token: continuous thoughts, pause steps, and recurrent depth. This note separates three risks on one latent process. The token risk $R_{\mathrm{tok}}$ scores a readout. The teacher-forced latent risk $R_1$ scores a one-step map that sees the true hidden state. The open-loop risk $R_H$ scores the same map after it has been iterated on its own outputs. If the Bayes next-token posterior is a function of a $k$-dimensional statistic with full-rank covariance, a width-$k$ latent, a linear least-squares transition, and a refit unembedding match the Bayes token predictor. The statistic is identified only up to an invertible gauge: whitening the residual stream does not change the token law once the unembedding is refit. The matching obstructions are sharp. A constant latent drives $R_1$ to zero while token cross-entropy falls back to the marginal entropy. A perfect token predictor can still hide a null-space walk whose open-loop error grows linearly in the horizon. A small next-latent loss does not certificate next-token prediction, and a small next-token loss does not certificate free latent rollout, unless a rank or injectivity condition is stated with the number.
bullets: Separates token risk, teacher-forced one-step latent risk, and open-loop rollout risk.
Shows that a full-rank k-dimensional sufficient statistic can support Bayes-optimal token prediction with a width-k latent, linear transition, and refit unembedding.
Establishes gauge freedom: invertible latent transformations, including whitening, preserve token predictions when the unembedding is refit.
Provides obstructions: constant latents can minimize one-step latent risk without predicting tokens, while perfect token prediction can conceal latent drift whose open-loop error grows with horizon.
Concludes that small latent-transition loss or token loss alone does not certify the other objective without stated rank or injectivity conditions.
papers.selection_reason: Theoretical analysis of predictive latents in autoregressive language models; relevant to LLM latent and continuous-thought mechanisms.
papers.title: Predictive Latents for Autoregressive Language Models: Possibility, Gauge, and Obstruction
papers.tldr: The note shows that accurate next-token prediction and stable autoregressive latent rollouts are distinct goals, linked only under explicit rank or injectivity conditions.

papers.abstract: For efficient deployment of large language models (LLMs), methods of ultra-low-bit backbones reduce weight storage, memory traffic, and linear-layer execution cost, while multi-token prediction (MTP) methods reduce sequential decoding steps by predicting multiple future tokens in parallel. Although complementary, the direct combination of these methods cannot accelerate decoding at comparable quality: masked drafting lacks intermediate token input supplied in next-token training, while wider computation and causal key-value (KV) updates can offset the savings from fewer steps. To address these challenges, we propose BitMTP, an algorithm-system co-design framework for efficient MTP on ultra-low-bit LLM backbones. A joint next-token prediction and MTP objective equips a single model with both autoregressive (AR) generation and block-causal drafting. Confidence-only decoding, speculative-only decoding, and hybrid decoding provide different quality-throughput operating points without using separate draft and verifier models. Accepted-prefix alignment keeps the committed prefix, materialized causal KV boundary, and CUDA Graph replay state consistent for continued generation. BitMTP uses this contract to select width-specialized low-bit execution and reuse captured graphs over shared KV storage. On NVIDIA H20, BitMTP with hybrid decoding achieves five-task mean speedups of 2.2x on BitNet b1.58-2B and 2.1-2.4x on 1.7B-4B Bonsai models at comparable task quality. On RTX 3090 and Jetson Orin, it further achieves up to 2.0x in five-task mean throughput and 3.3x on MBPP+, respectively. These results demonstrate that BitMTP accelerates ultra-low-bit LLM generation across backbones, model sizes, and GPU types. The source code is released at https://github.com/PolyU-VCLab/BitMTP
authors: Ning Zhang, Shihao Wang, Jinrui Zhang, Chaodong Xiao, Lei Zhang
bullets: Combines joint autoregressive and block-causal training so one model supports both regular generation and multi-token drafting.
Offers confidence-only, speculative-only, and hybrid decoding without separate draft and verifier models.
Uses accepted-prefix alignment, shared KV storage, and width-specialized CUDA Graph execution to reduce decoding overhead.
Reports 2.1–2.4× speedups on selected Bonsai models and up to 3.3× throughput on Jetson Orin across evaluated tasks and hardware.
papers.selection_reason: Co-design for multi-token prediction on low-bit LLMs, reducing decoding steps and KV/memory overhead in LLM inference.
papers.title: BitMTP: When Multi-Token Prediction Meets Low-Bit Large Language Models
papers.tldr: BitMTP co-designs multi-token prediction with ultra-low-bit LLM execution to accelerate generation while maintaining comparable task quality.

papers.abstract: People adapt how they talk to the person in front of them. However, chat models tend to respond in Standard English regardless of the dialect used by the user. A uniform answer can hide whether training treats these users alike, and output audits cannot tell as well. We trace how each post-training stage, from supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to preference optimization (DPO) and reinforcement learning, changes a model's tendency to match the user, and read what each update prefers from two content-matched replies, one matching the user and one not. Across 10 open model lineages, post-training standardizes replies to every informal cue, yet after adjusting for how likely each reply already was, the DPO update still favours matching British and Australian spelling over AAE and Singlish on 10 lineages, and models still produce AAE features when asked. We then introduce calibrated accommodation pairs (CAP), preference data that reward matching users' dialect density while preserving Standard English for Standard-English users. On a fully open model, CAP raises convergence on features it was not trained on without a detectable increase in dialect for Standard-English users or a cost in instruction following. In contrast, one-sided pairs reach a similar gain only by overshooting the user and imposing dialect. Our findings show that uniform replies can hide selective updates and audits should read the update as well as the output. Code: https://github.com/kouzhizhuo/cap-accommodation.
authors: Zhizhuo Kou, Heming Li, Jian Yang, Junyu Luo, Jingshu Peng, Sirui Han, Yike Guo
bullets: Post-training stages from SFT through DPO and reinforcement learning tend to standardize responses to informal dialect cues.
Update-level analysis finds DPO favors matching British and Australian spelling more than AAE and Singlish across 10 open model lineages, despite models producing AAE features when prompted.
CAP uses preference pairs that reward dialect matching while preserving Standard English for Standard-English users.
On a fully open model, CAP improves accommodation to unseen dialect features without detectable increases for Standard-English users or reduced instruction following.
One-sided preference pairs achieve similar gains only by overshooting users and imposing dialect.
papers.selection_reason: Studies dialect accommodation across post-training stages and introduces calibrated preference data, directly relevant to LLM post-training behavior.
papers.title: Answering in the User's Variety: Calibrated Accommodation Pairs for Post-Training
papers.tldr: Calibrated Accommodation Pairs (CAP) helps chat models match users’ dialect density without imposing dialect on Standard-English users, while revealing selective preferences hidden by uniform outputs.

papers.abstract: We present our solution to the AKBC LM-KBC 2026 Shared Task, where we achieved a score of 0.6836 on the official leaderboard, more than double the baseline of 0.2964. This task requires generating all possible objects for subject-relation pairs using a language model with up to 32 billion parameters, with no retrieval or fine-tuning involved. We show that the prompting methodology is as important as the model architecture: while the instruction-tuned model version achieves 0.5681 with its chat interface, the base model achieves 0.6836 when prompted using text completion. Thus, instruction tuning decreases factual recall; we refer to this effect as the instruction tax, which is caused by the model's weights rather than the prompting method. Our final solution is fairly straightforward: we prompt the base model with some examples from the training data, generate 64--256 outputs, and retain only the repeated ones. Two specialized methods are then applied for each relation: one improves the recall of large answer sets, and the other verifies a person's vitality before predicting their place of death.
bullets: Achieved 0.6836 on the AKBC LM-KBC 2026 Shared Task, over twice the 0.2964 baseline.
The base model scored 0.6836 with text-completion prompting, versus 0.5681 for the instruction-tuned model using chat prompting.
The approach uses training examples in prompts, generates 64–256 candidates, and keeps repeated answers.
Relation-specific methods improve recall for large answer sets and verify a person’s vitality before predicting their place of death.
The findings suggest reduced factual recall is caused by instruction tuning in the model weights, not merely by prompting.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes instruction tuning versus base LLM factual recall; relevant to LLM behavior.
papers.title: The Instruction Tax on Factual Recall: Base Models Can Beat Their Instruction-Tuned Counterparts
papers.tldr: For factual knowledge-base completion, a base model prompted as a text completer outperformed its instruction-tuned counterpart, revealing an “instruction tax” on recall.

papers.abstract: A growing body of work proposes dynamic expert-skipping methods for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models that adjust the number of experts activated per token during inference, aiming to preserve model quality while further reducing the number of active parameters. These methods have added calibrated importance scores, inter-expert similarity metrics, or learned per-token allocators in order to identify experts to skip. However, different calibration regimes, different reductions in the effective number of experts, and evaluation suites make comparisons difficult. We classify four representative prior methods into a unified taxonomy and benchmark them against a natural, simple baseline: statically reducing the number of experts $k$ (i.e., same reduced $k$ across all layers and tokens). We provide a fair comparison of these methods at matched expert-compute budget, on two modern MoEs (Gemma4-26B-A4B and Qwen3-30B-A3B) in a text-only setting and a contemporary vision-language model (Qwen3-VL) in a multimodal setting. Surprisingly, we find that the simple baseline is hard to outperform consistently across models, modalities, benchmarks, and calibration settings. The methods we benchmark often underperform the baseline and achieved gains, when present, are minor. We further find that the effective $k$ achieved (or optimized for) in calibration can diverge from the effective $k$ in testing, resulting in over- or under-estimating the compute at inference time. Based on these findings, we recommend a calibration-free per-modality static $k$ reduction and validate this on a held-out model and modality. We further argue that a static control at matched measured compute is the baseline any dynamic skipping method must beat.
authors: Jakob Steimle, Thomas Elsken, Daniel Ehrhardt, Lukas Rinder, Daniel Cremers, Xi Wang
bullets: Unifies four dynamic expert-skipping methods and compares them with using the same reduced expert count across layers and tokens.
Evaluates methods at matched measured expert-compute budgets across two text MoEs and one vision-language model.
The static baseline is difficult to consistently outperform across models, modalities, benchmarks, and calibration settings; observed gains are usually minor.
Calibration can produce an effective expert count that differs from testing, causing inference compute to be over- or underestimated.
Recommends calibration-free, per-modality static expert reduction and validates it on a held-out model and modality.
papers.selection_reason: Controlled comparison of dynamic expert skipping in modern MoE LLMs; relevant to efficient inference and LLM architecture.
papers.title: Don't Skip the Baseline: A Controlled Comparison of Dynamic Expert Skipping in MoEs
papers.tldr: A controlled study finds that simple static expert reduction is often as effective as dynamic MoE expert-skipping methods and should be the baseline for fair comparisons.

papers.abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) minimizes empirical risk over observed preference comparisons, implicitly assuming that the training preference distribution matches the deployment preference distribution. In practice, this i.i.d. assumption often fails, as preference distribution shift exhibits a natural hierarchical structure across three levels: group-level shift, prompt-level shift, and preference-level shift. Such multi-level distributional mismatch poses a critical challenge for safe LLM deployment, yet existing robust DPO methods typically either model uncertainty over the joint preference distribution or focus on individual sources of shift, leaving the hierarchical structure of OOD preference shifts underexplored. We propose TPO, a tri-level distributionally robust framework for OOD preference alignment, which jointly models all three levels of distributional uncertainty through a hierarchically structured rectangular ambiguity set. By instantiating it with Wasserstein distance, we derive a tractable and interpretable objective that combines a closed-form preference-level margin penalty, prompt-level adversarial embedding perturbation, and worst-case group reweighting, each governed by an independent radius. We establish finite-sample convergence guarantees and empirically validate the effectiveness of TPO over existing robust DPO methods.
bullets: Addresses DPO’s vulnerability to deployment preference shifts beyond the i.i.d. assumption.
Uses a hierarchically structured rectangular ambiguity set to jointly represent three shift levels.
Combines a closed-form preference-margin penalty, adversarial prompt-embedding perturbation, and worst-case group reweighting.
Provides finite-sample convergence guarantees.
Experiments report improved effectiveness over existing robust DPO methods, without details on datasets or numerical gains.
papers.selection_reason: Tri-level distributionally robust DPO framework for OOD preference alignment of LLMs.
papers.title: TPO: Tri-level Distributionally Robust Learning for OOD Direct Preference Optimization
papers.tldr: TPO improves OOD preference alignment by robustly modeling distribution shifts at the group, prompt, and preference levels.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) supervises student-generated responses using sampled-token student-teacher log-ratios. A positive log-ratio penalizes a token that the student assigns higher probability to than the teacher, but its current value does not distinguish sustained high penalties from abrupt increases along a response. We examine these local changes by comparing consecutive blocks of tokens within the same response. Our diagnostic identifies penalty jumps, abrupt increases in average penalty that persist on held-out tokens. Across these jumps, penalties rise while teacher confidence decreases. We call this pattern penalty-confidence tension. Boundaries into high-penalty blocks do not exhibit comparable confidence changes, showing that local changes provide information beyond the current penalty value. Motivated by this observation, we propose Adaptive Pullback OPD (AP-OPD). At each detected jump, AP-OPD uses the preceding block as a local reference and uniformly scales all supervision coefficients in the following block so that its weighted average penalty matches the preceding block's original mean. This reference determines the scaling factor without an additional strength constant. AP-OPD improves performance on both mathematical reasoning and code generation.
authors: Guangyu Liu, Siyuan Gan, Shilong Zhou, Linjian Meng, Boyan Wang, Jing Huo
bullets: OPD’s current penalty value does not capture abrupt local increases within a response.
Penalty jumps coincide with rising penalties and decreasing teacher confidence, a pattern termed penalty-confidence tension.
AP-OPD uses the preceding token block as a local reference at each detected jump.
It uniformly rescales supervision coefficients in the following block to match the reference block’s original mean penalty.
The method improves performance on mathematical reasoning and code generation.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive supervision reweighting for on-policy distillation of LLMs on reasoning and code generation.
papers.title: Adaptive Pullback: Reweighting Supervision at Penalty Jumps in On-Policy Distillation
papers.tldr: AP-OPD detects abrupt, persistent increases in token penalties and rescales subsequent supervision to match the preceding block’s average penalty, improving reasoning and code-generation performance.

papers.abstract: Multilingual evaluations often score a model's opening yes or no, a token that also carries model and language answering conventions. We ask when different ways of eliciting and reading an answer recover the same judgment, and when they measure an answer habit. We collect 1.1 million replies from eight models in six languages on up to 105 moral vignettes, varying the question's form, the answer constraint, and the reading of the reply, token or sentence, in both wordings (the FAR-6 battery). Story-level judgment profiles converge across the tested readouts and question forms, except for the yes/no token after a negative interrogative read under a preset mapping: on the same replies, token and sentence profiles agree at a median r = 0.67 across cells, while sentence profiles agree with free-sentence profiles at 0.94, a known linguistic variability. With each language's story consensus removed, a model's profile is nearest to its own in another language for 39 of 48 model-language cells under proposition labels and 15 under free sentences, against 5 expected by chance. Particle, position, and named-term preferences follow their own patterns. A model can keep its judgment and change its yes: scoring that token requires establishing which proposition it affirms.
authors: Haonan Huang, Yuwei Lu, Chengkun Cai
bullets: The study tests eight models in six languages across up to 105 moral vignettes, varying question form, answer constraints, and whether replies are read as tokens or sentences.
Story-level judgment profiles generally converge across readouts and question forms.

The main exception is a yes/no token following a negative interrogative under a preset label mapping; token and sentence profiles agree less strongly (median r = 0.67), while sentence and free-sentence profiles agree at 0.94.

After removing shared story consensus, models’ profiles are most similar to themselves across languages in 39 of 48 cells using proposition labels, versus 15 with free sentences; particle, position, and named-term preferences show distinct patterns.
Interpreting a yes/no answer requires identifying which proposition the model is affirming, rather than scoring the token alone.
papers.selection_reason: Multilingual LLM evaluation of judgment and answer conventions.
papers.title: Same Judgment, Different Yes: Measuring Multilingual Judgment Profiles in Language Models
papers.tldr: Language models largely preserve the same moral judgments across languages and elicitation formats, but a standalone yes/no token can reflect answering conventions rather than the affirmed proposition.

papers.abstract: The Reinforcement Learning (RL) paradigm has achieved remarkable success in enhancing the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, when applied to long-horizon tasks, it faces severe challenges: i) Due to the high task complexity, the model struggles to sample enough successful trajectories, resulting in slow convergence. ii) Relying solely on sparse final rewards causes all steps to be updated indiscriminately, encouraging redundant step generation. When both the quantity and quality of successful trajectories become difficult to guarantee, the performance is severely constrained. This dilemma stems from the limitations: existing RL paradigms rely entirely on the reasoning capability of base models, lacking the ability to actively optimize trajectories. To address the above issues, we propose a novel trajectory evolution paradigm with hindsight credit assignment, termed TrajEvolve. TrajEvolve not only relies on the trajectory inferred by the model but also generates ``evolutionary trajectories'' by refining low-quality steps in historical trajectories, thereby exposing the policy to high-quality compositions that lie within the base model's support but are rarely sampled within practical training budgets. Furthermore, TrajEvolve reformulates step-level continuous credit assignment as a binary classification task, whether each step is necessary for task completion. This simplification not only reduces the learning difficulty but also enables step labels to be obtained through counterfactual verification, achieving precise identification of redundant steps. Extensive experiments on two datasets demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method.
authors: Yi Wen, Hao Chen, Wanyu Wang, Maolin Wang, Pengyue Jia, Derong Xu, Huize Tan, Yingyi Zhang, Wenlin Zhang, Weihong Luo, Xiku Du, Xiangyu Zhao
bullets: Addresses sparse-success sampling and indiscriminate updates caused by final-only rewards.
Generates evolutionary trajectories by refining low-quality steps in historical trajectories.
Recasts continuous step-level credit assignment as binary necessity classification.
Uses counterfactual verification to label whether each step is required for task completion.
Experiments on two datasets report superior performance, without details in the abstract.
papers.selection_reason: Trajectory evolution with hindsight credit assignment for RL fine-tuning of LLM reasoning on long-horizon tasks.
papers.title: TrajEvolve: Trajectory Evolution for Reinforcement Learning with Hindsight Credit Assignment
papers.tldr: TrajEvolve improves long-horizon RL for LLMs by evolving low-quality trajectories and assigning hindsight credit to identify necessary reasoning steps.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) consolidates expert capabilities into a single student by matching teacher and student final-layer distributions on student-generated rollouts. We investigate whether depthwise prediction transitions, the changes in predictions between layers, can provide additional task-relevant supervision. Our diagnostic study finds that stronger teacher--student agreement in intermediate transitions is associated with higher answer correctness within questions, with correct responses exhibiting lower mean transition KL across all measured intermediate layer pairs. These observations motivate On-Policy Transition Distillation (OPTD), which augments final-layer distribution matching by aligning teacher and student layer-to-layer log-probability increments on student-generated rollouts. Evaluations across three backbones and eight benchmarks spanning mathematics, coding, and instruction following show that OPTD achieves the best or tied-best overall performance in both dual- and three-domain distillation. In the three-domain setting, OPTD recovers $\approx 90\%$ of the overall teacher--student capability gap, compared with $\approx 75\%$ for OPD.
authors: Runyang You, Yongqi Li, Tiezheng Yu, Wenjie Li
bullets: Intermediate teacher–student transition agreement correlates with answer correctness, with correct responses showing lower transition KL.
OPTD augments standard on-policy final-layer distribution matching with layer-to-layer log-probability increment alignment.
Evaluated across three backbones and eight mathematics, coding, and instruction-following benchmarks.
OPTD achieves the best or tied-best overall performance in both dual- and three-domain distillation.
In three-domain distillation, OPTD recovers approximately 90% of the teacher–student capability gap versus approximately 75% for OPD.
papers.selection_reason: LLM distillation method aligning layer-wise prediction transitions.
papers.title: On-Policy Transition Distillation
papers.tldr: On-Policy Transition Distillation improves expert-to-student knowledge transfer by matching how predictions change across layers, not just final outputs.

papers.abstract: Telecom language models must combine broad networking knowledge with specialist behavior across routing, broadband services, access technologies, and operational diagnostics while remaining practical to deploy as a single model. We present an end-to-end framework that builds source-grounded synthetic training data from structured networking taxonomies and expert graphs, materializes 212,559 routed training records across fourteen networking routes, trains six frozen specialist LoRA teachers over one shared continued-pretrained backbone, and consolidates their behavior into one deployable student adapter using Routed Specialist On-Policy Distillation (RSOD). In RSOD, the committed student generates each trajectory, the route-assigned specialist teacher-forces the exact native token sequence, compact teacher hidden states are reconstructed through the shared frozen output head, and only the student LoRA is updated. A controlled reconstruction validation shows mean absolute logit error of 7.26 x 10^-6 with 100% top-1 agreement between native and reconstructed teacher logits. On four RTX 6000 Ada GPUs, the completed 2,000-step run produced 16,000 trajectories with zero observed student-version or token- ID mismatches. Under the primary route-conditioned evaluation over 2,850 held-out questions, the raw Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct model scores 12.8661/25 micro (13.0172/25 macro), the combined routed six-teacher system scores 21.7641/25 micro, and the consolidated RSOD student, released as Llama-CalixCLM v1, reaches 21.7112/25 micro (21.8006/25 macro) on the same five dimension LLM-judge rubric. Under a separate neutral deployment-like prompt, the same student reaches 20.0028/25 micro (20.0778/25 macro). The consolidated student remains within 0.0529 micro-score points of the combined routed-teacher system while retaining a numerically validated and auditable train-serve execution path.
authors: Anil Srirangapatna Nagesh, Nitin Gupta, Anuj Taneja, Vivek Singh, Shane Eleniak, Theo Zhao, Moulidharan N, Shashank Keshetty
bullets: Addresses the challenge of combining broad networking knowledge with specialist behavior across routing, broadband, access technologies, and diagnostics in a single practical model.
Builds source-grounded synthetic data from networking taxonomies and expert graphs, yielding 212,559 routed records across 14 networking routes.
Uses Routed Specialist On-Policy Distillation: the student generates trajectories, route-specific teachers provide token-level supervision, and only the student LoRA is updated.
Teacher-logit reconstruction achieved 7.26 × 10^-6 mean absolute error and 100% top-1 agreement; the completed run reported zero student-version or token-ID mismatches.
On 2,850 held-out questions, Llama-CalixCLM v1 scored 21.7112/25 micro versus 21.7641/25 for the combined routed teachers and 12.8661/25 for the base model.
papers.selection_reason: End-to-end framework for domain-specialist post-training and distillation of deployable telecom LLMs.
papers.title: Building Telecom Language Models with RSOD: Domain Data, Specialist Post-Training, Memory-Conscious Distillation, and Networking Evaluation
papers.tldr: RSOD consolidates six telecom-specialist LoRA teachers into one deployable student while preserving nearly all of the routed system’s evaluated performance.

papers.abstract: Model compression makes large language models deployable, but today's evaluation tells an incomplete story. Standard practice measures retained task performance and stops there. This misses a critical fact: compression perturbs the distributed knowledge embedded across billions of weights, and task scores alone cannot reveal which underlying abilities survive and which quietly collapse. To solve this question, we introduce ACE-Compression, an ability-centric evaluation framework. Instead of asking only "does the compressed model still answer correctly?", we ask "which of its core abilities remain intact?" Our framework probes four deployment-facing dimensions: procedural reasoning and constraint execution, knowledge grounding and truthfulness, social cognition and affective understanding, and persona fidelity and stylistic consistency. Across more than 35 compressed checkpoints from six open-weight LLMs-covering quantization and pruning-we find that compression redistributes ability profiles. Coarse, local, and surface-level signals often persist, while fine-grained, long-tail, and context-dependent abilities become fragile. Quantization consistently outperforms pruning in retention, but the practical meaning of that gap depends entirely on which ability an application requires. Based on our findings, deployers can choose compression methods by the ability profile their application needs, not just by a leaderboard average. And algorithm designers gain diagnostic signals to build compression methods that preserve what matters. We believe that ACE-Compression turns compression from a black-box accuracy drop into an interpretable intervention-one we can measure, understand, and ultimately improve.
authors: Jiahui Ning, Liang Chen, Yuchen Liang, Yi Zhang, Fenglei Fan
bullets: Introduces an ability-centric framework covering procedural reasoning, knowledge grounding and truthfulness, social cognition, and persona/style consistency.
Evaluates over 35 compressed checkpoints from six open-weight LLMs using quantization and pruning.
Finds that compression redistributes ability profiles: coarse and surface-level abilities often persist, while long-tail and context-dependent abilities are more fragile.
Quantization generally retains abilities better than pruning, but the practical choice depends on an application’s required capabilities.
Supports capability-aware deployment decisions and provides diagnostics for designing more ability-preserving compression methods.
papers.selection_reason: Ability-centric evaluation of compressed LLMs, directly relevant to LLM efficiency and understanding how compression affects language model capabilities.
papers.title: ACE-Compression: An Ability-Centric Evaluation of Compressed Large Language Models
papers.tldr: ACE-Compression evaluates compressed LLMs by which underlying abilities they preserve—not just by aggregate task accuracy—revealing that compression selectively weakens fine-grained and context-dependent capabilities.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judgment assistants and as stand-in participants in psychology experiments, yet little is known about how much their probability estimates move in response to a single new piece of information. We pair premise-hypothesis items from $\delta$-SNLI with one strengthener and one weakener each, elicit the prior and the posteriors in separate calls, and measure the directional movement s: the mean posterior change signed by the annotated direction, so that the prior cancels out. We vary whether the update is stated ("Here is something else you learned") or reported ("Someone said that"), and whether the model gives one probability or five weighted estimates. We test seven configurations: two local models (Qwen3-8B, OLMo-2-7B; 240 pairs) and five configurations run through agent command-line harnesses (120 pairs), with hypotheses and analysis rules fixed before the formal runs (not publicly registered). Under stated, direct elicitation all seven move in the annotated direction (s = 18-28 percentage points). Reporting lowers s in all seven point estimates (significantly in six, by 2-5 points) and raises the share of reverse movements in all seven: the effect is consistent but small. Five weighted estimates lower the share of responses at $\leq$5% or $\geq$95% in all seven, but in the two local models they also reduce s by 43% and 68%, whereas in the harnessed configurations the point estimates of the change lie between -3.7 and +0.5 points. An elicitation format that reduces extreme values thus need not preserve sensitivity to evidence; the two should be tested separately. Because $\delta$-NLI annotates only direction, we make no claim about how large an update should be. Code, data and the frozen plan: https://github.com/asj252/llm-judgment-studies
bullets: Across seven model/configuration settings, directly stated information consistently shifted probabilities in the annotated direction.
Framing information as something someone said produced smaller updates and more reverse movements, though the effect was generally small.
Requesting five weighted estimates reduced near-certain responses across all settings.
This multi-estimate format sharply reduced update sensitivity in the two local models but had little effect in harnessed configurations.
The study measures only whether updates follow the annotated direction, not whether their magnitude is normatively correct.
papers.selection_reason: Studies how framing and elicitation affect LLM probability updates. This is a linguistic study, but the findings on probability updates are relevant to the reliability of LLMs used as judgment assistants in embodied systems.
papers.title: Hearsay or Fact? How Framing and Elicitation Shape LLM Probability Updates
papers.tldr: How an update is elicited substantially shapes LLM probability revisions: reported information weakens directional updating, while multiple estimates reduce extremes but may also reduce evidence sensitivity.

papers.abstract: Temperature scaling is typically applied as a post-hoc transformation of model probabilities. In posterior-induced flow language models, this creates two mismatches. First, posterior tempering implicitly changes both the endpoint distribution and the distribution of intermediate noisy states, while the denoiser remains trained on the original states. Second, the tempered posterior weights are combined with transport dynamics derived for the untempered flow. These mismatches are reflected empirically: lowering temperature improves GSM8K performance much less reliably in flow LMs than in discrete diffusion LMs. We introduce Bayes-Consistent Tempering (BCT), which makes temperature explicit in both the distributions and dynamics of the generative flow. Its learned realization trains the denoiser on tempered intermediate states and tempers the endpoint distribution using the corresponding tempered dynamics. We also derive training-free variants for conventionally trained checkpoints. Across hyperspherical flow LMs with two denoiser architectures and a von Mises--Fisher flow LM, BCT improves GSM8K generation across broad temperature ranges and achieves the strongest tempering performance. The gains also extend to Sudoku, demonstrating benefits on tightly constrained generation. At very low temperatures, the learned realization is also markedly more robust than the training-free variants, supporting temperature as a property of the generative flow across training and inference rather than a post-hoc probability adjustment. Code and model weights are available at https://daioba.github.io/bct .
authors: Daisuke Oba, Hiroki Furuta, Naoaki Okazaki
bullets: Post-hoc temperature scaling mismatches the intermediate noisy states and transport dynamics used by posterior-induced flow LMs.
BCT trains denoisers on tempered intermediate states and uses matching tempered endpoint distributions and dynamics.
Training-free BCT variants adapt conventionally trained checkpoints without retraining.
Across hyperspherical and von Mises–Fisher flow LMs, BCT improves GSM8K and Sudoku generation across broad temperature ranges.
The learned variant is notably more robust at very low temperatures, indicating temperature should be treated as part of the generative flow.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes Bayes-consistent tempering for flow language models, advancing training and controlled generation for language foundation models.
papers.title: BCT: Bayes-Consistent Tempering for Flow Language Models
papers.tldr: Bayes-Consistent Tempering (BCT) integrates temperature into both the distributions and dynamics of flow language models, improving low-temperature constrained generation over post-hoc tempering.

papers.abstract: As model parameters scale up, sparsely activated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) approaches have become essential for model scaling. However, mainstream models currently adopt hierarchical architectures, where experts in different layers, although topologically independent, exhibit substantial similarity and redundancy in their stored content. Compared to the hierarchically arranged \textbf{Local Expert} in existing mainstream models, we hypothesize that inter-layer shared \textbf{Meta Expert} hold greater potential. To this end, we conduct a multi-dimensional empirical comparison between Local and Meta Experts, and find that models incorporating Meta Experts exhibit lower parameter redundancy, together with lower cross-entropy loss and higher downstream task accuracy. With the activated quantity and the expert granularity held fixed, \textbf{our model matches the performance of Vanilla MoE using only 70--80\% of the experts}, substantially improving the model's scaling potential. Beyond removing inter-layer redundancy among experts and improving information storage efficiency, our theoretical analysis further shows that, compared with Local Experts, Meta Experts provide hidden states with more flexible residual pathways, thereby improving information retrieval efficiency.
authors: Ermo Hua, Xiangyu Hong, Baiting Wu, Che Jiang, Haozheng Hou, Yicheng Gu, Hanjing Wang, Qirui Zeng, Ming Zhang, Ning Ding, Qipeng Guo, Youbang Sun, Biqing Qi, Bowen Zhou
bullets: Problem: Hierarchically local experts across layers can store redundant information, limiting MoE scaling efficiency.
Method: Replace or augment layer-specific Local Experts with cross-layer shared Meta Experts and compare their properties empirically and theoretically.
Result: Meta Expert models show lower parameter redundancy, lower cross-entropy loss, and higher downstream task accuracy.
Efficiency: With fixed activation quantity and expert granularity, the approach matches Vanilla MoE performance using 70–80% of its experts.
Insight: Cross-layer Meta Experts provide more flexible residual pathways, improving hidden-state information retrieval.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes cross-layer expert sharing for MoE, reducing parameter redundancy and improving scaling; directly relevant to LLM architecture research.
papers.title: Meta Expert: Cross-Layer Expert Sharing for Storage- and Retrieval-Efficient MoE
papers.tldr: Meta Expert improves MoE storage and retrieval efficiency by sharing experts across layers, matching Vanilla MoE performance with only 70–80% as many experts.

papers.abstract: When unique pretraining data is scarce, models see the same tokens many times and are thought to memorize. Random-token replacement, an input-corruption augmentation, is one remedy reported to lower validation loss, but a lower loss alone does not reveal which source of error it reduces. On a controlled source whose entropy rate is known in closed form, we show that replacement shrinks predictions toward the corpus average. We also introduce a decomposition that separates validation loss into approximation, estimation, and memorization terms. This shrinkage view predicts that replacement's bias cost needs no memorization but its benefit does. Memorization raises validation loss after its minimum, so we report the effect at two points, the minimum validation loss and the end of a fixed budget. Where replacement helps, it reduces this rise by about 60%. At the end of the budget, it turns from harmful to helpful as the controlled source becomes less predictable; at the minimum, it helps at no predictability level under the fixed recipe. On Korean and Japanese web text, replacement removes about a third of the loss rise after the minimum by the end of the budget, but its effect at the minimum is much smaller. Across ten real corpora, replacement lowers the final loss on nine. It harms only the census corpus, program-generated JSON that is the most redundant of the ten and much more redundant than any of 64 further prose and code corpora we measure.
bullets: Repeated data causes memorization that raises validation loss after its minimum; random replacement counteracts part of this rise.
A known-entropy analysis decomposes loss into approximation, estimation, and memorization terms, showing replacement trades bias for reduced memorization.
At a fixed training-budget endpoint, replacement reduces the post-minimum loss rise by about 60% where it helps and becomes beneficial as the source becomes less predictable.
On Korean and Japanese web text, it removes about one-third of the post-minimum loss rise; across ten real corpora, it lowers final loss on nine.
The exception is highly redundant, program-generated JSON, indicating that extreme redundancy can make replacement harmful.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes random-token replacement augmentation under repeated pretraining data; relevant to LLM pretraining behavior and generalization.
papers.title: Benefit and Cost of Random-Token Replacement under Repeated Data: A Known-Entropy Decomposition and Evidence from Ten Real Corpora
papers.tldr: Random-token replacement can reduce memorization-driven loss growth on repeated data, but its benefit depends on predictability, training stage, and corpus redundancy.

papers.abstract: Factual recall is a lookup: some representation inside the network serves as the key, and what that key is made of decides which queries can retrieve the fact, what an edit must cover, and what a retriever can read. We call it the factual access state. In autoregressive (AR) models the subject position enriches attributes largely independently of the relation, and relation-specific selection happens later, at the readout position. In masked diffusion language models (DLMs) we find the state is assembled differently, and much earlier: in the first attention layer the wording of the relation is routed into the position of whichever entity is visible and the early feed-forward layers look the fact up on this fused representation. The state therefore varies with the relation's surface form and with the query direction, so the queries about one fact occupy a region of state space rather than a point, and an operation on the fact succeeds only for queries that enter it. We treat the state as an interface to a DLM's factual knowledge, and put it to two uses. Writing to the state gives a knowledge editor: from one declarative statement, Multi-View Edit fits one shared value per direction across that region and installs it in the early-MLP block, preserving source-prompt reliability while substantially improving paraphrase and reverse question answering, where AR editors gain near zero. Reading it suggests a complementary use: the state at each entity position can serve as a relation-specific retrieval vector with no training, returning both pieces of evidence for two-entity queries on which pooled, prompted and lexical retrievers almost never return both.
authors: Yuchen Guo, Zhuoyuan Mao, Yiwen Guo
bullets: In autoregressive models, relation-specific selection occurs late; in diffusion language models, relation wording is fused with entity representations in the first attention layer.
Because the access state varies across relation surface forms and query directions, one fact corresponds to a region of state space rather than a single point.
Multi-View Edit writes a shared value across this region in the early MLP block, improving paraphrase and reverse-question answering while preserving source-prompt reliability.
The same state can act as a relation-specific retrieval vector without training, retrieving both evidence pieces for two-entity queries where pooled, prompted, and lexical retrievers usually fail.
The findings are specific to masked diffusion language models and emphasize how their factual representation differs from autoregressive models.
papers.selection_reason: Mechanistic analysis of factual access states in diffusion language models enabling knowledge editing and retrieval; relevant to LLM foundations.
papers.title: Factual Access States in Diffusion Language Models: From Mechanism to Knowledge Editing and Retrieval
papers.tldr: The paper identifies a relation- and direction-dependent factual access state in diffusion language models and uses it for more robust knowledge editing and training-free retrieval.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used within everyday applications where their responses have significant downstream impacts. For responsible deployment of such systems, we desire insight into how much we can trust their individual outputs. A popular approach for estimating LLM confidence is to train probes on the hidden states of the LLM's tokens to predict the correctness of the model's output. These probes typically read hidden states from tokens that are already in the model's vocabulary. In this work, we introduce a new approach to confidence probes that learn a new readout token and utilize its hidden states to train the probe. We show that our learned readout approach ScratchProbe outperforms its existing-token counterpart on a variety of datasets and LLMs. We also extend our method to a multi-token approach which we show provides further performance improvements. Finally, since the learned readout changes only the position a probe reads from, any existing probe can adopt it. Applied to a state-of-the-art probe, it improves AUROC on every backbone, in domain and out of domain.
bullets: Addresses the need to assess whether individual LLM outputs can be trusted.
Introduces a learned readout token in place of hidden states from existing vocabulary tokens.
Extends the approach to multiple learned readout tokens for further improvements.
Outperforms existing-token probes across varied datasets and LLMs.
Improves AUROC for a state-of-the-art probe across every tested backbone, both in- and out-of-domain.
papers.selection_reason: Learned readout tokens improve LLM confidence probing; relevant to LLM reliability and interpretation.
papers.title: Learned Readout Tokens for Extracting Large Language Model Confidence
papers.tldr: ScratchProbe improves LLM confidence estimation by learning dedicated readout token(s) whose hidden states better predict output correctness.

papers.abstract: Safety pretraining has emerged as a promising paradigm for embedding safety deeply into a model during pretraining, yielding robustness to subsequent fine-tuning that conventional safety post-training often lacks. We refer to this safety acquired during model pretraining as native safety. Yet native safety is expensive to acquire, confined to the model in which it was pretrained, and often accompanied by lower general utility. In this work, we rethink the practical value of safety-pretrained models and introduce, for the first time, the native safety reuse problem: Can native safety be transferred from a specialized, potentially smaller, safety-pretrained "teacher" to standard-pretrained "students," enabling them to inherit its robustness while preserving their general utility? We show that native safety can "travel" through on-policy distillation. A standard-pretrained student generates responses to safety-pretraining prompts, while a small safety-pretrained teacher supervises the student's token-level predictions along its own generated trajectories; cross-tokenizer alignment further enables transfer across model families. The resulting students exhibit substantially greater safety robustness than their safety-post-trained counterparts while retaining higher general utility than the teacher: subsequent fine-tuning raises the average attack success rate (ASR) of the 1.7B student by only 5.00%, compared with 11.58% for safety post-training, and its average utility of 48.20% far exceeds the aligned teacher's 27.42%. Unlike conventional large-to-small knowledge distillation, our framework enables selective, small-to-large safety transfer: it reuses the robust safety expertise of a smaller pretrained teacher without inheriting its utility limitations. These findings establish native safety as a reusable model property rather than one permanently tied to the originally pretrained model.
authors: Bingqi Shang, Yang Zhang, Yiwei Chen, Changsheng Wang, Shiyu Chang, Bingquan Shen, Sijia Liu
bullets: Introduces the native safety reuse problem: transferring safety learned during pretraining across models.
Uses student-generated trajectories, teacher token-level supervision, and cross-tokenizer alignment for cross-family transfer.
Transferred students show greater safety robustness after fine-tuning than safety-post-trained counterparts.
The 1.7B student’s ASR increase after fine-tuning is 5.00%, versus 11.58% for safety post-training.
The student reaches 48.20% average utility, exceeding the aligned teacher’s 27.42%.
papers.selection_reason: Transfers safety pretraining across LLMs via on-policy distillation; directly relevant to LLM research.
papers.title: Can Native Safety Travel? Reusing Safety Pretraining Across Models via On-Policy Distillation
papers.tldr: On-policy distillation can transfer a small safety-pretrained model’s robustness to standard-pretrained students while preserving more general utility.

papers.abstract: Self-evolving agents aim to improve from their own experience rather than remain fixed after deployment, but naturally collected trajectories often lack ground-truth solutions or verifier-derived rewards. We introduce Retrospective Self-Distillation (RSD), a multi-round framework that turns such experience into dense supervision using privileged retrospective context. For each on-policy trajectory, the same underlying model acts as both student and teacher: the teacher re-scores the student's realized actions while conditioning on cross-task precedents and lessons, together with turn-level reflection and future hindsight from the completed trajectory. The resulting teacher distribution is distilled back into the policy through on-policy self-distillation. Across rounds, the experience bank grows and the retrospective context is refreshed, allowing the model, its data, and its supervision to co-evolve. We further introduce frontier-guided context-policy evolution, where a stronger frontier model proposes constrained edits to how privileged context is constructed. Across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and SearchQA with Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B, RSD improves performance by up to 59.7% relative to the base model, while frontier-guided context-policy evolution adds up to a further 44.7% relative improvement over a fixed context policy. These results show that naturally accumulated experience can be converted into persistent model capability without ground-truth trajectories or verifier-derived rewards for the core policy update.
authors: Yuhang Zhou, Yifan Wu, Bo Peng, Mingyi Wang, Jiayi Liu, Xiangjun Fan, Lizhu Zhang, Zhuokai Zhao
bullets: Addresses the lack of ground-truth solutions or verifier rewards in naturally collected trajectories.
Uses the same model as student and teacher: the teacher re-scores actions with precedents, lessons, reflections, and future hindsight.
Distills these teacher distributions into the policy across multiple rounds while the experience bank and supervision co-evolve.
Adds frontier-guided evolution to improve how privileged context is constructed.
Across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and SearchQA, RSD improves performance by up to 59.7% relative to the base model; context-policy evolution adds up to 44.7% further relative improvement.
papers.selection_reason: Self-evolving LLM agents that distill privileged retrospective context from their own trajectories into persistent policy improvements.
papers.title: Self-Evolving Agents through Privileged Retrospective Distillation
papers.tldr: Retrospective Self-Distillation enables agents to improve from their own unverified experience by using hindsight and privileged context to create training supervision.

papers.abstract: Mitigating catastrophic risks from large language models requires excising hazardous operational capabilities, such as cyberwarfare exploitation and pathogen enhancement, without degrading benign scientific utility. In these dual-use domains, legitimate defensive science and malicious attacks share vocabulary, syntax, and internal model representations, causing standard unlearning methods to induce severe collateral damage (concept bleeding). In this work, we present Orthogonal Boundary Unlearning (OBU), a mathematically grounded framework designed to eliminate collateral damage on benign dual-use capabilities. OBU extracts a domain-matched capability subspace from paired calibration queries via singular value decomposition on empirical activation covariances, and restricts parameter updates strictly to the orthogonal null space. This guarantees that benign representations experience zero parameter perturbation along the spanned calibration subspace. We present two complementary realizations of OBU: Projected LoRA, which applies the orthogonal constraint during iterative gradient-based fine-tuning, and Closed-Form Weight Surgery, which directly edits model weights in a single analytical step without training. Across four modern open-weight foundation models (Gemma-3-4B, Qwen3.5-4B, SmolLM3-3B, and Granite-4.2-3B), OBU achieves strong dual-use concept separation, substantially mitigates in-context priming attacks, and demonstrates durable resistance against adversarial relearning without degrading benign domain competence.
bullets: Targets concept bleeding, where malicious and defensive capabilities share language and internal representations.
Extracts a domain-matched capability subspace from paired calibration queries using SVD of activation covariances.
Restricts parameter updates to the orthogonal null space, providing zero perturbation along the spanned benign calibration subspace.
Implements the approach through Projected LoRA and training-free Closed-Form Weight Surgery.
Evaluated on four open-weight models, it mitigates in-context priming attacks and resists adversarial relearning without degrading benign competence.
papers.selection_reason: Orthogonal subspace unlearning method for LLMs that removes hazardous capabilities while preserving benign dual-use competence.
papers.title: Orthogonal Boundary Unlearning for Dual-Use Concepts in Large Language Models
papers.tldr: Orthogonal Boundary Unlearning removes hazardous dual-use capabilities while preserving benign scientific competence by constraining model updates away from benign capability representations.

papers.abstract: On-policy learning is central to post-training: training on a model's own generations limits distribution shift and helps preserve existing capabilities. On hard problems, however, on-policy RL provides no reward-based learning signal when all attempts fail. On-policy distillation provides next-token supervision from a teacher, but on hard problems, if a rollout goes wrong early, subsequent supervision is conditioned on prefixes that already contain the mistake. Correct behavior can instead come from a gold or teacher solution, but such off-policy targets can differ substantially from the model's generations and, as we show, may erode existing capabilities. We therefore treat on-policyness as a continuum and propose projected distillation, which minimally edits the student's failed attempts into correct targets. The method uses contrastive updates to favor corrections over failed attempts and refreshes these corrections as the student evolves, enabling near-on-policy learning even when all student attempts fail. Theoretically, we prove that the student's learning regret grows with the edit size: it scales linearly with the horizon under minimal correction, as in DAgger, and quadratically under full-answer replacement, as in behavior cloning. Empirically, across two students (Qwen3-8B and OLMo-2-7B) and five domains spanning math, code, science, and tool use, projected distillation gives the highest area under the specialization-retention frontier (best on 8 of 9 cells against GRPO and OPD, and 7 of 9 against SPOT and SODA). Our ablations highlight the importance of online corrections, the contrastive loss, and on-policyness: moving targets farther off-policy steadily worsens the specialization-retention trade-off, with retention falling from 0.916 to 0.744 when minimal corrections are replaced by student-agnostic gold solutions.
authors: Shripad V. Deshmukh, Christian Bock, Kangrui Ruan, Abhijeet Awasthi, Vijay Lingam, Rein Houthooft, Manish Prajapat
bullets: Hard problems can yield no reward signal when all on-policy attempts fail, while teacher or gold solutions may be too far off-policy and cause capability erosion.
The method edits failed student attempts into minimally corrected solutions, using contrastive updates and refreshing corrections as the student changes.
Theory links learning regret to edit size: minimal corrections scale linearly with horizon, whereas full-answer replacement scales quadratically.
Across two students and five domains, it achieved the best specialization–retention frontier in most reported comparisons against GRPO, OPD, SPOT, and SODA.
Ablations show that online corrections, contrastive loss, and on-policyness matter; farther-off-policy targets reduce retention.
papers.selection_reason: LLM post-training distillation method that minimally edits failed rollouts into correct targets, with theoretical regret analysis and retention trade-offs.
papers.title: Projected Distillation: On Learning to Solve Hard Problems from Close, Correct Targets
papers.tldr: Projected distillation minimally corrects failed model attempts to enable near-on-policy learning on hard tasks while better preserving existing capabilities than fully off-policy targets.

papers.abstract: Solving reasoning tasks supported on graphs typically requires providing a Language Reasoning Model (LRM) with a serialized description of the graph. This approach results in the input length growing with the number of edges, which limits the size of the problems that can be solved. Furthermore, even when graphs fit in context, performance sharply decays as the graphs grow. We propose to address this by augmenting LRMs with scalable and permutation equivariant graph positional encodings that modulate attention logits. An additional post-fusion-style module incorporates structural information into hidden states. We compute these positional encodings using a GNN followed by a Graph Transformer. This eliminates the need for serialized adjacencies, reducing the context burden to $O(N)$. We jointly fine-tune the positional encoder and the LRM LoRA adapters using optimal solutions generated by graph-theoretic solvers, resulting in a computationally efficient method. Trained on small graphs, the model exhibits improved size-generalization across graph-theoretic tasks on graphs with up to 1,000 nodes, and produces fewer tokens than a conventional LRM. Additionally, we observe that our model remains robust to node relabelings. Evaluations on graph-theoretic benchmarks also show that performance on small graphs is preserved.
authors: Javier Porras-Valenzuela, Arush Arora, Alejandro Ribeiro
bullets: Serialized graph descriptions scale with the number of edges and cause reasoning performance to degrade on larger graphs.
The method uses permutation-equivariant positional encodings from a GNN and Graph Transformer to modulate attention, plus a post-fusion module for structural information.
The positional encoder and LRM LoRA adapters are jointly fine-tuned using solver-generated optimal solutions.
Trained on small graphs, the model generalizes to graphs with up to 1,000 nodes, uses fewer tokens, and remains robust to node relabeling.
Performance on small graphs is preserved on graph-theoretic benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Augments language reasoning models with learnable graph positional encodings for scalable graph reasoning.
papers.title: Scaling Graph Reasoning in Language Models with Learnable Graph Positional Encodings
papers.tldr: A graph-aware positional encoding system enables language reasoning models to solve larger graph problems with linear context growth and improved size generalization.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models already make a sparse choice for every token: which experts should process it. We ask whether a sparse dictionary should reuse that choice. NR-SAE gives each routed expert a small dictionary and opens only those the frozen router selects. At block 15 of Gemma 4 26B-A4B, after ten million C4 training tokens and across three seeds, the expert-aligned autoencoder explains 0.518 of the variance in router-weighted expert outputs on a fixed evaluation capture. A rank-addressed control with the same parameters but sixteen times as many candidates reaches 0.481, a candidate-matched control 0.458, and an architecture-matched control with randomized expert identity 0.387. A transcoder variant also leads all three controls: 0.432, against 0.347, 0.371, and 0.118. Part of this advantage is architectural: each expert writes into a subspace of at most a quarter of the model width, so naming the expert names the subspace. How much it explains, we have not measured. At this layer and budget, the router already knows something a dictionary would otherwise have to learn. Our implementation did not train faster, and semantic interpretability, downstream loss, and causal faithfulness remain untested.
bullets: MoE routing decisions can be reused to select dictionary components, creating the Neural Router Sparse Autoencoder (NR-SAE).
At Gemma 4 26B-A4B block 15, NR-SAE explained 0.518 of router-weighted expert-output variance after training on 10 million C4 tokens across three seeds.
NR-SAE outperformed rank-addressed, candidate-matched, and randomized-expert controls; a similarly advantaged transcoder variant also led its controls.
Some gains may come from architecture: each expert writes to a subspace no wider than one-quarter of the model width.
The study did not find faster training, and semantic interpretability, downstream loss, and causal faithfulness were not evaluated.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates expert-routed sparse dictionaries in a large MoE language model, relevant to LLM internal representations.
papers.title: The Router Already Knows
papers.tldr: An expert-aligned sparse autoencoder leverages the MoE router’s existing expert choices to explain routed activations better than matched controls, though interpretability and downstream benefits remain untested.

papers.abstract: Test-case generation is critical but remains challenging for language models. Existing test-time scaling methods either isolate candidates or aggregate traces, which do not scale to long-horizon tasks. We present TEX, a collaborative test-time scaling framework based on execution-driven cross-validation. TEX parallelizes agents to generate tests and patches, cross-executing each test against every patch to form a $K \times K$ feedback matrix. Agents use their matrix slices for refinement, enabling objective validation without verbose trace sharing. On SWT-Bench Verified, TEX achieves 86.4%, establishing a new state-of-the-art and improving +9.0% over single-agent baselines. Moreover, even random selection from TEX outputs (84.4%) surpasses the previous SOTA (84.0%), showing collaborative execution feedback improves solution quality, not just best-case samples. Our results highlight execution-grounded feedback as an effective scaling mechanism for long-horizon agentic tasks.
authors: Akash Gokul, Srijan Bansal, Yingbo Zhou, Semih Yavuz
bullets: Addresses the scalability limits of existing test-time scaling for language-model test generation.
Parallel agents generate tests and patches, then execute every test against every patch to build a K×K feedback matrix.
Agents refine their outputs using matrix slices rather than sharing verbose execution traces.
Reaches 86.4% on SWT-Bench Verified, improving 9.0 percentage points over single-agent baselines.
Random TEX output selection achieves 84.4%, indicating execution feedback—not only best-sample selection—drives gains.
papers.selection_reason: Collaborative test-time scaling for LLM agents via execution-based cross-validation.
papers.title: TEX: Test-Time Scaling Testing Agents via Execution-based Cross-Validation
papers.tldr: TEX improves long-horizon code-agent test and patch generation by having agents cross-execute one another’s outputs for objective feedback.

papers.abstract: Large language models can detect vulnerable code, yet the form of vulnerability encoding in their representations remains unclear. We analyze 8 code models spanning 6.7B-15B parameters on C programs using three datasets (DELTASECOMMITS, SVEN, and PRECISE-BUGS), comparing two diagnostic tasks on the same representations: identifying what patterns the code instantiates, and determining whether it is vulnerable. Models encode the first with high fidelity. Under the studied paired C-code datasets and linear-probing setup, vulnerability information is more accessible as a paired relational signal-whether code A is riskier than code B-than as a globally separable categorical label. This structural difference has implications for classification: the model reliably ranks which code is riskier but standard classifiers on isolated samples achieve limited accuracy because vulnerable and secure samples form overlapping distributions in representation space.
authors: Rui Melo, Andre Catarino, Claudia Mamede, Corina Pasareanu, Rui Abreu
bullets: Analyzes 8 code models (6.7B–15B parameters) on C programs across three datasets.
Models represent code-instantiated patterns with high fidelity.
Vulnerability is more accessible through paired comparisons—whether code A is riskier than code B—than through globally separable labels.
Linear classifiers perform poorly on isolated samples because vulnerable and secure representations overlap.
Findings are scoped to the studied paired C-code datasets and linear-probing setup.
papers.selection_reason: Shows vulnerability information in code LLMs is encoded relationally rather than linearly separable; relevant to LLM representation analysis.
papers.title: When Models Know but Can't Linearly Say: Relational Encoding Limits Linear Vulnerability Classification in Code LLMs
papers.tldr: Code LLMs encode vulnerability information relationally, making them better at ranking which code is riskier than linearly classifying isolated samples as vulnerable or secure.

papers.abstract: Analyzing merchant transaction histories requires dynamic temporal filtering, entity resolution, and aggregation over irregular event streams--operations poorly captured by static tabular or time-series forecasting benchmarks. We introduce TxnQA, an analytical QA benchmark comprising 27 task families (81 templates) alongside a 5-scenario fraud-risk reasoning suite that evaluates both verdicts and supporting evidence over synthetic, privacy-mitigated transaction data. Ground-truth answers are computed programmatically, and model performance is decomposed into format-following rate (FFR), conditional content accuracy (CA), and end-to-end correctness (E2E). Evaluating prompted proprietary baselines and six LoRA-adapted open-weight models shows that adaptation reliably enforces output schemas but leaves arithmetic bottlenecks: Gemma-4-31B-IT and Qwen3-8B attain E2E scores of 0.867 and 0.816, whereas evaluated MoE checkpoints reach only 0.632-0.713. Furthermore, on the 500-instance fraud suite, verdict accuracy frequently exceeds 80%, yet joint accuracy (requiring exact evidence attribution) collapses to at most ~23%. These findings identify schema compliance, semantic calculation, and evidence attribution as three distinct bottlenecks in transaction-sequence QA.
authors: Rabimba Karanjai, Yiming Bian, Yun-Shiuan Chuang, Jenna L. Ballard, Zijie Pan, Shivani Shekhar, Yixi Li, Yirou Ge, Avinash Thangali, Richard Williamson, Linsey Pang, Prakhar Mehrotra
bullets: Introduces a benchmark with 27 analytical QA task families, 81 templates, and a five-scenario fraud-risk reasoning suite.
Tests temporal filtering, entity resolution, aggregation, verdicts, and supporting-evidence attribution over synthetic, privacy-mitigated transaction data.
Separates performance into format-following rate, conditional content accuracy, and end-to-end correctness using programmatic ground truth.
LoRA adaptation improves output-schema compliance, while arithmetic remains a bottleneck; evaluated models achieve E2E scores from 0.632 to 0.867.
Fraud verdict accuracy often exceeds 80%, but joint verdict-and-evidence accuracy reaches at most about 23%.
papers.selection_reason: Analytical QA benchmark for LLM reasoning and evidence grounding over transaction sequences.
papers.title: TxnQA: Benchmarking Analytical Reasoning and Evidence Grounding over Transaction Event Sequences
papers.tldr: TxnQA shows that transaction-sequence QA models can follow schemas and make fraud verdicts, but struggle with exact arithmetic and evidence attribution.

papers.abstract: Hallucination stress tests can yield similar average scores across language models even when different prompts elicit hallucinations in each model. We develop a procedure that iteratively edits source-grounded seed prompts to expose hallucinations in a target model. An LLM editor revises each prompt in response to the target's answer and a judge's category-specific score and explanation. In the main setting, the target also receives feedback on its previous response. Experiments cover 500 seeds from seven datasets and ten topics, with intrinsic and extrinsic hallucinations evaluated across open-weight and closed-source models. Editing substantially increases judge-rated severity over the seeds. In the baseline configuration, retained responses fall in the judge's strong-hallucination bin in 77.2% of runs targeting extrinsic hallucination and 74.2% targeting intrinsic hallucination. Later editing rounds account for more than half of the mean score increase. Among 219 prompts that pass model-assisted source-validity checks, 89 elicit responses containing unsupported claims. Across five models, 200 curated prompts yield similar average severity scores, although pairwise Spearman correlations between prompt-level scores are only $\rho=0.0387$ to $0.1897$. Curated prompts can be reused across models, but their diagnostic value depends on source validity and the failures they expose in each model.
authors: Jiho Lee, Bingquan Zhang, Lin Ting Liang, Soroush Vosoughi, Weicheng Ma
bullets: Curated prompts produce substantially more severe judge-rated hallucinations than source-grounded seeds.
The method targets both intrinsic and extrinsic hallucinations across seven datasets, ten topics, and open- and closed-source models.
Later editing rounds contribute more than half of the average severity improvement.
Across models, curated prompts have similar average severity but weak prompt-level score correlations, indicating model-specific diagnostic value.
Prompt usefulness depends on source validity and the particular failures exposed by each model.
papers.selection_reason: Target-aware curation of hallucination stress tests for LLMs; relevant to LLM evaluation and reliability.
papers.title: Target-Aware Curation of Hallucination Stress Tests for Large Language Models
papers.tldr: An iterative, target-aware prompt-editing procedure creates hallucination stress tests that expose model-specific failures more effectively than seed prompts alone.

papers.abstract: Enterprise adoption of LLMs in agentic workflows is gated by evaluations that span a wide arc of abilities: CRM operations, heterogeneous-document retrieval, personal data understanding, multi-turn planning, tool use, function calling, long-horizon research, and long-context software engineering. These evaluations live today in separate repositories with divergent runners, dependencies, and scoring conventions, which makes cross-benchmark comparison difficult and obscures what a single aggregate number actually represents. We release EGI-BENCH, a unified LLM agent benchmark suite that consolidates eight enterprise facing agent benchmarks (CRMARENA, HERB, PERSONABENCH, USERBENCH, MCP-UNIVERSE, MCPEVAL, BENCHFORCE, LOCOBENCH) behind a single command-line interface with two runtime-budgeted execution modes. On top of the suite we define the Enterprise General Intelligence (EGI) Score, a six-dimensional framework (M1-M6) whose buckets are populated by fine-grained sub-metrics routed from each benchmark rather than by benchmark-level averages. We describe the suite, the sub-metric routing, and the quick/deep budgets, and report results for fourteen frontier and cost-efficient LLMs spanning the GPT, Claude, and Gemini families under quick mode. Top-line EGI ranges from 39.6 (GPT-4o mini) to 65.6 (gpt-5.5), and no single model dominates every capability axis: gpt-5.5 leads task outcome, planning, and retrieval grounding; Claude Sonnet 4.5 leads tool actioning and safety/abstention; and Claude Haiku 4.5 leads engineering quality. Code is available at https://github.com/SalesforceAIResearch/egi-bench.
authors: Zhiwei Liu, Zhujun Lan, Jielin Qiu, Zixiang Chen, Liangwei Yang, Ming Zhu, Akshara Prabhakar, Wenting Zhao, John Emmons, Jason Wu, Shafiq Rayhan Joty, Junnan Li, Shelby Heinecke, Silvio Savarese, Huan Wang
