bullets: Covers CRM operations, document retrieval, personal-data understanding, planning, tool use, research, and long-context software engineering.
Provides a single CLI with quick and deep runtime-budgeted execution modes, replacing disparate runners and scoring conventions.
Routes fine-grained sub-metrics into six capability dimensions rather than averaging whole benchmarks.
Evaluates 14 GPT, Claude, and Gemini models; results show different models lead different capability axes rather than one universal winner.
Code is publicly available at github.com/SalesforceAIResearch/egi-bench.
papers.selection_reason: Unified benchmark suite for enterprise LLM agent capabilities.
papers.title: EGI-BENCH: An Enterprise General Intelligence Benchmark Suite
papers.tldr: EGI-BENCH unifies eight enterprise LLM-agent benchmarks and introduces a six-dimensional score to compare capabilities across diverse agentic workflows.

papers.abstract: Recent work has explored continuous representations in place of discrete tokens during Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, often referred to as soft CoT. This is motivated by the idea that a mixture of token embeddings can represent a superposition of multiple reasoning possibilities within a single step. However, it remains challenging to train large language models to realize this potential. Existing work has explored reinforcement learning (RL)-style training for soft CoT. However, these approaches treat soft tokens as actions in a Markov decision process rather than as differentiable intermediate computation steps. Thus, they do not propagate gradients across the soft tokens and miss out on the signal of how the choice of one soft token affects the next. In this paper, we propose a sparse relaxation method for RL (called SpaRLax), which leverages the differentiability of soft-CoT reasoning over time steps and makes training more stable and effective. We adopt an entmax sparsity method that adaptively determines the degree of softness, which truncates long-tail noise at confident steps while retaining multiple plausible candidates when uncertain. Across nine reasoning benchmarks, our method achieves the highest average performance compared with baseline methods. Further analyses validate the effective use of soft-token superposition in our approach, and also demonstrate the contribution of adaptive sparsity in our approach.
authors: Jiabin Fan, Matthias Lindemann, Zita Marinho, Andr\'e FT Martins, Lili Mou
bullets: Soft-CoT methods use mixtures of token embeddings to represent multiple reasoning possibilities, but are difficult to train effectively.
Prior RL approaches treat soft tokens as discrete-like actions, missing dependencies between successive soft tokens.
SpaRLax uses differentiable reasoning across time steps with entmax-based adaptive sparsity.
Adaptive sparsity suppresses noise at confident steps while preserving multiple candidates under uncertainty.
It achieves the highest average performance among compared baselines across nine reasoning benchmarks, with analyses supporting both soft-token superposition and adaptive sparsity.
papers.selection_reason: Sparse RL relaxation for soft chain-of-thought reasoning in LLMs.
papers.title: Sparse RL Relaxation for LLM Reasoning
papers.tldr: SpaRLax improves soft-CoT reinforcement learning by propagating gradients across reasoning steps and adaptively controlling token sparsity.

papers.abstract: Modern language models are increasingly asked to handle several tasks within a single prompt. Doing so requires solving each task correctly while integrating the resulting answers into a coherent response. In this paper, we identify a fundamental limitation in this process, where models make substantially more errors when tasks are composed, even when they can solve every constituent task reliably in isolation. This degradation cannot be fully explained by the accumulation of independent errors. Across both open-weight models and the frontier model Claude Opus 5, our findings instead point to an implicit thinking budget underlying this effect. In particular, under composition, models use substantially fewer tokens per task than in isolation, even when the full sequence remains well within the context window. Tasks that require longer solution traces in isolation are consequently more $\textit{fragile}$ under composition, i.e., models make more errors on prompts containing these tasks. In isolation, non-fragile tasks receive more reasoning than they need and waste compute. However, by grouping tasks according to their fragility, the implicit budgeting can be manipulated to reduce token usage by $43$\% across a range of math and linguistic tasks while also preserving accuracy.
authors: Chenpan Li, Thies Brockmoeller, Stefanie Jegelka, Sharut Gupta, Nikolaos Karalias
bullets: Models make substantially more errors on combined tasks even when they solve each task reliably in isolation.
The degradation is not fully explained by independent error accumulation.
Under composition, models spend fewer tokens per task despite having sufficient context-window capacity.
Tasks requiring longer reasoning in isolation are more fragile, while non-fragile tasks may receive excess computation.
Grouping tasks by fragility reduces token usage by 43% across math and linguistic tasks while preserving accuracy.
papers.selection_reason: Identifies implicit reasoning-budget effects in LLM task composition and a way to reduce token usage; relevant to LLM reasoning and efficiency.
papers.title: On the Fragility of Tasks under Composition: Implicit Budgeting in Language Models
papers.tldr: Composing multiple tasks makes language models fragile because they implicitly divide their reasoning budget, especially harming tasks that need longer solution traces.

papers.abstract: Clinical care, health-system operations and biomedical discovery depend on extracting reliable answers from patient records, yet applying diverse clinical questions across entire populations remains computationally expensive. Here we present Clinical System One (CS1), a 4-billion-parameter decision model for fast, typed judgments from clinical records, along with two agentic harnesses in which CS1 works together with a generalist language model. CS1-4B is trained on 12.4 million questions and answers from 3.6 million patients across a multi-hospital health system, combining structured-data keys, observed outcomes and language-model supervision across clinical notes, diagnostic reports and patient timelines. It answers multiple typed questions in a single forward pass without task-specific retraining, and each answer carries a probability that can route uncertain cases to human review. On 963,408 held-out patients, CS1-4B outperformed open decision models up to 27 billion parameters on 13 of 14 tasks scored independently of its training teacher. Across 21 external data sets, its aggregate performance approached that of the strongest tested 27-billion-parameter model, with 6.4-fold faster inference in a matched workload. Integrating CS1-4B with a language model agent produced cited answers over complete multi-year patient histories and screened a patient population against the eligibility criteria of 17 registered clinical trials, placing four times as many judged-eligible patients among its top 20 candidates as keyword search while using 690-fold fewer language-model tokens than a language model reading every record. These findings support a division of labour in clinical AI, with small decision models performing repeated record reading and generative models formulating questions and synthesizing evidence.
authors: Andrew Zhang, Trinh T. L. Vuong, Sophia J. Wagner, Dongmin Bang, Tong Ding, Yuchang Su, Mary Cipperman, Christina S. Chen, Judith Lefkes, Ramin Kahidi, Ming Y. Lu, Caiwei Tian, Tianhao Luo, Jingnan Ma, Rowland Pettit, Long Phi Le, Faisal Mahmood
bullets: Targets the computational cost of applying varied clinical questions across large patient populations.
Trained on 12.4 million question–answer examples from 3.6 million patients using structured data, outcomes, notes, reports and timelines.
Produces multiple typed judgments in one pass, with probabilities that can flag uncertain cases for human review.
Outperformed open decision models up to 27B parameters on 13 of 14 independently evaluated tasks; inference was 6.4× faster than a matched 27B model across 21 external datasets.
When paired with a language model, improved clinical-trial screening over keyword search and used 690× fewer language-model tokens than reading every record.
papers.selection_reason: Presents Clinical System One (CS1), a 4B parameter decision model for clinical records that performs fast, typed judgments in a single forward pass, integrated with an agentic harness.
papers.title: A general-purpose System One decision model for clinical records
papers.tldr: Clinical System One is a 4-billion-parameter model that rapidly answers diverse clinical-record questions and efficiently supports language-model agents.

papers.abstract: As AI systems begin to resolve open research problems, reliable verification becomes increasingly important. Formal mathematics provides a trusted framework for mathematical reasoning, enabling agents to produce machine-checkable proofs while conducting mathematical exploration. Existing formal mathematics benchmarks often focus on known results or a small set of prominent open problems, which can become difficult to evaluate reliably once solutions are discovered and widely disseminated. Existing evaluation protocols are also not always aligned with how modern coding agents operate. We therefore introduce ReuF2F, a Lean 4 benchmark of 244 formalized open problems drawn from Research Experiences for Undergraduates (REU), spanning entry-level open research problems across a broad range of mathematical subfields. We expect these less prominent open problems, which tend to attract less attention and may remain unsolved for longer, to be better suited for held-out evaluation of end-to-end open problem resolution in Lean. We adopt a standard coding-agent evaluation setting, placing each problem and its logical negation into a Lean project in a Docker container. We also build Leanimum-agent on mini-SWE-agent to provide a unified harness for fair comparisons across models. Our evaluation finds that even the best-performing model resolves only ~40% of the problems, leaving substantial room for improvement on formalized open research problems.
authors: Zeyu Zheng, Yiyang Liu, Yuyang Zhao, Congmin Zheng, Jiachen Zhu, Jianian Chen, Kangning Zhang, Kayue Daniel Wong, Lingyu Yang, Rong Shan, Shihao Chen, Thomas Zhu, Wentao Zhang, Xiaopeng Li, Yan Hu, Yongxi Lin, Yuxiang Chen, Zhuoying Ou, Jianghao Lin, Jeremy Avigad, Prasad Tetali, Jingbang Chen, Sean Welleck
bullets: Addresses the need for reliable, machine-checkable evaluation of AI systems attempting open mathematical research problems.
Introduces 244 Lean 4 problems from Research Experiences for Undergraduates across diverse mathematical subfields.
Uses a coding-agent setup with each problem and its negation in a Dockerized Lean project.
Provides Leanimum-agent, a unified evaluation harness built on mini-SWE-agent.
Finds substantial room for improvement in end-to-end formal open-problem resolution.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces ReuF2F, a benchmark for coding agents on formalized undergraduate research problems in Lean 4, evaluating end-to-end open problem resolution capabilities.
papers.title: ReuF2F: Benchmarking Coding Agents on Formalized Undergraduate Research Problems
papers.tldr: ReuF2F benchmarks coding agents on 244 formalized undergraduate-level open mathematics problems in Lean 4, finding that even the best model solves only about 40%.

papers.abstract: A poker agent can make a legal move and still make a strategically poor one. We ask whether compact AI agents can exhibit strategic behavior under hidden information and whether preference optimization can improve beyond static and zero-shot policies. We first evaluate a static baseline and three frozen language models: SmallThinker, Qwen3, and Gemma-3 whose performance varies substantially between exact-game and six-player evaluation. We therefore propose Strategic Preference Optimization with KL-anchored Equilibrium (SPOKE), combining teacher-relative value penalties, policy anchoring, risk constraints, and structured rationale supervision, and compare it with SFT, DPO, GRPO, and GSPO. Across three runs of a SmallThinker-4B-A0.6B policy, SPOKE achieves the lowest mean exploitability in Kuhn (0.213) and Leduc (1.081) and the highest six-max top-1 agreement (0.775), while maintaining teacher KL comparable to SFT (0.522 vs 0.523). These results provide preliminary evidence that strategic preference optimization can improve strategic quality while preserving teacher-consistent behavior.
authors: Phurinat Polasa, Thanapon Thanadunpremdet, Phatthanasak Kraiduang, Saksorn Ruangtanusak
bullets: Poker agents may make legal moves that are strategically weak, especially in multi-player settings.
The study evaluates a static policy and three frozen language models, finding performance varies between exact-game and six-player evaluation.
SPOKE combines teacher-relative value penalties, policy anchoring, risk constraints, and structured rationale supervision.
Compared with SFT, DPO, GRPO, and GSPO, SPOKE reports the lowest mean exploitability in Kuhn and Leduc and the highest six-max top-1 agreement.
Results are preliminary and focus on three runs of a SmallThinker-4B-A0.6B policy, with teacher-consistent behavior measured through KL divergence.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces SPOKE, a strategic preference optimization method for LLM agents in poker, combining value penalties and policy anchoring to improve strategic behavior under hidden information.
papers.title: Teaching AI Agent to Play Poker Strategically Through Preference Optimization
papers.tldr: SPOKE uses preference optimization with equilibrium and risk-aware constraints to improve compact language-model poker agents’ strategic play under hidden information.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems improve performance on clinical tasks, and that improvement is often read as evidence of a more trustworthy system. However, the two are not the same claim. A clinician acts on the stated reasoning and not only on the conclusion, so whether collaboration reduces hallucination, and what decides when it does, has to be measured in the reasoning too. Yet most evaluations score only the final answer. We evaluate four systems (a single-LLM baseline and three multi-agent topologies) across four models and three clinical tasks, scoring hallucination, under a factuality and faithfulness taxonomy, inside the rationale each system generates and reporting it alongside the task metric. We report that collaboration buys task performance but not lower hallucination as a rule, and no topology is reliably better than another. The effect differs by model: of the $36$ model--system--task comparisons, $12$ are large enough to resolve --- four decreases and eight increases, with no model on both sides. What sets the level, and the direction of any change, is the model rather than the topology or the number of agents. A self-correction experiment is consistent with this: shown its own flagged errors, every model except Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct reduces hallucination; the one model for which collaboration lowers hallucination gains the most, and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, the model whose hallucination it amplifies most, does not reduce its hallucination at all. We find that collaboration redistributes what its models can already do; it does not supply what they cannot.
authors: Won Seok Jang, Harry Bhaskar Joshi, Hong Yu
bullets: Evaluates a single-LLM baseline and three multi-agent topologies across four models and three clinical tasks.
Measures hallucination in generated rationales using factuality and faithfulness criteria, alongside final task performance.
Collaboration improves task performance but has no consistent effect on hallucination, with no topology reliably outperforming another.
Across 36 comparisons, notable effects included four decreases and eight increases in hallucination; effects varied by model.
Self-correction reduced hallucination for all but Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, suggesting collaboration redistributes existing model capabilities rather than adding missing ones.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates multi-agent LLM systems on clinical tasks, specifically analyzing hallucination in reasoning steps versus final answers, providing insights into the reliability of multi-agent collaboration.
papers.title: Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?
papers.tldr: Multi-agent collaboration can improve clinical task performance, but it does not reliably reduce reasoning hallucinations; the underlying model matters more than the collaboration topology.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon agents must learn heterogeneous capabilities from interleaved trajectories. Updating shared parameters to learn new capabilities can degrade previously acquired ones, resulting in catastrophic forgetting. As a trajectory unfolds, different stages may require different capabilities, yet conventional joint training and static adapter merging maintain a fixed parameter configuration throughout execution. We introduce WeAct (Weight-level Internal Actions), which trains independent capability-specific LoRA adapters over a frozen backbone and adds adapter selection to the agent's action space. These internal actions use the model's native tool-calling interface for on-demand capability composition in a shared context. Across eight deep-research benchmarks, Qwen3-32B with WeAct improves average accuracy by 6.2% relative to full fine-tuning counterparts despite using less compute, and by 27.5% relative to the strongest static LoRA-merging method. WeAct also supports modular continual adaptation, by adding a new code computation adapter to expand the agent's capabilities and updating the existing writing adapter to improve report quality. Both updates leave the backbone and other adapters unchanged, supporting modular continual adaptation in agents.
authors: Rui Shi, Xunjian Yin, Jiacheng Sang, Zichuan Liu, Shuyan Zhou
bullets: Addresses catastrophic forgetting and the need for different capabilities across long-horizon trajectories.
Trains independent LoRA adapters on a frozen backbone and exposes adapter selection as internal tool-calling actions.
Enables on-demand capability composition instead of fixed parameter configurations or static adapter merging.
On eight deep-research benchmarks, reports 6.2% higher average accuracy than full fine-tuning and 27.5% higher than static LoRA merging.
Supports modular continual adaptation by adding or updating individual adapters without changing the backbone or other capabilities.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes WeAct, a method for modular continual adaptation in agents using dynamic weight switching (LoRA adapters) as internal actions, directly addressing catastrophic forgetting in long-horizon agents.
papers.title: WeAct: Dynamic Weight Switching as Agent Actions
papers.tldr: WeAct lets agents dynamically switch among capability-specific LoRA adapters during execution, reducing forgetting and improving deep-research performance.

papers.abstract: We propose KronLSTM, a linear attention architecture based on the Kronecker Delta Rule, a novel update rule for associative matrix memories. KronLSTM extends the xLSTM family with a memory-revision mechanism that corrects targeted associations while modifying the memory only along a single direction in matrix space. This minimally invasive memory revision reduces interference with previously stored information compared with delta-rule updates, making it particularly well suited for long-context language modeling. The resulting memory dynamics can be mathematically described as a Markov chain that converges to a steady-state distribution, while the expected norm of the memory matrix remains uniformly bounded throughout the entire input sequence. Hence, KronLSTM ensures stable memory dynamics without requiring additional normalization and stabilization mechanisms for the memory state. Experiments show that KronLSTM is competitive with, and often outperforms, existing linear attention architectures, including models of the (Gated) DeltaNet family, with particularly strong performance on long context benchmarks. These results establish the Kronecker Delta Rule as an effective and analytically tractable foundation for stable associative memory in recurrent linear attention architectures. Our code (https://github.com/NX-AI/KronLSTM) and models (https://huggingface.co/collections/NX-AI/kronlstm) are open-source.
authors: Anamaria-Roberta Hartl, Levente Z\'olyomi, Michael List, G\"unter Klambauer, Sebastian B\"ock, Sepp Hochreiter
bullets: Extends the xLSTM family with memory revision that corrects targeted associations along a single matrix-space direction.
Reduces interference with stored information compared with standard delta-rule updates.
Its memory dynamics form a convergent Markov chain with uniformly bounded expected memory norm, without extra stabilization or normalization.
Experiments find performance competitive with or often better than linear attention baselines, especially on long-context benchmarks.
Code and pretrained models are publicly available.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces KronLSTM, a linear attention architecture based on the Kronecker Delta Rule, offering stable memory dynamics and improved efficiency for long-context language modeling.
papers.title: Kronecker Delta Rule for Long Context Linear Attention
papers.tldr: KronLSTM introduces a minimally invasive Kronecker Delta Rule for stable, high-performing long-context linear attention.

papers.abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) are powerful tools for protein annotation and mutation-effect prediction, but progress has largely depended on scaling model size and data, making them expensive and prone to memorization. Test-time scaling offers a complementary path, but methods developed for autoregressive LLMs do not transfer directly: masked encoders lack a generation loop, and amino acids do not verbalize in a reasoning language. Instead, we adapt recursive pretraining to masked pLMs, where a weight-tied Transformer core refines residue-aligned hidden states over an adjustable number of cycles. We instantiate this recipe as recAMPLIFY, a pLM with 155M unique parameters trained on the same 2T tokens as AMPLIFY-350M. Despite 56% fewer parameters, it improves CASP contact recovery and three out of four supervised tasks, notably raising fold accuracy by 22.5%. Because optimal depth for recAMPLIFY varies across tasks and assays, we then introduce Gated Mixture Recurrence (GMR), a framework that decodes each protein from a probability-weighted mixture of hidden states visited during recursion. GMR employs a learned residual gate at scalar, low-rank, or per-dimension resolution to control how much of each cycle's proposed update is accepted into the state. This unifies halting and gating into a single adaptive computation objective while recovering PonderNet-style halting as a special case without gates. Layered on top of recAMPLIFY, GMR further reduces expected layer depth by up to 37%, although the accuracy trade-off varies by task. Mechanistic analyses show that residual gating controls recurrence stability beyond the trained depth and that halt depth tracks biological properties.
authors: Saurav Jha, Qianli Liao, Robert Vernon, Sarath Chandar, Quentin Fournier
bullets: Addresses the cost and memorization risks of scaling protein language models, while adapting test-time scaling to masked encoders.
Uses a weight-tied Transformer core that repeatedly refines residue representations over an adjustable number of cycles.
With 155M unique parameters, recAMPLIFY outperforms the larger AMPLIFY-350M on CASP contact recovery and three of four supervised tasks, including a 22.5% fold-accuracy gain.
Introduces Gated Mixture Recurrence (GMR), which combines hidden states across recursion cycles using learned residual gates for adaptive depth.
GMR reduces expected layer depth by up to 37%, but accuracy trade-offs vary by task; halt depth also tracks biological properties.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces recursive pretraining for protein language models (recAMPLIFY) and a Gated Mixture Recurrence framework, representing a foundation model approach for biological sequences.
papers.title: recAMPLIFY: Large-Scale Pretraining of Recursive Protein Language Models
papers.tldr: recAMPLIFY scales masked protein language modeling through recursive, weight-tied refinement, achieving strong task performance with fewer parameters and enabling adaptive computation via GMR.

papers.abstract: Frontier LLMs can copy random text almost flawlessly, yet they often overrun or truncate long blocks of repeated characters. In repeated strings, matching local content no longer reliably identifies where copying should continue or when it should stop. Nevertheless, we show that a two-layer transformer with $O(\log\log N)$-bit precision and $O(\log N/\log\log N)$ width can copy every string up to a chosen design horizon $N$ and terminate correctly under arbitrary repetition. We use RoPE-style rotations of attention values and outputs (VO-rotations) with small prime periods to encode distances from delimiter anchors modulo those primes. By the Chinese Remainder Theorem, these periodic encodings jointly distinguish all required distances, allowing one retrieval rule to select either the next source token or the end marker. In contrast, we prove a width-independent impossibility result for copying under sequential finite-precision softmax accumulation. It applies to transformers whose only positional input is an additive attention bias that eventually becomes constant, including NoPE and a recursive implementation of ALiBi. Once an identical-token run exceeds the resulting saturation threshold, further repetitions leave the logits unchanged. If this threshold grows sublinearly with $N$, these models cannot both complete a long all-identical copy and stop correctly, a pattern resembling the termination errors of frontier LLMs. In synthetic copying experiments, baseline transformer models fail on long repeated strings even within the training range. Trained VO models, by contrast, generalize beyond the training lengths with near-perfect accuracy up to length $\approx 5005$, the selected primes' period product.
authors: Anxin Guo, Tianlong Huang, Chenxiao Yang, Zhiyuan Li
bullets: Repeated tokens make local content insufficient for determining copying position and termination.
A two-layer transformer uses small-prime periodic VO-rotations to encode delimiter distances modulo multiple primes.
The Chinese Remainder Theorem combines these encodings to distinguish distances up to a chosen horizon using low precision and width.
The paper proves saturation-based impossibility for models relying on eventually constant additive attention biases, including NoPE and recursive ALiBi.
In synthetic experiments, VO models generalize to near-perfect copying up to about length 5005, while baselines fail on long repeated strings.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes LLM copying behavior and introduces a novel Position Hashing mechanism using RoPE rotations to handle repetition, providing insights into LLM architecture and attention mechanisms.
papers.title: Copying Under Repetition: From Prefix Matching to Position Hashing
papers.tldr: VO-rotations with Chinese Remainder Theorem distance encoding enable compact transformers to copy and terminate correctly on highly repetitive strings, addressing failures of standard positional mechanisms.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive language models emit one token per forward pass. This causes high inference latency, in particular as models are scaled up for quality. In this paper, we introduce Parallel Language Models (PLMs), which generate mutually consistent tokens in one forward pass by routing dependencies through latent auxiliary variables. PLMs are trained using a variational bound that reduces to an autoregressive loss plus a parallel decoding loss. Empirically, PLMs are on a faster and better Pareto frontier than autoregressive and discrete diffusion baselines. Pretrained PLMs achieve near-autoregressive pretraining loss on model scales of 80M to 3B parameters, and speedup follows a power law in model size. When post-trained, our 1.3B model matches or exceeds an identically trained autoregressive model on math, coding, and instruction-following benchmarks, speeding up inference $2.3\text{-}5.7\times$. Together, we show that parallel generation can be trained from a single training objective at autoregressive quality. We will make our code available at https://github.com/mandt-lab/plm.
authors: Felix Draxler, Robin C. Geyer, Daniel Geyfman, Farrin Marouf Sofian, Justus Will, Philipp Hildebrandt, Giosue Migliorini, Prakhar Srivastava, Gagan Sai Trinadh Duggaraju Peddiraju, Kushagra Pandey, Jorge da Silva Gon\c{c}alves, Elijah Tavares, Jan Niklas Groeneveld, Yang Meng, Julia E. Vogt, Stephan Mandt
bullets: Addresses the latency of autoregressive models, which generate one token per forward pass.
Routes token dependencies through latent auxiliary variables so multiple tokens can be generated in a single forward pass.
Uses a variational objective combining autoregressive and parallel-decoding losses.
Achieves near-autoregressive pretraining loss from 80M to 3B parameters, with speedup increasing with model size.
A post-trained 1.3B model matches or exceeds an identically trained autoregressive model while providing 2.3–5.7× faster inference on math, coding, and instruction-following benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a parallel autoregressive language model architecture via variational decoding, a substantive LLM architecture contribution with inference speedup.
papers.title: Parallel Language Models via Variational Decoding
papers.tldr: Parallel Language Models use latent variables and variational training to generate mutually consistent tokens in parallel, achieving near-autoregressive quality with substantially faster inference.

papers.abstract: It has long been proposed that animals construct cognitive maps to support flexible behavior in novel environments. We tested whether large language models form similar representations using relational reasoning tasks and causal "mosaic experiments" that manipulate internal activations in open-weight language models. Models beyond the ten-billion-parameter scale successfully inferred unstated relationships between entities and generalized to synthetic entity names. Across model and task families, models generated abstract representations of relational structure and combined them additively with representations of entity identity, binding entities to roles within that structure. Models stored observed relationships as pairwise links that they composed retrospectively when queried, rather than prospectively positioning each entity in a global coordinate system. Binding was mediated by a sparse, distributed set of key--value pairs; by perturbing these pairs, we implanted "false memories" that altered model behavior in predictable ways. Overall, our findings reveal an internal organization analogous to a cognitive map that explains how language models reason with limited information.
authors: Albert Qin, Jonathan Cohen, Gautam Reddy
bullets: Models larger than 10 billion parameters inferred unstated relationships and generalized them to synthetic entity names.
Causal activation experiments found abstract relational structure combined additively with entity-identity representations.
Models represented relationships as pairwise links composed at query time, rather than as positions in a global coordinate system.
Entity–role binding relied on sparse, distributed key–value representations; perturbing them produced predictable false memories.
These findings suggest an internal organization analogous to a cognitive map for reasoning with limited information.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates internal relational representations and key-value binding in large language models, contributing to LLM understanding and interpretability.
papers.title: Cognitive Map in Large Language Models
papers.tldr: Large language models can build cognitive-map-like relational representations that support flexible inference and targeted memory manipulation.

papers.abstract: Hybrid architectures offer a promising approach to efficient language modeling by combining a small number of full-attention layers with a larger number of efficient sequence layers, such as sparse attention and recurrent layers. While full-attention layers maintain a KV cache that grows linearly with sequence length, efficient layers typically rely on separate, fixed-size states rather than accessing this richer existing memory. Recent work has begun exploring ways to allow efficient layers access to the KV cache, but the theoretical benefits of such access, and the extent to which existing approaches can realize them remain poorly understood. We investigate these questions by analyzing the expressive power of individual hybrid blocks on function composition, a well-studied task in sequence-model expressivity associated with multi-hop reasoning. We first establish that both conventional hybrid blocks and those with top-$\kappa$ KV-cache access require $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$ capacity to compute even two-function composition over a domain of size $n$. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the \emph{Multi-hop Retrieval Attention} (MuRA) hybrid block, a simple architecture that enables multi-hop retrieval from a shared KV cache while preserving asymptotic computational and memory efficiency. We prove that a single fixed size $m$-hop MuRA block can compute $m$-function composition, whereas computing $(m+1)$-function composition with the same retrieval depth requires polynomial model size, establishing a strict expressivity hierarchy in retrieval depth. Synthetic experiments support this hierarchy, showing that increasing retrieval depth enables learning progressively deeper compositions, substantially outperforming existing hybrid architectures. Together, our results identify multi-hop retrieval as a promising mechanism for improving the expressive power of efficient hybrid architectures.
authors: Yam Eitan, Gilad Yehudai, Haggai Maron
bullets: Hybrid models combine a few full-attention layers with more efficient sparse-attention or recurrent layers, but efficient layers typically cannot exploit the full KV cache.
Conventional hybrid blocks and top-κ KV-cache access require Ω(√n) capacity even for two-function composition over a domain of size n.
The proposed Multi-hop Retrieval Attention (MuRA) block supports multi-hop access to a shared KV cache while preserving asymptotic computational and memory efficiency.
A fixed-size m-hop MuRA block can compute m-function composition, while computing (m+1)-function composition at the same depth requires polynomial model size.
Synthetic experiments support a retrieval-depth hierarchy, with deeper retrieval enabling progressively deeper compositions and outperforming existing hybrid architectures.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a multi-hop retrieval attention block for efficient hybrid language architectures, improving expressivity while preserving asymptotic efficiency.
papers.title: Improving the Expressive Power of Hybrid Sequence Models via Multi-Hop Retrieval
papers.tldr: Multi-hop retrieval substantially increases the expressive power of efficient hybrid sequence models, enabling deeper compositional reasoning with fixed-size retrieval depth.

papers.abstract: Solving algorithmic tasks with many sequential steps typically requires scaling up transformer depth or chain-of-thought length, incurring unfavorable parameter and inference-compute costs, respectively. Looped transformers, which reuse one block of layers across many iterations, are poised to address this, since they scale effective depth without adding parameters or tokens. Yet, it remains unclear what each iteration is actually computing, or whether the loop merely simulates a deeper untied stack. Here, we study directed permutation traversal, in which a model follows $H$ hops from a starting node and reports the node it reaches, so every intermediate hop has a known ground truth. We find that a minimum effective depth is necessary to solve the task, beyond which the degree of weight tying becomes the determining factor. For instance, a looped transformer with a four-layer block iterated eight times solves the task in every seed, while an identically-trained untied transformer of the same effective depth never does, succeeding only with a lower learning rate or supervision of its intermediate layers. Probing and intervening on the residual stream, we find that the looped model advances through the intermediate nodes gradually, forming a staircase that adapts to its iteration budget, whereas the untied model, at that lower rate, exposes them only in its final layers. Taken together, our results recast looped transformers as iterative program learners, which allocate their iterations to successive steps of the algorithm and solve tasks that identically-trained untied models of the same effective depth do not. Code is available at https://github.com/magnus-sesodia/insidetheloop.
authors: Magnus Sesodia, Juil Sock, Philip Torr, Christian Schroeder de Witt
bullets: Studies directed permutation traversal, where each hop provides a known intermediate target.
Finds that sufficient effective depth is necessary, but weight tying strongly affects successful learning beyond that threshold.
A four-layer block looped for eight iterations solves the task across all seeds, while an equally deep untied model does not under identical training.
Residual-stream analysis shows looped models progressively represent intermediate nodes in an iteration-adaptive staircase.
Results support viewing looped transformers as iterative program learners rather than merely simulated deep stacks.
papers.selection_reason: Mechanistic study of weight-tied/looped transformer architectures and iterative computation, directly relevant to LLM architecture advances.
papers.title: Inside the Loop: A Mechanistic Study of Weight-Tied Transformers on Depth-Bound Algorithmic Tasks
papers.tldr: Weight-tied looped transformers learn algorithmic steps iteratively, solving depth-bound permutation tasks more reliably than equally deep untied models under the same training setup.

papers.abstract: Internal signatures could support monitoring, adaptive computation, and mechanistic analysis, but benchmark prompts can be separable without any shared computational distinction. We test whether a prespecified knowledge/reasoning label defines a reusable internal signature in five contemporary 7B to 31B models. We treat the \textbf{task} as the unit of inference probes hold out complete tasks, labels are permuted across tasks, and the best layer and stream are reselected for every permutation. Raw probes recover an eight-versus-eight-subject MMLU partition in all five models (macro-F1 $0.78$--$0.81$), but prompt text predicts it nearly as well: under an identical probe configuration, the activation advantage is only $0.017$--$0.070$ macro-F1 and is not significant. At the prespecified $0.01$ level, lexical adjustment removes significance while the adjusted states still identify individual subjects, and the selected site changes across task panels and selection rules. Additionally, two released base-training trajectories show no common direction. These pooled layerwise measures recover the task label but identify no transferable knowledge/reasoning signature at the tested sensitivity, which cannot exclude moderate effects. The resulting protocol gives future internal monitors and intervention studies a sequence of tests to pass. Project page: \url{https://parsa-ra.github.io/lmbehave/}.
bullets: Task-held-out probes recover the benchmark partition with macro-F1 0.78–0.81, but prompt text predicts it nearly as well.
Activation-based gains are small (0.017–0.070 macro-F1) and become nonsignificant after lexical adjustment at the prespecified 0.01 level.
The best layer and activation stream vary across task panels and selection rules, indicating poor stability.
Two base-training trajectories show no common direction, further weakening evidence for a shared signature.
The results do not rule out moderate effects, but define tests future monitoring and intervention studies should pass.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates internal representation signatures in modern LLMs, fitting LLM architecture and interpretability interests.
papers.title: Do Knowledge and Reasoning Oriented Benchmarks Induce Stable Representation Signatures in LLMs?
papers.tldr: Across five LLMs, knowledge-versus-reasoning benchmark labels are recoverable but do not produce a stable, transferable internal representation signature under the tested protocol.

papers.abstract: Latent reasoning replaces natural-language chains of thought with compact continuous "soft-token" representations, reducing the number of intermediate tokens that must be decoded autoregressively. We use a small external encoder to induce latent reasoning in a frozen backbone model. The encoder iteratively maps the backbone's hidden states to new latent blocks, constructing a latent reasoning prefix, after which the frozen model writes its remaining reasoning and its answer as text. Our method, INTACT, trains this encoder through distillation to reproduce the effect of written reasoning steps while keeping the model's behavior close to that of the frozen backbone, and then reinforces it on answer correctness. Across four frozen backbones from 1B to 8B, INTACT improves both GSM8K and average out-of-domain accuracy, including GSM8K gains from 75.8% to 79.3% on Llama-3.2-3B and from 77.6% to 79.7% on Qwen2.5-3B. It also reduces end-to-end latency per problem by 19% on Llama-3.2-3B and outperforms the evaluated latent-reasoning baselines at the 3B and 8B scales. Beyond the mathematics setting, the same recipe trained on a multi-domain corpus improves the frozen backbone on twelve evaluation benchmarks spanning mathematics, science, and commonsense, without task-specific adaptation.
bullets: Uses a small external encoder to iteratively transform frozen-backbone hidden states into a latent reasoning prefix.
Trains the encoder by distilling written reasoning, preserving the backbone’s behavior, then reinforces it using answer correctness.
Across four frozen backbones from 1B–8B parameters, it improves GSM8K and average out-of-domain accuracy.
On Llama-3.2-3B, GSM8K rises from 75.8% to 79.3% and latency falls by 19%.
A multi-domain version improves performance across twelve mathematics, science, and commonsense benchmarks without task-specific adaptation.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a method (INTACT) to induce latent reasoning in frozen LLM backbones to reduce latency, directly addressing LLM efficiency and reasoning architectures.
papers.title: INTACT: Inducing Latent Reasoning on a Frozen Backbone
papers.tldr: INTACT adds compact latent reasoning to frozen language models, improving accuracy while reducing inference latency.

papers.abstract: While LLM-based agent systems have demonstrated remarkable proficiency in reasoning and solving complex real-world tasks, they also come with substantial token consumption and inference latency, limiting their practical deployment. To enhance the efficiency of agent systems, recent efforts have focused on transferring agentic capabilities from large-scale models to small language models (SLMs) via supervised fine-tuning-based distillation. Nevertheless, as interaction trajectories grow longer, involving extended reasoning-action chains and extensive environmental feedback, distilled student agents tend to experience progress stagnation: becoming trapped in unproductive loops characterized by persistent failed strategies and difficulty making meaningful progress. Our systematic analysis shows that this phenomenon consistently occurs across diverse SLMs and task domains. To address this issue, we propose Progress-Aware Distillation (ProD), which explicitly detects and penalizes stagnation in student-generated trajectories. ProD encodes the stagnation gap between student and teacher into an adaptive margin for dynamically penalizing possible stagnation. By iteratively applying this procedure, ProD enables student agents to progressively approximate teacher behavior. Extensive experiments involving 8 SLMs, ranging from 0.6B to 8B parameters, on both in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks, demonstrate that ProD substantially mitigates progress stagnation while enhancing both the success rates and task-completion efficiency of distilled SLM agents.
bullets: Distilled SLM agents can become trapped in unproductive loops during long reasoning-action trajectories.
The stagnation problem appears consistently across diverse SLMs and task domains.
ProD detects stagnation and converts the student–teacher stagnation gap into an adaptive penalty margin.
Iterative progress-aware distillation helps students increasingly approximate teacher behavior.
Experiments across 8 SLMs (0.6B–8B) and in- and out-of-domain benchmarks show improved success rates and efficiency.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses a critical issue in LLM agents (stagnation) and proposes a novel distillation technique (Progress-Aware Distillation) to improve SLM agent performance.
papers.title: Progress-Aware Distillation for Mitigating Stagnation in Small Language Model Agents
papers.tldr: Progress-Aware Distillation reduces stagnation in distilled small language model agents, improving task success and completion efficiency across models and benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Standard positional encodings treat position as a one-dimensional reading-order coordinate, but reading order alone does not determine hierarchical textual structure. We use a hierarchical rotary positional encoding (hRoPE) that represents paragraph, sentence, and token indices as separate channels, hold the token sequence fixed, intervene on the paragraph coordinate $p_1$, and measure cross-paragraph attention with a token-distance-exact estimator. Attention is compressed in every corpus, but compression alone is not diagnostic of true structure: an architecturally identical channel with density-matched random labels is compressed too. What distinguishes real structure is the depth of compression: the real-versus-random depth gap is resolvable in two of three corpora and not in the third, and real-structure depth varies more strongly across corpora than the control's. Comparing eight corpus-only quantities across three constructs (lexical persistence, paragraph length, embedding-based coherence), none fully reproduces the cross-corpus ordering of depth, though embedding-based coherence comes closest. At the paragraph level that relation transfers as a common slope, but with the opposite sign to the corpus-level ranking: controlling for length, diversity, and position, paragraphs with more similar neighbors compress less deeply, with no detectable slope difference between any pair of corpora, while length, lexical-diversity, and position effects remain corpus-specific. Compression depth, not its location, is the reproducible signature of genuine paragraph structure in our setting.
bullets: Standard positional encodings capture reading order but not paragraph-level hierarchy.
The study uses hierarchical rotary positional encoding with separate paragraph, sentence, and token channels, intervening on paragraph indices while keeping tokens fixed.
Compression appears in all corpora, including random-label controls; the real-versus-random depth gap is detectable in two of three corpora.
Embedding-based coherence most closely tracks cross-corpus compression depth, but no corpus-only measure fully explains its ordering.
At the paragraph level, more similar neighboring paragraphs compress less deeply; length, lexical diversity, and position have corpus-specific effects.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes and analyzes hierarchical rotary positional encoding for LLMs, an architectural contribution to language foundation models.
papers.title: Paragraph Boundaries Are Not White Space:Compression Depth as the Signature of Hierarchical Structure
papers.tldr: Compression depth—not merely the presence or location of attention compression—best signals genuine hierarchical paragraph structure in this study.

papers.abstract: AI agents are usually evaluated by whether they complete a task. In interactive service settings, a successful agent can still frustrate users by asking repeated questions, performing redundant searches, or making avoidable revisions. We introduce RideWay, an efficiency-centered benchmark for ridehailing agents in a stateful tool-calling environment, together with Efficiency Utility, a success-gated metric that discounts successful trajectories for excess tool calls and user-facing turns relative to task-specific reference effort. Human paired preferences calibrate the relative penalties, reflecting an aggregate service-workflow trade-off: extra dialogue often creates visible friction, whereas extra tool use can sometimes verify constraints or preserve user intent. Across 58 tasks and 24 models, the fitted penalty for excess turns is about twice that for excess tool calls. On task-disjoint held-out preferences, Efficiency Utility achieves 78.7% accuracy overall: 90.6% when trajectories differ in turns, but chance-level accuracy when they differ solely in tool calls - the axis on which human annotators agree least. RideWay therefore makes interaction efficiency measurable alongside task success, while exposing the boundary of count-based tool-use evaluation.
bullets: Introduces a stateful ridehailing benchmark spanning 58 tasks and 24 models.
Proposes Efficiency Utility, a success-gated metric comparing excess turns and tool calls with task-specific reference effort.
Human preferences assign roughly twice as much penalty to excess user-facing turns as to excess tool calls.
The metric reaches 78.7% accuracy on held-out preferences, performing best when trajectories differ in turns.
Results show that count-based tool-use evaluation has limited validity when trajectories differ only in tool calls.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a benchmark for evaluating efficiency in tool-using language agents.
papers.title: RideWay: Benchmarking Efficient Task Completion for Tool-Using Language Agents
papers.tldr: RideWay benchmarks whether tool-using ridehailing agents complete tasks efficiently, not merely successfully, by penalizing unnecessary interaction and tool use.

papers.abstract: Many modern language models have adopted hybrid architectures that incorporate both linear-time recurrence and softmax attention. Modern recurrence layers provide a highly expressive mixing mechanism while ensuring high throughput by compressing contextual information into a fixed-size state, but underperform softmax attention in contextual information retrieval. In this paper, we reveal a Competing Learning phenomenon where different kinds of mixers compete to learn the same function, and when any layer learns a function, it suppresses the corresponding learning signal for other layers. Layer attribution analysis reveals that under typical data distributions, modern recurrence learns retrieval functions faster than softmax attention, causing attention to fail to learn retrieval in most cases. Stopping weight updates in recurrence in the middle of training helps attention learn retrieval. Based on these results, we propose a staged training procedure for pre-training hybrid architectures on natural language. Empirical results on models up to 1B parameters show that our method results in substantial improvement in language modeling loss, common-sense reasoning, as well as a wide range of retrieval-related tasks across different context lengths.
authors: Xingyu Shen, Yingfa Chen, Ziqing Qiao, Chaojun Xiao, Xu Han, Zhiyuan Liu
bullets: Modern recurrence offers efficient, expressive mixing but is weaker than softmax attention for contextual retrieval.
Different mixer types compete to learn the same functions, and early learning by one suppresses learning signals for others.
Recurrence typically learns retrieval faster than attention, often preventing attention from acquiring retrieval capabilities.
Freezing recurrence updates mid-training enables attention to learn retrieval; the paper uses this insight for staged pre-training.
Experiments up to 1B parameters report improvements in language modeling, commonsense reasoning, and retrieval tasks across context lengths.
papers.selection_reason: Studies training dynamics in hybrid LLM architectures, directly relevant to LLM architecture research.
papers.title: Competing Learning in Hybrid Architectures
papers.tldr: Hybrid language models can improve retrieval and overall performance by preventing recurrence layers from suppressing softmax attention during training.

papers.abstract: Memory-native evolution requires making memory an intrinsic capability of foundation models, enabling them to continuously accumulate and utilize information. To this end, we introduce MemT-1.0, a new architecture of memory foundation models that internalize memory as part of model computation. Building on Metis, MemT-1.0 employs Gated DeltaNet-2 with a stable token-level memory update mechanism within each turn. We further introduce Mixture-of-Storage to scale native memory capacity. Following a deliberate backbone preparation, we develop a two-stage training pipeline consisting of continued pre-training and post-training, supported by 34B tokens of training data and efficient training and inference infrastructure. We release a model family comprising MemT-1.0-Nano and MemT-1.0-Flash, and conduct a comprehensive evaluation of memory and general capabilities. The results show that they outperform the parametric memory baselines on average and remain competitive with retrieval-augmented methods, while largely preserving general capabilities. At a history length of 128K tokens, MemT-1.0-Nano achieves approximately $1.86\times$ end-to-end inference speedup and a $66\times$ reduction in persistent storage relative to full context KV cache. By internalizing retrieved procedural experience, MemT-1.0 improves task success on agentic tasks, providing a practical step toward memory-native evolution.
authors: Zhiyu Li, Zeyu Zhang, Linyun Liu, Yiwei Bu, Chenyang Xi, Xichong Zhang, Yi Yu, Yu Yu, Zhichen Liu, Yuxiao Yi, Chunyu Li, Haoran Liu, Zhenkai Ding, Le Zhou, Juncheng Zhang, Boyu Chen, Zehao Lin, Guorui Li, Renyu Fu, Ji Li, Youyang Xia, Jiajun Shen, Harvey Li, Jingsong Zhou, Helan Hu, Tong Shen, Tianxiao Xu, Chenye Han, Weijie Li, Zhongquan Zhou, Hongming Xu, Yuekeng Li, Erenkai Zhu, Peng Yu, Wenhao Li, Jingyi Kang, Xixuan Hao, Xuzhou Zhu, Can Chen, Jiawei Liu, Chen Jiang, Tao Jiang, Fangwei Xiang, Zepeng Yao, Kai Chen, Guang Yang, Mingfei Lu, Chunhui Li, Zhengxuan Jiang, Bo Tang, Shiyu Zhan, Yihang Sun, Jie Chu, Wenjun Xiong, Zhenxiang Hua, Chen Lin, Detong Su, Dongyu Deng, Qiuping Ding, Guofeng Ding, Si Chen, Guohua Wen, Xu Chen, Zhi-Qin John Xu, Ying-Cong Chen, Ningyu Zhang, Haofen Wang, Muning Wen, Haotian Chen, Wentao Zhang, Xuanhe Zhou, Rita Zhang, Junchi Yan, Feiyu Xiong
bullets: Introduces a memory-native architecture built on Metis and Gated DeltaNet-2 for stable token-level memory updates.
Uses Mixture-of-Storage to scale native memory capacity.
Trains the model through continued pre-training and post-training, yielding MemT-1.0-Nano and MemT-1.0-Flash.
Outperforms parametric-memory baselines on average and remains competitive with retrieval-augmented methods.
At 128K-token history, MemT-1.0-Nano provides approximately 1.86× faster end-to-end inference and 66× lower persistent storage than full-context KV cache.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a memory-native foundation-model architecture with internalized persistent memory, directly fitting LLM memory and foundation language model topics.
papers.title: MemT-1.0: Towards Memory-Native Evolution
papers.tldr: MemT-1.0 makes memory an intrinsic part of foundation-model computation, improving long-context efficiency and agentic task performance while preserving general capabilities.

papers.abstract: Safety alignment for large language models (LLMs) is primarily performed during post-training, while recent work has also begun incorporating safety data into pre-training. Yet safety can degrade when later training no longer includes safety data, and gains in safety often come at the cost of general capability. This tension suggests that safety and general reasoning should not be treated as separate training goals. We instead view safety as an LLM capability that can be learned through a reasoning structure shared with general tasks. Both require the model to understand intent or task goals, apply relevant knowledge, and reason about potential consequences. We introduce safety mid-training, a stage between pre-training and post-training that jointly develops safety and general reasoning through this shared structure. Given safety and utility prompts, the base model generates structured documents and reasoning traces that are then used for mid-training. Safety mid-training reduces average attack success rate (ASR) by 72% to 81% relative to Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B base models, while also improving general capability. The benefits persist through subsequent post-training. After general-only SFT, mid-trained models largely retain their safety, achieving lower ASR than the baselines without sacrificing general capability. They also retain safety under general-only GRPO without safety rewards, while subsequent RL reaches a better safety-utility frontier when initialized from the mid-trained models. Together, these results suggest that learning safety and general reasoning within a shared mid-training stage can reduce the safety-utility trade-off and make safety more robust to subsequent training.
authors: Zhengyue Zhao, Liwei Jiang, Yejin Choi, Chaowei Xiao1
bullets: Motivation: Safety learned mainly during post-training can be forgotten during later training and may reduce general capability.
Method: Between pre-training and post-training, models learn from structured safety and utility documents and reasoning traces generated by the base model.
Key result: The approach reduces average attack success rate by 72%–81% versus Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B base models while improving general capability.
Robustness: Models largely retain safety after general-only SFT and GRPO, even without safety rewards.
Implication: Treating safety and reasoning as shared capabilities can reduce the safety–utility trade-off and improve training robustness.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a training stage for LLM safety and reasoning, directly relevant to LLM foundation-model research.
papers.title: Safety Mid-Training: Internalizing LLM Safety as a Foundational Capability
papers.tldr: Safety mid-training jointly teaches LLMs safety and general reasoning before post-training, making safety more persistent while improving general capability.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation can transfer the reasoning capabilities of a strong teacher to a smaller student. However, distillation from a stronger teacher model faces two mismatches: its solutions may be difficult for a smaller student to imitate, and its token-level probabilities may be incompatible with, or even unavailable to, the student. Existing methods handle these settings through different forms of supervision. To this end, we propose Bridged Self-Distillation (BSD), a unified framework for distilling from any teacher that provides reasoning traces. The model to be distilled from, termed the external teacher, first provides a reasoning trace as privileged context, which can be generated in an offline fashion. The student generates rollouts without this context, while a copy of the student conditioned on it, serving as the self-teacher, scores the same rollouts in the student's own token space. BSD uses the resulting token-level guidance to adjust updates on unsuccessful rollouts, with a verifier providing the outcome signal. As the external teacher is queried only to produce text, the same training procedure applies to all teacher scenarios: shared-tokenizer, cross-tokenizer, and closed API teachers. Across these scenarios, BSD improves over the base model and outperforms baselines tailored to each scenario, offering a novel and unified pathway for distillation. Code is available: https://github.com/TUMLegalTech/Bridged-Self-Distillation
authors: Runsheng Chen (Technical University of Munich, Germany), Yihong Liu (LMU Munich, Germany, Munich Center for Machine Learning, Germany), Raoyuan Zhao (LMU Munich, Germany, Munich Center for Machine Learning, Germany), Michael A. Hedderich (LMU Munich, Germany, Munich Center for Machine Learning, Germany), Hinrich Sch\"utze (LMU Munich, Germany, Munich Center for Machine Learning, Germany), Matthias Grabmair (Technical University of Munich, Germany)
bullets: Addresses two challenges: teacher solutions may be hard to imitate, and teacher token probabilities may be incompatible or unavailable.
The external teacher supplies reasoning traces, which can be generated offline; the student then learns without access to those traces at rollout time.
A trace-conditioned copy of the student scores the student’s rollouts in the student’s own token space.
A verifier identifies unsuccessful rollouts, and BSD uses the self-teacher’s guidance to adjust their updates.
Works with shared-tokenizer, cross-tokenizer, and closed-API teachers, improving over the base model and scenario-specific baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a unified distillation framework for LLM reasoning traces, relevant to LLM training and model improvement.
papers.title: Bridged Self-Distillation for On-Policy Learning
papers.tldr: Bridged Self-Distillation transfers reasoning from diverse teachers to smaller students by using teacher-generated traces as context for a self-teacher that provides compatible token-level guidance.

papers.abstract: An inference budget is useful only when the system delivers an answer within it. We study a fixed-budget policy combining first-valid-box stopping with a charged finalization cue. On 100 fresh, independently audited GSM8K test questions per model, it improves delivered endpoint accuracy over first-box stopping by 8.0 percentage points for Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 and 7.0 for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B. A prelocked repeat on the same questions gives 7.0 and 10.0 points; neither seed shows a gross harm relative to first-box stopping. The point estimates of incremental physical-slot savings are below one percent. A finalization-only ablation separates cue recovery from stopping, and a fixed scalar reader tests extraction as an alternative explanation. The cue is prior art; the contribution is a component and readout analysis with charged injections and verified paths. Results cover two checkpoints, one task, one prompt family, and two fixed seed conditions.
authors: Yupeng Chang, Linyuan Gao, Zhiyuan Li, Yuan Wu, Yi Chang
bullets: Evaluated on 100 independently audited GSM8K test questions per model using Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B.
Improved endpoint accuracy over first-box stopping by 8.0 and 7.0 percentage points, respectively; a prelocked repeat yielded 7.0 and 10.0 points.
Finalization-only ablations and a fixed scalar reader distinguish cue recovery, stopping, and extraction effects.
Incremental physical-slot savings were below 1%, and no seed showed gross harm relative to first-box stopping.
Scope is limited to two checkpoints, one task, one prompt family, and two fixed seed conditions.
papers.selection_reason: Fixed-budget stopping and finalization policy for LLM answer delivery under shared token budgets.
papers.title: Answer Delivery Under a Shared Token Budget: An Audited Study of Stopping and Finalization
papers.tldr: A charged finalization cue combined with first-valid-box stopping improves delivered GSM8K endpoint accuracy under a shared token budget, though physical-slot savings are negligible.

papers.abstract: Test-time scaling can improve LLM reasoning, but existing approaches typically adapt generation or apply answer selection after a predetermined generation schedule. We study within-instance allocation: under a hard per-instance prompt-plus-completion token cap, when should inference stop, generate another candidate, or spend residual tokens adjudicating candidates already observed? BOSS is a training-free policy for this three-way decision, with worst-case budget checks before every generation and judge call. Its key contribution is online generation-adjudication allocation under one shared token ledger. Across two Llama-3.1 models and four reasoning benchmarks, BOSS attains the highest accuracy in 22 of 24 model-task-budget cells under the common hard cap. At Llama-3.1-8B and B=4k, it reaches 60.5 macro-average accuracy versus 58.6 for Adaptive-Consistency, 59.1 for TALE-EP, and 58.9 for fixed-schedule League. On identical Stage-I candidate pools, randomized A/B judging with repeated voting improves plurality from 58.4 to 60.3, with the full BOSS selector reaching 60.5. Approximately matched-cost controls further characterize how the benefit of adjudication changes with available inference budget. Together, these results establish generation-adjudication allocation as a distinct design axis for reasoning under strict per-instance caps.
authors: Yupeng Chang, Yahan Li, Chenlu Guo, Diana Inkpen, Yuan Wu, Yi Chang
bullets: Addresses within-instance inference allocation rather than relying on fixed generation schedules or post-hoc selection.
Uses a training-free policy with worst-case token checks before every generation and judge call.
Maintains one shared token ledger for online generation and adjudication decisions.
Achieves the highest accuracy in 22 of 24 model-task-budget settings across two Llama-3.1 models and four reasoning benchmarks.
At Llama-3.1-8B with a 4k-token cap, BOSS reaches 60.5 macro-average accuracy; its scope is reasoning under hard per-instance token caps.
papers.selection_reason: Token-budgeted online sampling and adjudication for LLM reasoning under hard per-instance caps.
papers.title: BOSS: Token-Budgeted Online Sampling and Selection for LLM Reasoning
papers.tldr: BOSS adaptively decides whether to stop, generate another reasoning candidate, or adjudicate existing candidates under a strict per-instance token budget.

papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods are critical for adapting large models under resource-constrained settings. However, as mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures, which offer efficient inference at massive parameter scales, gain increasing prevalence in the community, a critical gap arising from the lack of systematic recipes for applying PEFT to MoE models. To narrow this gap, we conduct a large-scale systematic study that investigates a set of essential design recipes, including which modules should be adapted, which granularity should be used to adapt MoE modules, which PEFT method to use, and to what extent should the load-balancing objective be used, across three MoE backbones on downstream tasks and general knowledge tasks. Our experiments yield several key insights. First, adapting MoE experts alone achieves the highest downstream performance with competitive general capability retention under a comparable parameter budget. Second, native expert-weight updates offer a better downstream--retention trade-off than adapters that bypass experts or entire MoE modules. Third, LoRA and DoRA together define the strongest operating region for high downstream accuracy among the evaluated PEFT methods. Fourth, no nonzero load-balancing coefficient Pareto-dominates the zero baseline. We finally evaluate a weight-level redesign of MoE$^2$-LoRA on Qwen3. Moving its module-level bypass pool into native expert weights improves all four upstream endpoints by 2.4 to 17.9 points with 17% fewer trainable parameters and a 3.2-point average downstream cost.
authors: Minglei Li, Peng Ye, Haonan He, Jingqi Ye, Qingyu Yang, Tao Chen
bullets: Studies PEFT design choices across three MoE backbones, downstream tasks, and general-knowledge tasks.
Adapting experts alone achieves the strongest downstream performance while retaining general capabilities under similar parameter budgets.
Native expert-weight updates provide a better performance–retention trade-off than bypassing experts or whole MoE modules.
LoRA and DoRA form the strongest operating region for downstream accuracy; nonzero load-balancing coefficients do not Pareto-dominate zero.
A redesigned MoE²-LoRA that moves its bypass pool into expert weights improves four upstream endpoints by 2.4–17.9 points with 17% fewer trainable parameters.
papers.selection_reason: Systematic PEFT study for MoE LLMs, directly relevant to LLM architecture and adaptation.
papers.title: An Empirical Study of Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
papers.tldr: A systematic study finds that PEFT for MoE LLMs works best when directly adapting native expert weights, especially with LoRA or DoRA, while omitting load-balancing objectives.

papers.abstract: When a user supplies a document and wants the answer drawn from it, a language model is expected to follow it even when it contradicts its parametric knowledge. Prior work has focused on making the model rely on context by steering activations, contrasting logits during decoding, or instructing it in plain language. We ask whether the document alone, with no instruction written into it and no access to the model at inference time, is enough. We optimize a document suffix by discrete token search, starting from the answer to a single question and extending the objective to a set of passages, to multi-hop questions that follow from the planted fact, and to later turns of a conversation. On counterfactual passages that contradict parametric knowledge of the model, the suffix flips nearly all items the model resists across three instruction-tuned model families, in most settings outperforms the decoding baseline and the strongest instruction we could write, and matches activation steering. Controls show that the suffix largely acts through the passage rather than injecting the answer, and a single suffix per model transfers to unseen passages. Each extended objective carries the effect to its target, so the objective, not only the document, sets how far the effect reaches.
authors: Gia-Bao Dinh Ho, Sekh Mainul Islam, Masahiro Kaneko, Timothy Baldwin, Isabelle Augenstein
bullets: The work studies whether a document alone can override a model’s parametric knowledge.
It uses discrete token search to optimize suffixes for single questions, passage sets, multi-hop reasoning, and later conversation turns.
On counterfactual passages, suffixes flip nearly all resisted items across three instruction-tuned model families.
They usually outperform decoding-based intervention and written instructions, and match activation steering.
Controls suggest the effect mainly operates through the passage; model-specific suffixes also transfer to unseen passages.
papers.selection_reason: Studies optimized suffixes to steer language-model context following, relevant to LLM behavior and instruction-following.
papers.title: Shaping the Document, Not the Model: Optimized Suffixes for Context Following
papers.tldr: Optimized document suffixes can make language models follow contradictory context without modifying the model or adding instructions at inference time.

papers.abstract: Tool-using voice agents often leave users waiting after speech ends, even when actionable information arrives earlier in the request. Speculative approaches begin work during speech, but chunk-bounded or interrupt-on-update generation can truncate a tool call before its arguments are complete. This couples computation time to speech updates, limiting useful work completed in advance. We introduce Heartbeat Thinking, which handles updated input through new Thinker invocations while allowing ongoing invocations and dispatched tools to finish. Periodic invocations read the latest partial transcript and a shared record of completed reasoning and tool results. These results help resolve missing arguments and initiate dependent calls, allowing preparation to progress across speech updates. Across SpeechFCEval, FDBench v3, and AudioCRAG, Heartbeat improves aggregate speculative tool coverage or retrieval reuse over a SHANKS-style windowed baseline, with benchmark-dependent effects on final task quality. On FDBench v3, it increases tool coverage by 16 percentage points and reduces mean final-response latency by 36.4\%. The results show that heartbeat thinking paradigm preserving ongoing computation during speech can turn listening time into reusable preparation for faster and more capable voice-agent responses.
authors: Zhenyu Zhang, Kewei Fu, Yongqi Tong, Chenzhi Zheng, Wei Wu, Jiang-Ming Yang, Jianshe Li
bullets: Addresses wasted listening time and truncated tool calls in realtime voice agents.
Starts new Thinker invocations on updated partial transcripts while preserving ongoing reasoning and dispatched tools.
Shares completed reasoning and tool results to fill missing arguments and launch dependent calls.
Across three benchmarks, it improves speculative tool coverage or retrieval reuse, with benchmark-dependent effects on final quality.
On FDBench v3, tool coverage rises by 16 percentage points and mean final-response latency falls by 36.4%.
papers.selection_reason: Concerns tool-using LLM voice agents with speculative execution and latency reduction, relevant to LLM deployment and reasoning.
papers.title: Heartbeat Thinking: Speculative Reasoning and Tool Execution While Listening in Realtime Voice Agents
papers.tldr: Heartbeat Thinking lets voice agents continue and reuse speculative reasoning and tool calls across speech updates, reducing post-speech response latency.

papers.abstract: Subword tokenization methods such as Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) are a core component of modern language models; yet, tokenizer capacity remains typically determined by a fixed merge budget, chosen heuristically. Since larger vocabularies increase memory usage and computational cost, selecting compact and effective token inventories is essential for efficient language modeling. We study the optimization of a BPE merge budget as a statistical model selection problem and investigate information-theoretic criteria for \emph{computing optimal merge sets} directly from corpus statistics. To further improve the merge selection in limited data conditions, we augment the BPE training corpora with synthetic texts generated from the original data, providing estimates for the unigram and bigram distributions. Experiments across multiple corpora and downstream tasks show that using a principled vocabulary selection technique reduces model size, with little degradation in performance. We further observe that synthetic data can yield better tokenizers, especially in low-resource settings.
bullets: Fixed BPE merge budgets are often chosen heuristically, despite their impact on memory and computation.
The study uses information-theoretic criteria and corpus statistics to compute effective merge sets directly.
Synthetic text augmentation improves unigram and bigram estimates for tokenizer selection in limited-data settings.
Experiments across corpora and downstream tasks find reduced model size with little degradation in performance.
Synthetic data is especially helpful for tokenizer quality in low-resource settings.
papers.selection_reason: The paper addresses the optimization of BPE merge budgets for language models, treating the selection process as a statistical model selection problem to reduce memory and computational cost. This is directly relevant to the architecture and efficiency of Large Language Models.
papers.title: Rethinking BPE: Merge Selection as Model Selection
papers.tldr: BPE merge budgets can be selected as a statistical model-selection problem to build smaller token vocabularies with little performance loss.

papers.abstract: While language models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities, their performance remains disproportionately skewed towards high-resource languages. This disparity is particularly acute for the 700 million inhabitants of Southeast Asia, where vast linguistic diversity remains under-represented in existing benchmarks, often suffering from limited language coverage or narrow task scopes. To address this, we introduce DeepSEA, a comprehensive benchmark constructed from established datasets through professional human translation into 12 Southeast Asian languages, spanning both high-resource (e.g., Indonesian, Thai, Vietnamese) and low-resource (e.g., Burmese, Khmer, Lao) tiers across five distinct tasks: mathematical reasoning, scientific reasoning, question answering, abstractive summarization, and machine translation. Extensive evaluation of frontier proprietary and open-weights models reveals that while frontier models like Gemini-3.7-Flash maintain robustness across resource tiers, smaller models face severe performance degradation on low-resource languages. Crucially, models perform better in reasoning and summarization when pivoted through English rather than target languages, exposing a critical dependency on English representations, especially for low-resource languages. Beyond these observations, we provide a cross-lingual error analysis and a cross-script tokenizer fertility analysis. We hope these findings shed light on the development of next-generation inclusive multilingual models.
authors: Jiuzhou Han, Abhishek Bijay Mishra, Trevor Cohn, Shubham Mittal
bullets: Covers five tasks: mathematical reasoning, scientific reasoning, question answering, abstractive summarization, and machine translation.
Includes professionally translated data across high-resource and low-resource Southeast Asian languages, including Burmese, Khmer, and Lao.
Frontier models are relatively robust across language-resource tiers, while smaller models degrade sharply on low-resource languages.
Reasoning and summarization improve when models pivot through English rather than using target languages directly.
Provides cross-lingual error analysis and cross-script tokenizer fertility analysis to diagnose multilingual limitations.
papers.selection_reason: Multilingual evaluation benchmark for Southeast Asian languages, relevant to LLM evaluation and multilingual capabilities.
papers.title: DeepSEA: A Multilingual Evaluation Benchmark for Southeast Asia
papers.tldr: DeepSEA benchmarks multilingual model performance across 12 Southeast Asian languages and shows that low-resource languages remain especially challenging, with models often relying on English for reasoning and summarization.

papers.abstract: External skills provide language-model agents with reusable procedural knowledge, yet how models use such knowledge after it is supplied remains poorly understood.
