We identify Procedural Exposure Bias (PEB), the tendency of language models to increasingly favor an action as its associated procedural pattern is repeatedly exposed in a skill, even when the interaction state and action relevance remain unchanged. We find that PEB strongly depends on how procedural knowledge is represented: presenting the same content visually substantially attenuates exposure-induced shifts in action preference relative to textual presentation. Further analysis shows that this attenuation primarily arises from visual encoding rather than structured layout. Although repeated procedural signals remain recoverable from Visual representations, they exert a weaker influence on downstream action prediction, distinguishing signal accessibility from its use as action evidence. This effect also extends to executable action selection, where increasing exposure more strongly favors the corresponding action under Text than Visual. Layer-wise analyses show that exposure-dependent action evidence becomes more pronounced toward the model output, with stronger evidence under Text, while activation interventions reveal architecture-specific roles of internal components in transmitting or counteracting the preference shift. Complete-agent evaluations across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and WebShop further show that Visual skills achieve higher macro-average task success than Text skills for all four evaluated models. These findings establish skill representation as an important factor governing how procedural knowledge is translated into agent decisions. All code is available at https://github.com/NEUIR/Vis-Skill.
authors: Qing Yang, Yuqi Xiong, Pengcheng Huang, Zhipeng Xu, Zhenghao Liu, Zulong Chen, Yu Gu, Ge Yu
bullets: Identifies Procedural Exposure Bias (PEB): repeated procedural patterns increasingly influence action preferences even when state and relevance are unchanged.
The bias is much stronger with textual than visual skill representations; visual encoding, rather than structured layout alone, drives the attenuation.
Visual representations preserve recoverable procedural signals but reduce their use as evidence for downstream action prediction.
Layer-wise and activation analyses show that exposure-dependent action evidence grows toward model output and involves architecture-specific components.
Across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and WebShop, Visual skills achieve higher macro-average task success than Text skills for all evaluated models.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates Procedural Exposure Bias in skill-augmented language model agents operating in embodied environments (ALFWorld, ScienceWorld). Relevant to both embodied AI and LLMs.
papers.title: Procedural Exposure Bias in Skill-Augmented Language Model Agents
papers.tldr: Repeated textual exposure to procedural skills can bias language-model agents toward associated actions, while visual representations substantially reduce this effect and improve task success.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models enable parallel token generation, offering a promising alternative to sequential autoregressive decoding. Existing acceleration methods use predictive confidence to enable parallel token commitment while preserving generation quality. However, confidence-based selection prioritizes reliable token predictions without explicitly considering how token positions shape the remaining decoding schedule. Moreover, such ordering does not always reflect inter-token dependencies, suggesting that confidence need not be the sole criterion for token selection. Motivated by this limitation, we propose Balance-Aware Pivot Decoding (BPD), which favors central pivots within contiguous masked intervals and decodes the selected positions in parallel. Balanced pivots yield logarithmic decoding depth in the interval length. Our practical method accounts for model uncertainty by combining confidence-based prefilling with confidence-thresholded center selection. We evaluate the resulting quality-efficiency tradeoff on LLaDA and Dream across five mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction-following benchmarks. Our implementation is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DLM_random_pivot-EE62/
authors: Yejin Lee, Hyundong Jin, Yo-Sub Han
bullets: Confidence-only decoding overlooks the structure of remaining masked intervals and token dependencies.
BPD selects central pivots within contiguous masked spans, decoding selected positions in parallel.
Balanced pivoting provides logarithmic decoding depth with respect to interval length.
The practical strategy combines confidence-based prefilling with confidence-thresholded center selection.
Evaluated on LLaDA and Dream across mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction-following benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Balance-aware pivot selection for parallel diffusion LLM decoding, improving efficiency via token selection.
papers.title: Balance-Aware Pivot Selection for Parallel Diffusion LLM Decoding
papers.tldr: Balance-Aware Pivot Decoding accelerates diffusion LLM generation by combining confidence with center-focused parallel token selection to reduce decoding depth.

papers.abstract: Looped transformers reuse a shared block of layers to increase computational depth without increasing the number of trainable parameters. They are trained with backpropagation through time (BPTT). To save training compute, BPTT is often truncated to the last few loops, although this may weaken the benefit of looping. To study this tradeoff systematically, we jointly vary model size, training tokens, and forward and backward loop counts across nearly 600 training runs and fit a unified scaling law that captures the effects of looping and truncation through effective parameters. Despite the training-compute savings of truncation, our fitted law favors full BPTT when forward and backward loop counts are jointly optimized. In matched-compute runs, full BPTT through fewer loops consistently outperforms truncated settings of the same compute. The law further shows that at fixed model size, the compute-optimal loop count and training-token budget both grow with compute. When model size is also free, the law identifies two fully trained loops as the best looped setting. Experimentally, this setting achieves lower loss than the compute-optimal non-looped model with about 27% fewer non-embedding parameters and only 8% more training compute.
authors: Xuyuan Xiong, Siyu Chen, Zihan Shao, Yue Su, Weiyang Jin, Ping Luo, Zhuoran Yang, Xihui Liu
bullets: Looped transformers reuse a shared layer block to add depth without adding trainable parameters.
The study varies model size, training tokens, and forward/backward loop counts across nearly 600 runs.
A unified scaling law models looping and truncation using effective parameters.
When compute is matched, full BPTT with fewer loops consistently beats truncated BPTT.
With model size optimized, two fully trained loops achieve lower loss than a compute-optimal non-looped model using about 27% fewer non-embedding parameters and 8% more training compute.
papers.selection_reason: Scaling study of looped transformers with truncated backpropagation; relevant to LLM architecture advances and training-efficiency tradeoffs.
papers.title: Truncate or Not? A Scaling Study of Looped Transformers with Truncated Backpropagation
papers.tldr: A large scaling study finds that full backpropagation through looped transformers is generally better than truncated training, with two fully trained loops offering an efficient tradeoff.

papers.abstract: Building capable language models for India requires scalable multilingual data and robust evaluation. We introduce Nemotron-Pretraining-Indic-v1, a synthetic pretraining corpus of approximately 2.83 trillion tokens covering all 22 scheduled Indian languages in native script and twelve in romanized form. It is the largest openly released Indic pretraining corpus. Using our GPU-accelerated pipeline, we translate curated English documents, assess translation quality, and repair low-quality outputs while preserving technical content and document structure and maintaining source traceability. Through continued-pretraining experiments across twelve languages, we show that combining our synthetic corpus with natural Indic text improves knowledge and reasoning over a public-corpus baseline. Additional experiments show how data volume, script coverage, and Indic training share affect English performance. We also introduce the Indic-LLM-Eval-Suite, a multilingual benchmark suite for evaluating Indic language models across chat, instruction following, reasoning, knowledge, code, and translation. The suite combines existing Indic benchmarks with task-aware translations of English benchmarks, using automated quality assessment, targeted correction, and native-speaker review in a human-in-the-loop pipeline. We use the suite to comprehensively benchmark contemporary open-weight Indic and multilingual models across capabilities and languages, revealing substantial variation across tasks and languages. Together, these resources provide a scalable foundation for developing and evaluating more capable Indic language models.
authors: Abhinav Khattar (NVIDIA), Aishwarya Chhabra (NVIDIA), Ameya Velingker (NVIDIA), Anusha Kamath (NVIDIA), Brandon Norick (NVIDIA), Kanishk Singla (NVIDIA), Kiran Praveen (NVIDIA), Markus Kliegl (NVIDIA), Mohammad Qazim Bhat (NVIDIA), Mostofa Patwary (NVIDIA), Niket Agarwal (NVIDIA), Rajpreet Thethy (NVIDIA), Ramani Akkati (NVIDIA), Raviraj Joshi (NVIDIA), Sai Nishanth Padala (NVIDIA), Shuoyang Ding (NVIDIA), Sriharsha Niverty (NVIDIA), Utkarsh Vaidya (NVIDIA), Vitaly Lavrukhin (NVIDIA), Yev Meyer (NVIDIA), Anoop Kunchukuttan (AI4Bharat), Mitesh Khapra (AI4Bharat), Mohammed Safi Ur Rahman Khan (AI4Bharat), Rudra Murthy (AI4Bharat), Sumanth Doddapaneni (AI4Bharat), Thanmay Jayakumar (AI4Bharat), Ujjwal Sharma (AI4Bharat)
bullets: The corpus contains approximately 2.83 trillion tokens across all 22 scheduled Indian languages in native scripts and 12 in romanized form.
A GPU-accelerated pipeline translates curated English data, evaluates and repairs low-quality outputs, preserves structure and technical content, and maintains source traceability.
Continued-pretraining experiments across 12 languages find that combining synthetic data with natural Indic text improves knowledge and reasoning over a public-corpus baseline.
The Indic-LLM-Eval-Suite covers chat, instruction following, reasoning, knowledge, code, and translation using translated benchmarks plus native-speaker review.
Benchmarking open-weight models reveals substantial variation across tasks and languages; experiments also examine data volume, script coverage, and Indic-data share effects on English performance.
papers.selection_reason: Large-scale synthetic pretraining corpus and evaluation suite for Indic LLMs, relevant to LLM pretraining and evaluation.
papers.title: Scaling Synthetic Pre-training Data and Evaluation for Indic LLMs
papers.tldr: The work releases a large synthetic Indic pretraining corpus and multilingual evaluation suite to support scalable development and assessment of Indic LLMs.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) enables constant-bit-size transformers to perform general-purpose computation through generated tokens (Li and Wang, 2025a), whereas looped transformers carry out the same computation by recurrence in hidden states (latent thought). We construct a family of constant-bit-size looped transformers that interpolates between CoT and latent thought. For a prescribed loop count $L=L(n)$ and a fixed integer $k\ge1$ satisfying $s(n)^{1/k}=\Omega(L)$, our transformer simulates a time-$t(n)$, space-$s(n)$ Turing machine using a context window of $O(s(n)/L)$ and $O(t(n)s(n)^{1/k}/L)$ generated tokens, reducing both resources by a factor of $L$ relative to the corresponding unlooped queue-machine simulation. The construction also holds with softmax attention at constant bit-size, under the finite-precision kernel specified in this paper.
bullets: Bridges explicit CoT, which uses generated tokens, and latent thought, which uses recurrence in hidden states.
For loop count L=L(n) and fixed k≥1 with s(n)^(1/k)=Ω(L), the model simulates a time-t(n), space-s(n) Turing machine.
Uses context window O(s(n)/L) and O(t(n)s(n)^(1/k)/L) generated tokens.
These resources are each reduced by a factor of L relative to the corresponding unlooped queue-machine simulation.
The construction also works with constant-bit-size softmax attention under the paper’s finite-precision kernel.
papers.selection_reason: Theoretical construction of looped transformers that internalize chain-of-thought, reducing context and generated tokens; relevant to LLM architecture and efficiency.
papers.title: Internalizing Chain-of-thought into Looped Transformers
papers.tldr: A constant-bit-size looped transformer can internalize chain-of-thought into recurrent hidden-state computation while reducing context and generated-token requirements by a factor of the loop count.

papers.abstract: Generative modeling of discrete data has two popular paradigms: autoregressive models such as GPT, which factorize a sequence in a left-to-right (L2R) order, and masked diffusion models, which are essentially any-order autoregressive modeling. Rather than competing methods, these are the two extreme points of a single axis -- the generation order. For structured discrete domains without a natural traversal, both extremes may be suboptimal, yet the intermediate choice -- a single well-adapted order -- remains largely unexplored. We introduce OrderGPT, which builds on Any-Order GPT to learn a task-level generation order without canonical-order supervision. Our key observation is that predicting variables from randomly sampled reveal prefixes produces recurring attention patterns in the backbone that provide a model-dependent signal of predictive dependencies. We aggregate this signal into a reciprocal dependency graph and use a spectral teacher to derive continuous generation priorities. A lightweight OrderMLP integrated into the GPT backbone learns to predict these priorities from attention, incorporating order learning into the architecture within a single training run. Training gradually shifts toward the learned order, which is then frozen for subsequent autoregressive training and generation. The same mechanism adapts across modalities: adaptively it recovers near-L2R dependency structure in language, learns anatomically organized factorizations on human pose, and discovers a factorization on tabular data that places statistically and semantically related fields nearby, while improving downstream modeling metrics across all domains. The code is available at https://github.com/Chenhe-yang/OrderGPT/.
authors: Chenhe Yang, Yuhuan Lyu, Tianyang Hu
bullets: Targets structured domains where neither left-to-right nor fully arbitrary generation order is ideal.
Extracts predictive dependencies from attention patterns under randomly sampled reveal prefixes.
Builds a reciprocal dependency graph and uses a spectral teacher to produce continuous generation priorities.
An OrderMLP learns these priorities within the GPT backbone during a single training run, after which the order is frozen.
Adapts across language, human pose, and tabular data, improving downstream modeling metrics across these domains.
papers.selection_reason: Learnable generation order for GPT-style models is a meaningful architectural contribution relevant to LLM foundation models.
papers.title: OrderGPT: Generation Order as a Learnable Modeling Choice
papers.tldr: OrderGPT learns a task-specific generation order for discrete data, bridging fixed-order autoregressive and any-order masked diffusion models.

papers.abstract: Inference-time sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) decoding can improve the reasoning accuracy of masked diffusion language models (diffusion LLMs) without post-training by resampling a population of partial generations according to a reward. Its effectiveness therefore depends on the resampling step, which must concentrate computation on promising candidates while retaining enough diversity to explore alternative reasoning paths. The reward can be internal, the decoder's own confidence on the committed prefix, or external, a process reward model scoring that prefix. Under either reward, multinomial resampling can disrupt this balance by duplicating high-weight particles and discarding lineages that may still reach a correct solution. The effective sample size (ESS) does not register this loss: multinomial resampling resets it to its maximum even as distinct lineages disappear. To retain such lineages, we introduce lineage-preserving SMC (LP-SMC), which combines Chopthin resampling with an input weight floor. Instead of equalizing weights, Chopthin bounds the ratio between the largest and smallest weights it returns and carries the unequal weights forward. The floor limits how far below the maximum a weight may fall before resampling so that lineages with low early weight keep a chance to recover. Across mathematical-reasoning and code-generation benchmarks on two base models, LP-SMC raises oracle coverage, the fraction of problems with at least one correct particle, in every setting, by 1.8 to 25.6 points, and raises end-to-end accuracy under a common reward-model selector in eleven of twelve settings, by up to 7.9 points on LLaDA-1.5 and 18.3 on Dream-7B. The coverage gain persists under the external reward model, which suggests that diversity-preserving resampling and the guidance signal contribute separately to inference-time search.
authors: Minoo Ahmadi, Seyedarmin Azizi, Mehdi Kamal, Massoud Pedram
bullets: SMC enhances inference-time search by resampling partial generations according to internal confidence or external process rewards.
Multinomial resampling can duplicate high-weight candidates and eliminate alternative lineages, while ESS may miss this diversity loss.
LP-SMC combines Chopthin resampling with a weight floor to preserve unequal weights and give low-scoring lineages opportunities to recover.
Across two base models and multiple reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, LP-SMC improved oracle coverage in every setting and end-to-end accuracy in 11 of 12 settings.
Coverage gains also persisted with an external reward model, indicating separate benefits from diversity preservation and reward guidance.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces diversity-preserving inference-time SMC decoding for diffusion LLMs, directly relevant to LLM decoding and reasoning.
papers.title: Keep the Lineages Alive: Diversity-Preserving SMC for Diffusion LLM Decoding
papers.tldr: Lineage-preserving SMC improves diffusion-LLM reasoning and code-generation decoding by maintaining diverse candidate trajectories during reward-guided resampling.

papers.abstract: Deep research agents are increasingly capable of searching the open web and synthesizing evidence, yet they remain poorly suited to controllable report generation in multimodal deep research. This task requires agents to handle interleaved textual and visual inputs, gather multimodal evidence through multi-step web search, and deliver comprehensive illustrated reports under user-specified requirements. Existing systems face two limitations. During reasoning, they often underuse images discovered along the search trajectory; during generation, they tend to produce fixed-form answers with limited control over report granularity, multimodal composition, and evidence grounding. We introduce MIRA, a Multimodal Illustrated Deep Research Agent for controllable reports. MIRA integrates textual and visual evidence throughout research and writing. At its core, MIRA-Harness translates user requirements into generation contracts and connects four stages: evidence collection, report submission, feedback-driven revision, and final delivery. Building on this harness, MIRA-Data constructs high-quality multi-hop multimodal research trajectories, and we post-train foundation models to operate within the workflow. Using Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, MIRA achieves state-of-the-art performance among open agents on 7 representative, established multimodal-search and deep-research-agent benchmarks, while producing user-aligned illustrated reports with traceable textual and visual evidence.
authors: Hongrui Wu, Kaiwen Tuo, Congcong Wang, Gen Li, Shuai Dong, Xinlei Yu, Yuqi Xu, Haowen Hou, Zelin Peng, Jiaqi Wang
bullets: Addresses weak image use during web research and limited control over report structure, granularity, and evidence grounding.
MIRA-Harness converts user requirements into generation contracts across evidence collection, submission, revision, and delivery.
MIRA-Data provides multi-hop multimodal research trajectories for post-training foundation models within this workflow.
Using Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, MIRA achieves state-of-the-art results among open agents on seven multimodal-search and deep-research benchmarks.
Produces user-aligned illustrated reports grounded in traceable textual and visual evidence.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces MIRA, a multimodal deep research agent for controllable reports. This involves multimodal reasoning and instruction following, relevant to multimodal and large language foundation models.
papers.title: MIRA: A Multimodal Illustrated Deep Research Agent for Controllable Reports
papers.tldr: MIRA is a multimodal deep-research agent that uses textual and visual evidence to generate controllable, illustrated reports with traceable citations.

papers.abstract: Sequential knowledge editing in Large Language Models (LLMs) often leads to a degradation of general capabilities due to cumulative parameter interference. In this paper, we revisit prominent projection-based methods like AlphaEdit and reveal a surprising mismatch: their robustness is primarily driven by update regularization rather than the intended null-space projection. Based on this insight, we propose FisherEdit, a theoretically grounded method built on Fisher geometry, which replaces coarse activation-space projections with importance-aware regularization in parameter space. It penalizes changes to sensitive parameters more strongly while retaining flexibility for new facts, and admits an efficient row-wise closed-form solution. Experiments on Llama-3, Qwen2.5, and Olmo-3 across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that FisherEdit achieves state-of-the-art performance while better preserving model stability and downstream task accuracy.
authors: Yizhou Yang, Jiahong Fu, Zhiwu Wang, Kailong Fan, Haokun Lin, Yichen Wu, Zhenan Sun, Renzhen Wang, Deyu Meng
bullets: Sequential editing can cause cumulative parameter interference and degrade general abilities.
The paper finds that projection-based methods’ robustness mainly comes from update regularization, not null-space projection.
FisherEdit penalizes changes to sensitive parameters more strongly while allowing flexibility for new facts.
Its Fisher-geometry formulation has an efficient row-wise closed-form solution.
Experiments across Llama-3, Qwen2.5, and Olmo-3 show strong performance and improved preservation of downstream accuracy.
papers.selection_reason: Fisher information-guided knowledge editing for LLMs, addressing sequential editing and stability, relevant to model adaptation and memory.
papers.title: FisherEdit: Fisher Information Guided Knowledge Editing for Large Language Models
papers.tldr: FisherEdit uses Fisher-information-guided parameter regularization to add knowledge while better preserving LLM stability and general capabilities.

papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) have achieved strong performance on challenging mathematical and scientific tasks through long chain-of-thought reasoning, but they often suffer from overthinking with unnecessary reasoning steps. Existing truncation-based methods typically detect consecutive trial-answer agreement and force early exit, yet such local stopping signals do not necessarily indicate final-answer stability and can disrupt useful subsequent reflection or verification, potentially leading to performance degradation. We propose consistency-aware logit masking (CALM), a training-free decoding intervention for mitigating overthinking in LRMs. CALM first monitors trial answers at step boundaries and then applies logit masking to action transition point (ATP) tokens such as "Wait", "Alternatively", and "Hmm", suppressing redundant transitional reasoning while allowing the model to continue its thought process more naturally. Experiments across four advanced LRMs and five benchmarks show that CALM reduces token consumption by 18.6%-25.0% compared with full CoT reasoning while maintaining performance, and can even improve accuracy by 0.07%-1.48% by reducing redundant reasoning. LLM-as-a-Judge results also demonstrate that CALM provides more coherent and concise results.
authors: Shengjing Liu, Feiyang Li, Yuxuan Yang, Yile Wang, Hui Huang
bullets: Targets overthinking caused by lengthy, redundant reasoning in large reasoning models.
Monitors trial-answer consistency at reasoning-step boundaries rather than forcing early termination.
Suppresses action transition point tokens such as “Wait,” “Alternatively,” and “Hmm” during decoding.
Training-free experiments across four models and five benchmarks reduce token use by 18.6%–25.0% while maintaining performance.
Results also report 0.07%–1.48% accuracy improvements and more coherent, concise outputs judged by LLMs.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free decoding intervention to reduce overthinking in large reasoning models, relevant to LLM reasoning and efficiency.
papers.title: CALM: Consistency-Aware Logit Masking in Decoding Space for Mitigating Overthinking of Large Reasoning Models
papers.tldr: CALM reduces large reasoning models’ unnecessary chain-of-thought steps by masking redundant transition tokens while preserving—and sometimes improving—accuracy.

papers.abstract: Large reasoning models often produce lengthy chain-of-thought (CoT) traces mixing useful intermediate steps with unnecessary ones. Recent methods explore step-level signals such as attention mass and step entropy to identify and suppress unnecessary steps. Despite their effectiveness, such signals reflect the model's behavior at a step rather than that step's contribution to the answer. To address this, we propose the interventional step credit (ISC), which takes a causal-intervention view and assesses step importance to the reasoning through targeted parameter-level interventions. Building on ISC, we further propose IGPO, which uses ISC to guide fine-grained advantage rescaling in reinforcement learning, reducing redundant steps while preserving the important ones. Experiments across two model scales and nine benchmarks show that IGPO achieves up to 62% average token reduction and better overall performance among compared methods.
authors: Guanda Li, Xuefeng Bai, Yulong Chen, Zhiyong Wang, Kehai Chen, Min Zhang
bullets: Long reasoning traces often mix useful and redundant intermediate steps.
Existing step signals describe model behavior but not each step’s causal contribution to the answer.
Interventional Step Credit (ISC) estimates step importance through targeted parameter-level interventions.
IGPO uses ISC to rescale reinforcement-learning advantages at fine granularity.
Across two model scales and nine benchmarks, IGPO reduces average tokens by up to 62% while improving overall performance versus compared methods.
papers.selection_reason: Reduces redundant chain-of-thought steps in large reasoning models via interventional step credit, directly relevant to efficient LLM reasoning.
papers.title: Learning to Reason Efficiently with Interventional Step Credit
papers.tldr: IGPO uses causal, intervention-based step credit to shorten chain-of-thought reasoning while preserving important steps and improving performance.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often generate more reasoning tokens than needed. Limiting the reasoning budget reduces cost, but forcing an answer from an incomplete trace can hurt accuracy. System-1 decision models select among candidate options without producing a reasoning response. We evaluate Jev as a decision reader of truncated reasoning across seven LLM reasoners and five multiple-choice benchmarks (35 pairs). Jev achieves higher mean accuracy than forced answering at tested budgets from 500 to 16,000 tokens, including the estimated costs of reasoning and answering. At a 1,500-token budget, it improves accuracy by 4.1 pp overall and 8.6 pp on truncated questions, with significant gains in 17 pairs under Holm-corrected bootstrap tests. Offline replay estimates 34.5% of the full-run cost, with a 1.13 pp accuracy loss. A policy selected on training folds saves 71.3% of the estimated full-run cost on held-out folds, with a 0.58 pp accuracy loss. We also find that Jev shows strong question-only accuracy, exceeding 500-token forced answering on average (68.0% vs. 65.5%), although this advantage varies by benchmark. These findings suggest that System-1 decision models can complement LLM reasoning and reduce the need for costly reasoning completion.
authors: Zhongyin Wang, Zhaoqian Xue, Junting Mu, Haozheng Liu, Ye Yuan, Haolun Wu, Lingyao Li
bullets: Evaluates Jev across seven reasoning LLMs and five multiple-choice benchmarks, covering 35 model–benchmark pairs.
Jev outperforms forced answering at tested budgets from 500 to 16,000 tokens, including reasoning and answer costs.
At 1,500 tokens, it improves accuracy by 4.1 percentage points overall and 8.6 points on truncated questions.
Offline replay estimates 34.5% of full-run cost with a 1.13-point accuracy loss; a learned policy saves 71.3% with a 0.58-point loss on held-out folds.
Jev also performs competitively using only the question, though its advantage varies across benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates system-1 decision models for truncated LLM reasoning under budget, relevant to efficient reasoning and LLM decision-making.
papers.title: Truncated Reasoning Under a Budget: Evaluating System-1 Models as Decision-makers
papers.tldr: Using a System-1 decision model to select answers from truncated LLM reasoning improves cost-adjusted accuracy over forcing incomplete reasoning traces to answer.

papers.abstract: Self-consistency answers a question by generating multiple responses and selecting the most frequent answer. Its evaluation requires both correctness labels and information about which responses agree; correctness labels alone generally determine neither voting accuracy nor the benefit of additional votes. For tasks in which all correct responses map to the same normalized answer, we derive sharp accuracy bounds using classical stochastic majorization, refined by abstention counts and answer-category limits. We also derive sharp bounds on accuracy changes across voting budgets that share a response pool. When answer-category counts are available, we introduce Plurality-U, a count-based dynamic program that exactly averages voting accuracy over all fixed-size subsets, eliminating finite-pool Monte Carlo error. On 1,403,520 stored outputs from recent reasoning models in Scorio Lite and Scorio Trace, recording abstention counts and answer options cuts the width of SuperGPQA accuracy intervals by more than half. For moving from 9 to 17 votes, our bounds reduce interval width by a median of 77.7% on SuperGPQA and 72.3% on 14 GPQA and Adaptive-Consistency pools, compared with a baseline that combines separate accuracy bounds. Exact computation has lower paired median runtime than 2,000-subset Monte Carlo in 14 of 15 tested pool-budget settings. These results clarify what incomplete logs can establish and provide an exact evaluation procedure when answer counts are retained.
authors: Zhengtao Gui, Zexi Chen, Weining Shen
bullets: Correctness labels alone are insufficient to determine voting accuracy or the value of additional votes; agreement information is needed.
For tasks with a shared normalized correct answer, the authors derive sharp bounds using stochastic majorization, abstention counts, and answer-category limits.
They introduce Plurality-U, a dynamic program that exactly averages accuracy over fixed-size response subsets when answer counts are available.
Across stored reasoning-model outputs, adding abstention and answer-option counts substantially narrows accuracy intervals, while exact computation often outperforms 2,000-subset Monte Carlo.
The analysis applies to incomplete logs and clarifies what can—and cannot—be established about self-consistency performance.
papers.selection_reason: Develops exact evaluation methods for self-consistency in LLMs using stochastic majorization and dynamic programming.
papers.title: Which Answers Agree? Evaluating Self-Consistency from Incomplete Logs
papers.tldr: The paper shows how to evaluate self-consistency voting from incomplete logs by deriving tight accuracy bounds and an exact count-based computation method.

papers.abstract: Catastrophic forgetting is a central obstacle in single-stage fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) on a new task, especially when the original pretraining data are unavailable. Synthetic data offers a practical mitigation path, but candidate pools are often noisy and redundant, making effective selection essential. Existing methods often rely on indirect proxy signals whose alignment with actual training benefit can be limited, while utility--diversity selection over large candidate pools remains computationally demanding. To address these challenges, we propose NAvigator-guided Data Selection (NADS), a fine-tuning framework for LLMs. NADS first follows the target fine-tuning recipe without preservation regularization to obtain a navigator model, whose deviation from the pretrained model exposes recipe-induced capability drift. It then uses the predictive divergence between the navigator and the pretrained model to score forgetting-aware utility for each synthetic candidate, and constructs a constraint set through an efficient utility--diversity selection strategy. Finally, NADS fine-tunes on the new-task data while distilling pretrained behavior on the selected constraints to preserve general capabilities. Experiments show that NADS delivers a stronger balance between new-task performance and general capability preservation, while reducing utility--diversity selection overhead. Code at: https://github.com/zjh-vinky/NADS.
authors: Jianhao Zhang, Ou Wu, Yi Du
bullets: Targets noisy, redundant synthetic candidate pools and the difficulty of preserving pretrained capabilities during single-stage fine-tuning.
Builds a navigator by applying the target fine-tuning recipe without preservation regularization, revealing recipe-induced capability drift.
Scores candidates by predictive divergence between the navigator and pretrained model to estimate forgetting-aware utility.
Efficiently selects a utility–diversity constraint set, then distills pretrained behavior on it during new-task fine-tuning.
Experiments report a stronger balance between new-task performance and general capability preservation with lower selection overhead.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces NADS for mitigating catastrophic forgetting in LLM fine-tuning using a navigator-guided data selection strategy.
papers.title: NADS: Navigator-Guided Data Selection for Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting in Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: NADS selects synthetic data using navigator-model drift to mitigate catastrophic forgetting during LLM fine-tuning without access to pretraining data.

papers.abstract: Scientific model discovery requires proposing candidate models of an unknown system and designing experiments that discriminate among them. However, LLM-based approaches typically rely on in-context learning to predict outcomes and select experiments, lacking explicit model evaluation to systematically guide hypothesis search, while Bayesian approaches enable principled model comparison but are confined to a predefined candidate set which results in limited search spaces. To this end, we introduce BMD, which closes the loop between LLM-driven hypothesis generation and Bayesian experimental design. Specifically, an LLM proposes model families, while a numerical engine fits their parameters, weighs them by model evidence, and averages their predictions. Then, BMD chooses the next experimental conditions by maximizing the joint expected information gain over families and their parameters, while feeding the updated beliefs and residual diagnostics back to the LLM to guide its next proposals. Across four scientific discovery benchmarks, BMD achieves lowest final prediction error than in-context learning and LLM-based scientific agents while recovering exact functional forms more often, with ablations supporting numerical feedback and the joint objective.
authors: JooKyung Yuh, Byungmin Park, Eunseo Choi, Jinheon Baek, Junmo Cho, Kyu Hyun Choi, Sung Ju Hwang, Kyong Hwan Jin, Hae Beom Lee
bullets: Targets the limitations of LLM methods lacking explicit model evaluation and Bayesian methods restricted to predefined candidates.
An LLM proposes model families, while a numerical engine fits parameters, computes model evidence, and averages predictions.
Experiments are selected to maximize expected information gain over both model families and parameters.
Updated beliefs and residual diagnostics guide subsequent LLM hypothesis proposals.
Across four benchmarks, BMD achieved the lowest final prediction error and more often recovered exact functional forms; ablations supported its numerical feedback and joint objective.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes BMD, a framework integrating LLMs with Bayesian experimental design for scientific model discovery, advancing LLM agent capabilities.
papers.title: Bayesian Model Discovery with Language Models: Closing the Loop between Hypotheses and Experiments
papers.tldr: BMD combines LLM-generated hypotheses with Bayesian model evaluation and experiment design to iteratively discover scientific models.

papers.abstract: Constraint pruning saves queries to a large language model (LLM) or another noisy oracle by skipping each yes/no question implied by answers accepted earlier, for example through transitivity. Entity-resolution systems and LLM-based rankers use this idea. However, their analyses typically assume a correct oracle. We argue that pruning should be judged by its risk when the oracle errs, since an accepted wrong answer spreads to every question it implies. When each answer is wrong independently with small probability $\varepsilon$, the first-order risk is set by how many facts one wrong answer corrupts on average. We consider two kinds of constraints. For implication rules, as in taxonomies, pruning in a random order adds no first-order risk: a wrong answer that would change $k$ facts is accepted with probability $1/k$, so it costs one fact on average. Rules with $s$ premises break this balance: a wrong answer at a premise shared by $r$ rules can cost order $r^{1-1/s}$ facts. For entity resolution with $m$ records of one entity, the first-order risk equals $\varepsilon$ times the Wiener index (the total pairwise distance) of the spanning tree built by the query order. Pivot orders, which first compare one record with all others, amplify errors by less than 2 and are optimal; random orders by order $m^{1/3}$; the common most-similar-first order is the worst in one dimension and, for large $m$, worse than random in two. With several entities, the cost of wrongly merging two does not depend on how many others exist. Simulations agree with every predicted constant within sampling error.
authors: Zhengtao Gui (University of California, Irvine), Weining Shen (University of California, Irvine)
bullets: For single-premise implication rules, random pruning order adds no first-order risk; multi-premise rules can amplify errors substantially.
In entity resolution, first-order error risk is proportional to the Wiener index of the query-order spanning tree.
Pivot query orders are optimal and keep error amplification below 2; random orders can be much worse as the number of records grows.
Most-similar-first ordering is worst in one dimension and can underperform random ordering in two dimensions.
Simulations match the abstract’s predicted risk constants within sampling error.
papers.selection_reason: Provides theoretical analysis of error propagation in constraint pruning with noisy LLM oracles, offering insights into LLM optimization and reliability.
papers.title: How Much Does One Wrong Answer Cost? Error Propagation in Constraint Pruning with Noisy LLM Oracles
papers.tldr: Constraint pruning can save queries but amplify a single noisy LLM error, with risk determined by how many implied facts that error corrupts.

papers.abstract: LLM unlearning is essential for removing sensitive or unwanted knowledge while preserving useful capabilities. As LLM teams are increasingly used to solve complex problems, forgetting must remain effective during collaboration. Despite advances in forgetting effectiveness, efficiency, and robustness to relearning, team deployment remains underexplored. We find that collaboration weakens forgetting: final-answer evaluations miss recoverable evidence in team messages, including complementary clues supporting joint recovery. We establish theoretically and confirm empirically that controlling final answers or individual messages does not ensure low recovery from their combination. To address this challenge, we propose Aggregation-Conditioned Unlearning (ACU). ACU trains a shared model using reconstruction feedback from individual and pooled messages, prioritizes views with higher recovery risk, and uses replacement-based credit assignment while protecting direct and collaborative utility. TOFU evaluates trajectory-level recovery, while WMDP-bio tests native forgetting and retained utility. On TOFU, ACU lowers full-trajectory recovery from 41.8% to 19.3% in ROUGE-L recall and factual recovery from 34.2% to 18.7% versus output-supervised training, with comparable retained-task performance. These results demonstrate that ACU curbs information leakage in LLM teams and generalizes across team sizes and readers.
authors: Hengsong Liu, Liangyu Teng, Jingnan Cai, Yuntian Shi, Jingyu Zhang, Yang Liu, Jing Liu, Liang Song
bullets: Final-answer or single-message evaluations can miss complementary clues that jointly recover forgotten information.
The paper formalizes and empirically validates that controlling individual views does not guarantee low recovery from their combination.
Aggregation-Conditioned Unlearning (ACU) trains on individual and pooled messages, prioritizes high-risk views, and uses replacement-based credit assignment.
On TOFU, ACU reduces full-trajectory recovery from 41.8% to 19.3% and factual recovery from 34.2% to 18.7% versus output-supervised training.
Retained-task performance remains comparable, with evaluation also conducted on WMDP-bio for native forgetting and utility.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses robust unlearning for shared-model LLM teams, relevant to LLM safety and adaptation.
papers.title: Does Unlearning Survive Collaboration? Robust Unlearning for Shared-Model LLM Teams
papers.tldr: Collaboration can reconstruct information that appears forgotten from individual LLM outputs, and ACU reduces this team-level recovery while preserving utility.

papers.abstract: Automated essay scoring (AES) using large language models (LLMs) offers promising use cases for language assessment, yet high-stakes testing requires scores that are both controllable and verifiable, which current LLM-based scorers lack. Given that, we investigate whether LLM-based scorers form distinct internal representations for individual scoring rubrics and whether these representations can be independently controlled. Probing and steering 25 open-weight base LLMs (0.13B-10.31B parameters; 14 families) on human-scored BESTEP English writing tasks, we find that holistic scores are decodable from model activations for the longer tasks (Parts 2 and 3) and only weakly for the shortest (Part 1). Furthermore, scoring rubrics have partly separable directions in representation space for the longer tasks, though not for short responses (Part 1). However, causal steering reveals a critical limitation: applying a matching intervention (e.g., steering "grammar" on a grammar-degraded response) yields only a negligible advantage (about 2% of the effect) over a mismatched intervention (e.g., steering "vocabulary"), and none that is detectable in any of the 10 testable comparisons across reliably measured rubrics. Rather than controlling distinct evaluative dimensions, the rubric directions share a dominant lever whose rubric-specific parts are not selective, which may mirror the halo structure of human ratings. Our contributions are two-fold. First, we show that analytic scoring rubrics designed for human raters do not behave as independent controls in base LLMs, even among the seven models whose scores agree best with human raters ($r \geq 0.6$). Second, we establish a methodology that shows that score agreement and decodability do not imply rubric-level control in LLM-based assessment.
authors: Chungche Huang, Po-Ya Angela Wang, Shu-Kai Hsieh
bullets: Holistic scores are more decodable for longer essays than for the shortest responses.
Rubric-related directions are partly separable in activation space for longer tasks, but not for short responses.
Causal steering shows negligible benefit from matching an intervention to the targeted rubric, with no detectable advantage across 10 comparisons.
The findings hold even among models with relatively strong agreement with human raters, indicating that agreement and decodability do not guarantee rubric-level control.
The shared rubric structure may reflect a dominant halo-like evaluation signal rather than independent scoring dimensions.
papers.selection_reason: Mechanistic analysis of rubric control in LLM-based essay scoring, relevant to LLM interpretability.
papers.title: Inside the Scorer: Mechanistic Evidence on Rubric Control in LLM-Based Automated Essay Scoring from 25 Base Models
papers.tldr: Across 25 base LLMs, essay scores and rubric signals can often be decoded, but rubric-specific steering does not provide reliable independent control over scoring dimensions.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models accelerate generation by predicting multiple tokens in parallel, but factorized denoisers treat simultaneous predictions as conditionally independent. Decoding heuristics reduce the resulting errors by controlling which tokens are committed, but leave the underlying distribution factorized. Joint modeling addresses the source of the problem, yet existing methods attach separately learned layers to frozen denoisers, leaving the backbone unadapted to the joint objective and the coupling parameters fixed across contexts. We propose Codpula, a context-parameterized denoiser combining a Transformer with a tractable probabilistic inference layer. Given a partially masked input, the Transformer produces token potentials that shape per-position predictions and compact gates that modulate the layer's coupling parameters, yielding a context-dependent joint distribution while retaining exact conditional inference. We jointly optimize both components under a conditional denoising objective using a dual-flow multiplicative update that preserves valid probabilistic parameters. At inference, Codpula supports standard heuristics and uses conditional queries to adapt commitments to dependencies among proposed tokens without extra Transformer evaluations within a step. Codpula sets new state-of-the-art results across a broad suite of reasoning benchmarks while advancing the accuracy-latency Pareto frontier in mathematical reasoning and code generation.
authors: Zilei Shao, Ian Li, Heng Zhao, Kewei Lian, Guy Van den Broeck, Zhe Zeng, Anji Liu
bullets: Factorized denoisers treat simultaneously predicted tokens as conditionally independent, leaving dependency errors unresolved.
Codpula combines a Transformer with a tractable probabilistic inference layer whose coupling parameters adapt to the input context.
The model jointly trains token potentials and coupling controls using a dual-flow multiplicative update that preserves valid probabilistic parameters.
Conditional queries adapt token commitments to dependencies without additional Transformer evaluations within a decoding step.
The method reports state-of-the-art results across reasoning benchmarks and advances the mathematical-reasoning and code-generation accuracy–latency frontier.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces Codpula, a context-parameterized denoiser for diffusion language models, advancing LLM architecture and accuracy-latency tradeoffs.
papers.title: Learning to Couple: Context-Adaptive Joint Denoising for Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: Codpula enables diffusion language models to make context-dependent joint token predictions, improving the accuracy–latency tradeoff for reasoning and code generation.

papers.abstract: Curriculum learning, which organizes training samples according to their learning priority, has been widely adopted in reinforcement learning to improve training efficiency. However, existing methods commonly construct curriculum units using predefined data properties and estimate their utility by simply aggregating a single proxy signal from recent training history.Such designs may group samples with different optimization effects and fail to anticipate how their utility evolves in relation to the policy. We propose Predictive Gradient-based Bandit (PGB) Curriculum, which first discovers optimization-aware learning units by clustering projected sample-level gradients. PGB then employs a lightweight temporal predictor to forecast the future utility of each unit and converts the predictions into a Boltzmann sampling distribution for adaptive data allocation. Experiments across multiple model scales and reasoning benchmarks show that PGB consistently outperforms standard GRPO, difficulty-based curricula, and history-based scheduling strategies, demonstrating improved data utilization and training efficiency.
authors: Liang Xu, Shufan Shen, Zhongni Hou, Chao Bi, Yufei Zhang, Wei Lin, Guojun Yin, Shuhui Wang
bullets: Addresses curricula that rely on predefined sample properties and single historical utility signals.
Clusters projected sample-level gradients to form optimization-aware learning units.
Uses a lightweight temporal predictor to forecast each unit’s future utility.
Applies Boltzmann sampling to adaptively allocate training data.
Outperforms standard GRPO, difficulty-based curricula, and history-based scheduling across model scales and reasoning benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces gradient-based curriculum learning for RL training of reasoning models, relevant to LLM post-training.
papers.title: Predictive Bandit Curriculum Reinforcement Learning via Gradient-Based Sample Group Discovery
papers.tldr: PGB Curriculum improves reinforcement-learning training efficiency by grouping samples by gradient behavior and predicting which groups will be most useful next.

papers.abstract: Inference-time steering is crucial for deploying Large Language Models (LLMs) in real-world applications, where they must flexibly adjust behavior preferences. For instance, a model should dynamically adjust its caution level based on the risk of the scenario. This requirement introduces a challenge: modulating the intensity of LLM preferences. Prompt engineering can require task-specific prompt design, while fine-tuning requires additional optimization and data. These requirements can make repeated behavioral adjustments costly. To address this, we introduce NeuroSteer, a plug-and-play framework that enables flexible, quantitative adjustment of LLM preferences at inference time. NeuroSteer employs a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) as its controller. Comparing neuron activation frequencies between positive and negative examples isolates "feature neurons" that correspond to target preferences such as politeness and positive sentiment. During inference, the activations of selected SAE features are amplified in the latent representations to steer the output distribution. Users can adjust the strength of this steering on a per-scenario or per-user basis, granting the LLM fine-grained, quantifiable trait modulation. Our experiments show that NeuroSteer can alter sentiment, toxicity, stance, and politeness at inference time. It achieves higher target-direction steering scores than the compared baselines in several settings, with task- and strength-dependent trade-offs in generation quality.
authors: Keqi Chen, Zekai Sun, Yuhua Wen, Tianyi Tian, Xinyang Huang, Huijun Lian, Yingming Gao, Ya Li
bullets: Targets preferences such as sentiment, toxicity, stance, and politeness through feature-level activation amplification.
Identifies preference-related “feature neurons” by comparing activations on positive and negative examples.
Lets users control steering strength per scenario or user for fine-grained behavior modulation.
Experiments demonstrate effective target-direction steering, with generation-quality trade-offs depending on the task and steering strength.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes NeuroSteer, a plug-and-play framework for inference-time steering of LLMs using Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) feature amplification to modulate behavior quantitatively.
papers.title: From Black Box to Controller: Inference-Time Steering of LLM via Feature Amplification
papers.tldr: NeuroSteer uses sparse-autoencoder features to quantitatively adjust LLM behaviors at inference time without prompt redesign or fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Large language models have recently been used to discover heuristics through iterative program search, offering a promising approach to automated algorithm design. However, candidates selected by average performance may degrade across instance families, random seeds, and problem scales because mean-based objectives can obscure rare but severe failures. We propose CVaR-RMD, a risk-sensitive evolutionary framework that uses an LLM to mutate executable heuristic programs and ranks candidates by empirical conditional value-at-risk over heterogeneous evaluation conditions. Across three combinatorial optimization domains, CVaR-based selection improves upper-tail performance and reduces failure rates while maintaining competitive mean performance. These gains persist on larger unseen instances and independently curated within-domain benchmarks
bullets: Targets weaknesses of mean-based selection, which can hide rare failures across instances, seeds, and scales.
Uses an LLM to mutate executable heuristic programs in an evolutionary search framework.
Ranks candidates by empirical conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) over heterogeneous evaluation conditions.
Across three combinatorial optimization domains, it improves upper-tail performance and reduces failure rates while preserving competitive mean performance.
Benefits persist on larger unseen instances and independently curated within-domain benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes CVaR-RMD, a risk-sensitive evolutionary framework using LLMs to discover heuristics, applying conditional value-at-risk selection pressure to improve robustness.
papers.title: CVaR-RMD: CVaR Selection Pressure for Robust Metaheuristic Discovery
papers.tldr: CVaR-RMD uses risk-sensitive selection to discover heuristics that are more robust to severe failures across varied conditions.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) enhances the capabilities of small language agents by providing dense, token-level supervision from a teacher model on student-generated trajectories. However, standard OPD implicitly assumes that credit is uniformly distributed across long-horizon trajectories, assigning the same strength of teacher supervision to different actions. Through credit-distribution analysis and outcome-reversal counterfactual experiments, we find that trajectory credit is concentrated on a small number of critical actions. Moreover, even when the trajectory is held fixed, reversing only the final outcome substantially changes the credit assigned to multiple interaction turns. These findings show that the uniform-credit assumption fails to identify critical decisions and ultimately degrades the model's reasoning accuracy. To address these challenges, we propose ToolOPD, an outcome-aware on-policy distillation framework designed for long-horizon tool use. ToolOPD first summarizes each completed trajectory and its outcome into a reusable hindsight skill. It then measures how this skill changes the teacher's probability of each student action token and converts the change into outcome-aware credit. The resulting credit preserves supervision that supports successful decisions or discourages failed ones, while suppressing irrelevant and conflicting signals. ToolOPD uses these credits to reweight the action-level distillation loss and jointly optimizes it with reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments across multiple long-horizon tool interaction benchmarks demonstrate that ToolOPD significantly outperforms existing reinforcement learning and self-distillation baselines.
authors: Chu Zhao, Lei Tang, Yanming Wang, Jianzhe Zhao, Guibing Guo, Zhengzong Chen, Yuanyuan Zhao, Fei Huang
bullets: Standard on-policy distillation gives uniform supervision across long trajectories, missing critical decisions.
Counterfactual outcome reversals show that action credit can change substantially even when the trajectory is unchanged.
ToolOPD summarizes each trajectory and outcome into a hindsight skill, then uses its effect on teacher probabilities to derive outcome-aware token credit.
The method reweights action-level distillation and jointly trains with reinforcement learning.
Experiments across multiple long-horizon tool-interaction benchmarks show significant gains over reinforcement-learning and self-distillation baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes ToolOPD, an outcome-aware on-policy distillation framework for long-horizon tool-use agents that addresses credit assignment issues in standard distillation.
papers.title: ToolOPD: Credit-Aware On-Policy Distillation for Tool-Use Agents
papers.tldr: ToolOPD improves long-horizon tool-use agents by assigning distillation credit to the actions that most influence outcomes, rather than treating all trajectory actions equally.

papers.abstract: Harmful fine-tuning can rapidly erode the safety alignment of large language models, creating substantial risks when aligned models are adapted to downstream tasks. Existing alignment-stage defenses use harmful examples and simulated harmful perturbations during safety alignment to prepare models for later harmful fine-tuning, yet the collective effects of harmful weight perturbations remain underexplored. We identify a collective failure pattern: disjoint parts of a harmful perturbation have limited effects in isolation, but their joint application increases the model's harmfulness beyond the sum of their individual effects. Guided by this observation, we propose Joint Weight Perturbations (JWP), an alignment-stage defense that masks different parts of a harmful perturbation estimated from the current model and trains the model to respond safely in the resulting states. This exposes the model to different combinations of harmful perturbations and reduces its sensitivity to their accumulation during subsequent harmful fine-tuning. Experiments across downstream tasks and model families show that JWP offers stronger resistance to harmful fine-tuning than prior defenses while largely preserving task performance.
authors: Zhiyuan Wang, Yuezhi Zhou, Zhu Zhang, Zhixing Tan
bullets: Harmful fine-tuning can erode the safety alignment of large language models.
Disjoint harmful weight perturbations may have limited individual effects but produce greater-than-additive harm when combined.
JWP masks different parts of an estimated harmful perturbation and trains the model to remain safe across the resulting states.
Across downstream tasks and model families, JWP resists harmful fine-tuning more strongly than prior defenses while largely preserving task performance.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes Joint Weight Perturbations (JWP), a defense mechanism for LLMs to resist harmful fine-tuning by training on masked perturbations.
papers.title: When Safety Fails Collectively: Robust Alignment Against Harmful Fine-Tuning via Joint Weight Perturbations
papers.tldr: Joint Weight Perturbations improve language models’ resistance to harmful fine-tuning by training them against combinations of harmful weight changes.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is increasingly used for language model post-training, yet how teacher supervision shapes learning and forgetting remains unclear. We present OPDArena, a framework comparing supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), and OPD across five pretrained models and diverse teacher sources. It jointly evaluates mathematical learning, general capability retention, and predictive distribution changes. Teacher choice strongly shapes retention: students of RLVR-trained teachers improve on the target task while retaining prior capabilities, whereas students of SFT-trained teachers incur greater capability loss. Across post-training methods, out-of-domain (OOD) distribution change shows a more consistent positive association with forgetting than in-domain change. To understand how teacher choice affects these changes, we examine the additional information teachers provide relative to the student's pretrained model. Controlled teacher comparisons show that the task-specific preferences teachers acquire through post-training make student updates more concentrated in-domain.
authors: Yuanze Xu, Tianzhu Ye, Hui Sun, Wenhui Wang, Li Dong, Furu Wei
bullets: Compares SFT, RLVR, and on-policy distillation across five pretrained models and varied teacher sources.
Evaluates mathematical learning, retention of general capabilities, and changes in predictive distributions.
RLVR-trained teachers improve target-task performance while better preserving prior capabilities; SFT-trained teachers cause more forgetting.
Out-of-domain distribution changes are more consistently associated with forgetting than in-domain changes.
Post-training gives teachers task-specific preferences that concentrate student updates more strongly in-domain.
papers.selection_reason: Studies learning and forgetting in on-policy distillation for LLM post-training, relevant to LLM training dynamics.
papers.title: OPDArena: Understanding Learning and Forgetting in On-Policy Distillation
papers.tldr: OPDArena shows that teacher training strongly influences what on-policy distillation helps models learn and what capabilities they forget.

papers.abstract: Looped (weight-tied) transformers enable adaptive computation by allocating more iterations to harder inputs. Fixed-Point Reasoners (FPRM) achieve this with a damped fixed-point solver, but operate in an unbounded Euclidean residual space with coupled rescaling and relative-norm halting. We introduce Spherical Fixed-Point Reasoners (SFPRM), which perform the same computation on the unit hypersphere of normalized transformers (nGPT). Input injection, damping, and halting become geodesic operations, yielding boundedness by construction and eliminating coefficient coupling. We prove fixed-point existence, local convergence under an explicit step-size condition, and global convergence under strong injection. On Sudoku-Extreme, Maze-Hard, and Mini-ARC, SFPRM achieves 96.6%, 87.9%, and 59.1% test accuracy, respectively, outperforming FPRM and other baselines while allocating test-time compute more effectively. Its converged geometry is also interpretable: token-input angles capture puzzle structure and predict correctness.
authors: Arber Zela, Artavazd Maranjyan, Pol Puigdemont, David Berghaus, Valentyn Boreiko, Volkan Cevher
bullets: Recasts Fixed-Point Reasoners in normalized-transformer geometry, replacing Euclidean residual updates with geodesic operations.
Hyperspherical updates provide boundedness by construction and remove coupled rescaling in input injection, damping, and halting.
Establishes fixed-point existence, local convergence under an explicit step-size condition, and global convergence under strong injection.
Reports 96.6% on Sudoku-Extreme, 87.9% on Maze-Hard, and 59.1% on Mini-ARC, outperforming FPRM and other baselines.
Converged token-input angles are interpretable, encoding puzzle structure and predicting correctness.
papers.selection_reason: Spherical fixed-point looped transformers with adaptive halting improve compute allocation and reasoning; relevant to transformer architecture and efficiency.
papers.title: Spherical Fixed-Point Reasoners: Adaptive Loop Halting on the Hypersphere
papers.tldr: SFPRM adapts looped-transformer computation on the unit hypersphere, offering theoretically grounded halting and strong puzzle-solving performance.

papers.abstract: LLMs "reason" by externalizing intermediate steps as tokens through chain-of-thought (CoT), yet even frontier reasoning models hit abrupt performance cliffs on long-horizon tasks. Implicit reasoning (reasoning within a single forward pass) is useful during CoT generation, as the model can "search ahead" to decide the correct next move without explicit search. Models with weak implicit reasoning are more likely to commit to wrong paths and must attempt to recover via backtracking, while models with strong implicit reasoning identify the correct proof strategy directly, shortening the CoT. However, prior work shows LLMs struggle to reason implicitly beyond shallow depths, with no relief from scale. We investigate whether curriculum learning can extend this depth by fine-tuning on examples with progressively increasing vocabulary size and lookahead (the number of steps a model must search ahead to identify the correct next move). At matched compute, curriculum-trained models achieve lookaheads where no-curriculum training fails. Qwen3-0.6B reaches 98% accuracy on problems with lookahead up to 256 with curriculum, compared to 45% without. However, progress slows as fine-tuning continues, following a saturating exponential that suggests a maximum intrinsic lookahead to which models can learn to reason implicitly. Larger models reach higher fitted ceilings, fine-tuning pretrained models far outpaces training from scratch, and curriculum step sizes that are too large stall progression. Finally, the capability acquired on synthetic data transfers to natural language reasoning, with curriculum-trained models outperforming models trained without curriculum at matched compute on 11 natural language reasoning benchmarks.
authors: Jimson Huang, Maxwell Nickell, Ruowang Zhang, Abulhair Saparov
bullets: Implicit reasoning lets LLMs search ahead within one forward pass, helping them choose correct proof paths and produce shorter CoT traces.
Fine-tuning on progressively larger vocabularies and longer lookaheads succeeds where matched-compute training without a curriculum fails.
Curriculum-trained Qwen3-0.6B reaches 98% accuracy at lookahead 256, versus 45% without curriculum.
Progress follows a saturating exponential: larger models have higher apparent ceilings, pretrained models improve faster, and overly large curriculum steps hinder learning.
Capabilities learned on synthetic tasks transfer to natural-language reasoning benchmarks, where curriculum training performs better at matched compute.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates curriculum learning to extend implicit reasoning in LLMs, directly relevant to LLM training and reasoning.
papers.title: Curriculum Learning Teaches LLMs Long-Horizon Implicit Reasoning, Up To A Limit
papers.tldr: Curriculum learning substantially extends LLMs’ implicit reasoning horizon, but improvements saturate at a model-dependent limit.

papers.abstract: Safety risks from fine-tuning are commonly characterized by the harmfulness of the training data:harmful fine-tuning is considered dangerous, while benign fine-tuning is often assumed to preservealignment. We argue that this view misses a more fundamental factor-the behavioral transition inducedby supervision. Harmful fine-tuning and safety-degrading benign fine-tuning can both be understoodas learning the same refusal-to-compliance transition, but on different data distributions. We studywhether such a transition learned on benign inputs can generalize to harmful requests. We constructbenign examples that an aligned model initially tends to refuse and pair them with their originalharmless responses, creating a discrepancy between the model's initial refusal and the supervisedanswer. Fine-tuning on these examples increases harmful compliance, but only when two conditionshold together: the discrepancy is large enough, and it cannot be resolved through a narrow surface-levelshortcut. With the induced discrepancy matched, varying only whether it is localized changes harmfulcompliance by an order of magnitude; raising the discrepancy does not help while a shortcut remainsavailable, and removing the shortcut does not help while the discrepancy is small. Building on thisobservation, we introduce SAFEOFF, a dataset of benign instructions rewritten to raise the alignedmodel's refusal likelihood and paired with their original answers. Across three aligned LLMs and threesafety benchmarks, SAFEOFF substantially weakens safety alignment despite containing no explicitharmful supervision, suggesting that fine-tuning safety depends not only on what data a model sees, butalso on which behavioral boundary the supervision moves.
authors: Jesson Wang, Zhanhao Hu, Minghao Lin, Yuchen Wu, Aylin Caliskan, Mengyuan Li
bullets: Safety degradation depends on the behavioral transition induced by supervision, not only on whether training data is harmful.
The key conditions are a large refusal–answer discrepancy and the absence of an easy surface-level shortcut.
With matched discrepancies, localized versus non-localized transitions can change harmful compliance by an order of magnitude.
The authors introduce SAFEOFF, benign refusal-triggering instructions paired with harmless answers.
Across three aligned LLMs and three safety benchmarks, SAFEOFF substantially weakens safety alignment without explicit harmful supervision.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes how benign fine-tuning can misalign LLMs, contributing to understanding of LLM behavior and safety.
papers.title: Safety Offset Learning: When Benign Fine-Tuning Misaligns LLMs
papers.tldr: Benign fine-tuning can weaken LLM safety when it trains a sufficiently large, non-localized shift from refusal to compliance, even without harmful examples.

papers.abstract: Moore's paradox \citep{moore1942} concerns sentences such as ``It is raining, but I don't believe that it is,'' which may well be true yet cannot be sensibly asserted. The absurdity lies not in the content but in the act, since to assert is to vouch for one's own belief. This makes the paradox a test of whether language models take the speech act into account when computing meaning. We present the first test of Moore's paradox in LLMs, evaluating 12 models on a curated set of Moorean sentences in varied contexts. We find that models largely recognize the infelicity of Moorean sentences, and that the judgement is not tied to a memorized form and tracks the speech act. Using the Rational Speech Act framework (RSA; \citealt{goodmanfrank2016}), we then test whether these judgements arise from a listener reasoning about a speaker. We find the models' own listeners do not reason about their own speakers, and their reasoning traces suggest that they instead recall knowledge about the paradox and apply rules therein. The models thus appear to have learned the paradox as a fact about sentences, not as a requirement on speakers.
authors: Anshun Asher Zheng, Weili Cao, Fangcong Yin, David Beaver, Junyi Jessy Li
bullets: Tests 12 language models on curated Moorean sentences across varied contexts.
Models generally detect the sentences’ infelicity, even when the wording is not a memorized form.
Using the Rational Speech Act framework, the study finds models’ listeners do not reason about their own speakers.
Reasoning traces suggest models treat Moore’s paradox as factual knowledge about sentences rather than a speaker-level constraint.
papers.selection_reason: Tests Moore's paradox in LLMs, probing speech act understanding and reasoning.
papers.title: Assertion and Belief: Moore's Paradox in Language Models
papers.tldr: LLMs recognize Moorean sentences as infelicitous, but appear to apply memorized rules rather than reason about speakers’ beliefs and speech acts.

papers.abstract: Recent work suggests that activation dynamics--how representations change during inference--might be more revealing about language model behavior than static readouts from individual layers. In this work, we investigate the layer-wise evolution of representations of factuality, using true and false statements when the model is prompted to either lie or to be honest. We report a geometric phenomenon in which the factuality directions extracted from the lying and honest conditions appear to rotate away from each other across layers. We find that such layer-wise rotation also occurs in a task that requires the model to take different visual perspectives in the 3D world, suggesting that the rotation phenomenon might be indicative of manipulating conceptual spaces in general, rather than unique to factuality. We then investigate the "real time" transformation of conceptual representations on a trial-to-trial basis. We show that it is possible to make strong predictions about the model's target task and behavior from trajectories alone. In addition, diverging points in single-trial trajectories correspond to the onset of rotation in aggregated-trial analysis. Finally, we show that both rotation and divergent trajectories occur in more naturalistic settings in which models are not overtly prompted to "lie" but rather report false statements in the course of completing a different task.
authors: Zhuonan Yang, Yik Siu Chan, Wannan Yang, Ellie Pavlick
bullets: Studies factuality representations when models are prompted to lie or tell the truth.
Finds that factuality directions in the two conditions rotate apart across layers.
Observes similar rotation during a 3D visual-perspective task, suggesting the effect may generalize beyond factuality.
Shows that single-trial representation trajectories can predict the model’s target task and behavior.
Finds rotation and trajectory divergence even in naturalistic false-reporting settings without explicit lying prompts.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates layer-wise representation dynamics and trajectory divergence in LLMs, relevant to LLM interpretability.
papers.title: Representations in Motion: Layer-wise Rotation and Trajectory Divergence in LLMs
papers.tldr: LLM conceptual representations evolve dynamically, with layer-wise rotation and diverging trajectories revealing task-dependent behavior beyond static layer readouts.

papers.abstract: A synopsis in novels folds a story into a few lines; a function in code gathers many steps with a single execution. Context editing is native to language itself. In this paper, we propose the Native Context Editing (NCE) framework, which gives language model agents a grammar for natively editing their own context. By encoding context-editing operations in a grammar of dedicated special tokens, we teach the agents to invoke edits through the language itself. We train agents on iteratively constructed trajectory segments, with each teacher edit conditioned on the evolving context. This establishes context editing as an atomic and inherent capability of LLM agents, enabling them to dynamically modify their context as they generate responses over long-horizon reasoning and interaction. Compared with context-editing methods that learn to generate tool-use code within specific external harness environments, our approach integrates context editing as an internal mechanism of the model's native generation process, enabling better generalization across diverse real-world workflows. On four long-horizon agentic benchmarks (Terminal-Bench 2.0, SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Multilingual, and SWE-bench Pro), NCE improves the average task success rate over the base model by 5.6 percentage points for LongCat-Flash-Lite-Sparse and by 4.5 for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, while reducing average token usage by 36% and 15%, respectively.
authors: Yunlong Deng, Yan Li, Xing Hu, Yida Zhu, Sean Du, Weiyang Liu, Guangyi Chen
bullets: Motivates context editing as a native language capability for managing long reasoning and interaction histories.
Encodes editing operations with dedicated special tokens, allowing agents to invoke edits during generation.
Trains agents on iteratively constructed trajectory segments, with edits conditioned on evolving context.
Evaluated on four long-horizon benchmarks, improving average success by 5.6 and 4.5 percentage points for two models.
Reduces average token usage by 36% and 15% for those models, respectively; scope is focused on long-horizon agentic workflows.
papers.selection_reason: Teaches LLM agents native context editing via special-token grammar, improving long-horizon reasoning and token efficiency.
papers.title: Editing as Language: Teaching LLM Agents a Grammar for Native Context Editing
papers.tldr: Native Context Editing teaches LLM agents a token-based grammar for editing their own context, improving long-horizon task success while reducing token use.

papers.abstract: Previous work has argued that multilingual LLMs encode language-specific features most strongly in their initial and final layers, implying that intermediate layers support language-agnostic representations. This paper reconsiders this finding by performing four different experiments: three that undertake a fine-grained analysis of representations of Portuguese and Spanish, two closely related languages, and one large-scale language identification experiment that covers over 200 languages. The results of these experiments challenge the strict separation between language-specific and language-agnostic layers in multilingual LLMs, using Llama 3.2 1B as a test case. By analyzing and manipulating contextual sentence embeddings, we demonstrate that language identity remains strongly recoverable throughout the model rather than being restricted to initial and final layers. Moreover, we find that the model tends to classify ambiguous strings as closer to Spanish than to Portuguese, revealing a skew in model behavior that differs from human judgments.
bullets: Analyzes Portuguese and Spanish representations with three fine-grained experiments.
Uses a large-scale language-identification experiment spanning over 200 languages.
Finds strong language-identity signals across the model, not only in initial and final layers.
Shows ambiguous strings are classified closer to Spanish than Portuguese, unlike human judgments.
Results are demonstrated using Llama 3.2 1B and do not establish that all multilingual LLMs behave identically.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes language-specific feature representation across layers in multilingual LLMs, relevant to LLM interpretability.
