papers.title: Where Are Language-Specific Features Represented in Multilingual LLMs? Everywhere
papers.tldr: Language identity remains recoverable throughout multilingual LLM layers, challenging the view that only the first and last layers encode language-specific features.

papers.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning treats the expert demonstration or gold response as a one-hot target, suppressing valid alternative continuations that the model would otherwise assign probability to. We propose Gold-Conditioned Distillation (GCD), a method that turns expert demonstrations into model-native supervision. GCD uses one model as both teacher and student: the teacher conditions on a prompt containing the gold response in context, the student conditions on the original prompt as at inference, and the student is trained to minimize the forward KL divergence to the teacher's next-token distribution at each gold response token. This lets the model use its prior knowledge to teach itself the new task: correctness is anchored by the gold response, while the soft target preserves plausible alternatives. Across various training tasks on Qwen and Llama models, GCD improves new-task accuracy over SFT and generally reduces degradation on general benchmarks.
authors: Wenxuan Zhu, Bang An, Shuming Liu, Wenqing Cui, Tianqi Xu, Bing Li, Yibo Yang, Peter Wonka, Bernard Ghanem
bullets: Standard supervised fine-tuning suppresses plausible alternative continuations by using one-hot gold targets.
GCD uses the same model as teacher and student: the teacher sees the gold response in context, while the student sees only the inference-time prompt.
The student matches the teacher’s next-token distributions via forward KL divergence at each gold-response token.
Across Qwen and Llama training tasks, GCD improves new-task accuracy over SFT and generally reduces degradation on general benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a self-distillation method for supervised fine-tuning of LLMs, improving task accuracy and reducing general degradation.
papers.title: Self-Distillation for Supervised Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: Gold-Conditioned Distillation replaces one-hot SFT targets with self-generated soft targets anchored to gold responses, improving task accuracy while preserving general capabilities.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) can improve reasoning in large language models, but specialized non-English domains expose a data mismatch. Raw English domain text is often available, while target-language RLVR tasks with verifiable rewards are scarce. We introduce code-switched task synthesis for cross-lingual RLVR, a data-centric approach that derives target-language and code-switched RLVR task variants from otherwise unverifiable English domain text. Using fill-in-the-middle multiple-choice QA as a seed task format, we synthesize automatically verifiable tasks from domain passages and reshape them into cross-lingual variants. These variants preserve the same evidence-answer relation but change how English and target-language evidence are presented during RLVR. On Korean medical benchmarks and cybersecurity benchmarks across four target languages, code-switched training outperforms matched monolingual and bilingual-mixture baselines on average target-language performance while maintaining comparable English performance. Additional analyses provide evidence of better target-language input understanding and stronger cross-lingual alignment in both model outputs and internal representations. These results suggest that code-switched training helps target-language inputs access domain reasoning learned more strongly in English.
authors: Cheonbok Park, Jihwan Kim, Shinyoung Joo, Joosung Lee, Hwiyeol Jo, Jeonghoon Kim, Jaegul Choo
bullets: Addresses the scarcity of verifiable RLVR tasks in specialized non-English domains despite abundant English text.
Synthesizes automatically verifiable fill-in-the-middle multiple-choice tasks from otherwise unverifiable passages, then creates target-language and code-switched variants.
Preserves the evidence–answer relationship while varying the languages used to present evidence during RLVR training.

Across Korean medical and four-language cybersecurity benchmarks, code-switched training improves average target-language performance over matched baselines while maintaining comparable English performance.
Analyses indicate stronger target-language understanding and cross-lingual alignment in outputs and internal representations.
papers.selection_reason: Code-switched task synthesis for cross-lingual RLVR improves LLM reasoning in non-English domains.
papers.title: From Unverifiable Domain Text to Cross-Lingual RLVR via Code-Switched Task Synthesis
papers.tldr: Code-switched task synthesis enables RLVR to transfer reasoning from English domain text to target-language inputs, improving cross-lingual performance without sacrificing English ability.

papers.abstract: Multi-head attention is a central component of the transformer architecture, yet how its expressivity depends on the number of heads remains poorly understood. We study a one-layer, attention-only transformer with additive positional embeddings and define the head complexity $H^\ast(f)$ of a Boolean function $f$ as the minimum number of attention heads required to represent it. We derive an exact linear-fractional normal form for head complexity, prove a general threshold-degree lower bound, and give an explicit ten-bit function for which this bound is strict. For symmetric Boolean functions, we independently show that head complexity equals the number of times the function changes value between consecutive Hamming-weight levels, even when positional embeddings are allowed. This agrees with the concurrent characterization of Hsu and Xu (arXiv:2608.04243) in a model without positional embeddings. The symmetric lower bound combines our general threshold-degree bound with the classical result of Aspnes et al. (1994). These results were discovered and formalized by a frontier model through conjecture generation, theorem proving, and machine verification, while human researchers asked the high-level questions and reviewed the generated theorems. We make the Lean formalization and research traces publicly available to support agent-assisted theorem proving and formal verification in mechanistic interpretability. This work provides a proof of concept for using the capabilities of frontier models, grounded by formal verification, to develop an understanding of transformer architectures.
authors: Karthik Viswanathan, Plamen Dimitrov, Stefano Rocca, Sarayu Sirikonda
bullets: Defines head complexity as the minimum number of attention heads needed to represent a Boolean function.
Derives an exact linear-fractional normal form and proves a general lower bound based on threshold degree.
Provides a ten-bit function showing that the threshold-degree lower bound can be strict.
For symmetric Boolean functions, characterizes head complexity by the number of value changes across consecutive Hamming-weight levels, including with positional embeddings.
Uses frontier-model conjecture generation and theorem proving, with Lean formalization and research traces released publicly.
papers.selection_reason: Formal analysis of multi-head attention expressivity, relevant to LLM architecture understanding.
papers.title: Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention
papers.tldr: This work formally characterizes the head complexity of Boolean functions in a one-layer attention-only transformer and demonstrates model-assisted, machine-verified theorem discovery.

papers.abstract: Recent test-time scaling methods improve model performance by increasing inference-time compute. One practical form of this is parallel scaling, where a model samples multiple independent reasoning streams and aggregates their answers using methods like voting, reranking, or verification. While effective, this approach leaves the streams uncoordinated, and a discovery made in one rollout cannot influence any other. Multi-Sequence Verifiers jointly score candidate answers after generation, but the reasoning streams remain independent during inference. ParScale takes a step toward model-internal parallel scaling by learning to aggregate multiple forward passes, but its streams still do not exchange information while processing a sequence. We introduce BatchParScale, an attention mechanism that allows parallel streams to exchange information through a small set of communication positions. We evaluate BatchParScale on a new Parallel Needle-in-a-Haystack retrieval benchmark and in pretraining, fine-tuning, and cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning. Across these settings, BatchParScale outperforms ParScale on language-model loss and remains competitive on coordination-sensitive MARL tasks. Masked pretraining runs beat an unmasked single-sequence baseline despite local sequence corruption, and LoRA fine-tuning shows the mechanism can be added to a pretrained Transformer. At the same time, fact retrieval performance for pretrained and finetuned BatchParScale models remains unclear.
authors: Hans Peter Lyngs{\o}e Raaschou-jensen (University of Copenhagen), M. Onurcan Kaya (Technical University of Denmark), Desmond Elliott (University of Copenhagen)
bullets: Addresses the limitation that parallel scaling streams reason independently and cannot share discoveries during processing.
Introduces an attention mechanism for sparse information exchange among parallel sequence streams.
Evaluated on a Parallel Needle-in-a-Haystack benchmark, pretraining, fine-tuning, and cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning.
Outperforms ParScale on language-model loss and remains competitive on coordination-sensitive MARL tasks.
Masked pretraining beats an unmasked single-sequence baseline, while fact-retrieval performance remains unclear.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces an attention mechanism for parallel sequence streams, applicable to LLM pretraining and fine-tuning.
papers.title: BatchParScale: Sparse Batch-Mixing for Sequence Models
papers.tldr: BatchParScale enables parallel reasoning streams to share information during inference through sparse communication positions, improving over ParScale while retaining competitive coordination performance.

papers.abstract: Advancing physics reasoning in large language models requires scalable training data that connect physical laws, concrete problem scenarios, and verifiable numerical answers. Expert-designed problems offer top-down control over physical laws, conditions, and scenarios, but require costly human effort. LLM-based synthesis from texts scales efficiently, but model-generated answers and assessments leave supervision vulnerable to hallucinations. We introduce TIRE, a framework for Top-Down Formula Instantiation with Reliable Execution that brings knowledge-driven problem construction to large-scale data generation. Top-down instantiation uses reusable physical formulas and their applicability conditions to control the physical relations and numerical configurations of generated problems. Reliable execution establishes reference answers before problem generation, providing a common numerical foundation for problem construction and teacher distillation. Together, these mechanisms combine control over problem content with execution-grounded supervision for both supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. Using TIRE, we construct TIRE-19k, spanning nine subfields of physics. Across 3 backbone LLMs and 4 benchmarks, TIRE-19k outperforms 5 representative datasets with equal amounts of SFT data, exceeding the strongest baseline by 2.86 percentage points on average. Further GRPO raises Qwen3-8B's average accuracy by 1.52 percentage points over its TIRE-19k SFT checkpoint. These results demonstrate the value of generating physics training data from explicit physical knowledge with reliable execution.
authors: Xiaoyu Wu, Zhaoxin Yu, Xinglin Xiao, Nan Xu
bullets: Addresses the cost of expert-designed problems and hallucination risks in LLM-generated supervision.
Uses reusable physical formulas and applicability conditions to control laws, scenarios, and numerical configurations.
Executes reference solutions before problem generation, grounding answers for SFT and reinforcement learning.
Produces TIRE-19k across nine physics subfields; it outperforms five equal-sized datasets across three LLM backbones and four benchmarks.
Further GRPO improves Qwen3-8B accuracy over its TIRE-19k SFT checkpoint.
papers.selection_reason: Generates verifiable physics training data for LLM reasoning via top-down formula instantiation, relevant to LLM training and reasoning.
papers.title: TIRE: Top-Down Formula Instantiation with Reliable Execution for Physics Problem Synthesis
papers.tldr: TIRE generates scalable physics reasoning data by instantiating explicit formulas and reliably executing them to produce verified answers.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning improves the reasoning capability of large language models through verifiable rewards for mathematical and coding tasks. In token-level methods such as GRPO, clipping acts on individual token ratios while the reward and advantage apply to a complete response. Recent sequence-level methods align these units but still use fixed clipping bands, whose tail probabilities change as the score distribution evolves. We propose Conformal Prediction-Enabled Sequence-level Policy Optimization (CSPO), which adaptively calibrates sequence-level clipping bounds using recent training statistics. The resulting band targets a specified marginal tail budget and adapts to policy drift; calibration conditional on response length requires additional assumptions. We bound the probability that a fresh score falls outside the band by the target miscoverage level plus explicit CDF discrepancy and drift terms. Under additional moment conditions, this bound also controls the objective and gradient error relative to the unclipped GSPO power surrogate. Experiments with the Qwen3-1.7B series show improvements over GSPO on difficult mathematical reasoning benchmarks and ALFWorld, with clipping endpoints that adapt during training.
authors: Hui Yang, Wan Tian, Tao Ren, Zhongyi Li, Yijie Peng
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between token-level clipping and response-level rewards, plus fixed clipping bands that fail to adapt as score distributions evolve.
Uses recent training statistics and conformal prediction to set sequence-level clipping bounds for a target marginal tail budget.
Provides bounds on out-of-band probability, with terms for target miscoverage, CDF discrepancy, and policy drift.
Under additional moment assumptions, also bounds objective and gradient errors relative to the unclipped GSPO power surrogate.
Experiments on Qwen3-1.7B models report improvements over GSPO on difficult math reasoning benchmarks and ALFWorld.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive conformal calibration for sequence-level policy optimization in reasoning LLMs; relevant to LLM reasoning and training methods.
papers.title: Conformal Prediction-Enabled Sequence-level Policy Optimization for Reasoning Language Models
papers.tldr: CSPO adaptively calibrates sequence-level clipping for policy optimization, controlling clipping errors under policy drift while improving reasoning-task performance over GSPO.

papers.abstract: Looped language models increase computational depth by repeatedly applying shared layers, offering a way to improve model quality without adding parameters. However, sequential dependencies between loop iterations increase autoregressive decoding latency. We introduce Dual-Slot, an architecture that reorganizes serial looped computation into parallel latent and prediction slots. Rather than waiting for the current token's latent computation to finish, the prediction slot combines the previous token's deep latent state with the current representation, while the latent slot produces a state for the next decoding step. This shifts the latent dependency across adjacent tokens, replacing two sequential module invocations with a single paired invocation while preserving standard autoregressive generation. To preserve token-level parallelism during training, we use a small number of Jacobi iterations to refine latent states across the sequence in parallel. Experiments on Qwen-style dense and mixture-of-experts (MoE) models show consistent improvements in language modeling and average downstream accuracy. On the 1B dense model, Dual-Slot reduces Pile validation perplexity from 7.25 to 7.00 and improves average five-shot accuracy across nine task configurations by 2.26 percentage points. After supervised fine-tuning, it improves zero-shot GSM8K accuracy by 5.83 and 3.49 percentage points for the 1B dense and A0.6B MoE models, respectively. Across the evaluated batch sizes, Dual-Slot retains 93.1-96.5% of vanilla decoding throughput for the dense model and 98.1-99.6% for the MoE model.
authors: Yiqin Hao, Zitong Wang, Boyi Zeng, He Li, Shixiang Song, Feichen Song, Yifan Liu, Zhouhan Lin
bullets: Addresses the decoding latency caused by sequential dependencies in looped language models.
Uses a prediction slot for the current token and a latent slot that prepares the next token’s deep state in parallel.
Applies a small number of Jacobi iterations during training to refine latent states across the sequence while retaining token-level parallelism.
Experiments on dense and MoE Qwen-style models report better language modeling and downstream accuracy, with high retained decoding throughput.
Scope: results are reported for the evaluated 1B dense and A0.6B MoE models and batch sizes.
papers.selection_reason: Parallel-slot looped architecture improving LLM quality without added parameters; relevant to LLM architecture.
papers.title: Dual-Slot: From Serial Loops to Parallel Slots in Language Models
papers.tldr: Dual-Slot converts serial looped computation into paired latent and prediction slots, improving language-model quality while largely preserving decoding throughput.

papers.abstract: Mathematical problem solving and autonomous agents are increasingly important applications of language models, demanding stronger reasoning capabilities. Computational depth is a key resource for such reasoning, but adding model layers increases both training and inference costs, while test-time scaling incurs substantial additional inference computation. We introduce P2N (Previous to Next), which reuses the previous token's deep representations, already available during generation, to increase effective computational depth with negligible decoding overhead. Specifically, P2N adds the previous token's deep hidden state to the current token's shallow representation, allowing subsequent layers to build on previously completed deep computation. This recurrence extends effective computational depth across tokens, while introducing only a single vector addition per decoding step. We train the recurrence using parallel Jacobi updates restricted to a middle-layer core. Experiments with Qwen-style models show that, at 1.5B parameters, P2N improves GSM8K accuracy by over 10 percentage points under both zero-shot and few-shot prompting, with nearly unchanged decoding latency. The benefits also extend to language modeling and average performance on general downstream benchmarks. on general downstream benchmarks.
authors: Yiqin Hao, Boyi Zeng, Zitong Wang, He Li, Shixiang Song, Feichen Song, Yifan Liu, Zhouhan Lin
bullets: Targets stronger reasoning for mathematical problem solving and autonomous agents without adding model layers or substantial test-time computation.
Adds the previous token’s deep hidden state to the current token’s shallow representation, creating cross-token depth recurrence.
Trains the recurrence with parallel Jacobi updates in a middle-layer core.
On 1.5B-parameter Qwen-style models, improves GSM8K accuracy by over 10 percentage points with nearly unchanged decoding latency.
Also reports benefits for language modeling and average performance on general downstream benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Recurrence architecture reusing previous token's deep representations; relevant to LLM architecture and efficient depth.
papers.title: P2N: Reusing Deep Representations for Greater Effective Depth
papers.tldr: P2N reuses previous-token deep representations to increase effective reasoning depth with nearly no additional decoding cost.

papers.abstract: A guardrail classifier is reported as if unsafe were a property of text. It is not: it is a property of a policy, and the policy enters the model through its labels. We exploit an accident of an industrial deployment in which the same ~53k prompts were labelled twice, under two operational definitions ("is this a request for harmful content?" and "would a moderator block this?"), and used to train ten guardrail arms sharing architecture, codebase and optimiser family, at two model scales. First, the guardrail's own training corpus already contained the benchmarks: JailbreakBench-benign is 88% and OR-Bench-hard 82% present in the training pools, two over-refusal benchmarks, the kind a guardrail reports to argue it does not over-block. Everything below is decontaminated. Second, safety benchmarks stratify sharply by how much of their score is decided by the label definition rather than by the model: with architecture and optimiser fixed, the range across the ten arms is 0.99 on HarmBench-copyright and 0.043 on WildGuard-benign, a 23x spread. Third, a benchmark score can be moved across its entire range by 0.03% of the parameters. Across these arms HarmBench-copyright spans 0-100 and OR-Bench-hard over-refusal 3.4-56.4%, and the four arms whose last supervision signal carries a given policy occupy one extreme of both (exact rank p=0.005, or 0.04-0.14 at worst), at unchanged detection capability. For a distilled student the teacher's soft labels do this even when every hard label carries the other policy, so teacher provenance is an unrecorded confound in any released checkpoint. Fourth, validation accuracy on the one split that grades all twenty arms tracks agreement with the annotator's policy (rho=+0.74), not detection capability (rho=+0.34). We argue that guardrail evaluations should report contamination, a seed floor and the definition they were graded against as first-class variables.
authors: Vahid Jebraeeli, Jonathon Romero, Yijin Wang, Adrian Chan, Jianbang Zhang
bullets: The study examines ten guardrail models trained with identical architectures and optimization families but two different operational definitions of “unsafe.”
Many benchmark prompts were already present in training data, including 88% of JailbreakBench-benign and 82% of OR-Bench-hard; analyses were otherwise decontaminated.
Benchmark outcomes varied dramatically by labeling policy: HarmBench-copyright ranged from 0–100, while OR-Bench-hard over-refusal ranged from 3.4–56.4%, despite unchanged detection capability.
Only 0.03% of parameters and teacher soft-label provenance were sufficient to shift benchmark scores across their range, making checkpoint lineage a potential confound.
The authors recommend reporting benchmark contamination, a seed floor, and the policy definition used for grading.
papers.selection_reason: Examines how label policy, contamination, and parameter changes affect safety benchmark scores for guardrail LLMs, relevant to LLM evaluation and training.
papers.title: Policy Is Not Capability: Some Safety Benchmarks Measure Which Definition of "Unsafe" You Trained On
papers.tldr: Safety-benchmark scores can primarily reflect the policy used to label training data rather than a guardrail’s underlying ability to detect harmful content.

papers.abstract: Large language models sometimes reply in an unexpected language, a failure known as language confusion. We ablate individual attention heads in 12 model checkpoints spanning seven model series, using FLORES-200 continuations in five languages and Language Confusion Benchmark (LCB) chat replies. In ten models, zeroing one head causes substantially more departures from the expected language than zeroing any other head in its layer; its LCB pass-rate drop persists, though reduced, under mean ablation. Seven heads move 8.0 to 51.5 percent of all FLORES continuations out of the prompt's language, versus at most 1.4 percent for other same-layer heads; the other three mainly affect explicitly requested languages. These seven heads matter less in base models given plain text. In two models, replacing the values a head reads at the requested-language name with another language's mean makes replies fail and shifts some into that language, unlike a random change of equal size. Replacing a head's output with another language's mean redirects 84 to 99 percent of scored non-English monolingual LCB replies into that language in five models. Yet the requested language's mean improves crosslingual replies beyond every control head only in the two Gemma models, whose baselines are low. Code and results are available in the public repository at https://github.com/christian-hoang-04/anonymous-release.
authors: Jiwon Jeong, Anjelo Jann Laroza, Chaewoon Yoon, Arjun Pillai, Pranav Kokati, Christian Hoang, Seunghyeok Hong
bullets: Across 12 checkpoints from seven model series, one head in many layers caused the largest language-confusion increase when ablated.
Seven heads shifted 8.0–51.5% of FLORES continuations out of the prompt language, compared with at most 1.4% for other same-layer heads.
The identified heads also reduced Language Confusion Benchmark pass rates, though their effects weakened under mean ablation and were smaller in base models.
Replacing language-related values or head outputs could make replies fail or redirect them into another language, supporting a causal role for these heads.
Improvements for crosslingual replies over control heads appeared only in the two Gemma models, limiting the generality of that effect.
papers.selection_reason: Mechanistic analysis of individual attention heads in LLMs across model families, directly relevant to LLM architecture and behavior.
papers.title: One Head Away from Language Confusion: Single Attention Heads Across Model Families
papers.tldr: A small number of attention heads strongly influence which language an LLM uses, with effects that generalize across several model families.

papers.abstract: Looped large language models trade parameter storage for recurrent computation, but most are trained from scratch. In practice, pretraining with looped depth is expensive, making post-training upcycling of a pretrained non-looped LLM an attractive alternative. We introduce \textbf{UpLoop}, a post-training recipe based on \emph{layer-wise} recurrence. Instead of looping a whole model or a middle block, UpLoop loops each selected layer locally, preserving the pretrained depth hierarchy and avoiding feature-space mismatch. To make loop execution useful, we add hidden-wise gates on the attention and MLP residual branches, so later loops act as progressive refinements rather than redundant rewrites. Empirically, UpLoop breaks the commonly observed saturation at two loops ($R=2$) in prior looped models. Starting from Qwen3-4B Base and applying SFT, UpLoop improves the average accuracy across 20 benchmarks by 6.17\% at $R=3$. We use $R=3$ as the main setting for the best accuracy--cost trade-off, while both native and extrapolated $R=4$ yield further gains.
authors: Tieyuan Chen, Huabin Liu, Yingtao Zhang, Shijie Li, Tengyu Pan, Weiyao Lin, Jianguo Li
bullets: Addresses the high cost of pretraining looped LLMs from scratch through post-training upcycling.
Uses layer-wise recurrence, preserving the pretrained depth hierarchy and avoiding feature-space mismatch.
Adds hidden-wise gates to attention and MLP residual branches so later loops progressively refine representations.
On Qwen3-4B Base with SFT, improves average accuracy across 20 benchmarks by 6.17% at three loops.
Three loops offer the main accuracy–cost trade-off, while four loops provide further gains in both native and extrapolated settings.
papers.selection_reason: Layer-wise looped LLM upcycling is an architectural advance for large language models.
papers.title: UpLoop: Upcycling Large Language Models with Gated Loop
papers.tldr: UpLoop converts pretrained non-looped LLMs into more effective recurrent models by looping layers individually with gated residual refinement.

papers.abstract: Recursive Transformers depend not only on how many parameters are shared, but also on how shared parameters are organized across depth. Existing static schemes adopt two extreme reuse topologies: layer-wise repetition, where each layer is reused independently, and global cyclic reuse, where the entire stack is repeatedly applied as a single shared function. We argue that sharing granularity is an important factor in recursive parameter sharing. This study proposes Block Recursive Transformers (BRT), which partition layers into contiguous blocks and recursively reuse each block before moving to the next. This intermediate topology enables local refinement within blocks while preserving depth-wise transitions, without adding routing modules, auxiliary states, or extra training objectives. Across decoder-only models up to 1.7B parameters, with additional encoder-decoder and encoder-only studies, BRT improves validation negative log-likelihood and downstream accuracy over static recursive sharing baselines. Ablations and representation analyses further show that intermediate block granularity better balances local refinement and depth-wise differentiation. Project website: https://aim-skku.github.io/BRT/
authors: Josep Marques, Hyunyoung A. Cho, Youngeun Kim, Youjia Zhang, Aecheon Jung, Kyuhong Shim, Sungeun Hong
bullets: Recursive Transformers depend on how shared parameters are organized across depth, not just how many are shared.
BRT partitions layers into contiguous blocks and recursively applies each block before progressing to the next.
The approach requires no routing modules, auxiliary states, or additional training objectives.

Experiments across decoder-only models up to 1.7B parameters, plus encoder-decoder and encoder-only settings, show improved validation negative log-likelihood and downstream accuracy over static recursive-sharing baselines.
Ablations and representation analyses indicate that intermediate block granularity provides a better balance between local refinement and depth-wise differentiation.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes block recursive parameter sharing for transformer architectures, relevant to LLM architecture research.
papers.title: Block Recursive Transformers for Structured Parameter Sharing
papers.tldr: Block Recursive Transformers improve recursive parameter sharing by reusing contiguous layer blocks, balancing local refinement with depth-wise differentiation.

papers.abstract: Muon has recently emerged as a strong optimizer for large language model pretraining by exploiting matrix structure through polar orthogonalization. However, it processes each parameter matrix independently, whereas recent tensor-aware extensions of Muon jointly update groups of eligible matrix parameters through matrix unfoldings. In contrast, we propose T-MUON, a t-SVD-based generalization that groups structurally related Transformer gradients into third-order tensors and defines the corresponding Muon-style update directly through the $M$-transform. We show that the exact T-MUON update is a steepest-descent direction under the $\star_M$-spectral norm and establish a convergence guarantee. Across GPT-2-style and LLaMA-style models from 51M to 1.3B parameters trained on FineWeb and FineWeb-Edu, head-wise T-MUON with the identity transform consistently achieves lower validation perplexity than AdamW, Muon, and variants using DFT, DCT, or DST transforms. These gains persist in additional experiments with longer context lengths and larger token budgets, although the preferred tensorization mode varies across settings.
authors: Dongyang Li, Mingsong Yan, Zheng Zhang, Sui Tang
bullets: Groups structurally related Transformer gradients into third-order tensors instead of updating parameter matrices independently.
Defines a Muon-style update through the M-transform; the exact update is a steepest-descent direction under the star_M spectral norm.
Provides a convergence guarantee for the proposed optimizer.
Head-wise T-MUON with the identity transform outperforms AdamW, Muon, and DFT-, DCT-, and DST-based variants in reported experiments.
Performance gains persist with longer contexts and larger token budgets, while the best tensorization mode varies by setting.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a tensorized Muon-style optimizer for LLM pretraining, directly relevant to large language model training methods.
papers.title: T-MUON: Tensorizing Muon via t-SVD for Large Language Model Pre-training
papers.tldr: T-MUON extends Muon with t-SVD tensor updates for jointly optimizing related Transformer gradients, achieving consistently lower validation perplexity than several optimizer baselines across tested language-model settings.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities across natural language tasks. But their ability to generate accurate written verbalizations of mathematical formulas has not been systematically evaluated. Such verbalization is important for text-to-speech systems supporting audio-based learning and visually impaired users. We evaluated five state-of-the-art LLMs across six scientific domains and constructed Read-Aloud Math, a balanced multi-domain corpus with LaTeX formulas, manually validated simple and extended transcriptions, multiple variants, textual context, domain labels, and formula complexity levels. Using multi-reference BLEU, GPT-5.2 achieved the highest score for simple transcriptions (75.9% without context, 64.9% with context), although without context it did not significantly outperform Grok 4.1 Fast or Claude Sonnet 4.5. Claude Sonnet 4.5 achieved the highest score for extended transcriptions without context (36.5%), and Grok 4.1 Fast with context (48.8%). For extended transcriptions, Statistics and Mathematics scored highest across the two context settings, while Physics scored lowest. Formula length was significantly negatively associated with BLEU for simple transcriptions without context, but not with context, whereas BLEU increased significantly with formula length for extended transcriptions in both settings. Grouping symbols were most frequently involved in transcription differences, while variable names, capitalization, and Greek letters were associated with lower BLEU scores. Overall, LLM-based formula verbalization is promising but remains sensitive to transcription type, textual context, and formula characteristics.
bullets: The study evaluates five LLMs across six scientific domains for spoken-style formula transcription.
It introduces Read-Aloud Math, a balanced corpus with validated simple and extended transcriptions, variants, context, domain labels, and complexity levels.
GPT-5.2 led simple transcriptions, while Claude Sonnet 4.5 and Grok 4.1 Fast led extended transcriptions under different context settings.
Extended transcription performed best in Statistics and Mathematics and worst in Physics.
Grouping symbols, variable names, capitalization, and Greek letters were common sources of differences; formula complexity showed type- and context-dependent effects.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates the ability of LLMs to verbalize mathematical formulas. This is a specific evaluation task for Large Language Models, relevant to their capabilities in structured reasoning and generation.
papers.title: How Well Can LLMs Verbalize Mathematical Formulas? A Multi-Domain Evaluation
papers.tldr: LLMs can verbalize mathematical formulas, but accuracy varies substantially with transcription type, context, domain, and formula characteristics.

papers.abstract: Explainable AI (XAI) often prioritizes model fidelity over user intelligibility, yielding explanations that satisfy technical transparency yet fail to support human sense-making. We propose a human-centered approach, MIND-X (Mental-model INtegrated Design for eXplainability), which aligns explanations with users' mental models, commonsense concepts, and judgment heuristics. Using fake review detection as a case study, we contribute: (1) a qualitative study (n=10) that elicits how people assess review credibility and produces an actionable, design-guiding taxonomy of perceptual cues; (2) a set of design principles that link those cues to explanation strategies and prompt LLMs to generate adaptive, language-based explanations; and (3) a quantitative evaluation (n=166) showing that these explanations offer distinct advantages over token-level transparency methods widely used in explainable text classification in terms of understandability, satisfaction, perceived trust, persuasiveness, and decision-making support. Rather than claiming general superiority, our evaluation illustrates how grounding explanations in users' everyday reasoning practices can produce more intelligible and context-sensitive accounts. Our findings advance human-centered explanation design beyond a mere "gloss of transparency," demonstrating that a mental-model-aligned design process can improve intelligibility and support accountability across user-centered explanation tasks.
authors: Sidra Naveed (University of Siegen, Germany), Md Shajalal (University of Siegen, Germany), Gunnar Stevens (University of Siegen, Germany, Hochschule Bonn-Rhein-Sieg), Alexander Boden (Hochschule Bonn-Rhein-Sieg)
bullets: Addresses the gap between technically faithful explanations and explanations people can understand and use.
Elicits how people judge review credibility through a qualitative study of 10 participants, yielding a taxonomy of perceptual cues.
Translates these cues into design principles that guide adaptive, language-based explanations generated with LLMs.
A quantitative study with 166 participants found advantages over token-level transparency methods in understandability, satisfaction, perceived trust, persuasiveness, and decision support.
The findings illustrate the value of mental-model alignment without claiming universal superiority or general applicability beyond the studied context.
papers.selection_reason: Focuses on improving the explainability of LLMs for text classification (fake review detection) by aligning with user mental models. This is relevant to Language Foundation Models, specifically regarding instruction tuning and user-centric design.
papers.title: Leveraging Mental Models for Human-Centered Explanations: A Systematic Design Approach Illustrated by Explainable Fake Review Identification
papers.tldr: MIND-X designs AI explanations around users’ mental models and everyday reasoning, producing more intelligible and context-sensitive explanations for fake review detection.

papers.abstract: Speech recognition in real time in far-field conversational settings still incurs significant errors. Identifying potential error spans during streaming ASR permits a recourse mechanism where the speaker can be asked to repeat the affected content under cleaner acoustic conditions. We propose \sysname, a new framework for online error localization, that identifies spans likely to benefit from this intervention. Our supervision uses clean audio to estimate how the recognizer's output might change under improved acoustic conditions. We probabilistically align noisy and clean decodes using a pair-HMM to obtain soft supervision. These soft targets train a counterfactual gain scorer by combining a suite of acoustic and language features to produce token-level scores, that are further grouped into spans for targeted recourse. An LLM uses the ASR transcript of the repetition to revise only the selected span. At a precision of $70\%$, \sysname achieves the highest recall by identifying up to 52\% more erroneous tokens compared to the strongest baseline. Targeted repetition yields relative WER reductions of up to 24\% under a budget that accounts for both interruption frequency and the lengths of re-uttered spans.
authors: Sankalp Parashar, Preethi Jyothi, Sunita Sarawagi
bullets: Targets far-field conversational speech errors through selective clarification rather than full re-utterance.
Uses pair-HMM alignment between noisy and clean decodes to create soft, counterfactual supervision.
Combines acoustic and language features into token-level gain scores, which are grouped into intervention spans.
An LLM revises only the selected span using the transcript of the repetition.
At 70% precision, it finds up to 52% more erroneous tokens than the strongest baseline and reduces WER by up to 24% under a recourse budget.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a framework for targeted clarification in ASR, using an LLM to revise specific error spans identified by a counterfactual gain scorer.
papers.title: Ask, Don't Guess: Targeted Clarification for Speech Recognition Errors
papers.tldr: A streaming ASR framework identifies error-prone spans worth asking speakers to repeat, then selectively revises those spans to improve recognition.

papers.abstract: We study how text serialization affects table lookup in instruction-tuned language models. Our diagnostic asks the model to find the row containing a specified value under one named column, then return the value under another named column in that same row. We render the same synthetic 256-cell tables in row-major form and in column-major form with each header placed beside its values, while varying the table aspect ratio across five shapes. Across three models, the better format changes with table shape: row-major performs better on tall tables, whereas column-major performs better on wide tables. At 64 x 4, row-major leads by 42.3-54.0 percentage points; at 4 x 64, column-major leads by 35.0-59.0 points. Mapping wrong answers back to their source cells reveals a complementary error pattern: row-major tends to preserve the correct row but lose the target column, while column-major tends to preserve the correct column but lose the row. We use the term relational locality to describe this pattern: serialization keeps one relation locally available while making the other depend on positional alignment. A separate non-tabular ordering experiment supports this interpretation. Thus, apparent width-related failures in text-serialized tables depend on linearization, not table shape alone.
authors: Junwei Ma, Arun Kumar Chithanar, Palash Goyal, Chul Lee
bullets: The study tests lookup in identical 256-cell tables rendered in row-major or column-major formats across five aspect ratios.
Row-major serialization works better for tall tables, while column-major works better for wide tables.
At 64×4, row-major leads by 42.3–54.0 percentage points; at 4×64, column-major leads by 35.0–59.0 points across three models.
Errors show that row-major tends to preserve the correct row but lose the target column, whereas column-major tends to preserve the correct column but lose the row.
The findings motivate “relational locality”: linearization makes one relation locally available while making the other depend on positional alignment.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates the impact of text serialization (row-major vs column-major) on table lookup in LLMs, identifying 'relational locality' as a key factor in preserving information.
papers.title: Table Serialization Determines Which Relations Language Models Preserve
papers.tldr: How a table is serialized determines which row–column relations language models preserve during lookup.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (dLLMs) generate by gradually unmasking a canvas, so their samplers decide not only which token to write but also when to commit it. We show that this second decision changes who appears in generated text, a sampler-induced bias on top of the model's own. Common commit rules, including LLaDA's default, commit the positions whose sampled tokens are most probable; this peeking favors majority options. To separate the sampler from the model, we read the model's belief about a fork, such as a protagonist's gender, in one forward pass, and show that this belief matches exact sampling from the model. Measured against it, peeking samplers on LLaDA and Dream amplify occupational gender stereotypes and collapse opinion distributions, and confidence-based ordering shifts gender-balanced occupations toward men, more so under faster parallel decoding. We propose Fork-First Sampling, which decides the fork before anything else is written: it follows the belief or any target distribution, improves fluency, and avoids the stories that remark on the protagonist's gender, which prompt-based fixes produce, at the cost of one forward pass. Fairness evaluations of dLLMs should report the commit rule.
authors: Xujun Che, Farsheed Haque, Depeng Xu, Xi Niu, Haopeng Zhang
bullets: Commit rules influence both which tokens are generated and when, introducing bias beyond the model’s own beliefs.
A single forward pass can estimate the model’s belief about a binary fork and provide a sampler-independent baseline.
Peeking and confidence-based samplers amplify occupational gender stereotypes and collapse opinion distributions.
Confidence-based ordering shifts gender-balanced occupations toward men, especially with faster parallel decoding.
Fork-First Sampling can follow the model’s belief or a target distribution and avoids explicit gender commentary induced by prompt-based fixes, at the cost of one forward pass.
papers.selection_reason: Shows sampler commit rules induce bias in diffusion language models and proposes fork-first sampling, relevant to LLM generation.
papers.title: Who Gets Unmasked? Sampler-Induced Bias in Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: Diffusion language model samplers can amplify social biases by committing high-confidence tokens first, and Fork-First Sampling reduces these effects while preserving fluency.

papers.abstract: Existing Multi-token prediction (MTP) methods are auxiliary by design: the multi-horizon loss mostly trains modules attached to the backbone, and each added horizon costs another module and another pass. We propose Efficient Causal Self-Recursion (ECHO), which removes both costs. The backbone's own final layer predicts every horizon, so the supervision lands on the parameters that generate the next token, and Dynamic Depth Sampling (DDS) keeps deeper horizons affordable by drawing the training depth with probabilities that decay along depth. Future prediction thus becomes part of the autoregressive objective rather than a task attached to it, and the gains follow on both sides of it. In pretraining, added depth converts into downstream accuracy where auxiliary modules saturate, concentrating on reasoning and code at half the MTP training overhead of training every depth. At inference, the pretrained model is its own drafter: it drafts beyond the depth it was trained for, and keeps its draft-target alignment on the open-ended, high-entropy generation where post-hoc drafters lose theirs. The advantage survives a doubled token budget, a repeated pretraining run, and supervised finetuning.
authors: Yuxuan Zhou, Junyuan Shang, Tianyu Wang, Chunrui Zheng, Zichang Liu, Wenbin Chang, Shuohuan Wang, Dianhai Yu
bullets: Existing MTP methods rely on auxiliary modules, adding parameters, passes, and limited supervision to the backbone.
ECHO uses the backbone’s final layer to predict every future horizon, directly training the next-token-generating parameters.
Dynamic Depth Sampling samples training depths with probabilities that decay by depth, reducing the cost of deeper-horizon supervision.
The approach improves downstream accuracy, especially on reasoning and code, at half the overhead of training every depth.

At inference, the pretrained model drafts beyond its training depth while maintaining alignment in open-ended, high-entropy generation; benefits persist with more tokens, repeated pretraining, and supervised fine-tuning.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes ECHO, which removes auxiliary costs from multi-token prediction by using the backbone's final layer for all horizons and employing Dynamic Depth Sampling.
papers.title: ECHO: Efficient Causal Self-Recursion Beyond Auxiliary Multi-Token Prediction
papers.tldr: ECHO turns multi-token prediction into an efficient self-recursive autoregressive objective that improves training and enables the model to draft its own future tokens at inference.

papers.abstract: Discrete diffusion language models (dLLMs) offer an attractive alternative to autoregressive generation by updating multiple tokens in parallel, but their inference efficiency is still limited by the cost of safely committing tentative predictions. In particular, speculative decoding for dLLMs is challenging because speculative tokens within the same diffusion block may depend on one another, making aggressive acceptance prone to error propagation and strict verification computationally expensive. We present PV-Decoding, a confidence-driven speculative decoding framework with progressive verification for block diffusion inference. PV-Decoding partitions masked positions into directly decoded tokens, speculative tokens, and unresolved tokens using two confidence thresholds, and then verifies speculative tokens with progressively stronger policies, including single-batch, dual-batch, and multi-batch verification. This design exposes a practical accuracy--efficiency trade-off: weaker verification minimizes overhead, whereas stronger verification improves acceptance precision and robustness. Experiments on three diffusion language models across GSM8K, MBPP, and HumanEval show that PV-Decoding reduces sequential model forward passes (MFPs) by 8%--37% relative to confidence-based decoding, while keeping the largest observed accuracy drop to 1.3%. On Dream-7B-Instruct/GSM8K, PV-Decoding (1-batch) and PV-Decoding (2-batch) improve throughput by 7.0%--13.6% under the same hardware budget, whereas PV-Decoding (multi-batch) is slower under the current runtime. These results suggest that confidence-guided speculation with structured verification is a practical path toward efficient and reliable dLLM inference.
authors: Renxi Liu, Yiming Li, Shengyin Sun, Chen Chen, Xian Wang, Shuai Yang, Huiling Zhen, Xianzhi Yu, Yaoyuan Wang, Weizhe Lin, Xiaosong Li
bullets: Addresses the efficiency challenge of safely committing parallel token predictions in discrete diffusion language models.
Uses two confidence thresholds to classify tokens as directly decoded, speculative, or unresolved.
Applies progressively stronger verification: single-batch, dual-batch, and multi-batch.
Across three models and three benchmarks, reduces sequential model forward passes by 8%–37% versus confidence-based decoding, with at most a 1.3% accuracy drop.
Improves throughput by 7.0%–13.6% for 1-batch and 2-batch variants on Dream-7B-Instruct/GSM8K; multi-batch is slower in the reported runtime.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces PV-Decoding, a confidence-driven speculative decoding framework with progressive verification to improve inference efficiency for discrete diffusion language models.
papers.title: PV-Decoding: Progressive Verification Decoding with Decode Gating for Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: PV-Decoding accelerates diffusion language model inference by speculatively decoding tokens and progressively verifying them, reducing forward passes with minimal accuracy loss.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (dLLMs) are emerging as an alternative to autoregressive (AR) language models, yet dLLM agents largely inherit an interaction protocol designed for AR generation: once intermediate state is written, later observations can only be incorporated by appending more text. This is a poor match to a defining capability of dLLMs -- reconstructing earlier text conditioned on context that appears both before and after it. We ask whether this capability can support a different agent-state paradigm in which intermediate planning state is directly revisable as evidence arrives. We introduce DiffuPlan, a diffusion search agent that maintains a single editable planning state and reconstructs only the affected steps when later evidence resolves an entity or changes the search route. To support variable-length revisions, we introduce Expansion-Partition Marginalization (EPM), which marginalizes over equivalent expansion paths. We further adapt diffusion trajectory RL to multi-turn search. Across four multi-hop QA benchmarks, DiffuPlan achieves 50.24 average F1, outperforming strong AR search agents. More importantly, under identical data and training, editable planning state improves the diffusion agent by 2.44 F1 versus only 0.47 for its AR source model. These results show that dLLMs need not imitate append-only AR agents: revising committed state is a distinct agentic advantage.
authors: Qisheng Zhou, Zhen Xiong, Qiaoyu Tan
bullets: Targets the mismatch between diffusion models’ bidirectional reconstruction ability and append-only AR-style agent state.
Maintains one editable planning state and reconstructs only steps affected by resolved entities or changed search routes.
Introduces Expansion-Partition Marginalization to handle revisions that change plan length.
Adapts diffusion trajectory reinforcement learning to multi-turn search.
Achieves 50.24 average F1 across four multi-hop QA benchmarks; editable planning improves the diffusion agent by 2.44 F1 under matched training.
papers.selection_reason: Diffusion language model agents with editable planning state, relevant to language foundation models.
papers.title: DiffuPlan: Editable Planning State for Diffusion Language Model Agents
papers.tldr: DiffuPlan enables diffusion language model agents to revise earlier planning steps as new evidence arrives, improving multi-hop search performance.

papers.abstract: Language models sometimes repeat verbatim until the generation limit. We study the exit rather than the entrance: given that a span has already been repeated $n$ times, when is escape still possible? Along the loop the context is deterministic, so loop survival under any sampler can be computed exactly from one forward pass. Pure sampling leaves a positive escape probability at every step; top-$p$ with threshold $\pi>1/2$ locks a position exactly when the continuation probability reaches $\pi$. A bounded penalty can leave a position locked; a penalty that outgrows the model's preference for the loop over unseen tokens guarantees escape under top-$p$. The same analysis predicts a blind spot in the widely deployed DRY sampler: its sequence breakers cap the penalty at $\lambda b^{g-1-a}$ for loops whose longest breaker-free run has $g$ tokens. On eleven open models, 66\% of locked units with $g=6$ stay locked under DRY and 1\% with $g=8$. In free generation with llama.cpp, all 109 loops that survive DRY have $g\le 7$. We propose DRY-C, which adds a term that grows exponentially with the number of verbatim recurrences, up to its look-back window. With it, none of 720 structured-output generations looped to the length limit, and task completion stayed close to DRY's.
bullets: Pure sampling always retains a positive escape chance, but top-p can lock a loop when its continuation probability reaches the threshold.
Penalties that do not outgrow the model’s preference for repetition may leave positions permanently locked.
DRY’s breaker-based penalty is capped for short breaker-free runs, so many locked loops remain locked.
Across 11 open models, 66% of locked units with run length g=6 stayed locked under DRY, versus 1% with g=8.
DRY-C adds recurrence-based exponential penalty growth; none of 720 structured-output generations looped to the limit while task completion remained close to DRY’s.
papers.selection_reason: Formal analysis of repetition-loop lock-in and sampler blind spots in LLM decoding, relevant to language model generation.
papers.title: When Do Repetition Loops Lock? Truncation Sampling, Bounded Penalties, and a Blind Spot in DRY
papers.tldr: Repetition loops can become mathematically unescapable under truncation sampling and bounded penalties, revealing a blind spot in DRY that DRY-C addresses.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) substantially improves mathematical reasoning, but what it adds to the base model remains unclear. We investigate this through a sequence of generation-time interventions on Qwen3-4B-Base, measuring how much of its RL-trained counterpart's gain each intervention recovers on 120 AIME problems. Power sampling with the same 8,192-token output limit brings no gain beyond greedy decoding. Yet borrowing the RL model's token only where the two models' greedy choices differ, roughly 4% of generated positions, recovers 90.5% of the pass@1 gain, with similar recovery across three model pairs on MATH-500. We find that even a single opening token has a substantial effect: forcing the base model to begin with "Alright" recovers 35% of the RL gain. The opening alone is insufficient, however. Later replacements after the same opening add another 5.2 percentage points to pass@1, and the fixed rules we test for inserting reflective words such as "Wait" do not reproduce this benefit. Sparse replacement also retains much of the base model's diversity while staying close to the RL model at pass@1. At k=256, it solves 67.5% of the problems, significantly more than the RL model (61.4%) and a mixture of whole responses matched in pass@1 (61.45%). The comparison is at equal attempt counts rather than equal compute, since rl-replace consults both models at every decoding step. These results show that the opening can recover a meaningful part of the RL gain, but a larger contribution comes from later choices, which can be borrowed while retaining much of the base model's diversity. Code is available at https://github.com/CyrusZhang04/WhatRLBrings.
authors: Siyu Zhang, Yuquan Lu, Yoshua Y. Li, Yifan Ding, Kun Zeng, Yu Huo, Yifu Guo, Rongxiang Weng, Xunliang Cai, Xiaoying Tang
bullets: On 120 AIME problems, power sampling within the same output limit adds no gain over greedy decoding.

Replacing the base model’s tokens only where its greedy choice differs from the RL model—about 4% of positions—recovers 90.5% of the pass@1 improvement; this also holds across three model pairs on MATH-500.

Forcing the opening token to “Alright” recovers 35% of the RL gain, while later replacements add a further 5.2 percentage points; fixed insertion rules for words like “Wait” do not reproduce this benefit.
Sparse replacement preserves much of the base model’s diversity and reaches 67.5% at k=256, versus 61.4% for the RL model and 61.45% for a matched whole-response mixture.
The comparison uses equal attempt counts rather than equal compute, because the replacement method consults both models at every decoding step.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes what RL adds to LLM reasoning through sparse token-level interventions, directly relevant to LLM training and decoding.
papers.title: What RL Brings to Reasoning: A Few Decisions the Base Model Would Not Make
papers.tldr: A small number of token-level choices—especially the opening token and later divergent decisions—accounts for much of RL’s reasoning improvement over the base model.

papers.abstract: The safety capabilities of large language models (LLMs) are highly uneven across different languages, often allowing cross-lingual attacks to bypass safety guardrails. Existing alignment methods predominantly rely on external alignment signals and provide limited insight into underlying neuron-level mechanisms, making it difficult to provide a unified internal target for cross-lingual safety interventions. To address this, we analyze cross-lingual safety behavior at the neuron level and identify a compact set of safety-related neurons shared across languages, termed the safety kernel (SK). Specifically, we first utilize multilingual parallel safe and unsafe prompts to compute safety contrast with activation responsiveness (SCAR) scores, identifying language-wise safety-neuron candidates from internal activation patterns. We then intersect the resulting language-wise safety-neuron sets to obtain the SK, and validate its functional relevance to cross-lingual safety behavior through activation suppression and activation-state transfer interventions. Finally, building on the SK coordinates, we introduce SK-Masked LoRA, which constrains LoRA adaptation to the feed-forward network (FFN) output dimensions corresponding to the SK, thereby focusing safety-related changes on the cross-lingually shared neuron coordinates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SK-Masked LoRA substantially reduces attack success rates across multiple languages, including languages excluded from SK discovery, while intervening on only a small fraction of internal neuron coordinates and producing generally limited changes in the model's general capabilities.
authors: Chengyu Xie, Fei Shen, Shuyi Miao, Yue Feng, Jian Yu, Pengyang Shao, Yijun Tian, Xiaoyu Du
bullets: Cross-lingual safety gaps can let attacks bypass LLM guardrails, while existing alignment methods offer limited neuron-level interpretability.
SCAR scores from parallel safe and unsafe prompts identify language-specific safety neurons; their intersection forms the shared Safety Kernel (SK).
Activation suppression and state-transfer interventions validate the SK’s role in cross-lingual safety behavior.
SK-Masked LoRA restricts adaptation to FFN output dimensions associated with the SK.
Experiments report lower attack success across multiple languages, including languages excluded from SK discovery, with generally limited effects on general capabilities.
papers.selection_reason: Identifies a cross-lingual safety kernel of neurons and constrains LoRA adaptation to these shared coordinates to improve defense.
papers.title: Safety Kernel: Mechanistic Alignment for Cross-Lingual Defense in LLMs
papers.tldr: The paper identifies a shared cross-lingual safety neuron subset and uses it to target alignment updates, improving multilingual defense with limited impact on general capabilities.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning LLMs with in-context examples (IC-Train) lets translation models adapt to new parallel data at deployment, but it is unclear whether they actually learn the translations of rare terms from those examples. We formalize this capability as in-context term learning (ICTL). We show that standard IC-Train develops this capability only weakly, and propose RareCipherFT, which strengthens it without any lexical resources. RareCipherFT pairs each training target with in-context examples that share a rare term with it. It then replaces that term with a character-shuffled cipher in both the context and the reference, so the term can only be recovered by copying from context. The ciphered fraction of training data is annealed to preserve translation quality. Across seven translation directions between English and Tamil, Assamese, Mizo, Nepali and Hausa, and four models from 1B to 7B parameters, RareCipherFT raises term recall over standard IC-Train by 5-15 absolute points without lowering COMET. Probes using synonyms, nonce words and controls for shared surface context show that these gains come from linking source terms to their in-context translations rather than from shortcuts.
authors: Deevyanshu Malu, Deeptanshu Malu, Sunita Sarawagi
bullets: Standard in-context training develops in-context term learning only weakly.
RareCipherFT pairs targets with context examples sharing rare terms, then replaces those terms with matching character-shuffled ciphers.
The cipher forces models to recover translations by copying from context rather than relying on lexical resources or shortcuts.
Across seven English–low-resource language directions and four 1B–7B models, term recall improves by 5–15 points without reducing COMET.
Probes with synonyms, nonce words, and surface-context controls support genuine source-to-translation linking.
papers.selection_reason: Directly studies LLM in-context terminology learning and fine-tuning for translation, relevant to language foundation models.
papers.title: Training with Ciphers to Enhance In-Context Terminology Learning For Translation from Rare Languages
papers.tldr: RareCipherFT improves rare-term learning from in-context translation examples by training models to copy ciphered term translations from context.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards assigns one terminal reward to an entire reasoning trajectory, obscuring how individual reasoning steps contributed to the outcome. GRPO broadcasts a group-normalized advantage to every response token, while finer-grained approaches often rely on dense auxiliary rollouts or branching schemes that can also alter the data used for policy updates. We cast the missing middle as budgeted measurement: with a limited rollout budget, which partial solutions should be evaluated, and how should their value estimates refine credit? ProbePO selects partial-solution states with a reward-free uncertainty score and estimates their expected verifier rewards under a capped continuation budget. ProbePO redistributes, rather than replaces, GRPO's trajectory-level advantage across tokens while preserving each trajectory's mean token-level advantage; probe continuations serve only as measurements. Across three DeepSeekMath and Qwen-family models spanning 1.5B-7B parameters, ProbePO consistently outperforms GRPO and achieves the highest accuracy among the four evaluated methods in 16 of 18 model-benchmark comparisons. Against dense-probing VinePPO on DeepSeekMath-7B, ProbePO achieves higher accuracy on all six benchmarks with 76% less end-to-end training time.
authors: Diyi Hu, Ruizhong Qiu, Lin Qiu, Hanghang Tong, Hanqing Zeng
bullets: Addresses the coarse credit assignment of terminal rewards and GRPO’s uniform token-level advantages.
Selects partial-solution states using a reward-free uncertainty score and estimates their verifier rewards with capped continuation probes.
Redistributes, rather than replaces, GRPO’s trajectory advantage while preserving each trajectory’s mean token-level advantage.
Outperformed GRPO across evaluated models and achieved the highest accuracy in 16 of 18 model-benchmark comparisons.
Beat dense-probing VinePPO on all six tested benchmarks while using 76% less end-to-end training time.
papers.selection_reason: LLM reinforcement learning with sparse probes and credit redistribution; relevant to language foundation model reasoning methods.
papers.title: ProbePO: Sparse Probes, Redistributed Credit for Critic-Free LLM Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: ProbePO improves critic-free LLM reinforcement learning by using a limited budget to probe uncertain partial solutions and redistribute trajectory credit across reasoning tokens.

papers.abstract: While a LLM's chain of thought (CoT) is a promising approach to interpreting model outputs, prior work shows CoT's content does not always accurately reflect the reasoning process. Emmons et al. (2025) finds that models can follow a question hint without revealing so in its chain of thought, but when the hint is sufficiently complex the computation is forced into the CoT. This claim, however, has only been tested on Gemini models, and the datasets and code is closed source. We replicate their proxy task across eleven models from six families and find the necessity effect generalizes. Every model follows simple cues above a no-hint baseline, while concealed complex-cue following falls back near baseline for most models. We also extend the study from Emmons et al. (2025) to measure CoT-necessity and unfaithfulness across five cue families (four of them new) and three difficulty levels. The relationship between when CoT is necessary and unfaithfulness is task-specific and model-specific. For some hint types, models often verbalize their hint-following behavior even when the hint can be decoded in a single forward pass. These results support the case for CoT monitoring when unsafe behavior requires non-trivial computation, and that properties of CoT unfaithfulness are sensitive to model and setting.
authors: Arav Dhoot, Yixiong Hao, Zephaniah Roe
bullets: Replicates the necessity effect across 11 models from six model families, beyond the originally tested Gemini models.
All models follow simple cues above a no-hint baseline, while following concealed complex cues generally returns near baseline.
Extends evaluation to five cue families and three difficulty levels, including four new cue types.
The link between CoT necessity and unfaithfulness varies by cue type and model; some models verbalize hint-following even when it is computationally simple.
Supports CoT monitoring for unsafe behavior requiring non-trivial computation, but cautions that monitoring reliability is context-sensitive.
papers.selection_reason: Empirical study of chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability across LLMs; relevant to LLM reasoning.
papers.title: CoTs remain monitorable when being unfaithful requires computation: Replicating and Extending the Necessity Effect Across Eleven Models
papers.tldr: Across 11 models, concealed cue-following usually breaks down when it requires complex computation, making chain-of-thought monitoring useful but strongly dependent on the task and model.

papers.abstract: Transformers have emerged as a dominant architecture in modern machine learning, with in-context learning (ICL) enabling models to adapt to new tasks by conditioning on prompts, without any parameter updates. To understand the attention mechanism in transformer blocks, a growing line of theoretical work interprets ICL through the lens of classical statistical estimators. Recent works have established a connection between the attention mechanism and kernel methods, while the kernel function is usually assumed to be fixed. In practice, the query and key matrices in the attention mechanism are trained, which allows the attention mechanism to serve as an adaptive kernel method. In this work, we demonstrate that transformers can act as adaptive anisotropic kernel learners. Specifically, we study ICL for low-rank linear and multi-index nonlinear regressions, and conduct numerical simulations to show that the learned attention scores closely resemble the oracle kernels for these function classes. We then develop a general framework to analyze the generalization error of ICL by connecting transformers to the oracle kernel estimator for each function class. Our theory gives an explicit and constructive implementation of the oracle kernel estimators for these function classes using a wide and shallow transformer architecture, illustrating how the prediction is carried out by the interaction between the query token and the context tokens. Our work complements existing studies by providing numerical and theoretical evidence of how the attention mechanism adapts to anisotropic kernels in both linear and nonlinear settings.
authors: Zhaiming Shen, Alexander Cloninger, Rongjie Lai, Wenjing Liao
bullets: Motivated by the gap between fixed-kernel interpretations of attention and the trainable query/key matrices used in practice.
Studies ICL for low-rank linear and multi-index nonlinear regression tasks.
Shows through simulations that learned attention scores closely match oracle kernels for these function classes.
Develops a generalization-error framework linking transformer ICL to oracle kernel estimation.
Provides a constructive implementation using wide, shallow transformers, explaining prediction through query–context interactions.
papers.selection_reason: Theoretical analysis of transformers as adaptive kernel learners for in-context learning; relevant to LLM reasoning and ICL.
papers.title: Transformers as Adaptive Kernel Learners across Tasks for In-Context Learning
papers.tldr: The paper shows that transformers can perform in-context learning by adapting attention into task-specific anisotropic kernel estimators.

papers.abstract: Pixel-based language models process rendered text without relying on a fixed subword vocabulary, offering a promising approach to noisy and multilingual inputs. However, their practical value depends on whether they can be reliably adapted to downstream tasks. To this end, we systematically examine this question through fine-tuning behavior, typographical robustness, and zero-shot crosslingual transfer. Under our tested settings, pixel-based models require longer training and broader labelled-data coverage than text-based models, while delayed learning and learning-rate-dependent failures make adaptation less reliable. Our analyses further suggest that task-relevant information is less readily accessible in pretrained pixel representations, placing greater demands on fine-tuning. Once successfully adapted, however, pixel-based models lose substantially less accuracy under typographical noise and achieve higher target-language accuracy than English-pretrained text-based counterparts on two crosslingual benchmarks, despite weaker clean English performance. Together, these findings reveal a central trade-off: replacing tokenization with rendering reduces sensitivity to corrupted and unfamiliar inputs, but shifts a central bottleneck to downstream adaptation.
authors: Haowen Tang, Wei Xia, Raoyuan Zhao, Hinrich Sch\"utze, Yihong Liu
bullets: They avoid fixed subword vocabularies by processing rendered text, benefiting typographical and multilingual settings.
Fine-tuning requires longer training and broader labelled-data coverage, with delayed learning and learning-rate-sensitive failures.
Pretrained pixel representations make task-relevant information less accessible during downstream adaptation.

After successful adaptation, they retain substantially more accuracy under typographical noise and outperform English-pretrained text models on two crosslingual benchmarks, despite weaker clean-English performance.
The central trade-off is reduced input sensitivity at the cost of a more difficult adaptation bottleneck.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes pixel-based language model adaptation, robustness, and crosslingual transfer; relevant to foundation LM architectures.
papers.title: Beyond Clean Accuracy: The Practical Challenges and Benefits of Pixel-Based Language Models
papers.tldr: Pixel-based language models are more robust to noisy and crosslingual inputs, but harder and less reliable to adapt than text-based models.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in annotation tasks with varying success. While several studies have demonstrated the opportunities and shortcomings of LLMs for annotation, a critical question remains unanswered: is it possible to predict how well they will perform on a new dataset? To answer this and related questions, we construct two task families which induce 461 text classification datasets. We find that it is possible to predict LLM performance - to a certain degree - and that contrary to other work which highlights the usefulness of LLM verbalizations of self-confidence, internal log-probabilities are the most predictive signal.
authors: Tong Lin, Grant Schoenebeck, Sabina Tomkins
bullets: Addresses whether zero-shot LLM annotation quality can be predicted before labeling a new dataset.
Constructs two task families yielding 461 text-classification datasets.
Finds that LLM performance is predictable, but only to a certain degree.
Internal log-probabilities are more predictive than verbalized self-confidence.
Scope is limited to the constructed text-classification task families and datasets.
papers.selection_reason: Predicts zero-shot LLM annotation performance using internal log-probabilities.
papers.title: Can This LLM Annotate My Data? Estimating Zero-Shot LLM Performance
papers.tldr: LLM annotation performance on new datasets can be estimated to some extent, with internal log-probabilities providing the strongest predictive signal.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but often reduces the diversity of their reasoning behaviors. We study this phenomenon from the perspective of finite-sample learning dynamics and show that limited on-policy rollouts can progressively suppress semantically distinct but equally rewarded reasoning modes. Once a mode becomes sufficiently under-sampled, standard on-policy RLVR rarely recovers it. Motivated by this observation, we propose TAR, a Targeted Adaptive Replay framework that preserves diverse correct reasoning behaviors already present in the base policy. TAR constructs a compact memory bank of diverse base-model solutions and selectively replays them through an adaptive mechanism that activates only when stored behaviors are being suppressed during RLVR. Across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks and two Qwen2.5 model scales, TAR consistently achieves a better balance between reasoning performance and diversity preservation than existing diversity-preserving post-training methods, while substantially reducing the forgetting of correct base-model solutions. Code is available at https://github.com/wenzhilics/tar.
authors: Wen-Zhi Li, Sainyam Galhotra, Claire Cardie
bullets: RLVR can reduce reasoning diversity because limited on-policy rollouts under-sample distinct but equally rewarded solution modes.
Under-sampled reasoning behaviors are difficult for standard on-policy RLVR to recover.
TAR stores a compact bank of diverse base-model solutions and selectively replays them when suppression is detected.
Across six math benchmarks and two Qwen2.5 scales, TAR improves the balance between reasoning performance and diversity preservation while reducing forgetting of correct base-model solutions.
papers.selection_reason: RLVR for LLM reasoning with adaptive replay to preserve reasoning diversity.
papers.title: Preserving Reasoning Diversity in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards via Adaptive Replay
papers.tldr: TAR preserves diverse correct reasoning behaviors during RLVR by adaptively replaying base-model solutions when they are being suppressed.

papers.abstract: We ask how much an autoregressive transformer retains of its prompt after generating $t$ tokens. Consider two different prompts followed by the same continuation text, so that any difference in their hidden states comes from the prompt alone, and we find that the distance between their hidden states decays approximately as a power law $t^{-\alpha}$, where $\alpha=1$ is the rate at which a fixed prompt's share of uniform attention shrinks and smaller values mean longer memory. Trained models forget fast ($\alpha\approx0.55$--$0.7$), untrained ones slowly ($\alpha\approx0.2$--$0.5$). We prove that this offset is $O\big(P(\log t)^{L-1}/t\big)$ for a prompt of length $P$ and depth $L$. The bound holds for finite-depth pre-LN softmax transformers with bounded attention logits, under one additional condition: the pre-norm activations stay away from zero. The mechanism is geometric: the prompt's direct influence is diluted as the context grows, and \emph{relay} --- continuation tokens passing on what earlier tokens read from the prompt --- can only add logarithmic factors.
