This is what we call the \emph{conditional no-hair theorem}: given the text generated so far, the prompt's influence on the next token vanishes as $t$ grows, so any property of the prompt that survives, such as its language, must be carried by the text itself. An exactly solvable linear relay model shows that the bound cannot be improved and reproduces the rise of the local exponent towards $1$ seen in untrained networks. Cancelling the dilution with a logit bias stops the decay early in training and reverses it after, so dilution is necessary for the forgetting we measure; untrained networks and the solvable model show it is also sufficient.
bullets: Prompt-dependent hidden-state differences decay approximately as a power law, t^-α.
Trained models forget faster (α≈0.55–0.7) than untrained models (α≈0.2–0.5).
A finite-depth pre-LN softmax transformer has a prompt-dependent offset bounded by O(P(log t)^{L−1}/t), under bounded logits and nonzero pre-norm activations.
An exactly solvable relay model matches the bound and reproduces the increasing local exponent observed in untrained networks.
Logit-bias experiments indicate that attention dilution is necessary—and, in the studied settings, sufficient—for the observed forgetting.
papers.selection_reason: Theoretical analysis of prompt retention and forgetting in autoregressive transformers, relevant to LLM architecture and context behavior.
papers.title: A Conditional No-Hair Theorem for Transformers: How Language Models Forget Their Prompt
papers.tldr: Transformers gradually forget prompt-specific information as generation continues, with direct dilution dominating and relay effects adding only logarithmic corrections.

papers.abstract: Prefix-tuning is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method for large language models (LLMs) that steers model outputs by prepending task-specific prefix representations to the input sequence. Despite its practical success, the theoretical understanding of the expressiveness of prefixes remains incomplete. In particular, the following question remains open: Given a pretrained autoregressive Transformer, for any input-output sequence pair $(\mathtt{x},\mathtt{y})$, does there always exist a prefix $\mathcal{S}$ such that prepending $\mathcal{S}$ to $\mathtt{x}$ induces the model to generate the target output $\mathtt{y}$? In this work, we prove that under the assumption that $\mathtt{y}$ is in the range of the pretrained Transformer, such a prefix $\mathcal{S}$ exists and can be explicitly computed by solving multiple linear systems. We further show that this assumption is necessary, in the sense that such a prefix may not exist when the assumption fails, thereby providing a complete answer to the above question. Our analysis is constructive and the obtained theoretical results hold under fairly general assumptions on model architecture. Extensive experiments on GPT-2 and Qwen3-4B demonstrate that our algorithm produces prefixes with strong control over model outputs.
authors: Peter Cho-Ho Lam, Ziyi Wang, Zirui Zhou
bullets: Establishes existence of a prefix for an input–output pair when the target is in the pretrained Transformer’s output range.
Computes the prefix explicitly by solving multiple linear systems.
Shows the range assumption is necessary: desired outputs may be unreachable otherwise.
Theoretical results apply under fairly general architectural assumptions.
Experiments on GPT-2 and Qwen3-4B show strong control over generated outputs.
papers.selection_reason: Theoretical and constructive analysis of prefix steering for pretrained autoregressive LLMs; directly relevant to LLM control and adaptation methods.
papers.title: Prefix-Tuning for Arbitrary Output Sequences on Pretrained Transformers
papers.tldr: The paper proves when prefix-tuning can force a pretrained autoregressive Transformer to generate any target sequence and gives a constructive way to compute such prefixes.

papers.abstract: Looped language models reuse physical Transformer blocks across logical depth, but established architectures entangle recurrence placement, input injection, and recurrent state organization. We isolate these axes in models trained from scratch at matched parameter scale, logical depth, and token budgets, and then test whether the resulting design principles transfer to resident- and active-parameter-matched Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models. The prelude-recurrent block-coda sandwich architecture consistently improves performance on context extraction and reasoning-intensive tasks. Input injection primarily enhances knowledge retrieval and context utilization, whereas random initialization and separate H/L recurrent states provide mixed or negative returns. Taken together, these results favor the Huginn-style design: at the 730M-parameter and 336B-token scale, the complete Huginn architecture outperforms Ouro across all ten benchmarks. The advantages of Huginn over Ouro transfer to MoE models. At the 8BA0.8B (32BA3B when unrolled) scale trained on 500B tokens, Huginn outperforms Ouro on nearly all benchmarks spanning knowledge, reasoning, and coding, while also exhibiting more balanced expert routing. Under matched training and inference FLOPs, the Huginn-style model uses 75% fewer resident parameters than a 112-layer feedforward MoE baseline. Despite its smaller physical parameters, it outperforms the feedforward baseline on DROP and GSM8K, matches it on MATH500, and remains competitive on the other benchmarks.
bullets: Separates recurrence placement, input injection, and recurrent-state organization under matched training conditions.
A prelude–recurrent block–coda sandwich consistently improves context extraction and reasoning tasks.
Input injection mainly helps knowledge retrieval and context utilization; random initialization and separate H/L states offer mixed or negative benefits.
At 730M parameters and 336B tokens, Huginn outperforms Ouro across ten benchmarks, with gains transferring to MoE models.
With matched FLOPs, the looped MoE uses 75% fewer resident parameters than a 112-layer feedforward MoE while outperforming it on DROP and GSM8K and matching it on MATH500.
papers.selection_reason: Looped LLM architecture and MoE design study directly relevant to LLM architecture research.
papers.title: Towards Looped Models Done Right, Part I: Topology, Input Injection, Recurrent-State Design
papers.tldr: The study identifies a Huginn-style looped Transformer design that improves reasoning and context use and transfers effectively to MoE models with fewer resident parameters.

papers.abstract: Self-distillation with privileged context adapts a language model from demonstrations by letting the model, once conditioned on a reference response, teach its context-free copy token by token. Our taxonomy reveals existing methods differ along three entangled axes: (i) the rollout source (student or teacher), (ii) the teacher coupling (frozen, or an exponential moving average of the student at some coupling rate) and (iii) the KL direction (reverse or forward), yet these axes are usually studied in fixed combinations and have led to conflicting conclusions. We formalize a unifying framework to encompass all self-distillation methods vs classic supervised fine-tuning: we train every combination of the three axes, on Qwen2.5-7B and Ministral-3-3B across ordinary and contradictory tasks, totaling 1,200 adaptation runs, to systematically investigate the impact of the above axes. We propose a controlled model of the same objective to explain the resulting acquisition-retention trade-offs. We find that (i) the rollout source matters mostly where the task contradicts the pretrained behavior: there teacher rollouts raise acquisition well above what student rollouts achieve, with almost no change in retention; (ii) the teacher coupling changes acquisition most, on every task: acquisition rises with the coupling rate, then falls past a task-specific rate; (iii) switching the KL direction costs retention in one model but not the other so which axis to tune first depends on the model. The controlled model reproduces the three trends.
bullets: Evaluates rollout source, teacher coupling, and KL direction across all combinations, rather than fixed method pairings.
Teacher rollouts improve acquisition especially on tasks contradicting pretrained behavior, with little retention change.
Teacher coupling has the largest acquisition effect: performance rises with coupling rate before declining beyond a task-specific optimum.
Changing KL direction harms retention in one model but not the other, so tuning priorities are model-dependent.
A controlled model reproduces the observed acquisition–retention trends.
papers.selection_reason: Systematically studies self-distillation and supervised fine-tuning for LLMs using Qwen2.5 and Ministral checkpoints, contributing to understanding and improving modern LLM training.
papers.title: Disentangling Self-Distillation: Measuring and Modeling Acquisition and Retention
papers.tldr: A systematic study disentangles three design choices in self-distillation, showing how rollout source, teacher coupling, and KL direction separately shape task acquisition and retention.

papers.abstract: Scientific discovery requires developing worthwhile hypotheses into practical investigations, yet learning from this evolving research process remains challenging. We introduce an operational definition of valuable and testable research hypotheses: evidence-grounded claims about consequential uncertainties, coupled with feasible investigations, explicit decision criteria, and alternative explanations. Our DiscoveryRSI framework develops hypothesis trees through multi-agent evolutionary search, compiles selected investigations into executable Harbor tasks, and recursively learns through three mechanisms: hypothesis credit optimization attributes scientific assessments to documented research contributions; harness replay identifies productive strategies and recurring failures to refine research workflows; and rediscovery applies accepted improvements to new investigations, generating further experience for subsequent learning. We also introduce DFM-Bench, which provides comprehensive assessment of hypothesis quality and cumulative research progress at the levels of hypotheses, revisions, development paths and research runs. Across four life-science domains, automated evaluation shows that hypothesis quality rises from 4.86 for the base model to 5.39 after two rounds of self-improvement, with the large gains in falsifiability and data resolvability. We further validate hypothesis quality through expert review, comparing our DiscoveryRSI-27B with other research agents. Preliminary human assessments show that DiscoveryRSI-27B scores higher than GPT-6 Luna on hypothesis importance and whether claims are plausible and evidence-bounded. DiscoveryRSI-27B achieved a 6.3% rate of hypothesis correspondence with research published after the model cutoff, largely outperform GPT-6 with 2.5% and Claude Opus 5 with 2.3%, while delivering greater human-rated improvement along research paths.
authors: Jianyuan Zhong, Chenwei Wu, Zhaochen Yu, Xixian Jiang, Xuewei Li, Hao Xiao, Xilin Dai, Junyang Wang, Jiaru Zou, Zhiqing Cui, Boyuan Zheng, Jing Xiong, Zhen Zhang, Qiang Gao, Michael Morley, Luis Nakayama, Qiang Xu, Liyue Shen, Tao Gui, Leo Anthony Celi, James Zou, Zhenfei Yin, Yingcheng Wu, Ling Yang
bullets: Defines valuable, testable hypotheses as evidence-grounded claims about consequential uncertainties paired with feasible investigations, decision criteria, and alternatives.
Uses multi-agent evolutionary search to build hypothesis trees and compiles selected investigations into executable Harbor tasks.
Recursively learns through credit assignment, workflow replay, and rediscovery of improved strategies for new investigations.
Introduces DFM-Bench to evaluate hypothesis quality and cumulative progress across hypotheses, revisions, development paths, and research runs.

Across four life-science domains, hypothesis quality improved from 4.86 to 5.39 after two self-improvement rounds; expert evaluations and post-cutoff correspondence also favored DiscoveryRSI in the reported comparisons.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces DiscoveryRSI, a multi-agent framework for scientific hypothesis discovery. It demonstrates recursive learning and self-improvement strategies for LLM-based research agents.
papers.title: DiscoveryRSI: Recursively Learning to Discover Valuable Hypotheses
papers.tldr: DiscoveryRSI recursively improves scientific hypothesis generation by evolving evidence-grounded research plans and learning from their outcomes, producing higher-quality hypotheses and stronger alignment with later research.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding typically characterizes speedup by draft tokens accepted per verification round. Lossless verification preserves the target model's output distribution and thus expected completion length, making this metric a meaningful efficiency proxy. Relaxed (lossy) verification accepts tokens that lossless verification would reject, potentially altering that distribution. We identify a length inflation phenomenon: relaxed verification lengthens completions, primarily by extending reasoning traces, largely offsetting apparent gains in accepted tokens per round. We evaluate existing training-free relaxed verification rules on twelve target-drafter pairs against lossless verification on identical prompts, measuring completion length, verifier rounds, wall-clock time, and task accuracy. At each rule's most relaxed evaluated setting, relaxed verification on average accepts $1.34\times$ as many tokens per round but produces $1.54\times$ longer completions. For rules with higher acceptance lengths, tokens accepted only under relaxed verification tend to have low target-model probability, contributing to length inflation. For rules that reduce verifier rounds, accuracy typically drops substantially. Further analysis traces some failures to continued reasoning that exhausts the budget needed to deliver a final answer. Overall, accepted tokens per round alone is an unreliable measure of decoding speed under relaxed verification. Completion length and verifier rounds must also be reported to assess actual efficiency.
authors: Chiatzen Wang, Bill Xu, Haochen Gu, Hongyang Zhang
bullets: Lossless verification preserves output distributions, making accepted tokens per round a useful efficiency proxy; relaxed verification does not.
Across twelve target–drafter pairs, the most relaxed settings accepted 1.34× more tokens per round but produced 1.54× longer completions on average.
Extra accepted tokens often had low target-model probability and contributed to length inflation, especially by extending reasoning traces.
Rules that reduced verifier rounds typically caused substantial accuracy drops, sometimes because continued reasoning exhausted the output budget.
Completion length, verifier rounds, wall-clock time, and accuracy should be reported alongside acceptance rates.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes the efficiency of speculative decoding, specifically identifying 'length inflation' in lossy verification. This provides important empirical findings regarding LLM decoding speed and verification mechanisms.
papers.title: Acceptance Is Not Speed: Length Inflation in Training-Free Lossy Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: Relaxed speculative decoding may accept more tokens per round but often generates much longer completions, undermining its apparent speed gains and sometimes reducing accuracy.

papers.abstract: While deriving text embeddings directly from frozen LLMs has emerged as a promising direction, existing methods focus almost exclusively on English, leaving multilingual settings largely unexplored. In this work, we present the first systematic study of multilingual training-free text embeddings in LLMs. Our analysis reveals a language-conditioned embedding geometry in which semantically equivalent sentences remain misaligned across languages. We hypothesize that language-specific variation can be disentangled from semantic content to improve embedding quality. To this end, we propose Paired-Residual Subspace Removal (PRSR), a training-free inference-time intervention that steers LLM representations toward a more language-invariant semantic space. PRSR first constructs paired residuals from multilingual parallel sentences to capture language-specific deviations. It then estimates layer-wise low-rank subspaces from these residuals and suppresses the corresponding components in the last-token hidden states. We conduct more than 200 monolingual evaluations across 18 languages using MTEB and MMTEB, along with cross-lingual bitext mining between English and over 200 other languages. Empirical results demonstrate that PRSR consistently improves the performance of existing training-free baselines in both monolingual and cross-lingual settings across different LLMs.
authors: Ailiang Lin, Zhuoyun Li, Yusong Wang, Keyu Mao, Kotaro Funakoshi, Manabu Okumura
bullets: Identifies language-conditioned embedding geometry that misaligns semantically equivalent sentences across languages.
Uses parallel multilingual sentences to construct paired residuals capturing language-specific variation.
Estimates layer-wise low-rank residual subspaces and suppresses them in last-token representations at inference time.
Evaluated across 18 languages with MTEB/MMTEB and in English-to-200+ language bitext mining.
Consistently improves existing training-free baselines across monolingual and cross-lingual tasks and multiple LLMs.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes Paired-Residual Subspace Removal (PRSR), a training-free inference-time intervention to improve multilingual text embeddings by removing language-specific variation. This is a direct technical contribution to LLM representation learning and multilingual capabilities.
papers.title: Steering beyond Language: Improving Multilingual Training-Free Text Embeddings via Paired-Residual Subspace Removal
papers.tldr: PRSR improves multilingual, training-free text embeddings by removing language-specific representation components from frozen LLMs.

papers.abstract: Teachers increasingly configure educational chatbots through natural-language instructions, but how these bots fail in real-world use remains poorly understood. We introduce EduWild, a dataset of 1,726 conversations with 217 teacher-configured chatbots, each paired with the instructions and configuration behind it, including 900 conversations from the intended end users of 35 deployed chatbots. We develop a 29-code taxonomy covering factual, workflow, diagnostic, and pedagogical failures and apply it using a human-calibrated LLM judge. The most frequent failures are lapses in following teacher intent --- bots skip required workflow steps (53.8% of end-user conversations), omit expectation setup (33.4%), and overload learners with information or questions (37.1%). Guided by these findings, we design a prompt-based harness targeting the six most frequent failure modes. In a study with 200 college students across ten bots, the harness reduces the mean number of target failure codes per conversation from 1.406 to 0.489, a 65.2% relative reduction with bots weighted equally. These findings show how real-world failure analysis can guide practical improvements to educational chatbots.
authors: Ziqi Liu, Ruiwei Xiao, Yuxuan Li, John Stamper
bullets: Introduces 1,726 conversations involving 217 teacher-configured chatbots, including 900 end-user conversations from 35 deployed bots.
Provides a 29-code taxonomy spanning factual, workflow, diagnostic, and pedagogical failures, applied with a human-calibrated LLM judge.
Frequent failures include skipped workflow steps, missing expectation setup, and excessive information or questioning.
A prompt-based harness targeting six common failure modes reduced target failures by 65.2% in a study with 200 college students across ten bots.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates and provides a prompt-based harness to fix real-world failures in teacher-configured educational chatbots.
papers.title: EduWild: How Teacher-Configured Chatbots Fail in Real-World Use and How to Fix Them
papers.tldr: EduWild shows that teacher-configured educational chatbots often fail to follow intended workflows and overwhelm learners, while a prompt-based harness substantially reduces these failures.

papers.abstract: In-Context Learning (ICL) enables pretrained LLMs to adapt to downstream tasks from a small set of input-output demonstrations, without parameter updates. Yet existing theory primarily explains ICL as identifying a latent task already represented in pretraining, leaving unclear whether ICL can succeed when either the instruction or the target task falls outside the pretraining support. We develop a theoretical framework under mild assumptions that separates these two forms of distribution shift. For target tasks represented in pretraining, we show that demonstrations can identify the task and reduce sensitivity to pretrain-supported prompt templates as their number increases. For an unsupported instruction, we show that under a fixed model-induced reference extension, demonstration evidence can dominate an $N$-independent instruction shift while preserving the exponential identification rate. We then use the same ICL framework as an interpretive lens for long-horizon target tasks that are not represented in pretraining but admit a plan that decomposes them into pretraining-supported subtasks. Applying the supported-task analysis step by step yields a standard accumulated-error bound and clarifies how invoking familiar subtasks along an intermediate-state trajectory can avoid directly selecting the unsupported complete task. Together, our results characterize when demonstrations, instructions, and task decomposition can support ICL beyond the corresponding pretraining supports.
authors: Xuhan Tong, Yuchen Zeng, Jiawei Zhang
bullets: Separates two shifts: unsupported instructions versus target tasks absent from pretraining.
For pretraining-supported tasks, more demonstrations identify the task and reduce dependence on prompt templates.
For unsupported instructions, demonstrations can overcome a model-induced instruction shift while retaining exponential task-identification behavior.
For unsupported long-horizon tasks, decomposing them into pretraining-supported subtasks yields an accumulated-error bound.
Characterizes when demonstrations, instructions, and task decomposition extend ICL beyond pretraining support.
papers.selection_reason: Provides a theoretical framework for In-Context Learning when instructions or tasks fall outside the pretraining support, analyzing distribution shifts and task decomposition.
papers.title: Out of Support, Not Out of Reach: In-Context Learning with Unsupported Instructions and Composed Tasks
papers.tldr: A theoretical framework explains how in-context demonstrations can support learning with unsupported instructions and unfamiliar composed tasks by identifying supported subtasks and overriding prompt shifts.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) encode substantial factual knowledge. Yet, estimating confidence in factual claims reliably remains challenging. We study likelihood-based factual confidence from the complementary perspectives of discrimination and calibration across multilingual factual statements. Specifically, we instantiate contrastive generative likelihoods as Contrastive Factual Evidence (CFE), which compares the likelihood of the same claim under competing factual and non-factual conditions, and derive its probabilistic counterpart, the Contrastive Factual Posterior (CFP). We show analytically that CFP calibration depends on the differential error between the two surrogate conditionals, allowing errors shared across them to cancel and yield tighter calibration bounds. Empirically, CFP substantially improves calibration while maintaining factual discrimination comparable to its strongest competitor. Nonetheless, discrimination is uniformly weak across methods in lower-resource languages, which simultaneously undermines the utility of the measured calibration. To this end, we interpret a likelihood geometry, within which an evidence-bearing direction is induced, along with an orthogonal evidence-invariant direction. In our investigation, we selectively align target-language claims with stronger English evidence only along the factual-evidence direction, improving discrimination and open-ended factual generation without target-language labels.
authors: Ponhvoan Srey, Jason Lucas, Pittawat Taveekitworachai, Junyoung Lee, Anh Tuan Luu
bullets: Frames factual confidence as both discrimination and calibration across multilingual claims.
Introduces Contrastive Factual Evidence (CFE) and its probabilistic form, Contrastive Factual Posterior (CFP).
Shows that shared errors between competing conditionals can cancel, producing tighter calibration bounds.
Finds CFP substantially improves calibration while preserving discrimination comparable to the strongest baseline.
Addresses weak lower-resource-language discrimination by aligning claims with English evidence only along a factual-evidence direction, improving discrimination and open-ended factual generation.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces Contrastive Factual Evidence (CFE) for improved calibration of factual confidence in LLMs.
papers.title: Truth in Contrast: Calibrated Factual Evidence from Language Model Likelihoods
papers.tldr: Contrastive likelihoods yield better-calibrated factual confidence, while evidence-direction alignment transfers English factual strength to weaker languages without target-language labels.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can now perceive, describe, and reason about images and audio, yet time series understanding remains underestimated: most work uses LLMs as forecasters and classifiers, reasoning studies are few and narrow, and no suite trains and evaluates the full range of capabilities. In this paper, we build the first such suite, with 337K training and 44K evaluation samples across three progressive capabilities, Perceive, Solve, and Reason, and use it to ask how time series should enter an LLM that must master all three, and in what order. We find that a dedicated encoder is essential: with one, a 4B model surpasses GPT-4o on every perception attribute we test, whereas textualizing the series costs 8--10 points in reasoning accuracy. The capabilities then build on one another: learning them in order beats mixing the same data and rivals reasoning-only training with over three times the reasoning data, but only when an encoder is used. Analyses further reveal that capabilities are transferred through distinct network depths rather than simply stacked, and that a stage converged on its own benchmark is not necessarily ready for the next. Distilled into a simple recipe, these findings yield 4B TS-LLMs that, without any target-domain data, outperform four recent 7B TS-LLMs on seven of eight out-of-domain metrics, by up to 11 points. We therefore advocate treating time series as a first-class modality for LLMs, read through dedicated encoders and taught to perceive before they reason.
authors: Xin Qiu, Junlong Tong, Wei Zhang, Xiaoyu Shen
bullets: Introduces a suite with 337K training and 44K evaluation samples spanning Perceive, Solve, and Reason capabilities.
Finds that dedicated encoders are essential: textualizing time series reduces reasoning accuracy, while a 4B model exceeds GPT-4o on tested perception attributes.
Shows that ordered capability training outperforms mixing the same data and can rival reasoning-only training with over three times the reasoning data.
Reports that capability transfer occurs across distinct network depths, and benchmark convergence at one stage does not guarantee readiness for the next.
The resulting 4B models outperform four recent 7B time-series LLMs on seven of eight out-of-domain metrics without target-domain data.
papers.selection_reason: Develops Time Series-LLMs with a dedicated encoder, treating time series as a first-class multimodal modality.
papers.title: Perceive, Solve, Reason: Progressive Capability Formation in Time Series-LLMs
papers.tldr: A dedicated time-series encoder and progressive training from perception to solving to reasoning substantially improve LLM-based time-series understanding.

papers.abstract: LLMs and LVLMs are increasingly deployed across heterogeneous hardware, ranging from data-center GPUs to resource-constrained edge devices. Their fixed-size architectures limit the ability to reuse a single model across deployment settings with different compute, latency, and model-size targets. We introduce HydraLLM, an elastic MQA-based architecture. Its number of active attention heads determines the effective widths of the embeddings, attention projections, feed-forward layers, and the output head, forming a nested family of subnetworks within a single parameter set. We introduce a static-to-elastic conversion pipeline that, starting from a pre-trained model checkpoint, includes importance-driven weight reordering and stochastic subnetwork training with knowledge distillation. We extend this principle to multimodal inference through an elastic projection module whose output width follows the active text width. HydraLLM covers a wider range of active parameter configurations than FFN-only elastic architectures. With 75% of heads active, HydraLLM achieves 2.2 percentage points higher TriviaQA accuracy than a state-of-the-art nested baseline configuration which has 17.25% more parameters. With 50% of heads active, our multimodal model achieves a CLIPScore comparable to that of the 7$\times$ larger Gemma 3 4B model. With only 25% of heads active, HydraLLM increases token-generation throughput by 75.3% over the full-width configuration.
authors: Oscar Kemme, Janek Haberer, Ali Hojjat, Olaf Landsiedel
bullets: Uses the number of active attention heads to jointly control embedding, attention, feed-forward, and output widths.
Converts pretrained checkpoints into elastic models through importance-based weight reordering and stochastic subnetwork training with knowledge distillation.
Adds an elastic multimodal projection whose width matches the active text-model width.
Reports higher TriviaQA accuracy than a larger-parameter nested baseline at 75% active heads, comparable CLIPScore to a much larger Gemma 3 4B model at 50%, and 75.3% higher token throughput at 25%.
papers.selection_reason: Elastic width slicing for efficient LLM/LVLM inference, fitting efficient AI and foundation-model topics.
papers.title: HydraLLM: Adaptive Width Slicing for Elastic Text and Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: HydraLLM turns one text or vision-language model into a flexible family of width-adjustable subnetworks for different hardware and efficiency targets.

papers.abstract: Efficient expert routing is a fundamental challenge in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) systems, particularly for heterogeneous collections of independently trained Large Language Mod els (LLMs). Existing routing approaches typically rely on jointly trained gating networks, prompt-based predictors, or computationally expensive multi-model inference, limiting their flexibility and efficiency. This paper presents ScoutRoute, a lightweight post-hoc routing framework that predicts expert competence using internal language model signals extracted from a single forward pass through an inexpensive scout model. Hidden-state representations are used to estimate cross-model competence through lightweight logistic probes, while logit-derived confidence measures are incorporated within a domain-aware routing strategy for efficient expert selec tion without modifying the underlying language models. ScoutRoute isevaluatedon fiveopen-weightlanguagemodels across fourbenchmark datasets covering mathematical reasoning, code generation, commonsense reasoning, and multidis ciplinary knowledge. Experimental results show that ScoutRoute consistently outperforms individual routing signals while requiring only a single scout-model inference. The proposed competence probes also achieve superior calibration compared with conventional confidence measures, demonstrating that internal language model representations provide transferable information for accurate and efficient expert routing across heterogeneous language models
bullets: Addresses the cost and inflexibility of jointly trained gates, prompt-based predictors, and multi-model inference.
Uses hidden-state representations with lightweight logistic probes and logit confidence signals for domain-aware routing.
Evaluated across five open-weight LLMs and four task domains, including math, code, commonsense reasoning, and knowledge.
Combining routing signals consistently outperforms individual signals while requiring only one scout-model inference.
Competence probes are better calibrated than conventional confidence measures, indicating transferable internal representations.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses efficient routing in mixture-of-experts LLMs using internal model signals, fitting the large language models subtopic.
papers.title: ScoutRoute: Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Routing Using Internal Language Model Signals
papers.tldr: ScoutRoute enables efficient post-hoc routing among heterogeneous LLM experts using competence signals from a single inexpensive scout-model pass.

papers.abstract: Large language models often answer factual questions incorrectly in closed-book settings, and such errors are usually attributed to missing knowledge. Yet models often encode answers they fail to produce. We show that many closed-book errors are first-token recall failures: the model commits to a wrong first token, but once given the right one it completes the answer and often recognizes it as correct. We study this with First-Token Cueing, a behavioral probe that prefills the response with the first token of the gold answer. Model uncertainty peaks at the first answer token, where it already predicts correctness, and among gold prefixes of any length the first token alone accounts for the largest share of recovered errors. Across 16 open models, this one token corrects between a fifth and a half of the errors on multi-token answers in English QA and improves accuracy in all seven languages of a multilingual benchmark. Most of the errors it corrects are also solved by the model's own sampled reasoning, a criterion for encoded knowledge, and models recognize correct starts they do not produce: they continue a correct start more confidently than an incorrect start of the same answer type and prior probability, yet rarely find it without the gold answer. These results locate a recoverable class of factual errors at the first decoding step, where inference-time methods may gain the most.
authors: Jaewon Sok, Jewon Yeom, Seonghyeon Park, Jeongjae Park, Hwiyeong Lee, Taesup Kim
bullets: Introduces First-Token Cueing, which prefills the response with the gold answer’s first token to probe recall failures.
Uncertainty peaks at the first answer token, and this token recovers more errors than longer gold prefixes.
Across 16 open models, cueing fixes roughly one-fifth to one-half of errors on multi-token English QA answers.
The method improves accuracy across all seven languages tested in a multilingual benchmark.
Models often recognize and complete correct starts they rarely produce spontaneously, suggesting a recoverable inference-time failure mode.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces First-Token Cueing as a behavioral probe to analyze and recover recall failures in LLMs.
papers.title: On the Tip of the Tongue: First-Token Cueing as a Behavioral Probe of Recall Failures in LLMs
papers.tldr: Many LLM factual errors reflect failure to generate the correct first answer token, not missing knowledge; cueing that token can recover the answer.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to automate AI research, including language-model (LM) development, offering a potential path toward recursive self-improvement. However, turning experimental feedback into a learned ability to propose effective improvements across models faces two challenges. First, training such an ability with real feedback is expensive: reinforcement learning (RL) requires evaluating tens of thousands of proposals, each potentially requiring a full model-training run. Even at ten GPU-hours per run, reward collection alone would consume hundreds of thousands of GPU-hours, motivating a cheaper surrogate. Second, surrogate feedback can become unreliable as policy optimization favors overestimated proposals when the proposal distribution shifts. To address these challenges, we propose LM2LM, which trains LLMs with RL to generate effective LM improvement proposals. To provide scalable feedback, we use a research world model (RWM), a frozen LLM that predicts proposal gains from real experimental records provided in context, as the reward model for RL. To maintain feedback reliability, we periodically execute current-policy proposals ranked highly by the RWM and add their measured outcomes to its context. Across eight autoregressive and diffusion LM development environments, real-execution evaluations on held-out tasks show that LM2LM enables Qwen3.8-27B to outperform GPT-6-sol, even when GPT-6-sol is given 300 real experimental records in context, while requiring 33% lower data-generation cost. LM2LM also generalizes to a model family unseen during training.
authors: Minhua Lin, Zijun Wang, Zewen Liu, Zhaotian Weng, Bing He, Zhan Shi, Benoit Dumoulin, Xiang Zhang, Suhang Wang, Hanqing Lu
bullets: Addresses the high cost of evaluating thousands of LM-improvement proposals with real training runs.
Uses a frozen LLM research world model to predict proposal gains from experimental records and provide RL rewards.
Periodically tests highly ranked proposals and feeds their measured outcomes back into the world model to reduce reward-model drift.
Across eight autoregressive and diffusion LM development environments, LM2LM outperformed GPT-6-sol on held-out tasks while using 33% lower data-generation cost.
The method generalized to a model family not seen during training.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes LM2LM for LLM self-improvement using a Research World Model (RWM) to predict gains from experimental records.
papers.title: Language Models Learn to Improve Language Models
papers.tldr: LM2LM trains language models to propose effective language-model improvements using a learned research world model as scalable feedback, with periodic real experiments to keep that feedback reliable.

papers.abstract: Native language identification (NLI) infers a non-native speaker's first language (L1) from their second language (L2) production. We investigate a token probability approach that scores each text sample as a continuation of a prompt prefix specifying a candidate L1, then predicts the candidate with the highest score. We evaluate our approach using Llama 3.1 8B and 70B on three datasets: TOEFL9, Write and Improve 2024, and BULATS-L1. We compare its performance with previous prompting-based classification approaches. Token-probability scoring substantially improves on direct classification, particularly with the 8B model, while the 70B model achieves state-of-the-art performance across all datasets. Our results indicate that pretrained LLMs' token probabilities contain information useful for distinguishing L1 backgrounds from L2 English production.
authors: Ahmet Yavuz Uluslu, Mark Gales, Kate Knill, Gerold Schneider
bullets: Frames NLI as choosing the candidate L1 with the highest token-probability score.
Evaluates Llama 3.1 8B and 70B on TOEFL9, Write and Improve 2024, and BULATS-L1.
Token-probability scoring substantially outperforms direct prompting-based classification, especially with the 8B model.
The 70B model achieves state-of-the-art performance across all three datasets.
Findings suggest LLM token probabilities encode information about L1 backgrounds in L2 English.
papers.selection_reason: Utilizes LLM token probabilities for Native Language Identification (NLI) tasks.
papers.title: Inferring L1 Backgrounds from L2 English with LLM Token Probabilities
papers.tldr: Scoring L2 English by how likely it is under prompts naming candidate L1s enables strong native-language identification with pretrained LLMs.

papers.abstract: Small differences between internal representations can shrink or grow as they pass through a Transformer layer, affecting how information is preserved and how sensitive the model is to perturbations. Yet it remains unclear when changes in attention weights can turn a representation difference that would otherwise shrink into one that grows. We develop a \textbf{Mixture-Gated Theory of Anisotropic Representation Dynamics} that separates self-attention into value transport, query gating, and key gating. Our analysis reveals how the geometry of attended representations constrains gating and how interactions between these mechanisms can reverse contraction induced by value transport. We formalize this phenomenon as gating-induced regime switching, where a representation difference contracts under fixed attention routing but expands under full attention. We derive a necessary and sufficient spectral criterion that certifies the existence or absence of switching and identifies switching directions without exhaustive search. Beyond existence, our theory characterizes maximum relative switching strength, certifies the severity of contraction that gating can overcome, and determines the largest dimension of a subspace in which every nonzero direction switches. Experiments across four Transformer architectures validate these predictions through analytical and finite-forward comparisons, revealing distinct and joint query--key gating mechanisms and nontrivial switching subspaces. Our results provide a mechanistic and spectral understanding of how attention routing can alter local representation dynamics.
bullets: Decomposes self-attention into value transport, query gating, and key gating to analyze anisotropic representation dynamics.
Defines gating-induced regime switching: differences that contract under fixed attention routing can expand under full attention.
Derives a necessary-and-sufficient spectral criterion for detecting switching and identifying switching directions without exhaustive search.
Also characterizes switching strength, the contraction gating can overcome, and subspaces where all nonzero directions switch.
Experiments across four Transformer architectures support the theory and reveal distinct, combined query–key gating effects.
papers.selection_reason: Develops a Mixture-Gated Theory of Anisotropic Representation Dynamics in Transformers, providing mechanistic understanding of attention routing.
papers.title: Anisotropic Representation Dynamics in Transformers
papers.tldr: A spectral theory explains when query–key attention gating can reverse contraction and amplify small representation differences in Transformer layers.

papers.abstract: Multi-turn LLM routing selects a model at every turn before its response is available, yet task success is revealed only when the interaction ends, leaving each intermediate choice without a label of its own. Logged trajectories, however, retain the response each call produced, which exposes what each turn required and how well the chosen model served it, evidence that outcomes alone hide. We introduce RIVET (Response-Informed Value Estimation for Turn-Level Routing), which exploits this post-call evidence during training while keeping routing strictly pre-call at deployment. RIVET jointly trains two value estimators over a shared state-model representation: a deployable Routing Value Estimator that scores candidate models from pre-call information, and a training-only Response-Informed Value Estimator that additionally observes the realized response. Conditioning on the response turns response-induced return variation from residual noise into an observed covariate, and we show that this reduces the leading asymptotic estimation error of the shared representation. On the MINT benchmark, RIVET solves more held-out tasks than the strongest multi-turn baseline while using 74.7% less total call cost.
authors: Haotian Yan, Jiaqi Liu, Bingyi Jing, Tianjun Yao
bullets: Multi-turn routing lacks turn-level labels because task success is known only after the interaction ends.
RIVET uses logged responses as training-only evidence while keeping deployment routing strictly pre-call.
It jointly trains a deployable Routing Value Estimator and a response-informed training estimator over shared representations.
Response conditioning reduces estimation error by explaining return variation otherwise treated as noise.
On MINT, RIVET solves more held-out tasks than the strongest multi-turn baseline while reducing total call cost by 74.7%.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces RIVET, a response-informed value estimation method for cost-aware multi-turn LLM routing.
papers.title: Response-Informed Value Estimation for Cost-Aware Multi-Turn LLM Routing
papers.tldr: RIVET improves cost-aware multi-turn LLM routing by using post-call responses during training to better estimate pre-call model values at deployment.

papers.abstract: Drifting Models generate a sample with a single function evaluation, making them attractive for fast parallel language generation, but their one-step formulation does not support iterative refinement. We propose Recurrent Language Generation via Drifting (ReLaDrift), which uses a shared Drifting Model to generate an initial draft from noise and iteratively refine it in a continuous latent space. We train this recurrence by sampling the number of rounds and applying the drifting loss only at the final round, stopping gradients through preceding rounds so that only one round requires backpropagation. Unlike the one-step Drifting Model, whose accuracy does not improve when iterated, ReLaDrift enables a trade-off between test-time computation and generation quality, as diffusion and flow language models do. On Sudoku Hard and GSM8K, it achieves competitive or superior performance compared with these iterative-generation approaches across a range of inference budgets. Our code is available at https://github.com/Yuki-Ots/ReLaDrift
authors: Yuki Otsuka, Daisuke Oba, Naoaki Okazaki
bullets: Drifting Models generate samples in one function evaluation but cannot benefit from iterative refinement.
ReLaDrift first creates a draft from noise, then repeatedly refines it using a shared model in continuous latent space.
Training samples different recurrence lengths and applies the drifting loss only at the final round, avoiding backpropagation through earlier rounds.
On Sudoku Hard and GSM8K, it performs competitively or better than iterative diffusion and flow language models across inference budgets.
The approach supports adjustable test-time computation while retaining the parallel-generation advantages of drifting models.
papers.selection_reason: Recurrent latent-space refinement for language generation enables test-time compute-quality trade-off, relevant to LLM architecture and generation methods.
papers.title: ReLaDrift: Recurrent Language Generation via Drifting for Test-Time Scaling
papers.tldr: ReLaDrift adds iterative latent-space refinement to one-step Drifting Models, enabling test-time compute to trade off against language-generation quality.

papers.abstract: Process Reward Models (PRMs) play a central role in test-time scaling for large language model (LLM) reasoning. However, PRMs may provide inaccurate process rewards for test-time scaling, which we identify as arising from two sources of uncertainty: (1) \textit{PRM uncertainty} that arises from insufficient supervision data and imperfect PRM training; and (2) \textit{policy uncertainty} that results from the mismatch between the policy to collect supervision data and the policy for test-time scaling, leading to systematic reward overestimation. Previous studies fail to jointly consider both uncertainties. To bridge this gap, we propose BayesianPRM, which treats the process reward as a random variable within a reward hypothesis space and maintains a Bayesian belief over it. Since exact Bayesian inference over the continuous hypothesis space is generally intractable, we discretize the reward hypothesis space with a reward ensemble and introduce two complementary belief updates, each targeting one source of uncertainty: (1) to address PRM uncertainty, we introduce \textit{reliability-aware belief updating} that measures how well each ensemble member explains the supervision data and updates the belief with an amortized belief network optimized by the evidence lower bound (ELBO); and (2) to tackle policy uncertainty, we propose \textit{conservatism-aware belief calibration} which further reweights the belief toward lower rewards to suppress overestimation. These two updates yield a reliability- and conservatism-aware Bayesian belief, whose expectation determines the process reward. Experiments on multimodal reasoning benchmarks indicate that BayesianPRM consistently yields more accurate process reward estimates while enhancing test-time scaling performance.
authors: Zhongjian Qiao, Zhixiang Zhou, Jiafei Lyu, Peisong Wang, Qiaosheng Zhang, Siyang Gao, Shuang Qiu
bullets: Identifies two PRM error sources: PRM uncertainty from limited or imperfect training and policy uncertainty causing systematic reward overestimation.
Represents process rewards with a Bayesian belief over a discretized reward hypothesis space using an ensemble.
Uses reliability-aware belief updating to assess ensemble members against supervision data via an ELBO-trained belief network.
Applies conservatism-aware calibration to shift belief toward lower rewards and reduce overestimation.
Experiments on multimodal reasoning benchmarks show more accurate process rewards and improved test-time scaling.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes BayesianPRM, a reliability- and conservatism-aware Bayesian belief for Process Reward Models to improve test-time scaling for LLMs.
papers.title: Process Reward Modeling with Reliability- and Conservatism-Aware Bayesian Belief
papers.tldr: BayesianPRM models process-reward uncertainty from both imperfect supervision and policy mismatch, improving reward accuracy and test-time scaling for multimodal reasoning.

papers.abstract: Neural combinatorial optimization (NCO) rapidly produces high-quality solutions for problem structures encountered during training, but operational requirements may change after deployment and be communicated in natural language. We propose LangNCO, a framework that compiles instance-specific requirements into structured inference-time interventions for a frozen NCO solver, without changing the pretrained policy's architecture, learned input representation, or parameters. A pretrained LLM serves as a replaceable semantic front end, translating each requirement into a schema-validated domain-specific language (DSL) rule set. A deterministic Rule Executor applies the rules as nonexpansive hard action masks. Because local masking prevents immediate violations but does not ensure that a complete feasible continuation remains reachable, Critical-Offset Decoding extracts rule-referenced critical nodes and reallocates part of a fixed rollout budget to multi-strength biased rollouts. Using controlled task-specific language to isolate solver adaptation from open-ended language robustness, we evaluate a CVRP policy on road closures, time windows, vehicle assignments, visit-order requirements, all pairwise combinations, and twelve additional constraint types. LangNCO achieves 100% feasibility on the four primary datasets with mean reference gaps of 1.63--3.26%, 97.33--100% feasibility when separately generated rules are composed for pairwise constraints, and 98.67% feasibility across the additional constraints. These results demonstrate modular post-training adaptation of a frozen NCO solver through inspectable language-derived rules, without retraining.
bullets: A pretrained LLM converts requirements into schema-validated domain-specific rules.
A deterministic executor enforces rules through hard action masks, while Critical-Offset Decoding preserves feasible continuations via targeted biased rollouts.
Evaluated on CVRP tasks including road closures, time windows, vehicle assignments, visit-order constraints, combinations, and additional constraint types.
The method reaches 100% feasibility on four primary datasets, 97.33–100% for composed pairwise constraints, and 98.67% across additional constraints.
Results use controlled task-specific language, so open-ended language robustness is not directly assessed.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces LangNCO, a framework for compiling natural language constraints into inference-time interventions for NCO solvers using LLMs.
papers.title: LangNCO: Compiling Natural-Language Constraints into Inference-Time Interventions for Neural Combinatorial Optimization
papers.tldr: LangNCO adapts a frozen neural combinatorial optimization solver to natural-language operational constraints at inference time, achieving high feasibility without retraining.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has substantially improved Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs, but its outcome-level rewards provide only sparse supervision. On-Policy Distillation offers dense token-level feedback, yet requires a stronger compatible teacher, while on-policy self-distillation relies on hand-designed privileged information. We observe that the MoE architecture itself offers a way to resolve this dilemma, as increasing the activation budget per token exposes latent expert capacity and yields a potentially stronger teacher within the model. However, naive expansion degrades performance because newly co-activated experts are not optimized to work together. We therefore propose MoEvolve, a bidirectional distillation framework following a recovery-then-improvement strategy: we first restore the activation-expanded high-$k$ model and further strengthen it by exploiting its additional active capacity, then reverse the direction of distillation to transfer the enhanced capabilities back into the original low-$k$ configuration, retaining its inference-time activation budget. Across diverse MoE models and benchmarks, MoEvolve improves the initial models by up to $22.2$ domain-average points and outperforms same-budget RLVR baselines by up to $6.5$ points. Notably, the final low-$k$ models often surpass their activation-expanded teachers.
authors: Haoyu Chen, Jun Bai, Yang Liu, Jianfei Zhang, Wenge Rong
bullets: RLVR provides sparse outcome-level supervision, while on-policy distillation offers denser token-level feedback but typically needs a stronger compatible teacher.
Activating more experts per token exposes additional capacity, yet naive expansion harms performance because the experts are not jointly optimized.
MoEvolve first recovers and improves the high-k expanded model, then reverses distillation to strengthen the original low-k model without increasing inference cost.
Across diverse MoE models and benchmarks, it improves domain-average performance by up to 22.2 points and exceeds same-budget RLVR baselines by up to 6.5 points.
Final low-k models often outperform their activation-expanded teachers.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes MoEvolve, a bidirectional distillation framework to strengthen MoE LLMs using on-policy RL and internal expert capacity.
papers.title: A Stronger Teacher Within: Strengthening MoE Models via On-Policy Bidirectional Distillation
papers.tldr: MoEvolve turns an MoE model’s activation-expanded version into a stronger internal teacher, then distills its improvements back to the original low-activation model.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has become a scalable post-training paradigm for large language models. However, training agents over long-horizon interactions presents two challenges: using only terminal rewards makes turn-level credit assignment sparse and high-variance, while sequential mini-batch updates on a fixed rollout batch introduce policy staleness as the current policy drifts from the behavior policy. Existing approaches obtain denser credit via learned critics, process reward models, or on-policy distillation, but they rely on a value network, step-level annotations, or a stronger external teacher that increase training complexity. Meanwhile, importance sampling and clipping mitigate policy drift, but they do not specify a finite target that stops sequential updates from overshooting. In this work, we introduce TreeOPSD, a critic-free, tree-aware posterior self-distillation framework for long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning. Treating each interaction turn as a tree node, TreeOPSD branches alternative continuations from shared prefixes and recursively backs up terminal rewards into implicit turn-level credit. It then maps each credit to a closed-form, bounded teacher distribution parameterized by the likelihood ratio relative to the frozen behavior policy. Minimizing the divergence between this teacher and the student policy recovers the policy-gradient direction as the tangent at the behavior policy while bounding updates toward a finite target across sequential mini-batches. Empirically, TreeOPSD improves agentic capabilities across several competitive benchmarks and model scales, especially for long-horizon tasks, e.g., raising the average accuracy of Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 by 4.97 points over GRPO on the Deep Research setting.
authors: Heming Zou, Qi Wang, Yixiu Mao, Yun Qu, Yuyi Guo, Zeyuan Liu, Chenglin Li, Weijie Liu, Saiyong Yang, Xiangyang Ji
bullets: Addresses sparse, high-variance credit assignment from terminal-only rewards and policy drift during sequential updates.
Builds a tree of alternative continuations from shared interaction prefixes and recursively backs up terminal rewards into implicit turn-level credit.
Converts credit into a closed-form, bounded teacher distribution based on likelihood ratios to the frozen behavior policy.
Distillation matches policy-gradient behavior near the behavior policy while limiting overshooting toward a finite target.
Improves agentic performance across benchmarks and model scales, including a 4.97-point average accuracy gain over GRPO for Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 on Deep Research.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces TreeOPSD, a critic-free tree-aware posterior self-distillation framework for long-horizon agentic RL applied to LLMs (Qwen models).
papers.title: Tree-Aware Posterior Distillation for Long-Horizon Agentic Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: TreeOPSD improves long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning by providing critic-free turn-level credit and bounded self-distillation targets that reduce policy staleness.

papers.abstract: Outcome-reward reinforcement learning such as GRPO gives every token of a search-agent rollout the same advantage, although the rollout exercises two capabilities: finding evidence and using it. We show that accuracy improves without grounding: Search-R1 raises accuracy on all seven QA benchmarks, yet on Bamboogle the evidence-supported share of correct answers falls from 84.0% to 42.9%. We attribute this to GRPO's credit assignment: rollouts that retrieve answer-bearing evidence are favoured in aggregate only in proportion to their accuracy gain over the rest, a grounding gap that answering from memory or misusing evidence shrinks or reverses. To address this, we propose Grounded Credit Assignment (GCA), which uses verifiable sub-outcomes (evidence retrieval and answer correctness) to correct search and answer credit separately: a wrong answer is blamed more than the search that found the evidence, and a correct answer that bypasses retrievable evidence is credited less. Never negative on evidence-finding search, the correction does not shrink with the grounding gap; capped at 10% of each token's advantage, it never overrides the outcome signal. Without extra models, rollouts, or training stages, GCA improves average EM over Search-R1 by 5.7 (Qwen2.5-3B) and 6.3 points (Qwen3-30B-A3B) and raises this share from 76.9% to 93.4%.
authors: Qirui Liu, Hao Chen, Yi Wen, Weijie Shi, Yao Zhao, Xianhe Chen, Hao Zhao, Xing Tang, Weihong Luo, Yuyu Luo
bullets: Outcome-only GRPO can improve QA accuracy while encouraging answers based on memory or misused evidence.
The proposed GCA separately credits evidence retrieval and answer correctness using verifiable sub-outcomes.
GCA penalizes unsupported correct answers and assigns more blame to incorrect answering than to successful evidence-finding search.
It requires no extra models, rollouts, or training stages, and its correction is capped so it cannot override the outcome signal.
Across two model settings, GCA improves average exact match by 5.7–6.3 points and raises evidence-supported correct answers from 76.9% to 93.4%.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes Grounded Credit Assignment (GCA) for RL in search agents, improving credit assignment for LLMs (Qwen models).
papers.title: Grounded Credit Assignment in Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Turn Search Agents
papers.tldr: Grounded Credit Assignment improves multi-turn search-agent accuracy while substantially increasing the share of answers supported by retrieved evidence.

papers.abstract: Alignment is known to change the output characteristics of large language models (LLMs). Base models tend to generate more diverse outputs, whereas aligned models tend to produce higher-quality outputs. The appropriate balance between the two depends on the task. Existing methods either require costly fine-tuning or, like temperature sampling, mainly improve lexical diversity rather than semantic diversity. We introduce a depth-aware FrankenMerging approach for controlling the diversity--quality trade-off between an aligned model and its base model without additional training. This approach combines the lower layers of an aligned model with the higher layers of its base model based on the hypothesis that lexical diversity is more closely associated with lower layers and semantic diversity with higher layers. Experiments showed that varying the number of layers taken from each model adjusts both diversity and quality. In most cases, the merged models exhibited higher semantic diversity than the aligned model, and at some split positions, they showed higher lexical diversity than both original models. They also demonstrated a better diversity--quality trade-off than temperature sampling in most settings. A supporting ablation, in which we reversed the merging order, yielded results largely consistent with the hypothesis.
authors: Yasuaki Sumita, Tomoharu Iwata, Toshiyuki Tanaka
bullets: Aligned LLMs generally favor quality, while base models favor diversity; the desired balance depends on the task.
The method merges lower layers from an aligned model with higher layers from its base model, motivated by links between lower layers and lexical diversity and higher layers and semantic diversity.
Changing the layer split controls both diversity and output quality.
Merged models usually achieved higher semantic diversity than the aligned model and sometimes higher lexical diversity than both source models.
Results generally showed a better diversity–quality trade-off than temperature sampling; reversed-order ablations supported the depth-based hypothesis.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a depth-aware model merging approach to control the diversity-quality trade-off between base and aligned LLMs without additional training.
papers.title: Controlling the Diversity-Quality Trade-Off of LLMs by Merging Models Before and After Alignment
papers.tldr: A depth-aware model-merging method adjusts LLM diversity and quality without additional training, often improving semantic diversity over aligned models and outperforming temperature sampling in trade-offs.

papers.abstract: Computer-use agents (CUAs) are commonly evaluated against fixed task specifications, but users may omit requirements, add constraints, or require approval before consequential actions. Completing the benchmark instruction does not guarantee serving the person who asked. We introduce PersonaCUABench, which holds 74 tasks across 11 domains fixed and varies only who asks. A persona agent, playing one of 44 personas in four groups, rewrites each instruction in that user's own words and answers the CUA's questions, while the CUA sees only the dialogue, never the profile or the original instruction. Across nine backbones (3,330 runs), mean task completion falls by 36% relative to the original requests. The losses have two sources: in 59.9% of cells that lose points, the agent engages with what the user asked for and still gets it wrong, and 11.2% are stops the user requested that the checker scores as failures. Even when a persona request is fully completed, the user gives the top satisfaction rating in only 62.7% of cells, against 84.1% for the original requests. CUAs should therefore be evaluated not only on task completion but also on whether they meet the requirements and constraints users express. Code: https://github.com/MatrAIx-ai/PersonaCUABench. Project page: https://matraix.ai/research/persona-cua.html
authors: Haoming Li, Defu Cao, Xu Hu, Yingtao Luo, Yiyang Wang, Xianghe Xu, Jiashu He, Wanting Jiang, Yifan Zhang, Yunhan Zhao, Siyang Wu, Chen Yang, Haixin Wang, Zheyuan Deng, Taoran Li, Jingwen Zhang, Zhejian Peng, Shushu Liang, Yue Zhao, Bingzhe Li, Feng Chen, Yifan Wang, Jintao Huang, Yijun Wang, Yuexing Hao, Xiaomin Li
bullets: Introduces a benchmark with 74 tasks across 11 domains and 44 personas in four groups.
Persona agents rewrite requests and answer CUA questions while CUAs see only the resulting dialogue.
Across nine backbones and 3,330 runs, mean task completion drops 36% versus original requests.
Many failures involve misunderstanding user needs, while some user-requested stops are scored as failures.
Full task completion does not ensure satisfaction: top ratings occur in 62.7% of persona cases versus 84.1% for original requests.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces PersonaCUABench, a benchmark for computer-use agents to evaluate their ability to serve diverse user personas, highlighting the gap between task completion and persona adherence.
papers.title: PersonaCUABench: Benchmarking Computer-Use Agents Serving Diverse Personas
papers.tldr: PersonaCUABench shows that computer-use agents often complete benchmark tasks without adequately serving users with diverse personas, requirements, and constraints.

papers.abstract: Brain alignment of large language models (LLMs) offers a way to investigate representational similarities between LLMs and the human brain during language processing. While previous studies have mainly focused on passive language comprehension, little is known about such alignment during dialogue, in which speakers engage in both language production and comprehension. In this study, using fMRI data collected during dialogue, we examine brain alignment during language production and comprehension across LLM layers and brain regions. We assess its association with the intrinsic dimension (ID) of LLM representations and the contributions of several interpretable linguistic and communicative features. Our results reveal distinct patterns of brain alignment between production and comprehension, as well as strong associations with ID in brain regions associated with each processing mode. Furthermore, we show that the contributions of linguistic and communicative features also vary across processing modes, LLM layers, and brain regions.
authors: Yuko Nakagi, Yuya Chiba, Yasue Kishino
bullets: Uses fMRI collected during dialogue to examine LLM alignment with the brain.
Compares alignment during language production versus comprehension across LLM layers and brain regions.
Finds distinct alignment patterns for the two processing modes.
Reports strong associations between alignment and the intrinsic dimension of LLM representations in mode-relevant brain regions.
Shows that linguistic and communicative features contribute differently across processing modes, layers, and regions.
papers.selection_reason: Examines brain alignment of LLMs during dialogue using fMRI data, providing insights into the representational similarities between LLMs and human language processing.
papers.title: What Shapes Brain Alignment of Large Language Models during Dialogue? Insights from Language Production and Comprehension
papers.tldr: LLM–brain alignment during dialogue differs between language production and comprehension and varies with representation dimensionality, model layer, brain region, and linguistic or communicative features.

papers.abstract: Small variations in prompt characteristics can meaningfully alter the semantics, tone, and contextual assumptions of large language model outputs. Such characteristics can involve group variables such as demographics or other sensitive latent attributes. Sensitivity to such input variables is undesirable when demographic information is causally irrelevant to the task, but might still be relevant for generation of semantically coherent responses. This makes the task of enforcing counterfactual invariance while preserving model utility difficult. To study this problem, we first show that standard model alignment recipes (such as reinforcement learning) increase differences in response quality across demographics, while improving overall response quality, ultimately amplifying what is known as counterfactual bias. To address this, we develop a policy gradient technique involving a group-level reward function that operates on matched pairs of counterfactual prompts. For completeness, we build a dataset of controlled counterfactual prompt pairs and design an evaluation that separately measures cases where demographic information is causally relevant to the answer. Finally, we validate our findings on several fairness benchmarks. We demonstrate that our methods reduce counterfactual differences while preserving overall response quality and that the models continue to adapt appropriately when such sensitive information is relevant.
authors: Basar Demir, Emily Shen, Ksheeraj Sai Vepuri, Sourabh Kulkarni, Harihar Subramanyam, Ankit Jain, Nan Jiang, Chirag Nagpal
bullets: Standard alignment methods can improve overall quality while increasing response-quality disparities across demographic counterfactuals.
The proposed approach trains on matched counterfactual prompt pairs using a group-level reward function.
The authors create controlled counterfactual prompt-pair data and an evaluation that distinguishes relevant from irrelevant demographic information.
Experiments on several fairness benchmarks show reduced counterfactual differences without sacrificing overall response quality.
Models still adapt appropriately when demographic information is causally relevant to the answer.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses counterfactual bias in LLMs during alignment by developing a policy gradient technique that enforces invariance to sensitive demographic variables while preserving utility.
papers.title: Aligning Language Models Towards Counterfactual Invariance
papers.tldr: A group-level policy-gradient method reduces counterfactual demographic bias in language-model outputs while preserving response quality and sensitivity when demographic information is relevant.

papers.abstract: Language models often abandon a correct answer when the prompt contains a cue, a hint toward a wrong option such as "I think the answer is B." Sycophancy and related biases show this failure. They are often studied separately and blamed on alignment. We test this view causally, tracing the attention heads behind these biases through the stages of two post-training pipelines. In multiple-choice tests on most models, four cue types rely largely on the same few heads, a shared circuit already present in pretrained models. Most base models follow cues in plain text. Fine-tuning a base model on about 200 generic assistant examples without cues activates these heads in chat format, so cue-following can be a side effect of assistant tuning. The final reinforcement learning (RL) stage strengthens the effect of cues in almost every comparison. In Tulu-3-8B and OLMo-2-7B, we swap the attention patterns of six middle layers between the RL checkpoint and its predecessor. For suggested-answer cues, this shifts each checkpoint's cue effect most of the way to the other's level. Post-training thus seems to change when and how strongly models use this circuit. Mitigation for these multiple-choice biases could target this circuit.
authors: Prakhar Gupta, Terry Jingchen Zhang, Zhijing Jin
bullets: Several cue-driven biases, including sycophancy-like behavior, rely on largely the same small set of attention heads.
This cue-routing circuit is already present in pretrained models, which often follow cues in plain text.
Generic assistant fine-tuning can activate the circuit in chat format even without training on cues.
Reinforcement learning generally strengthens cue effects across the tested comparisons.
Swapping attention patterns in six middle layers transfers much of the cue-following behavior between RL and pre-RL checkpoints.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes sycophancy and cue-following in LLMs, identifying a shared 'cue-routing' circuit in attention heads that is modified by post-training alignment.
papers.title: Many Biases, One Circuit: Post-Training Tunes a Pretrained Cue-Routing Mechanism
papers.tldr: Post-training appears to tune a shared pretrained attention circuit that makes language models follow misleading answer cues.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable success in complex reasoning through explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT), but the associated computational overhead and token verbosity remain significant barriers to efficiency. While implicit reasoning in continuous latent spaces offers a promising alternative, existing methods like Coconut and CODI often rely on fixed-length latent sequences and suffer from representational collapse. In this paper, we propose Sep-Latent, an adaptive implicit reasoning framework that utilizes separator tokens as structural semantic anchors. By introducing an Attention-Decay mechanism, we force the model to aggregate and compress reasoning logic into these anchors during training. We then align explicit and implicit pathways through multi-level distillation across all layers to ensure logical consistency. Crucially, Sep-Latent enables dynamic reasoning depth by adaptively terminating the latent thinking phase based on query complexity. Experimental results on the GSM8k-Aug benchmark show that Sep-Latent achieves an accuracy of 56.8\% with an average of only 5.4 tokens, significantly outperforming prior fixed-length implicit models in efficiency while narrowing the performance gap with explicit CoT. Further analysis via PCA and symbolic variant testing confirms that our method ensures semantic grounding and exhibits superior robustness to perturbations.
authors: Yinlong Xu, Jianfeng Huang, Zhengdong Zhou, Mingjie Lin, Fuyu Lv, Dan Ou, Hongxia Xu, Jian Wu
bullets: Targets the verbosity and computational cost of explicit Chain-of-Thought reasoning, while addressing collapse and fixed-length limitations in prior implicit methods.
Uses separator tokens as semantic anchors, with Attention-Decay to aggregate reasoning and multi-level distillation to align explicit and implicit pathways.
Adaptively terminates latent reasoning according to query complexity rather than using a fixed latent sequence length.
On GSM8k-Aug, reaches 56.8% accuracy using an average of 5.4 tokens, outperforming prior fixed-length implicit models in efficiency.
PCA and symbolic-variant analyses support semantic grounding and robustness to perturbations; scope is primarily demonstrated on GSM8k-Aug.
papers.selection_reason: Implicit reasoning with separator-token anchors and attention-decay; fits LLM architecture and reasoning research.
papers.title: Sep-Latent: Separator Tokens as Natural Compression Anchors for Implicit Reasoning
papers.tldr: Sep-Latent compresses implicit reasoning into separator-token anchors, enabling adaptive-depth inference with strong efficiency and improved robustness.

papers.abstract: Language models generalize beyond their training corpus to learn linguistic phenomena (Patil et al., 2024; Misra and Mahowald, 2024), showing that there exists indirect evidence driving learning. Prior work has inferred that indirect evidence exists without identifying its character or considered specific hypotheses about what it might be. We explore an alternative bottom-up method for identifying indirect evidence. We use influence functions (Koh and Liang, 2017) to measure how individual training sentences affect model predictions in 15 grammatical phenomena from BLiMP (Warstadt et al., 2020). We filter out a phenomenon's direct evidence using hand-constructed rules and take the 60,000 most influential remaining sentences as indirect evidence. This indirect evidence substantially affects learning: retraining without it lowers held-out accuracy more than removing a matched random group for every phenomenon across five models (by a median of 12 points). We characterize the indirect evidence by its similarity to our direct evidence filters: it (partially) meets the filters' structural conditions at a median of 4.7 times the rate of a matched random group. Finally, clustering phenomena by indirect-evidence overlap recovers three of the five BLiMP categories that include multiple phenomena, suggesting that this method can reveal linguistic relationships.
authors: William Dai, Zhenghao Herbert Zhou, Maya Viswanathan, Robert Frank
bullets: Studies indirect evidence for 15 grammatical phenomena from BLiMP across five language models.
Uses influence functions to rank training sentences, removes rule-defined direct evidence, and selects the 60,000 most influential remaining sentences.
Removing this indirect evidence reduces held-out accuracy more than removing matched random sentences for every phenomenon, with a median 12-point drop.
Indirect evidence partially shares structural properties with direct evidence, occurring at a median 4.7× the rate of matched random data.
Clustering phenomena by shared indirect evidence recovers three of five multi-phenomenon BLiMP categories.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates grammatical generalization in LLMs using influence functions to identify 'indirect evidence' driving learning, offering a methodological tool for analyzing LLM behavior.
papers.title: Where's the Indirect Evidence? Investigating Grammatical Generalization with Influence Functions
papers.tldr: Influence functions identify training sentences that indirectly support grammatical generalization, and removing them consistently harms language-model performance.

papers.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a powerful machine learning framework that allows building a global model from the contributions of multiple, distributed clients, while ensuring the privacy of their local data. However, its heavy computational and communication overheads challenge its use for contemporary AI workloads such as natural language processing (NLP) and multimodal analysis.
