For this reason, this paper presents a novel small language model that leverages byte-level text and multimodal data processing, enhanced by a linear attention mechanism, to enable manageable Federated Learning of NLP and multimodal analysis tasks. The proposed model, nicknamed FederatedBytes, manages to process text and any other data types, including images, by treating its input as a mere sequence of bytes, while its lean linear attention mechanism allows abating the overall memory and computational footprint. To prove the effectiveness of the proposed model we have carried out an extensive performance evaluation on sentiment analysis tasks in multilingual and multimodal settings over the Multilingual Amazon Reviews and ScienceQA datasets. The experimental results show that FederatedBytes has been able to outperform comparable models such as ByT5 and LSTM, achieving higher accuracy while significantly reducing memory and communication overheads.
authors: Ali Sarabadani, Massimo Piccardi, Mehran Abolhasan, Farzad Tofigh, Ian Zhou, Justin Lipman
bullets: Targets the computational and communication costs that hinder federated NLP and multimodal learning.
Processes text, images, and other modalities uniformly as byte sequences, without tokenization.
Uses lean linear attention to reduce memory and computational requirements.
Evaluated on multilingual and multimodal sentiment analysis using Multilingual Amazon Reviews and ScienceQA.
The abstract reports higher accuracy than ByT5 and LSTM, alongside substantially lower memory and communication overheads.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a tokenizer-free, byte-level small language model for efficient federated learning, utilizing linear attention to reduce memory and computational footprint.
papers.title: FederatedBytes: Tokenizer-Free, Byte-Level Small Language Models for Efficient Multimodal Federated Learning
papers.tldr: FederatedBytes is a tokenizer-free, byte-level small language model using linear attention to make multimodal federated learning more efficient while maintaining strong sentiment-analysis performance.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have brought impressive performance across diverse tasks; however, shortcomings remain in logical reasoning, including inconsistencies under linguistic variation. To improve the reasoning capacity of LLMs, we must be able to accurately measure their reasoning capacity. Current benchmarks primarily report single accuracy numbers on selected reasoning tasks. Such a performance-based evaluation methodology says little about a model's generalization capacity in reasoning. To address this limitation, we argue for a different evaluation paradigm, called competence-based evaluation (CBE), which tests whether models reliably apply the same competence across a family of problems. A parameterized generator scales complexity while keeping the required competence fixed, and matched answer-preserving presentations test correctness beyond one formulation. We instantiate CBE on elementary ordering tasks, scaling input size while varying presentations of the same ordering rule. Across six GPT and Qwen models, performance is reasonably good over bounded complexity ranges, but even strong models fail the competence condition across the tested family. Chain-of-thought and GRPO extend strong performance without resolving all tested failures; supervised LoRA shows little held-out transfer. CBE provides diagnostic profiles and an evaluation protocol that can grow with future models.
bullets: Standard benchmarks may overstate reasoning ability because they measure performance on selected tasks rather than generalization across a problem family.
CBE uses parameterized generators to increase complexity while preserving the required competence, plus answer-preserving reformulations to test robustness.
Applied to elementary ordering tasks across six GPT and Qwen models, the evaluation found good performance within bounded ranges but failures of consistent competence across the tested family.
Chain-of-thought and GRPO improved or extended strong performance but did not eliminate all failures; supervised LoRA showed limited held-out transfer.
The protocol produces diagnostic competence profiles and is designed to scale with future models.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes competence-based evaluation for logical reasoning in LLMs; directly relevant to language foundation model assessment.
papers.title: Competence-Based Evaluation of Logical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.tldr: Competence-based evaluation tests whether LLMs consistently apply the same reasoning skill across increasingly complex and differently phrased problems, revealing failures hidden by single accuracy scores.

papers.abstract: Tree search enhances multi-step reasoning in large language models (LLMs), yet prevailing methods expand every step with a fixed budget, irrespective of the marginal utility of expansion. We first show, across existing search algorithms, that continuations sampled from a shared intermediate state are largely duplicates and collapse to a few distinct answers. Critically, we find that the semantic dispersion of sibling actions predicts the redundancy of their downstream continuations, permitting a subtree's budget to be fixed before expansion. An information-theoretic analysis motivates this: treating the per-step budget as the Monte Carlo sample size for estimating a step's residual answer entropy, we derive a sufficient budget that shrinks with sibling dispersion. We accordingly propose $\textbf{Uncertainty-Aware Allocation}$ (UAA), a training-free framework that decouples value from uncertainty: values determine which candidates are promising, while uncertainty, estimated from sibling dispersion at no additional model cost, determines how many merit expansion, via uncertainty-aware pruning and uncertainty-aware budgeting. Across mathematical reasoning, logical reasoning, and planning benchmarks, UAA reduces token usage by up to $90\%$ and latency by up to $9\times$ at comparable accuracy, generalizing across four tree search algorithms and both open- and closed-source LLMs.
authors: Jianguo Huang, Zhiyi Lyu, Fuxiang Zhang, Yanchen Deng, Deheng Ye, Bo An
bullets: Sibling continuations from the same intermediate state are often redundant and collapse to a few distinct answers.
Semantic dispersion among sibling actions predicts downstream redundancy and can estimate uncertainty before subtree expansion.
UAA is training-free and separates candidate value from uncertainty: value selects promising candidates, while uncertainty controls pruning and expansion budgets.
Across reasoning and planning benchmarks, UAA reduces token use by up to 90% and latency by up to 9× at comparable accuracy.
The framework generalizes across four tree-search algorithms and both open- and closed-source LLMs.
papers.selection_reason: Uncertainty-aware budget allocation reduces token usage and latency in LLM tree search; fits efficient AI and LLM reasoning.
papers.title: Uncertainty-Aware Budget Allocation for Efficient LLM Tree Search
papers.tldr: UAA makes LLM tree search more efficient by allocating expansion budgets according to sibling-action uncertainty rather than using a fixed budget at every step.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) faithfulness matters for monitoring, explaining and safely deploying large language models, yet it has been studied mostly in English. Languages differ in level, the amount of text available to learn from, so models know less in lower-resource languages, which may change how much they rely on their reasoning. To our knowledge, we are the first to relate CoT faithfulness to both resource level and task type (knowledge- or reasoning-intensive). On parallel multiple-choice questions from Multilingual Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMMLU) in eight languages, faithfulness rises as resource level falls on knowledge-intensive tasks but not on reasoning-intensive ones, a gap that points the same way across four models and several faithfulness measures. We propose, and find support for, the Reliance Hypothesis: models rely more on their reasoning when they cannot recall the answer, as in lower-resource languages on knowledge-intensive tasks. Model confidence partly explains the effect of resource level, but not the knowledge-reasoning gap. Languages in which models are less confident rely more on reasoning, yet less confident answers within a language do not, a Simpson's paradox. In lower-resource languages, models rely on their reasoning for more answers, not more strongly for each. CoT monitoring may therefore be most informative in lower-resource languages, where it is least often validated.
authors: Lucas Resck, Jingyi Sun, Qianli Wang, Isabelle Augenstein, Anna Korhonen
bullets: Studies CoT faithfulness across eight languages, four models, and multiple measures using parallel MMMLU questions.
Faithfulness rises as language resource level falls on knowledge-intensive tasks, but not on reasoning-intensive tasks.
Findings support the Reliance Hypothesis: limited knowledge access increases reliance on stated reasoning.
Model confidence partly explains the resource-level effect, but not the gap between knowledge- and reasoning-intensive tasks.
Lower-resource languages may be especially valuable for CoT monitoring, despite receiving less validation.
papers.selection_reason: Chain-of-thought faithfulness across language resource levels; relevant to LLM reasoning and evaluation.
papers.title: The Reliance Hypothesis: Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness Rises as Language Resource Level Falls
papers.tldr: CoT faithfulness generally increases in lower-resource languages for knowledge-intensive tasks because models rely more on reasoning when they cannot recall answers.

papers.abstract: Standard autoregressive language models generate text sequentially, but revision requires referring back to tokens in the input context or those already generated. Causal Edit Serialization (CES) is introduced as a framework for expressing such revisions within the same causal token stream. Special pointer tokens are paired with predicted source addresses, allowing insertion, deletion, replacement, copying and movement to be localized explicitly. A lightweight localization head and dual-index rotary position encoding support both address prediction and conditioning on previously emitted pointers, while retaining a standard causal attention mask. A pretraining procedure combines ordinary language modeling with serialized repairs derived from random corruptions, model-generated edits and repeated text. Across model scales and editing baselines, CES models demonstrate complete applied edits with modestly higher clean-text bits per byte than clean autoregressive models. Supervised and reinforcement-learning post-training provide a grammatical-error-correction proof of concept, producing more beneficial than harmful changes under reference-blind model judging. Correct repair programs also improve subsequent text prediction while the original context and its cached states are retained. CES provides a common interface for generation and localized revision, with potential extensions to iterative refinement and additional pointer-addressed transformations.
bullets: Supports insertion, deletion, replacement, copying, and movement through explicit source-address pointers.
Uses a localization head and dual-index rotary position encoding while preserving standard causal attention.
Pretraining combines language modeling with repairs from random corruptions, generated edits, and repeated text.
Across scales and baselines, models complete edits with only modestly worse clean-text bits per byte than standard models.
A grammatical-error-correction proof of concept shows more beneficial than harmful edits, and correct repairs improve later prediction while cached context is retained.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces causal edit serialization with pointer tokens for autoregressive language models; a novel architecture and training contribution to language foundation models.
papers.title: Causal Edit Serialization
papers.tldr: Causal Edit Serialization lets autoregressive language models perform localized text revisions by encoding edits as pointer-addressed operations in the causal token stream.

papers.abstract: Recent studies have shown that position bias remains a critical vulnerability in large language models (LLMs), undermining both the integrity of multiple-choice evaluations and the reliability of retrieval-augmented generation. However, existing understanding of this phenomenon is largely derived from studies with limited model coverage and English-centric benchmarks, leaving the behavior of frontier models and diverse languages underexplored. In this work, we conduct a comprehensive investigation of position bias across model scales ranging from billion-level to trillion-level parameters, covering both multiple-choice and multi-document tasks in five languages. Our experiments reveal that while position bias remains noticeable in small-scale models and Non-English languages, increasing model scale and employing standard Chain-of-Thought prompting significantly mitigate this issue. Moreover, we demonstrate that emerging \emph{thinking models} with extended reasoning capabilities are nearly immune to position bias, suggesting a costly but general approach toward resolving this vulnerability.
authors: Yining Li, Huayang Li, Lemao Liu, Taro Watanabe
bullets: Studies position bias in multiple-choice and multi-document tasks across five languages.
Covers models ranging from billion-level to trillion-level parameter scales.
Finds position bias remains noticeable in small models and non-English languages.
Reports that larger models and standard Chain-of-Thought prompting significantly mitigate the issue.
Extended-reasoning “thinking models” are nearly immune, though this may be costly.
papers.selection_reason: Comprehensive study of position bias in LLMs across scales and languages; relevant to LLM behavior and evaluation.
papers.title: On the Position Bias of Large Language Models: A Comprehensive Study
papers.tldr: Position bias is strongest in smaller models and non-English settings, but is reduced by scaling and Chain-of-Thought prompting, with thinking models showing near immunity.

papers.abstract: Reusing a Transformer block across depth increases computation without replicating its parameters, but successive passes have no dedicated state through which positions can exchange compact summaries of their causal prefix. We introduce the causal latent workspace Transformer: an anchored, four-round shared-depth architecture in which each position writes gated vectors into prefix-specific latent slots and retrieves a content-addressed summary before the next shared block application. This path complements causal self-attention while the original input embedding remains accessible at every round. Across three byte-level corpora, three seeds, and two matched parameter budgets, the proposed model achieves the best mean held-out perplexity in five of six settings against five Transformer controls. At 101.71M parameters it leads on WikiText-103 raw, enwik8, and TinyStories, reaching perplexities 2.7820, 2.7843, and 1.6823; these improve upon the strongest non-workspace control on each corpus by 1.06%, 0.73%, and 1.01%. All nine seed-labelled comparisons at this budget favor the workspace. At 0.918M parameters it leads on WikiText-103 and TinyStories, whereas a conditioned loop is stronger on enwik8. Architectural ablations show that adding the workspace improves upon the anchored loop in all six settings and support refreshing its causal summaries at each round. Together, these results identify a causal, content-addressable prefix workspace as an effective structural augmentation of looped Transformers.
bullets: Addresses the lack of dedicated state for causal prefix information in parameter-shared Transformer loops.
Uses an anchored four-round architecture with gated writes to causal latent slots and content-addressed retrieval before each shared block pass.
The workspace achieves the best mean held-out perplexity in five of six settings across three byte-level corpora and two parameter budgets.
At 101.71M parameters, it leads on WikiText-103 raw, enwik8, and TinyStories; at 0.918M, it leads on WikiText-103 and TinyStories.
Ablations show consistent gains over the anchored loop and support refreshing causal summaries each round; a conditioned loop remains stronger on small-budget enwik8.
papers.selection_reason: Looped Transformer architecture with causal latent workspace memory; fits LLM architecture and memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Causal Latent Workspaces for Looped Transformers
papers.tldr: A causal latent workspace improves shared-depth looped Transformers by letting positions exchange compact, prefix-specific summaries across repeated block applications.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on proprietary records enables domain adaptation but introduces two challenges: (i) privacy leakage of memorized private data, such as personally identifiable information (PII), and (ii) balancing private data removal with utility preservation. Existing defenses, including data sanitization and differential privacy, often degrade performance, while privacy-neuron editing lacks a PII-free reference to distinguish identity-specific neurons from those supporting useful text. We propose JEPA-Prune, a post-hoc neuron pruning framework guided by a model trained exclusively on PII-free views. Alongside the fine-tuned private model, JEPA-Prune, trains a public model on surrogate and masked views of the same records using a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA), capturing domain knowledge without identifiers. A cross-model representation probe quantifies deviations between private representations of leaked records and this PII-free reference. Integrated gradients and a scale-invariant specificity score then identify PII-responsive neurons, which are pruned without retraining. Experiments show that pruning just 1.6% of neurons reduces PII inference accuracy by up to 7.4x and PII extraction recall by up to 13.9x, while keeping unseen-text perplexity within 16% of that of the unpruned model for most LLMs. In contrast, privacy-neuron editing increases perplexity by at least 26x.
bullets: Fine-tuning on proprietary records can memorize PII, creating a privacy–utility trade-off.
JEPA-Prune trains a PII-free public reference model on surrogate and masked views of the same records.
Cross-model representation probing, integrated gradients, and a scale-invariant specificity score identify neurons associated with PII.
Pruning 1.6% of neurons reduces PII inference accuracy by up to 7.4× and extraction recall by up to 13.9×.
Unseen-text perplexity generally remains within 16% of the unpruned model, outperforming privacy-neuron editing in utility preservation.
papers.selection_reason: Post-hoc neuron pruning for privacy in fine-tuned LLMs; relevant to LLM methods and model editing.
papers.title: Prune the Leaky Neurons: Mitigating Private Data Leakage in Fine-Tuned LLMs via Joint-Embedding-Guided Pruning
papers.tldr: JEPA-Prune reduces private-data leakage in fine-tuned LLMs by pruning a small set of PII-responsive neurons while largely preserving language-model utility.

papers.abstract: Split language models keep input text on a client but send intermediate representations to a server. Attacks can reconstruct text from these messages. Comparing privacy evaluations is difficult when attackers see different messages, know different model weights or use different datasets and recovery measures. We present LLM-Attacker, a framework that records these choices and lets researchers check, compare and extend an evaluation. Compatible attacks reuse recorded messages, and their predictions are saved for independent scoring. The scoring rule requires a linked undefended reference before a defence can pass. Reports also identify attacks that remain untested. In a controlled GPT-2 experiment, adding gradients returned during training increased token recovery from 94.20% to 97.38% and exact-document recovery from 13.71% to 37.77%. The 95% interval for the token gain lay above the two-percentage-point threshold fixed before testing. This experiment is shared with a companion study; here, it tests how the evaluation responds to a change in attacker access. Further studies measure how corpus choice and compression defences affect recovery, compare an adapted published attack with its reference implementation, and test the measurement code. The framework reports implementation checks separately from measured attack effectiveness. Each privacy claim should state the attacker, dataset and scoring rule, report its controls and identify untested attacks.
bullets: Addresses inconsistent evaluations caused by differing attacker access, model knowledge, datasets, and recovery metrics.
Records messages and attack settings so compatible attacks can be reused, independently scored, and compared.
Requires a linked undefended reference before a defence can pass and separates implementation checks from attack effectiveness.
In a controlled GPT-2 experiment, adding training-time gradients increased token recovery from 94.20% to 97.38% and exact-document recovery from 13.71% to 37.77%.
Supports further analysis of corpus choice, compression defences, attack implementations, and measurement code; claims should state controls and untested attacks.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces LLM-Attacker, a framework for evaluating privacy in split and distributed LLM systems. It provides a unified approach to red-teaming LLM architectures.
papers.title: The LLM-Attacker: A Unified Red-Team Framework for Privacy Evaluation of Split and Distributed LLM Systems
papers.tldr: LLM-Attacker standardizes and audits privacy evaluations for split and distributed LLMs by tracking attacker assumptions, enabling reproducible comparisons, and exposing untested attacks.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) unlearning aims to forget certain information while preserving others, without retraining from scratch. SoTA methods such as NPO, SimNPO, and SatImp balance forgetting and retain through whole model fine-tuning, while FOM-UL explores selective layer updates. Prior works show that suppressing target information can damage retained knowledge. This trade-off can vary across layers even under the same unlearning loss. In this work, we propose Confidence-Weighted Layerwise Unlearning (CoLU), which combines a novel confidence-weighted forgetting and retain regularization while updating a single selected transformer layer, rather than the whole model for unlearning. To reduce CoLU compute cost, we further propose Brief Layer Screening (BLS), which uses a newly defined normalized forgetting-retention (NFR) score to first rank layers through a brief unlearning trials using a subset of forgetting dataset and fewer epochs. BLS pre-selects top-k ranked layer candidates, which will then be fully profiled using full data analysis. BLS is proven to reduce the runtime of CoLU by 60.2-79.7% with almost the same performance. On TOFU dataset, CoLU improves both forgetting and retention over NPO, SatImp, and GA-based FOM-UL in all six TOFU settings, and over SimNPO in five of the six settings. On MUSE Books and News datasets, CoLU achieves the highest retained KnowMem and the PrivLeak closest to zero among the compared SOTA unlearning methods. CoLU presents a new record performance in both unlearning and retain in most settings up to date. Moreover, across the measured settings, average CoLU GPU memory usage is 77.4% to 79.5% lower than full-model unlearning.
authors: Jingkai Guo, Ziyi Zhao, Chaitali Chakrabarti, Deliang Fan
bullets: Addresses the risk that suppressing target information damages retained knowledge, with trade-offs varying across layers.
Uses confidence-weighted forgetting and retain regularization while updating only a selected layer.
Brief Layer Screening (BLS) ranks candidate layers using a normalized forgetting-retention score before full profiling.
BLS reduces CoLU runtime by 60.2–79.7% with nearly unchanged performance.
Across TOFU, MUSE Books, and News, CoLU generally improves forgetting and retention while using 77.4–79.5% less GPU memory than full-model unlearning.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes CoLU, a layerwise unlearning method for LLMs. It balances forgetting and retention by updating specific layers, contributing to the understanding of LLM memory and adaptation.
papers.title: CoLU: Confidence-Weighted Layerwise Unlearning for Large Language Models
papers.tldr: CoLU improves LLM unlearning–retention trade-offs by updating one confidence-selected transformer layer, while BLS sharply reduces layer-screening cost.

papers.abstract: Methods for training language models on sensitive data differ in how they balance capability gains against the risk of leaking private information. In this paper, we present a controlled comparison of data-level and training-level interventions for navigating the capability-privacy tradeoff on synthetic medical records with canaries to probe for leakage. Direct finetuning performs best on capability metrics but leads to the most privacy leakage, while DP-SGD reduces leakage at substantial cost to capabilities. Generating synthetic data from these records offers a more favorable balance, particularly when guided by a uniqueness-aware instruction to replace private details. Relative to naive paraphrasing, privacy-aware rewriting improves privacy protection across a variety of different rewriting models. We also find that more capable rewriting models generally reduce the risks of downstream privacy leakage, although held-out fit does not improve monotonically and increased test-time compute yields inconsistent gains. Overall, these results highlight privacy-aware rewriting as a promising direction for achieving a more favorable trade-off between capabilities and empirical privacy compared to other training-level methods, and our evaluation framework supports comparisons of future models and methods.
authors: Zihao Zhao, Avi Schwarzschild, Casey Meehan, Katherine Lee, Zhili Feng, Dylan Sam
bullets: Direct finetuning achieves the strongest capabilities but causes the most privacy leakage.
DP-SGD reduces leakage substantially, but with significant capability costs.
Synthetic-data generation, especially uniqueness-aware rewriting, provides a more favorable balance.
Privacy-aware rewriting outperforms naive paraphrasing for privacy protection across rewriting models.
More capable rewriting models generally lower downstream leakage, but held-out fit and extra test-time compute show inconsistent trends.
papers.selection_reason: Explores the empirical privacy landscape of training LLMs on synthetic data, comparing data-level and training-level interventions. This is relevant to LLM training methodologies and safety.
papers.title: Exploring The Empirical Privacy Landscape of Synthetic Data
papers.tldr: A controlled study finds that privacy-aware synthetic-data rewriting offers a better capability–privacy trade-off than direct finetuning or DP-SGD on synthetic medical records.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in AI make Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) increasingly plausible. Large Language Models (LLMs) can already propose, select, and run Machine Learning (ML) experiments. However, the space of possible design choices in ML is vast. An LLM that proposes an experiment needs a reliable intuition of whether it is worth running given the timing constraints of long training runs. In this work, we measure such intuition in current frontier LLMs by evaluating how accurately they predict the impact of self-generated ML experiment ideas before these are put into training runs. To this end, we construct a dataset of 288 LLM-proposed ideas on eight MLE-bench tasks. We then prompt five frontier LLMs (GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1, Kimi K3, and GLM-5.3) to predict the impact of each idea and compare their predictions with the actual outcomes after training. We report four main findings. First, LLM predictions are substantially better than random chance but far from accurate: even the best model, Claude Opus 5.5, explains only half of the variance in outcomes (R^2 = 0.49). Second, we notice that all tested models systematically underestimate the magnitude of the changes. Third, prediction quality varies widely across tasks. Finally, the choice of the coding harness that actually implements the ideas has little effect on outcomes, and we find no evidence of self-preference. Higher reasoning settings and additional context lead to modest gains. Overall, our results show that current LLMs have useful but limited intuition about which ML ideas will work. We release our dataset to support further study.
authors: Ayush Bansal, Aldo Pareja, Sean Klein, Serge Didenko, Artem Lukoianov
bullets: Evaluates predictions for 288 LLM-generated ideas across eight MLE-bench tasks using five frontier LLMs.
The best model explains 49% of outcome variance, indicating useful but imperfect predictive ability.
All tested models systematically underestimate the magnitude of experimental effects.
Prediction quality varies substantially by task; more reasoning and context provide modest improvements.
Coding-harness choice has little impact on outcomes, with no evidence of self-preference; the dataset is released.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates frontier LLMs' ability to predict ML experiment outcomes, relevant to LLM reasoning and self-improvement.
papers.title: Can LLMs predict the outcomes of machine learning experiments?
papers.tldr: Current frontier LLMs can predict the outcomes of ML experiments better than chance, but their intuition remains limited and task-dependent.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as formalizers: given a reasoning problem expressed in natural language, they produce a formal specification that a symbolic solver can then solve, with guarantees relative to that specification. Many specifications are runnable yet semantically wrong, encoding incorrect constraints, domains, objectives, predicates, or goals, and solver-error feedback dries up once execution succeeds. Purely LLM-based diagnosis, lacking a formal ground truth, often fails to spot these errors, and its ungrounded critiques cause regressions in 11.8% of initially correct specifications in our experiments. We propose DRAGO, a repair framework that replaces this ungrounded critique with deterministic, formalism-specific diagnosis, and retains a rewrite only when the diagnosed error weight strictly decreases under a reference-free acceptance predicate. Across five benchmarks spanning logical reasoning (SMT-LIB2), constraint programming (MiniZinc), and planning (PDDL), DRAGO cuts regressions by nearly an order of magnitude, to 1.3%, while improving answer accuracy by 12.9 percentage points over zero-shot formalization and 8.7 percentage points over LLM-diagnostic repair, averaged across benchmarks. We also uncover two rendering defects in Planetarium that cause 50% (3,086 instances) of its floor-tile split to be inconsistent with the reference formalizations, and release a corrected split.
authors: Giovanni Vaccarino, Emanuele La Malfa, Dehai Min, Hanrong Zhang, Pier Luca Lanzi, Lu Cheng, Michael J. Wooldridge, Philip S. Yu, Sara Bernardini
bullets: LLM-generated specifications can execute successfully while encoding incorrect constraints, domains, objectives, predicates, or goals.
DRAGO uses formalism-specific deterministic diagnosis instead of ungrounded LLM critique.
A rewrite is accepted only when a reference-free error-weight measure strictly decreases.
Across five SMT-LIB2, MiniZinc, and PDDL benchmarks, regressions fell from initially correct specifications to 1.3%, while accuracy improved by 12.9 and 8.7 percentage points over two baselines.
The work identifies and corrects rendering defects affecting 3,086 Planetarium floor-tile instances.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes DRAGO, a framework for repairing LLM-generated formal specifications using deterministic diagnosis. This addresses the issue of semantic errors in LLM formalization outputs.
papers.title: Repairing LLM-Generated Specifications with Deterministic Diagnosis
papers.tldr: DRAGO repairs runnable-but-semantically-wrong LLM-generated formal specifications using deterministic diagnosis, substantially reducing regressions and improving answer accuracy.

papers.abstract: While LLMs demonstrate strong capabilities in English Relation Extraction (RE) tasks, a significant gap remains in assessing their RE performance in low-resource languages, due to a lack of standardized benchmarks. Creating native, language-specific annotated RE benchmarks is expensive and requires human expertise, while relying on translation yields suboptimal, inaccurate datasets that introduce English-centric biases. To tackle this, we propose a scalable, language-agnostic methodology to create RE data by denoising naturally occurring yet noisy alignments of knowledge bases and corresponding texts. We define a proper alignment via a Natural Language Inference (NLI) task, where a relation triplet is entailed by an input text. We empirically assess five denoising strategies, and demonstrate that multilingual models outperform language-specific models in the few-shot LLM setting, while Hebrew-specific encoders remain competitive under NLI fine-tuning and are strongest in the label-free cross-training setting. We further find that prompting in the native language achieves performance on par with or slightly exceeding English prompts, confirming that the pipeline operates naturally in the target language. The best open-weights model, Gemma-4-31B-it (F1\,=\,0.915), matches the best API model, GPT-5.4 (0.921), and reaches F1\,=\,0.844 on a fully held-out, dual-annotated test set. Applying the optimized pipeline, we release HeRE: a novel, massive, 1.5-million-instance silver dataset for Hebrew RE, designed to support data-intensive experimentation and model fine-tuning. HeRE bridges a critical gap in standard Hebrew RE evaluation, while providing the NLP community with a reproducible, language-agnostic pipeline for RE dataset construction in other low-resource settings.
authors: Ron Keinan, Amir David Nissan Cohen, Reut Tsarfaty
bullets: Addresses the lack of standardized Hebrew and other low-resource-language RE benchmarks.
Frames alignment validation as an NLI task: whether a relation triplet is entailed by the text.
Evaluates five denoising strategies and compares multilingual, Hebrew-specific, and general LLM approaches.
Releases HeRE, a 1.5-million-instance silver Hebrew RE dataset, plus a reproducible construction pipeline.
The best open-weights and API models achieve F1 scores of 0.915 and 0.921, respectively; the dual-annotated held-out test reaches F1=0.844.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes HeRE, a benchmark for Hebrew Relation Extraction using LLMs. It utilizes LLMs for NLP tasks, fitting the 'Large Language Models' subtopic.
papers.title: HeRE: A Novel Benchmark for Hebrew Relation Extraction via LLM-Guided Denoising of Knowledge Graph Alignments
papers.tldr: HeRE introduces a scalable, language-agnostic pipeline that denoises knowledge-graph–text alignments to create a large Hebrew relation-extraction benchmark without relying on costly native annotation or biased translation.

papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) that leverage test-time computation achieve strong performance on mathematical and scientific benchmarks and are increasingly deployed in real-world applications. However, their ability to perform \textit{everyday logical reasoning}, which often departs from textbook formal logic, remains underexplored. In this work, we systematically evaluate how well reasoning models align with everyday reasoning patterns by introducing a benchmark based on linguistic and pragmatic reasoning phenomena. We also compare reasoning models with non-reasoning models under controlled prompting conditions. We find that, in many cases, (1) reasoning models show degraded performance in everyday reasoning when such reasoning deviates from formal logical rules, (2) some non-reasoning models with chain-of-thought prompting outperform comparable reasoning models in everyday reasoning, and (3) prompting with additional instructions provides limited control over reasoning behavior. These findings suggest that current reasoning models do not reliably capture everyday reasoning and point to limitations in post-training, motivating improved training objectives and evaluation across diverse forms of reasoning.
authors: Kentaro Ozeki, Risako Ando, Takanobu Morishita, Hirohiko Abe, Koji Mineshima, Mitsuhiro Okada
bullets: Introduces a benchmark targeting linguistic and pragmatic phenomena in everyday reasoning.
Systematically compares reasoning and non-reasoning models under controlled prompting.
Reasoning models frequently perform worse when everyday reasoning conflicts with formal logical rules.
Some non-reasoning models using chain-of-thought prompting outperform comparable reasoning models.
Additional instructions provide limited control, highlighting gaps in post-training and evaluation.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) on 'everyday logical reasoning' tasks, comparing them to non-reasoning models. This provides insights into the limitations and capabilities of LLMs in pragmatic reasoning.
papers.title: Are Large Reasoning Models Good Everyday Reasoners? A Comparison with Non-Reasoning Models on Logical Reasoning Tasks
papers.tldr: Current large reasoning models often struggle with everyday logical reasoning, especially when it departs from formal logic, and may be outperformed by prompted non-reasoning models.

papers.abstract: LLM agents are used to check records against an organization's requirements, for example whether a vulnerability report is ready for investigation. Requirements often allow several ways to be met, such as a severity rating with a curator-reviewed advisory or a published advisory link. Agents fail by accepting a report after a required check has failed, or by settling for a weaker conclusion without trying another way that could still succeed. We introduce PRIME (Precommitted Rules for Inference from Minimal Evidence). Before checking, it fixes evidence routes specifying how each conclusion may be justified. A separate program records each check result and refuses any conclusion the results do not justify. It also points the agent to checks that could justify a stronger conclusion, or runs them itself. PRIME reports only conclusions authorized by its rules and ledger. With correct requirements, exact checks at known locations, and sufficient budget at stopping, completion reaches the strongest supported conclusion. On 480 public-record tasks, an agent shown the requirements reported unjustified conclusions on 26.7% of tasks, while PRIME reported none. Its directions and added checks raised the average score for justified conclusions from 30.1, with refusal alone, to the maximum of 59.2 out of 100.
bullets: Targets agents that accept failed checks or stop at weaker conclusions without exploring valid alternatives.
Precommits rules for how each conclusion can be justified before evidence is checked.
A separate program records check outcomes, blocks unsupported conclusions, and guides or performs checks for stronger ones.
On 480 public-record tasks, PRIME eliminated the unjustified conclusions observed in 26.7% of baseline-agent cases.
Its guidance and additional checks improved justified-conclusion scores from 30.1 to 59.2/100; guarantees depend on correct requirements, exact check locations, and sufficient budget.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces PRIME, a framework for verifiable evidence-grounded reasoning in LLM agents using precommitted rules. It focuses on constraint-based verification of agent conclusions.
papers.title: PRIME: Towards Verifiable Evidence-Grounded Reasoning in LLM Agents
papers.tldr: PRIME makes LLM-agent decisions verifiable by predefining evidence routes and enforcing conclusions through a programmatic evidence ledger.

papers.abstract: LLMs can generate Lean specifications from task descriptions, but those descriptions are often underspecified or ambiguous and may omit verifier-relevant edge cases, yielding imperfect formal specifications. We study whether an elicitation agent (EA) can improve verifier-checked Lean specifications by seeking clarification from a reference-grounded simulated developer before formalization. The agent decomposes the task, identifies unresolved decisions, asks bounded clarification questions, and uses the answers to write a refined natural-language specification that an LLM formalizer then translates into Lean. On 189 Verina Lean 4 specification-generation tasks, we compare single-shot generation with elicitation under question budgets of k=3 and k=10, allowing at most three or ten EA questions per task, across same-model and cross-model configurations. The same-model Claude Sonnet 4.6 pipeline has negative strict pass@1 estimates at both budgets, showing elicitation is not a uniform accuracy booster. In contrast, the Sonnet 4.6-to-GPT-5.6 and Sonnet 4.6-to-Gemini 3.8 Flash pipelines have positive strict estimates. The largest strict result reaches 65.6%, a +6.3-point change (+12 tasks), in the Sonnet 4.6-to-GPT-5.6 pipeline. Six of eight conditions have positive compile-conditional estimates, with a maximum cross-model difference of +4.9 points among compiling outputs. Treatment estimates also differ across the basic and advanced splits; the largest advanced-task change occurs in the Sonnet 4.6-to-GPT-5.6 configuration at k=10, from 42.0% to 50.6%. Failure analysis identifies postconditions as the largest source of degradation. These findings suggest future autoformalization systems should treat elicited natural-language specifications as intermediate artifacts and optimize jointly for semantic correctness among compiling outputs and reliable translation of clarified information into Lean.
authors: Mowafak Allaham, Aditya Vempaty, Ashish Jagmohan, Prasenjit Dey, Ravi Kokku
bullets: Underspecified task descriptions can omit verifier-relevant edge cases, motivating clarification before formalization.
An elicitation agent decomposes tasks, asks up to 3 or 10 bounded questions to a reference-grounded simulated developer, and refines the natural-language specification before Lean translation.
Across 189 Verina Lean 4 tasks, same-model elicitation reduced strict pass@1 estimates, while several cross-model pipelines improved them.
The largest reported strict improvement was +6.3 percentage points in the Sonnet 4.6-to-GPT-5.6 pipeline; effects also varied between basic and advanced tasks.
Postconditions were the main source of degradation, indicating that clarified specifications must be translated reliably into Lean.
papers.selection_reason: Studies an elicitation agent that uses clarification questions to improve the quality of Lean specifications generated by LLMs. This explores interactive prompting and agent-based formalization.
papers.title: Eliciting Specifications: When Does Interactive Clarification Help?
papers.tldr: Interactive clarification can improve Lean specification generation in some cross-model setups, but its benefits are inconsistent and depend on the models, question budget, and task type.

papers.abstract: When a large language model solves a mathematical problem, its reasoning is largely hierarchical, and the solution often branches at a few tokens where the next-token entropy is high. Such tree-like structure embeds in hyperbolic space with far lower distortion than in Euclidean space. Activation steering, however, usually edits the hidden states of a pretrained model by adding one fixed Euclidean vector at every token, even though most tokens of a solution are already determined by the context. We propose Hyperbolic Entropy Steering (HEST), which embeds the hidden states in the Poincaré ball with a lightweight probe whose only label is the model's own next-token entropy. Where this entropy exceeds a threshold, HEST moves the embedded state along the geodesic of steepest descent of a readout of the probe and maps the change back to the hidden state. For the Busemann readout of a learned ideal point, we prove that a step of fixed length lowers it by the same amount at every state. On three instruction-tuned models from the Qwen2.5-Math and Llama-3.1 families, HEST with the Busemann readout improves greedy accuracy on MATH-500 and GSM8K in five of six settings, by up to 1.8 points, whereas a contrastive steering vector added at every token lowers accuracy. With a Euclidean probe trained in the same way, this gain disappears on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct. The gains are largest on problems where the model hesitates often, and accuracy on the remaining problems is almost unchanged.
bullets: Motivation: Mathematical reasoning is hierarchical and branches mainly at tokens with high next-token entropy, while standard steering applies the same Euclidean edit everywhere.
Method: A lightweight probe maps hidden states into the Poincaré ball using the model’s own entropy; above a threshold, it applies geodesic descent and maps the update back.
Theory: With a Busemann readout, a fixed-length hyperbolic step lowers the readout by the same amount at every state.
Results: Across three Qwen2.5-Math and Llama-3.1 models, HEST improves greedy accuracy on MATH-500 and GSM8K in five of six settings, by up to 1.8 points.
Scope: Gains are largest on problems with frequent hesitation, while other problems remain nearly unchanged; the gain disappears with a matched Euclidean probe on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct.
papers.selection_reason: Entropy-trained hyperbolic probes for sparse activation steering in instruction-tuned LLMs improve reasoning accuracy.
papers.title: Hesitation Has a Geometry: Entropy-Trained Hyperbolic Probes for Sparse Activation Steering
papers.tldr: HEST steers mathematical reasoning only at high-entropy decision points, using hyperbolic geometry to improve greedy accuracy without disrupting confident tokens.

papers.abstract: Text-to-SQL translates natural-language questions into executable SQL queries, but open-source large language models still require task-specific post-training for complex, real-world SQL generation. Effective post-training requires both training data that cover the capabilities demanded by the target task and a learning strategy that enables the model to acquire them. Existing datasets provide valuable supervision but incompletely cover SQL structures, while augmentation methods typically expand data without identifying structural gaps. Moreover, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) or reinforcement learning (RL) alone cannot dynamically address weaknesses exposed during training. We propose COAL-SQL, a unified framework combining Coverage-Guided Augmentation (CGA) and Failure-Driven Learning (FDL). CGA uses greedy selection to identify SQL structures missing from the original dataset and constructs complementary examples, improving structural coverage. FDL retains GRPO as the main optimization objective while supplying targeted supervision for unsolved examples. At the step level, it applies SFT to verified reasoning traces generated by a strong LLM for accumulated failures. At the epoch level, it retrieves structurally related examples based on accumulated failures to create targeted practice, helping the model acquire the corresponding SQL capabilities. With only 12,600 distinct post-training examples, COAL-SQL achieves 64.9% execution accuracy on the BIRD development set and outperforms baselines trained at comparable scale. The code is available at https://github.com/TechNomad-ds/COAL-SQL.
bullets: Addresses incomplete SQL-structure coverage and static training strategies in existing post-training data and methods.
Uses Coverage-Guided Augmentation to greedily identify missing structures and generate complementary examples.
Uses Failure-Driven Learning with GRPO, step-level SFT on verified reasoning traces, and epoch-level retrieval of structurally related practice examples.
With 12,600 post-training examples, reaches 64.9% execution accuracy on the BIRD development set and outperforms comparably scaled baselines.
Scope: focuses on complex, real-world Text-to-SQL generation for open-source language models.
papers.selection_reason: Post-training framework for open-source LLMs on text-to-SQL with coverage-guided augmentation and failure-driven learning.
papers.title: COAL-SQL: Coverage-Guided Augmentation and Failure-Driven Learning for Text-to-SQL Post-Training
papers.tldr: COAL-SQL improves Text-to-SQL post-training by filling SQL-structure coverage gaps and targeting examples the model repeatedly fails to solve.

papers.abstract: An agent that learns from rewards has to trust whatever reports those rewards. When the reports suddenly change, either the world changed or the reporter broke. From the reports alone these are indistinguishable, and reinforcement learning theory shows that no amount of further experience separates them. The prescribed escape is richer data about the reporter itself. We ask whether a frozen language model, handed exactly that data, uses it. We build a two-option game in which a payout swap and a lying reporter produce byte-identical histories. Then we add one verified record: an independent check of one round's real result, printed beside what the reporter said about that round. That single line settles the case. We ask three large models, from two families, to answer one question with one letter. Is the reporter honest or lying? They catch a lying reporter almost perfectly. At the 70B class that holds in every condition we tried; the 32B model slips in one wording. They clear an honest reporter far less often, and how often depends on things that should not matter. Averaged over rounds, letters, and wordings, a 72B model calls an honest reporter a liar 38% of the time when nothing has changed at all, and 58% of the time when the payouts moved. A 70B model from a second family calls an honest reporter a liar 26% and 48% of the time. The failure is not one of reading, because in the situation where nothing changed the same models score 0.96 to 1.00 with the answer printed in the prompt. Which surface feature drives it differs by family. For the Qwen models it is which round the record names, and for Llama it is which letter stands for "honest." Adding the record to a prompt that already states the answer makes Llama less likely to give that answer. We had registered a prediction for that 58% before the run: 35%. The failure is larger than we expected.
bullets: A payout change and a lying reporter can generate identical reward histories, making them indistinguishable from reports alone.
The study tests whether one verified comparison between the reporter’s claim and the real outcome resolves this ambiguity for language models.
Models nearly always identify lying reporters, but their accuracy for honest reporters varies substantially with wording and other irrelevant surface features.
False accusations are especially frequent when payouts changed, reaching 58% for one 72B-class model and 48% for another 70B-class model.
Providing the verified record alongside an answer can sometimes reduce, rather than improve, the likelihood of selecting that answer.
papers.selection_reason: Uses a large language model to diagnose corrupted reward channels in reinforcement learning agents, relevant to Test-Time Learning and LLM reasoning.
papers.title: Easy to Catch a Liar, Hard to Clear an Honest One: Language Models Diagnosing a Corrupted Reward Channel from a Verified Record
papers.tldr: Large frozen language models reliably detect lying reward reporters but often falsely accuse honest ones, even when given a verified record that resolves the ambiguity.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at programming tasks but frequently fail at deterministic, fine-grained reasoning in natural language, relying heavily on semantic approximations rather than robust symbolic execution. To bridge this gap, we propose MIMIC, a framework that leverages executable code as a rigorous medium for reasoning data synthesis. MIMIC fundamentally transforms algorithms into verifiable reasoning trajectories through narrative fusion, code-guided test synthesis, and dynamic code instrumentation. Crucially, these explicit intermediate execution states naturally form a Code-Instrumented Reward (CIR), providing dense, high-fidelity process supervision for reinforcement learning without external reward models. Extensive evaluations reveal that models trained via SFT and GRPO on our synthesized dataset achieve substantial, consistent gains. Our method significantly elevates accuracy across general reasoning, complex mathematical benchmarks, and fine-grained deterministic tasks, demonstrating that the procedural rigor of executable code can effectively unlock and enhance the generalized reasoning capabilities of LLMs. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/zjy1298/MIMIC.
bullets: Addresses LLMs’ tendency to rely on semantic approximations instead of robust symbolic execution in natural-language reasoning.
Transforms algorithms into reasoning data through narrative fusion, code-guided test synthesis, and dynamic code instrumentation.
Uses intermediate execution states as Code-Instrumented Rewards (CIR) for process supervision without external reward models.
Training with SFT and GRPO yields consistent gains across general reasoning, complex mathematics, and fine-grained deterministic tasks.
The approach is scoped to reasoning learned from executable, algorithmic procedures; the abstract does not specify quantitative results.
papers.selection_reason: Code-centric reasoning data synthesis and process reward for LLM reasoning, fitting LLM reasoning methods.
papers.title: The Imitation Game: When LLMs Learn to Reason Like Programs via Code-Centric Reasoning Data Synthesis
papers.tldr: MIMIC uses executable code to synthesize verifiable reasoning trajectories and dense process rewards, improving LLMs’ deterministic and general reasoning abilities.

papers.abstract: Retrieving relevant lemmas is crucial for formal theorem proving, enabling provers to build machine-checkable proofs from established mathematical results. Recent retrieval systems match library declarations to a target theorem or its intermediate proof steps, but make limited use of multi-hop dependencies among declarations. These dependencies can reveal supporting lemmas that are not necessarily lexically similar to the target theorem but recur in proofs of related problems. To this end, we propose LeanGraphSearch, a graph-based retrieval method for Lean 4 that constructs a graph from Mathlib's forward dependencies and traverses it to uncover supporting lemmas through multi-hop dependency chains. Specifically, LeanGraphSearch links each declaration to the premises it depends on, uses a graph-based ranking algorithm to propagate relevance from semantically matched declarations to their dependencies, and reranks the expanded candidates against the original query. Across two mathematical retrieval benchmarks, LeanGraphSearch improves recall by up to 12% over the strongest baseline, LeanSearch v2, on MathlibQR and increases coverage of complete annotated proof routes on MathlibMPR, covering up to 3.7% of extra groups. More importantly, we evaluate whether these retrieval gains translate into improved end-to-end theorem proving by integrating LeanGraphSearch into an iterative proving loop guided by Lean feedback. Across three theorem proving benchmarks, LeanGraphSearch improves pass rate at {8, 16, 32} reflection turns by as much as 40% compared to vanilla prover and at most 10% compared to LeanSearch v2, showing higher accuracy-cost efficiency. These findings highlight the value of dependency graph search for theorem proving and motivate further research on structure-aware search for proof discovery.
bullets: Targets a limitation of lexical or direct matching: useful supporting lemmas may be several dependency hops away from the target.
Builds a graph from Mathlib forward dependencies and propagates relevance from semantically matched declarations to their dependencies before reranking candidates.
Improves recall by up to 12% over LeanSearch v2 on MathlibQR and covers up to 3.7% more complete annotated proof routes on MathlibMPR.
In an iterative Lean-feedback proving loop, improves pass rate by up to 40% over a vanilla prover and up to 10% over LeanSearch v2 across reported reflection-turn settings.
Motivates further structure-aware search for proof discovery.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes LeanGraphSearch, a graph-based retrieval method to enhance formal theorem proving capabilities in LLMs by utilizing multi-hop dependencies in mathematical libraries.
papers.title: Lean Graph Search for Formal Theorem Proving
papers.tldr: LeanGraphSearch improves Lean 4 theorem proving by retrieving lemmas through multi-hop dependency graphs, raising retrieval recall and end-to-end proof pass rates.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are becoming prevalent in scenarios where honesty is critical. However, despite alignment training, these models still exhibit dishonest behaviour, such as outputting claims that contradict some knowledge or are not supported by what is accessible in context. We introduce Continuous Adversarial Training for Consistent Honesty (CATCH), inspired by a method originally developed to robustly refuse harmful queries. CATCH trains the model towards an honest answer and away from a dishonest one while maintaining the model's capabilities. We evaluate two architectures (Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and Qwen3-3.6-27B). We show that trained with only hundreds of targets built from self-reporting scenarios, CATCH learns an honest behaviour that robustly generalizes and transfers across distinct benchmarks. It consistently reduces dishonesty under pressure on MASK, increases confessions in the multi-agent game of Among Us, and improves the discovery rates of the model's hidden behaviours in AuditBench. We show that CATCH outperforms prompting and supervised fine-tuning in improving honesty, and it is on par with state-of-the-art honesty activation steering. However, CATCH surpasses honesty steering in maintaining utility, thanks to a novel choice of utility data.
bullets: Targets dishonest answers by training toward honest responses and away from dishonest alternatives.
Learns from only hundreds of self-reporting scenarios and transfers across distinct honesty benchmarks.
Reduces dishonesty under pressure, increases confessions in Among Us, and improves hidden-behaviour discovery in AuditBench.
Outperforms prompting and supervised fine-tuning, and matches honesty steering while better preserving utility.
Evaluated on Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and Qwen3-3.6-27B.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces CATCH, a continuous adversarial training method to improve LLM honesty and transferability across benchmarks, outperforming standard prompting and fine-tuning.
papers.title: CAT-alyzing Honesty: Continuous Adversarial Training for Transferable LLM Honesty
papers.tldr: CATCH uses continuous adversarial training to make LLMs more honest across tasks while preserving their general capabilities.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning has become a widely used approach to post-training large language models. In a typical implementation, learning is off-policy: The policy generating the responses differs from the policy being trained because of training-inference mismatch or policy staleness in asynchronous training. This discrepancy is commonly addressed by importance sampling, whose ratio is usually regularized in practice through truncation, masking, or clipping. Under regularized importance sampling, the importance-weighted policy gradient is no longer invariant to constant shifts in the reward. This invariance is recovered by using the covariance between the reward and the importance-weighted score as the estimand, which coincides with the policy gradient when the ratio is not regularized. This note develops this covariance perspective for both sequence-level and token-level importance sampling. The covariance perspective reveals the roles of the group-mean baseline and score centering in policy gradient estimation. Both perform centering in covariance estimation, but they differ in the mean being subtracted: The group-mean baseline uses a sample mean, whereas score centering uses a population mean. The two lead to distinct unbiased covariance estimators with different variances. Whether both forms of centering should be used simultaneously depends on whether importance sampling is applied at the sequence level or at the token level. With sequence-level importance sampling, score centering adds no benefit once the group-mean baseline is used; with token-level importance sampling, using the group-mean baseline without score centering generally introduces bias when the importance ratio is regularized.
bullets: Regularized importance sampling breaks the usual invariance of policy gradients to constant reward shifts.
Estimating the covariance between reward and importance-weighted score restores this invariance, matching the standard gradient without ratio regularization.
Group-mean baselines subtract a sample mean, while score centering subtracts a population mean; they produce different unbiased covariance estimators and variances.
For sequence-level importance sampling, score centering adds no benefit after applying a group-mean baseline.
For token-level importance sampling, omitting score centering while using a group-mean baseline generally causes bias under regularized ratios.
papers.selection_reason: Provides a theoretical perspective on policy gradient estimation for LLMs, clarifying the roles of group-mean baselines and score centering in importance sampling.
papers.title: Baselines and Score Centering in Policy Gradient Estimation
papers.tldr: A covariance-based view clarifies when reward baselines and score centering yield unbiased, shift-invariant policy-gradient estimates under regularized importance sampling.

papers.abstract: Verifying the final answer of a long reasoning trace may show that the trace is wrong but it does not distinguish three cases. The problem may lie beyond the model's capability, another attempt would succeed, or one step in an otherwise recoverable trace made the trace fail. Standard hidden-state probes are trained on final-answer correctness, a label that conflates these cases. Monte Carlo rollouts distinguish the cases and locate the failing step at additional inference cost. We test the hidden states of 4B and 8B reasoning models for the failure type and the failing step and compare each probe with the strongest baseline that uses no hidden states. On incorrect 8B traces, the confidence probe, a calibrated correctness probe at a midpoint cutoff, misses 81% of cases in which a single step makes the trace unrecoverable and 47% of cases in which another attempt would succeed. A probe with a different training design over the same states reverses the ordering of these two kinds of failure, so either ordering can be read from those states. At both scales, no single tested probe locates the failing step more accurately than a rule based only on trace length, and at 4B a probe trained to predict that step fails to outperform this rule in any of 10 runs on identical traces. The confidence probe therefore indicates that an answer is wrong, but its failure-type ordering depends on its training design.
bullets: Final-answer correctness labels conflate capability limits, recoverable failed attempts, and single-step failures.
The study evaluates probes on hidden states from 4B and 8B reasoning models, comparing them with non-hidden-state baselines.
Monte Carlo rollouts provide reference labels for failure type and failing step, but require extra inference cost.
A calibrated confidence probe misses many unrecoverable single-step failures and cases where another attempt would succeed; its failure-type ordering changes with training design.
No tested probe locates failing steps more accurately than a trace-length rule, including across 10 runs at 4B.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates the effectiveness of hidden-state probes for localizing reasoning failures in LLMs, finding that simple rules often outperform complex probes in this specific diagnostic task.
papers.title: Effectiveness of Hidden-State Probes for Localizing Reasoning Failures
papers.tldr: Hidden-state probes can signal incorrect reasoning traces and distinguish failure types, but tested probes do not reliably localize the specific failing step.

papers.abstract: We study sparse and continual reinforcement learning fine-tuning of language models through attention-head ranking and partitioning. For sparse learning, we rank attention heads by gradient norm to identify a small subset of heads that can be trained effectively. For continual learning, we partition heads across tasks to reduce cross-task interference and preserve previously learned capabilities. Theoretically, we relate gradient norm to training effectiveness, and further characterize why sparse, separated head updates can remain stable. Empirically, across math, instruction-following, and coding tasks, tuning higher-ranked heads consistently outperforms tuning lower-ranked ones while often matching denser baselines, and head partitioning improves retention while preserving adaptation to new tasks.
bullets: Targets efficient sparse and continual reinforcement-learning fine-tuning of language models.
Ranks heads by gradient norm to select a small, effective trainable subset.
Partitions heads across tasks to reduce interference and preserve prior capabilities.
Theory links gradient norm to training effectiveness and explains the stability of separated updates.
Across math, instruction-following, and coding tasks, higher-ranked heads outperform lower-ranked ones; partitioning improves retention while maintaining adaptation.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes sparse and continual reinforcement learning fine-tuning strategies for LLMs by ranking and partitioning attention heads to improve training efficiency and task retention.
papers.title: Ranking and Partitioning of Attention Heads for Sparse and Continual Reinforcement Learning Fine-tuning
papers.tldr: Ranking attention heads by gradient norm enables effective sparse fine-tuning, while partitioning heads across tasks improves continual-learning retention and adaptation.

papers.abstract: Current value alignment evaluations for large language models (LLMs) heavily rely on output compliance, overlooking whether LLMs maintain value consistency when alternating between generator and evaluator roles. Such consistency is increasingly important because modern LLM agents and alignment pipelines often rely on the same LLM to both generate actions and evaluate their acceptability. To mitigate this limitation, we propose VALCON, a role-driven data construction framework that operationalizes value consistency into three benchmark suites (VAB-Consistency, VAB-Boundary, VAB-Challenge) via dual-role variation. By systematically pairing an LLM's generative behavior with its evaluative judgments under identical principles, VALCON synthesizes target evaluation data that exposes hidden value discrepancies. Experiments on 28 LLMs reveal pervasive cross-role inconsistency: models with highly compliant outputs frequently fail to align their judgments with their own generations. To understand and address this gap, we perform mechanistic probing that uncovers a role-dependent representational decoupling associated with this behavioral asymmetry. Guided by these insights, we propose a representation-directed intervention that effectively mitigates consistency failures. Our work establishes value consistency as a distinct alignment dimension and provides a complete evaluation-analysis-mitigation pipeline. Code and data are available at https://github.com/tjunlp-lab/VALCON.
bullets: Existing alignment evaluations often measure compliance but overlook consistency across generator and evaluator roles.
VALCON constructs three benchmark suites—VAB-Consistency, VAB-Boundary, and VAB-Challenge—using dual-role variation.
Experiments across 28 LLMs find widespread cross-role inconsistency, including among models with highly compliant outputs.
Mechanistic probing links this asymmetry to role-dependent representational decoupling.
A representation-directed intervention reduces consistency failures, forming an evaluation–analysis–mitigation pipeline.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces VALCON, a benchmark and framework for evaluating value consistency in LLMs when acting as both generators and evaluators, addressing a gap in current alignment evaluations.
papers.title: VALCON: Benchmarking and Enhancing Value Consistency in Large Language Models via Dual-Role Variation
papers.tldr: VALCON benchmarks and mitigates whether LLMs maintain consistent values when generating outputs and evaluating them.

papers.abstract: Language models are often asked to make judgments: whether a proposed answer is correct, whether one statement follows logically from another, or whether a response is safe. Yet changing the instructions that specify how the judgment should be expressed can make the final answer less reliable, even for the same input. We ask whether this reflects a change in internal judgment or a failure to express it. Comparing hidden-state vectors for the same input under different instructions, we find that their differences concentrate in a low-dimensional expression subspace. We identify this subspace without benchmark labels and remove its contribution from a linear predictor to obtain an isolated judgment. Across correctness, entailment, and safety, the isolated judgment remains reliable under instructions not used to identify the subspace, even when the model's final answer and the original predictor degrade. When the judgment question is negated, isolation raises the predictor's AUROC from 0.504 to 0.825 for entailment and from 0.480 to 0.891 for safety. We also find that judgment is readable in earlier layers, before the expression subspace begins to disrupt the predictor. Together, these results provide a way to separate judgment from expression and recover internal judgments even when the model's final answers are unreliable.
bullets: Different instructions alter hidden states mainly along a low-dimensional expression subspace, suggesting changes in wording need not reflect changed judgment.
The method identifies this subspace without benchmark labels and removes its effect from a linear predictor.
Across correctness, entailment, and safety, the isolated judgment generalizes to unseen instructions more reliably than the original predictor or final answer.
Under negated judgment questions, AUROC improves from 0.504 to 0.825 for entailment and from 0.480 to 0.891 for safety.
Judgment is readable in earlier layers, before expression-related variation disrupts prediction.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a method to isolate a language model's internal judgment from its expression subspace using label-free analysis. This provides a technical insight into LLM reasoning and internal states, fitting 'Large Language Models'.
papers.title: Isolating a Language Model's Judgment with a Label-Free Subspace
papers.tldr: A label-free low-dimensional subspace method separates a language model’s internal judgment from instruction-dependent answer expression, improving judgment reliability when outputs degrade.

papers.abstract: Cyber threat intelligence (CTI) relies on the timely identification of emerging threats, enabling organizations and security analysts to support situational awareness and decision-making. Social media platforms such as X (formerly Twitter) have become valuable CTI sources because vulnerabilities and attack activities are often discussed there before appearing in formal reports. However, the rapid growth of cybersecurity discussions on social media has created more content than domain experts can realistically review and annotate, making labeled data a major bottleneck for developing supervised learning approaches. While large language models (LLMs) have shown promise as weak annotators in other domains, their effectiveness for cybersecurity tweet classification and downstream training of domain-specific pre-trained language models (PLMs) remains underexplored. To address this challenge, we propose a Teacher-Student weak supervision framework in which a selected LLM serves as a Teacher to generate weak labels for unlabeled cybersecurity tweets, enabling the training of cybersecurity-specific PLMs without large-scale manual annotation. Experimental results show that PLMs trained solely on LLM-generated labels consistently achieve F1 scores above 0.92, remaining within 3 percentage points of fully human-supervised models across all evaluated architectures. These findings suggest that LLM-based weak annotation offers a practical alternative for constructing cybersecurity-specific training data when expert annotation resources are limited.
bullets: Addresses the shortage of expert-labeled data for rapidly growing cybersecurity discussions on X.
Uses a Teacher–Student framework: an LLM generates weak labels, which train cybersecurity-specific PLMs.
PLMs trained only on LLM-generated labels achieved F1 scores above 0.92.
Results stayed within 3 percentage points of fully human-supervised models across evaluated architectures.
Supports weak annotation as a practical alternative when expert annotation resources are limited.
papers.selection_reason: Uses LLMs as weak annotators to generate labels for cybersecurity tweets, enabling training of domain-specific PLMs. This is a standard application of LLMs in the 'Large Language Models' topic.
papers.title: LLM-Based Weak Annotation for Cybersecurity Tweet Classification: A Teacher-Student Framework
papers.tldr: An LLM teacher can weakly label cybersecurity tweets to train domain-specific language models with performance close to human-supervised training.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models have become an important approach for scaling model parameters. Modern MoE architectures increasingly combine two design choices: fine-grained expert segmentation and shared experts. The former increases expressiveness by enabling more expert combinations at a fixed activation ratio, and the latter introduces experts that are active for every token. We identify an exploration dilemma between these designs: shared experts can make routing less exploratory by reducing the variability of token representations. This conflicts with the greater need for exploration induced by fine-grained expert segmentation due to the combinatorially enlarged routing space. Consequently, the additional expressiveness offered by fine-grained segmentation may not be fully realized in practice. MirrorMoE is proposed to reconcile this exploration dilemma by shrinking the exploration space through token-adaptive suppression of unnecessary experts. MirrorMoE consistently improves performance across model scales.
authors: Bingcong Li, Hao Ma, Michael Muehlebach, Niao He, Yi Ma
bullets: Fine-grained expert segmentation expands routing choices and potential expressiveness.
Shared experts reduce token-representation variability, creating an exploration dilemma.
MirrorMoE uses token-adaptive suppression to shrink the routing space and improve exploration efficiency.
The method consistently improves performance across model scales.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses routing exploration in mixture-of-experts LLM architectures.
papers.title: Rethinking Routing Exploration in Modern Mixture-of-Experts
papers.tldr: MirrorMoE addresses reduced routing exploration in fine-grained MoE models with shared experts by suppressing unnecessary experts per token.

papers.abstract: Continuous diffusion language models (CDLMs) offer an alternative approach to parallel language generation; however, most existing studies directly use transformer architectures from either causal large language models (LLMs) or Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) for image generation, which were not optimized for CDLMs. In this paper, we conduct a systematic study on Transformer architectures for CDLMs and introduce Language Diffusion Transformer (LangDiT), combining feature and query-key normalization, wider noise conditioning, likelihood-shortcut gradient routing and calibration, and confidence-gated training self-conditioning. LangDiT significantly reduces generation perplexity in matched LangFlow comparisons, establishing a new state of the art in continuous language generation across different model formulations. Using LangFlow as a representative CDLM, LangDiT as a plug-and-play backbone leads to a new state-of-the-art model with a generation perplexity (GenPPL) of 21.72 using 1024 NFEs and 44.72 GenPPL using 128 NFEs on the unconditional generation of 1024-token sequences on the OpenWebText dataset. When adapted to Plaid-style CDLM formulations, LangDiT results in a new leading GenPPL of 11.33 using 1024 denoising NFEs, and 27.51 GenPPL using 128 denoising NFEs. These gains are achieved while retaining each model's underlying representation, training objective, and inference sampler, isolating transformer architecture as a fundamental source of improvement. Our study identifies architectural design as an important source of improvement in continuous diffusion language models.
authors: Weijian Luo, Yujian Chen, Hao Jiang, Guang Cheng, Tianyang Hu
bullets: Existing CDLMs typically reuse architectures designed for causal LLMs or image-generation diffusion Transformers rather than language diffusion.
LangDiT combines feature and query-key normalization, wider noise conditioning, likelihood-shortcut gradient routing and calibration, and confidence-gated training self-conditioning.
As a plug-in backbone, it achieves leading generation perplexities in LangFlow and Plaid-style CDLMs at both high and low denoising-step budgets.
Improvements are isolated to the Transformer architecture while retaining each model’s representation, training objective, and inference sampler.
The study demonstrates that architectural design is a key source of performance gains in continuous language generation.
papers.selection_reason: Transformer architecture improvements for continuous diffusion language models.
papers.title: Designing Transformers for Continuous Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: LangDiT systematically redesigns Transformer architectures for continuous diffusion language models, substantially improving generation perplexity across CDLM formulations.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) acquire new skills through fine-tuning, but it can destroy capabilities they already have: catastrophic forgetting remains a central obstacle to continual learning in LLMs. Recent works connect forgetting to how far, and along which directions, fine-tuning moves the weights.
