On-policy methods such as reinforcement learning and on-policy distillation avoid updating the principal singular directions of weight matrices and thus forget less. In contrast, SFT concentrates updates along these directions and is susceptible to catastrophic forgetting. In this work, we introduce Subspace Tuning (SST), which restricts each weight update to the bottom singular subspace, eliminating changes along the principal directions. SST is optimizer-agnostic and composes well with fine-tuning recipes including SFT and self-distillation. SST combines tight subspace protection, dense gradient estimation, and a simple refresh mechanism, enabling stronger learning than prior orthogonal fine-tuning methods. With these mechanisms, protecting as much as 99\% of the weight subspace substantially improves retention while preserving strong target-task performance. This behavior strengthens with model and data size and nearly eliminates forgetting in the large-model regime. SST also keeps the model close to its base distribution, inducing $2$--$4\times$ less KL drift than the baseline recipes. Overall, SST advances the learning--forgetting Pareto frontier, making it a practical default for fine-tuning pre-trained language models.
authors: Arnav Chavan, Kusha Sareen, Rishabh Tiwari, Abhranil Chandra, Johan Obando-Ceron, Kurt Keutzer, Scott Niekum, Inderjit S Dhillon, Devvrit Khatri
bullets: Addresses capability loss when LLMs are continually fine-tuned, especially with supervised fine-tuning.
Restricts weight updates away from principal singular directions, which are associated with greater forgetting.
Is optimizer-agnostic and compatible with SFT and self-distillation, using dense gradient estimation and subspace refreshing.
Protecting up to 99% of the weight subspace substantially improves retention and can nearly eliminate forgetting for large models.
Produces 2–4× less KL drift than baseline recipes and improves the learning–forgetting tradeoff.
papers.selection_reason: Subspace tuning mitigates catastrophic forgetting in LLM continual learning, directly relevant to continual learning and language foundation models.
papers.title: Towards Continual Learning: Mitigating Forgetting With Subspace Tuning
papers.tldr: Subspace Tuning reduces catastrophic forgetting by confining fine-tuning updates to the bottom singular subspace while retaining strong performance on new tasks.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation consolidates specialist models into one student at the price of rollouts, teacher passes and gradient steps for every teacher. We show that the consolidation does not need training: with forward passes only, the capabilities of separately tuned specialists can be aggregated into one model that is, on average, more accurate than either specialist alone. When specialists share a base model, distillation has an exact layer-wise solution: each linear layer of the fused model must reproduce every specialist's output on the inputs that specialist receives while reading its own answers, a least-squares problem whose solution needs only the second moments of those inputs. One forward pass over a few hundred rollouts provides them. We call this training-free on-policy distillation (\method). What the rollouts contain matters more than the solver: answers truncated in repetition loops are few among a mathematics specialist's rollouts but carry a large share of their tokens, and removing them lifts the fused model on AIME25 from task arithmetic's level to the specialist's at matched precision. On Olmo~3 7B, a few GPU-hours of forward computation per specialist yield a generalist that keeps most of each specialist's gain on each of seven mathematics and code benchmarks.
authors: Bangji Yang, Jiajun Fan, Zhaoyu Zhu, Hongbo Ma, Ge Liu
bullets: Eliminates teacher-specific rollouts, gradient steps, and training during specialist consolidation.
For specialists sharing a base model, solves each fused linear layer via least squares using input second moments collected from a few hundred rollouts.
The composition of rollouts is critical: filtering repetition-loop truncations substantially improves mathematical performance.
On Olmo 3 7B, a few GPU-hours of forward computation per specialist produce a generalist that preserves most gains across seven math and code benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free on-policy distillation consolidates specialist LLMs with forward passes only, relevant to language foundation model efficiency and merging.
papers.title: Training-Free On-Policy Distillation
papers.tldr: Training-free on-policy distillation fuses specialist models into one generalist using only forward passes and rollout statistics, retaining most specialist gains across math and code tasks.

papers.abstract: We present a scalable framework for solving multi-step tasks through a decentralized market of self-interested agents. Prior theoretical work demonstrated that agents organized through sequential auctions can converge to a globally optimal policy in a Markov decision process (MDP), but relied on the restrictive assumption of the existence of perfect clones as a model of perfect competition. In reality, exact clones drive agent profit to zero, violating the natural risk-reward incentives of participants. Conversely, we empirically demonstrate that the opposite extreme, absence of competition, also leads to market failure and value extraction collapse. Between these two extremes, we investigate how heterogeneous agents can survive in markets that span the critical middle ground of imperfect competition. To be profitable, agents learn to strategically shade bids to secure positive individual profit margins, while still ensuring that the marketplace functions effectively enough so that collaborative tasks posed by market consumers can still be solved. We formulate and evaluate four bidding algorithms (Mirror Descent, Thompson Sampling, Bayes-Optimal, and PPO) across three auction protocols (1st-Price, 2nd-Price, and Credit-Conserving Vickrey). Across a diverse set of domains, we demonstrate that imperfect competition successfully sustains necessary agent profit margins while maintaining high task success rates at low costs.
authors: Ian Gemp, Shubhendu Trivedi, Adam Fisch, Fantine Huot, Michael Kaisers, Mirella Lapata, William W. Cohen, Alekh Agarwal, Kate Larson, Jacob Eisenstein
bullets: Addresses market failure at both extremes: perfect clones eliminate profits, while no competition collapses value extraction.
Studies the critical middle ground where heterogeneous agents strategically shade bids to earn positive margins.
Evaluates Mirror Descent, Thompson Sampling, Bayes-Optimal, and PPO bidding across three auction protocols.
Finds that imperfect competition preserves agent profitability while maintaining high task success at low cost across diverse domains.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a decentralized market framework for LLM agents to solve multi-step tasks via sequential auctions, relevant to LLM agents and multi-agent systems.
papers.title: Decentralized LLM Workflows via Sequential Auctions
papers.tldr: A decentralized auction market of heterogeneous LLM agents can balance profitable bidding with effective, low-cost completion of multi-step tasks under imperfect competition.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in computational social science to assign scalar scores to social and psychological constructs. However, studies use different rating scales, and whether their scores remain comparable across scale designs is understudied. To address this gap, we define and systematically investigate scale sensitivity, the variation in LLM-generated scores caused by rating scale design. We distinguish numerical sensitivity, changes in normalized scores, from semantic sensitivity, changes in score interpretation. To assess both, our experimental design crosses 2 formats (continuous vs. ordinal), 4 ranges (3, 5, 11, and 21 points), and 2 signs (signed vs. unsigned) across 3 tasks (political leaning, sentiment, and toxicity), 2 prompting strategies (zero-shot and rubric-based), and 5 LLMs. We find that changing one design element shifts normalized scores by about 0.10 on average and changes the category of roughly 20% of texts. Sensitivity is greatest for toxicity, the only unipolar construct examined. Also, rubric-based prompting does not reduce sensitivity compared with zero-shot prompting. We provide practical guidance for designing more reliable LLM-based text scoring and highlight the need for robustness checks across alternative scales.
authors: Wonjeong Jo, Gyuwan Kim, Ming Shan Hee
bullets: The study defines scale sensitivity as changes in LLM scores caused by rating-scale design, covering both numerical values and score interpretation.
It tests continuous versus ordinal formats, 3–21 point ranges, and signed versus unsigned scales across political leaning, sentiment, and toxicity tasks.
Changing one scale element shifts normalized scores by about 0.10 on average and changes the category of roughly 20% of texts.
Sensitivity is highest for toxicity, the only unipolar construct examined.
Rubric-based prompting does not reduce sensitivity relative to zero-shot prompting.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates the sensitivity of LLM-based text scoring to rating scale design, relevant to LLM evaluation and robustness.
papers.title: Change the Number, Change the Answer: Assessing Rating Scale Sensitivity in LLM-Based Text Scoring
papers.tldr: LLM-generated text scores can change substantially when the rating scale changes, even after normalization, so scale robustness checks are essential.

papers.abstract: The vocabulary of a language model is its native semantics: the embedding and the unembedding fix the meaning of a state at the two ends of the residual stream. Between them, existing methods either reuse a fixed lens or treat the states as a point cloud, and neither reads a state the way the model does. We argue that every hidden state has a native reference frame, induced by the layers that read it next and adaptive to the context. Lexical reference frames approximate it by reading a state through the model's own remaining layers with a stated number of rounds of attention between positions and a typical attention output for the rest, without fitting to the model's output. No lens, with fixed directions per layer, can exceed the square root of the native frame's coherence, 0.30 and 0.35 at mid-depth of SmolLM3-3B and OLMo3-7B, whereas the first-order frame, LexFrame[1], reaches 0.97 and 0.97 and reads a state within 0.16 nats of the model's output. Its coefficients attribute predictions more faithfully than attribution patching, its lexical basis steers a prediction while sparing other tokens, and its confident readings would let an early exit skip 0.45 and 0.42 of the layers, where lenses skip almost none. In this way, lexical reference frames make every hidden state of the model readable, attributable and steerable.
authors: Jian Gu, Hongyu Zhang, Chunyang Chen, Aldeida Aleti
bullets: Fixed lenses and point-cloud views do not capture the context-dependent semantics of intermediate states.
LexFrame approximates each state’s native reference frame by applying remaining layers, with configurable inter-position attention rounds and typical attention elsewhere.
The first-order LexFrame[1] achieves 0.97 coherence on both SmolLM3-3B and OLMo3-7B, reading states within 0.16 nats of the model output.
Its coefficients are more faithful than attribution patching, and its lexical basis can steer selected predictions while preserving others.
Confident readings support skipping 0.45 and 0.42 of layers on the two models, respectively, unlike conventional lenses.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces native lexical reference frames for interpreting and steering LM residual streams, relevant to LLM architecture and interpretability.
papers.title: Lexical Reference Frames: Interpreting LM Residual Streams in Native Semantics
papers.tldr: Lexical reference frames interpret language-model hidden states using the model’s own remaining computation, yielding highly faithful, attributable, steerable readings and enabling substantial early exits.

papers.abstract: Personalization of Large Language Models (LLMs) is increasingly important for user-centric applications, yet prior methods mainly adapt dense LLMs, whose polysemantic neurons, each encoding multiple unrelated concepts, hinder localizing the components behind personalization, and thus understanding and controlling it. We propose to personalize Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs, which sparsely route each token to a few specialized experts, reducing polysemanticity and enabling such localization. We adapt three open-weight MoE LLMs on a large-scale personalization dataset and train crosscoders on paired activations of the personalized and non-personalized models to learn interpretable personalized latents, from which we identify the experts encoding distinct personalization features. The personalized MoE LLMs perform competitively with dense LLMs while activating only a fraction of their parameters, exhibit lower polysemanticity than dense LLMs with similar active parameters, and, within the same model family, yield personalized latents that are less shared with the non-personalized model. Causal interventions show that these latents suffice to recover the personalized model's behavior and that boosting their associated experts moves the non-personalized model toward it, revealing distinct routing paths for different personalization features.
authors: Sekh Mainul Islam, Pepa Atanasova, Isabelle Augenstein
bullets: Dense LLMs are difficult to interpret for personalization because their neurons are polysemantic.
The authors personalize three open-weight MoE LLMs and train crosscoders on paired personalized and non-personalized activations.
Interpretable personalized latents identify experts associated with distinct personalization features.
Personalized MoEs perform competitively with dense LLMs while activating only a fraction of their parameters and show lower polysemanticity.
Causal interventions recover personalized behavior and shift non-personalized models toward it by boosting associated experts.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates personalization in Mixture-of-Experts LLMs by identifying specific experts responsible for personalization features using crosscoders, relevant to LLM architecture and personalization.
papers.title: Explaining the Roles of Experts in Mixture-of-Experts LLMs for Personalization
papers.tldr: Personalizing MoE LLMs makes personalization more interpretable by linking distinct user features to specialized experts and causal routing paths.

papers.abstract: Byte-level language models such as the Byte Latent Transformer (BLT) run their large global model once per patch and start a patch where a small model's next-byte entropy is high. This rule rarely starts a patch at in-line computed results, such as the number after "=" in a worked solution, and accuracy on them collapses under tight patch budgets. We propose novelty patching, motivated by LZ77-style compression: start a patch where the upcoming bytes are unlikely to repeat the recent context. The rule is a lookup table over the previous two bytes, fitted in seconds on raw text with no labels, reference model or losses. In BLT-style models trained from scratch on a 1.9 GB math corpus at a matched ~11% patch rate (3 seeds each), it has no clear effect at 1M parameters, raises final-answer accuracy from 47% to 72% at 12M, and at 50M raises computed-result accuracy from 21% to 57% and final-answer accuracy from 60% to 90%; a table fitted on the raw pretraining corpus keeps the gain. Outside math the advantage shrinks: novelty lowers bits per byte on prose and ties entropy on source code and on synthetic execution traces. An analysis of where boundaries fall explains the pattern. Computed results have ordinary surprisal for the patcher's model, so surprisal-seeking rules pass over them: entropy concentrates patch starts on high-surprisal bytes most strongly of all rules (boundary enrichment 1.61) and is the worst on computed results, while the best rules sit near chance enrichment. Novelty works where new content begins at segment starts close to the computation, as in written math; a learned chunker (H-Net) finds such structure on its own, in math and in code. We also report what did not work: typed uncertainty as a training rule, switching rules after training, and a context-aware novelty predictor.
bullets: Entropy-based patching often misses inline computed results because they have ordinary surprisal for the patching model.
Novelty patching starts patches where upcoming bytes are unlikely to repeat the recent two-byte context, using a label-free lookup table fitted on raw text.
At 50M parameters, computed-result accuracy rises from 21% to 57% and final-answer accuracy from 60% to 90% at a matched ~11% patch rate.
The benefit is strongest in written math, shrinks on prose, and ties entropy on source code and synthetic execution traces.
Typed uncertainty, post-training rule switching, and a context-aware novelty predictor did not work; learned chunking finds related structure in math and code.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes compute-efficient patch selection for byte-level language models, relevant to token-level efficiency and LM architecture.
papers.title: Patch where the text is new: a compression view of where byte-level models should spend compute
papers.tldr: Novelty-based byte patching directs compute toward new content near mathematical computations, substantially improving computed-result and final-answer accuracy under fixed patch budgets.

papers.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning datasets remain overwhelmingly English-centric and commercially restricted, as their content is frequently generated by proprietary models whose terms of service forbid training competing systems. We introduce Multi-SFT, a commercially permissive collection of 502,818 instruction-response pairs across five European languages, built via translation and regeneration pipelines for tasks where translation is insufficient. Human evaluation yields inter-annotator agreement of at least 0.87 across all datasets and languages. Fine-tuning nine models from three different families (EuroLLM, OLMo 2, Qwen3; 1B-32B) and evaluating them on 13 benchmarks shows that Multi-SFT alone is competitive with larger augmented mixes and official instruction-tuned releases, with decisive advantages on safety tasks.
authors: Daniela Baiamonte, Kamyar Zeinalipour, Elena Fano, Stefano Simonazzi, Andrea Zugarini
bullets: Addresses the lack of open, commercially usable multilingual supervised fine-tuning data.
Contains 502,818 instruction-response pairs in five European languages.
Uses translation and regeneration pipelines, with regeneration for tasks where direct translation is insufficient.
Human evaluations report inter-annotator agreement of at least 0.87 across datasets and languages.
Fine-tuning nine models across three families and evaluation on 13 benchmarks show competitiveness with larger mixtures and official instruction-tuned releases, with clear safety-task advantages.
papers.selection_reason: Multilingual permissively-licensed instruction-following dataset for SFT; fits LLM instruction tuning.
papers.title: Multi-SFT: Permissively-Licensed Multilingual Instruction-Following
papers.tldr: Multi-SFT is a commercially permissive multilingual instruction-tuning dataset that enables strong performance across five European languages, especially on safety tasks.

papers.abstract: Many hierarchical byte-level language models group bytes into patches using a learned boundary predictor whose view of the next codepoint depends on encoding and lookahead. In UTF-8, codepoints of many scripts take three bytes: 8 of 24 bits mark length and continuation, and the first byte carries only 4 high codepoint bits. After the same left context, a mark extending a grapheme cluster and a letter starting the next can thus share their first byte. Universal Byte-Level Encoding (UBE) keeps one- and two-byte UTF-8 encodings but writes these codepoints as two UTF-16 bytes, low byte first, so its first symbol carries 8 low codepoint bits that can distinguish such continuations. We train small causal predictors on matched FineWeb-2 text and evaluate on FLORES-200 under UTF-8, UBE, and UBE's same-length big-endian variant. At one-symbol lookahead, balanced grapheme-boundary error at codepoint boundaries across 17 languages in 13 Brahmic scripts is 8.76% with UTF-8, 8.62% with the big-endian variant, and 0.06% with UBE. When the target instead retains a parent tokenizer's subword cuts at grapheme boundaries, UBE lowers the mean error relative to UTF-8 at the same lookahead by 72.91% in Korean, 35.29% in Chinese, and 67.32-99.55% in eight more scripts. In the seven of them whose main Unicode block fits on one 256-codepoint page, the big-endian variant stays within 3.0% of UTF-8, so the gain follows byte order, not length. In Korean and Chinese, UBE's mean error falls below UTF-8's final mean error after only 25% and 37.5% of training. Which byte comes first thus affects how much lookahead a byte-level boundary predictor needs.
bullets: UTF-8 can make a grapheme continuation and a following letter indistinguishable from their first byte in many scripts.
Universal Byte-Level Encoding (UBE) retains short UTF-8 encodings but represents longer codepoints as low-byte-first UTF-16.
Across 17 languages and 13 Brahmic scripts, one-symbol balanced boundary error was 0.06% with UBE versus 8.76% with UTF-8.
For parent-tokenizer subword boundaries, UBE reduced mean error by 35.29–99.55% across the reported scripts, including Korean and Chinese.
The comparison with a big-endian variant indicates that byte order—not encoding length—drives the improvement; scope is focused on boundary prediction and the evaluated multilingual text settings.
papers.selection_reason: Studies byte-level tokenization and boundary prediction for hierarchical language models, relevant to LLM architecture and tokenization.
papers.title: The Right Byte First: How UTF-16 Helps Multilingual Boundary Prediction
papers.tldr: Putting the low UTF-16 byte first substantially improves multilingual grapheme-boundary prediction compared with UTF-8 at the same lookahead.

papers.abstract: Given a state and a set of options, such as intents, tools or interface elements, System One decision models return a distribution over the options in one forward pass, without generated reasoning. Web systems increasingly build them by reading decisions from language models. Two axioms of rational choice are natural requirements for such decisions, because in web systems the listing and the option set are determined by other components and can change or be manipulated: the order in which the options are listed should not matter, and adding an option should not change the relative odds of the others (Luce's choice axiom). We test the standard reads, namely single-choice question (SCQ) prompting, with shuffled-order training, order averaging or sorted options, and invariant set architectures, and find that each violates at least one axiom: one shuffle changes 12-20% of SCQ answers, sorting only freezes an arbitrary convention, and a well-chosen added option steers 4-34% of decisions. By Luce's theorem, a read satisfies both axioms only if it is a softmax over scores that each depend on one option alone, so in a transformer they hold by construction only if no token that scores an option sees another. We implement this as Prism-1 (Position- and Rival-Independent Scoring for System One Models): every option is read in its own block at shared positions, with the model's usual left-to-right attention, in one forward pass. On five benchmark sets with Qwen3-8B and Gemma 4 12B, SCQ prompting trained on the same data still changes 7% of its answers under one shuffle, and an added irrelevant option steers 12% of its decisions. Prism-1 stays within one point of that baseline's accuracy and is 2-4 points more accurate once only answers that survive a reordering are counted, while no shuffle changes any of its answers and no added irrelevant option moves its choice among the others.
authors: Yao Long Teng, Jianguo Huang, Yanchen Deng, Jiayi Cai, Bo An
bullets: Web System One models should be insensitive to option order and to adding competing options, as required by rational-choice axioms.
Standard SCQ prompting, even with shuffling, sorting, or invariant architectures, violates at least one axiom.
Prism-1 scores each option independently in separate blocks at shared positions, using one forward pass.
Across five benchmark sets with Qwen3-8B and Gemma 4 12B, Prism-1 had no changes under shuffling or irrelevant-option additions.
Its accuracy stayed within one point of the baseline and was 2–4 points higher when counting only reorder-stable answers.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a novel LLM scoring architecture satisfying rational-choice axioms, relevant to LLM architectural advances.
papers.title: Prism-1: Position- and Rival-Independent Scoring for System One Models
papers.tldr: Prism-1 enforces order- and rival-independent option scoring, eliminating choice changes caused by option reordering or irrelevant additions while preserving baseline accuracy.

papers.abstract: Self-evolving language models train on tasks they generate, so every round must decide which updated model the next round inherits. Current loops such as R-Zero, Agent0, and Skill Self-Play make this decision through the task, admitting tasks that look learnable and inheriting every resulting update. We identify a selection-to-update gap in these loops, where a task that looks learnable need not produce a useful update. Most updates on verified tasks fail to make correct answers more likely, yet these loops inherit them all. HeirCommit freezes the updated model and uses fresh evaluation questions to decide whether to inherit it or retain the current model. EvoHeir separates parameter inheritance from experience inheritance, using current and archived experience to repair failures and preserve successes before final confirmation. Our analysis characterizes selection-induced optimism and decomposes regret into selection, absorption, and confirmation errors. HeirCommit cuts the harmful share of accepted updates by 68-83% relative to random inheritance at the same acceptance rate. Across four backbones, EvoHeir achieves the best mathematics and general-reasoning averages, raising the math average by 5.3% relative to the strongest baseline, Agent0. The framework lets useful experience persist even when the model that produced it is not inherited.
authors: Haoyi Yang, Kshitij Mishra, Nils Lukas, Salem Lahlou
bullets: Self-evolving loops often inherit updates from tasks that appear learnable, even when those updates do not improve correctness.
HeirCommit evaluates frozen candidate models on fresh questions before deciding whether to inherit them.
EvoHeir separates parameter inheritance from experience inheritance, allowing useful experience to persist despite rejecting its originating model.
The analysis decomposes regret into selection, absorption, and confirmation errors and characterizes selection-induced optimism.
HeirCommit reduces harmful accepted updates by 68–83%; EvoHeir obtains the best reported mathematics and general-reasoning averages across four backbones.
papers.selection_reason: Selection mechanisms for self-evolving LLM training loops; fits LLM training methodology.
papers.title: Selection Is Not Learning: Choosing Model Futures
papers.tldr: HeirCommit and EvoHeir improve self-evolving language-model training by verifying whether updates are useful before inheritance and preserving valuable experience independently of model selection.

papers.abstract: Frontier models, general-purpose and domain-specific alike, now include a midtraining stage between pretraining and post-training, but little has been published about how this stage is built. We present an open midtraining recipe that primes base models for agentic post-training, and we show its effectiveness on two Nemotron models of different sizes. Pretraining typically runs at short context and sees almost no agent interactions, while SFT data is mostly synthetic, and very long SFT stages can hurt the model's later RL trainability. Our midtraining stage sits between the two. It trains at 256K context for hundreds of billions of tokens on a diverse mixture of natural software-engineering data like packed repositories, pull requests, commit histories, and build logs together with a small share of agentic traces. On Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, 500B midtraining tokens improve SWE-bench Verified from 60.7 to 64.5, SWE-bench Multilingual from 55.8 to 62.8, and SWE-bench Pro from 32.0 to 35.5 after identical full SFT. On the larger Nemotron 3.5 Super, 280B midtraining tokens improve DeepSWE, a harder benchmark of long-horizon tasks, from 11.7 to 15.7 and SWE-bench Verified from 72.9 to 74.3 after identical full SFT. Midtraining also improves robustness across agent harnesses on both models. We report the ablations behind the recipe and an evaluation protocol built on short fixed SFT runs, since base-model proxy metrics did not correlate reliably with post-training results.
authors: Soumye Singhal, Joseph Jennings, Ka Shun Shum, Alexander Bukharin, Khushi Bhardwaj, Zirui Liu, Venkat Srinivasan, Jonathan Li, Yash Jain, Kezhi Kong, Markus Kliegl, Olivier Delalleau, Sanjeev Satheesh, Mostofa Patwary
bullets: Addresses the underexplored midtraining stage between pretraining and post-training, where short-context pretraining and synthetic-heavy SFT may limit agentic capabilities.
Trains at 256K context on hundreds of billions of tokens from repositories, pull requests, commit histories, build logs, and a small amount of agent traces.
After identical SFT, gains appear across SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Multilingual, SWE-bench Pro, and the long-horizon DeepSWE benchmark on two Nemotron models.
The recipe also improves robustness across agent harnesses.
Proxy metrics from base models were unreliable; the authors instead use short fixed SFT runs and report supporting ablations.
papers.selection_reason: Open midtraining recipe for agentic post-training of LLMs at 256K context; fits LLM training and long-context.
papers.title: Priming Base Models for Agentic Post-Training: An Open Midtraining Recipe
papers.tldr: An open midtraining recipe using long-context software-engineering data and limited agent traces improves models’ subsequent agentic post-training performance and robustness.

papers.abstract: An agent that learns a user's preferences from their choices faces a cold start problem: before any choices are observed, it must rely solely on a prior. Informative priors are usually fitted to historical choice data, which new tasks and deployments lack. To address this, we present Agentic-Priors, which lets agentic systems use the implicit knowledge of large language models (LLMs) instead. Specifically, an LLM states a new user's trade-offs in interpretable terms, such as willingness to pay or value of time, which we map to a prior over multinomial logit coefficients. This prior is then refined by a Bayesian learner as choices are observed. Across seven choice datasets, Agentic-Priors improves cold start accuracy over an uninformed prior by 5-40 percentage points. It also outperforms AutoElicit, a state-of-the-art LLM prior-elicitation method, on three datasets and loses on one. It is up to 18 points more accurate than in-context learning, and never significantly worse. Against hierarchical Bayes models fitted to surveys of increasing size, our approach is worth roughly 6-40 surveyed users, in terms of log-loss, so its value is concentrated in a deployment's first users.
authors: Bruno Arcanjo, Zhaoxing Li, Sebastian Stein
bullets: Addresses preference elicitation when no user choices are yet available.
An LLM describes a new user’s trade-offs, which are mapped to priors over multinomial logit coefficients.
A Bayesian learner updates these priors as user choices accumulate.
Across seven choice datasets, it improves cold-start accuracy over an uninformed prior by 5–40 percentage points.
Its benefit is concentrated among early users, with performance comparable to information from roughly 6–40 surveyed users in log-loss terms.
papers.selection_reason: Uses LLMs to generate informative priors for test-time preference elicitation, addressing the cold start problem in adaptive systems.
papers.title: Agentic-Priors: Using Large Language Models to Address the Cold Start Problem in Preference Elicitation
papers.tldr: Agentic-Priors uses LLM-derived, interpretable preference trade-offs to provide informative priors that substantially improve cold-start preference learning.

papers.abstract: Sequence models can generalise in fundamentally distinct ways: extrapolating structures seen in training, or using their prompt to adapt to novel tasks. The prevailing strategy determines how the model behaves beyond its training distribution, controlling potential capabilities and risks. Recent work has characterised many different strategies theoretically, and empirically described the transition between them as the quality and quantity of pretraining data vary. However, there is no learning theory for this competition, hence no fundamental understanding of \textit{why} one solution might be favoured over another. Here we provide such a theory in a solvable topic model---documents drawn from a finite mixture of latent topics, mirroring the heterogeneity of modern pretraining data. The dataset comes with two distinct solutions: a specialised predictor, that stores the finite topic mixture, and an in-context one, optimal for topics never seen during training. Our theory predicts their emergence at distinct sample complexities: the in-context predictor is available early, while the specialised one emerges only after the training tokens outnumber the parameters of the data-generating process. Trained transformers reproduce both scales and the separating crossover in remarkable agreement with the theory, with no fitted parameters.
bullets: Studies the competition between distribution-extrapolating specialized predictors and prompt-adapting in-context predictors.
Uses documents sampled from a finite mixture of latent topics, yielding both solution types.
Predicts distinct sample-complexity thresholds: in-context learning appears early, while specialization requires tokens exceeding the data-generating process’s parameter count.
Transformer experiments reproduce both learning scales and their crossover without fitted parameters.
papers.selection_reason: Provides a theoretical analysis of in-context learning versus specialization in transformers, relevant to Large Language Model learning dynamics.
papers.title: In-Context Learning Before Specialisation: Theory of Learning in a Solvable Topic Model
papers.tldr: A solvable topic-model theory explains why sequence models first learn in-context adaptation and only later specialize as pretraining data grows.

papers.abstract: Machine unlearning aims to remove targeted information from large language models, but existing evaluations often measure forgetting only on a designated benchmark distribution. We argue that such behavioral forgetting is an insufficient standard for privacy-oriented unlearning, and that evaluation should instead test whether forgetting persists across the access paths through which the same information may be recovered. We demonstrate this with a controlled case study of cross-lingual querying: across multiple multilingual model families, forgetting varies substantially when semantically equivalent information is queried in different languages and scripts. A single access path is therefore enough to expose a real gap between behavioral forgetting and information inaccessibility, motivating broader evaluation of access-path generalization and adversarial recoverability alongside in-distribution forgetting.
bullets: Machine unlearning evaluations often test forgetting only on a designated distribution.
Privacy-oriented evaluation should examine whether forgetting generalizes across ways of accessing the same information.
A controlled cross-lingual case study finds substantial variation across languages and scripts in multilingual model families.
A single alternative access path can reveal residual information, motivating tests of access-path generalization and adversarial recoverability.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes access-path generalization for evaluating machine unlearning in LLMs, a meaningful contribution to LLM privacy and reliability.
papers.title: Behavioral Forgetting Is Not Privacy in Machine Unlearning
papers.tldr: Behavioral forgetting on one benchmark does not guarantee that private information is inaccessible through other query paths.

papers.abstract: Existing safety benchmarks rely largely on synthetic prompts with loosely grounded taxonomies and offer little focused analysis of severe crime categories. We introduce GUISE, a benchmark of criminal-assistance scenarios sourced from real-world cases and organised under a taxonomy from the UNODC International Classification of Crime for Statistical Purposes (ICCS). Each scenario is rendered under three linguistic framings and evaluated across five distinct cultures. Using our proposed two-tier evaluation framework, which judges both harmfulness and operational uplift, we find that: (i) framing alone drives unsafe compliance, with the mean unsafe compliance rate rising from 28.9% under direct requests to 66.4% under correction seeking (peaking at 97.3%; p < 0.05), as models correcting deliberately distorted details supply executable criminal steps; (ii) culturally adapted prompts elicit significantly more unsafe compliance than literal translations of the same requests in all four non-English languages (+7 to +18 points), a risk that translation-based benchmarks miss; and (iii) unsafe responses from the least-safe models carry strong Anglocentric registers, and the extent of this leakage increases monotonically with response harmfulness ($\rho$ = 0.46 to 0.63 across languages, all p < 0.001). GUISE offers a grounded resource and fine-grained diagnostics for strengthening refusal alignment across languages and cultures. We publish our code and data to facilitate future research.
authors: Mohsinul Kabir, Md. Tariquzzaman, Karam S. R. Elradie, Polydoros Giannouris, Yuechen Jiang, Shaoxiong Ji, Sophia Ananiadou
bullets: Introduces a real-world criminal-assistance benchmark grounded in the UNODC ICCS taxonomy.
Evaluates three linguistic framings across five cultures using a two-tier measure of harmfulness and operational uplift.
Correction-seeking prompts produced much higher unsafe compliance than direct requests, reaching a peak of 97.3%.
Culturally adapted prompts triggered 7–18 percentage points more unsafe compliance than literal translations in four non-English languages.
Harmful responses from the least-safe models showed increasingly strong Anglocentric language patterns as harmfulness rose.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates LLM safety and alignment through framing and cultural adaptation, relevant to Large Language Model research.
papers.title: In the Guise of Correction: How Framing and Cultural Adaptation Erode LLM Safety on Real-World Criminal Cases
papers.tldr: GUISE shows that correction-framed and culturally adapted criminal prompts substantially weaken LLM safety, exposing risks missed by standard translation-based benchmarks.

papers.abstract: When an LLM agent misbehaves, a human steps in, and that intervention is usually discarded or replayed as training data. We treat it instead as a measurement: a label pointing at the internal computation that failed. We study it in a controlled agent environment, on one failure (asking a clarifying question when the request was already unambiguous), with labels from a rule-based overseer validated against blind human judgment. Claims cover eligible models, which both over-ask and sometimes act on matched unambiguous requests: five of thirteen qualified (Qwen2.5-3B, gemma-2-2b, OLMo-3-7B, Mistral-Nemo-12B, Phi-4). Four findings. First, the ask-vs-act decision is causally localizable in every eligible family: a direction learned from intervention labels flips 72-100% of held-out over-asks at a definite residual-stream depth, with site and dose chosen on training data, and random directions under the same procedure flip at most one episode. Second, over-asking has two mechanistic signatures: in four families the model demonstrably knows the request is unambiguous (the belief is decodable, causally inert and orthogonal to the decision) and asks anyway; in the fifth, the rare over-asks track different world-representations. Third, steering gated on a probe readout removes most of the simulated oversight burden while legitimate questions survive (bootstrap 95% intervals exclude zero); a prompt instruction makes it worse. Fourth, consolidating the fix into the weights yields a map, not a rule: on one model a LoRA confined to the causal band passes every criterion fixed in advance while behavior cloning on identical data breaks retention; on three families the reverse holds; on the fifth the outcome crosses the boundary across seeds. A geometric rule written down in advance to predict the regime failed on two out-of-family tests; we report the failure and stop rather than fit a replacement.
authors: Cesare Zavattari, Alessandro Tommasi, Giuseppe Prencipe
bullets: Study focuses on one failure: asking for clarification when a request is already unambiguous, using rule-based oversight labels validated by blind human judgment.
Across five eligible model families, intervention-derived directions causally flipped 72–100% of held-out over-asks at specific residual-stream depths; random directions rarely did so.
Most families appeared to know the request was unambiguous but asked anyway, indicating a decision failure rather than missing world knowledge; one family showed different world representations.
Probe-gated steering reduced simulated oversight burden while preserving legitimate questions, whereas a prompt instruction worsened behavior.
Weight consolidation was model-dependent: LoRA and behavior cloning alternated in effectiveness across families and seeds, and a proposed cross-family geometric predictor failed out-of-family tests.
papers.selection_reason: Studies causal localization, steering, and editing of LLM agent computations, contributing to understanding and improving large language model behavior.
papers.title: Human Interventions as Labels: Localizing, Steering, and (Sometimes) Editing the Computations Behind LLM Agent Failures
papers.tldr: Human interventions can label and causally localize the internal computations behind some LLM-agent over-asking failures, enabling targeted steering but only inconsistent weight-based fixes.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can become off-policy due to training-inference mismatch, mini-batch updates, and asynchronous training.The resulting mismatch is especially harmful in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, where rollout--training discrepancies can change routing decisions and lead to router drift. Rollout Routing Replay (R3) mitigates this mismatch by reusing expert selections from the rollout stage during training. Our analysis shows that routing replay introduces gradient bias by losing contributions from experts selected by the training router but not the rollout router. To address this, we propose Router Drift Control (RDC), which uses routing disagreement between rollout and training as a signal of off-policy staleness and selectively rejects high-drift responses. The sequence-level filtering avoids gradient bias introduced by replay while preserving native expert selection and the associated learning signals for retained responses. Experiments show that RDC achieves larger gains as policy staleness increases and remains effective in asynchronous RL. In asynchronous training, RDC combined with Truncated Importance Sampling (TIS) improves the average peak validation accuracy across AIME 2024 and AIME 2025 by 5.5 points over TIS and 4.5 points over R3.
authors: Liangyao Jin, Zhixin Wang, Liming Liu, Mingjun Zhang, Zhengzhou Zhu, Fangcheng Fu, Jinlong Hou, Yuan Cheng, Xiaohe Hu, Ping Zhang, Siyuan Feng
bullets: Off-policy mismatch can cause MoE routing changes and router drift, especially with asynchronous or stale training.
R3 replays rollout-time expert selections but introduces gradient bias by omitting experts selected only by the training router.
RDC uses routing disagreement as a staleness signal and rejects high-drift responses at the sequence level.
This preserves native expert selection and learning signals for retained responses without replay-induced bias.
RDC becomes more effective as policy staleness increases and improves asynchronous RL when combined with TIS.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses off-policy degradation and router drift in Mixture-of-Experts RL, directly relevant to LLM training and MoE-based foundation models.
papers.title: Router Drift Control: Mitigating Off-Policy Degradation in Mixture-of-Experts Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: Router Drift Control reduces off-policy degradation in MoE reinforcement learning by filtering responses with high rollout–training routing disagreement.

papers.abstract: Data strategy plays a central role in training large language models (LLMs). It governs the selection, weighting, and scheduling of training data, thereby determining the capabilities a model can acquire from a fixed data budget. We treat high-quality data as having high training-dependent utility, which depends on the target objective, the model, and its training state rather than on the text alone. Research in this area now spans pretraining and post-training, but related ideas use inconsistent terminology and evaluation protocols. This work reviews data strategies across the training lifecycle and formulates them as policies that allocate a training budget over candidate examples. We organise methods by their decision granularity, model dependence, and temporal adaptivity, then compare their computational requirements and empirical support. Fine-grained or state-dependent policies offer more control but incur additional scoring, search, or rollout costs. Evidence for transfer across model scales and comparable end-to-end cost remains limited. A continuously updated list of papers, along with their public implementations, is available at https://github.com/xuyj233/data_strategy_survey.
authors: Yuanjian Xu, Jianing Hao, Tianze Sun, Yongyao Duan, Sam Chen, Jinyi Han, Wanbo Zhang, Yuxuan Sun, Guang Zhang, Zhong Li
bullets: Training-data utility depends on the objective, model, and training state—not text quality alone.
The framework covers data selection, weighting, and scheduling in both pretraining and post-training.
Methods are organized by decision granularity, model dependence, and temporal adaptivity.
Fine-grained, state-dependent policies provide more control but require greater scoring, search, or rollout costs.
Evidence for transfer across model scales and comparable end-to-end costs remains limited.
papers.selection_reason: Reviews and unifies data selection, weighting, and scheduling strategies across the LLM training lifecycle, directly relevant to LLM development.
papers.title: Data Strategies for Large Language Models: A Unified Perspective on the Training Lifecycle
papers.tldr: This survey unifies data strategies across the LLM training lifecycle as budget-allocation policies and compares their control, costs, and evidence.

papers.abstract: Tokenization is a critical component of the language modeling pipeline, but it is poorly understood. Tokenizers can impact downstream performance, but there is currently mixed evidence about which tokenizer features predict a better language model without requiring a full training run. In this paper, we analyze approximately 200 language models trained on nine different languages. We evaluate both models and their tokenizers and test whether there is a relationship between any proposed intrinsic tokenizer evaluations and model performance, as measured by a wide variety of benchmarks. Despite the quantity and variety of proposed intrinsic tokenizer metrics, we find that none consistently predicts downstream performance across model families, tasks, and languages. This motivates the need for novel tokenizer evaluation metrics and approaches. We propose novel linguistically grounded metric introduced in this work shows that new metrics can capture aspects of tokenizer quality that existing metrics miss, though their predictive power is likely to vary across model families, languages, and tasks.
authors: Antonio Lopardo, Luis Frentzen Salim, Shikhar Srivastava, Kevin Jiang, Mridul Sharma, Catherine Arnett
bullets: Analyzes approximately 200 language models spanning nine languages.
Compares proposed tokenizer evaluations with performance across diverse benchmarks.
Finds that existing tokenizer metrics lack reliable, general predictive power.
Introduces a linguistically grounded metric that captures tokenizer qualities missed by prior metrics.
Suggests tokenizer metrics may remain model-, language-, and task-dependent.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes tokenizer features against downstream LLM performance and proposes a new linguistically grounded tokenizer metric, relevant to LLM design and evaluation.
papers.title: No Single Tokenizer Feature Reliably Predicts Downstream Language Model Performance
papers.tldr: No single intrinsic tokenizer metric consistently predicts downstream language-model performance across languages, tasks, and model families.

papers.abstract: When code-repair agents fail, final tests reveal that a patch is wrong but not which earlier commitment caused it or which software obligation failed. Poison Valleys traces this path in 1,844 model requests on two synthetic Python cases: PersistQueue adds atomic batch claiming to a disk-backed queue, while Dijkstra adds source-sensitive filtering to shortest-path search. We define plausible but incorrect software mechanisms, place each in a model's hypothesis, implementation plan, or both, and evaluate the generated code with an Oracle and targeted diagnostic coordinates. Moving the misconception from hypothesis to plan increased failure by 32.2% in PersistQueue and 28.9% in Dijkstra after matching the experimental mix. Different misconceptions produced distinct, model-dependent patterns of violated obligations, although several could converge on the same behavior. This creates a measured connection from upstream misconception to code mechanism and failure form. Code, data, and demo: https://poisonvalleys.org.
bullets: Analyzes 1,844 model requests across two synthetic Python repair tasks: PersistQueue and Dijkstra.
Injects plausible but incorrect mechanisms into either the model’s hypothesis, implementation plan, or both.
Uses an Oracle and targeted diagnostic coordinates to identify violated software obligations, not just incorrect final tests.
Moving a misconception from hypothesis to plan increased failures by 32.2% and 28.9% in the two tasks.
Different misconceptions created model-dependent failure patterns, while some converged on the same behavior.
papers.selection_reason: Diagnoses path-dependent failure in LLM code repair by analyzing misconceptions in hypothesis and implementation plans.
papers.title: Poison Valleys: Diagnosing Path-Dependent Failure in LLM Code Repair
papers.tldr: Poison Valleys shows how early misconceptions in LLM code-repair workflows propagate into specific implementation mechanisms and failure patterns.

papers.abstract: Every story has two orders: the order in which its events happen and the order in which they are told. A story is nonlinear when the two differ. We introduce a benchmark of 83 published works that measures whether language models can tell nonlinear stories. For each work, we annotate one list of events in both orders, together with a story graph of causal dependencies, character knowledge, and the questions the telling raises and resolves. Given events in chronological order, all 19 models tell them, on average, more chronologically than the published works do; asked for a specific structure, they land within the human range about half the time. We then compare a model's stories of the same events under different conditions, using both an automated judge and 71 human readers. Both prefer the chronological story a model writes by default to the nonlinear one it writes on request, which readers find harder to follow in 81% of decisive judgments. Readers also prefer stories written from the story graph to stories constrained to the published telling order (72% of decisive judgments), a difference the judge does not detect. Our results suggest that following an instruction to reorder a story is not yet the same as telling it well out of order.
authors: Syed Rifat Raiyan, Md. Tariquzzaman, Md Farhan Ishmam, Tenghao Huang
bullets: Introduces a benchmark of 83 published works with event orders, causal story graphs, character knowledge, and narrative questions.
Evaluates 19 models on reconstructing published nonlinear structures from chronologically ordered events.
Models default to more chronological storytelling than humans and match requested human narrative structures only about half the time.
Human readers prefer models’ default chronological stories over their requested nonlinear versions in 81% of decisive judgments.
Readers prefer stories generated from causal story graphs over those constrained to the published telling order, suggesting graph-based planning may better support nonlinear narration.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a benchmark and corpus for nonlinear narrative generation to evaluate LLMs' ability to handle non-chronological storytelling.
papers.title: Can LLMs Tell Stories Out of Order? A Corpus and Benchmark for Nonlinear Narrative Generation
papers.tldr: LLMs can reorder story events on request, but generally struggle to produce nonlinear narratives that readers find coherent and engaging.

papers.abstract: Large language model agents solve tasks through long sequences of tool calls, and the prevailing design has a single strong model generate every step, although many steps are routine enough for a much smaller model. Existing ways of sharing this work keep the strong model as the generator: routers and collaborative agents decide which model handles each query or step, and speculative methods check a small model's drafts one step at a time, usually against the strong model's own action. We introduce SpecAgent, a collaboration protocol that turns the strong model from the author of each step into a reviewer of steps drafted by a weak model. The weak model executes read-only tool calls as it drafts, so that every step is grounded in real observations, and holds the first action that would modify the environment. The strong model then verifies the drafted segment in a single prefill pass, commits the longest prefix it judges semantically valid, and repairs the first rejected step. Because verification replaces autoregressive decoding with parallel prefill, the strong model decodes only short verdicts and occasional repairs rather than every step. On $\tau^2$-Bench, SpecAgent comes within one point of the strong model's success rate while roughly halving memory traffic and wall time, and on AutomationBench and VitaBench it recovers 44-75% of the quality gap while lowering both. In an edge-cloud deployment on MCP-Atlas with three cloud models, it closes 53-75% of the weak-strong quality gap while the strong model generates at most half as many tokens. These results suggest that a strong model need not author every step of an agent: reviewing grounded drafts retains most of its quality while cutting both latency and memory traffic.
authors: Zilin Wang, Yinhong Liu, Chao Chen, Qun Liu, Zhijiang Guo
bullets: Addresses the cost of having a strong model generate every tool-calling step in long agent trajectories.
The weak model executes read-only calls while drafting and pauses before environment-changing actions.
The strong model semantically verifies an entire drafted segment in one prefill pass, commits valid prefixes, and repairs rejected steps.
On τ²-Bench, it comes within one point of the strong model’s success rate while roughly halving memory traffic and wall time.
Across AutomationBench, VitaBench, and MCP-Atlas, it recovers substantial quality relative to weak-only agents while reducing strong-model token generation.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes SpecAgent, a speculative decoding protocol where a strong model reviews grounded drafts from a weak model to reduce latency and memory traffic.
papers.title: Trajectory-Level Speculation with Semantic Verification for Tool-Using Agents
papers.tldr: SpecAgent lets a weak model draft grounded tool-use trajectories while a strong model verifies and repairs them in batches, preserving much of the strong model’s quality with lower latency and memory traffic.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) reproduce a human working-memory signature on the N-back task: performance declines as memory load N increases, and errors concentrate on lures, items that repeat the current stimulus at a neighboring but incorrect serial position. We ask whether this shared behavioral signature reflects a shared mechanism. The literature offers two candidate accounts. On a precision account, softmax attention cannot concentrate its weight on the item N positions back, so adjacent items are retrieved instead. On an interference account, attention selects the correct item, but the content of competing items corrupts the decision. We dissociate these accounts in 15 pretrained LLMs from three families (70 million to 14 billion parameters) and in minimal transformers trained from scratch. In all three families, the attention heads that carry the task attend to the target on most missed matches. Linear probes decode near-perfectly whether a matching letter occurred at the target or at a lure position, even on trials where the model false-alarms to the lure, although its own decisions barely distinguish the two. Sharpening attention yields negligible gains, whereas suppressing the letter identity of non-target items improves sensitivity (d') in nearly all model-by-load conditions. In larger models the task is spread over more heads, and removing interference helps more. In minimal transformers, precision limits a single attention layer, but a second layer removes this constraint. The working-memory limit of LLMs therefore lies in reading items out under interference rather than in locating them, consistent with interference accounts of human working memory.
bullets: LLMs show human-like N-back behavior: performance worsens with load, especially lure false alarms.
Task-relevant attention heads usually attend to the correct target, including on missed matches.
Linear probes recover target and lure information even when the model’s decision confuses them.
Sharpening attention provides little benefit, while suppressing non-target letter identity generally improves sensitivity.
The finding holds across pretrained models and minimal transformers, with deeper layers alleviating single-layer precision limits.
papers.selection_reason: Mechanistic study of working-memory readout in LLMs; relevant to LLM architecture and memory behavior.
papers.title: Language Models Share a Readout Bottleneck in Working Memory
papers.tldr: Across language models, working-memory errors mainly arise from interference when reading out the correct item, not from failing to locate it.

papers.abstract: To address sparse terminal rewards in LLM arithmetic reasoning, we propose a Bellman-consistent trajectory RL method. Our framework introduces Trajectory Bellman Residual Minimization (TBRM) to transform sparse rewards into dense token-level signals. We integrate a Reinforce Leave-One-Out (RLOO) group strategy to reduce gradient variance of Bellman residuals and use hindsight goal relabeling to accelerate intermediate learning. Evaluated on the Countdown task, our method alleviates optimization bottlenecks and stabilizes gradient variance significantly better than GRPO. The TBRM-RLOO framework boosts Pass@1 to 0.55--0.64 and achieves a state-of-the-art Pass@16 accuracy of 76.0--84.0\%, outperforming the SFT, IPO/DPO, and RLOO baselines. Our approach demonstrates exceptional single-sample efficiency and successfully circumvents standard performance plateaus via test-time scaling.
bullets: Targets sparse terminal rewards and optimization bottlenecks in arithmetic reasoning.
Uses Trajectory Bellman Residual Minimization to generate dense token-level signals.
Combines RLOO grouping to reduce Bellman-residual gradient variance with hindsight goal relabeling.
On Countdown, reports Pass@1 of 0.55–0.64 and Pass@16 of 76.0–84.0%, outperforming SFT, IPO/DPO, and RLOO baselines.
Supports improved single-sample efficiency and test-time scaling beyond standard performance plateaus.
papers.selection_reason: Trajectory RL method for LLM arithmetic reasoning with dense token-level rewards and test-time scaling; fits LLM reasoning and training methods.
papers.title: Bellman-Consistent Trajectory RL for LLM Arithmetic Reasoning
papers.tldr: TBRM-RLOO provides dense, Bellman-consistent learning signals for LLM arithmetic reasoning, improving optimization stability and Countdown accuracy over several baselines.

papers.abstract: Machine learning models for tabular prediction typically assume that training data are representative of the population on which they will be deployed. In practice, however, data are often collected based on convenience, availability, or cost, resulting in systematic sampling biases that can distort feature--target relationships and undermine real-world generalization. Existing tabular distribution-shift benchmarks primarily construct out-of-distribution (OOD) settings by partitioning observations across naturally occurring domains. While such partitions may induce changes in P(Y | X), the resulting shifts are neither explicitly controlled nor isolated, and the evaluation distributions themselves are often not representative of the broader target population. We introduce INCONVENIENT, a benchmark designed to study robustness to convenience-sample bias. Rather than relying on naturally occurring domain partitions, INCONVENIENT directly perturbs feature--target relationships in the training distribution while preserving the original population distribution as the deployment environment. This setting more closely reflects real-world scenarios in which models are developed from unrepresentative samples and subsequently deployed on a broader population. The distinction is particularly relevant for large language models (LLMs), whose pretraining may encode population-level knowledge that extends beyond the relationships observed in a biased training dataset. Unlike existing distribution-shift benchmarks, INCONVENIENT provides explicit control over both the direction and severity of relationship shifts, enabling a systematic assessment of robustness to convenience sampling. The benchmark comprises 200 tabular classification and regression datasets spanning diverse application domains and generates around 15,500 shifted training distributions which lead to substantial downstream degradation.
authors: Sara Rezaeimanesh, Chad Klochko, Kundan Thind, Mohammad Ghassemi
bullets: Addresses the gap between representative-data assumptions and real-world training data collected for convenience, availability, or cost.
Creates shifted training distributions by directly perturbing feature–target relationships while keeping the original population as the deployment environment.
Allows explicit control over the direction and severity of relationship shifts, unlike benchmarks based mainly on naturally occurring domain partitions.
Includes 200 tabular classification and regression datasets across diverse domains and about 15,500 shifted training distributions.
The generated shifts cause substantial downstream degradation, supporting systematic robustness evaluation.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for LLM robustness to convenience-sample distribution shift; relevant to LLM evaluation.
papers.title: INCONVENIENT: A Benchmark to Assess LLM Generalization Capabilities from Convenience Samples
papers.tldr: INCONVENIENT benchmarks how well LLMs and other tabular models generalize when trained on systematically biased convenience samples but deployed on the broader population.

papers.abstract: When does a language model acquire a capability? Developmental studies usually answer this by tracking when models start producing the correct token. But that prediction passes through the unembedding matrix, or readout, which is itself still being learned during pretraining. We show that a model's hidden states can encode task information before its own readout expresses it, so timelines read from outputs conflate what the model encodes with what its readout expresses. To track the readout directly, we introduce parameter-trajectory crosscoding, which fits one sparse dictionary to every token's readout row at every checkpoint. Unlike crosscoders on activations, it needs only checkpoint weights. We use it to locate a narrow early window, 0.4-1.1% of the way through Pythia's pretraining, in which the readout reorganizes and WordNet word categories become decodable from its rows. By then, linear probes on the hidden states already decode task information that the model's own outputs do not yet show. To test whether such gaps depend on how fast the readout learns, we pretrain small models from scratch that differ only in the readout's learning rate. We find that raising it makes the readout develop earlier and the gap close sooner, with little effect on final loss. Together, these results imply that early in training, where many developmental transitions are dated, a behavioral date can reflect when the readout learns to express task information and not when the model learns it.
authors: Matteo He, William F. Shen, Alex Iacob, Andrej Jovanovic, Xinchi Qiu, Nicholas D. Lane
bullets: Output-based capability timelines can conflate internal knowledge with the readout’s development.
The authors introduce parameter-trajectory crosscoding, using checkpoint weights to track structure across every token’s readout row.
In Pythia, the readout reorganizes early in training, and WordNet categories become decodable from its rows during a narrow early window.
Hidden-state probes detect task information before the model’s own predictions do.
Increasing the readout learning rate advances its development and closes this gap sooner, with little change in final loss.
papers.selection_reason: Studies unembedding/readout dynamics during language-model pretraining, directly relevant to LLM capability acquisition and training dynamics.
papers.title: Learning to Read Out: Unembedding Dynamics in Language Model Pretraining
papers.tldr: Language models may learn task information in hidden states before the unembedding/readout matrix learns to express it in outputs.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents for health can accumulate reusable textual skills from task feedback, such as calculation criteria, measurement time points, and formula units. Deciding which skills to retain is consequential: useful rules improve later answers, while faulty generalizations propagate errors. We propose CausalEvo, a method for causal skill self-evolution that estimates the relative effects of deliberately changed skill sets while holding the model weights, feedback cases, and rule count fixed. At each evolution step, a frozen LLM proposes candidate rules, which are pooled with the incumbent skills so that the current skill set remains a feasible choice. Paired skill replacements against shared background rules are scored on the same feedback cases; least squares converts the score differences into relative skill values, and the top-ranked rules are retained, favoring incumbents on ties. A decision-loss bound separates candidate support, approximation, and estimation errors. On six MedCalc-Bench-Verified tasks with 120 held-out cases, CausalEvo achieves 60.00% accuracy, compared with 55.83% for SkillOpt and 51.67% without skills. Across the recorded training configurations, which use different optimization budgets, it consumes 55.6% fewer training tokens than SkillOpt. Gains concentrate in particular calculations alongside regressions on others, and paired accuracy intervals include zero. CausalEvo turns task feedback into controlled decisions about skill retention and replacement. Project repository: https://github.com/txbrook/CausalEvo
bullets: Targets the risk that faulty skill generalizations persist and propagate errors in health-agent answers.
Uses a frozen LLM to propose rules, compares paired skill replacements on shared feedback cases, and ranks rules via least-squares estimates.
Keeps the incumbent skill set as a feasible option and favors incumbents when scores tie.
On six MedCalc-Bench-Verified tasks and 120 held-out cases, it reports 60.00% accuracy versus 55.83% for SkillOpt and 51.67% without skills.
Reported gains are task-dependent, with regressions on some calculations; paired accuracy intervals include zero, and training configurations used 55.6% fewer tokens than SkillOpt.
papers.selection_reason: LLM agent skill self-evolution with controlled skill retention; relevant to agent memory and LLM research.
papers.title: CausalEvo: Causal Skill Self-Evolution for Health LLM Agents
papers.tldr: CausalEvo selects which textual skills health LLM agents should retain by estimating their causal value through controlled skill replacements.

papers.abstract: Decision models answer typed questions about an input with one probability per option, computed in a single forward pass without generating text. Like the fast System 1 of dual-process theory, they answer at once, but their depth is fixed at training time, so they spend the same computation on easy and hard questions. Models that reason in generated text can think longer, but they pay for every extra step in decoded tokens. We present LEV, a decision model that thinks deeper by rerunning its layers in a loop instead of generating tokens. LEV builds on a language model pretrained as a loop, reads the options after every loop step and trains all steps jointly, so one checkpoint can answer at any depth. On three looped backbones, accuracy rises with depth on the same weights, mostly on hard questions, and a 2.6B LEV goes from 63.2% at depth one to 76.2% at depth four on JevBench. On-demand depth, set per question by a small stopper with a threshold fitted on unlabelled requests, saves 15% to 24% of the computation at a cost of under one accuracy point, level with or slightly above a fixed mix of depths. On a locked test set, the 1.4B and 3B models are 5.4 to 8.8 points more accurate than dense (non-looped) models and cascades of the same latency below 50 ms.
authors: Dingjie Song, Zhiling Yan, Yuxuan Zhang, Lichao Sun
bullets: Decision models answer typed multiple-choice questions in one forward pass but use fixed computation for every question.
LEV reads answer options after each loop and trains all loop depths jointly, allowing one checkpoint to answer at different depths.
Accuracy increases with loop depth, especially on hard questions; a 2.6B model improves from 63.2% at depth one to 76.2% at depth four on JevBench.
A learned stopper saves 15–24% computation with less than one accuracy-point cost, using thresholds fitted on unlabeled requests.
On a locked test set, 1.4B and 3B LEV models outperform same-latency dense models and cascades by 5.4–8.8 points below 50 ms.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a novel architectural approach (looped decision models) for LLMs to balance speed and depth, fitting the large language models subtopic.
papers.title: LEV: Thinking Fast and Deep with Looped Decision Models
papers.tldr: LEV enables decision models to think longer by looping the same layers, improving hard-question accuracy while optionally reducing computation through adaptive stopping.

papers.abstract: Distillation of reasoning chains from Large Language Models (LLMs) into their smaller siblings is a standard training approach. Frequently, researchers do not have full access to a teacher model and its internal representations, which limits the resulting performance. We propose a recursive offline distillation method combining two components: entropy-based sampling for selective distillation and answer mixing. Specifically, for three open models (3-4B), at each epoch, we sample reasoning chains weighted by entropy difference with an auxiliary medium model (70-72B) and, next, supplement thinking traces with single-token ground truth answers. Our approach consistently outperforms naive distillation with comparable data budgets ($57.15 \pm 1.01$ vs 51.61 on average) and offers a much steeper learning curve. Additionally, we present a comparative analysis of methods to generate and normalize distillation traces.
authors: Andrey Goncharov, Daniil Vyazhev, Simon Epanov, Alexey Zaytsev
bullets: Addresses distillation when full teacher access and internal representations are unavailable.
Uses entropy-difference sampling with an auxiliary 70–72B model to select reasoning chains each epoch.
Mixes reasoning traces with single-token ground-truth answers in a recursive offline process.
Across three 3–4B open models, it reports higher average performance than naive distillation under comparable data budgets: 57.15 ± 1.01 vs. 51.61.
Also compares methods for generating and normalizing distillation traces.
papers.selection_reason: Recursive offline distillation of LLM reasoning chains; relevant to language foundation model training.
papers.title: Recursive Offline Distillation via Entropy Gain Sampling and Answer Mixing
papers.tldr: An offline distillation approach improves small-model reasoning by selecting informative chains with entropy gains and mixing in ground-truth answers.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning language models on narrowly defined harmful tasks can induce emergent misalignment (EM) across unrelated domains. While prior work has identified shared misalignment-associated representations across independently fine-tuned models, it remains unclear whether these models rely on common computational components. We investigate this question using three LoRA fine-tunes of Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct trained on harmful medical advice, risky financial advice, and extreme-sports recommendations. Using direction-based activation tracing, we identify three attention-head locations shared among the five highest-ranked heads of all three organisms. Replacing each organism's five selected head contributions with Base contributions reduces free-generation EM from 38.9% to 22.9% for medical, 50.7% to 12.5% for finance, and 41.7% to 11.1% for sports, outperforming layer-matched random interventions without reducing judged coherence. Cross-organism activation transfer further shows that the shared heads exhibit partially interchangeable effects on fixed-response preference. These findings provide evidence that representational convergence in EM extends to shared, causally relevant attention-head components within a common model architecture.
bullets: Three LoRA fine-tunes targeted harmful medical, financial, and extreme-sports advice.
Direction-based activation tracing found three attention-head locations shared among the top five heads across all models.
Replacing selected head contributions with base-model activations reduced free-generation misalignment while preserving judged coherence.
Cross-model activation transfer suggested these shared heads have partially interchangeable effects on response preferences.
The evidence is specific to these fine-tunes and the shared Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct architecture.
papers.selection_reason: LLM interpretability study of shared circuits underlying emergent misalignment; relevant to LLM research.
papers.title: Do Emergent Misalignment Models Share a Circuit?
papers.tldr: Emergent misalignment from different harmful-task fine-tunes appears to depend on shared, causally relevant attention heads.

papers.abstract: Evaluator-guided reasoning presents a local control problem at every step: trust the current answer, return a fallback, or spend more inference. We formulate this choice as a compute-aware three-action controller, scoring terminal actions by predicted answer success and expansion by a rollout-based continuation-success surrogate, with compute cost priced explicitly. A local action-gap analysis characterizes when score errors can change a decision, while an expected regret bound accounts for errors along the realized expansion path. Guided by this analysis, we learn and calibrate action-specific confidence estimates, with local uncertainty penalties for ambiguous decisions. On held-out width expansion and revision tasks, the controller improves observed utility over calibration-selected fixed policies while reducing normalized online compute by about 30% and 16%, respectively. Across four Qwen3-8B seeds, compute is lower than fitted Q in both settings, while utility differences are small and mixed. The results frame evaluator-guided reasoning as resource allocation under uncertainty, rather than a uniformly stronger reasoner.
bullets: Formulates inference control as a compute-aware three-action decision problem.
Scores terminal actions by predicted success and expansion by rollout-based continuation success, with explicit compute costs.
Uses action-gap analysis, pathwise regret bounds, calibrated action confidence, and uncertainty penalties to guide decisions.
Improves observed utility over calibration-selected fixed policies while reducing normalized online compute by about 30% and 16% on two task types.
Results across four Qwen3-8B seeds show lower compute than fitted Q, but only small and mixed utility differences.
papers.selection_reason: Confidence-calibrated compute allocation for evaluator-guided test-time reasoning in LLMs.
papers.title: Confidence-Calibrated Inference Expansion for Evaluator-Guided Test-Time Reasoning
papers.tldr: A confidence-calibrated controller allocates test-time compute among answering, fallback, and further reasoning, improving utility while reducing online computation on evaluator-guided tasks.

papers.abstract: Despite their extensive pretraining knowledge and strong reasoning capabilities, large language models (LLMs) struggle to adaptively gather information in experimental design tasks. We study how to amortize sequential Bayesian experimental design (BED) into an LLM by explicitly training the reasoning that guides action selection using information-gain rewards. Our approach specifies the experimental generative model independently of the LLM's own beliefs, allowing us to optimize expected information gain under a model of our choosing.
