We investigate the design choices for amortization, including alternative generative-model constructions, reward estimation, hypothesis-space specification, multi-step objectives, and computational costs relative to training- and inference-time BED baselines. On Twenty Questions, the resulting policies improve information acquisition and task performance, outperform inference- and training-time BED baselines at substantially lower computational cost, and generalize to unseen categories. We further demonstrate positive transfer from Twenty Questions training to Medi-Q, a real-world clinical dialogue benchmark. These results suggest that information gathering can be learned as a generalizable reasoning skill in LLMs.
authors: Anita Kriz, Antonin Berthon, Nicol\'as Astorga, Mihaela van der Schaar
bullets: LLMs often struggle to adaptively select informative actions despite strong reasoning and pretrained knowledge.
The method amortizes sequential Bayesian experimental design by training reasoning with information-gain rewards under an independently specified generative model.
The study evaluates generative-model design, reward estimation, hypothesis spaces, multi-step objectives, and computational costs.
On Twenty Questions, the learned policies improve information acquisition and task performance, generalize to unseen categories, and use less computation than BED baselines.
Training on Twenty Questions transfers positively to the real-world Medi-Q clinical dialogue benchmark.
papers.selection_reason: Trains LLMs to amortize sequential experimental design as a generalizable reasoning skill.
papers.title: Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs
papers.tldr: The paper trains LLMs to learn efficient, generalizable information-gathering strategies for sequential experimental design.

papers.abstract: Reasoning distillation requires chain-of-thought (CoT) data with correct answers, but obtaining such data efficiently remains challenging. Forward CoT generation (FCG) followed by rejection sampling (RS) produces verified, question-only responses, yet may require many teacher calls for difficult problems. Reverse CoT generation (RCG) is cheaper because it conditions on the known answer, but access to this answer can lead to post-hoc rationalization and a mismatch with the student's answer-free inference setting. We propose CoTranslator, which learns to translate reverse CoT responses toward the distribution of verified forward responses. Trained on a small set of paired reverse and rejection-sampled forward responses, it supports large-scale generation and verification of student training data. Across six student models evaluated on six mathematics benchmarks, CoTranslator improves average accuracy over semantic suppression by up to $5.82$ percentage points. For two 4B students, it retains $95.0\%$ of rejection sampling's average accuracy while using $35.9\%$ of its estimated compute. Without retraining, the same translator transfers to a new mathematics dataset, a different teacher, and STEM problems, improving average STEM accuracy by $4.88$ and $4.31$ percentage points for 4B and 8B students, respectively. These results show that CoTranslator offers an efficient and transferable approach to reasoning distillation.
authors: Zinan Tang, Zhuoshi Pan, Kairui Chen, Ze Yan, Shaomian Zheng, Yukun Zhang, Gang Wang, Biqing Huang
bullets: Problem: Forward CoT generation with rejection sampling is costly, while reverse CoT can rationalize from known answers and mismatch student inference.
Method: Train a translator on a small set of paired reverse and verified forward responses, then use it to generate and verify large-scale distillation data.
Results: Across six student models and six math benchmarks, it improves accuracy over semantic suppression by up to 5.82 percentage points.
Efficiency: For 4B students, it retains 95.0% of rejection sampling’s average accuracy using 35.9% of its estimated compute.
Transferability: Without retraining, it improves STEM accuracy by 4.88 points for 4B students and 4.31 points for 8B students on new settings.
papers.selection_reason: Efficient reasoning distillation method for LLMs via reverse-to-forward CoT translation.
papers.title: CoTranslator: Reverse to Forward Chain-of-Thought Translator for Reasoning Distillation
papers.tldr: CoTranslator makes cheaper answer-conditioned reasoning data more suitable for answer-free student training by translating it toward verified forward chain-of-thought responses.

papers.abstract: Wolof is spoken by 23M people, mostly in Senegal, but remains weakly supported by open-weight language models, while API models raise cost, governance, and sovereignty constraints for local deployments. In this paper, we present 0.6B-14B open-weight models adapted to Wolof through instruction tuning, preference alignment, and model merging. After presenting the pipeline and data, extensive experiments on 63~public and in-house tasks show good performance on Wolof understanding and generation while remaining effective on other languages and cross-lingual skills, with the 8B and 14B models being particularly competitive with substantially larger commercial systems. The models are currently being evaluated in internal customer-care pilots and are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/collections/Orange/wolof-lm .
authors: Gw\'enol\'e Lecorv\'e, Delphine Charlet, Pierre Adam, Floriane Behanzin, Lionel Delphin-Poulat, Johannes Heinecke, G\'eraldine Damnati, Pelin Kaytmaz, Nourredine Khaous, Charbel Kindji, Meriam Maadi, Abdoulaye Mbaye, Claire Perroux, Isma\"el Rousseau, Papa S\'ega Wad\'e, Gilles Xiberras, Olivier Zhang, Malek Zitouni
bullets: Addresses limited open-weight support for Wolof and the cost, governance, and sovereignty concerns of API-based models.
Adapts models using instruction tuning, preference alignment, and model merging.
Evaluates the models across 63 public and in-house tasks covering Wolof understanding, generation, multilingual, and cross-lingual capabilities.
Reports strong Wolof performance while retaining effectiveness in other languages; the 8B and 14B models are competitive with substantially larger commercial systems.
Models are undergoing customer-care pilot evaluations and are publicly available on Hugging Face.
papers.selection_reason: Open-weight LLMs adapted to Wolof via instruction tuning and alignment.
papers.title: Wolof-Adapted Industry-Ready Open-Weight Language Models
papers.tldr: This paper introduces open-weight Wolof language models from 0.6B to 14B parameters designed for practical, locally deployable use.

papers.abstract: A reasoning trace retained at answer time plays two roles: it can raise accuracy, and it can compete with the current evidence when the two disagree. We disentangle these roles by crossing verified evidence versions with the traces generated from each and answering from the same traces and evidence under two configurations: continuation of the model's own thinking and a separate answer call. Across three model families (gpt-oss, Gemma4, Qwen3) on HotpotQA and MuSiQue, the separate call raises evidence-following over continuation by 29.9 to 60.6 points. On the same pairs, removing the trace lowers accuracy by similar amounts under both configurations. Yet continuation repeats the stale conclusion in most conflicts, and the separate call follows the current evidence far more often. Benefiting from a trace and deferring to it are therefore distinct properties. Further analyses show that the final line of a trace carries most of its value, gold evidence helps most before the trace is written, distractors weaken correction under a separate call, and renewed reasoning, unlike a verification instruction, follows the current evidence in most conflicts. Because trace deletion alone cannot reveal which source an answer follows, evaluations should report both properties together with the answer configuration.
authors: Shaoang Li, Yanhang Shi, Jian Li
bullets: Reasoning traces can improve accuracy while also causing models to repeat stale conclusions.
Across three model families on HotpotQA and MuSiQue, separate calls improved evidence-following over continuation by 29.9–60.6 points.
Removing traces reduced accuracy similarly in both configurations, showing that benefiting from a trace differs from deferring to it.
The trace’s final line provides most of its value; gold evidence is most helpful before reasoning is written.
Renewed reasoning corrected conflicts more often than verification instructions, while distractors weakened correction.
papers.selection_reason: Studies reasoning-trace and evidence-following behavior in LLMs under different answer configurations.
papers.title: When Reasoning Traces Conflict with Evidence: How Answer Configuration Shapes Evidence Following
papers.tldr: Separate answer calls follow updated evidence far more reliably than continuing a model’s prior reasoning trace when the two conflict.

papers.abstract: Residual context is key to unlocking the speed-quality Pareto frontier of diffusion language models (DLMs) by carrying forward predictive distributions across denoising steps. Yet turning this seemingly simple mechanism into an effective learning paradigm is far from simple: there is no clear recipe for how residual context should be learned. We introduce ORL, a framework for on-policy residual learning in DLMs. Algorithmically, we identify that residual learning is inherently on-policy. ORL learns from model-induced residual trajectories on the fly and introduces an entropy-contraction objective that sharpens predictions as the model revisits its own predictions. System-wise, exact residual supervision requires capturing, retaining, and reprocessing many trajectory-dependent states. ORL co-designs the algorithm with asynchronous residual capture and transport, specialized block-diffusion attention, and packed compute-balanced training, making it practical at scale. On a 4B DLM converted from Qwen3-4B, ORL improves tokens per forward (TPF) by up to 6.2x and, with our dlmrt engine, end-to-end throughput by approximately 6.9x at comparable or better quality. In single-request serving on one H100, this mode achieves a stronger speed-quality Pareto frontier than autoregressive models with EAGLE3 and DFlash speculative decoding under both strict and relaxed verification, running 1.74x faster than DFlash at matched accuracy. ORL also transfers to existing DLMs: on LLaDA-2.1-mini, 36 H100-hours and 4.2M self-generated tokens, about 10x less data than prior LLaDA recipes, yield up to 1.5x higher TPF and up to 3x higher throughput at comparable quality, and on DiffusionGemma, ORL raises TPF by 1.1-1.2x. With dlmrt and NVFP4 quantization, ORL models decode a single request at up to 5,046 tokens/s on one B200, 7,708 on eight B200s, and 2,788 on a consumer RTX 5090, with comparable quality.
authors: Yifan Yu, Yuqing Jian, Jisen Li, Yuezhou Hu, Tianyi Zhang, Xiaoxia Wu, Rui-Jie Zhu, Junxiong Wang, Zhongzhu Zhou, Fan Lai, James Zou, Chenfeng Xu
bullets: Residual learning is inherently on-policy: ORL trains on residual trajectories generated by the model itself.
An entropy-contraction objective sharpens predictions as the model revisits its own outputs.
Asynchronous residual handling, specialized attention, and compute-balanced packing make training practical at scale.
On a 4B DLM, ORL achieves up to 6.2× higher tokens per forward and approximately 6.9× higher end-to-end throughput at comparable or better quality.
The method transfers across existing DLMs and reaches up to 5,046 tokens/s for single-request decoding on one B200 with NVFP4 quantization.
papers.selection_reason: Presents an on-policy residual learning framework for diffusion language models, improving speed-quality tradeoffs and transfer to existing DLMs.
papers.title: On-Policy Residual Learning for Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: ORL makes diffusion language models substantially faster by learning on-policy residual predictions and supporting them with a scalable systems design, while maintaining comparable quality.

papers.abstract: We introduce TurboMamba, a language-model architecture for faster inference, faster training, and better token prediction. A global Mamba-3 model runs once per completed token block. A small Transformer uses this global context and earlier tokens within the block to predict the next token. Three lightweight additions improve local predictions: direct access to the previous block's last token, a small correction to next-token scores, and a learned mixture with recent-token frequencies. We compare twelve small-scale implementations on public FineWeb-Edu, with comparable parameter counts and shared training-budget caps. The baselines include Transformer, Mamba-3, Jamba, and Zamba. The Jamba and Zamba versions use Mamba-3 in place of their original Mamba modules. TurboMamba achieves the lowest mean test prediction loss (negative log-likelihood, NLL) among all twelve models. Its mean NLL is 9.4% lower than that of Mamba-3, 7.3% lower than that of the Jamba version, and 18.3% lower than that of the Zamba version. End-to-end training throughput is 2.60x that of Mamba-3, 2.81x that of the Jamba version, and 4.82x that of the Zamba version. We measure end-to-end batch latency for a batch of 32 sequences, each with a 256-token prompt and 128 generated tokens. On this workload, TurboMamba achieves a 3.12x speedup over Mamba-3, a 3.53x speedup over the Jamba version, and a 6.21x speedup over the Zamba version.
bullets: Evaluated twelve small-scale models with comparable parameter counts and shared training budgets on public FineWeb-Edu.
Uses global Mamba-3 processing once per completed token block, while a small Transformer predicts tokens within each block.
Adds previous-block token access, a next-token score correction, and a learned mixture of recent-token frequencies.
Achieved the lowest mean test NLL, with reported reductions of 9.4% versus Mamba-3, 7.3% versus Jamba, and 18.3% versus Zamba.
Reported 2.60×–4.82× higher training throughput and 3.12×–6.21× lower batch latency than the compared baselines, depending on the baseline.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a new hybrid language-model architecture with lexical memory for faster inference and training, directly relevant to LLM architectural advances.
papers.title: TurboMamba: Faster Inference, Faster Training, and Better Prediction with Lexical Memory
papers.tldr: TurboMamba combines block-level Mamba-3 context with a small local Transformer and lexical-memory enhancements to improve prediction quality while substantially accelerating training and inference.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models reconstruct masked tokens in parallel, offering an alternative to autoregressive generation. Yet their Transformer backbones typically carry visible evidence and evolving masked predictions through a single residual stream. We equip masked diffusion models with multiple residual streams that persist through depth and adaptive routing between them, then investigate how they support these complementary roles. On the pretraining task, two streams reduce reconstruction perplexity by 5.71% on validation data and 5.13% on average across external corpora compared with standard residual connections. We observe that, without predefined roles, visible and masked positions learn distinct routing patterns. Causal interventions show that this distinction organizes read and write routing, while token-specific write strength remains important within each role. Guided by these findings, a model trained with role-conditioned routing recovers half the validation gain from adding a second stream. State interventions explain the benefit of the additional stream: it preserves early token representations for later reuse while evidence accumulates at masked positions. This mechanism recurs at a larger model scale, showing how persistent streams support context preservation alongside prediction refinement.
bullets: Targets the single-stream limitation in diffusion language models, where visible evidence and evolving masked predictions share one residual pathway.
Adds multiple residual streams with adaptive routing and finds distinct routing patterns for visible versus masked positions.
Two streams reduce validation reconstruction perplexity by 5.71% and by 5.13% on average across external corpora.
Interventions indicate that the extra stream preserves early token representations for later reuse as masked-token evidence accumulates.
Role-conditioned routing recovers half of the validation improvement, and the mechanism also appears at larger scale.
papers.selection_reason: Architectural study of multi-stream residual computation and routing in diffusion language models; relevant to LLM architecture.
papers.title: Multi-Stream Residual Computation in Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: Multiple persistent residual streams improve diffusion language model reconstruction by separating context preservation from masked-token prediction refinement.

papers.abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) pose a dual-surface safety challenge: both intermediate reasoning traces and final answers can contain harmful content. Existing alignment methods often operate at the whole-response level, allowing unsafe reasoning to be masked by a safe-looking final answer. We propose Segment-aware Listwise Target DPO (SaLT-DPO), which addresses this gap through three mechanisms: (1) segment-aware listwise alignment that decomposes responses into reasoning and answer segments, independently scores each segment's safety, and aligns length-normalized segment rewards with soft target distributions over multiple candidates; (2) joint safety coherence regularization that applies a weakest-link principle to promote safety consistency across both segments; and (3) utility anchoring on benign prompts to mitigate over-refusal and reasoning degradation. Experiments on three LRMs show that SaLT-DPO consistently reduces unsafe rates for both reasoning and answer segments while mitigating degradation in benign compliance and preserving general reasoning performance. Ablation studies demonstrate the complementary contributions of its components.
bullets: Targets a dual-surface safety problem: harmful content may appear in either intermediate reasoning or the final answer.
Decomposes responses into reasoning and answer segments, then applies length-normalized listwise alignment using soft target distributions over candidates.
Uses weakest-link safety coherence regularization to enforce consistency across both segments.
Anchors utility on benign prompts to reduce over-refusal and reasoning degradation.
Experiments on three LRMs report reduced unsafe rates in both segments while preserving benign compliance and general reasoning performance; ablations support complementary component effects.
papers.selection_reason: Safety alignment method for large reasoning models, directly relevant to LLM alignment and reasoning-model research.
papers.title: Beyond Safe Answers: Segment-Aware Listwise Alignment for Reasoning Safety in Large Reasoning Models
papers.tldr: SaLT-DPO aligns reasoning traces and final answers separately to improve end-to-end safety in large reasoning models without substantially harming benign usefulness or reasoning ability.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a central approach for improving mathematical reasoning in language models, but long-form completions introduce a difficult credit-assignment problem: different parts of a solution trace may contribute unevenly to final correctness. Existing policyoptimization objectives for RLVR commonly apply importance-sampling correction at either the token level (GRPO, DAPO) or the sequence level (GSPO), imposing different granularities for assigning credit across a response. We introduce Hierarchical Importance-Sampling Policy Optimization (HISPO), a segment-level policy-optimization method that constructs rollout-time entropy-derived contiguous segments, assigns soft entropy-based saliency weights, and applies clipped importance-sampling correction at the segment granularity. This provides an intermediate correction unit between token-level GRPO/DAPO and sequence-level GSPO. We evaluate HISPO by fine-tuning Qwen3-1.7B-Base on mathematical reasoning tasks. Across six benchmarks, HISPO improves Pass@8 over the strongest baseline on all benchmarks and matches or exceeds the strongest baseline in Acc@8 on five of them. On AIME25, HISPO improves over GRPO by +3.75 Acc@8 and +3.78 Pass@8, and over GSPO by +2.50 Acc@8 and +1.27 Pass@8. These results suggest that segment-level correction is a promising granularity for RLVR in long-form mathematical reasoning.
bullets: Addresses uneven credit assignment across parts of long solution traces.
Builds contiguous segments from rollout-time entropy and weights them by entropy-derived saliency.
Uses segment-level correction as an intermediate granularity between token-level and sequence-level methods.
On six math benchmarks, it improves Pass@8 over the strongest baseline on all tasks and matches or exceeds it in Acc@8 on five.
Scope: evaluated by fine-tuning Qwen3-1.7B-Base for mathematical reasoning.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces Hierarchical Importance-Sampling Policy Optimization (HISPO) for segment-level credit assignment in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards for LLMs.
papers.title: HISPO: Hierarchical Importance-Sampling Policy Optimization with Entropy-Derived Segments
papers.tldr: HISPO improves RLVR for long-form mathematical reasoning by applying entropy-guided, clipped importance sampling at the segment level.

papers.abstract: Tokenization determines both the physiological content presented to an ECG Transformer and the sequence over which attention operates. We compare eight tokenization strategies across Transformer, Informer, Reformer, and FEDformer on the nine-label CPSC2018 classification task. The input projection and principal backbone capacity are controlled to isolate the effect of token construction. Median-beat and HeartLang tokenization achieve mean macro-AUCs of 0.893 and 0.889 across the four backbones, compared with 0.822 and 0.824 for point-wise and patch-wise tokenization. Pooling the two physiology-aware representations yields an 8.2% relative improvement in macro-AUC. They also reduce mean sequence length from 1,250 to 158 tokens and mean peak training memory from 5.21 to 0.27 GB. The results show that aligning tokens with ECG morphology can improve both predictive performance and memory efficiency without increasing backbone capacity. The source code is available on https://github.com/LeeJarvis996/ecg_tokenizer.
bullets: Compares eight tokenization strategies across four ECG Transformer backbones on nine-label CPSC2018 classification.
Median-beat and HeartLang tokens outperform point-wise and patch-wise tokens in mean macro-AUC.
Pooling the two physiology-aware representations provides an 8.2% relative macro-AUC improvement.
Physiology-aware tokens reduce mean sequence length from 1,250 to 158 and peak training memory from 5.21 to 0.27 GB.
The findings support aligning tokens with ECG morphology without increasing backbone capacity.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes and optimizes tokenization strategies for ECG Transformer models to improve physiological representation, sequence length, and memory efficiency.
papers.title: On the role of the tokenizer in ECG transformer models
papers.tldr: Physiology-aware ECG tokenization substantially improves Transformer classification performance while reducing sequence length and memory use.

papers.abstract: We introduce Continuum Attention (CA), a causal Transformer attention operator that replaces discrete key and value lookup with integration over a continuous, piecewise linear memory curve. Each query induces an exponential relevance density along the curve. Integrating the density and interpolated values yields exact normalized attention from closed form exponential moments, including half token boundary contributions. The gradients follow analytically from moments of order at most two, enabling parallel GPU implementations while retaining quadratic sequence complexity and the standard Transformer decoder. Compared with ordinary softmax and focal attention, CA reduces mean validation negative log likelihood by 0.0200 and 0.0480 nats per byte, respectively, winning all paired comparisons. An additional disjoint validation slice yields a 0.0457 nats per byte advantage over the strongest selected softmax baseline, with a paired 95% confidence interval. These findings motivate continuous integration as a promising attention alternative while leaving larger scale generalization open.
bullets: Uses a continuous piecewise-linear memory curve instead of discrete keys and values.
Computes query-dependent exponential relevance densities and exact normalized attention via closed-form moments, including boundary contributions.
Provides analytic gradients using moments up to order two, supporting parallel GPU implementation.
Outperforms ordinary softmax and focal attention on reported validation comparisons.
Larger-scale generalization remains untested.
papers.selection_reason: Novel continuous attention operator for Transformers; relevant to LLM architecture advances.
papers.title: Continuum Attention
papers.tldr: Continuum Attention replaces discrete token lookup with analytically integrated continuous memory, improving validation likelihood over softmax and focal attention while retaining standard causal Transformer structure and quadratic complexity.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student model on its own rollouts with token-level supervision from a teacher, assuming that the teacher can reach a correct answer from any prefix the student writes. We call this property the recoverability of the teacher and show it fails on incorrect rollouts: the teacher follows student errors, although it recognizes them. We propose CriticOPD, using error recognition to restore recoverability. The teacher critiques an incorrect rollout, allowing the student to rewrite its solution following the error. The resulting output, including the critique as privileged information, is scored by the teacher while the student uses the revision without the critique for training. On two Qwen3 students and six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, CriticOPD improves OPD, with the largest gains on competition problems.
authors: Kaixiang Zhao, Tianrun Yu, Shangzhe Li, Yuxiao Yang, Amanda Hughes, Weitong Zhang, Taylor W. Killian
bullets: OPD assumes the teacher can recover from any student-generated prefix, but this fails when the teacher follows recognizable student errors.
CriticOPD uses the teacher’s error critique to guide the student in rewriting its solution.
The teacher scores the critique-assisted revision, while the student trains on the revision without access to the critique.
Across two Qwen3 students and six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, CriticOPD improves over standard OPD, especially on competition problems.
papers.selection_reason: Critique-guided on-policy distillation improves LLM mathematical reasoning; fits language foundation model methods.
papers.title: Recovering Reliable Supervision via Critique-Guided On-Policy Distillation
papers.tldr: CriticOPD improves on-policy distillation by having the teacher critique and help repair incorrect student rollouts before supervision.

papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation provides dense supervision for reasoning models via a privileged self-teacher. However, this supervision reflects local token preferences rather than the expected return of an unguided student continuation. Recent methods combine this signal with GRPO. They use GRPO for update directions and the teacher for signal scaling. However, we demonstrate a more effective integration within PPO. Specifically, we identify complementary positional dynamics: privileged information enhances a critic's value-prediction accuracy toward the response's end, whereas self-teacher guidance is strong initially, drops mid-generation, and rebounds finally. These insights motivate Value-Augmented Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (VASPO), wherein a self-teacher and critic evaluate identical privileged information at student-generated prefixes. The critic computes token-level PPO advantages from predicted continuation returns, while the self-teacher modulates selected positive advantages via bounded probability ratios. Across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, VASPO improves mean accuracy over PPO by 2.59 and 1.81 percentage points on Qwen3-4B and OLMo3-7B variants, respectively, and achieves the highest mean accuracy among evaluated methods on Knights and Knaves. Our code is available at https://github.com/cii030/VASPO.
authors: Fei Wu, Zhenrong Zhang, Jianshu Zhang, Jun Du
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between local self-teacher preferences and the expected return of student continuations.
Uses a critic and self-teacher on the same privileged information at student-generated prefixes.
The critic computes token-level PPO advantages, while bounded teacher probability ratios modulate selected positive advantages.
Across six math reasoning benchmarks, VASPO improves mean accuracy over PPO by 2.59 points on Qwen3-4B and 1.81 points on OLMo3-7B.
Achieves the highest mean accuracy among evaluated methods on Knights and Knaves.
papers.selection_reason: PPO-based self-distillation with privileged value estimation for reasoning LLMs; relevant to LLM training methods.
papers.title: VASPO: Self-Distillation with Privileged Value Estimation
papers.tldr: VASPO combines privileged self-teacher guidance with PPO value estimation to improve mathematical reasoning accuracy.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by drafting multiple tokens per step, yet feature-based drafters rely on target hidden features whose contextual emphasis may not align with the needs of subsequent draft positions. Hybrid linear attention (HLA) models maintain compact recurrent states that accumulate historical associations, offering an efficient source of complementary context for speculative drafting. We introduce ReaDy, the first speculative decoding method, to the best of our knowledge, to leverage HLA recurrent states for position-specific context retrieval during drafting. ReaDy equips each draft position with a learned query to retrieve supplementary context directly from the target's committed recurrent states. A lightweight state reader integrates this context into draft representations through residual updates, while low-rank state reads and fused operators keep additional computation and I/O overhead low. Building on DSpark's parallel backbone and sequential prediction head, ReaDy employs a lightweight two-stage adaptation strategy, with reader capacity, state sources, and residual placement examined through ablation studies. Across seven benchmarks spanning mathematics, code generation, and dialogue, ReaDy achieves an average $3.16\times$ decoding speedup over autoregressive decoding with Qwen3.8-27B on a single NVIDIA B200 GPU. It outperforms DSpark on every benchmark, improving throughput by 7.97% and acceptance length by 8.50% on average. Our code is available at https://github.com/StartLuxLabs/ReaDy.
authors: Bohan Sun, Zunhai Su, Xialie Zhuang, Jianjin Li, Ngai Wong, Chuan-Wei Kuo
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between target hidden features and the contextual needs of later draft positions.
Uses learned per-position queries and a lightweight state reader to retrieve and fuse supplementary context via residual updates.
Reduces overhead with low-rank state reads and fused operators, building on DSpark’s parallel backbone and sequential prediction head.
Across seven math, code, and dialogue benchmarks, reports a 3.16× average speedup over autoregressive decoding on Qwen3.8-27B.
Outperforms DSpark on all benchmarks, with average throughput and acceptance-length gains of 7.97% and 8.50%, respectively.
papers.selection_reason: Speculative decoding using recurrent states in hybrid linear attention LLMs; directly relevant to efficient attention, memory-efficient inference, and LLM architecture.
papers.title: ReaDy: Recurrent States as Dynamic Context for Speculative Drafting in Hybrid Linear Attention Large Language Models
papers.tldr: ReaDy accelerates speculative decoding in hybrid linear-attention LLMs by retrieving position-specific context from the target model’s recurrent states.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains language models from checked task outcomes, but assigning a terminal reward to individual reasoning tokens or actions remains difficult. Group-relative methods such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) sample several attempts per prompt, but lose their reward-based learning signal when all attempts receive the same outcome. We propose Hindsight-Privileged RLVR (HP-RLVR), a single-rollout method that turns a completed trajectory's own future into token-level update weights. The generating policy snapshot scores each eligible token under its causal history and under a hindsight context containing the realized future and verifier feedback. A normalized Jensen--Shannon divergence between the two views weights the reward relative to a historical baseline, yielding bounded token credit for both successful and failed attempts, with no reference solution or learned critic. In paired Qwen3-8B runs over a shared $100$-step schedule, HP-RLVR trains $1.21\times$, $1.46\times$, and $2.30\times$ faster than GRPO on mathematics, code generation, and ALFWorld, using one eighth the rollouts per prompt. Accuracy is comparable overall, with HP-RLVR ahead on mathematics at all three sizes and GRPO ahead on code and ALFWorld. In ALFWorld, $43.2\%$ (4B) and $49.0\%$ (8B) of GRPO's gradient-norm records are zero, versus none for HP-RLVR.
authors: Wei Chen, Yubing Wu, Zhou Xu, Haoyue Zhang, Delu Zeng, Jiahao Wang, Junmei Yang, Pan tiewen, Jingfeng Liu, Zhiheng Zhou, Bo Li, Min Chen
bullets: Addresses sparse terminal rewards and GRPO’s loss of learning signal when sampled attempts share the same outcome.
Scores tokens under causal versus hindsight contexts using normalized Jensen–Shannon divergence, then weights rewards relative to a historical baseline.
Uses one eighth the rollouts per prompt and trains 1.21×–2.30× faster than GRPO across mathematics, code generation, and ALFWorld in the reported schedule.
Achieves comparable overall accuracy: stronger on mathematics, while GRPO leads on code generation and ALFWorld.
Produces nonzero gradient-norm records in ALFWorld, unlike GRPO, where 43.2%–49.0% are zero in the reported settings.
papers.selection_reason: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for training language models, including embodied task evaluation.
papers.title: Hindsight-Privileged RLVR: Single-Rollout Token Credit Without Group Sampling
papers.tldr: HP-RLVR assigns bounded token-level credit from each rollout’s realized future, enabling single-rollout RLVR without group sampling or a learned critic.

papers.abstract: We study how to improve LLM reasoning at inference time without updating model weights or using external reward models. Recent reward-free power-sampling methods define the sequence-level power target $\pi_\alpha(y\mid x)\propto p_0(y\mid x)^\alpha$, where $\alpha>1$, which increases the relative probability of completions that are already likely under the base model. Existing methods use Metropolis--Hastings or Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) to approximately sample from this target. However, two challenges arise at different levels. At the target level, full-sequence sharpening can concentrate probability on a few exact reasoning--answer trajectories, suppressing alternative paths that support the same answer. At the sampler level, finite-particle SMC can suffer from path collapse when resampling repeatedly duplicates a few high-weight prefixes. To address these challenges, we propose Decoupled Marginal Sharpening (DMS), which separately controls how strongly the model favors particular reasoning paths and how strongly it favors final answers after aggregating support across those paths. At the target level, DMS first samples from a sharpened reasoning distribution, then marginalizes the model's answer probabilities over the resulting weighted reasoning population and sharpens the induced answer marginal. Separate exponents allow mild reasoning sharpening to encourage exploration of diverse paths, followed by stronger answer-marginal sharpening to concentrate probability on answers with greater aggregate support across those paths. At the sampler level, we develop Fully Adapted Annealed SMC, which combines an annealed sequence of power targets with locally fully adapted proposals and predictive ancestor resampling. Experiments on MATH500, GPQA-Diamond, HumanEval, and AIME24/25 across three base models show that DMS achieves the highest mean pass@1 among the compared methods in all tasks.
authors: Weixin Wang, Wei Deng, Anderson Schneider, Yuriy Nevmyvaka, Pan Xu, Andrew Bennett
bullets: Addresses two issues in reward-free power sampling: loss of alternative reasoning paths and SMC path collapse.
Separates reasoning-path sharpening from final-answer sharpening through independent exponents.
Introduces Fully Adapted Annealed SMC with adapted proposals and predictive ancestor resampling.
Evaluated on MATH500, GPQA-Diamond, HumanEval, and AIME24/25 across three base models.
Achieves the highest mean pass@1 among compared methods on all reported tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Inference-time sampling method to improve LLM reasoning without weight updates.
papers.title: Decoupled Marginal Sharpening for Training-Free Inference-Time Scaling
papers.tldr: DMS improves training-free LLM inference-time reasoning by mildly sharpening diverse reasoning paths, then more strongly sharpening answers supported across those paths.

papers.abstract: The scaling relationship of compute and performance for language models (LMs) has been extensively studied; more recently, models are being designed to scale memory use, as well. In particular, adding embeddings for n-grams scales memory separately from compute use, because each pass only processes individual embedding rows, which are much smaller than the storage used for the whole embedding table. However, existing methods train embeddings from scratch, which needs expensive GPU memory for fast reading and writing. Meanwhile, the ordinary memory of the host system is cheap and underutilized by these training methods. To scale on host memory, we introduce COUNT (Counting Offline Unlocks N-gram Transformers), which builds n-gram embeddings without adding learned parameters by storing precomputed n-gram counts on host. We use the corpus frequencies to weight together the LM's own unembeddings of the next tokens most often following the current n-gram history. At a fixed compute budget, COUNT can be added as an additional input embedding for pretraining 1B-parameter LMs to improve validation loss as much as an LM with 57% more compute. If GPU memory is limited, using COUNT to let backbone parameters fill GPU memory gives better performance than splitting memory with additional learned n-gram embeddings. Beyond efficiency, COUNT allows switching in a different table of n-gram counts from a domain-specific corpus at inference time to adapt to a new task without any training.
authors: Ian Magnusson, Noah A. Smith, Pang Wei Koh
bullets: Addresses the GPU-memory and training cost of learned n-gram embeddings.
Builds n-gram embeddings from corpus frequencies and the LM’s next-token unembeddings, without adding learned parameters.
Stores count tables in inexpensive host memory while accessing only relevant embedding rows during inference or training.
For 1B-parameter LMs at fixed compute, COUNT improves validation loss by as much as 57% more compute.
Supports training-free adaptation by swapping in n-gram counts from a domain-specific corpus at inference time.
papers.selection_reason: N-gram embedding memory that scales LM memory on host and enables training-free adaptation; fits LLM memory and architecture topics.
papers.title: The COUNT: Counting N-grams Unlocks Scaling on Host Memory and Training-Free Adaptation
papers.tldr: COUNT uses offline n-gram counts stored in host memory to provide training-free, domain-adaptable embeddings that improve language-model efficiency and validation loss.

papers.abstract: Momentum is a classical tool for accelerating convex optimization and a standard component of modern large language model training. Yet recent empirical work has questioned the usefulness of first-moment momentum in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). We study this question through a bandit formulation of RLVR with bias-corrected exponential moving average (EMA) momentum, where the EMA coefficient $\beta$ controls how quickly the weights on past gradients decay. When policy gradients are evaluated exactly, we prove that increasing $\beta$ within a range that prevents overshoot strictly accelerates optimization. When gradients are estimated from sampled responses, a positive expected gain can be obscured by sampling fluctuations. We show that as the learning rate $\eta$ decreases, the expected gain with fixed $\beta$ vanishes faster than these fluctuations, whereas increasing $\beta$ to keep $\eta/(1-\beta)$ within the safe regime preserves a nonvanishing gain that eventually dominates them. Bandit simulations quantitatively validate these predictions. RLVR experiments on Qwen3-4B-Base using SGD with EMA and AdamW support our principle of choosing larger coefficients in practical LLM post-training. On Qwen2.5-32B with AdamW, simply increasing $\beta_1$ improves mean validation accuracy by nearly $2$ percentage points over the conventional choice, demonstrating the principle's effectiveness at a larger model scale.
authors: Kaifei Wang, Zikang Shan, Liwei Wang, Yinyu Ye, Han Zhong
bullets: Models RLVR as a bandit problem using bias-corrected EMA momentum, with β controlling gradient-memory decay.
With exact policy gradients, increasing β within a safe, non-overshooting range strictly speeds optimization.
With sampled gradients, fixed-β gains can be hidden by sampling noise; scaling β to keep η/(1−β) safe preserves gains that eventually dominate fluctuations.
Bandit simulations and Qwen experiments support using larger momentum coefficients; increasing AdamW’s β₁ improved mean validation accuracy by nearly 2 percentage points on Qwen2.5-32B.
The analysis is scoped to the proposed bandit formulation and tested RLVR settings; larger momentum must remain within a safe regime to avoid overshoot.
papers.selection_reason: Momentum analysis for RLVR in LLM post-training, relevant to language foundation model training.
papers.title: When Does Momentum Help in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards?
papers.tldr: Momentum can accelerate RLVR when its coefficient is increased alongside a decreasing learning rate while avoiding overshoot, improving optimization and practical LLM post-training.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning makes language models better at solving tasks, but the same mechanism also rewards guessing. When success is the only way to earn reward, opting for a safe fallback is always worse than a long-shot attempt. When a wrong action can corrupt a database or ship broken code, that incentive can be costly. Therefore, we propose training models to fail gracefully: to preserve successful behavior whenever possible while learning to execute a safe fallback policy when acting would be unreliable. However, naively using policy gradients with intermediate reward for fallback behavior is brittle due to unfavorable optimization dynamics. We address this challenge with GracefulRL, which reshapes the optimization landscape to promote graceful failure. Importantly, this behavior emerges directly from outcome-level reward signals, without annotations specifying when to fall back or additional inference-time machinery such as a verifier. Across a range of tasks and scales, we train models that largely preserve their task-solving capability while selectively falling back when acting would be unreliable. More broadly, our results show that reinforcement learning can not only incentivize models to succeed, but also to reason about the limits of their capabilities and change course when they determine that success is out of reach.
authors: Daman Arora, Xuecheng Liu, Himanshu Gaurav Singh, Fahim Tajwar, Abitha Thankaraj, Ruslan Salakhutdinov, Haiwen Feng, Yuda Song, Andrea Zanette
bullets: RL can encourage risky guessing because success is rewarded more than safe abstention.
Graceful failure is important when incorrect actions could corrupt data or deploy broken code.
GracefulRL reshapes optimization to make fallback behavior easier to learn from outcome-level rewards.
The approach requires neither fallback annotations nor an inference-time verifier.
Across tasks and scales, models largely retain task-solving ability while selectively avoiding unreliable actions.
papers.selection_reason: RL training method for LLMs to reason about capability limits and fall back, relevant to language foundation models.
papers.title: Training Language Models to Fail Gracefully
papers.tldr: GracefulRL trains language models to preserve successful behavior while safely falling back when task completion is unreliable.

papers.abstract: Multilingual models share capacity across languages, so adding languages can hurt performance on existing ones. Mixture-of-experts models expand this capacity with little additional per-token computation. Given this extra capacity, does adding experts reduce what each additional language costs? To answer this question, we propose a repetition-aware joint scaling law relating number of active parameters, training tokens per language, number of experts, and language coverage. Fitted on 26,300 per-language loss observations from 64 pretrained configurations, our law reduces prediction error on held-out configurations by 28% relative to the strongest evaluated baseline. At matched number of active parameters and training tokens per language, 32 experts reduce the loss penalty of expanding from 12 to 200 languages by 83% compared with a dense model. Our law further shows that broader language coverage favors more experts across a wider range of compute budgets, guiding capacity allocation as multilingual models scale.
authors: Joel Dag, Nikit Srivastava, Hamada M. Zahera, Axel-Cyrille Ngonga Ngomo
bullets: Adding languages can degrade existing-language performance because model capacity is shared.
The study proposes a joint scaling law linking active parameters, per-language training tokens, expert count, and language coverage.
The law is fitted to 26,300 per-language loss observations from 64 pretrained configurations.
With matched active parameters and per-language tokens, 32 experts reduce the loss penalty of scaling from 12 to 200 languages by 83% versus a dense model.
Broader language coverage favors using more experts across a wider range of compute budgets.
papers.selection_reason: Scaling laws for multilingual Mixture-of-Experts; directly relevant to LLM architecture and scaling.
papers.title: Scaling Multilingual Mixture-of-Experts: How Language Coverage Changes Capacity and Compute Allocation
papers.tldr: A repetition-aware scaling law shows that adding MoE experts substantially reduces the per-language cost of expanding multilingual coverage and helps guide expert allocation.

papers.abstract: We investigate two aspects of multilingual pre-training with limited data, namely how language exposure is distributed across English, Dutch, and Chinese, and how that exposure is ordered during training. In particular, we compare balanced multilingual exposure to language-dominant exposure, where one language is exposed with more training data than the others. We also compare mixed training, where multilingual training data is used throughout training, with curriculum training, where monolingual exposure of the dominant language is followed by balanced multilingual exposure. Our results show that multilingual BabyLM performance varies with both the amount and order of language exposure. Mixed training outperforms curriculum learning across all 15 matched configurations, indicating that simultaneous multilingual exposure is more effective than staged exposure in our setting. Several language-dominant mixed training configurations achieve higher scores than the balanced configuration, suggesting that a balanced distribution is not necessarily the highest-performing configuration in our setting. Interestingly, the Dutch-primary configurations achieve the best overall performance.
authors: JiWoo Hwang, Lukas Edman, Alexander Fraser
bullets: The study examines English, Dutch, and Chinese under balanced versus language-dominant exposure.
It compares mixed multilingual training with a curriculum that starts monolingual and later becomes balanced multilingual.
Mixed training outperforms curriculum learning in all 15 matched configurations.
Some language-dominant mixtures outperform balanced exposure, with Dutch-primary configurations performing best overall.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates language exposure distribution and order in multilingual LLM pretraining; relevant to pretraining strategies.
papers.title: Language Exposure Matters: Distribution and Order in Multilingual BabyLM Pre-training
papers.tldr: Multilingual BabyLM performance depends on both how much exposure each language receives and when that exposure occurs.

papers.abstract: Synthetic data is increasingly used in language-model pretraining. Existing knowledge-corpus synthesis pipelines, including WRAP and Nemotron-CC, usually take a source passage or document segment as input and generate rewritten or QA-style samples from that text. This can improve surface form and prompt diversity, but it does not explicitly require fine-grained source facts -- especially secondary entities, list/table entries, and precise temporal attributes -- to appear in the synthesized corpus. We propose AFCS (Atomic-Fact-Conditioned Synthesis), a pipeline that first extracts source-supported atomic facts and then uses each retained fact to drive generation. AFCS uses structure-aware extraction over the document tree, source-grounded verification, local context expansion, and multi-format generation. In continued-pretraining experiments with OLMo-3-7B and a 32B base on the same FineWiki source corpus, AFCS outperforms WRAP and Nemotron-CC on SimpleQA, SimpleQA Verified, PopQA, and HotpotQA. Granularity ablations show that fact-level synthesis improves over chunk-level, paragraph-level, and entity-level synthesis; and a 100B-token mid-training integration improves factual benchmarks and raises the 12-task general benchmark average by +1.09.
authors: Yunhao Wang, Feng Zhang, Tinghao Yu, Xing Wu, Jiang Zhou
bullets: Targets missing fine-grained facts, including secondary entities, list/table entries, and temporal details.
Extracts source-supported atomic facts with document-structure awareness and verifies them against the source.
Expands local context and generates diverse samples in multiple formats from each retained fact.
Outperforms WRAP and Nemotron-CC on SimpleQA, SimpleQA Verified, PopQA, and HotpotQA in experiments with 7B and 32B models.
A 100B-token integration improves factual benchmarks and increases the 12-task general benchmark average by 1.09 points.
papers.selection_reason: Atomic-fact-conditioned synthesis improves factual knowledge pretraining; relevant to LLM pretraining methods.
papers.title: AFCS: Atomic-Fact-Conditioned Synthesis for Factual Knowledge Pretraining
papers.tldr: AFCS improves factual knowledge pretraining by generating synthetic data directly from verified atomic facts rather than only source passages or document segments.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently encounter conflicts between internal parametric knowledge and external contextual knowledge, yet the mechanisms governing this selection remain unclear. We show that the choice between context and parametric knowledge is linearly represented and can be controlled along a single direction in the model's residual stream. We first demonstrate that this direction generalizes across factual-conflict settings, including context formats, knowledge categories, and datasets, while consistently shifting behavior between parametric and contextual answers. We then transfer a direction learned from simple factual conflicts to three more complex task families: RAG, memory, and rule following, where models must acquire information from retrieved documents, interaction histories, or explicit rules. Across four model families and multiple transfer settings, steering consistently improves the use of prompt-provided information over the unsteered model. These results suggest that the direction captures a transferable preference for external knowledge rather than a mechanism specific to factual conflicts.
authors: Yibin Lou, Yi Hu, Jianhui Chen, Chenpeng Wang, Muhan Zhang, Liangming Pan
bullets: Knowledge selection between parametric and contextual information is linearly represented along a single model direction.
The direction generalizes across conflict formats, knowledge categories, and datasets.
A direction learned from simple factual conflicts transfers to RAG, memory, and rule-following tasks.
Steering consistently improves reliance on prompt-provided information across four model families and multiple settings.
The findings indicate a transferable preference for external knowledge, not merely a factual-conflict-specific mechanism.
papers.selection_reason: Shows a single steering direction controls context vs parametric knowledge in LLMs and transfers across tasks; relevant to LLM mechanisms.
papers.title: Which Knowledge Should LLMs Trust? Uncovering a Generalizable Steering Direction Across Knowledge Conflicts
papers.tldr: LLMs’ preference between internal and prompt-provided knowledge is encoded in a generalizable residual-stream direction that can be steered to favor external information.

papers.abstract: Looped Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models combine parameter reuse with sparse computation to improve performance under matched budgets. Prior work demonstrates that different loop visits can play different roles even when they share parameters. To probe the contributions of different loop visits, we learn separate residual coefficients in a model that applies a shared block twice, observing a smaller scale in the first visit. Fixed coefficient experiments show that reducing the first visit's scale preserves or improves performance, whereas the same reductions to the second hurt it. This asymmetry motivates us to explore asymmetric compute allocation. We propose \textbf{LatentLoop}, which compresses the first visit's sequence, retains full resolution in the second, and reallocates saved computation to increase the hidden size. We further learn how strongly the first visit updates the full sequence, and share MoE weights across visits while using separate attention parameters to accommodate their different sequence resolutions. Across 15 configurations spanning 1.3B--7B parameters, with the largest budget exceeding $10^{21}$ FLOPs, LatentLoop consistently lowers validation NLL. At a fitted NLL of 1.988, predicted compute savings are 19.0\% and 7.9\% relative to vanilla MoE and the looped baseline. It also improves average scores on nine benchmarks at all sizes in 0-shot and 5-shot settings. These results suggest asymmetric compute allocation is a promising direction for looped MoE models.
authors: Zefeng He, Yunkai Chai, Xiaoyang Chen, Tong Zhu, Zongliang Wu, Yun Luo, Yafu Li, Yu Cheng
bullets: Different loop visits contribute asymmetrically: reducing computation in the first visit is less harmful than reducing it in the second.
The method compresses the first visit’s sequence, keeps the second at full resolution, and increases hidden size with the saved compute.
It learns the first visit’s update strength, shares MoE weights across visits, and uses separate attention parameters for differing resolutions.
Across 15 configurations from 1.3B to 7B parameters, it consistently lowers validation NLL and improves average scores on nine benchmarks in 0-shot and 5-shot settings.
At fitted NLL 1.988, it predicts 19.0% and 7.9% compute savings versus vanilla MoE and the looped baseline, respectively.
papers.selection_reason: Looped MoE language model architecture with asymmetric compute allocation and sequence compression for efficiency.
papers.title: LatentLoop: Scaling Looped MoE Models with Asymmetric Compute Allocation
papers.tldr: LatentLoop improves looped MoE efficiency by compressing the first loop visit and reallocating its saved computation to model capacity.

papers.abstract: Weight pruning can degrade the accuracy of large reasoning models (LRMs), yet it remains unclear whether it damages reasoning itself. We find that much of this degradation stems from a failure to stop rather than to reason. As sparsity increases, pruned LRMs increasingly fail to terminate within the token budget, often after the correct answer has appeared in their reasoning, instead falling into repetitive loops, even though they still recognize where the dense model would stop. We further find that the hidden-state difference between terminating and looping continuations is consistent across pruned checkpoints, suggesting a shared direction associated with committing to an answer. Building on this, we propose Termination-Guided Activation Steering (TGAS), a training-free method that adds this direction to the residual stream at inference time. Across six LRMs, three pruning pipelines, and math and code benchmarks, TGAS improves termination and overall accuracy while reducing repetitive reasoning and generation length, showing that this failure is actionable.
authors: Minh-Anh Nguyen, Nguyen T. Ha Lan, Xiyan Fu, Dung D. Le, Wei Lu
bullets: Pruned models frequently continue reasoning past a correct answer and exceed the token budget through repetitive loops.
This degradation reflects impaired termination more than impaired reasoning: models often recognize where the dense model would stop.
Terminating and looping continuations show a consistent hidden-state difference across pruned checkpoints.
Termination-Guided Activation Steering (TGAS) adds this shared direction to the residual stream during inference.
Across six models, three pruning pipelines, and math/code benchmarks, TGAS improves termination and accuracy while reducing repetition and generation length.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes and recovers pruned large reasoning models via termination-guided activation steering.
papers.title: To Reason but Not to Stop: Understanding and Recovering Pruned Large Reasoning Models
papers.tldr: Pruning often makes large reasoning models loop instead of stop, and a training-free activation-steering method can recover termination and accuracy.

papers.abstract: LLMs absorb vast knowledge from training data, yet their inherently probabilistic nature offers no guarantee that this knowledge will surface in their outputs. To bridge this gap, Knowledge Extraction Enhancement (KEE) techniques such as activation steering, decoding adjustments, and prompting modify inference, potentially reinforcing existing predictions or surfacing less accessible answers. Yet their evaluations centered on aggregate accuracy, which obscures diverse effects by collapsing recovered failures and disrupted successes into a single score. We introduce MAPLE, a unified framework for characterizing how KEE techniques affect parametric knowledge extraction. Its diagnostic metrics disentangle these effects at the surface, probability, and beyond-sampling levels by measuring answer recovery and disruption, gold-token rank shifts on unrecovered failures, and recovery of answers missed by fixed-budget sampling. We evaluate six KEE techniques spanning decoding, activation steering, and prompting across three model families: OLMo2, Qwen2.5, and Llama3. Our analysis reveals distinct effects and trade-offs across techniques, highlighting the value of MAPLE for understanding and comparing KEE beyond aggregate accuracy.
authors: Minsuh Joo, Youna Kim, Choonghyun Park, Soo Kyung Kim, Hyunsoo Cho
bullets: Aggregate accuracy can hide whether a technique recovers failures, disrupts successes, or reveals answers missed by sampling.
MAPLE measures effects at surface, probability, and beyond-sampling levels.
Its metrics track answer recovery/disruption, gold-token rank shifts, and recovery beyond fixed-budget sampling.
The study evaluates six decoding, activation-steering, and prompting techniques across OLMo2, Qwen2.5, and Llama3.
Results show distinct trade-offs between techniques, supporting more informative KEE comparisons.
papers.selection_reason: Diagnostic framework for LLM parametric knowledge extraction techniques; fits LLM foundation model evaluation.
papers.title: MAPLE: A Multi-Axis Parametric Knowledge Extraction Lens for LLM Evaluation
papers.tldr: MAPLE provides a multi-axis framework for evaluating how knowledge-extraction enhancements recover, disrupt, or uncover LLM answers beyond aggregate accuracy.

papers.abstract: Soft spectral clipping (SSC) reduces gradient singular values, but its effect depends on the gradient scale and clipping threshold. We introduce CAST (Clipping with Adaptive Scales and Thresholds), a history-adaptive extension of SSC. AdamW's previous second moment sets row and column scales. An exponential moving average of the clipped output's estimated spectral norm sets each matrix's threshold. CAST restores the original coordinates before the AdamW update. We train a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model with 19.08B total parameters for 83.89B tokens. CAST achieves lower training and mean validation losses than nine gradient-processing baselines, with the fewest relative gradient spikes. It reaches the best baseline's final smoothed training loss in 7.2\% fewer steps.
authors: Jiacheng Li, Jianchao Tan, Kefeng Zhang, Yuchen Xie, Xunliang Cai
bullets: Addresses SSC’s sensitivity to gradient scale and clipping thresholds.
Uses AdamW’s previous second moment for row/column scaling and an EMA of clipped spectral norms for per-matrix thresholds.
Restores original coordinates before applying the AdamW update.
On a 19.08B-parameter MoE trained for 83.89B tokens, CAST had lower training and mean validation losses than nine baselines.
Produced the fewest relative gradient spikes and matched the best baseline’s final smoothed training loss in 7.2% fewer steps.
papers.selection_reason: History-adaptive spectral clipping for LLM pretraining; directly relevant to large language model training.
papers.title: CAST: History-Adaptive Spectral Clipping for LLM Pretraining
papers.tldr: CAST adaptively scales and thresholds soft spectral clipping to stabilize LLM pretraining and accelerate optimization.

papers.abstract: Visible reasoning traces of Chinese reasoning-oriented LLMs are typically written in modern vernacular Chinese, which may be verbose under limited decoding budgets. We ask whether the linguistic register of reasoning can be used to improve efficiency. We propose Wenyan Thinking, which emits intermediate reasoning in Classical Chinese (wenyanwen) while retaining a short direct-answer output. Starting from modern-Chinese reasoning traces, we rewrite only the reasoning field into wenyan and fine-tune Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 on the rewritten supervision. To distinguish register shift from generic compression, we construct a compact modern-Chinese control using the same source data, teacher family, base model, and SFT recipe. Across budget-sensitive evaluations on MMLU-ProX-Lite-ZH, CEVAL, and AGIEval-CN, Wenyan Thinking substantially reduces reasoning length and missing-answer rates under constrained decoding. Compact rewriting explains much of the efficiency gain, while wenyan consistently outperforms the compact modern-Chinese control on the primary benchmark and remains competitive across the additional benchmarks. These results identify linguistic register as a practical design axis for efficient visible reasoning in Chinese LLMs.
bullets: Modern vernacular reasoning traces can be verbose, motivating a more compact linguistic register.
The method rewrites only reasoning traces into wenyan while preserving short direct answers, then fine-tunes a Chinese reasoning model.
A compact modern-Chinese control separates register effects from generic compression.
Across three Chinese reasoning benchmarks, wenyan reduces reasoning length and missing-answer rates under constrained decoding.
Wenyan outperforms the compact modern-Chinese control on the primary benchmark and remains competitive elsewhere.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates linguistic register for efficient LLM reasoning, relevant to LLM training and efficiency.
papers.title: Does the Linguistic Register of Thinking Matter? Wenyan as a Compact Reasoning Register for Chinese LLMs
papers.tldr: Wenyan Thinking uses Classical Chinese for intermediate reasoning to make Chinese LLM outputs more compact and effective under limited decoding budgets.

papers.abstract: Multi-session agents can switch between LLMs to balance performance and inference cost. Such switches require transferring a history for continuity, yet their effects on the recipient remain underexplored. Through controlled experiments with multi-session tasks, we uncover behavior transfer: recipients tend to adopt reasoning and action patterns from the models that generated their histories. This effect is most evident with raw-history transfer but is substantially reduced by summarization. Based on these findings, we propose Direction- and Authorship-aware Summarization of History (DASH) that preserves stronger-model behavior while minimizing weak-to-strong transfer via summarization. Experiments with repeated swaps show that DASH outperforms raw-history transfer and naive summarization baselines. These results suggest that effective multi-model orchestration requires considering not only which model to use, but also which behavioral patterns to carry forward.
authors: Youngbin Choi, Sehyun Hwang, Suhyeon Jun, Seoyeon Lee, Sunghyun Choi, MoonJeong Park, Dongwoo Kim
bullets: Model swaps can cause recipient LLMs to adopt the reasoning and action patterns embedded in prior histories.
Behavior transfer is strongest with raw-history sharing and is substantially reduced by summarization.
DASH uses direction- and authorship-aware summarization to preserve desirable behavior and limit weak-to-strong transfer.
Across repeated swaps, DASH outperforms raw-history transfer and naive summarization baselines.
The findings highlight behavioral history—not just model selection—as a key factor in multi-model orchestration.
papers.selection_reason: Studies history transfer and summarization in multi-session LLM agents, relevant to LLM deployment and agent behavior.
papers.title: New Model, Old Habits: Behavior Transfer under Model Swapping in Multi-Session LLM Agents
papers.tldr: Switching LLMs in multi-session agents transfers behavioral patterns through shared histories, and DASH reduces unwanted transfer while preserving stronger-model behavior.

papers.abstract: Mamba models underperform Transformers on in-context retrieval. This gap is usually attributed to Mamba's fixed-size recurrent state, which loses information as the context grows. We challenge this assumption by focusing on query-first retrieval, a setup in which the query precedes the context and state capacity should not be the binding constraint. We show that even in this setting Mamba lags substantially behind Transformers, despite its selection mechanism, which was designed to distinguish relevant content from distractors. We then demonstrate that the Mamba selection gates have sufficient control over the state updates to influence the model output: intervening on specific gates alone can swing accuracy between extremes. However, as gates are input-dependent, they require the incoming token's representation to encode its relevance to the query. We therefore probe token representations across layers, and find that the relevance signal emerges only gradually with model depth, and that the gates begin to reflect it only several layers deeper. Crucially, we find that gates in retrieval-critical layers are not yet aligned with relevance. The selection mechanism is thus expressive enough to solve the task, but it commonly operates on a relevance signal that has not yet arrived. Mamba's retrieval bottleneck therefore extends beyond state capacity: even when capacity is sufficient, the delayed emergence of relevance information across depth often prevents successful retrieval.
authors: Nir Yarden, Amit Ben-Artzy, Roy Schwartz
bullets: Query-first retrieval removes state-capacity pressure, yet Mamba still substantially trails Transformers.
Mamba’s selection gates can strongly control outputs, showing that the mechanism is expressive enough for retrieval.
Gate decisions depend on token representations encoding relevance to the query.
Relevance signals emerge gradually across layers, while retrieval-critical gates often act before those signals are available.
The bottleneck is therefore delayed cross-layer relevance alignment, not capacity alone.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes Mamba's retrieval bottleneck and selection gates, relevant to LLM architecture.
papers.title: Beyond State Capacity: Why Retrieval Breaks in Mamba
papers.tldr: Mamba’s retrieval failures are not just caused by limited state capacity: relevance information often reaches its selection gates too late for effective retrieval.

papers.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enables parameter-efficient fine-tuning by learning low-rank weight updates. Increasing rank expands adaptation capacity, but does not guarantee that all learned directions improve downstream performance. In a diagnostic experiment with rank-16 LoRA, we show that retaining only the top singular components achieves the best performance, whereas adding further components degrades it. Motivated by this, we propose Residual-Gradient Adaptation (ReGRA), a two-stage method for making more effective use of a fixed rank budget. After the first stage, ReGRA estimates task gradients on a calibration set and removes their projections onto the two-sided subspace induced by the first-stage update. It then aggregates the residual-gradient directions to initialize a second-stage adapter without changing the first-stage update. An orthogonality regularizer encourages the two updates to capture complementary directions. Both updates can be merged into the pretrained weights, incurring no additional inference overhead. Across diverse benchmark sets, ReGRA achieves stronger performance than alternatives with the same total rank and even matches LoRA adapters with twice the rank. Ablation studies and further analysis support the contribution of its core design choices. Code is available at https://github.com/Fanyao-Li/ReGRA.
authors: Fanyao Li, Yuxi Liu, Xiaohao Liu, He Chang, Zhaoxin Wang, Zhulin Tao
bullets: Higher LoRA rank can introduce harmful directions: in a rank-16 diagnostic, keeping only top singular components performed best.
ReGRA uses a two-stage process: it projects calibration-set task gradients away from the first adapter’s induced subspace, then initializes a second adapter from residual directions.
An orthogonality regularizer encourages the two updates to learn complementary information.
Across diverse benchmarks, ReGRA outperforms same-total-rank alternatives and matches LoRA with twice the rank.
The two adapters can be merged into pretrained weights, adding no inference overhead.
papers.selection_reason: Low-rank fine-tuning method for pretrained models, transferable to LLM adaptation.
papers.title: ReGRA: Residual-Gradient Adaptation for Complementary Low-Rank Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: ReGRA improves fixed-rank LoRA fine-tuning by adding a gradient-derived, complementary adapter without increasing inference cost.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) improves reasoning in language models, but scalar outcomes provide coarse supervision over response trajectories. Self-distillation offers denser token-level guidance by comparing an unassisted policy with a feedback-informed self-teacher, yet the teacher evolves with the student, creating unstable targets and motivating additional regularization. We introduce Function-Space Policy Optimization (FSPO), a single-policy framework that combines current privileged adaptation with function-space temporal consolidation. FSPO stores sparse historical next-token distributions as fixed temporal targets, providing temporal separation without maintaining a persistent teacher model. It further introduces privileged disagreement correction to explicitly suppress locally overvalued actions, reliability-adaptive grounding that strengthens reference supervision when self-generated evidence repeatedly fails, and quality and coverage-aware temporal memory that retains verified behaviors and improves privileged demonstrations. Across reasoning and tool-use benchmarks, FSPO achieves the highest average accuracy under a 5-hour training budget, improving over the strongest baseline by approximately 4% points on average while reducing peak memory from about 70 GB to 56 GB on Olmo3-7B-Instruct.
authors: Aryan Das, Arnab Bhattacharya, Vinay Kumar Verma
bullets: Addresses coarse scalar supervision and unstable moving targets in RL with Verifiable Rewards.
Uses a single policy with sparse historical next-token distributions as fixed temporal targets, avoiding a persistent teacher model.
Adds privileged disagreement correction, reliability-adaptive grounding, and quality- and coverage-aware memory.
Reports the highest average accuracy under a 5-hour budget, with roughly 4 percentage points over the strongest baseline.
Reduces peak memory from about 70 GB to 56 GB on Olmo3-7B-Instruct.
papers.selection_reason: RLVR policy optimization for LLM reasoning with temporal self-distillation; relevant to LLM training methods.
papers.title: Function-Space Temporal Self-Distillation for Policy Optimization
papers.tldr: FSPO stabilizes self-distillation for reinforcement learning by using sparse historical policy targets and adaptive correction, improving reasoning and tool-use performance with lower memory use.

papers.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) changes logit margins among non-target tokens at teacher-forced prefixes. Matching a local reference distribution keeps those probabilities and also penalizes margin expansions. We ask whether a soft auxiliary can preserve selected local non-target margin relations without freezing that distribution. We introduce \textbf{Selective Rank-Preserving SFT (SRP-SFT)}, a soft margin target: a hinge on reference-scaled lower bounds for pairs from the reference's top-$K$ non-target tokens, applied at fixed teacher-forced prefixes. The hinge stops once the requested bound is met. We derive the KL cost of violating a margin, characterize the feasible region and its conditional utility, and give a finite-step condition for reducing aggregate violations. In one-epoch experiments on Qwen3-4B-Base and UltraFeedback, this target raises MATH-500 and code-generation scores over CE and LP-SFT at all three training seeds. At seed 1234, MATH-500 pass@1 rises from 49.56\% to 54.56\% and the four-metric code mean rises from 65.91\% to 69.50\% relative to LP-SFT. Ranking controls, held-out cache diagnostics, sensitivity sweeps, and six additional backbones show where these score changes appear.
authors: Yuxuan Wang, Guangxiang Zhao, Xinyu Tan, Yahui Han, Xinxiang Yin, Zhonghai Wu, Xiangzheng Zhang, Lin Sun, Tong Yang
bullets: SFT can alter non-target logit margins even when matching a local reference distribution.
SRP-SFT applies a hinge loss to reference-scaled lower bounds for pairs among the reference model’s top-K non-target tokens at teacher-forced prefixes.
The hinge stops penalizing a pair once its requested margin bound is satisfied, allowing distributional flexibility.
The paper derives the KL cost of margin violations, characterizes feasibility and utility, and provides a finite-step condition for reducing aggregate violations.
On Qwen3-4B-Base with UltraFeedback, SRP-SFT outperformed CE and LP-SFT across three seeds in the reported MATH-500 and code-generation evaluations.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a margin-preserving SFT objective for LLMs, directly relevant to LLM fine-tuning and training.
papers.title: Beyond Distribution Matching: Selective Margin Preservation for Supervised Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: SRP-SFT preserves selected non-target logit margins without forcing the full reference distribution, improving math and code-generation scores in reported one-epoch experiments.

papers.abstract: We propose DAGFormer, a Transformer language model whose cross-layer connections are planned by a jointly trained topology predictor. Beyond the residual connections in a standard Transformer, DAGFormer adds direct connections from earlier layers to later ones, and the predictor controls the strength of every connection based on input tokens. Unlike existing cross-layer routing architectures, which set each layer's connections separately, DAGFormer plans the routing of the whole model at once. On matched OLMo-2 pairs from 75M to 1B parameters, DAGFormer lowers WikiText-2 perplexity by 17% to 25% over the vanilla Transformer, and a 1B DAGFormer trained on 5B tokens outperforms the vanilla model trained on 10B. Against four routing baselines with the same data and budget, it reaches the lowest perplexity at 75M, 300M and 1B. The gain carries over to 13 commonsense, science, reading and math evaluation tasks (2.0 to 2.5 points higher mean accuracy at 300M and 1B) and to instruction finetuning (63% to 70% AlpacaEval win rate against the vanilla Transformer, leading every routing baseline), and under structured pruning DAGFormer degrades the least in five of six settings.
authors: Xiaocong Yang, Yuren Hao, ChengXiang Zhai
bullets: Adds direct connections from earlier to later layers beyond standard residual links.
A jointly trained topology predictor plans the full model’s routing at once, rather than layer by layer.
Reduces WikiText-2 perplexity by 17–25% over matched vanilla Transformers from 75M to 1B parameters.
Improves mean accuracy on 13 downstream tasks and achieves higher AlpacaEval win rates after instruction finetuning.
Shows greater robustness to structured pruning in five of six tested settings.
papers.selection_reason: Novel Transformer topology predictor for language models; directly relevant to LLM architecture.
papers.title: DAGFormer: Global Topology Prediction for Transformer Cross-Layer Connections
papers.tldr: DAGFormer jointly plans token-dependent cross-layer connections across the entire Transformer, substantially improving language modeling and downstream performance over standard and routed Transformers.

papers.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have advanced rapidly, yet strengthening their reasoning through reinforcement learning (RL) remains an open challenge.
