Any-order generation can suffer from entropy degradation, which narrows the reasoning paths available for exploration. Recent work mitigates this issue by applying standard GRPO with left-to-right generation. However, independently generating every rollout from the input prompt can leave alternative continuations from intermediate states underexplored, while trajectory-level advantages assign uniform credit to all tokens without distinguishing the contributions of individual reasoning segments. We propose ForkGRPO, an RL framework that couples efficient exploration with fine-grained segment-level credit assignment. It samples multiple continuations from high-entropy intermediate states along a reference trajectory, prioritizing textual boundaries and reusing shared prefixes. The continuations provide complementary learning signals: within-state group-relative advantages guide which continuations to reinforce, while Monte Carlo state-value differences indicate which reasoning segments improve expected outcomes. Among the evaluated architecture-preserving RL methods, ForkGRPO achieves the best performance on three of four benchmarks, while improving over the directly comparable JustGRPO by up to 1.2 percentage points and using up to 27.8% fewer generated tokens. ForkGRPO-Fast further achieves a $2.49\times$ training wall-clock speedup with negligible accuracy loss.
authors: Zhaoyan Jia, Chengwei Zhou, Gourav Datta, Massoud Pedram
bullets: Addresses entropy degradation and insufficient exploration in any-order diffusion generation.
Samples continuations from high-entropy intermediate states, prioritizing textual boundaries and reusing shared prefixes.
Uses group-relative advantages for continuation selection and Monte Carlo value differences for segment-level credit assignment.
Achieves the best results among evaluated architecture-preserving methods on three of four benchmarks, improving over JustGRPO by up to 1.2 percentage points.
Reduces generated tokens by up to 27.8%; ForkGRPO-Fast provides a 2.49× training speedup with negligible accuracy loss.
papers.selection_reason: Reinforcement learning method for diffusion LLMs, relevant to LLM architecture and training.
papers.title: ForkGRPO: Efficient Exploration and Fine-Grained Credit Assignment for Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: ForkGRPO improves reinforcement learning for diffusion language models by exploring alternative continuations efficiently and assigning credit at the reasoning-segment level.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for multi-turn agentic tasks that require interactions with users and environments over extended sequences of actions. A common approach to improving LLM agents is to use more capable expert models to provide training supervision, either by behavior cloning the expert's trajectories or by using the expert to correct the actions in trajectories generated by the weaker student model. However, expert LLMs can provide richer supervision than actions alone: they can directly generate textual critique that explain why specific actions are incorrect. We study whether training on such feedback benefits LLM agents and propose Critique-Augmented Agentic Fine-Tuning (CAFT), a framework that elicits textual expert feedback on student-generated trajectories. For each incorrect action, the expert yields both a corrected action and a textual critique explaining the student's mistake--which we then use as the training target for fine-tuning. Across four student models from the Nemotron 3 and Gemma 4 families on the agentic domains $\tau^2$-Bench Airline+Retail and WebShop, adding critiques to action-level supervision improves performance by 8% on average over action-only distillation. Additionally, CAFT checkpoints can also provide a better warm start for reinforcement learning than expert-trajectory distillation. Our results demonstrate that textual critiques can strengthen supervision for multi-turn LLM agents.
authors: Thomas Zeng, Zelei Cheng, Mingyang Zhou, Sambit Sahu, William Campbell, Genta Indra Winata
bullets: Expert feedback can explain why a student’s actions are incorrect, providing richer supervision than corrected actions alone.
CAFT elicits critiques and corrected actions from an expert on student-generated trajectories, then fine-tunes the agent on both.
Evaluated across four Nemotron 3 and Gemma 4 student models in Airline+Retail, WebShop, and related agentic settings.
Adding critiques improved performance by 8% on average over action-only distillation.
CAFT checkpoints also provided a stronger warm start for reinforcement learning than expert-trajectory distillation.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes Critique-Augmented Agentic Fine-Tuning (CAFT) using textual expert feedback to improve multi-turn LLM agent performance, contributing to agent training methodologies.
papers.title: Beyond Corrected Actions: Training LLM Agents on Textual Critiques
papers.tldr: Training LLM agents with expert textual critiques alongside corrected actions improves multi-turn agent performance over action-only supervision.

papers.abstract: This paper presents LLM-jp-4, a family of Japanese sovereign large language models (LLMs) developed with an emphasis on transparency, reproducibility, and practical usability. LLM-jp-4 comprises an 8B dense model and a 32B-A3B mixture-of-experts model, both trained from scratch on approximately 12 trillion tokens. To support independent verification and reproduction, we establish explicit criteria for selecting training data, external models, and software, and make the development process publicly available. Evaluation results demonstrate substantial improvements over previous LLM-jp models and competitive performance against open-weight models of similar scale. By documenting the development principles, training procedures, and empirical findings of LLM-jp-4, we aim to provide a reference for future sovereign AI development.
authors: LLM-jp, :, Chaoran Liu, Daisuke Kawahara, Hideyuki Tachibana, Hirokazu Kiyomaru, Jun Suzuki, Koshi Eguchi, Kouta Nakayama, Qianying Liu, Rio Yokota, Ryo Takahashi, Sadao Kurohashi, Sosuke Hosokawa, Taishi Nakamura, Takashi Kodama, Yun-Ang Wu, Yusuke Miyao, Yusuke Oda
bullets: Introduces 8B dense and 32B-A3B mixture-of-experts models.
Trains both models from scratch on approximately 12 trillion tokens.
Defines explicit criteria for training data, external models, and software selection.
Publicly documents development principles, training procedures, and empirical findings.
Reports substantial gains over previous LLM-jp models and competitive results against similarly scaled open-weight models.
papers.selection_reason: Technical report on LLM-jp-4, a Japanese sovereign LLM family featuring a dense 8B and MoE 32B model, contributing to LLM training and architecture (Mixture of Experts).
papers.title: LLM-jp-4 Technical Report
papers.tldr: LLM-jp-4 is a transparent, reproducible family of Japanese sovereign LLMs that achieves improved and competitive performance through large-scale from-scratch training.

papers.abstract: Jailbreak attacks against large language models (LLMs) are evaluated using attack success rate (ASR), which depends on correctly identifying responses that fulfill prohibited requests. Existing evaluators can mistake refusals or topically related responses for successful attacks. We show that changing only the judge LLM can alter reported ASR by up to $82$ percentage points. We introduce the semantic reconstruction game, a training-free evaluator that decomposes compliance judgments into constrained semantic comparisons. Given only a response, an LLM reconstructs the request answered by its substantive content, excluding information merely repeated or refused. The game compares this reconstruction against similar decoy requests to determine whether it matches the original request, allowing abstention when neither candidate matches. Across three off-the-shelf LLM judges, the game achieves the lowest mean error against human labels among evaluated methods and reduces variation in reported ASR. It prioritizes avoiding false positives, even at the cost of missing some successful jailbreaks.
authors: Liam Davis, Romain Emil-Popescu, Suman Jana
bullets: Existing jailbreak evaluation can misclassify refusals or merely related answers as successful attacks.
Changing only the judging LLM can shift reported attack success rates by up to 82 percentage points.
The method reconstructs the request answered by a response’s substantive content, excluding repeated or refused information.
It compares the reconstruction with the original and decoy requests, while allowing abstention when neither matches.
Across three off-the-shelf judges, it had the lowest mean error against human labels and reduced ASR variation, but may miss some successful jailbreaks.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free semantic reconstruction evaluator for LLM jailbreak compliance; relevant to LLM evaluation and safety.
papers.title: Did the LLM Answer the Question? A Semantic Reconstruction Game for Jailbreak Evaluation
papers.tldr: A training-free semantic reconstruction evaluator makes jailbreak success-rate judgments more reliable by reducing false positives and judge-dependent variation.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense token-level supervision on student rollouts, but this supervision can become unreliable when the student and teacher diverge, either because of a large initial policy gap or compounding errors in long-horizon reasoning and tool use. We introduce Divergence-Triggered Dynamic Distillation (DTDD), an adaptive OPD framework that uses segment-level student-teacher divergence to trigger teacher takeover during training. When divergence triggers an intervention during reasoning, the student prefix continues to receive standard OPD supervision. The teacher then generates a recovery suffix, which the student learns through behavior cloning, using cross-entropy on the teacher-generated tokens. We evaluate DTDD in three regimes: long-horizon reasoning, distillation from a base initialization without offline supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and multi-turn agents. We also compare alternative trigger designs and teacher-intervention rates. DTDD reduces the post-warmup peak gradient norm by $8.6\times$ and, from a base initialization, reaches $21.3\%$ held-out math accuracy in $2.6\times$ fewer optimizer updates than OPD; both methods finish near $22\%$. It improves best-observed performance by $4.8$ and $4.1$ percentage points on ALFWorld with LoRA and agentic code, respectively. Ablations show that segment-averaged triggers outperform token-spike triggers. Behavior cloning is also more effective than the tested OPD surrogate for training teacher-generated recoveries. Across 23 experimental arms, takeover tends to help when the teacher substantially outperforms the OPD-trained student, provided that the teacher can recover from student-visited states, the student can learn those recoveries, and teacher intervention is neither excessive nor insufficient.
authors: Qijia He, Zequn Li, Spencer Luo, Tianle Chen, Pradyumna Narayana, Zixian Ma, Ranjay Krishna, Lan Nie, Sugato Basu
bullets: Problem: OPD supervision can become unreliable after large policy gaps or compounding reasoning and tool-use errors.
Method: Segment-level divergence triggers teacher intervention; the student prefix receives OPD supervision, while a teacher-generated recovery suffix is learned via behavior cloning.
Results: DTDD reduced post-warmup peak gradient norm by 8.6× and reached 21.3% held-out math accuracy in 2.6× fewer updates from a base initialization, with similar final accuracy to OPD.
It improved best-observed ALFWorld and agentic-code performance by 4.8 and 4.1 percentage points, respectively.
Scope: Takeover helps when the teacher is substantially better and can recover from student states, while intervention rates must avoid being too high or too low.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive on-policy distillation for LLM reasoning and agentic training; relevant to LLM training methods.
papers.title: DTDD: Divergence-Triggered Dynamic Distillation for Reliable On-Policy Supervision
papers.tldr: DTDD stabilizes on-policy distillation by having the teacher take over when student–teacher divergence signals likely rollout failure, improving training speed and best observed performance in several long-horizon and agentic settings.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning for code usually rewards passing tests, which a model can do while remaining wrong on the inputs the tests do not cover. A program verifier instead decides whether a program satisfies a formal specification for all inputs. Language models are almost always paired with verifiers at inference time only, and turning a verifier into a reward raises two difficulties. It reports only acceptance or rejection, which gives no gradient when every attempt fails, and a policy can cheat it, most simply by telling it to assume what the proof was supposed to establish. We build an agentic environment and reward that address both. The reward reads the verifier's diagnostics rather than its verdict, scoring a candidate by the weighted fraction of proof obligations it discharges, extended with hidden probes from a reference proof's annotations. An integrity audit outranks the verifier, rejecting any candidate that alters the specification or assumes what it was meant to prove. The model works as an agent against a live verifier over many turns, with a separately trained proof specialist as a frozen collaborator. Across Qwen3 models from 1.7B to 14B and a 35B Qwen3.6 mixture-of-experts model, held-out verification on code generation rises from 66.1% to 93.5% on DafnyBench and from 56.3% to 100% on SWE-Proof. This reward leads every other training signal we compare, including a binary pass-or-fail reward trained under otherwise identical settings, with the widest margin on code generation. When the agent must also deliver the repository patch, graded by each project's withheld tests, the fraction of held-out issues it resolves rises from 59.6% to 72.5%. Evaluated unchanged on three verification suites withheld from training, the checkpoints improve on all of them, including one whose language and verifier are absent from training.
authors: George Ma, Yuhao Zhang, Bing He, Zeren Shui, Ferhat Erata, Murali Krishna Ramanathan, Somayeh Sojoudi, Hao Zhou
bullets: Addresses sparse verifier rewards and policies that exploit or weaken specifications.
Scores partial progress from discharged proof obligations, augmented with hidden reference-proof probes.
Uses an integrity audit to reject specification changes or circular assumptions.
Agents interact with a live verifier over multiple turns alongside a frozen proof specialist.
Verification improves across model sizes and unseen suites, while held-out issue resolution rises from 59.6% to 72.5%.
papers.selection_reason: Agentic RL with verifier-grounded rewards for code generation across Qwen LLMs; directly relevant to LLM training and reasoning.
papers.title: Verifier-Grounded Agentic RL for Provably Correct Code
papers.tldr: Verifier-grounded agentic RL substantially improves formally verified code generation and held-out software fixes by using diagnostic proof feedback and integrity checks.

papers.abstract: This work concerns our submission for the Multilingual track of the 2026 BabyLM Challenge. We improve on our baseline using data that has been summarized and translated by an LLM, showing that higher-quality data can come from synthetic sources. We further improve with 2 simple changes: using a larger model, and using a character-level vocabulary. Both of these changes require LoRA-style fine-tuning for realizing their full potential. We dub our final Qwen3-based model Qwenfant, which, at the time of submission, ranks 1st in the Multilingual track.
bullets: Uses LLM-generated summaries and translations as higher-quality synthetic training data.
Improves the baseline with a larger model and character-level vocabulary.
Finds that both changes reach their full potential with LoRA-style fine-tuning.
The submitted Qwenfant model ranked first in the 2026 Multilingual track at submission time.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a character-level BabyLM model (Qwenfant) trained on synthetic parallel text, contributing to LLM training methodologies and multilingual language modeling.
papers.title: Qwenfant: Train Big Character-level BabyLMs on Concise Parallel Text
papers.tldr: Qwenfant improves Multilingual BabyLM Challenge performance by training a larger, character-level Qwen3 model on concise LLM-summarized and translated text with LoRA-style fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: In so-called "Industry 4.0," integrated sensors, analytics tools, and other digital technologies supplement industrial workflows, potentiating enhanced visibility and automation. Prognostics and health management (PHM) and natural language processing (NLP) practitioners alike have explored the application of large language models (LLMs) to industrial asset management, but many prior works' focus on exam-like benchmarks has limited their assessment of LLMs' ability to automate practical operations. Herein, we introduce CoffeeBench, a fault diagnostics task for LLM agents, using a simulated appliance. The LLMs we evaluate struggle to consistently identify faults from the sensor information alone, but the best-performing ones can iteratively refine the fault-option space to eventually obtain a successful diagnosis. Our subsequent analyses, therefore, focus on: differentiating models by diagnostic efficiency (RQ1); examining the lagging performance of the three worst models (RQ2); and identifying viable heuristics for selective prediction (RQ3), including that initial diagnostic uncertainty and LLM-judged soundness of reasoning are high-signal predictors of diagnostic success. In addition to our benchmark results (Section 3.1), we provide practical insights for improving the performance of the open-weight models on CoffeeBench, such as by explicitly tracking episode state on their behalf to reduce timeouts (Section 3.2) or applying a deliberation loop to refine diagnostic hypotheses (Section 3.3).
authors: Lucas H. McCabe, Sarah Lukens, H. Howie Huang
bullets: Introduces CoffeeBench, a fault-diagnosis benchmark for LLM agents operating on a simulated appliance.
Evaluates diagnostic efficiency, poor-performing models, and heuristics for selectively trusting predictions.
The strongest models can narrow the fault-option space iteratively to eventually reach successful diagnoses.
Initial diagnostic uncertainty and the model’s judged reasoning soundness predict diagnostic success.
Practical improvements include explicitly tracking episode state to reduce timeouts and using deliberation loops to refine hypotheses.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces CoffeeBench for diagnosing appliance faults using LLM agents, focusing on agent reasoning and efficiency in a simulated industrial context.
papers.title: Can LLM Agents Efficiently Identify Appliance Faults? Insights From Diagnosing a Simulated Appliance
papers.tldr: CoffeeBench shows that LLM agents struggle to reliably diagnose simulated appliance faults from sensor data alone, but iterative hypothesis refinement and uncertainty-based selection can improve practical diagnosis.

papers.abstract: Understanding neural scaling laws is increasingly important for theory and practice, yet first-principles explanations remain limited even in simple settings. In this work, we study capacity-limited scaling in a bottlenecked bigram model with power-law (Zipf) token statistics, viewed as an analytically tractable toy model of a large language model. Fixed random embeddings serve as a proxy for representational capacity and induce an explicit bottleneck of width, allowing us to derive scaling laws for prediction regret as a function of model width, vocabulary size, and the Zipf exponent. Our results complement recent theoretical accounts based on optimization dynamics by isolating scaling due purely to representational constraints. In the appropriate regime, the theory recovers the functional form of classical neural scaling laws and suggests that heavy-tailed language statistics may underlie both optimization- and capacity-driven scaling. Experiments natural language datasets (WikiText2, OpenWebText) closely match the predicted curves.
bullets: Studies prediction regret under Zipf-distributed token statistics.
Uses fixed random embeddings to impose an explicit representational bottleneck of variable width.
Derives scaling with model width, vocabulary size, and Zipf exponent.
Recovers the functional form of classical neural scaling laws in an appropriate regime.
Predicted curves closely match results on WikiText2 and OpenWebText.
papers.selection_reason: Analytical scaling laws for a bottlenecked bigram model as an LLM toy model; relevant to LLM architecture and scaling understanding.
papers.title: Exact Scaling Laws for a Random-Features Bigram Model
papers.tldr: An analytically tractable random-features bigram model derives capacity-driven scaling laws that closely match experiments on natural-language data.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation provides dense supervision on the student's own samples, but its targets still come from the teacher. Verifier reinforcement learning (RL) instead uses an outcome signal, but it provides no direct constraint on capabilities outside the verifier. Combining the two is difficult for diffusion language models (dLLMs), because bidirectional denoising makes the policy likelihoods required by ratio-based RL unreliable. We develop a likelihood-free pipeline for a mixture-of-experts dLLM. Each rollout group is routed by verifier outcome. Mixed groups use ratio-free, group-centred REINFORCE. If every student rollout fails but a teacher succeeds, the model receives dense KL supervision on the student's denoising canvases. All other groups are skipped. A KL term anchored to the distilled checkpoint limits changes outside the verifier reward. The tool-calling teacher succeeds on only 18.6% of the training prompts. At 24 denoising steps, distillation exceeds the teacher by 6.77 percentage points, and routing improves the distilled checkpoint by a further 18.31 points. Routing lowers reasoning-trace accuracy by 0.71 points but raises direct-answer accuracy on the same items by 13.21 points. The anchored arm restores trace accuracy. Its tool-calling score differs by -0.16 points, with a confidence interval that includes zero, although this comparison also removes a small fallback distillation route. A domain-conditional recipe retains a 16.37-point tool-calling gain; a second seed gives 18.23 points and reproduces both preservation results, but the math result is seed-dependent. We pre-registered every arm and evaluated each comparison on paired items in a single sweep on one machine.
authors: Wentao Lu, Tianyu Zhu, Jesse Clark
bullets: Addresses unreliable policy likelihoods in bidirectional denoising, which hinder ratio-based RL for diffusion language models.
Routes rollout groups by verifier outcomes: mixed outcomes use group-centred, ratio-free REINFORCE; all-failure groups with teacher success receive dense KL distillation; other groups are skipped.
Anchors training to the distilled checkpoint with KL regularization to limit changes outside the verifier objective.
At 24 denoising steps, distillation beats the teacher by 6.77 points, while routing adds 18.31 points; direct-answer accuracy rises 13.21 points despite a 0.71-point drop in reasoning-trace accuracy.
The anchored variant restores trace accuracy, and domain-conditional training retains a 16.37-point tool-calling gain; math improvements are seed-dependent.
papers.selection_reason: Training method for diffusion language models combining distillation and verifier RL; relevant to LLM training/architecture advances.
papers.title: Outcome-Routed Distillation and Reinforcement Learning for Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: A likelihood-free, verifier-routed training pipeline combines distillation and reinforcement learning for diffusion language models, improving tool-calling performance while largely preserving broader capabilities.

papers.abstract: Transformers are intuitively considered to be efficient at copying from their inputs. We actually show that the ability of LLMs to copy in context can be improved through explicit modeling. We propose Copy-Paste Language Models (CPLMs), which add a lightweight Copy-Paste head to the conventional language modeling (LM) head. CPLMs improve training efficiency, downstream performance, and offer new operating points in long-context and retrieval setups. We validate our approach by pretraining models from 135M to 1.7B parameters, showing improvements across all scales and backbones with negligible training and inference overheads. We explain the success of CPLMs by showing that they partially mitigate the LM head gradient bottleneck through an alternative gradient path.
bullets: Transformers may copy from inputs inefficiently despite appearing naturally suited to copying.
CPLMs augment the standard language-modeling head with a lightweight Copy-Paste head.
The method improves training efficiency, downstream performance, and provides useful operating points for long-context and retrieval tasks.
Improvements hold across model scales from 135M to 1.7B parameters and across backbones, with negligible training and inference overhead.
The authors attribute the gains to an alternative gradient path that partially alleviates the LM-head gradient bottleneck.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a Copy-Paste head to explicitly model input copying in LLMs, improving training efficiency and long-context performance, which is relevant to LLM architectures and efficient attention.
papers.title: Copy-Paste Language Models
papers.tldr: Copy-Paste Language Models add a lightweight copy mechanism that improves in-context copying, efficiency, and downstream performance with negligible overhead.

papers.abstract: Large language models impose substantial memory demands and arithmetic costs during inference. Dense-to-mixture-of-experts (MoE) conversion is a model optimization technique that aims to reduce these arithmetic costs. Dense-to-MoE conversion partitions pretrained feed-forward network (FFN) neurons into experts and selects a subset for each token. Leading methods fall into two categories: analytic methods produce a converted model quickly using heuristics, while learning methods produce a model much more slowly by optimizing via gradients. Both approaches, however, fix the same active expert count, or "utilization," at every layer. We introduce Spectral-MoE, which learns to allocate a utilization budget heterogeneously across layers. Its name draws a metaphor between separating a dense FFN into experts and separating a light beam into its spectrum. Spectral-MoE consists of two distinct approaches: a static approach that uses a single per-layer scalar which is shared across tokens, and a dynamic approach which emits a per-token schedule. We demonstrate that both allocators improve performance over uniform on both the analytic-based and learning-based SOTA dense-to-MoE methods. At 25% FFN utilization, dynamic allocation reduces WikiText-2 perplexity relative to uniform by 1.04, 2.96, and 2.71 points on the learned base for Llama-2-7B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B, respectively. The corresponding reductions on the analytic base are 2.45, 6.26, and 2.17 points. On the learned base, dynamic allocation improves six-task mean accuracy over uniform by an average of 1.5, 4.2, and 3.6 percentage points across the three models at FFN utilizations of 12.5%, 25%, and 50%, respectively. These results establish per-layer expert utilization as a novel optimization axis in dense-to-MoE conversion.
authors: Zachary Broveak, Christian Kubicka, Thierry Tambe
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of fixed per-layer expert utilization in dense-to-MoE conversion.
Introduces static per-layer allocation shared across tokens and dynamic per-token allocation schedules.
Both approaches improve analytic- and learning-based conversion methods over uniform utilization.
At 25% FFN utilization, dynamic allocation lowers WikiText-2 perplexity by 1.04–6.26 points across the evaluated models and bases.
Dynamic allocation also improves six-task mean accuracy by 1.5–4.2 percentage points on the learned bases across tested utilization levels.
papers.selection_reason: Dense-to-MoE conversion reduces LLM inference cost; per-layer utilization is a novel optimization axis.
papers.title: Spectral-MoE: Heterogeneous Per-Layer Expert Utilization in Dense-to-MoE Conversion
papers.tldr: Spectral-MoE improves dense-to-MoE conversion by allocating different expert-utilization budgets across layers instead of using one uniform count.

papers.abstract: Transformer language models develop attention heads that specialize in syntactic relations, for example, attending from verbs to their subjects. Do these heads play a causal role in the model's syntactic predictions? Evidence for such a role is mixed to negative: even when we force these heads to attend to a distractor noun other than the subject, the model's syntactic predictions are still more consistent with the subject than with the distractor. Interventions on specialized syntax heads had a significantly stronger effect on syntactic predictions than interventions on random heads, but only in one of the two measures we propose.
bullets: The study tests whether heads attending along syntactic relations, such as verbs attending to subjects, causally influence syntax.
Forcing syntax heads to attend to distractor nouns does not shift predictions away from the true subject.
Intervening on syntax heads affects syntactic predictions more than intervening on random heads under one proposed measure.
The findings provide limited evidence for a causal role and differ across evaluation measures.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates the causal role of syntax-specialized attention heads in Transformer LLMs, contributing to the understanding of LLM architectures and behavior.
papers.title: Do Syntax Heads Influence Model Behavior?
papers.tldr: Syntax-specialized attention heads respond to interventions, but evidence that they causally drive syntactic predictions remains mixed and generally weak.

papers.abstract: While work on LLM-based regression has largely focused on scalar prediction, multi-output text regression remains less explored. We present DualView, a parameter-efficient approach to leverage LLMs for multi-output text regression. \method{} first extracts broad and output-specific representations from a frozen LLM, then uses a dual-branch architecture to produce the full score vector. Across five heterogeneous regression tasks and eight LLMs (up to 122B), DualView outperforms seven supervised regression baselines while requiring 82--1842 times fewer fitted parameters than the three strongest baselines. These improvements extend across individual output dimensions and persist even with limited training data. Notably, DualView using a smaller open-weight LLM can outperform unsupervised prediction with Gemini 3.1 Pro. Controlled ablations show that broad and output-specific evidence provide complementary predictive benefits, while lightweight shared predictors achieve strong performance with fewer trainable parameters.
authors: Yiheng Su, Junyi Jessy Li, Matthew Lease
bullets: Addresses the underexplored problem of predicting multiple regression outputs from text with LLMs.
Extracts broad and output-specific representations, then combines them through a dual-branch architecture.
Evaluated across five heterogeneous tasks and eight LLMs, including models up to 122B parameters.
Outperforms seven supervised baselines while fitting substantially fewer parameters; gains persist with limited training data.
Ablations show complementary value from both evidence types and effective lightweight shared predictors.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a parameter-efficient dual-branch architecture for multi-output text regression, which is a relevant methodological contribution to LLM architectures and efficiency.
papers.title: DUALVIEW: Leveraging Broad and Output-Specific Evidence for LLM-based Multi-Output Text Regression
papers.tldr: DualView enables parameter-efficient multi-output text regression by combining broad and output-specific evidence from a frozen LLM.

papers.abstract: With the growing number of LLMs available, selecting which one to use for a prompt has become a key question. A large part of the routing literature relies on semantically embedding prompts into a vector space and then applying a lightweight classifier to the embedded representations. These methods perform robustly in-distribution but they struggle to generalize to unseen tasks. By studying the geometry of semantic embeddings, we trace a clear failure mode: features that determine the neighbors of unseen prompts are an unreliable proxy for LLM selection. We therefore replace the semantic embedding with the following map: we run a partial forward pass of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on the prompt and use the hidden state of its last token at a deep layer as the representation. When applying kNN and other simple classifiers to this new representation, we obtain a clear result in generalization: on average across cost penalties, their performance improves. Moreover, kNN and another simple classifier that we propose outperform every evaluated semantic-embedding baseline. Our two simple methods also beat a recent SoTA hidden-states based router on RouterBench.
authors: Leonardo Torti, Emanuele Rimoldi, Tomer Galanti, Tomaso Poggio, Pierfrancesco Beneventano
bullets: Semantic-embedding routers work well in-distribution but struggle on unseen tasks.
Embedding geometry reveals that semantic neighbors are unreliable proxies for which LLM should answer a prompt.
The proposed representation uses the last-token hidden state from a deep layer of a partial Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct forward pass.
Simple kNN and a proposed classifier improve average generalization across cost penalties and outperform evaluated semantic-embedding baselines.
Both methods also outperform a recent hidden-state router on RouterBench.
papers.selection_reason: Studies LLM routing using hidden states and embedding geometry, directly relevant to LLM selection and generalization.
papers.title: Embedding Geometry Shapes LLM Routing: Tracing Failure Modes and Improving Generalization
papers.tldr: LLM routers generalize better to unseen tasks when they use deep hidden-state representations rather than semantic prompt embeddings.

papers.abstract: Evaluation of large language models (LLMs) remains largely pre-scientific: it involves many design decisions, with little guidance on how to make them. These choices can substantially affect measured performance and, consequently, decisions about subsequent pretraining. To identify effective evaluation setups, we investigate 8 aspects, such as task formulation or the number of in-context examples. We compare the setups using three widely-used signal criteria, repurposed as normative meta-measures: monotonicity, non-randomness, and ranking consistency of the evaluation scores across intermediate checkpoints. In an early pretraining scenario, we evaluate these setups on 26 monolingual 2B-parameter models trained on different types of data, using 80 tasks in four languages. We also examine the setups on three larger LLMs ($\geq$7B) in the same four languages and explore how the preferred setups change with model scale. Our results yield concrete recommendations: some choices, such as the use of multiple prompts, are consistently useful, whereas others, such as task formulation, depend on model scale. More generally, our framework serves as a recipe for the choice of evaluation setups in new scenarios.
authors: Shenbin Qian, David Samuel, Jind\v{r}ich Helcl, Andrey Kutuzov, Stephan Oepen
bullets: Studies eight evaluation aspects, including task formulation and the number of in-context examples.
Uses monotonicity, non-randomness, and ranking consistency as normative meta-measures.
Evaluates setups across 26 monolingual 2B-parameter models, 80 tasks, and four languages, plus three larger models.
Finds that multiple prompts are consistently helpful, while task formulation preferences vary with model scale.
Provides practical recommendations and a general recipe for choosing evaluation setups in new scenarios.
papers.selection_reason: Framework for selecting reliable evaluation setups for base LLM benchmarking; relevant to LLM research.
papers.title: How to Evaluate When You Don't Know How to Evaluate? Choosing Reliable Setups for Base Language Model Benchmarking
papers.tldr: The paper proposes a framework for selecting reliable base-LLM evaluation setups by comparing design choices against checkpoint-based signal criteria.

papers.abstract: Can AI agents carry out research on open scientific problems? We introduce Into the Unknown, a benchmark that provides an agent with a science paper along with a research direction to pursue and tasks it to write a follow-up paper. We work with scientists at US Department of Energy (DOE) national laboratories, who each contribute an unpublished follow-up direction from their own work together with the necessary conditions a submission must meet. While assessing the quality of a follow-up paper is challenging in general, using these conditions to form a rubric makes evaluation more tractable for research problems that have no reference answer. We have nine frontier agents write 15 follow-ups each, spanning quantum computing, plasma physics, computational chemistry, materials science, and scientific machine learning domains. None of the 135 submissions satisfies all the conditions, and 114 fail our integrity check, most often because the paper claims work that was never done or reports numbers that contradict the recorded evidence. Overall, agents readily produce papers that look like follow-ups, but none meets the standard of the domain scientist, leaving substantial headroom. Our code and data are publicly available.
authors: Seungone Kim, Jiayi Geng, Young-Jun Lee, Bo Liu, Juyoung Suk, Nicholas Lubbers, Mitchell Wood, Marcus Noack, Yong-Xin Yao, Yuan Shi, Roxana Bujack, Cristina Garcia Cardona, Austin Rodriguez, Ilon Joseph, Woojin Cho, Zora Zhiruo Wang, Chuanyang Jin, Ian Wu, Apurva Gandhi, Tianjian Li, Weiwei Sun, Carolin Lawrence, Kiril Gashteovski, Dongyeop Kang, Jay Shin, Akari Asai, Graham Neubig, Sean Welleck
bullets: Introduces a benchmark in which agents receive a scientific paper and research direction, then write a follow-up paper.
Uses unpublished research directions from DOE national-laboratory scientists and evaluates submissions against scientist-defined conditions.
Covers quantum computing, plasma physics, computational chemistry, materials science, and scientific machine learning.
Nine agents produced 15 follow-ups each; none satisfied all rubric conditions.
114 of 135 submissions failed integrity checks, commonly claiming unperformed work or reporting evidence-inconsistent numbers.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmarks AI agents on open scientific research, relevant to LLM agent capabilities and evaluation.
papers.title: Into the Unknown: Benchmarking AI agents on open scientific research problems
papers.tldr: Into the Unknown benchmarks AI agents on open-ended scientific research and finds that none of 135 generated follow-up papers met all domain-specific requirements, with many containing integrity failures.

papers.abstract: Generating novel molecules with desired properties is a central challenge in drug discovery. Although foundational work focused on de novo generation, practical use cases require a more complex setting: conditioning on an initial seed molecule, optimizing multiple properties, and operating in data-sparse regimes. We introduce PairIT, a flexible training framework for autoregressive transformers over SMILES sequences that enables seeded generation by learning from pairs of structurally similar molecules. By leveraging matched pairs, the model learns to generate local, chemically meaningful edits that improve a property of the seed molecule. Prompt tokens extend this framework by specifying the target property, desired direction, and approximate magnitude of change. Multiple prompt tokens can be concatenated to enable multi-property optimization at inference time. For properties where pair supervision alone is insufficient, reinforcement learning post-training can further improve optimization, providing a tunable trade-off between proximity to the seed and the optimization objective. PairIT naturally supports pretraining on a large dataset and fine-tuning on a smaller dataset, which is critical for performance in data-sparse regimes. Surprisingly, we observe diminishing returns to the scale of the pretraining dataset. We demonstrate empirically on MoleculeNet and Therapeutics Data Commons datasets that, with appropriate paired-data curation, a standard transformer model of modest size (68M parameters) can achieve robust seeded molecular optimization in low-data regimes.
authors: Hannah Lawrence, Bodhi P. Vani, Ji Won Park, Natasa Tagasovska, Samuel Don Stanton, Andrew Martin Watkins, Michael Maser, Ewa M. Nowara
bullets: Addresses molecule optimization with a starting seed, multiple property goals, and sparse training data.
Learns local chemical edits from structurally similar molecule pairs represented as SMILES sequences.
Uses prompt tokens to specify target properties, optimization direction, and approximate change; prompts can be combined for multi-property optimization.
Optional reinforcement-learning post-training improves optimization while controlling similarity to the seed.
Experiments on MoleculeNet and Therapeutics Data Commons show robust optimization with a modest 68M-parameter transformer; larger pretraining data offers diminishing returns.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces PairIT, an autoregressive transformer framework for low-data molecule optimization, demonstrating a method for sequence generation and optimization.
papers.title: PairIT: Autoregressive Transformers for Low-Data Molecule Optimization
papers.tldr: PairIT enables low-data, seeded molecular optimization by training autoregressive transformers on matched molecule pairs and prompting them for targeted property improvements.

papers.abstract: Structured pruning reduces LLM inference costs by removing model components to produce smaller dense models. However, existing methods can cause reasoning performance to collapse on long-form reasoning tasks such as AIME. We propose \textit{LayerTrim}, a training-free structured pruning method that identifies redundant decoder layers and selectively trims their MLP features while preserving attention and decoder depth. LayerTrim is the first training-free structured pruning method designed to preserve long-form reasoning without gradients or recovery training. Across three reasoning language models and five benchmarks, LayerTrim outperforms existing structured pruning methods in most evaluated settings, improving average accuracy by up to 21.4 percentage points over RESP. On \texttt{Qwen3-14B}, LayerTrim achieves 1.24$\times$ faster prefill and 19.7\% lower peak GPU memory than the dense model, while better preserving reasoning ability. It also achieves the shortest average generation length among evaluated pruned models, while retaining the highest average accuracy. These results demonstrate that LayerTrim improves reasoning efficiency through both structural compression and reduced token generation.
authors: Woosang Lim, Haneul Yoo, Vincent-Daniel Yun, Sungjoo Yoo
bullets: Targets reasoning degradation caused by conventional structured pruning on long-form tasks such as AIME.
Identifies redundant decoder layers and selectively trims their MLP features without gradients or recovery training.
Evaluated across three reasoning language models and five benchmarks, outperforming existing pruning methods in most settings.
Improves average accuracy by up to 21.4 percentage points over RESP.
On Qwen3-14B, delivers 1.24× faster prefill and 19.7% lower peak GPU memory than the dense model while preserving reasoning ability.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a training-free structured pruning method (LayerTrim) for LLMs that preserves reasoning ability, addressing efficiency and performance trade-offs.
papers.title: Unlocking Structured Pruning for Reasoning Language Models via Attention-Preserving MLP Trimming
papers.tldr: LayerTrim is a training-free structured pruning method that reduces reasoning-model inference costs while preserving long-form reasoning by trimming MLP features and retaining attention and decoder depth.

papers.abstract: Activation steering controls large language models at inference time, but its effectiveness depends on the choice of reference data. We introduce genesis steering, which derives a genesis vector from contrastive examples in the model's own fine-tuning data. When these data are unavailable, we draw on the membership inference literature to identify likely training examples and construct a proxy dataset. We establish two theoretical results on optimal displacement to the decision boundary and reduced proxy-estimation bias. We evaluate genesis steering and membership-based proxy construction on T\"ulu-3-8B, whose fine-tuning data are publicly available, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as a control. We find that safety data from T\"ulu-3-8B's training mixture yield stronger steering than external datasets on both models. On T\"ulu-3-8B, membership scores largely agree in identifying training examples, and vectors built from top-ranked examples achieve competitive performance against random subsets of the same size. In contrast, the results on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct hint that a MIA method will only have a positive effect if the mean direction shift with MIA-filtered in-distribution data is much less severe than the direction shift with OoD data.
authors: Tora Bodin, Eric Aubinais, Ilaria Torre, Chih-Hong Cheng
bullets: Activation steering is sensitive to the choice of reference data.
The method builds a genesis vector from contrastive examples in training data; membership inference identifies likely examples when the data are unavailable.
Theoretical analysis characterizes optimal displacement toward decision boundaries and reduced proxy-estimation bias.
On Tülu-3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, in-distribution safety data produced stronger steering than external datasets.
Membership-ranked examples were competitive on Tülu-3-8B, while benefits on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct depended on limiting the induced mean-direction shift.
papers.selection_reason: Improves activation steering for LLMs by utilizing training data, offering a method to control model behavior at inference time.
papers.title: Genesis Steering: Better Activation Steering Through Training Data
papers.tldr: Genesis steering improves activation steering by deriving control vectors from a model’s own fine-tuning data or membership-inference-based proxies.

papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) allows language models to adapt their behavior from instructions and demonstrations in a prompt, but accuracy alone does not reveal how contextual information controls their predictions. We study the acquisition and trainability of ICL with a controlled diagnostic that separates copying a nearby demonstration from integrating information across the prompt. Across 17 models, about a third prefer the copied answer, a few are undecided, and the rest prefer the rule-consistent answer, which goes with higher accuracy and with control by the requested value rather than the closest conflicting example. Checkpoint analyses show that models begin prioritizing task-relevant prompt tokens over conflicting examples long before their accuracy improves beyond chance level. In matched training experiments, synthetic documents that define endings and then query them shift models toward compositional responses on the controlled diagnostic, whereas fine-tuning on definition exercises built from rewritten real documents improves accuracy when prompts reassign label meanings. The results suggest that ICL is not acquired as a single, uniform capability. Instead, prompt control, answer preference, construction without candidates, and transfer can develop along distinct trajectories.
authors: Minglai Yang, Xinyu Guo, Renxiong Wang, Sunjie Hou, Daniel Yue Zhang, Yunzhong He
bullets: A controlled diagnostic distinguishes copying a nearby demonstration from integrating information across the prompt.
Across 17 models, many favor copied answers, while rule-consistent preferences align with higher accuracy and better prompt control.
Checkpoint analyses show sensitivity to task-relevant tokens emerges before accuracy rises above chance.
Synthetic training promotes compositional responses, while rewritten-document exercises improve accuracy when label meanings are reassigned.
ICL components—including prompt control, answer preference, candidate-free construction, and transfer—follow distinct developmental paths.
papers.selection_reason: Studies how language models develop in-context learning, a core capability of LLMs.
papers.title: From Copying to Composition: How Language Models Develop In-Context Learning
papers.tldr: Language models develop in-context learning through separable abilities, gradually shifting from copying nearby examples to composing answers from task-relevant prompt information.

papers.abstract: Group-based reinforcement learning enables large language model agents to learn from sparse outcome rewards in long-horizon tasks. Recent methods derive step-level credit by comparing observation-matched experiences across trajectories. However, identical observations can occur in different contexts, and matched peers are not equally informative for a given decision. Moreover, favorable terminal outcomes can obscure redundant actions or detours within successful trajectories. To address these two challenges, we propose Contextual Credit Policy Optimization (CCPO). For the first, CCPO weights observation-matched peers from other trajectories by contextual similarity, computed from frozen LLM representations and accumulated trajectory statistics, allowing peers from similar contexts to contribute more to a step's baseline. For the second, CCPO pairs historical credit, which compares the realized return against the weighted peer baseline, with future credit, which measures the change in contextual outcome value over a short realized continuation. A step is thus credited for the progress it makes, not only for its trajectory's eventual outcome. Both credits are computed in hindsight from rollouts already collected for training, enabling CCPO to address these challenges without an auxiliary value critic. Across two Qwen2.5-Instruct backbones (1.5B and 7B), CCPO achieves up to 97.4% success on ALFWorld and 79.4% on WebShop and outperforms GRPO by up to 21.6 and 18.5 points. Ablations show that contextual weighting outperforms uniform weighting, and that historical and future credit serve as complementary learning signals.
authors: Huiwen Han, Ziyao Zeng, Zihao Zhu, Sisong Bei, Hao Wang, Hongyu Xu, Yan Han, Degui Zhi, Zhiwen Fan
bullets: Addresses misleading peer comparisons across contexts and redundant actions hidden by successful final outcomes.
Weights observation-matched peers using frozen LLM representations and trajectory statistics.
Combines historical credit from peer baselines with future credit from short-term contextual value changes.
Computes both signals retrospectively from existing rollouts, avoiding an auxiliary critic.
Reaches up to 97.4% success on ALFWorld and 79.4% on WebShop, outperforming GRPO by up to 21.6 and 18.5 points.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses credit assignment in RL for LLM agents, proposing Contextual Credit Policy Optimization to handle sparse rewards in long-horizon tasks.
papers.title: Contextual Credit Policy Optimization
papers.tldr: CCPO improves long-horizon LLM agent learning by assigning context-sensitive, progress-based step credit without an auxiliary value critic.

papers.abstract: Chatbot Arena ranks language models with the Bradley-Terry model, which gives each model one score and so assumes Luce's choice axiom. Choice theory predicts where this fails: near-copies are told apart more decisively than their scores imply. On 1.8 million Arena votes, votes between versions of one model are 1.37 times as decisive as Bradley-Terry predicts, between sizes of one generation 1.26 times and between models of one lab 1.12 times; a release a year later gives consistent multipliers, and the effect survives alternative tie treatments, prompt subsets and topics, and timing checks. How alike two models' answers are worded and formatted tracks the effect. A correction with four to six parameters predicts held-out votes better than Bradley-Terry and than models with hundreds of parameters, mostly by modelling ties; frozen and carried to new releases in a test fixed in advance, its gains are concentrated in ties, and better head-to-head odds are not established. The leaderboard order barely moves. With language-model judges and three-answer menus, a near-copy takes votes mostly from its twin when choices are pooled over prompts (log-odds shift +0.10, 95% interval 0.05 to 0.16); within a prompt the shift is smaller and clear for two of four judges.
authors: Soovadeep Bakshi, Apurba Bose, Aishwarya Bose, Sandip Nandi
bullets: Near-duplicate models are distinguished more decisively than Bradley–Terry predicts: 1.37× for model versions, 1.26× for same-generation sizes, and 1.12× for models from the same lab.
The effect persists across release timing, tie treatments, prompt subsets, topics, and other checks, and is associated with similarity in answer wording and formatting.
A compact 4–6-parameter correction predicts held-out votes better than Bradley–Terry and much larger alternatives, mainly by modelling ties.
The correction’s gains carry to new releases, but improved head-to-head odds are not established and leaderboard rankings change little.
Language-model judges also favor a near-copy’s twin when votes are pooled across prompts, with weaker and less consistent within-prompt effects.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes LLM evaluation/ranking (Chatbot Arena) and Luce's axiom failure, directly relevant to LLM research and evaluation.
papers.title: Similar Models, Broken Odds: Where Luce's Axiom Fails in Chatbot Arena
papers.tldr: Chatbot Arena’s Bradley–Terry rankings miss systematic choice effects among similar models, especially in how ties are handled, though correcting them barely changes leaderboard order.

papers.abstract: Automatic prompt optimization (APO) uses feedback from model responses to improve prompts automatically. However, its effectiveness is usually measured through overall scores, which do not reveal which questions become correct, which previously correct answers become wrong, or whether improvements extend to unseen questions. We introduce Reflective Feedback-Driven Prompt Optimization (RFDPO), a tool that tracks recoveries (incorrect to correct), regressions (correct to incorrect), and churn (all changed outcomes). RFDPO uses this feedback to guide subsequent revisions and records prompt changes throughout optimization. We evaluate RFDPO across five benchmarks covering law, knowledge, instruction following, mathematics, and privacy, using GPT-5 as the optimizer and GPT-4o-mini and GPT-4.1 Mini as solvers. Our results show that overall accuracy can hide substantial changes: in five of nine configurations, churn was at least five times the absolute net change, and a single-item net change concealed up to 17 changed outcomes. Average validation gains were 7.9 percentage points, compared with 5.2 points on held-out tests. In a controlled ablation on LegalBench-Hearsay, item-level feedback reduced churn by 40% ($p=0.024$) while maintaining similar net gains. These findings motivate reporting recovery, regression, churn, and performance on unseen data alongside overall accuracy.
bullets: Overall accuracy may obscure substantial question-level changes: churn was at least five times the net change in five of nine configurations.
RFDPO uses item-level feedback to guide prompt revisions and records how prompts evolve.
Across five benchmarks, average gains were 7.9 percentage points on validation data and 5.2 points on held-out tests.
On LegalBench-Hearsay, item-level feedback reduced churn by 40% while preserving similar net gains.
The study recommends reporting recoveries, regressions, churn, and unseen-data performance alongside accuracy.
papers.selection_reason: Focuses on prompt optimization for LLMs, introducing item-level feedback metrics to track regressions and recoveries, which is relevant to LLM evaluation and optimization.
papers.title: Beyond Aggregate Accuracy: Item-Level Transitions in Prompt Optimization
papers.tldr: RFDPO improves prompt optimization by tracking item-level recoveries, regressions, and churn, revealing changes that aggregate accuracy can hide.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has substantially improved the reasoning of autoregressive and discrete-diffusion language models. Language models that generate continuous token embeddings are emerging as a strong alternative, but RL post-training for them remains understudied. We propose \method{}, a post-training framework for continuous flow language models. Such a model denoises token embeddings over multiple steps and decodes them into discrete tokens only at the last step. To obtain pathwise gradients, which backpropagate through continuous actions and have much lower variance than REINFORCE, we introduce a critic that estimates the value of intermediate token embeddings, bypassing the non-differentiable decoding step. The critic must also keep track of the value function as the policy changes; to this end, we design a critic that predicts a value from every token representation and improves policy optimization. Across four reasoning tasks, \method{} reliably improves a continuous flow language model through RL post-training and outperforms baseline methods of the same type.
authors: Xu Han, Jiajing Hu, Li-Ping Liu
bullets: Addresses the understudied problem of RL post-training for language models that generate continuous token embeddings.
Uses a critic to estimate values for intermediate embeddings, avoiding the non-differentiable final token-decoding step.
Employs pathwise gradients, which offer lower variance than REINFORCE for continuous actions.
Introduces a critic that predicts values from every token representation while tracking policy changes.
Reliably improves the model across four reasoning tasks and outperforms same-type baseline methods.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a post-training framework for continuous flow language models using RL, addressing a gap in RL for continuous token embeddings.
papers.title: Backpropagating Verifier Rewards Through Continuous Flow Language Models
papers.tldr: A reinforcement-learning framework improves continuous flow language models by backpropagating verifier rewards through intermediate token embeddings.

papers.abstract: Reliable uncertainty quantification remains an important challenge in AI. Hierarchical Bayesian methods provide a principled framework for this by representing unknown quantities through posterior distributions. Joint inference of neural-network parameters and prior hyperparameters is challenging for conventional Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods due to strong dependencies. In this work, we introduce the multilevel particle marginal Metropolis-Hastings (MLPMMH) method, which combines pseudo-marginal inference for the hyperparameters with coupled sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) across hierarchy of network-width truncations for conditional parameter inference. The hierarchy is induced by a trace-class neural network (TNN) prior with width-dependent decay, motivated empirically by the compressible structure observed in trained neural-network parameters. Under standard multilevel coupling assumptions, we establish that MLPMMH achieves mean-square error (MSE) $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^2)$ at expected computational cost $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-2})$, and verify the predicted rate on a Bayesian regression problem. To address larger-scale applications, we further introduce S-MLPMMH, a practical approximation that replaces the exact sampling components with a PCA-based hierarchy and scalable Bayesian Monte Carlo. Experiments on MNIST demonstrate competitive predictive performance and uncertainty quantification while exploiting the parallel structure of the approximation. Software has been made publicly available at https://github.com/submission-code-anon/mlpmmh-anon.
authors: Neil K. Chada, Simon Cotter, Kody J. H. Law, Xinzhu Liang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of jointly inferring neural-network parameters and prior hyperparameters with conventional MCMC.
Proposes MLPMMH, combining pseudo-marginal hyperparameter inference with coupled SMC over network-width truncations under a trace-class neural-network prior.
Provides a theoretical MSE–cost guarantee of O(ε²) error at O(ε⁻²) expected computational cost under standard coupling assumptions.
Introduces S-MLPMMH, a practical PCA-based approximation with scalable Bayesian Monte Carlo for larger applications.
Regression experiments verify the predicted rate, while MNIST experiments show competitive prediction and uncertainty quantification with parallelizable computation.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a new method (MLPMMH) for hierarchical Bayesian inference in neural networks, relevant for uncertainty quantification in LLMs.
papers.title: Theoretical and Practical Advances in Hierarchical Bayesian Deep Learning Methodology
papers.tldr: The paper introduces hierarchical particle-MCMC methods that make Bayesian neural-network inference more scalable while retaining principled uncertainty quantification.

papers.abstract: Training large language models (LLMs) across geographically distributed and poorly interconnected compute pools or data centers has become a topic of significant interest. This has led to increased study of local optimization methods such as DiLoco for LLMs, especially those that use local (or inner) adaptive or preconditioned optimizers, which are critical for high-performance LLM training. However, a central challenge remains: it is well known that increasing the number of model replicas (replica scaling) while fixing the total training budget leads to monotonically decreasing performance. Existing work has empirically demonstrated that the choice of inner optimizer (Muon v.s. AdamW) can significantly improve this trend, but offers only limited explanation of the performance difference. In this work, we consider a range of inner-optimizers and identify two important factors that impact replica scaling: (1) the covariance structure of the pseudo-gradients and (2) the impact of batch size on the pseudogradient's noise scale. Based on these insights, we theoretically and empirically demonstrate that whitening-based pre-conditioning is a powerful inner-optimizer desideratum. Our empirical evaluation extends the results to reveal that whitening-based inner-optimizers achieve strong replica scaling (for 8-96 replicas), with performance relative to DP improving as parameters and data are scaled.
authors: Eugene Belilovsky, Stefan Horoi, Edouard Oyallon, Benjamin Th\'erien
bullets: Replica scaling under a fixed training budget typically degrades performance as the number of replicas grows.
The study examines how different local or inner optimizers affect this scaling in methods such as DiLoCo.
Two key factors are identified: pseudo-gradient covariance structure and batch-size effects on pseudo-gradient noise.
Theory and experiments indicate that whitening-based preconditioning is a desirable inner-optimizer property.
Across 8–96 replicas, whitening-based optimizers show strong scaling, with relative performance improving as model and data scales increase.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses training LLMs across distributed compute pools, focusing on inner optimizers and replica scaling, which is core to LLM research.
papers.title: How Inner Optimizers Shape Replica Scaling
papers.tldr: Whitening-based inner optimizers improve the scalability of distributed LLM training across increasing numbers of replicas.

papers.abstract: Understanding the dynamics of language acquisition in Large Language Models (LLMs) is crucial for uncovering how statistical representations evolve into structured linguistic capabilities. However, most existing studies focus primarily on fully trained models, leaving the developmental trajectory across intermediate training stages largely underexplored. In this work, we leverage intermediate checkpoints from open-source models (e.g., Pythia and OLMo) under teacher-forcing evaluation to systematically investigate language acquisition across training steps and model scales. We focus on four core characteristics: morphological structure acquisition, embedding drift, repetition dominance, and co-occurrence effects. Our findings reveal that models acquire morphological structures well before semantic embeddings stabilize. Furthermore, we show that training dataset size has a positive impact on divergence recognition, while co-occurrence during pre-training and repetition during inference have a negative impact on divergence recognition and associative link generation.
authors: Forough Shirin Abkenar, Haoshuo Fu, Liang Feng, Ning Yan, Masood S. Mortazavi
bullets: Studies language acquisition across training stages and model scales rather than only at convergence.
Analyzes morphological structure acquisition, embedding drift, repetition dominance, and co-occurrence effects.
Finds morphological structures emerge earlier than stable semantic embeddings.
Larger training datasets improve divergence recognition.
Pre-training co-occurrence and inference-time repetition negatively affect divergence recognition and associative link generation.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes the training dynamics of LLMs, specifically tracing morphology, semantics, and divergence during language acquisition, providing insights into the developmental trajectory of foundation models.
papers.title: Tracing Morphology, Semantics, and Divergence in Language Acquisition
papers.tldr: Intermediate checkpoints reveal that LLMs develop morphological structure before semantic representations stabilize, while repetition and co-occurrence hinder divergence recognition and associative links.

papers.abstract: Pluralistic alignment needs to accommodate diverse preferences under limited human feedback. Using AI simulators to label preference comparisons reduces annotation costs, but variation in simulation accuracy across individuals can leave some people's preferences poorly represented in training. We study how to allocate human feedback across people to construct training data for pluralistic alignment, and how this allocation affects the trained policy. To make this allocation explicit and controllable, we define a social welfare objective over individual supervision utilities that measure label quality. Each query's marginal welfare gain depends on its expected supervision improvement, the recipient's current utility, and application-designated priority. Welfare-Aware Preference Acquisition (WAPA) uses auxiliary reference models to estimate query gains and individual utilities, then selects queries by estimated marginal welfare gain while updating recipient utilities. We prove exact optimality of the acquisition algorithm for the estimated welfare objective under a fixed query budget and model predictions. Experiments on six Roleplay collections and four OpinionQA regions demonstrate improved supervision and controllable allocation tradeoffs. Policy training on four Roleplay collections improves preference prediction for both seen and unseen individuals. When prioritizing a designated group and poorly represented individuals, acquiring human labels for 20% of comparisons recovers 75-86% of the average predictive utility gap between policies trained entirely on AI-generated labels and entirely on ground-truth labels.
authors: Ruomeng Ding, Tianwei Gao, Lianrui Geng, Mohit Bansal, Zhun Deng
bullets: Addresses uneven AI-simulator accuracy, which can leave some individuals’ preferences poorly represented in pluralistic alignment.
Defines social welfare over individual supervision utilities, incorporating expected label improvement, current utility, and application priorities.
Selects queries by estimated marginal welfare gain using auxiliary reference models and updates utilities after each acquisition.
Proves optimality for the estimated welfare objective under a fixed query budget and model predictions.

Across Roleplay and OpinionQA experiments, 20% human labels recovered 75–86% of the average predictive-utility gap between fully AI-labeled and fully ground-truth-trained policies when prioritizing designated or poorly represented groups.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses preference acquisition and alignment for LLMs using a welfare-aware objective to allocate human feedback, contributing to the robustness of LLM training data.
papers.title: Who Should We Listen to More? Welfare-Aware Preference Acquisition for Pluralistic Alignment
papers.tldr: WAPA allocates limited human preference feedback across people using a welfare-based strategy, improving representation of diverse preferences and enabling controllable prioritization.

papers.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) applies every rank-one component of its update to every token, and mixture-of-experts variants replace this with a learned router that activates a fixed number of components. We argue that the number of components a token needs is a detection question with a classical answer. A token's responses to the rank-one components of a trained LoRA consist of a few large values on a Gaussian noise floor whose width matches that of an untrained adapter, and the floor carries cross-talk rather than adaptation. We introduce SQUELCH, a router-free mixture of rank-one experts that (i) soft-thresholds each token's responses at a multiple of its own robust noise level, so the active rank varies per token; (ii) chooses that multiple for each module by Stein's unbiased risk estimate, so no rank budget is specified; and (iii) replaces the resulting marginal keep-or-drop decisions by one explaining-away step on the value Gram matrix, which suppresses redundant co-active components and recruits complementary ones. SQUELCH adds no trainable parameters to LoRA. We prove that the squelch is within a logarithmic factor of the oracle input-dependent allocation, that the selected threshold is risk-consistent, and that explaining away is a descent step toward the joint sparse code whose error is controlled by the coherence of co-active components. On commonsense reasoning, knowledge, math, code, and GLUE with LLaMA-3.1-8B, Qwen3, and DeBERTaV3, SQUELCH improves over LoRA by 2.2--3.2 points and over the strongest mixture baseline by 0.8--1.2 points while activating 8.6 of 32 components per token on average.
authors: Mei Okonkwo, Owen Castellanos, Ingrid Solberg, Yusuf Demirel
bullets: Motivation: LoRA applies every rank-one component to every token, although many responses appear to be cross-talk on a Gaussian noise floor.
Method: A router-free mechanism estimates each token’s robust noise level and soft-thresholds component responses, allowing the active rank to vary without a preset rank budget.
Thresholds are chosen per module using Stein’s unbiased risk estimate; an explaining-away step suppresses redundant components and favors complementary ones.
Theory: The method is near-optimal up to a logarithmic factor, has risk-consistent threshold selection, and provides coherence-based error control for joint sparse coding.
Experiments across reasoning, knowledge, math, code, and GLUE tasks report gains over LoRA and a mixture baseline while activating 8.6 of 32 components per token on average.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces SQUELCH, a router-free method for efficient token-level adaptation in LoRA, improving efficiency and performance in LLMs through noise-floor squelching and explaining-away mechanisms.
papers.title: How Many Ranks Does a Token Need? A Noise-Floor Squelch for Rank-One LoRA Experts
papers.tldr: SQUELCH dynamically selects only the rank-one LoRA components each token needs by thresholding noise and removing redundancy, improving performance while using fewer components.

papers.abstract: Token-selection methods for on-policy distillation (OPD) prioritize student-visited positions using diverse signals, including uncertainty, teacher-student disagreement, and mismatch direction. We instead derive token importance from the distillation objective itself: how much can each position's loss decrease under an equal local KL budget on the student's predictive distribution? The answer is the utility $s_t=g_t^\top F_t^\dagger g_t$, where $g_t$ is the logit gradient and $F_t$ is the categorical Fisher matrix. For reverse-KL it equals the student-weighted variance of the student-teacher log-probability ratio, and for forward-KL it equals the Pearson $\chi^2$ divergence, so the appropriate utility follows from the choice of objective. On shared training checkpoints, several independently motivated criteria, including student entropy, KL disagreement, and TIP, concentrate their importance on nearly the same positions as the derived utility at a 50\% selection fraction, while diverging at stricter fractions and for direction-specific criteria. We instantiate the utility as Fisher Utility Weighting (FUW), a continuous, mean-normalized token weighting. Across seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks and three Qwen3 student-teacher pairs, FUW improves over matched uniform OPD under both reverse-KL (1.35-4.0 macro points) and forward-KL (1.08-2.71 macro points), and is competitive with existing selective methods using a single closed-form score derived from the training objective.
authors: Narayanan Sadagopan, Yilan Chen, Vijay Lingam
bullets: Defines token utility as the loss reduction achievable under an equal local KL budget: $s_t=g_t^\top F_t^\dagger g_t$.
The utility has objective-specific forms: student-weighted log-ratio variance for reverse-KL and Pearson $\chi^2$ divergence for forward-KL.
Implements the score as continuous, mean-normalized Fisher Utility Weighting (FUW).
On seven math-reasoning benchmarks and three Qwen3 teacher–student pairs, FUW improves over matched uniform OPD for both KL directions.
Several existing criteria align with the derived utility at moderate selection rates but diverge under stricter selection or direction-specific scoring.
papers.selection_reason: Token utility weighting for on-policy distillation of reasoning LLMs.
papers.title: Token Utility for On-Policy Distillation via Local Trust-Region Optimization
papers.tldr: FUW derives token importance directly from the OPD objective and improves on uniform token weighting across multiple reasoning benchmarks and model pairs.

papers.abstract: Post-training reasoning LLMs often requires making a tradeoff between costly supervision and compute inefficiency: supervised finetuning typically requires reasoning traces, which is data inefficient since in many applications one only has prompt-answer tuples and lacks the groundtruth chain-of-thought (CoT) sequence. On the other hand, reinforcement learning (with verifiable rewards, for example) can operate without CoT data but it is much more compute-inefficient since it requires multiple autoregressive completions per optimization step, none of which are guaranteed to give a non-zero policy gradient. In this work we explore a middleground, a self-distillation technique that uses answer-only data, treating CoT as latent variables. This relies on training a partner ``inverse reasoning LLM" that generates the original's reasoning traces conditioned on the answer. The inverse model is trained once and reused across incoming batches of answer-only data, with all generation happening offline and up front, making the approach particularly suited to continual post-training. Using Qwen3-0.6B on the Countdown and GSM8K tasks, we show that after GRPO training has saturated, a single offline distillation round from the inverse model roughly doubles pass@1 on hard prompts and, on Countdown, outperforms rejection-sampling self-distillation on every hard-tail metric at every mix ratio (with smaller gains on GSM8K); rejection sampling by construction has no signal on problems the model never solves on its own. Continued GRPO on the fresh data retains an edge at hard pass@1 but trails distillation at pass@8 and pass@32 while regenerating rollouts at every step. As an added bonus we see that the inverse model has a second application as an accurate verifier of correctness. When used for best-of-$n$ selection at test time, it raises selection accuracy on Countdown from 0.753 (majority voting) to 0.969.
bullets: Addresses the tradeoff between trace-dependent supervised fine-tuning and compute-heavy reinforcement learning when only prompt–answer pairs are available.
Trains an inverse reasoning LLM to generate latent reasoning traces conditioned on known answers, then reuses it to produce offline data for self-distillation.
On Qwen3-0.6B evaluations, one distillation round after GRPO saturation roughly doubles pass@1 on hard prompts; gains are smaller on GSM8K.
On Countdown, inverse-model distillation outperforms rejection-sampling self-distillation across reported hard-tail metrics and mix ratios.
As a verifier for best-of-n selection, the inverse model improves Countdown selection accuracy from 0.753 with majority voting to 0.969.
papers.selection_reason: Inverse reasoning self-distillation for efficient post-training of reasoning LLMs.
papers.title: Inverse Reasoning Models for Efficient Post-Training and Verification from Answer-Only Data
papers.tldr: An inverse reasoning model turns answer-only data into offline reasoning traces for efficient post-training and can also verify answers accurately.

papers.abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) extends on-policy distillation (OPD) by routing domain-specific data to specialized teachers, integrating their capabilities through dense token-level supervision on student-generated trajectories. However, domain routing only distinguishes the supervision sources for different domains; updates from all domains still act on shared parameters. When teachers differ substantially in response style and domain expertise, supervision that is effective in isolation may still lead to persistent gradient conflicts and capability degradation during joint optimization. To address this challenge, we propose Cross-Teacher Guarding for MOPD (Road MOPD), which introduces non-routed teachers as auxiliary cross-domain critics on the same student trajectories and coordinates multi-teacher supervision through token-level credit assignment and gradient updates.
