Specifically, cross-teacher-guided credit assignment uses teacher agreement to strengthen token-level corrections jointly supported by the teachers and attenuate conflicting signals; preventive multi-teacher gradient projection uses auxiliary gradients from the same trajectories to constrain potentially conflicting updates and adaptively controls projection strength to retain target-domain learning signals. In experiments, Road MOPD mitigates degradation in the disadvantaged domain, gains over 5 percentage points under high conflict, and improves overall performance in low-conflict and three-domain settings.
bullets: MOPD routes domain data to specialized teachers, but shared student parameters can still suffer conflicting updates and capability degradation.
Road MOPD adds non-routed teachers as auxiliary cross-domain critics on the same student-generated trajectories.
Teacher agreement guides token-level credit assignment, emphasizing jointly supported corrections and downweighting conflicting signals.
Adaptive multi-teacher gradient projection constrains conflicting updates while preserving target-domain learning signals.
Experiments report reduced degradation in disadvantaged domains, gains exceeding 5 percentage points under high conflict, and improvements in low-conflict and three-domain settings.
papers.selection_reason: Multi-teacher distillation with gradient-conflict mitigation for LLM training.
papers.title: Beyond Domain-Routed Supervision: Cross-Teacher Guarding for Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
papers.tldr: Road MOPD reduces cross-domain gradient conflict in multi-teacher on-policy distillation by using auxiliary cross-teacher critiques for token-level supervision and gradient protection.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is now the standard way to ground Large Language Models (LLMs) in external knowledge, yet the design space of retrieval pipelines is large and the trade-offs between variants are not well understood, especially on domain-specific corpora at realistic scale. In this work, we present a controlled comparison of six retrieval strategies for scientific question answering: (i) classic top-k dense retrieval, (ii) LLM-based query rephrasing, (iii) query rephrasing followed by LLM-based reranking, (iv) multi-query fusion via Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), (v) an agentic tool-call pipeline in which the generator decides for itself whether to retrieve, and (vi) late-interaction retrieval with ColBERTv2. All six pipelines share the same generator (Meta-Llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), prompt, and evaluation protocol; the five single-vector pipelines additionally share SPECTER2 embeddings and a Chroma vector store; and all six retrieve from the full corpus of 463,971 arXiv papers dated 2024-2025. To support reproducible, large-scale evaluation, we also release a synthetic question dataset of 19,484 problem-statement and methodology questions generated by Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct from a random sample of 10,000 papers across academic domains (query generation succeeded for 9,742 of them), and every strategy is evaluated on this same query set. We describe the architecture and implementation of each pipeline, release the code and the synthetic question dataset, and evaluate each strategy with an LLM-as-a-judge protocol along multiple quality dimensions, together with direct gold-paper retrieval metrics. The result is an open testbed for studying the cost and quality trade-offs of RAG design choices on a research-literature corpus, and a basis for future work on faithfulness, retrieval robustness, and agentic retrieval.
bullets: Compares dense top-k retrieval, query rephrasing, reranking, RRF multi-query fusion, agentic retrieval, and ColBERTv2 late interaction.
Uses the same Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct generator, prompt, and evaluation protocol across pipelines.
Evaluates retrieval over 463,971 recent arXiv papers using synthetic problem-statement and methodology questions.
Releases code and a synthetic dataset of 19,484 questions generated from 9,742 papers.
Assesses answer quality with LLM-as-a-judge and retrieval performance with direct gold-paper metrics; results emphasize a testbed rather than a single best strategy.
papers.selection_reason: Provides a controlled comparison of RAG strategies for scientific question answering, offering insights into retrieval quality and cost trade-offs for LLMs.
papers.title: Re-ranking and Late Interaction Drive Retrieval Quality: A Controlled Comparison of RAG Strategies for Scientific Question Answering
papers.tldr: A controlled evaluation of six RAG retrieval pipelines for scientific QA establishes an open testbed for comparing retrieval quality and cost trade-offs at large scale.

papers.abstract: Discrete diffusion models and flow matching have emerged as powerful frameworks for generative modeling over discrete state spaces, yet efficient few-step generation remains a fundamental challenge. In this work, we introduce the Discrete Average Generator, a principled extension of MeanFlow to Continuous-Time Markov Chains (CTMCs). Analogously to how MeanFlow defines an average velocity field over a time interval in continuous spaces, we define an average generator as the normalized increment of the transition kernel over a time interval. We show that this average generator satisfies a self-consistency identity, which provides the foundation for our training objective. We further develop training strategies that align with the standard training paradigm of diffusion language models while keeping the resulting objective tractable. When projected onto per-coordinate marginals, the self-consistency identity admits a closed-form expression, enabling efficient training and inference. In Potts model simulations, our objective reduces the total variation distance of the $K$-step sampler by up to 67%. On OpenWebText, our method achieves the lowest generative perplexity among the evaluated methods for 8 to 64 sampling steps while enabling a $16\times$ acceleration, and achieves comparable performance to existing methods on ImageNet.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of efficient few-step generation in discrete diffusion and flow-matching models.
Defines an average generator for continuous-time Markov chains as a normalized transition-kernel increment.
Derives a self-consistency identity and tractable training objective compatible with standard diffusion-language-model training.
A closed-form per-coordinate marginal formulation supports efficient training and inference.
Reduces total variation distance by up to 67% in Potts simulations and achieves the lowest evaluated generative perplexity on OpenWebText for 8–64 sampling steps; results are comparable on ImageNet.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a Discrete Average Generator for efficient few-step generation in discrete diffusion language models, offering acceleration and improved quality.
papers.title: Acceleration of Diffusion Language Model through Discrete Average Generator
papers.tldr: The Discrete Average Generator extends MeanFlow to discrete diffusion language models, enabling up to 16× faster sampling while maintaining strong generation quality.

papers.abstract: Recent work on anchored diffusion language models improves denoising by shaping an intermediate latent space with supervised important-token targets. In this work, we introduce time-based (self-supervised) anchoring, which learns and reuses latent anchors without requiring such targets. Our key observation is that anchors encode persistent properties of the clean sequence, such as its semantic intent, global structure, or intermediate plan. Although their hidden representations become stale as the token canvas evolves, their semantic content remains useful across nearby diffusion times. This is implemented through a two-stage architecture consisting of a relatively expensive anchor network that generates the latent cache state and a lightweight denoising network that intelligently combines the cached latent state with the current state at each reverse step using a fusion module. This gives anchoring a latent-space caching interpretation: the anchor network is evaluated periodically, while its cached representation is reused across multiple reverse steps. We instantiate this framework as TADM:Post-train, which time-anchorizes pretrained DLMs, and TADM:Pretraining, which learns time-based anchors during pretraining. Applied to DiffusionGemma-26B, TADM:Post-train improves throughput by approximately 49% to 79% on several math, code, and STEM benchmarks (GSM8K, AIME26, GPQA-Diamond, LiveCodeBench-v6, HumanEval, MMLU-Pro). TADM:Pretraining reduces Transformer-layer computation by up to 38% relative to a standard single-stage DLM, achieves up to 73% higher measured throughput than ADLM.
bullets: Addresses the high per-step computation of diffusion language models and the need for supervised important-token targets in prior anchored approaches.
Uses a two-stage architecture: an expensive anchor network periodically creates a latent cache, while a lightweight denoiser fuses the cache with the current state across reverse steps.
Introduces TADM:Post-train for adapting pretrained DLMs and TADM:Pretraining for learning time-based anchors during pretraining.
On DiffusionGemma-26B, TADM:Post-train improves throughput by about 49–79% across math, code, and STEM benchmarks.
TADM:Pretraining cuts Transformer-layer computation by up to 38% and reaches up to 73% higher measured throughput than ADLM.
papers.selection_reason: Time-anchored diffusion language models with latent-space caching for faster generation, relevant to efficient inference and LLM architectures.
papers.title: Time-Anchored Diffusion Language Models: Latent-Space Caching for Fast Generation
papers.tldr: Time-based latent anchoring caches persistent sequence information across diffusion steps, substantially accelerating diffusion language model generation without supervised anchor targets.

papers.abstract: Interpretable machine learning for Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly relies on sparse probing methods that identify small sets of neurons claimed to detect and causally influence behaviors such as factuality recall, safety alignment, and hallucination. These claims have important implications for model auditing and behavioral steering, yet they are rarely tested against known failure modes of $L_1$-regularized probing in correlated, high-dimensional feature spaces. We propose a five-step diagnostic protocol covering feature correlation, bootstrap stability, sparse versus dense ranking disagreement, intervention baselines, and cross-dataset evaluation as a minimum standard for sparse-neuron localization claims. We investigate prior work using our proposed approach, specifically on H-neurons using open-source LLMs across TriviaQA, BioASQ, and NQ-Open datasets. Our results demonstrate detection replicates across both models and datasets, and exceeds the original reported AUROC gaps for TriviaQA and BioASQ datasets. Gemma 3 4B consistently outperforms MedGemma 4B on matched datasets, with AUROC gaps of +0.311 versus +0.235 on TriviaQA, +0.474 versus +0.455 on BioASQ, and +0.128 versus +0.112 on NQ-Open respectively. Causal validation at $n = 500$ with five random seeds shows statistically significant effects beyond random same-layer baselines. At the same time, the diagnostic results indicate that the selected neurons are not uniquely localized. Across the three Gemma 3 4B settings, 19 of 22 selected H-Neurons have Pearson $|r| > 0.7$ with other features, bootstrap selections show only moderate stability, and sparse and dense rankings overlap only weakly. Our findings show that sparse predictive structure can coexist with non-unique neuron selection. Routine diagnostic validation is necessary to distinguish detection claims from localization claims in mechanistic interpretability.
bullets: The paper proposes a five-step diagnostic protocol for testing sparse-neuron localization claims in correlated, high-dimensional settings.
Across open-source LLMs and TriviaQA, BioASQ, and NQ-Open, H-neuron detection replicates and shows significant causal effects beyond same-layer random baselines.
Gemma 3 4B achieves larger reported AUROC gaps than MedGemma 4B on all three matched datasets.
Many selected neurons are highly correlated with other features, show only moderate bootstrap stability, and have weak agreement with dense rankings.
The results distinguish predictive detection from unique mechanistic localization and support routine diagnostic validation.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates hallucination neurons in LLMs with a diagnostic protocol, relevant to LLM reasoning and interpretability.
papers.title: Hallucination Neurons and Where to Find Them: An Investigation into the existence of Hallucination Neurons
papers.tldr: H-neurons can predict hallucination-related behavior and show causal effects, but sparse probing does not uniquely identify the responsible neurons.

papers.abstract: Multi-objective molecular optimization is a critical process in drug discovery that aims to modify a given molecule to simultaneously improve multiple properties while maintaining a similar overall structure. This process often requires iterative modifications guided by computational or experimental feedback. Recent large language model (LLM)-based methods have begun to explore this iterative approach; however, these methods are not explicitly trained to leverage such feedback, while existing approaches primarily focus on single-turn molecular optimization. To address this gap, we introduce Multi-turn Feedback Guided (MFG) molecular optimization, a reinforcement learning framework that trains an LLM to progressively optimize molecules using feedback from previous turns. MFG introduces a feedback vector capturing both property improvements and source molecule similarity, alongside a feedback-aligned reward function that promotes progressive improvement across turns. We apply MFG over $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O}$, a state-of-the-art LLM model for multi-objective molecular optimization, evaluate $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O-MFG}$ on ten multi-objective molecular optimization tasks. The results demonstrate that $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O-MFG}$ achieves the highest average similarity-constrained success rate ($81.50%$), outperforming the base model $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O}$ ($70.81%$).
authors: Trieu Nguyen, Frazier N. Baker, Ruoxi Gao, Daniel Adu-Ampratwum, Xia Ning
bullets: Addresses the gap between iterative molecular optimization and methods not explicitly trained to use feedback across turns.
Uses reinforcement learning with a feedback vector capturing property improvements and similarity to the source molecule.
Introduces a feedback-aligned reward that encourages progressive improvement over successive optimization turns.
Evaluated on ten multi-objective molecular optimization tasks using GeLLM³O.
GeLLM³O-MFG achieves an 81.50% average similarity-constrained success rate versus 70.81% for the base model.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces MFG, a reinforcement learning framework for LLMs to perform multi-turn molecular optimization using feedback from previous turns, improving success rates.
papers.title: MFG: Multi-turn Feedback Guided Molecular Optimization
papers.tldr: MFG trains an LLM with multi-turn feedback to progressively optimize molecules across multiple objectives while preserving structural similarity.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) generally rely on sampling temperature to regulate the amount of randomness in their outputs. Mainstream methods for selecting temperature typically involve fixed, heuristic global settings and context or token-level calibration, rather than a geometrically interpretable representation of the communicative scenario. In this work, we introduce a simple and interpretable temperature selection framework, the \textbf{Scenario-Actor}, which adapts decoding to the inferred situational characteristics. Scenario-Actor extracts scenario-relevant structures from Transformer hidden states and determines the temperature from scenario embedding, a structured geometric representation of the communicative setting. Empirical results show that on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Scenario-Actor achieves strong goal-completion performance in interactive social scenarios, significant gains on open-ended instruction following, and competitive performance on multi-turn conversation compared to multiple baselines.
bullets: Addresses the limitations of fixed heuristic temperatures and context- or token-level calibration.
Extracts scenario-relevant structures from Transformer hidden states.
Represents the setting as a structured scenario embedding and derives temperature from it.
Shows strong goal completion in interactive social scenarios and gains in open-ended instruction following on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct.
Achieves competitive multi-turn conversation performance against multiple baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces Scenario-Actor, a temperature selection framework for LLMs that adapts decoding based on inferred situational characteristics from hidden states.
papers.title: Read the Room Before Your Model Generates
papers.tldr: Scenario-Actor selects LLM decoding temperature from an interpretable geometric representation of the communicative situation, improving performance across several interaction and instruction-following settings.

papers.abstract: Harness self-evolution revises an agent's software scaffolding, including prompts, memory, workflows, and executable components, while keeping model weights fixed. We formalize a feedback-driven process in which accepted revisions persist across runs. The framework separates update targets from proposal and admission mechanisms. It distinguishes changes to interpreted state from revisions to tools and code, repository-level control logic, and plugin composition. We characterize search through evolutionary optimization and examine its reliability through continual PAC-learning. Under explicit assumptions, the analysis yields an expected generalization bound, a retention bound conditional on historical regression budgets, and a high-probability admission rule using fresh, independent validation data. We examine how persistent harness revisions affect knowledge sharing and organizational workflows, with implications for scientific reliability, physical safety, and institutional accountability. Cases from prior work illustrate model--harness co-design, distributed execution, and plugin reuse. Reliable deployment requires continual validation as task distributions and evaluators change, with independent safeguards for learning, runtime privileges, and consequential actions. We provide a comprehensive 66-page discussion of related work, theory, algorithms, evaluation, applications, and the broader impact of Harness RSI, together with continuously updated code and supplementary materials, at https://github.com/zgcagi/Harness-RSI.
authors: Chuyang Wei, Haoxiang Guan, Minghang Zhu, Kexin Zhou, Jiyan He, Xiren Zhou, Huanhuan Chen, Yifei Shen
bullets: Separates what is updated from how revisions are proposed and admitted.
Models harness evolution as evolutionary search and analyzes reliability with continual PAC-learning.
Derives theoretical bounds for generalization and revision retention, plus a high-probability admission rule using fresh validation data.
Discusses impacts on knowledge sharing, organizational workflows, scientific reliability, safety, and accountability.
Emphasizes independent safeguards and continual validation as tasks, evaluators, and deployment conditions change.
papers.selection_reason: Formalizes a framework for self-evolving agent harnesses (prompts, memory, workflows) with theoretical analysis, focusing on reliable deployment and co-design.
papers.title: Self-Evolving Agent Harness
papers.tldr: A framework for safely evolving an agent’s prompts, memory, workflows, tools, and code without changing its model weights, using persistent feedback-driven revisions and continual validation.

papers.abstract: Residual connections propagate information through a network by additively accumulating layer outputs. Recently proposed alternatives, such as Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) and Attention Residuals (AttnRes), instead use more expressive depth aggregation mechanisms that improve language modeling performance at scale. In this work, we consider the mixing of representations over depth as a problem of storing and retrieving information across layers. Formalizing this perspective, we introduce Depth Memory (DM), a unified framework that describes the standard pre-layer-norm (PreLN) transformer, mHC, and AttnRes in terms of streams that carry representations through the network. One such stream, for example, could be an explicit memory stream that is queried to enrich the input to every layer, and whose output is subsequently written back into the memory for use by later layers. For AttnRes, this memory stream is a growing cache of explicit layer representations. For mHC, it is an expanded residual stream. Building on this view, we propose Linear Depth Memory (LDM), which formulates information retrieval across depth as a regression problem solved using recursive least squares. The resulting architecture propagates three streams across depth: the standard residual stream, a linear associative memory stream, and an inverse covariance stream. For high-throughput training and inference, we propose a hardware-aware implementation of LDM that reduces peak activation memory and memory traffic. LDM consistently achieves the lowest perplexities among PreLN, mHC and AttnRes baselines at the 400M and 1.5B parameter scales, alongside competitive zero-shot accuracy.
authors: David Gonz\'alez-Mart\'inez, Philipp Nazari, T. Konstantin Rusch, Shiwei Liu
bullets: Frames representation mixing across layers as storing and retrieving information through depth.
Unifies PreLN Transformers, mHC, and AttnRes as stream-based memory mechanisms.
Introduces LDM, using recursive least squares to retrieve information across depth.
LDM propagates residual, associative-memory, and inverse-covariance streams.
At 400M and 1.5B parameters, LDM reports the lowest perplexities among the compared baselines and competitive zero-shot accuracy.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a unified depth-memory framework and linear associative memory stream for transformer architectures, improving language modeling and memory efficiency.
papers.title: Depth Memory
papers.tldr: Depth Memory unifies residual-style depth aggregation as information storage and retrieval, and its Linear Depth Memory variant improves language-model perplexity with hardware-efficient execution.

papers.abstract: Large language model multi-agent systems extend individual agents' capabilities through collaboration across specialized roles, tools, and workflows. Yet collaboration makes failures harder to diagnose: one agent may misinterpret a correct result while others carry the mistake forward. Failure attribution therefore seeks to identify the responsible agent and decisive error step. Recent methods trace dependencies, but knowing where information came from is not the same as knowing where it went wrong. We introduce BLADE (Blame Localization via Audited Dependency Evidence), a training-free framework that moves beyond tracing information to auditing its use. Using Jev for structured probabilistic judgments, BLADE uses dependency probabilities to select relevant source-decision handoffs for auditing. At these handoffs, it examines whether receiving decisions use their sources faithfully and within task requirements, distinguishing error introduction, propagation, and repair. These findings inform a global diagnosis that considers all execution steps. Without reference answers, BLADE achieves the best or tied-best step accuracy among eight strategies under a shared Jev decision interface on 1,228 failed runs across five Who&When and Who&When Pro subsets, outperforming All-at-once by 2.2-11.1 percentage points. Making responsibility evidence explicit offers a path toward more interpretable and reliable agentic systems.
authors: Xiaoguang Guo, Yaohao Long, Chuxu Zhang
bullets: Targets the difficulty of identifying which agent and decision step caused a collaborative failure.
Uses dependency probabilities to select source–decision handoffs for structured auditing with Jev.
Checks whether receiving agents use source information faithfully and within task requirements, distinguishing error introduction, propagation, and repair.
Builds a global diagnosis across the full execution without requiring reference answers.
Achieves the best or tied-best step accuracy among eight strategies on 1,228 failed runs, outperforming All-at-once by 2.2–11.1 percentage points.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a training-free framework (BLADE) for failure attribution in LLM multi-agent systems by auditing information use rather than just tracing dependencies.
papers.title: BLADE: Auditing Information Use for Failure Attribution in LLM Multi-Agent Systems
papers.tldr: BLADE improves failure attribution in LLM multi-agent systems by auditing how agents use exchanged information, rather than only tracing where it originated.

papers.abstract: System one models enable direct, low-latency decision-making. Yet recent practice of predicting an answer from serialized text does not, by itself, respect the structure of a decision problem. We argue that current designs underemphasize four important structural requirements. (i) null-aware: Models should distinguish answer absence from uncertainty among candidates; (ii) permutation-invariant: Reordering alternatives should not change the decision; (iii) option-scalable: Growing candidate sets should not require redefining the output space; (iv) cacheable: Request-independent computation over recurring alternatives should be reusable across requests. We introduce Jeva, a decision-native architecture that addresses these requirements jointly. A shared encoder independently represents the request and each option, while a compact decision stack refines only the request state against immutable option memory. Symmetric aggregation yields permutation-equivariant probabilities; shared scoring accommodates variable-size candidate sets. A separate coverage estimate distinguishes answer absence from candidate competition, enabling explicit null outcomes. Request-independent option representations and layer projections support reuse across newly assembled sets. These mechanisms unify Choice, Noul, and Score outputs. Across evaluations, Jeva combines strong typed-decision performance with near-perfect null detection and no decision flips under any tested permutations. It scales to thousands of candidates and substantially reduces latency through cross-request reuse without changing decisions.
bullets: Targets four structural needs: distinguishing no valid answer from uncertainty, ignoring candidate order, scaling to variable-size option sets, and caching recurring option computations.
Encodes the request and each option separately, then refines the request against immutable option representations with symmetric aggregation and shared scoring.
Uses a separate coverage estimate to produce explicit null outcomes and unifies Choice, Noul, and Score outputs.
Evaluations report strong typed-decision performance, near-perfect null detection, no tested permutation-induced decision flips, scaling to thousands of candidates, and lower latency through reuse.
Scope: the reported permutation and latency findings are based on the tested evaluations and reuse setting described in the abstract.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces Jeva, a decision-native architecture for System 1 models that addresses structural requirements like null-awareness and permutation invariance, improving decision-making efficiency.
papers.title: Jeva: System One Models from First Principles
papers.tldr: Jeva is a decision-native architecture designed for fast, reliable choices over variable candidate sets while handling null answers, permutation invariance, and reusable computation.

papers.abstract: Test-time scaling for large language models (LLMs) can involve generating multiple candidate solutions for selection or revising an earlier attempt. To guide selection and revision, we need a verifier that can estimate candidate correctness and provide evidence of failure. In competitive programming, however, official judging systems provide authoritative verdicts under finite submission budgets, without revealing failure explanations or failing inputs. To provide informative feedback without consuming official submissions, we formulate a task in which a model judges and diagnoses a candidate program using only the problem statement and source code, with generated counterexamples serving as checkable evidence. To evaluate this task, we build USACO-JUDGE from the USACO 2026 contests, using accepted and unaccepted programs written by human experts and multiple LLMs. We then train ARBITER, a 35B mixture-of-experts (MoE) agentic verifier, with reinforcement learning in a generic execution sandbox. Training raises counterexample success on incorrect programs from 40.61% to 62.67% and mean binary verdict accuracy on USACO-JUDGE from 71.41% to 87.41%, approaching frontier verification performance. Beyond verification, ARBITER outperforms baselines in both code selection and refinement. In an IOI 2026 case study, ARBITER-guided refinement raises GPT-OSS-120B's expected score above the gold-medal threshold under the official submission limit.
authors: Zheye Deng, Sha Li, Changlong Yu, Xin Liu, Qin Lu, Priyanka Nigam, Yangqiu Song
bullets: Addresses the lack of failure explanations and inputs from official judges while avoiding extra official submissions.
Uses only the problem statement and candidate source code, with generated counterexamples as evidence.
Introduces USACO-JUDGE, built from accepted and unaccepted human- and LLM-written programs from USACO 2026 contests.
Trains a 35B mixture-of-experts verifier with reinforcement learning in an execution sandbox.
Improves counterexample success from 40.61% to 62.67% and verdict accuracy from 71.41% to 87.41%; also benefits code selection and refinement.
papers.selection_reason: Develops an agentic verifier (ARBITER) for LLM code generation and refinement using reinforcement learning, improving verification accuracy and feedback quality.
papers.title: Beyond the Verdict: Agentic Code Judging with Verifiable Feedback
papers.tldr: ARBITER is an agentic verifier that diagnoses competitive-programming solutions by generating checkable counterexamples, improving correctness judgments and supporting code selection and refinement.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose an extremely efficient, training-free method to extract token-level reward signals directly from an existing deep reward model. Our core idea is to attribute the overall process reward to individual tokens by estimating each token's influence. This influence is defined as the change in the final macroscopic reward (e.g., the process reward) when a token is replaced with a semantically null token. Naively calculating this influence is computationally infeasible, requiring N forward passes through the PRM for an N-token sequence. We overcome this bottleneck by proposing a highly efficient gradient-based estimator. Specifically, we use a first-order Taylor approximation, which simplifies the influence calculation to the inner product of the difference between the token embedding and the null token embedding, and the gradient of the reward with respect to the token embedding. This requires only a single forward and backward pass. The resulting token-level rewards enable standard RL algorithms to perform precise credit assignment without requiring additional reward model training. Experiments on challenging reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that our method substantially improves policy optimization efficiency and enhances the generalization of LLM reasoning capabilities. Our P2T outperforms the outcome reward by +4.9% on MathVista for Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, and +11.5% on AIME24 for Qwen2.5-Math-7B. The code will be released via https://github.com/stonewst/P2T.
authors: Sitong Wu, Haoru Tan, Bin Xia, Xichen Zhang, Jingyao Li, Shaofeng Zhang, Xiaojuan Qi, Bei Yu, Jiaya Jia
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of assigning a sequence-level process reward to individual tokens, where exact influence estimation would require one model evaluation per token.
Defines each token’s influence by replacing it with a semantically null token and measuring the resulting reward change.
Uses a first-order Taylor approximation to estimate influence from the token–null-token embedding difference and the reward gradient.
The resulting token rewards can be used with standard reinforcement-learning algorithms for credit assignment.
Experiments report improved policy optimization and reasoning generalization, including gains over outcome rewards on MathVista and AIME24.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a training-free method for token-level credit assignment in LLMs using gradient-based influence estimation, improving policy optimization efficiency on reasoning benchmarks.
papers.title: Unlocking Token Rewards via Training-Free Reward Attribution
papers.tldr: P2T extracts token-level rewards from an existing process reward model in one forward–backward pass, enabling more precise credit assignment without reward-model retraining.

papers.abstract: Combining pretrained models is a common strategy for building AI systems, whether by aligning a vision encoder with a language model or merging fine-tuned checkpoints. However, finding compatible pairs typically requires costly empirical search, as compatibility is known only after alignment or merging. We propose COMPASS (COMPatibility ASsessment Score), a theoretically motivated diagnostic that estimates whether a model pair will be compatible prior to alignment or merging. Building on the observation that representational convergence is most robust at the level of local neighborhoods, COMPASS decomposes model compatibility into two cheap-to-compute axes: a pair-specific ease, defined as the $k$-NN overlap between the two encoders, and a paradigm-level ceiling, capturing the maximum overlap their training paradigms allow. Together, these two axes provide a ranking of candidate model pairs and prescribe how to act on each pair: (i) prioritize pairs that already agree and whose paradigms are compatible, (ii) invest additional compute on pairs with compatible paradigms but low initial agreement, (iii) switch the pretraining paradigm when it cannot support sufficient agreement, or (iv) deprioritize pairs that score poorly on both axes. We apply COMPASS to $72$ cross-modal alignment experiments and $392$ task-arithmetic model merges and show that compatibility estimates by COMPASS strongly correlate with downstream success, achieving average Pearson correlation of $0.91$ on cross-modal alignment tasks and $0.70$ on model merging.
authors: Fabian Gr\"oger, Petar Damjanovi\'c, Maria Brbi\'c
bullets: Addresses the costly trial-and-error needed to identify compatible model pairs.
Measures compatibility using two axes: pair-specific k-NN overlap and a training-paradigm compatibility ceiling.
Ranks candidate pairs and recommends whether to proceed, spend more compute, change the paradigm, or deprioritize the pair.
Across 72 cross-modal alignment experiments and 392 model merges, COMPASS correlated strongly with downstream success.
Reported average Pearson correlations were 0.91 for alignment and 0.70 for merging.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes COMPASS, a diagnostic tool to assess model compatibility for alignment/merging based on representational convergence (k-NN overlap), a spatial/structural metric.
papers.title: To Align or Not To Align: Check Your COMPASS Before You Train
papers.tldr: COMPASS cheaply predicts whether pretrained model pairs will align or merge successfully before expensive training or merging.

papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly tackle tasks that require multi-step reasoning, where errors in intermediate claims can affect the final answer. Self-consistency (SC) improves reasoning by voting over sampled final answers, but its vote leaves intermediate disagreements unresolved. To address this problem, we introduce DDRG (Disagreement-Driven Verification Guided by Reasoning Graphs), a framework for selective correction from a frozen bank of reasoning traces. Our insight is that graph alignment can expose claim-level disagreements and provide correction evidence without expanding the sampled trace bank. DDRG builds source-grounded claim graphs and sends localized conflicts to an answer-blind verifier. A verifier-supported refutation that reaches the majority answer's supporting path triggers one focused repair; otherwise, DDRG returns the exact SC vote. Experimental results across five benchmarks show that native zero-shot DDRG improves macro-average accuracy over direct answering by 8.65 and 15.83 percentage points for Qwen2.5-7B and Llama3.1-8B. It also exceeds CoT, the evaluated GoT and GoV question-answering adaptations, and SC on this macro metric. DDRG links local verification to selective correction without enlarging the initial candidate bank.
authors: Haotian Liu, Yingjian Chen, Xiaohang Xu, Lang Huang, Yusuke Iwasawa, Yutaka Matsuo, Irene Li
bullets: Targets unresolved intermediate errors that final-answer voting in self-consistency cannot correct.
Builds source-grounded claim graphs and sends localized conflicts to an answer-blind verifier.
Applies one focused repair only when verifier-supported refutation connects to the majority answer’s supporting path; otherwise preserves the SC vote.
Across five benchmarks, zero-shot DDRG improves macro-average accuracy over direct answering by 8.65 points for Qwen2.5-7B and 15.83 points for Llama3.1-8B.
Outperforms the evaluated CoT, GoT, GoV, and self-consistency baselines without expanding the initial trace bank.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces DDRG, a framework for fine-grained correction of LLM reasoning using graph alignment on sampled traces, improving upon standard self-consistency voting.
papers.title: Beyond Answer Voting: Fine-Grained Correction of LLM Reasoning through Graph Alignment across Sampled Traces
papers.tldr: DDRG improves self-consistent LLM reasoning by aligning sampled reasoning graphs to detect and selectively repair intermediate claim disagreements.

papers.abstract: Sampling-based test-time scaling enhances LLM reasoning by aggregating multiple reasoning paths for the same query. Existing methods use answer frequencies or path confidence to compute candidate scores, which do not explicitly characterize comparisons between competing answers. Inspired by the Condorcet principle in social choice theory, we introduce pairwise confidence comparisons between paths supporting different answers to capture answer-level comparative advantage. We combine this comparative evidence with voting support through a KL-regularized objective. Theoretically, we show that this comparative-advantage is equivalent to the adjustment to the traditional voting logits. In this way, our proposed Pairwise-Guided Logit Adjustment (PGLA) framework allows comparative evidence to compensate for weaker voting support and correct voting-based ranking errors. Experiments on 10 challenging benchmarks including mathematical reasoning, knowledge reasoning, and code generation with 7 models ranging from 1.7B to 32B parameters speak to the effectiveness of this plug-and-play term. Additional evaluations with external reward scores and online sampling further demonstrate its applicability.
authors: Cong Hua, Qianqian Xu, Zitai Wang, Zhiyong Yang, Shilong Bao, Linchao Zhang, Qingming Huang
bullets: Existing methods rank candidate answers mainly by frequency or path confidence, missing direct comparisons between alternatives.
PGLA adds pairwise confidence evidence for paths supporting different answers, inspired by the Condorcet principle.
A KL-regularized objective combines comparative evidence with voting support and yields an equivalent logit adjustment.
The framework is evaluated across 10 reasoning and code-generation benchmarks with 7 models, plus external-reward and online-sampling settings.
The method is presented as a plug-and-play way to compensate for weaker vote counts and correct ranking errors.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes Pairwise-Guided Logit Adjustment (PGLA) to improve LLM reasoning at test time by comparing paths supporting different answers, a novel technique for test-time scaling.
papers.title: Compare to Correct: Pairwise-Guided Logit Adjustment for LLM Test-Time Scaling
papers.tldr: PGLA improves sampling-based LLM test-time scaling by using pairwise comparisons between competing answers to correct voting-based rankings.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive language models produce, at every prediction step, a vocabulary-sized logit vector whose structure determines the conditional next-token distribution. We empirically identify that the ordered vocabulary-head logits follow a remarkably consistent log-linear relation \[ z_{(r)} \approx \mu - \alpha \log r. \] across prediction contexts, architectures, and scales, emerging progressively during pretraining. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic analysis of the logit geometry underlying the distributional assumptions used in the prior decoding work. While controlled order-statistic baselines spanning bounded, light-tailed, and heavier-tailed distributions can largely explain the observed log-linear geometry, they do not explain the systematic shift in the slope $\alpha$: trained language models exhibit $\alpha \approx 1.4$--$1.7$, sitting well above the initialization baseline ($\alpha \approx 0.2$) . Moreover, $\alpha$ correlates with predictive performance, suggesting that it captures learned structure beyond generic extreme-value effects.
authors: Swathi Shree Narashiman, Aravind Ramana Venkatramanan, Nambi Seshadri
bullets: Ordered logits approximately satisfy $z_{(r)} \approx \mu - \alpha \log r$ across contexts, architectures, and scales.
This geometry emerges progressively during pretraining.
Order-statistic baselines explain much of the pattern but not the learned slope shift.
Trained models show substantially larger slopes than initialization, with $\alpha$ linked to predictive performance.
papers.selection_reason: Provides a systematic analysis of the log-linear geometry of LLM logits, contributing to the understanding of LLM architectures and decoding mechanisms.
papers.title: The Geometry of Language Model Logits: Generic Structure and Learned Departures
papers.tldr: Language-model logits generally follow a log-linear rank pattern, but training shifts the slope in a way associated with predictive performance beyond generic statistical effects.

papers.abstract: The safety of LLM-based agents currently rests on alignment training and safety classifiers, neither of which can rule out that a sophisticated indirect prompt injection (IPI) goes through and causes significant harm. Recent work therefore builds agents with information-flow guarantees that rely on structured tool interfaces to interact with the environment. Computer Use Agents (CUAs) act visually on the computer screen, which does not provide a boundary between trusted first-party interfaces and untrusted, potentially attacker-authored content. Actions are equally ambiguous: a click may land on an application toolbar or a button controlled by an attacker. Treating the user as the source of trust and confirming each sensitive decision produces confirmation fatigue, with the risk of missing harmful actions. We introduce SA-CUA, a dual-LLM framework that generates a reliable trust boundary for CUAs by deriving conservative deterministic rules from the accessibility tree for unmasking trusted regions from the privileged LLM's screenshot, keeping trusted and untrusted content separated. Human interaction is only required for proper task specification in the beginning. During the task a robust endorsement channel allows values to pass from the untrusted to the trusted domain by verifying information via trusted channels. This allows the agent to autonomously handle tasks involving untrusted information. SA-CUA maintains much higher utility than CaMeL-CUA while keeping the attack success rate at zero.
authors: Dominik Seip, Bartol Markovinovi\'c, Matthias Hein
bullets: Computer-use agents lack clear trust boundaries because screenshots mix trusted UI with attacker-controlled content and actions are ambiguous.
SA-CUA uses a dual-LLM design and conservative deterministic rules from the accessibility tree to identify trusted regions.
A robust endorsement channel verifies values from untrusted content through trusted channels.
Human input is limited to initial task specification rather than repeated confirmations.
The abstract reports zero attack success while retaining substantially higher utility than CaMeL-CUA.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses safety for LLM agents acting on computers, proposing a dual-LLM framework to establish a trust boundary and prevent prompt injection.
papers.title: Towards Safe Autonomy for Computer Use
papers.tldr: SA-CUA enables safer autonomous computer-use agents by separating trusted interface regions from untrusted content and verifying cross-boundary information.

papers.abstract: Recently, Morris et al. introduced TinyLoRA, a strategy for LLM fine-tuning which introduces arbitrarily few parameters, and demonstrated accuracy improvements using less than $10$ parameters rather than the ${\gtrsim 10,000}$ typically demanded by LoRA-based methods. However, that study continued to use gradient-based local search methods of the kind deployed for training multi-billion parameter LLMs in the first place. This article is predicated on the observation that, in the low dimensional setting, global optimization methods become tractable, unlocking Large language Model Bayesian Optimization (LlMBO). LlMBO is sample-efficient, gradient-free, memory-light, parallelizes across devices without synchronization, and, unlike policy-gradient methods, can optimize greedy-decoding accuracy directly. We describe numerical experiments comparing LlMBO against GRPO on fine-tuning tasks for a variety of models on a math benchmark suite which show that LlMBO can be a suitable alternative in this regime, matching or exceeding GRPO's fine tuning gains, while using a fraction of the compute and memory.
authors: Aditya Kulkarni, Davide Sartor, Carlos Soto, Nathan Wycoff
bullets: Targets the low-dimensional regime enabled by TinyLoRA, where only a handful of parameters are tuned.
Replaces gradient-based local search with global, gradient-free Bayesian optimization.
Is sample-efficient, memory-light, parallelizable without synchronization, and directly optimizes greedy-decoding accuracy.
Experiments across models and math benchmarks find LlMBO competitive with or better than GRPO while using a fraction of the compute and memory.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a novel fine-tuning approach (Bayesian Optimization) for LLMs, contrasting with standard gradient-based methods and offering a sample-efficient alternative.
papers.title: How Low Can You Go: Fine-Tuning LLMs with Bayesian Optimization (LlMBO)
papers.tldr: LlMBO uses Bayesian optimization to fine-tune LLMs with extremely few parameters, matching or surpassing GRPO gains with lower compute and memory.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are becoming an integral part of the software development lifecycle, and the capabilities granted to them allow an agent to act with the user's authority on any resource it can access. The reach that gives an agent its utility is equally available to an attacker who can steer it. Anything an agent ingests can carry an injected instruction, and since the model does not reliably distinguish instructions from data, indirect prompt injection should be mitigated by mediating the effects the agent produces. Such mediation faces a structural difficulty. Legitimate work and the first step of an attack often look alike when an individual action is observed, and what separates them lies later in the trace, so a monitor limited to allow and deny is forced to decide before the evidence accumulates. We present Kairos, a reference monitor at the isolation boundary of an unmodified, opaque agent, where a tool call, a shell command, and a script the agent writes all cross the boundary as the same file and network operations, so that confinement holds regardless of the agent's behavior. A declarative policy that states which sources are trusted decides most effects deterministically and defers the rest, which are held while the agent continues speculatively. A decision oracle with bounded authority, such as a language model or a human, releases or refuses each deferred effect on the trace. Across three benchmarks and three agent models, Kairos outperforms existing defenses in the trade-off between attack success and utility. In particular, on AgentDojo, it reduces attack success from 47.0\% to 2.7\% while its benign utility stays at the level of the undefended agent.
authors: Kristoffer Hempel, Nils Loose, Lorenzo Cavallaro, Thomas Eisenbarth
bullets: Agents can be steered by malicious instructions embedded in ingested data, while individual legitimate and attack actions may initially look identical.
Kairos confines an opaque, unmodified agent by mediating all file and network effects at the isolation boundary.
A declarative policy deterministically permits trusted effects and defers uncertain ones while the agent continues speculatively.
A bounded-authority oracle, such as an LLM or human, decides whether deferred effects are released.

Across three benchmarks and agent models, Kairos improved the attack-success/utility trade-off; on AgentDojo, attack success fell from 47.0% to 2.7% with benign utility maintained at the undefended level.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses security enforcement for LLM agents using a reference monitor, a critical aspect of deploying LLMs, though the focus is on system-level policy rather than model architecture.
papers.title: Kairos: Transactional Security Enforcement at the System Boundary for LLM Agents
papers.tldr: Kairos protects LLM agents from indirect prompt injection by enforcing transactional, trace-aware security at the system boundary without modifying the agent.

papers.abstract: Referees increasingly use large language models (LLMs), while finance and accounting journals disagree about whether to allow it. We ask which part of a referee's job the models can do. GPT-4o, whose training data end before the 2024 conference season, referees the papers presented at the 2024 AFA and NBER finance meetings, and we compare its verdicts with publication in the top-three finance journals over the next two years. Papers the model scores one standard deviation higher are 44\% more likely to be published, net of author reputation. The result is not driven by look-ahead bias, as the model does not recall the outcomes. The information comes from its judgements of correctness and exposition. Its judgements of originality and significance carry none, and a referee guide that stresses importance does not help. The split between correctness and contribution holds for accounting papers and for a newer model, GPT-5. LLMs can check whether research is right, but not whether it matters. The technical check can go to the model, while the judgement of contribution stays with people.
authors: Hai Lu, Yichen Luo, Luping Yu
bullets: Studies GPT-4o reviews of papers presented at the 2024 AFA and NBER finance meetings.
Model scores predict publication in top-three finance journals over the following two years, controlling for author reputation.
The predictive signal comes from judgments of correctness and exposition, not originality or significance.
Results are not explained by look-ahead bias and also hold for accounting papers and GPT-5.
Implication: LLMs may handle technical checking, while humans should assess research contribution.
papers.selection_reason: Empirically evaluates LLM performance in peer review for finance and accounting, fitting the Language Foundation Models category.
papers.title: How Well Do LLMs Perform in Peer Review? Evidence from Finance and Accounting
papers.tldr: LLMs appear effective at evaluating research correctness and exposition, but not its originality, significance, or broader contribution.

papers.abstract: Federated fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) allows multiple clients to collaboratively adapt models without sharing raw data, offering strong privacy benefits. However, this setting is highly vulnerable to backdoor attacks, in which malicious clients manipulate their updates to induce targeted behaviors while maintaining normal performance on benign inputs. In this work, we make a key observation specific to federated LLM fine-tuning: malicious clients tend to exhibit strong consistency in their model updates, whereas benign clients produce more diverse and dispersed updates. This structural difference is not well captured by existing defense methods, which typically rely on direct anomaly detection in high-dimensional parameter space and therefore struggle in the presence of entangled LLM updates. Motivated by this observation, we propose FedGraph, a graph-based aggregation framework that explicitly models relationships among client updates. By representing clients as nodes in a dynamically constructed graph and extracting structural features that characterize their relative positions and interactions, FedGraph derives compact client representations that effectively separate malicious and benign behaviors. These representations are then used to identify and suppress malicious contributions during aggregation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FedGraph significantly improves backdoor defense. It consistently reduces attack success rates to below 10% while achieving high detection accuracy (95.5% on average) and a low false positive rate (2.33%), substantially outperforming existing federated learning defenses.
authors: Xi Chen, Chunyi Zhou, Rui Zeng, Xiaogang Xu, Zhe Liu, Shouling Ji
bullets: Targets backdoor attacks that preserve benign-input performance while inducing malicious behaviors.
Exploits the observation that malicious clients’ updates are more consistent, while benign updates are more diverse.
Builds a dynamic client-update graph and extracts compact structural representations to distinguish client behaviors.
Uses these representations to identify and downweight or suppress malicious updates during aggregation.
Experiments report attack success rates below 10%, 95.5% average detection accuracy, and a 2.33% false positive rate.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses backdoor attacks in federated LLM fine-tuning using a graph-based aggregation framework, fitting the Language Foundation Models category.
papers.title: FedGraph: Defending Federated Large Language Model Fine-Tuning Against Backdoor Attacks via Graph-Based Aggregation
papers.tldr: FedGraph defends federated LLM fine-tuning from backdoors by using graph-based relationships among client updates to detect and suppress malicious contributions.

papers.abstract: We trained Agaram 2.5B, a 2.5-billion-parameter Tamil-English language model, from scratch on about 50 billion tokens (58% Tamil, the rest English, math, code and parallel text) on one node of eight H100 GPUs in about six days, with a new tokenizer that, unlike our first model's, keeps line breaks. Supervised fine-tuning on 134,428 conversations, whose replies an open-weight teacher model wrote, and three short targeted rounds turned it into a chat model that answers in Tamil script, romanized Tamil (Tanglish) and English and can call tools: on 25 tool prompts whose schemas appear in training it picks the right tool 23 times and gives exactly the expected arguments 13 times. The released model translates better than Sarvam-1, a 2B Indic base model, in all six FLORES and IN22 directions (FLORES chrF 54.3 into Tamil and 55.2 into English, against 49.2 and 44.2), and nearly doubles its base model on native-Tamil IndicIFEval (19.3% from 10.0%). It is weak on knowledge: reading-comprehension and knowledge benchmarks sit near chance, and on 50 held-out everyday questions written by one native speaker, one LLM judge rated 46% of its replies usable (22-24 of 50 over three passes; 95% interval for 23 of 50, 33-60%), with nearly every failure a wrong fact. Our two further SFT experiments changed answer format but not the knowledge measures. We also describe our first model, Agaram 1.5B, whose failures shaped the choices here; how the judge's scores varied between passes on identical replies; and, item by item, what the targeted rounds trained against and where frontier-model text entered the data. The project ran on compute credits and our own funds, about USD 13,300 across both models; the weights are released (licence to be announced after legal review), with GGUF files for llama.cpp, at https://huggingface.co/murai-labs/agaram-2.5b-instruct; code at https://github.com/Murai-Labs/Agaram2.5b
authors: Ramchand Kumaresan, Madhusudhanan G, Kaushik Kezendirane
bullets: Trained on about 50B tokens with 58% Tamil data using eight H100 GPUs for roughly six days.
Supervised fine-tuning enabled multilingual chat and tool use; it selected the correct tool on 23/25 prompts and exact arguments on 13/25.
Outperformed Sarvam-1 on all six reported FLORES and IN22 translation directions and nearly doubled its native-Tamil IndicIFEval score.
Knowledge and reading-comprehension performance stayed near chance; 46% of answers to 50 everyday questions were judged usable, with most failures involving incorrect facts.
Weights and GGUF files are released, while the licence was pending legal review.
papers.selection_reason: Details the training and evaluation of a Tamil-English language model, fitting the Language Foundation Models category.
papers.title: Agaram 2.5B: The First Tamil-First Language Model Trained from Scratch with Tool Calling. A Playbook for Under-Represented Languages
papers.tldr: Agaram 2.5B is a Tamil-first model trained from scratch that supports Tamil, Tanglish, English, and tool calling, but remains weak on factual knowledge.

papers.abstract: Applying process-based Earth science models to new sites and questions often requires expert calibration decisions. Reliable delegation to language-model agents must preserve scientific competence and reproducibility. Here we develop a general calibration harness (GCH) for end-to-end delegation from a calibration request to assessed results. Constrained by a knowledge infrastructure (KI) and a validation convention, agents define parameter domains, observation mappings and objectives, and generate model-specific code. GCH checks the formulations against the same declarations and freezes them before numerical search and assessment, which require no further agent judgement. Agent-authored workflows executed across six model families, with assessment identifying unmet criteria. In snow-model tests, five of five knowledge-guided specifications executed on the first attempt, compared with none of five given only the model name, achieving validation Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) of 0.81-0.94 against 0.57 for defaults. Under a common objective, independent GR4J formulations yielded scores within 0.001 NSE; re-evaluating eleven saved parameter vectors reproduced their metrics. In ten paired VIC tests with matched budgets, fixed search was non-inferior to continuing agent proposals (margin, -0.02 NSE; median difference, -0.003). This separation enables end-to-end calibration delegation with inspectable scientific choices and reproducible numerical evaluation.
authors: Zhanliang Zhu, Ziwei Li, Liujun Zhu, Yuchen Liu, Junliang Jin, Jianyun Zhang
bullets: Targets reliable delegation of site-specific, expert calibration decisions for process-based Earth science models.
Agents use a knowledge infrastructure and validation convention to define parameter domains, observation mappings, objectives, and model code.
The harness checks and freezes these declarations before agent-independent numerical search and assessment.
Across snow-model tests, all five knowledge-guided workflows ran successfully on the first attempt and achieved NSE values of 0.81–0.94, versus 0.57 for defaults.
Common-objective GR4J workflows were highly consistent, and fixed search was non-inferior to continued agent proposals in paired VIC tests.
papers.selection_reason: Delegates Earth science model calibration to LLM agents using a general harness, demonstrating end-to-end delegation and reproducible scientific choices.
papers.title: Delegating Earth science model calibration to knowledge-guided LLM agents
papers.tldr: A knowledge-guided calibration harness enables LLM agents to make inspectable Earth-model calibration choices while keeping numerical search and evaluation reproducible.

papers.abstract: Game-theoretic benchmarks claim that large language model (LLM) strategic decision-making varies across game types, interaction structures, and capability dimensions. However, they only evaluate strategic performance across individual fixed models. In parallel, contemporary LLM routers pick models under quality-cost trade-offs, but with no notion of a strategic structure. They do not account for an opponent that might be unknown, and that can adapt over time and shift the feedback signal. To address this, we extend the game-theoretic evaluations and define strategic selection as the meta game layered on top of the base game. In each round, a strategic selector fields an LLM from a portfolio of models to navigate a game payoff matrix that is latent and learned online. We find that the evaluation signal is game-specific, and that extracting a reliable signal requires a much higher number of seed runs $N$ compared to traditional benchmarking setups. Evaluating across 5 games and 10 LLMs, we show a model's strategic competence varies significantly depending on the game setup and the opponent faced. Building on this, we implement a suite of selector methods and find that approaches that rely on query embeddings or LLM self-reflection do not consistently capture the underlying strategic signal. A lightweight multi-armed bandit algorithm performs more reliably across games, though it still falls short of the best fixed model. Finally, we show that simple non-stationary and adversarial bandit variants fail to outperform a stationary bandit baseline, pointing to a gap in how current methods handle a shifting opponent in strategic settings.
authors: Arastun Mammadli, Herbert Woisetschl\"ager, Jawad Fayaz, Shiqiang Wang
bullets: Strategic selection is formulated as a meta-game: each round chooses an LLM from a portfolio for a game with a latent payoff matrix learned online.
Reliable evaluation requires substantially more seed runs than traditional fixed-model benchmarking because the signal is game-specific.
Across 5 games and 10 LLMs, strategic competence varies significantly with both the game and the opponent.
Query-embedding and LLM self-reflection selectors do not consistently identify the best strategic model; a lightweight multi-armed bandit performs more reliably.
Non-stationary and adversarial bandit variants fail to improve over a stationary baseline, highlighting difficulty handling shifting opponents.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates strategic agent interactions and model selection in game-theoretic settings, analyzing how LLM strategic competence varies across different opponents and game setups.
papers.title: Choosing LLMs for Strategic Agent Interactions
papers.tldr: Selecting an LLM for strategic interactions is game- and opponent-dependent, and simple bandit selectors are more reliable than embedding or self-reflection methods but still do not beat the best fixed model.

papers.abstract: Training business automation agents requires executable tasks that connect a natural-language request to an application state and a verifiable end state. Traditional Rubrics requires Authors to recreate application interfaces, initial records, policy evidence, and outcome checks for each task, entangling business logic with repeated infrastructure work. We introduce AssetForge, an asset-augmented task-construction pipeline that pairs a reusable construction-asset library with task-specific Rubrics. The assets provide application interfaces, world-state components, policy/evidence carriers, and native assertion definitions; the Rubric directs their instantiation for a particular business task. Executable checks and an additional model-based review validate each candidate, return targeted feedback, and support bounded repair before acceptance. On AutomationBench v1.0.6 public-600, fine-tuning Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on 6,000 AssetForge examples yields 41.17% on the official strict pass@1 metric, 4.4 times the 9.33% base score (+31.83 points). With the same backbone and GLM-5.3 supervision, AssetForge reaches 41.17% versus 30.33% for traditional Rubrics, a 10.84-point gain (35.7% relative) at the same accepted-example scale (6,000 versus 6,000 examples). Both DeepSeek- and GLM-supervised AssetForge models improve AppWorld completion over the base model on Test-Normal and Test-Challenge. These results establish the advantage of AssetForge's complete construction pipeline on AutomationBench public: the coupled asset-Rubric interface directs Authors toward business logic, while executable checks and model-based review validate their tasks.
authors: Xiangrui Liu, Shuo Tang, Siheng Chen
bullets: Addresses the repeated infrastructure work required to build executable business-automation tasks.
Pairs reusable assets—interfaces, world state, policy evidence, and assertions—with task-specific Rubrics.
Uses executable checks and model-based review to provide feedback and support bounded task repair.
On AutomationBench public-600, AssetForge fine-tuning reached 41.17% strict pass@1 versus 9.33% for the base model.
At the same accepted-example scale, it outperformed traditional Rubrics by 10.84 percentage points and also improved AppWorld completion.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces AssetForge, an asset-augmented pipeline for synthesizing executable tasks for business automation agents, fitting LLM agent protocols and task synthesis.
papers.title: AssetForge: Asset-Augmented Task Synthesis for Business Automation Agents
papers.tldr: AssetForge improves business-automation agent training by combining reusable construction assets with task-specific Rubrics and validation, substantially boosting benchmark performance over base models and traditional Rubrics.

papers.abstract: Guardrail approaches that rely on reasoning-based large language models (LLM) improve safety decisions, but come with substantial inference overhead due to the explicit reasoning. We introduce LR-Guard (Latent Reasoning Guardrail), an efficient and explainable guardrail that jointly learns structured latent reasoning and on-demand reasoning reconstruction. Our method distills a frozen teacher's analysis of safe and unsafe prompt interpretations and their comparison into compact latent representations. Joint training optimizes these representations for both safety prediction and reconstruction of the teacher's explicit reasoning traces, enabling human-readable explanations without requiring intermediate text generation for every decision. Experiments show that LR-Guard outperforms its explicit-reasoning teacher in most in-domain and out-of-domain settings on safety classification and explanation extraction, while achieving a 19.4x inference speedup at batch size one. Further, reconstructed reasoning traces from the latent information exhibit high semantic similarity to the teacher's explicit reasoning.
authors: Md Asiful Islam, Fahmida Alam, Mihai Surdeanu
bullets: Addresses the inference overhead of reasoning-based LLM guardrails.
Distills a frozen teacher’s safe/unsafe interpretations and comparisons into compact latent representations.
Jointly trains latent representations for safety prediction and on-demand reconstruction of human-readable reasoning traces.
Outperforms its explicit-reasoning teacher in most reported in-domain and out-of-domain safety classification and explanation-extraction settings.
Achieves a 19.4× inference speedup at batch size one, with reconstructed traces showing high semantic similarity to the teacher’s reasoning.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces LR-Guard, an efficient safety guardrail that achieves 19.4x inference speedup via latent reasoning and reconstruction, fitting both efficiency and LLM safety domains.
papers.title: Efficient Safety Guardrails through Latent Dual-Hypothesis Reasoning with On-Demand Trace Reconstruction
papers.tldr: LR-Guard delivers fast, explainable safety guardrails by replacing routine explicit reasoning with structured latent reasoning and reconstructing explanations only when needed.

papers.abstract: What binds large language models on auditable, hypothesis-driven decision tasks, where every candidate can be checked against the evidence? On the public TCMEval-SDT benchmark for Traditional Chinese Medicine syndrome differentiation (200 cases), the binding constraint is output discipline and reasoning structure, not model capability alone: two years of model scaling move zero-shot scores by only -0.03 to +0.08, while output-discipline failures (non-terminating reasoning, format non-compliance, large run-to-run spread) persist even in frontier models. We test this with a model-agnostic agent framework formalizing decision making as a five-stage closed loop, enforced by a candidate x evidence matrix falsification protocol: every candidate is judged against every evidence item, at least half of the candidates must be falsified before a conclusion is licensed, and survivors are emitted in a machine-verifiable single-line format. Across five base models, the effect is sign-conditional on zero-shot output discipline: it rescues models whose discipline fails (DeepSeek-V4-Flash: +0.267/+0.271, entirely termination rescue), reduces a high-variance model's run-to-run standard deviation from 0.218 to 0.007 (Kimi K3), and significantly costs already-disciplined models (-0.087 to -0.120 on budget-matched Qwen3-4B/32B). Ablations attribute the cost to the candidate-bounded format layer and show the effect is independent of injected knowledge content (protocol-knowledge decoupling). The protocol also transfers to misinformation-robust mathematical reasoning, detecting injected false premises at 89.8% recall with a 6.8% false-positive rate (MCC 0.54; a flag-everything baseline scores 0) and restoring accuracy to the no-misinformation ceiling. Where zero-shot output discipline is weak, the reasoning protocol sets the floor; base-model capability always sets the ceiling.
authors: Jing Liu, Yongxing Qi, Ping Yao, Ting Wu
bullets: On the 200-case TCMEval-SDT benchmark, scaling alone changed zero-shot scores by only −0.03 to +0.08, while termination, format, and variance failures persisted.
The five-stage protocol evaluates every candidate against every evidence item, requires at least half the candidates to be falsified, and emits machine-verifiable conclusions.
It improved DeepSeek-V4-Flash by about 0.27 through termination rescue and reduced Kimi K3’s run-to-run standard deviation from 0.218 to 0.007.
It lowered scores for already-disciplined Qwen3-4B/32B models by 0.087–0.120; ablations linked the cost to the candidate-bounded format layer, not injected knowledge.
On misinformation-robust mathematical reasoning, it detected false premises with 89.8% recall and 6.8% false-positive rate, restoring accuracy to the no-misinformation ceiling.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a model-agnostic agent protocol for auditable decision-making that enforces output discipline and falsification, addressing reasoning structure in LLM agents.
papers.title: Output Discipline Sets the Floor: A Falsification-Guided, Model-Agnostic Agent Protocol for Auditable Hypothesis-Driven Decision Making
papers.tldr: A model-agnostic, falsification-guided protocol improves auditable reasoning mainly by enforcing output discipline, helping undisciplined models while sometimes hurting already-disciplined ones.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent debate (MAD) aims to improve large language model reasoning by exposing agents to alternative solutions and enabling iterative revision. However, standard broadcast-style MAD makes peer answers visible without requiring agents to engage with a particular peer claim. As a result, reliable reasoning may be suppressed by conflicting or majority responses, limiting achievable performance, while erroneous reasoning may persist and degrade final predictions without actionable feedback. We propose TrueMAD, a backbone-agnostic test-time plug-in that introduces one-to-one, free-form peer advice between answer broadcasting and self-revision. Each source agent responds to a target's current reasoning through support, rebuttal, refinement, or further questions, while the target retains control over how to revise. The same mechanism can augment standard MAD and its improved variants without parameter updates. Across AIME, GPQA-Diamond, and TruthfulQA with Qwen3-30B-A3B, TrueMAD improves agent-level and strict-majority accuracy over MAD by 3.62 and 3.52 percentage points on average, while TrueDMAD improves DMAD by 4.72 and 4.06 points, respectively. Analyses at the utterance, agent-transition, and group levels further show more peer-specific deliberation, more correction-oriented revisions, and more favorable consensus dynamics.
authors: Dezheng Bao, Sihang Du, Renhong Huang, Zhizhang Yuan, Yifei Sun, Yang Yang
bullets: Standard broadcast debate can leave agents disengaged from peer claims, allowing errors or majority influence to persist.
TrueMAD adds one-to-one, free-form peer advice—including support, rebuttal, refinement, or questions—between answer sharing and self-revision.
It is a backbone-agnostic, parameter-free test-time plug-in that can augment standard MAD and improved variants.
On AIME, GPQA-Diamond, and TruthfulQA using Qwen3-30B-A3B, TrueMAD improves agent-level and strict-majority accuracy over MAD by 3.62 and 3.52 percentage points on average.
The method produces more peer-specific deliberation, correction-oriented revisions, and favorable consensus dynamics.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes TrueMAD, a test-time plug-in for multi-agent debate that improves LLM reasoning through targeted peer engagement, fitting both LLM agent interaction and test-time adaptation.
papers.title: Beyond Answer Sharing: TrueMAD for Targeted Peer Engagement in Multi-Agent Debate
papers.tldr: TrueMAD improves multi-agent debate by directing each agent to give targeted, actionable feedback to a specific peer before revision.

papers.abstract: System One models answer typed questions in a single forward pass and promise the same answer for the same input. For choice questions, this promise fails: the answer depends on the order of the options, increasingly so as they grow in number, and averaging over their cyclic shifts reduces this dependence without removing it. Scoring each option alone, which the order cannot affect, shows that the order changes the answer mostly when the model is unsure among its top few options, even though the listwise answer looks confident. We therefore propose $\textbf{Runoff}$, which considers, then chooses: it scores each option alone to keep a few candidates, then compares them in listings where each candidate takes every position. It needs no training and can run in two forward passes, and its answer does not depend on the option order by construction. On two open models and five datasets, it changes no answer under shuffling, against 9.3% for cyclic averaging, and with 20 options it is about as accurate and three to four times faster. Wrapped around eight System One models, it removes the order dependence of the five benchmarks, while cyclic averaging changes up to 15.4%.
authors: Jianguo Huang, Yao Long Teng, Yanchen Deng, Bo An
bullets: Option order can change answers substantially, especially when models are uncertain among their top few choices despite appearing confident listwise.
Runoff requires no training and can operate in two forward passes.
It is order-invariant by construction and produced no answer changes under shuffling in the reported evaluations.
Across two open models and five datasets, Runoff was about as accurate as cyclic averaging with 20 options and ran 3–4× faster.
Applied to eight System One models, it removed order dependence on all five benchmarks, whereas cyclic averaging changed up to 15.4% of answers.
papers.selection_reason: Order-invariant decision method for System One LLMs; relevant to LLM inference behavior.
papers.title: Consider, Then Choose: Order-Invariant Decisions in System One Models
papers.tldr: Runoff makes System One models’ multiple-choice decisions order-invariant by first narrowing candidates individually, then comparing them across reordered listings.

papers.abstract: Parallel generation is widely regarded as an inherent advantage of diffusion large language models. Yet our fixed-quota evaluation of four representative models reveals severe degradation across mathematics and code, with all scores below 15% at 16 tokens per step. Token-level probes identify local predictive potential near the observed prefix, especially in mathematical text. We propose RePara, which reinforces short consecutive token blocks through group-relative policy optimization and reduces rollout and log-probability recomputation costs. On LLaDA and SDAR, \ours improves GSM8K and MATH-500 accuracy over JustGRPO under reduced denoising budgets, with a 1.96x training-step speedup in our LLaDA/MATH setup.
authors: Jiahao Kuang, Yangfan Gao, Tao Gui, Yuanbin Wu, Qi Zhang, Xuanjing Huang, Tao Ji
bullets: Fixed-quota evaluation finds severe degradation on math and code, with all tested models scoring below 15% at 16 tokens per step.
Token-level probes show useful local predictive potential near the observed prefix, particularly in mathematical text.
RePara applies group-relative policy optimization to reinforce short consecutive token blocks.
On LLaDA and SDAR, RePara improves GSM8K and MATH-500 accuracy over JustGRPO under reduced denoising budgets.
The method achieves a reported 1.96× training-step speedup in the LLaDA/MATH setup.
papers.selection_reason: Improves parallel generation and training efficiency in diffusion LLMs; directly relevant to LLM architecture and reasoning.
papers.title: A Few More Tokens Ahead: Reinforcing Parallelism in Diffusion LLMs
papers.tldr: RePara improves diffusion LLM parallel generation by reinforcing short token blocks, boosting math performance under limited denoising budgets while accelerating training.

papers.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive LLMs, yet remain susceptible to hallucination. Activation steering offers a promising mitigation approach by guiding parallel token predictions through internal representations.
