However, existing steering methods largely overlook two characteristics of dLLMs: dynamic denoising states and temporal hallucination risks, which challenge predefined steering vectors and uniform intervention strengths. We propose TRACESTEER, a trace-driven activation steering framework that uses preceding denoising predictions as feedback to jointly adapt steering direction and strength. Specifically, Denoising Feedback Steering (DF-Steering) constructs step-specific steering vectors from preceding predictions and current hidden states. Trajectory-Guided Steering Gate (TS-Gate) regulates their strength using prediction uncertainty and the denoising timestep. With the backbone frozen, factual supervision and magnitude regularization jointly guide the learning of adaptive steering interventions, promoting factual reliability and stability throughout denoising. Experiments on two dLLMs show improved factual reliability on TruthfulQA and generalization across five downstream benchmarks.
authors: Xin Zhang, Yili Wang, Yue Tan, Xin He, Rui Miao, Yixin Liu, Yi Chang, Xin Wang
bullets: Targets dLLM-specific challenges: changing denoising states and time-varying hallucination risk.
Uses Denoising Feedback Steering to derive step-specific steering vectors from prior predictions and current hidden states.
Uses a Trajectory-Guided Steering Gate to adjust intervention strength based on uncertainty and denoising timestep.
Learns adaptive interventions with the backbone frozen, combining factual supervision and magnitude regularization.
Improves factual reliability on TruthfulQA and generalizes across five downstream benchmarks in experiments on two dLLMs.
papers.selection_reason: Activation steering for diffusion LLMs with inference-time adaptation, fitting language foundation models and test-time learning.
papers.title: TRACESTEER: Trace Driven Activation Steering for Hallucination Mitigation in Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: TRACESTEER reduces hallucinations in diffusion language models by adapting activation-steering directions and strengths throughout the denoising process.

papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation improves a model using guidance from the model itself, but it still requires a teacher that provides more useful predictions than the student. Existing approaches obtain such guidance by giving the teacher additional context or instructions. We ask whether it can instead come from changing how the same model uses its own layers. To address this, we introduce LoOPSD, which searches over a model's layer execution order to construct a stronger teacher and distills its advantage into the student. Specifically, we keep the model weights unchanged while searching for layers to repeat, and use the resulting teacher's predictions on student-generated prefixes to guide learning. We then alternate search and distillation, rebuilding the teacher from the updated student in each round so that the student progressively absorbs the gains from alternative layer execution. Experiments on mathematical and logical reasoning tasks show improvements across models. On GSM8K with a 400-token thinking budget, LoOPSD raises Qwen3-1.7B accuracy from 42.30% to 79.61%; subsequent distillation rounds yield further gains beyond the first round. Together, these findings show that by searching layer execution to construct teachers, we can turn a model's additional computation into improved student capabilities, opening a new avenue for self-distillation to derive supervision from the model's own computation.
authors: Wei Fan, Qingyue Yang, Chao-Hong Tan, Qian Chen, Wen Wang, Xiangang Li, Kejiang Chen, Weiming Zhang, Nenghai Yu
bullets: Addresses the need for a more capable teacher in on-policy self-distillation.
Searches for repeated layers and altered execution orders to construct a stronger teacher from the same model.
Distills teacher predictions on student-generated prefixes, alternating teacher search and student updates.
Improves mathematical and logical reasoning across models; on GSM8K, Qwen3-1.7B rises from 42.30% to 79.61% with a 400-token budget.
Further distillation rounds provide gains beyond the first round.
papers.selection_reason: Self-distillation via looped layer execution improves LLM reasoning; relevant to LLM architecture and training methods.
papers.title: LoOPSD: On-Policy Self-Distillation with Looped Teachers
papers.tldr: LoOPSD improves a model through self-distillation by creating stronger teachers via alternative layer execution, without changing model weights.

papers.abstract: Looped language models (LMs) reuse one block of layers several times per token generation, promising more latent computation at no additional storage cost. Despite their rising popularity, the analysis of looped LMs is still in its infancy: little is known about whether the iterative transformations actually improve their capabilities, or whether these models remain stable under prompt perturbation. We construct an inspection protocol rooted in Mechanistic Interpretability comprising five diverse lenses. We apply it to examine eight looped LMs from four families. Models differ in many aspects but the key one is whether the prompt is transmitted only within the looped state (carry loops: Ouro, LoopUS) or re-supplied at every iteration (re-read loops: Parcae, and Rec-OLMo & Huginn from the Raven family). The results of our study provide valuable insights concerning safety and efficient use of looped language models.
authors: Pawel Olszowiec, Paulina Tomaszewska, Maciej \.Zelaszczyk, Michal Byra, Neo Christopher Chung
bullets: Studies eight looped LMs spanning four model families.
Introduces an inspection protocol using five complementary analytical lenses.
Compares carry loops, which retain prompts only in the looped state, with re-read loops, which re-supply prompts each iteration.
Investigates whether iterative transformations improve capabilities and whether models remain stable under prompt perturbations.
Provides insights relevant to the safety and efficient use of looped language models.
papers.selection_reason: Looped LM architecture and latent reasoning inspection; relevant to LLM architecture advances.
papers.title: Monitoring latent reasoning in looped language models
papers.tldr: A mechanistic-interpretability protocol examines how looped language models reason, improve across iterations, and respond to prompt perturbations.

papers.abstract: Do language models carry information about narrative events before writing them, and how far ahead? We examine narrative lookahead through salient, state-changing events rather than tokens or response-level attributes. We extract 23,355 LLM-annotated events from 2,000 stories generated by four open-weight LLMs, labeling them along three nonexclusive dimensions of change: within agents, between agents, and in the story world, with human validation on a subset. Event segmentation and plot-independent labels enable comparisons across stories at horizons measured in events rather than in tokens. At event ends, we probe hidden states for upcoming event types and compare predictions with text-only predictors using matched prefixes. Across four models, future event types are decodable above prevalence baselines for at least four subsequent events, but probes significantly outperform both primary text-only predictors only for the next event. In exploratory steering with OLMo-3.1-32B, a probe-derived direction shifts the proportion of the target event type in both intended directions at higher strengths. Our event-level approach links the prediction of future narrative developments to interventions that reshape subsequent event composition.
authors: Donghoon Jung, Min Kim, Seojin Choi, Songeun Chae, Seohyon Jung
bullets: Studies 23,355 annotated events from 2,000 stories generated by four open-weight LLMs, using event-level rather than token-level horizons.
Future event types are decodable above baseline for at least four events ahead.
Hidden-state probes outperform matched text-only predictors significantly only for the immediately upcoming event.
In exploratory steering with OLMo-3.1-32B, probe-derived directions shift the frequency of target event types in both intended directions.
Human validation supports the event labels, but steering results are exploratory and demonstrated with one model.
papers.selection_reason: Studies event-level predictive lookahead and activation steering in LLM hidden states, fitting language foundation model research.
papers.title: Narrative Lookahead in LLMs: Event-Level Decodability, Predictive Advantage, and Steering
papers.tldr: LLMs encode information about upcoming narrative events, with reliable next-event prediction and limited ability to steer what happens next.

papers.abstract: AI companions provide users with emotional support and ongoing companionship, but their sustained relational interactions also introduce distinct safety risks. Prior work largely targets general harms or specific companion platforms and risk categories, while relying on manually collected conversations, limiting scalable and user-grounded evaluation and mitigation. To address this, we introduce CompanionSafe, a unified evaluation-to-mitigation framework for AI companion safety. Its evaluation component, CompanionEval, provides scalable multi-turn evaluation by constructing 1,300 relationally grounded settings from diverse personas, matched companion characters, and dialogue scenarios across four turn tiers. Its mitigation component, CompanionGuard, converts benchmark-exposed failures into turn-localized supervision for companion-specific risk detection. Our results show that even strong LLMs and existing guard models remain vulnerable to companion-specific relational harms, while both closed- and open-source models exhibit increasing safety risks as interactions become longer. Together, CompanionEval and CompanionGuard form a practical evaluation-to-mitigation loop for AI companion safety, turning relational safety failures exposed during multi-turn interaction into supervision for companion-specific guardrails.
authors: Xinyang Liao, Lingyu Li, Kaicheng Shen, Yang Yao, Na Lu, Yan Teng, Xia Hu
bullets: Targets relational harms in sustained AI companion interactions, which general safety evaluations may miss.
CompanionEval constructs 1,300 settings using diverse personas, companion characters, scenarios, and four dialogue-length tiers.
CompanionGuard turns benchmark-identified failures into turn-localized supervision for companion-specific risk detection.
Experiments find vulnerabilities in both strong LLMs and existing guard models, with risks increasing over longer interactions.
Provides a practical evaluation-to-mitigation framework, though its scope is limited to the risks and settings represented in the benchmark.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces CompanionSafe, a framework for evaluating and mitigating safety risks in AI companions through multi-turn interaction analysis, focusing on relational harms.
papers.title: CompanionSafe: From Multi-turn Safety Evaluation to Guardrails for AI Companions
papers.tldr: CompanionSafe introduces a scalable multi-turn benchmark and guardrail-training loop for detecting and mitigating safety risks specific to AI companion relationships.

papers.abstract: Deep research (DR) agents address open-ended information needs through multi-step reasoning, long-horizon web search, and evidence synthesis. However, existing benchmarks primarily focus on academic research or synthetic tasks, leaving DR agents' capabilities in real-world life and professional productivity settings insufficiently evaluated. To bridge this gap, we introduce LifeSearch, a challenging benchmark comprising 203 Chinese and English tasks derived from real-user query seeds across 7 concrete life and productivity domains. With more than 4,500 hours of human annotation, we construct over 4,000 expert-written, fine-grained rubrics, covering both report-content criteria for coverage and accuracy and concrete criteria specifying values, units, dates, and URLs. We conduct extensive experiments on 12 advanced DR agents under a unified evaluation harness, systematically analyzing their performance patterns and failure modes. We find that even the best-performing frontier agent, GPT-5.6 Sol, achieves a score of only 63.4%, leaving substantial room for improvement on realistic life and professional DR tasks. We select the grading configuration by comparing candidate LLM judges against human rubric labels, and a human ranking study shows strong alignment between aggregate benchmark scores and human judgments (Spearman's $\rho = 0.89$, Kendall's $\tau = 0.81$). LifeSearch provides a rigorous evaluation framework and foundation for advancing DR agents toward real-world life and productivity.
authors: Yibo Wang, Senjie Jin, Yansong Ning, Xinbing Liang, Haotian Luo, Jiazheng Zhang, Yuxuan He, Will Wu, Clarenceai
bullets: Covers 203 Chinese and English tasks across 7 real-world life and professional productivity domains.
Uses over 4,000 expert-written rubrics and more than 4,500 hours of human annotation to assess coverage, accuracy, and concrete details such as dates, units, values, and URLs.
Evaluates 12 advanced deep research agents with a unified harness and analyzes their performance patterns and failure modes.
The top-performing reported agent scores 63.4%, indicating substantial room for improvement.
Benchmark scores align strongly with human judgments, supporting LifeSearch’s evaluation validity.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces LifeSearch, a benchmark for evaluating deep research agents on real-world life and productivity tasks, addressing a gap in current evaluations focused on academic or synthetic tasks.
papers.title: LifeSearch: Benchmarking Deep Research Agents for Real-World Life and Productivity
papers.tldr: LifeSearch is a human-annotated benchmark showing that deep research agents still struggle with realistic life and productivity tasks.

papers.abstract: Ambiguous or incomplete task specifications complicate both execution and clarification for language-model agents. Yet agents' responses to these information gaps remain poorly characterized across models and execution harnesses. We present AM-Bench, a benchmark built from 48 tasks adapted from Terminal-Bench 2.0 and Harness-Bench. Each task includes a fully specified reference and six variants spanning ambiguous or missing goals, context, and constraints. We evaluate every pairing of five models and four harnesses over 20,160 runs. Our results reveal distinct execution deficits: goal gaps hinder completion, context gaps increase token use, and constraint gaps weaken compliance without necessarily preventing completion. Missingness lowers success more than ambiguity in all three domains. These effects also reshape system comparisons: advantages under complete information need not persist, and rankings depend on model $\times$ harness pairings and the evaluation criterion -- completion, success, or repeat consistency. Estimates based on observed clarification requests and matched fully specified runs further suggest that clarification could recover unfinished work while leaving most constraint violations unresolved. Together, these findings motivate joint model-harness evaluation across information conditions and targeted clarification of unresolved requirements before dependent actions. To support future research on agents under task underspecification, we provide the AM-Bench project repository at https://github.com/s4-lab-cuhksz/AM-Bench.git.
authors: Kaiyu Huang, Yiting Li, Angyang Gu, Pinjia He, Minchen Yu, Qingjiang Shi
bullets: Introduces 48 tasks with fully specified references and six variants covering ambiguous or missing goals, context, and constraints.
Evaluates five models across four execution harnesses in 20,160 runs.
Goal gaps reduce completion, context gaps increase token use, and constraint gaps weaken compliance without always blocking completion.
Missing information harms success more than ambiguity across all three domains.
Clarification may recover unfinished work but is unlikely to resolve most constraint violations; joint model–harness evaluation is therefore needed.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces AM-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents under task underspecification, providing insights into how agents handle ambiguous or incomplete task specifications.
papers.title: AM-Bench: Understanding Agents under Task Underspecification across Models and Harnesses
papers.tldr: AM-Bench shows that task underspecification affects agent completion, efficiency, and compliance differently, with outcomes varying substantially by model–harness pairing and evaluation criterion.

papers.abstract: AI has become increasingly helpful in scientific discovery, yet human expert review remains essential for those problems without reliable automated evaluation, posing a fundamental challenge as candidate generation scales beyond available review capacity. This paper studies verification under limited human effort, where rare valid solutions need to be prioritized while invalid candidates should be filtered out to reduce human workload. We adopt the one-sided verification objective that maximizes the rejection rate of invalid solutions (TNR) under a constraint on the false-rejection rate of valid ones (FNR), making human review cost an explicit term to minimize. Drawing on the intuition that verifying a specific error can be easier than discovering one, we introduce OSVerify, an algorithmic framework that decouples error proposal from error validation. The error proposer searches for errors in solutions across different granularities by hierarchical decomposition, while the validator distinguishes substantial errors from minor or hallucinated ones. Experiments on competition- and research-level benchmarks show that OSVerify reduces the number of human reviews of invalid solutions by 46% on average compared to voting baselines under the same empirical low FNR constraint. Our post-training of the validator further improves the reduction to 57%. As high-impact real-world use cases, we apply OSVerify to identify errors in published research papers that are subsequently confirmed by the original authors and help resolve three Langlands open conjectures that are confirmed by experts, demonstrating its utility to facilitate human-AI research collaboration.
authors: Fan Nie, Haotian Ye, Shurui Liu, Zihao Wang, Stefano Ermon, James Zou
bullets: Targets one-sided verification: maximize rejection of invalid candidates while constraining false rejection of valid solutions.
Separates error proposal from error validation using hierarchical search across solution granularities and a validator that filters substantial from minor or hallucinated errors.
Reduces human reviews of invalid solutions by 46% on average versus voting baselines, improving to 57% with validator post-training under the same empirical low-FNR constraint.
Demonstrated on competition- and research-level benchmarks, published papers, and three Langlands open conjectures confirmed by experts.
Scope: designed for settings where reliable automated evaluation is unavailable and expert review is limited.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces OSVerify, an algorithmic framework for efficient error validation in AI-assisted scientific discovery that decouples error proposal from validation to minimize human review effort.
papers.title: One-Sided Verification Under Limited Expert Review
papers.tldr: OSVerify reduces scarce expert-review effort by finding and validating errors in candidate solutions while maintaining a low false-rejection rate for valid ones.

papers.abstract: Autoresearch systems increasingly undertake entire research projects. In practice, scientific research requires systems to pursue multiple interdependent claims through a continuous, multi-stage workflow and revise experiments as evidence accumulates. Existing evaluations of autoresearch systems, however, typically score isolated tasks or final artifacts, leaving these process-level capabilities largely unmeasured. We therefore introduce ResearchFlow-Eval, a fine-grained framework for assessing continuous scientific execution and iteration at both the stage and claim levels. Each evaluation is grounded in a published anchor paper, from which we derive stage-specific rubrics that decompose each research stage into dimensions and separately scored rubric items. Using these rubrics, we score each research stage and examine experimental execution in detail, focusing on multi-claim completion and revisions across attempts. We apply the evaluation framework to general-purpose agent harnesses, skill-augmented harnesses, and systems with research-specific orchestration. Across all evaluated systems, experimental execution consistently lags behind design and planning. Within execution, systems struggle to produce high-quality results and meet claim requirements, and repeated attempts rarely yield measurable improvements. Moreover, neither skill augmentation nor research-specific orchestration reliably yields higher scores. ResearchFlow-Eval thus extends autoresearch evaluation beyond isolated, single-objective runs to continuous workflows in which systems pursue multiple claims and refine their work across iterations.
authors: Peng Jiang (Tsinghua University), Dongyang Li (Tsinghua University), Quanying Liu (Southern University of Science,Technology), Xiaoxuan Jia (Tsinghua University)
bullets: Evaluates continuous scientific execution at both research-stage and claim levels.
Derives fine-grained, stage-specific rubrics from published anchor papers, with separately scored items.
Assesses general-purpose, skill-augmented, and research-orchestrated agent systems.
Finds consistent gaps in experimental execution, including weak results, unmet claim requirements, and limited gains across repeated attempts.
Skill augmentation and research-specific orchestration do not reliably improve evaluation scores.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces ResearchFlow-Eval, a fine-grained framework for evaluating the execution capabilities of autoresearch systems, specifically focusing on multi-claim workflows and iteration.
papers.title: ResearchFlow-Eval: Tracing the Execution Gap in End-to-End Multi-Claim Autoresearch
papers.tldr: ResearchFlow-Eval shows that autoresearch systems remain much weaker at executing and iteratively refining multi-claim research workflows than at planning them.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own rollouts under a frozen teacher, mitigating the distribution mismatch of off-policy supervision. While prior work has primarily trained on problems a student can largely solve, we ask whether OPD can improve a student when training is restricted to problems it currently fails. We evaluate five representative OPD mechanisms with Qwen-3 and Phi-4 models under a unified competition-mathematics protocol. We find that OPD does not improve accuracy on this hard subset, with most mechanisms instead degrading performance despite continued decreases in training KL divergence. All eight configurations show a decline, and the two-sided sign test gives p=0.0078. In contrast, the same pipeline improves accuracy by 4.6 percentage points when training is not concentrated on failures, showing that the failure is conditional on the training regime rather than systematic. These findings suggest that OPD is effective when supervision is dominated by correct student prefixes, but can reinforce existing errors when training is concentrated on problems the student currently fails.
authors: Shuo Yang, Zheyu Zhang, Mahito Sugiyama, Gjergji Kasneci
bullets: Evaluated five OPD mechanisms with Qwen-3 and Phi-4 under a unified competition-mathematics protocol.
Failure-focused OPD reduced accuracy in all eight configurations despite continued decreases in training KL divergence.
A two-sided sign test found the degradation statistically significant (p=0.0078).
When training was not concentrated on failures, the same pipeline improved accuracy by 4.6 percentage points.
The results suggest OPD benefits from correct student prefixes but can amplify errors in failure-heavy regimes.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes on-policy distillation training dynamics for large language models on reasoning tasks, relevant to language foundation model training.
papers.title: Correcting or Continuing? What On-Policy Distillation Learns from Student Errors
papers.tldr: On-policy distillation can reinforce student mistakes rather than correct them when training focuses on problems the student already fails.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) enable flexible parallel generation by resolving tokens according to the model's evolving predictability rather than a fixed left-to-right order. This flexibility, however, introduces training choices absent from standard autoregressive teacher forcing: which reference tokens are visible when a target is supervised and how much generation space is allocated. Standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) typically makes these choices through random masking, independently of inference. Our analysis shows how this training-inference mismatch can misdirect supervision. Random masking can conceal prediction errors or penalize uncertainty that decoding would otherwise resolve, while the attention-visible input length can change which response formulations the model favors, even when the underlying solution is unchanged. Motivated by these findings, we propose Predictability-Aware Canvas Selection and Supervision (PACS), an SFT method. PACS uses the model's own predictability to select each example's attention-visible input length and supervises reference tokens immediately before their confidence-guided revelation. Across reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, PACS consistently achieves the highest mean accuracy among the compared SFT methods, with gains of up to 12.84 percentage points over vanilla SFT on individual benchmarks. Code will be released upon publication.
authors: Miao Li, Hanyang Jiang, Hengyu Fu, Baihe Huang, Yating Liu, Yuhang Cai, Changkun Guan, Zhongzhu Chen, Jiecheng Lu, Michael A. Boateng, Pascal Van Hentenryck
bullets: DLMs generate tokens in flexible, predictability-driven orders, making visibility and generation-space choices important during training.
Random masking can mismatch inference by hiding errors or penalizing uncertainty that decoding would resolve.
PACS selects the attention-visible input length using the model’s predictability and supervises tokens just before their confidence-guided revelation.

Across reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, PACS achieved the highest mean accuracy among compared SFT methods, with gains of up to 12.84 percentage points over vanilla SFT on individual benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Develops a supervised fine-tuning method for diffusion language models, a class of language foundation models.
papers.title: Match the Canvas, Not Just the Answer: Predictability-Aware SFT for Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: PACS aligns diffusion language model fine-tuning with confidence-guided inference, improving reasoning and code-generation accuracy over standard SFT.

papers.abstract: Modern Transformers rely on many scale-control mechanisms, including normalization, residual scaling, attention temperatures, loss weighting, and adaptive updates. To explain how these mechanisms maintain scale consistency, we introduce Neural Dimensional Analysis (NDA), a unified framework based on dimensional consistency. We define neural units that specify how tensors rescale and which quantities can be added, just as physical units do in physics. Our rules match residual units, nondimensionalize attention and gate inputs, combine losses across units, and convert gradient units into parameter units. We implement NDA through dimensionless Unit Violation Indices (UVI) for diagnosing scale mismatches within Transformers, a unit-consistent multi-loss objective, and the Gauge-Canonical Transformer (GCT) with normalized coordinates and orthogonalized residual additions. In language-model experiments spanning 51M to 1B parameters, GCT remains stable during training across a broad sixteenfold learning-rate range, outperforming Pre-LN, LLaMA-style, and QK-Norm in 124M validation loss at tuned learning rates. GCT's normalized residual stream also shows improved robustness to quantization. At 1B parameters, calibrated per-tensor int8 quantization increases GCT's validation loss by only 0.009 nats, compared with up to 5.51 nats for the baselines. Vision and physics-informed neural network experiments further confirm NDA's benefits beyond language modeling. These results establish dimensional consistency as a neural network design principle.
authors: Bum Jun Kim, Makoto Kawano, Yusuke Iwasawa, Yutaka Matsuo
bullets: Motivated by the many scale-control mechanisms required in modern Transformers, including normalization, residual scaling, attention temperatures, and loss weighting.
Defines neural units and dimensional-consistency rules for tensor rescaling, valid additions, attention and gate inputs, multi-loss objectives, and gradient-to-parameter conversion.
Introduces Unit Violation Indices for diagnosing scale mismatches and the Gauge-Canonical Transformer with normalized coordinates and orthogonalized residual additions.
Across language, vision, and physics-informed experiments, the approach supports stable training over a broad learning-rate range and improved quantization robustness.
In the reported 1B-parameter experiment, calibrated per-tensor int8 quantization increased validation loss by 0.009 nats for GCT versus up to 5.51 nats for baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Transformer architecture design for scale consistency, validated on LLMs up to 1B; relevant to LLM architectures.
papers.title: Neural Dimensional Analysis: Foundations of Dimensionless and Scale-Consistent Computation
papers.tldr: Neural Dimensional Analysis (NDA) treats tensor scales like physical units, providing a framework and architectures for more consistent and robust neural-network computation.

papers.abstract: The design of attention mechanisms in long-context large language models faces an ``impossible triangle'' among KV cache size, training and prefill FLOPs, and model quality. GQA achieves strong quality but incurs high KV cache overhead; alternative approaches such as MLA and MFA can compress the cache, but MLA suffers from quality loss while MFA substantially increases training and prefill compute. We propose Virtual Head Attention (VHA), which simultaneously improves all three vertices through two lightweight linear operations: Q Premix applies a near-identity transformation to queries within each KV group to recover virtual head diversity from halved physical query heads, and Linear Postmix fuses inter-head features via a low-rank $I + AB^\top$ residual structure. Since VHA introduces no nonlinear operations, Premix can be folded into the query projection and Postmix into the output projection at inference time, reducing the model to a standard GQA-2 architecture that directly reuses all existing GQA inference optimizations. With only two KV heads, the group size in large models readily reaches 64, fully exploiting Tensor Core parallelism during decoding. Across four scales with 4K-context 50B-token pretraining, VHA consistently surpasses the standard GQA baseline at every scale ($+$0.05\% to $+$0.81\%), while reducing KV cache by $4\times$ vs.\ GQA-8 at dense scales and $2\times$ vs.\ GQA-4 at the MoE scale, and lowering training and prefill FLOPs by 7.9\% (1.7B, $S{=}4096$). On an industrial 30B-A3B MoE model trained on 500B tokens at 8K context, VHA outperforms both MLA and GQA-4 by $+$0.70\,/\,$+$2.60\,\% on a 12-benchmark base-model evaluation suite; in a separate matched 10B-A1B MoE comparison after long-context mid-training, VHA attains an average RULER score of 84.4 over 8K--128K versus 73.0 for GQA, while using two rather than four KV heads in the full-attention layers.
authors: Xibo Ding, Guoxia Wang, Jinle Zeng, Jiabin Yang, Sirui Tao, Chao Yang, Dianhai Yu
bullets: Targets the trade-off among KV-cache size, training/prefill compute, and model quality in long-context LLMs.
Uses two lightweight linear operations: Q Premix restores virtual query-head diversity, while Linear Postmix fuses inter-head features with a low-rank residual structure.
The operations can be folded into existing projections at inference, yielding a standard GQA-2 model compatible with GQA optimizations and Tensor Core decoding.
Across four model scales, VHA improves over GQA while reducing KV cache by 2–4× and training/prefill FLOPs by 7.9% in one reported setting.
On industrial MoE evaluations, VHA outperforms MLA and GQA and achieves higher long-context RULER scores than GQA while using fewer KV heads.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a linear attention variant that reduces KV cache size and training/prefill FLOPs for long-context LLMs, directly advancing efficient attention and KV-cache efficiency.
papers.title: Virtual Head Attention
papers.tldr: Virtual Head Attention (VHA) reduces KV-cache and compute costs while maintaining or improving long-context language-model quality over standard attention alternatives.

papers.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have attracted increasing research attention due to their bidirectional attention and arbitrary order decoding. However, there are two issues in dLLMs inference: the decoding difficulty is dominated by the tokens on the right side of the block, and the block-wise decoding inherently suffers from boundary contextual discontinuity. To tackle these limitations, we propose HaloBlock, a difficulty-aware adaptive halo mechanism for dLLM inference. We first leverage bidirectional cumulative entropy to characterize block decoding difficulty. Then, based on the bidirectional decoding difficulty, we adaptively allocate bidirectional halo regions on both sides of each block to mitigate boundary contextual discontinuity. The difficulty-aware design of HaloBlock smooths cross-block context propagation and lowers decoding difficulty for hard tokens, yielding better generation quality and faster convergence. Evaluated on LLaDA-8B-Instruct, Dream-7B-Instruct and LLaDA-1.5 across mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks, HaloBlock demonstrates consistent accuracy improvements and higher inference efficiency. Source codes are publicly available at https://github.com/PolyU-VCLab/HaloBlock.
authors: Zhaohui Zheng, Chenhang He, Jinrui Zhang, Ming-Ming Cheng, Lei Zhang
bullets: dLLM block-wise decoding is challenged by difficult right-side tokens and discontinuous context across block boundaries.
It estimates block difficulty using bidirectional cumulative entropy.
It adaptively allocates halo regions on both sides of each block to improve cross-block context propagation.
Experiments on LLaDA-8B-Instruct, Dream-7B-Instruct, and LLaDA-1.5 show consistent accuracy gains and higher inference efficiency on math and code-generation benchmarks.
Source code is publicly available.
papers.selection_reason: Improves decoding efficiency and quality for diffusion large language models, relevant to LLM inference and architecture.
papers.title: HaloBlock: Faster and Better Decoding for Diffusion Large Language Models
papers.tldr: HaloBlock improves diffusion LLM decoding by adaptively adding context around block boundaries based on token difficulty, achieving better quality and faster inference.

papers.abstract: Theory of mind (ToM), the ability to reason about others' mental states, underlies effective communication and coordination. Its higher-order form enables reasoning over nested perspectives in strategic interactions. However, existing evaluations often equate belief-nesting depth with reasoning order, allowing nominally higher-order questions to admit lower-order shortcuts. We formalize effective order through the distinct events supporting successive belief prefixes, revealing widespread order inflation across existing benchmarks. We introduce HopToM, with certified full-order questions and controls for lower-order alternatives. Under direct prompting, mean accuracy across four frontier LLMs falls from 73.5% at first order to 20.0% at fourth order, and human participants also struggle. Causal interventions link a recurring class of errors to evidence for shallower belief prefixes. We introduce HopTrace, a plug-and-play inference-time method that encodes each interaction once into perspective records and resolves nested queries deterministically. On certified narrative questions, it improves fourth- and fifth-order accuracy by 22.0 and 38.5 percentage points over strong prompting baselines, while using 20-39 times fewer tokens than multi-call methods. These results sharpen how higher-order ToM is evaluated and offer a practical way to improve perspective reasoning in interactive agents.
authors: Shanshan You, Zhengqi Wang, Hao Liu, Yuqin Liu, Ya He, Xin Hao, Liyuan Wang
bullets: Existing benchmarks can mistake belief-nesting depth for genuine reasoning order because lower-order shortcuts remain possible.
HopToM certifies full-order questions and controls for lower-order alternatives, exposing widespread order inflation.
Across four frontier LLMs, mean accuracy drops from 73.5% at first order to 20.0% at fourth order; humans also struggle.
HopTrace improves fourth- and fifth-order accuracy by 22.0 and 38.5 percentage points over strong prompting baselines while using 20–39× fewer tokens than multi-call methods.
Error analyses link recurring failures to reliance on shallower belief prefixes.
papers.selection_reason: Formalizes and improves higher-order theory-of-mind reasoning in LLMs, fitting the language foundation model reasoning focus.
papers.title: Beyond Belief Nesting: Rethinking Higher-Order Theory of Mind in Large Language Models
papers.tldr: Higher-order Theory of Mind is often overestimated in LLM benchmarks, but certified tests reveal sharp performance declines that HopTrace substantially mitigates with efficient perspective tracking.

papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) achieve strong performance by externalizing explicit reasoning traces before producing the answer, yet suffer from overthinking challenge that allocates uniformly heavy computation to queries of varying difficulty. While proprietary models mitigate this via opaque routing, open-source LRMs still lack an efficient mechanism to internalize adaptive reasoning due to both expensive training cost and limited disclosure of training recipes. In response, we introduce RPO (Root-token Policy Optimization), a framework that enables LRMs to self-determine when to reason by training only the initial root token (e.g., whether to invoke the tag) via group relative reward and group-wise advantages. By focusing on this pivotal branching point, RPO drastically reduces training overhead and VRAM usage. Across multiple model families and scales, RPO learns difficulty-aware adaptive thinking at just ~2% of the training compute of prior adaptive-reasoning methods.
authors: Taehyeon Kim, Hyunsoo Lee, Youngsoo Jang, Moontae Lee
bullets: Addresses overthinking caused by applying equally heavy reasoning to queries of different difficulty.
Optimizes only the initial root token that decides whether to invoke explicit reasoning.
Uses group-relative rewards and group-wise advantages to learn difficulty-aware routing.
Reported across multiple model families and scales, with substantially lower training overhead and VRAM use.
The abstract does not specify detailed datasets, baselines, or inference-time gains.
papers.selection_reason: Tackles adaptive reasoning in LRMs with minimal training/inference compute; directly contributes to efficient AI and large reasoning model methodology.
papers.title: Efficiently Learning To Reason or Not to Reason: Root-token Policy Optimization for Adaptive Thinking
papers.tldr: RPO trains a reasoning model to decide when to think, reducing adaptive-reasoning training compute to about 2% of prior methods.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) have attracted wide attention for their fast, parallel decoding, but they are believed to be far less efficient to train than autoregressive language models (ARMs): a widely cited study reports that a DLM needs roughly 16x the training compute of an ARM to match its likelihood, a figure that has made pretraining DLMs from scratch look prohibitive at scale. We find that the methodology behind this figure has fallen out of step with current DLM practice: it scores the model with its evidence lower bound (ELBO) and trains a full-sequence, decoder-only model. We therefore revisit the scaling laws of DLMs, adopting the exact likelihood under the model's own decoding order, block diffusion training, an encoder-decoder architecture, and a sweep over the block sizes used in practice. Under this new protocol, we study across ten model variants, about 1,700 models in total, and find that pretraining DLMs is far cheaper than previously thought. Concretely, scoring with the exact likelihood reduces the compute multiple to 12.8x; block diffusion training and an encoder-decoder architecture further reduce it to 7.8x at block size 32, and smaller block sizes narrow it to 4.6x at block size 8 and 3.0x at block size 4. We complement these scaling analyses with an empirical rule for the optimal decoder depth of encoder-decoder block diffusion, a held-out compute budget beyond the fitting range at which the gap between variants persists, and downstream benchmark results where likelihood improvements carry over to accuracy. Overall, the 16x figure substantially overstates the pretraining cost gap between DLMs and ARMs, and pretraining DLMs from scratch is far more viable than previously assumed.
authors: Guanghan Wang, Bing He, Zhan Shi, Benoit Dumoulin, Hanqing Lu, Volodymyr Kuleshov
bullets: The prior estimate used ELBO scoring and full-sequence decoder-only training, which do not reflect current DLM practice.
Using exact likelihood, block diffusion training, encoder-decoder models, and practical block sizes reduces the compute gap from 16× to 3.0×–12.8×.
The study evaluates about 1,700 models across ten variants and tests scaling behavior beyond the fitting range.
Likelihood gains also transfer to downstream accuracy, supporting the practical relevance of the revised scaling results.
Overall, training DLMs from scratch appears substantially more viable than previously assumed.
papers.selection_reason: Revisits pretraining compute scaling of diffusion versus autoregressive language models, relevant to LLM architecture research.
papers.title: Revisiting the 16x Pretraining Compute Gap between Diffusion and Autoregressive Language Models
papers.tldr: A revised evaluation and training protocol shows that diffusion language models require far less extra pretraining compute than the previously reported 16× gap suggests.

papers.abstract: In humans, proprioception corresponds to the sense of self-movement or position, e.g. understanding the position of one's arm. This sense is often less well-understood and in popular understanding sometimes conflated with introspection. But, notably, proprioception is a separate sense, with dedicated receptors and verifiable outcomes. On the other hand though, language models cannot observe their own internal states during training (and for example answer the question which experts activated in a certain layer of an MoE) and so cannot accurately report on them. Yet, such information is, by virtue of being internal to the model, both accessible, and readily constructed into verifiable signals. We argue that this provides the basis for a digital analog of proprioception. As such, we train models through SFT and on-policy training to equip them with this ability. We show that modern models can be trained to understand a range of subtypes of proprioception, such as routing decision awareness, token entropy, decision depth or logit lens information, without affecting model capabilities. We then run these models through a broad evaluation of situational awareness, legibility, and epiphenomenality, to evaluate in what ways access to proprioception changes model behavior.
bullets: Defines model proprioception as awareness of internal signals, distinct from introspection.
Trains models using supervised fine-tuning and on-policy training.
Covers routing decisions, token entropy, decision depth, and logit-lens information.
Evaluates effects on situational awareness, legibility, and epiphenomenality.
Reports that this internal-state awareness can be added without affecting model capabilities.
papers.selection_reason: Training language models to report internal states, relevant to LLM capabilities and behavior.
papers.title: A Sense of Proprioception in Language Models
papers.tldr: The paper develops a digital analog of proprioception that lets language models report verifiable information about their internal states without reducing their capabilities.

papers.abstract: Training large language models is constrained by both wall-clock time and memory footprint, and recent matrix-aware optimizers sharpen this tradeoff: Muon can improve optimization but its dense polar update remains expensive. We propose Monarch-Muon, a structured matrix-aware optimizer for weights parameterized by Monarch factors. The resulting structure reduces weights, gradients, and optimizer state, and exposes small independent update subproblems in place of a single dense orthogonalization; we formalize this through a blockwise trust-region interpretation. In quality runs, Monarch-Muon improves over Monarch-AdamW at fixed structure: 3.06 vs. 3.09 in the dense 257M model and 2.68 vs. 2.77 in the 1B MoE model; the two-block MoE variant also matches dense AdamW while using 15% fewer active and 25.4% fewer total parameters. In 6.89B-parameter systems measurements, Monarch-Muon reduces peak memory from 68.9 to 52.9 GB, Muon optimizer state from 14.60 to 6.77 GB, and the Muon optimizer step from 1288 to 304 ms.
authors: Alexander Miasnikov, Ruslan Kabirov, Gleb Molodtsov, Dmitrii Vlashchuk, Vladimir Aletov, Nail Bashirov, Daniil Tikhonov, Maxim Krutikov, Aleksandr Shestakov, Aleksandr Beznosikov
bullets: Targets the compute and memory costs of dense Muon updates for large language models.
Parameterizes weights with Monarch factors, reducing weights, gradients, and optimizer state.
Replaces dense orthogonalization with independent blockwise update problems, formalized via a trust-region view.
Improves over Monarch-AdamW in reported dense and MoE quality runs, and matches dense AdamW with fewer parameters in a two-block MoE.
For 6.89B-parameter systems, reduces peak memory from 68.9 to 52.9 GB and the Muon optimizer step from 1288 to 304 ms.
papers.selection_reason: Memory-efficient structured optimizer for LLM pretraining, relevant to both efficient AI and language foundation models.
papers.title: Monarch-Muon: Structure-Aware Muon for Fast and Memory-Efficient Pretraining
papers.tldr: Monarch-Muon makes Muon-style pretraining more memory- and time-efficient by exploiting structured Monarch factorization while maintaining or improving model quality.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is a post-training approach for large language models (LLMs) that enables a student model to learn a teacher model's distribution from sequences sampled from the student's own policy. Despite its promising capability, OPD for diffusion language models (DLMs) remains underexplored and existing studies primarily focuses on DLM-to-DLM distillation. The limited availability of strong teacher DLMs and the flexible generation order of DLMs impose additional technical challenges as well. However, it remains unclear how to effectively distill knowledge from a strong autoregressive language model (ARM) into a weaker DLM, given the mismatch between the left-to-right decoding of ARMs and the flexible decoding order of DLMs. Inspired by Ni et al. (2026), we propose JustOPD, an ARM-to-DLM on-policy distillation method that uses autoregressive rollouts during training to align the student's generation process with the ARM teacher's left-to-right decoding. This alignment enables effective distillation from ARM teachers while preserving the DLM's flexible generation-order capability at inference time. Experiments using Qwen3-14B as the teacher and Dream-7B as the student demonstrate that JustOPD consistently improves mathematical reasoning performance over the base DLM across multiple divergence choices.
authors: Zikun Zhang, Jiayuan Sheng, David D. Yao, Wenpin Tang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of ARM-to-DLM distillation caused by mismatched decoding orders.
Uses autoregressive rollouts to align the DLM student’s training process with the teacher’s left-to-right generation.
Retains the DLM’s flexible generation-order capability during inference.
Experiments with Qwen3-14B as teacher and Dream-7B as student show consistent mathematical-reasoning gains across multiple divergence choices.
papers.selection_reason: On-policy distillation from autoregressive to diffusion language models, relevant to LLM training and foundation language model development.
papers.title: JustOPD: On-Policy Distillation from Autoregressive to Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: JustOPD distills knowledge from autoregressive teachers into diffusion language models by using autoregressive student rollouts during training while preserving flexible decoding at inference.

papers.abstract: Formal verification proves that a program satisfies its specification, but says nothing about whether the specification captures what the author meant. As LLMs increasingly write both code and specifications, a gap between the author's natural-language requirement and the specification becomes a live risk. A machine-checked proof of a property narrower than the one requested is worthless but passes every check. Closing this gap is solving the spec formalization problem: given a natural-language requirement, produce a formal artifact whose meaning matches it. To measure the gap, we curate an end-to-end benchmark for spec formalization spanning four formal languages: Dafny contracts and Lean 4, Isabelle and Rocq theorem statements. Each of its 3,234 rows pairs a natural-language requirement with a formal artifact and a label established by execution, by proof, or by the benchmark it is drawn from. A third of the rows are meaning-preserving rewrites of the artifact that keep the faithful label, so a judge cannot score by detecting that a row was edited. We introduce claimcheck, a tool that detects incorrect formalizations: the formal artifact is translated back into plain English by a model that never sees the requirement, and a separate model, the judge, decides whether the informalization and the requirement express the same guarantee. On all four languages it gains 8.2 to 9.8 points of macro recall over a single call shown the requirement and the artifact, and 4.2 to 6.0 over that call handed the same list of meaning-preserving rewrites. Showing the judge the artifact as well costs 1.4 to 4.5 points. Across four judges that also see the artifact, the gain shrinks as the judge gets stronger, to within a point of the informed single call for the strongest.
authors: Martin Amster, One An, Holly Baker, Fernanda Graciolli, Simon Henniger, Nada Amin
bullets: Addresses the risk that verified code satisfies a formal specification narrower than the author’s intent.
Introduces a 3,234-row benchmark covering Dafny, Lean 4, Isabelle, and Rocq formalizations.
Uses a two-model pipeline: one translates the formal artifact into plain English, and another judges semantic agreement with the requirement.
Improves macro recall by 8.2–9.8 points over a single informed call, and by 4.2–6.0 points against meaning-preserving rewrites.
Benefits diminish for stronger judges, approaching informed single-call performance within one point.
papers.selection_reason: LLM-based tool for measuring specification faithfulness via informalization and judging, relevant to LLM reasoning and evaluation.
papers.title: claimcheck: Measuring and Improving Specification Faithfulness
papers.tldr: claimcheck measures whether formal specifications faithfully capture natural-language requirements and improves detection of mismatches across four formal languages.

papers.abstract: We revisit the statistical mechanics of Transformer attention via modern Hopfield models. We present a free-energy formalism to characterize parameter regimes and critical thresholds for robust attention inference. The resulting free-energy landscape incorporates randomness in query states and attention weights. Attention then emerges as the equation of motion of the corresponding statistical-mechanical system (i.e., modern Hopfield model) through the standard free-energy minimization principle. This allows us to identify first-order phase transitions in attention between glassy and robust-inference phases. We further extend to attentions with stochastic queries and keys. Together, our results provide a rigorous statistical-mechanics framework for characterizing phase structure and inference reliability across a family of Transformer attention mechanisms.
authors: Jerry Yao-Chieh Hu, Yu-An Chen, Maojiang Su, Han Liu
bullets: Formulates attention through a free-energy landscape with random queries and attention weights.
Derives attention as the system’s equation of motion via free-energy minimization.
Characterizes parameter regimes and critical thresholds for robust attention inference.
Identifies first-order transitions between glassy and robust-inference phases.
Extends the analysis to stochastic queries and keys across multiple attention mechanisms.
papers.selection_reason: Statistical-mechanics analysis of Transformer attention via Hopfield models, relevant to LLM architecture and reasoning.
papers.title: On the Statistical Mechanics of Attention
papers.tldr: A statistical-mechanics framework models Transformer attention as modern Hopfield dynamics and identifies phase transitions governing inference reliability.

papers.abstract: We introduce StartLux-Decision, decision models from 0.8B to 27B parameters that combine efficient single-pass prediction with adaptive, confidence-guided reasoning. The Instant models use bidirectional attention in full-attention layers to improve decision accuracy while keeping single-pass inference. The AutoThink models invoke explicit reasoning for uncertain decisions and answer confident cases directly. A three-stage training pipeline establishes shared decision capabilities, specializes the two variants, and equips AutoThink with reasoning through reasoning supervision and reinforcement learning. We introduce Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Deliberative Decisions (RLCD$^2$), which uses a frozen model and proper scoring rules to reward improvements in decision probability quality and applies a soft penalty to overlong reasoning traces. RLCD$^2$ raises the share of reasoning traces that terminate within the generation limit by up to 48 percentage points and cuts average reasoning length by up to 65%, while largely preserving decision accuracy. On the public subset of Decision Index 0.3, the Instant models outperform the strongest evaluated comparable-scale open-weight decision models by 7.4-16.9 points, and the 27B AutoThink model reaches 73.4. We also introduce DecisionPivot, a programmatically verifiable benchmark of computational decisions built from contrast pairs that differ in a single answer-changing detail. On DecisionPivot, AutoThink outperforms its Instant counterparts by 11.5-18.4 points in pair accuracy and leads among evaluated systems. The models run on vLLM, llama.cpp and MLX, with quantized variants for lower memory use.
authors: Xialie Zhuang, Zunhai Su, Jia Pan, Ngai Wong, Guanhua Chen, Chuan-Wei Kuo
bullets: Offers Instant models for efficient single-pass decisions and AutoThink models that reason only when uncertainty warrants it.
Trains the models in three stages, adding reasoning supervision and reinforcement learning to AutoThink.

RLCD² uses proper scoring rules and a soft length penalty, reducing average reasoning length by up to 65% and increasing within-limit termination by up to 48 percentage points while largely preserving accuracy.
Instant models outperform comparable open-weight models by 7.4–16.9 points on the public Decision Index 0.3 subset; the 27B AutoThink model scores 73.4.
Introduces DecisionPivot, where AutoThink exceeds Instant models by 11.5–18.4 points in pair accuracy; models support common inference runtimes and quantization.
papers.selection_reason: LLM-based decision models with reinforcement learning for calibrated deliberative reasoning.
papers.title: StartLux-Decision: AutoThink Decision Models with Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Deliberative Decisions
papers.tldr: StartLux-Decision combines fast single-pass prediction with adaptive, confidence-guided reasoning, using RLCD² to make deliberation shorter, more calibrated, and effective on computational decision tasks.

papers.abstract: The success of autoregressive language models trained with Chain-of-Thought~(CoT) supervision raises a fundamental question: How simple can a next-token predictor be while still enabling the efficient simulation of general computation through its autoregressively generated CoT? Surprisingly, we show that a single neuron suffices. For a broad family of activations, including threshold and ReLU, a single autoregressive neuron can simulate any feedforward circuit with the same activation. Specifically, a size-$s$ circuit on $n$ inputs can be simulated by a neuron of dimension $O(ns+s^2)$ using $O(s^2)$ generation steps, with both bounds independent of circuit depth and tight under natural assumptions. For threshold activations, this improves upon the simulation of Joshi et al. (COLT 2025), whose bounds scale exponentially with circuit depth. Consequently, autoregressive threshold neurons can simulate polynomial-time Turing machines, while remaining efficiently learnable from CoT supervision. Our main expressivity result relies on a novel connection to Sidon sets from additive combinatorics. As an experimental illustration, we efficiently train a single autoregressive ReLU neuron to mimic a neural network teacher with nontrivial test accuracy on CIFAR-10.
authors: Roey Magen, Nirmit Joshi, Gal Vardi
bullets: Shows that one autoregressive neuron with threshold or ReLU activation can simulate any same-activation feedforward circuit.
A size-s circuit on n inputs is simulated in dimension O(ns+s²) and O(s²) generation steps, independently of circuit depth.
For threshold activations, the result improves prior bounds that grew exponentially with circuit depth.
The construction uses a novel connection to Sidon sets from additive combinatorics.
Experiments train a single autoregressive ReLU neuron to imitate a neural-network teacher with nontrivial CIFAR-10 test accuracy.
papers.selection_reason: Theoretical expressivity of autoregressive chain-of-thought predictors is directly relevant to LLM reasoning and architecture.
papers.title: The Surprising Expressivity of a Single Neuron with Autoregressive Chain-of-Thought
papers.tldr: A single autoregressive neuron, when guided by Chain-of-Thought, can efficiently simulate broad classes of neural circuits and even polynomial-time computation.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models are a promising and more efficient alternative to autoregressive models. However, most RL post-training techniques are not easily adapted to these models. One issue is that diffusion language models generate answers through many intermediate states, deciding at each step which masked positions to reveal and which tokens to place in them. Many existing RL methods used in this setting approximate intractable sequence likelihoods or weight every denoising step by the same advantage, without explicitly distinguishing how these intermediate states of the denoising trajectory affect the expected reward. To address this issue of trajectory blindness, we introduce PACT (Potential-Anchored Consistency of Transitions). Motivated by a reward-tilted reference distribution, PACT jointly learns the policy and a scalar potential that scores each intermediate state, anchored by terminal reward. For each sampled denoising transition, a consistency loss matches the policy-to-reference log-probability ratio of revealed tokens to the change in this potential. This formulation requires neither sequence-likelihood estimation nor importance-ratio clipping. On four tasks, PACT improves LLaDA-8B-Instruct by +9.9 points on GSM8K, +12.0 on MATH500, +55.7 on Countdown, and +72.6 on Sudoku, and reaches the best average accuracy across the four tasks reported for this model, +3.7 points over the next best method. Further compared to AGRPO, it reaches that baseline's best accuracy in about half the training compute on GSM8K.
bullets: Diffusion language models generate through multi-step denoising trajectories, making standard RL methods difficult to apply.
PACT addresses trajectory blindness with a learned scalar potential over intermediate states, anchored by terminal reward.
A consistency loss matches revealed-token policy/reference log-ratio changes to potential changes, avoiding sequence-likelihood estimation and importance-ratio clipping.
On four tasks, PACT improves LLaDA-8B-Instruct by 9.9–72.6 points and achieves the best reported average accuracy for this model.
On GSM8K, PACT reaches AGRPO’s best accuracy with about half the training compute.
papers.selection_reason: RL post-training method for diffusion language models, relevant to language foundation model training and improvement.
papers.title: RL Post-Training Diffusion Language Models Along Their Own Generation Paths
papers.tldr: PACT enables effective RL post-training for diffusion language models by learning how each denoising transition contributes to final reward.

papers.abstract: Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) compresses the KV cache into a latent representation, reducing inference memory and bandwidth. Existing MHA2MLA/TransMLA methods do not support QKNorm and require costly recovery on modern LLMs, especially MoE. We present MLAfication, a QKNorm-compatible, parameter-efficient extension of MHA2MLA. It combines calibrated KNorm, parameter-efficient distillation, contribution-aware Partial-RoPE, and activation-aware joint KV initialization. Across MHA and GQA models, including QKNorm- and MoE-equipped variants, MLAfication preserves performance under substantial KV-cache compression, surpasses the current SOTA on commonsense and long-context benchmarks, and extends MLA conversion to modern architectures. On Qwen3-30B-A3B, MLAfication delivers up to $5.35\times$ the serving throughput of BF16 GQA and, combined with 4-bit KV quantization, reduces the KV-cache footprint by $94.73\%$. Our code is available at https://github.com/JT-Ushio/MLAfication.
authors: Zile Wang, Zhide Xie, Tao Ji
bullets: Addresses the limited compatibility and costly recovery of existing MHA-to-MLA methods, especially for QKNorm and MoE models.
Introduces calibrated KNorm, parameter-efficient distillation, contribution-aware Partial-RoPE, and activation-aware joint KV initialization.
Preserves model performance across MHA and GQA models under substantial KV-cache compression.
Surpasses prior state of the art on commonsense and long-context benchmarks.
On Qwen3-30B-A3B, achieves up to 5.35× BF16 GQA serving throughput and reduces KV-cache footprint by 94.73% with 4-bit KV quantization.
papers.selection_reason: Converts modern LLMs to MLA with large KV-cache compression and throughput gains, directly relevant to efficient LLM inference.
papers.title: MLAfication: Efficiently Enabling High-Fidelity MLA for Modern LLMs
papers.tldr: MLAfication efficiently converts modern LLMs to high-fidelity MLA, supporting QKNorm and MoE architectures while sharply reducing KV-cache costs.

papers.abstract: Soft tokens have so far been used to replace discrete chain-of-thought in latent reasoning methods. These approaches typically require multi-stage training and, in some cases, auxiliary modules, yet they still underperform supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on triples. In this paper, we ask whether soft tokens can be used to improve SFT itself, instead of as an avenue for latent reasoning. We introduce Soft Teacher Forcing (Soft-TF), a simple training algorithm that combines teacher-forced embeddings with soft tokens through random convex combinations. The soft tokens are computed in a single parallel forward pass over the ground-truth sequence. Soft-TF adds no parameters, no external model and no curriculum, and leaves inference unchanged. Experiments show that Soft-TF improves over SFT on GSM8K, MATH, MathQA and AQuA, by +2.1 to +4.1 points on GSM8K across seven Gemma, Llama and Mistral models.
authors: Mohammad Fahes, Cordelia Schmid, Anurag Arnab
bullets: Targets the underperformance and complexity of prior soft-token latent-reasoning methods.
Combines teacher-forced embeddings and soft tokens using random convex combinations.
Computes soft tokens in one parallel forward pass over the ground-truth sequence.
Requires no additional parameters, external model, or curriculum; inference remains unchanged.
Improves SFT across GSM8K, MATH, MathQA, and AQuA, including +2.1 to +4.1 GSM8K points across seven models.
papers.selection_reason: Training algorithm for LLM supervised fine-tuning, relevant to language foundation models.
papers.title: Soft Teacher Forcing
papers.tldr: Soft Teacher Forcing improves supervised fine-tuning by mixing teacher-forced embeddings with learned soft tokens during training, without changing inference.

papers.abstract: Tool-augmented language models ground their responses in external tool outputs, improving reliability beyond parametric knowledge alone. However, even when the correct tool is called and returns accurate information, models may still contradict such outputs, omit critical details, or generate unsupported claims. Existing hallucination benchmarks for tool-augmented dialogue primarily focus on the tool-calling stage, evaluating whether the correct tool and arguments are selected, while overlooking errors that arise during post-tool response generation. To address this gap, we introduce ToolHACE, a span-level benchmark for hallucination detection in tool-augmented LLM responses, covering five fine-grained hallucination categories. Through extensive experiments with modern hallucination detectors, we show that post-tool-call hallucinations are widespread and remain challenging to detect. Our results further demonstrate that effective detection requires training on specialized tool-augmented corpora, while transfer from tool-agnostic hallucination datasets performs poorly in this setting. These findings highlight the need for dedicated benchmarks and models for reliable hallucination detection in tool-augmented language systems.
authors: Nikolay Ivanov, Sergey Pletenev, Elisei Rykov, Anatolii Frolov, Bogdan Monogov, Alexander Potekhin, Maria Marina, Daniil Moskovskiy, Viktor Moskvoretskii, Alexander Panchenko, Ilseyar Alimova
bullets: Targets post-tool response errors such as contradictions, omissions, and unsupported claims.
Covers five fine-grained hallucination categories at the span level.
Experiments find post-tool hallucinations are widespread and challenging for current detectors.
Detectors trained on specialized tool-augmented data outperform transfer from tool-agnostic hallucination datasets.
Scope: focuses on hallucination detection after tool calls, not tool selection or argument accuracy.
papers.selection_reason: Span-level benchmark for hallucination detection in tool-augmented LLM responses, relevant to LLM reliability.
papers.title: ToolHACE: A Dataset for Detecting Hallucinations in Tool-Based LLM Responses
papers.tldr: ToolHACE is a span-level benchmark showing that hallucinations after correct tool use are common, difficult to detect, and require tool-specific training.

papers.abstract: How do language models reconcile conflicting contextual evidence within a prompt? We study this question using lexical redefinition, where an explicit instruction specifies how a word should be interpreted and a subsequent sentence provides additional evidence through its usage. Across 870 word pairs, we find that lexical redefinitions are not applied as fixed rules. Instead, the behaviour depends systematically on the relationship between the explicit instruction and the intervening sentence: the contextualised usage can preserve, weaken, or completely reverse the instruction. These results suggest that the interpretation of an explicit instruction remains sensitive to subsequent contextual evidence. Lexical redefinition therefore provides a controlled behavioural paradigm for studying how language models integrate multiple sources of information within a prompt.
bullets: Studies how models reconcile conflicting evidence within prompts.
Uses lexical redefinition: an instruction assigns a word’s meaning, followed by a sentence using the word.
Evaluates 870 word pairs across different relationships between the instruction and intervening sentence.
Finds that redefinitions are not applied as fixed rules; subsequent context systematically changes their effect.
Proposes lexical redefinition as a controlled paradigm for studying prompt-level information integration.
papers.selection_reason: Studies context-sensitive instruction following in LLMs via lexical redefinition, relevant to LLM reasoning and context.
papers.title: Lexical Redefinition Reveals Context-Sensitive Instruction Following
papers.tldr: Language models interpret lexical redefinitions context-sensitively, with later usage evidence sometimes preserving, weakening, or reversing an explicit instruction.

papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) applies large language models to new tasks by prepending a few labeled demonstrations to a query. Prior work has studied how demonstration ordering affects ICL, but the interaction between label arrangement patterns and model biases has not been systematically examined. We define label collapse as the failure mode in which the model generates query-independent labels, and show that it is architecturally universal at the tested 8-9B scale: five models spanning autoregressive (Llama-3, Qwen3.5) and discrete diffusion (LLaDA, iLLaDA, LLaDA-Instruct) families all exhibit label collapse even under the class-balanced alternating arrangement, with some label word pairs collapsing in virtually every tested condition and others flipping their collapse direction with arrangement. Critically, accuracy alone cannot detect this collapse: models can achieve near-chance accuracy while generating query-independent labels, a score indistinguishable from balanced performance, so the failure can persist undetected in deployment. We measure separation, the log-odds of the two label words at the query position (the quantity that label-bias calibration operates on), as a complementary diagnostic that exposes collapse hidden beneath surface accuracy, together with a measurement protocol that guards label extraction against tokenizer and formatting artifacts. For autoregressive models, collapse persists where the majority-label-bias account does not apply, and arrangement patterns can reverse the collapse direction; for diffusion models, we present a systematic evaluation of ICL failure modes, complementing contemporaneous studies of dLLM context comprehension and demonstration-order sensitivity, and identify open questions about how iterative denoising interacts with label biases.
bullets: The study examines how label arrangement patterns interact with model biases in in-context learning.
Five 8–9B autoregressive and discrete diffusion models exhibit label collapse, including under balanced alternating demonstrations.
Some label pairs collapse consistently, while others reverse collapse direction depending on arrangement.
Near-chance accuracy can hide query-independent predictions, so accuracy is not a sufficient diagnostic.
Separation—query-position log-odds between label words—combined with artifact-aware label extraction reveals the collapse.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes in-context learning failure modes in diffusion language models; relevant to language foundation model behavior.
papers.title: Label Collapse in Diffusion Language Model In-Context Learning
papers.tldr: Label collapse causes language models to produce query-independent ICL labels, and accuracy alone may miss this failure, making separation a necessary diagnostic.

papers.abstract: Syntactic language models (SLMs) that generate sentences along with their syntactic tree structures have shown promise in both syntactic generalization and downstream tasks. Prior studies, however, have mostly evaluated smaller models trained on less pretraining data and tested on narrower task suites. In addition, the design space of tree linearization and attention masks remains underexplored. We conduct a large-scale empirical study of 12 controlled configurations---one terminal baseline and 11 SLM variants spanning different linearizations and masks---at scales up to 1B parameters and 100B training tokens, evaluated across 11 downstream tasks and two syntactic benchmarks. The experimental results show that SLMs with standard causal attention match or exceed structural-mask variants across downstream and syntactic benchmarks. They require no architectural modifications and remain compatible with FlashAttention. We also observe that when scaling up to the 1B-parameter scale, the top-performing SLM variant no longer shows a clear advantage over a compute-matched non-structural baseline, suggesting that SLMs may become less competitive with scale. Our code is available at https://github.com/qlwpc/TG-Interpolation.
authors: Pengcheng Wang, Zhexuan Zhang, Chao Lou, Kewei Tu
bullets: Evaluates 12 controlled configurations, including one terminal baseline and 11 SLM variants.
Tests models up to 1B parameters and 100B training tokens on 11 downstream tasks and two syntactic benchmarks.
Standard causal attention matches or exceeds structural attention masks without architectural changes and remains compatible with FlashAttention.
At the 1B-parameter scale, the best SLM shows no clear advantage over a compute-matched non-structural baseline.
The study covers different tree linearizations and attention masks, addressing an underexplored design space.
papers.selection_reason: Empirical study of syntactic language model architectures and scaling, relevant to LLM architecture research.
papers.title: A Scaled-Up Empirical Study of Syntactic Language Models
papers.tldr: A large-scale study finds that syntactic language models with standard causal attention perform as well as or better than structural-mask variants, but lose their relative advantage over non-structural models at 1B parameters.

papers.abstract: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) is widely used in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for language-model reasoning. While \emph{value evolution along trajectory} characterizes relative token-level credit, yet standard critics often fail to track it under sparse terminal rewards. To model this evolution, we analyze the relation between successive prefix values and show that they admit a Bayesian decomposition with additive updates in log-odds space. We use this additive structure to construct Tracking-Value PPO (\method), a cumulative value parameterization that sums position-wise scalar outputs into value logits. These outputs are learned through terminal-outcome supervision on the reconstructed values. \method improves aggregate mathematical reasoning scores over PPO by 7.0 and 8.4 points on Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base, respectively, while improving out-of-distribution generalization. Gains extend to Qwen3-4B, Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, Qwen3.5-9B and to countdown, and scientific coding tasks. Further analysis shows more accurate tracking of value evolution and more reliable advantage estimates. Our code is publicly available in https://github.com/LINs-lab/TPPO.
authors: Futing Wang, Chenxi Li, Jianhao Yan, Yun Luo, Zhi Wang, Yizhuo Li, Runzhe Zhan, Yu Cheng, Tao Lin
bullets: Addresses inaccurate token-level credit assignment under sparse terminal rewards.
Derives a Bayesian decomposition showing that successive prefix values can be updated additively in log-odds space.
Parameterizes values as cumulative sums of position-wise scalar outputs, trained with terminal-outcome supervision.
Improves aggregate mathematical reasoning scores by 7.0 and 8.4 points on Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base, respectively.
Also improves out-of-distribution generalization, advantage estimates, and performance across additional models and countdown and scientific coding tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Improves PPO-based reasoning for language models via better value tracking, directly relevant to LLM reasoning methods.
papers.title: TPPO: Tracking-Value PPO For Language Model Reasoning
papers.tldr: TPPO improves PPO-based language-model reasoning by tracking token-level value evolution through cumulative log-odds updates.

papers.abstract: Parallel token proposals in language-model decoding need a joint law, not merely accurate token marginals. We construct a family of coordinate-Bethe-ansatz laws from the periodic XXZ chain and compare each with its maximum-entropy pairwise projection at identical one- and two-site moments. In the eight-site, three-excitation sector, symmetry makes their entire probability-law difference one-dimensional, determined by a contiguous three-site moment. Along the Bethe branch, this gap varies with anisotropy, changes sign, and vanishes exactly at $\Delta=(3+\sqrt{3})/2$, where the eigenstate law becomes exactly pairwise. A nonlinear readout transfers a nonzero gap into the first two token positions while preserving their separate marginals. At $\Delta=1.5$ the deterministic binary token laws differ by 0.02654573 in total variation. Exact speculative verification then gives a strict accepted-prefix advantage for a constructed target and a neighborhood within targets sharing its first-token marginal. This is a mathematical existence result. It does not establish a language-model gain or wall-clock speedup.
bullets: Parallel decoding requires a joint token law, not just accurate marginals.
Coordinate-Bethe-ansatz laws from the periodic XXZ chain are compared with maximum-entropy pairwise projections having identical one- and two-site moments.
For an eight-site, three-excitation sector, the law difference is one-dimensional and controlled by a contiguous three-site moment; it changes with anisotropy and vanishes at a specific value of Δ.
A nonlinear readout transfers this higher-order gap to the first two token positions while preserving their individual marginals.
At Δ=1.5, the constructed binary laws differ by 0.02654573 in total variation and yield a strict accepted-prefix advantage for a constructed target and nearby targets.
papers.selection_reason: Constructs joint laws for parallel token proposals in language-model decoding; relevant to language foundation model decoding, though theoretical.
