papers.title: A Bethe-Ansatz Source of Early Token Correlations: A marginal-preserving construction for parallel proposals
papers.tldr: A Bethe-ansatz construction shows that parallel token proposals can share one- and two-token marginals yet differ in higher-order dependencies that affect speculative decoding.

papers.abstract: Attention sinks are usually studied after they have formed. We ask whether a measurable hidden-state change appears beforehand and whether changing that geometry alters what happens later. To remove network depth as a shortcut, we compare prompts in the same model and at the same layer. When sink timing varies across prompts, simple spectral summaries of the hidden states add information beyond current attention, with the clearest prompt-specific signal in a short window about two to three layers before sink formation. The predictive strength varies across cohorts, so we treat the spectrum as a readout of a pre-sink state change rather than a universal warning statistic. The signal is broader than one measured extreme activation. We then modify only the singular values of the post-layer hidden states after current attention has already been computed. These interventions change later sink behavior in Qwen2.5, GLM-Z1, and GPT-OSS relative to norm-matched random spectral perturbations. In Qwen2.5, the immediate suppressive effect is accompanied by a reduction in next-layer query--key preference for position~0, and the learned spectral directions remain stable when estimated from substantially less training data. Together, the results show that attention sinks are preceded by a short spectral reorganization of hidden states, and directly perturbing this geometry can causally alter subsequent sink formation.
bullets: Spectral summaries provide prompt-specific information about sink timing beyond current attention, especially two to three layers beforehand.
The predictive signal varies across prompt cohorts, so it is a pre-sink state-change indicator rather than a universal warning statistic.
The effect reflects broader spectral structure, not just a single extreme activation.
Post-attention singular-value interventions alter later sink behavior across Qwen2.5, GLM-Z1, and GPT-OSS, compared with norm-matched random perturbations.
In Qwen2.5, suppression reduces the next-layer query–key preference for position 0; learned spectral directions are stable with substantially less training data.
papers.selection_reason: Studies hidden-state geometry preceding attention-sink formation in LLMs; fits LLM architecture/behavior.
papers.title: Before Attention Sinks Form: Hidden-State Geometry Reveals and Modulates Their Formation
papers.tldr: A short-lived reorganization in hidden-state spectra precedes attention-sink formation, and modifying this geometry can change later sink behavior.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) implemented with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has driven substantial progress in training reasoning language models. However, verifiable outcome rewards provide an imperfect measure of reasoning quality: a correct final answer may not be supported by the reasoning trace, whereas an incorrect rollout may contain a nearly correct reasoning trajectory. We present empirical evidence for this mismatch and hypothesize that the resulting reward noise contributes to instability in reinforcement learning for both reasoning accuracy and token efficiency. To address this credit assignment challenge, this paper proposes double-rollout reinforcement learning. For each sampled rollout, we truncate its reasoning trace, sample multiple continuations from the truncated prefix, and replace the original reward with the mean continuation reward, yielding a more robust estimate of reasoning quality. This double-rollout algorithm incurs only a moderate increase in compute cost and yet reaches substantially higher accuracies across math and coding tasks and across Qwen and Nemotron models than baseline algorithms with fewer RL steps. For example, using only DAPO data it trains Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B to reach 95.4% on AIME 2026, versus 91.5% by GRPO and substantially above state of the art for this model size, within 30 RL steps. When combined with length-based rewards, the same algorithm further improves the accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier over existing efficiency optimizations. These findings suggest that the double-rollout reward estimation is an effective and cost-efficient way to improve both the accuracy and token efficiency of reasoning RL.
authors: Haifeng Qian, David Mosallanezhad, Christian Munley, Adithya Renduchintala, Oleksii Kuchaiev
bullets: Verifiable final-answer rewards can misrepresent reasoning quality, creating noisy credit assignment and unstable RL.
For each rollout, the method truncates the reasoning trace and samples multiple continuations from the prefix.
It replaces the original outcome reward with the mean continuation reward as a more robust quality estimate.
The approach adds moderate compute cost and improves math and coding performance across Qwen and Nemotron models.
Combined with length-based rewards, it further improves the accuracy–efficiency trade-off.
papers.selection_reason: Double-rollout reward estimation improves RL training of reasoning language models; relevant to LLM reasoning methods.
papers.title: Double-Rollout Reinforcement Learning with Sampling-based Reward Estimation
papers.tldr: Double-rollout reinforcement learning improves reasoning accuracy and token efficiency by estimating reward from multiple continuations of truncated reasoning traces.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is reshaping how large language models (LLMs) acquire reasoning capabilities, yet the optimizers used remain largely inherited from teacher-forcing training. This raises a fundamental question: does RLVR induce a distinct optimization geometry that calls for a different optimizer? We investigate this question through the spectral structure of LLM gradients and find that gradient energy progressively concentrates into a shrinking effective subspace, which is characteristic of RLVR, as it is absent under supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and is largely removed when the verifiable reward is replaced by a random one. Moreover, the rank required to capture a fixed fraction of gradient energy steadily decreases over training, revealing that the effective dimensionality of useful updates itself evolves with training. These findings motivate a new optimization principle: rather than prescribing the update rank externally, an optimizer should adapt its rank to the evolving spectral structure of the gradient. We introduce Ares (Adaptive Rank-Effective Spectral Optimization), which estimates the effective update rank from the gradient's spectral energy distribution, tracks its evolution, and confines the gradient signal driving each update to the resulting low-rank subspace. Across LLMs of different scales, Ares improves accuracy over widely used optimizers and generalizes across RLVR algorithms and tasks. Results suggest that effective optimization may require optimizers to be designed around the geometry and dynamics of the training process. We release the code and data at https://github.com/RUCAIBox/Ares.
authors: Zhipeng Chen, Wayne Xin Zhao, Ji-Rong Wen
bullets: RLVR gradients progressively concentrate energy in a shrinking effective subspace, unlike gradients from supervised fine-tuning or random-reward training.
The rank needed to capture a fixed share of gradient energy decreases during training, indicating that useful update dimensionality evolves over time.
Ares estimates gradient spectral energy, tracks effective rank, and restricts each update to the resulting adaptive low-rank subspace.
Across LLM scales, RLVR algorithms, and tasks, Ares improves accuracy over commonly used optimizers.
The findings suggest RLVR may benefit from optimizers designed for its specific gradient geometry and dynamics.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive spectral low-rank optimizer for LLM reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards directly addresses LLM optimization and reasoning training.
papers.title: Spectral-Driven Adaptive-Rank Optimizer for Large Language Model Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
papers.tldr: RLVR creates an evolving low-dimensional gradient structure, motivating Ares, an optimizer that adapts update rank to this spectral geometry and improves accuracy across models, algorithms, and tasks.

papers.abstract: In parallel decoding, diffusion language models commit several tokens per forward pass, so co-committed tokens cannot see each other, breaking multi-token format units that parsers need. On ECHO, an open-weight one-step chest X-ray (CXR) report generator, 32.7-36.7% of evaluation reports lack a parseable Impression heading and score as empty. We propose intent-triggered anchoring, a training-free decoding rule that completes a format unit once the model commits its first token, inserting only units with a unique, content-free completion; fallbacks write the unit when the model stops or loops without starting it. On three CXR evaluation sets, the rule raises readable rates from 63.3-67.3% to 100.0% with no regressions and a 95th-percentile latency ratio of 0.68-1.28 against official decoding. Broken headings state findings absent from the reference; adding the heading at the end leaves them in 15.5-31.0% of reports, our rule in at most 0.6%. For math answer markers, the rule raises accuracy in the most parallel setting of five diffusion language models by 5.8-20.8 points on GSM8K and 5.1-17.1 on GSM-Symbolic, held out from tuning. With lenient answer extraction, gains are 3.3-12.5 and 2.7-6.3 points; the rule adds 1.4-8.6 points over a stop-only fallback for four of the five models.
bullets: Parallel decoding can commit tokens simultaneously, preventing tokens within required format units—such as headings or answer markers—from attending to one another.
The training-free rule completes a format unit after its first token when the completion is unique and content-free, with stop-or-loop fallbacks.
Across three CXR evaluation sets, readable reports increase from 63.3–67.3% to 100.0%, with no regressions and latency ratios of 0.68–1.28 at the 95th percentile.
For math answer markers, accuracy improves by 5.8–20.8 points on GSM8K and 5.1–17.1 points on GSM-Symbolic in the most parallel setting.
The approach reduces broken headings that state unsupported findings to at most 0.6% of reports; scope is limited to format units with unique, content-free completions.
papers.selection_reason: Decoding rule for diffusion language models to preserve format units; relevant to language foundation model behavior.
papers.title: Intent-Triggered Anchoring for Multi-Token Format Units in Parallel Decoding of Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: Intent-triggered anchoring fixes multi-token format units during parallel diffusion decoding, substantially improving parseability and math-answer accuracy without training.

papers.abstract: Improving an agent through successive revisions requires balancing exploration and evaluation under a limited budget. A narrow search can miss useful sequences of edits, while fully evaluating every intermediate version can exhaust the budget before those sequences yield a verified improvement. We introduce Speculative Recursive Self-Improvement (SpecRSI), which drafts executable successor agents before their predecessors are fully evaluated, while requiring complete verification before adoption. Verification-Aware Tree Search (VATS) allocates the budget between further edits and outstanding checks using the predicted verified return of a continuation. Group Verification Optimization (GVO) learns the improver from completed searches while keeping the real evaluator fixed. In the main scientific comparison, terminal gains exceed Janus by 33.3%--40.0%. Additional evaluations show that SpecRSI outperforms Janus in all 50 scientific backbone--task pairs and exceeds MetaRSI-v1 by 1.85%--2.38% in macro-average system score across twenty backbones. Coding-validation success reaches 69.4% versus HGM's 64.3% at a 20.8% lower target-cost index.
authors: Xin Xu, Ke Cheng, Hao Wang, Yangru Huang, Yanghao Xiao, Zhichao Chen, Zhisheng Zhong, Xun Liu, Yi Li, Qian Li, Haibin Lv, Jun Zhang, Jie Jiang, Zhouchen Lin
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between exploring edit sequences and spending limited budget on evaluating intermediate agents.
Uses Verification-Aware Tree Search to allocate resources between further edits and pending verification based on predicted returns.
Uses Group Verification Optimization to train the improver while keeping the evaluator fixed.
Terminal gains exceed Janus by 33.3%–40.0%; SpecRSI wins across all 50 scientific backbone–task pairs.
Coding-validation success is 69.4% versus HGM’s 64.3% at a 20.8% lower target-cost index.
papers.selection_reason: Focuses on improving agent systems through speculative recursive self-improvement, relevant to LLMs and adaptation.
papers.title: Drafting Agents, Not Just Tokens: Speculative Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Systems
papers.tldr: SpecRSI improves agentic systems by drafting successor agents speculatively while requiring full verification before adoption.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can substantially improve the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but an effective training run requires considerable resources. Reusing the computation acquired through RL across models would extend the value of that training. We propose GrowRL, an RL method that organizes learned updates into compact computational pathways through structural growth. GrowRL freezes the pretrained backbone and adds an independent causal attention branch and a feed-forward network branch at each Transformer layer. Zero-initialized output projections preserve the pretrained policy at initialization, and RL updates only the added pathways. The learned pathways remain explicit after training, allowing transfer to structurally compatible target models and subsequent adaptation with the target backbone frozen. The architecture also supports sequential transfer of additional pathways. By keeping the learned attention and feed-forward computation separate from the pretrained weights, GrowRL provides an explicit structure for preserving and reusing the outcome of an RL run. Experiments across five backbones show competitive mathematical reasoning and out-of-distribution performance with a small number of trainable parameters. Learned pathways provide immediate gains across all three transfer directions, with performance after only 10 target-side updates already close to that after 100 updates in every case. These results support computational pathways as parameter-efficient and reusable units of reinforcement learning adaptation.
authors: Haolin Tian, Yikang Li, Tonghan Wang
bullets: Freezes the pretrained backbone and trains added attention and feed-forward branches at each Transformer layer.
Uses zero-initialized output projections to preserve the original policy at initialization.
Keeps learned pathways explicit, supporting transfer across models and sequential addition of further pathways.
Across five backbones, achieves competitive mathematical reasoning and out-of-distribution performance with few trainable parameters.
Transferred pathways provide immediate gains, reaching near-100-update performance after only 10 target-side updates in all tested transfer directions.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a method for RL adaptation of LLMs using structural pathways, relevant to LLMs and adaptation.
papers.title: Growing and Transferring Pathways for LLM Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: GrowRL makes RL adaptations into compact, transferable Transformer pathways, enabling parameter-efficient reuse across compatible LLMs.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale model capacity efficiently by activating only a small subset of experts for each input, while still requiring all parameters to be stored in memory, resulting in substantial memory overhead. Expert merging techniques have recently emerged as a promising compression paradigm that reduces this overhead by consolidating multiple experts into a smaller set. However, existing approaches have two key limitations: (i) direct convex interpolation in parameter space is not generally guaranteed to yield meaningful interpolation of expert functions; and (ii) estimating expert similarity or merging coefficients often relies on calibration data, introducing dependence on the calibration distribution. To address these limitations, we propose Spectrum-Aware Latent Expert Merging (SLEM), a calibration-free expert merging framework that occurs in a structured latent representation of expert weights using a VAE. SLEM groups experts within and across layers based on latent similarities and derives merging coefficients from expert weight spectra. It then performs geometry-aware latent interpolation and decodes the resulting representations into merged expert weights. Compared with existing expert merging methods, SLEM achieves comparable or better performance on general knowledge benchmarks and higher average performance on generation benchmarks involving mathematical reasoning and code generation.
authors: Dohyeon Kim, Bedionita Soro, Bruno Andreis, Sung Ju Hwang
bullets: MoE models reduce computation but retain all expert parameters, creating substantial memory overhead.
Existing merging methods may produce poor function interpolation and depend on calibration data.
SLEM uses a VAE-based latent representation, grouping experts by latent similarity within and across layers.
It derives merge coefficients from expert weight spectra and applies geometry-aware latent interpolation.
The method achieves comparable or better general-knowledge performance and higher average performance on math-reasoning and code-generation benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses memory efficiency in Mixture-of-Experts models through expert merging in a latent space, relevant to efficient AI and LLMs.
papers.title: SLEM: Spectrum-Aware Latent Expert Merging
papers.tldr: SLEM compresses Mixture-of-Experts models without calibration data by merging experts in a spectrum-aware latent space.

papers.abstract: Preference alignment enables language models to better reflect human values, but the preference data contains sensitive information, especially when derived from surveys about political beliefs, social norms, religion, gender attitudes, and cultural values. This paper studies privacy-preserving alignment on questionnaire-derived data from the World Values Survey, where supervision takes the form of ordinal labels rather than standard pairwise rankings. Existing efforts mainly focus on general privacy protections upon model training, while data-specific methods for survey data remain unexplored. We first show the vulnerability of aligned models, then formulate the task as rating prediction and introduce label differential privacy. Building on this formulation, we construct a differential private pipeline utilizing three privacy mechanisms: randomized response, exponential mechanism, and DP-SGD. Experiments show that simple label-level mechanisms outperform gradient-level methods, and proper aggregation function for preprocessing also make large contribution. The new fine-grained private comparison motivates explorations toward language model alignment with formal privacy guarantees.
authors: Xiuyuan Qi, Yi Wang, Wenjie Wang
bullets: Survey-based preference data can reveal sensitive political, religious, social, gender, and cultural beliefs.
The study formulates alignment as rating prediction rather than pairwise preference comparison.
It evaluates randomized response, the exponential mechanism, and DP-SGD for privacy protection.
Label-level mechanisms outperform gradient-level protection in the reported experiments.
Preprocessing and label aggregation choices substantially affect privacy-preserving alignment.
papers.selection_reason: Privacy-preserving preference alignment of language models with differential privacy directly fits LLM alignment and training.
papers.title: Differential Privacy Protected Preference Alignment on Survey Derived Data
papers.tldr: The paper introduces a differential privacy pipeline for aligning language models with sensitive, survey-derived preference data using ordinal labels.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large language models at scale is increasingly limited by the memory cost of backpropagation. Zeroth-Order (ZO) optimizers reduce this burden by relying only on forward function evaluations, but they still exhibit a substantial performance gap to first-order (FO) optimizers such as Adam. We argue that this gap does not arise solely from the absence of explicit gradients: FO fine-tuning also benefits from informative low-rank optimization geometry, large-scale signal aggregation, and well-conditioned update directions. Motivated by this, we introduce StructZO, a structured Zeroth-Order optimization framework for memory-efficient LLM fine-tuning. StructZO performs large-query ZO estimation within an activation-induced informative subspace and applies spectral control to the resulting reduced-space update before mapping it back to the original parameters. This lets ZO aggregate useful directional signals in a compact, geometry-aware space while avoiding the activation and optimizer-state memory costs of backpropagation. We show theoretically that, when the induced subspace captures concentrated optimization-relevant directions, StructZO reduces the effective ZO estimation dimension from $mn$ to $mr$, with the remaining projection error governed by the spectral tail of the activation Gram matrix. Empirically, across OPT-series and Llama3.1-8B on diverse downstreamtasks, StructZO improves over the strongest existing ZO baselines by up to $8.7%$ relative on average and up to $26.9%$ relative on individual tasks, while remaining within $1.5%$ of FO-Adam on average. These results suggest that structured and spectrally controlled ZO updates can substantially narrow the gap between ZO and FO optimization.
authors: Xuanlin Yang, Jia Li, Zhouchen Lin
bullets: Targets the high memory cost of backpropagation and optimizer states in large-language-model fine-tuning.
Uses large-query zeroth-order estimation within an activation-induced informative subspace, then spectrally controls and maps updates back to the full parameter space.

Theoretical analysis reduces the effective estimation dimension from $mn$ to $mr$ when optimization-relevant directions are concentrated; projection error depends on the activation Gram matrix’s spectral tail.
Across OPT-series and Llama3.1-8B downstream tasks, it improves over existing ZO baselines by up to 8.7% on average and 26.9% on individual tasks, while staying within 1.5% of FO-Adam on average.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a memory-efficient fine-tuning method using structured zeroth-order optimization, directly addressing memory efficiency in LLMs.
papers.title: StructZO: Structured Zeroth-Order Optimization for Memory-Efficient LLM Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: StructZO narrows the gap between memory-efficient zeroth-order and Adam fine-tuning by estimating updates in a compact, activation-informed subspace with spectral control.

papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed in morally and legally sensitive contexts, yet little is known about how they internally represent distinctions between moral reasoning styles. We ask whether a model's differential response to rule-framed and consequence-framed moral questions reflects distinct internal structure or merely surface lexical sensitivity. We construct a 2$\times$2 factorial dataset crossing reasoning style (rule-based vs. consequence-based framing) with judgment polarity (permissive vs. prohibitive), drawn from three established moral reasoning benchmarks and evaluated on a cleanroom test set of novel phrasings that includes conflict pairs where the two framings predict opposite labels. Using linear probing and activation steering, we identify two orthogonal directions in the residual stream: Dir-A tracks reasoning style and Dir-B tracks judgment polarity, each near-blind to the other factor (cross-correlation $|r| < 0.04$). This double dissociation replicates across three instruction-tuned models from different developers at comparable proportional depth, and it is not knife-edged in layer: the directions are recoverable and causally effective throughout an extended band of the network. Dir-A can causally change judgments, and in conflicting scenarios, it selectively corrects errors in rule-based judgments without changing consequence-based judgments, suggesting that it does not simply make the model more likely to accept everything. Generalization beyond the training templates is partial: the direction transfers across benchmark sources, but its advantage over lexical baselines on novel phrasings is modest. We therefore frame the result as moral reasoning style sensitivity, a geometrically dissociable and causally effective structure, rather than internalized normative reasoning.
bullets: A 2×2 dataset separates rule- versus consequence-based framing from permissive versus prohibitive judgments, including conflicting cases.
Linear probes identify two largely orthogonal residual-stream directions: one for reasoning style and one for judgment polarity.
The dissociation replicates across three instruction-tuned models and across a broad network layer range.
Steering the style direction changes judgments and selectively improves rule-based responses in conflicts without broadly increasing permissiveness.
Transfer across benchmarks occurs, but gains over lexical baselines on novel phrasings are modest; the findings do not establish internalized normative reasoning.
papers.selection_reason: Identifies dissociable internal representations for moral reasoning styles (rule vs. consequence) in LLMs using linear probing and activation steering. Relevant to LLM interpretability and internal representations.
papers.title: Rule vs.Consequence: Dissociable Internal Representations of Moral Reasoning in LLMs
papers.tldr: LLMs encode moral reasoning style and judgment polarity as distinct, causally manipulable internal directions, but generalization to novel wording is only partial.

papers.abstract: Looped Language Models (LoopLMs) improve parameter efficiency by recursively reusing shared Transformer modules, yet their repeated computation over evolving recurrent states poses new challenges for low-bit deployment. Existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods, largely designed for feed-forward Transformers, fail to account for cross-loop activation dynamics, heterogeneous loop sensitivity, and recursive error propagation, leading to substantial performance degradation at low precision. To address these challenges, we propose LoopQuant, a loop-aware PTQ framework for accurate and efficient low-bit quantization of LoopLMs. LoopQuant is built on three core components: 1) Cross-Loop Distribution Canonicalization (CLDC) learns a shared quantization-friendly representation across recurrent states while preserving parameter sharing; 2) Interaction-Aware Loop-wise Precision Allocation (ILPA) allocates activation precision under a fixed bit budget by modeling task-level loop sensitivity and cross-loop interactions; and 3) Loop-Conditioned Task Calibration (LCTC) further aligns quantized inference with the low-bit recursive trajectory through lightweight task-space calibration. Extensive experiments across LoopLM architectures demonstrate that LoopQuant consistently outperforms existing low-bit PTQ methods. On Ouro-2.6B, LoopQuant under W4A4 surpasses all W4A8 baselines in performance, while reducing model memory by 65.3% with only 3.4% additional storage overhead over naive INT4 and achieving a 1.7 times decoding speedup over BF16. These results demonstrate a strong balance among accuracy, compression, and inference efficiency, providing a practical and deployment-friendly solution for low-bit LoopLM inference. The code is available at [https://github.com/Kishon-zzx/LoopQuant].
authors: Zhixiong Zhao, Zukang Xu, Xing Hu, Lifeng Liu, Guangyu Sun, Dawei Yang
bullets: Addresses activation shifts, heterogeneous loop sensitivity, and recursive error propagation that undermine standard PTQ methods.
Uses Cross-Loop Distribution Canonicalization to learn a shared quantization-friendly representation while preserving parameter sharing.
Allocates activation precision through interaction-aware, loop-wise sensitivity modeling under a fixed bit budget.
Applies lightweight loop-conditioned task calibration to align quantized inference with low-bit recursive trajectories.
On Ouro-2.6B, W4A4 surpasses W4A8 baselines, cuts memory by 65.3%, and achieves 1.7× BF16 decoding speed with 3.4% storage overhead over naive INT4.
papers.selection_reason: Loop-aware quantization for efficient LLM inference; fits efficient AI and language models.
papers.title: LoopQuant: Accurate and Efficient Post-Training Quantization for Looped Transformers
papers.tldr: LoopQuant enables accurate, efficient low-bit post-training quantization for recursively computed LoopLMs by modeling cross-loop dynamics and sensitivity.

papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) trains a large language model using supervision from a teacher instantiated from the same model as the student. The teacher is conditioned on privileged information (PI), such as verified solutions. The student, which does not observe PI, learns from the teacher's next-token distributions along its own sampled responses. However, PI can bias supervision toward shortcut reasoning with limited verification or reconsideration, accompanied by a sharp drop in the entropy of the output distribution. To address this challenge, we introduce self-distillation with verbal regularization (VRSD), which uses system prompts to regulate how the teacher uses PI, thereby encouraging rethinking and exploration to counteract premature commitment. Theoretically, we model prompting as attenuating the influence of PI on the teacher distribution and derive conditions for entropy preservation. Across three models and four tasks, VRSD improves Pass@1 over OPSD in 11 of 12 model-task settings, by 3.9 percentage points on average, while generally maintaining higher token entropy.
authors: Jiazheng Li, Yawei Li, Junru Lu, Zhenyi Shen, Di Yin, Lin Gui, Xing Sun, David R\"ugamer, Xinpeng Wang, Yulan He
bullets: OPSD trains a student from a same-model teacher conditioned on privileged information, such as verified solutions.
Privileged information can encourage shortcut reasoning, premature commitment, and sharply reduced output entropy.
VRSD uses system prompts to make the teacher rethink and explore rather than over-rely on privileged information.
A theoretical analysis models prompting as reducing privileged-information influence and derives conditions for preserving entropy.
Across three models and four tasks, VRSD improves Pass@1 over OPSD in 11 of 12 settings by 3.9 percentage points on average, while generally maintaining higher token entropy.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces Verbal Regularization for Self-Distillation (VRSD) to prevent shortcut reasoning in LLMs by regulating the use of privileged information. Relevant to LLM training and self-distillation.
papers.title: Self-Distillation with Verbal Regularization
papers.tldr: Verbal regularization improves on-policy self-distillation by prompting teachers to use privileged information less rigidly, promoting exploration and better task performance.

papers.abstract: Self-attention assigns two functions to one mechanism-where to read and how to mix-at the price of O(L^2) training, an O(T) decode state, and position signals bound to the training length. Existing attention-free alternatives all optimize the single function of generation. We propose FON (Fusion-Organ Network), which differentiates one weight stack into a drafting organ (multi-tap learnable delays + content-adaptive recursion; causal, O(S) training, O(1) decode state, no sequence-level quadratic attention) and a revision organ that re-processes the written prefix through multi-scale ripple kernels injected via weak gates, never generating. At 30M parameters, iso-parameter and iso-token budget, FON reaches perplexity 131.03 on WikiText-103, beating Transformer (197.73) and Mamba2 (152.53); the advantage persists under all depth-aligned baselines and at the 70M tier (-20.8%). At 8x length extrapolation FON degrades by ~8-9% without positional-encoding engineering, between ALiBi and RoPE. The revision channel provides a structural pathway for in-domain infilling that causal architectures lack in principle (+19% over on-demand coupling), at a perplexity cost indistinguishable within measurement precision. We report all costs and boundaries: impaired long-range retrieval, synthetic-task disadvantages, weaker out-of-domain code infilling than a same-recipe Transformer, and a 6.5-12.3x wall-clock gap.
authors: Helong Hu (Zhanjiang Campus, Guangdong Ocean University, Zhanjiang, Guangdong, China), Hongdan Pan (Maoming Administrative Service Center, Maoming, Guangdong, China), Shuiqing Hu (China Pacific Insurance)
bullets: Drafting uses learnable delays and content-adaptive recursion with O(S) training and O(1) decode state; revision reprocesses prefixes via gated multi-scale ripple kernels.
At 30M parameters, FON achieves 131.03 perplexity on WikiText-103 versus 197.73 for Transformer and 152.53 for Mamba2; gains persist at 70M parameters.
At 8× length extrapolation, perplexity degrades by about 8–9% without positional-encoding engineering.
Revision enables in-domain infilling, improving performance by 19% over on-demand coupling at no measurable perplexity cost.
Limitations include impaired long-range retrieval, weaker synthetic-task and out-of-domain code-infilling performance, and a 6.5–12.3× wall-clock gap.
papers.selection_reason: Attention-free LLM architecture with efficient training/decode; fits language foundation models and efficient AI.
papers.title: FON: A Draft-Revise Dual-Organ Language Model without Sequence-Level Quadratic Attention
papers.tldr: FON combines causal drafting with non-generative prefix revision to avoid sequence-level quadratic attention while improving language-modeling perplexity under matched budgets.

papers.abstract: Deep-search agents are commonly trained by distilling tool-use trajectories from stronger teacher models. However, structurally complex questions may remain relatively easy for teachers familiar with key entities in the underlying entity graph, resulting in lower search demand and weaker supervision. We refer to this teacher-specific variation in question difficulty as teacher-relative difficulty and investigate entity familiarity as an early predictor. We first introduce Evidence-Verified Entity Familiarity (EVF), which estimates familiarity by verifying a teacher-generated factual brief against online evidence. Across multiple teachers, EVF is significantly correlated with teacher-relative difficulty with AUCs of 0.60--0.70. However, its high cost makes it impractical for constructing entity graphs at scale. To address this limitation, we propose Self-Reported Entity Familiarity (SEF), a lightweight gating signal that directly asks a teacher whether it is familiar with an entity before admitting that entity into the graph. Across multiple teachers, trajectories from SEF-gated synthesis exhibit greater observed search demand and yield higher downstream student accuracy than those from ungated synthesis. Because familiarity is teacher specific, we further study cross-teacher reuse. We screen graphs collected for other teachers using Kimi-K3's SEF judgments and use the retained graphs to produce 5,411 additional trajectories. Combined with 2,200 trajectories from newly constructed, SEF-gated graphs, these data improve Qwen3.8-27B's accuracy from 44.10% to 66.41% on a BrowseComp subset, and achieving state-of-the-art performance among models of comparable size on BrowseComp, SEAL-0, HLE-text, and xbench. Overall, SEF provides a low-cost way to synthesize more informative supervision for deep-search distillation.
authors: Yifei Liu, Zhixiang Liang, Wentao Tan, Yicheng Wang, Jiaqi Wang, Nan Duan, Qiong Cao
bullets: Teacher familiarity can make complex questions easier for the teacher, reducing search demand and weakening training signals.
Evidence-Verified Entity Familiarity (EVF) predicts teacher-relative difficulty, but its online verification cost limits scalability.
SEF cheaply asks teachers about entity familiarity before including entities in search graphs.
SEF-gated trajectories show greater observed search demand and improve downstream student accuracy.
Combining newly collected and cross-teacher-reused data raises Qwen3.8-27B accuracy on a BrowseComp subset from 44.10% to 66.41%.
papers.selection_reason: Entity-familiarity gating for deep-search distillation; relevant to LLM training and data synthesis.
papers.title: Avoiding What Your Teacher Already Knows: Entity Familiarity for Deep-Search Distillation
papers.tldr: Self-Reported Entity Familiarity (SEF) filters out entities teachers already know, producing more search-demanding supervision and improving deep-search distillation.

papers.abstract: This manuscript presents DeepThink, a knowledge-addressable framework for recurrent language modeling. A Knowledge Bank stores typed Knowledge Units, a Knowledge Activator selects units from the current execution state, Knowledge Assembly produces an executable configuration, and a Shared Thinking Operator updates that state. An output stage then organizes generation. This organization exposes knowledge capacity, activation width, and recurrent depth as separate design variables, supporting both complete parameter packages and fine-grained expert or low-rank modules. We formalize the interfaces and their execution semantics, including state-dependent selection, parameter-space assembly, and thinking followed by generation. For compatible templates and complete runtime-state configurations, we establish an exact Fixed-Schedule Realization of an existing fixed-depth model. Exact shared-base reparameterization and pretrained output-tail reuse provide complementary initialization constructions. Together, these results define a route from pretrained models to dynamically selected and assembled recurrent computation. A synthesis of conditional computation, recurrent models, modular parameters, and knowledge interfaces positions DeepThink within the research landscape and identifies the design questions arising from their integration.
bullets: Separates knowledge capacity, activation width, and recurrent depth as independent design variables.
Uses a Knowledge Bank, state-dependent Knowledge Activator, Knowledge Assembly, Shared Thinking Operator, and output stage.
Supports complete parameter packages as well as fine-grained expert and low-rank modules.
Proves exact realization of compatible fixed-depth models under fixed schedules and gives reparameterization and output-tail reuse initialization schemes.
Frames open design questions at the intersection of conditional computation, recurrence, modular parameters, and knowledge interfaces.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a knowledge-addressable recurrent language modeling framework with a Knowledge Bank and modular parameter assembly, relevant to LLM architecture and memory.
papers.title: DeepThink: A Conceptual Model for Knowledge-Addressable Recurrent Language Modeling
papers.tldr: DeepThink proposes a modular recurrent language-modeling framework that dynamically selects and assembles knowledge and computation during generation.

papers.abstract: Although post-training significantly enhances model performance, the use of massive undisclosed data raises concerns about benchmark contamination and copyright infringement. This drives growing interest in training data detection for post-trained models. Existing evaluations for training data detection often leverage benchmarks constructed post hoc, which can introduce distribution shifts. Alternatively, controlled evaluations rely on small-scale training setups that diverge from realistic post-training settings. As a result, their reported performance may not faithfully reflect the effectiveness of detection methods in real-world scenarios. To this end, we introduce \textsc{\method}, a reliable benchmark designed to evaluate detection methods in realistic, large-scale post-training settings. Built on a multi-stage pipeline, \method\space encompasses stage-specific models throughout the post-training lifecycle, spanning SFT, DPO, and RL. To perform a reliable evaluation, we construct model-specific evaluation sets across four diverse tasks, featuring distribution-matched members and non-members with verifiable membership labels. Our results reveal that even the best-performing method achieves an average AUC of only 0.529 on our benchmark, which approaches random-guessing level (0.5). Furthermore, our analysis suggests that evaluation protocols can significantly affect measured detection performance. These findings highlight the significant potential for developing effective, practical, and robust detection methods under realistic scenarios.
authors: Hengxiang Zhang, Junxian Liu, Hongxin Wei
bullets: Existing evaluations may misrepresent detection performance because of post hoc distribution shifts or small-scale training setups.
WildTrace evaluates detection across SFT, DPO, and RL stages using model-specific, distribution-matched member and non-member sets.
The benchmark covers four diverse tasks with verifiable membership labels.
The best method reaches only 0.529 average AUC, close to random-guessing performance.
Evaluation protocols substantially influence measured detection results.
papers.selection_reason: Focuses on post-training evaluation and training data detection for LLMs. While the application is evaluation, it relates to the robustness and knowledge boundaries of LLMs.
papers.title: WildTrace: Evaluating Training Data Detection in Realistic Large-Scale LLM Post-Training
papers.tldr: WildTrace shows that detecting whether data was used in realistic, large-scale LLM post-training remains nearly as difficult as random guessing.

papers.abstract: Puzzles offer a natural testbed for Large Language Models (LLMs) reasoning because they pose verifiable goals under partial information and require multi-step decisions to reach a solution. However, existing puzzle benchmarks typically focus on narrow environments with rigid mechanics and tightly constrained solution targets. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Active Probing Benchmark (APB), which generalizes puzzle-solving by casting concept identification as an interactive reasoning task that integrates specialized knowledge assessment into the puzzle setting. Specifically, APB evaluates whether models can acquire information via multi-turn active probing and inference to pinpoint 960 target concepts of specialized difficulty across eight diverse academic domains. Our evaluation reveals a counter-intuitive phenomenon: most open-source reasoning models significantly underperform their standard instruction counterparts. This finding suggests that in interactive settings, these models struggle to leverage procedural reasoning to reliably access and apply specialized domain knowledge. Beyond these empirical insights, APB provides a scalable pipeline for generating benchmarks that probe knowledge reasoning under interaction across diverse settings.
authors: Xin Cheng, Junming Yang, Ning Xu
bullets: Reframes puzzle solving as interactive concept identification under partial information and verifiable goals.
Evaluates multi-turn probing and inference over 960 specialized concepts across eight academic domains.
Finds that most open-source reasoning models underperform their standard instruction-tuned counterparts in this setting.
Suggests reasoning models struggle to use procedural reasoning to access and apply specialized knowledge interactively.
Provides a scalable pipeline for generating interactive knowledge-reasoning benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a benchmark for multi-turn active probing and knowledge reasoning in LLMs, contributing to LLM reasoning evaluation.
papers.title: Query Your Way Out: Benchmarking Multi-Turn Knowledge Reasoning through Generalized Puzzle Solving
papers.tldr: APB benchmarks whether LLMs can identify specialized concepts by actively querying for information and reasoning across multiple turns.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success across a wide range of language tasks. At their core, autoregressive LLMs are conditional probability models that learn to approximate the next-token distribution given the preceding context. Despite this probabilistic nature, the stochastic dynamics of autoregressive decoding have rarely been investigated from a rigorous probabilistic perspective. In this work, we define the per-step prediction error as the difference between the sampled token indicator and the model's conditional predictive distribution, and prove that the cumulative error process is a martingale with respect to the decoding filtration, implying that its conditional first-order moment is identically zero. Beyond this first-order property, we derive a closed-form expression for the second-order behavior of the martingale sequence: its predictable quadratic variation reduces to $\sum_t\left(1-p(y_t\mid y_{<t})\right)$, computable from realized token probabilities alone. This identity establishes a direct theoretical connection between sequence fluctuations and predictive uncertainty during autoregressive decoding. White-box experiments on Llama-3.x and Qwen2.5 families (1B to 72B parameters) verify that the empirically measured second-order moments closely match the theoretical predictions derived from our martingale analysis. These results provide a probabilistic framework for analyzing autoregressive LLM decoding, reveal intrinsic probabilistic fingerprints of different language models, and establish a rigorous mathematical foundation for LLM-generated text detection and uncertainty quantification.
authors: Xiahui Zhu, Zhenyi Qi, Wanwei Liu, Haoang Chi, Yang Tan, Xinyu Sun, Ji Wang
bullets: Defines per-step prediction error as the sampled-token indicator minus the model’s conditional token distribution.
Proves that cumulative prediction error is a martingale with zero conditional first-order moment.
Derives predictable quadratic variation as \(\sum_t(1-p(y_t\mid y_{<t}))\), computable from realized token probabilities.
Experiments on Llama-3.x and Qwen2.5 models from 1B to 72B parameters closely match the theoretical second-order predictions.
Provides a framework for studying model-specific probabilistic fingerprints, text detection, and uncertainty quantification.
papers.selection_reason: Provides a martingale-based probabilistic analysis of autoregressive LLM decoding, relevant to LLM uncertainty quantification and generated-text detection.
papers.title: Autoregressive Decoding as a Martingale: Characterizing the Stochastic Dynamics of LLM Generation
papers.tldr: Autoregressive LLM decoding can be modeled as a martingale whose predictable fluctuations are determined by the probabilities assigned to the generated tokens.

papers.abstract: We study pretraining when compute is abundant but unique training data are finite, requiring repeated training on the same data. We first revisit infinite-compute pretraining (Kim et al. 2026) and show that its frontier depends critically on choices previously fixed or studied only in isolation. In particular, optimizing batch size together with epoch counts reveals a U-shaped relationship between validation loss and batch size, favoring smaller batches than typical pretraining, likely because small-batch gradient noise provides implicit regularization. We further find that training recipes, previously optimized under a single-pass assumption, can be tuned, e.g., repacking documents into new sequences every epoch, weight tying, and positive embedding weight decay. We then relax the infinite-compute assumption. In particular, smaller-than-typical batch sizes can require prohibitively long sequential training, motivating to treat GPUs and time as separate resources. Tighter deadlines favor larger batches, and latency-oriented parallelism can trade additional GPUs for shorter training. Nevertheless, even under a fixed time budget, a smaller batch with fewer GPUs can achieve lower validation loss than a larger batch with more GPUs, challenging the common practice of increasing data parallelism to maximize GPU utilization under a deadline. Together, our results identify underexplored factors in repeated-data training and provide concrete guidance on how training recipes and resource allocation should change from single-pass pretraining.
bullets: Validation loss follows a U-shaped curve with batch size, with smaller-than-typical batches often performing best due in part to implicit gradient-noise regularization.
Repeated-data training benefits from recipe changes such as reshuffling document packing each epoch, weight tying, and positive embedding weight decay.
When time is limited, larger batches can reduce sequential training time, while extra GPUs can trade cost for lower latency.
Even under a fixed deadline, a smaller batch using fewer GPUs may outperform a larger batch using more GPUs, challenging GPU-utilization-focused scaling.
The study focuses on finite-data, repeated-training regimes rather than standard single-pass pretraining.
papers.selection_reason: Studies pretraining recipes and resource tradeoffs for repeated-data LLM training.
papers.title: Scaling Repeated-Data Pretraining: Batch Size, Regularization, and GPU-Time Tradeoffs
papers.tldr: For pretraining on finite data with repeated passes, smaller batches and revised regularization can improve validation loss, but deadlines and GPU-time constraints may favor larger batches or different parallelism choices.

papers.abstract: With ever increasing personalized large language model (LLM) services, the next question to answer is how to improve the quality of services/users' experiences, which is indicated by personalized LLM generation accuracy/quality and inference latency. Although state-of-the-art designs, e.g., parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) or Full PEFT+RAG, can help, they largely ignore the heterogeneous semantic concentrations of users' historical data and cannot fully unleash the potential of personal data for personalized LLM performance enhancement. In this paper, we propose PEFT Union RAG (PUR), a novel ``fast and accurate'' approach that exploits the semantic concentration of users' personal historical data to split workload between PEFT and RAG, aiming to improve personalized LLM performance in terms of better generation accuracy/quality and lower inference latency. Briefly, PUR partitions user's personal historical data and assigns semantic concentrated ``core'' information to PEFT for offline parametric fine-tuning, while retaining dispersed information for RAG. During the online LLM inference, PUR directly generates responses for ``core'' queries covered by the PEFT region and invokes RAG only for sporadic ``peripheral'' queries. Experimental results show that, by appropriately splitting workload between PEFT and RAG, PUR consistently achieves the best generation accuracy/quality for various users across multiple tasks, while reducing inference latency by 14.4%--46.6% compared with the best performed method.
authors: Xingke Yang, Sicong Li, Lingfeng Yao, Rui Chen, Changqing Luo, Xin Fu, Miao Pan
bullets: Targets the limitations of using PEFT or RAG alone, or combining them without considering users’ heterogeneous data semantics.
Partitions personal historical data into a concentrated “core” region for offline PEFT and a dispersed “peripheral” region for RAG.
During inference, core queries are answered directly through the fine-tuned model, while RAG handles sporadic peripheral queries.
Across multiple tasks and users, PUR reports the best generation accuracy/quality and reduces inference latency by 14.4%–46.6% versus the best-performing comparison method.
papers.selection_reason: Improves personalized LLM accuracy and latency via semantic-concentration-based PEFT/RAG workload split.
papers.title: Fast and Accurate: Improving Personalized LLM Performance by Semantic Concentration Inspired Workload Split between RAG and Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: PUR improves personalized LLM quality and latency by assigning semantically concentrated user information to PEFT and dispersed information to RAG.

papers.abstract: Qwen3-8B reviewing Llama-3.1-8B in math adds 33.2 points, yet Qwen3-8B alone is 6.4 points more accurate than the result. Reviewing another model's answer is usually judged by its gain over the generator. We show that this confuses verification, which adds accuracy beyond either model alone, with capability transfer, where a stronger reviewer supplies answers it could have given on its own. Measured against the stronger model alone, across 48 pairs of 12 open-weight models (3B to 72B) in math, knowledge, code and reasoning, review beats it in only 9 of 96 review directions, and does worse the larger the capability gap. The reason is that the reviewer mostly follows the generator, discarding its own correct answers. Review costs 2.6 to 2.8 times as much as the stronger model alone, while a selector using the same two calls is 2.7 to 4.2 points more accurate than review and cheaper. Studies of verification should report the stronger model alone, not only the gain over the generator. Code and per-question results: https://github.com/Kamilaabb/verification-or-capability-transfer
bullets: Across 48 model pairs and 96 review directions, review outperformed the stronger standalone model only 9 times.
Review performance declines as the capability gap between generator and reviewer grows.
Reviewers often follow the generator and discard correct answers they could have produced independently.
Review costs 2.6–2.8× as much as using the stronger model alone.
A selector using the same two calls was 2.7–4.2 points more accurate than review and cheaper.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes verification versus capability transfer in LLM pipelines, relevant to LLM evaluation and reasoning.
papers.title: Review Rarely Beats the Stronger Model: Separating Verification from Capability Transfer in LLM Pipelines
papers.tldr: LLM review often transfers a stronger model’s capability rather than adding verification, making it less accurate and more costly than simply using that stronger model.

papers.abstract: Large-scale personalization is shifting from embedding-table retrieval to LLM-based recommenders that generate the Semantic ID (SID) of the item to recommend, where each SID is a short sequence of discrete hierarchical content codes. A single instruction-tuned model can then unify retrieval, content understanding, and language, and recommend brand-new titles from their content alone using SID; then, how should the model generate the SID? Traditionally, models rely on a single language modeling head that generates tokens autoregressively, typically using constrained beam search. In contrast, an emerging body of work explores multi-token prediction (MTP), where dedicated heads predict all tokens in parallel, substantially reducing the decoding latency associated with beam search. We report an industry-scale, apples-to-apples comparison of these two generation paradigms: single-head autoregressive decoding vs. MTP. We introduce a new auxiliary ranking loss, defined over the joint SID score, to train the MTP objective. We evaluate the SID training objectives on both quality and training/inference cost, inside a multi-task LLM that jointly does personalized retrieval, content question-answering (QA), and instruction following over a large streaming-media catalog. Our experiments show single-head beam search consistently beats MTP on most product-critical metrics: ranking and content QA, and trains at roughly 2.6x lower dollar cost on Qwen3-8B scale; MTP wins only on raw inference throughput. Around this finding, we detail an efficient training and inference stack and report end-to-end gains over the previous non-SID baseline equipped with an auxiliary ranking head: +77% item cold-start ranking, +22% content-QA accuracy, +2.8x faster training, with language metric regression traced to SID vocabulary expansion. We address the language regression by reinforcement learning post training.
authors: Sejoon Oh, Fernando Amat Gil, Evan Smothers, Dan Iter, Mark Thornburg, Dawit Mureja Argaw, Sourabh Medapati, Thea Wang, Ria Verma, Qiuling Xu, Harshit Syal, Ehsan Gholami, Moumita Bhattacharya, Ashish Rastogi
bullets: Semantic IDs let a unified instruction-tuned LLM recommend new items from content alone while supporting retrieval, QA, and instruction following.
The study compares single-head autoregressive SID generation with parallel multi-token prediction (MTP), introducing an auxiliary loss based on joint SID scores for MTP.
Beam search performs better on ranking and content QA and costs about 2.6× less to train at Qwen3-8B scale; MTP wins only on raw decoding throughput.
Compared with a prior non-SID baseline, the stack improves cold-start ranking by 77%, content-QA accuracy by 22%, and training speed by 2.8×.
SID vocabulary expansion causes language-metric regression, which the authors address through reinforcement-learning post-training.
papers.selection_reason: Compares autoregressive and multi-token prediction paradigms for LLM-based recommendation, relevant to LLM generation and training.
papers.title: Personalized LLM Recommendation with Semantic IDs: Autoregressive Beam Search vs. Multi-Token Prediction
papers.tldr: In an industry-scale comparison, autoregressive constrained beam search outperforms multi-token prediction for most recommendation and content-QA metrics, while MTP provides higher raw inference throughput.

papers.abstract: When told that robins have sesamoid bones, people are far more prone to extend the property to sparrows than to whales. This behavior, called category-based property induction, is well documented in humans, but whether and how it develops in language models trained only to predict the next token is unclear. To shed light on this, we construct a hierarchical taxonomy of synthetic entities grouped by the properties they share. We then inject facts from this latent taxonomy into the continued pre-training of Pythia and OLMo 2 models from 70M to 7B parameters, and track the development of inductive behaviors. We find that taxonomically aligned induction emerges from next-token prediction alone: a property learned for one entity transfers more strongly within its taxonomic category than across categories. Internally, entities that share a deeper category become more similar in activation space, and clustering recovers the full taxonomic tree from entity representations. Contrary to the usual expectation that scale helps, we find that induction weakens with model size when the data budget is fixed, suggesting that larger models memorize individual facts rather than compress them into shared structure. Induction also strengthens with more pre-training before the taxonomy injection, transfers to novel in-context properties, and can be overridden by a latent taxonomy implied by the prompt. Together, these results show that a model's inductive generalization reflects the latent organization of its training data, with implications for data curation and for predicting how far a learned fact will spread.
authors: Jan Sobotka, Ekaterina Goliakova, Marcin Detyniecki, Antoine Bosselut, Xavier Renard
bullets: Researchers test whether language models transfer properties more strongly among taxonomically related entities.
Synthetic hierarchical taxonomies were injected during continued pre-training of Pythia and OLMo 2 models ranging from 70M to 7B parameters.
Taxonomically aligned induction emerges without explicit supervision; activation representations recover the underlying taxonomic tree.
With a fixed data budget, induction weakens as model size increases, while more prior pre-training strengthens it.
Induction transfers to novel in-context properties and can be redirected by a taxonomy implied in the prompt.
papers.selection_reason: Studies inductive generalization and latent taxonomy formation in LLM pre-training, relevant to language foundation model reasoning and data curation.
papers.title: Latent Taxonomies: How Property Induction Develops in Language Model Pre-training
papers.tldr: Next-token pre-training can produce human-like, taxonomy-based property induction, but fixed-data scaling may favor memorization over shared structure.

papers.abstract: Large language model agents are emerging as an important new class of users of desktop applications. However, existing desktop interfaces were designed for human end users or application developers, leaving agents to interpret visual controls or discover and compose low-level software operations. This mismatch can hinder even capable agents, yet it remains unclear what interface properties make desktop software easier for agents to use. To study this question, we treat software evolution as a natural source of interface variation and introduce DeskIF-Bench, a benchmark of 255 artifact-verified tasks across six desktop applications. By holding the task, agent, and verifier fixed while varying the software release, we measure how interface changes affect agent performance. Across two models and six applications, the newest release consistently outperforms the oldest. Trajectory analysis identifies three relevant interface properties: discoverability, granularity, and observability. Guided by these properties, we develop ANIS, a framework that synthesizes agent-native interfaces from the capabilities of installed applications. On an expanded evaluation of 368 tasks across eight applications, atomic interfaces improve success over native SDK use by 3.8 and 3.5 percentage points with DeepSeek V4 Flash and Claude Haiku 4.5, respectively, while reducing online token usage by approximately 73%. Goal-level commands further raise success to 74.5% and 67.4%, respectively.
authors: Alan Wu, Wei Tao, Yiwen Guo
bullets: Desktop software was built for humans or developers, creating a mismatch for LLM agents.
DeskIF-Bench contains 255 artifact-verified tasks across six applications and isolates the effect of software releases on agent performance.
Analysis highlights discoverability, granularity, and observability as key agent-facing interface properties.
ANIS synthesizes atomic and goal-level interfaces from installed application capabilities.

Across expanded evaluations, atomic interfaces improved success by 3.8 and 3.5 percentage points and reduced online token usage by about 73%; goal-level commands achieved 74.5% and 67.4% success for the two models.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses the interaction of Large Language Model agents with software interfaces, relevant to the development of LLMs and agent capabilities.
papers.title: A Decade in a Day: Synthesizing Agent-Native Interfaces from Human-Oriented Software Evolution
papers.tldr: DeskIF-Bench shows that newer desktop interfaces better support agents, while ANIS synthesizes agent-native interfaces that improve task success and sharply reduce token use.

papers.abstract: A central desideratum in model editing is generalization to complex tasks, which prior work formalizes under a direct generalization paradigm: treating and evaluating LLM behavior as an input-output mapping and expecting a factual update to alter outputs on reasoning tasks. Yet despite substantial empirical effort, the field consensus remains that such generalization is highly challenging and elusive. However, when we deploy the latest models in an in-the-wild chatbot-user setting, we surprisingly find that even classical editing methods exhibit remarkably fluent generalization behavior. This motivates us to revisit the obstacles to generalization and the limitations of the prevailing paradigm. We find that direct generalization is fundamentally constrained both theoretically and practically: theoretically, it suffers from an identifiability issue; and practically, existing approaches attempting to circumvent this are further hindered by the ambiguity of their constructed biases and by vulnerability to being overridden by other factors such as optimization dynamics. We instead identify compositional generalization, empowered by the increasingly strong reasoning and composition abilities of modern LLMs, as a theoretically grounded and empirically validated alternative. We validate this phenomenon across multiple models and editing methods, showing that such generalization behavior is widespread. Overall, we argue that generalizable model editing could be more than direct generalization, and call for a paradigm shift toward more generalizable and practically deployable knowledge update techniques.
authors: Xiaotian Ye, Chunyao Yang, Xiaohan Wang, Junkai Chen, Yongqi Duan, Mengqi Zhang, Shu Wu
bullets: Direct generalization—expecting factual edits to reliably change reasoning-task outputs—is theoretically and practically constrained.
In-the-wild chatbot evaluations reveal fluent generalization even with classical editing methods.
Theoretical analysis identifies an identifiability problem in direct generalization.
Attempts to address this face ambiguous constructed biases and interference from factors such as optimization dynamics.
Compositional generalization is supported theoretically and empirically across multiple models and editing methods.
papers.selection_reason: Examines generalization of LLM model editing and proposes compositional generalization, directly relevant to LLM knowledge-update research.
papers.title: Generalizable Model Editing Could Be More Than Direct Generalization
papers.tldr: Model editing may generalize more effectively through compositional reasoning in real chatbot interactions than through the conventional direct input-output update paradigm.

papers.abstract: India's Eighth Schedule recognises 22 languages, yet parallel data is uneven across them, and many language pairs, especially among lower-resource languages such as Bodo, Dogri, Santali and Kashmiri, lack direct bitext. We present BharatSetu 22-Indic 1M, a row-aligned table of 984,764 English sentences, each paired with machine translations into all 22 scheduled languages (21,664,808 Indic cells), generated with the sarvamai/sarvam-translate model family. Because every Indic cell in a row translates the same English sentence, any two columns form a translation pair: 462 directed Indic-to-Indic pairs, or 506 including English, without direct bitext. We call these pivot-derived pairs and propose a confidence layer that lets users choose how strictly each pair is connected. The corpus is machine-generated and not human-verified; quality is expected to vary by language, domain and sentence style, and pivot-derived pairs can inherit errors from both sides. We therefore release BharatSetu as a machine layer and propose a human-correction layer keyed to the same row identifiers, so that each corrected column upgrades every pair that uses it, together with an evaluation protocol. We report no translation-quality results.
authors: Haq Nawaz Malik, Nahfid Nissar, Faizan Iqbal
bullets: Addresses uneven parallel data and missing direct bitext, especially for lower-resource Indic languages.
Contains 984,764 English sentences translated into all 22 languages, yielding 21.7M Indic cells.
Row alignment enables 462 directed Indic-to-Indic pairs, or 506 pairs when including English.
Adds a confidence layer for controlling pair connectivity and proposes row-keyed human corrections that can improve multiple pairs.
The corpus is machine-generated, unverified, and reported without translation-quality results.
papers.selection_reason: Provides a large-scale translation dataset for Indian languages, relevant to the development and evaluation of Large Language Models.
papers.title: bharatSetu: a 1M x 22 bridge for indic translation
papers.tldr: BharatSetu provides nearly 1M English-aligned machine translations across all 22 scheduled Indian languages to enable broad pivot-derived translation pairs, while highlighting the need for human correction.

papers.abstract: Structural pruning followed by a recovery stage is the standard recipe for compressing large language models (LLMs), yet the two stages are typically designed and tuned in isolation. In this work, we study how their interaction shapes the compressed model, sweeping ordering, the data that drives each stage, and the alignment of their training objectives. We find that instruction-following is the first capability to collapse under pruning, well before knowledge, reasoning, or core language modeling, and that much of the pruning in-domain loss is likely not knowledge loss but a domain-agnostic failure to respond coherently to the prompt. We find in our setting that in-domain data is the strongest pruning signal, whereas instruction-style data recovers the most. Stage order matters little, but only marginally. We further analyze how the importance ranking drifts before and after pruning. Together these results give practitioners a concrete recipe for composing pruning and recovery.
authors: Luis Frentzen Salim, Komang Rinartha, Chia-Chun Wu, Tran Van Nhiem, Lun-Wei Ku, Yung-Hui Li
bullets: Instruction-following collapses before knowledge, reasoning, or core language modeling during pruning.
Much of the in-domain loss appears to reflect incoherent prompt responses rather than knowledge loss.
In-domain data provides the strongest pruning signal in the studied setting.
Instruction-style data delivers the strongest recovery.
Pruning and recovery alter parameter-importance rankings, while reversing their stage order has only a marginal effect.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes interaction of structural pruning and recovery in LLMs, yielding a practical recipe for efficient compression.
papers.title: The Fragility and Dynamics of LLM Pruning-Recovery Steps
papers.tldr: LLM pruning primarily disrupts instruction-following, while instruction-style recovery data most effectively restores behavior, making pruning–recovery design choices important even when stage order has limited impact.

papers.abstract: Settling one comparison between two truncation samplers has cost six thousand A100-hours, and nothing says in advance how far apart two samplers can be. We observe that almost every deployed truncation rule keeps a prefix of the probability-sorted vocabulary, so any two such rules are nested at every decoding step. Nesting yields a closed-form per-step distance and a coupling under which both samplers emit identical text until they first disagree. Accumulated over a generation, this gives a separation certificate that bounds the difference between two samplers on any bounded outcome, is computable from logs a comparison already produces, and equals their sequence-level total variation distance exactly when neither rule ever overtakes the other. Two consequences follow without measurement: exactness is fragile, and certifying a small difference requires the two retained masses to agree to very high precision at every step. On six open-weight models over four math and science benchmarks, the certificate for every hyperparameter grid we tested is at least 0.998, so a bound alone rarely settles a comparison, although two members of one family can be far closer. What remains useful is the coupling, which gives an unbiased paired estimator that cuts variance $1.2$-$3.8\times$ against prompt-level pairing. Read against benchmark sizes at the default pair's variance and our point estimate of its between-prompt component, resolving a one-point difference needs 8 to 32 samples per prompt on GSM8K, MATH-500 and GPQA-Diamond and about 210 on AIME 2025; at that component's upper confidence bound GPQA-Diamond needs more than 32 and AIME 2025 cannot be resolved at any sample count. Choosing a truncation sampler is a measurement problem at least as much as a design one. The code is available at https://github.com/KurbanIntelligenceLab/truncation-samplers.
bullets: Most deployed truncation rules retain a prefix of the probability-sorted vocabulary, making sampler supports nested at each decoding step.
Nesting provides a closed-form per-step distance and a coupling under which generated texts match until the first disagreement.
The accumulated certificate bounds differences on bounded outcomes, is computable from comparison logs, and can equal sequence-level total variation under a no-overtaking condition.
Across six open-weight models and four benchmarks, tested certificates were at least 0.998, so bounds rarely resolve comparisons; exactness is also highly fragile.
The coupling enables unbiased paired estimation with 1.2–3.8× lower variance than prompt-level pairing, but resolving small performance gaps may still require many samples.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes nested truncation samplers for LLM decoding and provides a coupling-based measurement framework, directly relevant to language model generation.
papers.title: Truncation Samplers Are Nested: Comparing Decoding Rules Is a Measurement Problem
papers.tldr: Truncation samplers are usually nested, enabling exact coupling-based comparison certificates, but the resulting bounds are often too loose—so reliable sampler comparisons remain a costly measurement problem.

papers.abstract: Language models are becoming infrastructure, and infrastructure built in the open, by public institutions, on documented data, is the alternative to dependence on a few providers; Apertus shows this is viable at scale. Apertus 1.5 extends the fully open Apertus family from text to multimodal reasoning. Continued pretraining of the Apertus 1.0 models, on 4T additional tokens for the 8B and 2T for the 70B, adds image and audio understanding and extends the context window fourfold to 262,144 tokens; multimodality enters through the tokenizer, the language-model head remains restricted to text, and the architecture is unchanged. Supervised finetuning, long-context finetuning, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, and preference alignment complete the released models. Thinking is a flag of the chat template rather than a separate model, and lifts mathematical reasoning by up to 20 points on the 8B model. The released models improve over their predecessors on nearly every benchmark; among fully open models of its class, the 8B leads on knowledge, instruction following, and cultural benchmarks, and its instruction following surpasses all compared models, including open-weight ones. On image and audio understanding, a first for the family, the models are competitive with fully open multimodal models, strongest on document understanding and long-form and lower-resource speech recognition, while specialized vision and audio models remain ahead on perception and transcription of English and other high-resource languages. As in Apertus 1.0, we train only on openly available data, respect crawler opt-outs retroactively, and exclude restrictively licensed material. We release the model weights, data preparation and training recipes, and evaluation suites under permissive licenses; openness extends to values, with the Apertus charter guiding alignment stages published alongside the models.

bullets: Continued pretraining adds multimodality and expands context to 262,144 tokens without changing the architecture; multimodality is introduced through the tokenizer.
Training combines supervised and long-context finetuning, verifiable-reward reinforcement learning, and preference alignment; “thinking” is controlled by the chat template.
The models improve over Apertus 1.0 across nearly every benchmark; the 8B model leads comparable fully open models in knowledge, instruction following, and cultural benchmarks.
Image and audio capabilities are competitive among fully open multimodal models, especially for document understanding, long-form speech, and lower-resource speech recognition.
The project uses openly available data with crawler opt-outs and restrictive licenses excluded, and releases weights, recipes, evaluation suites, and alignment guidance permissively.
papers.selection_reason: Open multimodal LLM with image/audio understanding, long context, and RL-trained reasoning; fits multimodal and language foundation model interests.
papers.title: Apertus 1.5: From Open Text Models to Open Multimodal Reasoners
papers.tldr: Apertus 1.5 extends a fully open text-model family into multimodal reasoning with image/audio understanding, much longer context, and publicly released models, data practices, recipes, and evaluations.

papers.abstract: Large language models make decisions through parallel prefill and sequential decoding. Although effective, this approach incurs decoding costs and does not explicitly expose decision probabilities. Existing task-specific classifiers require per-task training and offer limited generalization to unseen decision schemas. We propose Large Decision Models (LDMs), repurposing language models to return explicit probabilities over labels specified at run time using one prefill forward pass. We first adapt models to this interface through Diverse Decision Supervision (DDS), covering varied domains, rules and labels. To further narrow the performance gap to a reasoning model, Self-Posed Reasoning Distillation (SPRD) adds tasks generated by a frozen teacher, filters them for answer consistency, and trains on label distributions obtained from repeated teacher reasoning. We evaluate on DecisionVista, pairing new-schema tests with held-out human-labelled sources. Across three base models, the recipe improves accuracy over a step-matched baseline by 1.8 and 1.5 percentage points, respectively, achieving a 182-fold speedup in latency over reasoning rollout on Gemma-4-31B. Reasoning remains stronger on the new-schema test, motivating a confidence router for uncertain decisions. On development sets, routing recovers a median 92% of reasoning's accuracy advantage while generating 27-58% of its tokens. Code is available at https://github.com/JianhuiWei7/LDM.
authors: Ziyi Chen, Yan Zhang, Jianhui Wei, Jianing Yin, Daoan Zhang
bullets: LDMs support run-time-specified labels, improving generalization beyond task-specific classifiers.
Diverse Decision Supervision trains the model across varied domains, rules, and decision schemas.
Self-Posed Reasoning Distillation uses teacher-generated, consistency-filtered tasks and label distributions to narrow the reasoning gap.
Across three base models, LDMs improve accuracy over a step-matched baseline by 1.8 and 1.5 percentage points, with up to a 182× latency speedup over reasoning rollout on Gemma-4-31B.
A confidence router recovers a median 92% of reasoning’s accuracy advantage on development sets while using 27–58% as many tokens; reasoning remains stronger on new schemas.
