papers.selection_reason: Repurposes LLMs as single-pass decision makers with large latency gains, relevant to LLM methods and efficient inference.
papers.title: Large Decision Models: Repurposing Large Language Models as Single-Pass Decision Makers
papers.tldr: Large Decision Models turn language models into fast, single-pass classifiers that output explicit label probabilities while retaining much of the accuracy of slower reasoning models.

papers.abstract: Large reasoning models generate reasoning trajectories token by token. At a given prefix, multiple next-token candidates may be plausible, yet shape subsequent reasoning and differ in their chances of leading to the correct answer. Whether these differences are reflected in internal representations remains unclear. To study this question, we define relative long-horizon candidate value to quantify within-prefix differences and construct the Reasoning Candidate-Token Value (RCTV) dataset, pairing mathematical reasoning prefixes with plausible next-token candidates and their empirical long-horizon candidate values. Using RCTV, we examine hidden states, multilayer perceptron outputs, and attention outputs at candidate positions with sparse linear probes. Experimental results provide evidence that relative long-horizon candidate value is linearly decodable from these representations at multiple layers. Candidate-value probes can also outperform probability- and embedding-based baselines. Furthermore, a controlled online intervention experiment shows that using the decoded signals to guide token selection during generation can improve the chances of eventual success. Our findings provide evidence that internal representations encode information about relative long-horizon candidate value, offering insights into how local candidate-level representations relate to long-horizon reasoning outcomes.
authors: Yixin Yang, Yue Wang, Fandong Meng, Zhifang Sui
bullets: Introduces relative long-horizon candidate value to measure within-prefix differences among plausible next tokens.
Builds the RCTV dataset of mathematical reasoning prefixes, candidate tokens, and empirical long-horizon values.
Uses sparse linear probes on hidden states, MLP outputs, and attention outputs across layers.
Candidate-value signals are linearly decodable and can outperform probability- and embedding-based baselines.
An online intervention suggests decoded signals can improve eventual generation success.
papers.selection_reason: Probes LLM internal representations to decode long-horizon candidate value and improve reasoning token selection.
papers.title: From Candidate Tokens to Final Outcomes: Decoding Relative Long-Horizon Candidate Value from Reasoning Model Representations
papers.tldr: The study finds that reasoning-model representations encode how promising different next-token candidates are for eventual success, and that probing this signal can improve token selection.

papers.abstract: We adapted Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B for eight Indian languages without changing its backbone architecture. We expanded the vocabulary in place from 131,072 to 163,072 entries using continued byte-pair encoding and AdaptMix rebalancing, reducing tokens per word by 38.6%. We initialized new input and output rows by averaging their original constituent rows, then trained them on 90% Indic and 10% English text before updating the backbone. Continual pretraining then progressed through broad training, high-quality annealing, and long-context training over approximately 1.27 trillion tokens. The annealed checkpoint gained 12.9 points on the Indic MILU benchmark but lost 3.4 on English MMLU. We also report practical negative results. Direct token addition underperformed continued byte-pair encoding. AdamW weight decay changed rows intended to stay fixed. Perplexity on an Indic-heavy holdout did not select the learning rate that best preserved English performance.
authors: Avinash Benki, Prasanjith Pasunuti, Sutanshu Saksena Raj, Parijat Chatterjee, Nayanjit Sarkar, Daksh Maan
bullets: Expands the tokenizer in place from 131,072 to 163,072 entries using continued byte-pair encoding and AdaptMix, reducing tokens per word by 38.6%.
Initializes new input/output rows from constituent embeddings and trains with 90% Indic and 10% English text before updating the backbone.
Continual pretraining uses broad training, high-quality annealing, and long-context training over approximately 1.27 trillion tokens.
The annealed checkpoint improves Indic MILU by 12.9 points but decreases English MMLU by 3.4 points.

Negative results show direct token addition underperforms continued BPE, AdamW alters supposedly fixed rows, and Indic-heavy perplexity does not reliably select the best learning rate for English retention.
papers.selection_reason: In-place tokenizer expansion and continual pretraining for a large language model.
papers.title: In-Place Indic Tokenizer Expansion and Continual Pretraining of Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B
papers.tldr: The study expands and continually pretrains Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B for eight Indic languages, improving Indic benchmark performance while reducing English performance.

papers.abstract: Gnani-Evon-v3.3-30B-A3B is a long-context hybrid Mamba-Transformer mixture-of-experts model for reasoning, instruction following, and tool use in English and eight Indian languages. Starting from NVIDIA's Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B checkpoint, it retains the 52-layer backbone and changes the vocabulary, training data, and post-training objectives. An in-place expansion from 131,072 to 163,072 tokens reduces mean Indian-language fertility by 38.6%. The new embedding rows are initialized from their upstream decompositions and warmed before the backbone is updated. Continual pretraining then adds broad English-Indic data, high-quality annealing, and direct training at a 131,072-token sequence length. The central result appears after post-training. Reinforcement learning across four verifiable task environments improves mathematics, graduate-level science, and instruction following, but degrades Indic extractive question answering because the rewards do not require an answer in the requested language. The share of Indic extraction items answered in English rises from 8.7% to 91.7%. Accuracy conditional on answering in the target script roughly doubles, which is consistent with preserved reading ability but is measured on a self-selected subset. Two unreleased studies test repairs. A scoped Indic reward restores the language convention. A 26B-A4B generative judge outperforms a 235B-parameter model on RM-Bench, and distillation restores 81% of the capabilities displaced by optimizing against it. Relative to the architecture-identical starting checkpoint, the released model gains 5.2 points on an Indic aggregate while giving up 1.7 points of English retention. The unreleased Indic-aware branch trades further, gaining 14.6 Indic points at a cost of 5.4 in English. A planned FP8 release reduces the artifact to 32GB with near-zero mean change across 32 paired benchmarks.
authors: Sutanshu Saksena Raj, Prasanjith Pasunuti, Parijat Chatterjee, Daksh Maan, Purusharth Malik, Nayanjit Sarkar, Avinash Benki
bullets: Supports reasoning, instruction following, and tool use across English and eight Indian languages with a 163,072-token vocabulary/context expansion.
Vocabulary expansion reduces mean Indian-language fertility by 38.6%; continued pretraining adds broad English–Indic data and long-context training.

Reinforcement learning improves mathematics, graduate-level science, and instruction following but causes Indic extraction answers to shift from 8.7% to 91.7% English when rewards omit language constraints.
Relative to its starting checkpoint, the released model gains 5.2 Indic-aggregate points while losing 1.7 English-retention points.
Unreleased repairs include scoped Indic rewards and a smaller generative judge that recovers capabilities through distillation; an FP8 release is planned.
papers.selection_reason: Indic-first reasoning LLM with hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE architecture and RL post-training.
papers.title: A Sovereign, Indic-First, Reasoning Model
papers.tldr: Gnani-Evon-v3.3-30B-A3B is an Indic-first hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE that improves Indic performance through vocabulary expansion, continued pretraining, and reinforcement learning, while exposing reward-design trade-offs in language adherence.

papers.abstract: A recurrent-depth language model reuses one block of weights several times in a row. The number of repetitions, which we call loops, is chosen when the model runs, not when it is trained, and running fewer is cheaper and faster, so a deployment may choose to do it. Running fewer loops also makes these models less safe, and the loss of safety is larger than the loss of anything else we measured. We study four released Ouro checkpoints and Huginn-0125. At half of its trained depth, Ouro-1.4B-Thinking still solves 0.692 of the GSM8K maths problems, against 0.775 at full depth, keeping 89% of its accuracy. Over the same reduction, the rate at which it helps with harmful requests rises from 0.038 to 0.205, 5.3 times higher. The information is not lost: a linear classifier reads whether a request is harmful from the model's internal state after a single loop, with an ROC AUC of 0.967 against 0.986 at full depth. What the missing loops remove is the refusal that should follow. We measure the effect with four instruments, one generating no text at all, and reproduce it on a second model family. Removing a single direction from Ouro-1.4B's internal state at full depth drops its refusal rate on harmful prompts from 0.950 to 0.130, identifying what the shallow model is missing. Two run-time repairs do not help: the models' early-exit rules do not spend more loops on harmful requests, and choosing a depth per request does not recover the loss. Changing the training does. Standard safety training makes the shallow model safe only by refusing 0.865 of harmless requests, while training at randomly chosen depths reaches a separation of +0.399 between harmful and harmless refusal at one loop, against +0.118. On Huginn-0125 it keeps harmful help at or below 0.040 at every depth from 1 to 32 loops, where standard training reaches 0.194, and it costs no accuracy at full depth.
authors: Seyedarmin Azizi, Erfan Baghaei Potraghloo, Arya Fayyazi, Saeid Shokoufa, Massoud Pedram
bullets: At half depth, Ouro-1.4B-Thinking retains 89% of its GSM8K accuracy, but harmful-request assistance rises 5.3×.
Harmful intent remains encoded after one loop, indicating that shallow execution removes the refusal response rather than the safety signal.
Ablating one internal direction at full depth similarly reduces refusal, identifying a component linked to refusal behavior.
Early-exit rules and per-request depth selection do not restore safety.

Training across randomly sampled depths improves harmful/harmless refusal separation and keeps Huginn-0125’s harmful assistance at or below 0.040 across 1–32 loops without reducing full-depth accuracy.
papers.selection_reason: Studies recurrent-depth LLM architecture and safety/refusal behavior across loop counts; fits LLM architecture research.
papers.title: Running Fewer Loops Removes Refusal Behaviour in Recurrent-Depth Language Models
papers.tldr: Reducing inference loops preserves much of recurrent-depth models’ reasoning ability but sharply removes their refusal behavior, while depth-diverse safety training can maintain safety across loop counts.

papers.abstract: As agentic AI systems take on increasingly complex and consequential tasks, securing them against prompt injection becomes critical. Existing defenses often rely on detecting or reasoning about injected malicious instructions and can therefore remain vulnerable to adaptive attacks that optimize the injection itself. Diffusion language models (dLLMs), an emerging framework for language generation, offer a new opportunity for security enforcement: by iteratively refining their sequence wide predictions, they enable broader-scope constraint enforcement throughout generation. This paper introduces Policy-Constrained Diffusion Agents (CoDA), a framework that enforces task dependent security policies directly within the denoising process of diffusion language models. At each denoising step, CoDA projects token distributions onto a policy-compliant set, maintaining constraint satisfaction throughout generation. We evaluate CoDA across state-of-the-art diffusion language model families under both static and adaptive prompt-injection attacks. Results demonstrate substantial reductions in attack success rate with competitive task utility and practical inference overhead.
authors: Michael Cardei, Anjun Hu, Chenrui Ma, Francesco Pinto, Chawin Sitawarin, Chulin Xie, Ferdinando Fioretto
bullets: Addresses adaptive prompt-injection attacks that can evade defenses based on detecting malicious instructions.
Projects token distributions onto a policy-compliant set at every denoising step.
Evaluated across multiple diffusion language model families under static and adaptive attacks.
Substantially reduces attack success while preserving competitive task utility with practical inference overhead.
papers.selection_reason: Policy-constrained denoising for diffusion language models advances secure and controllable language generation.
papers.title: Only What You've Signed up For: Secure Workflows with Constrained Diffusion Agents
papers.tldr: CoDA secures diffusion-based agents against prompt injection by enforcing task-specific policies throughout generation.

papers.abstract: Existing depth-compression methods for large language models (LLMs) score layers individually or group only adjacent or contiguous layers, implicitly assuming that functional redundancy is local. We test this assumption by computing full pairwise Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) similarity matrices for thirteen LLMs from six architecture families (1.6B-14B parameters). Non-adjacent layers have 3.6-15.9x more high-similarity pairs than adjacent ones, a structure that prior similarity-based layer merging has not systematically exploited. We propose Fusion via Community Mining (FCM), which builds the full L x L similarity graph, uses spectral community detection to find clusters of functionally equivalent layers, keeps the highest-Block-Influence layer in each cluster, and applies LoRA recovery; a pre-specified rule computed only on calibration data chooses between cosine and CKA similarity. At 2x compression, FCM lowers mean perplexity below ShortGPT on twelve of thirteen models, significantly on ten (Welch's t-test with Holm-Bonferroni correction; up to 50% on Qwen3-4B), with Mistral-7B the only loss (+13.4%). Against FlattenGPT, SWM, and DeltaLLM under matched calibration and recovery, FCM gives the best perplexity on ten of thirteen models (mean rank 1.15), and it also outperforms MKA on three anchor models. FCM matches or exceeds ShortGPT on 15 of 20 zero-shot reasoning cells and also improves MMLU, LAMBADA, HumanEval pass@1, and free-form generation quality. The 2x-compressed Qwen2.5-7B has 46% fewer parameters, 42% lower peak VRAM, and 84% higher decode throughput on a single A100. Spectral grouping outperforms Fisher contiguous segmentation by 41% and uniform partitioning by 51%, and FCM's advantage grows beyond a 2x crossover up to 3x and persists at the 14B scale. Code: https://github.com/Usama1002/fcm-layer-fusion
bullets: Full pairwise CKA analysis across 13 LLMs finds substantially more high-similarity non-adjacent than adjacent layer pairs, challenging local-redundancy assumptions.
FCM constructs a layer-similarity graph, detects functional communities spectrally, retains the highest-Block-Influence layer per cluster, and applies LoRA recovery.
At 2× compression, FCM beats ShortGPT in mean perplexity on 12 of 13 models and is best among several baselines on 10 of 13.
It matches or exceeds ShortGPT on 15 of 20 zero-shot reasoning evaluations and improves several downstream generation and language benchmarks.
For compressed Qwen2.5-7B, FCM reports 46% fewer parameters, 42% lower peak VRAM, and 84% higher decode throughput on one A100; Mistral-7B is the main exception, with a perplexity loss.
papers.selection_reason: Graph-guided layer fusion compresses LLMs, reducing memory and improving inference throughput.
papers.title: Beyond Adjacent Layers: Graph-Guided Layer Fusion for Compressing Large Language Models
papers.tldr: FCM compresses LLM depth by grouping functionally similar non-adjacent layers, achieving strong perplexity and efficiency improvements at up to 3× compression.

papers.abstract: Spiking neural networks target energy-efficient language modeling through sparse, binary activations, but the efficiency-accuracy tradeoff of spiking language models is uncharacterized at scale. We present the first Chinchilla-style IsoFLOP scaling study of a spiking language model, sweeping SpikeGPT-family models (RWKV backbone) from width 384 to 1536 across compute budgets from $3\times10^{17}$ to $10^{19}$ FLOPs on FineWeb-EDU. We report two findings. First, the compute-optimal frontier is $N_{opt} \propto C^{0.56}$, close to the 0.50 that Hoffmann et al. report for dense Transformers, so spiking does not change how parameters and data should be traded off under a compute budget. Second, against non-spiking RWKV and Transformer baselines trained the same way, the loss gap splits into a backbone cost of about 0.16 nats that does not change with compute and a spiking cost that falls from 0.34 to about 0.23 nats and then levels off. These results give the first compute-optimal recipe for spiking language models and quantify the accuracy cost of their sparsity.
authors: Dan Saunders, Benjamin Ren, Catherine He
bullets: Studies SpikeGPT-family models with an RWKV backbone across widths 384–1536 and compute budgets of 3×10^17–10^19 FLOPs.
Finds the compute-optimal parameter scaling exponent is 0.56, close to the 0.50 reported for dense Transformers.
Decomposes the loss gap versus non-spiking baselines into a roughly compute-invariant backbone cost of 0.16 nats and a spiking cost that decreases before leveling off near 0.23 nats.
Provides a compute-optimal scaling recipe and quantifies the accuracy cost associated with spiking activations.
papers.selection_reason: Compute-optimal scaling laws for spiking language models inform efficient language model design and scaling.
papers.title: Compute-Optimal Scaling Laws for Spiking Language Models
papers.tldr: A large-scale scaling study finds that spiking language models follow dense-model compute-optimal parameter–data tradeoffs while incurring a persistent accuracy penalty from sparsity.

papers.abstract: Foundation models need to support diverse inference budgets, yet training a separate model for each budget duplicates pretraining effort. Elastic models train several nested sub-networks inside one weight-shared supernet, but existing recipes face three obstacles: variable per-step workloads that hinder distributed scaling, limited hyperparameter (HP) transfer across model sizes, and no guarantee that all sub-networks are maximally updated at once. We present \Ours, an elastic transformer that organizes hidden dimensions into a dense core and successive shells, so that every hidden matrix is block lower triangular. One full-width forward pass contains every sub-network's exact hidden states as prefixes, so joint training keeps a fixed computation graph and costs about as much per step as training the widest sub-network alone. We further introduce \muE, an extension of maximal update parameterization (\mup) to \Ours and other elastic architectures. Its scaling rules provably keep all sub-networks of a supernet maximally updated simultaneously (\muI), and keep doing so when the supernet is widened or given more shells; sweeps confirm that HPs tuned on a small non-elastic proxy stay near-optimal for elastic families and larger supernets (\mbox{\muT}). A single \Ours run produces sub-networks that outperform MatFormer and fully elastic baselines at matched parameter counts, and approach separately trained models that together take several times the steps.
authors: Can Jin, Yan Kang, Yifan Gong, Chongjian Ge, Mingze Xu, Yuanjun Xiong, Dimitris N. Metaxas, Hongwu Peng
bullets: Organizes hidden dimensions into a dense core and successive shells with block lower-triangular matrices.
A single full-width forward pass contains the exact hidden states of all nested sub-networks, keeping computation fixed and scalable.
Introduces μE, extending maximal update parameterization so all sub-networks remain maximally updated simultaneously as the supernet scales.
Hyperparameters tuned on small non-elastic proxies transfer near-optimally to elastic families and larger supernets.
One training run outperforms MatFormer and fully elastic baselines at matched parameter counts, approaching separately trained models with several-times more total steps.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes an elastic transformer training method (ShellElastic) with hyperparameter transfer, which is a significant architectural and training advance for LLMs.
papers.title: ShellElastic: Scalable Elastic Pretraining with Simultaneous Maximal Updates and Hyperparameter Transfer
papers.tldr: ShellElastic enables one efficiently trained supernet to produce strong models across multiple inference budgets while transferring hyperparameters reliably across sizes.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought prompting enables reasoning in large language models but produces explanations that are difficult to verify, expensive to generate, and not always faithful. We introduce a Structural Chain-of-Thought framework where models generate executable computational graphs instead of free-form reasoning. The final answer is obtained by deterministically executing the graph. The model is trained using graph-based reinforcement learning that rewards structural validity, answer correctness, and node overlap with reference graphs. Experiments across five benchmarks and four model families show that our method consistently improves accuracy over supervised graph training and can reduce generation length by up to 5-6x compared with standard GRPO and chain-of-thought supervised training. Our faithfulness experiments reveal that models trained with our approach tend to rely on deriving their answers from the generated graphs rather than producing post-hoc rationalizations as usually in chain-of-thought reasoning.
authors: Petr Senatorov, Karim Vafin, Elena Tutubalina, Oleg Somov
bullets: Addresses unverifiable, costly, and potentially unfaithful chain-of-thought explanations.
Generates computational graphs whose final answers are obtained by deterministic execution.
Uses graph-based reinforcement learning to reward valid structure, correct answers, and overlap with reference graphs.

Across five benchmarks and four model families, improves accuracy over supervised graph training and cuts generation length by up to 5–6× versus standard GRPO and supervised chain-of-thought training.
Faithfulness tests suggest models derive answers from their graphs rather than merely producing post-hoc rationalizations.
papers.selection_reason: LLM reasoning method generating executable computational graphs, with large generation-length reductions.
papers.title: Structural Chain-of-Thought: Reasoning with Executable Computational Graphs
papers.tldr: Structural Chain-of-Thought replaces free-form reasoning with executable graphs that improve accuracy, reduce generation length, and make reasoning more verifiable.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer new opportunities for controllable text generation. However, their controllability, defined as the ability to satisfy task constraints while preserving their original capabilities, remains underexplored. DLMs' bidirectional attention allows control tokens to guide generation from arbitrary positions in the output sequence, but effective guidance depends on the compatibility between their content and placement. To this end, we propose AnchorDLM, a framework in which an anchor generator produces an anchor consisting of a short output fragment and its position for each query. The anchor is placed as control tokens at the specified position to initialize the output sequence of a frozen DLM and guide subsequent denoising. We train the anchor generator with reinforcement learning (RL) to jointly optimize anchor content and placement, using rewards computed from the DLM's generated outputs based on answer correctness and constraint satisfaction. Moreover, through the lens of discrete flow matching (DFM), we interpret anchor placement as helping to reshape the initial velocity field that guides generation. Experiments on code generation and mathematical reasoning across five DLM backbones show that AnchorDLM improves controllability and further yields gains in reasoning performance across diverse benchmarks.
authors: Feiyu Qu, Zheng Huang, Andrea Zanette
bullets: Addresses the challenge of satisfying task constraints without degrading DLM capabilities.
A learned anchor generator produces a short output fragment and its insertion position for each query.
The anchor initializes a frozen DLM, guiding subsequent bidirectional denoising.
Reinforcement learning optimizes anchor content and placement using answer correctness and constraint-satisfaction rewards.
Experiments across five DLM backbones show improvements in controllability and reasoning for code generation and mathematics.
papers.selection_reason: Diffusion language model controllability via RL-generated anchors is a meaningful contribution to language model generation and reasoning.
papers.title: Anchors Enhance Controllability and Reasoning of Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: AnchorDLM improves diffusion language models’ controllability and reasoning by learning what short anchor to insert and where to place it before generation.

papers.abstract: LLM multi-agent systems split work across agents that communicate through text. An agent summarizes its findings, another agent receives the text. This constrains communication to discrete tokens and costs redundant compute, limiting bandwidth and capabilities of multi-agent systems. Recent works demonstrate KV-cache transfer between LLMs but they either require the LLMs to be within the same family or cannot function across context, thus requiring the receiver to prefill text. We present SwaT (Swarm Telepathy), the first cross-family KV-cache transfer method that allows prefill-free communication in multi-family multi-agent systems. In an agent-to-agent communication setting, combining SwaT with recent advances in KV-cache compaction beats text-to-text communication in both accuracy and speed, with a mean of $40\%$ higher accuracy and a mean of $4\times$ faster wall-clock time. Experiments show SwaT achieves high performance on 17 benchmarks across 12 LLMs and 6 families. Additionally, given a sender Vision-Language Model (VLM), SwaT is able to transfer the vision capabilities to a text-only receiver LLM exceeding text-to-text communication despite SwaT being trained on text-only data. SwaT keeps both sender and receiver models frozen without fine-tuning and only requires $<50M$ tokens and $<1$ GPU-day to train.
authors: Abdulrahman Alabdulkareem, Irene Tenison, Yang Zhang, Yada Zhu, Boris Katz, Dan Gutfreund
bullets: Addresses the bandwidth, redundant-compute, and context limitations of text-only communication between agents.
Transfers KV caches across model families without requiring the receiver to prefill the communicated text.
Combined with KV-cache compaction, it reports 40% higher mean accuracy and 4× faster mean wall-clock time than text-to-text communication.
Evaluated across 17 benchmarks, 12 LLMs, and 6 model families.
Can transfer a sender VLM’s vision capabilities to a text-only receiver, while keeping both models frozen.
papers.selection_reason: Cross-family KV-cache transfer for prefill-free multi-agent LLM communication; directly targets KV-cache efficiency and LLM systems.
papers.title: Swarm Telepathy: Prefill-Free KV-Cache Transfer Across Families
papers.tldr: SwaT enables fast, prefill-free KV-cache communication between different LLM families, outperforming text-based agent communication in accuracy and speed.

papers.abstract: Argument structures represent how individual arguments interact within a discourse. However, leveraging these structures to infer meaningful knowledge remains challenging, as it requires a formal representation of how argumentative influence propagates across the structure. We propose Neuro-symbolic Argumentation Reasoning System (NARS) for performing persuasiveness detection directly from online discussions. The neural component employs retrieval-augmented iterative LLM reasoning to extract bipolar argument structures, while the symbolic component applies gradual argumentation semantics to propagate argumentative influence over the structure. Using the Webis-CMV-20 corpus, we construct CMV2BAS, a dataset of long, multi-threaded ChangeMyView discussions annotated with LLM-derived bipolar argument structures and labeled with delta events (view change vs.\ no change). We investigate whether gradual argumentation semantics can effectively detect persuasiveness, whether augmenting them with argument quality and graph-based centrality improves performance, and whether symbolic reasoning remains necessary in the presence of modern LLMs. NARS achieves F1=0.57 and AUC=0.56 under its best configuration, outperforming zero-shot Qwen3.6:27B and GPT-oss:20B. We identify support-dominant discussions and long argumentative chains as key failure modes limiting attack influence propagation. Our work demonstrates the feasibility of operationalizing formal gradual argumentation semantics over noisy real-world discourse for scalable macro-level persuasion analysis, while highlighting key challenges and directions for future research in neuro-symbolic argumentation reasoning. We release both CMV2BAS dataset and the NARS framework for public use.
authors: Siddharth Bhargava, Sara Tonelli, Patricia Mart\'in-Rodilla
bullets: Addresses the challenge of modeling how argumentative influence propagates through complex online discussions.
Uses retrieval-augmented iterative LLM reasoning to extract argument structures, then applies gradual argumentation semantics.
Introduces CMV2BAS, a dataset of long, multi-threaded discussions annotated with argument structures and view-change labels.
Best configuration reaches F1=0.57 and AUC=0.56, outperforming the reported zero-shot Qwen3.6:27B and GPT-oss:20B baselines.
Support-dominant discussions and long argumentative chains limit attack-influence propagation; the dataset and framework are publicly released.
papers.selection_reason: Utilizes LLMs and neuro-symbolic reasoning to analyze online discussions, relevant to LLM capabilities in reasoning and argumentation.
papers.title: Have You Been Convinced? A Neuro-symbolic Argumentation Reasoning Approach to Detecting Persuasiveness in ChangeMyView Discussions
papers.tldr: NARS combines LLM-extracted bipolar argument structures with symbolic argumentation semantics to detect view changes in ChangeMyView discussions.

papers.abstract: Larger sample budgets benefit from higher sampling temperatures in LLMs, but what temperature tuning optimizes and why it works remain poorly understood. We seek to answer these questions: we pose decoding as pass@$k$ maximization subject to two constraints that encode critical decoding failure modes: an entropy floor preventing diversity collapse, and a cross-entropy ceiling preventing implausibility. We prove that this maximization takes the form of a single closed-form conditional sampling rule, the \emph{tilted temperature} $q^\star \propto \bigl(p e^{\eta V}\bigr)^{1/T}$. Here, the tilt comes from a verifier potential $V$ that quantifies how likely a partial generation is to eventually pass. Ordinary temperature sampling, verifier-greedy decoding, and reward-tilted policies represent special cases. We further show that, under a natural rule for scaling the diversity budget with sample size $k$, the resulting optimal temperature increases with $k$, turning empirical choice into a theorem. The optimum still needs the unknown verifier potential, which we estimate using two design approaches. In the online setting, our J-EOS algorithm jointly tracks the two constraint multipliers and learns the verifier potential from binary pass/ fail feedback alone. In the offline setting, we show that when the model is calibrated, its log-probability tracks correctness up to an affine map. Under this condition, the tilt collapses into the exponent and the optimum reduces to ordinary temperature sampling. Calibrated Temperature Decoding (CTD) then fits one scalar offline and samples with zero additional inference-time overhead relative to temperature sampling. Building on these decision rules, we design a practical decoding algorithm for code generation and evaluate it alongside CTD on benchmarks including HumanEval and MBPP, showing improvements over standard and adaptive decoding baselines.
authors: Nikolaos Papagiannis, Ananth Grama, Wojciech Szpankowski
bullets: Frames decoding as maximizing pass@$k$ under an entropy floor and cross-entropy ceiling to preserve diversity and plausibility.
Derives the closed-form rule q⋆ ∝ (p e^{ηV})^{1/T}, where V estimates a partial generation’s likelihood of eventually passing.
Proves that the optimal temperature increases with sample budget k under a natural diversity-scaling rule.
Introduces J-EOS for online learning from binary pass/fail feedback and CTD, which fits one offline scalar with no extra inference-time overhead.
Reports improvements over standard and adaptive decoding baselines on code-generation benchmarks including HumanEval and MBPP.
papers.selection_reason: Optimal decoder rule for LLM sampling with verifier tilt; relevant to LLM decoding and temperature tuning.
papers.title: The Optimal Decoder is Tilted Temperature
papers.tldr: The paper derives a theoretically optimal decoding rule—verifier-informed tilted temperature sampling—and shows how to estimate it online or reduce it to ordinary temperature sampling when model probabilities are calibrated.

papers.abstract: Large language models can post-edit ASR by using linguistic context to compare N-best hypotheses and rewrite the transcript when needed, often improving WER without retraining the recognizer. However, prompt-only correction is brittle: it may over-edit when top-1 is correct and hallucinate when the reference is absent, and often needs very large models. We propose oracle-guided fine-tuning that turns N-best lists into supervision via three curated pools: corrections (reference in the list but not top-1) to teach selection, regularizers (top-1 correct) to discourage unnecessary rewrites, and hard negatives (reference absent) to suppress hallucination. Fine-tuning on this data provides more effective supervision than random subset fine-tuning for learning a hybrid select-or-rewrite policy, with the clearest gains from around 3B parameters on the proprietary dataset but less conclusive results on CommonVoice, a divergence suggesting that public read-speech text may overlap with LLM pretraining and mask genuine post-editing gains.
authors: Shiran Liu, Gaohui Xu, Sergio Burdisso, Thibault Ba\~neras-Roux, Shashi Kumar, Petr Motlicek
bullets: Prompt-only ASR post-editing can over-edit correct top-1 hypotheses, hallucinate when the reference is absent, and require very large models.
The method builds three supervision pools from N-best lists: corrections, regularizers, and hard negatives.
Fine-tuning learns a hybrid select-or-rewrite policy and is more effective than random subset fine-tuning.
The clearest gains appear with models around 3B parameters on a proprietary dataset, while CommonVoice results are less conclusive.
The CommonVoice divergence may reflect overlap between public read-speech text and LLM pretraining data.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a fine-tuning method for LLMs to perform post-editing on ASR N-best hypotheses, a relevant application of LLMs in language processing.
papers.title: Select or Rewrite: Oracle-Guided Fine-Tuning for Generative ASR Post-Editing from N-Best Hypotheses
papers.tldr: Oracle-guided fine-tuning teaches language models to select correct ASR hypotheses or rewrite them only when needed, reducing brittle corrections and hallucinations.

papers.abstract: Repetitive, degenerate generation is a persistent failure of LLM decoding, and the standard remedies (temperature, nucleus, and top-$k$ sampling) are static heuristics. By Kac's lemma and the AEP, a stationary source takes time exponential in its entropy to repeat a block. We therefore maximize the entropy of the sampling distributions under one cross-entropy budget that keeps the output plausible under the model. Offline, the solution is temperature sampling, with the inverse temperature as the budget's Lagrange multiplier. \emph{Our contribution is the online problem}: the conditionals $p_1, p_2, \dots$ are revealed one at a time, and the sampling distribution $q_t$ must be chosen causally from $p_1, \dots, p_t$ while the budget couples the entire horizon. The optimal temperature is thus a global shadow price that must be estimated from a prefix. We propose Entropic Online Sampling (EOS), which re-solves for the temperature on each prefix. We prove it loses $O(R\log n)$ entropy against the offline optimum while overshooting the budget by $O(R\log n)$, with $R$ an instance-dependent drift parameter. A budget-tightened variant is exactly feasible at the same rate. Conversely, every exactly feasible online algorithm must lose $\Omega(R)$, so EOS is optimal up to a $\log n$ factor. When the conditionals are drawn from a finite mixture, $R=\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n})$. Experiments confirm that EOS tracks the offline temperature and beats fixed-temperature sampling in entropy.
authors: Jin Sima, Nikolaos Papagiannis, Ananth Grama, Wojciech Szpankowski
bullets: Static temperature, nucleus, and top-k sampling can cause repetitive generation and do not adapt to changing token distributions.
The method maximizes sampling entropy subject to a horizon-wide cross-entropy budget, selecting temperature causally from the observed prefix.
EOS loses only O(R log n) entropy relative to the offline optimum and overshoots the budget by the same order; a tightened variant is exactly feasible.
No exactly feasible online method can avoid an Ω(R) entropy loss, making EOS optimal up to a logarithmic factor.
Experiments show EOS tracks the offline temperature and achieves higher entropy than fixed-temperature sampling.
papers.selection_reason: Online temperature sampling for LLM decoding with entropy guarantees; relevant to LLM generation methods.
papers.title: Information-Theoretic Foundations of Online Temperature Sampling
papers.tldr: Entropic Online Sampling (EOS) adaptively estimates a globally optimal temperature online, improving diversity while controlling plausibility and achieving near-optimal theoretical guarantees.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models combine specialized experts through an input-dependent routing mechanism, and their sparse variants underpin many modern large-scale systems. Yet the statistical cost of adaptive routing remains only partially understood. We study the estimation error of least-squares MoE estimators when both the experts and the gating network are Lipschitz in their parameters. We represent each MoE as a gate--expert pair in a Gated Hilbert Space, whose norm $\|\cdot\|_\Delta$ separates the contributions of routing and expert discrepancies. Using its empirical representation, we derive an oracle inequality with a fast rate of order $\tilde{\mathcal O}\big((Kd_{\mathrm{pr},e}+d_{\mathrm{pr},g})/n\big)$ for dense MoEs with $K$ experts. For sparse Top-$k$ and Top-$p$ routing, the selection map is discontinuous in the gating parameters. We handle this by partitioning the gating class according to the selection patterns it induces on the sample. The resulting bounds match the dense rate up to an additive routing cost governed by the Natarajan dimension of the selector. We show that such a routing-complexity condition cannot be dropped: Lipschitz continuity in the parameters alone does not suffice. For linear softmax gating, the routing cost is of the same order as the gating term. Finally, for linear experts, we establish a matching minimax lower bound of order $Kd_{\mathrm{pr},e}/n$, showing that the rates are optimal up to logarithmic factors.
authors: Sagar Ghosh, Huy Nguyen, Alessandro Rinaldo
bullets: Derives fast-rate oracle inequalities for least-squares MoE estimators with Lipschitz experts and gating networks.
Dense MoEs achieve rates of order Õ((K d_pr,e + d_pr,g)/n).
Sparse Top-k and Top-p routing incur an additional cost tied to the selector’s Natarajan dimension because routing is discontinuous.
Shows Lipschitz parameterization alone is insufficient to control sparse-routing complexity; linear softmax gating has routing cost comparable to its gating term.
For linear experts, a matching minimax lower bound establishes optimality up to logarithmic factors.
papers.selection_reason: Theoretical analysis of sparse MoE routing and estimation rates; directly relevant to MoE-based LLM architectures.
papers.title: Sparsity Saves Compute, Not Samples: Oracle Inequalities for Dense and Sparse Mixture of Experts
papers.tldr: Sparsity reduces MoE computation but does not eliminate the statistical cost of learning adaptive routing.

papers.abstract: Recent bidirectional encoders have been modernized with innovations from causal large language models (LLMs). However, the pretraining recipe itself remains inherited from small-scale conventions, leaving encoders underoptimized, with no single model performing competitively across both classification and retrieval tasks. In this work, we investigate how far encoder performance can be pushed by revisiting core design choices in training, revealing three key findings: (1) Encoders saturate on downstream tasks beyond a few trillion tokens, indicating that additional compute past this point does not help. (2) Across model sizes, lower masking ratios benefit classification while higher ones benefit retrieval, contradicting prior work suggesting larger ratios for larger models. (3) Distillation with pruning improves classification at low masking ratios but degrades retrieval at high ones. Guided by these findings, we present UltraBERT, a single encoder that assigns separate LM heads to low and high masking ratios within a batch and restricts the distillation objective to the low ratio. To our knowledge, UltraBERT is the first encoder to achieve state of the art on both classification and retrieval tasks, reaching 91.0 on GLUE and 47.7 on BEIR. Together, these results show how far encoder performance can be pushed and provide a principled basis for compute allocation, masking ratio design, and knowledge transfer in bidirectional models.
authors: Jungwoo Park, Taewhoo Lee, Jaewoo Kang
bullets: Encoder performance saturates after a few trillion pretraining tokens, limiting the value of additional compute.
Lower masking ratios favor classification, while higher ratios favor retrieval across model sizes.
Distillation with pruning helps classification at low masking ratios but harms retrieval at high ratios.
UltraBERT uses separate language-modeling heads for low and high masking ratios and applies distillation only to the low ratio.
It reports state-of-the-art results on both GLUE (91.0) and BEIR (47.7).
papers.selection_reason: Advances bidirectional encoder pretraining with masking-ratio-specific heads and distillation; relevant to language foundation model design.
papers.title: UltraBERT: Beyond the Limit of BERT Pre-Training
papers.tldr: UltraBERT improves bidirectional encoder pretraining by tailoring masking and distillation to jointly achieve strong classification and retrieval performance.

papers.abstract: WavePhaseNet introduced frequency-resolved semantic representations, QuantumPhaseNet introduced gauge-covariant phase connections, and ModularPhaseNet made a finite cyclic phase channel and its cycle holonomy computable in an ordinary Transformer. These constructions are complementary, yet they do not by themselves separate an observed collection of pairwise relations into a globally consistent direction, circulation around local compositions, and circulation that persists around a larger unfilled cycle. HodgePhaseNet addresses this separation by representing semantic transitions as an antisymmetric real-valued 1-cochain on a finite oriented simplicial complex. With vertex-edge incidence matrix $B_1$ and edge-face incidence matrix $B_2$, every such field has a unique orthogonal decomposition $\Omega = B_1^T\Phi + B_2\Psi + H$, where $B_1H=0$ and $B_2^TH=0$. The three component fields are unique even when their potentials are not. We give explicit projectors, a sparse implementation, integrability and gauge results, a verified numerical example, and a redesigned attention interface. The attention bias is defined on allowed ordered query-key pairs, remains consistent under arbitrary choices of edge orientation, and preserves a decoder's causal information boundary by constructing its complex from the visible prefix. Gauge invariance of the attention output is conditional on using invariant or appropriately compensated features. A simple difference of vertex embeddings has no coexact or harmonic component; a genuine relation encoder is therefore indispensable. Local circulation is not automatically contradiction, and harmonic flow is not automatically missing knowledge. These interpretations and any reduction in factual error require controlled empirical evaluation. This paper presents a mathematical and architectural proposal, not external natural-language performance results.
bullets: Represents semantic transitions as an antisymmetric real-valued 1-cochain on an oriented simplicial complex.
Uses incidence matrices to obtain a unique orthogonal decomposition into exact, coexact, and harmonic components.
Provides explicit projectors, sparse implementation, integrability and gauge results, and a verified numerical example.
Introduces an orientation-consistent attention bias built from the decoder’s visible prefix to preserve causal information boundaries.
Presents a mathematical and architectural proposal; factual-error reductions and other language-performance benefits remain unevaluated.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a Hodge-decomposition-based attention interface for Transformers, relevant to LLM architecture research.
papers.title: HodgePhaseNet: Discrete Hodge Decomposition of Semantic Flows in Transformer Attention
papers.tldr: HodgePhaseNet decomposes Transformer semantic relations into globally consistent flow, local circulation, and larger-cycle circulation using discrete Hodge theory.

papers.abstract: Bengali has no grammatical gender, but honorificity is obligatory: every third-person reference must choose ordinary or respectful register. English has no such signal, so the system must choose a level of deference that the source never specified. We use this property to measure how large language models (LLMs) allocate respect in English--Bengali translation. Our evaluation set contains 2{,}016 sentences across 72 occupations. Each appears in seven sentence frames under four pronoun conditions. Masculine and feminine versions differ by one word, forming counterfactual pairs. We report a single Honorific Bias Score (HBS) for each model on a 0--100 scale, covering both the gender and occupation axes. A lower score means that respect is allocated more evenly. For the occupation analysis, we compute each occupation's honorific rate across the seven no-pronoun sentence frames. The standard deviation of these 72 occupation-level rates ranges from 17.2 to 35.5 percentage points across models, showing substantial variation in how honorifics are allocated across occupations. Occupation is associated with 3.2\% to 51.5\% of the variance in register choice, compared with at most 1.2\% for gender. Gender effects are much smaller overall: only two of the nine models show significant directional gender gaps, and they favor opposite genders. HBS ranges from 19.9 to 70.1 across the nine models, showing substantial variation in how evenly the models allocate respect.
authors: Ajwad Abrar, Md Kamrul Hasan, Hasan Mahmud
bullets: Bengali requires choosing ordinary or respectful register, although English source text does not specify deference.
The benchmark contains 2,016 sentences spanning 72 occupations, seven frames, and four pronoun conditions, including one-word-difference gender counterfactuals.
It reports a 0–100 Honorific Bias Score (HBS), where lower scores indicate more even respect allocation.
Across nine models, HBS ranges from 19.9 to 70.1; occupation explains 3.2%–51.5% of register-choice variance, versus at most 1.2% for gender.
Occupation-level honorific-rate variability is substantial, while only two models show significant directional gender gaps, favoring opposite genders.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a counterfactual benchmark to measure honorific allocation bias in LLMs for Bengali/English translation.
papers.title: Who Receives Respect? A Counterfactual Benchmark for Honorific Allocation Bias in Bengali
papers.tldr: A counterfactual benchmark finds that Bengali honorific choices in English–Bengali translation vary substantially by occupation and model, while gender effects are generally small.

papers.abstract: Nheengatu (yrl), the Amazonian L\'ingua Geral, has 6--10 thousand speakers and is co-official in S\~ao Gabriel da Cachoeira (Brazil), yet remains poorly served by evaluated Portuguese--Nheengatu MT resources. We present the largest parallel corpus assembled for the language (14.5k Portuguese--Nheengatu pairs), anchored by the 2023 official translation of the Brazilian Federal Constitution; the first MT evaluation set built from transcribed spontaneous speech; and, to our knowledge, the first open-weight MT models dedicated to bidirectional Portuguese--Nheengatu translation. Three findings organize the paper. First, translation into Nheengatu on held-out constitutional articles plateaus on development data regardless of training length or model size, and much of the remaining error sits in conventional legal terms that the written sources do not attest consistently; a terminology success rate over a frozen lexicon shows that glossary mechanisms at training time and lexical constraints at decoding each raise term realization, the latter at a cost in repetitive output that chrF++ barely registers. Second, a corpus expansion that adds transcribed conversation raises speech chrF++ by 24--27 points while leaving written domains unchanged, a register gap that written-only benchmarks cannot see. Third, a larger NLLB model helps translation into Portuguese but not into Nheengatu on legal or speech text. For Portuguese-to-Nheengatu translation, our final systems reach 31.7--32.8 chrF++ on article-disjoint constitutional text, 64.1--64.5 on the near-domain set (62.1 after removing items with target-side content overlap), and 45.2--47.5 on speech.
authors: Fabr\'icio Carraro, Rodolfo Joel Zevallos, Rodrigo Gon\c{c}alves de Souza, Caio Henrique Faustino da Silva, John E. Ortega
bullets: Assembles a 14.5k-pair parallel corpus centered on the 2023 Portuguese translation of Brazil’s Federal Constitution, plus the first spontaneous-speech MT evaluation set.
Releases the first open-weight bidirectional Portuguese–Nheengatu MT models, with evaluations on constitutional, near-domain, and speech text.
Glossary training and constrained decoding improve realization of legal terminology, though decoding constraints increase repetitive output.
Adding transcribed conversation improves speech chrF++ by 24–27 points without improving written-domain performance, exposing a register gap.
Larger NLLB models help translation into Portuguese but not into Nheengatu; remaining errors include inconsistently attested legal terms.
papers.selection_reason: Presents an open MT system and corpus pipeline for the low-resource Amazonian language Nheengatu.
papers.title: The Constitution Speaks Nheengatu: An Open MT System and Reproducible Corpus Pipeline for the Amazonian L\'ingua Geral
papers.tldr: The paper introduces an open, reproducible Portuguese–Nheengatu MT resource and shows that conversational data and terminology controls substantially improve coverage of this under-resourced language.

papers.abstract: The predominance of English-language Web content creates an information-access barrier for speakers of low-resource languages such as Amharic. This paper presents the design, imple-mentation, and evaluation of a bidirectional Amharic-English cross-language question answering (CLQA) system that allows a user to formulate a natural-language question in either Amharic or English and retrieve an answer from documents written in the other language. The system integrates a statistical machine translation (SMT) component for query translation, a maximum-entropy named entity recognition (NER) component for Amharic text processing, semantic-based indexing, question analysis, passage retrieval, and answer extraction. A domain-diverse Amharic-English parallel corpus was used to train the SMT component, while monolingual cor-pora supported language modeling. Documents were normalized, tokenized, stemmed, indexed, and semantically enriched before retrieval. The original evaluation used precision and recall as the principal effectiveness measures. For Amharic-to-English retrieval, the system achieved 72% precision and 79% recall; for English-to-Amharic retrieval, it achieved 65% precision and 70% recall. These findings show that a modular translation-and-retrieval architecture can provide useful cross-language access even under low-resource conditions. This revised article preserves the original experimental claims while situating them in the context of subsequent multilingual transformer and Amharic QA research.
bullets: Addresses the information-access barrier caused by limited Amharic Web content.
Translates user questions with statistical machine translation and processes Amharic text using maximum-entropy NER.
Uses normalization, tokenization, stemming, semantic indexing, question analysis, passage retrieval, and answer extraction.
Reports 72% precision and 79% recall for Amharic-to-English retrieval, and 65% precision and 70% recall in the reverse direction.
Demonstrates useful cross-language QA under low-resource conditions; the article also contextualizes the work alongside later multilingual transformer research.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a cross-language QA system for low-resource languages (Amharic/English) using traditional NLP components.
papers.title: Amharic-English Cross-Language Question Answering Using Statistical Machine Translation, Named Entity Recognition, and Semantic Indexing
papers.tldr: A bidirectional Amharic–English question-answering system combines translation, named-entity recognition, semantic indexing, and retrieval to improve access to cross-language information for Amharic speakers.

papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed in applications that act on users' long-term behavior histories, from personal assistants to recommendation and advertising systems. These applications demand the user dimension of LLM intelligence: inferring a person's preferences, intent, and likely future actions from weeks to years of behavior data. Yet current models are trained on static text or synthetic data, neither of which captures how user behavior evolves over time. Real-world behavior records, already available at scale on content platforms and in personal-assistant agents, offer a natural supervisory signal. We propose user behavior as supervision and introduce Vela, a framework that converts real user behavior data into trainable tasks and trajectories. From the anonymized behavior records of 100,000 users, Vela generates 100,000 tasks across 91 real-world task templates; difficulty-based filtering and trajectory acceptance criteria retain approximately 75,000 tasks with selected training trajectories. Fine-tuning Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on these trajectories improves performance over the base model by up to 11.5 points on user-related tasks and by an average of 4 points on general benchmarks. Training on more user behavior data further improves user-related performance, and reinforcement learning after fine-tuning outperforms reinforcement learning from the base model by up to 7.7 points. These gains suggest that real-world user behavior is a scalable source of supervision for both user-centered capabilities and the broader intelligence of LLMs.
authors: Yang Xiao, Yusong Sun, Haoyi Wu, Wenyang Hui, Weiqiang Hang, Luqing Wang, Zejian Wang, Zirui Tu, Jingsheng Mao, Shaobo Hu, Yang Luo, Jiale Guo, Jin Zhang, Yudan Liu, Zhaokai Luo, Ren Huan, Yao Hu, Chengyue Jiang, Wenjie Li, Chuan Mu
bullets: Addresses the gap between static or synthetic training data and the evolving behavior needed to infer users’ preferences, intent, and future actions.
Converts anonymized behavior records from 100,000 users into 100,000 tasks across 91 templates, retaining approximately 75,000 tasks with selected trajectories.
Fine-tuning Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on Vela trajectories improves user-related task performance by up to 11.5 points and general benchmark performance by an average of 4 points.
Additional user behavior data provides further gains, while reinforcement learning after fine-tuning outperforms reinforcement learning from the base model by up to 7.7 points.
papers.selection_reason: Uses user behavior data as supervision to improve LLM intelligence, fitting LLM training.
papers.title: Vela: User Behavior as Supervision Sparks LLM Intelligence
papers.tldr: Vela turns real-world user behavior histories into training tasks and trajectories, improving LLM performance on user-centered and general capabilities.

papers.abstract: Large language models have advanced medical reasoning, but clinically grounded reasoning in traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) remains challenging because prescription decisions require integrating domain knowledge, syndrome differentiation, treatment principles, herbal prescription composition, and dosage determination. We develop a TCM language model family comprising models with 4 billion, 8 billion, and 14 billion parameters. The artificial intelligence contribution is a staged clinical alignment framework integrating large scale continued pretraining on TCM and clinical records, complementary reasoning supervision, and prescription-centered reinforcement learning (RL). We further formulate herbal prescription generation as a structured RL problem with prescription-level feedback, enabling direct optimization of clinical decision outputs beyond knowledge reproduction and generic instruction following. The engineering application is TCM clinical decision support, particularly herbal prescription recommendation. We evaluate the models on a public benchmark containing 25,620 expert-verified items across 13 TCM knowledge and clinical reasoning tasks and on a private retrospective dataset of 4,348 spleen and stomach disease prescription cases. The 14 billion parameter reinforcement aligned model achieves a prescription generation F1 of 37.0 on the public benchmark, compared with 32.3 for DeepSeek-R1 with 671 billion total parameters, and a herb-level F1 of 52.8 on the clinical dataset with improved dosage agreement. Reinforcement post-training consistently improves prescription recommendation across all scales, while physician-source analysis shows that expert heterogeneity affects reward stability. These findings demonstrate a scalable pathway from domain grounding and reasoning supervision to clinically oriented prescription decision support.
authors: Rui Hua, Yu Wei, Ziri Jin, Zhuo Sun, Kai Chang, Jianan Xia, Zixin Shu, Xiaodong Li, Dongmei Jia, Fei Dong, Runshun Zhang, Jian Yu, Hao Xu, Haibin Yu, Jiansheng Li, Baoyan Liu, Wenjia Wang, Xuezhong Zhou
bullets: Addresses the challenge of integrating TCM knowledge, syndrome differentiation, treatment principles, prescription composition, and dosage.
Uses continued pretraining on TCM and clinical records, reasoning supervision, and prescription-level reinforcement learning.
Includes 4B, 8B, and 14B-parameter models evaluated on public TCM tasks and a private spleen-and-stomach prescription dataset.
The 14B reinforcement-aligned model achieved 37.0 prescription-generation F1 on the public benchmark and 52.8 herb-level F1 on the clinical dataset, with improved dosage agreement.
Expert heterogeneity affected reward stability, indicating a limitation for prescription-focused reinforcement learning.
papers.selection_reason: Develops TCM-specific LLM family with clinical alignment and reinforcement learning, fitting LLM research.
papers.title: Lingdan-V2: Large language models for clinically grounded reasoning in traditional Chinese medicine
papers.tldr: Lingdan-V2 is a family of TCM language models trained with staged clinical alignment and prescription-focused reinforcement learning to support herbal prescription recommendation.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained mixture-of-experts (MoE) models commonly increase expert count by narrowing each expert, treating expert shape as a by-product of routing granularity. LatentMoE moves expert computation into a lower-dimensional space, exposing the input dimension and intermediate width of each expert as explicit design choices. We show that an expert's local Jacobian rank is jointly bounded by these two dimensions, and that balancing them maximizes the rank ceiling at fixed per-expert parameters. Controlled shape sweeps across model scales and routing granularities consistently favor near-square experts. We further use layerwise intrinsic dimension (ID) to guide capacity allocation across depth, co-varying the number and shape of experts while keeping per-layer parameter count, activated FLOPs, and communication volume constant. Compared with layer-homogeneous baselines, our ID-guided allocation achieves lower validation loss and stronger downstream performance. These results establish expert shape and layerwise allocation as practical design axes for MoEs.
authors: Yaoxiang Wang, Kai Zhang, Ruobing Xie, Lanrui Wang, Guoliang Zhao, Junhui Li, Jinsong Su
bullets: MoE expert geometry is made explicit by computing expert transformations in a lower-dimensional latent space.
An expert’s local Jacobian rank is bounded by its input dimension and intermediate width; balancing these dimensions maximizes the rank ceiling for a fixed parameter budget.
Controlled experiments across model scales and routing granularities favor near-square expert shapes.

Intrinsic-dimension-guided layerwise allocation, while holding per-layer parameters, activated FLOPs, and communication constant, improves validation loss and downstream performance over homogeneous baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Expert shape and layerwise capacity allocation in MoE LLMs; relevant to LLM architecture and efficiency.
papers.title: Shaping Latent Mixture-of-Experts: From Expert Geometry to Layerwise Capacity Allocation
papers.tldr: LatentMoE shows that expert shape and layerwise capacity allocation are key design choices for improving mixture-of-experts models.

papers.abstract: To enable large language models to generate outputs that align with human preferences, optimization algorithms based on the comparison between chosen and rejected output pairs have been developed and been proven effective. Some recent endeavors have utilized certain linguistically-derived assumptions about the preference pairs to guide the design of more precise optimization directions. However, human preferences are complex and hard to measure by simplistic criteria, and it is important to incorporate broader and more sophisticated insights about preferred vs. not-preferred language. In this study, we adopt a well-established psycholinguistic theory, Uniform Information Density, to develop a novel preference optimization algorithm, UIDPO. The basic assumption is that humans prefer to produce language in which information is uniformly distributed, because uniformity induces less cognitive processing effort. To implement this idea into the algorithm, we derive a compound metric for information uniformity by combining the global standard deviation and the local second-order difference, and integrate it to the objective of preference optimization. We compare UIDPO with SimPO, a previous state-of-the-art method, obtaining comparable and sometimes better performance on AlpacaEval2, ArenaHard, and MT-Bench. Additional linguistic analysis on complement clauses also shows that UIDPO can better reflect the tendencies of keeping information uniform in natural language than baselines. Our results show that the subtle human preference over the information rate in language is a helpful source for achieving better human alignment for LLMs. The code repository is published here: https://github.com/CLCS-SUSTech/UIDPO.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of simplistic linguistic assumptions in preference optimization, given the complexity of human preferences.
Combines global information-rate variability with local second-order differences into an information-uniformity metric.
Integrates this metric into a preference-optimization objective based on chosen and rejected outputs.
Achieves comparable and sometimes better performance than SimPO on AlpacaEval2, ArenaHard, and MT-Bench.
Linguistic analysis suggests UIDPO better captures human tendencies toward uniform information distribution, though its scope is tied to this psycholinguistic assumption.
papers.selection_reason: Develops a preference optimization algorithm (UIDPO) based on psycholinguistic theory to improve human alignment.
papers.title: Uniform Information Density-Based Preference Optimization
papers.tldr: UIDPO uses Uniform Information Density to improve LLM preference optimization by favoring outputs with more uniformly distributed information.

papers.abstract: Real-world business requests often leave key requirements unstated because frontline practitioners struggle to articulate rules they know from experience. Forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) must elicit these requirements through dialogue and iteratively optimize solutions until they meet customer acceptance criteria. Existing optimization benchmarks typically start from explicit objectives, while clarification benchmarks often introduce information gaps into existing tasks. We introduce FDE-Bench, the first benchmark built from real customer projects to evaluate agents on end-to-end delivery tasks that require interactive requirement clarification and iterative optimization. Its 49 cases span combinatorial optimization and machine learning. Clarification targets are distilled from discussions between frontline practitioners and FDEs. Agents elicit missing requirements from a simulated customer, and case-specific evaluators assess final artifacts against acceptance criteria using customer-accepted FDE solutions as quality references. Across 18 agent configurations, the highest mean delivery score is only 0.5510, compared with an FDE reference of 1.0. The highest delivery success rate (DSR), defined as the fraction of planned runs reaching this reference, is only 6.12%. These results show that reliable FDE-level end-to-end delivery remains out of reach for the evaluated agents on underspecified real-world business tasks. The benchmark project page is available at https://baidubce.github.io/FM-Agent/FDE-Bench/.
authors: Huaiming Li, Can Huang, Chufan Wu, Danyu Liu, Xiaomin Yuan, Qinze Li, Yui Lo, Wenhui Bai, Qianlong Wang, Zengle Ge, Xiyu Yan, Yuheng Cheng, Jinhui Ren, Guokai Chen, Jiaqun Liu, Haoran Li, Qianhui Liu, Annan Li, Jianmin Wu, Dawei Yin, Dou Shen
bullets: Introduces 49 real-world cases spanning combinatorial optimization and machine learning.
Agents interact with simulated customers to elicit missing requirements, then optimize final artifacts iteratively.
Case-specific evaluators compare outputs with customer-accepted FDE solutions.
Across 18 configurations, the best mean delivery score is 0.5510 versus an FDE reference of 1.0.
The best delivery success rate is 6.12%, indicating that reliable FDE-level delivery remains challenging.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces FDE-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating agents on end-to-end delivery tasks involving requirement clarification and iterative optimization, relevant to LLM agent capabilities.
papers.title: FDE-Bench: Evaluating End-to-End Delivery from Underspecified Real-World Business Requests
papers.tldr: FDE-Bench evaluates whether agents can clarify underspecified business requests and iteratively deliver solutions that meet customer acceptance criteria.

papers.abstract: In Chinese content governance, large language models are increasingly used to identify toxic and discriminatory expressions, yet both task operationalization and ironic expression can alter bias measurement readings. We conducted a preregistered multi-task behavioral audit of multiple Chinese large language models. In the content classification experiment, the core panel's classification error rate rose from 10.9% in the formal register to 23.5% in the yinyang (an echoic-irony register) version, a risk difference of +12.7 percentage points. (95% CI [+9.7, +15.7]). Inter-rater agreement was lower in the yinyang register (majority-vote kappa = 0.299), so the increase contains a component of label uncertainty propagation, but the direction of increase was consistent under both adjudicated and majority-vote reference standards. Explicit irony-aware prompts reduced the intervention panel's error rate by 9.6 percentage points. We operationalized the 29 shared proposition anchors into three task forms: social consensus estimation (Form A), high-stakes decision (Form B), and controlled association rating (Form C); independent manipulation checks found that all 58 A-C comparison units received unanimous agreement, whereas the low A-B convergence was confirmed by calibrated majority adjudication (87.8% supporting the minority judgment); on the irony-probe materials, the interactions of B and C relative to A were +0.577 and +1.121, respectively. Thus, when evaluating large language models for Chinese content governance, the effect of task operationalization on bias readings is an empirical question that requires data to answer, and safety evaluation should incorporate the ironic register as a test condition.
bullets: Classification errors increased from 10.9% in formal Chinese to 23.5% in the yinyang (echoic-irony) register, a +12.7-point risk difference.
Lower agreement in the ironic condition indicates some label-uncertainty propagation, but the increase persisted under both reference standards.
Explicit irony-aware prompts reduced intervention-panel errors by 9.6 percentage points.
Across 29 proposition anchors, task forms for consensus estimation, high-stakes decisions, and association ratings produced differing bias readings, especially for irony probes.
The findings support including ironic registers and multiple task forms in Chinese content-governance evaluations.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates bias in Chinese LLMs across different registers and task operationalizations, relevant to safety and evaluation.
papers.title: Evaluating Bias in Chinese Large Language Models across Tasks and Registers: Task Operationalization Effects and Irony Classification Risks
papers.tldr: A preregistered audit finds that Chinese LLM bias measurements worsen under ironic language and vary substantially with task operationalization.

papers.abstract: Semantic relations organise word senses and are fundamental to lexical semantics. In order to evaluate semantic relation knowledge of large language models (LLMs), we propose a challenging task in which an LLM predicts the relation between two glosses (definitions of senses) presented in two different orders. The predictions for the two orders are evaluated for consistency with the symmetry or asymmetry of semantic relations. Our task is designed for both monolingual and cross-lingual evaluation, allowing us to examine whether relation knowledge remains accessible when the same senses are verbalised through glosses in different languages. We construct a dataset of 3,069 sense pairs, with each sense verbalised in English, Greek, Romanian, Turkish, and Japanese. Experiments with 17 LLMs in zero-shot and five-shot settings reveal generally poor performance. In each setting, only eight LLMs achieve a macro-averaged F1 score significantly above a random baseline, and only one (zero-shot) and two (five-shot) significantly outperform a neural baseline. In particular, LLMs often fail to generate bidirectionally consistent predictions for hypernymy and to make correct predictions for holonymy in either direction. Our results suggest limitations in current LLMs' semantic relation knowledge, both in identifying relations and in respecting asymmetry.
authors: Zhihan Cao, Adam Nohejl, Hitomi Yanaka
bullets: Evaluates whether LLMs identify semantic relations consistently when gloss pairs are presented in both orders.
Supports monolingual and cross-lingual testing across English, Greek, Romanian, Turkish, and Japanese.
Uses 3,069 sense pairs to evaluate 17 LLMs in zero-shot and five-shot settings.
Most models perform poorly; only a minority exceed random or neural baselines significantly.
Models particularly struggle with bidirectional hypernymy consistency and holonymy prediction.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates semantic relation knowledge in LLMs through bidirectional prediction, highlighting limitations in handling asymmetry.
papers.title: Evaluating Semantic Relation Knowledge through Bidirectional Relation Prediction from Gloss Pairs
papers.tldr: A bidirectional gloss-pair task reveals that current LLMs have limited and inconsistent knowledge of semantic relations, especially across relation directions.

papers.abstract: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) genuinely grasp the truth conditions of plural descriptions, or do they force every sentence into true or false? We investigate the Homogeneity Gap, a semantic phenomenon where a plural definite (e.g., the kids laughed) and its negation (the kids didn't laugh) are both neither true nor false when only some of the kids laughed, whereas their quantified counterparts (all, not all) remain strictly bivalent. We introduce HomogeneityNLI, a diagnostic dataset of 1,000 minimal-pair items crossing determiner, polarity, and group composition across ten logical conditions. Evaluating seven open-weight models, we uncover a pervasive Bivalence Bias: models assign plural definites their homogeneous truth conditions, reading the kids as all of them and the kids didn't as none of them, yet collapse the truth-value gap into falsity. In the zero-shot setting, no model recognizes the gap for both polarities in more than 15% of scenarios, and negated definites are judged False in 84% of cases. Explicit linguistic rules, chain-of-thought, and enumeration prompts produce unstable, model-specific effects that often entrench the bias. Taken together, our findings indicate that current open-weight LLMs have acquired the truth conditions of plural predication but not its trivalent logic.
authors: Duaa Nakshbandi, Zhiyu An, Yiping Li, Sachin Giri, Wan Du
bullets: The study tests whether LLMs distinguish plural definites from quantified expressions under partial group membership.
It introduces HomogeneityNLI, a 1,000-item diagnostic dataset spanning determiners, polarity, and ten logical conditions.
Across seven open-weight models, a pervasive Bivalence Bias treats “the kids” as all and “the kids didn’t” as none.
In zero-shot evaluation, no model identifies the gap for both polarities in over 15% of scenarios; negated definites are judged false in 84%.
Rules, chain-of-thought, and enumeration prompts have unstable effects and often reinforce the bias.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates logical reasoning capabilities (truth conditions) in LLMs, introducing a diagnostic dataset for trivalent logic.
papers.title: Neither True nor False: Do LLMs Represent Truth-Value Gaps in Plural Predication?
papers.tldr: Open-weight LLMs largely understand homogeneous plural predication but fail to represent its truth-value gap, forcing mixed cases into false judgments.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance in mathematical and logical reasoning, yet they still suffer from the curse of complexity and struggle as problem difficulty increases with the number of constraint interactions and the size of the search space. In contrast, satisfiability solvers such as Z3 provide scalable and verifiable reasoning through constraint solving under formal theories, but lack the flexibility to interpret natural-language problem descriptions. In this work, we propose SAT-RL, a reinforcement-learning (RL) framework that trains LLMs to interact with symbolic solvers through multi-turn tool execution. SAT-RL leverages synthetic data generation with verifiable solutions, supervised warm-up on solver-augmented traces, and solver-grounded reinforcement learning with tool-aware rewards. Experiments show that SAT-RL substantially improves symbolic reasoning with tools on both in-domain and out-of-domain logic tasks. Our code is available on https://github.com/sunjia72/SAT-RL.
bullets: Targets LLM difficulty with growing constraint interactions and search spaces.
Uses multi-turn tool execution to connect natural-language reasoning with solvers such as Z3.
Combines synthetic verifiable data, supervised warm-up on solver traces, and solver-grounded RL.
Reports substantial gains on both in-domain and out-of-domain logic tasks.
Scope: focuses on symbolic reasoning with external solver tools.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a reinforcement learning framework for LLMs to interact with symbolic solvers (Z3) for logical reasoning, addressing the complexity of LLMs through tool-augmented execution.
papers.title: SAT-RL: Training Language Models for Logical Reasoning with Symbolic Solvers
papers.tldr: SAT-RL trains language models to solve increasingly complex logic problems by combining reinforcement learning with symbolic solver interaction.

papers.abstract: Scientific research increasingly depends on curating experimental data from literature. Scientific data curation requires verifying exact experimental conditions (e.g., specific assays, clinical outcomes, and data availability) across long, heterogeneous files, which is a highly time-consuming process. Existing benchmarks evaluate only broad relevance on short queries, failing to capture this complexity. We introduce SciCurateBench, a benchmark of 200 expert-annotated papers from major life-science journals that challenges systems to verify conjunctive biological experimental criteria from raw, unprocessed scientific literature. We show that plain LLMs and popular reasoning, tool-using, and feedback-based agents all struggle with this task.
