To study what makes the task tractable, we further propose LangPoli, an integrative system in which a policy agent generates natural language action guidelines that actor agents convert into executable tools. LangPoli showed strong performance on both Paper Classification (83.16% F1 vs. 58.22% for its base LLM) and Structured Information Retrieval, and also improves re-ranking on the public benchmarks of LitSearch, BEIR, and TREC. We further explore curriculum transfer, a method that distills generalizable strategies from solved tasks to accelerate the solving of related problems. We hope this work facilitates research in truly practical scientific AI assistance. The anonymized pre-release can be found from https://anonymous.4open. science/r/scicuratebench-D885/.
authors: Minuk Ma, Kaiyun Guo, Jiarui Ding
bullets: Presents 200 expert-annotated papers from major life-science journals for evaluating experimental-data curation.
Targets verification of specific assays, clinical outcomes, and data availability across long, heterogeneous documents.
Finds that plain LLMs and existing reasoning, tool-using, and feedback-based agents struggle with the task.
LangPoli achieves 83.16% F1 on Paper Classification, compared with 58.22% for its base LLM, and improves performance on LitSearch, BEIR, and TREC re-ranking.
Explores curriculum transfer to reuse strategies from solved tasks for related curation problems.
papers.selection_reason: Focuses on LLM agents (LangPoli) for scientific data curation, addressing agent design and test-time learning strategies.
papers.title: SciCurateBench: Curating Experimental Data from Heterogeneous Scientific Literature with Verbal-Action Agents
papers.tldr: SciCurateBench evaluates whether AI systems can verify detailed, conjunctive experimental criteria in messy scientific literature, and introduces LangPoli, which uses natural-language action policies to improve curation and retrieval.

papers.abstract: Hybrid reasoning models such as the Qwen3 series switch between a THINK mode and a NO-THINK mode through a few chat-template tokens. A popular recipe trains such models with reinforcement learning in NO-THINK mode and reports improved reasoning performance. We provide evidence that much of this gain can be explained by thinking leakage: the gain comes largely from partially reactivating the reasoning abilities of the original model's THINK mode instead of learning enhanced reasoning behavior. We train Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B with GRPO in NO-THINK mode. As accuracy improves, responses become longer and more reflective, are increasingly judged by the original model to resemble its own thinking, and the model's internal activations shift toward its THINK mode. We then investigate at the level of weights, activations, and attention heads: scaling the RL update further elicits THINK-mode behavior and approaches THINK-mode accuracy but does not exceed it; in Qwen3-8B, replacing a low-dimensional THINK-related activation subspace of the RL-trained model with its original-model value removes most of the RL gain, and the reverse exchange transfers a considerable fraction of the gain to the original model; and the RL-induced shift passes through the attention heads that read the empty think block. We further identify a possible mechanism in the GRPO training signal: responses favored by the advantage-weighted update are more THINK-like, and a gradient step computed from this signal moves the model toward its THINK state. Thus, gains in NO-THINK mode can largely reflect reactivation of reasoning abilities already present in the original model.
authors: Wenxuan Zhu, Shuming Liu, Bang An, Aznaur Aliev, Bing Li, Yibo Yang, Bernard Ghanem
bullets: The study examines Qwen3 models trained with GRPO in NO-THINK mode.
Improved accuracy coincides with longer, more reflective, THINK-like responses and activations.
Stronger RL shifts the models toward THINK-mode behavior and accuracy but does not surpass the original THINK mode.
Activation-subspace and attention-head interventions transfer or remove much of the RL gain, linking it to THINK-related components.
The GRPO signal may favor THINK-like responses, causing updates toward the model’s existing THINK state.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes RL-induced thinking leakage in Qwen3 hybrid LLMs via weights, activations, and attention heads; directly relevant to LLM training and reasoning.
papers.title: The Thinking Leakage in Reinforcement Learning for LLMs
papers.tldr: Reinforcement learning gains in Qwen3’s NO-THINK mode largely come from reactivating existing THINK-mode reasoning rather than learning substantially stronger reasoning.

papers.abstract: Looped transformers reuse the same layer multiple times, allowing inference compute to be adjusted without changing the model. Recent adaptive-depth methods train the model across multiple loop depths from the beginning of training. We introduce fixed-first training, which varies model depth only during a short final phase of training. At 200M parameters, training a model of fixed-depth 2 for the first 67% of the run reduces modeled training compute by 45% while keeping mean negative log-likelihood (NLL) across inference depths within 0.5% of training across depths throughout. At 1B parameters, training initially at depth 4 reduces modeled compute by 31% to 37% and wall-clock time by 32% to 39%, while keeping final NLL within 0.8% and downstream differences within the observed seed variation. These results show that training over the full range of depths can be reserved for a short finishing phase with only small changes in performance.
authors: Andrei Piterbarg, Sean McLeish, Dhruv Pai, Benjamin Keigwin
bullets: Trains at one fixed loop depth for most of training, then varies depth only near the end.
At 200M parameters, it reduces modeled training compute by 45% while keeping mean NLL within 0.5% of full multi-depth training.
At 1B parameters, it reduces modeled compute by 31–37% and wall-clock time by 32–39%.
Final NLL remains within 0.8%, and downstream differences stay within observed seed variation.
Scope: results concern looped transformers and the tested 200M- and 1B-parameter settings.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive-depth training for looped transformer language models is an architectural and training-efficiency contribution relevant to LLM foundation models.
papers.title: Adaptive-Depth Is a Finishing Stage
papers.tldr: Fixed-first training lets looped transformers defer multi-depth training to a short finishing phase, substantially reducing training cost with little performance loss.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer parallel sampling for faster generation than autoregressive models, an increasingly important advantage as inference becomes a dominant computational workload. However, DLMs degrade quickly with fewer sampling steps, process the full sequence at every step, and require many passes over the dataset to reach good quality. We introduce Next-Concept Modeling (NCM), a two-stage, coarse-to-fine framework: a multiscale residual VQ-VAE encodes text into a hierarchy of discrete codes, and a transformer generates one level at a time, predicting all codes within a level in parallel. At matched parameter scales, NCM achieves better generative perplexity than the strongest DLM baseline on LM1B while running $21\times$ faster. On OpenWebText, NCM is competitive with the strongest DLM while running $10\times$ faster; on XSum, it matches the strongest DLM's ROUGE-L while being $31\times$ faster. On the reasoning task of Sudoku, NCM outperforms autoregressive and diffusion baselines across all difficulty levels, using fewer function evaluations. On the reasoning task of Sudoku, NCM outperforms autoregressive and diffusion baselines across all difficulty levels, using fewer function evaluations.
authors: Hermann Kumbong, Ishan S. Khare, Iddah Mlauzi, Andrew Woen, Charles Ding, E. Kelly Buchanan, Simran Arora, Azalia Mirhoseini, Christopher R\'e
bullets: Addresses diffusion language models’ slow sampling, full-sequence processing, and training inefficiency at few sampling steps.
Uses a multiscale residual VQ-VAE to encode text into hierarchical discrete codes.
A transformer predicts all codes within each hierarchy level in parallel.
Reports faster generation than diffusion baselines across LM1B, OpenWebText, and XSum while maintaining or improving quality.
Outperforms autoregressive and diffusion baselines on Sudoku reasoning across difficulty levels with fewer function evaluations.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a parallel coarse-to-fine text generation architecture, relevant to language model architectural advances.
papers.title: Next-Concept Modeling: Fast, Parallel Coarse-to-Fine Text Generation
papers.tldr: Next-Concept Modeling enables fast, parallel coarse-to-fine text generation by predicting hierarchical discrete representations level by level.

papers.abstract: Large language models typically support different inference budgets through separate model sizes or fixed compute configurations. In multi-turn interactions, however, compute demand can vary substantially across turns. Using a high-compute model for every turn wastes computation, while routing among independent models may require rebuilding model-specific history states after switches. We therefore ask whether a single shared model can support multiple compute budgets that can be flexibly assigned across turns. We introduce Multi-Ratio ConceptMoE, which jointly supports token-to-concept compression ratios of 2, 4, and 8 (CR2/CR4/CR8) within a shared backbone. Lightweight full-token modules reduce compression-independent cost, ratio-specific boundary routers support distinct compression levels, and cross-ratio training enables mixed-ratio processing within the same context. Across PTBench and SFTBench, the three fixed modes outperform their compute-matched MoE baselines in all 6 comparisons while remaining competitive with independently trained fixed-ratio specialists. On CodeChat and CoSQL, mixed-ratio inference improves the accuracy--compute trade-off, outperforming the Large MoE by 5.87 and 2.68 percentage points while reducing FLOPs by 41.1% and 12.3%, respectively. Under the same turn-wise budget schedule, Multi-Ratio ConceptMoE further reduces FLOPs by 78.4% and 46.9% relative to routing among independent models. These results demonstrate that a single shared model can provide multiple compute budgets for flexible compute allocation across turns.
authors: Yiyang Fu, Zihao Huang, Dongchen Han, Shukai Gong, Zhen Dong, Qiyang Min, Daquan Zhou
bullets: Addresses variable per-turn compute needs without using separate models or rebuilding history states when switching.
Uses lightweight full-token modules, ratio-specific boundary routers, and cross-ratio training in a shared backbone.
Fixed-ratio modes outperform compute-matched MoE baselines in all six reported comparisons and remain competitive with specialists.
Mixed-ratio inference improves the accuracy–compute trade-off on CodeChat and CoSQL, with lower FLOPs than the Large MoE.
Under matched turn-wise budgets, it reduces FLOPs versus routing among independent models, demonstrating flexible shared-model inference.
papers.selection_reason: Single shared MoE model supporting multiple compute budgets via token-to-concept compression, fitting efficient AI and LLM architecture topics.
papers.title: One Model, Multiple Compute Budgets: Multi-Ratio ConceptMoE for Flexible Compute Across Turns
papers.tldr: Multi-Ratio ConceptMoE enables one shared model to flexibly use 2×, 4×, or 8× token-to-concept compression across conversation turns, improving accuracy–compute trade-offs while avoiding model-switching overhead.

papers.abstract: Looped transformers reuse one shared block across many recurrent steps, so depth becomes a quantity that can be spent at runtime rather than a stack of distinct layers. Those extra steps help only if a write made on one recurrent step is still readable on later ones, and that depends on the linear map applied to the residual between recurrent steps. We show that whether the loop learns to track state is a geometric question about the form of this map, and we propose blockwise conformal injections: the residual splits into coordinate-aligned groups and rotates inside each one, so every group has its own timescale while the geometry stays exact within it. Our experiments show a performance increase on a demanding form of state tracking - last-token accuracy when the rest of the prefix is already correct - and on language modelling, where a signal written earlier has to be retrieved at the end of the sequence.
authors: Alexey Zemtsov, Albina Klepach, Vadim Lomshakov, Andrei Polubarov, Nikita Lyubaykin, Alexander Derevyagin, Vladislav Kurenkov, Alexander Nikulin
bullets: Looped transformers reuse one block, making runtime depth dependent on how well state persists between steps.
State tracking depends on the geometry of the residual map used between recurrent iterations.
The proposed blockwise conformal injections split residuals into coordinate-aligned groups and rotate each group independently.
This gives each group a distinct timescale while preserving exact within-group geometry.
Experiments show gains in last-token state-tracking accuracy and language modeling with delayed signal retrieval.
papers.selection_reason: Looped transformer architecture for state tracking, relevant to LLM architectural advances.
papers.title: Rotate the Loop: Blockwise Conformality for Looped Transformers
papers.tldr: Blockwise conformal residual rotations improve state tracking and language modeling in looped transformers by preserving readable information across recurrent steps.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards improves mathematical reasoning when a final answer can be checked, but a correct answer does not certify the derivation behind it, and proof problems offer no answer to check. Replacing the check with a reasoning model as an in-loop verifier faces a fundamental obstacle: the policy must already produce occasional correct attempts for any reward to exist, which it may never do at olympiad level. We instead move verification and repair out of the training loop and into offline data generation with SPLICE, a workflow in which a second model, given only a reference solution, edits a reasoning model's traces as they are generated: it verifies progress, truncates a failed trace at its last verified step, and splices in an adaptively strengthened hint until progress resumes. The resulting dataset includes repaired examples whose sampled unaided trajectory failed, with failed continuations removed and progress repeatedly checked against the reference solution. A model finetuned on SPLICE traces outperforms the same model distilled from the reasoning model's unedited traces on AIME and, under a grading protocol validated against human grades, on olympiad proofs. The trained model's own traces show a corresponding behavioral signature: at difficult points it announces a branch in the style of the spliced hints and takes riskier steps, with predictive entropy rising there and just after, a pattern absent from the model trained on unedited traces.
authors: Hamed Mahdavi (Pennsylvania State University), Pouria Mahdavinia (Pennsylvania State University), Majid Farhadi (Google), Vasant Honavar (Pennsylvania State University)
bullets: RL with verifiable rewards struggles when correct solutions are too rare or proofs lack checkable final answers.
SPLICE performs verification and repair offline using a reference solution rather than relying on in-loop rewards.
A second model truncates failed traces at the last verified step and inserts increasingly strong hints until progress resumes.
Finetuning on these repaired traces outperforms training on unedited traces on AIME and human-validated olympiad-proof grading.
The resulting model exhibits hint-like branching and increased predictive entropy at difficult reasoning points.
papers.selection_reason: Offline data generation with spliced hints to improve reasoning model training; relevant to LLM post-training.
papers.title: Splicing Hints into Reasoning Traces: Learning from Demonstrator Failures
papers.tldr: SPLICE trains mathematical reasoning models from repaired failure traces, improving performance on answer-checked problems and olympiad proofs.

papers.abstract: Post-training large language models (LLMs) on two-player zero-sum games provides a verifiable reward, and the gains have been shown to transfer to general reasoning. Existing pipelines, however, rely on a handful of hand-written games and on advantage estimators tied to them, so both the supply of games and the advantage estimate on a large corpus limit scaling. We present GameSmith, which scales both. An LLM synthesises games inside templates whose reward, observation, and hidden-information code is fixed. Each game is verified by seed-paired replay and by an independent re-implementation of its specification, then expanded into encoding, rule, and size variants, giving 26 new games in 29 families and 336 verified variants from the three SPIRAL templates. The model is distilled from the self-play of a larger teacher (Qwen3-32B) on these games and then trained by self-play reinforcement learning with CRAB, an advantage estimator that credits each decision against a shrinkage estimate of the expected return of its position and is defined on every variant. On Qwen3-4B-Base, distillation raises the 13-benchmark mean pass@1 from 45.5 to 62.5, above the three SPIRAL games at the same budget, and self-play with CRAB reaches 64.9. The ordering holds across models, and transfer grows with the number of game families.
authors: Weixian Waylon Li, Jiaxin Zhang, Han Zhou, Chengzu Li, Ke Wang, Fengxiang He, Yiwen Guo
bullets: Addresses the limited supply of hand-written games and game-specific advantage estimators in LLM self-play.
Synthesises games within fixed reward, observation, and hidden-information templates, then verifies and expands them into variants.
Produces 26 new games across 29 families and 336 verified variants from three templates.
Introduces CRAB, which estimates advantages for decisions across all game variants using shrinkage-based position returns.
On Qwen3-4B-Base, distillation improves mean pass@1 from 45.5 to 62.5, while CRAB self-play reaches 64.9; transfer increases with game-family count.
papers.selection_reason: Scaling LLM post-training via synthesized zero-sum games and self-play; relevant to language foundation model training.
papers.title: GameSmith: Scaling Zero-Sum Self-Play with Synthesised Games
papers.tldr: GameSmith scales zero-sum self-play by automatically generating and verifying diverse games and using a game-agnostic advantage estimator, improving LLM reasoning transfer.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have emerged as an effective paradigm for scaling large language models, yet their massive parameter footprint poses severe memory challenges for deployment. Existing compression methods typically treat expert pruning and merging as disjoint operations and rely on greedy heuristics, often leading to irreversible information loss or representational pollution. In this paper, we propose PRIME, a unified optimization framework for MoE compression via adaptive PRunIng and MErging. PRIME casts the discrete prune-merge assignment step as a global Integer Linear Programming over a frequency-weighted surrogate objective, jointly selecting pruning and merging decisions while accounting for expert usage. We motivate the frequency-aware objective through an error-bound analysis under fixed representative assignments, and show that the formulation favors high-frequency experts as centroids, promoting routing stability. Extensive experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B and Qwen3.5-122B-A10B demonstrate that PRIME achieves strong accuracy retention across knowledge, coding, math, and long-context tasks, while serving benchmarks of merged models quantify the memory and throughput benefits of expert compression in vLLM.
authors: Shanfeng Huang, Rongqian Zhang, Zhou Fang, Song Xiao, Hai Du
bullets: Addresses memory challenges from the large parameter footprint of MoE models.
Jointly optimizes prune-and-merge assignments with global Integer Linear Programming rather than separate greedy decisions.
Uses expert-usage frequency in a surrogate objective to favor frequently used experts as merge representatives and improve routing stability.
Experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B and Qwen3.5-122B-A10B show strong accuracy retention across knowledge, coding, math, and long-context tasks.
Serving benchmarks with vLLM quantify memory and throughput benefits after compression.
papers.selection_reason: MoE LLM compression via expert pruning and merging for memory and throughput, relevant to efficient AI and large language models.
papers.title: PRIME: Frequency-Aware Unified Pruning and Merging for MoE Compression
papers.tldr: PRIME unifies frequency-aware expert pruning and merging for MoE compression, preserving accuracy while reducing deployment costs.

papers.abstract: Power-law learning curves are often treated as fixed properties of a model and its data, although learning-rate and batch-size schedules can change the observed loss. We study this dependence in noisy online SGD with linear random features. Conditional on the representation, an exact Volterra equation separates two response components: a forcing term that propagates unresolved target error and a memory kernel that propagates stochastic-error injections. We prove that either component follows a power law if and only if its cumulative weighted spectral mass has the corresponding low-spectrum scaling; individual eigenvalues and target coefficients need not obey coordinatewise power laws. Under a joint schedule, intrinsic time $T_t=\sum_{s<t}η_s$ controls optimization progress, while $r_t=B_t/η_t$ controls noise injection. Their interaction yields sharp conditions under which a schedule preserves, changes, or destroys the clean power law, together with a memory ceiling on noise reduction. The power-law random-feature model realizes this mechanism in $3+3(+2)$ propagation regimes with phase-dependent compute rates. Controlled nanoGPT experiments show that (1) learning-rate and batch-size schedules with matched $B/η$ paths are nearly equivalent in intrinsic time, (2) a forcing-memory surrogate accurately predicts loss across schedules, and (3) its fitted exponents across real-world datasets identify the regime of LLMs in $3+3(+2)$ map. The source code for reproducing our experiments is available on https://github.com/yichenblue/spectra-to-schedules-in-pretraining.
bullets: An exact Volterra equation separates loss dynamics into unresolved-target forcing and stochastic-error memory components.
Power laws arise from low-spectrum scaling of cumulative weighted spectral mass, not necessarily from individual eigenvalues or target coefficients.
Intrinsic time $T_t=\sum_{s<t}η_s$ governs optimization progress, while $r_t=B_t/η_t$ governs noise injection.
Joint schedules can preserve, alter, or destroy clean power laws; noise reduction is limited by a memory ceiling.
Experiments find near-equivalence for schedules with matched $B/η$ paths and show that a forcing-memory surrogate predicts loss and maps real-world datasets to the proposed regimes.
papers.selection_reason: Provides a theoretical analysis of scaling laws in LLM pre-training, linking spectral properties to optimization dynamics and schedule regimes.
papers.title: From Spectra to Joint Schedules in LLM Pre-training: 3+3(+2) Scaling-Law Regimes
papers.tldr: Learning-rate and batch-size schedules reshape observed power-law scaling through intrinsic optimization time and the noise-injection ratio, yielding a unified $3+3(+2)$ regime map validated in controlled nanoGPT experiments.

papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to simulate response distributions in social surveys. Prior work has achieved accurate population-level simulation for individual questions. Real questionnaires, however, ask each respondent a sequence of related questions. A simulated respondent should show coherent preferences across the whole questionnaire, not merely accurate distributions for isolated items. Existing single-item methods cannot accurately reproduce how the same person answers a complete survey. We propose FullRespondent-LLM (FR-LLM), which fine-tunes two specialized LLMs: a marginal model for each item's response distribution and a respondent-level autoregressive model for dependencies across answers. Marginal-Constrained Joint Projection (MCJP) then projects the autoregressive joint distribution onto the set satisfying the item-level marginals learned by the first model. This yields complete questionnaires with realistic cross-item relationships while retaining strong item-level accuracy. On two real-world social survey datasets, FR-LLM more accurately reproduces multi-question response patterns, maintains competitive single-item accuracy, and generalizes better to unseen populations and questions. In a small commercial-survey dataset, we use simulated responses to make pricing and stocking decisions; FR-LLM achieves the highest realized profit.
bullets: Problem: Single-question simulators fail to capture how one respondent answers related questions across a questionnaire.
Method: Fine-tunes a marginal model for item-level distributions and an autoregressive respondent model for cross-answer dependencies.
MCJP projects the joint respondent distribution to satisfy the learned item-level marginals.
Across two real-world social survey datasets, FR-LLM better reproduces multi-question patterns while retaining competitive single-item accuracy.
It generalizes better to unseen populations and questions, and achieved the highest realized profit in a small commercial-survey application.
papers.selection_reason: Demonstrates an application of LLMs to simulate coherent survey responses, showcasing complex reasoning capabilities beyond single-item generation.
papers.title: Simulating Respondents, Not Single Questions: Coherent Survey Generation with Large Language Models
papers.tldr: FR-LLM generates complete, internally coherent survey responses while preserving accurate answer distributions for individual questions.

papers.abstract: How many dimensions does a language model's computation actually use? The question is ill-posed until one names a functional. Task-weighted charts make it well-posed: low-dimensional coordinate systems fit against a chosen functional of the representation, under the functional's own metric, turning distillation into plain least squares. Across six models from three families, spanning 70m to 7B parameters, next-token prediction needs 70--90% of the residual stream's width to stay within 5% of intact perplexity, a width consumed by the rare tail of language, and the variance profile predicts none of it: two directions carry 90% of GPT-2's activation variance and almost none of its function. Dimension is per-functional: the model's own uncertainty reads from six coordinates where the full predictive distribution needs hundreds; and it grows with depth. The dissociation is exploitable: when only a few dimensions can be kept, charts trained under the functional's metric preserve the model's predictions better than variance-based or optimal linear compression.
bullets: Next-token prediction requires 70–90% of residual-stream width to remain within 5% of intact perplexity across six models.
The needed dimensions are driven by the rare tail of language, not dominant activation-variance directions.
Two directions explain 90% of GPT-2’s activation variance but capture almost none of its predictive function.
Dimensionality depends on the functional: model uncertainty uses six coordinates, while the full predictive distribution needs hundreds, and dimensionality grows with depth.
Functional-metric charts preserve predictions better than variance-based or optimal linear compression when dimensions are limited.
papers.selection_reason: Task-weighted low-dimensional charts compress LM representations while preserving function, relevant to efficient AI and LLM analysis.
papers.title: Function Lives Where Variance Doesn't: Task-Weighted Charts of a Language Model's Computation
papers.tldr: Task-weighted charts reveal that a language model’s functional computation is often high-dimensional and poorly predicted by activation variance.

papers.abstract: Linear RNNs with input-dependent Householder-product transitions (DeltaNet/DeltaProduct-class) can provably represent hard state-tracking automata, yet trained models fail to length-generalize -- a gap recent work attributes to optimization, without a causal account. We give one, in a pre-registered, within-architecture causal ablation: the same model with one term deleted -- the additive input injection $b_t = W_b e_t$. With $b_t$, models fit length 32 and collapse out-of-distribution on parity, $S_4$, $A_5$, and non-solvable $S_5$ word problems (0.20 at position 512 on $S_5$). Without it -- input acting only through the orthogonal transitions -- the same architecture learns the exact automaton: median accuracy 1.00 at 16x the training length, at every width admitted by a representation law we state and test: the minimal number of Householder factors per token equals the maximal reflection length of the task's generators in the format-pinned representation (parity 1, $S_4$ 3, $A_5$ and $S_5$ 4); below it, nothing fits. The contrast with DeltaProduct's $S_4$/$A_5$ at $n_h{=}2$ (group-element classification, $SO(3)$ realization) shows the law is representation-relative: task format is a hidden variable in state-tracking benchmarks. Two pre-registered arms locate the mechanism. (i) Initialized at a verified-exact solution with $W_b{=}0$, Adam grows the additive path and pulls the model off the exact solution; $-b$ controls stay at 1.00. (ii) Our registered prediction that the fit routes through $b_t$ fired its kill criterion: all 49 fitting seeds retain in-domain fit under $W_b{:=}0$ -- and at law-minimal width, zeroing $W_b$ at inference restores exact generalization (parity 5/5, $S_5$ 5/5, $S_4$ 4/5, $A_5$ 4/5). The additive pathway is parasitic: it destabilizes, then conceals, a correctly learned automaton. All 202 runs pre-registered; all numbers regenerate from artifacts.
bullets: Adding $b_t=W_b e_t$ lets models fit short sequences but causes out-of-distribution collapse on parity and permutation-group tasks.
Removing the additive pathway yields exact automaton behavior, with median accuracy 1.00 at 16× the training length.
Generalization requires a task- and representation-dependent number of Householder factors: 1 for parity, 3 for $S_4$, and 4 for $A_5$/$S_5$.
Mechanistic ablations show Adam grows the additive path away from exact solutions, while zeroing it preserves or restores exact generalization.
The findings indicate that benchmark task format is a hidden variable and that the additive pathway can conceal a correctly learned automaton.
papers.selection_reason: Causal analysis of Householder linear RNNs informs recurrent LLM architecture design and length generalization.
papers.title: The Automaton Underneath: The Additive Input Pathway Is a Parasitic Attractor for State Tracking in Householder Linear RNN
papers.tldr: A causal ablation shows that additive input injection destabilizes Householder linear RNNs, while transition-only input enables exact automaton learning and long-range generalization.

papers.abstract: This paper provides a self-contained proof of the rank of the pathlifting Jacobian of a DAG ReLU network by performing an induction on the network's number of hidden nodes. In fact, the induction is elementary, and the key recipe is to consider the skeleton matrix of the network, a sparse matrix encoding the network paths, and transform the representation of one of its hidden neurons into an output node. The proof relies on intermediate propositions which link the pathlifting, its Jacobian, the network parameters, and its skeleton matrix, which, on top of permitting to conclude on the rank of the pathlifting Jacobian, also provide a way to compute it without backpropagation and whose computation cost is super efficient in practice compare to usual backpropagation. The paper is provided with a Python module that implements the different propositions of the paper for feed forward networks and is used to experimentally quantifies the computational gain of computing the pathlifting Jacobian with the proposed theory.
bullets: Motivation: determine the rank of the pathlifting Jacobian and make its computation practical.
Method: use the network’s sparse skeleton matrix and induct on the number of hidden nodes, replacing a hidden neuron with an output node.
Theoretical links connect the pathlifting, its Jacobian, network parameters, and skeleton matrix.
The resulting propositions enable Jacobian-rank computation without backpropagation.
A Python module implements the theory for feed-forward networks and experimentally evaluates its computational efficiency.
papers.selection_reason: Provides a theoretical and computational framework for analyzing the rank of Jacobians in ReLU networks, contributing to the understanding of neural network architectures.
papers.title: Rank and computation of the pathlifting Jacobian of a DAG ReLU network
papers.tldr: A self-contained inductive theory characterizes and efficiently computes the rank of the pathlifting Jacobian for DAG ReLU networks without backpropagation.

papers.abstract: We propose a compact NISQ-compatible quantum transformer architecture for synthetic QNLP sequence modelling. The model preserves the autoregressive next-token interface of a classical transformer, but replaces attention and feed-forward sublayers with variational quantum encoder blocks, connector circuits, decoder blocks and a direct two-qubit measurement readout. Token contexts are angle-encoded into small quantum registers, processed by parallel variational heads and encoder integration circuits and conditioned through decoder ancillae to produce a distribution over a four-token vocabulary. We evaluate several architecture variants on deterministic and lexicographic grammar-generation tasks against a compact classical transformer baseline. The quantum models are trainable end-to-end and learn nontrivial grammar structure, including perfect deterministic generation in individual runs and high lexicographic validity in the strongest variant. The classical baseline remains more accurate and stable and the quantum models are sensitive to initialization. The contribution is therefore not a claim of quantum advantage, but a concrete architecture and evaluation of transformer-inspired QNLP sequence modelling under near-term quantum constraints.
bullets: Targets synthetic quantum natural language processing (QNLP) sequence modelling under near-term hardware constraints.
Replaces classical attention and feed-forward layers with variational quantum encoder, connector, and decoder circuits.
Uses angle-encoded token contexts, parallel variational heads, decoder ancillae, and two-qubit measurement to predict a four-token vocabulary.
Evaluated on deterministic and lexicographic grammar-generation tasks; some runs achieved perfect deterministic generation and the strongest variant showed high lexicographic validity.
Quantum models were sensitive to initialization, and the classical baseline was more accurate and stable; no quantum advantage is claimed.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a variational quantum transformer architecture for sequence modeling, contributing to the architecture of language foundation models.
papers.title: Variational Quantum Transformer Architecture for Synthetic Language Generation
papers.tldr: A compact NISQ-compatible variational quantum transformer can learn nontrivial synthetic grammar generation, but remains less accurate and stable than a classical transformer baseline.

papers.abstract: An ideal (language) model must continually update its knowledge. Existing work largely focuses on making these updates efficient after training. We investigate how the organization of time-varying knowledge during pre-training shapes the efficiency of subsequent updates. Models trained on chronologically ordered knowledge specialize in the most recently encountered knowledge; we call them specialists. In contrast, models trained on the same knowledge in randomly shuffled order perform well across all represented time periods; we call them generalists. Surprisingly, specialists require far fewer update steps than generalists to acquire new knowledge. To explain this advantage, we derive a law from first principles that relates update cost to the model's optimization dynamics and that closely predicts empirical results. Guided by these findings, we design a strategy for organizing pre-training data that preserves stable historical knowledge while enabling efficient updates to current knowledge. We also show that the benefits of temporal knowledge organization extend to real-world pre-trained models and existing knowledge update tools, and generalize to other knowledge orderings. Project page: https://horizon-lab.org/specialist/
bullets: Chronological training makes models specialize in recently encountered knowledge, whereas shuffled training produces broader generalists.
Specialists need far fewer update steps to learn new knowledge than generalists.
The paper derives a first-principles law linking update cost to optimization dynamics and predicting empirical behavior.
A data-ordering strategy preserves stable historical knowledge while facilitating updates to current knowledge.
The findings extend to real-world pre-trained models, existing knowledge-editing tools, and other knowledge orderings.
papers.selection_reason: Studies how pre-training knowledge organization affects update efficiency, relevant to continual learning and LLM training.
papers.title: Specialists Learn Faster: Knowledge Organization in Pre-training Shapes Knowledge Update Efficiency
papers.tldr: Organizing pre-training knowledge chronologically creates specialists that update substantially more efficiently than generalists while preserving historical knowledge.

papers.abstract: Continuous diffusion language models (CDLMs) promise to bring the benefits of continuous flow modelling to language, including accelerated sampling and controllable generation. The field has grown rapidly, and the capabilities of CDLMs have begun to rival those of discrete diffusion. Yet, unlike for continuous modalities such as images or videos, our grasp of the levers that matter when training CDLMs remains limited. In this work, we focus on two of these levers, namely self-conditioning and embedding geometry, and shed light on some of the mechanisms behind them, which in turn suggest cheaper and more effective designs. We begin by showing that self-conditioning corrects a train/inference mismatch by exposing the model to inference-like states that are otherwise rare during training. These gains can be recovered without an extra forward pass by a two-level interpolant, coined $\mathrm{DoubleCat}$, which improves TinyGSM accuracy more than threefold. Self-conditioning also aids in recognising tokens dominated by large-norm Gaussians$\unicode{x2013}$an issue known as token identifiability. To address it directly, we introduce discrete reveals to $\mathrm{DoubleCat}$, yielding $\mathrm{SemiCat}$, which achieves discrete diffusion-level performance on TinyGSM, reaching $49.94\%$ with standard training hyperparameters and a tuned sampler. At the $1.7$B scale, $\mathrm{SemiCat}$ outperforms discrete diffusion on four of six likelihood-based evaluations, and surpasses one-hot flows on unconditional generation. On embedded spaces, we find that cross-entropy drives embeddings towards a geometry whose decoding error rate closely matches the one-hot one. We briefly explore a range of further options, such as hybrid corruption processes and noise schedules, including asynchronous ones. We believe this exploration can help the community better understand and advance the design space of CDLMs.
bullets: Studies self-conditioning and embedding geometry as important but underexplored CDLM design levers.
Explains self-conditioning as correcting a train–inference mismatch and helping identify tokens obscured by large-norm Gaussian noise.
Introduces DoubleCat, a two-level interpolant that recovers self-conditioning gains without an extra forward pass.
Extends DoubleCat with discrete reveals in SemiCat, reaching discrete diffusion-level TinyGSM performance and outperforming discrete diffusion on several likelihood evaluations at 1.7B parameters.
Also examines hybrid corruption processes and noise schedules, including asynchronous schedules.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes design choices for continuous diffusion language models, directly relevant to LLM architectures.
papers.title: On the Design Space of Continuous Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: This work analyzes key design choices in continuous diffusion language models and introduces cheaper interpolants that improve token identifiability and achieve competitive performance with discrete diffusion.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have taken the world by storm. Their ability to communicate with us in our own language, and to reason about our world, has made them a favorite tool for writing, answering questions, and much more. Their answers already influence our decisions and our actions. What would happen if LLMs themselves could act in the world directly? What would happen if LLMs could interact with each other? Agentic LLMs combine the power of large language models with the ability to act in the real world. In this book we will discuss how agentic LLMs work, how they act, how they interact, and what this means for us, as users.
bullets: Motivated by LLMs’ growing influence on human decisions and actions.
Explores how LLMs can act directly in the world and interact with one another.
Covers the workings, behaviors, and interactions of agentic LLMs.
Discusses implications for people who use these systems.
papers.selection_reason: Book-level treatment of agentic LLMs, relevant to large language model research and agent architectures.
papers.title: Agentic Large Language Models
papers.tldr: Agentic LLMs extend language models from generating responses to acting in and interacting with the real world.

papers.abstract: Designing tool-integrated reasoning agent systems for complex chemical tasks remains a fundamental challenge. Although recent chemical agents have demonstrated promising performance through the integration of external tools, they are still built on the autoregressive paradigm, which is inherently constrained by causal attention and left-to-right generation. As a result, they often struggle with bidirectional molecular understanding, global coordinated tool planning and multi-source evidence integration. To address this challenge, we introduce ChemDiffAgent, the first masked diffusion language agent for tool-integrated chemical reasoning. It reformulates chemical reasoning as iterative denoising over interleaved reasoning and tool-use trajectories, enabling tool-use decisions to be jointly determined under full-trajectory context and thereby better aligning the agent's decision boundary with its knowledge boundary. We further analyze how this paradigm benefits agentic reasoning through harder infilling subproblems during training and flexible arbitrary-order decoding during inference. Then we develop a two-stage post-training framework, comprising agentic supervised fine-tuning and variance-reduced preference optimization, to enhance tool-use and reasoning capabilities. We also construct a comprehensive benchmark covering six chemistry tasks across both single-turn and multi-turn tool-use scenarios. Under matched budgets and evaluation, ChemDiffAgent consistently outperforms autoregressive agents, achieving an overall improvement of approximately 20%. Notably, our 8B model achieves performance comparable to, in some cases surpassing, significantly larger frontier models, such as GPT 5.5 and Claude Opus 4.7. Code is available at https://github.com/bilemond/ChemDiffAgent.
bullets: Targets limitations of left-to-right agents in bidirectional molecular understanding, global tool planning, and multi-source evidence integration.
Reformulates chemical reasoning as iterative denoising over interleaved reasoning and tool-use trajectories, with arbitrary-order decoding at inference.
Uses two-stage post-training: agentic supervised fine-tuning followed by variance-reduced preference optimization.
Evaluated on six chemistry tasks spanning single-turn and multi-turn tool use, with approximately 20% overall improvement under matched budgets.
The abstract reports that the 8B model performs comparably to or sometimes better than substantially larger frontier models.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a masked diffusion language agent for tool-integrated reasoning, relevant to LLM architecture and reasoning research.
papers.title: Masked Diffusion Language Agents for Tool-Integrated Chemical Reasoning
papers.tldr: ChemDiffAgent uses masked diffusion to jointly plan reasoning and tool use with full-trajectory context, improving chemical agent performance over autoregressive approaches.

papers.abstract: Training long-horizon language model agents requires assigning credit to intermediate decisions from sparse terminal feedback. Within a finite group of sibling rollouts, useful action comparisons depend on their context, evidence for both alternatives, and how that evidence enters learning. We propose Matched-Context Group Policy Optimization (MCGPO), a procedure for constructing weighted action preferences from already collected trajectories. MCGPO defines comparison contexts with pre-action state summaries and observed rubric progress, annotated by task rules. Two-action support selects among ordered exact and coarse matching rules. Fixed folds separate candidate decisions from the terminal outcomes used to orient their preferences, and support-dependent evidence weights scale an auxiliary pairwise objective alongside shared GraphGPO task learning. MCGPO reuses rollout data and each response's original history, preserving critic-free training. Across six environment-backbone settings with three training seeds each, MCGPO improves mean success over matched GraphGPO: by 0.47-1.46 percentage points on ALFWorld and WebShop with Qwen2.5-1.5B and 7B, and by 3.96 and 5.16 points on WebShop with Qwen3-4B and 8B. The ALFWorld gains build on baseline success above 92%, where remaining headroom is limited. Integrated success improves in three of four Qwen2.5 settings. Three-seed factorial controls support opposite-fold evidence and evidence weighting; joint state-rubric matching achieves the highest mean in all four representation-control settings.
authors: Chenxu Zhang, Yaorui Shi, Wenlong Zhang, Jianchao Tan, Zihan Wang, Yiming Cheng
bullets: Addresses credit assignment when agents receive feedback only at the end of long tasks.
Builds weighted two-action comparisons using pre-action state, rubric progress, and exact or coarse context matching.
Uses fixed folds to prevent candidate decisions from being oriented by the same terminal outcomes, while retaining critic-free training.
Improves mean success over matched GraphGPO across six environment–backbone settings, with gains ranging from 0.47 to 5.16 percentage points.
Joint state–rubric matching performs best across the tested representation controls; gains are smaller where baseline success already exceeds 92%.
papers.selection_reason: Group policy optimization for LLM agent training fits LLM reasoning and decision-making methods under language foundation models.
papers.title: Matched-Context Group Policy Optimization for LLM Agent Training
papers.tldr: MCGPO improves long-horizon LLM agent training by learning context-matched action preferences from existing rollouts and sparse terminal feedback.

papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation promises to replace the sparse outcome signal of verifiable-reward RL with dense token-level credit: a teacher conditioned on the reference solution scores the student's own rollout, and the resulting distributional shift is distilled back into the policy. We investigate whether this scoring signal actually contains corrective credit. Using gold error spans in student rollouts, we test the two signals consumed by self-distillation objectives, the full-distribution KL and the token log-ratio, for two properties: whether they localize errors and whether they push probability away from erroneous student tokens. They exhibit neither of these properties nor can they reliably distinguish correct from incorrect rollouts within the same problem. We argue that this failure is structural: locating an error in a reasoning trace is itself a search problem, while a scoring teacher is never explicitly asked to perform that search. The same model, with the same privileged information, localizes errors substantially better when allowed to generate a critique. This forms the motivation for \emph{critique-conditioned self-distillation}: first generate a critique of the current rollout, then condition the scoring teacher on that critique. The resulting signal localizes errors, is corrective within error spans, and shifts probability toward tokens that initiate backtracking such as ``Wait'', ``But'', and ``Actually''. We further show that the critique is useful both at test time, where resuming a wrong rollout with the critique in context converts math problems the model cannot solve by sampling, and in cold-start GRPO, where it provides an advantage signal on prompts for which verifiable rewards alone provide none.
authors: Mayug Maniparambil, Ayush Rai, Ekansh Verma, Noel E. O'Connor, Fergal Reid
bullets: Full-distribution KL and token log-ratio signals neither localize errors nor reliably distinguish correct from incorrect rollouts.
The failure is structural: error localization requires search, which a teacher asked only to score does not perform.
Critique-conditioned self-distillation generates a critique before scoring the rollout, producing corrective signals within error spans.
The critique shifts probability toward backtracking tokens such as “Wait,” “But,” and “Actually.”
At test time and in cold-start GRPO, critiques help recover from wrong rollouts and provide useful advantages when verifiable rewards are absent.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces critique-conditioned self-distillation for reasoning LLMs, improving training signals and test-time reasoning; relevant to LLM training and reasoning.
papers.title: A Privileged Teacher That Only Scores Cannot Search: Critique-Conditioned On-Policy Self-Distillation for Reasoning
papers.tldr: Scoring-only privileged teachers fail to find and correct reasoning errors, while generating a critique first enables effective error localization and corrective self-distillation.

papers.abstract: Large language models struggle to reliably identify and correct errors in their own reasoning. Unlike prior training-based approaches that fine-tune an LLM to generate revisions or feedback, we learn where to intervene in failed rollouts and determine how to redirect them. To choose where to intervene, we train a 130K-parameter MLP head on a frozen encoder using only final-answer correctness. For redirection, we find that under a fixed generation budget, the tested inline injections fail to reliably redirect reasoning, whereas presenting the same instruction in a new user turn changes the model's course. The resulting correction framework, UPTURN (User-Prompt TURN injection at a learned position), requires no LLM fine-tuning: it retains a selected prefix, injects an instruction as a new user turn, and regenerates the suffix. Across four reasoners and six math benchmarks, UPTURN improves average accuracy in every setting over a 32-rollout baseline. It outperforms self-correction and reflection-token injection baselines under matched correction budgets, transfers across reasoners and to GPQA-Diamond without retraining, and complements GRPO and self-correction methods.
authors: Jiwon Jeon, Myungsik Cho, Jeonghye Kim, Youngchul Sung
bullets: Trains a small MLP intervention head on a frozen encoder using only final-answer correctness.
Retains the reasoning prefix, inserts an instruction as a new user turn, and regenerates the remainder.
Inline instruction injections did not reliably redirect reasoning under a fixed generation budget.
Improves accuracy across four reasoners and six math benchmarks over a 32-rollout baseline.
Transfers to GPQA-Diamond without retraining and complements GRPO and self-correction methods.
papers.selection_reason: Learned intervention-position redirection for LLM self-correction fits LLM reasoning methods under language foundation models.
papers.title: Inject a Turn, Not a Token: Learning Where to Redirect LLM Reasoning for Self-Correction
papers.tldr: UPTURN learns where to interrupt failed LLM reasoning and redirects it with a new user turn, improving self-correction without fine-tuning the LLM.

papers.abstract: Curriculum learning typically organizes training samples from easy to hard. In GRPO, medium-difficulty samples are attractive for online selection because they are more likely to yield informative group-relative learning signals, and prioritizing them can improve training efficiency. However, it remains unclear whether persistently selecting such samples also leads to the strongest final model performance, or whether training can benefit from progressing toward harder samples. Meanwhile, sample difficulty changes as the policy evolves, so fixed difficulty estimates can become misaligned with the current policy. We therefore re-estimate sample difficulty under the current policy and, inspired by the easy-to-hard principle of curriculum learning, design and evaluate a staged curriculum that progressively shifts the active difficulty band toward harder samples. Experiments on GSM8K show that persistent medium-difficulty selection does not achieve the strongest observed performance. Across three random seeds, progressing to a moderately harder difficulty band improves test accuracy to $0.6591 \pm 0.0077$, compared with $0.6449 \pm 0.0024$ for the fixed-medium curriculum. However, further progression to a harder difficulty band reduces accuracy to $0.6405 \pm 0.0053$. These results show that staged difficulty progression can outperform persistent medium-difficulty selection, but its benefit is non-monotonic. Effective GRPO curricula can therefore benefit from progressing beyond medium difficulty, while avoiding excessive progression toward overly difficult samples.}
authors: Ronghan Li, Fei Chen, Mingyu Lu
bullets: Persistent medium-difficulty selection is efficient for generating informative group-relative signals but is not optimal for final performance.
The method re-estimates sample difficulty under the evolving policy and progressively shifts the active difficulty band.
On GSM8K, the moderately harder curriculum reached 0.6591 ± 0.0077 test accuracy versus 0.6449 ± 0.0024 for fixed-medium selection.
Further progression to a harder band reduced accuracy to 0.6405 ± 0.0053 across three random seeds.
The benefit of difficulty progression is non-monotonic, indicating a need to avoid overly difficult samples.
papers.selection_reason: Studies curriculum difficulty progression in GRPO for LLM reasoning training, directly relevant to LLM training methodology.
papers.title: A Step Harder, Not a Step Too Far: The Benefits and Limits of Curriculum Difficulty Progression in GRPO
papers.tldr: A staged GRPO curriculum that gradually shifts from medium to moderately harder samples improves performance, but progressing too far toward hard samples hurts accuracy.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are rapidly improving on long-horizon scientific and olympiad tasks. Recent systems have produced a Lean-formalized resolution of the Navier--Stokes problem and autonomous solutions to four open questions in the Erd\H{o}s Conjectures database. Yet neither system releases both its underlying model and complete inference stack. More broadly, a single agent session remains brittle on difficult problems: early errors can propagate, missing domain knowledge can stall progress, and apparent success can mask a misinterpretation or weakening of the original task. We introduce HOA (Humanize Olympiads Agent), an open, flow-level framework that coordinates multiple agent sessions through three complementary feedback channels. First, an independent reviewer evaluates each candidate and provides actionable feedback. Second, a structured wiki supplies task-specific knowledge that may be missing or unreliable in model pretraining. Third, a verifier checks generated Lean proofs against trusted challenge statements. With GPT-5.6 Sol, HOA achieves perfect scores on the IMO, IPhO, and IOI 2026, near-full marks on the IChO 2026 problem set, and solves all 672 problems (100%) on PutnamBench. On the Lean-Eval leaderboard, HOA ranks first, solving 251 of 304 problems (82.6%). We further evaluate HOA with open models. Using Kimi-K3, HOA achieves full scores on the IMO, IPhO, and IOI, and a gold-level score of 97.1% on the IChO. These results closely match the closed-source GPT-5.6 Sol + /Goal baseline on the IMO and IPhO, while exceeding it on the IChO and IOI, demonstrating that systematic feedback can help bridge substantial differences in base-model capability.
authors: Zhengyang Zhang, Jing Xiong, Hongzhou Lin, Juihui Chung, Zijian Zhang, Song Han, Sihao Liu, Ligeng Zhu
bullets: Targets brittleness in single-session agents, including error propagation, missing knowledge, and task misinterpretation.
Uses three feedback channels: actionable independent review, a task-specific structured wiki, and trusted Lean-proof verification.
With GPT-5.6 Sol, reports perfect scores on IMO, IPhO, and IOI 2026, near-full IChO marks, and 672/672 PutnamBench problems.
Ranks first on Lean-Eval, solving 251/304 problems (82.6%).
With Kimi-K3, achieves full IMO, IPhO, and IOI scores and 97.1% on IChO, suggesting feedback can compensate for weaker base models.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a multi-session LLM-agent workflow for long-horizon reasoning and formal verification, relevant to LLM-based reasoning systems.
papers.title: Humanize Olympiad Agents: A Multi-Session Workflow for Olympiad Problem Solving with Solve, Review, Wiki, Verify
papers.tldr: HOA improves difficult olympiad solving by coordinating independent solving, review, knowledge retrieval, and Lean verification across multiple agent sessions.

papers.abstract: Attention Residuals (AttnRes) enables content-dependent retrieval over network depth, which can be viewed as single-stream softmax attention along the depth axis. Inspired by the success of multi-head attention along the sequence axis, we introduce Multi-Stream Attention Residuals (MSAR), an extension of AttnRes that generalizes this mechanism to multi-head depth attention, yielding substantial performance gains with minimal additional overhead. MSAR draws stream diversity from sequence context through multi-scale causal convolutions, allowing different heads to retrieve historical representations through distinct contextual views while preserving the integrity of the hidden representation. The retrieved streams are combined through lightweight adaptive mixing to generate the single-stream layer input. By retaining single-stream sources and expanding them on demand, MSAR supports multi-stream computation without requiring persistent multi-stream storage or communication. Across all 12 downstream benchmarks at the 18B and 28B MoE scales, MSAR consistently outperforms prior residual variants, including standard residual connections, manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC), and AttnRes. Scaling-law experiments yield an iso-loss compute speedup of $1.58\times$ over the standard residual baseline, compared with $1.35\times$ for AttnRes and $1.30\times$ for mHC. These results make MSAR a promising residual architecture for large-scale pre-training.
authors: Xiaohan Qin, Xiangdong Zhang, Tuo Dai, Sunan Zou, Huaijin Wu, Yebin Yang, Zhuo Xia, Lin Yao, Yuliang Liu, Junchi Yan
bullets: Addresses the limited single-stream retrieval of prior residual architectures across network depth.
Uses multi-scale causal convolutions to give attention heads distinct sequence-context views.
Adaptively mixes retrieved streams into a single layer input while avoiding persistent multi-stream storage or communication.
Outperforms standard residuals, mHC, and AttnRes across 12 downstream benchmarks at 18B and 28B MoE scales.
Achieves a reported 1.58× iso-loss compute speedup over standard residuals, versus 1.35× for AttnRes and 1.30× for mHC.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a novel residual architecture for large-scale LLM pretraining, directly relevant to LLM architecture advances.
papers.title: Multi-Stream Attention Residuals
papers.tldr: MSAR extends Attention Residuals with multi-head depth attention, improving large-scale language-model performance with little extra overhead.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) is a key driver for Large Reasoning Models, but it is vulnerable to "zero-reward collapse", a training failure where a sudden increase in task difficulty causes the learning signal to vanish. We argue that the conventional approach of discarding these failed trajectories is wasteful, as they contain valuable diagnostic information about the model's cognitive gaps, a bright side that can be leveraged for recovery. Existing solutions, however, often regress to static, "off-policy-style" interventions like pre-defined hint libraries or perform post-hoc refinement, failing to provide the adaptive, forward-looking guidance needed to escape the collapse. To address this, we propose a paradigm shift towards on-policy pedagogical intervention and introduce MENTOR, a multi-agent framework that acts as a live mentor. MENTOR diagnoses the root cause of failure in real-time and dynamically generates targeted, instructional prompts to guide the learning agent's next attempt. As a plug-and-play module, MENTOR integrates seamlessly into existing policy optimization pipelines like GRPO without modifying the training infrastructure. Extensive experiments on math and code generation show that MENTOR effectively mitigates zero-reward collapse, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines. Notably, it achieves massive average relative gains of up to 78.3% on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct over its base model.
authors: Guanlan Yue, Hang Yu, Xiaoyong Huang, Ruipeng Li, Wei Zhang, Bingchang Liu, Rui Wang
bullets: Zero-reward collapse can occur when task difficulty rises sharply, causing learning signals to disappear.
Failed trajectories contain diagnostic information but are often discarded or handled with static, off-policy interventions.
MENTOR is a multi-agent live mentor that identifies failure causes and generates adaptive guidance for the next attempt.
It is designed as a plug-and-play module for policy optimization pipelines such as GRPO.
Experiments in math and code generation report improved recovery and gains of up to 78.3% on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct over its base model.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses RLVR training dynamics and failure recovery for large reasoning models, directly relevant to LLM training and reasoning.
papers.title: MENTOR: Learning from Failure with On-Policy Pedagogical Intervention
papers.tldr: MENTOR uses real-time, on-policy diagnosis and targeted instructional prompts to help reasoning models recover from zero-reward collapse in RLVR.

papers.abstract: In machine learning, a self-attention dynamics describes the attention mechanism of transformers, and is obtained treating the layer index of a transformer as time index. Even though naturally discrete-time, this dynamical system is most often studied in continuous-time. Scope of this paper is to provide a thorough investigation of the discrete-time version of the self-attention dynamics: a complete classification of its equilibria is given, and their stability properties are studied, in both the single-head and the multihead case. We show that in both cases the main attractor of the dynamics is a consensus equilibrium aligned with the principal eigenvector of the value matrix (in the single-head case, a corresponding matrix of weights in the multihead case), even though other locally asymptotically stable bipartite equilibria can be show to exist at least in the single-head situation. The behavior is confirmed by looking at the learned weight matrices of a real transformer.
bullets: Studies self-attention dynamics using the transformer layer index as discrete time.
Classifies equilibria and analyzes their stability for both single-head and multihead attention.
Identifies consensus equilibria aligned with the principal eigenvector of the value matrix or a related multihead weight matrix as the main attractors.
Shows that locally asymptotically stable bipartite equilibria can also occur, at least in the single-head case.
Observations are supported by examining learned weight matrices from a real transformer.
papers.selection_reason: Provides a theoretical analysis of self-attention dynamics in Transformers, contributing to the understanding of LLM architectures.
papers.title: Asymptotic Analysis of Discrete-Time Self-Attention Dynamics in Transformers
papers.tldr: This paper rigorously analyzes discrete-time self-attention as a dynamical system, classifying its equilibria and showing that consensus aligned with a principal eigenvector is the main attractor.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have become the standard architecture for frontier LLMs. The multiple parallel experts in each transformer block theoretically enable expert specialization according to categories such as domains, languages, or modalities during pretraining. However, when data is imbalanced across categories, minority categories can become concentrated in a small fraction of the expert pool or spread inefficiently across them, effectively limiting their available capacity. In this work, we demonstrate that category-conditioned expert-selection biases can preferentially route tokens from different categories toward specialized expert pools. By applying biases based on input category, we provide a simple way to induce soft category-aligned specialization. This intervention encourages categories toward distinct expert subsets while retaining cross-category sharing when useful. More importantly, it enables the over-allocation of expert capacity to categories that would otherwise be disadvantaged by data scarcity. We observe performance improvements across modalities, low-resource languages, and code in models up to 10.6B parameters. At our smallest and largest model scales, these gains are equivalent to allocating 18.5% and 2.7% additional baseline training tokens, respectively. Overall, our results show that expert biases can serve as a lightweight control for category-level expert allocation, making room for low-resource categories while retaining standard MoE inference.
authors: Ayush K. Tarun, Clara Meister, Antoine Bosselut
bullets: Data imbalance can leave minority categories with too little effective expert capacity or inefficiently distributed experts.
The method applies input-category biases to expert selection, inducing soft specialization into category-aligned expert pools.
The approach supports over-allocation of experts to disadvantaged categories without changing standard MoE inference.
Improvements are reported across modalities, low-resource languages, and code for models up to 10.6B parameters.
Reported gains correspond to the benefit of 18.5% and 2.7% additional baseline training tokens at the smallest and largest scales, respectively.
papers.selection_reason: Category-conditioned expert selection biases improve MoE LLM routing for imbalanced data.
papers.title: Overcoming Data Imbalances with Expert Selection Biases
papers.tldr: Category-conditioned routing biases help MoE models allocate more expert capacity to data-scarce categories while preserving useful cross-category sharing.

papers.abstract: Cross-tokenizer on-policy distillation (OPD) requires aligning teacher and student sequences before their scores can be compared. Decoded-text alignment provides such correspondence at the chunk level, but leaves a distinct problem unresolved: credit alignment. A chunk-level signal specifies how much a span should change, but not how that signal should be distributed across student tokens, while tokens without teacher correspondence remain unconstrained. We propose CAST (Chunk-aware credit Assignment with Selective Token Anchoring), a shift-or-stay framework that addresses both issues. For aligned chunks, CAST redistributes each chunk's advantage across student tokens using predictive uncertainty and local teacher-signal smoothness, emphasizing learning opportunities supported by locally consistent teacher feedback while preserving the chunk's total advantage. The resulting weights exactly solve a KL-regularized credit-allocation problem. For unaligned positions, CAST selectively anchors the student to its initial policy through a KL penalty, limiting drift where teacher supervision is unavailable. Because credit assignment is separated from chunk construction, CAST also applies to punctuation-defined or fixed-length chunks under shared tokenization. Across six mathematics, science, and code benchmarks, CAST improves the average over the strongest evaluated baseline by $2.45$ and $1.32$ points for cross-tokenizer transfer from Qwen3-8B to Mistral-7B and Llama-3.1-8B, respectively, and by $2.10$ points for shared-tokenizer transfer to Qwen3-1.7B.
authors: Jingru Yang, Jinhang Wu, Minjing Shi, Shengfeng He, Xuyan Li, Man Tan, Biye Li
bullets: Addresses the unresolved credit-alignment problem: distributing chunk advantages across student tokens and constraining unaligned positions.
Redistributes each chunk’s advantage using predictive uncertainty and local teacher-signal smoothness, while preserving the total advantage.
Uses selective KL anchoring to the student’s initial policy where teacher supervision is unavailable.
Separates credit assignment from chunk construction, supporting decoded-text, punctuation-defined, and fixed-length chunks.
Across six math, science, and code benchmarks, improves over the strongest evaluated baseline by 2.45, 1.32, and 2.10 points in the reported transfer settings.
papers.selection_reason: Cross-tokenizer distillation with credit alignment improves LLM reasoning transfer; relevant to language foundation models.
papers.title: CAST: Credit Alignment for Cross-Tokenizer On-Policy Distillation
papers.tldr: CAST improves cross-tokenizer on-policy distillation by assigning chunk-level teacher feedback to student tokens and anchoring tokens without teacher correspondence.

papers.abstract: On-Policy Distillation (OPD) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for transferring reasoning capabilities from frontier models to smaller models, while extending its success to multi-turn agentic environments remains challenging. We study agentic OPD through interaction states, distinguishing the objective task and executed action-observation record from the internal semantic trajectory of student reasoning. Through this lens, we identify two roles of student reasoning in multi-turn OPD: prior reasoning distorts teacher supervision, while current reasoning shapes the action alternatives sampled at the same state. Specifically, at matched interaction states, removing prior student reasoning improves teacher continuation success and changes the teacher's token-level targets, with larger continuation gains at later turns. Meanwhile, resampling complete reasoning-action responses yields greater action diversity at the same state than resampling actions under a fixed reasoning trace. We introduce State-Grounded On-Policy Distillation, a framework that grounds teacher supervision in interaction states and reallocates the sampling budget to generate multiple complete reasoning-action responses at states with high response entropy, while retaining full-history student generation. Comprehensive evaluations across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld and WebShop demonstrate that State-OPD achieves the highest macro-average success rate among the evaluated methods for both Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B students. Notably, for Qwen3-4B, State-OPD raises macro-average success from 26.07\% with the strongest baseline to 31.74\% and surpasses its Qwen3-32B teacher on ALFWorld Seen. Further analyses reveal that State-OPD achieves higher task success with fewer supervised turn responses and substantially reduces persistent failed-action repetition; qualitative traces illustrate decision revision based on interaction feedback.
authors: Zhentao Zhang, Yanzhao Zheng, Yanlin Liu, Yuanqiang Yu, Tianze Xu, Chao Ma, Jihuai Zhu, Lelun Wu, Baohua Dong, Hangcheng Zhu, Ruohui Huang, Gang Yu
bullets: Problem: Standard on-policy distillation struggles in multi-turn agents because prior student reasoning can distort teacher supervision and fixed reasoning traces limit action diversity.
Method: Separate interaction states from internal reasoning, remove prior student reasoning when querying teacher continuations, and allocate sampling to high-entropy states.
The framework retains full-history student generation while generating multiple complete reasoning-action responses at selected states.
Across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and WebShop, State-OPD achieves the highest macro-average success among evaluated methods for both Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B.
For Qwen3-4B, macro-average success increases from 26.07% with the strongest baseline to 31.74%; analyses also show fewer supervised turn responses and less repeated failed actions.
papers.selection_reason: On-policy distillation for multi-turn LLM agents; directly relevant to language foundation model training and reasoning.
papers.title: State-OPD: State-Grounded On-Policy Distillation for Multi-Turn Agents
papers.tldr: State-OPD improves multi-turn agent learning by grounding teacher supervision in interaction states and sampling diverse complete reasoning-action responses.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a target policy on its own rollouts using token-level supervision from a stronger teacher, but typically relies on the teacher being substantially more capable than the target. Recent work relaxes this requirement by transferring the relative policy difference between an expert and a reference policy rather than the expert's absolute distribution. Yet it remains unclear which differences provide useful supervision and which targets can benefit from them. We develop a unified view in which the log-probability ratio between a proxy expert and a proxy reference defines an implicit reward for KL-regularized policy optimization. This formulation induces an on-policy update for the target, recovers conventional OPD as a special case, and enables any-to-any transfer across models that differ in scale, training stage or generation. Our systematic experiments yield three findings. First, a stronger expert is not necessarily a better source of supervision: differences induced by task-specific training, including reinforcement learning and supervised fine-tuning, transfer consistently, whereas those arising from model scale alone transfer weakly or not at all. Second, the expert and reference serve complementary roles: the expert provides the capability to be transferred, while the reference filters out shared behavior and isolates the relevant residual. Third, even a useful difference does not transfer to every target: success requires the induced update to move the target toward the expert and generalize beyond sampled rollouts. Raw policy distance does not predict transferability, whereas an appropriate reference can rescue otherwise unsuccessful transfer. These results characterize when relative policy differences provide effective supervision for OPD.
authors: Rong Wu, Daocheng Fu, Yu Yang, Xuemeng Yang, Siqi Li, Shu Zou, Yao Zhu, Botian Shi, Bo Zhang, Cong Zhang, Pinlong Cai, Jianbiao Mei
bullets: Frames the log-probability ratio between a proxy expert and reference as an implicit reward for KL-regularized target updates.
Generalizes conventional on-policy distillation and supports transfer across models differing in scale, training stage, or generation.
Task-specific changes from reinforcement learning or supervised fine-tuning transfer more reliably than differences caused by model scaling alone.
The expert supplies transferable capability, while the reference removes shared behavior and isolates useful residuals.
Transfer succeeds only when the update moves the target toward the expert and generalizes beyond sampled rollouts; suitable references can rescue failed transfers.
papers.selection_reason: Rethinks on-policy distillation by transferring relative policy differences rather than absolute distributions. A significant technical contribution to LLM training methods.
papers.title: Rethinking Relative Policy Differences Transfer of On-Policy Distillation
papers.tldr: Relative policy differences can enable on-policy distillation across diverse models, but transfer depends more on what the expert–reference difference captures than on expert strength or raw policy distance.

papers.abstract: We present Neurograf v1, an experimental end-to-end Romanian-first language-model pipeline developed to investigate the feasibility of training language models from scratch for a lower-resource European language. The pipeline comprises RoSfera, a 635 GB Romanian corpus containing 175.7 million documents; an 80k byte-level BPE tokenizer; five decoder-only models ranging from 160M to 6B parameters, trained on 131 billion tokens; three instruction-tuned assistants; and two contrastively trained embedding models. Training and evaluation were conducted using computing infrastructure at ELI-NP/IFIN-HH. The model family exhibits consistent scaling of validation loss and increasing Romanian factual and cultural knowledge with model size. On the 1,000-question WWTBM benchmark, Neurograf-6B achieves 69.89% accuracy on Romanian-context questions, while Neurograf-3.2B reaches 67.38%. Compute-optimal analysis yields a parameter-scaling exponent of approximately 0.423. Neurograf v1 serves as an experimental demonstrator rather than a production system. The study identifies practical challenges involving diacritic preservation, corpus quality, data composition, and tokenization efficiency, while demonstrating the feasibility of developing Romanian-first base models, instruction-following assistants, and semantic embedding models within a unified training pipeline.
bullets: Introduces a unified pipeline for developing models tailored to the lower-resource Romanian language.
Uses the 635 GB RoSfera corpus, an 80k byte-level BPE tokenizer, and five decoder-only models from 160M to 6B parameters.
Includes three instruction-tuned assistants and two contrastively trained embedding models.
