On the 1,000-question WWTBM benchmark, the 6B and 3.2B models achieve 69.89% and 67.38% accuracy on Romanian-context questions, respectively.
Identifies challenges in diacritic preservation, corpus quality, data composition, and tokenization efficiency; the system is an experimental demonstrator, not a production model.
papers.selection_reason: End-to-end Romanian-first LLM family trained from scratch with scaling and instruction tuning.
papers.title: Neurograf v1: An End-to-End Romanian-First Language Model Family
papers.tldr: Neurograf v1 demonstrates that Romanian-first language models can be trained from scratch across base, instruction-tuned, and embedding models, with larger models showing stronger Romanian knowledge.

papers.abstract: AI agents depend on repeated decisions to accomplish tasks, with large language models (LLMs) commonly serving as their core decision makers. The recent emergence of Jev offers an opportunity to make these decisions faster and at lower cost. However, it remains unclear whether such local savings can be translated into efficient and reliable task completion. In this paper, we investigate this efficiency transfer across five agents in two representative application settings, embodied tasks in ALFWorld and mobile app use in AndroidWorld. Across 4,500 task executions, we jointly evaluate task effectiveness, decision-level and task-level resource use, and execution behavior. Experimental results show that Jev integration substantially reduces decision cost and latency across all five agents, with task-level gains varying by workflow. Task success remains close to baseline levels on ALFWorld and declines more substantially in two mobile agents. Auxiliary reasoning and additional interactions absorb decision savings, while failed recovery and premature completion limit successful delivery. Mean cost per successful outcome increases in one agent even as spending per attempt falls. These findings highlight the importance of preserving progress, supporting recovery, and verifying completion when integrating efficient decision models into agent workflows. Their practical value should be assessed through successful task delivery, recovery behavior, and resources per delivered outcome.
authors: Yuchen Ling, Shengcheng Yu, Zhenyu Chen, Chunrong Fang
bullets: Evaluates Jev across five agents and 4,500 executions in ALFWorld and AndroidWorld.
Jev substantially reduces decision-level cost and latency across all agents.
Task-level benefits depend on the workflow: success stays near baseline in ALFWorld but declines more in two mobile agents.
Auxiliary reasoning, extra interactions, failed recovery, and premature completion can absorb savings or reduce delivery success.
Efficiency should be measured by successful outcomes, recovery behavior, and resources per delivered task—not per-attempt spending.
papers.selection_reason: Empirical study of efficient decision models in LLM agent workflows, relevant to efficiency and agent reliability.
papers.title: When Faster Decisions Do Not Make Better Agents: An Empirical Study of Jev in Agent Workflows
papers.tldr: Jev makes agent decisions faster and cheaper, but workflow overhead and weaker recovery can prevent those savings from improving successful task completion.

papers.abstract: Safety-aligned large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreaks and can over-refuse benign requests. Understanding these failures requires distinguishing harmfulness recognition from the computation that writes refusal. We reframe this as a pathway question and make it measurable on residual-stream updates in decoder-only Transformers, separating the harmfulness information a module update exposes from the change it produces in readable refusal evidence. Across 18 Base-Instruct pairs spanning Qwen, Llama, and Gemma, harmfulness is decoded more readily from attention updates, particularly in early layers, whereas MLP updates contribute more strongly to harm-selective refusal writing in aligned models. Post-training strengthens MLP refusal writing in all 18 pairs without systematically improving harmfulness decodability, while positive MLP writing becomes more concentrated in deeper layers after post-training. Across six reasoning-enabled models, harmfulness remains decodable during reasoning while strong refusal writing concentrates at answer onset, a pattern that persists with reasoning disabled. Causal interventions further support this pathway: resetting downstream MLP updates to their clean values substantially reduces the refusal shift caused by upstream attention interventions. Building on these findings, we introduce Sentinel, which combines an attention-derived perception score P with an MLP-derived decision score D. Their joint profiles characterize jailbreaks and over-refusals, and conditional routing with both signals achieves a lower aggregate error rate than single-signal routing and evaluated fixed reminders across eight models.
authors: Zixuan Weng, Haoqi He, Weifei Jin, Yue Huang, Yang Bai
bullets: Frames jailbreaks and over-refusals as failures in the pathway from harmfulness recognition to refusal writing.
Across 18 Base–Instruct model pairs, harmfulness is more decodable from attention updates, especially early in the network.
MLP updates contribute more strongly to harm-selective refusal writing; post-training strengthens this writing without consistently improving harmfulness recognition.
In reasoning-enabled models, harmfulness remains detectable during reasoning, but refusal writing concentrates near answer onset.
Causal interventions support attention-to-MLP dependence, and Sentinel’s combined perception and decision signals outperform single-signal routing and evaluated fixed reminders across eight models.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes attention-to-MLP safety pathways in LLMs and proposes a routing method, relevant to LLM interpretability and safety.
papers.title: Attention Sees, MLP Refuses: Tracing the Attention-to-MLP Safety Pathway in LLMs
papers.tldr: The study finds that attention mainly recognizes harmfulness, while MLPs convert that signal into refusal behavior, enabling a two-signal safety monitor called Sentinel.

papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in tackling complex tasks through agentic workflows. However, manually designing these workflows is labor-intensive and lacks flexibility to adapt to diverse queries. While automated workflow optimization is a promising direction, existing methods often incur expensive API costs during training-phase feedback collection. Furthermore, they fail to adaptively reuse high-quality workflows, which creates a bottleneck for both performance and cost-effectiveness. To address these limitations, we propose CB-Orchestrator, an adaptive framework that decouples workflow generation from selection. In the first stage, we construct a diverse pool of candidate workflows via evolutionary search. In the second stage, we formulate workflow selection as a Contextual Bandit problem, which enables sample-efficient learning by balancing exploration and exploitation, thereby significantly reducing the feedback required for training. During inference, the model adaptively selects the optimal workflow tailored to each query. Evaluations across five diverse benchmarks demonstrate that CB-Orchestrator consistently outperforms all baselines. Notably, on the MATH dataset, CB-Orchestrator achieves better performance than strong recent baselines while reducing training-phase API token overhead by no less than 40.55% and total end-to-end training (including workflow pool generation) token overhead by no less than 29.73%.
authors: Jiahang Sun, Zhiwei Shang, Zhipiao Liu, Hongwei Yang, Guoqing Xie, Shuang Qiu, Zhongxiang Dai
bullets: Addresses the cost and inflexibility of manually designed or automatically optimized agent workflows.
Generates a diverse workflow pool through evolutionary search, then decouples selection from generation.
Uses contextual bandits to balance exploration and exploitation and reuse effective workflows per query.
Evaluated on five benchmarks, it consistently outperforms reported baselines.
On MATH, it reduces training-phase token overhead by at least 40.55% and total training overhead by at least 29.73%.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces CB-Orchestrator for optimizing LLM agent workflows using Contextual Bandits. This is a methodological contribution to improving the efficiency and performance of LLM agents, fitting the 'Language Foundation Models' topic.
papers.title: CB-Orchestrator: Adaptive Workflow Optimization for LLM Agents via Contextual Bandits
papers.tldr: CB-Orchestrator adaptively selects among evolved LLM-agent workflows using contextual bandits, improving task performance while reducing API-token costs.

papers.abstract: Large language model agents increasingly operate in long-horizon environments where early mistakes can trigger cascading failures and trap agents in dead-end trajectories. Agents must therefore be able to proactively recover from such states and turn their exploratory experience into guidance for subsequent decisions. We introduce ReTRAIL, a framework that enables agents to rewind the environment to earlier states while preserving valid progress and carrying forward knowledge learned from abandoned exploration. The environment state moves backward while the agent's knowledge continues to move forward. ReTRAIL trains a shared policy with two complementary signals: State-Anchored GRPO compares alternative continuations from revisited states to improve execution, while a branch-advancement reward guides reflection through the progress of subsequent exploration. Experiments across four interactive benchmark MineSweeper, Sokoban, ALFWorld and ScienceWorld show that simply adding a rewind primitive provides limited benefit and can even degrade performance. In contrast, ReTRAIL enables agents to rewind from unproductive states and use insights from abandoned branches to guide subsequent exploration. These results demonstrate the value of coupling environment rewinding with experience reuse within an ongoing task for long-horizon task solving. The code is available at https://github.com/whi497/ReTRAIL.
authors: Ziang Ye, Wentao Shi, Lei Chen, Zhengzhou Cai, Yu Wang, Zhiyuan Yao, Zihan Wang, Xierui Song, Fuli Feng, Yixin Cao
bullets: Long-horizon agents can suffer cascading failures when early mistakes lead to unproductive trajectories.
ReTRAIL rewinds environments to earlier states, preserves valid progress, and carries learned experience forward.
It trains a shared policy using State-Anchored GRPO for comparing alternative continuations and a branch-advancement reward for guiding exploration.
Across MineSweeper, Sokoban, ALFWorld, and ScienceWorld, rewind alone offered limited or harmful benefits, whereas ReTRAIL improved recovery and exploration.
The approach focuses on coupling environment rewind with experience reuse within the same task.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a framework for long-horizon LLM agents to rewind environments and reuse exploration knowledge, relevant to agentic LLM reasoning.
papers.title: Travel Back To Move Forward: Retrospective Exploration and Evolving for Long Horizon Agents
papers.tldr: ReTRAIL helps long-horizon agents recover from dead ends by rewinding the environment while retaining and applying knowledge from abandoned explorations.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a dominant paradigm for enhancing LLMs' reasoning capabilities. Yet long-horizon autoregressive rollouts introduce a fundamental limitation: local policy mismatch can compound into severe state distribution shift over trajectories. Existing LLM RL methods, such as GRPO and GSPO, control policy mismatch at the token or sequence level, but overlook this trajectory-induced shift, causing training instability and eventual collapse as the horizon grows. To close the state distribution gap, we propose Trajectory-Aware Policy Optimization (TAPO), a principled framework that theoretically derives the state-distribution correction from the off-policy policy gradient and incorporates it into the RL objective. TAPO further employs a geometric-mean estimator for variance reduction, together with a length-aware dynamic clipping that prevents overly deviated updates across the trajectory. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TAPO significantly surpasses existing LLM RL algorithms across eight competition-level benchmarks, achieving up to 48% and 12% improvement over GRPO on mathematical reasoning and algorithmic coding, with substantially enhanced training stability.
authors: Zhicheng Cai, Weinan Dai, Yuyan Zhou, Wei-Ying Ma, Ya-Qin Zhang, Hao Zhou
bullets: Long autoregressive rollouts amplify small policy mismatches into severe state distribution gaps.
Existing methods such as GRPO and GSPO mainly constrain token- or sequence-level mismatch, leaving trajectory-induced shift unaddressed.
TAPO derives a state-distribution correction from the off-policy policy gradient and adds it to the RL objective.
A geometric-mean estimator reduces variance, while length-aware dynamic clipping limits overly large trajectory-level updates.
Across eight competition-level benchmarks, TAPO improves over GRPO by up to 48% on mathematical reasoning and 12% on algorithmic coding, with more stable training.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses training instability in Long-Horizon LLM Reinforcement Learning by correcting state distribution shift. This is a methodological contribution to training LLMs via RL, fitting the 'Language Foundation Models' topic.
papers.title: Trajectory-Aware Policy Optimization: Closing the State Distribution Gap in Long-Horizon LLM RL
papers.tldr: TAPO stabilizes long-horizon LLM reinforcement learning by correcting trajectory-level state distribution shifts that cause policy collapse.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning has become the foundational paradigm for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of LLMs. Yet the dominant approach, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), relies on a geometrically degenerate clipping proxy that cannot adapt its resistance to policy shifts, leading to premature clipping and degraded exploration. Subsequent variants alleviate these issues through fragmented and heuristic modifications. We propose Generalized Proximal Policy Optimization (GPPO), a principled and unified framework for understanding and designing LLM RL algorithms through the lens of divergence. We establish a generalized $f$-divergence trust-region theory with a monotonic performance improvement guarantee, and show that different $f$-divergences induce distinct geometries and policy update dynamics. We further introduce novel estimator topologies that provide more faithful divergence estimates than the conventional single-sample Monte Carlo estimation. Under this framework, PPO and recent variants such as DAPO, DPPO, and RIPO emerge as special cases, establishing a principled two-dimensional design space of {Divergence $\times$ Estimator}. Extensive experiments on eight competition-level math and coding benchmarks show that both dimensions are critical. The best-performing GPPO instantiation surpasses standard GRPO by up to 50% and 14% on math and coding, delivering SOTA performance.
authors: Zhicheng Cai, Xinyuan Guo, Hanlin Wu, Weinan Dai, Yuyan Zhou, Wei-Ying Ma, Ya-Qin Zhang, Hao Zhou
bullets: PPO’s fixed clipping proxy can cause premature clipping, limiting policy adaptation and exploration.
GPPO develops an $f$-divergence trust-region theory with a monotonic performance-improvement guarantee.
It introduces improved estimator topologies for more faithful divergence estimation than single-sample Monte Carlo methods.
PPO, DAPO, DPPO, and RIPO are framed as special cases in a two-dimensional Divergence × Estimator design space.
Experiments across eight competition-level math and coding benchmarks show gains of up to 50% and 14% over standard GRPO, respectively.
papers.selection_reason: Unifies LLM reinforcement learning algorithms through f-divergence theory, with direct implications for LLM reasoning training.
papers.title: Generalized Proximal Policy Optimization: Unifying LLM RL Algorithms from the Perspective of Divergence
papers.tldr: GPPO unifies LLM reinforcement-learning algorithms through generalized divergence-based trust regions and achieves strong gains on math and coding benchmarks.

papers.abstract: In repeated human-AI interaction, a single observation can be quoted, summarized, and returned to a model as multiple reports, making repetition look like independent corroboration. We study whether language models can use supplied report lineage to update according to evidence provenance rather than report count. We introduce Latent Quotient Evidence Training (LQET), a relational objective that combines sparse Bayesian supervision with constraints that encourage stable predictions when reports add no new evidence and consistent updates to the same new evidence across relay histories. On a controlled binary benchmark, LQET reduces new-evidence update RMSE by 41-44% and log-odds drift after eight relay steps by 89-91% relative to task-only training across Qwen3-4B and Phi-4-mini, with three paired training seeds per backbone. The gains extend to a closed-loop simulation in which model confidence controls how many relayed reports re-enter the model's context in later rounds. By grounding belief updates in supplied provenance, LQET offers a route toward dynamic human-AI systems in which influence follows new evidence, not the number of times the same evidence returns.
authors: Tianyi Huang, Eric Liu, Jay Chong, Emily Yin, Wanqi Zhao
bullets: Addresses repetition bias in human-AI feedback loops, where one observation may appear as multiple corroborating reports.
Uses report lineage with sparse Bayesian supervision and relational consistency constraints.
Encourages stable predictions when relays add no evidence and consistent updates across different relay histories.
On a controlled binary benchmark, LQET reduced new-evidence update RMSE by 41–44% and eight-step log-odds drift by 89–91% versus task-only training.
Benefits also extended to a closed-loop simulation where model confidence controls future report relaying.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a training objective for provenance-aware belief updating in LLMs, relevant to reliable LLM reasoning in human-AI loops.
papers.title: Provenance-Aware Belief Updating in Human-AI Feedback Loops
papers.tldr: LQET helps language models update beliefs based on genuinely new evidence rather than repeated, relayed reports.

papers.abstract: Language-model agents are used for specialized work such as financial research, healthcare and law. Such agents are often capable enough for a task but still miss its details. In finance, for example, these details include which filing reports a figure or how a company discloses a metric. Retraining the agent to learn these details is expensive, and often impossible when the agent is a closed or shared system. Writing the missing know-how into the agent's prompt makes the prompt long and identical for every input, although different inputs need different guidance. We propose to learn to generate this guidance instead. A small advisor model reads each input and writes structured advice, which is appended to the prompt of a frozen executor. The advisor is trained with hindsight, following work on distillation with privileged information. On a training pool with graded answers, we analyse the executor's failures, run it under several strategies to see which one worked on each input, and let a teacher that sees the grades and the traces write the advice that would have helped. The advisor then learns, by supervised fine-tuning, to write that advice from the input alone. Because the student is a separate small model rather than the executor, it is cheap to train and adds little latency. We call this approach hindsight structured advice distillation (HSAD). On FrontierFinance, a public benchmark of expert-written financial research queries, an 8B advisor raises the qualification rate of Samaya's proprietary research agent, which already leads the benchmark's leaderboard, from 52.9% to 56.6%. This is above the agent's own high-effort configuration, at 37% lower cost per query. We study the generalization of the proposed approach, and in particular show that HSAD also improves results on WebShop, BIRD text-to-SQL and ExpertLongBench.
bullets: Targets specialized tasks where agents miss domain-specific details and full retraining is costly or impossible.
A teacher analyzes graded answers, executor traces, and strategy outcomes to create helpful structured advice.
A separate advisor learns to generate this advice from the input alone, then appends it to the frozen executor’s prompt.
On FrontierFinance, an 8B advisor raises qualification from 52.9% to 56.6% and exceeds the executor’s high-effort setting at 37% lower query cost.
The approach also improves results on WebShop, BIRD text-to-SQL, and ExpertLongBench.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a small advisor model that generates structured advice for a frozen LLM executor via hindsight distillation, directly relevant to LLM agent improvement.
papers.title: Hindsight Structured Advice Distillation: Steering Executor Agents with Advisors Trained on Their Failures and Task Characteristics
papers.tldr: HSAD trains a small advisor to generate input-specific advice from an executor’s past failures, improving a frozen research agent’s performance without retraining it.

papers.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) remains a widely used approach for post-training large language models, because fixed demonstrations can directly introduce desired reasoning strategies and behavioral patterns. Yet forcing a model to imitate externally provided trajectories may also interfere with behaviors already supported by pretraining, limiting generalization beyond the training distribution. Recent dynamic SFT methods mitigate this issue by reweighting token-level supervision according to model-side signals such as predictive probability, prior support, or distributional compatibility. However, model compatibility is not equivalent to learning value: a token that is weakly supported by the current model may either be an undesirable mismatch or precisely the task-specific decision that the demonstration is intended to teach. We propose CIG-SFT, an information-theoretic framework that estimates the task-conditioned information carried by each demonstrated token. Under teacher forcing, we compare the token likelihood from a frozen reference model with and without access to the task input while keeping the gold solution prefix fixed. The resulting conditional information gain quantifies how much the task itself reduces uncertainty about the demonstrated decision. We then convert this information into a KL-regularized projection of the current policy and derive an equivalent scalar-weighted SFT objective whose logit gradient exactly matches that of the projected target. Across mathematical reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, CIG-SFT consistently outperforms standard SFT and recent adaptive fine-tuning baselines, with particularly strong improvements in generalization to challenging evaluation distributions, while requiring neither additional training data nor online rollouts.
authors: Yuxuan Gu, Kequan Niu, Xiaocheng Feng, Yun Li, Yiqiao Yang, Bing Qin
bullets: SFT can over-imitate demonstrations and disrupt useful behaviors learned during pretraining.
CIG-SFT estimates each token’s task-conditioned information gain using a frozen reference model with and without task input, while fixing the gold prefix.
These information scores define a KL-regularized target and an equivalent scalar-weighted SFT objective.
Across math reasoning and code generation benchmarks, it outperforms standard SFT and adaptive fine-tuning baselines, especially on challenging distributions.
The method does not require additional training data or online rollouts.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes an information-theoretic SFT objective for LLM post-training, improving generalization on reasoning and code tasks.
papers.title: What Should SFT Learn? Conditional Information Gain for Generalizable Post-Training
papers.tldr: CIG-SFT weights demonstrated tokens by how much task context informs their decisions, improving post-training generalization without extra data or online rollouts.

papers.abstract: This paper introduces MathVis, a benchmark designed to evaluate LLMs' ability to visualize frontier mathematical problems and perform diagram-assisted reasoning. The benchmark consists of 512 tasks, each comprising a mathematical statement, a reference diagram, executable TikZ or SVG code, a Gold Intermediate Representation (IR), atomic rubrics, and error codes. Through rigorous evaluation, GPT-6-Astra, Claude Fable 5, and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview achieve pass@1 scores of 31.25%, 26.56%, and 22.85%, respectively. We found that although the tasks require visualization, LLMs produce outputs dominated by formal languages, symbols, and graphics programs, rather than explicit diagram-mediated reasoning. Furthermore, while the solutions generated by LLMs may contain all the necessary elements, they are often visually confusing to humans. Ultimately, this benchmark aims to visualize mathematical problems and promote research on enabling LLMs to simplify their reasoning via visual diagrams.
authors: Jingjing Wei, Hao Zhao, Xinke Li, Linxi Yu, Xiaosong Gao, Shanshan Xiao
bullets: Introduces 512 tasks for visualizing frontier mathematical problems and performing diagram-assisted reasoning.
Each task includes a mathematical statement, reference diagram, executable TikZ/SVG code, Gold IR, atomic rubrics, and error codes.
Reported pass@1 scores are 31.25% for GPT-6-Astra, 26.56% for Claude Fable 5, and 22.85% for Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview.
LLM outputs are dominated by formal language, symbols, and graphics programs rather than explicit diagram-mediated reasoning.
Generated solutions may include required elements but remain visually confusing to humans.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for LLM diagram-assisted mathematical reasoning and visualization.
papers.title: MathVis: Can AI Reason through Drawing? A Benchmark for Mathematical Figure Generation
papers.tldr: MathVis benchmarks whether LLMs can generate and reason through mathematical diagrams, revealing low success rates and limited explicit use of visual reasoning.

papers.abstract: Large language models have achieved remarkable advances in complex reasoning. However, scaling reasoning post-training with ever-larger corpora can substantially increase training cost without proportional performance gains. In this study, we therefore ask: how far can reasoning supervision be compressed without sacrificing capability? To this end, we propose an uncertainty-guided progressive contraction framework that concentrates supervision and optimization on the reasoning trajectories most valuable for learning. Specifically, rather than treating a teacher-generated chain-of-thought (CoT) as a single realized path, we construct uncertainty-profiled reasoning supervision by building Monte Carlo reasoning trees around intermediate reasoning states to expose process-level uncertainty. This uncertainty first contracts the original corpus into a compact teacher-informed pool. A second, learner-aware contraction then performs online routing during SFT, concentrating optimization according to the student's evolving learning state. Together, the two stages progressively contract both supervision and optimization, substantially reducing the student training budget. Experiments across diverse reasoning benchmarks and LLM families show that our method uses as little as 0.22% of the optimization budget of full-data SFT, over 450x less training exposure, while maintaining or improving reasoning performance. Notably, our framework generalizes well across heterogeneous student families, black-box teachers, and weak-to-strong transfer. This indicates that it is not only a way to accelerate training but can also enhance reasoning capability.
authors: Suorong Yang, Jiaxin Wang, Jiaming Su, Chentao Yue, Furao Shen, Peng Ye, Soujanya Poria
bullets: Targets the high cost and diminishing returns of scaling reasoning post-training data.
Builds Monte Carlo reasoning trees to estimate process-level uncertainty around teacher-generated chains of thought.
Progressively contracts training in two stages: teacher-informed data selection, then learner-aware online routing during SFT.
Uses as little as 0.22% of the full-data SFT optimization budget—over 450× less training exposure—while maintaining or improving performance.
Works across diverse benchmarks, LLM families, black-box teachers, and weak-to-strong transfer.
papers.selection_reason: Uncertainty-guided contraction drastically reduces LLM reasoning post-training budget.
papers.title: Learning More by Training Less: Uncertainty-Guided Progressive Contraction for Efficient Reasoning Post-Training
papers.tldr: Uncertainty-guided progressive contraction compresses reasoning supervision and training exposure while preserving or improving LLM reasoning performance.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel across diverse tasks, benefiting from knowledge priors, in-context reasoning, and test-time computation. Despite these strengths, single-model reasoning remains vulnerable to error propagation, as later steps depend on the model's earlier outputs, leaving reasoning blind spots difficult to independently reassess. To address this limitation, we develop \textit{collaborative learning}, encompassing the construction of heterogeneous collaborators and the learning of effective cross-model collaboration. Specifically, \textit{model slicing} replaces a large model with smaller, heterogeneous models under a comparable parameter budget, enabling prior reasoning to be reassessed across distinct model parameterizations. \textit{Pyramid supervision} combines protocol distillation with step-level supervision to refine reasoning and interaction decisions throughout collaboration. We evaluate our approach across four task categories: multi-hop question answering, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and open-ended constrained generation. The trained heterogeneous models achieve comparable or better task performance than the original large model and established multi-agent baselines, including reinforcement-learning-based methods, while also achieving higher inference efficiency than the multi-agent baselines and exhibiting differentiated collaboration patterns across tasks. These findings show that learned collaboration turns model heterogeneity into complementary reasoning capabilities.
authors: Yuheng Wang, Runde Yang, Zhuohan Bao, Qiran Zhang, Huatao Li, Yiyang Zheng, Lin Wu, Jingru Fan, Shu Yao, Yihan Li, Zhi Li, Chen Qian
bullets: Targets error propagation and blind spots in single-model reasoning.
Uses model slicing to create heterogeneous collaborators within a comparable parameter budget.
Applies pyramid supervision combining protocol distillation with step-level supervision.
Evaluated on multi-hop QA, math reasoning, code generation, and constrained generation.
Reports comparable or better performance than the original large model and established multi-agent methods, with higher inference efficiency than those baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Improves LLM reasoning through heterogeneous model collaboration and model slicing.
papers.title: Collaborative Learning and Reasoning over Model Slices
papers.tldr: A collaboration framework splits one large LLM into heterogeneous smaller models and trains them to reassess reasoning, improving or matching performance while using inference more efficiently than multi-agent baselines.

papers.abstract: Federated Direct Preference Optimization (FedDPO) enables privacy-preserving alignment of language models across distributed agents without centralizing sensitive preference data. However, existing FedDPO analysis assumes all clients converge to a single shared policy, which is fundamentally at odds with the heterogeneous preference distributions present in practice. We propose Personalized FedDPO (pFedDPO), in which each client maintains a small private LoRA adapter atop a shared global base model. In pFedDPO, the base model is synchronized via FedAvg each round, while LoRA adapters remain local and capture client-specific preference patterns. We prove that this decomposition replaces the gradient diversity $\kappa^2$ in the FedDPO bound with a residual heterogeneity $\kappa^2_{\mathrm{eff}}$, which is no larger than $\kappa^2$ when adapters absorb client-specific directions, at the cost of an additive adapter-bias term that vanishes as adapters converge. Experiments on preference datasets show that pFedDPO consistently attains a lower gradient norm than vanilla FedDPO while remaining competitive in training loss and per-client reward accuracy.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between single-policy FedDPO and heterogeneous client preferences.
Synchronizes a shared base model with FedAvg while keeping small client-specific LoRA adapters private.
Theoretical analysis replaces gradient diversity with lower residual heterogeneity, plus an adapter-bias term that vanishes as adapters converge.
Experiments report lower gradient norms than vanilla FedDPO while remaining competitive in training loss and per-client reward accuracy.
papers.selection_reason: Personalized federated DPO for LLM alignment; relevant to language foundation model training.
papers.title: Personalized Federated Direct Preference Optimization via LoRA Adapters
papers.tldr: Personalized FedDPO uses local LoRA adapters to capture heterogeneous client preferences, improving optimization while preserving federated privacy.

papers.abstract: Existing sequence models share a critical limitation: they lack an explicit, interpretable mechanism for content-aware temporal recall. LSTMs compress everything into a single hidden state, thereby losing information about specific past events. Transformers attend to all tokens indiscriminately at quadratic cost, while state-space models like Mamba compress history into a fixed-dimensional state without explicit content-addressable memory. To address this gap, we introduce a novel framework grounded in nonlinear time-delay systems, in which the effective delay is dynamically estimated based on the semantic similarity between current and historical inputs. Our approach features three key innovations: (i) a differentiable semantic lag estimator that computes content-aware soft attention weights over history, producing a weighted historical context and similarity score; (ii) a diagonal state space with closed-form cumulative sum solution, achieving O(1) per-step complexity with no sequential loops; and (iii) an interpretable fuzzy semantic modulation mechanism that learns context-dependent rules for balancing instantaneous processing versus historical recall, where rule centers correspond to prototypical semantic contexts. Experimental results on text classification and generation outperform state-of-the-art methods.
bullets: Addresses the lack of explicit, content-aware temporal recall in LSTMs, Transformers, and state-space models.
Uses a differentiable semantic lag estimator to assign soft attention weights over historical inputs.
Employs a diagonal state space with a closed-form cumulative-sum solution for O(1) per-step computation without sequential loops.
Adds fuzzy semantic modulation to balance current-input processing with historical recall using interpretable context rules.
Outperforms state-of-the-art methods on text classification and generation tasks, according to the abstract.
papers.selection_reason: Novel sequence model architecture with content-aware temporal recall and O(1) per-step complexity; transferable to LLM architecture research.
papers.title: Time Delay System for Sequence Modeling
papers.tldr: A sequence model uses semantic similarity to dynamically recall relevant past information through an interpretable, efficient time-delay mechanism.

papers.abstract: Reasoning post-training draws on offline demonstrations and policy-generated rollouts, yet conventional supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by reinforcement learning (RL) separates their objectives and limits continued reuse of collected responses. We propose \textbf{Cross-Behavior Policy Optimization} (CBPO), which makes these sources compatible with one regression loss through a fixed-reference target. Because the generating policy does not enter this target, positive and negative offline completions, reference responses, and current and historical rollouts can share a common reward-labeled record format and replay buffer. As new responses enter the buffer, optimization retains the same regression objective without coordinating separate SFT and RL objectives or requiring stored behavior-policy probabilities, importance weighting, or a learned critic. Restricting the available sources gives offline, on-policy, and off-policy variants, while CBPO-Unified combines them. Across two model scales and four mathematical reasoning benchmarks, CBPO delivers leading \texttt{avg@32} and \texttt{pass@32} performance across benchmarks and data regimes. On Qwen3-1.7B, CBPO-Unified improves benchmark-averaged \texttt{avg@32} and \texttt{pass@32} over SFT DAPO by 2.33 and 4.44 percentage points, respectively. In the replay ablation, retaining historical rollouts improves these metrics by 1.87 and 3.72 percentage points over the no-history configuration.
authors: Du Cheng, Junyu Lu, Jingfan Zhang, Yuzhuo Zhang, Haoxuan Jia, Shichao Weng
bullets: Addresses the separation between supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, which limits reuse of collected responses.
Uses a generating-policy-independent target so positive/negative completions, reference responses, and current or historical rollouts share one reward-labeled replay format.
Supports offline, on-policy, off-policy, and unified training variants without stored behavior-policy probabilities, importance weighting, or a learned critic.
Across two model scales and four mathematical reasoning benchmarks, CBPO reports leading avg@32 and pass@32 performance across tested benchmarks and data regimes.
For Qwen3-1.7B, CBPO-Unified improves benchmark-averaged avg@32/pass@32 over SFT DAPO by 2.33/4.44 percentage points; retaining historical rollouts adds 1.87/3.72 points over no history.
papers.selection_reason: Unified regression objective for LLM post-training from demonstrations and rollouts; relevant to LLM reasoning and alignment.
papers.title: Cross-Behavior Policy Optimization: Unified Learning from Offline Demonstrations and On- and Off-Policy Rollouts via a Shared Regression Target
papers.tldr: CBPO unifies offline demonstrations with on- and off-policy rollouts through a shared fixed-reference regression target, enabling replay-based reasoning post-training without importance weighting or a learned critic.

papers.abstract: Outcome-supervised group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) assigns the same advantage to every token in an LLM agent trajectory, leaving useful and unhelpful decisions undifferentiated. Hindsight credit assignment (HCA) can refine this feedback, but its estimates rely on trajectories containing informative alternatives at consequential histories. We introduce TreeHCA, which couples hindsight-guided exploration with hindsight credit assignment. TreeHCA uses changes in reference-answer likelihood to revisit intermediate histories and sample alternative continuations, forming a tree of reasoning and tool interactions. Because this exploration changes the distribution of sampled continuations, we derive the corresponding inverse-hindsight importance correction, including an exact finite-pool identity. We use this structure in a normalized tree backup that propagates terminal outcomes into turn-level advantages. This shared hindsight structure is TreeHCA's central design principle, linking informative exploration with hindsight-guided credit assignment. Across seven question-answering benchmarks and three Qwen backbones, TreeHCA outperforms all baselines in aggregate exact match, validating the effectiveness of paired exploration and credit assignment for multi-turn LLM agent training. Our code is available at github.com/TheBlackCat22/TreeHCA.
authors: Debajoy Mukherjee, Jeremy Carleton, Sushil Vemuri, Srinivas Shakkottai, Dileep Kalathil
bullets: Addresses GRPO’s limitation of giving every trajectory token the same advantage, which obscures useful versus unhelpful decisions.
Revisits intermediate reasoning and tool-use histories using changes in reference-answer likelihood to sample alternative continuations.
Introduces inverse-hindsight importance correction to account for the altered continuation distribution, including an exact finite-pool identity.
Uses normalized tree backups to propagate terminal outcomes into turn-level advantages.
Outperforms all baselines in aggregate exact match across seven question-answering benchmarks and three Qwen backbones.
papers.selection_reason: Hindsight-guided exploration and credit assignment for multi-turn LLM agent RL; relevant to LLM reasoning and training.
papers.title: TreeHCA: Hindsight-Guided Exploration and Credit Assignment for Multi-Turn LLM Agents
papers.tldr: TreeHCA improves multi-turn LLM agent training by jointly exploring alternative continuations and assigning more precise credit to consequential decisions.

papers.abstract: We study byte-level autoregressive language models whose hidden state is a small quantum register, whose transitions are learned token-conditioned quantum channels, and whose next-byte probabilities come directly from Born-rule measurements without a learned classical vocabulary projection or softmax. In the fixed-width recurrent setting, unitary dynamics cannot contract or reset stored distinctions; experimentally, unitary recurrence loses to its retrained one-token control in every tested variant. Introducing learned dissipation, then token-conditioned dissipative gating, yields useful memory beyond one token. The gated model improves test negative log-likelihood by 0.20 +/- 0.03 nats/byte over retrained parameter-matched one-token controls at context length 12, and by 0.29-0.33 at longer contexts, but never beats retrained two-token controls. A key-value recall benchmark shows a width-dependent threshold: one stored pair meets the pre-registered accuracy bar at 4-5 memory qubits, two pairs at 6-7, and three pairs remain unsolved. This is consistent with, but does not establish, a capacity explanation for the short effective memory horizon. As a secondary result, one-qubit models reach lower stationary memory entropy than a heuristically optimized classical predictive frontier at matched error in 9/9 seeds. On IBM Heron hardware, computational-basis memory-register distributions show signal against a uniform null in 12/12 circuits across prefixes of up to 12 tokens, next-bit probabilities pass pre-registered accuracy bars at four-token prefixes, and bytes are generated autoregressively by sampling physically measured bit probabilities. The tested models are classically simulable and substantially worse than classical n-gram baselines. We claim no computational quantum advantage.
bullets: The models use small quantum registers with token-conditioned quantum channels and Born-rule measurements for next-byte prediction, without a classical vocabulary projection or softmax.
Unitary-only dynamics fail to contract or reset memory and underperform retrained one-token controls; learned dissipative gating provides useful longer-context memory.
At context length 12, gating improves test negative log-likelihood over matched one-token controls, but never surpasses retrained two-token controls.
Recall capacity grows with memory width: one key-value pair succeeds at 4–5 qubits, two at 6–7, while three remain unsolved; this supports but does not prove a capacity-based memory limit.

IBM Heron experiments detected memory signal and generated bytes autoregressively from measured probabilities, but the models showed no claimed quantum advantage and remained worse than classical n-grams.
papers.selection_reason: Explores quantum-native language models with dissipative memory, contributing to the 'Large Language Models' topic.
papers.title: Trainable Quantum-Native Language Models: Dissipative Memory, Capacity Limits, and Hardware Validation
papers.tldr: Trainable dissipative quantum language models can retain information beyond one token and operate on IBM hardware, but remain short-memory, classically simulable, and inferior to classical n-gram baselines.

papers.abstract: We interpret Transformer networks as learned approximations to a hybrid probabilistic-inference procedure that combines max-product Loopy Belief Propagation (LBP) with Expectation--Maximization (EM). In this view, a Transformer performs inference in partially observed Markov Random Fields (MRFs) whose structure and parameters are not given a priori but are inferred from data. We show that self-attention implements a differentiable approximation to max-product LBP on an input-conditioned, dynamically structured MRF, with attention weights encoding learned structural affinities. We further establish an EM correspondence at the level of depth: each layer updates latent representations in an E-step-like forward pass, while the transition $\theta^{(l)} \to \theta^{(l+1)}$ across layers acts as an implicit M-step. Building on this interpretation, we introduce \emph{meta-models}, a design paradigm in which inputs generate instance-specific parameters, unifying mechanisms such as self-attention, mixture-of-experts, and gated units within a single framework. Empirical results support the proposed perspective.
bullets: Reinterprets self-attention as differentiable max-product LBP on input-conditioned Markov Random Fields.
Maps Transformer depth to EM: layerwise representation updates resemble E-steps, while parameter transitions resemble implicit M-steps.
Introduces meta-models, where inputs generate instance-specific parameters.
Unifies self-attention, mixture-of-experts, and gated units under this meta-model perspective.
Reports empirical support for the proposed interpretation, without specifying results in the abstract.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a unifying view of Transformer architectures and meta-models, relevant to LLM architecture research.
papers.title: Neural expectation-maximization and meta-models
papers.tldr: Transformers can be viewed as learned, input-adaptive EM and max-product LBP procedures over dynamically structured probabilistic models.

papers.abstract: Large language models are stochastic by nature. Repeated executions under the same experimental conditions may produce different responses. We propose a framework that can be applied across the model lifecycle, from task design to residual behavior and continuous monitoring. The method consists of building an empirical response distribution estimated through Monte Carlo simulation. Semantic interventions are introduced to study how these distributions change. We illustrate the framework with two different tasks, borrower classification and music album recommendation, and quantify the resulting distributional changes. The framework is linked to model risk management and governance by measuring robustness and control effectiveness, and characterizing residual behavior. Since it relies only on observed responses, it can also be applied to black-box models accessed through commercial APIs.
bullets: Addresses variability in LLM outputs across repeated executions under identical conditions.
Estimates response distributions via Monte Carlo simulation across the model lifecycle.
Uses semantic interventions to measure changes in behavioral distributions.
Demonstrates the approach on borrower classification and music album recommendation tasks.
Connects distributional measurements to robustness, control effectiveness, governance, and residual behavior.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a distributional framework for characterizing LLM behavior and risk management, fitting the 'Language Foundation Models' topic.
papers.title: A Distributional Framework for Behavioral Characterization and Risk Management of Large Language Models
papers.tldr: A black-box-compatible framework uses empirical response distributions to characterize, test, and manage the stochastic behavior and risks of large language models.

papers.abstract: Continual learning (CL) seeks to adapt pretrained models while preserving prior capabilities. Yet the tasks supplied for preservation cover only part of what a model knows, while forgetting can extend beyond them. Recent work shows that language models can supplement this limited evidence by generating useful replay without access to their original training data. This raises a question about self-preservation: can a model help choose preservation targets that protect its own capabilities more broadly? To study this question, we organize task descriptions and their examples into Task Banks, whose entries can be selected and combined to guide replay generation by a frozen model. Continual instruction tuning with Qwen models of varying sizes yields three findings. First, the new task and learning rate shape which prior capabilities degrade, while tracking previously correct answers reveals losses that average accuracy can conceal. Second, generated replay reduces forgetting on tasks outside the bank. Combining partial banks strengthens this protection, improving mean retention of previously correct answers over either bank alone across the tested sizes. Third, the model can also help choose replay targets: selection informed by the new task improves mean held-out retention over random selection at 4B, with similar new-task gains, although smaller models show no corresponding advantage. Under a fixed example budget, however, replacing new-task examples with replay improves preservation at the cost of smaller new-task gains. Together, these findings show that models can support broader self-preservation by generating replay data and, in some settings, choosing which tasks to replay.
authors: Dongkyu Cho, Rumi Chunara, Ali Behrouz
bullets: Continual learning may forget capabilities not represented in the available preservation tasks.
Task Banks organize task descriptions and examples to guide replay generation by a frozen model.
Generated replay reduces forgetting on held-out tasks, and combining partial banks improves retention across tested Qwen model sizes.
New-task-informed replay selection outperforms random selection at 4B, but smaller models show no comparable benefit.
Using a fixed example budget, more replay improves preservation while reducing gains on the new task.
papers.selection_reason: Continual learning with replay for LLM self-preservation; fits continual learning and LLM topics.
papers.title: Self-Preservation in Language Models
papers.tldr: Language models can use generated replay—and sometimes select replay targets—to preserve capabilities beyond the tasks explicitly monitored during continual learning.

papers.abstract: Sparse computation can scale the parametric capacity of LLMs without proportionally increasing active computation, but pretraining sparse architectures remains expensive and data-hungry. Existing sparse upcycling methods mainly target Mixture-of-Experts models, where expert homogeneity, sample inefficiency, and system overheads can limit practical scalability. Static sparse memory offers predictable access and token-specific updates that can help address these challenges, but naively integrating it into pretrained computation yields poor returns. In this work, we introduce STAPLE, a recipe built upon STEM for integrating static sparse memory into pretrained models. Whereas STEM replaces FFN up-projections with token-indexed embeddings, STAPLE retains them and adds the embeddings as a residual pathway, preserving pretrained computation while learning complementary token-specific information in a scalable manner. On OLMo-2 1B, STAPLE improves over continued dense training by 4.27 points on HumanEval, 2.80 on MBPP, 2.27 on GSM8K, and 1.65 on DROP. Average performance increases with static capacity, and improvements persist on the larger OLMo-2 7B backbone. STAPLE also outperforms static sparse baselines such as STEM and an Engram-style model, and achieves a higher average score than an MoE upcycling baseline while decoding 2x faster with less than half its GPU model memory and measured GPU energy per token in our throughput-oriented decoding evaluation. Importantly, despite introducing billions of parameters late in training, our host-offloaded implementation keeps generation throughput within 1.5% and training throughput within 3% of the dense baseline, while caching only the ~5% most frequent embeddings on GPU. These results show that static sparse memory can provide a sample-efficient, scalable, and sustainable path for expanding pretrained models without sparse pretraining from scratch.
authors: Ranajoy Sadhukhan, Euijin Hong, Sheng Cao, Zechun Liu, Shuowei Jin, Sha Li, Changlong Yu, Xin Liu, Qin Lu, Zhenyu Shi, Priyanka Nigam, Beidi Chen
bullets: Addresses the cost and data demands of pretraining sparse architectures, especially limitations of MoE upcycling.
Retains pretrained FFN up-projections and adds STEM-based token-indexed embeddings as complementary residual information.
Performance improves with static memory capacity and transfers to both 1B and 7B OLMo-2 backbones.
Outperforms dense continued training and static sparse baselines across coding, math, and question-answering benchmarks.
Compared with an MoE upcycling baseline, achieves higher average performance while decoding 2× faster and using less GPU memory; throughput stays close to dense training and generation baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Static sparse memory upcycling improves LLM capacity and inference efficiency.
papers.title: STAPLE: Static Sparse Upcycling of Pretrained Checkpoints via Embedding Modules
papers.tldr: STAPLE efficiently expands pretrained LLMs by adding token-indexed static sparse embeddings as a residual pathway, improving task performance with minimal training and decoding overhead.

papers.abstract: A latent recurrent language model applies a shared block of layers repeatedly, so one checkpoint can trade inference compute for accuracy by changing the loop count. At one loop, however, such models typically fall well short of a non-recurrent model of the same size, a one-loop tax that makes a separate non-recurrent model the better choice whenever latency matters. We present Elastic Latent Recurrence (ELR), a recipe for training looped language models without this tax. At one loop, an ELR model costs the same to serve as a non-recurrent model of the same size and, trained on the same data, reaches similar accuracy. Each additional loop then buys more accuracy for more inference compute. Three choices make this work: a gated state update with a learned step size, loop counts mixed within each optimizer update, and conditioning each pass on its loop index and budget. The first two preserve one-loop accuracy, and the third lowers loss at every additional loop. Mixed depths can be introduced late in pretraining to limit the added training cost, and with zero-initialized conditioning added at the switch, this late schedule reaches lower loss than mixed-depth training from scratch. In MoE models, reusing first-loop expert routes on later loops cuts mixed-depth update time by 11.7% with no measurable change in accuracy. At inference, keeping only the last loop's attention KV cache holds attention KV memory at its one-loop level while retaining most of the gain from additional loops. On 4B dense and 30B-A3B MoE hybrid models, ELR at one loop is 0.52 points below and 1.04 points above its matched baseline on a ten-task average, and four loops add 7.25 and 4.75 points. Carried through post-training, the recipe yields Koi-4B, a single checkpoint that scores an estimated 18 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at one loop, matching Qwen3.5-4B, and 29 at four loops.
authors: Faisal Ladhak, Shantanu Acharya, Santiago Akle Serano, Simeng Sun, Boris Ginsburg, Krishna C Puvvada
bullets: Addresses the one-loop accuracy tax that often makes recurrent models unattractive under latency constraints.
Uses gated state updates with learned step sizes, mixed loop counts during training, and loop-index/budget conditioning.
Late mixed-depth training can reduce added training cost; reusing MoE expert routes cuts update time by 11.7% without measurable accuracy loss.
Retaining only the final loop’s attention KV cache keeps KV memory at the one-loop level while preserving most multi-loop gains.

On 4B dense and 30B-A3B MoE models, four loops improve ten-task averages by 7.25 and 4.75 points, respectively; the post-trained Koi-4B reaches estimated Intelligence Index scores of 18 at one loop and 29 at four.
papers.selection_reason: Elastic latent recurrence for looped LLMs with one-loop tax removal and KV-cache memory savings; strong architectural and efficiency contribution.
papers.title: One Model to Loop Them All: Elastic Latent Recurrence for Language Models
papers.tldr: Elastic Latent Recurrence trains one language-model checkpoint to match non-recurrent accuracy at one loop while gaining accuracy as additional loops increase inference compute.

papers.abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization offers a memory-efficient alternative to backpropagation for fine-tuning large language models. However, existing ZO methods typically sample training examples uniformly, overlooking their evolving importance and leaving avoidable estimation variance. To address this limitation, we propose Sample-Adaptive Zeroth-Order Optimization (SAZO), which learns sample importance online and adaptively allocates queries to accelerate convergence. SAZO extracts gradient-norm information from existing directional differences to estimate sample importance without access to true gradients. Furthermore, to track evolving importance from sparse minibatch feedback, SAZO maintains per-example exponential moving averages that aggregate observations across updates. The method requires no additional model evaluations and only $O(N)$ additional scalar state compared with MeZO. We prove that SAZO asymptotically matches the leading convergence term of the minimum-variance sampling oracle, and achieves a strictly faster convergence rate than standard methods. Extensive experiments across four model families demonstrate improved average downstream performance and up to $6\times$ faster convergence to the same training loss in terms of query count.
authors: Haiyuan Wan, Yanyi Li, Weicheng Lin, Cong Fang
bullets: Uniform sampling in existing zeroth-order methods can waste queries and increase estimation variance as sample importance changes.
SAZO estimates sample importance from directional differences, without requiring true gradients.
Per-example exponential moving averages track importance under sparse minibatch feedback.
It adds only O(N) scalar state over MeZO and theoretically approaches minimum-variance sampling convergence.
Experiments across four model families show improved average downstream performance and up to 6× faster convergence by query count.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces Sample-Adaptive Zeroth-Order optimization for fine-tuning large language models, relevant to efficient LLM training and adaptation methods.
papers.title: Sample-Adaptive Zeroth-Order Post-Training
papers.tldr: SAZO improves zeroth-order fine-tuning by adaptively prioritizing important training examples without extra model evaluations.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive decoding is less suited to non-causally ordered data, e.g., cross-references or future dependencies, since their outputs cannot be revised post hoc, unlike iterative human reasoning. Diffusion LLMs partially mitigate this limitation but still cannot flexibly insert or remove arbitrary numbers of tokens from a pre-generated context. We design AutoIndexer as a generative model with a novel training and decoding mechanism that simulates a Chain of Edits, allowing the model to flexibly modify its prior outputs in hindsight via token insertions, substitutions, and deletions. The model learns to predict marker tokens for opening and closing edits, simultaneously moving a cursor to positions in the existing token sequence, analogous to a text editor. Training sequences are obtained by perturbing ground-truth labels with inverse chained edit operations, and the model learns to edit by undoing those inverses. The perturbation training allows AutoIndexer to be robust to erroneous context and adaptable to editing tasks such as code correction. We demonstrate that our method exhibits post-generation context-editing capabilities that most autoregressive and diffusion models lack without compromising performance on standard LLM benchmarks. The code is available at https://github.com/AutodeskAILab/autoindexer.
authors: Shu Ishida, Aliasghar Khani, Tianyu Zhang, The Cong Luong, James Seale Smith, Adam Gaier
bullets: Addresses causal decoding’s difficulty with non-causal dependencies and outputs that require hindsight revision.
Trains models on perturbed sequences created through inverse chained edits, teaching them to undo errors.
Predicts edit markers while moving a cursor through the existing token sequence, like a text editor.
Supports flexible post-generation context editing and potential applications such as code correction.
The abstract reports retained performance on standard LLM benchmarks, but gives no quantitative results or detailed scope limits.
papers.selection_reason: Novel decoding mechanism for LLMs with edit operations; fits language foundation model architecture research.
papers.title: AutoIndexer: Flexible-Order Decoding by Training Causal Models on Chains of Edits
papers.tldr: AutoIndexer augments causal language models with chain-of-edit decoding so they can revise generated text through insertions, substitutions, and deletions.

papers.abstract: Sequence models with a fixed-size state avoid the quadratic cost of attention, but face a design choice. An input-dependent state transition gives content-dependent memory at the cost of FFT-based training, while a fixed transition keeps the O(T log T) convolutional path but reads memory the same way for every input. ResonatorLM, a recent model of the second kind, reads a bank of damped complex oscillators through a fixed learned phase per head. We make that readout phase a function of the current token, which adds input dependence to the read only, keeps the convolution exact, and costs 0.2 percent more parameters. An analysis of the untrained bank shows that phase does encode elapsed time, but an ordinary token falls below the background within 2-8 steps and no choice of damping extends linear reconstruction beyond about 16 tokens. In 6M-parameter character-level models on WikiText-2, the input-dependent phase matches the original at the training length and removes its failure beyond it: trained on 256 tokens and tested on 1024, perplexity falls from 12.81 to 3.76. We trace the failure to long-memory heads that accumulate more history than training exposed them to. The learned phase tracks the current character rather than distance and does not improve retrieval.
bullets: Fixed-state sequence models retain efficient O(T log T) convolution but normally read memory identically for every input.
The proposed input-dependent readout changes only the phase, preserving exact convolution and adding 0.2% parameters.
Untrained oscillators lose ordinary-token information after 2–8 steps, with linear reconstruction limited to about 16 tokens regardless of damping.
In 6M-parameter WikiText-2 character models trained on 256 tokens and tested on 1024, perplexity drops from 12.81 to 3.76 versus the original model.
The learned phase follows the current character rather than elapsed distance and does not improve retrieval; long-memory heads explain the baseline’s extrapolation failure.
papers.selection_reason: Improves the long-context capabilities of ResonatorLM sequence models by making the readout phase input-dependent, relevant to LLM architecture and context handling.
papers.title: An Input-Dependent Readout Phase for Resonant Sequence Models
papers.tldr: Making ResonatorLM’s oscillator readout phase depend on the current token preserves efficient convolution while substantially improving extrapolation to longer sequences.

papers.abstract: We introduce a post-training method for diffusion language models (DLMs) that minimizes Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) between generated and reference distributions in the feature space of a frozen pretrained DLM. To estimate MMD, we retain contextual features at individual token positions, obtaining multiple observations per sequence from a single extractor pass. We optimize this objective using policy gradients for discrete models and direct differentiation through generated latents for continuous models. In both cases, computing the loss directly from these features enables efficient post-training without full sampling trajectories or jointly trained auxiliary models. Experiments show lower generative perplexity at comparable entropy on OpenWebText and better accuracy-computation trade-offs on GSM8K. On 16B DMax-LLaDA2.0 models with hybrid masked-uniform diffusion, we increase decoding parallelism with similar or higher accuracy on math and code benchmarks.
bullets: Matches generated and reference distributions using contextual token features from a frozen pretrained DLM.
Uses policy gradients for discrete diffusion models and latent differentiation for continuous models.
Avoids full sampling trajectories and jointly trained auxiliary models during optimization.
Reports lower generative perplexity at comparable entropy, improved GSM8K accuracy–compute trade-offs, and higher decoding parallelism with similar or better math/code accuracy.
Demonstrated on OpenWebText, GSM8K, and 16B DMax-LLaDA2.0 models with hybrid masked-uniform diffusion.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a post-training method for diffusion language models, a language foundation model architecture, with accuracy and decoding improvements.
papers.title: Representation-Space MMD for Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: A feature-space MMD objective enables efficient post-training of diffusion language models, improving generation quality and decoding efficiency without auxiliary models or full sampling trajectories.

papers.abstract: Agentic pipelines for structured-query generation are rapidly expanding, but it is unclear which part of the loop produces the gain. We use LAST-CQ -- a five-agent, training-free, execution-grounded Text-to-Cypher framework -- as an instrumented testbed, running three counterfactuals over 2,471 live-database queries and six backbones spanning three vendor scale tiers. Removing correction is worth between 3.1% aggregate execution-BLEU against the single-pass system and 12.3% against a no-refinement counterfactual (up to 80.7% for the weakest backbone). Replacing schema-grounded, LLM-synthesised feedback with raw database error strings costs almost nothing (20.9% vs. 19.9% naive exact match; <0.2% end-to-end; equivalent within $\pm 0.075$ set-F1 by two one-sided tests). Spending the same call budget on parallel sampling degrades quality by 10-11%. What works is detecting failure and routing it to a retry, not the feedback sophistication or number of samples. LAST-CQ itself recovers 91.7% of queries that fail under single-pass generation, while a query that succeeds first time still costs exactly one LLM call. We also show that n-gram overlap on serialised results is not a bound in either direction: it over-scores against set equivalence on 65.9% of results while under-scoring against judged semantics. Finally, we calibrate our LLM judge against blind human labels and find it optimistic by 9 points.
bullets: Evaluates five-agent, training-free, execution-grounded Text-to-Cypher refinement using 2,471 live-database queries and six backbones.
Removing correction reduces execution-BLEU by 3.1% versus single-pass generation and 12.3% versus no refinement, with larger effects for weaker backbones.
Raw database error messages perform nearly as well as schema-grounded synthesized feedback, while allocating calls to parallel sampling lowers quality by 10–11%.
LAST-CQ recovers 91.7% of queries that fail under single-pass generation, while successful first-pass queries use one LLM call.
Serialized-result n-gram overlap poorly reflects set equivalence and judged semantics; the LLM judge is 9 points more optimistic than blind human labels.
papers.selection_reason: Focuses on LLM agent self-refinement for Text-to-Cypher generation, analyzing the agent loop and recovery mechanisms.
papers.title: What Drives Recovery in Agentic Text-to-Cypher? LAST-CQ: An LLM Agent Self-Refinement Framework
papers.tldr: LAST-CQ’s recovery gains mainly come from detecting failed queries and retrying them, rather than sophisticated feedback or parallel sampling.

papers.abstract: Multivariate ordinal data along with covariates are commonly collected in problems ranging from alignment of language models with human preferences, as well as in recommender systems. For example, data sets such as MovieLens contain several movies rated on a scale 1--5 by human users, along with their demographic information such as age or gender. Similarly, data sets such as HelpSteer collect human feedback on several attributes such as "helpfulness" or "verbosity" of LLM response on an ordinal scale, with covariates depending on the LLM prompt--response pairs. Unfortunately, the standard approaches for modeling these data (a) look at the attributes individually rather than jointly, and (b) often convert the data into pairwise or list-wise win--loss comparisons for fitting models such as Bradley--Terry and Plackett--Luce. Both of these lead to a coarsening of what is actually observed, which we address via a joint covariate-dependent consecutive ratio Markov random field model. We also show pairwise or listwise comparison models are obtained under restrictions of our joint model, and that joint modeling improves comparisons. We also develop a maximum likelihood inference procedure even in the presence of an intractable normalizer.
bullets: Addresses the loss of information from modeling ordinal attributes separately or reducing them to win–loss comparisons.
Introduces a joint covariate-dependent consecutive ratio Markov random field for multivariate ordinal data.
Shows Bradley–Terry- and Plackett–Luce-type comparison models arise under restrictions of the joint model.
Develops maximum-likelihood inference despite an intractable normalizing constant.
Reports that joint modeling improves comparisons, without specifying quantitative results in the abstract.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a joint model for multivariate ordinal preferences with covariates, providing a statistically rigorous approach relevant to LLM alignment and human feedback.
papers.title: Covariate-dependent Joint Modeling of Multivariate Ordinal Preferences and Its Connections with Comparison Models
papers.tldr: A joint covariate-dependent model preserves multivariate ordinal preference information while encompassing common pairwise and listwise comparison models as special cases.

papers.abstract: As small language models (SLMs) are increasingly deployed on resource-constrained and on-device platforms, including as components of agentic systems, the integrity of locally stored model parameters becomes an important safety concern. We investigate whether safety-sensitive behavior in LLaMA-2-7B-Chat is concentrated within a sparse subset of parameters, creating a reduced fault surface for targeted analysis. We study two complementary localization methods: low-rank safety-associated subspace analysis and parameter-level safety--utility importance filtering. Both approaches reveal highly non-uniform safety sensitivity across the network, with the MLP down_proj consistently emerging as a prominent safety-sensitive component and o_proj providing a smaller contribution. Using parameter-level localization, modifying only 0.19% of model weights in down_proj yields 53% Basic ASR and 56% GCG ASR, while tinyBenchmarks accuracy remains at 51.6% compared with a 52.2% unmodified baseline. These results motivate targeted fault analysis and selective integrity protection for language models deployed in resource-constrained, on-device, and agentic settings.
bullets: Safety sensitivity is highly uneven across the network, with the MLP down_proj most prominent and o_proj contributing less.
The study uses low-rank safety-subspace analysis and parameter-level safety–utility importance filtering.
Changing only 0.19% of down_proj weights produces 53% Basic ASR and 56% GCG ASR.
tinyBenchmarks accuracy remains nearly unchanged: 51.6% versus 52.2% for the unmodified model.
The findings support selective integrity protection for on-device and agentic deployments.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates safety in on-device LLMs and localizes safety-critical parameters, addressing a key concern for resource-constrained deployment.
papers.title: How Fragile Is On-Device Language Model Safety? Localizing Safety-Critical Parameters for Sparse Fault Analysis
papers.tldr: Safety behavior in LLaMA-2-7B-Chat is concentrated in a tiny subset of parameters, enabling targeted fault analysis with minimal utility loss.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems are expected to be more reliable because agents can catch each other's mistakes. But peer pressure cuts both ways: the same correction that fixes a wrong answer can overturn a right one. The tempting safeguard is a brake that keeps the beneficial revisions and blocks the harmful ones. We show this brake is hard to build, for a simple reason: a revision is harmful exactly when the original answer was right, so deciding whether to block it is the same as knowing whether the model was already correct. This turns the open-ended hunt for a brake into one measurable quantity, the model's self-knowledge: any brake built from a deploy-time signal is a correctness probe in disguise, and self-knowledge is far from perfect (AUROC $\approx 0.64$--$0.89$ across six model families). We call this ceiling the wall. Even white-box steering of the model's own correctness direction does not breach it: it changes how often the model revises, but harmful and beneficial revisions move together. At population scale the wall becomes the cliff: when most agents start wrong, debate amplifies the shared mistake into a confident, wrong consensus. In our multiple-choice societies, more agents, more model diversity, and a stronger member do not fix it. What helps is adding information before the revision, not filtering after it. Local agreement is not global correctness.
bullets: Peer correction can help fix wrong answers but can also overturn correct ones.
Any deploy-time filter for harmful revisions effectively probes whether the original answer was correct.
Self-knowledge is imperfect, with AUROC around 0.64–0.89 across six model families.
White-box steering changes revision frequency but does not separate harmful from beneficial revisions.
When most agents are initially wrong, debate can amplify shared errors into confident consensus; adding information before revision helps more than filtering afterward.
papers.selection_reason: Studies LLM self-knowledge and revision filtering in multi-agent systems, directly relevant to LLM reasoning and reliability.
papers.title: One Axis, No Brake: Self-Knowledge Limits the Filtering of Harmful Peer Conformity in LLMs
papers.tldr: Filtering harmful peer conformity in LLM societies is fundamentally limited by imperfect self-knowledge: models cannot reliably tell when their original answer was already correct.

papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) scores student-generated prefixes with a solution-conditioned self-teacher, yet transfers supervision only through next-token probabilities. We ask whether the aligned final-layer discrepancy offers a useful second channel, and how to test that channel without confusing its geometry with auxiliary strength. SCOPE-OPSD projects the privileged teacher-student residual onto a frozen rank-64 factor estimated from residual covariance and language-model-head Fisher sensitivity. It reuses the forwards already required by OPSD and adds neither rollouts nor inference-time modules. A matched Random control preserves the structured factor's rank and nonzero spectrum and uses per-arm gradient-RMS calibration, isolating the effect of the data-dependent orientation. Across the complete 25/50/75/100-step trajectories for Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B, Structured is never below Pure OPSD, with strict gains in 11 of the 12 model-checkpoint combinations and an exact tie at 4B step 25. Structured also exceeds matched Random in 10 of the 12 combinations. At step 75 on Qwen3-1.7B, Structured exceeds matched Random by 1.39 Macro Avg@12 points in each of two independent training reruns. A cross-fitted diagnostic also shows 4.40 times greater held-out privileged-gap capture than the matched random orientation. The results support a compact, Fisher-conditioned privileged subspace for short-budget OPSD.
bullets: Addresses whether final-layer teacher–student discrepancies can provide a useful supervision channel beyond next-token probabilities.
Uses a frozen rank-64 factor derived from residual covariance and language-model-head Fisher sensitivity, reusing existing OPSD forwards without extra rollouts or inference modules.
A matched Random control preserves rank, spectrum, and gradient-RMS calibration to isolate the effect of the learned orientation.
Across 12 model-checkpoint combinations, Structured never underperforms Pure OPSD, improves in 11, and exceeds matched Random in 10.
The method is supported by a 4.40× higher held-out privileged-gap capture in a cross-fitted diagnostic and is presented for short-budget OPSD.
papers.selection_reason: Improves on-policy self-distillation for LLMs using a Fisher-conditioned privileged subspace.
papers.title: SCOPE-OPSD: Fisher-Conditioned Privileged Subspaces for On-Policy Self-Distillation
papers.tldr: SCOPE-OPSD improves on-policy self-distillation by projecting teacher–student residuals into a compact Fisher-conditioned privileged subspace.

papers.abstract: Existing model marketplaces typically trade and select individual models as indivisible units, limiting their ability to exploit complementarities among heterogeneous experts. This paper proposes an MoE-based model market framework that lifts Mixture-of-Experts from a model-level learning architecture to a market-level coordination mechanism. In this framework, brokers use gating networks to coordinate multiple heterogeneous experts and deliver a composite model service. We formalize the market participants, service workflow, expert cost structure, and a welfare objective that combines predictive utility with heterogeneous execution costs.
